Initially created: 2026-02-03T11:00:52.898+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: The Tathāgata manifested in response to conditions,
expounding teachings according to opportunities.
His compassion extended to dragons and spirits,
not only to humans and devas.
His transformation began with Ājñātakauṇḍinya,
and concluded with Subhadra.
The texts accumulated tens of thousands of scrolls, filling the great cosmos,
and from west to east, it is truly difficult to exhaustively study them.
As for Liú Xiàng collating texts,
profound teachings had long been amassed.
Emperor Míng of Hàn, moved by a dream,
made spiritual evidence even more evident.
From then on, translations and transmissions followed one after another.
Although the profound canons of the Tripiṭaka were roughly complete,
the miscellaneous words of the nine divisions had not yet been systematically compiled.
The emperor, in harmony with enlightenment and equal in virtue to omniscience,
greatly propagated the sūtras and teachings, benefiting both the Dharma and the laity.
He broadly invited experts in antiquity and extensively collected lost texts.
Thus, scattered verses and chapters frequently emerged.
What we have obtained now is indeed abundant.
The imperial decree considered that
as the Dharma’s semblance and true periods declined, faith and joy increasingly waned,
and the texts were vast and extensive, with few able to master them comprehensively.
In the seventh year of the Tiānjiàn era,
he ordered the monk Shì Sēng Mín and others
to compile extracts from all the canons,
revealing evidence of profound texts and connecting with the essential meaning,
with concise wording and clear intent.
For those seeking to delve, this already provided more than half the benefit.
However, rare and extraordinary phenomena were still scattered among various chapters,
and difficult-to-hear secret teachings had not been highlighted.
Then, at the end of the fifteenth year,
he ordered Bǎo Chàng to extract essential matters from the sūtras and vinaya,
all arranged by category,
so that readers could easily understand.
Furthermore,
he ordered Shì Sēngháo of Xīn’ān Temple
and Shì Fǎshēng of Xīnghuáng Temple, among others,
to assist in reviewing and reading.
Thus, they broadly synthesized the scriptures and selected secret essentials,
consulting divine considerations and following established rules.
In total, it comprises fifty scrolls,
plus a catalog of five scrolls,
divided into five bundles,
titled *Jīnglǜ Yìxiàng* (Strange Phenomena from Sūtras and Vinaya).
Future learners
may thus gain broad knowledge without toil.
The Four Heavenly Kings reside on the four sides of Sumeru,
each forty-two thousand yojanas high. The eastern heavenly king,
named Dhr̥tarāṣṭra,
has a city called Shàngxián.
The southern heavenly king,
named Virūḍhaka,
has a city called Shànjiàn.
The western heavenly king,
named Virūpākṣa,
has a city called Zhōuluó.
The northern heavenly king,
named Vaiśravaṇa,
generally dwells in three cities:
the first called Kěwèi,
the second called Tiānjìng,
and the third called Zhòngguī.
The four kings are each half a yojana tall,
with robes one yojana long,
half a yojana wide,
and weighing two fen.
Their heavenly lifespan is five hundred years,
with slight variations.
Fifty human years
equal one day and night in heaven,
also thirty days make a month,
and twelve months make a year. They eat pure food, and bathing and clothing serve as subtle nourishment.
Men marry women, and they engage in intercourse just like humans.
Due to past good karma, they are born as devas,
spontaneously manifesting on the knees of heavenly beings.
Their size at birth is like a two-year-old human child, and soon after birth, they naturally know hunger.
A seven-jeweled exquisite vessel holds food of a hundred flavors.
If one has abundant merit, the rice is white;
if moderate merit, the rice is blue;
if little merit, the rice is red.
After the child digests the food, if thirsty,
a jeweled vessel contains nectar matching the color of the food.
Drinking it leaves no residue, like ghee thrown into fire.
When the body grows to full size, equal to other devas, they enter pools to bathe.
Approaching fragrant trees, the branches hang low,
and they take incense to anoint themselves, wearing adornments.
Garlands, jeweled vessels, fruits, and musical instruments each come from trees.
They go everywhere, taking whatever they wish, entering various gardens where countless heavenly maidens play music, sing, and converse with laughter.
Deep attachment arises,
and looking west, they forget east.
Amidst their play and joy, they forget the initial thoughts and knowledge from birth.
Relying on past good deeds, they are born in heaven, where ponds are clear, flowers and fruits flourish.
Their city has seven walls, each six thousand yojanas wide.
Balustrades, nets, palace walls, and rows of trees are all sevenfold.
Vaiśravaṇa
constantly has five great spirits:
first, Nàshélóu;
second, Tántuóluó;
third, Xīmóbátuó;
fourth, Tíjìluó;
fifth, Xiūyìlùmó.
They always attend by his side.
Twice a month, on the three fast days—
the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth—
the Four Heavenly Kings always on the eighth day command their messengers:
"You, inspect the world and observe the people—
whether they honor parents, revere śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, elders,
observe fasting precepts, and give alms or not."
The messengers, receiving the order, report all good and evil.
Hearing evil displeases them; hearing good delights them.
On the fourteenth day, the four kings often send their princes to inspect the world.
On the fifteenth day, the four kings personally tour,
then go to the Hall of Good Dharma to report to Śakra.
Hearing evil saddens them; hearing good gladdens them.
They recite verses praising those who uphold fasting precepts, saying, "They walk the same path as we."
The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven resides atop Mount Sumeru,
with thirty-three heavenly palaces.
The king, named Śakra Devānām Indra, is one yojana tall, with robes two yojanas long,
two yojanas wide, weighing six zhu.
Heavenly lifespan is a thousand years, with slight variations.
When about to die, five signs appear:
first, clothes become soiled;
second, flowers on the head wither;
third, the body emits foul odor;
fourth, sweat flows from the armpits;
fifth, displeasure with one’s own seat.
Seeing these five things, the mind is greatly tormented, like the suffering of hell.
Eating, drinking, and marriage are like those of the Four Heavenly Kings.
Bodies draw close, and through breath, yin-yang union occurs. Through good deeds of body, speech, and mind, one is born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Spontaneously manifesting on the knees of heavenly beings like a three-year-old child,
the deva immediately acknowledges, saying,
"This is my son, my daughter."
They themselves remember past lives of giving and upholding precepts.
Desiring food and drink, golden vessels are filled accordingly.
Merit varies in depth, and food differs in quality.
As in the Heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings,
the city measures eighty thousand yojanas in length and width, with seven walls,
nine hundred ninety-nine gates.
Each gate has sixty blue-clad yakṣas guarding it. The thirty-three heavens
have golden walls with silver gates, silver walls with golden gates,
and so on, with seven jewels alternating as city gates.
Towers, pavilions, terraces, and observatories surround them.
Gardens, bathing pools, and precious flowers are interspersed.
Precious trees stand in rows, with abundant flowers and fruits.
Fragrant breezes blow from all directions, delighting the mind.
Rare and exotic birds, countless in number, sing in harmony.
In its four gardens, each has two stone platforms,
each fifty yojanas in length and width.
Made of seven jewels, soft as heavenly garments. The Rough Garden, the Exhausted Garden, and the Joyful Garden have the Lake of Nanda in between,
one hundred yojanas in length and width, its water clear and pure.
Sevenfold precious moats produce four kinds of flowers:
blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and light blue in mixed colors.
Their fragrance pervades, detectable from one yojana away.
Roots like chariot hubs, sap white as milk, taste sweet as honey.
There are also the Miscellaneous Garden and the Great Joy Garden.
In between is a tree named Zhòudù,
seven yojanas in circumference, one hundred yojanas tall,
with branches and leaves spreading fifty yojanas.
Its fragrance against the wind reaches one hundred yojanas.
South of the Trāyastriṃśa Hall is another tree,
named Bōzhìjūqíluó,
four thousand li tall,
with branches and leaves spreading two thousand li.
When the wind blows its floral fragrance, it travels against the wind for two thousand li.
When the tree blooms, the devas gather beneath it for joy.
Traveling through heaven lasts one hundred twenty days.
Śakra has thirty-two ministers,
hence called the Thirty-Three Heavens.
Each has a palace within the city.
Playing in the gardens always lasts seven days.
In the Rough Garden, upon entering, bodies become rough.
In the Painted Garden, upon entering,
bodies naturally display various painted colors for mutual delight.
In the Miscellaneous Garden, often on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month,
heavenly maidens are released to mingle and play with the devas.
Śakra alone with Śacī in one place is called "miscellaneous."
In the Great Joy Garden, upon entering, hearts are greatly delighted.
The Heaven of Yāma’s palace
is upheld by wind wheels in empty space.
The king, named Shànshí, is two yojanas tall,
with robes four yojanas long, two yojanas wide,
weighing three zhu, emerging from trees,
bright, pure, and luminous with various colors.
The body emits light, needing no sun or moon.
Good deeds of body, speech, and mind,
or offerings like lamps, candles, and bright pearls,
and practices such as upholding precepts and meditation lead to birth in the Yāma Heaven.
Heavenly lifespan is two thousand years, with slight variations.
Eating, drinking, marriage, and desire are like in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. The initial form at birth is like a four-year-old human.
The light of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven cannot reach here.
The Tuṣita Heaven Palace.
Held in empty space by the wind-wheel.
The king is named Shànxǐ.
Bodhisattvas in their final rebirth are often born in this heaven.
Because those in the lower heavens are indulgent and those in the higher heavens are dull, they are born in this heaven. Their bodies are four yojanas tall.
Their garments are eight yojanas long.
And four yojanas wide.
Their garments weigh one and a half zhū.
Their heavenly lifespan is four thousand years, mostly less, rarely exceeding.
Their food is the same as in the lower heavens.
They also have marriages; holding hands fulfills desire.
When first born in this heaven, they resemble a five-year-old human.
They themselves know their past lives' deeds of giving, upholding precepts, and such.
They eat natural food and drink, wear caps, and sing and dance.
Their bodies emit light surpassing that of the Yāma Heaven.
The Nirmāṇarati Heaven Palace.
Also held in empty space by the wind-wheel.
The king is named Shànhuà.
They themselves transform the five sense objects for their own amusement.
Their bodies are eight yojanas tall.
Their garments are sixteen yojanas long.
And eight yojanas wide.
Their garments weigh one zhū.
Their heavenly lifespan is eight thousand years, mostly less, rarely exceeding.
Their food is the same as below.
They also have marriages; a deep gaze fulfills desire. When first born in this heaven, they resemble a six-year-old human.
Their own light is exceptionally superior to Tuṣita.
The Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven Palace.
Also held in empty space by the wind-wheel.
The king is named Zìzài.
They gather and transform what others have transformed for their own amusement.
It is called the Heaven of Loving One's Body.
Within the desire realm, it alone attains mastery.
Their bodies are sixteen yojanas tall.
Their garments are thirty-two yojanas long.
And sixteen yojanas wide.
Their garments weigh half a zhū.
Their heavenly lifespan is sixteen thousand years, mostly less, rarely exceeding.
Their food is as in the lower heavens.
They also have marriages; a momentary glance fulfills desire. When first born in this heaven, they resemble a seven-year-old human and know their own past lives.
Because of giving, upholding precepts, and abandoning evil.
Natural food, drink, clothing, jade maidens—all matters are as before.
Their light surpasses that of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
The Māra Heaven Palace is located between the desire and form realms.
Māra is like a millstone.
It grinds down merit.
It measures six thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
The palace walls are sevenfold.
All adornments are like those of the lower heavens.
They also possess ten dharmas.
First, flying away without limit.
Second, flying here without limit.
Third, going unobstructed.
Fourth, coming unobstructed.
Fifth, the heavenly body has no skin, flesh, bones, marrow, sinews, vessels, blood, or flesh.
Sixth, the body has no impurities like urine or feces.
Seventh, the body knows no fatigue.
Eighth, heavenly women do not give birth.
Ninth, the heavenly eye does not blink.
Tenth, the body follows the mind's preference: if blue is desired, it becomes blue; if yellow, yellow; if red, white, or any color, it appears as desired.
These are the ten dharmas of the heavens.
Furthermore, there are ten things upheld.
First, flying without limit.
Second, coming and going without limit.
Third, among the heavens, there are no thieves.
Fourth, they do not speak of their own goodness.
Nor do they speak of others' evil.
Fifth, there is no mutual encroachment.
Sixth, all heavenly beings have equal teeth and communicate.
Seventh, their hair is dark blue, smooth, glossy, and eighty zhàng long.
Eighth, heavenly beings with blue hair.
Their bodies are also blue.
Ninth, if they desire whiteness, their bodies become white.
Tenth, if they desire blackness, their bodies become black.
The Brahmakāyika Heaven Palace.
The palace is pure gold.
Their bodies are silver-colored, wearing golden garments.
Practicing meditation, detached from desire, cultivating the fire-light samādhi.
Therefore, their bodies emit wondrous light surpassing the sun and moon.
Neither male nor female.
They feed on the joy of meditation.
Lifespan one kalpa, some less.
Body length half a yojana.
Lifespan half a kalpa.
The Brahmapurohita Heaven is the same as the previous heaven.
If one cultivates middling meditation, it is the noble Brahmā's birth place.
Body length one yojana, lifespan one kalpa.
The Brahmāpāriṣadya Heaven.
Same as the previous heaven.
If one cultivates lower meditation, it is the birth place of lesser Brahmās.
Body length one and a half yojanas.
Lifespan one and a half kalpas.
The Great Brahmā Heaven King.
Named Śikhin, same as the previous heaven.
If one cultivates superior meditation, one is born here.
Among the Brahmā assembly, he utters a great voice.
All the great assembly knows it.
The Brahmakāyika gods each think to themselves.
The Great Brahmā Heaven King speaks only to me, not to others.
I attain naturally, without receiving from others.
In the thousand-world system, he is most sovereign.
Rich, abundant, able to create all things.
I am the parent of all sentient beings.
The later-arrived Brahmās respect him foremost.
His face is like a youth's.
He is named Youth.
Holding a rooster and a bell, grasping a red banner, riding a peacock.
The first dhyāna is named Brahmakāyika.
Its palace is distant from the Paranirmitavaśavartin palace.
By one yojana multiple.
The Ābhāsvara Heaven.
They feed on the flavor of meditation.
Lifespan two kalpas, some less.
Parīttābha.
Briefly same as before.
Apramāṇābha.
Briefly same as before.
The Ābhāsvara Heaven King is named Lèguāng. He observes the foul, evil stench of Jambudvīpa.
Rising to seventy million lǐ.
Therefore, bodhisattvas are not born in Ābhāsvara. The second dhyāna is collectively named Ābhāsvara.
Its palace is distant from the Brahmakāyika palace by one yojana multiple.
The Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
They feed on the bliss of meditation.
Lifespan three kalpas, some less.
Parīttaśubha.
Briefly same as before.
Apramāṇaśubha.
Briefly same as before.
The Śubhakṛtsna Heaven King is named Jìngzhì.
Four arms, holding implements, holding a wheel.
Riding a golden-winged bird.
The third dhyāna is collectively named Śubhakṛtsna.
Also named Śuddhāvāsa.
Its palace is distant from the Ābhāsvara palace by one yojana multiple.
The Bṛhatphala Heaven.
They feed on the joy of meditation.
Lifespan forty thousand kalpas, some less.
Parīttabṛhatphala.
Roughly same as before.
Apramāṇabṛhatphala.
Roughly same as before.
The Bṛhatphala Heaven of Adornment.
The king is named Fǎhuáguāng. The fourth dhyāna is collectively named Bṛhatphala.
Its palace is distant from the Śubhakṛtsna palace by one yojana multiple.
The Asaṃjñika Heaven feeds on the bliss of meditation.
Lifespan five hundred kalpas.
Some less.
Still counted within the form realm.
Its light surpasses Bṛhatphala.
Non-Buddhists consider it nirvāṇa.
The Avṛha Heaven feeds on the bliss of meditation.
Lifespan one thousand kalpas.
Some less.
Its light surpasses Asaṃjñika.
The Atapa Heaven.
Body length four thousand yojanas.
Fine and soft, drooping to the ground, unable to stand independently.
If descending to see the Buddha, they transform into a coarse form.
They take meditation as flavor.
Heavenly lifespan two thousand kalpas.
Some less.
Its light surpasses Avṛha.
The Sudarśana Heaven, body length four thousand yojanas.
Also feeds on the bliss of meditation.
Lifespan three thousand kalpas, some less.
Its light surpasses Atapa.
The Sudṛśa Heaven, body length eight thousand yojanas.
Also feeds on the bliss of meditation.
Lifespan four thousand kalpas, some less.
Its light surpasses Sudarśana.
The Akaniṣṭha Heaven, body length sixteen thousand yojanas.
Also feeds on the bliss of meditation.
Lifespan five thousand kalpas, some less.
These five heavens are collectively named Śuddhāvāsa.
Where the anāgāmins dwell.
Their light is most supreme.
The Maheśvara Heaven is also called Śuddhāvāsa.
Beyond the five Śuddhāvāsas are eight places, all empty and tranquil.
They are the dwelling places of the ten abiding great beings.
The Dharma Cloud Bodhisattva often becomes this heaven king.
His form has eight arms, three eyes, riding a great white ox.
Great clouds rain, showering the great thousand-world system.
All sentient beings cannot know the count.
Only this heaven king alone can know it.
The Ākāśānantyāyatana.
Or called the Heaven of Space Wisdom.
Lifespan ten thousand kalpas.
Some slightly less.
The Sphere of Infinite Consciousness.
Also called the Heaven of Wisdom of the Sphere of Consciousness.
The lifespan of its gods is twenty-one thousand kalpas.
Or slightly less. The Sphere of Nothingness.
Also called the Heaven of Wisdom of the Sphere of Nothingness.
Or called the Sphere of No-Perceiving.
There was Youtálán.
He did not accept the Buddha's teachings and died naturally.
The Buddha predicted this person would be reborn in the Sphere of No-Perceiving.
If further, after abandoning his body, he becomes a borderland king who harms people,
he will later be born in hell.
The lifespan of its gods is forty-two thousand kalpas.
Or slightly less.
The Sphere of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception.
Also called the Heaven of Perception and Non-Perception.
There was Fúluólèjiālán.
He did not accept the Buddha's teachings and died.
The Buddha predicted he would be born in the Heaven of Perception and Non-Perception.
Later, he will again become a winged, evil wildcat.
No flying or running beast will escape it.
After death, he will be born in hell.
The lifespan of its gods is eighty-four thousand kalpas.
Or slightly less.
At the beginning of the kalpa, human lifespan was forty thousand years.
Later it gradually decreased and shortened, stopping at one hundred years.
Gradually it became incomplete until, at ten years old, girls at five months were all already married.
The time of ten years is called the three small kalpas.
First, the kalpa of swords.
Second, the kalpa of famine. Third, the kalpa of disease.
The kalpa of swords:
People are mostly greedy, coarse, and practice the ten evil deeds.
If someone practices one good deed, the crowd mocks and laughs at him.
They consider him foolish and strive to oppress and destroy him.
They imitate each other in doing evil; there is not a single good person.
The five grains do not produce delicious flavors and vanish.
Silks, fine cloths, and karpāsa cotton naturally come to an end.
They only eat weeds and coarse grains, weaving grass for clothing.
The seven treasures sink and disappear; sand and stones fill everywhere.
The ground grows thorns and brambles; branches and leaves, large and small, all become swords. Trees fall and decay.
The land is full of ditches and pits; waves surge and banks collapse.
Rivers and streams gradually widen; flat land gradually decreases.
Once the conflict of swords arises, it lasts for seven days.
In their hands, grass, wood, tiles, and stones all turn into swords.
They plunder from each other, trembling in fear, only wanting to kill one another.
It is like a hunter encountering a herd of deer.
Among them, the wise hide far away in mountain valleys and uninhabited places.
They eat fruits and drink water until the ten years of mutual killing are over. Those who kill each other to the end are born in hell.
This is called the kalpa of swords.
The kalpa of famine:
People mostly follow wrong ways, are foolish, ignorant, and hold wrong views.
Stingy, greedy, jealous, guarding wealth and not giving.
Floods and droughts are irregular; fields yield no harvest.
Rice and grains gradually run out; food grains become frighteningly expensive.
They sweep and gather chaff and husks, leaves fallen in streets and alleys, to sustain their lives.
When chaff and leaves are exhausted, they dig underground to eat grass and tree roots.
Those unable to compete die first.
They carve up dead people and again eat them.
As this consumption gradually exhausts, at slaughtering places,
and even in graveyards, they pick up various bones.
They boil them to make soup and drink it to survive.
Those who die of starvation are all born among hungry ghosts.
This is called the small kalpa of famine.
The kalpa of disease:
People all hold right views and practice the ten good deeds.
Diseases are numerous; there is no other method, and medicine is scarce.
Although they practice many good deeds, they cannot ward off adversity.
Due to their meager virtue, they die whenever illness strikes.
Spirits come together to harass, beat, and strike them with sticks.
They disturb their minds, seize their vitality, kill them, and take them away.
After human life ends, they are all born in the heavens.
This is called the kalpa of disease.
If one can uphold the precept of not killing for one day and one night,
one will ultimately not be born in the kalpa of swords.
If one offers a single myrobalan fruit to the monastic community,
one will ultimately not be born in the kalpa of epidemics.
If one offers a single meal to the monastic community,
one will ultimately not be born in the kalpa of famine.
In this Jambudvīpa, evil kalpas arise alternately; in other realms they are fewer.
When the kalpa of swords arises here, there it is only heavy anger.
When the kalpa of epidemics arises here, there it is only weakness of vitality.
When the kalpa of famine arises here,
there it is only slight thirst and scarcity.
The beginning and end of heaven and earth is called one kalpa.
When the kalpa is exhausted and destruction approaches, the fire calamity will arise.
All the people will turn their backs on righteousness and incline toward evil, competing to commit the ten evils.
Heaven will not rain for a long time, and what is planted will not grow.
All the springs and sources of water,
even the four great swift rivers, will all dry up.
After a long time, the wind will enter the sea floor,
take the great city above the sun,
and place it on the path of the sun by the side of Mount Xūmí. When one sun appears,
all grasses, trees, and plants will wither and fall at once.
When two suns appear,
the waters of the four great seas, from a hundred yojanas,
up to seven hundred yojanas within,
will naturally dry up.
When three suns appear,
the waters of the four great seas, for a thousand yojanas,
up to seven thousand yojanas within,
will gradually diminish and exhaust.
When four suns appear,
the waters of the four great seas will be a thousand yojanas deep.
When five suns appear,
the waters of the four great seas will still extend for seven hundred yojanas,
until they are completely exhausted.
When six suns appear,
this earth, sixty-eight thousand yojanas thick, will all emit smoke.
From Mount Xūmí,
up to the three-thousand-great-thousand world systems,
and the eight hells,
nothing will remain unburned, reduced to ashes without a trace.
When the people's lives end, they all gather at Mount Xūmí.
The five kinds of devas,
the Trāyastriṃśa devas,
the Yán tiān up to the Paranirmitavaśavartin devas,
will all perish, and their palaces will become empty.
All is impermanent and cannot long endure.
When seven suns appear,
the great earth and Mount Xūmí will gradually collapse and be destroyed.
For a hundred yojanas, nothing will remain.
Gold, silver, copper, iron, and the like will all melt and flow,
dissolving and drying up, and the mountains will all become hollow.
All treasures will burst and shatter, collapsing with a thundering crash, and the smoke and flames will shake up to the Brahmā heavens.
All evil realms and asuras will be completely swept away.
When sins end and blessings arrive, all gather in the fifteenth heaven.
Below the fourteenth heaven, all becomes scorched and blackened.
The newly born devas, having never seen this before, are filled with fear.
The older devas each come to console them,
saying, "Do not be afraid; this will not reach you."
When the people's lives end, they are born in the Ābhāsvara heaven, where they feed on mindfulness.
They illuminate themselves with light, travel with supernatural feet, and fly.
Some are born in other lands or in hells.
When their hellish sins are completed, they are also born in the heavens.
If their sins are not yet completed, they are also born in the heavens.
If their sins are not yet completed, they move to other realms where there are no sun, moon, or stars, nor day or night.
There is only great darkness, called the fire kalpa and fire calamity.
Causes, conditions, and karmic retribution lead to this destruction.
When the kalpa is about to form, the fire will naturally extinguish.
Great clouds will rise again, gradually bringing heavy rain, with drops as large as cart axles.
At that time, this three-thousand-great-thousand world system
will be filled with water up to the Brahmā heavens, called the water kalpa and water calamity.
Again, there are four winds that hold the water and prevent it from scattering.
The first is called "dwelling,"
the second "assisting,"
the third "immovable,"
and the fourth "firm."
After thousands of billions of years,
the foam on the water transforms into the palaces of the thousand fourteenth heavens, all made of various treasures.
The water gradually recedes as the wind blows and drums,
successively forming the palaces of the various heavens, the sun, and the moon.
Next, the thousand Mount Xūmí are formed,
and successively, up to the thousand four-continent worlds.
Mountains, rivers, cities, and moats are clean and pure on the water.
Initially, the heavenly palaces are made of various treasures,
with the most brilliant light, but as they diminish, they become turbid.
The palaces of the devas, with their seven treasures and light, gradually descend and deteriorate.
When the earth is about to be exposed, the water and sand flow swiftly,
rushing downward and competing to advance, thus forming rivers that flow into the sea. The sea is eighty-four thousand yojanas deep,
and its breadth is boundless. Mount Xūmí is in the sea,
rising eighty-four thousand yojanas above the sea.
The water tastes salty and bitter.
When the kalpa first forms, clouds naturally rise up to the Ābhāsvara heaven,
spreading everywhere and raining to wash the heavenly palaces,
cleansing all things of their impure juices.
These flow down into the sea, making it salty and bitter.
Also, there are great immortals
who cast spells to make it salty and bitter, so that people will not drink it.
Also, there are various kinds of beings living there,
who defecate and urinate in it, making it salty and bitter.
This is called the wind kalpa and wind calamity. These three, together with the earth, are the four calamities and four kalpas.
Except for the earth, the other three are called the great kalpas.
As for the earth seed kalpa,
the destruction of the kalpa reaches
only up to the fourth dhyāna heaven,
for the sake of the Śuddhāvāsa devas.
There is no higher realm to be born in,
so they attain nirvana there and do not descend to be reborn.
Not due to numerical decrease, they transform into heaven and earth.
Heaven and earth begin anew, vast and empty,
with nothing at all, and no sun or moon.
Sweet springs well up from the earth, tasting like ghee and honey.
At that time, the devas of the Ābhāsvara heaven,
some with exhausted blessings, come to be born,
or delight in observing the new earth. Being by nature light and restless, they taste it with their fingers.
Repeating this, they gradually acquire the taste,
and eating it without cease, they gradually develop coarse flesh.
They lose their heavenly marvelous form, supernatural feet, and light, and become plunged into great darkness.
Later, a great black wind blows the seawater, causing the sun and moon to emerge,
and places them by Mount Xūmí, setting them on the path of the sun.
They revolve around Mount Xūmí, illuminating the four continents.
At that time, when people see them rise, they rejoice; when they see them set, they fear.
From then on, day and night, dark and bright,
spring and autumn, years and ages,
suddenly begin again.
Those who eat much become ugly in appearance,
while those who eat little still retain their marvelous form.
Beauty and ugliness gradually arise,
arrogance, jealousy, and envy successively emerge.
Anger, contention, and competition continue without end.
The sweet springs dry up naturally, and fertile soil grows on the earth.
Its taste is fragrant and delicious, like nectar.
At that time, the beings again eat it together.
Those who eat much suddenly lose their majestic light, and their bodies become heavy with bones.
Those who eat little remain light and unburdened, still able to fly.
The heavy ones, seeing this, all cry out loudly,
saying, "We are destitute and unfortunate, dwelling in this world."
Disputes and lawsuits become even more intense than before.
Relying on the fertile soil for food, they look at each other's appearances.
Those with many desires become women,
and together they develop affection and engage in sexual desire.
Thus it spreads.
The remaining Ābhāsvara devas see all the devas falling,
and come together to rebuke them, saying,
"Why are you engaging in impure conduct?"
The fertile soil turns into the earth, and rice grows naturally.
It is fresh, clean, without husks, fragrant, and delicious.
Those who eat it become plump and fair; it is gathered in the morning and grows again by evening.
People gradually become lazy and gather enough for many days.
Indulging in extreme desires, there is no restraint.
Women become pregnant and give birth to more beings.
Others, seeing this, drive them out,
expelling them from the community, allowing them to return after three months.
Knowing shame, they devise a plan together,
gathering grass and wood to build houses,
covering their bodies so others cannot see.
Accustomed to sexual desire, it increases even more.
They gather many grains to store as provisions.
Learning from each other, the rice becomes wild and overgrown,
producing husks and chaff, and after harvesting, it does not grow again.
Seeing this, the beings become greatly distressed.
There is a great calamity in the world, and the rice is no longer as it was before.
Each thinks to themselves,
"When I was first born, I fed on mindfulness,
traveled with supernatural feet and flew, illuminating myself with light.
Dwelling here in laziness has led to this."
They also say to each other,
"Now let us divide the land and set up markers.
Establishing boundaries and borders begins from this."
Hiding their own share, they steal others' rice and grains.
The owners of the rice, seeing this, say,
"We forgive you this time, but do not do it again."
As this increases, they rebuke them even more severely.
When rebukes are not enough, they resort to physical force.
They tell the others, saying,
"This person is a thief."
The thief also says,
"This person hit me."
Seeing this, the people become sorrowful and unhappy.
They all gather and discuss, saying,
"Beings are becoming worse; this is the source of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Troubled by suffering and retribution, they fall into the three evil realms.
Because there is land, disputes arise.
Now, it would be better to jointly appoint one intelligent and talented person as ruler,
to govern according to the law, protecting what should be protected,
rebuking what should be rebuked,
and expelling what should be expelled.
We should gather rice together to supply him.
Selecting a wise, dignified, and virtuous person,
they say to him,
"Be our impartial ruler."
With kind words, they console him, and all are joyful.
Together they proclaim,
"Excellent, great king!"
Thus, he governs the people with righteous law,
and is called a kṣatriya.
All this is according to the old ways.
Later, when people encroach on others' property, they are punished.
For repeated offenses, restraints are imposed.
Whipping and caning are still not enough to stop them, so prisons, knives, clubs, and other tools are made.
Torture and killing are used to instill fear.
At that time, one person, thinking that family life is full of troubles like poisonous thorns,
abandons his wife and children and dwells alone in the mountain forest.
He builds a grass hut, calms his mind,
and practices brahmacarya, becoming a brāhmaṇa.
Later, some brāhmaṇas, not fond of quietude and seated meditation,
enter human society and make recitation their livelihood.
They also declare,
"I am a non-meditator."
Thus, people call them non-meditating brāhmaṇas.
At that time, among the beings, there are those
who are fond of managing households and accumulating wealth, called householders.
There are also many who are skilled in craftsmanship.
Named Shūtuóluó.
There were also those who, weary of worldly ways, shaved off their hair and beard, donned the robes of the Dharma, and cultivated the Path.
They were called Shāmén.
At that time, people's minds harbored thoughts of killing and theft.
Moreover, they lost the fragrant rice.
They established five kinds of seeds.
The first are root seeds.
The second are leaf seeds.
The third are flower seeds.
The fourth are fruit seeds.
The fifth are stem-born and other seeds.
These are called the five kinds of seeds.
All were seeds blown by the wind from other realms to aid the beings of this land.
Such was the auspicious sign.
There was birth, old age, sickness, and death.
There were the five aggregates.
The end of suffering was not reached.
At the end of the water kalpa, the devas of Ābhāsvara entered the water to bathe.
The essences of the four great elements entered their bodies.
Their bodies gave rise to tactile pleasure, and essence flowed into the water.
The eight winds blew and tossed them, and they fell into the mud.
Naturally, an egg formed, and after eight thousand years,
the egg split open and gave birth to a woman.
Her form was blue-black, like mud.
She had nine hundred and ninety-nine heads.
She had a thousand eyes and nine hundred and ninety-nine mouths.
Each mouth had four teeth, and fire issued from the teeth, like lightning.
She had twenty-four hands, each grasping all kinds of weapons.
Her body was as tall and large as Mount Sumeru.
She entered the great ocean, slapping the water for her own amusement.
There was a whirlwind that blew the waters of the great ocean.
The essence of the water entered her body, and she immediately became pregnant.
After eight thousand years, she then gave birth to a boy.
His body was tall and large, four times greater than his mother.
The child had nine heads, each head had a thousand eyes, and fire issued from his mouths.
He had nine hundred and ninety-nine hands and eight feet.
In the ocean waters, he proclaimed himself:
"I am Vemacitrin, the Asura King."
He only ate mud and lotus roots.
Such were the transformations at the beginning of the earth kalpa. When the kalpa burns to an end, everything becomes empty.
Due to the power of the beings' merit and causal conditions,
winds from the ten directions arrived, wind following wind, able to hold the great waters.
Above, there was a person with a thousand heads and two thousand hands and feet.
Named Veṇu, from this person's navel grew a thousand-petaled golden lotus.
Its light was greatly bright, like ten thousand suns shining.
Within the flower was a person sitting cross-legged.
This person also had immeasurable light.
Named Brahmā Devarāja.
He properly gave birth to eight sons.
The eight sons gave birth to heaven, earth, and people.
This is Brahmā Devarāja.
Having exhausted lust and anger, he sat upon the lotus flower.
All Buddhas, following convention, manifest upon precious lotus flowers.
Sitting cross-legged, they preach the six pāramitās.
Those who hear this Dharma
will certainly attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said:
Suppose there is a city one hundred yojanas square, filled with mustard seeds.
There is a long-lived person who lives a hundred years.
He takes one mustard seed each time until they are all exhausted.
The kalpa would still not be exhausted.
Again, suppose there is a stone one hundred yojanas square.
Taking a light, soft Kāśī cloth,
and wiping it once every hundred years, when the stone is worn away, the kalpa would still not be exhausted.
This is called a great kalpa.
Again it is said:
One yojana square, and likewise in height,
an iron city filled with mustard seeds.
Taking one every hundred years until exhausted constitutes one kalpa.
Again, a stone mountain one yojana square.
A man with a Kāśī cloth wipes it once every hundred years.
Wiping without cease, when the stone mountain is worn away,
the kalpa would still not be completed.
One thought within sixty thoughts
is called an extremely small kalpa.
The city-wall of the sun,
square, two thousand and forty li,
its height likewise.
Its light shines into people's eyes, so it appears round.
The palace-city is pure gold, adorned with the seven treasures, radiant and beautiful, without any flaws.
It is upheld by five winds.
The first upholds.
The second nourishes.
The third receives.
The fourth turns.
The fifth regulates.
The Sun King's throne is twenty li square.
His body emits light, illuminating the palace.
The light of the palace illuminates the city-wall.
The light of the city-wall shines down upon the lower earth.
Countless devas guide and follow before and after.
Music entertains itself without rest.
Its groves, pavilions, and bathing pools are like those in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
The devas' lifespan is five hundred years.
Descendants succeed each other to complete one kalpa.
The sun-city circles Mount Sumeru.
When it rises in the east,
it is daytime in the south.
It is midnight in the west.
The sun sets in the north.
Thus, rotating to the right, it alternates day and night.
Furthermore, there are lengths and shortness.
When the sun travels slightly south, the days in the south gradually lengthen.
After sixty li,
for one hundred and eighty days, the days in the north gradually shorten.
Again, traveling slightly north, the days in the north gradually lengthen.
For one hundred and eighty days, the days in the south gradually shorten.
The city-wall of the moon,
broad and long, one thousand nine hundred and sixty li,
its height likewise.
Majestically square, but seen from afar, it appears round.
Two parts celestial silver, one part lapis lazuli.
Inside and out, clear and translucent, its light shines far.
It is upheld by five winds.
The Moon King sits in a seven-treasure palace twenty li square.
Immeasurable devas, with light and music, guide and follow before and after.
Gardens, pools, and other amusements are like those in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
The devas' lifespan is five hundred years.
Descendants succeed each other to complete one kalpa.
The moon has waxing and waning.
The waning: one corner travels at night, gradually hidden and tilted, thus appearing diminished.
It is also said:
Beside the moon-city there is a deva.
His color is pure blue, his clothes also blue.
The side where he is located shines blue light upon the city, thus it appears diminished.
The full moon: the moon's travel gradually turns toward the correct position.
Moreover, the blue deva on the fifteenth day enters the moon-city and meets with the king.
Furthermore, south of Mount Sumeru, on the ground, there is a great tree.
The tree is named Jambudvīpa.
Forty thousand li high, its branches shade two thousand li, and its shadow appears in the moon.
Solar and lunar eclipses:
The Asura king is named Rāhu.
His body is twenty-eight thousand li tall.
On the fifteenth day of the month, he stands in the center of the ocean.
The ocean water reaches only to his navel.
Bowing his head, he obstructs the Sumeru jewel,
the Tiṣya mountain, and the four directional guardian mountains.
With his finger, he covers the sun and moon, and the world becomes dark.
Or he covers the sun, making day into night.
This is what is called the time of solar and lunar eclipses, when the light is endangered.
The city-walls of the constellations,
are the dwellings of the devas.
With crystal as the walls, the seven treasures as the palaces,
suspended in empty space, great winds uphold them like floating clouds.
Moving with the sun's course, they are seen by the eye.
The large ones are seven hundred li,
the medium ones five hundred li, the small ones one hundred and twenty li.
Palaces, chambers, gardens, and pools are like those in the Cāturmahārājika heaven.
Their lifespans are likewise.
In the clouds of empty space,
sometimes the earth element comes into contact with water.
Sometimes it comes into contact with the fire and wind elements, etc.
The water, fire, and wind elements come into contact with each other.
All give rise to thunder sounds in the clouds of empty space.
Lightning has four kinds.
The eastern one is named Body Light.
The second, southern one is named Hard to Destroy.
The western one is named Flowing Flame.
The northern one is named Steady Brightness.
Why is there this lightning in the clouds of empty space?
The lightnings of the four directions also come into contact with each other.
This light arises.
Clouds have four kinds.
First, white.
Second, black.
Third, red.
Fourth, pink.
White ones have predominantly the earth element.
Black ones have predominantly the water element.
Red ones have predominantly the fire element.
Pink ones have predominantly the wind element.
They are ten li above the ground,
or twenty, thirty,
up to forty li.
Except at the beginning of the kalpa, they extend up to the Ābhāsvara heaven. Clouds have four colors.
First, blue.
Second, red.
Third, yellow-white.
Fourth, black.
Blue ones have mostly the water element within.
Red ones have mostly the fire element within.
Yellow-white ones have mostly the earth element within.
Black ones have mostly the wind element within; dragon energy becomes clouds.
When the world is destroyed, a great wind arises named Destroying Scatterer.
It can completely blow away and destroy the great thousand-world system.
The Vajra Iron Ring Mountains and all the ten thousand things.
At that time, outside the great thousand-world system,
another wind arises named Obstructing Destroying Scatterer.
It can block the wind calamity from reaching other regions.
If there were no this obstructing wind,
the immeasurable, countless worlds in the ten directions,
would all be scattered and destroyed.
The astrologer predicts rain.
There are five reasons why it cannot be determined with certainty.
They cause the predictor to be confused.
First, when clouds have thunder and lightning, the prediction says it should rain.
But due to excessive fire, the clouds are burned and it does not rain.
Second, when clouds have thunder and lightning, the prediction also says it will rain.
But a great wind arises, scattering the clouds into the mountains.
Third, when clouds have thunder and lightning, the prediction also says it will rain.
At that time, the Asuras gather the floating clouds and place them in the great sea.
Fourth, when clouds have thunder and lightning, the prediction also says it will rain.
But the rain deity indulges in debauchery and disorder, ultimately not releasing rain.
Fifth, when clouds have thunder and lightning, the prediction also says it will rain.
But the beings of the world act unlawfully and recklessly, defiling pure conduct.
They are stingy, greedy, jealous, and their views are perverted.
Therefore, heaven does not send rain.
Due to these five things, the prediction cannot be certain.
The dragon king Anàodá raises great heavy clouds.
Filling Jambudvīpa, he pours down heavy rain.
All grains, grasses, and trees flourish.
Rivers, streams, and marshes are all filled.
This great rain water emerges from the dragon king’s body and mind, benefiting countless beings.
The dragon king Mónàsī, about to send rain,
first raises heavy clouds covering the sky.
Out of compassion, he holds back for seven days.
First, he allows beings to complete their various activities.
Then gradually sends light rain, universally moistening the earth.
Formerly, in the country of Bǐmó, on Cóngtuó Mountain, there was a wild fox.
Chased by a lion, it fell into a dry well in the wilderness.
After three days, its heart was open, partly dead.
It spoke a verse.
Śakra heard it.
With eighty thousand gods, he sought its location and flew to the side of the well.
He said, “I have not heard the holy teaching for long; in darkness, there is no guide.
What you just said is no ordinary speech; I wish you would expound the Dharma.”
It replied,
“Heavenly Emperor, you lack instruction.
Greatly ignorant of what is timely.
The Dharma teacher is below, you place yourself above.
Initially, you do not show respect.
Yet ask for the essentials of the Dharma.”
Śakra lowered a heavenly garment to lift the wild fox, who bowed and repented.
The Heavenly Emperor said,
“I recall that in the past I saw people who wished to hear the true Dharma.
First, they prepared a high seat, adorned it purely, then invited the Dharma teacher.”
The gods each took off their heavenly jeweled garments and piled them into a high seat.
The wild fox ascended the seat and said,
“There are two great reasons.
First, to teach the Dharma and enlighten gods and humans brings immeasurable merit.
Second, to repay the kindness of giving food—how could I not speak?”
Śakra said,
“Being saved from the well’s peril, the merit and reward should be great.
How is it that teaching the Dharma to repay kindness is not as good as this?”
It replied,
“Life and death each have their appropriateness.
Each has its people.
Some people cling to life.
Some delight in death.
There are foolish people.
Who do not know that after death there is rebirth.
They turn away from the Buddha’s Dharma.
Do not encounter a wise teacher.
Killing, stealing, debauchery, deceit.
Only associate with evil.
Such people,
greedy for life, fear death.
After death, they fall into hell.
There are wise people.
Who serve the Three Jewels.
Encounter a wise teacher.
Reform evil and cultivate good.
Filially support parents.
Respectfully serve teachers and elders.
Harmonize with relatives.
Humbly respect those below.
Such people,
detest life and delight in death.
After death, they are born in heaven.”
Śakra said,
“As you have instructed,
preserving the body and life
has no merit.
I wish to hear about giving food and giving Dharma.”
The wild fox replied,
“Giving food and drink
sustains life for one day.
Giving precious treasures
relieves poverty for one lifetime.
But it increases birth and death.
Bonds of karma.
Teaching the Dharma and instructing
is called Dharma giving.
It enables beings to attain the path beyond the world.
Some become Arhats.
Some become Pratyekabuddhas.
Some attain Buddhahood.
These three kinds of joyful people
all come from hearing the Dharma.
Practicing as taught.
Moreover, all beings
avoid the three evil paths.
Enjoy human and heavenly blessings and happiness.
All due to hearing the Dharma.
Therefore, the Buddha said,
Giving Dharma
has immeasurable merit.”
Śakra said,
“Teacher, your current form,
is it karmic retribution,
or an emanation body?”
It replied,
“It is retribution for sins,
not an emanation.”
The god said,
“I thought
you were a Bodhisattva or sage manifesting to save beings.
Now I hear it is the fruit of sin.
I do not know the reason.
I wish to hear the cause.”
The wild fox said,
“In a past life, in Bōluónà Bōtóumó City,
I was the son of a poor family.
Of the Kṣatriya caste.
From childhood, intelligent and bright.
Especially fond of learning.
At age twelve,
I followed a wise teacher.
In the deep mountains,
I served diligently with hardship.
Striving tirelessly.
The teacher also, day and night,
instructed and guided me.
Never missing the proper time.
After fifty years,
the ninety-six kinds
of scriptures, prophecies, treatises,
medical formulas, spells,
divining auspicious and inauspicious signs,
disasters, anomalies, misfortunes, and blessings,
there was nothing I did not master.
With high talent and wisdom,
my fame spread far and wide.
Then I thought to myself:
‘Now that I have attained salvation,
it is all due to the teaching kindness of my master.
Such merit is hard to repay.
My family is poor,
with nothing to offer.
I must sell myself to repay my teacher’s kindness.’
The teacher said,
‘A mountain-dwelling ascetic
begs for food to survive.
Truly, I lack nothing.
Why destroy and sell your precious body to provide for me?
Now you have achieved wisdom and eloquence.
You should turn to teach and transform the people of the world.
Be a lamp of the Dharma.
The merit of teaching and transforming
is surely enough to repay my kindness.’
So I stayed in the mountains,
begging for food to support myself.
Not long after, the king died.
The ministers gathered over five hundred scholars from the country.
They debated for seven days.
The winner would become king.
This poor family’s son
received the king’s position.
Using all the country’s wealth and power,
he made offerings to his teacher and parents.
Later, the country of Āntuóluó
and the country of Móluópóyē
fought and punished each other for many years without victory.
The king of Āntuóluó
summoned his ministers:
‘What plan should we adopt
to obtain the country of Móluópóyē?’
The ministers replied,
‘Only Bōluónà Bōtóumó country.”
The king was born into humble poverty.
He upheld the ten precepts.
He did not violate external desires.
Although there were palace women,
they were all of advanced age and long-standing.
Searching throughout the country,
regardless of nobility or lowliness,
he selected renowned women,
totaling one hundred,
young, upright,
and capable of pleasing the mind.
Carrying precious treasures,
along with these palace women,
he offered them as tribute.
If the other accepted them,
he would borrow troops from him,
and with combined strength attack in battle,
there would be no place he would not subdue.
He then followed his minister’s plan.
At that time, he offered everything.
The king was greatly delighted.
He selected and reviewed a million strong soldiers
to send as assistance.
After a hundred days of bitter fighting,
more than half had died.
King Móluópó
was completely executed and beheaded.
Only then did he achieve victory.
Because of these beautiful women,
he forgot his original aspirations.
Indulging in luxury and pleasure,
he neglected the governance of the state.
The hundred officials and all the courtiers
together rose in rebellion.
The children of good people
were seized as slaves and maidservants.
Wind and rain were untimely,
and starvation filled the roads.
Resentful enemies from other regions
then came to invade and plunder.
From then on, his country
consequently perished and was lost.
He was reborn in hell,
suffering numerous torments.
Relying on the power of wisdom from previous learning,
he himself recognized his past lives,
his heart repented and blamed himself,
he reformed his past and cultivated the future.
In a moment, he relinquished his life,
and was reborn among hungry ghosts.
Again he repented and confessed,
cultivating mindfulness of the ten good deeds.
In a moment, he relinquished his life,
and received the body of a wild fox.
Still recognizing his previous connections,
he again practiced the ten good deeds.
Recently encountering a lion,
he fell into this well.
Opening his heart, prepared to die,
hoping to be reborn in heaven, leaving suffering and receiving joy.
Because you saved me,
you thwarted my original wish.
Now I must endure hardship,
when will I ever be free?
Therefore, I say
that you saving my life
is of no merit.
The reason I entered the robe and could emerge
is, first, not to violate the heavenly aspiration.
If the aspiration is not fulfilled,
great suffering arises.
Inflicting suffering on others,
in every rebirth,
one’s wishes are not attained.
Second, for the devas who wish to hear the Dharma.
If one is stingy with the Dharma,
in every lifetime,
one is born deaf, blind, mute, or dumb,
with faculties blocked,
born in borderlands,
foolish and ignorant.
If born in a good place,
the mind is dull and obtuse,
what is learned does not succeed,
bringing suffering upon oneself.
Third, to propagate the Dharma,
enlightening devas and humans.
This is the gift of Dharma.
The benefit of the gift of Dharma
enables beings to know that death leads to rebirth,
doing good brings blessings,
doing evil brings calamity,
cultivating the path leads to attaining the path.
In future rebirths,
wisdom becomes clear,
always recognizing past lives.
If born in heaven,
one becomes a teacher of the devas.
If born among humans,
one becomes a golden-wheel-turning king,
transforming the world with the ten good deeds,
wisdom and light gradually increasing,
accomplishing the practices of a bodhisattva,
reaching the patience of non-arising.
The gift of material wealth is like a lamp,
only illuminating a small room.
The gift of Dharma is like the sun, shining far across the world.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, with eighty thousand devas, received the Dharma of the ten good deeds.
First, with ten skillful means, he subdued his faculties,
namely the six pāramitās, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Then the devas asked:
“Now we return to the heavenly palace.
When will you, O teacher, abandon this retribution of offenses and be reborn in heaven?”
The wild fox said:
“Exactly seven days from now, I will abandon this body and be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.
You all may then aspire to be reborn in that heaven.
There are many bodhisattvas teaching and transforming beings.”
After seven days, his life ended, and he was reborn in the Tuṣita heavenly palace.
Again recognizing past lives, he practiced the ten good paths.
In a past world,
there was Śakra, Lord of the Devas,
who said to the Buddha:
“I now receive the precept
that as long as the Buddha’s Dharma remains in the world,
for the rest of my life,
if anyone troubles me,
I vow not to retaliate
or cause trouble to them.”
At that time, King Vemacitrin of the asuras,
hearing that Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had received such a precept,
upon hearing it, took up a sharp sword and came against him on the road.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saw him from afar,
and from afar declared:
“Asura, stop!
Be bound and do not move!” And he could not move.
Śakra said: “If you vow not to cause trouble, then I will release you.”
King Asura then spoke a verse:
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again declared:
“I release you to go wherever you wish.”
He went to the Buddha and fully reported this.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent!
In the past, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, when the five virtues left his body, knew his life was ending.
He was to be reborn in a potter’s family, in the womb of a donkey.
Worried and reflecting to himself,
‘In the three realms, only the Buddha can save people from suffering and distress.’
He rushed to the Buddha, bowed with his head to the ground, and with utmost sincerity took refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
Before he could rise, his life suddenly ended, and he entered the womb of a donkey mother.
At that time, the donkey broke loose and destroyed pottery vessels.
Its owner struck it, immediately injuring the fetus.
His spirit then returned to his former body,
the five virtues were restored,
and he again became Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
The Buddha praised him: ‘Excellent!
At the moment of death, you took refuge in the Three Jewels.
Your karmic retribution ended, and you did not undergo further suffering.’
The Buddha spoke a verse:
Śakra, hearing this, understood the transformation of offense and blessing,
comprehended the root of rise and decline,
followed the practice of cessation,
and attained the path of stream-enterer.”
At that time, the deva Sivipili said to the Buddha:
“In my past life, I was a king named Sivipili.
At the four city gates, I universally performed acts of generosity.
At the crossroads within the city, I also gave alms.
Then the first queen said:
‘The king performs great meritorious deeds, but I am first.’
The king said: ‘The almsgiving and meritorious deeds at the eastern city gate all belong to you.’
The princes again said:
‘The almsgiving and meritorious deeds at the southern city gate all belong to you.’
Then a minister again said to the king:
‘The almsgiving and meritorious deeds at the western city gate all belong to you.’
Then the generals and soldiers again said to the king:
‘The northern city gate, together—’
Then the common people again said to the king:
The king replied:
‘The almsgiving and meritorious deeds at the four crossroads within the city all belong to you all.’
At that time, the king, queen, ministers, generals, soldiers, and common people all performed acts of generosity.
Among all meritorious deeds, I was the first to act.
The merit of generosity was thus cut off for me.
Then those I had sent to perform meritorious deeds returned to me, paid homage, and said to me:
‘Great King, you should know
that at all places of meritorious deeds, the queen, princes, ministers, generals, soldiers, and common people
each occupy their places, performing almsgiving and meritorious deeds.
The king’s almsgiving is thus cut off.’
I then replied:
‘Of the annual tributes from all regions that should come to me,
half shall enter the treasury, and half shall be given in alms there.’
For a long time, I thus performed generosity, always obtaining lovely, desirable, and pleasing karmic rewards.
I always experienced happiness without end.
Through this karmic fruit of meritorious deeds, I entered the great accumulation of merit.
It is like five great rivers merging into one stream,
such as the Ganges, which no one can measure.
The amount of its water in hundreds of thousands, millions, billions of bushels and pecks—
the karmic fruit of merit is immeasurable.
All enter the great accumulation of merit.’
At that time, the deva Sivipili, hearing the Buddha’s words,
joyfully paid homage at his feet and then vanished from sight.”
One day, the Sun Deva King, accompanied by countless heavenly beings, came to where the Buddha was, bowed his head, and said:
"Through what actions does one become the Sun Deva, illuminating the four quarters of the world?
And through what causes and conditions does one become the Moon Deva, dispelling the darkness of night?"
The Buddha said:
"There are four deeds.
First, always delighting in giving alms.
Second, cultivating one's conduct and being careful in one's actions.
Third, upholding the precepts without transgression.
Fourth, lighting lamps in Buddha's temples.
If one does so for parents, śramaṇas, or practitioners, one plants the seeds of light.
Furthermore, practicing the ten wholesome deeds with body, speech, and mind, such as not killing, and so forth."
The Buddha said:
"There are also four deeds through which one becomes the Moon King.
First, giving alms to the poor and destitute.
Second, upholding the five precepts.
Third, reverently serving the Three Jewels.
Fourth, setting up lamps in the dark for one's ruler, father, teacher, and temples."
In the past, in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven palace, there was a deva
whose lifespan was about to end, and seven omens appeared:
first, the light on his neck extinguished;
second, the flowers on his head withered;
third, his complexion changed;
fourth, dust appeared on his clothes;
fifth, sweat emerged from his armpits;
sixth, his body shape changed;
seventh, he left his original seat.
He then thought to himself:
"After my life ends, I will descend to be born in the country of Kauśāmbī, in the womb of a scabby, leprous sow, becoming a piglet.
I am deeply distressed and sorrowful, not knowing what plan to make."
A deva said to him:
"The Buddha is now here, preaching the sūtra for his mother.
Only the Buddha can free you from your transgressions."
He immediately went to where the Buddha was, bowed his head in reverence, and before he could even ask a question,
the Buddha addressed the deva:
"All things in the world are impermanent.
You have always known this; why are you sorrowful?"
The deva explained everything to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If you wish to escape being born as a piglet, you should recite the Threefold Refuge.
Do this three times a day."
The deva followed the Buddha's teaching, taking refuge morning and night.
After seven days, the deva's life ended.
He descended and was born in the country of Vaiśālī as the son of a wealthy elder.
While in his mother's womb, he took the Threefold Refuge three times daily.
When he was born and fell to the ground, he also knelt and took refuge.
His mother gave birth easily and without any foul discharge.
The maidservants attending his mother were terrified and fled.
His mother was also deeply astonished.
The child spoke as soon as he fell to the ground.
They called him an ominous spirit and wanted to kill him.
But then she thought to herself:
"I have few sons.
If I kill this child, my husband will surely punish me.
I will slowly inform the elder; it is not too late to kill him then."
The mother then took the child and went to tell the elder.
"The boy I gave birth to fell to the ground and immediately knelt with hands folded, taking refuge in the Three Jewels."
The whole household was amazed and called him an ominous spirit.
The father said:
"Stop, stop.
This child is no ordinary person.
Ordinary people live a hundred years without understanding to take refuge in the Three Jewels.
How much more so a newborn who can utter 'Namo Buddha'!
Take good care of him and be careful not to slight or disrespect him."
The child grew up and was nearly seven years old.
He was playing by the roadside with his companions
when he encountered Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
The child went forward and paid respects to them. The holy ones were astonished that one so young could pay such respects.
The child said:
"Venerable ones, do you not recognize me?"
He then recounted in detail how he had met the Buddha in heaven and how they had met before.
"I was originally in heaven and was destined to be reborn in an evil path.
But I encountered the Buddha's compassion and pity; he taught me to take refuge, and thus I was able to become a human."
The bhikṣus then uttered a blessing for him, saying:
"Zhélíqí'ér spoke to Maudgalyāyana and the others, including Śāriputra:
'I wish to use my words to invite the World-Honored One, the bodhisattva-saṅgha, and you venerable ones.'"
They accepted and returned, fully informing his parents.
"I wish to prepare offerings for them, making them sweet and delicious."
His parents loved him and complied with his words.
They marveled at his young age and his profound understanding.
They were also amazed by his actions and his knowledge of past lives.
They prepared the most exquisite delicacies, the finest flavors in the world.
The offerings were so refined and exquisite that they surpassed the child's expectations.
The Buddha and the assembled saṅgha each used their supernatural powers to come to the child's house for the meal.
The Buddha preached a sūtra for them.
The child, his parents, and all his relatives, both internal and external, attained the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika).
In the past, there was a guide
who traveled with five hundred merchants on a trading journey.
They came to a great wilderness, where they were extremely hungry, thirsty, and exhausted.
They took refuge in the World-Honored One, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings, but were terrified and at a loss for what to do.
At that time, the guide climbed high to look into the distance.
He saw a grove of trees with birds flying toward it, hoping there would be water there.
They all rushed there and soon arrived.
They only saw trees surrounded by grass, and the ground was clean.
The guide then said to the merchants:
"Let us all dig here to get water; we are sure to find it."
Just as they were discussing this,
a deva from afar in heaven observed this guide and the five hundred people suffering from lack of water.
In the time it takes to stretch out an arm, he arrived at their location and stood atop a tree.
He stretched out his right hand, and from his
five fingers flowed water of eight flavors, sweet and delicious,
providing for the guide and the five hundred people.
Each took and used it without exhaustion, and all were fully satisfied.
Why was this?
In past lives, they had all together planted seeds of kindness and merit.
Thus, the deva remembered them and descended to provide them with fine water, so that each could be safe and secure."
In the past, when a deva of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven was about to die,
five auspicious signs appeared before him:
flowers withered;
clothes became soiled and defiled;
sweat emerged from the armpits;
heavenly maidens decreased;
he lost pleasure in his original seat.
It was as if his body had developed scabies, sores, boils, or ulcers.
Among the thirty-three devas, there was one deva
who manifested five unusual signs and was sorrowfully moaning.
At that time, Śakra heard this and asked:
"In that heavenly palace, which deva is sorrowfully moaning?"
A deva replied:
"There is a deva manifesting five auspicious signs."
"Excellent! For that deva,"
Śakra went to where he was and said:
"Why are you sorrowfully moaning?"
He then slapped his thigh and replied:
"There are strange disasters and anomalies."
Śakra then spoke a verse to him:
The deva said:
"I have not heard this."
Śakra said:
"All affectionate attachments involve separation."
The deva said:
"How can I not feel sorrow?
Now, in this heavenly palace, all the various five desires will be left behind.
When my life ends, I will be born in the womb of a sow in the city of Rājagṛha.
What I will eat is feces.
I will then be slaughtered by butchers.
Seeing this now, I am filled with sorrow."
At that time, Śakra said to the deva:
"You should now take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
The reason is this:
The Buddha spoke a verse, saying:"
The deva folded his hands and then said:
"The World-Honored One is omniscient,
seeing and observing with perfect clarity.
I wish to be saved and aided.
I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, take refuge in the Bhikṣu-Saṅgha."
Thus, he did not end up in a sow's womb.
He was born into the household of the foremost elder in the city of Rājagṛha.
Upon seeing him, they were overjoyed and could not contain themselves."
There was a heavenly maiden
sitting on a lotus flower one hundred yojanas in breadth and length.
This flower was uniquely exquisite, surpassing all others.
Whatever necessities for life she desired would appear from the flower according to her thoughts.
It moved with her as she went or stayed.
Maudgalyāyana asked:
"What wholesome deeds did you perform to receive such a reward?"
The heavenly maiden replied:
"After the parinirvāṇa of Buddha Kāśyapa,
his complete bodily relics remained.
Together with the Buddha's disciples, a seven-jeweled stūpa was built,
forty li high and wide.
At that time, I was a woman and went out to see the image in the jeweled stūpa.
Faith and reverence arose in my heart, and I reflected on the Buddha's merit.
I removed the flowers from my head and offered them to the image."
In the Heaven of the Lord of the Sense Desires (Paranirmitavaśavartin), there was a jeweled maiden named Shànkǒu.
With a single utterance, she could produce hundreds of thousands of delightful sounds.
And from each one of those sounds,
hundreds of thousands more sounds would emerge.
Children of the Buddha, you should know:
from one Shànkǒu sound,
innumerable sounds are born,
each according to what is appropriate, enabling all to understand."
In a past age,
in the country of Kośala, there was a man who played the lute,
named Lùniú.
While resting in the wilderness, there were six vast heavenly palaces.
Heavenly maidens came and said to Lùniú:
"Uncle, uncle, play the lute for me,
and I will sing and dance."
Lùniú played the lute, and the six devas sang and danced.
The first song's lyrics said:
The lyrics of the other devas were roughly similar. Lùniú also paid his respects.
After paying respects, the devas suddenly vanished.
Within Jambudvīpa,
there are sixteen great kingdoms, eighty-four thousand cities, eight royal states, and four celestial sons.
To the east is the Jìn Kingdom, whose celestial son and people are prosperous and flourishing.
To the south is the Tiānzhú Kingdom, whose celestial son's land is abundant with elephants.
To the west is the Dàqín Kingdom, whose celestial son's land is rich in gold and jade.
To the north is the Yuèzhī Kingdom, whose celestial son's land is known for fine horses.
Among the eighty-four thousand cities,
there are six thousand four hundred kinds of people.
Ten thousand kinds of sounds.
Five hundred and sixty trillion settlements.
Fish have six thousand four hundred kinds.
Birds have four thousand five hundred kinds.
Beasts have two thousand four hundred kinds.
Trees have ten thousand kinds.
Grasses have eight thousand kinds.
Miscellaneous medicines have seven hundred and forty kinds.
Miscellaneous incenses have forty-three kinds.
Treasures have one hundred and twenty-one kinds.
True treasures have seven kinds.
In the seas, there are two thousand five hundred kingdoms.
One hundred and eighty kingdoms consume the five grains.
Two thousand three hundred and twenty kingdoms consume fish, turtles, and soft-shelled turtles.
There are five kings.
One king rules over five hundred cities.
The first king is named Sīlí.
His kingdom entirely serves the Buddha and does not serve various heretics.
The second king is named Jiāluó.
His land produces the seven treasures.
The third king is named Bùluó.
His land produces forty-three kinds of incense and white glass.
The fourth king is named Shéyé.
His land produces pepper and long pepper.
The fifth king is named Nàpō.
His land produces white pearls and seven-colored glass.
The five great kingdoms' cities are mostly dark, short, and small, separated by six hundred and fifty thousand lǐ.
From here, there is only seawater, with no people.
It is one million four hundred thousand lǐ from the Iron Encircling Mountains.
Among them, the place where Āngulimāla killed people is eighty thousand lǐ east of Shèwèi Kingdom.
The place where the Buddha transformed is also one place.
Jūyínàjié Kingdom is one thousand lǐ southeast of Jiāwéiluó Kingdom.
Wángshè Kingdom is two thousand two hundred lǐ southeast of Jiāwéiluówèi Kingdom.
The place where the Buddha attained enlightenment is two hundred lǐ southeast of Wángshè City.
Wéiyélí Kingdom is one thousand eight hundred lǐ east of Jiāwéiwèi Kingdom.
Nǚ Kingdom is three lǐ south of Wéiyélí City, west of the road.
Jūshǎnmí Kingdom is one thousand two hundred lǐ southwest of Jiāwéiluówèi Kingdom.
Yèbō Kingdom is one thousand two hundred eighty lǐ east of Jiāwéiluówèi Kingdom.
Nán Kingdom is three thousand two hundred lǐ east of Jiāwéiluówèi Kingdom.
Shèwèi Kingdom is five hundred lǐ west of Jiāwéiluówèi.
Bōluónà Kingdom is nine hundred sixty lǐ west of Jiāwéiwèi Kingdom.
The place where the Buddha turned the Dharma wheel is twenty lǐ north of Bōluónà Kingdom.
The tree is named Xiāngjìng.
It is the place where he subdued Māra.
Bōluónàsī Kingdom is one thousand four hundred lǐ south of Shèwèi Kingdom.
In between, the Ganges River flows southeast.
Qíshéjué Mountain has five hundred peaks.
The Buddha recited scriptures at the central peak.
Wángshè Kingdom is below the central peak.
Question:
Such as Shèpótí, Jiāpíluópó,
Bōluónà City,
all have kings and royal residences.
Why is this city alone named Wángshè (Royal Residence)?
Answer:
Some say:
The king of Mójiātuó had a son with one head, two faces, and four arms.
People at the time considered it inauspicious.
The king tore apart his body and head and abandoned them in the wilderness.
A rākṣasī demoness named Líluó
reassembled his body and nursed him.
Later, he grew into a great man of strength and annexed various kingdoms.
He captured eighteen thousand kings and placed them in the five mountains named this mountain.
With great power, he ruled Jambudvīpa.
Therefore, this mountain was named Wángshè City.
Furthermore, some say:
The king of Mójiātuó's previously inhabited city caught fire.
Once burned, once rebuilt, thus up to seven times.
The kingdom's people were exhausted by labor.
The king assembled wise men to ask the reason; some said:
It is appropriate to change location.
The king saw these five mountains encircling like a city.
He then built palaces and resided there.
Hence, it is named Wángshè City.
Furthermore, in ancient times,
this kingdom had a king named Pó sǒu.
Weary of worldly affairs, he left home to become an immortal.
At that time, householder brāhmaṇas and various ascetic immortals debated.
The householder brāhmaṇas said:
In heavenly sacrifices, one should kill and eat meat.
The ascetic immortals said one should not.
They argued back and forth.
The ascetic brāhmaṇas said:
There is a great king who left home to become an immortal; do you believe it or not?
The householder brāhmaṇas said:
The ascetic immortals said:
I take this person as witness.
Tomorrow I will ask.
The householder brāhmaṇas first went to Pó sǒu's place.
They said to the immortal Pó sǒu:
Tomorrow we debate.
You should assist me.
The ascetic immortals asked:
In heavenly sacrifices, should one kill and eat meat or not?
The immortal Pó sǒu said:
One should kill and eat meat.
Those killed in heavenly sacrifices are thus reborn in heaven.
The ascetic immortals said:
You are greatly wrong.
You speak great falsehoods, and they spat, saying:
Sinner, perish!
Then the immortal Pó sǒu
immediately sank into the ground up to his ankles.
This was the first opening of the gate of great sin.
The ascetic immortals said:
You should speak truthfully.
If you persist in falsehood,
your body will sink into the ground.
Pó sǒu said:
I know that killing sheep and eating meat for heaven's sake is without sin.
He sank to his knees.
Thus gradually sinking to his waist, then to his neck.
The ascetic immortals said:
You now receive the present retribution for falsehood.
If you speak truthfully, even if you sink underground, I can pull you out and spare you from sin.
Pó sǒu thought:
I am an honorable man and should not speak two kinds of words.
Moreover, the four Vedas praise the method of sacrificing to heaven.
What does my death alone matter?
With single-mindedness, he said:
In heavenly sacrifices, killing and eating meat is without sin.
Thereupon, his entire body plunged into the ground.
From then on, they always used the method of the immortal Pó sǒu.
In heavenly sacrifices, when killing sheep,
at the moment of wielding the knife, they say Pó sǒu kills you.
Sǒu's son was named Guǎngchē.
He succeeded to the throne as king.
He too was weary of worldly ways but could not leave home.
Thus he thought:
My father left home and sank alive into the ground.
If I rule the world, I will also commit great sins.
How should I now conduct myself?
Then a voice in the sky said:
If you travel and see a rare, hard-to-find place, you should build a dwelling there.
Not long after,
the king went hunting and saw a deer running swift as wind.
The king chased it; none of the officials or attendants could keep up.
Ahead, he saw five mountains encircling, steep and solid.
The land was adorned with heavenly flowers and incense, and heavenly music was heard.
This place was rare, never seen before.
Now I should dwell here.
He then abandoned his original city and dwelt in these mountains.
From then on, they successively dwelt there; hence, it is named Wángshè City.
There was a wealthy elder,
named Jiā lán tuó.
He regretted giving his garden to the Nirgranthas.
Unable to offer it to the Buddha and his monks,
he could not rest peacefully.
There was a great ghost general,
named Bàn shī.
Receiving the Buddha's divine command,
he summoned yakṣas to expel the Nirgranthas.
Naked and shameless, they should not stay here.
The ghost master, receiving the order,
beat the Nirgranthas and dragged away their utensils.
The Nirgranthas fled in terror, saying:
What evil men are these, acting so violently?
The ghost master replied:
The elder Jiā lán tuó will offer the bamboo grove to make a vihāra for the Buddha.
The great ghost general Bàn shī was ordered to expel you.
The next day, the Nirgranthas together reproached the elder.
The elder was pleased: my wish is fulfilled.
He answered the Nirgranthas:
These ghosts are violent and wrathful; I fear they will cause harm.
It is better to leave and seek another place.
The Nirgranthas, resentful, all left that day.
The elder repaired and established the vihāra.
Monks' quarters, sitting mats, and all adornments were completed.
He went to the tree and invited the Buddha and his monks.
The World-Honored One accepted the offering, stayed, transformed, and aided.
All were joyful and delighted.
Xūdáduō addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The people of Shèwèi City mostly believe in heresies.
May the Tathāgata, in his great compassion, deign to come to Shèwèi City."
The Buddha said:
"There is no monastery there; how can I go?"
Xūdá said:
"Your disciple will build one; I beg you to grant permission."
The World-Honored One remained silent.
"I wish to send Shèlìfú to instruct on the design."
