He was then ordered to go together to survey the area, but after searching everywhere, no suitable place was found.
Only Prince Jītuó's garden was level and even, with lush trees and forests, and the distance was just right.
Xūdá informed the prince.
The prince laughed and said:
"Do you wish to use it for amusement?"
Xūdá earnestly pleaded again and again.
The prince said:
"If you can cover the ground with gold, leaving no gaps, then I will give it to you."
Xūdá said:
"Agreed; I will pay the price as you say."
Prince Jītuó said:
"I was only joking."
Xūdá said:
"A prince should not speak falsely," and they began to dispute.
At that time, a deity from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven transformed into a person, descended to mediate, and said:
"A prince, by law, should not speak falsely.
Since the price has been settled,
it is not right to go back on it."
Thus, it was decided to give it to him.
Elephants were then sent to carry out the gold.
Over eighty qǐng of land,
were soon about to be filled.
Only a small area remained, and Xūdá thought to himself:
"Where can I get enough gold?"
Jītuó asked:
"Are you finding it too expensive? Then stop."
He replied: "No."
Jītuó thought to himself:
"The Buddha must be of great virtue to make this man regard treasure so lightly."
He then told Xūdá: "The garden land belongs to you.
The trees belong to me.
I will offer them to the Buddha myself," and so the work began.
The six teachers heard of this and went to inform the king:
"The elder Xūdá has bought Prince Jītuó's garden to build a monastery for Gautama.
Allow our followers to compete with his disciples in skills.
If the śramaṇa wins, permit the monastery to be built.
If not, it must not be built."
The king summoned Xūdá and asked him:
"These six teachers say
you bought the garden to build a monastery for Gautama.
They request to compete with the śramaṇa's disciples
in their skills.
If they win, the monastery may be built.
If not, it must not be built."
Xūdá returned home, put on dirty clothes, and was filled with sorrow and distress.
The next day, when the time came, Shèlìfú put on his robe, took his bowl, and went to Xūdá's house.
He asked him:
"Why are you unhappy?"
Xūdá explained in detail.
"These six teachers have been ordained for a long time, are sincere and experienced, and their skills are unmatched.
I wonder if your honor's skills can compete with them?"
Shèlìfú said:
"Even if the number of these six teachers
filled Jambudvīpa like a bamboo forest,
they could not move a single hair on my foot.
Let them choose whatever they wish to compete in; I will allow it."
Xūdá was overjoyed, changed into new clothes, bathed, and applied fragrant water.
He then went to inform the king:
"I have asked him, and he allows them to choose."
The king told the six teachers:
"Now you may compete with the śramaṇa in skills."
The six teachers announced to the people:
"In seven days, we will compete with the śramaṇa outside the city."
In the kingdom of Shèwèi, there were 1.8 billion people.
According to the law of that country, drums were beaten to assemble the people.
If a bronze drum was beaten, 800 million people gathered.
If a silver drum was beaten, 1.4 billion people gathered.
If a gold drum was beaten, everyone gathered.
When the seven days were up, at a flat and open place, the gold drum was struck.
Everyone gathered.
The six teachers had 300 million followers.
At that time, the people set up high seats for the king and the six teachers.
Then Xūdá set up a high seat for Shèlìfú.
At that time, Shèlìfú was under a tree, entering various meditative concentrations.
He thought to himself:
"This assembly has long been accustomed to heresies, arrogant and self-important, treating all beings as mere grass. By what virtue shall I subdue them?"
After thinking this, he made a vow:
"If, over countless kalpas, I have been filial to my parents and revered śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas,
then when I first enter the assembly, all the people shall bow to me."
The six teachers saw that the assembly had gathered, but Shèlìfú had not yet arrived.
They said to the king:
"Gautama's disciple knows he has no skills.
Since the assembly has gathered, he is afraid and will not come."
The king told Xūdá:
"The time for the competition has come.
The Buddha's disciple should come to debate."
Xūdá then went to Shèlìfú, knelt down, and said:
"Venerable One, the assembly has gathered.
Please come to the meeting."
Shèlìfú rose from meditation,
adjusted his robes,
placed his sitting cloth over his left shoulder,
and walked calmly, like a lion king, to the assembly.
At that moment, the people and the six teachers suddenly stood up, as grass bends before the wind, and unconsciously bowed.
Shèlìfú then ascended the seat prepared by Xūdá.
Among the six teachers' followers was one named Láodùchā,
skilled in illusion.
Before the assembly, he chanted and created a tree,
which naturally grew large, shading the assembly, with lush branches and leaves, and various flowers and fruits.
Everyone said:
"This transformation was made by Láodùchā."
Shèlìfú then used his supernatural power to create a whirlwind,
which uprooted the tree, threw it to the ground, and shattered it into dust.
Everyone said Shèlìfú had won.
Láodùchā again chanted and created a pond,
its four sides adorned with the seven treasures.
In the pond water grew various flowers.
Shèlìfú transformed into a large six-tusked white elephant.
On each tusk were seven lotus flowers,
and on each flower were seven jade maidens.
The elephant walked calmly to the pond's edge,
sucked up the water with its trunk, and the pond immediately vanished.
Láodùchā created a mountain,
adorned with the seven treasures, with ponds, trees, and lush flowers and fruits.
Shèlìfú transformed into a vajra-wielding warrior,
who pointed his vajra pestle from afar,
and the mountain was destroyed without a trace.
Láodùchā created a dragon with ten heads,
raining down various treasures from the sky,
with thunder and lightning shaking the earth, startling the assembly.
Shèlìfú transformed into a golden-winged garuḍa king,
which tore the dragon apart and devoured it.
Láodùchā created an ox,
tall and strong, with powerful legs and sharp horns, pawing the ground and bellowing, charging forward.
Shèlìfú transformed into a lion,
which tore the ox apart and ate it.
Láodùchā transformed himself into a yakṣa demon,
tall in form, with fire burning on his head,
eyes red as blood, four long sharp fangs, fire spewing from his mouth and eyes, leaping and charging.
Shèlìfú transformed himself into Vaiśravaṇa,
and the yakṣa, terrified, tried to flee, but fire sprang up on all sides, leaving no escape.
Only near Shèlìfú was it cool and without fire.
The yakṣa immediately prostrated himself,
begging for mercy to spare his life, his arrogance gone, and the fire vanished.
Everyone exclaimed:
"Shèlìfú has won.
Láodùchā is no match."
Shèlìfú then rose into the air, displayed the four dignified postures, and performed eighteen transformations.
After these transformations, he withdrew his supernatural powers and sat back on his seat.
The assembly, seeing his supernatural powers, was filled with joy.
Shèlìfú then preached the Dharma, and according to their merits, each attained the path.
The six teachers' 300 million followers took refuge with Shèlìfú and entered the monastic life to study the Dharma.
Elder Xūdá and Shèlìfú went to plan the monastery.
As Xūdá held the measuring rope,
Shèlìfú smiled joyfully.
Xūdá asked:
"Venerable One, why do you smile?"
He replied:
"As you begin to plan this land,
palaces have already been completed in the six desire heavens."
He then lent him the divine eye, and Xūdá saw it all.
He asked Shèlìfú:
"Among the six desire heavens, which is the most blissful?"
Shèlìfú said:
"The fourth heaven, where desires are few and contentment is known.
There is always a bodhisattva in his last rebirth
born there, and the Dharma teachings never cease."
Xūdá said:
"I shall be born in the fourth heaven."
As soon as he spoke, the other palaces vanished.
He took up the rope again,
and Shèlìfú looked sad and worried.
Xūdá asked: "Venerable One, why do you look worried?"
He replied:
"Do you see the ants in this ground?
In the past, at the time of Buddha Vipaśyin,
you also built a monastery for that World-Honored One on this land.
And these ants were already born here.
Up to the time of Buddha Kāśyapa, it was the same.
For ninety-one kalpas, they have received the same form.
When building the monastery and making a cave for the Buddha,
using fine sandalwood as fragrant clay,
with separate dwellings in twelve hundred places,
and after striking the ghaṇṭā in each of the one hundred twenty places,
he informed the king:
'I beg Your Majesty to send an envoy to invite the Buddha.'
The king sent an envoy to Rājagṛha to invite the Buddha and his monks.
'We beg the World-Honored One to come to Shèwèi.'
The Buddha, surrounded by the fourfold assembly,
emitted great light, shook heaven and earth, and arrived in the kingdom of Shèwèi.
Along the way, they stopped at guesthouses.
Countless people were converted along the road.
Gradually, they approached the edge of Shèwèi City.
Everyone gathered, holding various offerings to welcome the World-Honored One.
When the World-Honored One arrived in the kingdom, he emitted great light, illuminating the three-thousandfold world system.
He pressed the ground with his toe,
and the earth shook.
Musical instruments in the city played by themselves.
The blind could see, the deaf could hear, the mute could speak, the hunched could stand straight.
The lame, the paralyzed, the crippled, and the disabled were all healed.
All the people, men and women, young and old, witnessed these auspicious signs.
They joyfully leapt and came to where the Buddha was.
Eighteen koṭis of people all gathered together.
At that time, the World-Honored One, prescribing medicine according to the illness, expounded the wondrous Dharma for them.
Each attained the path.
Mount Kūnlún
is the center of the Jambudvīpa continent.
The mountain is entirely of precious stones.
It is surrounded by five hundred caves.
The caves are all of gold.
Constantly, five hundred arhats dwell there.
The Anavatapta Great Spring encircles the mountain from outside.
Within the mountain, on level ground, a river flows through its midst.
On the riverbanks are four golden animal heads.
From their mouths water flows out.
Each flows around one circuit and returns to its direction, then enters the four seas.
That which flows from the elephant's mouth
is the Yellow River.
The spring is twenty-five yojanas square on each side.
It is twenty-one li deep.
In the spring there is a golden platform.
The platform is one yojana square.
On the platform is a golden lotus flower.
Its stem is made of the seven treasures.
The Tathāgata, leading five hundred arhats, constantly on the fifteenth day of the month, expounds the precepts there.
The great earth has ten great mountain kings.
The first is the Snow Mountain King.
The second is the Fragrant Mountain King.
The third is the Kharira Mountain King.
The fourth is the Mountain King of Immortals and Sages.
The fifth is the Yugandhara Mountain King.
The sixth is the Horse-Ear Mountain King.
The seventh is the Nimindhara Mountain King.
The eighth is the Cakravāḍa Mountain King.
The ninth is the Mountain King of Ancient Wisdom.
The tenth is the Sumeru Mountain King.
The Buddha was in Śrāvastī and addressed the bhikṣus:
There are eight causes and conditions for the great shaking of the earth.
This earth is sixty-eight thousand yojanas deep.
It is upheld by water.
The water rests upon space.
Or again, at that time, when the wind in space moves, the water also moves.
When the water moves, the earth then greatly shakes.
This is the first shaking.
If a bhikṣu attains spiritual powers and can act according to his will,
viewing the earth like the palm of his hand, he can cause the earth to greatly shake.
This is the second shaking.
If again, the devas have great spiritual powers and great might,
they can cause the earth to tremble.
This is the third shaking.
If again, a bodhisattva is in the Tuṣita heaven,
and wishes to descend with his spirit to be born, at that time the earth shakes.
This is the fourth shaking.
If a bodhisattva himself knows he is in his mother's womb, the earth greatly shakes.
This is the fifth shaking.
If a bodhisattva knows that after ten full months he is about to emerge from his mother's womb, the earth greatly shakes.
This is the sixth shaking.
If a bodhisattva leaves home and sits at the site of enlightenment,
subdues the māra enemies, and finally attains perfect enlightenment,
the earth greatly shakes.
This is the seventh shaking.
If the Tathāgata, in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder,
enters parinirvāṇa,
this is the eighth shaking.
In the past, there was a Buddha named Lion's Roar Drum Sound King.
His country was called Thousand Lights.
Trees were formed of the seven treasures.
The trees emitted sounds of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, nothingness, and non-grasping at signs.
Such were the sounds of these dharmas.
There were divine medicinal trees.
One was named Madhagī, which subdues
all poisons in the world, preventing them from acting recklessly.
There was a great divine serpent, its body one hundred and twenty zhang long.
The serpent moved about seeking food.
There was a black-headed insect, its body five zhang long.
The insect was walking on the road and encountered the serpent.
Just as it was about to raise its head to sever the great insect,
the serpent smelled the medicinal fragrance, bent its head, and wished to flee.
The serpent's body brushed against the medicinal tree.
Its body was immediately cut in two, splitting into two sections.
The front half lived and fled.
The tail then putrefied and rotted.
All poisons, hearing the stench of this serpent,
all evil poisonous vapors were extinguished.
On the peak of the Snow Mountain is a medicinal king tree.
It is named "Not Born from the Root, Not Not Born from the Root."
It is six million eight hundred thousand yojanas in breadth and length.
Below, it reaches the adamantine base.
When this tree takes root,
all trees in Jambudvīpa take root.
When it produces a stem, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits,
all trees in Jambudvīpa produce branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
This tree's root can produce a stem.
The stem can produce roots.
Therefore it is named "Not Born from the Root, Not Not Born from the Root."
It can grow in all places.
Only excepting the deep pits of hells,
and within the water element, it cannot grow.
In the past, there was a king.
The king's name was Wùliè. In his country was a tree named Xiūbōtíhuán.
It was five hundred and sixty li in circumference.
Its spreading roots extended eight hundred and forty li around.
It was forty thousand li high.
Its branches spread out, covering two thousand li.
The tree had five kinds of fruit.
The path had five sides.
On one side, the king of the country, with the palace women and entertainers, together ate its fruit.
On the second side, the great ministers and all officials all ate together.
On the third side, the common people ate together.
On the fourth side, all śramaṇas and ascetics ate together.
On the fifth side, flying birds, insects, and beasts ate together.
The fruits were all like two-dǒu jars.
Their flavor was like honey.
The tree had no guardian.
The fruits were distributed among beings without encroachment.
People at that time all lived for eighty-four thousand years.
People at that time had nine kinds of illnesses.
The first: cold.
The second: heat.
The third: hunger.
The fourth: thirst.
The fifth: defecation.
The sixth: urination.
The seventh: desire for love.
The eighth: eating too much.
The ninth: old age.
Women were five hundred years old,
and only then did they marry.
Among people, there was an incense.
Named Great Elephant Treasury.
It was produced because of dragons fighting.
If one burned a single pellet,
a great radiance arose, with fine clouds covering above.
Its flavor was like amṛta.
For seven days and seven nights, a fragrant rain fell.
If it touched the body, the body became golden-colored.
If it touched clothing, palaces, towers, or pavilions,
they also all became golden-colored.
If any being obtained and smelled this incense,
for seven days and seven nights they were joyful and happy.
All illnesses were extinguished, without any untimely death.
They were far removed from minds of fear, terror, and harm.
They turned single-mindedly toward great compassion, universally mindful of all beings.
I, knowing them thus, expounded the Dharma for them.
Causing immeasurable beings to attain non-retrogression.
Gośīrṣa candana incense.
Grows from the Vimala Mountain.
If one anoints the body with it,
fire cannot burn it.
South of Mount Sumeru is a great tree.
Forty thousand li high.
Various Bhāṣā birds constantly perch upon it.
The tree is always unmoving.
There is a small bird.
Its form resembles a quail or a sparrow.
When it alights upon it,
the tree then shakes and trembles.
The Bhāṣā bird asked the tree spirit, saying:
"You are ignorant.
My body is heavy and large, yet you do not move.
When the small bird comes, you instead shake and sway."
The spirit said:
"This bird, though small,
ate a vajra from the ocean's depths.
The vajra, as an object,
wherever it falls, nothing is not shattered and dispersed.
Therefore I am greatly terrified and cannot remain at ease."
In the country of Śrāvastī was a royal garden.
A poisonous tree grew there.
Men and women, while touring and viewing, would stop and rest beneath it.
Some would have headaches, feeling as if splitting.
Or pain in the waist and spine.
Or would die beneath the tree.
The garden keeper,
using a long-handled axe,
over one zhang long,
chopped at it from a distance to remove it.
Before ten days had passed,
it had grown again as before.
This happened many times.
Branches and leaves subsequently
became rounded and full as before.
The tree's appearance was fine.
People who saw it,
none were not delighted.
Not knowing the danger,
all who came encountered this.
The garden keeper's relatives,
greedily enjoying the tree's shade,
all met their end.
The garden keeper stood alone,
day and night sorrowful and worried,
wailing and weeping as he walked about.
Someone asked.
A wise person told him:
"You must eradicate its roots."
Just as he was about to dig up the roots,
he again feared he would certainly die.
Advancing further in thought,
he left home to study the path.
The Buddha said.
The mind awakened and reproached itself.
Immediately, the first fruit was attained.
Furthermore, there are four great rivers.
They flow out from Lake Anòu and head towards the great sea.
The first is named Héngjiā.
The second is named Xīntóu.
The third is named Bǔchā.
The fourth is named Sītuó.
That Héngjiā flows from the mouth of a golden elephant.
It circles the lake once and flows towards the Eastern Sea.
That Xīntóu flows from the mouth of a silver ox.
It circles the lake once and flows towards the Southern Sea.
That Bǔchā flows from the mouth of a lapis lazuli horse.
It circles the lake once and flows towards the Western Sea.
That Sītuó flows from the mouth of a crystal lion, circles the lake once, and flows towards the Northern Sea.
Those four great rivers.
Each has four rivers as its retinue.
Only the vast and named ones are mentioned.
However, each of those four rivers has five hundred retinue rivers.
Together, there are two thousand rivers.
Ultimately, they all head towards the great sea.
The one flowing west is named Héng.
The one flowing south is named Yéyún.
The ones flowing east are two.
One is named Shālù.
The other is named Āyíyuè.
The one flowing north is named Mò.
All flow and pour into the sea.
Since the establishment of heaven and earth, rain falls and rivers pour, yet the water neither increases nor decreases.
Shedding their old names.
They merge into one sea water.
The Buddha traveled to the land of Wúshèng.
Always on the fifteenth day.
He would sit in meditation to preach the precepts for the śramaṇas.
The Buddha remained silent.
Ānán said.
"Sit in meditation."
The World-Honored One then said.
"Among the śramaṇas.
There are those whose minds engage in perverse actions and violate.
It is not something that those of lowly status can practice.
The pure and the turbid are incompatible.
I will not speak of it."
Mùlián entered meditation and observed.
He then said to him.
"Rise, this is not a seat for a worldly person like you."
When he refused to rise, he grabbed his arm and pulled him out, saying, "You lack supreme virtue.
Your mind harbors six perversities.
How dare you, with your foul and defiled body,
sit upon the seat of heavenly fragrance?
You are a rejected person.
Not a śramaṇa."
The Buddha told the śramaṇas.
"Observe that vast sea; it possesses eight kinds of virtues.
Its breadth is boundless and shoreless.
Its depth has an unfathomable bottom.
Gradually entering, it gradually deepens, with nothing obstructing ahead.
This is the first virtue.
The tides never miss their time.
This is the second virtue.
The sea contains all treasures, encompassing everything.
Yet it does not tolerate dead, foul, and decaying corpses.
This is the third virtue.
The sea holds numerous jewels.
There is nothing sought that cannot be obtained.
This is the fourth virtue.
Under the entire heaven, there are five great rivers.
They flow into the sea.
All shed their old names.
Merging into one sea.
This is the fifth virtue.
The five rivers and myriad streams, with rain constantly pouring.
Yet the water in the sea remains as before, never increasing or decreasing.
This is the sixth virtue.
The sea has many fish, their bodies immense and towering.
The first fish's body is four thousand lǐ long.
The second fish's body is eight thousand lǐ long.
The third fish's body is twelve thousand lǐ long.
The fourth fish's body is sixteen thousand lǐ long.
The fifth fish's body is twenty thousand lǐ long.
The sixth fish's body is twenty-four thousand lǐ long.
The seventh fish's body is twenty-eight thousand lǐ long.
This is the seventh virtue.
The seawater is uniformly salty, the edges and center are the same; this is the eighth virtue.
The bright moon and maṇi pearls.
Are mostly found within dragon brains.
If beings have merit and virtue.
They naturally obtain them.
Just as in hell.
Instruments for punishment arise spontaneously.
This treasure is also called the wish-fulfilling pearl.
It constantly produces all kinds of treasures.
Clothing, food, and drink according to one's wishes.
Those who obtain this pearl.
Cannot be harmed by poison.
Cannot be burned by fire.
Some say.
It is what Śakra holds.
When the vajra fought with the asuras.
It shattered and fell upon Jambudvīpa.
Others say.
It is the śarīra of all past, distant Buddhas.
After the Dharma was extinguished.
They transformed into this pearl to bring benefit.
In the great sea, there are four treasure pearls.
All treasures are born from them.
If there were no four pearls.
All treasures would gradually be extinguished.
The minor dragon spirits cannot see them.
Only Sāgara, the Dragon King, secretly places them in a deep treasure store.
This deep treasure store has four names.
First, it is called the Accumulation of All Treasures.
Second, it is called the Inexhaustible Treasure Store. Third, it is called the Distant Blazing.
Fourth, it is called the Gathering of All Adornments.
Within the great sea.
There are four blazing, luminous great treasures.
The first is named the Sun-Store Luminous Great Treasure.
The second is named the Drought-Averting Luminous Great Treasure.
The third is named the Fire-Pearl Luminous Great Treasure.
The fourth is named the Ultimate, Nothing-Remaining Luminous Great Treasure.
If the great sea lacked these four treasures.
The vajra encircling mountains of the four continents.
Even up to the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, all would be submerged.
The Sun-Store Luminous.
Can transform seawater into curd.
The Drought-Averting Luminous.
Can transform sea curd into ghee.
The Fire-Pearl Luminous.
Can ignite the sea ghee.
The Ultimate, Nothing-Remaining Luminous Great Treasure.
Can burn the sea ghee completely, leaving nothing behind.
In Jambudvīpa.
When a child is born and falls to the ground.
Up to three years old.
How much milk does the mother's embrace provide?
Maitreya replied.
"They drink one hundred eighty hú of milk.
Excluding the four parts consumed in the mother's womb."
In Purvavideha.
When a child is born and falls to the ground.
Up to three years old.
They drink one thousand eight hundred hú of milk.
In Aparagodānīya.
When a child is born and falls to the ground.
Up to three years old.
They drink eight hundred eighty hú of milk.
In Uttarakuru.
When a child is born and falls to the ground.
They sit at the head of a path.
Passersby offer their fingers, and the child sucks the finger.
After seven days, they become an adult.
That land has no milk.
Beings in the antarābhava drink and suck the wind.
The lifespan of beings in Jambudvīpa is one hundred years.
The lifespan of beings in Purvavideha is two hundred fifty years.
The lifespan of beings in Aparagodānīya is five hundred years.
The lifespan of humans in Uttarakuru is one thousand years.
The lifespan of beings in the antarābhava is seven days.
The faces of beings in Jambudvīpa are broad above and narrow below.
The faces of people in Purvavideha are perfectly round.
The faces of people in Godānīya are narrow above and broad below.
The faces of people in Uttarakuru are square in shape.
The facial appearance of beings in the antarābhava.
Is like that of the Paranimmitavaśavartin Heaven."
The Northern Uttarakuru continent.
Its circumference is vast and long.
Each side is four hundred thousand li.
There are various mountains.
On both banks of its rivers,
there are various trees and various flowers.
In the water are boats,
made of four precious substances.
There is a bathing pool named Nanda.
Its water is cool and moist.
The sand at its bottom is all gold.
Around it are steps,
made of four precious substances.
Gold steps with silver railings, silver steps with gold railings.
Lapis lazuli steps with crystal railings.
Crystal steps with lapis lazuli railings.
There are various lotus flowers.
If a flower is broken,
its sap flows out like milk, sweet as honey.
Its light shines for forty li.
Its fragrance is also smelled for forty li.
East of the pool is a river,
named Yǐwèi.
South of the pool is a river,
named Xiūjié.
West of the pool is a river,
named Dàtǔ.
North of the pool is a river,
named Shànzhǒng.
In all these rivers, there are flowering trees,
formed from four precious substances.
East of the pool is a garden,
named Xiánshàng.
Its railings and rows of trees are also made of four precious substances.
In the garden, fragrant trees emit various scents.
There are clothing trees,
and necklace trees,
producing various garments and necklaces.
There are music trees,
producing various music.
The trees are seven li high.
There are those six li, five li, four li, three li, and two li high.
South of the pool is a garden-park,
named Yǔxián.
West of the pool is a garden-park,
named Luóyuè.
North of the pool is a garden-park,
named Chángyǒuhuá.
What the trees produce,
and their heights, high and low,
are also like the eastern garden.
In the Northern continent, the trees are curved and interwoven over the roads.
Celestial beings dwell above.
Men and women are in separate places.
There is pure, clean rice,
growing by itself without planting.
It yields all flavors.
If they wish to engage in sexual union,
their minds stir, they gaze at each other without speaking.
The man then goes forward first,
the woman follows behind.
They go to a garden-park and enjoy themselves together.
Sometimes for two or three days,
sometimes up to seven days,
they part as they wish,
with no attachment.
When a woman becomes pregnant,
she gives birth after seven or eight days.
The child is placed at a four-way crossroads.
If people come from the four directions,
they give their fingers for the child to suckle milk.
After seven days pass,
by their own virtue,
they grow up by themselves,
like Jambudvīpa people at age twenty,
or twenty-five.
All around the four directions,
there is water named Anuttara.
In the latter part of the night, clouds arise and rain water of eight flavors,
like people's food and drink.
The ground is as if oiled, so dust does not rise.
Grasses and trees are always present.
Flowers and fruits are all fragrant.
When the fragrant heat arrives,
a chaotic wind blows and sweeps the Xiánshàng garden-park.
The Ela wind arises,
blowing fallen flowers up to people's knees.
The people of this continent all enter the gardens to play and amuse themselves, with no attachments.
When people wish to eat,
they take pure, clean rice,
and cook it below with the light of a flame-flavor pearl.
When the rice is cooked, people from all directions come and all eat it.
The food is also never exhausted.
There is a tree named Xiàngdōu,
its branches curved and interwoven above like a woven canopy.
People dwell upon it to rest.
Men and women are in separate places.
People's teeth and hair are dark blue, eight inches long.
People's facial complexions are the same, their height equal.
All live for a thousand years.
After death, they are born in the heavens of the desire realm.
When their heavenly life ends,
they are born in Jambudvīpa in great, wealthy, and noble families.
For urination and defecation,
the ground splits open to receive it, and after receiving, it closes again.
When dying, they are adorned with fine clothes and do not weep.
They are placed at a four-way crossroads.
The Yùzhē birds lift and place them outside the Northern continent.
Long ago, in a distant kalpa, the Tathāgata,
practicing the Bodhisattva path,
was a great king.
His parents passed away.
He abdicated the kingdom to his younger brother.
He went alone to seek the path.
He met a Brahmin,
of the Gautama clan.
He studied under him.
Therefore, he took the same clan name.
He entered deep into the mountains,
meditating and contemplating the path.
Begging for food, he returned to the kingdom.
The people of the kingdom did not recognize him,
calling him 'Little Gautama'.
In a sugarcane garden outside the city walls,
he built a vihāra.
There were five hundred great bandits,
who robbed official wealth.
Passing by the edge of the garden,
the next day, following their tracks, they arrested the Bodhisattva.
They impaled him with a wooden stake under a great tree, his blood flowing on the ground.
The elder Gautama flew over and asked:
"What crime was so cruel as to bring you to this state?"
The officials released crossbow bolts and killed him.
The elder Gautama wept, his tears staining the coffin.
He took the blood-soaked earth to make mud balls.
Carrying them back to the vihāra,
he placed them in two vessels, left and right, saying:
"If this ascetic is sincere,
the devas should cause the blood to transform into people."
After ten months, the left one became a boy,
the right one became a girl.
Their clan name was Gautama.
The boy was named Shèyí.
In the Bhadrakalpa, during the time of Ratna Buddha, he was also called Śākya.
He who surpassed a lifespan of five million years is the one. The Buddha was in the Magadha realm,
under the auspicious tree at the Shànshèng practice ground.
With the power of virtue, he subdued Māra.
He converted two merchants.
Only Dipaṃkara Tathāgata,
predicted my Buddha-name, saying:
"You, in a future time, after ninety-one kalpas,
shall attain Buddhahood.
Your name will be Śākyamuni.
Complete with the ten epithets,
as I am now."
From that time onward,
I accumulated merit and cultivated practices,
diligently practicing the six pāramitās and the four immeasurables without weariness.
The reward of merit was not lost; the great vow bore fruit.
Ultimately, the Bodhisattva.
In the Tuṣita Heaven,
he inquired with the gods and held discussions.
It was decided that the Bodhisattva should manifest in which clan.
Zhòng Yīng Tiānzǐ asked:
"In which lineage will the One-Life Successor descend with his divine spirit?"
The answer was:
"The lineage must possess sixty virtues.
I shall descend into it. Only the Śākya clan has long cultivated virtuous roots.
The people of Kapilavastu,
great and small are harmonious and respectful, superiors and inferiors support each other.
The country is prosperous, the people are joyful, and they thirst for the One Vehicle.
Moreover, King Śuddhodana's nature and conduct are benevolent and virtuous.
His wife is of the Gautama clan.
Gentle, loyal, and good, she guards her body, speech, and mind.
For five hundred lifetimes she has been the mother of Bodhisattvas.
The queen was resting peacefully.
The Bodhisattva transformed, riding a white elephant,
crowned with the essence of the sun,
entered into her womb.
Her body and mind were at ease and joyful, as if in deep meditation.
She went to the foot of the Aśoka tree.
Messengers were sent to inform the king.
At that time, the Aśoka grove displayed ten auspicious signs:
First, it suddenly became vast and extensive.
Second, the earth and stones turned into vajra.
Third, jeweled trees stood in rows.
Fourth, it was adorned with aloeswood.
Fifth, it was filled with floral garlands.
Sixth, various treasures flowed forth.
Seventh, lotuses bloomed in the ponds.
Eighth, gods, dragons, and yakṣas stood with palms joined.
Ninth, heavenly maidens showed reverence.
Tenth, all Buddhas radiated light, illuminating everywhere.
The king was greatly delighted.
The queen's body became light and soft.
She had no thoughts of the three poisons.
All who were ill would be cured by the touch of her hand.
When the ten months were fulfilled and the time of birth approached,
there were thirty-two auspicious signs:
First, the trees in the rear garden naturally bore fruit.
Second, blue lotuses as large as cartwheels emerged from the ground.
Third, withered trees bloomed with flowers.
Fourth, a seven-jeweled carriage arrived.
Fifth, treasures from the earth naturally welled up.
Sixth, famous incense and fine flowers spread far and wide.
Seventh, five hundred lions from the snowy mountains gathered outside the city gates.
Eighth, five hundred white elephants all stood before the palace.
Ninth, a fine, fragrant rain moistened the earth.
Tenth, food and drink of a hundred flavors were provided to the hungry and thirsty.
On the night of the eighth day of the fourth month, when the morning star appeared,
the queen, wishing to stroll in the garden, went to the foot of the Lumbinī tree.
Three thousand lands trembled six times.
The constellation fell, and the tree bent its branches.
The mother then grasped hold.
The gods scattered flowers.
He was born from her right side.
His body was sixteen feet tall.
Immediately he took seven steps.
Precious flowers supported his feet.
Raising his hand, he stood and said:
"In heaven and on earth, I alone am honored.
The three realms are all suffering; what is there to delight in?"
Śakra and Brahmā served him.
The Four Heavenly Kings presented a golden tray.
Dragons poured down fragrant water for his bath.
Five hundred attendants each gave birth to strong men.
A white horse gave birth to a foal.
Yellow sheep gave birth to lambs.
After seven days, his mother passed away.
She was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The prince was young and needed care.
Someone then said:
"Only Mahāprajāpatī is the prince's aunt.
Pure and without a husband, she can raise him."
Then King Śuddhodana
went to Mahāprajāpatī to request her to nurse him.
Prajāpatī complied.
A Brahmin from the snowy mountains named Ājīta Keśakambala
saw the prince and wept with sorrowful sighs.
The king asked the reason.
He replied:
"I congratulate Your Majesty
for giving birth to this divine being.
Yesterday heaven and earth greatly shook;
it was precisely for this.
According to my physiognomy,
the prince possesses thirty-two marks:
First, his body is golden-colored.
Second, he has a fleshy protuberance on his head.
Third, his hair is dark blue.
Fourth, between his eyebrows is a white curl.
Fifth, light radiates from his head.
Sixth, his eyelashes are dark blue.
Seventh, his upper and lower eyelids blink together.
Eighth, his mouth has forty teeth.
Ninth, his teeth are white and even.
Tenth, he has square jaws.
Eleventh, he has a broad, long tongue.
Twelfth, his voice fills the hall.
Thirteenth, he has a lion's chest.
Fourteenth, his body is upright and square.
Fifteenth, his arms are long.
Sixteenth, his fingers are long.
Seventeenth, his heels are full.
Eighteenth, his feet are level and even.
Nineteenth, his hands grasp inward and outward.
Twentieth, his palms are joined and full.
Twenty-first, the palms of his hands have thousand-spoked wheel lines.
Twenty-second, the soles of his feet have thousand-spoked wheel lines.
Twenty-third, he has a concealed male organ like a horse.
Twenty-fourth, his calves are like those of an antelope.
Twenty-fifth, he has hook-shaped collarbones.
Twenty-sixth, his body hair curls to the right.
Twenty-seventh, each pore grows one hair.
Twenty-eighth, his skin and hair are fine and soft.
Twenty-ninth, dust and water do not adhere to him.
Thirtieth, on his chest is the svastika mark.
One who possesses these marks,
if he remains at home,
will become a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
The seven treasures will come to him of themselves.
If he leaves home, he will become a Buddha spontaneously.
I grieve that my years are late and declining,
and I will not see the Buddha arise.
That is why I am sad."
The king richly rewarded him.
He instructed Mahāprajāpatī:
"Deeply respect and protect the prince." At age seven,
riding a goat cart,
with many Śākyas leading and following,
he went to visit a writing teacher.
The teacher's name was Xuǎnyǒu.
The prince asked:
"Teacher, what writing will you teach me?"
He replied:
"There is the Brāhmī and Kharoṣṭhī scripts;
I can teach you these."
The prince said:
"There are sixty-four different scripts;
why only these two?"
The teacher said:
"I wish to hear their names."
The prince answered:
"Brāhmī script, Kharoṣṭhī script,
Hùzhòng script,
Jíjiān script,
Dragon-ghost script,
Gandharva script,
Asura deer-wheel script,
Tiāncháng script,
Zhuǎnshù script,
Guānkōng script... Which script will you use to teach me?"
The teacher could not understand,
and could only praise him.
The prince, for the other boys,
explained the fundamentals and details,
encouraging them to develop the mind for the Path. When the prince reached seventeen years of age,
the king arranged a marriage for him.
After selecting from several thousand,
finally a daughter of a minor king
of the Gautama clan,
the daughter of Bóxūfú named Gopī,
incomparably beautiful and pure as a lotus, was chosen.
Eight kingdoms contended for her hand, but none had been accepted.
The king summoned her father and said:
"Now I betroth your daughter to the prince."
Suprabuddha was worried:
"If I do not consent, I will surely be attacked.
If I consent, I will incur the enmity of the eight kingdoms."
His daughter said:
"King Śuddhodana's country
is most superior in martial arts;
all other countries fear it."
The king commanded the country:
"After seven days,
the prince will demonstrate his skills.
Those who are able should assemble." Devadatta struck and killed an elephant.
The prince threw it outside the city walls.
In astronomy, geography, and eighty thousand different arts,
none could match the prince.
Devadatta wrestled with the prince briefly.
The prince lifted him and threw him into the air three times without harming him.
They also competed in archery at a drum.
Devadatta hit
a drum forty li away, but could not surpass the difficulty.
The prince drew a bow, but the bow was soft and broke.
He asked if there was another bow he could use.
The king said:
"My late grandfather's bow is extraordinary and peerless; no one can use it.
It is in the heavenly temple."
It was fetched for the prince.
None of the Śākyas could surpass him.
The prince used it to shoot a drum a hundred li away.
The arrow disappeared into the ground, causing a spring to well up, reaching the Iron Ring Mountains.
Three thousand lands trembled six times.
Thus Gopī
became the prince's first wife.
Following worldly customs, he displayed signs of enjoyment. He also took the daughter of the elder Yíshī,
named Yaśodharā.
She was made the second consort.
He also took the daughter of an elder of the Śākya clan,
named Lùyě,
as the third consort.
The crown prince was destined to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
He established three seasonal palaces,
and placed sixty thousand court ladies within them.
Luóyún descended from heaven, transformed, vanished, and manifested to be born.
Later, the crown prince went out through the eastern city gate.
The king ordered the roads to be strictly maintained,
so that nothing impure would be seen.
Through the majestic spiritual power established by the crown prince,
a heavenly being transformed into an old man,
with white hair and fallen teeth,
dim eyes and deaf ears,
leaning on a staff and walking hunched over.
The crown prince, knowing full well, deliberately asked,
"What kind of person is this?"
The charioteer replied,
"This is called an old man."
The crown prince said,
"Human life flows like a stream, difficult to obtain a second time.
This is not unique to humans; all under heaven are thus."
He turned the chariot back to the palace, filled with compassion and sorrow, finding no joy.
Later, he went out through the southern city gate
and encountered a sick person,
with a swollen belly, emaciated and thin, lying by the roadside.
He asked the charioteer,
who answered,
"A sick person."
The crown prince said,
"All things are impermanent; having a body entails suffering.
I too am certainly thus."
He immediately returned to the palace.
Later, he went out through the western city gate
and saw a dead person,
with his family weeping in grief.
The charioteer said,
"A dead person.
Life entails death,
just as spring has winter.
Humans and all things share this same principle."
The crown prince said,
"Death is painful indeed.
The spirit is severely afflicted.
I see the deceased:
their form decays and their body transforms,
yet the spirit does not perish.
I can no longer take birth through death,
wandering through the five paths, exhausting my spirit.
He turned the chariot and returned.
Again, on another day,
he went out through the northern city gate
and saw a śramaṇa,
neatly dressed in robes and holding religious implements.
The charioteer said,
"This is called a bhikṣu.
He renounces and abandons desires and passions,
his heart delights in all beings,
seeking to liberate all in the ten directions."
The crown prince said,
"Excellent!
This is what I delight in.
If I do not renounce the kingship and leave home,
this would not be fitting."
Immediately, in the quiet of the night, he entered the king's palace.
Light shone far and near.
His father the king awoke and rose.
He then addressed his father, saying:
"The gods urge and assist me;
now is the time to leave home."
His father the king wept sorrowfully,
"What is your aspiration?
When will you return?"
The crown prince wished to obtain four vows:
first, not to grow old;
second, to be free from illness;
third, not to die;
fourth, not to be separated.
If his father the king could grant these four vows,
he would not leave home.
The king said,
"From ancient times to the present, no one has obtained these."
This only increased his great sorrow and grief.
He then commanded five hundred Śākya youths of great courage and strength
to guard the four gates day and night.
The sound of the city gates opening and closing could be heard for forty li.
Qiúyí, suspicious in her thoughts, never left his side.
The crown prince contemplated that the path is pure and it is not fitting to remain at home.
He should dwell in the mountains and forests, diligently practicing meditation.
At that time, he was twenty-nine years old.
On the night of the seventh day of the fourth month, after midnight,
Qiúyí then had five dreams.
She immediately awoke with a start.
The crown prince asked her about them.
She replied,
"I dreamed that Mount Sumeru collapsed,
the bright moon fell to the ground,
the light of pearls suddenly extinguished,
my hair fell out by itself,
and someone snatched away my parasol."
The Bodhisattva, knowing the dreams pertained to his own person, said:
"Mount Sumeru does not collapse,
the bright moon continues to shine,
the light of pearls does not extinguish,
hair does not fall out,
the parasol still remains.
Rest peacefully for now,
take care not to worry or feel loss."
At night, he observed the female entertainers; all their joints were empty,
like plantain trees.
Snot and tears from their eyes,
musical instruments scattered about.
He looked at his wife
and fully saw her bodily form:
brain, marrow, skull, heart, liver, intestines, stomach—
externally a leather bag, inside filled with foul filth.
It was as if borrowed,
and must be returned, nor can it last long.
The three realms offer no refuge; only the Path is to be relied upon.
The gods of the desire realm dwell in the sky.
The god Dharmacārin,
from afar, addressed the crown prince:
"The time has come.
The Buddha-star has just appeared."
He called Chànì to rise,
and saddled Kanthaka.
The Four Heavenly Kings, along with countless yakṣas, nāgas, and others,
all clad in armor,
came from the four directions,
bowing their heads in reverence.
The gods, fearing there might be obstacles,
immediately dispatched a sleep-inducing deity
to enter the palace and induce deep sleep.
All the men and women in the city fell into profound slumber.
Peacocks and flocks of birds, none failed to lie down exhausted.
Chànì wept in sorrow.
The gate locks would not open.
Four deities lifted the horse's hooves,
and they leaped over the palace walls.
Śakra led the way in front,
emitting a great pure light, proceeding to the Bodhi tree.
The next morning, the king inquired.
He did not know where he was.
The king then followed his tracks.
He went forward to the royal fields.
From afar, he saw the crown prince.
The trees bent their branches.
Following the shade, he sat upon them.
The king was startled and awakened.
Without recognizing him, he dismounted and paid respects.
The crown prince bowed and said:
Now that I have come here,
why should you trouble yourself to come?
The king, thinking of the crown prince,
could not let go of his heart's longing.
He returned and summoned his ministers:
"You all play with your sons and hold your grandsons,
enjoying mutual comfort and joy.
I have but one son,
and I see him separated, dwelling in the mountains.
I will take five of your sons
to follow and serve him.
If he does not return,
I will exterminate your clans."
The crown prince took off his precious robe and gave it to Chànà.
"Return and inform my father, the king,
and also Bóqiúyí:
When I attain the Way, I shall return.
I will not forget this vow."
Chànà received his words,
tears falling like rain.
The white horse knelt down,
licking the Bodhisattva's feet.
The king and the capital returned the items,
sighing and prostrating on the ground.
Bóqiúyí embraced the horse,
"The crown prince rode you;
why have you come back alone?"
"Sweet fruits and fine springs are not lacking."
The Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"I wish to become a śramaṇa and go to the mountain stream's edge."
The heavenly king knew his mind,
and descended with a knife.
The Bodhisattva shaved his own head and hair.
Śakra received the hair,
leaving only the uṣṇīṣa.
He became a great śramaṇa.
He went to the edge of the Nairañjanā River,
dwelling in serene seclusion.
He encountered a hunter,
wearing a dharma robe that resembled a śramaṇa's.
The crown prince asked him:
"What is this dharma robe called?"
He replied, "Kaṣāya."
"Deer, thinking I am a student of the Way,
feel no fear,
and come close to me.
I kill them one by one,
using them to sustain myself."
The crown prince felt even greater compassion.
He sought to trade his own robe
for the hunter's.
The hunter said:
"The king grew up in a deep palace,
his body soft and delicate.
Unaccustomed to cold and hardship,
I fear it would harm the king's body,
and moreover, it is unclean."
The crown prince said:
"This is the mark of sages and worthies.
Just trade it without worry."
"I will wash it myself."
The devas offered food,
but he refused to accept it.
He went forward to the kingdom of Magadha.
The people saw him,
thinking he was Śakra, Brahmā, or other devas.
The crown prince knew their thoughts,
and sat under a tree.
King Bimbisāra
went with his ministers to see the ascetic.
From afar, they saw his radiant form.
They asked, "What deity is this?
From which kingdom do you come?
What is your name?"
The crown prince replied:
"I come from east of the Fragrant Mountains, north of the Snowy Mountains.
The kingdom is called Kapilavastu.
My father's name is Śuddhodana.
My mother's name is Māyā."
Bimbisāra asked:
"Could it be Siddhārtha?"
He replied, "It is."
The king then bowed at his feet and said:
"Your appearance is radiant and distinguished.
You should rule over the four directions,
becoming a Cakravartin king.
The four seas look up with reverence,
hoping for the divine treasure to arrive.
Why abandon your heavenly position
to wander in the mountains and wilderness?"
He replied:
"Birth leads to death, and there are four great pains:
birth, old age, sickness, and death, from which one cannot escape.
The body is a vessel of suffering,
with endless worries and fears.
If one is in a position of honor and favor,
then pride and arrogance arise.
Greed and seeking pleasure bring suffering and affliction to the world.
I am weary of this,
and so I entered the mountains."
For six years, he diligently practiced austerities,
eating only one sesame seed and one grain of rice per day.
Sitting in full lotus posture without leaning or tilting,
he remained unchanged through wind, rain, thunder, and lightning, through all seasons.
He never raised his hand to shield himself.
People found it strange.
They took grass and twigs and threw them into his ears and nose,
but he did not remove them.
His body became emaciated,
yet his golden complexion grew even more radiant,
his light shining far and wide.
After six full years,
he thought to himself:
"Being so emaciated like this,
if I go to the Bodhi tree,
later generations might mock,
saying I attained the Way through starvation.
I would rather eat soft food,
restore my body,
and then attain enlightenment."
At that time, there was an elder's daughter.
She married and gave birth to a son,
her heart filled with great joy.
She gathered a thousand cows, having them drink each other's milk in succession,
taking the purest milk to make porridge,
intending to offer it to the tree deity.
She sent a maidservant to sweep and clean.
The maid saw the Buddha but did not recognize him.
She returned and reported to her mistress:
"Under the tree, there is a deity, upright and wonderfully beautiful."
The woman heard this and rejoiced.
She intended to take the porridge,
but the porridge leaped out of the pot over ten feet high,
and she could not take it.
The woman found it very strange.
A deva in the sky said:
"There is a great Bodhisattva
who has already risen from his seat.
You originally made a vow
to first offer him food.
Then he will attain perfect enlightenment."
The woman heard the deva's words,
and took the milk porridge,
filling a golden bowl to the brim.
She went to the edge of the Nairañjanā River.
The Bodhisattva, with his supernatural power,
entered the water to bathe.
A deva from the Tuṣita Heaven
took a heavenly robe and kaṣāya,
and offered them to the Bodhisattva.
He then took them and put them on.
He stayed by the edge of the Nairañjanā River.
The elder's daughter offered the milk porridge.
The Bodhisattva ate it,
and his strength gradually recovered.
He went to the Bodhi tree.
On the left side of the road,
there was a man named Jíxiáng.
He cut fresh kuśa grass,
soft and smooth, not tangled.
The Bodhisattva said to Jíxiáng:
"I wish to have grass to sit on."
The earth then shook greatly.
The devas transformed into eighty thousand lion thrones under Bodhi trees.
The devas each saw the Bodhisattva sitting alone on his throne.
Those with little merit still saw him sitting on grass.
The beings of the three realms saw the Bodhisattva sitting under the Bodhi tree, emitting great light,
obscuring the demon's palace.
Māra, while asleep, dreamed of thirty-two changes:
his palace darkened, he entered evil paths,
the pond water dried up,
musical instruments were destroyed,
yakṣas and malevolent ghosts' heads all fell to the ground,
the devas abandoned him and did not obey his words.
He gathered his ministers and told them what he saw in the dream.
He raised various weapons,
and summoned his thousand sons.
Five hundred of his sons,
led by the guide and others, believed in and delighted in the Bodhisattva.
The other five hundred sons,
led by Èmù and others, followed Māra to cause chaos.
They wished to subdue him.
Māra had four daughters:
the first named Yùfēi,
the second named Yuèbǐ,
the third named Kuàiguān,
the fourth named Jiàncóng.
They went to the Bodhisattva,
speaking charming words and flirting,
using thirty-two kinds of allurements.
With graceful demeanor and eloquent speech, they offered themselves as attendants, hoping to serve day and night by his side.
He replied,
"Though your form is beautiful, your heart is not upright.
You are but a leather sack filled with excrement.
What do you seek to achieve by coming here?
Leave, I have no use for you."
The three jade maidens then transformed into old women.
Unable to restore themselves, they returned to the demon king, whose malice grew even fiercer.
He summoned eighteen hundred million troops,
transforming them into various monstrous forms:
lions, bears, beasts with human bodies and insect heads, serpents and vipers.
They carried mountains and breathed fire,
with thunder and lightning crashing.
They brandished spears and halberds,
yet the Bodhisattva, with a joyful heart, remained unmoved, not a single hair stirring.
The demonic troops could not approach him.
At that moment, the Bodhisattva slowly raised the white hair between his eyebrows.
He directed it toward the Avīci Hell,
allowing the sinners there to see it.
From the white hair flowed a radiance as large as a chariot wheel.
The fires of hell temporarily ceased.
The sinners recalled the evil deeds of their past lives,
and their hearts became cool and serene, calling out "Námó Fó."
Due to this cause and condition, when their punishment ended,
they were to be reborn among humans.
Seeing this spectacle, the demon king
became haggard and distressed.
He retreated back to his palace.
The white hair then withdrew
and ascended to the sixth heaven.
There, within the pores of the white hair,
precious lotus flowers appeared,
upon which sat the seven Buddhas of the past.
Thus, the white hair ascended even to the formless realms,
illuminating all like a crystal mirror.
Eighty-four thousand heavenly maidens,
gazing upon Pāpīyas's form,
saw it as withered wood.
But beholding the radiant light of the Bodhisattva's white hair,
countless heavenly sons and maidens
awakened the mind of Bodhi.
The demon king again challenged the Buddha.
The Buddha, using his power of wisdom, stretched out his hand and touched the earth.
Immediately, the earth shook.
The demon king and his retinue
all tumbled and fell.
Having subdued the demonic foe,
he attained perfect enlightenment.
With a following of tens of millions,
he entered the city of Rājagṛha.
Those who saw him from afar
raised their hands in praise.
Some said, "Welcome!"
Some called him the sun and moon.
Some took refuge in him,
while others greeted him.
"Is he a deva?"
"Is he Śakra?"
The crowd followed him.
King Bimbisāra, from his high tower,
asked his attendants,
"What is happening?"
One minister replied,
"The Śākya prince left home and has been wandering abroad.
He may plot against the state.
We should go and execute him."
The king said,
"This prince, if he were to inherit the throne, would become a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
We would all serve as his ministers.
If he renounces the world to study the path and attains Buddhahood,
I wish to be his foremost disciple.
When he first expounds the Dharma,
may I be by his side."
The king loaded food and drink
and went to the eastern mountain to await him.
Approaching, he bowed at his feet,
declaring, "I am King Bimbisāra of Magadha.
That is who I am now."
The Buddha said,
"I recognized you earlier.
There is no need for such reverence."
The king then pleaded,
"Now I offer this humble provision
to express my sincere heart.
I hope you will accept it."
The Buddha silently accepted.
The king said,
"If you attain the unsurpassed path,
I wish to be the first you liberate."
At that time, the disciples of Ārāḍa Kālāma,
seeing the World-Honored One from afar,
said to their teacher,
"There is a person now,
of exceptionally dignified and splendid appearance,
heading toward your gate.
He must be seeking to become your disciple."
Ārāḍa then spoke a verse:
Ānanda asked about burial.
The Buddha said,
"The method of my burial
is like that of a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
First, bathe the body with fragrant water.
Wrap it in karpāsa cloth.
Then, wind it with five hundred layers of white cotton.
Place it inside a golden coffin.
Pour sesame oil over it.
Then place the golden coffin inside an iron outer coffin.
Surround it with sandalwood fragrant coffins.
Pile fragrant wood around the outside.
Cover it thickly with layers of cloth,
and then cremate it.
When the wood is consumed and the fire extinguished,
collect the relics.
At the crossroads,
erect a stūpa and temple.
Raise a flagpole and hang banners,
so that those who see it may remember and admire,
bringing great benefit."
The Buddha said,
"There are four kinds of people for whom stūpas should be built:
first, the Tathāgata;
second, the Pratyekabuddha;
third, the Śrāvaka;
fourth, the Wheel-Turning King.
All should be honored with incense, flowers, banners, canopies, and music."
The Buddha, between the twin trees,
laid out a bed and seat.
He lay with his head to the south and face to the north.
The reason for this is
that the Dharma will spread
and long endure in the north.
The Buddha himself folded his saṅghāṭī robe,
lay on his right side like a lion king,
with his feet placed together.
Ānanda asked further,
"How many kinds of burial are there in Jambudvīpa?"
The Buddha said,
"Countless.
In this land of ours,
there are water burials, fire burials, and stūpa burials.
In the land of Zhèndàn, the method of burial
involves gold, silver, treasures, carved chariots,
flying celestial musicians, bells, and songs,
to please the deceased.
The body is dressed in fine clothes,
placed in a coffin and outer coffin.
Fragrant incense perfumes the air.
Hundreds of thousands of people escort it to the mountains and wilderness,
adorning the place.
Those who see it are filled with joy.
Among the border kings of Zhèndàn,
the people under their rule,
when wishing to bury, place the coffin
inside a stone chamber.
In times of illness, they open it to view the bones,
wash them, and seek blessings to cure the disease.
There are also those who, at life's end, have no coffin.
They simply place the corpse on a high platform.
In times of urgent illness,
they lower the corpse and chant prayers,
seeking blessings and protection."
The Buddha said,
"In my Dharma, those who wish to cultivate merit
should diligently strive,
practice the six pāramitās,
uphold the ten wholesome deeds.
They may then be reborn in heaven
and progress toward the unsurpassed path."
The Buddha was in the city of Kuśinagarī, at the place of the Mallas, between the twin śāla trees by the river Ajiravatī.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of eighty kotis and one hundred thousand bhikṣus.
They surrounded him front and back.
On the fifteenth day of the second month, as he was approaching parinirvāṇa,
by the Buddha's spiritual power, a great sound was emitted.
It reached even the highest heaven.
According to the kinds of beings,
it universally announced to all:
"Today the Tathāgata,
out of compassion for sentient beings,
acts as their refuge.
The World-Honored One, the Greatly Awakened, is about to enter parinirvāṇa.
If any sentient being has doubts,
now you may all ask.
This is the final opportunity to question the Buddha." At dawn,
from the gate of his face, he emitted various lights,
illuminating the great chiliocosm,
reaching even the ten directions.
Sentient beings of the six destinies,
those who encountered this light,
had all their sins, defilements, and afflictions eliminated.
Sentient beings who saw or heard this felt great sorrow and distress.
Simultaneously raising their voices,
they wailed and wept bitterly.
The great earth, mountains, and seas all shook.
People said to one another:
"Quickly go to the Buddha's place.
Urge and entreat the Tathāgata
not to enter parinirvāṇa.
May he remain in the world for a kalpa." The great disciples such as Kātyāyana,
those who encountered the Buddha's light,
their bodies trembled and shook, unable to control themselves.
Raising their voices, they cried out loudly, experiencing various sufferings.
Furthermore, there were eighty hundred thousand bhikṣus,
sixty koṭis of bhikṣuṇīs,
all arhats.
The hairs all over their bodies stood on end, and blood appeared throughout their bodies,
like the flowers of the Pālaśa tree.
Furthermore, there were one koṭi of Gaṅgā-sands of bodhisattvas,
whose stages reached the ten abodes.
Two Gaṅgā-sands of upāsakas,
three Gaṅgā-sands of upāsikās,
four Gaṅgā-sands of Licchavis,
five Gaṅgā-sands of elders,
six Gaṅgā-sands of various kings,
seven Gaṅgā-sands of queens,
eight Gaṅgā-sands of heavenly maidens, etc.,
reaching even the Buddhas and disciples of the ten directions,
the great assembly of the six paths,
seeing the signs of nirvāṇa,
wailed and wept, unable to control themselves.
In the assembly, there was also the son of an artisan from Kuśinagarī,
named Cunda,
who, together with fifteen others, paid homage to the Buddha and said:
"We only pray, World-Honored One,
and the assembly of bhikṣus,
compassionately accept our final offering.
From now on, we
will have no master, no relatives, no savior, no protector.
Poor and hungry,
we wish to seek future sustenance from the Tathāgata.
We only pray you compassionately accept our meager offering,
and then enter nirvāṇa."
The Buddha said:
"I now for your sake
cut off poverty.
The unsurpassed Dharma rain rains on your field of body,
causing the Dharma sprout to grow.
Causing you to perfect the pāramitā of dāna."
The assembly rejoiced,
praising in unison, saying:
"Rare is Cunda!
The Buddha accepts your offering.
You are truly a son of the Buddha."
The Buddha said:
"Cunda,
now is precisely the time.
The Tathāgata is just about to enter parinirvāṇa.
A second and third time it is also thus."
Cunda raised his voice and wept bitterly.
He further addressed the great assembly:
"Let us now together,
with our five limbs touching the ground,
in unison urge the Buddha
not to enter parinirvāṇa."
The Buddha told Cunda:
"Do not weep greatly and disturb your own mind.
Out of compassion for you and all beings,
therefore today I wish to enter nirvāṇa.
Why is this?
All Buddhas are thus; conditioned things are also thus.
Quickly prepare the offering.
It is not suitable to delay long."
The Buddha again emitted five-colored light from the gate of his face,
illuminating Cunda's body.
Cunda, holding the food offerings,
quickly went to the Buddha's place.
Sorrowful and distressed,
he still wished for compassion, that he might remain for a kalpa.
The Buddha said: "If you wish me to remain long,
you should now present the final perfect pāramitā of dāna."
All the bodhisattvas, devas, humans, and mixed kinds,
with different mouths but the same sound, exclaimed:
"How wonderful, Cunda!
You have accomplished great merit.
We, lacking virtue,
our prepared offerings are then in vain."
The World-Honored One, wishing to satisfy the hopes of all beings,
from his own body,
from each and every pore, manifested immeasurable Buddhas.
Each of those Buddhas each had immeasurable bhikṣu saṅghas.
All were shown receiving their offerings.
Śākyamuni Tathāgata
himself accepted what Cunda presented and offered.
The food Cunda held was ripe rice,
from Magadha, filling eight hu.
By the Buddha's spiritual power,
it was all sufficient for the entire great assembly. He lay on his right side, as if ill,
like other sick people.
He told the bodhisattva Kāśyapa:
"These sentient beings,
not knowing the secret words of the Mahāyāna vaipulya sūtras,
then say:
'The Tathāgata truly is ill.'
Now, between the twin śāla trees,
I manifest reclining on the lion's couch, about to enter nirvāṇa,
causing those disciples who have not yet attained the fruit of arhatship and the various Mallas to produce great sorrow and suffering,
causing devas, humans, asuras, etc., to make great offerings,
and also causing various people
to wrap his body with a thousand lengths of cloth,
to wrap his body,
with a coffin of seven treasures filled with fragrant oil,
piling up fragrant wood,
to burn it with fire.
Only except for two ends,
which cannot be burned:
one is the innermost cloth against the body,
the other is the outermost.
For the sake of sentient beings,
the relics are divided,
into eight portions.
All the śrāvaka disciples all say:
'The Tathāgata has entered nirvāṇa.'
You should know the Tathāgata
also does not definitely enter nirvāṇa.
Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata is eternal and unchanging."
"Having wished to hear the true Dharma,
you should abandon greed and lust.
Follow and uphold my teaching,
diligently practice the path.
This is the Buddha's final bequest.
You should all be careful of it."
"You bhikṣus,
behold the Buddha's dignified appearance.
It is difficult to encounter seeing it.
After more than one koṭi and four thousand years,
only then will there be Maitreya Buddha."
As the Buddha approached nirvāṇa,
the earth greatly shook.
Devas and humans were all frightened.
All dark places,
where the light of sun and moon
does not reach,
were all illuminated by a great light,
and they could see each other.
Devas scattered flowers and incense.
When the Buddha passed into extinction,
the kings of the six desire heavens,
the god Kumbhīra,
the strong man Guhyapāda,
the Buddha's mother Māyā,
the garden deity of the twin śāla trees,
each spoke verses.
The bhikṣus were grief-stricken,
each sighing and saying:
"How swiftly the Tathāgata has passed into extinction!
Living beings decline long; the eye of the world is extinguished."
Aniruddha told the bhikṣus:
"Enough, enough, do not grieve.
The devas are above;
perhaps they will blame us."
The bhikṣus asked:
"How many devas are above?"
He answered:
"Filling the empty space, how could they be counted?"
They were all in the air, pacing about,
agitated, wailing,
beating their breasts, sighing, and saying:
"How swiftly the Tathāgata has passed into extinction!
Living beings decline long; the eye of the world is extinguished. Where is the bhikṣu Ānanda now?"
Mañjuśrī said:
"Outside the śāla grove,
twelve yojanas from here,
he is being harassed by sixty-four thousand koṭis of māras.
These māra hosts all transform themselves,
into the likeness of the Tathāgata,
expounding various dharmas, manifesting variously."
Ānanda thought to himself:
What had never been seen before.
Who created it?
Could it not be Śākyamuni?
Wishing to utter these words.
Yet none followed his intention.
Ānanda endured great suffering.
Unable to come.
The Buddha spoke the great dhāraṇī mantra.
Mañjuśrī received it.
Went to where Ānanda was.
Recited it for the demons.
The various demon kings and others gave rise to the bodhi mind.
Mañjuśrī then returned with Ānanda to where the Buddha was, the Mallas.
Gathered various offerings.
After a full day, with the Buddha's relics.
Placed upon a bier.
The Malla youths lifted the bier.
All unable to bear its weight.
Aniruddha said.
You all stop for now.
The devas wish to keep it for seven days.
So that all the people may make offerings.
The Tathāgata three times extended his golden arm from within the golden coffin.
Asked Ānanda if he had arrived.
Leveled the roads, swept, scattered incense, not yet?
How is it, Ānanda?
All that I have previously expounded.
The Vaipulya Mahāyāna.
Have you received it all?
Ānanda replied.
Only the Buddha knows.
The Buddha said, thus it is.
The various sūtras are now ultimately complete.
On the seventh day, the Malla youths lifted the four corners and carried it.
You may hold banners and canopies.
Burn incense, scatter flowers.
Make various music, leading before and following behind.
Proceed calmly and peacefully.
Enter the city's east gate.
Pass through all the streets and alleys.
Exit the city's north gate.
Cross the Hiraṇyavatī River.
Arrive at the Tiānguàn Temple.
The Malla envoys.
Piled up sandalwood.
The fire would not ignite.
Aniruddha said.
The devas intend to extinguish the fire.
Kāśyapa, leading five hundred disciples, returned from the country of Pópó.
Wishing to see the Buddha's body.
Kāśyapa met a Nirgrantha.
Holding a mandāra flower in hand.
Asked.
Do you know where my teacher is?
Answered.
Passed away seven days ago.
I obtained this flower from there.
Kāśyapa was displeased.
The five hundred disciples wailed and sobbed.
Unable to control themselves.
Sorrowfully sighing, they said.
How swiftly has the Sugata entered nirvāṇa!
Then Udāyin said.
Do not weep now.
We, by the side of the Mahallaka.
May attain liberation.
Kāśyapa urged the bhikṣus.
Quickly take up robes and bowls.
Go to Kuśinagara.
Upon seeing the relics.
Asked Ānanda.
May we see the World-Honored One's relics?
Answered.
Wrapped in karpāsa cloth.
Bound with white cotton.
Placed inside the golden coffin.
Enclosed within the iron outer coffin.
Covered with fragrant wood.
About to be cremated, difficult to see.
Kāśyapa requested three times.
Answered as before.
Proceeded to the pyre.
The Buddha's feet pressed the double coffin, revealing the wheel marks on both soles with various extraordinary colors.
Then asked Ānanda.
Answered.
Women's hearts are soft.
Previously paying respects to the Buddha.
Tears fell, hands touched.
Kāśyapa made obeisance.
The great assembly bowed together.
Circumambulated the tree three times.
Each offered verses of praise.
The pyre everywhere ignited spontaneously, the fire extremely fierce.
Difficult to extinguish.
The śāla tree deity extinguished it with power.
The Buddha entered parinirvāṇa.
Mahāmāyā, the mother, was in heaven.
The five signs of decay appeared.
First, the flowers on her head withered.
Second, sweat emerged under her arms.
Third, the light from her neck vanished.
Fourth, her eyes blinked frequently.
Fifth, she felt no joy in her original seat.
Also, she had five dreams.
First, Mount Sumeru collapsed.
The waters of the four seas dried up.
Second, rākṣasas ran about plucking out people's eyes.
Third, the heavens lost their jeweled crowns, bodies without light.
Fourth, the jeweled banner pole fell, losing the wish-fulfilling pearl.
Fifth, a lion bit her body, pain like being cut by a knife.
Having these dreams, she immediately awoke startled.
This is not auspicious.
I once, in King Śuddhodana's palace.
While sleeping during the day.
Had a rare dream.
Saw a deva.
Body golden in color.
Riding a white elephant king.
Followed by various devas.
Making wonderful music.
Observing the essence of the sun.
Entered my right side.
Mind and body at peace and joyful.
Then became pregnant.
Siddhārtha, the prince, illuminated the world.
These five dreams are extremely terrifying.
Surely they are signs of my son's nirvāṇa.
Then Aniruddha, after the Buddha's funeral rites were completed.
Ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Verses informed Mahāmāyā.
Mahāmāyā fainted for a long while, then descended with her retinue between the twin trees.
Saw the saṅghāṭi robe, bowl, and staff.
Held them, wailing in grief.
Fainted and revived, saying.
My son blessed and liberated devas and humans.
Now these objects are empty, without an owner.
The Buddha, through supernatural power, caused the coffin lids to open naturally.
The Buddha joined his palms and rose.
Emitted great light.
Greeted his mother, saying.
You have come from afar, descending.
All conditioned things are thus.
I pray you do not weep.
Ānanda, though restraining himself.
Addressed the Buddha.
Beings of later times will certainly ask me.
What did the Buddha say upon nearing extinction?
How should I answer?
The Buddha told Ānanda.
You should answer thus.
The Buddha has already entered nirvāṇa.
Mahāmāyā, the mother, descended.
The Tathāgata, for the sake of future unfilial beings.
Emerged from the golden coffin, joined palms in greeting.
And spoke the verses above, all respectfully.
This sūtra is named "The Sūtra of the Buddha Approaching Nirvāṇa and the Mother and Son Meeting."
Thus receive and uphold it.
The Tathāgata traveled to the Wonderful Joy World.
Wishing to manifest wisdom, broadly saving without limit.
With disciples, bodhisattvas, Brahmā, Śakra, devas, nāgas.
Gathered in a vihāra.
Emitted the svastika light and sound.
Pure, penetrating far.
Five great Dharma sounds.
First, the sound of leading people to the Mahāyāna.
Second, the sound of leading people without self and other.
Third, the sound of leading people beyond the pratyekabuddha path.
Fourth, the sound of leading people without severing thoughts, skillful means.
Fifth, the sound of leading people to enter birth and death, liberating them from toil and dust, expounding the Dharma.
The king named Chùliú.
With the various people.
Approached the Buddha, paid respects, saying.
Long have we heard of the Tathāgata.
Proclaiming the Way, teaching and transforming.
Saving and liberating from birth and death.
Without limit.
We, our retinue, drift in birth and death.
Have not yet attained liberation.
May the Honored One bestow teaching, enabling us to understand the bright Dharma.
Heaven and earth shook, cultivating the bodhisattva path.
What is meant by the mind's secrecy?
It is the four practices being pure and not losing supernatural powers, establishing the great compassion and boundless deeds.
Through supernatural transformations, all is universally revealed.
Thus, the abode of the true path and wisdom is accomplished.
Beholding all dharmas,
this is the correct penetration that universally governs all.
The true dharma reveals all forms through wisdom-spirit and wisdom-penetration.
It thoroughly comprehends all colors.
It thoroughly comprehends all Buddhadharmas.
It enlightens all sentient beings in the ten directions.
Causing them to enter the dharma and precepts,
reaching the stage of Avivartanī.
Turning all dharmas,
this is the bodhisattva's deed of the mind's secrecy. The bodhisattva abides in this Vajra Samādhi.
With a single sound proclaiming teachings,
all sentient beings each, according to their kind, understand.
Manifesting a single color,
all sentient beings each see various colors and forms. Abiding in one place,
the body unmoving,
yet able to cause sentient beings to see according to their respective directions.
Expounding a single dharma,
whether realms or entrances,
all sentient beings each hear according to their original understanding. The Buddha with one sound expounds the dharma.
Sentient beings, according to kind, each gain understanding.
All say the World-Honored One speaks their language.
Sentient beings each, according to their understanding,
universally receive, practice, and obtain its benefit.
Some may feel fear
or joy,
some may generate aversion,
some may cut off doubts.
This is the supernatural power, the uncommon dharma, the mark of all dharmas.
Practicing without grasping,
erecting the supreme precious banner,
issuing one great sound:
If those who delight in hearing of generosity gain liberation,
they then hear the Tathāgata speak of the benefits of generosity.
Likewise for those who delight in precepts, wisdom, and so forth.
Expounding the Mahāyāna dharma, there is not a single sentient being who does not gain liberation.
The Buddha with one word speaks all dharmas.
Sentient beings of the great thousand worlds, with immeasurable sounds, pose difficult questions simultaneously.
All are different.
In a single thought-moment,
with one sound answering,
all are caused to understand.
In the country of Suíluórán, there was a Brahmin king.
His name was Āqídá.
He was intelligent and wise.
He went to visit Ānànbīndī and engaged in extensive discussion with him. After the conversation ended,
he asked Sudatta,
"In this land, are there any divine beings or sages worthy of reverence?"
Sudatta replied, "There are.
Prince Siddhartha left home and attained Buddhahood.
His features are exceptionally majestic, revered by gods and humans alike."
Āqídá immediately ordered his carriage
and went to the Jetavana to see the Buddha's dignified bearing.
A feeling of reverence arose from within his heart.
He then stood up and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I wish for the Buddha and the Sangha
to accept my invitation for the three-month summer retreat."
The Buddha said,
"My assembly is large,
and you hold different views and faith."
The king said,
"I do not consider it too many."
This was repeated three times.
The Buddha, along with five hundred bhikkhus, accepted the invitation at once
and went to his country.
The cities and towns were narrow and impoverished, and the people had little faith.
Alms were difficult to obtain.
There were no viharas beforehand.
North of the city, there was a forest
with lush and dense foliage.
The ground was flat and broad.
They settled there with the assembly.
The Buddha instructed the bhikkhus,
"You should know
that this region is poor and narrow, and the people largely lack faith, making alms difficult to obtain.
If you wish to stay here
for the retreat, you may do so.
If not, you may leave as you please."
At that time, Śāriputra alone went to the Āmóujiāmòjiā Mountain
to accept offerings of heavenly food from Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the daughters of the asuras.
They provided heavenly sustenance.
At that time, there was a heavenly demon
who deluded the king's mind,
causing him to return to his palace and indulge in the five desires:
first, precious ornaments;
second, female entertainers;
third, fine clothing and food;
fourth, fame and profit;
fifth, sensual pleasures.
He returned to the inner palace
and ordered the gatekeepers,
"For three months, regardless of rank or status,
no external matters, big or small, are to be reported to me."
He forgot about the offerings and also gave no constant orders for provisions.
After six days, the offerings ceased.
The bhikkhus found it extremely difficult and arduous to obtain alms.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying,
"There is a tree called the Udumbara,
and I wish to take its fruits to provide for the assembly.
There are groves of harītakī
and āmalakī.
In Uttarakuru, there is naturally grown rice;
in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, there is the food of exquisite flavor.
I wish to take all of these to provide for the assembly.
There is also sweet earth.
With one hand,
I can lift all beings,
and with the other hand, turn the earth over,
allowing the bhikkhus to take and eat for themselves.
I hope you will permit this."
The Buddha said,
"You possess great supernatural powers yourself,
but the karmic retribution for the evil deeds of these bhikkhus has ripened and cannot be transferred.
I do not permit any of this."
In this country, there was clear water and fine grass.
There were people from the country of Bōluó
who followed the water and grass to pasture horses,
wishing to fatten them and thus came to this place.
