The horse herders had pure faith in the Buddha.
They addressed the bhikkhus, saying,
"We know that the Sangha is extremely hungry, and their food is exhausted.
We only have horse barley.
Can you eat it?"
The bhikkhus reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"The horses belong to the horse herders, who can feed them good grass and salted water.
This barley is freely available and should be accepted."
There were five hundred horses.
Each horse ate two shēng per day.
They divided half to give to the bhikkhus. There was one fine horse
that ate four dǒu per day.
They divided half to offer to the Buddha. Ānanda took the Buddha's portion along with his own
and entered a village.
In front of a woman,
he praised the Buddha's virtues.
"Due to a minor circumstance,
we are staying here for the retreat.
Can you prepare dried rice for us?"
The woman said,
"My household has many affairs;
I cannot do it."
Another woman nearby heard this
and said to Ānanda,
"Bring the barley, and I will prepare rice for you.
If there are other gentle, wise, and disciplined bhikkhus,
I will also prepare for them."
The woman then prepared rice and gave it to Ānanda.
Ānanda, with deep reverence for the Buddha, thought to himself:
"The Buddha is of royal lineage.
He usually eats fine delicacies.
This rice is coarse and poor, unable to benefit the body."
He served water and offered the rice.
Seeing the Buddha eat it,
he was overwhelmed with sorrow and choked with emotion.
The Buddha knew his thoughts
and wished to dispel them.
"Can you eat it?"
Ānanda said,
"I can accept and eat it."
The flavor was extraordinary.
Indeed, the devas had added flavor to it.
He felt boundless joy, and his sorrow and choking immediately vanished.
He fully recounted the incident of the two women.
The Buddha said,
"If the first woman had prepared the rice,
she would have become the chief consort of a wheel-turning king.
As for the one who prepared it without being asked,
her merit is immeasurable."
At that time, the nobles, wealthy householders,
great rich merchants, and others from various countries
heard that the Buddha had eaten horse barley for three months.
They prepared various offerings and delicacies,
filling the roads with carriages and horses,
and came to present them.
The World-Honored One's pavāraṇā was approaching, with seven days remaining.
He told Ānanda,
"Go into the city
and inform Āqídá:
'The retreat has ended.
We will now travel to other countries.'"
Ānanda went with one bhikkhu
to the king's place
and fully conveyed the Buddha's words.
The king still had not realized
and asked,
"Where is the Buddha now?"
Ānanda said,
"He accepted your three-month invitation, which has just ended, and is still in the country."
The king asked Ānanda again,
"Who provided for him?"
Ānanda said,
"In extreme poverty and hardship,
the Buddha and the Sangha ate horse barley for three months."
Only then did the king awaken to the situation.
"How could I have let the Buddha and the Sangha
eat horse barley for three months?
This evil reputation and ugly name will spread throughout all countries."
He was filled with worry, shame, and distress.
Together with his relatives,
he went to see the Buddha,
deeply repenting,
and further invited the Buddha to stay.
The Buddha accepted for seven days, during which various foods were prepared.
Four pieces of karpāsa cloth
and one pair of leather sandals were offered to the Buddha.
Two pieces of karpāsa cloth
and one pair of leather sandals were given to the Sangha. The king took his offerings
and scattered them all over the road,
wishing for them to be trodden upon.
The Buddha said,
"Food and provisions should be eaten;
reverence should not be shown by trampling underfoot." The Buddha then accepted them.
He bestowed blessings upon all.
The king's heart was joyful, his knots untied,
and he attained the pure Dharma eye.
In a distant past age,
there was a Buddha named Pípóyè.
He was in the city of Pántóumóbá.
The king was named Pántóu.
There was a Brahmin
named Yīntíqílì,
who was well-versed in the four Vedas,
various calculations,
and Brahmin precepts.
He taught five hundred youths.
The king held a feast and invited the Buddha, offering exquisite delicacies.
Among the assembly, there was one bhikkhu
named Maitreya,
who was ill and unable to go for alms.
After the meal, they requested food for the sick monk.
The Brahmin refused and scolded, saying,
"These shaven-headed śramaṇas should only eat horse barley;
they should not eat such sweet and fine offerings."
His disciples at that time said,
"Indeed."
Śāriputra,
that Brahmin was myself.
The five hundred youths
are now the five hundred arhats.
The sick bhikkhu is now Maitreya.
In the city of Shèwèi, there were twenty people.
There were also another twenty people who were their sworn enemies.
At that time, these forty people each wished to harm one another.
They sought opportunities.
Relying on the Buddha's majestic spiritual power, they soon went to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha transformed these forty people.
There would be an iron spear that would naturally appear and pierce the Buddha's right foot big toe.
Before the words were finished, the spear was before the Buddha.
Mùlián addressed the Buddha.
"Now I will pull out the iron spear and cast it into another world."
The Buddha said.
"Using the power of diligence to try to pull out the iron spear,"
"the three-thousandfold great thousand world would be greatly shaken,"
"yet it could not move the spear even a hair's breadth."
The Buddha went to the Brahma Heaven.
The spear followed him.
He returned to the city of Shèwèi.
The spear was also before him.
The Tathāgata took the spear and trod upon it with his foot.
Mùlián addressed the Buddha.
"What offense did the Tathāgata commit to incur this spear calamity?"
The Buddha said.
"In the past, five hundred merchants had one evil thought."
"I then harmed them."
"This is the remaining retribution."
The forty people, hearing this,
said to each other,
"Even the King of Dharma is thus,"
"how much more so for us?"
"Should we not receive punishment?"
They repented their faults and confessed.
They entered into the wisdom of equality.
In the past, there were four brāhmaṇas.
All had attained spiritual powers.
Their bodies could fly, and their spiritual feet were unimpeded.
These four brāhmaṇa ascetics said to each other,
"If there are people"
"who offer delicious food to the śramaṇa Gautama,"
"they will be born in heaven, never leaving the hall of blessings."
"Those who hear the Dharma enter the gate of liberation."
"Today, our minds covet heavenly blessings,"
"we do not wish for liberation, we do not need to hear the Dharma."
At that time, the four each held four jars of sweet, delicious rock sugar.
The first one came forward and offered it to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa,
"What is done is impermanent."
The brāhmaṇa, hearing this, covered his ears.
The second one in turn spoke,
saying, "The Dharma arises and declines."
The brāhmaṇa, hearing this, also covered his ears.
The third one in turn spoke,
saying, "Birth leads to death."
The brāhmaṇa, hearing this, also covered his ears with his hands.
The fourth one in turn spoke,
saying, "This cessation is bliss."
The brāhmaṇa, hearing this, also covered his ears.
They each abandoned it and left.
They said to each other,
"What teachings did the śramaṇa Gautama have?"
The first one replied,
"I heard one phrase: 'What is done is impermanent.'"
The second, third, and fourth,
each stated in turn.
After speaking this verse,
their minds opened, their thoughts were liberated, and they attained the Anāgāmin path.
At that time, the four people,
knowing they had each attained the proof of the path,
returned and earnestly reproached themselves.
They went to where the Tathāgata was.
They bowed their heads at his feet.
They stood to one side.
They addressed the World-Honored One, saying,
"We only wish, Tathāgata,"
"to be allowed to join the order and become śramaṇas."
The World-Honored One told them,
"Welcome, bhikṣus."
"Quickly cultivate the holy life."
At that time, the four people,
their hair and beards fell off by themselves.
The clothes they wore transformed into monastic robes.
Soon before the Buddha, they attained Arhatship.
In the past, there was a brāhmaṇa country,
named Duōwèixiàng.
Its king served heterodox paths.
The king suddenly one day gave rise to a good thought.
He wished to make a great offering.
According to the brāhmaṇa method,
he piled up the seven treasures like a mountain.
Those who came to beg
were allowed to take for themselves,
one handful's weight to take away.
Thus for several days,
the pile did not diminish.
The Buddha knew that this king, due to past blessings, should be saved.
He transformed into a brāhmaṇa and went to that country.
The king came out to meet him.
He greeted him and asked about his well-being, saying,
"What do you seek?"
"Do not hesitate or find it difficult."
The brāhmaṇa replied,
"I have come from afar,"
"wishing to beg for precious jewels to build a house."
The king said, "Very good."
"Take for yourself one handful's weight and go."
The brāhmaṇa took one handful, walked seven steps,
and returned it to its original place.
The king asked why.
The brāhmaṇa replied,
"This is only enough to build a house."
"I will also have to take a wife."
"I fear it is not enough."
"Therefore I do not take it."
The king said,
"Take three handfuls more."
The brāhmaṇa then took them.
He walked seven steps and again returned them to their original place.
The king said, "Why?"
He replied,
"This is enough to take a wife."
"But there is still no land, servants, slaves, oxen, or horses."
"Therefore I have given up the thought."
The king said,
"Take seven handfuls more."
The brāhmaṇa then took them.
He walked seven steps and again returned them to their original place.
The king said,
"What is the reason again?"
The brāhmaṇa replied,
"If I have sons and daughters, they will also have to marry."
"The expenses for auspicious and inauspicious occasions, when calculated, are insufficient."
"Therefore I do not take it."
The king said,
"Take all the piled treasures, I give them to you."
The brāhmaṇa accepted them and then discarded them and left.
The king found it very strange.
He asked again the reason.
The brāhmaṇa replied,
"Originally I came begging to use for livelihood."
"But upon careful reflection, human life in the world is brief,"
"all things are impermanent, difficult to preserve even for a morning or evening."
"Causes and conditions are heavy, worries and sufferings deepen daily."
"Piling treasures like a mountain is of no benefit to oneself."
"Coveting and scheming is but vain toil."
"It is better to cease thoughts and seek the unconditioned path."
"Therefore I do not take it."
The king's mind opened and he received the teaching.
Then the brāhmaṇa revealed the Buddha's radiant form.
He rose up and stayed in the air.
He spoke a verse, saying:
The king saw the Buddha's light.
And heard this verse.
The king and his ministers
then received the five precepts.
They attained the Srotaāpanna path.
In the southern part of India, there was a great city.
It was named Shǒubōluó.
In the city, there was an elder.
His name was Lúzhì.
He served as a guide and leader for the people.
He had, in the past, at the places of countless Buddhas,
planted various virtuous roots.
All the people of that great city,
believed in and submitted to heretical paths, serving the Nirgranthas.
At that time, wishing to convert that elder,
I traveled from Rājagṛha to that city.
The Nirgranthas, hearing that I was coming to that city,
then thought thus:
"If the Śramaṇa Gautama comes here,
these people will then abandon us and no longer provide for us."
They told the people of that city:
"The Śramaṇa Gautama now wishes to come here.
However, that Śramaṇa,
abandoned his parents and roamed east and west.
Wherever he goes, he can cause the land's five grains not to ripen.
The people will suffer famine and many will die; there will be no peace or happiness from the start."
Those people, hearing this, were then filled with fear.
They said:
"Great Teachers,
what plan should we devise?"
The Nirgranthas replied:
"The Śramaṇa Gautama
has a fondness for groves, flowing springs, and clear water.
If there are any outside, they should be destroyed.
You all should then go out of the city together and cut down the trees and forests.
Do not leave any behind. The flowing springs, wells, and ponds,
fill them with foul and filthy things.
Firmly close the city gates.
Each of you prepare your weapons.
Guard the walls and defend them.
Diligently fortify and hold them.
If he should come,
do not let him advance.
We will also perform various arts,
to make that Gautama turn back on the path and leave."
Those people reverently carried out their instructions.
At that time, I,
arriving at that city,
seeing these things already done,
immediately felt compassion.
With a mind of loving-kindness towards them,
all the trees grew back as before, countless and immeasurable.
The rivers, ponds, wells, and springs had their water clear and pure, filling them completely.
Like blue beryl.
Various flowers grew, covering them above.
I transformed the city walls into deep blue beryl.
The people inside the city all could see through to me and the great assembly.
The gates opened by themselves, with none able to restrain them.
The weapons they had prepared turned into various flowers.
The elder Lúzhì, as the foremost,
together with his people, all followed one another,
and came to where I was.
I then expounded for them various essential teachings of the Dharma.
Causing all those people to generate the mind of Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Formerly, in the country of Vārāṇasī, there was a mountain.
Forty or fifty *li* from the city.
There were five Śramaṇas.
Dwelling on the mountain, studying the Path.
In the morning, they would leave the mountain to beg for food among people.
After eating, they would return to the mountain, arriving only in the late evening.
The going and returning was extremely tiring; they could not bear to sit in meditation.
Contemplating correct concentration year after year like this,
they could not attain the Path.
The Buddha, compassionate towards them,
toiling without gain,
transformed into a Daoist.
Went to where they were.
Asked the Daoists:
"Living in seclusion and cultivating the Path, are you not weary?"
The Śramaṇas said:
"We are here,
too far from the city.
These bodies of the four great elements require food.
Going and returning daily,
we are fatigued year after year,
unable to cultivate the Path.
We are just like this until the end of our lives."
The Daoist said:
"Those who practice the Path take precepts as fundamental.
Restraining the mind is the practice.
Devalue the body, value the true.
Decay and discard the physical life.
Eat only to support the body.
Guard the mind in correct concentration.
Internally study cessation and contemplation.
Extinguish thoughts to attain the Path.
Nourishing the body and following desires,
how can one avoid suffering?
I wish, you Daoists,
tomorrow do not go.
I will provide for you."
The Daoists rested for a day.
At that time, the five Śramaṇas were greatly joyful.
Marveling at what had never been before.
Settling their minds in concentration,
no longer worrying about going.
The next day at noon, this transformed Daoist brought food.
After eating, peaceful and harmonious, their minds serene and tranquil.
The transformed Daoist, having spoken a verse, revealed the Buddha's body, the appearance of his light.
The five Śramaṇas, their spirits shaken and stirred,
all contemplated the precepts,
and immediately attained Arhatship.
In the country of Śrāvastī, there was a poor family.
The husband and wife were stingy and greedy, not believing in the Path and virtue.
The Buddha, compassionate towards their foolishness, manifested as a Śramaṇa.
Went to their door to beg for alms.
At that time, the husband was not home.
His wife reviled him,
saying it was unreasonable.
The Śramaṇa said:
"I am a Daoist,
living by begging.
I do not revile in return.
I only hope for a meal."
The woman said:
"Even if you were to drop dead,
you still wouldn't get food.
How much more now, being healthy, do you expect food from me?
You're just wasting time; better leave early."
Then the Śramaṇa,
stood still in front of her,
eyes staring upward, gasping for breath,
and then manifested standing dead.
His body swelled up, worms came out of his nose and mouth.
His belly burst, intestines rotted, filth flowing out.
The woman, seeing this, terrified, lost her voice and ran away.
Then the Daoist,
suddenly left.
Several *li* from the house,
he sat under a tree to rest.
Her husband came home.
On the road, he saw his wife.
Surprised at her fright.
His wife told her husband,
fully relating this event.
The husband was greatly angry.
Asked where he was.
The wife said:
"He has left.
I think he is not far."
The husband then took his bow, brought his knife, and followed the tracks in pursuit.
Drawing his bow, pulling out his knife, running straight ahead,
wanting to chop the Daoist.
The Daoist then transformed into a small city of beryl.
Surrounding himself with it; the man circled several times but could not enter.
He then asked the Daoist:
"Why don't you open the gate?"
The Daoist said:
"If you want the gate to open, discard your bow and knife."
The man thought to himself:
"I should follow his words.
If I can get my hands on him, I'll wring his neck."
He then discarded his bow and knife.
The gate still did not open.
He again said to the Daoist:
"I have discarded my bow and knife.
Why doesn't the gate open?"
The Daoist said again:
"I told you to discard the bow and knife of malice in your heart.
Not the bow and knife in your hand."
Then that man,
heart startled, body trembling,
thought, "The Daoist is divine and sage-like,
he even knows my mind."
He then kowtowed, repented of his faults, and blamed himself.
Said to the Daoist:
"I have a foolish wife who did not recognize a true person.
She made me generate evil.
I beg you to bestow a little compassion.
Do not abandon me now.
I wish to bring her here to urge her to cultivate the Path."
He then got up and returned.
His wife asked:
"Where is the Śramaṇa?"
Her husband fully described his divine transformations and virtue.
"He is now over there.
You should go yourself,
repent and eliminate your sins."
Then husband and wife went to where the Daoist was.
Prostrating with their five limbs, they repented of their faults.
Wishing to become disciples.
They asked about the beryl city:
"Firm and solid, difficult to surpass.
With determined will and settled mind,
eternally without worry or distress.
By what virtue did you attain such divine wonder?"
The Daoist replied:
"I studied broadly without weariness.
Served the Dharma without slackening.
Diligently upheld the precepts.
Mind not indulging in negligence.
Because of this, I attained the Path.
And reached Nirvāṇa by myself."
In the past, there were five hundred Brahmins.
They constantly sought an opportunity against the Buddha.
Wishing to slander him.
They discussed among themselves, saying:
"We should have a butcher, who kills living beings,
invite the Buddha and all the monks.
The Buddha will certainly accept the invitation.
He will then praise the butcher.
We will then step forward and together ridicule him."
The Buddha accepted the invitation.
He told the butcher:
"When fruit is ripe, it falls by itself.
When merit is ripe, one liberates oneself."
The butcher returned home to prepare food and drink.
The Buddha led his disciples to the butcher's village.
Arriving at the donor's house,
the Brahmins, young and old, were all delighted.
"Today we have finally found an opportunity against the Buddha!
If he praises the merit,
we will use his past and present killing and sins
to ridicule him.
If he speaks of his past sins,
we will challenge him with today's merit.
In either case, we now have our opportunity."
The Buddha arrived and sat down.
Water was offered for washing, then food was served.
Then the World-Honored One,
observing the minds of the assembly,
saw those who should be liberated.
He then extended his tongue, covering his face and licking his ears,
and emitted a great light illuminating the entire city.
Then, with a Brahmā-like voice, he spoke verses of blessing.
The five hundred Brahmins' minds opened in understanding.
They stepped forward, bowed to the Buddha,
prostrating themselves with five limbs touching the ground.
Seeking the sage's instruction,
they said: "We only wish for your compassionate guidance to become śramaṇas."
The Buddha immediately accepted them.
They all became śramaṇas.
The villagers, young and old,
witnessing the Buddha's transformation,
were all filled with joy.
All attained the path.
The village was praised as a virtuous place,
and the name "butcher" was no more.
To the southeast of Śrāvastī was a great river,
both deep and wide.
Over five hundred families lived along its banks.
They had not heard of the path of virtue or the practice of liberating the world.
They were accustomed to being stubborn and deceitful as their way of life,
greedy for profit, self-indulgent, seeking only pleasure and satisfaction.
The Buddha knew these families had the merit to be liberated.
He went to the riverbank
and sat under a tree.
The villagers saw the Buddha's extraordinary light,
and all were awed and respectfully went to pay homage.
Some bowed, some saluted, inquiring after his well-being.
The Buddha instructed them to sit and preached the Dharma to them.
The people listened, but their minds still did not believe.
The Buddha manifested a person
coming from the south bank of the river.
He walked on the water,
with the water just covering his ankles.
He came before the Buddha, bowed his head, and paid homage.
Everyone who saw this was astonished.
They asked the manifested person:
"Our ancestors have lived by this riverbank for generations,
and we have never heard of anyone walking on water.
Who are you?
What spiritual power do you have to tread on water without sinking?"
The manifested person replied:
"I am a simple, straightforward man from the south bank.
Hearing the Buddha was here,
I longed for the Dharma and virtue.
I came to the southern bank,
but could not cross at the usual time.
I asked people on the other shore
how deep the water was.
They told me,
'The water only reaches your ankles.'
I believed their words,
and thus came across.
I have no other special power."
The Buddha praised him, saying: "Excellent!
Holding firm to sincere faith can cross the abyss of birth and death.
A river of several miles is nothing extraordinary."
Hearing this, the villagers
opened their minds and their faith became firm.
They all received the Five Precepts
and became pure lay devotees.
At that time, the kingdoms of Shèwèi and Píshělí
harbored grievances against each other.
They engaged in mutual raids and attacks.
The king of Shèwèi thought to himself:
"I am the king.
I should repel enemies and bring peace to the people.
How can I allow bandits to plunder and seize people and goods?"
He then commanded his generals and soldiers:
"I order you to pursue and capture them.
You must ensure they are apprehended."
At that time, the bhikṣus of Shèwèi had completed their summer retreat.
They intended to go to Píshělí.
The bhikṣus lost their way
and fell among those bandits.
The bhikṣus asked:
"Venerable ones, where are you going?"
They replied:
"To Píshělí."
The bhikṣus said further:
"Let us travel together as companions."
They then answered:
"We are bandits.
We traverse through brambles and woods,
walking without choosing paths.
You are good people.
How can you follow us?"
The bhikṣus pleaded again:
"Please take us with you."
Before their words were finished,
the pursuers arrived in search.
They seized the bhikṣus along with them
and brought them before the king.
"These are the bandits."
The king said:
"Bring the bhikṣus forward first."
The king said:
"You are renunciants.
How could you become bandits?"
They replied:
"I am not a bandit."
"Then why did you accompany them?"
The bhikṣus fully explained the above events to the king.
The king said, "Release them."
The king asked the bandits:
"Is this renunciant your companion?"
They replied:
"He is a companion."
The king said:
"Take the bandits away and summon the bhikṣus again."
The king asked:
"Bhikṣu, you speak falsely and deceive the authorities.
The bandits say you are their companion.
Why do you say you are not?"
The bhikṣu answered as before.
The king then ordered the bandits to be released and dealt with according to the law.
They seized five hundred bandits,
placed garlands of Kapila flowers on them,
beat drums and paraded them through the streets,
intending to execute them.
The bandits wailed and wept loudly.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked:
"What is this sound of many people?"
A bhikṣu replied:
"World-Honored One,
these are five hundred bandits
whom the king has ordered to be killed.
That is the sound."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Go and tell the king:
'You are a king among men.
You should cherish the people like your own children.
How can you kill five hundred people at once?'"
Ānanda received the instruction
and went to the king's place.
He fully relayed the Buddha's words.
The king said:
"Venerable One,
I know this matter.
Killing one person incurs much guilt,
let alone five hundred.
But they repeatedly destroyed villages
and plundered the people.
If the World-Honored One can make them cease being bandits,
I can spare their lives."
Ānanda returned and fully reported to the Buddha.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Tell the king to simply release them.
I will cause these people from this day forth to never again become bandits."
Ānanda received the instruction.
He first went to the execution ground
and said to the execution supervisor:
"These criminals
have been saved by the World-Honored One.
Do not kill them yet."
He then went to the king's place:
"The World-Honored One says to the king
that he can make these people never again become bandits."
The king then spared their lives.
However, he did not yet untie their bonds,
but sent them to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One,
wishing to liberate those people,
was sitting in an open area.
The bandits saw the Buddha from afar,
and their bonds untied themselves.
They bowed their heads at his feet,
then stepped back and stood to one side.
The Buddha observed their predispositions
and accordingly preached the Dharma to them:
the karmic retribution of giving, upholding precepts, and actions;
the Four Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Right at that time,
they attained the path of the Stream-enterer.
He asked:
"Do you wish to leave home and become monks?"
They replied:
"World-Honored One,
if we had left home earlier, we would not have suffered this misery.
We now beseech you to ordain us as monks."
The Buddha said:
"Come, bhikṣus."
Then the five hundred bandits' entire bodies and garments transformed into the three robes.
Alms bowls and utensils appeared naturally, and their dignified demeanor was serene and orderly,
as if they were bhikṣus of a hundred years.
They all became Arhats.
In the kingdom of Jiāosàluó,
there were five hundred bandits.
King Pōsīnì
was troubled by their rampant violence.
He dispatched troops to lie in wait and capture them.
Once captured, their eyes were gouged out,
and they were abandoned in a dark, dense forest.
These bandits
had planted many roots of virtue with a previous Buddha.
Having lost their eyes, they suffered great agony.
Each said these words:
"Námó Fótuó (Homage to the Buddha)."
I was staying at the Jetavana Monastery at that time.
Hearing their voices,
I immediately gave rise to a mind of compassion.
At that moment, a cool breeze
blew various fragrant herbs from the incense mountains,
filling their eye sockets.
Their eyes were immediately restored as before, no different.
The bandits opened their eyes and saw the Tathāgata
standing before them, preaching the Dharma.
Hearing the Dharma,
the bandits aroused the mind of Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
In the kingdom of Píshělí,
there was a brāhmaṇa
who held firmly to wrong views.
He had no offspring.
Fearing sudden death,
his wealth would be confiscated by the state.
He made offerings to various mountains
and tree spirits.
He perceived his wife was pregnant.
When the months were full, she gave birth to a boy.
The child was handsome.
His parents loved and cherished him.
When he reached twelve years of age,
he went out for an excursion.
On the road, he encountered a drunken elephant,
was trampled, and died immediately.
His parents were grief-stricken and distressed,
their minds becoming deranged and insane.
They ran about naked.
The Tathāgata, with compassionate thought,
manifested as their son.
The parents embraced him,
experiencing immeasurable joy.
Their derangement and insanity immediately ceased,
and they regained their original minds.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to them,
and they aroused the mind for the Path.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the past, during the summer retreat,
in the city of Bālínàtuó,
there was a courtesan
named Miàoyì.
She had a connection with the Buddha.
The Buddha, along with Nàntuó,
went to the courtesan's dwelling
to beg for alms daily.
This woman never showed reverence toward me,
but toward Nàntuó alone she felt deep affection and attachment.
After seven days had passed,
the woman thought to herself:
'If the ascetic Gautama
could send Nàntuó and Ānanda
to fulfill my wish,
I would make all kinds of offerings.'
The Buddha told Ānanda and Nàntuó:
'From today onward, do not go to that village.'
The World-Honored One alone went to the woman's chamber.
From the first day to the third day,
he emitted golden light
and transformed into various heavenly beings.
This woman did not awaken.
On a later day, the World-Honored One
again took Ānanda and Nàntuó
and walked beneath a tree.
Because the courtesan loved and revered the two bhikkhus,
she scattered many flowers from afar toward the Buddha and the two bhikkhus.
Ānanda said to her:
'You should pay homage to the Buddha.'
The woman, loving Ānanda,
immediately made obeisance.
The Buddha transformed into three youths,
all fifteen years old,
with handsome faces.
The woman saw them and rejoiced.
For the sake of the transformed youths,
she prostrated herself in reverence.
She addressed the youths, saying:
'Sirs, my dwelling here is like the goddess of merit—
rich, powerful, and free,
adorned with all kinds of treasures.
I now offer myself, along with my servants,
to you, sirs.
They can serve for cleaning and sweeping.
If you would kindly accept,
and grant my wish,
I will provide everything without any reluctance.'
The transformed beings sat on the bed.
Before even a mealtime had passed,
the woman approached intimately and said:
'Please fulfill my desire.'
The transformed beings did not refuse.
For one day and one night, their minds did not grow weary.
By the second day, her affection gradually subsided.
By the third day,
she said:
'Sirs, you may rise and eat.'
The transformed beings then rose.
They clung to her incessantly.
The woman grew disgusted and regretful.
She said:
'Sirs, how can people be like this?'
The transformed beings replied:
'According to my former ways,
whenever I consort with a woman,
it takes twelve days before I rest.'
Hearing these words,
the woman felt as if she had choked on food—
unable to spit it out,
and unable to swallow it.
Her body suffered pain,
as if pounded by a pestle.
By the fourth day,
it was as if she had been run over by a cart.
By the fifth day,
it was as if iron pellets had entered her body.
By the sixth day,
all her limbs and joints ached,
as if arrows had pierced her heart.
The woman thought:
'I have heard that the son of King Jìngfàn
always rescues suffering people.
Why does he not come to save me today?'
Having thought this,
she felt deep remorse and blamed herself.
'From this day until the end of my life,
I will not crave sensual desires.
I would rather share a room with tigers, wolves, lions, and fierce beasts
than endure this suffering.'
After saying this,
she rose again to eat and drink.
Walking and sitting together, there was nothing she could do.
The transformed beings also grew angry and spat, saying:
'Wretched woman!
You have ruined my affairs.
I now wish to join with you
as one body.
It would be better to die early.
If my parents and relatives
come looking for me,
where shall I hide myself?
I would rather hang myself
than endure such shame.'
The woman said:
'Wretched creature, I want nothing to do with you.
If you wish to die, do as you please.'
The transformed being took a knife and stabbed his own neck.
Blood stained the woman's body.
He collapsed to the ground,
and the woman could not overcome him,
nor could she avoid death.
After two days, the body turned blue, putrid, and black.
On the third day, it swelled up.
On the fourth day, it festered and burst open.
Feces and urine,
along with various vile insects,
gushed blood and pus,
smearing the woman's body.
The woman was utterly disgusted but could not escape.
By the fifth day,
the skin and flesh gradually rotted away.
By the sixth day,
the flesh had completely fallen off.
By the seventh day,
only foul bones remained,
sticky like glue or lacquer,
adhering to the woman's body.
The woman made a vow:
'If any heavenly deity
or immortal,
or the son of King Jìngfàn,
can free me from this suffering,
I will offer this dwelling
and all its treasures
as alms.'
Just as she thought this,
the Buddha, accompanied by Ānanda and Nàntuó, with Indra in front
holding a precious incense burner
burning priceless incense,
and Brahmā behind
holding a great precious canopy,
along with countless heavenly musicians,
the Buddha emitted his constant light, illuminating heaven and earth.
All the great assembly saw the Tathāgata
approaching this woman's chamber.
When the woman saw the Buddha,
she felt shame and embarrassment.
Having nowhere to hide the bones,
she took countless white cloths and much incense
to wrap the foul bones,
but the stench remained as before,
impossible to conceal.
When the woman saw the World-Honored One,
she paid homage to him.
Out of shame,
her body covered the bones,
but the foul bones suddenly appeared on her back.
The woman wept and said:
'The Tathāgata's merit and compassion are immeasurable.
If you can free me from this suffering,
I vow to become your disciple and never retreat from this resolve.'
By the Buddha's supernatural power,
the foul bones disappeared.
The woman was overjoyed
and paid homage to the Buddha.
She addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One,
I now offer all my treasures to you.'
The Buddha pronounced a blessing in his Brahmā-like voice, flowing smoothly.
The woman heard it and rejoiced,
and immediately attained the fruit of Stream-Entry.
Good man,
when I entered the great city of Rājagṛha
to beg for alms in sequence,
Devadatta
instructed King Ajātaśatru
to release the maddened, drunken elephant named Hùcái,
intending to harm me and my disciples.
At that time, I entered the meditation of loving-kindness,
extended my hand, and showed it.
From my five fingers emerged five lions.
When the elephant saw them, its heart was terrified,
it lost control of its bowels,
threw its whole body to the ground,
and reverently bowed at my feet.
Good man,
at that time, my fingers actually had no lions;
it was due to the power of cultivating the wholesome roots of compassion
that I subdued it."
Furthermore, good man.
I wish to enter Nirvāṇa.
At the very beginning of my journey,
heading towards Kuśinagara,
there were five hundred strongmen.
On that middle road,
they were leveling, repairing, sweeping, and sprinkling it.
Among them was a large stone.
The crowd wanted to lift and move it,
but despite exhausting their strength, they could not.
At that time, I felt compassion,
and immediately gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
Those strongmen then saw
me use my big toe
to lift this great stone,
toss it into the empty sky,
catch it again with my hand,
place it on my right palm,
blow on it, reducing it to fine dust,
and then reassemble it.
I did this to subdue their arrogant minds.
Then I briefly explained various essential teachings to them.
I caused them all to arouse the mind of Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
After the Buddha's Nirvāṇa,
the Malla people of the country of Pāpā and the Vajjī people of the country of Cārapa,
the Koliya people of the country of Rāmaga,
the Brāhmaṇa people of the country of Vṛji,
the Śākya residents of the country of Kapilavastu,
the Licchavi people of the country of Vaiśālī,
and King Ajātaśatru of the country of Magadha, each with their fourfold army prepared, sent the Brāhmaṇa Droṇa to speak to the strongmen of Kuśinagara, saying:
"The Buddha is our teacher, the one we revere.
He attained Parinirvāṇa within your country.
Therefore, we have come from afar to request a portion of the relics to take back to our countries to build stūpas.
If you give us a portion, our entire countries will treasure it and share it with you."
The strongmen replied:
"The World-Honored One condescended to come to this land and attained Parinirvāṇa here.
The officers and people of our country should naturally make offerings.
You gentlemen have labored from afar, but it cannot be granted."
The kings consulted together:
"We have humbly requested in peace, but since it is not given,
we will not spare our lives and bodies; we shall take it by force."
The king of the strongmen said:
"If you wish to raise troops, we have sufficient strength to resist.
In the end, you will not succeed."
The Brāhmaṇa Droṇa loudly proclaimed among the eight assemblies:
"The Buddha accumulated and cultivated goodness, enduring for immeasurable kalpas.
You gentlemen have also heard him praise forbearance.
How can you raise armies to contend and seize from each other?
This is not a reverent act.
Now the relics are present; we should simply divide them into eight portions,
so that people everywhere may all make offerings.
You gentlemen have all also received the Buddha's precepts and recite his teachings with your mouths.
How can you fight over the relics and thereby harm each other?"
The strongmen reported:
"We respectfully agree with your proposal."
At that time, the Brāhmaṇa Droṇa
immediately divided them into eight portions.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra manifested as a human and said to the kings:
"We gods should also have a portion.
If we contend by force, there will be victors and vanquished.
We hope you will give it to us; do not make it difficult."
At that time, the Nāga King Anavatapta, the Nāga King Vāsuki, and the Nāga King Elāpattra said to the eight kings:
"We also should have a portion of the relics.
If you do not give it to us, we have sufficient strength to subdue you."
At that time, Upagupta said:
"Gentlemen, please stop; it is fitting to share them together."
He then divided them into three portions:
one portion for the gods,
one portion for the nāga kings,
and one portion belonging to the eight kings.
They smeared a jar with honey, measured with the jar.
The gods, obtaining their portion, returned to heaven and built a seven-jeweled stūpa.
The nāgas, obtaining their portion, returned to the nāga palace and also built a jeweled stūpa.
King Ajātaśatru counted the portions; each obtained eighty-four thousand relics.
There remained one tooth of the Buddha that no one dared to take.
Because King Ajātaśatru was the first to seek the relics, throwing himself to the ground in exhaustion, his sincerity was the most profound, so they all held it and gave it to him.
Ajātaśatru was joyful; drums and music shook the heavens.
The Nāga King Ghaṭīkarṇa met him on the road and said:
"The Buddha left relics; give one portion to me."
The king said:
"It cannot be granted."
The nāga said:
"I am Ghaṭīkarṇa.
I can lift your country and cast it eighty thousand li away, grinding it to dust."
The king, terrified and alarmed, gave the Buddha's tooth to him.
The nāga built a stūpa beneath Mount Sumeru.
It was eighty-four thousand li high,
a towering stūpa of crystal and lapis lazuli.
King Ajātaśatru passed away.
Aśoka obtained his kingdom.
At that time, a minister reported to King Aśoka:
"The Nāga King Ghaṭīkarṇa previously intimidated Ajātaśatru and took the Buddha's tooth away."
Aśoka heard this,
and immediately commanded the king of ghosts and spirits to make iron nets and iron traps,
placing them in the water beneath Mount Sumeru, intending to capture the nāga king.
The nāga king was greatly afraid and together they devised a plan, saying:
"Aśoka serves the Buddha; wait until he is sound asleep, then take his palace and move it to the water beneath Mount Sumeru,
beneath the crystal stūpa. He will come out himself to meet us; we will explain the whole story, and his anger will surely cease."
They then dispatched nāgas to lift and take Aśoka's palace.
He awoke from sleep, not knowing where he was.
He saw a crystal stūpa eighty-four thousand li high.
Joy and fear intermingled in his heart.
The Nāga King Ghaṭīkarṇa himself came out and apologized, saying:
"King Ajātaśatru himself gave it to me; I did not seize it.
Śākyatathāgata formerly made an agreement with me, saying:
'After my Nirvāṇa, when the kalpa is about to end, all the sūtras, vinaya, robes, and alms bowls should be taken and stored in this stūpa.
When Maitreya descends, they shall be brought out again.'"
The nāga returned the king to his palace, placing it in its original location.
The Brāhmaṇa Droṇa said:
"Please give me the relic urn; I will return to the village of Hiraṇyavatī and build an urn stūpa."
The strongmen gave it to him.
With the urn and the relics placed in the urn, they together built a jeweled stūpa.
The Brāhmaṇa and householders of Pāṭaliputra also said:
"Give us the charcoal from where the Buddha was cremated.
We will return to our country and build a charcoal stūpa."
Foreign ascetics from another country requested the ashes from the ground to take back to their country to build a stūpa.
The strongmen all agreed.
There were also those who built a jeweled stūpa at the cremation site.
The ashes, charcoal, and earth amounted to forty-nine hu.
The jeweled stūpas built numbered forty-nine.
All were adorned with tall flagpoles, Dharma wheels, and silk banners.
King Aśoka, with his fourfold army arrayed,
went to open the seven stūpas to take the relics, leaving only the nāga stūpa.
The nāga led the king into his palace, saying:
"This stūpa is what I make offerings to; I wish for it to be left."
The king immediately consented.
Returning to his country, he made eighty-four thousand jeweled caskets, distributed the relics, filling each casket.
He further made eighty-four thousand jeweled vases and various banners and canopies,
entrusting them to yakṣas to build stūpas everywhere in Jambudvīpa, all over the land, even to the great sea.
He first consulted the Arhat Yaśas, saying:
"I wish in one day, in a single thought, to build eighty-four thousand stūpas, causing them all to be completed simultaneously."
The Arhat Yaśas greatly praised him.
The king later compared his merit with the nāga's.
They weighed two statues together,
and the nāga's was heavy, the king's light.
The king extensively invited the saṅgha and tirelessly planted merit.
Later, they weighed again.
The weight was balanced.
The king further cultivated and practiced,
knowing his merit increased daily.
He raised troops to go and subdue [the nāga].
Just as he set out on the road,
the nāga king, great and small, all came forth to welcome him.
The relics of one stūpa were respectfully presented to the king.
Later, observing the places where the Buddha attained the Way and converted people, he accordingly built stūpas again. Within the king's realm there were one thousand two hundred monasteries.
He also made woven gold-threaded banners, also one thousand two hundred.
Also, thousand-petaled golden flowers he wished to scatter with his own hand.
Just as he prepared them, he encountered a severe illness.
Fearing to contradict his original intent, tears streamed down.
A śramaṇa said to the king:
"The merit you have cultivated is incalculable.
You should simply open your mind; why be sorrowful?
Just single-mindedly [focus].
I will enable the king to achieve his wish."
The śramaṇa then used his spiritual power to cause all one thousand two hundred monasteries to appear before the king.
His illness and suffering immediately vanished.
Wishing to attach the banners,
all the stūpa finials lowered to the king's hand.
His original wish was fulfilled.
His lifespan was extended twenty-five years, and for twenty more years he promoted merit.
At the time of his approaching death,
he continuously recollected the Three Jewels, thought after thought unceasing.
Without any stinginess, he fully accomplished Bodhi.
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
"What cause did he previously create,
that his bodily relics gave rise to eighty-four thousand jeweled stūpas?"
The Buddha said:
"In the past, there was a king named Prasenajit, ruling over eighty-four thousand countries in Jambudvīpa.
At that time, there was a Buddha named Puṣya.
The king, with his ministers and people, made offerings to the Buddha and the bhikṣu saṅgha.
At that time, the king thought:
'The border small countries, their places remote and偏僻, the people there have no means to cultivate merit.'
He then summoned painters to paint images of the Buddha.
He distributed them to distant countries, so all could make offerings.
At that time, the painters, looking at the Buddha's marks and characteristics,
would just get one part right and forget the rest, unable to complete it.
At that time, King Prasenajit,
mixing the various pigments, painted an image himself to serve as a model.
The masters copied and learned, painting eighty-four thousand images.
He distributed them to eighty-four thousand small countries.
The kings of those small countries all were able to make offerings.
King Prasenajit is now me.
Due to this merit, my body possesses the thirty-two marks.
After Nirvāṇa, I again obtained eighty-four thousand various stūpas."
King Āyù passed away.
The ministers wished to establish the crown prince to succeed the throne.
There was one minister,
named Ātúluódì,
who said:
"Great King Āyù
vowed to donate a full hundred thousand million in gold
to perform various meritorious deeds.
He was still short by four million.
The crown prince sealed the treasury and would not give it.
The king relinquished the land of Jambudvīpa
to bestow upon the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha,
wishing to fulfill the vow.
Now the great land all belongs to the Three Jewels.
How can we simply make the crown prince king?"
The ministers then raised four million in gold and sent it to the monasteries before jointly establishing him.
It is known that this was the fourth-generation king,
named Fúshāmìduōluó.
He asked his ministers:
"What kind of deeds should I perform
so that my name and legacy will endure for a long time?"
A minister addressed the king:
"The former king Āyù
built eighty-four thousand stūpas of the Tathāgata
and further revived various offerings.
His name and virtue have been passed down without interruption."
The king said:
"The former king possessed great majesty and virtue;
he was capable of accomplishing such deeds.
I cannot do that.
Consider other matters."
Another minister said:
"There are two kinds of deeds
by which a name is passed down without perishing:
one is doing good,
the other is doing evil.
The former king built stūpas;
now the king may destroy stūpas.
Both will be immortal."
The king then followed this advice.
He immediately raised the fourfold army and went to the monasteries.
First arriving at the Jīquè Monastery, before the middle gate,
there was a stone lion
that immediately roared like a lion.
Hearing it, the king was terrified
and returned to the city.
This happened repeatedly.
Summoning the bhikṣus, he asked:
"If I destroy stūpas or destroy monastic dwellings, which is better?"
The bhikṣus replied:
"Neither should be done.
If absolutely unavoidable, rather destroy the monastic dwellings than the stūpas."
The king then killed the bhikṣus
and destroyed various stūpas and monasteries.
Arriving in the country of Pójiāluó,
he again proclaimed:
"Whoever obtains the head of a śramaṇa will be rewarded with a thousand pieces of gold."
In this country, there was an arhat
who transformed into many bhikṣu heads
and distributed them to the common people to send in and claim the gold.
The king's treasury of gold and treasures was exhausted.
Later, learning of the arhat's deed, he became even more furious.
The arhat entered the nirodha-samāpatti (cessation attainment).
The king went to kill him but ultimately could not succeed,
for by the power of nirodha-samāpatti, his body was not harmed.
Thus gradually advancing to the stūpa gate, at the Yáchǐ Stūpa,
a deity said:
"A crawling spirit previously sought my daughter;
I did not give her.
Now, to protect the Dharma, I shall call my daughter and give her to him."
Together they made a vow:
"You subdue this king; do not let him destroy the true Dharma."
At that time, the crawling spirit went to the southern sea, pushed apart a great mountain, and crushed the king and his fourfold army.
None survived.
The people exclaimed:
"Excellent! Excellent!
The lineage of the Peacock has here come to an end forever."
The bhikṣus such as Mahinda,
having received the three-month summer offerings of the four requisites from the king of Siṃhala named Devānampiya Tissa,
upon completion of the offerings,
took leave of the king, saying:
"In the past, we relied on our teacher's presence,
serving him morning and evening,
making offerings and paying respects.
It has been a long time since we parted,
and now we wish to return."
The king said:
"Relying on the Dharma master,
we have received the refuges and precepts.
With the four requisites provided, what is there to be dissatisfied with?
Previously, you said
the Buddha had already attained parinirvāṇa.
Now you say
you wish to return to inquire after him."
The bhikṣus said:
"Although the Buddha has attained parinirvāṇa,
his relics still remain."
The king said:
"Venerable ones,
do you wish for me to build a stūpa? Where is a suitable place for measurement?"
He then went to where the śrāmaṇera Sumana was
and asked:
"How can we obtain the Tathāgata's relics?"
The śrāmaṇera replied:
"Simply purify the roads, burn incense, and scatter flowers.
The king, together with his retinue, should observe the eight precepts.
Depart from the Nāga Garden,
and they will naturally arrive."
The king then made the preparations.
Sumana returned to inform his grandfather, fully reporting the above matters,
saying they wished to build a stūpa
and hoped he would bestow the relics.
Aśoka said: "You may go to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven palace and inform Śakra.
Śakra has two relics:
one is the right tooth, kept by Śakra for worship,
and the other is the right collarbone, which he will certainly give to you.
Open the casket, take the relics, place them in a bowl,
fill the bowl with white light like pearls, and give them to the śrāmaṇera."
The śrāmaṇera again went to Śakra's palace to request the right collarbone.
Śakra said:
"Excellent."
He opened the casket and gave it to him.
The śrāmaṇera gave the relics from his grandfather to the king.
The king thought:
"I should place the Tathāgata's relics on top of my head."
Before the thought was complete,
the elephant knelt on the ground,
a white canopy descended,
and the casket rose to the top of his head.
The king's entire body was filled with joy as if he had obtained ambrosia.
A fine rain fell, and the earth trembled.
The king asked the venerable ones:
"Where should we place them now?"
They replied:
"Place them on the elephant's head."
The elephant made sounds, worshipping the relics.
Devas, nāgas, and ghosts and spirits all rejoiced greatly.
They then entered the city, where the people worshipped them.
Exiting through the southern gate, they circumambulated and took them to the stūpa.
In the past, the relics of the three Buddhas were also in this stūpa garden.
They then cleared away thorns and brambles and first built the stūpa base,
making it level with the elephant's head.
The king said to the venerable ones:
"What should the stūpa's shape be?"
Mahinda replied:
"Like a heap of rice."
The king said:
"Excellent."
They then built a small stūpa and prepared to enshrine the relics.
All the people of the country gathered.
The relics rose from the elephant's head into the sky,
reaching the height of seven tāla trees, manifesting various miraculous transformations.
They displayed five colors, dark and yellow,
sometimes emitting water,
sometimes emitting fire.
They then took the relics and placed them in the stūpa.
Heaven and earth trembled.
The king's consort,
named Anulā, requested
to take ordination under Mahinda.
Mahinda said:
"I cannot ordain women.
My sister, named Saṅghamittā,
is in Pāṭaliputra.
The king may go to invite her, along with the Bodhi tree."
The king sent his nephew named Ariṭṭha.
Mahinda, using his supernatural power, caused the ship to arrive in one day.
He reported to King Aśoka:
"Mahinda sent me to fully convey his intentions."
The king said:
"My son Mahinda
and grandson Sumana—
after parting, I have been sorrowful and unhappy at heart,
troubled day and night as if my limbs were severed.
Now seeing this nun would relieve my heart.
If she leaves again, I will surely die."
He told the nun not to go.
The nun said to the king:
"It is difficult to go against your will,
but the kṣatriya lady awaits ordination.
The king permits the Bodhi tree, but it cannot be divided with an axe."
Moggaliputta Tissa said:
"When the Tathāgata was in the world, he already gave five instructions:
First, Aśoka should take the Bodhi tree to Siṃhala without using an axe.
The southern branch will break off by itself and enter a golden urn.
Second, it will rise into the sky and remain among the clouds.
Third, after seven days, it will descend by itself back into the golden urn.
Its leaves will flourish luxuriantly, bearing fruit abundantly, with dark yellow leaves.
Fourth, when Siṃhala first wishes to obtain my relics,
they should perform various miraculous transformations.
Fifth, all marks of excellence
will go to Siṃhala as if I were in the world."
The king, hearing this, rejoiced and made a vow:
"If the branch is permitted to be taken, may the tree display branches on all sides.
If it is permitted to go to Siṃhala, may it fall by itself into the golden urn, and the tree return to its original state."
He then filled the golden urn with fragrant clay.
On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, in the afternoon,
he drew lines on the curved part of the tree branch, making ten lines in total.
The first line grew roots,
and the last line broke off.
The roots grew four inches long and produced fine roots,
crisscrossing and sprouting branches like a net.
The main branch was ten cubits long,
and there were five branches, each four cubits long.
Each of the five branches bore one fruit.
There were also a thousand small branches.
The king, seeing the miraculous transformations, rejoiced greatly.
He shouted toward the tree,
and the monks chanted "sādhu."
The minor kings and their retinues, along with the entire assembly, all shouted.
The earth deities, startled, also shouted, their voices reaching the sky.
Thus, the sound spread all the way to the Brahmā heaven.
The tree branch, from where it was cut, immediately produced a hundred roots.
Ten roots went straight down to the bottom of the urn, piercing through it,
while ninety fine roots grew around it.
In this way, they grew day and night.
At that time, the earth shook in six ways.
Devas in the sky played various musical instruments.
Mountains and trees danced like people.
Devas and humans clapped their hands,
yakṣas laughed joyfully,
and the asura kings sang praises.
Brahmā was delighted.
In the sky, thunder and lightning crashed.
Four-legged creatures ran about, crying out.
Birds flew, producing various sounds.
The Bodhi tree fruit emitted light of six colors,
illuminating the entire sahā world up to the Brahmā heaven.
At that time, the Bodhi tree rose into the sky
and remained there for seven days.
The assembly saw only the light, not the urn or the tree.
The king then descended from his seat and worshipped the Bodhi tree.
After seven days, the tree again emitted light,
illuminating the sahā world up to the Brahmā heaven.
The light withdrew, and the sky became clear again.
The leaves spread, and fruit formed as it descended from the sky back into the golden urn.
The king, seeing this, rejoiced and again worshipped the small Bodhi tree as the ruler of Jambudvīpa for seven days.
The king paid homage to the Bodhi tree for seven days as the ruler of Jambudvīpa.
On the fifteenth day of the ninth month, the monks held the uposatha.
The Bodhi tree, from its original place of growth,
came to the east of the city of Pāṭaliputra
and stayed under a sāla tree, its branches lush and dense.
The king, seeing this, rejoiced
and again paid homage to it as the ruler of Jambudvīpa.
He said to Saṅghamittā:
"It is time to go."
She replied:
"Excellent,
great king."
He then assigned eight classes of ghosts and spirits to protect the Bodhi tree,
along with eight great ministers,
eight brāhmaṇas,
eight householders,
eight Bhārgavas,
eight Śākyas,
and eight Kaliṅgas.
The king, with eight golden jars and eight silver jars, poured water to bathe the Bodhi tree.
Having received the king's instructions, they acted accordingly.
The king and the great assembly circumambulated the Bodhi tree and escorted it on the road.
Devas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and asuras worshipped it day and night.
When they reached Tāmraliptī,
the kings themselves carried the Bodhi tree,
entering the water up to their necks.
They then boarded the ship with Saṅghamittā.
The king called Ariṭṭha and said:
"The Bodhi tree was in my country.
I paid homage to it three times as the ruler of Jambudvīpa.
I myself carried the Bodhi tree into the water up to my neck
and placed it on the ship.
I command you, Ariṭṭha:
When the Bodhi tree arrives in that country,
you may tell your king
to enter the water himself,
with the water reaching his neck,
to welcome the Bodhi tree and carry it on his head,
just as I performed various acts of worship here."
Having issued this command, the ship immediately set sail.
At that time, in the sea where the ship was located, for an area one yojana in length and breadth, there were no waves.
The king thought to himself,
"The Bodhi tree of the Buddha is now leaving my kingdom."
As he thought this, tears flowed and he wept with sorrow.
After the ship departed, the king gazed into the distance and saw
various flowers emerging from the seawater, following behind the ship to make offerings.
Moreover, in the empty sky, various flowers and music were scattered as offerings.
The water deities also made offerings with various flowers and incense.
Thus, in succession, it reached all the way to the dragon king's palace.
The dragon king then emerged, intending to seize the Bodhi tree.
At this time, the bhikṣuṇī Sēngqiémìduō
transformed into a golden-winged garuḍa king.
The dragon king bowed his head and said,
"Now I wish to invite the Bodhi tree and the great virtuous one
to return to my palace for seven days of offerings."
Thereupon, the Bodhi tree and the great assembly all entered the dragon palace.
The dragon king offered his royal throne to the tree, honoring it as king, and made offerings for seven days.
After seven days had passed,
the dragon king personally escorted the Bodhi tree to the island of Jùnàwèi in Jambudvīpa.
King Āyù, gazing into the distance and no longer seeing the Bodhi tree,
wept and returned.
At that time, the heaven-beloved King Dìxū
leveled and repaired the road from the city to the Jùnà island.
The ground was as flat as a palm.
Sēngqiémìduō, through supernatural power,
enabled the king to see from within the palace city the Bodhi tree approaching from afar.
The king went out to the island to welcome it into Jambudvīpa.
At Jùnàwèi, the water reached up to his neck.
The tree emitted light of six colors.
Seeing this, the king rejoiced.
Then, lifting it upon his head, he brought it ashore.
In the country, there were sixteen great clans of elders,
who together with the king welcomed the Bodhi tree.
When the tree reached the shore,
for three days, offerings were made to the Bodhi tree in the Lion Continent.
The sixteen great clans managed the affairs of the king's country.
When the three days ended and the fourth day arrived,
they carried the Bodhi tree in succession to the country of Ānóuluótuó.
All the people of the country rejoiced, bowed, and made offerings.
On the fourteenth day of the tenth month, after midday,
the Bodhi tree entered through the northern city gate to the center of the city.
Then it again exited through the southern city gate.
Five hundred bow-lengths from the southern city gate,
at this place, the past Buddhas had also all entered samādhi.
The Bodhi tree of Buddha Jùnàwèi
was named Mahāśālipa.
The Bodhi tree of Buddha Kanakamuni was named Udumbara.
The Bodhi tree of Buddha Kāśyapa was named Nyagrodha.
In the country of Jiāmí,
the śrāmaṇera Xiumónà had a foundation laid.
The entire area was measured, and gates, buildings,
and the place where the Bodhi tree would reside were all made square and orderly, with a royal gatehouse established.
At that time, the sixteen great clans all submitted.
They surrounded and planted the ground of the royal gatehouse.
Then they released the tree.
The tree rose into the empty sky, eighty cubits high.
Immediately, it emitted light of six colors, illuminating the Lion Country.
It spread everywhere.
Up to the Brahma heavens.
The multitude, seeing the transformation of the tree, greatly rejoiced in their hearts.
Ten thousand people in the assembly simultaneously recollected the Buddha.
In succession, they left home and attained the path of arhatship.
Before the sunlight had faded, the tree was still in the empty sky.
After the sun set, the constellations all descended, and the earth greatly shook.
At that time, Mǎshéntuó,
together with Sēngqiémìduō, the king, and the people of the country,
gathered beneath the Bodhi tree.
A seed from a northern branch ripened and fell from the branch, offered to Mǎshéntuó.
Mǎshéntuó gave the pit to the king, instructing him to plant it.
The king then received it in a golden vessel.
He covered it with fertile soil.
And also covered it with fragrant paste.
In a moment, eight saplings grew.
Each was four cubits long.
Seeing this, the king was amazed and sighed.
He covered them with a white parasol.
And honored the small trees as king.
The king took one sapling
and planted it on the island of Jùnàwèi in Jambudvīpa.
He also took one sapling and planted it in the village of Bójūluópómén.
He also took one sapling and planted it within the gate.
He also took one sapling and planted it in the stūpa garden.
He also took one sapling and planted it at the Mahēshǒuluó temple.
He also took one sapling and planted it in the center of Zhīdìyē mountain.
He also took one sapling and planted it in the village of Lóuxīnà.
He also took one sapling and planted it in the village of Wǎngluó.
The remaining four seeds on the tree
ripened and fell in succession, producing thirty-two saplings.
All were taken and planted in the Yóuxún garden.
Thus, stūpas multiplied and filled the Lion Country.
Because of the Bodhi tree, the country was peaceful and secure, without disasters or suffering.
At that time, the wife of Ānóuluó, together with a thousand women,
went to Sēngqiémìduō to become bhikṣuṇīs.
After receiving ordination, they successively attained arhatship.
The king's nephew Ābiāochā, together with five hundred people, left home and successively attained arhatship.
Again, one day, the king went with Mǎshéntuó to pay respects to the Bodhi tree.
Arriving at the place of the Iron Hall,
the people offered flowers to the king.
The king offered the flowers to his teacher Mǎshéntuó to make offerings at the Iron Hall; as the flowers fell to the ground, it shook.
Seeing the ground shake, the king immediately asked the great virtuous one,
"Why did the ground suddenly shake?"
He replied,
"Great King, in the future, the assembly of monks will recite the precepts in this hall.
Therefore, the earth manifests this auspicious sign."
They proceeded in succession to the place of the āmra trees.
Someone offered the king āmra seeds, complete with fragrance and flavor.
The king offered them to Mǎshéntuó. Mǎshéntuó,
after eating the pit, said to the king,
"You may plant this pit."
The king then planted it.
When he sprinkled water on the ground,
the earth shook.
The king asked,
"Why did the ground shake?"
He replied,
"Because in the future, this will be a place where the assembly of monks will gather, thus manifesting this auspicious sign."
The king then scattered flowers, paid respects, and departed.
Arriving at the place of Zhīdìyē,
someone offered the king campaka flowers.
The king offered them to Mǎshéntuó.
The ground shook.
The king asked,
"Why did the ground shake?"
He replied,
"Because in the future, a great stūpa of the Buddha will be erected here, thus manifesting this auspicious sign."
The king said,
"I shall now erect a stūpa."
Mǎshéntuó replied,
"It is not necessary for the king to erect it.
The king has many constructions.
In the future, there will be a king's descendant,
named Mùchājiāmóní Āpóyē,
who will erect a great stūpa."
The king asked, "Is he my descendant? Will I obtain the merit?"
He replied,
"You will not obtain it."
The king took a stone pillar twenty feet high,
and engraved on the stone pillar a record:
"My descendant named Mùchājiāmóní Āpóyē
will in the future erect a great stūpa here."
In the past, in King Āyù's country, there was a householder
who made offerings to twenty thousand bhikṣus.
He invited them for a long period of one year, and his fame reached the king.
The king summoned him for an audience.
"I have heard that your family is greatly wealthy. What do you possess?"
He replied,
"In truth, I possess nothing."
The king did not believe him.
He detained the householder and sent someone to inspect his home.
They saw that his gate had seven layers of houses and mansions.
The halls and buildings were all made of the seven treasures.
They surpassed the king's palace.
The women also surpassed.
But there was no grain, cloth, or money.
They returned and reported to the king.
The king's mind gradually understood.
The householder laughed.
The king asked,
"Why do you laugh?"
He replied,
"The king did not believe me."
The householder pointed with his finger to the eastern sky, and immediately the seven treasures rained down.
Pointing to the south, treasures also rained down without limit.
The king then sent him back.
And the monks' vihāra was not far from the palace.
The king then prepared his carriage and went to the vihāra.
Seeing the assembly of bhikṣus, he bowed respectfully and asked the senior monk,
"What past merit did that householder have, that treasures naturally come when he thinks of them?"
The senior bhikṣu entered samādhi and saw the thoughts of beings within four hundred yojanas.
He saw that in the past, during the time of Buddha Vipaśyin, there were four people who together built a stūpa and temple.
Among them, one person was diligent and earnest in his intention.
After the stūpa and temple were completed, he took gold, silver, the seven treasures, and various fine flowers, mixed them together,
and ascended to the top three levels of the stūpa.
He scattered them to the four directions,
vowing that his future enjoyment of blessings would never cease.
The one who now obtains natural treasures is this person."
Hearing this, the king greatly cultivated merit.
The Buddha traveled for a long time through various countries.
The elder Sudatta, longing and yearning with thirst,
said to the Buddha,
"I wish you would leave a small object so that I may always make offerings."
The Buddha gave him hair and nails.
He requested permission to erect a stūpa.
The Buddha then permitted it.
In Śrāvastī, he constructed brackets and arches,
adorned with painted decorations.
The Buddha arrived in the country of Yuèzhī.
To the west, he subdued a female rākṣasī.
At that time, he stayed overnight in a stone cave.
To this day, the Buddha's shadow remains there.
If someone looks inside,
they cannot see it.
But if they step outside the opening, the luminous form appears just like the Buddha.
Sometimes, he flew to the mountain of the hermit Lìbátuó in the country of Jìbīn.
He remained in the empty sky,
and descended to this hermit.
The hermit said,
"I delight in dwelling here.
I wish the Buddha would give me his hair and nails to build a stūpa for offerings."
The stūpa still exists today at the foot of this mountain.
There is a Líyuè Temple.
Líyuè should be pronounced as Lìbátuó.
The Buddha's right tooth and right parietal bone
are in the stūpa erected in Tuṣita Heaven on the Lion Island.
They obtained two parietal bones and a tooth,
which are now in the Śakra Palace.
When the Buddha traveled to Bōluónài,
five hundred young children formed a group
and played together by the riverbank, piling sand to make stūpas.
Each said,
"My stūpa is very good; you should learn from me and make one like it."
Although these five hundred children had good intentions, their past-life blessings were meager.
Heaven sent a great rainstorm, and the river suddenly swelled.
All five hundred children drowned at once.
Their parents wailed and searched for their corpses,
but could not find them.
The Buddha said,
"Do not harbor resentment over past-life karma that was not sought.
These children's past-life karma was thus destined.
Now they are born in Tuṣita Heaven."
The Buddha emitted light,
enabling their parents to see their children from afar.
Immediately, they all came to scatter flowers as offerings.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent!
Because they built sand stūpas, they were able to be born in heaven and see Maitreya Buddha."
The five hundred heavenly sons each addressed their parents, saying, "Do not grieve any longer.
Just strive diligently.
They circumambulated the Buddha three times, paid homage, and flew away.
When the Buddha was in the country of Luóyuèzhī,
he sent an arhat named Xū Màn
to take the Buddha's hair and nails to the southern mountains of Jìbīn to build a stūpa.
A temple with five hundred arhats constantly resided there.
Morning and evening, they burned incense, circumambulated the stūpa, and paid homage.
Five hundred monkeys saw the monks making offerings,
went to the deep ravine, carried mud and stones, and erected a Buddha stūpa.
They set up a wooden pole as a flagstaff and tied a worn banner to it.
Morning and evening, they paid homage.
A sudden flood surged and swept them all away to their deaths.
They were born in Tuṣita Heaven.
Using their divine eyes, they saw their own past and present.
Each took flowers, incense, and music, descended to their former corpses, and circumambulated them seven times.
The heavenly beings from afar saw them scattering flowers and playing music around the monkey corpses.
There were five hundred brahmins who studied heterodox views.
They asked the heavenly beings,
"Why do you humble yourselves to make offerings here?"
They replied,
"These are our former bodies.
In the past, while in the world, we imitated the śramaṇas and playfully built stūpas and temples.
Because of this, we were born in heaven, and now we repay this kindness.
You, with your heterodox views, toil diligently for a hundred kalpas without gaining anything.
It would be better to go together to Qíshéjué Mountain to pay homage and serve, for the blessings are limitless."
Then the brahmins all rejoiced
and went together to the Buddha's place, prostrated themselves with five limbs touching the ground, and scattered flowers as offerings.
In the eastern Illumination Garden of the Tuṣita Heaven city, there is a stūpa of the Buddha's hair.
In the southern Rough Garden, there is a stūpa of the Buddha's nails.
In the western Joy Garden, there is a stūpa of the Buddha's alms bowl.
In the northern Chariot Garden, there is a stūpa of the Buddha's tooth.
In the country of Jiāwéiluówèi, considered the center of heaven and earth, a stūpa was erected at the birthplace.
In the country of Mójiétí, at the site of the Victorious Path,
under the Auspicious Tree, a stūpa was erected for the attainment of enlightenment.
In the country of Bōluónài, at the dwelling place of sages in the Deer Park, a stūpa was erected for turning the Dharma wheel.
In the country of Jūshīnà, at the place of the strongmen, between the twin śāla trees in the Beautiful Grove, a stūpa was erected for parinirvāṇa.
In the past, there was a prince
named Mahāsattva.
He went out to roam the forest wilderness,
and saw a tigress who had newly given birth to seven cubs, starving for many days and on the verge of death.
He immediately removed his clothes, pierced his neck with bamboo, threw himself down from a height, and lay before the tigress.
The tigress licked his blood and gradually ate him entirely.
The great king and the palace heard that the prince had not returned,
and immediately sent people to search for him.
The messengers returned and reported in detail.
The king ordered the collection of his relics,
and a seven-jeweled stūpa was erected.
There is a seven-jeweled stūpa
that emerged from the ground.
The Buddha rose from his seat,
and paid homage to the stūpa.
At that time, the deity of the bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment asked,
"Tathāgata, you are the most supreme and revered; why do you pay homage to this stūpa?"
The Buddha replied,
"In the past, when I practiced the bodhisattva path, there were whole-body relics in this stūpa.
Because of this body, I attained Buddhahood early.
He had Ānanda open the stūpa to take the relics and show them to the great assembly.
Ānanda opened the stūpa and the seven-jeweled casket.
The relics were red and white.
The Buddha said,
"These are the results of cultivating precepts, meditation, and wisdom.
They are extremely difficult to obtain and are the supreme field of merit."
The great assembly rejoiced, reverently paid homage, and bowed their heads.
In a past age, there was King Jinmei.
After Kāśyapa Tathāgata attained parinirvāṇa,
this king used gold and silver to build a stūpa,
measuring a thousand yojanas in length and width, and one yojana in height.
He piled silver and gold as a moat, which remains in the ground to this day.
At that time, the Tathāgata revealed this stūpa to the fourfold assembly.
Kāśyapa's whole-body relics were solemn and intact as before.
After Kāśyapa Buddha's parinirvāṇa and cremation,
a seven-jeweled stūpa was erected with the Buddha's relics.
They reverently made offerings.
After passing through several generations,
the stūpa decayed and deteriorated.
No one repaired it.
There was a righteous community of ninety-three thousand people.
At that time, King Píngshā was their leader.
He addressed the crowd, saying,
"Each of you should encourage yourselves.
Together, let us create blessings and virtue.
The Buddha's era is difficult to encounter.
Human birth is difficult to obtain.
Even if one is born human,
they may fall into borderlands,
or be born into households of heterodox views.
What are we doing?
Greedy for this worldly pleasure?
It would be better to willingly repair the decaying stūpas and temples."
They all repaired them together.
They also made a vow together:
"If there is any merit,
may we not fall into the three wretched destinies or the eight difficult circumstances.
May we be born together among humans and devas,
see Śākyamuni,
and at his first assembly where he preaches the Dharma,
all attain liberation."
With the king as their leader,
when their lives ended,
they were born in Tuṣita Heaven.
After passing through several generations,
when Śākyamuni appeared in the world,
the ninety-three thousand people
were born in the country of Mójiétí, with Píngshā becoming king.
In a past age,
there was a wheel-turning king
named Dézhǔ.
Once, in a single day,
he erected five hundred stūpas,
each five hundred yojanas high.
At that time before the Buddha,
there was a seven-jeweled stupa,
five hundred yojanas high,
two hundred and fifty yojanas wide and deep,
which sprang up from the earth
and remained suspended in the air,
adorned with
all kinds of precious objects.
It had five thousand railings, millions of niches and chambers,
countless banners and streamers,
serving as ornaments,
with precious necklaces hanging down
and ten thousand million jeweled bells suspended
from it.
From all four sides emerged the fragrance of tamālapatra candana incense,
pervading the whole world.
All its banners and canopies
were made of the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, carnelian, pearls, and amber—combined together.
It rose up to the palace of the Four Heavenly Kings
and the Heaven of the Thirty-Three Gods,
where mandārava flowers rained down
as offerings to the jeweled stupa.
Down to the eight kinds of beings,
all offered flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, and music
to the jeweled stupa.
At that time, from within the stupa
came a great voice praising,
"Excellent, Śākyamuni Buddha!
With impartial wisdom,
you teach the Dharma to bodhisattvas."
The fourfold assembly, hearing the voice from the stupa,
all attained Dharma joy
and marveled at this unprecedented event.
Within this jeweled stupa
is the complete body of a Tathāgata.
In the past, in the east, beyond measureless thousands of ten thousands of asaṃkhyeya worlds,
there was a land named Bǎojìng,
and a Buddha named Duōbǎo.
When that Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path,
he made a great vow:
"If, after I attain Buddhahood and enter parinirvāṇa,
in any land in the ten directions
where the Lotus Sūtra is preached,
for the sake of hearing the sūtra, my stupa
will spring forth and appear before them to bear witness."
If there is one who preaches the Lotus Sūtra,
my whole-body relics will be within the stupa,
praising, 'Excellent!'"
The bodhisattva Mahāpratibhāna
addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One,
we wish to see this Buddha's body."
The Buddha said,
"Buddha Duōbǎo has a profound and weighty vow:
if my jeweled stupa,
for the sake of hearing the Lotus Sūtra, appears before the Buddhas,
and if one wishes to show my body to the fourfold assembly,
then that Buddha's emanated Buddhas
in the ten directions
must all gather in one place,
and only then will my body appear."
Mahāpratibhāna said,
"We also wish to see the World-Honored One's emanated Buddhas."
The Buddha emitted a white hair-mark light,
and the Buddhas in the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below
each addressed their assemblies of bodhisattvas, saying,
"Good sons,
I should now go to the Sahā world, to where Śākyamuni Buddha is,
and also make offerings to the jeweled stupa of Tathāgata Duōbǎo."
At that time, the Sahā world instantly became purified,
with lapis lazuli for ground,
adorned with jeweled trees.
Golden cords
marked off the eight paths.
There were no villages, hamlets, cities, towns, great seas, rivers, mountains, forests, or thickets; great precious incense was burned,
and the gods and humans were transferred to other lands.
At that time, each Buddha brought one great bodhisattva as an attendant
and came to the Sahā world.
Each arrived beneath a jeweled tree.
Beneath each tree was a lion seat
five hundred yojanas high.
The Buddhas from the ten directions all gathered
and sat in the eight directions.
The Buddhas wished to open the jeweled stupa together.
