They then rose from their seats and stood in the empty space.
The entire fourfold assembly stood up, joined their palms, and with one mind gazed at the Buddha.
Thereupon, Śākyamuni Buddha
used his right finger to open the door of the seven-jeweled stupa.
A great sound issued forth,
like the unlocking of a bolt.
The entire assembly
saw Tathāgata Duōbǎo sitting on a lion seat inside the jeweled stupa,
his whole body intact as if in meditation.
They also heard him say,
"Excellent, excellent!
Śākyamuni Buddha,
you have well preached this Lotus Sūtra.
I have come here for the sake of hearing this sūtra."
At that time, the fourfold assembly and others saw a Buddha who had entered parinirvāṇa measureless thousands of ten thousands of kalpas ago
speak such words,
and they marveled at this unprecedented event.
They gathered heavenly jeweled flowers and scattered them over Buddha Duōbǎo and Śākyamuni Buddha.
At that time, Buddha Duōbǎo,
inside the jeweled stupa,
shared half his seat with Śākyamuni Buddha.
Then Śākyamuni Buddha sat on that half-seat.
With his supernatural power, he lifted the great assembly,
and all were in empty space.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly,
"Reflect on the merits you have practiced in ancient times.
The bodies you have relinquished and received are not one, not two.
I will now speak of this.
The earth element of this great land is eighty-four trillion yojanas thick.
Below it is wind, eighty-four trillion yojanas thick.
Below the wind is water, eighty-four trillion yojanas thick.
Below the water is fire, eighty-four trillion yojanas thick.
Below the fire is sand, eighty-four trillion yojanas thick.
Below the sand is vajra, eighty-four trillion yojanas thick.
The whole-body relics and fragmented-body relics of all Buddhas are within the vajra realm.
The vajra realm is again eighty-four trillion yojanas thick,
named Miàoxiāng.
The Buddha's name is Bùzhù,
fully endowed with the ten epithets,
and is now teaching the Dharma.
In the past, there was a śramaṇa whose family was very wealthy.
He built a stupa and temple,
using sandalwood for pillars and the seven treasures for the spire.
Before it was completed, five hundred śramaṇas came from afar.
In that country, there were five hundred virtuous men.
Each gave robes and bedding.
The people of the country said to the temple master,
'The visitors will leave soon.
We will send them off first.
You, Ācārya, who dwell here permanently, should distribute it yourself.' The temple master
thought,
'My accumulated merit is as great as Mount Sumeru, immeasurable.
Yet the people of the country do not assist me.
I will do this for all, whether lowly or noble, near or far.'
He then set fire to the temple and stupa.
Afterward, he fell into hell and the animal realm for ninety kalpas each.
Later, he became a great fish
in the sea,
four hundred thousand yojanas long,
with eyes like the sun and moon,
teeth twenty thousand yojanas long,
pure white like snow mountains,
a tongue forty thousand yojanas wide,
bright red like a fiery mountain,
and a mouth fifty thousand yojanas wide.
At that time, there were five hundred men
who entered the sea to seek treasures.
They were precisely those who had given robes to the five hundred śramaṇas in a previous life.
Due to karmic retribution from past lives, the fish opened its mouth to drink water.
At that moment, the boat was carried by the current very swiftly.
All were greatly terrified
and together called out, 'Namo Buddha!'
Hearing their voices, the fish closed its mouth to listen.
The water stopped flowing.
Hearing the sound of sūtra recitation on the boat,
the fish shed tears.
It reflected, 'I have not heard this sound for a very long time.'
Thereupon, it ceased eating and after seven days died in the sea.
Its corpse floated ashore, and its spirit was reborn in a Dharma family.
Upon falling to the ground, it could speak
and immediately knew its past lives.
At the age of eight,
it attained arhatship.
It then went to the seashore and saw its former body.
The accumulated bones were like a mountain; gazing inside the skull, it could not finish in seven days.
Due to burning the temple and stupa, for one hundred and eighty kalpas it remained in the evil paths.
The fourfold assembly was negligent in seeking and listening to the Dharma.
Śakra Devānām Indra invited the Buddha
to ascend to the Heaven of the Thirty-Three Gods
to teach the Dharma to his mother for three months during the summer retreat.
The Tathāgata, wishing to generate people's longing and reverence,
did not bring attendants and left without saying anything.
At that time, King Prasenajit of Śrāvastī and King Udayana of Kauśāmbī went to Ānanda
and asked where the Buddha was.
Ānanda replied,
'I also do not know.'
The two kings, longing to see the Tathāgata, then fell physically ill.
King Udayana then ordered all skilled craftsmen in his country
to make an image of the Tathāgata from gośīrṣa candana sandalwood,
five feet tall. King Udayana asked the Buddha,
'After the Tathāgata's parinirvāṇa, if one makes a Buddha image,
and reverently serves it, what merit will one obtain?'
The Buddha said,
'If one makes a Buddha image,
in every lifetime one will be born with a handsome body and appearance; after death, one will be born in the seventh Brahma heaven.
Furthermore, one will surpass all heavens in excellence, incomparably upright.
One will always be born into noble and wealthy families,
with exceptional strength,
loved and respected by all,
and immeasurable wealth.
Or one will be born into royal, ducal, or virtuous families in Jambudvīpa.
Or one will be born as a wheel-turning king, flying through the heavens and earth.
Or one will be born into a family that follows filial piety and virtue.
After death, one will not fall into the three wretched paths.'
The Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
King Udayana, overwhelmed with longing and admiration,
cast a golden statue.
Hearing that the Buddha was about to descend, he loaded it on an elephant and gazed upward, awaiting the World-Honored One as if the Buddha were alive.
Then, from afar, he saw the Buddha's feet treading the empty sky, stepping upon twin lotus flowers, emitting a great radiant light.
The Buddha addressed the statue, saying:
"In the future, you shall perform great Buddha-work.
After my parinirvāṇa, I entrust my disciples to you.
If there are beings who create images and make various offerings,
these people in future lives will certainly attain the pure samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Take my words and proclaim them widely to the disciples.
After my parinirvāṇa, create Buddha images.
[Let them be] complete with the marks and minor characteristics.
Also make immeasurable transformation Buddhas,
and paint the Buddha's footprints with subtle
colors and place crystal beads on the spot of the ūrṇā.
This will cause people who see them to give rise to joy in their hearts.
It can eradicate the karmic offenses of birth and death accumulated over hundreds of millions of nayutas of Gaṅgā-sands kalpas."
At that time, King Prasenajit heard that King Udayana had made a Tathāgata image and was making offerings to it.
He also summoned skilled craftsmen to cast a Tathāgata image from purple-refined gold,
over five feet tall.
At that time, within Jambudvīpa, there began to be two images.
The Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven
to preach the Dharma for his mother,
for ninety days.
King Prasenajit longed to see the Buddha.
He carved a sandalwood image of the Tathāgata from ox-head sandalwood and placed it on the Buddha's seat.
Later, when the Buddha returned and entered the vihāra, the image came out to welcome the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Return to your seat."
And said:
"After my parinirvāṇa, you shall serve as the model for the fourfold assembly."
The image then returned to its seat.
This image was the very first of all images,
the one later people followed as a model.
The Buddha then moved to reside in a small vihāra on the two sides,
in a different place from the image,
twenty paces away.
The Jetavana Vihāra originally had seven stories.
Various countries vied in making offerings without cease.
A mouse carried a lamp wick and burned a banner and canopy,
which then spread to the vihāra, completely consuming all seven stories.
The kings and people of the various countries were greatly grieved and distressed,
thinking the sandalwood image had been burned.
Four or five days later, when they opened the door of the small vihāra on the east side,
they suddenly saw the original image.
The multitude was greatly delighted.
Together they repaired the vihāra,
managing to build two stories and moved the image back to its original place.
King Śubhakara entered the mountains to hunt.
He saw some brāhmaṇas
naked and exposed,
some eating leaves,
some inhaling wind and subsisting on breath,
some lying on thorns,
inflicting various hardships upon themselves to seek immortality.
Śubhakara asked:
"How can there be no accomplishment?"
A brāhmaṇa replied:
"There is a herd of deer that often gathers together.
When I see them, my mind is stirred and I cannot control myself."
The king said:
"Even while practicing austerities and emaciated, you still have lustful desires.
The Śākya ascetics,
who eat delicious food,
sit on fine seats,
wear clothes according to the season,
and perfume themselves with incense and flowers—
how could they be without it?"
Aśoka heard this and became worried and distressed.
"I have only one younger brother.
He has suddenly given rise to wrong views.
I fear he will be forever lost and confused; it is right to eliminate the evil."
He ordered female entertainers to be provided to amuse him together.
The king personally addressed his brother:
"Why do you take your elder brother's female entertainers and concubines,
indulging yourself in pleasure?"
He then wanted to kill him.
A minister remonstrated:
"Your Majesty has only one younger brother and also few heirs.
I beg you to grant him seven days,
and he will comply with your command."
The king then fell silent.
He said to the ministers:
"Allow my brother to wear my robes and crown, enter my palace, and amuse himself with music and entertainment."
When the seven days were up,
the king sent a messenger to ask:
"Is your will free and are you happy?"
Śubhakara said:
"I neither see nor hear; what happiness is there?"
The king said:
"Experiencing things as I do, how can you say you neither hear nor see?"
The younger brother said:
"A man condemned to death, though his life is not yet ended, is no different from dead.
How could he have any attachment to the five desires?"
The king said:
"Now, one body is beset by ten thousand worries.
One body should perish.
Amidst desires, there is no joy.
The Way speaks of ascetics who worry about the three periods of time.
When one body dies and decays, it receives another body.
For hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, body after body suffers pain,
immeasurable afflictions and troubles.
Even if reborn as a human,
one serves others,
poor and lacking in food and clothing.
Reflecting on this bitterness, they therefore leave home to practice the Way,
seeking the essential of the unconditioned for transcending the world.
If they are not diligent, they will again undergo the suffering of countless kalpas."
Śubhakara then had his mind opened and his understanding resolved.
He addressed the king:
"Now, hearing your instruction, I have gained awakening.
Birth, old age, sickness, and death are truly detestable and distressing.
Sorrow, worry, suffering, and affliction revolve endlessly.
I only wish Your Majesty would permit me to practice the Way."
The king said:
"You should know the time is right."
The younger brother then left home, upheld the precepts, diligently practiced day and night, and attained the path of an arhat. The Aśokarāja Sūtra says:
King Aśoka heard that his younger brother had attained the Way,
deeply rejoiced in his heart, bowed his head in reverence, and requested to provide long-term support.
The younger brother vowed to rely on forests and wilderness to sustain his remaining life.
Aśoka then had spirits construct a mountain inside the city, several tens of zhang high,
cutting off external people and things, severing all comings and goings.
Only then did he comply with the king's request.
He pooled his clothing and resources to create one stone image,
sixteen feet tall, using the mountain as a niche chamber.
There was a nāga king who requested the Buddha to permanently reside in his place.
"If you do not stay, I will give rise to an evil mind and have no means to attain the Way."
The Brahmā kings also earnestly urged and requested,
wishing [the Buddha] for the sake of all beings, not to dwell alone here.
The nāga offered a seven-jeweled palace to the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said:
"It is not needed; just give me the rākṣasa stone cave."
The Buddha gathered his supernatural powers and alone entered the stone chamber.
He spread his sitting mat and sat in full lotus posture.
At that time, the rākṣasī and the nāga,
for the four great disciples and Ānanda,
also created five stone chambers.
The Buddha accepted the invitations of the king of Nāgasenahrada City and various countries.
Everywhere they saw the Buddha, empty thrones of flowers were filled with transformation Buddhas.
The nāga king rejoiced and made a great vow:
"May I in future lives attain Buddhahood like this."
The Buddha accepted the king's invitation for seven days.
He gathered his supernatural powers,
emerged from the stone cave,
and traveled to various places with the bhikṣus.
The nāga followed along.
Later, when the Buddha returned to the country, [the nāga] wept tears like rain,
and said:
"I beg you, do not abandon me."
The World-Honored One comforted him, saying:
"I shall sit in your cave for fifteen hundred years."
At that time, the various nāga kings joined their palms and requested the Buddha to enter the cave.
The Buddha sat in the cave and performed eighteen transformations.
He leaped into the stone,
like a bright mirror.
Being inside the stone, his reflection appeared outside.
From afar it could be seen,
but up close there was nothing.
The devas in hundreds of thousands made offerings to the Buddha's shadow.
The shadow also preached the Dharma.
The stone cave was eighteen feet high,
twenty-four paces deep,
and the stone was pure white in color.
The Buddha said:
I entrust the true Dharma to humans and devas.
My Dharma will remain unshaken for a thousand years.
He told Śakra and the Four Heavenly Kings:
After my nirvāṇa, each of you shall protect and uphold the true Dharma in your respective realms.
After a thousand years have passed,
there will be fierce winds, torrential rains, and many disasters and calamities.
People will suffer famine, and all things will be worn away and destroyed.
Food and drink will lose their flavor, and precious treasures will sink into oblivion.
In the west, there will be a king named Bōluópó.
In the north, a king named Yépónà.
In the south, a king named Shìjiā.
In the east, a king named Dōushāluó.
These four kings will all have many followers.
They will kill bhikṣus and destroy stūpas and monasteries.
Chaos will spread throughout the four directions.
At that time, the bhikṣus will gather in the central region.
In the kingdom of Kuśāmbī, there will be a king named Móyīntuóluóxīnuó.
He will have a son.
The child’s hands will appear as if smeared with blood.
His body will resemble armor.
He will possess great courage and strength.
On the same day, five hundred ministers will also have sons.
All with blood-stained hands and armored bodies.
At that time, blood will rain down in the kingdom of Kuśāmbī for a day.
The king, seeing these evil omens, will be greatly terrified and ask an astrologer about them.
The astrologer replied:
The son born to the king now
will rule Jambudvīpa and kill many people.
He will be named Nándāng.
As he gradually grows older,
the four evil kings
will come from the four directions.
The king will be greatly worried and afraid.
A deva then told him:
Great king, simply establish Nándāng as king.
He will be able to subdue the four great evil kings.
Following the deva’s words, he abdicated the throne to his son.
Taking a precious pearl from his topknot,
he placed it on his son’s head.
He assembled the five hundred ministers.
With fragrant water, he performed the abhiṣeka.
He ordered them to go forth and wage war.
The sons of the ministers, clad in armor,
followed the king on the campaign.
They fought the four evil kings
and annihilated them completely.
He ruled over Jambudvīpa,
governing from the kingdom of Kuśāmbī.
The Buddha told the Four Heavenly Kings:
In the country of Pāṭaliputra,
there will be a brāhmaṇa
named Āqínídáduō.
He will be well-versed in the Vedas and śāstras.
This brāhmaṇa will take a wife.
His wife will become pregnant.
He then wished to engage in debates,
so he asked an astrologer.
The astrologer replied:
The child in the womb
will thoroughly master all scriptures and śāstras.
The child born will clearly understand all scriptures and śāstras, as well as various medical methods.
He will teach five hundred disciples.
In my Dharma, he will renounce and study the path.
He will master the Tripiṭaka.
He will be skilled in expounding the Dharma.
With eloquent and skillful speech, he will attract many followers.
In this city of Pāṭaliputra,
there will be a great merchant
named Xūtuónà.
His wife will become pregnant.
She will then become honest, gentle, and serene in all her faculties.
The merchant then asked an astrologer.
The astrologer replied:
The child in the womb is extremely virtuous.
When the month is full, she will give birth to a son named Xiūluótuó.
As he gradually grows older, he will renounce and study the path in my Dharma.
Diligently practicing with vigor, he will attain the fruit of arhatship.
However, he will be of limited learning, few desires, content,
and with little knowledge of his former dwelling.
He will reside on Mount Jiàntuómóluó.
He will constantly expound the Dharma to King Nándāng.
When King Nándāng saw his father pass away,
he embraced his father’s corpse with both hands, wailing and crying in grief and sorrow.
At that time, the Tripiṭaka master expounded the Dharma to the king.
The king’s grief immediately ceased.
He developed great reverence and faith in the Buddha’s Dharma.
And he proclaimed aloud:
From now on, I will provide for the bhikṣus without fear, allowing them to dwell in comfort and joy.
He then asked the bhikṣus:
How many years did the previous four evil kings spend destroying the Buddha’s Dharma?
The bhikṣus replied:
Twelve years.
The king thought to himself:
I will roar like a lion.
For twelve years,
I will provide the fivefold assembly with abundant offerings of all kinds.
On the day of offering,
the heavens will send down fragrant, moistening rain.
Throughout Jambudvīpa, all crops will flourish.
People from all directions will bring offerings
to the kingdom of Kuśāmbī to make offerings to the saṅgha.
At that time, the bhikṣus were not diligent in the threefold practice.
They passed their days in idle talk.
Greedy for offerings, they adorned themselves well, wearing fine garments, departing from the renunciant’s way, though appearing as bhikṣus.
They were great thieves within the Dharma.
They toppled the banner of the true Dharma.
They raised the flag of Māra.
They extinguished the torch of the true Dharma.
They kindled the fire of afflictions.
They dried up the ocean of the true Dharma.
They destroyed the bridge of the true Dharma.
They sank the ship of the true Dharma.
They felled the tree of the true Dharma.
At that time, devas, nāgas, and other spirits developed ill will toward these bhikṣus.
Disgusted, they distanced themselves.
They no longer protected them.
Instead, they proclaimed in unison:
After seven days, the Buddha’s Dharma will be completely extinguished.
They wept and wailed in sorrow.
They said to one another:
On the uposatha day, the bhikṣus will quarrel.
The Tathāgata’s true Dharma will then perish.
The upāsakas, hearing the words of the devas,
went together to the assembly to admonish the quarreling bhikṣus.
On the fifteenth day, the uposatha was to be observed.
At that time, the arhat Xiūluótuó from Mount Jiàntuómóluó
surveyed Jambudvīpa,
wondering where today
there might be a saṅgha to attend for the uposatha.
He then went to Kuśāmbī.
At that time, the saṅgha assembly numbered a hundred thousand.
Only this arhat Xiūluótuó came.
There was also a Tripiṭaka master named Dìzǐ.
This was the Tathāgata’s final great assembly gathering.
Then the karmadāna distributed the śalākā counting sticks.
He addressed the Tripiṭaka master:
The saṅgha has assembled.
Now, please recite the Prātimokṣa.
The senior monk then replied:
The Tathāgata’s disciples from Jambudvīpa have all gathered here, numbering a hundred thousand.
In such an assembly, I am the foremost.
I have mastered the Tripiṭaka but have not studied the Vinaya.
How much less have the others studied it.
For whom, then, should I recite the Vinaya?
At that time, the arhat Xiūluótuó stood before the senior monk.
With palms joined, he addressed the senior monk:
Simply recite the Prātimokṣa.
As when the Buddha was present,
the great bhikṣus such as Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana studied the Dharma—I have now studied it all.
Although a thousand years have passed since the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa,
the precepts he established, I have fully upheld.
The senior monk Dìzǐ, hearing Bhikṣu Xiūluótuó declare that he had fully upheld the precepts established by the Tathāgata,
arose with an intolerant mind.
He had a disciple named Ānjiātuó.
Extremely enraged,
he rose from his seat and insulted that saint.
You are a junior bhikṣu, foolish and ignorant, yet you insult my teacher.
He then took a sharp knife and killed that saint.
At that time, there was a demon named Dàtímùfǎ.
He thought to himself:
In the world, there remains only this one arhat,
and he has been killed by an evil bhikṣu disciple.
Seizing a vajra pestle, he struck his head, killing him.
At that time, the disciples of the arhat,
seeing their teacher killed, were filled with rage and could not bear it.
They then killed the Tripiṭaka master.
At that time, devas and humans wept in sorrow.
Alas, how bitter!
The Tathāgata’s true Dharma is now completely extinguished.
Immediately, the great earth shook in six ways.
Countless beings cried out and wept.
Each dispersed.
At that time, the king of Kuśāmbī,
hearing that the bhikṣus had killed the arhat and the Tripiṭaka Dharma master,
felt deep distress and regret.
Followers of heterodox views competed to destroy stūpas and temples,
and to harm bhikṣus.
From then on, the Buddha’s Dharma suddenly vanished completely. The Buddha told Ānanda:
After my nirvāṇa,
when the Dharma is about to perish,
in the evil age of the five turbidities, the māra-path will flourish.
Māra-śramaṇas will corrupt and disrupt my path.
They will wear secular garments, adorned with fine robes of five colors.
They will drink alcohol, eat roasted meat, kill living beings, and crave flavors.
They will have no compassion, but instead harbor mutual hatred and jealousy.
At that time, there will be bodhisattvas who diligently cultivate virtue.
All will respect and treat them well, and they will be revered by people.
They will teach with equality.
They will pity the poor and remember the aged.
They will rescue and nurture the destitute.
Constantly using sūtras and images,
they will lead people to serve and make offerings.
They will perform various meritorious deeds.
Their nature will be gentle and kind.
They will not harm others.
They will sacrifice themselves to aid beings.
They will not cherish themselves.
They will be patient, benevolent, and harmonious.
If there are such people.
All the demonic bhikkhus were jealous of him.
They slandered and spread evil, expelled and drove him away, not allowing him to stay.
Afterwards, they themselves no longer cultivated virtue.
The temples became empty and desolate, no longer repaired.
They gradually fell into ruin.
They only coveted wealth and possessions.
Accumulating without dispersing.
They did not perform meritorious deeds.
They traded in slaves, plowed fields, and planted crops.
They burned forests and harmed living beings.
They had no compassion.
Male slaves became bhikkhus.
Female slaves became bhikkhunīs.
They had no virtue.
They were lustful and corrupt, causing chaos.
Men and women were not kept separate.
This caused the Way to become shallow and faint.
All of this was due to such people.
Some, to avoid government officials,
relied on my teachings,
seeking to become bhikkhus.
They did not uphold the precepts.
On the full and new moon days,
they nominally gave lectures on the precepts.
They were weary and lazy,
unwilling to listen.
They summarized parts from the beginning and end,
unwilling to explain fully.
They did not recite the scriptures.
Even if there were those who read,
they did not recognize the characters or sentences.
They forcefully claimed to be correct without consulting those who understood.
Arrogant and seeking fame, they boasted and made predictions,
considering it honorable and noble, expecting others to make offerings to them.
After the demonic bhikkhus passed away,
their spirits would fall into the Avīci Hell.
Among the five heinous crimes, they would experience rebirth as hungry ghosts and animals without exception.
After kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, their sins would be exhausted,
and they would be reborn in borderlands without the Three Jewels.
When the Dharma was about to perish,
women would be diligent and constantly perform meritorious deeds.
Men would be lazy and slow, not following the Dharma's teachings.
They would regard śramaṇas as dung and dirt.
They would have no faith.
The Dharma wheel would be extinguished, and the devas would weep.
Floods and droughts would be irregular, and the five grains would not ripen.
Epidemics would spread, and many would die.
The people would suffer hardships, and government officials would exploit them.
They would not cultivate the right path, all thinking of enjoying chaos.
Evil people would increase, and the good would be very few.
Days and months would become shorter, and human lifespans would shorten.
At forty, hair would turn white, and lifespan would be cut to sixty.
Men's lifespans would be short.
Women's lifespans would be long.
Seventy, eighty, ninety, or even a hundred years.
Great floods would suddenly arise, arriving unexpectedly.
People of the world would not believe it, saying it was constant.
Beings of all kinds, without distinction of noble or lowly,
would drown and float.
Drifting, fish and turtles would devour them. Bodhisattva bhikkhus would be driven away by demons and not participate in assemblies.
Bodhisattvas would enter mountains, places of merit, living in tranquility and contentment, finding joy.
Their lifespans would be extended, protected by devas.
When the Moonlight Bodhisattva appeared in the world, they would encounter him.
Together they would revive my teachings for fifty-two years.
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra,
the Pratyutpanna Samādhi,
would first vanish and transform away.
The twelve divisions of scriptures would subsequently vanish and transform, completely disappearing, no longer appearing, and no written words would be seen.
The robes of śramaṇas would naturally turn white.
After the Holy King departed, my Dharma would be completely extinguished.
Just as an oil lamp, when about to go out, its light flares up brightly,
and then it extinguishes.
When my Dharma ends, it will also be like the lamp extinguishing.
After this, it will be difficult to maintain order.
After such a long time, Maitreya will descend into the world and become a Buddha.
The world will be at peace, and poisonous influences will be eliminated.
Rain will be harmonious and timely, and the five grains will flourish.
Trees will grow tall, and people will be eighty feet tall.
All will live for eighty-four thousand years.
The number of beings who attain liberation will be
incalculable.
In the past, there was a king named King Yùmó.
He had four sons by concubines.
The first was named Zhàomù,
the second Cōngmù,
the third Tiáofú Xiàng,
and the fourth Nílóu, all intelligent, divine, martial, and greatly virtuous.
The chief queen had a son named Chángshēng.
He was stubborn, inferior, and ugly, despised by everyone.
The queen said to the king,
"The four sons are divine and outstanding, but my son is stubborn and inferior.
If they succeed to the throne, they will surely compete and seize power.
If the king expels the four sons, my heart will be at peace."
The king said,
"The four sons are benevolent and filial, and have committed no fault.
How can I expel them?"
The queen said again,
"My heart is weary, and it concerns the state as well.
The four sons are heroic and martial, and the people each long for their rule.
If factions are established, once they compete, they will surely destroy each other.
The great kingdom's fortune will then belong to others.
I hope the king considers this."
The king said,
"Your words are correct."
He then summoned the four sons.
And commanded them,
"You have offended me.
I cannot bear to have you killed.
Each of you must leave the kingdom quickly.
Restrain yourselves and plan for your livelihood.
Do not linger and bring regret upon yourselves later."
The four sons received the command.
They immediately prepared.
Their mother and their sisters,
all requested to go with them.
At that time, many warriors and all the people
gladly followed them.
The king permitted all of them.
They reached the edge of the Snowy Mountains and settled in the Zhíshù Forest.
Their mother arranged marriages for them, and they settled themselves.
Within a few years, those who submitted to their virtue came like a market crowd.
Thus they became greatly prosperous.
Yù became a powerful kingdom.
Several years later, their father longed to see them.
He sent messengers to summon them.
They all declined and did not return.
The king then sighed three times,
"My sons are capable,
able to establish themselves."
Because of this, he named the clan Shì, hence there is the Shì clan.
Their ancestor was King Nílóu.
He gave birth to Wūtóuluó.
Their great-grandfather Wūtóuluó became the king of Jiāwéiluówèi Kingdom.
He gave birth to Qútóuluó.
Their great-great-grandfather King Qútóuluó
gave birth to Shīxiūluó. Their grandfather King Shīxiūluó
gave birth to four sons, the eldest being Jìngfàn.
King Śuddhodana fell ill.
His limbs felt as if they were coming apart.
His breathing was like a rushing stream.
All treatments were of no avail.
His two younger brothers, the various princes, ministers, and others said:
"Great King, you have never done evil.
You have cultivated virtue tirelessly.
You have nurtured and cared for all, ensuring none lacked peace.
Why then are you distressed and troubled?"
The King said:
"I regret not seeing Siddhārtha,
and Nanda, Ānanda, Rāhula, and the others.
To dispel my clinging desires."
Tears fell like rain.
At that time, the Buddha was in Rājagṛha,
fifty yojanas away.
The King was growing increasingly weak.
I fear we will not make it in time.
The Buddha knew his father's heart.
He immediately commanded Nanda, Rāhula, and the others.
Then, using his spiritual power, he soared into the empty sky.
Suddenly appearing in Kapilavastu,
he emitted a great radiant light.
The people of the country saw it from afar.
Raising their voices, they wept, saying:
"If the Great King passes away,
surely this Śākya kingdom will be severed and lost."
The people within the city
turned towards the Buddha, weeping sorrowfully, writhing and striking themselves.
The Buddha said:
"Impermanence and separation have existed since ancient times until now.
Birth and death are suffering; only the Path is true."
The Buddha's light shone brilliantly, illuminating everything inside and out.
It shone upon the King's body.
The King said:
"What light is this?
As soon as it touches my body, my suffering and illness are relieved.
Is it not my Siddhārtha?" Those who had come from outside reported:
"The Buddha, Ānanda, Rāhula, and others have come through the sky."
The King's heart leapt with joy, and unconsciously he sat up.
He said: "I only wish for the Tathāgata to touch my body with his hand.
My body feels as if being pressed for oil; the pain is unbearable.
Upon seeing the World-Honored One, my suffering will surely cease."
The Buddha told Nanda:
"Observe the King's original form: upright, majestic, his fame spread far and wide.
Now, gravely ill, emaciated and weak, he is almost unrecognizable.
Where now are his appearance, strength, and fame?"
The King, with single-minded devotion, joined his palms.
"I only wish you not to grieve.
Your virtue is pure and flawless." The Buddha placed his hand on the King's forehead and said:
"The King is a person of pure moral conduct.
The defilements of the mind have already been abandoned.
You should only rejoice, not be sorrowful or troubled.
You should deeply contemplate,
reflect on the meaning of the various sūtras and Dharma.
From that which is not firm and secure,
attain a firm and secure resolve.
Plant roots of goodness.
The King should rejoice."
The great King Śuddhodana made a vow:
"The Buddha, along with Nanda, Ānanda, and Rāhula,
my four sons who have destroyed Māra's net, have caused the King to rejoice."
The Buddha preached the Jātaka of King Mahāprabhāsa.
The King attained the fruit of Anāgāmin.
He took the Buddha's hand and placed it upon his heart.
The Buddha preached the Dharma further.
He attained the fruit of Arhat.
His life ended, his breath ceased.
The Śākyas wailed and lamented.
They bathed his body with fragrant water.
Wrapped him in karpāsa cotton and silk, and placed him in a coffin.
Adorned with the seven treasures, with pearl nets hanging around it.
They lifted the coffin and placed the body on a lion throne, scattering flowers and burning incense.
The Buddha and Nanda stood at the head,
Ānanda and Rāhula at the feet.
Nanda and the others addressed the Buddha:
"Recalling his nurturing and care,
we beg to carry the coffin ourselves."
For the sake of future unfilial beings who do not repay the care of their parents,
the Buddha himself wished to carry it.
The great thousand-world system trembled.
All mountains swayed like boats on waves.
The six heavens of the Desire Realm, with their countless retinues, all came to attend the funeral.
The Four Heavenly Kings led ghosts and spirits, hundreds of millions in number, all joining in mourning.
The kings said to the Buddha:
"We are disciples of the Buddha.
Having heard the Dharma from the Buddha,
we have attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
We should carry it."
The Buddha permitted the Four Heavenly Kings to carry it.
They all transformed their bodies to appear human.
With their hands, they lifted the coffin
and placed it upon their shoulders.
The Buddha's majestic light was like ten thousand suns.
Holding an incense burner,
he led the procession at the very front.
They arrived at the burial ground.
A thousand Arhats from Vulture Peak arrived through the sky.
They bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet, wishing for his command on what to do.
The Buddha said:
"Go to the great sea isle and fetch sandalwood from the ox-head tree and various fragrant woods."
In the snap of a finger, they obtained the fragrant firewood.
The great assembly gathered and used it to burn the coffin.
Seeing the fire rise,
the crowd wept even more sorrowfully.
The Buddha said:
"Suffering, emptiness, impermanence—
they are like illusions, the moon in water, an image in a mirror."
When the body was completely burned,
they extinguished it with milk.
They collected the bones and placed them in a vajra casket.
Then together they erected a stūpa.
The great assembly inquired where his spirit had been reborn.
The Buddha said:
"He has been born in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens."
The Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
Entering the Garden of Joy,
beneath the Pārijāta tree,
he observed the three-month rainy season retreat.
He emitted light from his pores, illuminating the great thousand-world system.
The various heavenly sons did not know the reason.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Go to my mother and tell her I am here.
I wish my mother to condescend to come."
Queen Māyā went herself.
Māyā's breast milk flowed spontaneously.
"If this is Siddhārtha,
let the milk enter his mouth."
Two streams of milk issued forth,
flowing from afar into the Buddha's mouth.
Māyā was filled with joy.
The entire earth quaked.
Wonderful flowers and fruits ripened out of season.
She then said to Mañjuśrī: "For mother and son to come together, such joy and bliss has never been known until now."
Together they went to where the Buddha was.
Seeing his mother from afar, the Buddha said:
"The body's experiences are mingled with suffering and pleasure.
One should cultivate Nirvāṇa to seek eternal liberation."
Māyā, with single-minded devotion, prostrated herself with her five limbs on the ground, concentrating her correct mindfulness; her defilements subsided and were subdued.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to her, and she immediately remembered her past lives.
She attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
She then addressed the Buddha:
"The prison of birth and death is now liberated."
The great assembly all said:
"May all living beings attain liberation."
Widely transforming devas and humans, he brought great benefit.
As the three months were nearing their end,
he told Kumāra:
"You may now descend to Jambudvīpa.
The Tathāgata will soon enter Parinirvāṇa."
The assembly was distressed and troubled.
"Had we not known sooner that he would soon enter Nirvāṇa!
The eye of the world is about to be extinguished.
How bitter this is!"
Śakra had ghosts and spirits create a triple jeweled staircase.
Māyā shed tears,
and thus they parted.
His feet trod the jeweled steps.
Brahmā held a canopy.
The Four Heavenly Kings attended, standing to his left and right.
The fourfold great assembly sang hymns and offered praises.
Devas performed music that filled the empty sky.
Scattering flowers and burning incense, they descended to Jambudvīpa.
The Buddha returned to the country of Jiāwéiluówèi.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī requested the Buddha to allow her to renounce the household life, pleading sorrowfully three times.
The Buddha did not permit it.
She withdrew and stood outside the gate.
Wearing soiled and tattered robes,
barefoot,
she sobbed and wept in grief.
Ānanda asked,
"Why are you weeping?"
She replied,
"Because women are not allowed to renounce the household life; I am grieving for myself."
Ānanda stopped her and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I have heard from the Buddha
that women, through diligent effort, can attain the four fruits.
Now Mahāprajāpatī
sincerely wishes and delights in this." The Buddha said,
"Do not allow
women to enter my Dharma and discipline as śramaṇās.
For example, if a household has many women and few men, the household will certainly decline.
If women renounce the household life, the pure and holy life will not endure long.
It is like weeds mixed among the grain, harming and ruining the good crops.
Women entering the Dharma are also like this."
Ānanda said,
"Mahāprajāpatī has shown much goodwill.
When the Buddha was first born, she herself nurtured and raised you until adulthood."
The Buddha said,
"She has shown much faith and goodwill, and has been kind to me.
I, too, have shown much kindness to Mahāprajāpatī.
Through me, she has taken refuge in the Three Jewels, has no doubts about the Four Truths, has established the five faculties, and faithfully upholds the five precepts.
Even if someone were to offer their body in供养, it would not surpass this.
If women wish to become śramaṇās,
they must not transgress the eight rules of respect.
They must study them for their entire lives.
It is like preventing water from leaking by diligently maintaining the dikes and ponds.
Do not allow any leakage.
If they can do this,
they may enter the Dharma and discipline."
Ānanda fully reported this to Mahāprajāpatī.
Mahāprajāpatī rejoiced and was then able to renounce the household life.
She became a great bhikṣuṇī,
upholding the Dharma and discipline,
and eventually attained arhatship.
Later, she and the elder bhikṣuṇīs
went to where Ānanda was and said,
"We have long cultivated the holy life
and have already realized the truth.
Why should we pay respects to young and junior bhikṣus?"
Ānanda reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"Enough, enough, do not speak of this.
If women had not renounced the household life,
all the sages of heterodox paths and different schools
would make the four kinds of offerings.
They would spread their hair on the ground and humbly request to tread upon it.
My true Dharma would endure for a thousand years.
But because women have been admitted, it will now last only five hundred years."
Hearing this, Mahāprajāpatī rejoiced and upheld it. Residing in the Jetavana Monastery, she was about to pass away.
She said,
"I cannot bear to see the world without the Tathāgata and the arhats passing into nirvāṇa.
I will first extinguish my spirit in the original non-existence."
The Buddha, knowing her mind,
told Ānanda.
Ānanda's body wilted, his heart was blocked, and his mind was without awareness.
The Buddha said,
"Do you think she is taking away the five parts of the Dharma, the four foundations of mindfulness, and the eightfold noble path?"
Ānanda replied,
"No.
I only think that seven days after the Buddha's birth, the queen mother passed away,
and she was a compassionate mother who showed kindness to the World-Honored One."
The Buddha said,
"You speak of the heavy kindness of nursing; this favor is difficult to repay.
But I have already shown her the way,
to take refuge in the Three Jewels,
to hear the truths of suffering, its origin, cessation, and the path,
so that her wisdom eye becomes clear,
all bonds of existence are exhausted,
and she attains non-attachment.
This kindness surpasses Mount Sumeru."
Mahāprajāpatī, together with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, went to where the Buddha was.
She fully expressed her intention,
touched the Buddha's feet with her hands, and said,
"From now on, I will no longer see the Perfectly Enlightened One."
She circumambulated the Buddha three times and returned to the monastery.
Together with the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, she performed eighteen transformations,
illuminating the heavens above, and simultaneously entered nirvāṇa.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"Go into the city to the householder Yéyóu's place and inform him that the Buddha's mother and the five hundred elders have passed into nirvāṇa."
Ānanda entered the city at dawn and arrived at the householder's gate.
He fully related the matter.
Upon hearing it, the listeners wailed in grief, fell to the ground, and said with tears,
"From now on, we will no longer behold their supernatural powers. How painful this is!"
Ānanda said,
"The Buddha says that although heaven and earth endure for a long time, they must eventually come to an end.
The three realms are impermanent,
like an illusion or a dream.
To seek immortality in life,
to hope that meetings will never part—
in the end, this cannot be attained."
The householder's mind was liberated. He then went to the Brahmin householders
and told them,
"The Buddha advises you, virtuous ones, to prepare five hundred funeral items
for the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs."
The Brahmin householders prepared and delivered them to the monastery.
The gate of the monastery was closed; they opened it and entered.
They intended to go to the lecture hall.
A novice nun
said,
"My teacher is in meditation.
Be careful not to disturb her."
They replied,
"She is dead, not in meditation."
The novice nun fell to the ground, fainted,
and after a long time, revived.
She wailed and cried out, saying,
"Who will teach and guide us now?
The holy instruction has ceased!"
The householders said to the novice nun,
"Although affection and love meet,
they must eventually part.
You should only resolve to strive and attain arhatship."
After the cremation, they brought the relics to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"Face east, join your palms, and kneel on your right knee, saying,
'Those with straight faith, straight action, the three spiritual faculties, the six higher knowledges, and whose path and spiritual power are complete, all come.'"
The five hundred bhikṣuṇīs have now all well departed.
It is fitting to hold a Dharma assembly."
It was so in all four directions.
From each of the four directions, two hundred and fifty arhats flew in.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"Fill a bowl with the relics and place it in my hands."
Ānanda handed it to the Buddha, who received it with both hands.
He addressed the bhikṣus and householders, saying,
"This was originally a defiled body,
foolish, fierce, and violent,
envious, scheming,
ruining the path and destroying virtue.
Yet they were able to uproot fierceness and foolishness, to act as true men,
attaining the path of arhatship,
transferring their spirits to the original non-existence.
How strong they were!
You should together erect a shrine and make offerings accordingly."
All said,
"So be it." Then the four assemblies, gods, humans, nāgas, and spirits
each erected shrines and made various offerings.
Prince Siddhārtha had two wives.
One was named Qúpíyé.
The other was named Yéshūtuóluó.
Qúpíyé, being a maiden of precious virtue, never became pregnant.
On the night that the Bodhisattva renounced the world,
Yéshūtuóluó herself became aware that she was with child.
The Bodhisattva practiced austerities for six years.
Yéshūtuóluó did not give birth for six years.
The Śākyas questioned her,
saying, "How could this be, since the Bodhisattva has left home?"
Yéshūtuóluó replied,
"I am guilty of no other fault.
The child I carry is truly the Bodhisattva's own flesh and blood."
The Śākyas said,
"Why has it been so long without birth?"
She answered,
"That is not for me to know."
The Śākyas gathered to deliberate.
Hearing that the king intended to punish her according to the law,
Qúpíyé addressed the king,
"I have always lived together with Yéshūtuóluó.
I can testify on her behalf and know she is innocent.
Wait until her child is born.
See if he resembles his father or not.
What harm is there in delaying punishment?"
The king then set the matter aside.
When the Bodhisattva's austerities were complete and he first attained Buddhahood that very night,
Rāhula was born.
The king saw that he resembled his father,
and his affection and fondness made him forget his sorrow.
He said to his ministers,
"Although my son has gone, now I have gained his child, which is no different from having my son."
Yéshūtuóluó's ill repute had become widespread, and she wished to clear her name.
The Buddha returned to Kapilavastu
to guide the Śākya youths.
At that time, King Śuddhodana and Yéshūtuóluó
often invited the Buddha to the palace for meals.
On one occasion, Yéshūtuóluó prepared a hundred-flavored delight-ball and had Rāhula present it.
The Buddha, using his supernatural power, transformed the five hundred Arhats,
making them all appear in the form of the Buddha, indistinguishable from one another.
Rāhula was just seven years old.
Holding the delight-ball, he went straight before the Buddha and offered it to the World-Honored One.
At that moment, the Buddha withdrew his supernatural power, and the monks returned to their original forms.
Their bowls were all empty.
Only the Buddha's bowl was filled with the delight-ball.
Yéshūtuóluó asked,
"What was the cause in the past that made me carry the child for six years?"
The Buddha answered,
"In a past life, Rāhula
was once a king.
At that time, a sage with the five supernatural powers came to the king's realm.
He said to the king,
'Your Majesty governs thieves according to the law.
I request that you punish my crime.
I once stole Your Majesty's water
and used Your Majesty's tooth-cleaning twig—
this was taking what was not given.'
The king said,
'When I first ascended the throne, I decreed that water and tooth-cleaning twigs
be provided to all.'
The sage said,
'Although Your Majesty has granted them, my mind remains troubled.
I beg you to punish me now, so that I may avoid future offenses.'
The king said,
'If you insist, please wait a moment while I go into the palace.'
He entered the palace and did not emerge for six days.
The sage grew hungry and thirsty.
The sage said,
'I fear the king is using this very method to punish me.'
When the king came out, he apologized but forgot to let him go.
Because of this, for five hundred lifetimes, he was always in the womb for six years."
The Buddha told Mùlián,
"Go to the city of Jiāpíluó.
Inquire after my father, mother, my uncle, and my aunt.
Console Ráhula's mother.
Instruct her to sever her affection.
Release Ráhula to become a śrāmaṇera.
The joy of mother and son's affection lasts but a moment.
Upon death, falling into hell, they will not know each other.
When Ráhula attains the Way, he will return to ferry his mother across.
Forever ending birth and death, as I have now."
Mùlián arrived in the kingdom.
He fully conveyed the Buddha's intent.
Yéshūtuóluó, hearing that the Buddha had sent an envoy,
took Ráhula and ascended a high tower.
She ordered the guards to securely close the gates and make them all firm.
Mùlián flew up.
Yéshūtuóluó, having no alternative, paid her respects.
She asked,
"Is the World-Honored One well?
For what purpose has he sent the Venerable One here?"
Mùlián said, "The crown prince Ráhula is now nine years old.
He should be allowed to leave home to cultivate and study the holy path."
He fully conveyed the Buddha's intent.
She replied,
"When Śākya Tathāgata was crown prince, he took me as his wife.
I served the crown prince as if serving a heavenly deity.
Before three years were fulfilled, he abandoned the pleasures of the five desires.
Soaring over the palace walls,
he fled to the royal fields.
He promised that upon attaining the Way,
he vowed to return.
Having attained the Way, he returned to the kingdom,
yet did not see his kin at all.
He forgot and disregarded past kindness and old ties,
worse than a stranger.
He left me to guard my solitude and embrace poverty.
Now he seeks to take my son to join his retinue.
What cruelty is this!
The crown prince, having attained the Way, claims to be compassionate.
What compassion is there in separating mother and son?
Return and tell the World-Honored One what I have said."
Mùlián took his leave and departed.
He returned to King Jìngfàn and fully reported the above matters.
The king, hearing these words, then told Lady Póshépótí,
"My son Siddhārtha
has sent for Ráhula to cultivate and study the holy Dharma.
His mother, being a woman, is foolish, entangled, and attached with love, unable to let go.
You should go and advise her, to make her mind awaken."
The lady advised her repeatedly, again and again.
Yéshūtuóluó still would not listen.
She said to the lady,
"When I was at home,
the kings of eight kingdoms
competed to seek me.
My parents did not consent.
Because the crown prince's talents surpassed others,
therefore my parents gave me to him.
If the crown prince did not wish to remain in the world,
why did he diligently and earnestly seek me?
A man takes a wife
precisely for affection and harmony,
for descendants to continue the lineage.
This is the proper custom of the world.
The crown prince has already left,
and now he seeks Ráhula.
This forever cuts off the kingdom's heir.
What principle is this?"
The lady, hearing this,
remained silent, saying nothing.
The Buddha sent a transformed being,
who spoke from the sky, saying,
"Do you remember the ancient vow or not?
When I was a bodhisattva,
I bought five stems of flowers from you with five hundred silver coins to offer to Dìngguāng Buddha.
You asked to entrust two flowers, begging that in every life hereafter you would always be my wife.
I said to you,
'As a bodhisattva, I practice all giving.'
You then made a vow,
saying that in every life hereafter, your kingdom, city, wife, children, even your own body,
would be given to me as I wish.
Why do you now cling to Ráhula?"
Yéshūtuóluó suddenly awakened, as if recalling yesterday's event.
Her attachment to her son gradually subsided.
She summoned Mùlián, apologized repeatedly,
took Ráhula's hand, and earnestly entrusted him.
Weeping tears, she bid farewell.
Ráhula addressed his mother,
"I will pay my respects to the World-Honored One.
I wish Mother not to grieve.
I will soon return to see you."
King Jìngfàn told the noble clans,
"Each of you send one son
to accompany my grandson."
Immediately, fifty men
followed him to where the Buddha was.
They bowed their heads to the ground in reverence.
The Buddha had Ānanda shave Ráhula's head and those of the fifty young nobles.
He had them all leave home.
He appointed Śāriputra as their upādhyāya.
Mahā-Maudgalyāyana served as ācārya, conferring upon them the ten precepts.
The Buddha, for the fifty śrāmaṇeras,
spoke of the karmic retribution from past lives, such as that of Shàntíluó, and they all became greatly distressed.
They all said to the Buddha,
"Our upādhyāya possesses great wisdom and virtue, receiving the highest offerings.
We children are foolish and without virtue.
To consume people's good offerings,
and suffer in later lives like Shàntíluó—
therefore we are truly filled with worry.
We beseech the Buddha, in his compassion, to allow us to renounce the path.
Hoping to avoid sin and blame."
The Buddha said,
"Suppose two men are starving.
Suddenly they encounter a king's feast with fine food and drink.
Greedily eating to excess,
one man has wisdom.
He takes medicine to induce vomiting,
regulates and moderates himself,
thereby avoiding calamity and preserving his life span.
The other man lacks wisdom.
He kills living beings to make sacrificial offerings, seeking to save his life.
The undigested food causes severe pain,
his heart aches, and he dies.
He is reborn in hell.
Fearing retribution, he returns home.
This is the unwise man.
You have good causes from the past.
Having encountered me,
taking the medicine to relieve suffering,
you will certainly not die."
Ráhula, hearing this,
felt his heart open and his mind liberated.
Later, when the Buddha returned to the palace,
people doubted Gòuyí.
"The crown prince abandoned the kingdom for twelve years.
How then did she bear a child?"
The Buddha addressed his father the king, saying,
"Gòuyí has guarded her purity and chastity; her integrity is flawless.
I transformed the assembly of bhikṣus to all be like the Buddha.
When Ráhula was seven years old, he was asked, 'Who is your father?'
Ráhula immediately stepped forward, approached the Buddha, and paid his respects.
With his mother's seal-ring,
he presented it to the World-Honored One."
In the past, Luóyún,
before attaining the Way,
was crude and rough in nature, with little sincerity or trustworthiness in his words.
The Buddha instructed Luóyún:
"Go and dwell in the Xiántí Monastery.
Guard your speech, restrain your mind, and diligently cultivate the scriptures and precepts."
Luóyún, receiving the teaching, bowed and departed.
He stayed for ninety days,
ashamed and remorseful,
ceaseless day and night.
The Buddha went to see him.
Luóyún was joyful.
He came forward, bowed at the Buddha's feet, prepared a rope-bed, and arranged the sitting mat.
The Buddha sat on the rope-bed
and said to Luóyún:
"Take the washbasin, fetch water, and wash my feet."
After washing the feet was finished,
the Buddha said to Luóyún:
"Can this water be used for drinking, eating, washing, or rinsing?"
Luóyún replied:
"This water was originally pure and clean,
but now it has washed feet and received dust and grime.
It cannot be used again."
The Buddha said to Luóyún:
"You are also like this.
Although you are my son and the grandson of a king,
having renounced worldly glory and wealth to become a śramaṇa,
you do not think of diligence, restraining your mind, or guarding your speech.
The defilements of the three poisons fill your breast.
This too
is like water that cannot be used again."
The Buddha further said to Luóyún:
"Although the washbasin is empty, can it be used to hold food or drink?"
He replied: "It cannot."
"Why is that? Because it bears the name 'washbasin,'
having once received impurities."
The Buddha said to Luóyún:
"You are also like this.
Although you are a śramaṇa,
your speech lacks sincerity and trustworthiness,
your nature is stubborn and rigid,
you do not strive for diligence,
and you have borne an evil reputation.
Just like the washbasin,
you are not fit to hold food."
The Buddha used his toe
to kick over the washbasin.
Immediately it spun around, jumping and falling several times before stopping.
The Buddha said to Luóyún:
"Would you regret this washbasin being broken?"
Luóyún replied to the Buddha:
"It is a vessel for washing feet, a thing of little value.
Although in my mind I might regret it, I am not deeply concerned."
The Buddha said to Luóyún:
"You are also like this.
Although you are a śramaṇa,
you do not restrain your body and speech, uttering coarse words and evil talk that often wound others.
You are not accepted by the multitude, nor cherished by the wise.
When your body dies and your spirit departs, you will revolve through the three wretched paths,
being born and dying on your own, suffering immeasurably.
The Buddhas, sages, and worthies do not cherish you either,
just as you said you do not regret the washbasin."
Luóyún, hearing this,
was ashamed, fearful, and trembling.
The Buddha told Luóyún:
"Listen as I tell you a parable.
In the past, a king had a great elephant,
fierce and strong, capable of battle.
The king raised an army to attack a rebellious country.
He armored the elephant and sent it into battle to enforce strict discipline.
The elephant only hid its trunk, afraid to use it in combat.
The elephant-keeper was delighted, knowing the elephant protected its body.
Why was this?
Because the elephant's trunk is soft and fragile; if struck by an arrow, it would die.
One should guard one's mouth just so.
The great elephant protected its trunk and did not fight."
Luóyún, hearing the Buddha's earnest and compassionate teaching,
was deeply moved and spurred himself on.
He attained the path of an arhat.
The Buddha's younger brother, Sūntuóluó Nántuó,
was fifteen feet four inches tall.
The Buddha and Ānán entered the city of Jiāwéiluójié to beg for food.
Nántuó saw from a high tower,
descended, and bowed, saying:
"The Tathāgata should become a wheel-turning sage king.
Why do you humble yourself, holding a bowl to beg for food?"
He took the bowl and filled it with fine food.
The Buddha then returned to the Nyagrodha Garden and told the attendants:
"When Nántuó comes out, do not take it; let him bring it himself."
Nántuó delivered it to the Buddha.
His wife came out and urged him to wait until he returned to eat.
He handed over the bowl, urging the Buddha to quickly accept it.
The Buddha said:
"Since you have come here,
you should now leave home."
Using his spiritual power, he confined him in a quiet room.
After a long time, it was his turn to be on duty.
Nántuó happily thought:
"I can take advantage of this free time to escape and return home."
At that time, Nántuó performed all his assigned tasks without fail.
Heavenly spirits followed him.
When he drew water, it would overflow and spill by itself.
The ground he cleaned would sprout grass and soil again.
When he closed doors,
they would open again.
Nántuó thought:
"Even if something is lost, my family has enough to compensate."
He removed his three monastic robes,
put on other clothes,
secretly followed a small path,
avoiding the Buddha to return home.
He had not gone far
when he encountered the Tathāgata.
He ran to a large tree,
wanting to hide himself.
The tree moved behind him.
The Buddha, using his spiritual power,
uprooted the tree and suspended it in the air.
Nántuó went to the tree's roots.
The Buddha said:
"Why have you come here?"
He remained silent, ashamed.
The Buddha asked him repeatedly:
"Where do you wish to go?"
He replied:
"To return home and see my wife."
The Buddha said:
"When people study the Way,
their minds cling to greed and desire, heedless of the calamity of burning their bodies in future lives.
I will now take you to tour the heavens.
Focus your mind and do not harbor fear."
The Buddha lifted him up to the heavens.
They saw a palace
adorned with the seven treasures, attended by jade maidens beyond count.
Only there was no master.
Nántuó asked the Buddha:
"What heavenly palace is this,
with no master?"
The Buddha said:
"You may ask yourself."
Nántuó asked,
and the heavenly maidens replied:
"The Buddha's brother Nántuó,
if he upholds the precepts, will be reborn here."
He reported this fully to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Quickly cultivate pure conduct, and you will surely be reborn here soon."
Again using his spiritual power,
he took him to the hells.
Passing by the surface of the Iron Ring Mountains,
they saw a blind monkey.
The Buddha asked Nántuó:
"How does your wife Sūntuólì compare to this monkey?"
He replied:
"Sūntuólì
is supremely beautiful among women.
How can she be compared to this?"
The Buddha said:
"Compared to the heavenly maidens, she is like this a hundred million million times over."
They went everywhere in the hells,
seeing all kinds of suffering and pain.
There was a cauldron of fire,
surrounded by hell guards,
the boiling water fierce, the flames blazing.
But no sinner was seen.
Nántuó said to the Buddha:
"Why is there no sinner here alone?"
The Buddha said:
"Ask yourself."
The hell guard replied:
"The prince of sweet dew, Nántuó,
heavy with lustful desires,
relying on his nobility and looking down on others,
will be reborn here after death."
Nántuó turned pale.
He urgently asked the World-Honored One
to leave the hells.
The Buddha expounded the subtle and wonderful Dharma,
enabling him to reach the place of enlightenment.
King Báifàn had two sons.
One was named Ānán.
His height was one zhang, five chi, and three cun.
The other was named Tiáodá.
His height was one zhang, five chi, and four cun. King Báijìng went to the Buddha's place.
Seeing that Kāshè's followers were ugly in appearance,
he immediately gathered his clan and said:
"The sage Āyí prophesied that
if the Buddha did not leave home, he would become a sage king ruling over the four directions.
His left and right attendants would be extremely handsome.
But now his disciples are utterly lacking in dignified appearance.
If one wishes to follow the path, one's demeanor and bearing should be sufficient.
Allow them to complete the number of monks, bringing glory to the World-Honored One."
All said:
"Excellent."
Tiáodá said: "I am a prince's descendant; now I abandon worldly glory, leave home, and follow the path. My proper attire and ornaments are the finest in the world.
My elephants, horses, and carriages are worth ten thousand gold.
On that day, I set out in grandeur.
Onlookers filled the roads, and caps and headscarves fell to the ground.
The horse ridden by Qúhéli placed its four feet on the ground and made a bird's cry.
A diviner interpreted this,
saying the others would attain the Way,
but these two were inauspicious.
They all went to the Buddha's place,
seeking to become śramaṇas.
Their stubbornness was subdued, and none were unwilling to accept them.
King Húfàn had two sons.
One was named Mónán.
The other was named Ānàlǜ.
Ānàlǜ was beloved by his mother.
Mónán said:
"Many of the Śākyas have taken to the path.
Our family alone has not.
One manages worldly affairs,
the other seeks to leave home."
Ānàlǜ, finding household matters troublesome and trivial,
asked his mother to let him leave home.
His mother said:
"If Bátí leaves, then I will allow you."
He pleaded incessantly, and both were permitted.
Bátí requested to delay for seven years to enjoy the five desires.
Ānàlǜ said:
"Human life is impermanent and hard to preserve."
He then asked for one year, and even down to seven days.
After seven days, eight Śākya sons,
with Yōubōlí as the ninth,
each adorned a precious elephant
and rode out of the city.
They removed their clothes and gave up their elephants and horses,
handing them to Yōubōlí, saying:
"You rely on us for your livelihood.
Now that we are leaving home, we give these clothes and elephants to you as capital."
Yōubōlí then hung the clothes on a tree,
thinking:
"Whoever takes them, give them."
They all went to the Buddha's place and also sought to leave home.
They begged the Buddha to ordain Yōubōlí first,
to remove their arrogance.
Next was Ānàlǜ.
King Gānlùfàn had two sons.
One was named Típó.
The other was named Bátí.
Bátí was cherished by his mother.
He asked his mother to let him leave home.
His mother said:
"If Ānàlǜ leaves home, I will also allow you."
Later, it indeed happened so.
They went to the Buddha's place, seeking to leave home.
"Our parents have already permitted us; we wish for your salvation."
At that time, Bátí was alone under a tree in a graveyard, contemplating.
In the middle of the night, he exclaimed loudly: "Very joyful, very joyful!"
A nearby bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha called Bátí and asked: "What joy?"
Bátí said:
"When I was at home,
inside and outside, I always had to guard myself with knives and staffs, yet still felt fear.
Now, alone in the graveyard, not a hair on my body stands on end; liberation is very joyful."
The Buddha said: "Excellent."
King Prasenajit had newly ascended to the throne.
He then thought to himself:
"I should first take a Śākya woman."
He immediately told a minister:
"Take my name to Kapilavastu
to request marriage with one of their women."
The five hundred Śākyas gathered in one place were all greatly enraged.
"We are a great clan;
why should we form a marriage alliance with the son of a slave girl?"
Some said he should be given one,
others said he should not.
At that time, Mahānāman said to the Śākyas:
"King Prasenajit is a violent and cruel man;
he might destroy our kingdom."
At that time, Mahānāman had a daughter born of a slave girl,
with a beautiful and dignified appearance.
He bathed her, dressed her in fine clothes,
placed her in a carriage adorned with feathers and jewels,
and personally escorted her,
presenting her to King Prasenajit.
He then said to the king:
"This is my daughter;
you may marry her."
The king was delighted
and immediately made this woman his chief consort.
After a short while, she became pregnant
and gave birth to a son,
of unparalleled beauty, extraordinary in the world.
The king assembled fortune-tellers to name the child.
The fortune-tellers said:
"When seeking a consort, the Śākyas deliberated together;
some gave her the name Bìliúlí.
Now let the crown prince be named Bìliúlí." When he was nearly eight years old,
the king told him:
"You may go to Kapilavastu to learn various archery skills."
Riding a great elephant with many attendants,
he went to Mahānāman's residence.
Five hundred youths were gathered there to study together.
A new lecture hall had been built,
resembling a heavenly palace.
"We should first invite the Buddha and his monastic community to make offerings here and receive immeasurable blessings."
Seats were spread out,
banners and canopies were hung,
fragrant water was sprinkled on the ground,
and various precious incenses were burned.
Crown Prince Bìliúlí went to the lecture hall
and ascended the lion throne.
When the Śākyas saw him, they called him "son of a slave girl"
and dragged him outside, throwing him to the ground.
Crown Prince Bìliúlí turned and said to the ascetic Brahmin:
"These Śākyas have greatly insulted me.
When I later ascend the throne, you must remind me of this matter."
When his father the king passed away,
the crown prince succeeded him.
The ascetic reminded the king,
and the king ordered his ministers
to assemble the fourfold army
to campaign against the Śākyas.
Arriving at Kapilavastu,
the World-Honored One went to meet them and sat under a withered tree,
in full lotus posture.
Seeing him from afar, the crown prince dismounted and paid his respects,
asking:
"There are better trees; why sit under this one?"
The Buddha said:
"The shade of one's own clan is better than that of outsiders."
At that time, the king said:
"Today, the World-Honored One is here for his clan; I should not campaign against them."
The Brahmin insisted,
and the king again raised his army.
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha:
"Bìliúlí King is going to attack the Śākyas.
I wish to move his fourfold army and cast it to another realm.
Or pull it out into empty space,
or move it into the ocean,
or place it between the Iron Ring Mountains,
or move the people to another great land.
Or cover the city with an iron cage."
The Buddha said:
"You have wisdom and virtue,
but you cannot ultimately protect them.
The people of the Śākya country
are among the seven things
that cannot be avoided:
birth, old age, sickness, death, sin, blessings, and causes and conditions.
Though one may wish to avoid them, one ultimately cannot escape.
How can one cover up their past karma?"
Maudgalyāyana remained unsettled.
He took four or five thousand of his acquaintances
and placed them all in his alms bowl,
lifting it into the sky among the stars.
The Śākyas also assembled a fourfold army
and marched one yojana out
to meet Bìliúlí King.
Within one yojana,
the Śākyas saw Bìliúlí King from afar.
Some pierced their ears or topknots;
bowstrings, weapons, banners, and standards were all destroyed,
but no one was harmed.
At that time, Bìliúlí King was greatly terrified
and said to his ministers:
"Look at these arrows—where do they come from?
If they intended to harm us, we would surely all be dead."
He ordered a return to Śrāvastī.
The ascetic Brahmin said:
"Great King, do not fear.
The Śākyas uphold precepts; they do not even harm insects,
let alone people.
Now we should advance."
The king followed his advice.
The Śākyas indeed retreated back into the city.
Bìliúlí King said:
"Quickly open the city gates;
if not, I will kill you all."
In the city was a youth, only fifteen years old,
named Shémó.
He climbed the city wall and fought alone,
injuring many.
The enemy army scattered
and hid in earthen holes.
At that time, the Śākyas
said to the youth:
"You disgrace our clan.
Who does not know how to fight?
We Śākyas cultivate goodness;
we do not kill even insects or ants,
let alone human lives.
Each of us could face ten thousand enemies
and easily destroy an army,
but killing people
leads to falling into hell after death.
Even if reborn as humans, their lifespans would be short.
You must leave now; do not stay."
Shémó then left the country.
Bìliúlí King's army returned to the gate.
The demon Pāpīyas took the form of a Śākya
and called for the gates to be opened quickly.
The Śākyas opened the gates.
Bìliúlí King said:
"The Śākyas are numerous;
bury them all up to their feet
and have wild elephants trample them to death."
He selected five hundred Śākya women
and brought them before the king.
At that time, Mahānāman made a request of the king,
and the king granted it.
Mahānāman said:
"I will now submerge myself in water; however long I remain submerged, allow
the Śākyas to escape as they wish.
When I emerge, you may kill those who remain."
The king said, "Excellent."
Mahānāman entered the water,
tied his hair to a tree root, and ended his life.
The Śākyas in the city
rushed out through the four gates.
The king said to his ministers:
"Mahānāman, my grandfather, has not yet emerged."
They entered the water
and brought him out—he was already dead.
The king felt remorse:
"My maternal grandfather
has now died because of his love for his clan.
If I had known earlier,
I would never have attacked."
Bìliúlí killed ninety-nine million nine hundred ninety thousand people.
Their blood flowed into a river
encircling Kapilavastu.
After the army left,
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha:
"By the Buddha's spiritual power,
I saved four or five thousand people."
The Buddha said:
"Go and look at them."
Maudgalyāyana lowered his alms bowl,
and the people were all already dead.
Going to the Nyagrodha Garden,
he said to the five hundred Śākya women:
"Do not grieve or worry.
I am your husband."
Grabbing one Śākya woman, he said:
"Why should I now have relations with a slave girl?"
The king then cut off her hands and feet
and threw her into a deep pit.
The five hundred Śākya women all cursed the king:
"Who would give our bodies to have relations with a slave's son?"
The king ordered the five hundred Śākya women to be punished as before.
Returning to Śrāvastī,
Crown Prince Jeta was in the inner palace playing music.
Hearing the sound, the king turned his carriage and went to him.
Jeta came out to meet him and said:
"Welcome, Great King.
Please stay a while."
Bìliúlí King said:
"Have you not heard that I was fighting the Śākyas?
You were enjoying music and did not come to help."
Jeta replied:
"I heard, but I am incapable of killing living beings."
Bìliúlí King struck Jeta with his own hand.
The Buddha saw Jeta reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.
At that time, the five hundred Śākya women took refuge and called upon the name of the Tathāgata.
Born of the same Śākya clan.
He left home and attained Buddhahood.
Enduring this severe torment, yet they did not remember him.
The Buddha, together with the bhikṣus,
went to Kapilavastu.
The women, seeing from afar, were all filled with shame.
The World-Honored One turned and said to Śakra Devānām Indra,
"These women are ashamed.
Indra then covered these women with heavenly garments.
The Buddha addressed Vaiśravaṇa,
"These women have long been hungry and thirsty." Immediately, heavenly food was prepared, and all were fully satisfied.
The Buddha expounded the path of suffering, its origin, cessation, and the way.
The defilements of all the women were completely eradicated, and they attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Each, in her own place, passed away.
All were reborn in the heavens.
The Buddha proceeded to the eastern gate and saw within the city,
flames raging intensely.
He turned and said to the bhikṣus,
"I once preached the Dharma here with the bhikṣus.
Now it is like an empty ruin, devoid of people.
From now on, I shall not come here again."
He returned to the Jetavana Grove in Śrāvastī.
Addressing the bhikṣus, he said,
"King Virūḍhaka and his troops,
after seven days, will all be utterly destroyed."
The king, hearing this, was terrified.
He engaged in severe ascetic practices; the Brahmin, internally and externally free from dust, the king merely amused himself.
The king had people count the days until the morning of the seventh day.
The king was greatly delighted.
Leading his troops, army, and concubines,
he went to the side of the Aciravatī River.
Together they feasted and reveled.
Suddenly, great thunder roared.
Untimely clouds gathered.
A violent storm with fierce rain arose.
Causing injury, sweeping away, and drowning them,
all perished in an instant.
The king was born alive into the Avīci Hell.
Moreover, heavenly fire burned and destroyed the palace city.
A bhikṣu asked the Buddha,
"For what reason do the Śākyas now suffer this torment?"
The Buddha said,
"In the past, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a fishing village.
At that time, the world was plagued by famine, and people ate grass roots.
A peck of gold was traded for a liter of rice.
The village had a large pond,
teeming abundantly with fish.
The people caught and ate them.
There were two kinds of fish:
one named Kuṣa, the other named Duōshé.
They said to each other,
'We are aquatic creatures.
We do not dwell on dry land.
Yet these people all come to devour us.'
In the village, there was a child,
only eight years old.
Although he did not catch fish,
upon seeing them, he was delighted.
The people of Rājagṛha village are now the Śākya clan.
The Kuṣa fish is now King Virūḍhaka.
The two-tongued fish is now the severe ascetic Brahmin.
The child who laughed upon seeing the fish is now myself.
The sin of taking the fish resulted in suffering in hell for countless kalpas.
Now, this residual retribution remains.
Having rejoiced and laughed at the sight,
I now suffer from headaches as if crushed by a stone,
or as if bearing Mount Sumeru." Many who heard the Buddha expound the Dharma of impermanence,
attained the fruit of Stream-enterer.
A Buddhist nun told five hundred women:
"I once heard from the Buddha:
If a person, in a moment of extreme crisis,
single-mindedly recites the Buddha's name,
wholeheartedly taking refuge,
they will immediately attain peace and security."
At that time, the five hundred women, with different mouths but the same voice, wholeheartedly recited the Buddha's name.
They cried out: "Námó Shìjiāmóuní! How bitter! Alas, how painful!"
Then, in the sky, through the Tathāgata's power of compassionate roots,
a great cloud of compassion arose,
raining down a great rain of compassion.
The women's hands and feet were restored.
The women thought:
"How can we repay the Buddha's compassionate kindness?"
They immediately took their robes and alms bowls,
and went to the King's Garden Monastery,
seeking to leave the household life.
At that time, there were six groups of bhikṣuṇīs.
Seeing these women of the Śākya clan were young, beautiful, and graceful,
they intended to tell them of the pleasures of worldly desires,
saying: "Wait until you pass the age limit, then leave home—wouldn't that be joyful?
If you all return to lay life, you will surely give your robes and bowls to us."
Hearing this, the women felt bitter distress and said:
"It is like mixing delicious food and drink with poison.
The five worldly desires are full of many faults and calamities.
We have already fully understood this.
How can you praise their beauty
to persuade us?"
They raised their voices and wept loudly.
The bhikṣuṇī Huásè asked the reason.
They replied they wished to leave home,
but had not been granted permission.
Huásè then ordained them as her disciples.
At that time, the Śākya women, with mixed feelings of sorrow and joy,
fully recounted the loss of their clan and the mutilation of their bodies,
reporting to their preceptress.
She replied: "Your hardships are hardly worth mentioning.
In the past, when I was a laywoman,
I was from Shèwèi country.
My parents married me
to a man from the north.
The custom of that country
was that when a woman was about to give birth,
she would return to her parents' home.
Later, when the time of birth was near,
the husband and wife both rode in a carriage.
On the way, there was a river whose waters had suddenly risen.
The road was desolate and cut off, with many bandit dangers.
Reaching the river, they could not cross.
They stayed overnight on the bank.
In the first watch of the night, she gave birth to a boy.
A large venomous snake, smelling the scent of fresh blood,
came straight for me.
First, it bit and killed the servant.
I called my husband, but he did not answer.
Soon it also killed my husband.
Next, it killed the oxen and horses.
By sunrise,
my husband's body was swollen and rotting.
Overwhelmed with grief and terror,
I raised my voice and wept loudly.
After staying several days,
alone on the riverbank,
the water gradually receded.
Carrying the infant on my back,
holding him with my hands,
using my skirt to hold the afterbirth,
and holding it in my mouth,
I then entered the water ahead.
Having crossed half the river,
I looked back at my older child,
and saw he was being chased by a tiger.
I cried out and lost my skirt,
causing the infant to drown.
I tried to feel for him with my hands,
but ultimately could not find him.
The one on my back
slipped from my hands and fell.
The one on the bank
was eaten by the tiger.
My heart and liver felt torn apart,
and I vomited hot blood.
Reaching the shore, I fainted.
