A large group arrived.
Among them was an elder
who was an acquaintance of my parents.
I asked for news.
The elder replied:
'Last night, a fire destroyed your home completely.
Both your parents perished.'
Hearing this, I collapsed in a faint,
and after a long while, revived.
There were five hundred bandits
who then attacked the group,
and took me away,
making me a bandit's wife.
I was often made to guard the gate.
If there was an emergency,
and they were being pursued by people,
I had to open the gate during the day.
Later, the bandits went out plundering together.
The wealthy householder reported to the king and the village.
They then returned to their dwelling.
I had given birth inside the house.
He called three times, but no one opened.
So he climbed over the wall and entered, asking.
I replied I had given birth.
The bandit said:
'For the sake of a child, you endangered me. What use is the child to me?'
He drew his sword, cut off the child's limbs, and ordered his wife to eat them.
Out of terror, the wife ate.
His anger then subsided.
The husband continued robbing,
was captured by the king's men,
who cut him in half at the waist, executing him,
and buried him alive together with his wife.
Someone coveted the fine jewels on my body,
opened the grave to take them,
and also took me away.
After a short time,
the king, lying in wait, captured him,
executed the bandit companion,
and again buried them together.
The burial was not secure.
At night, a tiger dug it up to eat,
and thus I managed to get out.
Lost and confused, not knowing east from west,
I hurried along the road.
Seeing many people,
I asked:
'Where, O people, is there one who can remove these sorrows and afflictions?'
At that time, there were elders, brāhmaṇas, and others
who, with compassionate hearts, asked:
'Have you heard of the Dharma of Shìjiāmóuní?
It brings much peace and security, free from all decline and distress.'
Hearing this, my heart rejoiced.
I went to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, the bhikṣuṇī,
and gradually cultivated and practiced, finally attaining the fruit of the path.'
Hearing this, the Śākya women
were greatly joyful,
and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Then Gautamī said:
"The Tathāgata's ocean of Dharma
is accessible to all sentient beings.
All have a share in it.
But we women,
the Tathāgata does not readily permit,
because we have many doubts, attachments, and find it difficult to renounce,
with foolish affection covering our minds, submerged in the waters of desire,
unable to free ourselves,
indolent and lazy.
In this present life, we cannot adorn bodhi and attain the three vehicles.
Ānanda made a request, saying:
'Gautamī nursed and nurtured the Tathāgata's physical body until he attained buddhahood.'
The Buddha said: 'If women are permitted into the Dharma, it will gradually decline.'
Ānanda again requested:
'Past buddhas all had the fourfold assembly.
But now you alone do not have a complete assembly.'
The Buddha told Ānanda:
'If Gautamī
loves and delights in the Buddha-Dharma, arouses great vigor,
and purely cultivates and practices the eight rules of respect,
then she may be permitted to enter the Buddha-Dharma.'
I was thus able to leave home.
Imbued with great compassion,
I universally made a plea for all future women,
earnestly addressing the Buddha:
'For future virtuous women
who believe, delight in, love, and revere the Tathāgata's Dharma,
I only wish you would grant permission.'
The Buddha said:
'If there are women
who protect and uphold the Buddha-Dharma, gradually cultivating and studying,
observing precepts, giving, and much learning, taking the three refuges and five precepts,
up to the full precepts,
and all auxiliary dharmas of the path,
they are also permitted.
They should always wholeheartedly remember Ānanda's kindness,
making offerings and showing reverence,
day and night, at the six times,
never forgetting it in their minds.'
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What merit did Channa accumulate in a previous life that he was able to lead the Bodhisattva into the mountains to attain Buddhahood?"
The Buddha said:
"Channa not only possesses this merit in the present life.
In the past, when I was a Bodhisattva,
in the country of Shīhēbiànyíng,
King Xūtánmótí heard that some people in the world either practiced the Way to ascend to heaven or performed sacrifices to ascend to heaven.
The king always wished to ascend to heaven but did not know the method.
In the country, there were Brahmin practitioners,
numbering over forty thousand in total.
Among them was a great elder Brahmin.
The king respectfully inquired of him.
He replied:
'Do you wish to ascend to heaven in your living body or after death?'
The king said:
'To ascend to heaven in my living body.'
He continued:
'Great King, you should perform a sacrifice.'
The king, delighted, brought out treasures from his storehouse and gave them to the Brahmins.
He sought one hundred handsome boys and one hundred beautiful girls from the country,
and one hundred elephants, horses, and livestock each.
First, he fed the four Brahmins,
then killed the people and animals,
using them to sacrifice to heaven.
He took their blood to make steps,
for the Brahmins to ascend.
They further sought a divine maiden named Zhēntuóluó from the Fragrant Mountain,
wishing to obtain her blood to mix and use for making steps.
Upon hearing this, the king joyfully said, 'Why didn't you tell me earlier?'
The king then issued an order throughout the country, asking who could obtain Zhēntuóluó.
One person told the king:
'In the seventh mountain, there are two men,
one named Shélí, the other named Yōulí.
They know the whereabouts of Zhēntuóluó.'
The king said:
'Quickly summon those men.'
They were brought.
The king was greatly pleased and immediately set out wine and food, allowing them to indulge in pleasure for seven days and seven nights, rewarding them lavishly and satisfying their desires.
The king said to Shélí and the other man:
'If you can bring the maiden Zhēntuóluó to me so that I may ascend to heaven,
I will entrust this country to you two.'
The men accepted the command and exerted themselves fully to seek Zhēntuóluó.
After more than two months, passing through eight layers of mountains,
they reached the Fragrant Mountain and found a large pond.
They saw Śakra Devānām Indra,
with countless heavenly maidens and a vast multitude,
leaving the city to play, bathing in the pond, and then all flying up to heaven.
At that time, by the pond, there was a Brahmin
who had attained the four dhyānas and the path of the pañcābhijñā.
Then Shélí and the others approached, bowed, and asked:
'What kind of joyful sounds are these here?'
He replied:
'King Tóumó and over a thousand people are in this city,
playing and bathing. They will come to pay respects to me.
You should leave.'
Shélí and the others then left.
Hiding, they discussed:
'This is a great divine sage. How can we obtain this divine maiden from him?'
The man himself thought to take grass, make knots, and throw them into the water to bind it,
causing the Brahmin to be unable to move.
He also bound the heavenly maidens so they could not fly.
After completing the binding spell,
Śakra Devānām Indra and the heavenly maidens all flew up to heaven.
Only the king, the maiden, and the king's attendant Mónàhēluó remained in the water, unable to fly.
They then went forward, bound the maiden, and brought her to the original country.
The king invited them into the palace, fed them, and rewarded them.
The crown prince, Nánluóshī, became king of another country.
The king had a crown prince named Xūluó,
who was originally the king's eldest grandson.
He possessed great compassion and practiced the Bodhisattva path.
He sent someone to summon him to see this maiden, wishing to take her as his wife.
The king said:
'I will find another wife for you.
This maiden is from heaven; we will take her blood for the sacrifice to ascend to heaven.'
The Bodhisattva replied:
'If you do not give her to me, I will die of longing.'
The king, fearing his death, gave the maiden to him.
After more than four months, the Brahmins came and told the king:
'We previously obtained the maiden Zhēntuóluó; now we should kill her.
With the people and livestock, dig a pit eight cubits square.
We should take her blood and choose a day to perform the sacrifice.'
The king said:
'Excellent.' The Bodhisattva heard this and asked what was happening.
The Brahmins replied:
'Performing the sacrifice will allow us to ascend to heaven.'
The Bodhisattva said:
'Killing people and animals will lead to hell.
How could that lead to heaven?'
The Brahmins said:
'You are still young; this is not your concern.'
The Bodhisattva said:
'I fully understand your methods.'
The Brahmins said, 'If you know, try to explain.'
The Bodhisattva explained their practices.
The Brahmins, ashamed, bowed and left.
The Bodhisattva then explained the scriptures to the king, saying:
'Those who wish to ascend to heaven should uphold the five precepts, practice the ten good deeds,
give alms generously, support their parents, serve śramaṇas,
and have compassion for all beings, providing them with whatever food they need. Then they can ascend to heaven.'
The king, hearing this, followed the Bodhisattva's words.
He then brought out gold, silver, and treasures from the storehouse,
and gave them to the crown prince to distribute as he wished for seven days.
Then, bidding farewell to his wife, he left and returned to his original country.
Day and night, gold, silver, and jewels rained down.
The Bodhisattva and the maiden lived together for a year without attending to state affairs.
The ministers told the king:
'We should kill Zhēntuóluó.
Then the crown prince will attend to the country.'
The king, hearing this, ordered the crown prince to be captured and bound.
The maiden immediately flew away.
Passing by the place of Shélí and the other man,
she said to them:
'The crown prince will come chasing.
I trouble you to send him.
I leave a ring as a token.'
She gave it to the ascetics.
The king released the crown prince.
Not seeing Zhēntuóluó,
he fell to the ground and said:
'How can I find the maiden?'
A deity spoke to him:
'You need not weep.
I will tell you where she is.
Go to the seventh mountain; quickly chase her.'
He then put on a pearl garment, belted a sword, and took a bow.
The light of the pearl garment illuminated forty li.
The crown prince left the country; at dawn, he reached the seventh mountain and saw the two men from before.
He immediately said:
'Have you seen the maiden Zhēntuóluó?'
They replied they had.
They gave the ring to the crown prince.
They then proceeded together.
Ascending the eighth Fragrant Mountain,
they saw the four-dhyāna Brahmin and bowed to him.
At that time, the heavenly king Śakra transformed into a fearsome monkey that shook the mountain.
The Bodhisattva was greatly terrified.
The Brahmin said:
'This is usual; my monkey sees you and refuses to come down.'
The Brahmin said:
'You come down; the monkey will come and offer fruit.'
The Brahmin received it and shared it with the three men. After eating,
he said to the monkey:
'Take these three men to where the heavenly maidens are.'
The monkey said:
'What kind of people are these, that I should take them to heaven?'
The Brahmin said:
'This is the crown prince of a country.
They are Bodhisattva persons who will attain Buddhahood and liberate all heavenly beings and sentient creatures.'
The monkey said, 'Excellent.'
He then took them to heaven.
On the way, they passed by five hundred Pratyekabuddhas.
The three men sent the monkey back to fetch flowers to scatter upon the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
They made a vow, saying:
'May I quickly attain Buddhahood.'
The monkey also said:
'May I become the Buddha's horse.'
Shélí also said:
'May I become the Buddha's servant.'
The other man said, 'I wish to attain Arhatship.'
They arrived at Zhēntuóluó's place.
The monkey bowed and left.
The Bodhisattva and the two men sat together outside the gate.
A maidservant came to fetch water.
The Bodhisattva asked her what the water was for.
She replied:
'For Zhēntuóluó to bathe.'
The Bodhisattva removed his ring and secretly dropped it into the water.
When the maiden bathed and saw the ring, she stopped.
She went in and reported to her parents:
'My husband is outside.'
Her parents were delighted.
Her father's name was Tóumó.
He came out to meet him.
He bowed to the Bodhisattva.
Shélí and the other man also bowed and left.
The king invited them into the city, exchanged greetings,
washed the Bodhisattva's hands with water,
and entrusted the maiden and over a thousand maidservants to the Bodhisattva.
They stayed for seven years.
The Bodhisattva said to the king:
'I wish to return to see my parents.'
The king said, 'Stay a while.'
Seven days later, a ghost came to the king and said:
'I previously heard that Your Majesty's daughter was lost; congratulations on her return and on gaining a noble son-in-law.'
The king said:
'My daughter is fine, but my son-in-law is greatly honored.
He is the crown prince of a country and has long wished to return; I trouble you to send him.'
The ghost king said, 'Agreed.'
He then took a country's seven treasures and made a seven-storied tower.
The ghost placed it in his palm and sent them back to their original country, then bowed and left.
The Bodhisattva went forward, bowed to his parents, and inquired about their well-being.
The king, having regained the crown prince,
entrusted the country's treasures, gold, and silver to him.
The king ordered his ministers and attendants:
'From all four directions, those who wish to obtain gold, silver, rice, or grain,
let them all come to the palace gate and take whatever they desire.'
Later, when the king's life ended, he was reborn in heaven.
The crown prince at that time is my present self.
The four-dhyāna Brahmin at that time is Śāriputra.
Shélí at that time is now Channa."
At that time, one person who vowed to become an arhat is today's Mùjiànlián.
At that time, the heavenly king Śakra transformed into a monkey who vowed to become a horse, which is today's Kanthaka.
At that time, the king father is today's my father, Śuddhodana.
At that time, the mother is today's my mother, Māyā.
The Gandharva is today's Gopikā.
The bodhisattva Sadāprarudita practiced the bodhisattva path at the place of the Buddha Mahābhīṣmagarjitasvara.
Originally seeking the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) at that time,
he did not spare his body or life, nor did he seek fame or profit.
A voice in the sky admonished and instructed him:
"I shall seek the perfection of wisdom everywhere."
Immediately, he grieved and wept for seven days.
His body became extremely fatigued, even suffering hunger, thirst, cold, and heat.
A Buddha in the sky spoke to him, saying:
"Good man, past Buddhas practicing the bodhisattva path sought to hear the perfection of wisdom.
Just as you today, due to such diligent vigor and love for the Dharma,
make offerings to the perfection of wisdom.
The bodhisattva Dharmodgata on this seat expounds the perfection of wisdom.
If there are those who uphold, recite, and practice as taught,
from now on, do not ask day or night; you shall soon hear the perfection of wisdom."
"I am now poor and have nothing with which to make offerings to the perfection of wisdom and the Dharma teacher.
I should not go empty-handed.
I shall sell my body to obtain wealth for the sake of the perfection of wisdom and to make offerings to the Dharma teacher.
I have lost my body countless times over many lifetimes.
In beginningless saṃsāra, I have died or been sold.
Or for the sake of greed and desire, I have endured immeasurable suffering in hell over many lifetimes.
Never have I lost my body or life for the sake of the pure Dharma or making offerings to a Dharma teacher."
He then entered a great city and went to the marketplace.
Raising his voice, he cried out:
"Who needs a person? Who needs a person?"
At that time, the evil demon thought:
"Is Sadāprarudita, for the sake of the Dharma, about to sell himself?
I shall now ruin him."
The demon obscured the people so they could not hear his voice.
Unable to sell himself, he became deeply distressed.
Śakra, lord of the devas, transformed into a Brahmin and said:
"I now wish to perform a sacrifice to the heavens and need a human heart, human blood, and human marrow.
Can you provide them?"
He replied:
"I now obtain great good benefit."
He immediately took a knife, pierced his left arm to draw blood, cut flesh from his right thigh, and was about to break the bone to extract marrow.
At that time, a wealthy man's daughter, from a high tower, saw from afar and came down to ask the bodhisattva:
"Why do you torment yourself so? What do you intend to do with your heart, blood, and marrow?"
He replied:
"To sell to the Brahmin for the perfection of wisdom and to make offerings to the bodhisattva Dharmodgata."
The girl asked what merit he would gain.
He replied:
"This person skillfully learns the perfection of wisdom and its expedient means.
I learn this Dharma to attain the supreme path.
To become a refuge for all beings.
To obtain a golden-colored body endowed with all merits.
To distribute these benefits equally to all beings."
The girl said: "Subtle and hard to encounter are such merits.
One should sacrifice bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
What do you need? I shall give it all.
I also wish to go to Dharmodgata to plant good roots together."
Śakra, lord of the devas, then resumed his original form.
Praising, he said:
"Excellent, good man.
Past Buddhas practicing the bodhisattva path also sought thus.
I truly do not need human heart, blood, or marrow.
I only came to test you.
What do you wish?
I shall give it to you."
"I wish for my body to be restored as before."
He went to the wealthy man's daughter's home.
The girl's parents gave various wonderful flowers, incense, garlands, perfumes, burning incense, banners, canopies, clothing, the seven treasures, and music.
The girl, with her attendants, went together to make offerings to the sutra and to Dharmodgata.
Dharmodgata expounded the perfection of wisdom and its expedient means.
Sadāprarudita sought water to sprinkle the ground but could not obtain any.
He then pierced his own body and sprinkled the ground with his blood so that there would be no dust when approaching the great teacher.
The bodhisattva King of Constellations (Sugandhakuṣa) addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, how did the Medicine King (Bhaiṣajyarāja) roam this Sahā world?
He performed hundreds of millions of nayutas of difficult and arduous practices.
Please briefly explain."
The Buddha said:
"In the past, as many kalpas ago as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha named Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī.
In his land, there were no women.
The bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana diligently practiced and walked in meditation with single-minded pursuit of Buddhahood under this Buddha's Dharma.
After twenty thousand years, he attained the samādhi of manifesting all forms.
All this was due to the power of hearing the Lotus Sutra.
In the sky, he rained down mandārava flowers and the fragrance of sandalwood from the seashore.
Wrapping his body in heavenly garments and anointing it with fragrant oil, he set himself on fire.
The light illuminated eighty billion Ganges-sands of worlds.
This is true diligence, true Dharma offering.
His body burned for twelve hundred years, and after that, his body was completely consumed.
After the bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana made this Dharma offering,
he was reborn by transformation in this land, in the household of King Śubhavyūha.
He spoke a verse to his father:
'The Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī still exists now.
I shall return there to make offerings to this Buddha.'
Seated on a seven-jeweled platform, he ascended into the sky.
Going to the Buddha's place, he joined his palms and praised the Buddha.
The Buddha told Sarvasattvapriyadarśana:
'The time of my extinction is near.
Tonight I shall enter nirvāṇa.
I entrust my Dharma to you; I hand over the relics to you. You should cause them to spread widely and establish abundant offerings.'
Sarvasattvapriyadarśana then burned them with sandalwood from the seashore.
Collecting the relics, he made eighty-four thousand jeweled urns.
He erected eighty-four thousand stūpas.
Although he made these offerings, his mind was still not satisfied.
Then before the eighty-four thousand stūpas,
he burned his arms adorned with a hundred merits for seventy-two thousand years,
and thus made offerings.
Countless seekers of the śrāvaka vehicle and immeasurable people aroused the bodhi mind.
All attained and abided in the samādhi of manifesting all forms.
The bodhisattvas, devas, humans, and others, seeing him without arms, grieved and lamented, saying:
'The bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana is our great teacher who taught and transformed us; now he is incomplete.'
The bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana made a vow in the great assembly:
'I have sacrificed both arms; I shall certainly attain Buddhahood.
If this is true and not false, may my arms be restored.'
At that moment, the three-thousandfold world system shook in six ways, and devas rained down jeweled flowers.
At that time, his two arms were restored as before.
The Buddha told the bodhisattva King of Constellations:
'That Sarvasattvapriyadarśana of that time is today's Medicine King.
If there are those who arouse the mind desiring to attain the supreme bodhi path,
they can burn a finger, even a toe, to make offerings to a Buddha stūpa.

This surpasses offering kingdoms, cities, wives, children, and the three-thousandfold world's mountains, forests, rivers, lakes, and various precious jewels to Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, arhats, and others.'
In the distant past, there was a Buddha
named Meghaśrīgarbha.
There was a king named Śubhavyūha.
His queen was named Vimaladattā.
They had two sons:
one named Vimalagarbha,
the second named Vimalanetra.
These two sons possessed great supernatural powers,
merit, virtue, wisdom, and practiced the bodhisattva path.
The Buddha, wishing to guide King Śubhavyūha and compassionate toward beings, expounded this Lotus Sutra.
At that time, Vimalagarbha and Vimalanetra addressed their mother:
'We wish our mother to go to the Buddha Meghaśrīgarbha.
We shall also attend, make offerings, and pay homage.'
The mother told her sons:
'Your father believes in and accepts non-Buddhist paths and is deeply attached to Brahminical practices.
You should go tell your father and go together with him.'
The mother also said:
'You should consider showing your father supernatural transformations.'
Thereupon, the two sons leaped into the sky, as high as seven tāla trees, and displayed eighteen transformations.
The father, seeing their supernatural powers, greatly rejoiced, joined his palms toward his sons, and said:
'Who is your teacher?'
The two sons replied:
'The Buddha Meghaśrīgarbha is now seated on the Dharma seat under the seven-jeweled bodhi tree, expounding the Lotus Sutra.
He is our teacher.'
The father said to his sons:
'I now wish to see him.'
The two sons descended from the sky and told their mother: 'Our father the king now has faith, understanding, and has aroused the bodhi mind.
We have performed Buddha-work for our father.
We wish our mother's permission
to leave home and cultivate the path at that Buddha's place.'
The mother said: 'I permit you.
Buddhas are hard to encounter.'
Thereupon, the two sons addressed their parents:
'We wish to go now to the Buddha's place to personally behold and make offerings.'
Thereupon, King Śubhavyūha, with his ministers and retinue,
Queen Vimaladattā, with the palace maidens and her two sons, forty-two thousand people in all,
simultaneously went to the Buddha.
The Buddha expounded the Dharma for them, teaching, instructing, benefiting, and delighting them.
The king greatly rejoiced.
At that time, the king and his queen
removed their necklaces of genuine pearls and garlands and scattered them over the Buddha.
In the sky, they transformed into a four-pillared jeweled platform.
In the middle was a great jeweled bed spread with hundreds of thousands of heavenly garments.
Upon it sat a Buddha in full lotus posture, emitting great light.
At that time, the Buddha Meghaśrīgarbha addressed the fourfold assembly:
'Do you see this King Śubhavyūha standing before me with joined palms?
This king, in my Dharma, shall become a bhikṣu, diligently cultivate and practice, assist the Buddha's path-Dharma, and shall become a Buddha named Śālaphalarāja.
His land will be named Mahāprabhā, and the kalpa will be named Mahādhvaja.'
The king immediately entrusted the kingdom to his younger brother.
The king, with his queen, two sons, and various retinue, left home and cultivated the path within the Buddha's Dharma.
After the king left home, for eighty-four thousand years he constantly diligently practiced the Wonderful Dharma Lotus Sutra.
After that, he attained the samādhi of the adornment of all pure merits.
He then ascended into the sky as high as seven tāla trees.
King Śubhavyūha of that time is today's bodhisattva Puṣyacandra.
Queen Vimaladattā is today's bodhisattva Vairocanaraśmipratimaṇḍitadhvaja.
Those two sons are today's bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata."
In the past, when the Bodhisattva was a Brahmin ascetic named Chàntíhé, he dwelled in the mountains.

He lived beneath a tree, eating fruits and drinking from springs, his inner defilements completely eradicated. He had fully mastered the six supernatural powers and attained the wisdom of omniscience.
His renowned fragrance spread everywhere, reaching all eight directions and the realms above and below.
Sages and ordinary people alike praised and protected his country.
Wind and rain came in their proper seasons, the five grains ripened abundantly, and calamities and poisons were eliminated.
There was a king named Jiālí.
He entered the mountains to hunt, chasing after deer.
Following their tracks, he passed by the front of the Bodhisattva.
The king questioned him.
The Bodhisattva remained silent.
The king said:
"You deserve death, beggar! I am the sovereign of a nation.
When questioned, you do not answer promptly. The animal tracks lead here,
yet you pretend to lower your head. By my power, I can kill you."
The Bodhisattva said:
"I hear you, O King."
The king said: "Who are you?"
He replied: "I am one who endures humiliation."
The king, enraged, drew his sword and cut off the Bodhisattva's right arm.
The Bodhisattva said:
"My aspiration is for the supreme Way; I contend with nothing in this world.
If even this king can inflict such endurance upon me, how much more so can ordinary people?
I vow that when I attain Buddhahood, I will first liberate him,
so that living beings will not emulate his evil deeds."
The king said:
"Who are you?"
He answered:
"I am one who endures humiliation."
The king then cut off his left hand, and even his two feet, ears, and nose.
Blood flowed like a spring, and his pain was immeasurable.
Heaven and earth quaked, the sun and moon lost their light.
The Four Heavenly Kings all arrived together and spoke in unison with anger:
"This king is cruel and violent.
They said to the ascetic:
"We shall execute him, along with his wife and children,
and destroy his entire kingdom to make his evil known."
The ascetic replied:
"What words are these?
This is due to my actions in a past life when I did not follow the Buddha's teachings and inflicted poison upon him.
Evil brings misfortune in pursuit, just as a shadow follows a form.
The common people, witnessing the changes, rushed to confess their faults, saying in unison:
"The ascetic dwells here to avert disasters and bring liberation.
Our foolish ruler does not recognize good and evil, does not know what to accept or reject.
He has inflicted harm upon the supreme sage.
We only pray that the sage will not use us to seek retribution from the heavenly rulers."
The Bodhisattva replied:
"The king has treated me with cruelty, yet my heart pities him like a mother's care for her infant.
What fault have the common people committed? Do not harbor doubts."
The Bodhisattva had a younger brother dwelling in another mountain.
With his divine eye, he observed.
At that time, heavenly gods and dragons gathered to discuss the king's evil, and none were without indignation.
Fearing that his elder brother might harbor thoughts damaging to virtue,
he used his supernatural power to come to his brother's place.
He took the severed hands, feet, ears, and nose and placed them back in their original positions.
The brother then rejoined them, and they were restored as before.
The elder brother said:
"My universal compassion and faith are now clearly manifested."
Heavenly gods and earth spirits were all moved to sorrow and joy.
They bowed their heads in praise, encouraged one another, received the precepts, and withdrew.
Chàntíhé was myself.
The younger brother was Maitreya.
The king was Kauṇḍinya.
At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, the household of General Siṃha gave birth to a son.
At the moment of his birth, the various gods in the sky spoke thus:
"Child, always remember the Dharma, contemplate the Dharma. In all your speech, do not speak of worldly affairs.
Always proclaim the Dharma that transcends the world.
Always guard your mouth, be careful with words, speak little.
Do not give rise to perceptions and thoughts about worldly matters.
Rely on the meaning, not on the words."
Hearing this, the child ceased crying and displayed no infant-like behavior.
For up to seven days, his complexion was serene and joyful; seeing people, he was happy, and his eyes never blinked.
At that time, someone said to his parents:
"This child is inauspicious and should not be raised."
The parents replied:
"Although this child makes no sound,
his physical faculties are complete.
You should know that this child surely has merit and virtue; he is not an inauspicious cause."
They gave him the name Wúyán (Speechless).
The child Wúyán gradually grew up, like an eight-year-old.
People delighted in seeing him.
Wherever the Dharma was expounded and the Wheel of Dharma turned,
he delighted in the Dharma, listened and received it, but uttered nothing.
At that time, Wúyán, along with his parents, relatives, and clan members,
went from between the realms of form and desire to the jeweled precincts,
saw the Buddha and the bodhisattvas who had come from the ten directions, and gave rise to great joy.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
the son born to General Siṃha,
his physical faculties are complete, yet he cannot speak. What karma caused this?"
The Buddha said:
"You should not slight this child.
Why?
This person is a great bodhisattva.
He has planted roots of goodness at the feet of immeasurable buddhas.
He is on the irreversible path to enlightenment.
When this child was born, many gods came to admonish him as before.
Following the gods' instruction, he silently contemplated and attained the four dhyānas.
Manifesting such a body, he is able to tame and guide immeasurable living beings.
Through the power of his vows and supernatural power,
he caused the eight kinds of beings and the fourfold assembly each to see in his right hand a great lotus flower like a chariot wheel,
complete in color and fragrance, supremely subtle and excellent,
a delight for people to behold.
On each lotus pedestal sat a bodhisattva in full lotus posture, adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty excellent characteristics.
Wúyán, seeing this great supernatural power,
lowered his head, joined his palms, and uttered, "Namo Buddha."
All the bodhisattvas on the lotus pedestals spoke in unison:
"The worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions trembled in six ways.
The gods in the sky made offerings to the Buddha with wonderful fragrant flowers and various kinds of music.
At that time, Wúyán and the bodhisattvas leapt into the sky,
rising to the height of seven tāla trees,
and spoke verses praising the Buddha.
The World-Honored One in the past, as a bodhisattva,
was named Chángbēi (Constant Sorrow).
He saw that in the world, the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha
were as if the world were defiled and turbid.
People turned their backs on the right and followed the wrong, pursuing profit with flowery deceit,
like moths drawn to a flame.
He took the four immeasurables and the six pāramitās as the eternal abode of well-being.
Yet the world abandoned the Buddha and approached that perilous destruction, breaking themselves.
The bodhisattva was constantly sorrowful, distressed, and mournful.
In the past, there was a buddha named Jǐngfǎ Wúhuì (Pure Dharma Without Defilement).
He had not long passed into nirvāṇa.
The sūtras and Dharma had all been lost.
Chángbēi dreamed that this buddha expounded the Dharma for him.
Hearing it, the bodhisattva's mental defilements were eradicated, and he entered a state of pure concentration.
He then left his wife and children and entered the mountains in solitude.
He sustained himself with fruits and water.
He beat his breast and wailed in grief:
"I have not encountered a buddha, I do not see the Dharma and Saṅgha.
The ultimate goal of the Great Way!" As his mournful cry just ended,
a heavenly god descended and said: "O luminous one,
do not wail anymore.
The Buddha has a great Dharma called the illumination of the perfection of wisdom, the illumination of the ultimate.
All buddhas of the three times have achieved enlightenment through this.
You should seek it, recite and study its text, keep its meaning in mind,
and practice it accordingly.
You will certainly attain buddhahood."
Chángbēi looked up and said:
"From whom shall I hear this venerable Dharma?
By what means, to which land, and what is the name and clan of the teacher?"
The heavenly being replied:
"Go straight east.
Have no thought of form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness.
Let your mind be free from all desires, hold your mind without opposition.
I instruct you to behold the sacred text of the perfection of wisdom, the ultimate illumination."
Chángbēi said: "Yes.
I will remember it from beginning to end."
The heavenly being reiterated:
"Be diligent and keep it in mind."
Then he suddenly vanished.
The bodhisattva received the instruction and went eastward, seeking it.
After several days, he stopped.
He deeply reflected, thinking:
"My past merits are meager.
Rulers and ministers are confused and chaotic.
There is no one who knows the Buddha.
Except for the venerable teacher who dispels darkness,
how many miles away is he?"
Through the utmost sincerity,
he moved the buddha from above to appear before him, with gods attending on both sides.
The buddha praised the bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, excellent! You are rare in the world."
The bodhisattva saw the buddha and felt both joy and sorrow.
Bowing his head, he said:
"I pray the Buddha pities me and expounds the sūtra for me."
The Buddha told him:
"The three realms are all empty.
What exists must cease to be; all things are like illusions. Their arising and ceasing are like waves on water. Seeing the world as such, be careful not to forget."
From here, go east for twenty thousand leagues.
There is a country named Jiàntuóyuè.
It is a city of bodhisattvas.
Within the entire country, all are superior beings; there are no ordinary people.
I wish to tell you of the virtues of a bodhisattva.
Even when the kalpa has ended, his virtues remain abundant.
The bodhisattva is named Fǎlái (Dharma-Come).
Among those sages, he is like the moon among stars.
He holds various classic texts and repeatedly teaches people.
The bodhisattvas and others receive, recite, copy, and read them.
The source of this sūtra will certainly be your teacher. I urge you to go to him; he will expound it for you."
Chángbēi awoke from concentration and looked around.
He no longer saw the buddha.
His heart grieved, and tears flowed.
He said: "From where did the buddhas' spiritual radiance come, and now where has it gone?"
The Bodhisattva Shànxìn, in an age devoid of the Dharma, sought the True Dharma. A voice in the sky said:
"East from here, ten thousand yojanas away, there is a kingdom. Its king is named Shànzhù.
Long ago, a Tathāgata appeared in the world, but has long since entered Parinirvāṇa.
The Semblance Dharma has declined. There is a woman.
Born of lowly station, her form and appearance are ugly, unmatched in the human world.
Yet, as if by chance, she can recognize half a verse, a single gāthā.
It is shown she has received a transmission; you can go and ask to resolve your doubts.
There is a stretch of mud, ten thousand li across. Whoever treads upon it will sink.
Even birds in flight cannot cross it; a single hair cannot bear its weight.
You are now exhausted and ill, your hands and feet broken and torn.
How can you possibly proceed further?"
Hearing this, I leapt up joyfully and hastened eastward until I reached the muddy expanse.
Renouncing my body and life, I threw myself upon it, fully expecting to sink and disappear.
As I cast my body down,
wherever my body touched,
a small path emerged.
Pure white, long and straight.
I trod upon it and encountered no further difficulties.
Directly I reached that kingdom and entered the city of Shànzhù.
Wailing in sorrow and blaming myself for not having seen the World-Honored One,
I beheld this woman dwelling in a lowly, wretched place.
Her hut was full of holes.
Her human form was ordinary and base.
Yet I regarded her with reverence, viewing her as I would a Buddha.
I gazed upon her with respect, bowed in worship, circumambulated her, and praised her.
Looking up, I requested the woman to be my great teacher.
I wished she would bestow teaching and instruction, allowing me to fulfill my profound faith."
The woman replied:
"The wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas is immeasurable and boundless. What I have heard is but half a verse.
If you wish to hear it, I will now recite it."
Hearing these words, my body and mind became cool and clear; all my faculties became tranquil, naturally subdued and tamed.
I recited and practiced it in my mind, contemplating its meaning, thoroughly penetrating its purport.
Immediately I attained supernatural powers, flew back to my own country, and everywhere proclaimed this verse.
Through this merit, I gained in the Buddha-Dharma a firm faith that cannot be destroyed or obstructed.
All demons submitted, and all were converted.
Without this faith, I would always remain in birth and death.
For the sake of sentient beings, I reveal this faith so they may receive and practice it."
North of Shèwèi City, not far from the city, was a village named Sànà. There lived a poor Brāhmaṇa woman.
Her name was Bátuóluó.
She gave birth to a son from her womb.
His name was Yīqiè Shìjiān Xiàn (Manifest to All Worlds).
He lost his father while young.
At the age of twelve,
his beauty, strength, and human marks were supreme and foremost.
He was intelligent, eloquent, wise, skilled in subtle speech and good discourse.
There was another village named Pōluóhēsī.
There lived an old Brāhmaṇa teacher.
His name was Móníbátuóluó.
He was well-versed and proficient in the four Vedas.
Yīqiè Shìjiān Xiàn received instruction from him.
He was humble, obedient, respectful, served with utmost devotion, his faculties pure and gentle, retaining all he was taught.
The teacher accepted a king's invitation.
He left Yīqiè Shìjiān Xiàn to guard the house and departed.
The Brāhmaṇa's wife was young and beautiful.
She developed a deep, defiled passion for Shìjiān Xiàn.
Suddenly forgetting propriety and shame, she stepped forward and grasped his robe.
Then Shìjiān Xiàn said:
"You are now like my mother.
How can you act contrary to the Dharma?"
Feeling inner shame and fear, he released his robe and fled far away.
The teacher's wife, her desire inflamed, wept tears and thought to herself:
"He suddenly rejects and severs ties, not following my will.
If he certainly will not comply, I must end your life."
Thereupon, she used her fingernails to scratch her own body.
She employed a woman's deceit to adorn her person.
She tied a rope around herself, her feet not leaving the ground.
When her husband returned and saw his wife, he cut the rope with a knife.
Crying out loudly, he asked what had happened.
The wife answered:
"It was Shìjiān Xiàn who forcibly assaulted and violated me, doing such a thing."
Her husband thought to himself:
"On the day Shìjiān Xiàn was born, all the swords of the Kṣatriyas spontaneously drew themselves from their scabbards.
Their blades all curled up and fell to the ground.
At that time, all the Kṣatriyas were greatly terrified.
On his birth day, there was such an omen.
One should know this man possesses great virtuous power."
He said to Shìjiān Xiàn:
"You are an evil man who has defiled and insulted your superior.
You are no longer a true Brāhmaṇa.
You must kill a thousand people to atone for your crime."
Shìjiān Xiàn, by nature respectful and obedient, honored his teacher's instruction.
He then said to his teacher:
"Alas, Reverend! Killing a thousand people is not what I should do."
The teacher then said to him:
"Are you an evil man who does not desire to be born in heaven as a Brāhmaṇa?"
He replied:
"Reverend, very well. I accept the command." He then killed a thousand people and returned to pay homage at his teacher's feet.
The teacher, hearing and seeing this, gave rise to a rare thought:
"You great evil man, why are you not dead yet?"
He thought further: "Now I must cause his death."
And he told him:
"Kill one person, take one finger from each.
After killing a thousand, take the fingers, make a garland, wear it on your head, and then return.
Only then will you become a Brāhmaṇa."
Because of this cause, he was named Yāngjuémóluó (Aṅgulimāla).
He then said to his teacher:
"Very well, Reverend. I accept the instruction."
He then killed a thousand people, still short by one.
At that time, Yāngjuémóluó's mother, thinking her son must be hungry,
personally brought four kinds of delicious food to deliver to him.
Seeing his mother, the son thought thus:
"I must cause my mother to be reborn in heaven."
He immediately grasped his sword and stepped forward, intending to take her life.
Ten yojanas and one zhang short from Shèwèi Country,
there was a tree there named Āshūjiā (Aśoka).
At that time, the Buddha, with his omniscience, came like an elephant king.
Yāngjuémóluó, having seen the World-Honored One, grasped his sword and hurried towards him.
He thought thus:
"Now I shall also kill this śramaṇa."
The World-Honored One manifested avoiding him.
Yāngjuémóluó then spoke a verse:
The World-Honored One spoke a verse in reply:
At that time, the mother saw the Buddha and Yāngjuémóluó engaged in a difficult debate back and forth.
The son's mind became subdued; he released his body and turned his thoughts downward, therefore a verse was spoken:
Innumerable kalpas in the past, there was a seeker of learning,
named Yànguāng.
He dwelt in a forest grove, practicing auspicious vows.
For four million two hundred thousand years, he practiced without obstruction.
Entering the country of Shājié, there was a potter's daughter.
Seeing this seeker's handsome and fine appearance,
her desire swelled intensely, and she threw herself at him.
The seeker replied:
"I do not delight in desire."
The woman said:
"If not, I will harm myself."
Yànguāng thought to himself: "I uphold the precepts.
If I break them now, it would be inauspicious.
Stepping seven paces away, he then gave rise to compassionate pity.
To violate the precepts incurs the sin of falling into hell.
If I do not do this, the woman will harm herself.
Better to let this woman attain peace and safety.
I shall patiently endure the pains of hell."
Yànguāng then returned and complied with the woman's desire.
He withdrew from his ascetic practice and engaged in household life for twelve years.
After his life ended, he was reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
The Buddha said:
"Know that the seeker Yànguāng of that time,
was none other than my own body.
The potter's daughter was Jūyí."
Long ago, there were two Bodhisattvas whose aspirations were pure and conduct clean.
Internally serene and free from desire, outwardly like heavenly gold.
They carved a stone chamber and dwelt in seclusion, calming their minds.
Wearing garments of reeds, sitting on grass mats, eating and drinking spring water.
Pure and non-active, their minds like empty space.
They fully possessed the four dhyānas and attained the five supernatural knowledges.
All gods, immortals, sages, heavenly dragons, spirits, and ghosts bowed their heads in reverence.
They dwelt in the mountains and marshes for over sixty years.
Compassionate towards sentient beings, reverently serving the Three Jewels.
One was named Tíqíluó.
The second was named Nàlài.
Tíqíluó rose at night to recite scriptures; weary and exhausted, he lay down and fell asleep.
Nàlài, also reciting scriptures at the time, accidentally stepped on Tíqíluó's head.
Tíqíluó immediately rose and said:
"Who stepped on my head?
At sunrise tomorrow, I will split your head into seven pieces."
Nàlài said: "I accidentally stepped on your head; why is your curse so severe?
Even among ordinary utensils, there are accidental collisions.
How much more so for people living together for years—can there be no accidental mistakes?
Your words shall truly be tested. At sunrise tomorrow, my head will surely split.
I shall restrain the sun and not let it rise."
The sun then did not rise. For five days, the entire country was plunged into darkness.
Torches were sought one after another; officials did not perform their duties; ruler and people were alarmed and confused.
All assembled the officials and invited various Daoist masters.
The king said:
"The sun not rising—where does the fault lie?"
Among the Daoist masters, one with the five supernatural powers said:
"Two ascetics in the mountains have a slight dispute; one restrains it and does not let it rise."
The king said: "What is to be done?"
He replied:
"Your Majesty should lead all officials and people, great and small, hasten to them, bow in homage, and seek reconciliation. They will certainly be compassionate and harmonious."
The king then issued an edict and went to the mountains and marshes. Knocking his head on the ground, he said:
"The country's prosperity and the people's peace are moistened by the grace of you two venerable ones.
Yet now you are not harmonious, causing the entire land to lose its proper state.
The fault lies with me; the common people are without blame.
I beg your compassionate forgiveness."
Nàlài said:
"The King persuades and enlightens him regarding my intention.
If his mind is resolved, I will release the sun to rise."
The King went to Tíqíluó's place and conveyed Nàlài's intent.
That day, Tíqíluó, mindful of him, smeared mud on his head and allowed the sun to be released and rise.
His mud-covered head immediately split into seven pieces.
Nàlài, acting without striving, caused the king, ministers, and common people all to rejoice and be happy.
The two ascetics extensively expounded to the king on governing the country.
One should encourage the people with the Four Immeasurables of limitless compassion.
Uphold the Five Precepts and practice the Ten Wholesome Deeds.
The king and his ministers and people all received the precepts.
The king returned to the country and issued an edict:
"People, regardless of rank, shall carry the scriptures of the Five Precepts and Ten Wholesome Deeds.
to serve as the country's standard."
From that time onward, the king's benevolence extended even to plants and trees.
Ministers were loyal and pure.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Nàlài was my own body.
Tíqíluó was Maitreya."
In a past age, there was a bodhisattva.
His name was Lèfǎ.
Born into a royal family, he would copy down and recite all the good words he heard.
In his quest for the Dharma, he traveled through various kingdoms and cities.
At that time, there was a man living by the side of a deep pit who said to Lèfǎ,
"Come, come, I will give you a verse spoken by the Buddha."
The bodhisattva replied,
"You give it to me."
The man said again,
"Give me your precious robe and jeweled necklace,
then I will give it to you."
The bodhisattva agreed.
The man's greed grew,
and he said, "If you can jump into this deep pit for the sake of hearing the Buddha's verse,
and if you can do this, you must first make a vow, and then I will tell you."
The prince replied,
"Alas, good sir!
What benefit do you gain by making me jump into this deep pit?"
The man answered,
"I gain nothing.
I only fear that you, the prince, might now give up these treasures,
but after hearing the verse, you might regret it,
and relying on your royal power, take them back from me."
The prince replied,
"Just say it.
I will never regret giving you the treasures or jumping into the deep pit."
Hearing his vow, the man recited the Buddha's verse.
The bodhisattva then gave him the precious robe and jeweled necklace.
He also made this vow:
"If my heart is sincere in giving this without regret,
may this truthful speech cause me to fall from this height and land safely and unharmed."
After making this vow, he threw himself down.
Before he reached the ground, the Four Heavenly Kings came and gently caught him, placing him on the ground, saying,
"The verse spoken by the Buddha is profound, subtle, and of great benefit."
The man also descended from the height and came to where the bodhisattva was.
He spoke thus:
"Prince, it is rare that you can do such a difficult thing. What Dharma do you seek?"
The bodhisattva replied,
"Through this act, I shall attain Buddhahood."
He then uttered the Four Great Vows.
Hearing this, the man developed faith.
He said to the bodhisattva,
"Take back your royal robe and jeweled necklace."
The prince replied appropriately,
"It is like vomit that has been discarded—how can one eat it again?"
The man said,
"If you will not take them back, I beg you to accept my repentance.
When you later attain Buddhahood, may you save and aid me."
Prince Lèfǎ was none other than Śāriputra.
The one who spoke the verse at that time was Líqiélì.
Good man, in the distant past, before the sun of the Buddha had risen,
I was a Brahmin at that time.
Cultivating the bodhisattva path,
I was fully versed in the scriptures and treatises of non-Buddhist paths.
I practiced the path of quiescence and possessed perfect deportment.
My mind was pure and could not be corrupted by external desires.
I extinguished the fire of anger and hatred.
I upheld the Dharma of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
I sought everywhere for the Mahāyāna sutras.
Yet I did not even hear the name of the Vaipulya sutras.
Dwelling in the Snowy Mountains, I focused my mind in seated meditation for countless years.
I practiced difficult and austere practices.
At that time, Śakra, lord of the devas, transformed himself into the form of a rākṣasa.
His appearance was very fearsome.
He descended to the Snowy Mountains and stood not far from me.
This rākṣasa was fearless, brave, and formidable.
His eloquence was orderly, and his voice clear and elegant.
He proclaimed half a verse spoken by past Buddhas.
Having said it, he stopped.
The form he displayed was extremely terrifying.
He rolled his eyes and looked all around in every direction.
Hearing this half-verse, the ascetic felt great joy in his heart.
He immediately rose from his seat, lifted his hair with his hand, and looked all around.
He spoke these words:
"Who spoke the verse I just heard?"
Looking all around, he saw no one else.
He only saw the rākṣasa.
He then said,
"Who has opened such a door of liberation?
Who can thunder forth the voice of the Buddhas?
Who, amidst the slumber of birth and death, alone awakens
and proclaims such words?
Who can here reveal the supreme taste of the path to beings starving in birth and death?
Countless beings are sinking in the sea of birth and death.
Who can be their great captain?
These beings are constantly entangled by the heavy illness of afflictions.
Who can be their good physician among them?
Speaking this half-verse has enlightened my mind,
like a half-moon gradually opening a lotus flower."
At that time, I also thought,
"Could it be this rākṣasa who spoke the verse?"
I again harbored doubt, thinking it was not something he could have said.
Why?
This person's appearance was extremely terrifying.
If one hears this verse,
all fear and ugliness are immediately removed.
How could one with such a form speak this verse?"
Good man,
at that time, I thought further,
"Perhaps this rākṣasa may have seen past Buddhas
and heard this half-verse from them."
I then went to the rākṣasa and said,
"Excellent, great being!
Where did you obtain this half-verse spoken by those past ones who were free from fear?"
He replied to me,
"Great Brahmin,
you should not ask me about this now.
Why?
I have not eaten for many days.
I have searched everywhere but found nothing.
Tormented by hunger and thirst, my mind is confused, and I speak nonsense.
It is not something known by my original mind."
I then said to the rākṣasa,
"Great being, if you can recite the complete verse for me,
I will be your disciple for life.
What you have spoken is incomplete in name and meaning.
For what reason do you not wish to speak it?
Material gifts can be exhausted,
but the causes and conditions of Dharma-giving are inexhaustible.
Dharma-giving is inexhaustible and brings much benefit."
The rākṣasa replied,
"You are too clever.
You only worry about yourself and do not consider that I am pressed by hunger and suffering and truly cannot speak."
I then asked,
"What do you eat?"
The rākṣasa replied,
"You need not ask.
If I tell you, it will frighten many people."
I said again,
"We are alone here; there is no one else.
I am not afraid of you.
Why not tell me?"
The rākṣasa replied,
"What I eat is only the warm flesh of humans.
What I drink is only the hot blood of humans.
Although there are many people in the world, they all have merit and are protected by various devas.
I lack the power to kill them."
I said again,
"If you will fully recite that half-verse,
I will offer my body to you as alms.
If I die, this body of mine is of no further use.
It will be eaten by tigers, wolves, owls, hawks, and vultures,
and yet I will not gain even a hair's breadth of merit.
I seek Buddhahood; I give up this impermanent body to obtain a permanent one."
The rākṣasa replied,
"Who would believe that for the sake of eight words you would abandon your cherished body?"
I replied,
"It is like someone who gives away a clay vessel and receives a vessel of the seven treasures.
I give up this impermanent body to obtain a vajra body.
Mahābrahmā, Śakra, lord of the devas,
and the Four Heavenly Kings can bear witness to this matter.
Furthermore, there are devas with the divine eye and bodhisattvas who, wishing to benefit countless beings,
cultivate the Mahāyāna and perfect the six pāramitās—they too can bear witness, as can all Buddhas of the ten directions."
The rākṣasa then said,
The rākṣasa spoke:
"Mahāsattva bodhisattva, you have now heard the complete meaning of the verse.
Your wish is fully satisfied.
If you truly wish to benefit all beings, now give me your body."
At that time, I deeply pondered the meaning of this.
Then, everywhere—on rocks, walls, trees, and paths—
I wrote down this verse.
I then tightened the clothes I was wearing,
fearing that after death my body would be exposed.
I climbed a tall tree and threw myself down.
Before I reached the ground, various sounds arose in the empty sky.
The sounds reached even the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
At that time, the rākṣasa resumed his form as Śakra.
He caught me in midair and placed me safely on level ground.
Because of this cause and condition, I was able to transcend
twelve kalpas.
I attained Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi before Maitreya.
Question:
The bodhisattva's body is not made of wood or stone.
How is it that when sentient beings come to cut and slice it, he does not give rise to a different mind?
Answer:
Some say:
Because the bodhisattva has long cultivated the pāramitā of patience, he is able to not be distressed.
Just as when the ṛṣi Kṣānti had his hands and feet cut off, his blood all turned to milk.
Some say:
Because the bodhisattva has deeply cultivated great compassion over countless lifetimes, even when cut and sliced, he does not grieve or worry.
It is like plants and trees, which have no mind of anger.
Some say:
The bodhisattva deeply cultivates the pāramitā of wisdom.
Through transformation, he attains the karmic result of the pāramitā of wisdom.
Because his mind is empty, he clearly knows emptiness.
When his body is cut and sliced, his mind also does not move.
Just as external things do not move, so too internally.
Due to the karmic result of wisdom, there is no discrimination among all dharmas.
Some say:
This bodhisattva is not a body bound by birth and death.
It is a body born from the Dharma-nature beyond the three realms.
Because he abides in the karmic result of the sagely mind free from outflows.
His body is like wood or stone, yet he can compassionately think of those who cut and slice him.
Because this bodhisattva is able to give rise to such a mind.
When internal and external dharmas are cut, sliced, robbed, or plundered,
his mind does not move.
This is the rare Dharma of the bodhisattva.
With my Buddha-eye, I see in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions,
bodhisattvas entering hells,
causing the fires to extinguish and the boiling cauldrons to cool.
They teach and transform sentient beings with three things.
Over immeasurable, incalculable kalpas,
deeply practicing the mind of compassion, giving external possessions.
Their intention is still not satisfied.
Only by giving their bodies in almsgiving is it fully satisfied.
Just as the bodhisattva Medicine King, offering external treasures to the Buddha,
his intention was still not satisfied; only by using his body as a lamp was it fully satisfied.
External possessions, though many, are not considered a great kindness.
Why is that?
Because they are not what is valued.
Only when obtaining their body can one be profoundly moved.
Therefore, the giving of the body.
I recall in the past, over immeasurable kalpas,
at that time, the world was named Sāha.
A Buddha appeared in the world,
named Śākyamuni.
For the great assembly, he preached the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
At that time, I,
from a good friend,
hearing that I should preach the Dharma,
upon hearing this, my heart was filled with joy.
Wishing to make offerings,
living in poverty and having no possessions, I went around selling my body, hoping for a small gain.
Then on the road, I saw a person.
I wish to buy myself.
But in my household, there are tasks, and no one is capable.
I have a severe illness; a good physician prescribed medicine.
I must daily consume three liǎng of human flesh.
If you can give me three liǎng of your flesh daily,
I will then give you five gold coins.
Hearing this at the time, my heart was greatly joyful.
I then said to him: You give me the money, grant me seven days.
Wait until my matters are finished,
then I will return to you.
That person replied:
Seven days is not possible.
If you can truly do it,
I grant you one day.
At that time, I,
took the money,
returned to where the Buddha was,
prostrated with head and face at his feet, and offered it all to the Buddha.
Then with a sincere mind, I listened to and received this sūtra.
At that time, I was dull and dim-witted; although I heard the sūtra,
I could only receive and retain one verse.
I then returned to that sick person's house.
At that time, although I daily gave flesh,
because I was mindful of the verse, I did not feel pain.
After a full month,
because of this cause and condition, his illness was cured.
My body recovered and also had no wounds or scars.
At that time, seeing my body complete and whole,
I aroused the mind of supreme bodhi.
The power of one verse could still be like this,
how much more so by fully receiving, retaining, reading, and reciting? I see this sūtra has such benefits.
Again, I doubly aroused the mind,
vowing that in the future I would become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.
At that time, the Tathāgata preached the Lotus Sūtra.
The other bodhisattvas requested to protect and uphold it.
The Buddha then stopped them, saying:
From the lower region, bodhisattvas, immeasurable and countless,
due to the earth quaking and splitting, simultaneously emerged and appeared, abiding in empty space.
They went to the seven-jeweled stūpa of Prabhūtaratna Tathāgata and Śākyamuni Buddha.
Facing the two World-Honored Ones, they prostrated with head and face in reverence.
Formerly, when the World-Honored One was traveling in Rājagṛha,
the king sent several tens of people to constantly gather fine flowers.
One day later, the great and small nobles and the gathering women all went outside the city to gather flowers.
Wishing to return and enter the city,
from afar they saw the World-Honored One, with his magnificent marks, majestic radiance, lofty and immeasurable,
like the moon among stars, or the sun first rising, shining upon the world.
With his disciples and bodhisattvas surrounding him before and after,
they went to where the Buddha was, bowed their heads in reverence.
In their minds, they thought:
Human life is hard to preserve; encountering a Buddha in the world is hard; encountering sūtras and Dharma is hard.
Now encountering this great sage is like a sick person finding a physician.
I am poor and lowly, and moreover belong to the county officials, with the suffering of forced labor.
Constantly not free to follow my own will.
The king is strict and urgent.
The master supplies gathered flowers, always requiring early presentation.
If the time is missed, perhaps I will be executed.
Encountering the sagely assembly is hard.
It occurs once in a billion eons.
I would rather abandon body and life,
to offer flowers to the Buddha and scatter them upon the sagely assembly.
Thereby receiving the sūtra precepts, listening to and examining the profound Dharma of inexhaustible wisdom.
I, from countless kalpas, have been harmed by people, beyond reckoning.
Never for the sake of the Dharma have I not cherished my life.
Now making offerings to the World-Honored One and the Three Jewels is the karma.
Even if I am killed, I will not fall into suffering and pain, but will certainly be born in a peaceful place.
They then took refuge with single-mindedness and again reverently bowed.
The Buddha knew their thoughts.
They aroused the intention for the great path, and he was greatly compassionate toward them.
Fully for them, he expounded the Dharma of great joy.
The six pāramitās, the four immeasurables, the four kindnesses, the three liberations of the bodhisattva.
All the flower gatherers aroused the intention for the path.
Their minds understood the Buddha's wisdom, reaching the irreversible stage of non-arising.
The Buddha then bestowed predictions.
In the future they will attain Buddhahood.
Their name will be Wonderful Flower.
Complete with the ten epithets.
Those nearby hearing this were all joyful.
They requested to receive the great Dharma and make offerings to the Three Jewels.
At that time, the flower gatherers returned to their homes.
They bade farewell to their parents, wives, and children.
My life now ends, for the king will kill me.
The parents were shocked and asked what crime they had committed.
The sons fully explained.
The king is extremely strict and urgent.
Having already missed the time,
and also having no flowers,
I will certainly face danger to my life, therefore I bid farewell.
The parents hearing this were even more sorrowful and distressed.
What can be done?
Opening the basket to look, it was filled with fine flowers.
With filaments and mixed fragrances, their scent permeated far in all four directions.
The parents said:
You can present these to the king.
The sons each reported.
If people see this, they will certainly report to the king.
Moreover, we have missed the time; I fear we cannot be safe.
At that time, the king was greatly angry.
Seeing they did not come on time and also scattered the flowers,
he sent soldiers to arrest them.
They then received the king's order, were bound and taken to the palace.
Their crime deserved execution in the marketplace.
The people were not afraid, their complexions did not change.
The king, finding it strange, asked them:
Your crime is grave; your lives are in jeopardy; bound and brought here to be killed.
Why are you not fearful, your complexions unchanged?
They then said to the king:
In life there is death; when things form, there is destruction.
I, from countless kalpas, have often, through unwholesome actions, not cherished body and life.
This morning gathering flowers, I encountered the World-Honored One.
Offering flowers to him, I bowed my head and took refuge.
Knowing that violating the command warrants death,
I would rather die with virtue,
than live without virtue.
Looking back at the flower basket, it continued to be full as before.
All this is due to the covering of the Tathāgata's kindness and benevolence.
The king asked the Buddha about this.
The Buddha indicated it was so.
The king said:
These people, with utmost sincerity, wishing to save the ten directions, did not cherish body and life.
Therefore they took the flowers to scatter and offer to the Buddha.
Their intention without thought of reward has already received predictions.
In the future they will become Buddhas, named Wonderful Flower.
The king was greatly joyful.
Quickly he released their bonds, repented his faults, and blamed himself.
My foolish intention did not realize I was binding bodhisattvas.
The Buddha said:
Excellent, excellent.
Those who can reform themselves are the same as those without faults.
Good man, when a bodhisattva upholds and observes the precepts,
he makes this vow:
"I would rather cast this body into a fiery pit
than ever violate the precepts established by the Buddhas of the three times and engage in impurity with women.
I would rather have red-hot iron wrap around my body
than dare to accept clothing from faithful donors with a body that has broken the precepts.
I would rather have this mouth swallow red-hot iron pellets
than dare to eat the food and drink of faithful donors with a mouth that has violated the precepts.
I would rather lie upon a great bed of red-hot iron
than dare to accept beds, bedding, and furnishings from faithful donors with a body that has broken the precepts.
I would rather have this body receive three hundred spear thrusts
than dare to accept medicine and treatment from faithful donors with a body that has violated the precepts.
I would rather cast this body into a cauldron of molten iron
than dare to accept houses, dwellings, and buildings from faithful donors with a body that has broken the precepts.
I would rather have an iron hammer smash this body from head to foot into fine dust
than receive the reverence and bows of kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and householders with a body that has broken the precepts.
I would rather have red-hot iron gouge out both my eyes
than gaze upon beautiful forms with a lustful mind.
I would rather have iron awls pierce my entire body
than listen to pleasing sounds with a lustful mind.
I would rather have a sharp knife cut off my nose
than greedily smell various fragrances with a lustful mind.
I would rather have a sharp knife slice apart my tongue
than greedily savor delicious flavors with a lustful mind.
I would rather have a sharp axe chop my body
than greedily indulge in various tactile sensations with a lustful mind.
Why is this?
Because such causes and conditions
can cause practitioners to fall into hell, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts.
Kāśyapa, this is called the great bodhisattva's protection and upholding of the precepts.
He fully dedicates them to all sentient beings.
Through these causes and conditions, he vows that sentient beings may protect and uphold all precepts and attain pure precepts.
Good man, when a bodhisattva cultivates these precepts,
he immediately attains abiding in the first immovable ground.
Like Mount Sumeru,
even the fierce winds of a hurricane cannot move it.
A bodhisattva abiding in this ground
is not moved by forms, sounds, smells, or tastes.
He does not fall into hell, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts.
He does not regress to the level of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
He is not scattered by the heterodox winds of wrong views.
There are two kinds of bodhisattvas who arouse the mind:
one practices the pāramitās,
the other merely arouses the mind in emptiness.
Those who practice the bodhisattva path,
even if their tasks are not yet accomplished, can surpass all others.
Like the kalaviṅka bird,
even while still in the egg, it can produce sounds that already surpass those of other birds.
Once, an arhat with the six superknowledges
had a śrāmaṇera carry his robe and bowl.
The śrāmaṇera thought:
"I shall enter nirvāṇa via the Buddha vehicle."
The master, knowing his thought, took the robe and bowl and carried them himself,
pushing the śrāmaṇera to walk in front.
The śrāmaṇera again thought:
"The Buddha path is very difficult.
It requires dwelling for a long time in saṃsāra, enduring immeasurable suffering.
I should instead enter nirvāṇa early via the lesser vehicle."
The master again gave the robe and bowl bag back to the śrāmaṇera to carry and told him to walk behind.
This happened three times.
The śrāmaṇera said to his master:
"Master, you are old and senile, acting like a child."
The master immediately replied:
"When you first aroused the mind to become a Buddha, that mind was noble and weighty, and its status made you my teacher.
Even pratyekabuddhas should make offerings to it,
how much more so an arhat?
Therefore, I pushed you to walk in front.
When your mind regretted and you wished to take the lesser vehicle,
and before you could attain it,
you were far distant from me.
Therefore, I told you to walk behind."
The śrāmaṇera, startled and awakened, then abided in the great vehicle.
In past countless kalpas, there was a Buddha
named Yīqiè Dù.
He and his retinue were going on alms round.
There were three noble boys, finely dressed, playing together.
Seeing the Buddha and the various bodhisattvas, radiant and majestic,
they pointed with their hands and said to each other:
"We should together make offerings."
Two boys replied:
"Since we have no flowers or incense, what should we use?"
One boy took off the white pearl from his head and held it in his hand.
He then said to the two boys: "We can use this to make offerings to the Buddha."
The two boys imitated him, removing the white pearls from their heads and placing them in their hands.
They then went to the Buddha.
One boy again asked the two boys:
"What do you seek by means of this merit?"
One boy said:
"I wish to be like the venerable bhikṣu on the Buddha's right side."
The other boy said:
"I wish to be like the bhikṣu with spiritual powers on the left side."
They together asked the one boy.
He replied:
"I wish to be like the Buddha."
Eight thousand devas all said: "Excellent!
If it is as you say, all beings in heaven and on earth will receive grace."
The three boys went before the Buddha.
Each scattered their white pearls upon the Buddha.
For the two boys who aroused the intention for the śrāvaka path,
their pearls landed on the Buddha's shoulders.
For the one boy who aroused the bodhi mind,
his pearl landed on the Buddha's head.
It transformed into a pearl flower canopy with a jeweled net, within which was a Buddha.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "The boy in the middle is my former body.
The boy on the right is Śāriputra.
The boy on the left is Maudgalyāyana.
Śāriputra, because you originally feared birth and death,
you did not arouse the bodhisattva mind, wishing to quickly attain nirvāṇa.
Observe this one boy who aroused the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
In the past, a bodhisattva,
then an ordinary person,
just sixteen years old,
his aspiration for learning was vast and profound, and he mastered many scriptures.
He sighed and said:
"Only the Buddha's scriptures are the truest and most wonderful.
I shall embrace their truth and dwell in their peace."
His parents wished to arrange a wife for him.
He said sorrowfully:
"No calamity is greater than sensual desire.
If the calamity of seduction arrives, morality and virtue are lost.
If I do not flee far away, will I not be devoured by wolves?"
Thereupon, he went to another country.
He labored for hire to support himself.
At that time, there was an old farmer who had no heir.
While gathering firewood, he obtained a girl.
Her beauty surpassed the nation, and he joyfully raised her as his heir.
He sought a man as a match, but in the whole country, none was suitable for the old man.
He said:
"Young man, I have a dwelling and sufficient means. I will give you my daughter in marriage to be my heir."
The girl had divine virtue and confused the bodhisattva's mind.
Not long after marrying her,
he became self-aware and said:
"I have seen the clear teachings of the Buddhas.
They regard sensual desire as fire,
and people as moths.
Moths are greedy for the fire's light,
and their bodies are seen to be burned and boiled.
This old man uses the fire of sensual desire
to burn my person,
uses wealth as bait to hook my mouth,
and uses family ties to destroy my virtue."
At night, he silently fled on the road, traveling over a hundred li.
He took shelter in an empty pavilion.
The pavilion keeper said:
"Who are you?"
He replied: "I wish to lodge here."
Entering, he saw the bed and mat,
and there was already a woman there beforehand.
Her appearance resembled his own wife.
She confused the bodhisattva's mind, and he lived with her.
Again, after five years had accumulated,
his enlightened mind awakened and he said:
"Lust is like a poisonous insect that harms and endangers body and life."
Silently, he quickly fled.
Again, he saw a woman and lived with her for ten years.
Again, his enlightened mind awakened and he said:
"My calamity is heavy indeed!
Fleeing, yet I cannot avoid it."
Deeply, he made a vow:
"I will never again seek lodging."
Again, he fled and escaped.
From afar, he saw a large house and, avoiding it, walked through the grass.
The gatekeeper said:
"Who travels at night?"
He replied:
"I am heading to the village ahead."
The gatekeeper also said:
"There is a woman inside who summons you." He saw the one mentioned before,
the same woman as above, who said:
"For countless kalpas, I have vowed to be your wife. Where can you run to?"
The bodhisattva thought:
"Is the root of desire so difficult to uproot as this?"
Immediately, he aroused the contemplation of the four impermanences.
He extinguished all afflictions of the three realms.
How could any remaining defilement not be annihilated?
The demon-wife immediately vanished.
Then he saw the Buddhas standing before him.
They expounded the concentration of no-thought, bestowed the śramaṇa precepts, and became his unsurpassed teachers. The bodhisattva's universal salvation is boundless.
Shàng Jīnguāngshǒu and the elder's son Wèi Wén
were together in the pleasure garden scattering flowers, burning incense, adorned with music and dance.
At that time, that woman observed the elder's son and considered her desire satisfied.
Wénshūshīlì transformed this woman's body, and she immediately died.
Her complexion turned foul.
Pus and blood flowed from her eyes, ears, nose, and mouth.
Her body putrefied and could no longer be looked upon.
Blue flies flew over and gathered to feed upon it.
At that time, the elder's son saw this woman's body transformed and ruined thus.
Terrified and agitated, he sought refuge to save himself from this affliction.
From where could he escape this suffering?
Then Wénshūshīlì, with the majestic spiritual power of a youth,
caused the trees in the garden to spontaneously utter praises.
When the elder's son heard the trees' eulogies,
he rejoiced and leapt for joy, and a wholesome mind arose.
He wrapped the woman's corpse in his robe, discarded it among the thicket of trees, and left it there.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, wishing to enlighten that elder's son,
emitted light from his body, its radiance universally illuminating the realm of Mójié.
The elder's son beheld the Tathāgata's majestic spiritual power, lofty and grand.
Joy arose in his mind.
The Lord Śakra then stood before him.
Seeing the elder's son, he praised him, saying:
"Young one, with good causes and conditions,
you have obtained blessings and benefits,
that you are able to see the Buddha."
Hearing this encouragement and praise, that youth
went together with Śakra to where the Buddha was.
Śakra's intention
was to give flowers to the youth, saying:
"Take these flowers and scatter them upon the Tathāgata."
Having scattered them, he prostrated at the Buddha's feet, stood before him and declared:
"Now I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
There was a frivolous woman, Shàng Jīnguāngshǒu,
with whom I indeed sported and went to the pleasure garden.
Then today, her appearance turned foul and she immediately died.
She abandoned all her clan and relatives.
I was seized with great fear,
thinking, 'Will not the king interrogate me?'"
The Buddha said, "Enough."
At that time, Shàng Jīnguāngshǒu,
seeing the elder's son had been enlightened,
following the Vinaya teachings,
went together with musicians to where the Buddha was.
She prostrated at the Buddha's feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Then Wénshūshīlì said to the elder's son:
"Do you recognize this elder sister?"
He replied,
"I already know."
He asked again,
"How do you know?"
Thereupon, the elder's son reported to Wénshūshīlì,
and spoke a verse, saying:
"Form is like a mass of foam,
sensation like a bubble arising momentarily,
conception like a wild horse,
thus I understand and know."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Wénshūshīlì, in a past age, urged and transformed this woman, causing her to arouse the mind for the Path.
I, in a former life, urged and transformed her, causing her to arouse the mind for the Path.
Shàng Jīnguāngshǒu, after ninety-two hundred thousand kalpas,
will attain Buddhahood,
named Bǎo Guāngmíng.
The elder's son will become a Bodhisattva,
named Déguāng Yàoyào.
He will also become a Buddha.
Before his parinirvāṇa,
he will confer the prediction upon Bodhisattva Déguāng Yàoyào,
and then attain parinirvāṇa, named Chí Yàn.
There were two hundred devas who aroused the Bodhisattva mind,
but it was not yet firm and they were all about to fall away.
Each thought to themselves, 'The Buddha-Dharma is difficult to attain.
We now certainly will not study the Bodhisattva path.
It is better to attain Arhatship or Pratyekabuddhahood and enter parinirvāṇa.'"
The Buddha knew these people could become Bodhisattvas,
but their minds were regressing.
The Buddha then magically created a householder
holding a bowl filled with food of a hundred flavors, who came before the Buddha.
He then made obeisance and offered the bowl to the Buddha.
The Buddha accepted the bowl.
Wénshūshīlì addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One,
you should repay the kindness."
Śāriputra, doubtful, immediately asked the Buddha.
The Buddha then threw the bowl to the ground.
The bowl then descended, passing through many Buddha-lands,
directly passing through seventy-two Ganges' sands of Buddha-lands,
named Ōu Hē Shā,
whose Buddha is named Guāngmíng Wáng,
now present in the world.
The bowl in that Buddha-land remained suspended in the air, with no one holding it.
The bowl passed through many Buddha-lands.
The attendants of those Buddhas all asked their Buddhas,
and the Buddhas replied, 'Above there is a Buddha named Shìjiāwén.
