The bowl came from there,
to rescue and protect the regressing Bodhisattvas' minds.'"
The Buddha said to Śāriputra,
"Go seek the bowl and bring it."
Śāriputra, relying on the Buddha's majestic spiritual power,
with his own wisdom power and ten thousand samādhis, passed through ten thousand Buddha-lands but did not see the bowl.
Rising from samādhi, he returned and reported to the Buddha, saying:
"I sought it but did not see it."
He then sent Maudgalyāyana, who also did not see it.
Subhūti and five hundred other venerable ones all could not see it.
Maitreya Bodhisattva also could not see it.
He ordered Wénshūshīlì to seek the bowl.
Wénshūshīlì, without rising from his seat, immediately entered samādhi.
With his right hand pointing downward,
he traveled through all Buddha-lands, none not hearing and knowing.
The Buddha-lands he passed through all trembled and shook.
In all those Buddha-lands, all saw Wénshūshīlì.
Passing through seventy-two Ganges' sands,
on the hairs of his arm, each single hair emitted hundreds of millions of thousands of lights and hundreds of millions of thousands of lotus flowers.
On each lotus flower was a seated Bodhisattva,
all praising the merits of Buddha Shìjiāwén, the voice-hearers, Bodhisattvas, and the Buddha-land.
Then Shìjiāwén emitted light from the soles of his feet,
illuminating below, passing through seventy-two Ganges' sands of Buddha-lands.
Those who saw his light all attained the samādhi of mó pí dī.
Wénshūshīlì took the bowl with his right hand,
and came together with immeasurable Bodhisattvas.
The bowl in his hand, he made obeisance and offered the bowl.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Now I will tell you of a matter from a past kalpa.
In the past, there was a Buddha
named Yǒng Mò Néng Shèng.
There was a bhikṣu-saṅgha,
named Huì Wáng,
who took his bowl and entered the country of Wéizhì to beg for alms.
He obtained food of a hundred flavors.
At that time, there was a venerable's son named Lígòu Wáng,
held by his wet nurse,
on the city gate tower.
The child saw the bhikṣu from afar,
and getting down from her embrace, he went running towards him,
seeking his food.
The bhikṣu then gave him a honey cake.
The child ate it, knowing its taste was sweet and delicious.
He followed the bhikṣu, not heeding his wet nurse.
He then followed him to where Buddha Yǒng Mò Néng Shèng was.
He paid homage to the Buddha and sat to one side.
The bhikṣu gave the bowl of food he held to this child, instructing him to offer it to the Buddha.
The child then offered it to the Buddha.
The Buddha ate, and it was always full.
With this, he fed eighty-four thousand bhikṣus and twelve thousand Bodhisattvas,
each and every one being satisfied.
The food the child held did not decrease or diminish.
The Buddha, with his majestic spiritual power, caused the child to rejoice.
Following the bhikṣu, he received the five precepts and aroused the mind for enlightenment.
The child's parents sought their son and paid homage to the Buddha.
The son addressed his father, saying:
'I have now entered the Bodhisattva Dharma.
I wish to become a śramaṇa.'
His parents immediately consented,
saying, 'We also will arouse the mind and follow you.'"
The Buddha said:
"The bhikṣu Huì Wáng is Wénshūshīlì.
That child at that time is my own body.
Like my own body, they are immeasurable and countless.
The Buddhas of asaṃkhyeya Buddha-lands
were all aroused by Wénshūshīlì.
We all received the kindness of Wénshūshīlì."
Those two hundred devas immediately thought to themselves:
"Buddha Shìjiāwén was aroused by Wénshūshīlì and attained Buddhahood by himself.
Why are we indolent?"
Because of this thought, their minds became firm.
Pǔxián Bodhisattva,
with his sovereign supernatural powers, majestic virtue, and renown,
together with immeasurable, countless great Bodhisattvas, came from the east.
The countries he passed through all trembled and shook.
Precious lotus flowers rained down, and various musical performances were made.
Also, together with countless eightfold divisions of ghosts and spirits and other great assemblies surrounding him,
he paid homage to Buddha Shìjiāmóuní.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I, in the Buddha-land of Bǎo Wēidé Shàng Wáng Buddha,
heard from afar that in this Sahā world the Lotus Sūtra is being expounded, and have come together to listen and receive it.
I only wish the World-Honored One would expound it."
The Buddha told Pǔxián:
"If there are good men and women
who accomplish four dharmas,
after the Tathāgata's extinction, they will obtain this Lotus Sūtra."
Pǔxián Bodhisattva said:
"If there are those who walk, stand, diligently recite this sūtra, and contemplate this sūtra,
if someone forgets or loses a single phrase or verse of this sūtra,
the great Bodhisattva assembly will together go to that place,
and manifest themselves to make offerings, protect, guard, and comfort their minds.
Also, for the sake of making offerings to the Lotus Sūtra, they will cause them again to become fluent and proficient.
Those who see them will rejoice and again redouble their vigor.
Because of seeing me, they will immediately attain samādhi and dhāraṇī.
If in the later evil age, the fourfold assembly comes seeking,
those who uphold,
those who recite,
those who copy,
who wish to cultivate and practice this Lotus Sūtra,
for twenty-one days they should single-mindedly be diligent and vigorous.
After the full twenty-one days, I will also manifest before that person and expound the Dharma for them."
In a past kalpa, there was a Buddha named Guǎngguāngmíng. The king’s son was named Cáigōngdé. At the age of sixteen,
he relied on his handsome appearance and became arrogant.
Initially, he did not pay respects or bow to the Buddha.
The Buddha then distributed tallies, asking who could teach and transform him.
Eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas did not accept the tally.
There was one bodhisattva named Jìngjīngjìn.
He said,
“I can.”
Immediately, the great thousandfold world shook six times.
He then went and stood at the king’s gate.
When the prince saw him, he spoke evil words, slandered him,
threw dirt in his face,
and struck him with knives, sticks, tiles, and stones.
At that time, the bodhisattva did not become angry, did not leave, and his mind did not grow weary or resentful.
For a thousand years, he endured such suffering.
After twenty thousand years, he finally reached the second gate.
For eighty-four thousand years, before seven days had passed, he reached the seventh gate.
At that time, the prince saw this bodhisattva and said,
“Ascetic, why have you come today? What do you seek?”
Immediately, he felt an inconceivable thought toward the bodhisattva.
“What kind of person is this?
After enduring so much suffering for so long,
his mind does not grow weary.”
At that time, the bodhisattva knew that the prince’s mind had already been tamed.
He then spoke a verse, instructing him to go to the Buddha.
At that time, the prince renounced his royal position,
left home under the Buddha’s Dharma, listened to the teachings, dwelled according to the Dharma, and attained the patience of non-arising.
At that time, Jìngjīngjìn was my own body.
Cáigōngdé was Mílè.
Shùtímónà
stood before Buddha Bǎozàng,
placed his right knee on the ground, knelt with hands clasped,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
I now generate the mind of supreme bodhi and accomplish wholesome roots.
Regarding the three vehicles, if my aspiration is to attain benefit for myself,
may white dragon-elephants naturally emerge from my two hands.”
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, dragon-elephants emerged from his two hands.
Their color was pure white, and they touched the ground in seven places.
Seeing this, he declared:
“Dragon-elephants,
now you may ascend into the sky and go not far from here,
raining down throughout this realm the fragrant water of eight virtues,
awakening all beings in this realm.
If any being encounters even a single drop
and smells its fragrance, they will sever the five hindrances:
namely, sensual desire, anger, sloth, restlessness, and doubt.”
At that time, the dragon-elephants were in the sky,
circling swiftly like a strong archer shooting an arrow.
After the two dragon-elephants accomplished all these tasks,
they returned and stood before Shùtímónà.
Seeing this, Shùtímónà’s heart was greatly joyful.
In the past, a bodhisattva was born into a family of the four castes.
As soon as he fell to the ground, he said:
“I shall save all beings from their myriad calamities.
I shall remove their ignorance and lack of Dharma, dispel their blindness and deafness, and enable them to hear and see the bright examples of the sages.”
His nine relatives exclaimed in astonishment:
“We have never heard of an infant who can speak.
Could this be the spirit of a heavenly dragon, ghost, or deity?
We must divine it.”
He replied:
“I am transformed by the supreme sage,
endowed with universal wisdom.
I am not one of those many demons; do not doubt.”
After speaking, he fell silent.
His relatives said:
“This child has the ambition to encompass heaven and earth with vast compassion.
Surely he is no ordinary person.”
They named him Pǔshī.
When he reached the age of ten,
he had thoroughly mastered all the Buddhist scriptures, secular texts, and various arts.
He bid farewell to his family to aid the masses, giving alms to the poor.
His family said:
“We possess the wealthiest name.
You may act as you wish.”
He replied:
“That is not enough; I beg to become a śramaṇa.
Bestow upon me the Dharma robe, alms bowl, and staff, so that with these I may aid the masses.”
His parents consented.
Traveling to teach, he passed through a great kingdom.
In that kingdom was a wealthy family who also understood many texts.
Observing Pǔshī’s dignified appearance, his mind serene and pure like heavenly gold,
possessing the marks of a supreme sage,
destined to be a hero of the world,
they said to Pǔshī:
“I have an unworthy daughter; I wish to offer her to serve you.”
He replied:
“Very well.
Wait until I return.”
He then boarded a ship, crossed the sea, landed, and entered the mountains.
Reaching a deserted place, he saw in the distance a silver city.
A poisonous snake encircled the city seven times,
its body a hundred arm-spans thick, raising its head to look.
Pǔshī thought:
“This one has harmful intent; I shall generate compassion.”
The snake’s poison immediately ceased, and it lowered its head to sleep.
He stepped on its head and entered the city.
The celestial beings in the city saw him
and joyfully said:
“We have long revered your sage virtue; now you have come soaring here.
Truly our heartfelt wish.”
They asked him to stay for thirty days.
Pǔshī entrusted his affairs to the nearby ministers.
He personally received offerings and meals.
When the offerings were completed, they presented him with a bright moon pearl.
The pearl illuminated forty thousand li.
If he made a wish, all treasures would be fulfilled.
“If you later attain Buddhahood, may I become your disciple.”
Pǔshī said: “Agreed.”
He then proceeded further.
He saw a golden city, with a poisonous snake encircling it fourteen times,
its massive body twice as large as before, raising its head several zhang high.
Pǔshī again entered a state of compassionate concentration, and the snake lowered its head.
He stepped on it and entered the city.
The celestial beings inside met him joyfully, saying:
“We have long revered your spiritual radiance; your arrival here is excellent.
We wish you to stay for one hundred eighty days.
We shall provide offerings.”
After this period, he bid farewell.
The celestial beings again gave him a divine pearl,
illuminating two hundred thousand li.
Whatever he wished, all treasures would fill it.
“If you attain the Way, may I become your disciple, possessing supreme spiritual powers.”
He then proceeded further and saw a lapis lazuli city.
There was another poisonous snake, its body encircling the city twenty-one times,
raising its head, glaring angrily at the city gate.
Again, he generated compassionate concentration, vowing to save all beings.
The poison subsided, and it lowered its head. He stepped on it and entered the city.
The celestial beings rejoiced as before.
They requested him to stay for three periods.
“We wish to fulfill your aspirations.” When the period ended, he bid farewell.
They again gave him a divine pearl, illuminating one million six hundred thousand li.
Wherever the pearl was, all treasures followed,
filling its radiance; whatever he desired, nothing was unobtainable.
“When you attain right enlightenment, may I become your disciple, possessing the brightest wisdom.”
He said: “You shall certainly attain your wish.”
Pǔshī obtained the pearls and returned to his former dwelling.
The sea deities all gathered and deliberated:
“In our vast sea, only these three pearls are our glory and splendor.
The ascetic has obtained them all.
We would rather lose all our treasures than lose these pearls.”
The sea deities transformed into ordinary people
and stood before Pǔshī, saying:
“I have heard that the benevolent one has obtained the world’s treasures.
May I see them?”
He showed them.
The deity clapped his hands and snatched them away.
Pǔshī said:
“I endured dangers and crossed the sea to obtain these treasures, wishing to aid the destitute.
How can they be snatched away by this deity?”
He said: “Return my pearls, or I will drain your sea.”
The deity said:
“The vast sea is deep and wide; who can empty it?”
Heaven urged the wind to blow.
Pǔshī said:
“Before Buddha Dìngguāng,
I vowed to attain the power of the Way, to overturn all seas,
to lift Mount Sumeru, shake heaven and earth, and move all realms.
The Buddha granted my aspiration.
Now I have attained it.
Today, you ghostly creature, with your hair-thin strength,
how can you withstand my power of true reality?”
He then joined his two feet, scooped up the sea water, and cast it beyond the Iron Ring Mountains.
The god Biànjìngtiān said:
“In the past, before Buddha Dìngguāng, I heard his vow:
‘He will certainly become a World-Honored One and deliver us beings.’”
He descended to assist in scooping the water, removing eight-tenths of it.
The sea deity, terrified, said:
“This water is nearly gone!
My dwelling is ruined!”
He immediately returned the pearls.
Pǔshī followed the path, giving alms.
In every country he passed, there were no longer any poor people.
Everywhere, kings reformed their conduct,
adopting the five precepts and ten good deeds as the state’s law and governance.
They opened prisons and granted great amnesties.
Their compassion reached all beings, and they eventually attained Buddhahood.
Pǔshī was my own body.
The father was King Báijìng.
The mother was my mother Shěmiào.
The ascetic’s daughter at that time is now Qiúyí.
The celestial being in the silver city at that time is now Ānán.
The celestial being in the golden city is Mùlián.
The celestial being in the lapis lazuli city is Shèlìfú.
Ānán addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, when I entered the city of Shèwèi,
I saw the Bodhisattva Zhòngshèng Wáng sharing a bed with a woman.
I thought he had committed impurity, and my mind was filled with doubt, wondering if he was no different from an ordinary person.
Could it be that those who practice the pure life, under the teachings of the Tathāgata, might still harbor thoughts of seeing, hearing, and thinking?
At the moment I spoke these words, the three-thousand-great-thousandfold world shook six times.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Zhòngshèng Wáng immediately sprang up and remained suspended in mid-air,
forty-nine feet above the ground.
He replied to Ānán, saying:
'Could one who has violated precepts and committed impurity possibly leap up and remain suspended in the void?
In the presence of the Tathāgata...'
Ānán prostrated himself and repented of his fault.
'How could I have been so prejudiced as to seek out the shortcomings of a great dragon?'
The Buddha told Ānán:
'That woman
was, in a past life, the partner of Zhòngshèng Wáng for a hundred lifetimes.
Her old affections were not yet severed, and she was deeply attached to Zhòngshèng Wáng's appearance.
She uttered a vow, saying:
"If Zhòngshèng Wáng grants my wish and allows me to have my pleasure, I will follow his teachings."
At that time, Zhòngshèng Wáng knew her thoughts in his mind.
In the early morning, properly attired, he entered her chamber.
Immediately, he recited a verse.
The woman, overjoyed,
rose from her seat and threw herself to the ground.
She paid homage, blamed herself, confessed her fault, and repented.
For Zhòngshèng Wáng, she praised him with a verse, saying:
At that time, Zhòngshèng Wáng imparted to that woman the essential teaching.
After this woman's body, in ninety-nine kalpas, she will attain Buddhahood,
and be named the Tathāgata Who Has Transcended Countless Hundreds of Thousands of Sufferings.
When Śākyamuni Buddha was a bodhisattva,
he was named Dà Sàtāpó.
While crossing the great sea, a fierce wind wrecked the ship.
He said to the merchants: "Hold onto my hair, hands, and feet, and I will ferry you across."
After everyone had hold of him, he killed himself with a knife.
The law of the sea water does not retain dead bodies.
Immediately, a swift wind blew him to the shore.
The bodhisattva was on a mountain,
sitting upright with a compassionate mind, meditating without moving.
A bird nested on his head. He felt the bird on his crown,
and fearing the eggs would fall, he did not shift or sway his body.
He abandoned his body and remained motionless in that place until the birds grew wings.
But as long as they could not yet fly, he never left.
Knowing this himself, he then spoke this verse:
'For countless kalpas, I have diligently sought the Way.
From the beginning, I never slackened or rested until I attained Buddhahood.
Transcending nine kalpas, I appeared before Maitreya.
I recall in the past, when the people of the country were poor, I felt compassion in my heart.
I then wished to enter the sea to seek the wish-fulfilling pearl.
A great assembly of people gathered, raised the sails to catch the wind,
and went to the Dragon King of the sea to request the wish-fulfilling pearl from his head.
The Dragon King, hearing that he wished to aid the poor, gave him the pearl.
At that time, the various merchants each gathered treasures, all obtaining what they needed, and returned by ship.
The various dragons and spirits of the sea all discussed together, saying:
"This wish-fulfilling pearl is the supreme treasure of the sea.
It is not something that ordinary worldly people should obtain.
How can we allow the sea to be diminished for the benefit of Jambudvīpa?
It would truly be a pity.
We must devise a plan to take back the pearl; we cannot lose it."
At that time, the dragons and spirits surrounded them day and night, wanting to seize the pearl.
The guide, virtuous and venerable, by the power of the wish-fulfilling pearl, could not be robbed.
After crossing the sea,
the bodhisattva leaped for joy and stood by the seashore.
Bowing his head and lowering his hands, he invoked a blessing for the sea gods.
He placed the pearl around his neck.
At that time, the sea dragon spirits, finding an opportunity, caused the pearl to fall into the sea.
The guide, stirred with emotion, thought: "I journeyed into the sea,
braved difficulties by ship, endured countless hardships, and only then obtained this treasure.
It should save the multitude from want.
But now the sea gods have instead caused it to fall into the sea."
He ordered his attendants by the shore to bring vessels.
"I will scoop up the sea water until I reach the muddy bottom.
If I do not retrieve the pearl, I will never rest."
Immediately, he began scooping the water, disregarding his own life.
The water naturally flowed and all entered the vessels.
The various sea dragon spirits saw this and were filled with fear.
"This person's majestic power and diligent strength
are truly unparalleled in the world.
The water will soon be exhausted."
They immediately brought the pearl and returned it with apologies.
"We merely tested you, not expecting such diligent strength and power.
In heaven and on earth, none can surpass you."
The guide obtained the treasure and brought it back to the country.
He caused it to rain down the seven treasures to supply the world, bringing peace and stability to all.
That guide was my own body.
In the past, the bodhisattva entered the sea with five hundred merchants to gather treasures.
After several months at sea, they obtained a heavy load of treasures.
As they were about to return to their homeland, they encountered a storm on the way.
Thunder shook the earth, and water spirits gathered like clouds.
They surrounded them like a city, fire shot from their eyes, and waves surged, flooding the mountains.
The people cried out:
'We are going to die!'
Their faces changed with terror as they looked up to heaven, begging for mercy.
The bodhisattva, sorrowful, thought to himself:
'My quest for Buddhahood is solely for the sake of all beings.
The sea gods detest corpses.
To save the multitude by risking my life—
this is the noble work of an enlightened being.
If I do not shed my blood and pour it into the sea,
to appease the sea gods' displeasure, the people on the ship will never reach the shore.'
He said to the people:
'All of you, join hands and hold onto me.'
The people obeyed his command.
The bodhisattva then drew a knife and harmed himself.
The sea gods, moved by his virtue, drifted the ship to shore.
All the people were saved.
The people on the ship embraced the corpse and wailed, saying:
'This must be a bodhisattva, no ordinary person.'
They stamped their feet and cried out to heaven:
'We would rather our lives end here
than lose such a supremely virtuous one.'
Their sincere words moved the heavens above.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, witnessed the bodhisattva's great compassion.
Śakra descended and said:
'This supremely virtuous bodhisattva will become a holy hero.
I shall now revive him.'
He poured divine medicine into his mouth
and anointed his entire body with it.
The bodhisattva immediately revived, suddenly sat up, and greeted the people.
Śakra filled his ship with precious treasures,
a thousand times more than before.
They then returned to their homeland, where relatives met, and all were joyful.
They aided the poor and relieved the needy, bestowing kindness upon all beings.
They propagated the Buddhist scriptures, enlightening the ignorant and deluded.
The king of that country, impressed by the bodhisattva's virtue, came to receive his pure teachings.
The ruler was benevolent, the ministers loyal, the whole land upheld precepts, and every household had filial sons.
The country prospered, poisons ceased, and the common people rejoiced.
After death, they were reborn in heaven, forever free from all sufferings.
The bodhisattva, through countless kalpas of diligent effort without rest, finally attained Buddhahood.
The one who killed himself to save the multitude—that was my own body.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, is Maitreya.
The five hundred merchants are the five hundred Arhats now seated here.'
At that time, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the dust particles of a thousand worlds
sprang up from the earth, united in mind, joined their palms, and gazed up at the Honored One's countenance.
They addressed the Buddha, saying:
'After the Buddha's nirvāṇa,
wherever the World-Honored One's manifested bodies are, in the lands and places of parinirvāṇa, we will extensively preach this sūtra.
We ourselves also wish to obtain this true, pure, great Dharma, to receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, write, and make offerings to it.'

At that time, the World-Honored One, in the presence of Mañjuśrī and others—immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas who long resided in the Sahā World, as well as all the śrāvakas, humans, non-humans, and all beings—
extended his broad, long tongue upward to the Brahma-world.
From all his pores, he emitted immeasurable colored lights,
all illuminating everywhere throughout the ten-direction worlds.
The Buddhas seated on lion thrones under various jeweled trees did likewise.
Once there was a monk who was diligent and upheld the precepts, never violating them from the start.
He lived in a monastery.
What he recited was the Prajñāpāramitā.
All who heard this monk’s voice rejoiced.
There was a young boy, just seven years old, herding cattle outside the city.
From afar he heard the monk chanting the sūtra.
Following the sound, he went to the temple to listen and understood immediately.
His expression showed great joy, and he asked the monk.
The monk’s answer did not satisfy him.
The boy, in turn, explained its meaning, which was so profound and wonderful, something he had never heard before.
Hearing this, the monk sighed in admiration of the boy.
He possessed such wisdom—he was no ordinary person.
At that time, the boy left and returned to where the cattle were.
The calf he was herding had scattered and run into the mountains.
The boy followed its tracks and encountered a tiger, which killed him.
He was reborn as the son of the chief wife of a wealthy elder.
While the wife was pregnant, she could speak the Prajñāpāramitā from her mouth.
From morning till night, she never ceased.
The elder’s household had never before followed the Dharma.
They found the wife strange, saying she was speaking nonsense and calling it a ghost sickness.
They consulted diviners and exorcists, but none could understand it.
Everyone inside and outside the household was worried and fearful.
At that time, the monk entered the city to beg for alms and came to the elder’s gate.
From afar, he heard the sound of the sūtra and was greatly delighted.
He asked the elder, “Who inside is reciting such a profound sūtra with such a wonderful voice?”
The elder replied,
“My wife has a ghost sickness.
Day and night she speaks nonsense without ceasing.”
The monk replied,
“This is not a ghost sickness.
She is reciting a profound sūtra with deep meaning.
I suspect the child she is carrying is a disciple of the Buddha.”
The elder’s mind was set at ease.
He then invited the monk to stay and provided him with food.
When the months were fulfilled, she gave birth to a boy.
There was no foul discharge.
As soon as the boy was born, he joined his palms, knelt upright, and recited the Prajñāpāramitā.
After giving birth, the wife returned to her original state.
It was as if she had awakened from a dream, remembering nothing.
The elder gathered the monks to see the boy reciting the sūtra without any hindrance.
At that time, all the monks focused their minds on observing this boy.
The elder asked,
“What is this?”
The monk replied,
“He is a true disciple of the Buddha.
Do not be alarmed or doubtful.
Take good care of him.
When this boy grows up, he will become a teacher for all people.
We will all learn from him.”
By the age of seven, he fully understood the subtle and profound teachings.
He surpassed all others with his boundless wisdom.
All the monks studied under him.
If there were errors or omissions in the sūtras,
he would revise and complete what was lacking.
Whenever the boy went out or stayed somewhere,
he would teach people, inspiring them to aspire to the Great Vehicle.
All five hundred members of the elder’s household, both inside and outside,
studied under the boy, aspired to the Great Vehicle, and all engaged in Buddhist practices.
Wherever the boy taught—in the city, suburbs, or markets—
eighty-four thousand people were inspired to seek the supreme path.
Five hundred became his disciples.
When the monks heard this, their minds were set at ease, they aspired to the Great Vehicle, and all attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
“That boy was I in a past life.
The monk at that time was the Buddha Kāśyapa.
The Bodhisattva was Śakra, the lord of gods.
He focused on suffering, emptiness, and the mark of no-self.
When sitting, he contemplated;
when traveling, he taught.
He pitied the foolish and loved the wise, diligently and tirelessly.
Seeing his old friend reborn as a woman,
the wife of a wealthy man, deluded by wealth and beauty,
unaware of impermanence, living in the market and sitting in a shop,
Śakra transformed into
a merchant and sat beside the woman.
The merchant gazed intently and smiled.
The woman found it strange.
Beside her, a child was playing with a drum.
The merchant smiled again.
Someone’s father was ill, and the son sacrificed an ox.
The merchant also smiled.
There was a woman holding a child.
The child scratched its mother’s cheek until blood flowed down her neck.
The merchant smiled again.
The wealthy man’s wife asked,
‘You sit before me, smiling incessantly.
While I am playing with my child, why do you laugh?’
The merchant replied,
‘You are my good friend—have you forgotten me now?’
The woman was puzzled and grew even more displeased.
She found the merchant’s words strange.
The merchant continued,
‘The reason I smiled at you playing with your child
is that the child was your former father.
His spirit is now reborn as your son.
In one lifetime, you do not recognize your father—how much more so over many lifetimes?
The child playing with the drum was originally an ox.
After the ox died, it was reborn as its owner’s son.
The family used the ox’s hide to make this drum.
Now the child beats it, unaware it was once his own body.
The one sacrificing the ox for his father’s illness hopes for a cure,
but it is like taking poison to heal a disease.
The father will become an ox and be slaughtered for many lifetimes.
Now this sacrificial ox will again take on a human form.
The child scratching its mother’s face—
the child was originally a concubine.
The mother was the principal wife.
Out of jealousy, the wife often treated her cruelly.
The concubine harbored resentment.
The wife was later reborn as the principal wife’s child.
Now she scratches her face and injures her body but dares not resent it.
The husband’s heart is fickle.
Once hated, now loved—what constancy is there?
If one does not know even one lifetime, how much less many kalpas?’
The sūtra says,
‘Those who are blinded by form obstruct the great path.
Those devoted to false sounds do not hear the Buddha’s voice.’
That is why I smiled.
Worldly glory is like lightning, vanishing in an instant.
You should realize it is impermanent and not associate with fools.
Cultivate virtue and the six pāramitās.
I will return someday and surely visit your home.’
Having said this, he vanished.
The woman, bewildered, returned home.
With a purified heart, she respectfully awaited.
Later, he indeed appeared at her gate.
His appearance was ugly, and his clothes were ragged.
He said, ‘My friend is inside.
Call her out.’
The gatekeeper went in to report, describing his appearance.
The woman came out and said,
‘You are not my friend.’
Śakra smiled and said,
‘I have changed my form and clothes, and you do not recognize me.
How much less over different lifetimes?’
He added,
‘Diligently serve the Buddha.
The Buddha is hard to encounter.
It is difficult to make offerings to monks of high conduct.
Life lasts but a breath—do not fall into worldly delusions.’
Having spoken, he vanished.
The whole country rejoiced and sighed in admiration.
Each took up the practice of the six pāramitās, the supreme conduct.
The Buddha told Śāriputra,
‘The woman was Maitreya.
Śakra, the lord of gods, was I.’
In a past age, in the country of Yōubōluóyuè,
the five grains were abundant and the people were numerous.
In that country was a king named Bōluó.
Earlier, there was a courtesan of beautiful appearance.
She went to another house and encountered a woman who had just given birth and wanted to eat her own child.
The courtesan asked her.
She replied, "I am hungry."
The courtesan said,
"Wait, and I will find food for you."
She answered,
"I am desperately hungry.
Before you leave the house, I will starve to death.
How can I wait for you?"
The courtesan thought,
"If I take her child away, the mother will starve to death.
If I leave it, she will eat it. I must ensure both are saved."
The courtesan cut off her own breasts and gave them to the woman to eat.
The mother then ate them.
The courtesan asked,
"Are you full now?"
She replied, "I am full."
The courtesan returned home.
A man came to the courtesan's house.
Seeing her, he said,
"Who cut your breasts?"
He felt great pity and no longer desired her.
The man asked,
"Sister, please show me this utmost sincerity."
The courtesan said,
"If my sincerity is true, let my breasts be restored."
Immediately, both breasts were restored as before.
Śakro Devānām Indraḥ saw the merit of this courtesan's generosity.
Fearing she might take his throne,
he transformed into a Brahmin and went to her house.
The courtesan then filled a golden bowl with rice and gave it to the Brahmin.
But the Brahmin refused to accept it.
The woman asked, "Venerable one, why do you not accept?"
He replied,
"I do not need food.
I heard you gave your breasts in generosity. Is this true?"
She replied, "It is true."
The Brahmin said,
"Do you regret giving your breasts in generosity?"
The woman said,
"If my sincerity in giving my breasts was without any other thought,
may I be reborn as a man."
As soon as she spoke, she transformed.
At that time, the king of Yōubōluóyuè,
having ruled the country for fifty years,
died when his lifespan ended.
The ministers and attendants heard that the courtesan had been reborn as a man.
They thought,
"He should be made king."
So they invited and established him as king.
After being established, he delighted in generosity,
giving whatever was needed to all.
He taught the entire country to observe the Eight Precepts.
Thus the country was well-governed, the people were joyful, and lifespans were extended.
The king then thought,
"Although I have given generously, I have not yet given my body.
Giving one's body is truly difficult."
Then the king anointed his body with fragrant ghee,
entered an empty mountain, and lay upon a rocky cliff.
All kinds of birds came to peck at him.
After his death, he was born into a Brahmin family.
He was handsome and beautiful.
When he grew up, he secretly went to the market.
Seeing the poor begging and being sold, he sorrowfully said,
"If these people were wealthy and happy, they would not be sold."
He hurried to tell his parents, begging to become a monk.
His parents did not permit it.
So he did not eat for five days.
Relatives and friends came to persuade him.
The youth would not agree.
The relatives advised his parents to allow him to pursue the path.
His parents looked at each other, wept sadly, and allowed it.
The youth cared for his parents for six or seven days,
then circumambulated them three times, paid his respects, and left.
He went to a grove and saw two ascetics.
They had attained the five supernatural powers and sat in the open practicing the path.
They performed arduous practices for the sake of the people.
The youth then sat beneath a tree in the grove.
Through meditation and arduous practice, he attained the five supernatural powers.
His diligence and vigor surpassed those of the two ascetics.
According to the ascetics' practice, when fruits fell from the trees by themselves, they would eat them, but they would not pick them from the trees.
The ascetics went together to seek fruits and melons.
They saw a pregnant tigress.
The youth ascetic said to the two ascetics,
"The tigress will soon give birth.
Having been hungry for days, she may eat her own cubs.
Who will offer his body to feed her?"
Maitreya said,
"I will offer my body to feed her."
When they returned from gathering fruits, they saw the tigress had already given birth.
She was extremely hungry and about to eat her cubs.
The youth ascetic said to the two ascetics,
"The tigress has given birth and is hungry, about to eat her cubs.
Who will offer his body to save her from hunger and suffering?" They went together to where the tigress was.
The tigress opened her eyes and bared her teeth toward the two ascetics.
The ascetics, afraid, flew into the sky.
One of them said,
"Is this your utmost sincerity?
You vowed to offer your body to the tiger, so why are you flying away now?"
The other ascetic felt pity for him and shed tears.
Looking around, he saw nothing.
The youth ascetic then took a sharp knife, cut his arm, and let the blood flow.
He did this in seven places, letting the blood flow into the tigress's mouth for her to drink, then threw himself before the tigress, offering his body to feed her.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Know that the courtesan of that time, the one who was made king, and the Brahmin's son who offered his body to feed the tiger were all my former selves.
The two ascetics of that time were the two Bodhisattvas Kāśyapa and Maitreya.
I diligently practiced generosity with my body for sixty kalpas.
Thus I surpassed Maitreya by nine kalpas and attained Buddhahood.
Long ago, Śākyamuni Bodhisattva was a great king
named Sàpódá.
He generously gave to all beings, granting whatever they sought, and compassionately relieved their hardships.
The gods, spirits, and dragons all said,
"The position of Lord of the Gods is not permanently held by anyone.
Recognizing his lofty conduct, great compassion, wisdom, and abundant merit,
he should become it after death."
Fearing the king would take his heavenly position, [Indra] went to test him to verify the truth.
Indra appeared and commanded a border king,
"Now that human king's compassion is vast and profound, his merit and virtue are lofty.
I fear he aspires to take my position as Lord of the Gods.
He then transformed into a hawk,
and the border king became a dove.
The dove fled under the king's feet, trembling and saying,
"Great King, have pity! My life is at its end!"
The king said,
"Do not fear, I will save you now."
The hawk soon arrived and said,
"That dove came from me.
The dove is my food. I beg the king to return it."
The king said,
"The dove came seeking to save its life. I cannot break my promise from beginning to end.
If you desire meat, I will give you a hundred times its weight."
The hawk said,
"I only wish to have the dove, not other meat."
The king said,
"What can I give you to make you release the dove and leave happily?"
The hawk said,
"If the king is compassionate and merciful to all beings, then cut flesh from your own body and exchange it for the dove. I will gladly accept."
The king was greatly pleased.
He cut flesh from his own thigh and weighed it against the dove to make them equal.
The dove was heavier, so he cut flesh from his entire body,
but still could not balance the scale. The pain of his wounds was immeasurable.
The king, with compassionate endurance, commanded a nearby minister,
"Kill me and weigh my marrow to make it equal to the dove.
I uphold the Buddha's profound precepts to save beings from danger and hardship.
Though there are many afflictions, they are like a slight breeze—how can they move Mount Tai?"
The hawk, seeing the king's resolve, both resumed their original forms.
Bowing their heads to the ground, they said,
"Great King, what is your aspiration that you endure such suffering?"
He said, "I do not aspire to be Indra, Lord of the Gods, or a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
I see beings sunk in blindness and darkness, not seeing the Three Jewels,
indulging in evil deeds and casting themselves into the hell of no choice.
I feel compassion for them.
I vow to seek Buddhahood
to rescue beings and enable them to attain Nirvāṇa."
Indra, astonished, said,
"I foolishly thought the king desired to take my position.
Thus I disturbed you. How can I repent?"
The king said,
"If my body's wounds heal and become as before, my aspiration to always give generously remains."
Indra sent a heavenly physician with divine medicine to apply to him.
His wounds immediately healed, and his strength and appearance surpassed before.
Indra bowed, circumambulated the king three times, and joyfully departed.
The Buddha was traveling in the city of Wángshèchéng.
There was a woman of pleasure.
Named Shàng Jīnguāng Shǒu.
She was upright, beautiful, and exquisite, with a complexion like polished purple gold.
The king, the crown prince, great ministers, elders, and others developed lustful minds; wherever she went, they would follow her.
Men and women, young and old, all pursued her.
At that time, on another day, Shàng Jīnguāng Shǒu
went with the son of Elder Wèi Wén to the market to buy goods.
They presented offerings, prepared fine food, and together went to the pleasure garden.
At that time, Wénshū Shīlì emerged from his quiet chamber.
He gave rise to great compassion, grieving for all living beings.
"Who among the people can be persuaded and transformed to arouse the Great Vehicle?"
He saw Shàng Jīnguāng Shǒu
riding in the same carriage with the son of Elder Wèi Wén, heading to the pleasure garden, and thought she could be transformed.
Wénshū Shīlì then transformed his body into that of a youth.
Upright and supremely exquisite, his countenance surpassing that of a heavenly being, all who saw him were delighted.
The robes he wore illuminated forty *li*.
Observing the path along which the pleasure woman was traveling, he stood before it.
The robes and carriage of the elder's son and Shàng Jīnguāng Shǒu,
compared to those of Wénshū Shīlì,
were like gathering ink beside a bright pearl.
Shàng Jīnguāng Shǒu saw Wénshū Shīlì's countenance, heroic and exquisite like that of a heavenly son.
The radiance of his body was dazzling and hard to match.
Coveting his robes and their brilliant light,
she thought to herself:
"Now I wish to abandon this elder's son,
dismount from the carriage, leave him, and amuse myself with this one.
I would obtain these clothes."
As soon as this thought arose,
Wénshū Shīlì established his majestic spiritual power to pacify her mind.
A heavenly king transformed into a man
and said to that woman:
"Stop, stop!
Why do you give rise to such a frivolous, pleasure-seeking mind?
For what reason?
Such a person as this does not aspire to sensual desires."
The woman said, "Why?"
The heavenly king replied:
"This person is named Wénshū Shīlì, a Bodhisattva.
He is able to fulfill the wishes of all people.
Seeing the minds of sentient beings and what they seek, he does not oppose their will."
The woman thought:
"From what I have now heard, he will certainly bestow upon me exquisite and fine robes."
She dismounted from the carriage and said respectfully:
"Benevolent one,
I wish that you would kindly bestow these robes upon me."
Wénshū Shīlì replied:
"Elder sister,
if you can arouse the mind of unsurpassed, true, and right enlightenment,
then I will bestow the robes upon you."
The woman said, "Very well,"
and immediately aroused the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment, upholding the five precepts.
In a past age,
in the country of Jiāyí, there was an elder.
He had no sons.
Both husband and wife had lost their sight.
Their heartfelt wish was to enter the mountains to seek the supreme truth.
They cultivated purity of mind and delighted in solitude.
At that time, there was a Bodhisattva named Yīqiè Miàojiàn.
He thought to himself:
"These people have raised a profound aspiration, yet their eyes see nothing.
If they enter the mountains, they are sure to encounter harm."
When the Bodhisattva's life ended, he vowed to be reborn into the elder's family and be named Shǎn.
He was supremely filial, benevolent, and upheld the ten virtues.
Day and night, with diligence, he served his parents,
as people serve the heavens.
When he passed ten years of age,
Shǎn knelt and said to his parents:
"You originally conceived the great resolve to enter the deep mountains,
seeking the aim of emptiness, tranquility, and the supreme, true path.
How can you abandon your original vow because of your son?
People in the world are impermanent and ever-changing.
Life is not like metal or stone; when its end arrives, there is no postponing it.
I wish you would follow your original intent and, while it is still timely, enter the mountains for purity.
I myself will provide for you without missing the proper times."
His parents then entered the mountains.
Shǎn gave all the family's wealth and possessions to the various poor people of the country.
Then he went with his parents and together they entered the mountains.
Shǎn, upon reaching the mountains, made a hut of cattails and prepared bedding, so it was neither cold nor hot, always just right.
In the first year in the mountains, the wild fruits were abundant, fragrant, and sweet to eat.
Spring water gushed forth, clear and cool.
In the ponds, lotuses bloomed in five colors, bright and pure.
Sandalwood and various trees were fragrant beyond the ordinary.
Different kinds of birds made musical sounds.
Lions, brown bears, tigers, wolves, and poisonous beasts
treated each other with kindness and no longer had harmful intent.
They ate grass and fruit without giving rise to fear.
Shǎn was so filial and compassionate he feared treading the ground would cause it pain.
Heavenly spirits and mountain spirits often took human form to comfort and assist him day and night.
Shǎn wore a deerskin garment and carried a pitcher to fetch water.
Deer and flocks of birds would also come to drink, unafraid and unhindered.
At that time, the king of Jiāyí country entered the mountains to hunt.
The king saw a flock of birds and deer by the water and drew his bow to shoot them.
The arrow mistakenly struck Shǎn in the chest.
Shǎn was struck by the poisoned arrow.
Raising his voice, he cried out loudly:
"Who has shot one arrow and killed three practitioners of the Way?"
The king, hearing a human voice, dismounted and went to Shǎn.
Shǎn said to the king:
"The elephant dies because of its tusks.
The rhinoceros dies because of its horn.
The kingfisher dies because of its feathers.
The deer dies because of its skin and flesh.
For what, then, do I now rightly die?"
The king asked Shǎn:
"Who are you, sir,
wearing a deerskin, no different from the birds and beasts?"
Shǎn said:
"I am a person of your kingdom.
I came with my blind parents to study the Way over twenty years ago.
Never before have we been harmed by tigers, wolves, poisonous creatures, or seen injustice.
Now I am further shot by the king."
At that very moment, a violent storm suddenly arose in the mountains, breaking trees.
A hundred birds mourned sorrowfully; lions, brown bears, running beasts, and their kind all cried out loudly.
The sun lost its brilliance; flowing springs dried up.
Flowers withered and died; thunder shook the earth.
Then the blind parents, startled, rose and said to each other:
"Shǎn went to fetch water long ago and has not returned.
Surely he has not been harmed by poisonous creatures?
The sounds of beasts and flying birds crying out are not as usual.
Winds rise from all sides; trees are broken and destroyed.
There must be some calamity."
The king at that time was terrified and greatly reproached himself.
"What I have done is without form.
I intended to shoot a deer.
The arrow mistakenly struck and killed a practitioner of the Way. My sin is very grave.
Because of my greed for a little meat, I receive great calamity.
I now offer all the treasures and stored wealth of my country,
my palaces, courtesans, mounds, walls, and cities to save this son's life."
Then the king went forward and with his hand tried to pull the arrow from Shǎn's chest.
It was too deep and could not be removed.
Flying birds and running beasts gathered like clouds from all sides, their cries shaking the mountains.
The king grew even more terrified.
His three hundred sixty joints, joint by joint, all trembled.
Shǎn said to the king:
"It is not the king's fault, but caused by my own past transgressions.
I do not begrudge my body and life.
Only I pity
my blind parents, already aged and declining, their two eyes again blind.
Once without me, they too will surely perish, with no one to care for them.
Because of this, I am distressed,
not because of the poison and pain."
The king spoke again:
"I would rather enter the hells for a hundred kalpas, receiving punishment, so that Shǎn may live."
He knelt toward Shǎn and repented his fault.
"If this son's life ends, I will not return to my country but will stay in the mountains to serve your parents as you did in your time. Do not be concerned.
All the heavenly dragons and spirits shall bear witness; I will not break this vow."
Shǎn, hearing the king's vow,
though struck by a poisoned arrow, felt joy and delight in his heart; even in death he held no regret.
"I entrust my parents to the great king.
Serving practitioners of the Way, sins of the present life are extinguished, and immeasurable merit is gained."
The king said:
"Tell me where your parents are, and before you die, let me inform them."
Shǎn then pointed the way.
"Go from here; it is not far.
You will see a grass hut.
My parents dwell there.
Go slowly, so as not to startle or frighten my parents.
Use skillful means to enlighten their understanding.
For me, thank my parents.
Impermanence has now arrived; I am about to pass to the next life.
I do not begrudge my life, but think of my parents, aged, their two eyes again blind.
Once without me, they will have nothing to rely on.
Because of this I am distressed, tormenting myself bitterly.
Death is the common lot, caused by past transgressions from which none escape.
Now I confess before my parents
all the evils I have committed since countless kalpas past.
Through this, sins are extinguished and merit arises.
May I and my parents meet life after life, never far apart.
May my parents preserve their years and longevity, free from worry and suffering.
May heavenly dragons, ghosts, and spirits always follow, protect, and assist; may calamities
and harms be dispelled."
The king then took several men and went to where the parents were.
After the king left,
Shǎn then breathed his last.
Birds and beasts cried out, circling over Shǎn's corpse.
They licked the blood from Shǎn's chest with their mouths.
The blind parents, hearing these sounds, grew even more fearful.
The king, walking swiftly, disturbed the grass and trees, rustling with human sound.
The parents said in alarm:
"Who is this? These are not my son's footsteps."
The king said: "I am the king of Jiāyí country.
Hearing that practitioners of the Way were in the mountains studying the Way, I have come to serve them."
The parents said:
"The great king's coming is good.
We trouble your majestic dignity to come far to this wild grassland.
Is the king's body well?
Are the palace ladies, the crown prince, the officials, and the people of the country all well?
Are the winds and rains harmonious, the five grains abundant and full, and neighboring countries not invading or harming?"
The king replied to the practitioners:
"By the grace of the practitioners, all is peaceful."
The king inquired of the blind parents:
"Coming to dwell in the mountains, your hearts must labor diligently and suffer hardship.
Among the trees, have flying birds and running beasts not harmed the practitioners?
In the mountains, with cold and heat following the seasons, are you presently at peace?"
The blind parents said:
"By the great king's profound grace, we are always at peace.
We have a filial son named Shǎn.
He always gathers fruit and fetches spring water for us, so we are constantly well-supplied.
In the mountains, winds and rains are harmonious; we lack nothing.
We have grass mats to sit on and fruit to eat.
Shǎn has gone to fetch water and should return soon."
The king, hearing this, was heartbroken and tears fell.
He then said:
"I, sinful and without form, entered the mountains to hunt.
Seeing a flock of deer by the water, I drew my bow and shot.
The arrow mistakenly struck Shǎn, so I have come to tell you."
The parents, hearing this, threw themselves to the ground as if
a great mountain had collapsed and the earth had shaken.
The king then went forward to help and support them.
The parents wailed, looking up to heaven, saying themselves:
"Our son was filial and compassionate, fearing to tread the ground would cause it pain.
What crime did he have that you shot and killed him?
Earlier, the wind rose, trees [broke], and a hundred birds mourned sorrowfully.
We suspected our son had died."
The parents wept and wailed.
The father said:
"Enough.
Human life must end; it cannot be turned back.
Now let us ask the king:
Where did you shoot Shǎn? Is he now alive or dead?"
The king recounted Shǎn's words. The parents fainted from emotion.
"Once without our son, we too shall surely die.
We beg the king to lead us two to go to the corpse."
The king then led the blind parents to the corpse.
The father embraced his feet, the mother embraced his head, and looking up to heaven they cried out loudly.
The mother then licked the wound on Shǎn's chest with her tongue.
"May the poison enter my mouth.
I am already old.
My eyes see nothing.
Let my body substitute for my son's.
Let Shǎn live and me die.
In death I hold no regret.
If Shǎn's supreme filial piety is known by heaven and earth,
then the arrow should be drawn out, the poison removed, and Shǎn should live again."
Then the seat of Śakra, Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, immediately shook.
With his heavenly eye, he saw the two practitioners embracing their son and wailing.
The news reached even the fourth heaven, Tuṣita.
All the heavenly palaces shook.
Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings, from the fourth heaven,
in the time it takes a man to bend or stretch his arm, descended before Shǎn.
They poured a divine elixir into Shǎn's mouth.
As the medicine entered Shǎn's mouth, the arrow drew itself out, and he revived as before.
The parents were startled and overjoyed.
Seeing Shǎn, who had died, come back to life, their two eyes both opened.
Flying birds and beasts all rejoiced greatly.
The wind ceased, clouds dispersed, and the sun regained its double brilliance.
Spring water gushed forth; flowers bloomed in five colors; trees and flowers flourished twice as much as usual.
The king was overjoyed, unable to contain himself.
He bowed to Śakra, Lord of the Devas, then bowed again to the parents and to their son Shǎn.
"I wish to offer the wealth of my country to serve the practitioners."
Shǎn said:
The king then returned to comfort the people, instructing them all to uphold the precepts.
The king must no longer hunt and kill living creatures.
In this present life, his body will find no peace, and when his lifespan ends, he will fall into hell.
People dwell in the world where affection and love are but temporary.
Separation is long-lasting; nothing can be preserved forever.
The king, due to past meritorious virtues, has now become king.
Do not, because of attaining freedom, become self-indulgent and unrestrained.
The king repented and blamed himself.
From now on, he would follow Shǎn's teachings.
The several hundred followers all greatly rejoiced and upheld the Five Precepts.
The king then ordered that throughout the country, all blind parents like Shǎn's should
be supported and cared for, not abandoned.
Those who violate this will now be severely punished.
Thus, because Shǎn had brought life, the people of the country,
from high to low, taught each other to cultivate the Five Precepts and Ten Good Deeds.
Upon death, they would be reborn in heaven, with none falling into the three evil paths.
The Buddha told Ānán,
"The Shǎn of past destiny was my own body.
The blind father is now King Śuddhodana.
The blind mother is Queen Māyā.
The king of Jiāyí Country is you, Ānán.
The heavenly king Śakra at that time is Maitreya.
What enabled me to swiftly achieve the unsurpassed, true, and right enlightenment
was entirely due to the kindness of my parents' support and compassionate grace.
From death to life, it moved the heavens, dragons, spirits, and ghosts.
The profound kindness of parents is what filial children bring about.
Now I have become a Buddha and can liberate the people of the country,
all due to filial piety and the cultivation of virtue."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Kuàngyě manifested as a ghost body.
The Bodhisattva Sànzhī manifested as a deer body.
The Bodhisattva Huìjù manifested as a macaque body.
The Bodhisattva Lí'ài manifested as a goat body.
The Bodhisattva Jìnlòu manifested as a goose-king body.
Thus, these five hundred bodhisattvas,
each manifested and received various bodies.
Their bodies all emitted great fragrant light.
Each bodhisattva held a lamp in hand,
wishing to make offerings to the buddhas of the ten directions.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Yíxīn observed the five hundred people
and immediately knew they were all bodhisattvas.
He said to the ghost Kuàngyě,
"Good man,
why do you manifest such bodies to make offerings to the buddhas?"
The ghost Kuàngyě said,
"Good man,
in the distant past, ninety-one kalpas ago, there was a Buddha, the World-Honored One,
named Vipaśyin.
At that time, I,
together with these others, shared the same parents, were brothers, upheld the Five Precepts, and aroused the mind of enlightenment.
Wishing to tame and subdue all sentient beings,
we also made offerings to Śikhin, Viśvabhū, and Krakucchanda Buddha.
The great being Sànzhī, before that Buddha, made a great vow:
'May I, in future lives, use a ghost or spirit body to teach and transform sentient beings.
If there are wicked, evil ghosts,
I shall preach the Three Vehicles to tame and subdue them.
Only then shall I achieve the path of enlightenment.'
Also, twelve thousand great ghosts
in this world made great vows to tame and subdue sentient beings.
They further made a great vow:
'If there are evil ghosts who wish to destroy the true Dharma,
I shall subdue them.'
Therefore, I receive such a ghost body to tame, teach, and transform, establishing them in the Three Vehicles.
If there are sentient beings who stray from wholesome dharmas,
engaging in unwholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind,
this body will already be born in the three evil paths.
Or, due to mixed wholesome and unwholesome karma, they receive a ghost body.
Evil ghosts proliferate, while good ghosts are few.
I wish to tame and subdue them, manifesting and receiving this body.
I also cause kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras to abandon evil minds.
Good man,
there is a Vajra Hammer Dhāraṇī that causes all evil ghosts to be unable to do evil to those four castes.
Even birds and beasts all give rise to wholesome minds,
far removed from all evil and fear.
I made a great vow wishing to preach this dhāraṇī.
The Buddha was formerly in the Tuṣita Heaven.
At that time, the sage Vasu was in Jambudvīpa,
with six million two hundred thousand merchants, often acting as the caravan leader, entering the sea to seek treasures.
Sailing on a great ship, they wished to return to their homeland.
Midway, they encountered difficulties with a makara fish, great wind waves, and yakṣas.
These six million two hundred thousand people
immediately each made a vow to Maheśvara,
each promising one animal sacrifice.
Then they escaped the four difficulties
and reached their homeland.
Each prepared a sheep
to go to the heavenly temple.
At that time, Vasu silently thought,
'How can I now teach these merchants to do unwholesome deeds?'
He should devise a skillful means.
Immediately, he transformed into two people:
one a śramaṇa who had left home,
the other a brāhmaṇa householder. The brāhmaṇa then proclaimed among the crowd,
'The heavenly lord and the six million two hundred thousand people wish to go to the heavenly temple.'
At that time, the śramaṇa, from a distance on the road, saw this brāhmaṇa.
He asked,
'You and this great crowd, where do you intend to go?'
The householder said,
'I go to the heavenly temple to seek great benefit.'
The śramaṇa replied,
'I observe that you all wish to incur great misfortune.
How can this be great benefit?
Disputes and quarrels will not cease.'
At that time, the crowd asked the brāhmaṇa,
'Who is this person,
with such an appearance?'
The brāhmaṇa said,
'This is called a śramaṇa.'
The people asked,
'What does the śramaṇa say?'
He replied,
'Killing living beings to sacrifice to the heavens will incur great sin.'
The people said,
'This foolish śramaṇa, why speak such words?
Quickly go to the heavenly temple to gain great benefit.'
At that time, the brāhmaṇa said,
'Our great teacher is now at the heavenly temple; there is nothing he does not understand. We can go together to inquire.'
All said, 'Excellent!'
The śramaṇa, the brāhmaṇa, and the crowd went to the great sage's place.
At that time, the śramaṇa asked the great sage,
'Does killing living beings to sacrifice to the heavens lead to rebirth in heaven or falling into hell?'
The great sage replied,
'What foolish śramaṇa! Killing living beings to sacrifice to the heavens will certainly cause one to fall into hell.'
Vasu said,
'No.'
The śramaṇa said,
'If it does not cause one to fall, you should bear witness.'
At that time, Vasu immediately sank into the Avīci Hell.
The people, seeing this, cried, 'Alas, what a disaster! Such a thing has happened!
The great sage's wisdom and intelligence are now extinguished.
How much more will we not fall into hell?'
At that time, the people each released their sheep and fled in all directions.
They went to the mountains seeking various sages.
Having found sages, they received the sage's teachings.
After twenty-one years, each died and was reborn in Jambudvīpa.
At that time, I descended from the Tuṣita Heaven and was born in Jambudvīpa, in the pure white lineage of the king.
At that time, the six million two hundred thousand people were born in Śrāvastī, obtaining human bodies.
In the past, I first went to Śrāvastī, subdued these six million two hundred thousand people, caused them to leave home, and aroused the mind of enlightenment.
They were the merchants of old.
Good man,
the sage Vasu possessed such majestic spiritual power,
transforming such people to come to me.
In the past, in the eastern Jambudvīpa, there was a bodhisattva named Lúpóluó.
Due to the power of his vows, he was born here,
becoming a wheel-turning sage king ruling the four continents,
named Xūkōngjìng.
He told all sentient beings,
'Dwell securely in the Ten Good Deeds and the Three Vehicles.'
At that time, he gave alms to all without discrimination.
The beggars were innumerable, and treasures were insufficient.
He then asked his ministers,
'From where do such treasures arise?'
The ministers replied,
'Though dragons have them, they are only for sage kings.'
The five turbidities are heavy, afflictions are deep.
When human lifespan is one hundred years, he will certainly achieve anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
He will become a great dragon king, manifesting various treasuries.
In the chosen evil worlds,
in every place within the four continents,
in each continent, he will receive bodies seven times.
In each body, he will manifest immeasurable hundreds of thousands, millions, nayutas of treasuries.
Thus, in sequence, he will pervade the ten directions.

In the time of the five turbid evil ages, the various gods and humans, hundreds of thousands, millions, nayutas, in the sky, rain flowers, praise goodness, proclaiming as the heart wishes. The great crowd hears the sound.
The wheel-turning sage king Xūkōngjìng, the gods gave him the name 'All-Giver.'
At that time, the people each asked the king for his wives, court ladies, children, and so forth.
The king gave them all.
There was a beggar named Qīngguāngmíng,
who upheld the dog precept, asking the king for Jambudvīpa.
The king joyfully gave it, anointing him with fragrant water, and he succeeded to the sage kingship.
Moreover, he gained the people's support in serving this king.
The king's lifespan was no different.
'When I achieve Buddhahood, I shall give him a prediction, making him a one-life successor.'
The brāhmaṇa Lúzhì asked for his two feet.
The brāhmaṇa Yá asked for his two eyes.
The brāhmaṇa Jìngjiānláo asked for his two ears.
The Nirgrantha Xiǎng asked for his male organ.
The brāhmaṇa Mìwèi asked for his two hands.
He immediately cut and plucked them, giving them at that moment.
At that time, the various minor kings and ministers all said,
'Alas, foolish man!
How can you cut yourself? What value remains in the remaining flesh?'
They placed him in the wilderness; worms, beasts, vultures, and eagles all came to devour him.
'If my vow is to be accomplished,
may this body become a great mountain of flesh.
Blood-drinking, flesh-eating sentient beings all come here, freely drink and eat; the body will grow larger.'
The tongue root he gave up, due to the power of his vow,
'May I, in future lives, obtain a broad, long tongue.'
At that time, I died in Jambudvīpa.
Due to the power of my original vow, I was born as a dragon king,
named 'Manifesting Treasury.'
Immediately on the night of birth, I manifested hundreds of thousands, millions, nayutas of kinds,
various treasuries myself.
I proclaimed, 'Possessing all kinds of rare treasures, even mani pearls,
use them as you wish.'
Fully practicing the Ten Good Deeds,
arousing the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.
Thus, seven times receiving bodies,
each lifespan seventy-seven thousand million nayutas of hundreds of thousands of years.
Immeasurable treasuries were also like this.
The Buddha spoke to the Venerable Ānán.
In the past, there was a king
named Yuèmíng.
He was handsome and majestic, with awe-inspiring dignity.
Once, leaving his palace, he saw a blind man on the road.
Destitute and starving, the man was begging along the way.
He approached the king
and said, "Your Majesty, you alone are noble, secure, and happy.
I am poor and, moreover, blind."
The king, pitying him, asked the blind man, "What medicine can cure your ailment?"
The blind man replied,
"Only the king's eyes can heal my eyes."
Then the king removed his own two eyes and gave them to the blind man.
His heart was pure, without a trace of regret.
That King Yuèmíng was I myself.
The Buddha said, "The weight of Mount Sumeru can still be measured,
but the merit of my eye-giving cannot be calculated."
Once, a Bodhisattva was a great king.
He took refuge in the Three Jewels and fully upheld the Ten Virtues.
Weapons were not used, and there were no prisons.
The seasons were timely, grains were abundant, and the people were prosperous.
Even children recited them as small texts, and the entire country refrained from harmful speech.
The true teachings of the Six Perfections were recited by everyone.
At that time, there was a Brahmin who upheld pure conduct, dwelling peacefully in the mountains, aloof from worldly customs.
Thirsty at night, he went to drink
and mistakenly drank from a lotus pond cultivated by a citizen.
After drinking, he realized his mistake.
He went to the officials to confess, saying he had committed theft.
"I only beg Your Majesty to punish me according to the law."
The king said,
"This is natural water, not a tangible possession. What crime is there?"
The Brahmin replied,
"I drank without permission.
Is that not theft?
I beg the king to judge me."
The king said, "State affairs are numerous; please wait in the garden."
The prince had him wait deep inside the garden.
The king, overwhelmed by affairs, forgot for six days.
Suddenly remembering, he said,
"Where is the Brahmin?"
He urgently summoned him.
The Brahmin, upholding his precepts, had starved and thirsted for six days.
His body emaciated, he stumbled when rising.
The king saw him and wept, saying,
"My fault is grave!"
The queen laughed at this.
The king sent people to bathe him, prepared a feast, personally served him, bowed in repentance.
From then on, through endless cycles of birth and death, until just before attaining Buddhahood, he fasted for six years.
The Buddha told the bhikkhus,
"That king was I.
The queen was Jūyí.
The prince was Ráhula.
The king forgot the ascetic, causing him to starve for six days, and thus endured six years of retribution, ending only when the famine ceased.
After the six days, the king personally made offerings.
Therefore, after six years, the retribution ended and the Way was attained.
Jūyí laughed at it.
Thus, she now carries Ráhula for six years with a severe illness, and the prince, because the Brahmin was deeply confined in the garden,
spent six years in obscurity."
Once, a Bodhisattva was a great king.
He ruled the people with kindness, touring monthly.
For the poor, widowed, orphaned, and sick, he provided medicine and gruel.
Each time he toured, he ordered his attendants to carry clothing and medicine as needed.
The dead were buried.
His fame spread in all directions.
Indra, seeing his virtue, feared he would usurp his throne and sought to ruin him.
He transformed into an old Brahmin and begged the king for a thousand silver coins.
The king gave them.
The Brahmin said, "I live in hardship and fear theft; I wish to entrust them to the king."
The king said,
"There is no theft in my kingdom; I accept this heavy trust."
Indra then transformed into another Brahmin,
went to the palace gate,
and the king received him.
The Brahmin sighed, "Your Majesty's fame spreads everywhere; your virtue is rare.
I, a commoner, admire such nobility and wish to beg for this kingdom."
The king said, "Very well."
He then left with his wife and children, traveling lightly.
Indra again transformed into yet another Brahmin
and begged the king for his carriage.
The king gave him the carriage and horses.
He and his family proceeded on foot, resting by a mountain.
There was a monk with the five supernatural powers, a friend of the king.
Suddenly recalling the king's virtue and seeing he had lost his kingdom, he calmed his mind in meditation.
He saw Indra, greedy and jealous, seizing the kingdom, leaving the king exhausted and emaciated.
The monk, using his supernatural powers, suddenly appeared before the king and said, "What do you seek, toiling so?" The king replied,
"My intentions are already fully known to you."
The monk then transformed into a single-yoke carriage to send the king on his way.
Indra, as the Brahmin, again begged for this carriage.
Before reaching that country, still thousands of miles away,
Indra transformed into the previous Brahmin to demand the silver coins.
The king said,
"I gave away my kingdom and forgot about your money."
The king then pawned his wife and son to obtain a thousand coins to repay the Brahmin.
The wife served in the pawnbroker's household.
While bathing, she removed her pearls and jewels.
Indra transformed into a hawk and snatched the clothing and jewels away.
The woman said, "How could a servant steal?" She was arrested and imprisoned.
Her son slept with the pawnbroker's son.
Indra, at night, killed the pawnbroker's son.
The household seized the king's son and delivered him to prison.
Mother and son were imprisoned.
Starving, their forms ruined, they cried for help with no rescue.
Weeping all day, they were convicted and sentenced to execution.
The king earned a thousand silver coins
to ransom his wife and son.
Passing through the market, he saw them.
He then recalled the Buddhas, repented, and said,
"Is this due to my past karma?"
Calming his mind, he entered clarity and saw Indra's deeds.
A voice from the sky said,
"Why not kill him quickly?"
The king said,
"I have heard that Indra universally saves all beings, his sincere heart compassionate, nurturing more than a loving mother; all living beings receive his protection.
You, committing such evil, obtained the position of Indra.
Indra, harboring deep poison, his evil ripened, his crimes formed.
He will fall into the Great Hell.
Gods, dragons, and spirits all praised this."
The local king then released the wife and son from their crimes.
The two kings met and inquired about the origins.
Throughout the country, great and small, all shed tears.
The local king divided his kingdom to rule jointly.
The subjects of the former kingdom sought out their king and welcomed him back with the whole land.
The residents of the two kingdoms were both sorrowful and joyful.
That king was I.
The wife was Qiúyí.
The prince was Ráhula.
Indra was Devadatta.
The mountain-dwelling Brahmin was Śāriputra.
That other king was Maitreya.
The Buddha was in the kingdom of Shèwèi and addressed the bhikkhus.
In the past, a bodhisattva was a great king.
His name was Pǔmíng.
His compassion and kindness shone upon the ten directions, and he was praised and admired.
The people wished for his well-being as a filial son wishes for the peace of his parents.
In a neighboring kingdom, there was a king.
Named Āqún.
He governed with strict laws.
His strength was like that of a lion, swift enough to seize a flying eagle.
His cook, seeking meat, rushed to the market in the morning.
On the way, he saw a fresh corpse and took it to prepare a delicacy, mixing it with other meat.
The next day, when he prepared the meal, it was not as sweet as before.
The king reprimanded the head cook.
The cook confessed sincerely, bowing and knocking his head.
The king felt ashamed and said,
"Is human flesh sweet?"
He then ordered the cook to make this a regular practice.
Thus it is said:
Those who indulge in flavors have little benevolence.
When benevolence is thin, the heart of a wolf arises.
Wolves and dogs are greedy for the taste of meat,
and they harm living beings.
Therefore, the world hates them.
The cook, following the order, secretly killed people to supply the king's meals.
The ministers and people cried out in unison, driving him away.
The king fled into the mountains, waiting for other kings to come out.
He captured them with his followers,
like an eagle seizing sparrows.
He captured ninety-nine kings.
At that time, King Pǔmíng went out to observe the suffering and happiness of his people.
On the way, he met a Brahmin,
who said, "King, do not go out."
The king said,
"I have made a vow to go out; it is difficult to break my word."
Thus, he went out.
He was captured by Āqún.
The king said,
"I do not fear losing my life, but I regret breaking my promise."
Āqún said,
"What do you mean?"
The king explained in detail.
The Brahmin had seen him and warned him not to go out.
"I wish to see him once more and receive his solemn warning,
to fulfill my promise.
Even if I die afterward, I will have no regrets."
Āqún released him, allowing him to return briefly.
After seeing the Brahmin and offering him gold coins, the king received the warning and returned to Āqún with a smile.
Āqún asked,
"Your life is in danger today; why are you so joyful and smiling?"
He replied,
"The words of the World-Honored One are rarely heard in the three realms.
Now that I hold them in my heart, how can I regret losing my life?"
Āqún said again,
"I wish to hear this revered teaching."
The king took it and taught him.
Āqún was astonished and delighted, saying,
"The majestic World-Honored One expounds the four impermanences.
Not hearing or seeing this is called delusion and madness."
He immediately released all one hundred kings and allowed them to return to their countries.
Āqún repented and reformed, dwelling by a tree and reciting four verses daily.
After his death, his spirit was reborn as a crown prince.
He took a wife but was impotent, causing the king great worry.
The king then sought women from the country to transform him into a man.
Later, he became licentious and did not follow the path of chastity.
The king had him executed and displayed at a crossroads.
He ordered passersby,
"Poke his head with your fingers to humiliate him."
After ninety-nine people had done so, the crown prince died.
His soul underwent transformations, revolving endlessly.
He encountered the Buddha during his lifetime and was born in the kingdom of Shèwèi.
He lost his father early and lived alone with his mother, following the Brahmin path.
He was sincere in speech, trustworthy, and strong enough to defeat an elephant.
His teacher loved him, his friends respected him, and he was praised far and wide for his virtue.
Whenever his teacher traveled, he entrusted him with the household.
The teacher's wife, harboring lust, took his hand and tempted him with seductive words.
Āqún declined, saying,
"In this world, elders
are like fathers to me,
and women are like mothers to me.
How much more so the wife of my teacher?
I would rather burn my body than violate this command."
The teacher's wife, angered, pretended to retreat and plotted a scheme.
She said to her husband,
"Your disciple praises his own virtue, but it is enough to expose his faults." She fabricated his wrongdoing, and the Brahmin believed her.
The teacher asked Āqún, "Do you wish to become an immortal?"
He replied, "Yes."
"Then kill one hundred people and cut off their fingers,
and you will attain immortality."
Following the order, he took up his sword and killed everyone he met.
He obtained the fingers of ninety-nine people.
The people fled, and the kingdom was in turmoil.
Seeing his mother, he joyfully said,
"Mother, the number is complete; I will now become an immortal."
The Buddha, thinking that evil teachings were misleading the masses, made a universal vow.
He transformed into a śramaṇa and walked in front of Āqún.
Āqún said, "The number is complete."
The śramaṇa continued walking without stopping.
Āqún said, "Śramaṇa, stop!"
The śramaṇa replied, "I have stopped.
It is you who have not stopped."
Āqún's heart opened like clouds dispersing.
He prostrated himself on the ground, bowing and repenting.
With hands joined, he followed the śramaṇa back to the monastery and became a monk.
The Buddha explained his past actions and the four impermanences, and he attained the stream-entry path.
The king wished to punish him but, upon hearing this, sighed and told the Buddha he wished to see him. The Buddha said,
"A virtuous sage may open one eye to see him."
This was repeated three times.
Āqún replied,
"The light from my eyes is dazzling and hard to bear."
The king bowed and said,
"Tomorrow, I will prepare a humble meal and hope you will grace us with your presence."
Āqún replied,
"If it is in a latrine, I will go.
If it is in a palace, I will not."
The king said,
"As you command."
He returned and had the latrine torn apart, digging up the ground.
He used new camphorwood and catalpa for the pillars and beams.
He washed the ground with fragrant water and mixed sandalwood, storax, turmeric, and other fragrances into mud.
He used fine wool and silk for the seats.
He carved patterns and inlaid them with precious gems.
It shone brightly, surpassing the palace hall.
The next day, the king personally held an incense burner to welcome him.
Āqún took his seat.
The king lifted his robe and knelt to offer alms.
He then expounded the sutra, saying,
"The latrine was filthy yesterday.
Could one eat on it?" Āqún replied, "No."
"Can one do so now?"
He replied, "Yes."
Āqún said,
"Before I saw the Buddha, I was like that filthy latrine.
Thanks to past merits, I was born during the Buddha's time.
Bathing in his pure teachings, I removed the stench and embraced fragrance.
Inside and out, I am as pure as a genuine pearl."
He went to the market and heard a woman
having a difficult childbirth, her life hanging by a thread.
He reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"Go and assist her in childbirth."
Āqún received the instruction and went to proclaim the Buddha's grace.
Both mother and child survived.
The Buddha told Āqún,
"The day you received the Dharma can be considered your true birth.
Without seeing the Three Jewels and receiving the precepts,
you are like a child in the womb: though you have ears and eyes, what can you hear or see?"
Āqún said, "I was not yet born."
His heart opened, and he attained arhatship.
The Buddha told the bhikkhus,
"King Pǔmíng at that time was I.
In a past life, I taught him four verses,
saving one hundred kings and now enabling him to attain the path.
He will no longer suffer from various sins."
Āqún, in a past life, had been a bhikkhu.
