He carried a bushel of rice to offer at the monastery.
He offered a knife to the Buddha.
He rejoiced, praised the Buddha, bowed, and left.
Carrying rice brought him great strength.
Offering a knife brought him many treasures.
Rejoicing brought him a handsome appearance.
Praising the Buddha brought him kingship.
Bowing brought him the respect and worship of the people.
Ninety-nine people poked his head, leading to his death.
Thus, he killed his former enemies and cut off their fingers.
Later, people wanted to poke him but saw he was already dead.
Seeing the śramaṇa, he felt compassion.
The later person was his mother.
Initially having evil intentions, Āqún's mind was also evil.
Seeing the śramaṇa's compassion, he became filial upon seeing the Buddha.
Planting purity yields purity.
Planting impurity yields impurity.
Good and evil deeds bring their corresponding rewards.
Shadows follow forms, echoes follow sounds; all have their causes.
They do not arise spontaneously.
Ānanda,
in a past life,
there was a crown prince.
Named Liánhuā Wáng.
He was handsome and majestic, with awe-inspiring dignity.
While traveling, he saw a person
suffering from leprosy.
Seeing him, he felt compassion.
He asked the sick person, "What medicine can cure you?"
The sick person replied,
"If I can have the marrow from the king's body to smear on myself, my illness will be cured."
The prince then broke his own body to extract marrow and gave it to the sick person, joyfully bestowing it without regret.
That prince was I.
The water of the great ocean can be measured by the bushel,
but the merit of giving one's body marrow cannot be calculated.
Ānán.
When I originally sought the Way, I endured countless hardships.
In a past life, I was a crown prince,
named Xiànzhòng.
My appearance was upright and handsome.
As I was leaving the royal gardens,
I encountered a person on the road
who was suffering from a severe illness.
I approached and asked the sick person,
"What medicine can cure your illness?"
The sick person replied,
"Only the blood from the king's body can cure my illness."
The prince immediately used a sharp knife to pierce his body and gave the blood to the sick person.
He gave with utmost sincerity, without any regret or resentment.
That prince was my former self.
Ānán,
the waters of the four great seas can still be measured by the bucket,
but the blood I gave in charity cannot be quantified.
All for the sake of attaining perfect enlightenment.
In the distant past, during countless kalpas,
there were five ascetics.
They dwelled in mountain forests.
Four were masters,
and one served and attended to them, never failing in his duties—gathering fruits, drawing water, and presenting them at the proper times.
One day, while gathering fruits and sap far away, he grew weary and fell asleep.
He did not return at the appointed time.
The sun had already passed midday.
The four masters missed their meal.
Harboring resentment, they uttered a malevolent curse.
The attendant heard this and retreated beneath a tree.
Reflecting and blaming himself, he thought of his years of diligent service.
Now he had failed to provide the four ascetics with their timely meal.
Having lost the guidance of the Dharma and failing to follow the path of equality,
he died from the distress.
His feet always wore sandals of the seven treasures.
He sat with one foot raised.
One of the precious sandals fell into the water and was lost.
After his life ended, he was reborn among non-Buddhists.
He became the son of a malevolent curse.
When he was over ten years old,
he was playing with his companions by the roadside.
At that time, a Brahmin
encountered the playing children.
Observing the many children thoroughly,
he noticed that the cursed son possessed particularly noble features.
He was destined to become a king.
His countenance was extraordinary, surpassing that of ordinary people.
The Brahmin addressed him, saying,
"You bear the marks of a king; you should not mingle with the crowd."
The boy replied,
"I am the son of a curse; how could I have the marks of a king?"
The Brahmin said further,
"According to my scriptures,
your appearance and form match the prophecies in the treatises.
You correspond to them.
When the king of this country passes away, the throne will surely be passed to you."
The boy said,
"If what you say is true, I will remember your great kindness."
After the Brahmin finished speaking,
he immediately fled and went into hiding.
He traveled to another country.
Not long after,
the king died without an heir.
They sought a worthy man to become the royal successor.
Messengers were dispatched in all directions.
From afar, they saw this boy with the bearing of an extraordinary person.
They immediately sent someone back to report to the ministers,
urging them to prepare the royal carriage and come to welcome him.
All the ministers and officials rejoiced with great enthusiasm.
He was bathed in fragrant water, dressed in royal attire for the five times,
crowned with a precious diadem, girded with a sword, and enthroned in the palace.
Facing south, he assumed rule.
The land was peaceful, and the people were joyful and content.
At that time, the Brahmin,
observing the celestial signs above and examining the terrestrial patterns below,
knew that the boy had ascended the throne.
He went to the palace gate, seeking an audience with the king.
The Brahmin paid his respects and offered blessings, saying,
"As sworn, it has indeed come to pass."
The king said,
"Truly so.
You may have whatever you desire."
The Brahmin replied,
"I ask only for two wishes.
First,
that my food, movements, clothing, and lodging be equal to the king's.
Second,
that I participate in state affairs, and decisions be made with mutual agreement, not by your sole authority."
The king said,
"Very well."
The king ruled with righteous law, never wronging the people.
The Brahmin, however, became arrogant and contemptuous toward the senior ministers.
The ministers grew resentful and angry.
Together, they remonstrated, saying,
"Your Majesty's position is exalted.
You should consult with the state ministers and elders.
Placing blind trust in this beggar has allowed him to become insolent and insult the officials.
Neighboring countries will hear of this and mock us, which may lead to invasion and calamity."
The king said, "I made an oath with him; how can I break it?"
The ministers persisted in their remonstrance.
"If Your Majesty dines without him,
he will surely change his ways."
The king agreed to this.
When the Brahmin was away, the king ate first.
The Brahmin angrily said,
"What was our agreement? Why do you eat alone first?"
He cursed, saying,
"You cursed son!
Just provide supplies and banish him from the country."
Alone, he journeyed a long road, enduring cold and heat.
Exhausted and haggard, he reached another country.
He went to the home of a different Brahmin, an old acquaintance.
The host asked him,
"Where have you come from? What have you studied?
Which scriptures have you mastered? Can you recite them all?"
He replied,
"I have come from afar, driven by hunger and cold.
I have forgotten what I studied and recited."
The Brahmin thought to himself,
"This man is incapable of any work.
I will put him to work in the fields."
He provided him with a servant boy, an ox, a plow, and farming tools.
The Brahmin engaged in farming, harshly driving the servant boy.
He forced him to level the ground, running east and west.
The servant boy, distressed and with no recourse,
thought to drown himself and went to the riverbank.
There, he found a single sandal of the seven treasures.
He thought to himself,
"The Brahmin oppresses me with relentless labor.
If I present this sandal to him, perhaps I will be forgiven."
He took the sandal back and offered it to him.
The Brahmin was delighted and thought to himself,
"This sandal of the seven treasures is of priceless value.
If I present it to the king, whom I have offended, my transgression may be pardoned."
He returned to the kingdom
and presented the sandal to the king,
deeply confessing and repenting his previous offenses,
hoping for forgiveness.
The king said,
"Very well."
He placed it inside a curtain,
invited him to sit,
and assembled all the ministers.
He proclaimed,
"Have you not seen the former Brahmin?"
They replied,
"We have not."
The king said,
"If you saw him, what would you do?"
They all said,
"We would punish him with the five tortures."
The king brought out the precious sandal to show the ministers.
He summoned the Brahmin to come out and meet the ministers.
"Since he has presented this rare treasure, we should pardon him."
The ministers petitioned, saying,
"This Brahmin's crimes are as great as mountains and seas.
Presenting one sandal—what does that remedy?
If he obtains the pair, his crimes could be forgiven."
The king agreed to this.
He again expelled the Brahmin,
ordering him to find the other sandal.
The Brahmin, distressed, returned to his former host.
He asked the servant boy,
"Where did you previously obtain that precious sandal?"
The servant boy went with him to show him the place where he found the sandal.
At the riverbank, they searched everywhere but could not find the other sandal.
The servant boy left.
The Brahmin thought,
"This sandal must have come from upstream."
He went upstream against the current.
He saw a large lotus flower
caught in the swirling currents, held in a fish's mouth.
The lotus had over a thousand petals.
The Brahmin thought,
"Even if I do not find the sandal, if I present this flower,
perhaps I can atone for my offense and regain former favor."
He took the flower
and then saw four ascetics sitting beneath a tree.
The ascetics asked,
"Where have you come from?"
He replied,
"I have lost the king's favor.
Although I presented one sandal, it was insufficient to atone for my offense.
So I came upstream to search for it but have not found it."
The ascetics told him,
"As a learned man, you should know your place.
That king is our disciple.
He served us with love and respect, sharing meals and discussions.
How could you once curse him as a cursed son?
Your crime deserves punishment.
Now, without further inquiry, we point beneath this tree.
The king in his previous life was our attendant.
He died with one foot raised.
The precious sandal fell into the water, and one remained on his foot."
The Brahmin took the sandal, bowed in apology for his offense,
returned to his own country, and presented it.
The king was delighted, and the ministers were appeased.
He restored the Brahmin to his favored position.
The Buddha said,
"The king was myself in a past life.
The four ascetics were
Buddha Krakucchanda,
Buddha Kanakamuni,
Buddha Kāśyapa,
and Buddha Maitreya.
The Brahmin was Devadatta."
In the past, there were two bodhisattvas who were uncle and nephew.
Each carrying goods from their country, they went together to the Land of Nudity.
The nephew said,
"When entering another country, follow its customs; in all actions, seek propriety.
With a humble heart and modest words, conceal your wisdom and feign ignorance."
The uncle said,
"Rituals must not be compromised, virtue must not be abandoned.
How can we go naked and destroy our long-held principles?"
The nephew said,
"The sages of old upheld their conduct even at the cost of their lives.
Following the times, they were initially ridiculed, yet later praised for the greatness of their expedient means."
Thus, they proceeded together to that land.
The uncle said,
"You go first to observe the gains and losses, then send a messenger to inform me."
The nephew said,
"As you command."
Within ten days, the messenger returned to report.
The uncle said,
"We must follow their customs."
The uncle angrily said,
"Abandoning benevolence to follow beastly ways—is this the conduct of a gentleman?
I will not do as you do."
The custom of that country was that on the fifteenth night of the lunar month,
they would gather in circles for revelry.
They anointed their heads with sesame oil, painted their bodies with white clay,
adorned their necks with strings of mixed bones,
clapped stones together, and men held hands,
dancing and singing freely.
The bodhisattva followed along.
The people of the country rejoiced and praised him.
The king showed compassion, and the people respected him.
The guest king took all the goods and paid him tenfold.
The uncle entered the country in a carriage,
speaking with strict laws, which offended the people's sentiments.
The king grew angry, the people became disrespectful, and his wealth was seized and he was beaten.
Only after the nephew pleaded was he released.
They returned together to their own country.
Those who saw off the nephew filled the roads, while those who cursed the uncle covered their ears.
The uncle, ashamed and angry, said,
"What kinship do they have with you?
What enmity do they have with me?
You receive favor while I am robbed—is this not slander?"
He swore an oath to the nephew, saying,
"From now on, for countless lifetimes, I will torment you and never forgive you."
The bodhisattva, sorrowful and weeping, vowed,
"May I, for countless lifetimes, encounter the Buddha, see the Dharma, and personally serve the monastic community.
May the four kindnesses universally cover and nourish all sentient beings.
I will serve my uncle as myself and not violate this vow."
From that time onward,
the uncle constantly oppressed the nephew, while the nephew always aided him.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus,
"The nephew at that time was I,
and the uncle was Devadatta.
Innumerable, immeasurable kalpas in the past,
this world was then called Vimala Sumeru.
Human lifespan was one hundred years.
A Buddha appeared in the world,
named Fragrant Lotus Flower.
After his parinirvāṇa, during the period of the semblance Dharma,
I, at that time,
was a great and powerful cakravartin king,
named Durdharsha,
ruling over Jambudvīpa.
I had a thousand sons, all complete.
I exhorted and transformed them all,
causing them to generate the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
I wished to leave home and cultivate the path during the semblance Dharma period,
vigorously enhancing the Buddha's remaining teachings.
Only six sons remained
unwilling to leave home and generate the bodhi mind.
I spoke to them with kind and gentle words,
but they still would not leave home.
I questioned them again,
urging them to generate the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment.
The six sons replied,
'If you can give us Jambudvīpa,
then we will generate the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.'
Hearing this, my heart was filled with joy.
I thought to myself,
'I have already transformed the people of Jambudvīpa.
Now I should divide this Jambudvīpa
into six parts
and give them to these six sons,
so that they may generate the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment.
Then I can leave home and cultivate the path.'
I immediately divided Jambudvīpa into six parts and bestowed them upon the six sons.
Soon after, I left home.
At that time, the six sons
turned against each other, plundering and attacking.
Then, throughout Jambudvīpa,
crops failed, and the people suffered famine.
Rain did not fall in season, and all trees withered,
bearing no flowers or fruit.
Birds and beasts were all starving,
their bodies burning with hunger.
At that time, I gave up my own body,
skin, flesh, blood, and marrow to feed sentient beings and satisfy their hunger.
At that time,
I cast my own body down,
and through the power of my vow, it became a mountain of flesh,
one yojana high,
and equally broad in length and width.
At that time, the people,
birds, and beasts
began then
to eat the flesh and drink the blood.
Due to my original vow,
my body gradually grew larger,
until it was a thousand yojanas high,
and equally broad in length and width—also a thousand yojanas.
On its sides, human heads naturally grew,
complete with hair, eyes, ears, noses, mouths, lips, and tongues.
Each of those heads had a voice,
and they proclaimed, saying,
'All sentient beings,
each of you, take freely as you wish.
Drink the blood, eat the flesh,
take the eyes, ears, noses, tongues, teeth, and so on, all to your satisfaction.'
Then, I caused them all to generate the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi,
or the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha,
or to seek wealth and happiness in the heavens or among humans.
Due to my original vow, my body did not diminish,
even for ten thousand years.
Throughout Jambudvīpa,
humans and various spirits,
birds and beasts,
were all fully satisfied.
You should now know
that in the past, for ten thousand years,
I gave up immeasurable, boundless, countless bodies,
flesh and blood, to feed immeasurable, boundless beings, satisfying them all.
Not even for a single thought did I feel regret.
In this way, successively filling the ten directions, like the sands of the Ganges, in all Buddha lands,
I gave up my body, flesh, and blood to feed sentient beings, satisfying them all,
for the perfection of dāna.
In the past, there was a Bodhisattva.
He was a great householder.
He had accumulated wealth amounting to billions.
He constantly revered the Three Jewels.
His compassion extended to all living beings.
He went to the market to watch a performance.
There he saw a turtle and immediately felt pity for it.
He asked its price, whether high or low.
The turtle's owner knew that the Bodhisattva possessed the virtue of universal compassion, constantly saving all beings, and that his wealth was beyond measure, never refusing any price, high or low.
He replied,
"One million.
If you can take it, good.
If not, I will eat it."
The Bodhisattva replied,
"Very good."
He took the turtle home, bathed and cared for it without harming it.
He took it to the water's edge and released it, watching it swim away.
With mixed sorrow and joy, he vowed:
"May the hungry ghosts of Mount Tài, and all kinds of beings,
those imprisoned by the Lord of the World, be swiftly freed from hardship.
May they be safe and their lives preserved, as you are now."
He bowed to the ten directions, joined his palms, and made a wish:
"Living beings are in turmoil, their suffering immeasurable.
I shall be the earth.
For drought, I shall be the moisture.
For floods, I shall be the raft.
For the hungry, food; for the thirsty, drink.
For the cold, clothing; for the hot, coolness.
For the sick, a physician; for the darkness, light.
If there is an age of turbidity, a time of inversion,
I shall become a Buddha therein to liberate those beings."
The Buddhas of the ten directions all praised his vow.
They exclaimed:
"Excellent!
You shall certainly attain your aspiration."
Later that night, the turtle came and gnawed at his door.
Surprised by the noise at the door,
he sent someone to look and saw the turtle.
The servant returned and reported the matter.
The Bodhisattva looked at the turtle, and it immediately spoke in human language:
"I received your profound kindness; my life was saved.
I have no way to repay you.
But as a creature of the water, I know the rise and fall of its levels.
A great flood is coming; it will certainly cause great disaster.
I urge you to quickly prepare a boat and, when the time comes, I will come to meet you."
He replied,
"Very good."
The next morning, he went to the palace gate and informed the king of the matter.
The king said,
"The Bodhisattva has long had a reputation for goodness.
I trust his words." He ordered people to move from low areas to higher ground.
Then the turtle came and said,
"The flood is here.
Quickly board the boat.
Follow where I go.
You will certainly be safe."
The boat followed behind it.
A snake approached the boat.
The Bodhisattva said,
"Take it aboard."
The turtle said,
"Very good."
Then they saw a fox floating by.
He said, "Take it aboard."
The turtle also said it was good.
Then they saw a man floating,
slapping his cheeks and crying to heaven, begging to be saved: "Have pity, save my life!"
Again he said,
"Take him aboard."
The turtle said,
"Be careful, do not take him.
Human hearts are treacherous and false.
Rarely are they ultimately trustworthy.
They betray kindness and pursue power.
They are prone to malice and wicked rebellion."
The Bodhisattva said,
"We have saved even creatures.
To abandon a man seeking help—
how can that be humane?
I cannot bear to do it."
So he took the man aboard.
The turtle said,
"You will regret it." They then reached fertile land.
The turtle took its leave, saying:
"My debt of gratitude is repaid; I beg to withdraw."
He replied,
"If I attain Buddhahood, becoming the Tathāgata, the Unattached, the Perfectly Enlightened One,
I shall certainly liberate you."
The turtle said,
"Very good."
The turtle withdrew.
The snake and the fox each went their own way.
The fox, whose dwelling was a burrow,
found an ancient hidden treasure of a hundred catties of purple-gold.
Joyfully, it said:
"I shall use this to repay his kindness."
It rushed back and reported:
"A small creature received your kindness and was saved, its humble life preserved.
I, a burrow-dwelling creature, sought a burrow for shelter and found a hundred catties of gold.
This burrow was not tilled land, nor a home,
nor was it obtained by robbery or theft.
It was obtained through my sincere intent.
I wish to offer it to you, worthy one."
The Bodhisattva pondered deeply but was unwilling to accept it.
"It would merely be hoarded without benefiting the poor.
If taken to give alms, the masses would be saved.
Would that not be good?"
So he then took it.
The floating man saw this and said:
"Give me half."
The Bodhisattva immediately gave him ten catties.
The floating man said:
"You dug up and stole this gold.
What should your punishment be?
If you don't give me half,
I will certainly report you to the authorities."
He replied:
"I intend to distribute it equally among the poor and needy.
You wish to monopolize it.
Is that not unfair?"
The floating man then reported him to the authorities.
The Bodhisattva was arrested and had no one to appeal to.
He only took refuge in the Three Jewels, repented his faults, and blamed himself.
With compassionate wishes for all beings to soon escape the eight calamities,
and that none would have grievances as he did now.
The snake and fox met and said:
"What shall we do about this matter?"
The snake said:
"I will save him."
It then took a potent medicine in its mouth, opened the prison gate, and entered the jail.
Seeing the Bodhisattva's condition, his complexion impaired, it was grieved and saddened at heart.
It said to the Bodhisattva:
"Keep this medicine with you.
I will bite the crown prince.
The poison will be especially severe; no one will be able to cure him.
You, worthy one, apply the medicine to yourself and you will be healed."
The Bodhisattva remained silent.
The snake did as it said.
The crown prince was about to die.
The king proclaimed:
"Whoever can save him
will be appointed prime minister.
He will participate in governing."
The Bodhisattva, hearing of this, applied the medicine and the prince was cured.
The king, delighted, asked how it came about.
He recounted the whole story from beginning to end.
The king was dismayed and blamed himself.
He immediately executed the floating man.
He granted a great amnesty throughout the country.
He appointed the Bodhisattva as prime minister.
Taking his hand, he led him into the palace.
They sat together, and the king said:
"What texts do you, worthy one, expound?
What path do you embrace,
that you show the benevolence of heaven and earth,
reaching all living beings?"
He replied:
"I expound the Buddhist scriptures and embrace the Buddhist path."
The king said:
"Does the Buddha have essential teachings?"
He answered:
"He does."
"The Buddha speaks of the Four Impermanences.
Those who keep them will have abundant blessings and prosperity."
The king said:
"Excellent!
I wish to grasp their true meaning."
The Bodhisattva explained them.
The king said:
"Excellent!
The Buddha's teaching of non-self—my heart believes it.
If even the body cannot be preserved,
how much less the country and land?
How lamentable that former kings
did not hear the supreme, true, right awakening, the teachings of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self."
The king then emptied his treasury to give alms to the poor and destitute.
Widowers, widows, orphans, and the childless—he pitied them as his own children.
The whole country rejoiced, smiling and going about their lives.
Looking up to heaven, he sighed:
"The Bodhisattva's divine transformation has reached even this."
All quarters praised his virtue, and thus peace prevailed.
The Buddha told the monks:
"The Bodhisattva was myself.
The king was Maitreya.
The turtle was Ānanda.
The fox was Qiūlùzǐ.
The snake was Mùlián.
The floating man was Tiáodá."
In the past, a bodhisattva
was once a lion
living in a forest.
He was close friends with a macaque.
The macaque entrusted his two children to the lion.
At that time, a hungry vulture was flying around searching for food.
It happened that the lion was asleep.
The vulture took the macaque's children and perched in a tree.
When the lion awoke,
he could not find the macaque's children.
He saw the vulture holding them in the tree
and said to the vulture:
"I accepted the macaque's entrustment of his two children.
I was not careful enough in protecting them,
allowing you to take them away.
I have failed my promise.
I beg you to return them to me.
I am the king among beasts,
you are the lord among birds.
Our noble status is equal.
It is fitting that you return them."
The vulture said:
"You do not understand the situation.
I am now hungry and exhausted; what does it matter if we are equal or not?"
The lion knew he could not get them back.
He used his sharp claws
to cut the flesh from his own flank
to trade for the macaque's children.
Also, in a past age,
people suffered many illnesses,
with yellow and white fevers.
At that time, the bodhisattva was incarnated as a red fish.
He gave his own flesh to the sick people,
to cure their diseases.
Also in the past, a bodhisattva
was incarnated as a bird living in a forest.
He saw a person enter deep water,
a place not meant for humans, and was ensnared by a water spirit.
The water spirit's
snare was fastened and could not be undone.
If one could go to the Fragrant Mountain
and fetch a medicinal herb to place on the snare,
the rope would immediately rot and the person could escape.
There are countless such past lives (jātaka),
which have brought much aid; these are called the Jātaka Sūtras.
Subhūti asked:
"The bodhisattva has perfected virtuous roots.
Why is he born as an elephant or horse?"
The Buddha said:
"The bodhisattva truly possesses merit and virtue,
with perfected virtuous roots.
For the benefit of sentient beings, he takes the form of an animal,
but is without the faults of an animal.
When a bodhisattva is among animals,
he shows compassion even to enemies and wrongdoers—
something not found among arhats or pratyekabuddhas.
When arhats or pratyekabuddhas
are harmed by enemies,
though they do not retaliate,
they cannot feel loving-kindness or provide for them.
Like in a past life of the bodhisattva,
when he was a six-tusked white elephant.
A hunter shot him in the chest with a poisoned arrow.
At that time, the bodhisattva elephant used his trunk to embrace the hunter,
not allowing other elephants to harm him.
He said to the female elephant:
'You are the bodhisattva's wife.
Why do you harbor ill will?
The hunter's action is due to afflictions and karma,
not a personal fault.'
'When I attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi,
I will eradicate his afflictions,
just as when a ghost possesses a person, the exorcist treats the ghost without blaming the person.'
Gently, he asked the hunter:
'Why did you shoot me?'
The hunter replied:
'I need your tusks.'
The elephant immediately went to a rock and pulled out his tusks to give to him.
Blood and flesh came out together, but he felt no pain.
He provided him with food and showed him the path.
Such compassion as this
is not found among arhats or pratyekabuddhas."
A question was asked:
"Why does he not take a human form to preach the Dharma,
but instead takes this animal form?"
The answer was:
"Sometimes, when sentient beings see a human form, they do not believe or accept it.
When they see an animal form preaching the Dharma,
they give rise to faith and joy,
and accept its teachings.
The bodhisattva
wishes to fully embody great compassion,
and to practice true deeds.
When sentient beings see this, they are amazed and delighted, and all can enter the Path."
In the past, a bodhisattva
and Ānanda together
had finished their retribution.
Each became a nāga (dragon).
One nāga said:
"Only you and I are together in the sea,
and there is nothing we have not seen.
Shall we both go up to the land to play?"
The other replied:
"People on land are wicked; if we encounter something unusual, we cannot go out."
The first nāga said again:
"We can transform into small snakes.
If the road is empty of people, we can play along the main path.
If we meet people, we will hide; what is there to worry about?"
So they agreed
and both ascended to travel and look around.
Not long after leaving the water,
on the road they encountered a venomous snake.
The snake saw the two serpents and, with malicious intent, wanted to harm them.
It then spat venomous foam.
One serpent wanted to kill the venomous snake.
The other serpent, with compassionate forbearance, advised against it,
saying:
"A noble person should forgive the multitude of fools.
Enduring the unendurable—
this is the sage's precept."
He then spoke a verse:
The serpent praised forbearance.
One serpent respectfully accepted this and thus did not harm the snake.
One serpent said:
"Let us return to the sea."
They agreed and went together.
Then they exerted their majestic spiritual power,
shaking heaven and earth,
raising clouds and sending rain.
Humans and ghosts were all alarmed.
The venomous snake was terrified,
lying as if dead, unaware.
For seven days it abstained from food, desiring to harm.
The forbearing nāga was Ānanda.
The serpent who spoke of forbearance was myself.
The venomous snake was Devadatta.
There was a man.
He entered the forest to cut wood.
He became confused and lost his mind.
At that time, heavy rain fell.
As evening came, he was hungry and cold.
Vicious insects and poisonous beasts sought to harm him.
This man entered a stone cave.
There was a large bear inside.
Seeing him, the bear was frightened and came out.
The bear spoke to him, saying:
"Do not be afraid.
This dwelling is warm; you may stay here for the night."
At that time, the rain continued for seven days.
The bear constantly provided this man with sweet fruits and fine water.
After seven days, the rain stopped.
The bear showed this man the path.
The bear said to the man:
"I am a sinful being; men are my enemies.
If anyone asks,
do not say you have seen me."
The man replied, "Yes."
This man went on his way.
He saw some hunters.
The hunters asked:
"Where have you come from?
Have you seen any animals?"
He replied:
"I saw a large bear.
It was kind to me.
I cannot show you where it is."
The hunters said:
"You are a human, one of us.
You should view things from a human perspective.
Why spare a bear?
If you miss this chance now,
when will it come again?
If you show us,
we will give you a large share."
This man's heart changed.
He immediately led the hunters to where the bear was.
The hunters killed the bear.
They then gave him a large share.
As this man stretched out his hands to take the meat,
both his elbows fell off.
The hunters said:
"What crime have you committed?"
He replied:
"That bear cared for me
as a father cares for his son.
Now I have betrayed its kindness.
This is the retribution for my crime."
The hunters were terrified.
They dared not eat the meat.
They offered it to the community of monks.
The elder was an Arhat with the six supernatural powers.
He said to the junior monks:
"This is a Bodhisattva.
In a future age, it will become a Buddha.
Do not eat this meat."
They immediately built a stūpa and made offerings.
The king heard of this matter.
He issued an edict throughout the country:
"Those who betray kindness shall not be allowed to dwell here."
Through various circumstances,
people praised those who know gratitude.
In the past, when the Buddha was in the Deer Park at Isipatana in Bālánài Guó,
all the ṛṣis with the five supernatural powers
traveled to study in this country.
It was not a place where ordinary people dwelled.
The king went out hunting.
He encountered a herd of a thousand deer, all caught in his nets.
The king deployed foot soldiers to surround them in a circle.
The herd of deer was terrified.
Some lost their voices in panic, some lay on the ground trying to hide themselves.
Śākyamuni Buddha,
in a past life when he was a Bodhisattva,
was the king of the deer herd.
The Buddha himself told the herd of deer:
"Be at ease, do not be afraid.
I will devise a means
to plead with the king for mercy; surely our lives will be spared.
Each of you, do not worry."
The deer king went and knelt before the human king, pleading for mercy.
The human king saw him from afar.
He ordered his attendants, "Do not harm the deer."
The deer said:
"Now I observe the king's intention
is to kill a thousand deer in one day to supply the kitchen.
But now the weather is extremely hot.
Meat cannot be kept for long.
I beg the king to have compassion.
Let one deer be killed each day to supply the kitchen.
The king need not trouble his messengers.
The deer will come to the kitchen of its own accord,
to receive death.
Thus the meat supply will not be interrupted,
and the deer will have time to multiply."
The king asked the deer:
"Are you the eldest and leader among the herd of deer?"
He replied:
"Yes."
The king asked the deer again:
"Are you certain of this?"
He replied:
"I am certain."
The king then released the deer, withdrew his troops, and returned to the city.
At that time, the Bodhisattva led five hundred deer,
and Devadatta also led five hundred deer.
Each day, one deer was sent
to the king's kitchen.
When it was Devadatta's turn to send a deer to the king,
there was a pregnant doe who was due to give birth in a few months.
It was her turn to be sent to the kitchen.
The doe said to the king:
"I am about to give birth.
It is my turn to go,
but my fawn's turn has not yet come.
I beg you to change the order and allow me to go later."
Devadatta angrily said:
"Why don't you go quickly?
Who can die in your place?"
The doe wept sorrowfully, crying out in distress.
She then went to the Bodhisattva and explained her situation.
"I beg the king to be lenient
and allow me to go later."
The Bodhisattva asked the doe:
"Did your master listen to your plea?"
She replied:
"My master would not listen."
The Bodhisattva comforted her, saying:
"Do not be afraid.
I will now take your place
to be sent to the kitchen."
The Bodhisattva, the deer king,
then summoned the thousand deer.
He earnestly admonished them:
"Do not become lax or negligent.
Also, do not encroach upon the king's autumn crops and grain."
Devadatta angrily said to the doe:
"It is your turn to go; what excuse do you have?"
The Bodhisattva said to Devadatta:
"Enough, enough, do not speak such words.
It is true the doe's turn has come to die,
but out of compassion for her unborn fawn, she should not die yet.
I will take her place to save the fawn's life."
The herd of deer pleaded:
"We are willing to take our king's place and die.
If the king lives, we can
eat grass and drink water,
roam freely at will,
without fear or hindrance."
The king then went to the kitchen.
The herd of deer followed him to the king's palace.
The deer king went to the kitchen to offer himself for slaughter.
The kitchen workers saw the deer king.
They went to report to the king:
"The deer king has entered the kitchen.
It is his turn to be slaughtered.
We are not sure, great king,
whether we should kill him or not."
The king ordered his ministers:
"Quickly bring the deer king to me."
The king asked the deer:
"Have all the thousand deer been killed?
Why have you come?"
The deer said to the king:
"The thousand deer have given birth and multiplied into a large herd.
Their numbers increase daily,
with no decrease.
He then explained the whole matter.
The king reproached himself,
regretting his own shortcomings.
"I, a beast, could not distinguish truth from falsehood,
and wrongly killed living beings,
to this extent."
The king told his ministers:
"Proclaim throughout the land that anyone who hunts and kills deer
shall be executed.
He then sent the deer king back.
He decreed that no one in the country should eat deer meat.
Anyone who eats deer meat
shall be beheaded.
Because of this, it was named the Deer Park."
The Buddha said:
"In a past age, near the Snowy Mountains,
there was a deer king
named Wēidé.
He was the leader of five hundred deer.
At that time, there was a hunter
who set up grain and snares.
The deer king went ahead,
and his right foot fell into a hair snare.
The deer king thought to himself:
'If I show my distress,
then the other deer will not dare to eat the grain.
They must eat their fill of the grain,
and only then will I show my foot.'
At that time, all the deer left.
One doe stayed behind.
She spoke a verse, saying:
At that time, the deer king replied with a verse, saying:
"Female deer,
seeing the hunter has arrived,
I speak to him with a verse."
The hunter, hearing this,
felt compassion in his heart.
He replied with a verse, saying:
The hunter immediately released the deer king.
The Buddha said:
"The deer king of old is now my body.
The five hundred deer are the five hundred bhikkhus.
In the past, the Bodhisattva
was a nine-colored deer.
Its fur had nine kinds of colors,
and its horns were white as snow.
It dwelled by the Ganges River, drinking water and eating grass.
It often kept company with a crow as a friend.
At that time, there was a drowning man in the water,
carried downstream by the current,
sometimes surfacing, sometimes sinking.
He lifted his head and cried out to heaven:
'Mountain spirits, tree spirits, devas, dragon spirits—
why do you not pity me?'
The deer, hearing this, entered the water and said:
'You may ride on my back and hold my horns.
I will carry you out to the shore.'
The drowning man came ashore.
He circled the deer three times,
bowed his head to the deer,
and begged to become its servant,
to serve it and gather water and grass.
The deer said: 'There is no need.
Just go your own way.
If you wish to repay my kindness,
do not speak of my presence here.
People covet my skin and horns,
and will surely come to kill me.'
At that time, the king's consort
dreamed at night of the nine-colored deer.
She then feigned illness and refused to rise.
The king asked why.
She replied:
'Last night I dreamed of an extraordinary deer.
Its fur had nine kinds of colors,
and its horns were white as snow.
I desire to have its skin made into a sitting mat
and its horns made into a fly-whisk handle.
You must obtain them for me.
If you cannot, I will die.'
The king offered a reward throughout the kingdom:
'If anyone can obtain it, I will share the kingdom and rule with them,
bestow upon them a golden bowl filled with silver millet,
and a silver bowl filled with golden millet.'
The drowning man, hearing this, desired to gain wealth and honor.
He thought:
'The deer is but an animal.
What does its life or death matter?'
He went to the king and said he knew the deer's location.
The king was greatly pleased and said:
'If you can bring its skin and horns,
I will reward you with half the kingdom.'
Leprous sores immediately appeared on the drowning man's face.
The drowning man said:
'Great King, though this deer is an animal,
it possesses great divine power. You should send many troops to capture it.'
The king then dispatched a great host of people.
They proceeded to the Ganges River. The crow was atop a tree
and, seeing the troops approach, called out to the deer:
'Friend, rise! The king has arrived.'
The deer was sound asleep and unaware.
The crow pecked its ear,
and the deer, startled awake, looked around but had nowhere to flee.
It then approached the king's chariot.
The ministers beside him wished to shoot it,
but the king said:
'Do not shoot!
This deer is extraordinary;
it must be a heavenly deity.'
The deer said:
'Great King,
do not shoot me.
I once saved a man from your kingdom.'
The deer then knelt and asked the king:
'Who told you I was here?'
The king pointed and said:
'The man with the leprous face beside the chariot.'
The deer lifted its head,
looked at this man's face,
and tears fell from its eyes,
unable to contain itself.
'This man was drowning in the water.
I, disregarding my own life,
plunged into the water
and carried him out.
We agreed he would not speak of me.
He is without gratitude, worse than a floating log in the water.'
The king felt ashamed.
He rebuked his subject three times:
'You received his kindness.
How could you instead seek to kill him?'
He then decreed throughout the kingdom:
'If anyone drives away this deer,
their five clans shall be executed.'
Thousands of deer came to rely on it.
They drank water and ate grass without encroaching on crops.
The seasons brought timely wind and rain, the five grains flourished,
people had no illnesses,
and the world was at peace.
The nine-colored deer of that time is now my body.
The crow is Ānanda.
The king of that time is now my father, King Śuddhodana.
The king's consort of that time is now Sundarī.
The drowning man of that time is Devadatta.
Though I had a kind heart toward him,
he still sought to harm me.
Ānanda had sincere intent.
In a past age,
there was the city of Vārāṇasī.
Outside the city was a pond,
named 'Rain-formed.'
In this pond were many fish, turtles, geese, ducks, and other creatures.
Among them was a goose king,
named Zhìguó,
who led five hundred geese.
At that time, a hunter
had previously set a hair snare.
The goose king, walking ahead,
caught its right foot in the snare.
It thought:
'If I pull my foot out of this snare,
the other geese will not dare to eat the grain.'
After they had all eaten, it then revealed its foot.
The flock of geese flew away,
except for one goose,
named Sūmó,
who would not leave the king.
The king said to the minister:
'I give you the duty to be king
and lead the geese.'
The minister replied:
'I cannot.'
The king asked:
'Why is that?'
At that time, the minister
replied with a verse, saying:
At that time, the goose king
replied with a verse, saying:
Minister Sūmó,
seeing the snare-setter arrive,
spoke to him with a verse.
At that time, the snare-setter
said to the minister:
'I will not kill you.
I release you and the king
to go wherever you wish.'
The hunter then freed the goose king.
Both geese departed together.
They said to each other:
'This hunter has done an extraordinary deed,
granting us our lives.
We should repay him generously with our livelihood.'
The hunter asked:
'You are but animals.
What possessions do you have to repay me?'
The two geese replied:
'The king of Vārāṇasī is named Fàndé.
Take us to the hunter.'
Carrying the geese on his shoulders,
he arrived at the city streets.
The geese were handsome,
and people delighted in seeing them.
Some offered five coins, ten coins, twenty coins,
all saying, 'Do not kill them.'
By the time this man reached the palace,
he had obtained great wealth.
The hunter arrived at the palace gate,
placed the geese on the ground.
The goose king said to the gatekeeper:
'Inform King Fàndé
that Goose King Zhìguó is now outside the gate.'
He went and informed the king.
The king then permitted them to enter.
He provided a golden seat.
Minister Sūmó, as was fitting, exchanged greetings with him,
and then took his seat.
He addressed King Fàndé with a verse, saying:
At that time, King Fàndé
replied with a verse, saying:
Thus they conversed in response.
He spoke five hundred verses.
The minister Sūmó remained silent at that time.
King Fàndé said,
"Why are you silent?"
The minister replied,
"You are the king of men, the lord of the state.
This goose king is the lord of the marshlands.
How dare I interject when two kings are speaking?"
The king said,
"I have a fine garden.
Can you dwell there?"
He replied,
"I cannot."
The king asked,
"Why?"
The goose said,
"If the king should wake from sleep
and forget not to spare me,
ordering goose meat to be prepared for food,
and if the butcher cannot obtain other geese,
he might kill us to supply the royal kitchen."
The goose king who governed the flock entered the king's palace.
The geese, following the rain, emerged from the pond and flew above the king's palace.
They circled and cried mournfully.
Their wings were wet, sprinkling water that soiled the palace halls.
The king asked,
"What is this?"
The goose king replied,
"These are my kin."
The king said,
"Do you wish to leave?"
He replied,
"I wish to leave."
The king said,
"What do you need?"
He replied,
"I was captured by a hunter.
He performed a rare deed for us,
granting us life.
If he first kills one and later kills another, who can prevent it?"
The king said,
"How should he be repaid?"
The two geese replied,
"Give him gold, silver, chariots, horses, agate, clothing, food, and drink."
Having spoken these words, they soared into the sky.
The Buddha said,
"The goose king was my former self.
The five hundred geese
are the five hundred bhikkhus.
The hunter is the elephant keeper Shǒucái.
King Fàndé is King Jìngfàn.
The minister Sūmó is Ānán."
In the past, the Bodhisattva,
manifesting as a parrot, often dwelled in a tree.
The wind blew the trees, causing them to rub against each other,
and fire emerged.
The fire gradually grew fierce,
eventually burning a mountain.
The parrot thought,
"Even a flying bird that perches in a tree
should repeatedly arise with a mind of gratitude.
How much more so for me, who has long dwelt here?
Yet I cannot extinguish the fire."
He then went to the sea,
using his two wings to take seawater,
carried it to the fire, and sprinkled it on the flames.
Sometimes he sprinkled it with his beak, rushing east and west.
At that time, a benevolent deity,
moved by his diligence and hardship,
promptly extinguished the fire.
In the past, the Bodhisattva was a sparrow king.
With a compassionate heart, he saved many, protecting even his own wounds.
A tiger, having eaten an animal, got a bone stuck in its teeth.
It was afflicted and near death.
The sparrow entered its mouth and pecked at the bone daily, continuing thus.
The sparrow's beak developed sores, and its body grew thin and weak.
The bone came out of the tiger's mouth.
The sparrow flew up into a tree
and spoke the Buddha's sutra, saying:
"Killing is a grave evil; its wickedness is immense."
The tiger, hearing the sparrow's admonition,
flared up in anger and said,
"You have just left my mouth,
yet you dare to speak so much?"
The sparrow, seeing it could not be transformed,
swiftly flew away.
The Buddha said,
"The sparrow was my former self.
The tiger was Tiáodá."
In the past, the Bodhisattva was poor and destitute.
He traveled with merchants to another country.
The Bodhisattva saw fish in the sea, large ones swallowing small ones.
He gave his own body in place of the small ones, allowing them to live a little longer.
He threw himself into the sea; the large fish were satiated, and the small ones survived.
His spirit transformed into the king of the whales,
with a body several miles long.
A coastal country suffered drought, and the people were starving.
They began to devour each other.
The whale then washed its body ashore in that country.
Those who ate it survived.
They carted away its flesh for months, yet the whale remained alive.
A heavenly deity descended and said,
"For the sake of compassion, how can you endure such suffering?
Why not end your life and leave this pain?"
The whale said,
"If my spirit departs and my body rots,
and the people later starve again,
they will again devour each other.
I cannot bear to see it."
The deity said,
"You will certainly attain Buddhahood and save suffering beings."
Someone took its head, and the whale died at that time.
Its spirit became a prince,
possessing supreme sage-like wisdom.
His compassion and kindness, vast as the four graces, moistened and equaled heaven and earth.
He pitied the people's hardship and poverty,
speaking with choked sobs.
Yet the country still suffered drought.
With a tranquil heart, he observed purity and reverence,
abstaining from food and ceasing offerings.
Bowing his head, he repented his faults, saying:
"The people's misfortunes
are the fault of my own person.
I wish to forfeit my life to bring rain and moisture to benefit the people."
Month after month, he grieved and mourned,
like a filial son bereaved of a sage father.
His sincerity reached far and wide, and his fame spread.
The Buddha, with five hundred followers, came to the borders of his country.
The king heard and rejoiced in his heart.
He welcomed them, bowing and prostrating, knocking his head, weeping tears.
"My heart is defiled, my conduct turbid,
not fitting the teachings of the Three Jewels and the Four Graces.
I have harshly afflicted the people,
causing drought for many years.
The common people starve,
lamenting in pain and sorrow.
I pray to remove the people's calamities and bring the disaster upon myself."
The Buddhas replied,
"You, as a ruler of men,
are compassionate, benevolent, and virtuous, equal to Indra.
All Buddhas know this universally.
May the king receive blessings; do not grieve."
He ordered the people to plant grain.
Every household cultivated diligently.
The rice transformed into abundance.
The king said,
"It must ripen."
The grain covered the country,
all containing rice husks,
each holding several hu measures.
The rice was fragrant, and the whole country rejoiced happily.
They praised the king's virtue.
Throughout the land, they upheld the precepts,
taking refuge in the Three Jewels.
The king and his subjects, at life's end, were reborn in heaven.
The poor man at that time was my former self.
In the past, there was a Bodhisattva.
He once was a Turtle King.
He grew in the great sea and transformed his fellow creatures.
His subjects and the multitude all cultivated benevolence and virtue.
The king himself practiced compassion, loving-kindness, joy, and equanimity.
He pitied all living beings like a mother loves her child.
The sea was deep and vast, its boundaries difficult to limit.
Yet he traveled everywhere, leaving no place unvisited.
At that time, the Turtle King emerged from the sea.
He rested on the shore, having been there for many days and months.
His back was dry and hard, like dry land.
Merchants came from afar and stopped upon it.
They split firewood, lit a fire, and cooked their meals.
They tethered their oxen, horses, carts, and loaded stones, all placed upon him.
The Turtle King wished to go into the water.
But he feared the merchants would fall.
He tried to endure it forcibly, but the pain was unbearable.
So he devised a skillful means, entering shallow water.
He extinguished the fire’s harm, not endangering the merchants.
The merchants were terrified, thinking the tide had suddenly risen.
They wailed in sorrow, calling upon all the heavens.
Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, the sun, moon, and divine spirits.
They prayed for their majestic power to save and rescue them.
The Turtle King’s heart grew even more compassionate toward them.
Thus he addressed the merchants:
“Do not be afraid.
I am burned by the fire, so I entered the water.
I wished to ease the pain.
Now I will keep you safe and will not harm you.”
Hearing this, the merchants knew there was hope to live.
Together they cried out:
“Námó Fó!”
The turtle, with great compassion,
Carried the merchants back and moved them to the shore.
Everyone was saved, and all rejoiced.
From afar they bowed to the Turtle King and praised his virtue.
“You are a noble bridge, carrying many across.
Your conduct is a great vessel, ferrying beyond the three realms.
If you attain Buddhahood, you will again save us from the perils of birth and death.”
The Turtle King replied:
“Excellent, excellent!
It shall be as you say.”
Then they each went their separate ways.
The Buddha said:
“The Turtle King at that time was I myself.
The five hundred merchants
Were the five hundred disciples such as Śāriputra.
In the time of Buddha Krakucchanda,
There was a bhikṣu.
His name was Wúgòu.
He dwelled in seclusion.
In a mountain cave within the country’s borders.
Not far from there,
Were five ascetics.
A woman encountered heavy rain on the road.
She entered the bhikṣu’s cave and left after the rain stopped.
The five ascetics saw this.
Each said:
‘The bhikṣu is impure.’
Wúgòu heard this.
Immediately he leaped into the air.
Four zhàng and nine chǐ above the ground.
The ascetics saw him flying in the sky.
Each said:
‘According to our scriptures,
One who is defiled by desire cannot fly.’
They prostrated themselves, touching the ground with five limbs, bowing their heads in repentance.
Had the bhikṣu not displayed his spiritual power,
Those five ascetics would have fallen into the great hells.
That bhikṣu Wúgòu
Is now the Bodhisattva Maitreya.
In the past, there was a Buddha.
His name was Mònéngshèng.
There was a bhikṣu.
His name was Huìwáng.
In the morning, he went on alms round and obtained a meal of a hundred flavors and various foods.
On the road was a venerable’s son.
His name was Lígòubì.
He was being carried by his wet nurse.
From afar he saw the bhikṣu.
He got down from the wet nurse’s arms.
He followed the bhikṣu, asking for food.
Then the bhikṣu gave him a honey cake.
The child ate it and knew its sweetness.
So he followed the bhikṣu until the honey cake was almost finished.
The bhikṣu gave him more.
They went to where the Buddha was.
He bowed at the Buddha’s feet.
Huìwáng took the food he had obtained.
And gave it to the child to offer to the Buddha.
To inspire his aspiration for the Way.
The Buddha accepted it, and it filled the Buddha’s bowl.
The food did not diminish.
Then he gave to the śrāvakas, eighty-four thousand,
And to the bodhisattvas, twelve hundred million.
The Buddha and the holy assembly
Were all fully satisfied.
Such offerings continued for seven days.
The food remained as before, undiminished.
The child rejoiced and recited verses praising the Buddha.
He then aroused the unsurpassed true Dharma mind.
At that time, his parents searched for their son.
They went to where the Buddha was.
The child greeted them and praised his parents with verses.
At that time, the child
Converted his parents and five hundred others.
Causing them all to aspire to the unsurpassed true Dharma.
They all renounced their homes and became śramaṇas.
Practicing the bodhisattva path, they attained Buddhahood themselves.
That Huìwáng was Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
That Lígòubì was I myself.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva.
His name was Shàngshǒu.
He became a mendicant.
Entering the city to beg for food.
There was a bhikṣu.
His name was Héngqié.
He said to the mendicant:
“Where do you come from?”
He replied:
“I come from truth.”
Héngqié asked:
“What is called truth?”
He answered:
“The characteristic of extinction is called truth.”
Héngqié said:
“Where should one seek the true Dharma?”
He answered:
“One should seek it within the six pāramitās.”
Héngqié rejoiced.
He bowed at Shàngshǒu’s feet.
And then asked:
“With what food should one make offerings to such a person?”
Shàngshǒu answered:
“With the flavor of srotāpanna.”
Héngqié then went to the city market.
And proclaimed aloud:
“I wish to sell my body.
Who has need of it?”
There was a householder.
His name was Pínúlǜ.
He asked me:
“I wish to buy it.
What do you ask in return?”
Héngqié replied, asking for:
“Xūtuónàluó.”
He said:
“How many do you ask for?”
Héngqié replied:
“I wish for five.”
The householder bought this monk with five coins to serve him.
Héngqié said to his master:
“My body belongs to you.
Lend me seven days.
I wish to make offerings to the bhikṣu Shàngshǒu.”
The householder told Héngqié:
“I will show you the house.
Then I will release you to return.”
When Héngqié saw the house, he set out on the road back.
He saw this Shàngshǒu.
Who had not yet obtained alms food.
He then took Shàngshǒu.
To the city market.
Bought a hundred-flavored meal.
Brought it to a monastery.
The monastery was named Sìwáng.
Prepared seats, burned incense, scattered flowers.
And set out various foods.
Xūmótí addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
the forty matters of the bodhisattva that you have spoken of,
I shall uphold and practice them,
ensuring they are not lacking or diminished."
At that time, the elder Mùlián asked:
"These forty matters are practiced by great beings.
How can you, a young woman, accomplish them?"
She replied:
"I truly can practice them.
If you do not believe me, let the three thousand great-thousandfold world all shake six times for me,
rain down heavenly flowers,
and all musical instruments sound without being struck."
Immediately, it happened as she said.
The girl said:
"To verify my utmost sincerity,
if I will later attain Buddhahood without falsehood,
let all in the assembly turn golden in color."
Following her words, their color became like gold.
Mùlián addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For one who first resolves the great mind to become a bodhisattva,
I pay homage.
Why is this?
An eight-year-old girl can evoke such responses—
how much more so for a lofty great bodhisattva?"
Wénshūshīlì asked:
"How is it that you do not transform the body of a woman?"
Xūmótí replied:
"In this, there is nothing attained.
Why is this?
The Dharma has no male or female.
Now I shall resolve your doubt.
Xūmótí said:
'May I soon attain true enlightenment.
I shall now transform into a man.'
As soon as she spoke these words,
she became a male body.
Her hair fell off, and a monk's robe covered her body,
and she became a śrāmaṇera.
She further said:
'When I become a Buddha,
may my land be without three things:
first, demonic affairs;
second, hells;
third, feminine forms.
If I am sincere,
my body shall be like that of a thirty-year-old monk.'
As soon as she spoke these words,
her form and complexion became like that of a thirty-year-old.
She further said to Wénshūshīlì:
'When I become a Buddha,
may the people of my land all be golden in color,
the ground and city walls have seven-jeweled trees,
jeweled ponds and jeweled flowers, neither too many nor too few,
all uniformly even.'
She also said, 'May all in the assembly turn golden.'
Immediately, the entire assembly took on golden countenances.
At that time, the earth-holding deity emerged from the ground,
transformed into a heavenly body,
raised his voice in praise,
extolling Xūmótí,
saying three times her virtue,
that she would soon become a Buddha.
The bhikṣu Mahālu,
the king, believing he greatly recited the Mahāyāna,
often loosened his hair for him to tread upon.
Another bhikṣu
then said to the king:
'This Mahālu does not recite many sūtras.
Why do you make offerings to him like this?'
The king said:
'Day and night, I wish to see this bhikṣu.'
He then went and saw him in a cave reciting the Lotus Sūtra.
He saw a golden bright light,
a person riding a white elephant, with hands joined in offering.
As the king approached, it vanished and was no longer visible.
He then asked:
'Venerable One,
I came, and the golden bright person vanished. Why?'
The bhikṣu said:
'That was the bodhisattva Samantabhadra, who came to teach and guide me in reciting this sūtra.'
The bhikṣu Shànhuì
addressed the Buddha Pǔguāng Rúlái, saying:
'In the past, I was in a deep mountain,
and had five kinds of dreams.
First, I dreamed of lying on the great ocean;
second, I dreamed of using Mount Sumeru as a pillow;
third, I dreamed of all beings in the ocean entering my body;
fourth, I dreamed of holding the sun in my hand;
fifth, I dreamed of holding the moon in my hand.
I beseech the World-Honored One to explain them for me.'
At that time, the Buddha replied:
'Dreaming of lying on the great ocean means
your body is at that time within the great ocean of birth and death.
Dreaming of using Mount Sumeru as a pillow means
you will emerge from birth and death and attain the mark of nirvāṇa.
Dreaming of all beings in the ocean entering your body means
you will, within the great ocean of birth and death,
become a refuge for all beings.
Dreaming of holding the sun in your hand means
the light of wisdom universally illuminates the Dharma realm.
Dreaming of holding the moon in your hand means
with expedient wisdom, you enter birth and death,
and with the cool Dharma, guide and transform beings.'
The elder Xūfú had a daughter,
named Lóngshī,
who was fourteen years old.
At that time, she was in the bathhouse, having bathed, anointed with incense, and put on fine clothes.
The Buddha and his retinue emitted light from the ūrṇā between his eyebrows,
illuminating within the sevenfold doors,
making the halls and rooms all bright.
The girl saw the light surpassing the sun and moon,
and knew in her heart it was not ordinary.
She then ran up to the seventh story of the tower,
looked eastward, and saw the Buddha standing outside the door.
The girl was greatly joyful,
and thought to herself:
'Now I can make offerings to the Buddha and his disciples.
With the resolve to practice the bodhisattva path,
may I later attain the Way like the Buddha.'
Māra, seeing the girl resolve the great mind, was displeased.
He then descended and transformed into her father,
saying to Lóngshī:
'What you aspire to is too great.
The Buddha Way is difficult to attain.
This age is fortunate to have a Buddha,
but it is better to seek arhatship.
Moreover, both deliver from the world, and nirvāṇa is no different.'
Lóngshī replied:
'It is not as you say, Father.
The Buddha's wisdom is vast, saving beings without limit.
The arhat's wisdom is small, like a speck of dust.
Why would a noble person delight in the lesser?'
Māra again said:
'It has never been heard that a woman becomes a wheel-turning king,
much less becomes a Buddha.
It is better to seek arhatship and quickly attain nirvāṇa.'
Lóngshī replied:
'I have also heard
that a woman cannot become a wheel-turning king,
nor become a Buddha.
I shall diligently strive to transform this woman's body into a man's body.
I have heard
that in the world, one who practices the bodhisattva Dharma
without slackening for billions of kalpas,
will later become a Buddha.'
Māra, seeing the girl's mind unshaken,
became even more vexed and poisonous.
He further gave a harsh instruction:
'If you practice the bodhisattva path,
you should not cling to the world,
nor cherish your life.
Now, if you are diligent,
can you jump from the tower to the ground?
Then you may later become a Buddha.'
Lóngshī thought to herself:
'Now I see the Buddha,
I aspire to the bodhisattva path.
My father also instructs me to be diligent.
Through this body, I can attain Buddhahood.
Why should I cherish this fragile life?'
She then stood by the railing,
faced the Buddha with hands joined, and said:
'I take refuge in the Supreme among Gods.
With omniscient wisdom,
know what I seek.
I abandon my body and life, not forsaking the bodhisattva path.
I offer my body to the Buddha,
like scattering flowers.'
She then leaped from the tower.
Before reaching the ground,
she transformed into a man.
The Buddha smiled.
Five-colored light issued from his mouth, illuminating a Buddha-land,
then circled his body three times and entered through the top of his head.
'Do you see this girl leaping into the air and transforming into a man?
This girl, in a past life,
had already served ten thousand Buddhas.
She will later make offerings to as many future Buddhas as the sands of the Ganges.
After seventy-six million kalpas, she will become a Buddha,
named Míngshàng.
Her lifespan will be one kalpa.
After her parinirvāṇa,
the Dharma will flourish
for half a kalpa before ceasing.'
Then Lóngshī, standing before the Buddha, said to her parents:
'I wish to be released to become a śramaṇa.'
Her parents then consented.
All her relatives, both inner and outer, resolved the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.
The Buddha was in Rājagṛha.
Bodhisattvas and the great assembly of the fourfold community gathered.
The Buddha was expounding the Dharma.
There was a woman of the Kālā caste who was pregnant, seated in the assembly.
In her womb was a child.
With hands folded in reverence, she listened to the sutra.
The Buddha, wishing to make the assembly see this,
caused a great radiance to appear, illuminating the seat of the Kālā woman.
Everyone saw the girl in the womb with hands folded, listening to the sutra,
as clear as looking in a mirror.
The Buddha, with his eightfold voice,
asked the girl in the womb, "For what reason do you fold your hands and listen to the sutra?"
By the Buddha's majestic power, she immediately replied to the Buddha, saying,
"Because people in the world all practice the ten evils.
I wish to make them practice the ten good deeds.
Also, because the births and deaths of people in the world never cease.
Moreover, people in the world are not filial to their parents.
They do not make offerings to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or practitioners of the Way.
Therefore, I fold my hands and listen to the sutra."
When the girl finished speaking these words, she was born.
Like a crown prince born from the right side,
the earth shook in six ways.
In the sky, there was spontaneously heavenly music.
Heavenly flowers rained down.
A thousand-petaled lotus flower, large as a chariot wheel,
with a stem made of jewels,
resembling blue lapis lazuli, appeared.
The girl then sat upon the lotus flower.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, held out a heavenly garment
to give to the girl to wear.
The girl replied, saying,
"You are an Arhat.
I am a Bodhisattva.
You are not of my kind.
You are not my equal.
I have my own garment."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"From which land does this girl come,
that she should send for a garment?"
The Buddha said,
"This girl comes from the Pure Land of the Buddha in the southeast direction.
It is one hundred thousand Buddha-lands away from here.
The garment from her original land then spontaneously appeared in the sky, arriving with a rustling sound."
The girl, seeing the garment arrive, put it on.
She immediately attained the five supernatural powers.
Moreover, all the people of her original land attain the five supernatural powers.
After the girl finished putting on the garment,
she descended from the lotus flower and walked before the Buddha.
As the girl took a single step,
the earth shook in six ways.
She touched her head to the ground, making obeisance to the Buddha.
Three times she said, "Námó Fó."
Then, kneeling upright, she addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Now, in this assembly, there are many women of the Kālā caste.
I pray that the Buddha will expound a sutra for them,
enabling them to obtain male bodies."
The Buddha said,
"I do not cause you to become a man,
nor do I cause you to become a woman.
All is obtained from one's own bodily actions."
The Buddha said,
"There is one thing that can swiftly lead to obtaining a male body.
What is that one thing?
To arouse the mind for the Bodhisattva Path."
"Furthermore, a woman should inwardly contemplate her own body:
It is like a mechanical device,
bones and joints propping each other up,
with only sinews and skin covering them."
"Women are constantly afraid of people,
like poisonous snakes and toads,
not daring to come out during the day."
At that time, seventy-five women of the Kālā caste in the assembly,
hearing the Buddha expound the sutra, rejoiced and leapt for joy.
They came forward, touched their heads to the ground,
made obeisance to the Buddha, and addressed him, saying,
"We vow to arouse the Bodhisattva mind and become men.
If we do not obtain male bodies,
we will never rise up."
At that time, seventy-five Kālāpati (householders)
came from Śrāvastī to where the Buddha was.
Seeing their wives all before the Buddha,
they thought to themselves,
"We have already lost our wives."
They then asked Śāriputra,
"These women are our wives.
Why are they here?"
Śāriputra replied, saying,
"They wish to become bhikṣuṇīs.
Will you gentlemen consent or not?"
The Kālāpati answered, saying,
"First, let us become bhikṣus."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"These seventy-five Kālāpati
all wish to become bhikṣus."
The Buddha called out,
"Come, good men."
They all became bhikṣus.
Their hair naturally fell away.
Kaṣāya robes came and covered their bodies.
They held alms bowls in their hands.
They all came forward and made obeisance to the Buddha.
At that time, the seventy-five women,
each removing their pearl bracelets, scattered them above the Buddha.
They then spontaneously, in the sky,
transformed into seventy-five jeweled canopies with pearl necklaces.
Within the canopies were seven-jeweled couches,
upon which were seats.
Beside the Buddha were countless Bodhisattvas listening to the sutra.
The seventy-five women,
seeing these transformations,
greatly rejoiced and, by the Buddha's majestic power, flew up and dwelt in the sky.
Spontaneously, flowers rained down, scattering upon the Buddha.
Descending from the sky,
they then obtained male bodies.
They came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"We wish to become bhikṣus."
The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Maitreya,
"Take them and confer the precepts."
Bodhisattva Maitreya then conferred the precepts,
and they became bhikṣus of the Saṅgha.
The girl spontaneously had a transformed flower canopy with seven layers, its stem like a lotus.
She immediately took it and said to her mother,
"The Buddha is the teacher who saves people in heaven and under heaven.
Mother, offer this flower canopy to the Buddha.
It is fitting to offer it to the teacher of heaven and under heaven.
Afterwards, mother shall also become a canopy for all under heaven."
The girl said to her mother,
"Now you should arouse the Bodhisattva mind."
The mother replied to her daughter, saying,
"When I first conceived you,
in dreams I constantly saw the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Bhikṣu Saṅgha.
I had no mind of the three poisons.
My body was at ease and peaceful.
I knew the child in my womb was this Mahāsattva Bodhisattva.
Because of this, I was at ease and peaceful."
At that time, she aroused the Bodhisattva mind.
Having obtained the flower canopy from her mother,
she offered it to the Buddha.
The earth shook in six ways.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra,
"The stars in the fourfold world system
can still be known in number.
But the number of parents this girl has saved, past and future,
cannot be known."
Once there was a kingdom.
Grain and rice became extremely expensive.
The people suffered from hunger.
At that time, there was a śramaṇa.
He entered the city to beg for alms.
He obtained nothing at all.
Next, he came to the gate of a wealthy and noble elder.
There he received coarse and poor food.
Just as he was about to leave the city,
at the gate he encountered a hunter who killed living beings, a butcher.
The butcher was carrying a puppy, taking it home to kill.
Seeing the śramaṇa, he joyfully approached and paid his respects.
The śramaṇa chanted blessings for long life and longevity.
The śramaṇa knew there was a puppy that the man intended to kill and eat.
He asked the man what he was carrying.
The man replied,
"Nothing."
The śramaṇa asked again,
"I have already seen the sin of killing living beings.
It is very unwholesome.
I wish to trade my food for this puppy,
so that its life may be spared, and your merit will be immeasurable."
The man refused.
The śramaṇa earnestly explained and pleaded, but the man would not comply with his words.
The śramaṇa then said,
"If you refuse,
at least show it to me."
The man then brought it out
and showed it to the śramaṇa.
The śramaṇa offered the food to the puppy.
He stroked it with his hand, chanted blessings, and tears fell.
"Due to your past offenses, you have obtained this dog's body.
You are not free, about to be killed and eaten.
May you, through this, have your offenses eradicated and merit arise in life after life.
May you leave this dog's body and be reborn as a human.
Wherever you are, may you encounter the Dharma."
The puppy, having received the food, gave rise to a wholesome mind.
It leaped and rejoiced, and after this, it was taken away.
The man returned home, killed, and ate it.
The puppy's life ended.
It was reborn into the household of a wealthy and noble elder.
As soon as it was born and fell to the ground,
it possessed a compassionate heart.
At that time, that śramaṇa,
while begging for alms, next arrived at the elder's gate.
When the elder's son saw that śramaṇa,
he remembered his past connection.
He immediately approached, bowed his head to the śramaṇa's feet,
and invited him forward to make offerings of a hundred flavors of food and drink.
He then addressed his parents,
"Now I wish to follow this great upādhyāya,
to respectfully receive the sūtras and precepts and become his disciple."
His parents, loving and cherishing him, would not consent.
"Now, in our entire family, we have only you, one son.
You are to continue our lineage.
You are the master of our household—why do you wish to abandon us and leave?"
The child wept and cried, refusing to eat or drink.
"If you do not allow me, I will go to my death."
Seeing this, his parents consented and allowed him to go.
He followed his teacher to study the path.
He removed his hair and beard, donned the three Dharma robes,
recited the Buddhist sūtras,
deeply understood their meaning,
and then attained samādhi.
He established irreversible progress.
He taught and transformed all beings,
arousing the intention for the great path.
The śramaṇa then recognized his past lives.
He aroused the bodhisattva mind.
He established irreversible progress.
How much more so for someone who
serves and makes offerings to the Three Jewels,
and recites the Mahāyāna sūtras?
The father of Jiāyè
was named Níjùlǜtuó.
He was a man of the Mójié Kingdom.
He came from the Brahmin caste.
Due to blessings from past lives, he was born into great wealth in this world.
His rare treasures were the finest in the kingdom.
His wealth was comparable to that of the king,
lacking only one part in a thousand.
The couple was lonely and lacked children.
Nearby, beside their dwelling, was a great tree spirit.
At that time, the couple, desiring a child,
offered sacrifices of three types of livestock for years without success.
The man grew furious and set a deadline of seven days,
saying, "If there is still no result, I will cut you down
and burn you in the public square."
The spirit heard this and was terrified.
It went up to report to the King of the Xīyì Heaven.
The heavenly king then took the spirit
to inform Lord Indra.
Indra, using his heavenly eye, surveyed the realm of desire
but found no one suitable to be their child.
He then informed Lord Brahmā.
Brahmā looked everywhere and saw
a Brahmā Heaven being whose life was about to end.
He told him,
"You may be born in Jambudvīpa
as the son of Níjùlǜtuó."
The Brahmā Heaven being replied,
"Brahmins hold many wrong views.
If I am born below, I cannot become their son."
Lord Brahmā answered,
"That Brahmin possessed great virtue in the past.
Among the beings in the realm of desire, none are suitable to be his child.
If you go to be born,
I will command Lord Indra to protect you,
so that you do not fall into wrong views along the way."
The Brahmā Heaven being said, "So be it."
Indra then informed the tree spirit,
and the tree spirit returned to tell the elder,
"Do not be angry.
After seven days, you will surely have a son."
When the seven days had passed, the wife became pregnant.
After ten months, she gave birth.
The child's body was golden and radiated light.
A diviner prophesied,
"This child, due to past blessings, possesses great majesty and virtue.
His aspirations are pure and far-reaching; he does not crave worldly affairs.
If he later leaves home, he will certainly attain the holy path."
Upon hearing this, the parents were greatly distressed
and worried that their son would leave home. When he reached the age of fifteen,
they wanted to arrange a marriage for him.
Jiāyè heard this and repeatedly pleaded with his parents,
"My aspiration is for purity; I do not need a wife."
His parents would not listen. Jiāyè then said,
"If so, I will not take an ordinary woman.
Only if I find a woman with a purple-gold complexion, incomparably beautiful,
will I marry her."
He intended to make this impossible.
His parents ordered a search throughout the kingdom.
The Brahmins then devised a plan.
They cast a golden statue of a goddess,
with a beautiful face and exquisite radiance,
resembling a heavenly being.
From kingdom to kingdom, they loudly proclaimed,
"Any woman who sees the golden goddess
and makes offerings to her will, when she later marries,
obtain a good husband
with a golden body, a handsome and marvelous appearance,
and unparalleled wisdom."
Women in villages and cities everywhere,
hearing this proclamation, were all eager.
They came out to welcome it, making offerings and paying respects.
Only one woman, with a golden body,
beautiful and graceful, remained alone in her quiet room, unwilling to come out.
The other women advised her,
"Those who see the golden goddess
all get their wishes fulfilled.
Why do you alone refuse to come out?"
She replied,
"My aspiration is for tranquility; I do not desire other wishes."
The women said again,
"Even if you have no wishes, just come look with us.
What harm could it do?"
The women took her by the hand and together they went out to see.
The golden woman's radiance outshone the golden goddess.
The Brahmins returned to report to the elder in detail.
He immediately sent matchmakers to the woman's home
to convey his intention.
The woman's parents had also heard of Jiāyè's reputation.
Respectfully accepting the proposal, they agreed. The woman, hearing this, was greatly distressed and troubled.
Pressured by her parents and unable to avoid it,
she eventually married Jiāyè.
The two faced each other, each firm in their resolve.
Though husband and wife, they felt no affection.
They then made a vow together:
"You and I will each sleep on separate beds.
We must not touch each other."
At that time, the couple each slept on their own bed.
When Jiāyè's parents heard that although he shared a room with his wife,
they slept in separate beds,
his father soon had someone remove one of the beds.
Thus, the couple shared only one bed.
The wife then made another vow with her husband:
"When I am asleep,
you must walk about."
Once, when the wife was sleeping,
one arm fell to the ground.
A large venomous snake was about to bite it.
Seeing this, Jiāyè, out of compassion,
wrapped his hand in cloth and lifted her arm onto the bed.
She immediately awoke and was greatly angry,
saying to Jiāyè,
"We had an agreement.
How could you violate it?"
Jiāyè replied,
"Your arm fell to the ground, and a snake was about to bite it.
That is why I helped you; it was not intentional contact."
He pointed to the snake to show her.
The wife then understood.
Thereupon, the couple discussed together,
"Why don't we leave home to cultivate the path?"
They then bid farewell to their parents
and together left home,
entering the mountains to practice the path.
At that time, there was a Brahmin
with five hundred disciples
also dwelling in these mountains.
Seeing Jiāyè and his wife following each other,
Jiāyè then left his wife,
using five hundred taels of gold
to trade for a monastic robe and dwelled separately in another grove.
His wife then took refuge with the Brahmin,
seeking to become his disciple.
The Brahmin's five hundred disciples,
seeing this woman's beautiful appearance,
engaged in lustful acts with her daily.
The woman had no freedom
and could not endure it.
She then told her teacher.
The teacher then
admonished his disciples,
ordering them to restrain their desires.
