Jiāyè later encountered the Buddha's appearance in the world,
heard the Dharma, and received transformation,
immediately attaining Arhatship.
Hearing that his former wife was with the Brahmin,
he brought her to the Buddha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to her,
and she attained Arhatship.
Her hair fell out by itself, and the monastic robe appeared on her body.
She became a bhikṣuṇī.
Traveling to teach and transform others,
she happened upon the great assembly of King Pòsīnì.
The bhikṣuṇīs were then able to enter the king's palace,
teaching the king's wives,
persuading them all to observe a one-day fast.
When the king returned to the palace in the evening
and summoned his wives,
they all said they were fasting
and none were willing to come.
The king became greatly angry
and said to his attendants,
"Who taught the wives to fast?"
The attendants replied,
"A certain bhikṣuṇī."
The king then summoned her
and ordered her to receive the king's lustful desires for ninety days in place of the wives.
All of this was due to past causes and conditions
created by vows.
Therefore, even though she attained Arhatship,
she could not avoid it.
Kāshè abandoned great wealth to follow the path of a poor mendicant.
Entering the city of Rājagṛha, he saw a solitary old woman.
She was in extreme poverty.
On a large dung heap in the alley,
she had dug a cave beside the dung heap to serve as her dwelling.
Weak, sickly, and afflicted by illness, she often lay within it.
She had neither clothing nor food.
A small bamboo fence was set up to conceal her form.
Her life was nearing its end.
A maidservant of a wealthy elder,
while discarding some fermented rice water that was foul and unspeakably putrid,
was begged by the old woman for it.
The old woman then used a broken tile to hold it, placing it beside her.
Kāshè, pitying her, went to beg for a little of it.
The old woman spoke a verse,
saying it was foul and putrid.
Yet Kāshè, out of compassion,
endured and begged for it.
The old woman, overjoyed, then gave it to him.
Kāshè feared the old woman might not believe he would actually consume it.
So, in front of the old woman, he drank it and rinsed his bowl.
He displayed his spiritual power.
The old woman was greatly elated.
With single-minded focus, she gazed from afar.
Kāshè asked her,
"What is your wish now, mother?"
At that time, the old woman, weary of the suffering of this world,
upon hearing of the joys of heaven, wished to be reborn in heaven.
A few days later, her life ended,
and she was immediately reborn in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
Remembering her former kindness, she sought to make offerings.
Śakra, lord of the devas, hearing of this matter,
together with his queen, took a hundred-flavored food contained in a small bottle,
descended to the leaky hut,
changed their forms,
to resemble an old couple,
poor weavers of mats.
Kāshè, while seeking alms, saw them and went to beg.
The couple told him,
"We are now poor and suffering, yet we will cut from our own share
to give to the worthy one,
so that we may gain merit."
Kāshè lowered his bowl.
They then opened the small bottle,
and its fragrance pervaded the great city.
Kāshè, displeased by this,
entered into samādhi,
and his body flew away.
Snapping his fingers in joy,
the devas bowed at Kāshè's feet,
speaking verses in praise.
"Great virtuous one, do you not know?
The Dharma ship is about to break,
the Dharma city is about to collapse,
the Dharma ocean is about to dry up,
the Dharma banner is about to fall,
the Dharma lamp is about to be extinguished,
the preachers of Dharma are about to depart,
those who practice the Path are gradually decreasing,
while evil people are increasing.
You must, with great compassion, establish the Buddha-Dharma."
Kāshè's mind was like the great ocean,
clear and unmoving.
After a long while, he replied,
"The world will not last long;
it is without wisdom, blind and dark."
Kāshè reflected,
"What should I do now?
How can I make the Dharma, so difficult to attain over three asamkhyeya kalpas, endure long?
Only by compiling the Tripiṭaka
can it endure long.
Future generations will then be able to receive and practice it.
The Buddha, through countless lifetimes of arduous toil,
with compassion for sentient beings, learned this Dharma
and expounded it for people.
We too should uphold and propagate it."
Ascending to the summit of Mount Sumeru,
he struck the bell and sounded the ghaṇṭā,
and spoke a verse, saying:
This is the sound of the gavel.
And Kāshyapa spoke.
His voice reached throughout the three thousand great thousand worlds.
All heard and knew.
All disciples who had attained supernatural powers
gathered at Kāshyapa's place.
Kāshyapa addressed them in divine language, saying:
"The Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa; all disciples who know the Dharma
will also follow into extinction.
The Buddha's Dharma is about to perish.
Future sentient beings are truly pitiable.
They will lose the eye of wisdom.
They will be foolish, blind, and ignorant.
We should uphold the Buddha's teachings.
Wait until the compilation of the Dharma treasury is completed,
then enter extinction at will."
Kāshyapa selected a thousand people.
Except for Ānanda, all had attained arhatship.
King Bimbisāra,
having attained the Way, often ordered the palace to provide meals for a thousand people.
King Ajātaśatru did not discontinue this practice.
Kāshyapa considered:
"If we always beg for food,
there may be outsiders who forcefully come to challenge and question,
disrupting the Dharma affairs."
He went to Rājagṛha to inform the king of the matter.
The king should provide food,
sending it daily.
During the three-month summer retreat,
Kāshyapa observed who still had afflictions.
Only Ānanda remained.
Mahākāshyapa then enumerated his faults, saying:
"You have committed six dushkṛta offenses.
You should confess them all before the saṅgha."
Ānanda immediately followed the instruction,
kneeling with palms together,
baring his right shoulder, removing his sandals, and confessing.
Kāshyapa rose from the saṅgha,
took him by the hand and led him out,
saying:
"You should exhaust your defilements.
If any residual bonds remain,
do not come back."
Then he closed the door himself.
Together with the arhats, he deliberated:
"Who can compile the Vinaya Dharma treasury?"
Elder Aniruddha said:
"Śāriputra was the second Buddha.
Gavāṃpati is gentle and refined,
skilled in seclusion and tranquility, and knows the Vinaya treasury well.
He is now in the Śirīṣa tree garden in heaven.
Send a junior bhikṣu to summon him."
Kāshyapa's intention was:
"All arhats who have exhausted defilements should gather in Jambudvīpa.
The saṅgha has a great Dharma matter.
Come quickly now."
Gavāṃpati was suspicious,
asking:
"Is it because of disputes and schisms?
Or has the Buddha's sun set?"
The answer was:
"The great teacher has entered nirvāṇa."
"Where is my preceptor Śāriputra now?"
The answer was:
"He entered nirvāṇa earlier."
Gavāṃpati asked:
"What are Maudgalyāyana, Ānanda, and Rāhula doing now?"
The answer was:
"Maudgalyāyana has already entered nirvāṇa.
Ānanda still has sorrowful bonds,
grieving and weeping, unable to console himself.
Rāhula has attained arhatship and is free from sorrow and suffering."
Gavāṃpati said:
"My preceptor and the great teacher have both entered nirvāṇa.
I cannot descend now."
He then entered nirvāṇa.
Ānanda contemplated the Dharma, seeking to exhaust his residual defilements.
Sitting in meditation and walking in contemplation, his concentration power was insufficient, and he did not attain the Way in time.
In the latter part of the night, exhausted and wanting to rest,
before his head touched the pillow, he suddenly attained enlightenment.
He became a great powerful arhat.
That night, he went to the saṅgha hall and knocked on the door,
calling for Mahākāshyapa.
Mahākāshyapa said:
"Why have you come?"
He replied:
"I have exhausted my defilements tonight."
Kāshyapa said:
"I will not open the door for you.
Enter through the keyhole."
Ānanda then entered through the keyhole and confessed,
saying, "Mahākāshyapa, please do not blame me further."
Kāshyapa placed his hand on his head,
saying, "I deliberately made you attain the Way.
Do not resent me.
I am the same."
Mahākāshyapa said to Ānanda:
"From the Dharma Wheel Sutra
to the Mahāparinirvāṇa,
compile them into the four Āgamas.
The Aṅguttara, Ekottara, Dīrgha, and Saṃyukta.
This is called the Sūtra Dharma treasury."
The arhats further asked:
"Who can clearly compile the Vinaya Dharma treasury?" All said:
"Elder Upāli,
among the five hundred arhats,
is foremost in upholding the Vinaya.
We now invite him."
Upāli accepted the instruction,
sat on the lion seat, and said:
"Where was the Buddha
when he established the Vinaya precepts?"
At that time, Sudinna, the son of the Kalandaka elder,
first violated the rule of sexual misconduct.
Thus began the establishment of major offenses.
The arhats considered:
"Who can clearly
study the Abhidharma treasury?"
They thought:
"Elder Ānanda, among the five hundred arhats,
is foremost in understanding the meaning of the sūtras.
We now invite him."
Ānanda accepted the invitation.
The Buddha was in Śrāvastī,
speaking of the five fears, five offenses, five removals, and five extinctions.
Because of these causes and conditions,
in this life, body and mind experience immeasurable joy.
Yet they again fall into evil paths.
Such teachings are called the Abhidharma treasury."
After Kāshyapa compiled the Dharma treasury,
he entered the Kukkuṭapāda Mountain,
split it into three parts,
spread grass on the ground inside,
and then thought to himself,
speaking to his body:
"In the past, the Tathāgata covered you with rag robes.
You should remain here
until the time of Maitreya's Dharma treasury."
Then he spoke a verse:
Immediately he entered the three samādhis.
As if entering nirvāṇa, with three mountains covering his body,
like a child entering its mother's womb,
he remained undestroyed.
Second, if King Ajātaśatru comes,
having previously agreed to meet,
the mountain should open for him.
If Ajātaśatru does not see me,
he will vomit hot blood and die."
Third, when Ānanda comes, the mountain will open.
Maitreya will come here with ninety-six million disciples,
take Kāshyapa's body to show his retinue,
and have them all learn my merit of upholding precepts.
Maitreya Buddha
will also teach my disciples
with the three vehicles.
Mahākāshyapa
will assist Maitreya in teaching and transforming."
Also, the bhikṣu Kaṇṭhaka,
the bhikṣu Piṇḍola,
the bhikṣu Rāhula,
the four great śrāvakas,
vowed not to enter nirvāṇa
until the Buddha's Dharma is completely extinguished,
and only then enter nirvāṇa.
Mahākāshyapa dwells in the mountain of the village of Vidi in the kingdom of Magadha.
Maitreya will go there with several thousand people.
Various spirits and others
will open the stone gate to reveal his meditation cave.
At that time, Maitreya Buddha
will extend his right hand
to point at Kāshyapa,
telling the people:
"A disciple of the ancient Buddha Śākyamuni,
named Kāshyapa,
foremost in ascetic practices,
still exists today."
Maitreya Buddha
will then take Kāshyapa's saṅghāṭī robe and wear it.
Kāshyapa's body will suddenly scatter like stars.
Maitreya will take various flowers
to make offerings to Kāshyapa,
out of reverence.
In the city of Rājagṛha, there was a layman named Shùtí.
A merchant who had traveled overseas returned
and presented him with a sandalwood alms bowl.
He placed it in a net bag
and hung it high on a post, declaring:
"If any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa
can obtain it without using a ladder or staff,
they may take it."
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra and others all said,
"They wish to see supernatural powers," and turned their heads away, departing.
Piṇḍola
(whose surname was Bhāradvāja) went to Shùtí.
Shùtí said,
"Welcome, Bhāradvāja.
If you can take the bowl without using a ladder or staff, it is yours."
Piṇḍola entered meditation,
stretched out his hand, and took the bowl.
The layman then filled it with rice and offered it to him.
After eating, Piṇḍola took it away.
There was a monk
of few desires and contentment
who asked where he had obtained it.
Piṇḍola recounted the above events in detail.
The monk of few desires rebuked him, saying:
"For accepting an object from a naked ascetic,
how can you be called a monk?
Before those who have not received the full precepts,
you displayed transcendent holy powers."
After the rebuke, he reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha assembled the saṅgha
and asked Piṇḍola,
"Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
"Indeed, I did."
The Buddha said to Bhāradvāja,
"You are banished for life.
You shall not dwell in Jambudvīpa."
Piṇḍola
respectfully accepted the instruction, returned to his quarters,
handed over his bedding, bed, and couch to the saṅgha,
took his robe and bowl,
vanished from Jambudvīpa,
and appeared in Godānīya,
teaching the fourfold assembly and widely promoting the Buddha's work.
The Buddha was in Kapilavastu,
at the Nyagrodha Monastery.
The Śākyas asked the Buddha,
"What past causes
did Kauṇḍinya and the others have,
that when the Tathāgata appeared in the world and the Dharma drum was first sounded,
they were the first to hear it; when the nectar first descended, they received its moisture?"
With different mouths but the same voice, they praised immeasurably.
The monks heard this
and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"It is not only today that I first liberated these five men.
In the distant past, I also saved these ones.
Using my body as a boat,
I rescued them from drowning and preserved their lives.
Now that I have attained Buddhahood, I first liberate them."
The monks said to the Buddha,
"How was this matter?"
The Buddha said,
"In the past, in Jambudvīpa,
in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī,
there was a king named Brahmadatta.
At that time, there was a merchant leader
named Ratnājaya.
While wandering in an outer forest, he saw a man
weeping bitterly in sorrow.
He had tied a rope to a tree,
put his head into the noose,
and was about to kill himself.
Ratnājaya approached and asked him,
'Why are you doing this?'
He persuaded him to let go of the rope.
The man replied,
'I am poor and in debt.
My creditors seize everything,
pressing me day and night.
Though heaven and earth are vast, there is no place for me to hide.
Therefore, I seek to escape this suffering.'
At that time, the merchant leader
said to him,
'You just release yourself.
However much you owe, I will repay it all for you.'
After saying this,
that man desisted.
Overjoyed and elated,
he followed the merchant leader to the marketplace.
[Ratnājaya] announced to all,
'I wish to repay debts.'
At that time, the creditors
rushed together in a crowd, coming without limit.
He exhausted all his wealth but still could not settle the debts.
His wife and children were impoverished, freezing, and had to beg to survive.
At that time, there were many merchants
who urged the merchant leader,
wishing to go to sea together.
He replied to them,
'I am now destitute and have nothing left.
How can I follow?'
The others told him,
'There are five hundred of us in total.
We will contribute money, share the costs, and together prepare the ship and equipment.'
The group pooled their resources and obtained three thousand taels of gold.
The merchant leader used one thousand taels to prepare the ship,
one thousand taels for provisions,
and one thousand taels for necessities on the ship, with the remainder given to his wife and children.
Then at the seashore,
they constructed a large ship; when the ship was completed, they set sail.
But on the way,
they suddenly encountered a black storm,
which shattered the ship.
The people had nothing to rely on.
Among them, five men
together said to the merchant leader,
'We followed you here.
Now we are about to drown and die.
Peril is upon us.
We beg you to save us.'
The merchant leader replied,
'I have heard that the ocean does not harbor dead bodies.
All of you now, hold onto me.
I will kill myself to save you from this calamity.
I vow to attain Buddhahood.
When I later become a Buddha,
I shall use the supreme Dharma ship to liberate you from birth and death.'
After saying this,
he cut his own throat with a knife.
After his life ended,
a sea deity raised a wind that blew them to the far shore.
They crossed the great sea and all attained safety.
Know that the Ratnājaya of that time
is my present self.
The five men of that time
are Kauṇḍinya and the others."
The Buddha was in Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove.
Ānanda again asked the Buddha,
"What past causes did Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya and his five companions have,
that when the Dharma drum was first sounded,
they alone were the first to hear it?"
The Buddha said,
"In a past life, they ate my flesh and thereby attained safety.
Therefore, today they are the first to receive the Dharma food and thereby attain liberation.
In a past kalpa, in this Jambudvīpa,
there was a great king
named Śītārṣabha.
He ruled over Jambudvīpa's eighty-four thousand countries.
A fiery star appeared.
Astrologers told the king,
'There will be a drought.'
Indeed, heaven did not rain for twelve years.
The king was greatly distressed.
He calculated the current population
and counted the granaries; if all the people received one liter per day,
it would still be insufficient, and many were dying.
The king thought to himself,
'What plan can I devise to save the people's lives?'
He then made a vow:
'Now the people of this country are starving and have no food.
I relinquish this body and vow to become a great fish.
May my flesh suffice to save all.'
He then climbed to the top of a tree and threw himself to the ground.
He died immediately.
In a great river, he was reborn as a miraculously born fish.
Its body was five hundred yojanas long.
At that time, there were five woodcutters
who each carried axes and went to the riverbank
intending to cut timber.
The fish said,
'If you need food,
come take my flesh, eat your fill, and take some back.
When I later become a Buddha, I shall use the Dharma food to save and liberate you all.
Tell the people of the country that those who need food should come.'
The five men rejoiced and did exactly as told.
They told the people of the country; word spread, and throughout Jambudvīpa, all came together.
They ate its flesh until one side was completely consumed.
Then it turned over and offered the other side.
When that was eaten, it grew back again.
Thus turning back and forth,
it constantly used its body's flesh to provide for all.
For twelve years,
all those beings who ate its flesh developed minds of compassion.
After death, they were reborn in heaven.
The king Śītārṣabha of that time
is my present self.
The five woodcutters of that time
are Kauṇḍinya and the others.
As for the people who later ate the flesh,
they are now the eighty thousand devas
and the disciples who have attained liberation."
In the land of Yùbìluópó, there was a Brahmin.
His name was Bìluó Jiāyè.
He led five hundred Brahmin disciples who wore coiled topknots.
He was already revered as an Elder.
Throughout the country of Āngqié Mójié, he was proclaimed an Arhat.
The Buddha arrived at Jiāyè's place and said to him,
"I wish to lodge here for one night."
He replied,
"I do not begrudge it.
But there is a poisonous dragon in this chamber, and I fear it may harm you."
The Buddha said,
"It is no trouble."
Jiāyè said,
"As you wish."
The Buddha then entered the stone chamber.
He sat cross-legged, straightened his body, and focused his mind.
The dragon saw this and emitted smoke; the Buddha also emitted smoke.
The dragon then emitted fire; the Buddha also emitted fire.
At that time, smoke and fire arose together within the stone chamber.
Jiāyè saw this from afar and thought,
"What a pity for Qútán to be harmed by the poisonous dragon."
The Buddha then subdued the dragon and placed it in his alms bowl.
The next morning, he took it and went to Jiāyè's place.
He announced,
"The poisonous dragon is now inside the bowl."
Jiāyè thought to himself,
"Although Qútán has attained Arhatship and possesses great spiritual power,
he is still not equal to me."
He said to the Buddha,
"You may stay; I will provide food."
The Buddha said,
"If you can personally come at the appointed time, I will accept your invitation." Jiāyè said,
"I will come myself to serve the Buddha food."
After eating, the Buddha returned to the stone chamber to spend the night.
That night, he entered the Samādhi of Fire Light, illuminating the stone chamber.
Jiāyè immediately gathered his disciples and surrounded it.
He said to the Buddha,
"The time has now come.
Please return to partake of the meal.
Why was there such a great fire last night, O Śramaṇa?"
The Buddha told Jiāyè,
"Last night, I entered the Samādhi of Fire Light,
causing this stone chamber to be brightly illuminated."
Jiāyè marveled at his great majestic virtue,
but still thought, "He is not equal to me, who has attained Arhatship."
After the Buddha finished eating, he spent another night in a grove.
The next day, Jiāyè again welcomed him back for a meal.
The Buddha said,
"You go ahead; I will follow shortly."
He first went to the Jambū tree,
took its fruit, and sat on Jiāyè's seat.
When Jiāyè arrived later, he said,
"How is it that you have already arrived first?"
The Buddha said,
"This fruit is of fine color, fragrant, and delicious; you may eat it."
Jiāyè thought,
"This Śramaṇa possesses great spiritual powers,
but he is still not equal to me, who has attained Arhatship."
After the Buddha finished eating, he returned to his grove and sat.
He then displayed various spiritual powers,
intending to subdue Jiāyè.
The Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra, and others
all brought offerings to make offerings to the Buddha.
Jiāyè, along with his five hundred disciples,
discarded their fire-worship implements, clean robes, and water vessels,
throwing them into the Nairañjanā River.
They went to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha, in turn, preached the Dharma to the five hundred people.
Right on their seats, their defilements were exhausted, and they attained the pure Dharma-eye.
They all said to the Buddha,
"We wish to leave home."
The Buddha said,
"Come, Bhikṣus!
Diligently cultivate the holy life
to reach the end of suffering."
He then conferred upon them the full precepts.
Jiāyè's middle brother was named Nátí.
He lived downstream on the Nairañjanā River,
with three hundred disciples.
Jiāyè's youngest brother was named Jiāyé.
He lived on Elephant Head Mountain,
with two hundred disciples.
The two brothers saw that their elder brother had taken up the Path.
They went together and asked him,
"Is it superior to cultivate the holy life
under this great Śramaṇa?"
He replied,
"It is extremely superior and wonderful."
Each, along with their followers, went together to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to them.
On their seats, they awakened to the Path and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
They said to the Buddha,
"We wish to cultivate the holy life within the Buddha's Dharma."
The Buddha said,
"Come, Bhikṣus! Diligently cultivate the holy life to reach the end of suffering."
In the country of Śrāvastī, there was an elder,
named Jūliú.
He had no sons.
He prayed to the gods, seeking one.
A deity spoke to him from the sky, saying,
"Elder, your blessings are so great that no one is worthy to be born to you.
Therefore, you have no son.
There is a heavenly king whose life is ending and who should be born in your household."
Later, a son was born, named Xūpútí.
He was handsome, intelligent, eloquent, compassionate, benevolent, and broadly loving.
He said to his parents,
"Now I wish to invite the Buddha."
His parents consented.
He then invited the Buddha and extensively prepared offerings.
He further said to his parents, requesting to become a Śramaṇa.
His parents allowed it.
He then followed the Tathāgata back to the Jetavana and became a Śramaṇa.
Immediately, he attained the Avinivartanīya stage.
Endowed with complete spiritual powers, he taught according to worldly customs.
Among the disciples, he manifested as an Arhat.
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
"What merits did this Xūpútí cultivate in the past?"
The Buddha said,
"In countless past lives, this person was the son of a poor family.
He encountered a Bhikṣu entering the city to seek alms but obtaining nothing at all.
At that time, the youth saw that his bowl was empty.
He bowed and said,
'Please follow me home; I will make offerings to you.'
He then followed him home, took his own portion of food, and offered it to the monk.
And he himself did not eat.
After the monk finished eating, he manifested flying and departed.
The youth rejoiced and then aroused the mind for the Path.
Due to this merit,
he was later born in the heavens for ninety-one kalpas.
Now he has again been born into an elder's household.
That youth of that time is the present Xūpútí.
The merit of a single offering is still like this,
how much more so with many offerings?"
In the past, in the country of Śrāvastī, there was a great elder,
named Jiūliú.
His wealth was immeasurable, but he had no offspring.
He prayed extensively to various gods but could not obtain one.
A deity in the sky said,
'You shall obtain a blessed son.
There is a heavenly king whose life is about to end and who will be born in the elder's household.'
The elder was greatly delighted.
After seven days, the first wife felt she was pregnant.
When the months were fulfilled, she gave birth to a boy named Xūpútí.
His appearance was foremost, and he was intelligent and eloquent.
He was broadly loving, knowledgeable, and respected by both nobles and commoners.
Those who saw or heard him, in whatever they did,
he would turn them toward the joy of the Dharma, benefiting all.
His paternal uncles and brothers all became jealous and resentful of him.
They said to his mother,
'This son is not mindful
of managing the household; he wanders without restraint.'
His mother said,
'This son's blessings and virtue are not the same as ordinary people's.'
Later, Xūpútí asked for food, and his mother told a maidservant to wash an empty vessel in advance.
She replied that there was none.
Xūpútí opened the vessel and looked inside.
Naturally, there were a hundred flavors of rice, fragrant and delicious.
Everyone ate together and all attained peace and security.
Only then did his paternal uncles and brothers realize he was no ordinary person.
They invited the Buddha and the assembly of Bodhisattvas and great beings to a meal.
After eating, the son requested from his parents to become a Śramaṇa.
His father immediately allowed it.
He followed the Buddha back to the Jetavana,
and became a Śramaṇa.
Immediately, he attained the Avinivartanīya stage.
Among the disciples, he manifested as an Arhat."
Ānāthapiṇḍada had already attained Arhatship.
He had a beautiful countenance, resembling a woman.
Once, walking alone in the grass,
a youth saw him.
Thinking he was a woman,
his lustful mind was stirred, and he wanted to approach and violate him.
Upon realizing it was a man,
he looked at his own body and found it had transformed into a woman.
Ashamed, depressed, and poisoned,
he fled deep into the mountains, not daring to return.
After several years had passed,
his family and wife did not know his whereabouts.
They thought he had died.
Ānāthapiṇḍada, while seeking alms, went to his household.
The woman wept and told him that her husband had not returned,
begging for blessings and power so that he might live.
Ānāthapiṇḍada remained silent and did not respond.
Out of compassionate concern, he went to the mountains to seek and meet him.
This person then repented and blamed himself.
His body returned to being a man.
He was then able to return home, and the family was reunited.
The Buddha was in the Jeta Grove.
At that time, Ānàlǜ [Aniruddha]
was traveling to the Kingdom of Kausala.
There was no dwelling place for monks along the way.
There was a young prostitute who accommodated guests.
Ānàlǜ then went and said to her,
"Elder sister, I wish to lodge here for one night."
The woman replied,
"At this time, there is an elder householder
who is also lodging here.
Since the dwelling is cramped,
the woman invited Ānàlǜ into her inner quarters.
At that time, the Venerable One, in his seated place,
sat cross-legged with mindfulness established before him.
At that time, the unchaste woman lit a lamp and finished,
and at the end of the first watch, she went to where Ānàlǜ was and said,
"Recently, there have been many elders and Brahmins
with abundant wealth and treasures
who have all come to tell me,
'You can become my wife.'
I then said to them,
'You are all ugly;
I cannot become your wife.
I observe that the Venerable One's appearance is upright; you can become my husband.'"
At that time, Ānàlǜ remained silent and did not answer.
The woman came again in the same manner during the later watch.
He still remained silent.
At that time, this unchaste woman, having removed her clothes, came to embrace and hold him.
At that time, Ānàlǜ, with his supernatural power,
leapt into the air.
The unchaste woman, seeing this, felt ashamed,
immediately hurriedly put on her clothes, joined her palms together,
and looked upward, repenting thus three times:
"May the Venerable One return to his original seat."
At that time, Ānàlǜ then descended to his original seat.
This woman paid homage at his feet and sat to one side.
Ānàlǜ expounded various wonderful teachings for her, condemning desire as impure and praising detachment from desire.
The woman, while seated, had all her defilements exhausted and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
When the woman saw the Dharma and had attained it,
she said, "I only wish to be permitted to become a lay female disciple."
She then received the five precepts and became a disciple of the Buddha.
"I earnestly wish that the Venerable One would accept my offerings."
He silently accepted.
After she prepared various sweet delicacies and the meal was finished,
he expounded the Dharma, causing her mind to rejoice.
Ānán addressed the Buddha,
"The divine eye of Ānàlǜ—what he sees—
how does it differ from the Buddha's?"
The Buddha said to Ānán,
"What the Tathāgata sees
is not known by Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas,
let alone you, a monk still bound by birth and death.
How could you know that I, the Tathāgata, with penetrating vision, see from here eastward as many lands as the sands of the Ganges?
'Ganges' refers to rivers, lakes, and ponds up to the great ocean,
forty li wide.
The sand in the middle, measured from the surface to the bottom,
is one hundred and twenty hu.
Passing one land, place one grain of sand; exhaust that many sands.
All beings and things in the Buddha-lands,
the hidden and deep places, the obscure and dim things,
the minute forms of sentient beings—all are seen.
Encircling the ten directions, it is also thus.
What Ānàlǜ sees—
how could it be compared to the Buddha's?
Ānán said,
"What past cause did Ānàlǜ have that his vision is like this?"
The Buddha said,
"In the past, after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Vipaśyin,
there was a robber who, after committing a robbery, passed by a stupa.
He intended to steal objects from the divine monastery.
At that time, the lamp before the Buddha was about to go out, and it was dark, so he could not see.
The robber used an arrow to straighten the lamp wick,
causing the lamp to become bright.
Seeing the majestic light, his eyes were dazzled, and his hair stood on end.
He thought to himself,
'People even hold precious objects to seek blessings.
How could I steal them?'
He then abandoned the idea and left.
For ninety-one kalpas, his various evils gradually diminished,
and his blessings and protection increased daily.
That robber was Ānàlǜ.
Due to the merit of straightening the lamp, he was always reborn in good places,
encountered the Buddha, left home, attained the Way, and became foremost in penetrating vision.
How much more so for one who wholeheartedly cuts off what is cherished and precious
and offers a lamp before the Buddha—the merit is immeasurable."
The Buddha was in the Deer Park.
Ānàlǜ said to the monks,
"I recall in the past,
here in Varanasi, I was a poor man
who worked as a laborer carrying loads to sustain myself.
At that time, grain was expensive, and many people died of starvation.
Alms food was difficult to obtain.
There was a Pratyekabuddha
named Pilièzhā [Pilindha?],
who also resided here.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha went out early in the morning to seek alms.
I also went out early to carry loads.
I saw the Pratyekabuddha.
When I returned carrying my load, I saw him again.
I then thought,
'This person went out early when I saw him;
now I see him going out again—he must not have obtained food.'
He then followed behind me to my home.
I then thought,
'I wish to invite him.'
I then divided my food and brought it to where he was.
Upon arriving, I said, 'O ascetic,
this is my portion.
Please, out of compassion for me, accept this food.'
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha accepted half with his bowl.
'You eat half; that will be sufficient for both.'
I replied,
'O ascetic,
I have a household and can eat at any time.
O ascetic, please, out of compassion, fully accept this offering.'
This Pratyekabuddha, out of compassion,
fully accepted it.
Because of this offering, I was reborn in the heavens seven times,
becoming a heavenly king.
I was reborn among humans seven times, also becoming a human king.
In this life, I was born into the Śākya clan, with immeasurable wealth.
I abandoned this to leave home, learn the Way, and attain realization."
Ānàlǜ,
Mahākāśyapa,
Maudgalyāyana,
and Piṇḍola deliberated together:
"Now in the city of Rājagṛha,
there are those who do not believe in and take delight in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
We should together make them believe and take delight."
Having made this deliberation,
they looked all around, far and near.
They saw only the elder Bhadrī and his elder sister who did not believe in the Three Jewels.
The first three Śrāvakas said:
"We can convert Bhadrī."
At that time, that elder had made seven layers of gates.
There were three groups of entertainers.
When he wished to eat, all seven gates were closed.
For one meal, one group of entertainers performed.
Ānàlǜ, at his mealtime, went before him to beg.
The elder asked, saying:
"From where did you enter?"
He replied: "I entered from the gate."
He immediately asked the gatekeeper.
The gates were closed as before.
No one was seen entering.
The elder then placed a piece of hemp cake into his bowl.
Having received it, he immediately left.
Later, at mealtime,
Kāśyapa again begged, and it was also like this.
He received a piece of fish placed into his bowl.
His elder sister asked, saying:
"Do you think the bhikṣus cannot get [food] and thus come to beg?" He replied saying it was so.
The sister said:
"The bhikṣu who came before is named Ānàlǜ.
He is the son of a Śākya clan member.
He abandoned his three-season palace and the pleasures of the five desires
to leave home and study the path.
The later bhikṣu is this Pippalāyana,
the son of a great brahmin family.
He abandoned nine hundred and ninety fields, estates, and plow oxen
to leave home and study the path.
Out of compassion for you, they came to beg for food."
Hearing this, the elder inwardly felt reverence and submission.
Then Maudgalyāyana,
flying in the sky, expounded the Dharma, instructing, teaching, benefiting, and delighting him.
Immediately on his seat, he became free from dust and defilement, attained the pure Dharma-eye, saw the Dharma, and attained the fruit.
He then received the refuges and precepts.
The first three Śrāvakas said to Piṇḍola:
"We now
have converted Bhadrī, making him believe in the Dharma.
You should now go next to convert his sister."
At that time, Piṇḍola, in the morning, took his bowl and went to her house.
At that time, the elder's sister was making cakes by hand.
Suddenly seeing him come to beg, she
said to him:
"I will not give to you.
Why are you staring intently at the bowl?"
Piṇḍola then emitted smoke from his body.
She again said:
"Even if your whole body emits smoke, I still will not give to you."
Piṇḍola then caused his whole body to blaze with fire.
She again said:
"Even if your whole body blazes with fire, I still will not give to you."
Piṇḍola then soared into the empty sky.
She again said:
"Even if you soar into the empty sky, I still will not give to you."
Piṇḍola then hung upside down in the air.
She again said:
"Even if you hang upside down in the air, I still will not give to you."
Piṇḍola thought thus:
"The World-Honored One does not permit us to forcibly beg from people."
He then went out by himself.
Not far from Rājagṛha was a large rock.
Piṇḍola sat upon it.
He joined with the rock and flew into Rājagṛha.
The people in the city saw this and were all greatly terrified.
Fearing the rock would fall to the ground, none did not run away.
[The rock] reached above the elder's sister and then stopped, not leaving.
Seeing this, she was greatly terrified.
She said:
"I beg you to spare my life, return the rock to its former place.
I will give you food."
Piṇḍola then took the rock and placed it back in its original spot, then stood before her.
The elder's sister thought thus:
"I cannot give her a large cake.
I should make a small one and give it to her."
She then made a small ball, but it immediately turned into a large one.
Like this three times, each time it turned larger than before.
She then thought:
"Whenever I intend to make a small one, it turns into a large one.
I should now just quickly give one cake."
She then took one cake and gave it to her.
All the cakes became connected, reaching even to the cake container.
She grabbed the container with her hand, and her hand also stuck to it.
She then said to Piṇḍola:
"If you need cakes, I will give them all to you.
I will give them all out without regret.
Why do you need me?
And cause my hand to stick?"
He replied, saying:
"I do not need cakes.
I also do not need the container.
I also do not need you.
The four of us deliberated together
to save you and a second person.
We have already converted your younger brother.
I should save you.
That is the reason for this."
She asked, saying:
"What do you want me to do now?"
He replied, saying:
"Sister, you can carry these cakes
and follow me to make offerings to the Buddha and the 1,250 bhikṣus."
They were all completely full, yet [the cakes] were still not exhausted.
She took them and went to tell the Buddha:
"These few cakes of mine,
offered to the Buddha and the Saṅgha,
caused them all to be completely full.
Yet they are still not exhausted.
Where should I put these now?"
The Buddha said:
"You can put them on lifeless grass ground,
or in water without insects."
That woman then put them in water without insects.
The water boiled with a sound as if hot iron had been thrown into a small amount of water.
She then became terrified.
She returned to the Buddha's place.
The Buddha expounded the Dharma for her; she attained the pure Dharma-eye.
She then received the refuges and precepts, no different from a disciple.
The elders reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha then reprimanded the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I do not permit you to display supernormal powers again."
Śāriputra, for sixty kalpas, practiced the Bodhisattva path.
When he wished to cross the river of giving, a person came to beg for his eye.
Śāriputra said:
"The eye is of no use; why do you ask for it?
If you need my body or material possessions, I will give them to you."
He replied:
"I only want the eye."
Śāriputra took out one eye and gave it to him.
The beggar, having obtained the eye, spat on it and trampled it.
Śāriputra said:
"Such people as this are difficult to save.
It is better to discipline oneself and early subdue birth and death."
He then turned towards the Lesser Vehicle.
In Southern India, there was a Brahmin.
His name was Tíshè.
He was a great master of debate.
His wife became pregnant.
She dreamt of a person clad in armor, holding a vajra.
He shattered all mountains and stood by the mountain's edge.
Tíshè, upon hearing this, said:
"You will give birth to a son who will defeat all masters of debate.
Only one person will surpass him, and he will become that person's disciple."
After she became pregnant,
the mother became exceptionally intelligent and highly skilled in debate.
Her younger brother, Jūtuóluó, conversed with his elder sister,
but was repeatedly defeated in every topic.
He knew that the child she was carrying must possess great wisdom.
He left home to pursue learning, not even having time to trim his nails.
People of the time called him the Long-Nailed Brahmin.
His sister gave birth to a son after seven days.
He was named Yōubōtíshè, and people of the time, because he was born from his mother,
collectively gave him the name Shèlìfú.
At the age of eight, he recited the eighteen divisions of scriptures.
He thoroughly understood all books and texts.
At that time, in the country of Mójiātuó, there were two dragon king brothers.
One was named Jílì,
the other was named Āgāluó.
They brought rain in due season, so the country had no years of famine.
The people were grateful to them.
Often in the mid-spring month,
everyone would gather.
They would go to the dragons' dwelling place to hold a great assembly.
They would make music and discuss principles, spending the entire morning thus.
From ancient times to the present, this gathering had never ceased.
Four high seats were spread out.
One for the king,
one for the crown prince,
one for the chief minister,
and one for the debater.
Shèlìfú, at the age of eight,
observed the expressions and inclinations of the people of the time.
He saw no one superior to himself.
He then ascended the debate seat and sat cross-legged.
The crowd was suspicious and surprised.
Some said he was foolish and young, without wisdom.
Some said his intelligence surpassed others.
Although they admired his extraordinary nature,
they still felt a sense of shame.
Because of his youth, they did not speak to him directly.
They all sent their young disciples to relay questions to him.
His responses flowed smoothly, his reasoning was transcendent and exceptional.
The masters of debate at that time marveled, saying they had never seen such a thing.
Foolish and wise, young and old, all were subdued.
The king was greatly delighted.
He immediately ordered the officials to grant him a village to provide for him regularly.
Everyone in the country, great and small, rejoiced.
At that time, there was a fortune-teller's son named Jūlǜtuó.
His clan name was Dàmùjiānlián.
Shèlìfú and he were close friends.
Shèlìfú was esteemed for his brilliance and insight.
Mùjiānlián was known for his forthrightness and profound knowledge.
Their talents and wisdom were comparable, and their actions were always together.
They formed a bond that lasted from beginning to end.
Later, they both grew weary of the world and left home to study the path.
They became disciples of the Brahmin Shànshéyé.
They asked their teacher:
"What is attained by the path you seek?"
The teacher answered them:
"Since I sought the path, many years have passed.
I do not know whether the fruit of the path does not exist,
or whether I am not the right person,
but I have not attained it."
Another day, their teacher fell ill and lay in bed.
Shèlìfú stood by his head.
Dàmùjiānlián stood by his feet.
Gasping, he was nearing his end.
Then, with compassion, he smiled.
The two asked the meaning of his smile.
The teacher answered them:
"Worldly people are blind, invaded by affection and love.
I see that the king of the Golden Land died,
and his chief queen threw herself into the funeral pyre, seeking to be together in one place.
But these two people,
due to their different karmic retributions, were born in utterly separate places."
At that time, the two recorded their teacher's words.
They wished to verify their truth or falsehood.
Later, merchants from the Golden Land
came from afar to the country of Mójiātuó.
The two used their notes to verify it.
It was indeed as their teacher had said.
They then sighed with regret:
"Are we not the right people?
Or did our teacher conceal it from us?"
The two made a vow to each other:
"Whoever first attains the nectar of immortality must share the taste."
The Buddha converted the thousand brothers of the Kāshyapa clan.
Next, he traveled to the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, a bhikṣu named Āshuōshì, wearing robes and holding a bowl, entered the city to beg for food.
Shèlìfú saw his dignified appearance, surpassing others, and his senses calm and quiet.
He asked:
"Who is your teacher?"
He answered:
"The prince of the Shakyas,
who, weary of the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death, left home to study the path and attained unsurpassed enlightenment.
He is my teacher."
Shèlìfú said:
"Explain to me the teaching method of your teacher."
He answered:
"My years are still young,
and my learning is still shallow.
How can I proclaim the ultimate truth,
the vast meaning of the Tathāgata?"
Shèlìfú said again:
"Briefly state its essence."
He answered:
"All dharmas arise from causes and conditions.
These dharmas cease due to causes and conditions."
Shèlìfú immediately attained the first stage of the path.
Returning, he explained it to Mùjiānlián, who also attained the first stage.
The two teachers, each with two hundred and fifty disciples, went together to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha saw them from afar.
Pointing to Shèlìfú,
he said, "He is foremost in wisdom among my disciples."
Then pointing to Mùjiānlián, he said:
"Foremost in supernatural powers."
"Now they come with their disciples and a great assembly."
They addressed the Buddha:
"We wish to follow the Buddha's Dharma and leave home."
The Buddha said:
"Welcome, bhikṣus."
Immediately, their beards and hair fell off.
The Dharma robes adhered to their bodies.
Robes and bowls were fully provided.
They received the complete precepts.
After more than half a month,
hearing the Buddha expound the Dharma to the Long-Nailed Brahmin,
they attained Arhatship.
The Buddha resided in the city of Shèwèi.
Shèlìfú requested the Buddha to establish precepts.
The other bhikṣus said:
"Why establish precepts when there have been no transgressions?"
The Buddha said:
"Shèlìfú not only today, when there have been no transgressions, requested the establishment of precepts.
In a past time,
in a certain village,
when the people and householders had no faults or troubles,
he also once requested me to establish punishments."
At that time, the country was named Kāshī,
the city was named Bōluónài.
The king was named Jìngchēng.
Jìngchēng governed with the Dharma.
He practiced giving, upheld precepts, and with the path, loved all broadly.
The people attained great prosperity, happiness, and abundance.
Villages, hamlets, towns, and houses were so close that chickens could fly from one to another.
The whole country respected each other, often performing various arts and entertainments together for mutual enjoyment.
At that time, there was a chief minister,
named Táolì.
He had many strategies and plans.
He addressed the king:
"Today, within our borders, there is natural wealth and happiness.
The people respect each other.
I wish the king would establish punishments and penalties.
Do not let extreme joy give rise to faults."
The king said:
"The chief ministers are intelligent and wise,
and have many factions; they cannot be suddenly controlled.
If one reprimands them, conflict and blame may arise."
The king wished to gently enlighten him.
He then spoke a verse:
The chief ministers were all pleased.
They also spoke a verse:
The Buddha said:
"Jìngchēng was my former self.
The chief minister was Shèlìfú."
Śāriputra.
During the peak of summer's heat,
he was wandering in the Āmra Garden.
A hired laborer was drawing water from a well to irrigate the trees.
He did not have great faith in the Buddha,
but upon seeing Śāriputra, he developed a small measure of faith.
He called out to Śāriputra, saying,
"Venerable One, come here.
Take off your robe and sit beneath this tree.
I will water you without neglecting the irrigation,
and we can both benefit."
Śāriputra removed his robe and received the washing.
His body felt cool and comfortable, and he continued his wandering at ease.
That hired laborer passed away that very night.
He was immediately reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
He possessed great power,
second only to Śakra Devānām Indra.
He then thought to himself,
"By what cause was I born here?"
Observing his past lives,
he saw that his faith had been slight.
Because he was hired to irrigate,
he drew water and bathed Śāriputra's body.
"If my faith had been pure and deep,
knowing there would certainly be a reward, I would have prepared bathing utensils as an offering.
I reflect that although my merit was small,
because I encountered a fertile field, the reward I obtained was great."
He then went to where Śāriputra was,
scattered flowers as an offering.
Śāriputra, because of his pure faith,
expounded the essential Dharma to him, and he attained the fruit of Stream-enterer.
In the past, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, blood once rained down,
covering an area forty *li* in length and breadth.
The king and his ministers were all greatly alarmed and perplexed.
He immediately summoned various masters of arts and those skilled in divination to deduce whether it was auspicious or inauspicious.
The diviners replied,
"Ancient records state:
The calamity of raining blood
portends the birth of a venomous creature, a human *nāga*, that brings harm.
We should investigate within the country to clearly identify this calamity."
The king said,
"How can we identify it?"
The chief diviner said,
"This human *nāga* is difficult to identify.
Command throughout the country
that all newborn infants be brought here.
Use an empty jar and have each child spit into it.
Among them, there will be one child whose saliva turns into flame.
You will know this child is precisely the human *nāga*."
They deliberated, saying,
"This one cannot remain among humans."
They immediately relocated him to a secluded, uninhabited place.
Those in the country who were condemned to death could be sent to him.
The human *nāga* would spew venom and kill people in this way.
Subsequently, seventy-two thousand people were killed by his poison.
Later, a lion appeared, roaring with a thunderous voice.
Within four thousand *li*, people and creatures were terrified and subdued.
It roamed about causing violent harm, and no one could control it.
Thereupon, the king offered a reward throughout the land for anyone who could repel the lion,
promising a thousand catties of gold and the grant of a large district.
No one responded.
The assembled ministers addressed the king,
"Surely only the human *nāga* can repel it."
An order was sent to summon the human *nāga*.
The human *nāga*, encountering the approaching lion,
went and stood before it, blowing his poisonous breath.
The lion immediately died, and the country was restored to peace.
Later, the human *nāga* grew old, fell ill, and his life was about to end.
The Buddha, taking pity on the gravity of his sins—that once fallen into the evil paths, he would have no chance of escape—
told Śāriputra,
"Go and instruct him,
so that he may be freed from this heavy calamity."
Śāriputra then suddenly appeared before him.
The *nāga* was greatly enraged,
thinking,
"I am not yet dead,
and people treat me lightly, coming without any announcement
directly before me."
He then released his poisonous breath, thinking he could harm him.
Śāriputra,
with compassionate wisdom, warded it off.
His radiant countenance was serene and joyful, not a single hair moved.
Three times he released his poisonous breath, yet could not harm him.
Then he knew his venerability.
His mind was liberated and good thoughts arose.
With a compassionate mind, he looked up and down at Śāriputra seven times.
Śāriputra then returned to the monastery.
The human *nāga* drew his last breath and died that very day.
Immediately, heaven and earth greatly shook.
The supremely virtuous can cause movement,
the supremely evil
can also cause movement.
At that time, the king of Magadha
went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head to the ground,
and asked the World-Honored One,
"Where will the human *nāga* be reborn after his death?"
The Buddha said, "He is now born in the First Heaven."
Hearing the Buddha's words,
the king, astonished, asked further,
The Buddha said,
"How can one with such great sins be born in heaven?"
The Buddha said,
"Because he saw Śāriputra and with a compassionate mind looked up and down at him seven times.
By this merit, he was born in the First Heaven.
When that merit is exhausted, he will be born in the Second Heaven.
After seven such rebirths, he will become a Pratyekabuddha and attain Parinirvāṇa."
The king said to the Buddha,
"Will the debt for the seventy-two thousand people not be repaid?"
The Buddha said,
"When he finally becomes a Pratyekabuddha, his body will be like purple-gold.
At that time, he will be sitting in meditation under a tree by the roadside.
Then a great army of over seventy thousand men
will encounter the Pratyekabuddha, mistaking him for a golden man.
They will take him, hack him to pieces, and divide him among themselves.
The pieces will fall into their hands, and seeing it is flesh,
they will gather and leave it there.
Through this, he will attain Parinirvāṇa.
The sins of this present life will thus be thinly repaid and concluded."
The Buddha told the king,
"For one who encounters a good spiritual friend,
even sins piled high as a mountain can be eradicated.
And one can also attain the Path."
The Buddha was in the city of Rājagṛha, in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was in the Vulture Peak Mountain.
He entered the Vajra Samādhi. At that time, there were two spirits.
One was named Jiāluó.
The second was named Yōupójiāluó.
They were messengers dispatched by Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King.
They were going to the place of Virūḍhaka, the Heavenly King,
to discuss matters concerning humans and devas.
At that time, these two spirits
were passing through the sky.
From afar, they saw Śāriputra sitting cross-legged, his mindfulness gathered before him, his mind serene and concentrated.
The spirit Jiāluó said to the other spirit,
"I am now capable of striking this śramaṇa's head with my fist."
The spirit Yōupójiāluó said to the second spirit,
"Do not give rise to this intention to strike the śramaṇa's head.
The reason is this:
This śramaṇa possesses immense spiritual virtue and great majestic power.
Among the World-Honored One's disciples, he is foremost in intelligence and wisdom.
You would suffer immeasurably for a long, long time."
At that time, that spirit said repeatedly,
"I am capable of striking this śramaṇa's head."
The spirit Yōupójiāluó replied,
"If you do not follow my words now,
you stay here.
I will leave you."
This evil spirit said,
"Are you afraid of the śramaṇa?"
Yōupójiāluó said,
"I truly fear him. If you strike this śramaṇa with your hand,
the earth will split into two parts.
There will be violent storms and torrential rain, and the earth will also quake.
The devas will be alarmed and frightened; the Four Heavenly Kings will know,
and we will not be at peace in our abode."
At that time, the evil spirit said,
"I am now capable of insulting this śramaṇa."
Hearing this, the good spirit abandoned him and left.
Then that evil spirit struck Śāriputra's head.
At that moment, heaven and earth greatly shook; violent storms and torrential rain immediately came from all directions.
The earth split into two parts.
The evil spirit's entire body fell into the hells.
Śāriputra arose from his samādhi,
straightened his robes, and went to the Bamboo Grove.
He arrived at the place of the World-Honored One, paid homage at his feet, and sat to one side.
Then the Buddha said to Śāriputra,
"Is your body free from illness now?"
Śāriputra said,
"My body is fundamentally without ailment, only I suffer from a headache."
The World-Honored One said,
"The spirit Jiāluó struck your head with his hand.
If that spirit
were to strike Mount Sumeru with his hand,
the mountain would split into two.
The reason is this:
That spirit possessed great power.
Now, this spirit, receiving the retribution for his offense, has had his entire body enter the Avīci Hell."
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus,
"How exceedingly rare and special is the power of the Vajra Samādhi!
It is even to this extent. By this samādhi, one receives no harm.
Even if Mount Sumeru were to strike one's head, it could not move a single hair.
The reason is this:
Bhikṣus, listen.
In this Bhadrakalpa, there was a Buddha
named Krakucchanda.
That Buddha had two great śrāvakas.
One was named Equal Life.
The second was named Great Wisdom.
Equal Life was foremost in spiritual powers.
Great Wisdom was foremost in wisdom.
Just as today, my Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom,
and Maudgalyāyana is foremost in spiritual powers.
At that time, the two bhikṣus, Equal Life and Great Wisdom,
both attained the Vajra Samādhi.
Once, Equal Life, in a quiet place, entered serene concentration.
Cowherds and grass-gatherers,
seeing him, said to each other,
'This śramaṇa has now died.'
They gathered grass and wood together,
piled it on his body, set it on fire, and left him.
Then Equal Life soon arose from concentration,
straightened his robes, and entered the village to beg for food.
The grass-gatherers, returning, saw the bhikṣu.
They said to each other,
'This bhikṣu died yesterday.
We burned him with fire.
Today he is alive again.
We should now give him the name "Revived."'
If a bhikṣu attains the Vajra Samādhi,
entering fire, water, swords, and blades cannot harm him.
Such is the majestic power of the Vajra Samādhi.
Now, Śāriputra has attained this samādhi.
He often dwells in two places: the Samādhi of Emptiness and the Vajra Samādhi.
Śāriputra and others accepted an invitation from the group of six bhikṣuṇīs.
They prepared much delicious food.
For the lower seats and the śrāmaṇeras,
they gave sixty-day-old rice cooked with sesame dregs and vegetables.
The Buddha asked Rāhula,
"Are the saṅgha's meals sufficient?"
He answered in detail.
He asked again, "Who is the senior seat?"
He answered again, "The preceptor Śāriputra."
The Buddha said,
"Śāriputra has eaten impure food."
Śāriputra vomited what he had eaten.
He vowed that for the rest of his life he would stop accepting outside invitations and always practice begging for food.
Later, various great nobles, wishing to offer meals to the saṅgha,
desired to have Śāriputra.
They petitioned the Buddha to issue an order
for Śāriputra to again accept outside invitations.
The Buddha said, "Do not ask.
His nature is stubborn and harsh.
In a past time, there was a king
who was bitten by a poisonous snake.
A master who could cure poison performed the Śakara spell to summon the snake.
He first made a fire and said to the snake,
'Will you enter the fire, or will you suck back the poison?'
The snake thought,
'I have already spat it out.'
Then it threw itself into the fire.
That poisonous snake was Śāriputra."
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"One who attains the Four Bases of Supernormal Power
can prolong his life for one kalpa.
How long should the Tathāgata now live?"
He asked this three times.
Ānanda, deluded by Māra, remained silent and did not reply.
Again he told Ānanda,
"You may rise and go to a quiet place to contemplate."
He then rose and went to the forest.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān came to where the Buddha was
and said,
"World-Honored One,
you have dwelled in the world, taught and transformed beings, and saved people to completion.
Those liberated from the cycle of birth and death are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Now you are also old and may enter Nirvāṇa."
The Buddha then told Māra,
"After three months, I shall attain Parinirvāṇa."
Hearing this, Pāpīyān rejoiced and departed.
Ānanda, in his sleep, dreamed of a great tree that universally covered the sky.
All the masses relied upon it without exception.
Suddenly, a whirlwind arose, blowing fiercely against the tree,
destroying it in the land where the mighty ones dwell.
All living beings mourned without exception.
Ānanda awoke in alarm, terrified and unsettled.
Pondering the dream,
he thought, "Could it be that the World-Honored One wishes to attain Parinirvāṇa?"
He came to where the Buddha was and said to the Buddha,
"I just now dreamed such a thing.
Could it be that the World-Honored One wishes to attain Parinirvāṇa?"
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"It is as you say.
After three months, I shall attain Parinirvāṇa.
I earlier asked you,
'If one attains the Four Bases of Supernormal Power,
he can prolong his life for one kalpa.
I have fully cultivated the Four Bases of Supernormal Power to the utmost.'
I asked this three times, yet you did not reply.
Māra came and urged me to attain Nirvāṇa,
and I have consented."
Ānanda wept bitterly, unable to control himself.
The disciples relayed the news to one another.
Each filled with sorrow and reverence, they came to where the Buddha was.
"Who can exist forever?
For your sake,
what should be done, I have done;
what should be spoken, I have spoken.
You should only diligently cultivate vigor; why grieve and lament?"
Śāriputra, hearing of the Buddha's Nirvāṇa, deeply felt sorrow and lamentation.
Unable to bear seeing the World-Honored One attain extinction,
he wished to enter Nirvāṇa first.
He entreated the World-Honored One to grant him permission.
He asked this three times.
The World-Honored One said,
"You should know it is the time.
All sages and saints must eventually enter extinction."
Śāriputra then straightened his robes, made offerings with body, speech, and mind, and withdrew, walking backward.
Taking the novice monk Juṇḍī,
he went to Rājagṛha, to the city of his birth.
He then instructed Juṇḍī,
"Go into the city and to the villages,
and inform the king, ministers, old acquaintances, and lay devotees to come and bid farewell."
Juṇḍī announced,
"Venerable Śāriputra is about to attain Parinirvāṇa.
Those who wish to see him should go now."
King Ajātaśatru and people from the four groups rushed there.
Śāriputra extensively taught the people according to their afflictions, prescribing the appropriate medicine.
Some in the assembly attained the first fruit up to the third fruit.
Some left home and became Arhats.
Others vowed to seek the Buddha Way.
After hearing the Dharma, they paid homage and departed.
In the last watch of the night,
he straightened his body and mind, focused his thoughts, and entered the first dhyāna.
From the first dhyāna, he entered the second dhyāna.
Thus, in sequence, he entered the cessation of perception and feeling.
From the cessation samādhi, he arose and attained Parinirvāṇa.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, with many heavenly beings, came to where he was, praising and making offerings.
Śakra also commanded Viśvakarman
to gather various jewels to adorn a high chariot and send it to a level, broad ground.
He commanded the yakṣas
to go to the seashore and fetch sandalwood from the ox-head mountain, piling it into a large pyre.
Placing the body upon it, they poured ghee and oil and lit the cremation fire.
After the fire extinguished,
Juṇḍī
collected the relics, placed them in a bowl, gathered his three robes, and carried them to the Buddha.
Ānanda lamented sorrowfully,
"The great general of the Dharma-wheel has attained Nirvāṇa; upon whom shall I rely?"
The Buddha said,
"Although he has passed into extinction, the fivefold Dharma-body does not perish."
Śāriputra, in a past life,
also could not bear to see me die and died before me.
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
"I do not know about that past event of him dying first; how did it happen?"
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"In the distant past, an inconceivable number of kalpas ago,
in this Jambudvīpa, there was a king
named Candrabala.
The king had twenty thousand consorts and court ladies.
His chief queen was named Sumati. He had ten thousand ministers.
The chief minister was named Macchanda.
The king had five hundred princes.
The eldest prince
was named Śīlabhadra.
The city where the king resided was named Bhadrajīva.
The city was four hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
It had one hundred twenty gates all around.
He proclaimed a great almsgiving, granting whatever the people desired.
He also issued decrees to the eighty-four thousand small countries,
ordering them to open their treasuries and give alms.
All the ministers acted according to his instruction.
They erected a golden banner, struck a golden drum, and widely proclaimed the king's compassionate edict.
Far and near, inside and out, all heard of it.
At that time, within the country, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas,
the poor, orphans, the elderly, and those in need,
the strong supporting the weak, gathered like clouds and rain, and he gave according to their wishes.
The people of Jambudvīpa received the king's kindness.
There was a small country.
Its king was named Vimalasena.
Hearing of King Moonlight's excellent reputation and high renown,
he harbored jealousy and could not rest peacefully.
He then thought to himself,
"Unless Moonlight is removed, my name will not become known.
I should devise a means.
I will invite various ascetics and recruit people."
The brāhmaṇas said,
"What worries the king? Please tell us."
The king said,
"That Moonlight King's reputation and virtue are widely renowned; all follow his influence.
I alone am lowly and lack such fine repute.
I wish to remove him. What means can be used?"
The brāhmaṇas said,
"Moonlight is compassionate and benevolent, nurturing the poor and distressed like a parent to the people.
How could we, in good conscience, follow this evil scheme?
We would rather kill ourselves than do this."
They then dispersed, disregarding the king's support.
Then Vimalasena became even more distressed and agitated.
He issued a widespread recruitment, proclaiming everywhere,
"Who can get me Moonlight's head?
I will give half the kingdom to rule and give him my daughter in marriage."
At that time, in a mountain crevice, there was a brāhmaṇa
named Raudrākṣa.
He came to answer the king's recruitment.
The king was very pleased and said to him again,
"If you can accomplish this, I will not break my pledge.
If you go, on what day will it be?"
The brāhmaṇa said,
"Prepare my travel provisions and necessities.
After seven days, I will set out."
The brāhmaṇa performed incantations for self-protection.
When the seven days were completed,
he came to bid farewell to the king.
The king provided what he needed, and he set off on his journey.
At that time, in Moonlight's country, there were omens of change.
The eighty-four thousand small kings
all dreamed that the great king's golden banner suddenly broke and his golden drum suddenly cracked.
The great minister Moon dreamed that a ghost snatched the king's golden crown.
Each was filled with sorrow and could not be at peace.
Then the city gate deity, knowing the brāhmaṇa intended to beg for the king's head, blocked him and would not let him enter.
The brāhmaṇa circled the city several times but could not proceed.
The Śuddhāvāsa gods knew that King Moonlight would perfect his giving by offering his head.
They then awakened the king in a dream, saying,
"You vowed to give alms without opposing the wishes of the people.
A beggar is at the gate but cannot enter.
If you wish to be a donor, this should not be so."
The king awoke startled.
He then commanded Great Moon,
"Go to the gate and order them not to block anyone."
Great Moon the minister went to the city gate.
The city gate deity then manifested in form
and said to Great Moon,
"There is a brāhmaṇa from another country
who harbors evil intent and wishes to beg for the king's head; therefore, I did not let him in."
The minister replied,
"This is a great disaster.
However, the king has given an order; in principle, it cannot be disobeyed.
What can be done?
We should make five hundred heads each of the seven treasures to trade for it."
He then ordered them made.
The brāhmaṇa went straight to the palace hall and loudly proclaimed,
"I, from a distant land, have heard of Your Majesty's merit and virtue,
that you give alms in all things without opposing people's wishes.
Therefore, I have come from afar wishing to obtain something."
Hearing this, the king joyfully welcomed him and paid him respect.
He inquired, "Are you not weary from the journey?
Whatever you wish, I will grant."
The brāhmaṇa said,
"All external things, though given as alms, are not what I need.
I have come from afar solely to beg for Your Majesty's head.
If you do not disappoint me, please give it to me."
Hearing these words, the king was exceedingly joyful.
The brāhmaṇa said,
"If you give me your head, when will you give it?"
The king said,
"After seven days, I will give you my head."
At that time, the chief minister brought a head made of seven jewels.
He approached the Brahmin and said,
"This king's head is an impure thing of bone, flesh, and blood—why do you seek it?
Now I bring this head of seven jewels to trade with you.
You may take it.
Exchanging it will bring you enough wealth for a lifetime."
The Brahmin said,
"I do not want this.
I wish to obtain the king's head to fulfill my purpose."
At that time, the chief minister Dàyuè tried every means to persuade him, but he would never change his mind. In anger and grief, the minister's heart split into seven pieces and he died.
The king then issued a command,
saying to his ministers, "Ride an elephant that travels eight thousand lǐ and announce to all the kingdoms:
'King Yuèguāng, after seven days, will offer his head to a Brahmin.
If any wish to come, hurry and arrive quickly.'"
At that time, eighty-four thousand kings rushed by post-horse and arrived.
They all saw the great king and, beating their chests, prostrated before him, saying,
"The people of Jambudvīpa rely on Your Majesty's grace.
How can you, for the sake of one person in a single day, forever abandon the multitude and show no more compassion?
We beg you to take pity and not give your head away."
Ten thousand ministers threw themselves to the ground, beating their chests before the king, pleading, "Only show compassion and pity for us.
Do not give your head away."
Twenty thousand consorts also threw themselves to the ground, looking up and saying to the king,
"Do not forget and abandon us; only extend your shelter over us.
If you give your head away, on whom shall we rely?"
Five hundred princes wept before the king,
saying, "We are still young children; to whom shall we turn?
We beg you to show compassion and not give your head away.
Nurture and raise us until we reach adulthood."
Then the great king addressed the ministers, people, consorts, and princes:
"Consider that since I first received this body,
I have traversed birth and death for a very long time.
If in the three wretched destinies my head were cut off, I would die and be reborn again.
Countless times like this, yet there would be no merit.
If born among humans, I would contend for wealth and sensual pleasures,
and due to greed, anger, and delusion, constantly kill many beings.
Never have I given up this life for the sake of merit.
Now this body of mine, filled with various impurities, will eventually be discarded and cannot last long.
If I give up this foul head to trade for great benefit, why should I not do so?
I will give this head to the Brahmin.
By this merit, I vow to attain Buddhahood and deliver you all from suffering.
Now my intention to give is about to be fulfilled.
Do not obstruct my supreme aspiration for enlightenment."
All the kings, ministers, people, consorts, and princes, hearing the king's words, fell silent and spoke no more.
Then the king said to the Brahmin,
"If you wish to take my head, now is the time."
The Brahmin said,
"Now the king's ministers and people surround you in great numbers.
I am alone and weak in strength; I cannot chop off the king's head here.
If you wish to give it to me, let us go to the rear garden."
Then the king addressed the various kings, princes, ministers, and people:
"If you truly love and respect me,
be careful not to harm this Brahmin."
After saying this,
he went with the Brahmin into the rear garden.
Then the Brahmin said to the king,
"Your body is strong, with the strength of a warrior.
If you feel the pain of being chopped, you might regret it.
Tie your hair tightly to a tree, then I can chop."
Then the king said to the Brahmin,
"When you chop off my head, let it fall into my hands, then take it.
Now I give my head, seeking the supreme, right, and true Way, vowing to save all beings."
As the Brahmin raised his knife to chop,
the tree spirit saw this and was greatly distressed.
"How can such a person be killed?"
So he struck the Brahmin's ear with his hand.
The Brahmin's head twisted backward, his hands and feet contorted.
He dropped the knife to the ground and could not move.
Then the king looked up and said to the tree spirit,
"In the past, under this tree,
I have given away nine hundred and ninety-nine heads in charity.
Now, giving up this head will make it a full thousand.
After giving this head, my perfection of giving will be complete.
Do not obstruct my supreme aspiration for enlightenment."
Hearing the king's words,
the tree spirit restored the Brahmin to his original state.
Then the Brahmin rose from the ground,
took up the knife again, and chopped off the king's head. The head fell into his hands.
At that moment, heaven and earth shook violently six times; the palaces of the gods trembled unsteadily.
All were filled with terror, wondering why this was happening.
Soon they saw the Bodhisattva giving his head in charity for the sake of all beings.
They all descended, moved by this extraordinary act, shedding tears like rain.
Together they praised, saying,
"King Yuèguāng has given his head in charity.
His perfection of giving is now complete."
The sound spread everywhere.
When King Pímóxiàn heard these words,
he was overjoyed, astonished, and his heart split open, and he died.
Then the Brahmin carried the king's head away.
The kings, ministers, people, consorts, and princes,
seeing the king's head, threw themselves to the ground.
They wailed in unison, fainted, and revived.
Then the Brahmin, finding the king's head foul-smelling, threw it to the ground, kicked it, and left.
Some people said to the Brahmin,
"Your cruelty is extreme indeed.
Since it is of no use, why did you ask for it?"
Then the Brahmin went on his way.
People saw him and reproached him; no one gave him food.
He became hungry, emaciated, exhausted, and utterly miserable.
On the road, someone asked for news,
and learned that King Pímóxiàn had already died.
Disappointed and exhausted, he died.
Both fell into the Avīci hell.
The remaining ministers and people, remembering the king's kindness and moved by grief, died and were reborn in heaven.
Thus, Ānanda,
know that the King Yuèguāng of that time
is now myself.
King Pímóxiàn is now Māra.
The chief minister Dàyuè of that time is now Śāriputra.
At that time, he could not bear to see me die and died before me.
Even now, he cannot bear to see me enter Nirvāṇa
and passed away first.
The Buddha was in Śrāvastī, at the Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One was giving the precepts on the fifteenth day.
Then the community of bhikṣus and five hundred bhikṣus vanished from the Jetavana and went to Lake Anavatapta.
Then the dragon king Anavatapta came to the World-Honored One, bowed at his feet, and sat to one side.
He observed the Tathāgata's countenance and the bhikṣus,
and said to the Buddha,
"Looking at this assembly, it seems empty and lacking something.
The bhikṣu Śāriputra is not in this seat."
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana,
"Go quickly to Śāriputra and convey my message."
Maudgalyāyana received the instruction.
He went to Śrāvastī and said to Śāriputra,
"The Buddha summons you; the dragon king Anavatapta wishes to see you."
Śāriputra untied his robe belt and placed it before Maudgalyāyana,
saying to Maudgalyāyana,
"You have supernatural powers; lift this belt and tie it around a Jambudvīpa tree."
Maudgalyāyana took the belt but could not move it.
He exerted all his strength to lift it, causing the earth to shake greatly.
Śāriputra then had Maudgalyāyana tie it around a tree in Aparagodānīya.
Then he had it wrapped around Mount Sumeru.
Maudgalyāyana then moved Mount Sumeru.
Śāriputra again had this belt wrapped around the Tathāgata's seat.
Maudgalyāyana could not move it and returned the belt to the dragon king.
From afar, he saw Śāriputra had already arrived first,
sitting cross-legged, upright, with proper mindfulness focused before him.
He went to the World-Honored One, bowed at his feet, and said,
"Have I lost my supernatural powers?
Why is it that
I vanished from the Jetavana and appeared later at this lake,
while Śāriputra vanished later and arrived first to take his seat?
The World-Honored One always says I am first; why did I arrive later?"
The Buddha said, "You have not regressed.
The bhikṣu Śāriputra has great wisdom."
Returning to Śrāvastī, the assembly also had doubts.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana,
"Many bhikṣus lack respect for you, saying Śāriputra's supernatural powers surpass yours.
You may display your power before this assembly."
He replied, "I receive your instruction."
He then rose from his seat and went to the summit of Mount Sumeru.
With one foot, he stepped on the summit of Mount Sumeru,
and raised the other foot to the Brahma heaven.
He kicked Mount Sumeru, causing the earth to shake violently six times.
Then, in a Brahma voice, he spoke this verse.
The bhikṣus marveled at this unprecedented event.
When Mahāmaudgalyāyana spoke this verse,
sixty bhikṣus thereby ended their defilements and attained liberation.
In Śrāvastī, a great assembly was convened for almsgiving.
They offered food to ninety-six kinds of ascetics.
They also invited King Prasenajit, the crown prince, ministers, various village heads,
elders, and caravan leaders.
The day before, they gathered on the bank of the Aqì River.
The first to arrive would be the senior seat, Maudgalyāyana.
He caused the river to swell violently, with foam covering the banks.
The non-Buddhists competed to tie rafts,
intending to cross first and take the senior seat.
But the water was swift and turbulent, capsizing and sweeping them back.
All night they toiled in exhaustion; their rafts broke apart, and they drowned or froze.
They climbed onto the bank and crouched facing the sun.
At that time, someone from the Jetavana monastery invited the saṅgha.
The Buddha waited for the right time.
A young bhikṣu said,
"The World-Honored One is leaving late; I fear the non-Buddhists will take the senior seat."
The Buddha knew the time had come.
With the great assembly, dignified and orderly, they went to the river.
The non-Buddhists said,
"We cannot cross.
What will these śramaṇas do?"
Maudgalyāyana transformed a jeweled bridge, adorned with various flowers, incense, and music.
The non-Buddhists, seeing this, each said,
"The śramaṇas are late; we will cross first."
Stepping onto the bridge, they fell into the water, their bodies soaked, their robes flowing with the current.
The Buddha, with his divine power, ensured none died.
The Buddha and the bhikṣus advanced solemnly.
In orderly sequence, wherever they stepped, the jeweled bridge vanished.
Maudgalyāyana withdrew his divine power,
and the ground returned to its original state.
He allowed all the non-Buddhists to proceed.
The Buddha spoke a verse.
Mùlián had just attained enlightenment.
He wished to liberate his parents to repay the kindness of their nurturing.
He saw his deceased mother reborn among the hungry ghosts.
