She saw no food or drink, her skin and bones clinging together.
Mùlián was filled with sorrow.
He immediately filled his alms bowl with rice and went to offer it to his mother.
When his mother received the bowl of rice, before it could enter her mouth, it transformed into burning coals.
Mùlián hurried back and reported this matter in detail.
The Buddha said:
"Your mother's roots of sin are deeply entrenched.
It is not something your strength alone can remedy.
It requires the majestic spiritual power of the monastic community to achieve liberation.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month,
for the sake of parents of seven generations who are in distress and hardship,
prepare food, five kinds of fruits, water jars, basins, fragrant oil, candles, beds, bedding, and all the finest delicacies of the world to make offerings to the monastic community.
On that day, holy beings with the six supernatural powers—śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas—manifest as bhikṣus among the great assembly.
All are of one mind, receiving the alms bowl and observing pure precepts.
Those who make offerings to such monks,
their parents of seven generations and five kinds of relatives,
will be liberated from the three wretched paths, immediately freed, with clothing and food naturally provided."
The Buddha instructed the monastic community:
"All should, for the sake of the donors' parents of seven generations,
practice meditative concentration before partaking of the offerings."
Mùlián traveled by night.
An evil demon transformed into a clear shadow and entered Mùlián's abdomen.
Mùlián thought to himself:
"Why is my belly rumbling like thunder, as if hungry and burdened?"
Entering meditative concentration, he observed and saw it.
He then said to it:
"Evil demon, come out at once.
Do not harass the Tathāgata and his disciples."
The demon, terrified, transformed the clear shadow to emerge and stand before him.
Mùlián had a younger brother born of the same mother.
He was wealthy, possessing abundant treasures, his storehouses overflowing.
His servants, attendants, and slaves were beyond count.
Mùlián said to his brother:
"I have heard that you are miserly and jealous, not fond of charitable giving.
The Buddha often proclaims that those who practice charity receive immeasurable rewards."
His brother, hearing his elder brother's teaching, opened his storehouses and practiced charity.
He even built new storehouses, hoping to receive the rewards.
Before ten days had passed,
his wealth and treasures were exhausted; the old storehouses were completely empty, and the new ones yielded no reward.
His heart vexed, he said to his elder brother:
"Previously, you instructed me that charity brings great reward.
I dared not disobey, exhausting my storehouses in charity.
All the poor, past and future, were thoroughly assisted.
Now my treasures are exhausted, and the new storehouses bring no reward.
Could it be that I have been misled by you?"
Mùlián said:
"Enough, enough. Do not speak such words.
Do not let followers of other teachings or those with wrong views hear this coarse talk.
If meritorious virtue were to take physical form,
the realm of empty space could not contain it.
I will now temporarily show you a small portion of the reward.
If you wish to see it, follow me."
Mùlián, using his supernatural power,
took his brother by the hand and brought him to the sixth heaven.
There was a palace there, formed of seven treasures.
Before and after it were bathing pools, fragrant breezes spreading far.
Storehouses overflowed, beyond count.
Jade maidens attended in numbers of tens of millions.
They were all women, with no men or husbands.
The brother asked Mùlián:
"What palace is this, so majestic?
I see no men, only women."
Mùlián told his brother:
"Go and ask yourself."
He asked: "What palace is this?"
The heavenly maidens replied:
"In Jambudvīpa, in the country of Jiāpí,
there is a disciple of Śākyamuni Buddha with supernatural powers,
named Mùlián.
He has a younger brother who is very wealthy and delights in charity, aiding the poor and relieving the needy.
After his life ends, he will be reborn here to become our husband."
Hearing this, the man felt joy and a mind of goodness arose.
Returning to his elder brother, he was filled with shame.
He bowed his head in repentance, returned to the world, and practiced extensive charity without weariness.
Mùlián, receiving the Buddha's holy instruction,
went to a world in the west,
named Guāngmíng Fān.
The Buddha there was named Guāngmíng Wáng.
He was presently teaching the Dharma.
Mùlián went there to listen to the Buddha's words.
The Buddha's body was four thousand miles tall.
The bodies of the bodhisattvas were two thousand miles tall.
The alms bowls of those bodhisattvas
were one mile high.
Mùlián walked along the rim of a bowl.
Then the bodhisattvas addressed the World-Honored One:
"O Great Sage,
what insect is this that comes here?
Wearing the robes of a śramaṇa,
he walks on the rim of a bowl."
At that time, that Buddha said:
"Noble sons, be careful not to give rise to a mind that looks down upon this worthy one.
Why?
This youth is named Mahā-Maudgalyāyana.
He is the foremost in supernatural powers among the śrāvaka disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha."
Then Buddha Guāngmíng Wáng said to Mahā-Maudgalyāyana:
"The bodhisattvas and śrāvakas of my land,
seeing your small body, all give rise to contempt.
You should display your supernatural powers, relying on the majestic virtue of Śākyamuni."
Maudgalyāyana bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated to the right seven times, and stood again before the Buddha.
He said:
"May I now sit cross-legged upon this ground?"
The Buddha said:
"As you wish."
Then Mahā-Maudgalyāyana leapt into the empty space hundreds of millions of fathoms high.
Above that jeweled city, he created a seat.
He sat cross-legged upon it.
From his seat hung hundreds of millions of thousands of billions of jeweled pearls.
From each pearl radiance streamed forth hundreds of thousands of lights.
From each light emerged a lotus flower.
Upon every lotus flower appeared the form of Śākyamuni Buddha, seated upon the lotus.
His speech was like that of Śākyamuni.
The sound was pure, proclaiming the sutras, no different from the original.
After Maudgalyāyana displayed his supernatural powers,
he again stood before the Buddha.
The bodhisattvas exclaimed that this was unprecedented.
They addressed the Buddha:
"For what reason has this Maudgalyāyana come to this world?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"He came to this land to test how far the sound of Śākyamuni Buddha's voice reaches."
Then Buddha Guāngmíng Wáng said to Mahā-Maudgalyāyana:
"O Virtuous One, you should not test the Tathāgata's voice.
The Tathāgata's voice is without far or near; it is vast, immeasurable, and beyond analogy."
Then Mahā-Maudgalyāyana threw himself at the Buddha's feet, repenting of his fault.
"O World-Honored One,
I am not wise.
The Buddha's voice is immeasurable, yet I presumptuously sought to know its limit."
Buddha Guāngmíng Wáng said to Mahā-Maudgalyāyana:
"Although you have come far to this Buddha-land,
he again addressed the Buddha:
"It is extremely far, O God of Gods.
My body is utterly weary; I cannot return to my original land."
The World-Honored One said:
"How did you, by your own power, come to this world?
It was by the majestic virtue of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni Buddha that you were established here.
You should from afar take refuge, bow, and pay homage to Śākyamuni Buddha.
Then you will naturally return.
If you were to rely on your own supernatural power to return to your original land, you would not arrive even in an eon."
Maudgalyāyana placed his right knee on the ground, faced east toward Śākyamuni Buddha, joined his palms, and took refuge.
In the time it takes to bend and stretch an arm, he immediately arrived.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
"There is a great kingdom,
eight thousand yojanas from here, located in a border region.
They do not behold the Three Jewels and are accustomed to perverted views.
The king and his subjects serve Brahmin ascetics.
There are five hundred men who have attained the five supernatural powers.
They can move mountains, stop rivers, divide their bodies, and transform themselves.
In the kingdom, there is a great mountain blocking the people's path; the whole country is troubled by it.
The king spoke to the Brahmin ascetics.
The Brahmin ascetics then sat surrounding the mountain.
Each with a single mind, using the power of meditative concentration, caused the mountain to rise, intending to move it.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"Go to that kingdom, manifest supernatural transformations, and liberate the Brahmin ascetics, the king, and the people.
Cause them to be far from the three wretched paths and eternally dwell in the hall of blessings."
Maudgalyāyana emitted light, blocking the sun and moon, and hung suspended in empty space.
He positioned himself atop the mountain; the mountain did not move.
The Brahmin ascetics exclaimed in surprise:
"This mountain had risen; who is suppressing it?
The sun has lost its brilliance; there must be a reason."
Among them, one with clear vision observed the disciples:
"Who is impure, causing the mountain not to move?"
Looking up, they saw a śramaṇa atop the mountain.
The Brahmin ascetics all said:
"It must be the doing of Gautama's disciple."
The Brahmin ascetics called out:
"The king ordered us to remove the people's affliction.
Why are you suppressing it?"
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"I am merely suspended in emptiness; who is suppressing your mountain?"
The Brahmin ascetics exerted their spiritual power three times, trying to move the mountain.
The mountain sank three times and became level ground.
The Brahmin ascetics looked at each other and said:
"He who possesses clear understanding and profound virtue shall be our teacher."
All respectfully adjusted their garments, bowed, and reverently said:
"We wish to become your disciples.
Show us the ultimate spiritual path."
Maudgalyāyana said:
"If you wish to leave darkness and approach light, that is good.
I have a revered teacher,
called the Unsurpassed, Rightly Awakened, God of Gods.
He is omniscient.
You should all go to the Buddha."
The Brahmin ascetics said:
"Can the Buddha's teachings surpass yours?"
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"The Buddha's virtue is like Mount Sumeru;
we are like mustard seeds.
Follow behind me."
They immediately went before the Buddha and fully explained their situation.
"Internally and externally purified,
we only pray, O World-Honored One,
to cleanse our slight defilements and make us truly pure."
The Brahmin ascetics saw the Buddha,
their hearts opened, their minds liberated, and all became śramaṇas.
In the past, Maudgalyāyana went to the Snowy Mountains.
He converted various ghosts, spirits, and dragons,
yakṣas, asuras, gandharvas, and others.
At that time, there was a gandharva spirit
who dwelled in a palace of seven treasures.
He was extraordinary among the multitude, with a dignified form and exceptional intelligence.
However, he had a human body and a dog’s head.
Maudgalyāyana, finding this strange, asked,
"Why is it like this?"
He replied,
"I was a wealthy elder during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha.
I delighted in offering food to bhikṣus and brahmins and providing for the poor.
But I was impatient and irritable by nature,
uttering coarse words and curses directly, without regard for age or youth.
When guests or visitors were slightly displeasing in their eating or drinking, I would say,
'It would be better to feed this to dogs.'
Because of these words, I now have a dog’s head on a human body.
Yet, because of my generosity in giving and offering, I enjoy this blessed palace."
The Buddha instructed Elder Anāthapiṇḍada,
"You should practice almsgiving."
He immediately rose, knelt with hands clasped, and addressed the Buddha,
"May the Buddha and the monastic community
descend to my house tomorrow
to partake of a simple meal."
The Buddha silently accepted.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus,
"Tomorrow morning, we will ascend to the heavens and descend at noon to gather at Anāthapiṇḍada’s house for the meal."
The next morning, the Buddha and the bhikṣus
rose into the sky in the blink of an eye.
At that time, there was an arhat
named Hongtán,
who adjusted his robes and said to the Buddha in the sky,
"I have ascended to the heavens many times, but never has it been as dark as it is now."
The Buddha said,
"Two dragon kings are greatly angered and spewing mist,
hence the darkness."
Another arhat named Shòubǐ
then addressed the Buddha,
"I wish to stop them."
The Buddha said,
"The dragons possess great divine power.
If you go, they will surely stir up evil and spew water.
They might even kill people and all living creatures."
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha,
"I wish to go and admonish them." The Buddha said, "Excellent."
Maudgalyāyana immediately went to where the dragons were.
Upon seeing Maudgalyāyana, the dragons emitted smoke from their mouths, and moments later, fire,
encircling Maudgalyāyana in one layer.
Maudgalyāyana, through the power of his spiritual intent, also transformed and emitted fire, encircling the dragons in three layers.
He further transformed his body and entered the dragons’ eyes,
entering from the left and exiting from the right, entering from the right and exiting from the left.
In this manner, he successively entered and exited their ears and nostrils, or flew into their mouths.
The dragons thought Maudgalyāyana was inside their bellies.
Maudgalyāyana then transformed his body to encircle the dragons in fourteen layers, using his body to restrain the two dragons.
The dragons were greatly terrified, thrashing their tails and stirring the sea, shaking Mount Sumeru.
The Buddha, from afar, told Maudgalyāyana,
"These dragons are still capable of spewing water to flood and kill all under heaven.
You must be cautious."
Maudgalyāyana replied to the Buddha,
"I possess the four dhyānas and supernatural powers, which I constantly practice with faith.
I can take this Mount Sumeru and the two dragons,
place them in the palm of my hand, and toss them to another realm.
I can also grind Mount Sumeru with my hand into dust,
without any devas or humans being aware of it."
Hearing this, the two dragons immediately submitted.
Maudgalyāyana resumed his form as a śramaṇa.
The dragons transformed into humans, bowed their heads, paid respects, and repented to Maudgalyāyana,
"We were foolish, deluded, and reckless, not recognizing your venerable divinity.
We offended with our mist; we beg for mercy and forgiveness of our sins."
The two dragons repented and received the five precepts.
They bowed at the Buddha’s feet, paid their respects, and departed.
At that time, Anavatapta, along with his retinue,
invited the Buddha for three months
to enter the Anavatapta Great Lake to receive offerings,
along with all the spiritually accomplished bodhisattvas and disciples, agreeing to half a month.
The dragons rejoiced, raising clouds, thundering, and raining, showering the entire world.
In an instant, they returned to their palace and summoned their five hundred eldest sons,
named Shànyá, Shànshī, and others.
The five hundred eldest sons,
"I have now invited the Equal and Rightly Awakened One, along with the bodhisattvas and disciples,
for half a month.
You must unite in heart, encourage one another, and increase your reverence for the World-Honored One.
Diligently contemplate impermanence and each maintain tranquility.
Be humble, respectful, and solemn, attending upon the Tathāgata.
Abandon desires and the dragon’s playful pleasures.
Eliminate greed, anger, and harm.
Separate from sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile sensations.
Why is this?
The World-Honored One is desireless, serene, benevolent, and elegant.
He is discerning, harmonious, and compliant; uphold the Buddha’s essential precepts.
For this half month, do not enter the palace, free from lust, hatred, and ignorance.
As the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma, there will surely be spiritually accomplished bodhisattvas from other realms,
Śakra, Brahmā, world-protectors, and pure celestial beings who will universally gather.
You must diligently remember to give generously and be careful not to slacken midway.
Let all the assembly witness transformations and leap with joy."
At the Snowy Mountains, in the Anavatapta Lake,
they manifested flawless lapis lazuli seats,
seven hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
All around, they arrayed eighty-four thousand jeweled coral trees.
On the various platforms were eighty-four thousand lion seats, all vast and lofty.
There were two thousand dragon maidens each,
of exquisite beauty and boundless charm.
Their mouths emitted fragrant incense, and they held various flowers, powdered incense, and paste incense.
They performed music and songs to praise the Buddha’s virtues, delighting the assembly.
In the sky, banners and streamers hung, with jeweled bells harmoniously ringing, their sound surpassing all others.
They offered a hundred flavors of food along with their retinue,
remotely inviting the World-Honored One.
The Buddha, along with eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas of great spiritual power,
and two thousand disciples also possessing supernatural abilities,
arrived at the palace of King Anavatapta.
Maudgalyāyana, following the Buddha’s divine will,
moved the Anavatapta Lake, manifesting in the sky seven zhang above the ground.
He transformed his appearance like that of a golden-winged garuḍa king, dwelling above the dragon palace.
He then announced to the king,
"The Tathāgata has arrived."
The dragon multitude was terrified, their hair standing on end, fleeing and hiding in all directions.
The dragon king comforted them, saying,
"Be at ease, do not fear.
This is the work of the virtuous Mahāmaudgalyāyana."
Musicians played in harmony, welcoming the Rightly Awakened One and his disciples to the Anavatapta Lake.
They set up a vast arena with lion seats.
The dragons and their retinue personally served, offering the prepared food,
surpassing worldly sweetness and richness,
presenting celestial flavors for the offering.
After the meal, when the vessels were washed,
the Buddha preached the Dharma.
All in the assembly were filled with joy.
The Buddha was dwelling in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣus gathered in one place
and discussed among themselves,
"Are the pillars of the Good Dharma Lecture Hall connected to the beams or not?"
Maudgalyāyana said,
"They are connected."
Another bhikṣu, who was without years, said,
"They are not connected."
They sent a bhikṣu with supernatural powers to go and see.
He returned and said, "They are not connected."
The bhikṣus said to Maudgalyāyana,
"You did not know,
so why did you say they are connected?
False speech is untrue; you should be expelled and driven out."
They then assembled the monastic community.
The Buddha, with his supernatural powers, came from the sky.
Knowing yet asking intentionally,
"Bhikṣus,
what are you doing?"
They replied,
"Maudgalyāyana, when asked if they are connected, answered that they are,
though they are not. This false speech is untrue; we intend to perform a karmavācanā."
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu without years,
"How do you know they are not connected?"
He replied, "World-Honored One,
I once
practiced meditation in the Good Dharma Lecture Hall."
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana,
"Why did you not look for yourself?
You should have ascertained the truth."
Maudgalyāyana’s mind was truthful, and he did not violate the precepts.
Someone asked Maudgalyāyana,
"Where does the water of Lake Duōfú come from?"
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"This water comes from the Anavatapta Lake."
The bhikṣus said,
"The water of Anavatapta Lake is sweet and delicious, possessing eight qualities.
This water is boiling hot, salty, and bitter.
How can this be?
Maudgalyāyana,
you falsely claim supernatural powers beyond human capacity.
Therefore, you have spoken falsely and should be expelled and driven out."
They brought the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus,
"Do not accuse Maudgalyāyana of wrongdoing.
Why?
The dwelling place of the Anavatapta dragon is extremely far from here.
This water originally had eight qualities and was sweet and delicious.
It passed through five hundred small hells,
and because of this, it became salty and hot.
If you had asked Maudgalyāyana why this water is salty and hot,
he would have been able to answer accordingly."
Another time, there was a great drought with no rain.
Maudgalyāyana entered meditation and saw
that after seven days, heavy rain would fall,
filling all ditches and pits.
Cities, towns, and villages all heard this and rejoiced greatly.
The people in the country abandoned their tasks, covering and storing their belongings.
When the seventh day arrived,
the bhikṣus said to Maudgalyāyana,
"You said that in seven days, heavy rain would fall, filling all ditches and pits.
Now there is not even wind, let alone rain.
You falsely claim supernatural powers beyond human capacity; therefore, you have spoken falsely and should be expelled and driven out."
The Buddha heard of this matter.
He told the bhikṣus,
"Maudgalyāyana sees the front but not the back.
The Tathāgata sees both the front and the back.
Heavy rain did fall after seven days,
but the asura king Rāhu
caught it with his hand and placed it in the great sea.
Maudgalyāyana spoke according to what he perceived in his mind,
thus he is without fault."
The Buddha was in Rājagṛha, and no one dared to shave his head.
There was only one youth,
named Upāli,
who shaved the Buddha’s head.
The child’s parents, before the Buddha, joined their palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“He is quite capable of shaving hair, but his body is too bent.”
The parents instructed the child to straighten up a little.
“But do not be too straight, so that his breathing is not rough.”
They also said:
“He is good at shaving the head, but his body is too straight.”
The parents said:
“Do not be too straight.”
The Buddha said:
“He is good at shaving hair,
but his inhalation is too rough.”
The parents said:
“Do not inhale roughly, lest the Buddha be disturbed.”
They also said:
“He is good at shaving hair,
but his exhalation is too rough.”
The parents said:
“Do not exhale roughly, lest the Buddha be disturbed.”
At that time, Upāli
regulated his inhalation and exhalation and entered the fourth dhyāna.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Upāli has entered the fourth dhyāna.
You take the razor.”
Ānanda complied with the instruction.
Ānanda took the old container that held hair and collected the World-Honored One’s hair.
The Buddha said:
“It should not be placed in an old container.”
At that time, there was Prince Gopāli,
who, leading an army on an expedition, came to request the Buddha’s beard and hair.
The Buddha gave them.
The prince, having obtained them, did not know where to place them.
The Buddha said:
“Place them in a golden stūpa, a silver stūpa, a jeweled stūpa, or a stūpa of various treasures.
Wrap them in silk cloth, a bowl, a dānāṃbara robe, or a tūlā robe.”
He also said:
“I do not know how to carry them.”
The Buddha said:
“By elephant, horse, chariot, carriage, or palanquin,
or carry them on the head or shoulders.”
At that time, the prince took the World-Honored One’s hair and left.
Wherever he went on the expedition, he was victorious.
At that time, that prince returned to his country and erected a stūpa for the Buddha’s hair.
This was a stūpa built during the World-Honored One’s lifetime.
Later, when the bhikṣus traveled, they also used the aforementioned items to carry it.
The Buddha said:
“It should not be carried on the head.
Nor should the stūpa be taken to places for defecation or urination.”
The bhikṣus, out of reverence, did not dare to sleep in the same room as the stūpa.
They placed it in a separate room.
The Buddha said:
“Place it on a high peg or beside the head.”
In the country of Avanti, there was an elder
who was wealthy and rich but miserly, greedy, violent, wicked, and without compassion.
At that time, there was a maidservant
who worked day and night without rest.
If she made even a small mistake, she would be whipped and beaten.
Her clothes did not cover her body, her food did not fill her stomach, and in her old age, she was exhausted and miserable, wishing for death but unable to die.
At that time, she happened to take a pot to the river to fetch water.
Reflecting on this suffering, she cried out loudly.
At that time, Kātyāyana came to where she was.
He asked:
“Old mother, why are you crying?”
She replied:
“Venerable one,
I am already old and constantly perform hard labor.
Moreover, I am poor, with insufficient clothing and food, and I wish for death but cannot die.”
Kātyāyana said:
“If you are poor, why not sell your poverty?”
The woman said:
“How can poverty be sold? Who would buy poverty?”
Kātyāyana said:
“Poverty can indeed be sold.” He said this three times.
The woman said she would sell it.
Kātyāyana said:
“If you truly wish to sell it, follow my words.”
She replied:
“Yes, I will.”
He instructed her:
“First, bathe.”
After she finished bathing,
he said:
“You should make an offering.”
She said:
“Venerable one,
I am extremely poor. Now, I do not have even a hair’s breadth of intact cloth.
I only have this pot, which belongs to my master. With what can I make an offering?”
He then gave her a bowl.
“Take this bowl and fetch a little clean water.”
As instructed, she fetched it and offered it to Kātyāyana.
Kātyāyana received it and immediately chanted blessings for her.
Next, he taught her to observe the precepts.
Later, he taught her to contemplate the Buddha’s various merits.
He then asked:
“Do you have a place to stay?”
She replied: “No.”
“When grinding, I sleep under the millstone.
When pounding rice or cooking, I sleep there.
Sometimes, when there is no work, I sleep on a dung heap.”
Kātyāyana said:
“You should maintain a good mind, be respectful and diligent in your work.
Do not harbor resentment.
Wait until your master and everyone else have gone to sleep,
secretly open the door,
spread clean grass in the corner of the doorway, and sit there.
Contemplate the Buddha and do not give rise to evil thoughts.”
At that time, the old mother respectfully complied and carried out the instructions.
In the latter part of the night, she passed away and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
Her master had people tie a rope around her feet and drag her body to the charnel ground.
There was a deva with five hundred devas as his retinue.
When his merit was exhausted, his life ended.
This old woman took his place.
In the way of rebirth in heaven,
those with sharp faculties know the cause of their rebirth.
Those with dull faculties only know how to enjoy pleasures.
At that time, this woman, having been reborn in heaven,
along with five hundred devīs,
enjoyed pleasures and did not know the cause of her rebirth.
At that time, Śāriputra was in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
Knowing the cause of this deva’s rebirth in heaven,
he asked:
“Deva,
by what merit were you reborn in heaven?”
She replied that she did not know.
At that time, Śāriputra lent her the divine eye to see her former body.
She realized that she had been reborn in heaven due to Kātyāyana.
She then led the five hundred devas to the charnel ground.
They scattered flowers, burned incense, and made offerings to the corpse, illuminating it with light.
Her master saw this and wondered about the reason.
He ordered people from near and far to come to the charnel ground to see.
They saw the devas making offerings to this corpse.
He asked the devas:
“This maidservant was ugly and filthy.
When she was alive, people could hardly bear to look at her.
Why do the devas now make offerings to her?”
At that time, the deva explained the whole story.
The Buddha was in Vaiśālī.
At that time, Ambapālī, riding in a carriage adorned with feathers and jewels, came to the Tathāgata’s place.
She paid her respects, inquired after his well-being, alighted from the carriage, and approached the Buddha.
At that time, Nanda was walking not far from the Buddha.
Ambapālī then went to where Nanda was walking.
She touched Nanda’s feet with her hand.
She then said:
“Nanda,
I am Ambapālī.”
At that time, Nanda immediately emitted semen, which soiled her hand.
Ambapālī then placed it on her head
and went to the World-Honored One, saying:
“World-Honored One, should such a person be allowed among the assembly?”
The Buddha said to Ambapālī:
“Such a person should be allowed among the assembly.
The reason is this:
Nanda will soon attain the state of no outflows.”
Ambapālī remained silent and left without responding.
Not long after Ambapālī left,
the Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Gather all the bhikṣus in the lecture hall.”
After they had assembled,
the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“I have observed among the bhikṣus
that all should wear a saṅghāṭī to cover their inner form.
Thus, all bhikṣus should learn this.”
The Buddha said to Nanda:
“What is this, Nanda?
How could you behave in such a manner?”
Nanda felt ashamed within.
He said:
“Excellent, World-Honored One.
I wish you would quickly teach me the Dharma.
So that I may hear the Dharma,
dwell in a quiet place, and observe reality as it is, finding joy in it.”
The Buddha said to Nanda:
“Observe this body.
As it moves,
from head to foot, the hair, nails, and teeth—
all kinds of impurities fill the body.
Observe it as it truly is.
Is it pure or impure?
Observe those defilements.
Where do they come from? Where do they arise?”
At that time, Nanda received the Buddha’s instruction, paid homage at his feet, and left.
He observed this body, from head to foot, all kinds of impurities.
He knew that all these places arose from combination.
“I should now detach myself.
Then there will be no desire.”
He then spoke a verse:
At that time, Nanda,
dwelling alone in a quiet place,
became an arhat.
When the Buddha first attained enlightenment,
his body radiated light that illuminated the great chiliocosm.
People, heavenly dragons, and bodhisattvas from the ten directions
all came to listen to his teachings and were greatly joyful.
Each, according to their own practice, attained the Way.
Only the Buddha's brother Nántuó did not receive the teachings.
Instead, he opposed the Buddha's teachings and wished to practice the Way himself.
He possessed thirty marks.
Leading a number of disciples,
he wore robes of fine cloth and his countenance resembled the Buddha's.
There were bhikṣus who had not yet attained the Dharma-eye.
Seeing Nántuó from afar, they bowed to him.
The Buddha told Nántuó,
"From now on, you must not wear fine cloth robes; wear black monastic robes instead.
Why?
You oppose my precepts and accept bows from bhikṣus.
You will fall into hell."
Bìlíngjiāpócuō was in Rājagṛha.
As mealtime approached, he intended to go on alms round.
He came to a herder's house for food.
The woman of the house was weeping.
He asked the woman,
"Why are you weeping?"
She replied,
"Venerable,
today is a festival day, and everyone has gathered for amusement.
I have no fine clothes and cannot go alone."
Then the Venerable One transformed and created various clothes, jewels, necklaces, and gold and silver ornaments.
He gave them to her and then left.
People saw her and asked, "Where did you get these?"
She explained the circumstances in detail.
The news reached the king.
The king summoned the cowherd woman and the bhikṣu.
He asked the Venerable One,
"Where did you obtain such fine gold, not of this world?"
The bhikṣu then took his staff, struck the wall, and tapped the bed—everything turned into gold.
He spoke thus:
"Śūdra, where would one get gold? This is it."
The king said, "Venerable,
you possess great supernatural powers; please each return."
The Buddha was in the kingdom of Kośala.
He was in retreat with many bhikṣus.
Various lay devotees, seeing the large assembly of monks,
built dwellings and provided robes for them.
The following year, the Buddha returned to the Jetavana for retreat.
In that place, there remained two elder bhikṣus.
The lay devotees thought to themselves,
"This year, let us give alms as we did last year,
so that the bhikṣus may receive robes and we may continuously gain merit."
They brought many robes and offered them to the two elders.
The elders thought,
"These robes are many.
If we divide them, we do not know what offense we might incur," and ultimately did not dare to divide them.
Bànántuó traveled about, observing everywhere the amount of offerings.
The two elders saw him from afar,
rose from their seats, welcomed him, offered him a seat, and inquired after him.
Bànántuó asked,
"Has the monastic assembly received any offerings during the retreat?"
They replied, "Yes."
He asked, "Have they been divided?"
They replied, "Not yet."
"Why?"
The elders replied,
"These robes are many, and we are few.
If we divide them, we do not know what offense we might incur."
Bànántuó said,
"It is good that you have not divided them."
The two elders said to Bànántuó,
"Can you divide them?"
He replied, "I can." Bànántuó said,
"Here, a formal act (karman) should be performed; they cannot be divided directly."
Then the two elders brought out all the robes and placed them before Bànántuó.
Bànántuó divided the robes into three portions.
He said,
"You two sit beside one pile."
He himself sat between two piles.
He said,
"Elders, listen single-mindedly to the formal declaration.
You two have one pile of robes, which is called 'three.'
I alone have two piles of robes, which is called 'three.'
Is this formal act good?"
They replied, "Good."
He bundled up the robes and prepared to carry them away.
The two elders said,
"These piles of robes—we have not yet divided them.
How can you just leave?"
Bànántuó said,
"If I were to divide them with you,
one fine robe among them should be given to the one who knows the Dharma.
Then they can be divided."
They replied, "Give it." So he took out one superior precious robe and set it aside.
He divided the remaining robes into two portions and gave them to the two elders.
Bànántuó then bundled up the many robes,
carried them on his shoulder, and went to the Jetavana.
Various bhikṣus were walking in meditation.
Seeing Bànántuó from afar,
they said to each other,
"This shameless, unconscientious one,
who has seen, heard, and suspected offenses,
this insatiably greedy man is coming."
As he gradually drew near,
they asked,
"Bànántuó,
where did you get so many robes from?"
Bànántuó recounted the above events in detail.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires, content, practicing asceticism.
Hearing this, he felt resentment and reproached him in various ways.
"How can one be called a bhikṣu?
He deliberately took the possessions of the two elders."
He reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha also reproached him in various ways.
He told the bhikṣus,
"This Bànántuó
not only in this life took the possessions of these two elder bhikṣus;
in a past life, in a river bend,
there were two otters living in the river.
They caught a carp by the riverbank.
Unable to divide it, the two otters guarded it.
A jackal came to drink water.
Seeing them, he asked,
"Uncle, what are you doing?"
The otter said,
"Nephew,
we caught this big fish but cannot divide it.
Can you divide it for us?"
He replied, "I can.
This should be divided according to scriptural sayings; it cannot be divided directly."
Then the jackal divided the fish into three portions: the head as one portion, the tail as one portion,
and the middle, fleshy part as one portion.
He asked,
"Who likes to move near the shore?"
They replied,
"This one does."
"Who likes to go into deep water?"
They replied,
"This one does."
Then the jackal said,
"Listen single-mindedly.
The scriptures say,
'The one who moves near the shore gets the tail.
The one who goes into deep water gets the head.
The middle body portion goes to the one who knows the Dharma.'"
Then the jackal took the big fish's body in his mouth and returned.
His wife saw him and asked,
"Where did you get this?"
He replied,
"I got it from some foolish ones who do not know how to settle matters."
O bhikṣus,
these two otters
are now the two elder bhikṣus.
The jackal at that time
is now Bànántuó.
The Buddha was in the kingdom of Shèwèi.
At that time, the elder Jiāliútuóyí had attained the fruit of an Arhat.
He thought to himself:
"Previously, I was among the six groups of monks.
In the kingdom of Shèwèi, I defiled many households.
I think I should now return and make them pure."
He then entered the kingdom and converted nine hundred and ninety-nine households.
If the husband attained the Way but the wife did not,
or if the wife attained the Way but the husband did not,
they were not counted.
At that time, in the city of Shèwèi, there was a Brahmin household.
They were to be converted through the voice-hearer method.
Jiāliútuóyí thought:
"If I convert this household as well,
in the city of Shèwèi, it will make a full thousand households."
In the morning, he took his bowl and entered the city to beg for food.
He arrived at the Brahmin's house, but the master was not home.
His wife had closed the door and was frying pastries.
Jiāliútuóyí then entered meditative concentration and, upon arising, snapped his fingers.
The wife turned to look, but the door was still closed.
She thought to herself:
"From where did this monk enter?
He must have come because he craves pastries.
I will definitely not give him any.
Even if his eyes fall out, I still will not give."
Then, through supernatural power, both his eyes popped out.
She thought again:
"Even if his eyes come out like bowls, I still will not give."
He then used his supernatural power to transform his eyes into bowls.
She thought again:
"Even if he stands upside down before me, I still will not give."
He then used his supernatural power to stand upside down before her.
She thought again:
"Even if he dies, I still will not give."
He again used his supernatural power to enter the concentration of cessation of perception and feeling.
His mind and thoughts all ceased, and he was without any awareness.
The Brahmin's wife tried to pull and move him but could not.
She then became greatly frightened.
She thought: "This monk often visits the palace of King Pòsīnì,
and is the teacher of Queen Mòlì.
If they hear he died in my home,
we will suffer great misfortune."
"If he revives, I will give him one pastry."
Jiāliútuóyí then emerged from concentration.
The wife looked at the pastries.
The ones fried earlier were of good quality, and she was reluctant to give them.
She scraped the edges of the pan and made one small pastry, frying it until it turned out even better.
She intended to give the earlier one.
As soon as she picked up one pastry, the rest all stuck together.
Jiāliútuóyí said:
"Sister, give me as much as you wish."
She picked up four pastries to give him.
Jiāliútuóyí did not accept them and said:
"I do not need these pastries. If you wish to make an offering,
you can give them to the monks at the Jíyuán Monastery."
This woman had already planted good roots in previous lives.
She then thought to herself:
"This monk truly does not crave pastries.
He only came begging out of compassion for me."
She then took a basket of pastries and went to the Jíyuán Monastery.
She offered them to all the monks.
After giving the pastries to the monks,
she sat before Jiāliútuóyí.
At that time, Jiāliútuóyí,
observing her conditions, expounded the wonderful Dharma for her. She immediately, while seated, became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
She took refuge in the Three Jewels and became a lay disciple.
Only then did she return home.
Later, when her husband returned, she told him everything in detail.
She said: "I have now attained the fruit of Stream-enterer.
You should go now."
The Brahmin then went to visit.
Jiāliútuóyí expounded the wonderful Dharma for him.
He attained the pure Dharma-eye and became a lay disciple.
He always exhausted his wealth and efforts to support his teacher.
Even until his death, he instructed his son to continue just as before without difference.
His son obeyed the command and made offerings according to the Dharma.
Later, the daughter-in-law was weaving at the loom.
She encountered a young, handsome bandit leader.
The woman called to him, and the woman spoke to him, telling him to come and enjoy themselves together.
At that time, Jiāliútuóyí went to their house for food.
He spoke to the Brahmin's wife about the faults of sexual desire and condemned the sin of breaking precepts.
The wife then became suspicious, fearing he knew about this matter or might tell her husband.
She then devised a scheme, pretending to be ill and inviting him.
Jiāliútuóyí stayed to expound the Dharma for her.
She bitterly detained him until sunset.
At that time, Jiāliútuóyí went out to the dung heap.
The bandit leader used a sharp knife to cut off his head and buried it in the dung.
On the day of the confession ceremony, when counting the tallies, one was found missing.
They inquired among each other.
The Buddha said:
"Jiāliútuóyí has already entered Nirvana."
The night passed, and it was morning.
The Buddha and the assembly of monks entered the city of Shèwèi and arrived at the dung heap.
Through the Buddha's supernatural power, the corpse leaped out and hung in the air.
The monks took it and placed it on a bier.
They carried it out of the city, cremated the body, built a stupa, and made offerings.
King Pòsīnì heard that Jiāliútuóyí had died at a certain Brahmin's house.
He then exterminated seven generations and ten households on each side, seizing all their property.
He captured five hundred bandits.
He cut off all their hands and feet and threw them into the moat of the Jíyuán Monastery.
The monks, while begging for food, heard about this matter.
They reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"The fault of the transgression was all due to entering the settlement at an improper time."
The Buddha traveled to the country of Bōluónài.
He sat under a tree and smiled joyfully.
Five-colored light emanated.
Ānán knelt and asked.
The Buddha said:
"In the time of the Buddha Kāshyapa,
there was a monastery here.
In the monastery, there were twenty thousand monks.
The Buddha Kāshyapa constantly expounded the true Dharma.
Ānán then offered a rope-bed and knelt, urging:
'I pray you take this honorable seat.'
This land has blessings, thus attracting two Buddhas."
The Buddha took his seat.
He raised his hand and pointed, saying:
"There is a large district there named Wéilíng.
At that time, there was a potter
named Huānyù.
Out of love for his son, he frequently visited the Buddha to receive the Buddha's pure teachings.
Although he was a potter, he never dug up earth,
fearing harm to insects and creatures.
He only took soil from collapsed riverbanks and rat holes.
He mixed it to make pottery.
He traded it for the five grains.
The amount was up to the other party; he never haggled over price.
He used it to support his elderly parents.
His parents were old, weak, and had already lost their eyesight.
Huānyù's benevolence and filial piety were hard to match.
One morning, the Buddha Kāshyapa arose, arranged his robe, took his bowl, entered the city, and came to Huānyù's house.
He asked his parent:
'Where is the filial son?'
The parent replied:
'The Buddha's disciple has just stepped out.'
'There is good rice and bean soup in the house.'
The Buddha received it in his bowl, sat down, finished the meal, and then left.
When the son returned and saw the soup and rice were reduced,
he said:
'Who took this rice?'
The parent said:
'The Lord of Gods came to visit you.
He himself took the soup and rice, finished the meal, and then left.' Huānyù was both sad and overjoyed.
He said:
'The Buddha is the Tathāgata, the Unattached, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Dharma King, the Teacher of gods and humans.
Heavenly kings and emperors reverently offer feasts, often fearing they are not worthy of the World-Honored One.
I live in such lowliness, and the food is not fine.
He only took it out of compassion for my lowly state.'
Overwhelmed with both sorrow and joy, he bowed his head to the ground.
Reflecting on the Buddha's kindness, so vast and universal,
he was so joyful he forgot hunger for fifteen days.
His parent, sharing in the joy, forgot hunger for seven days.
A little over a month later, the Buddha again came to his house.
The son was again not home.
The Buddha again took the soup and rice, finished the meal, and then left.
The son soon returned, and the parent again told him what happened.
Huānyù and his parent
were again so overjoyed they forgot hunger for the same number of days as before.
At that time, dragons rained day and night without cease, and the monastery was leaking and damaged.
The Buddha told the monks:
'Huānyù has newly built a dwelling.
You all go and remove its tiles to protect the monastery.'
The monks went.
The son was again not home.
The parent said:
'Who is removing the tiles of my house?'
The monks replied:
'The Buddha's monastery is leaking.
He sent us to remove the tiles of this house to repair the monastery.'
The parent said:
'Excellent!
My son's virtue is so great that it has led to this!'
Overjoyed, he bowed his head and said:
'Please take more.
My blessings are immeasurable.'
As soon as the monks left,
the son returned and saw it, saying:
'Who removed the tiles?'
The parent said:
'The Buddha's monastery was leaking. He sent monks to take tiles to repair it.'
Huānyù, wherever he was, bowed his head to the ground toward the Buddha.
'The Honored One's wisdom is immeasurable.
Kings and lords build halls of the seven treasures and offer them in abundance.
Yet the Buddha does not dwell in them.
He takes these crude tiles only wishing to bless me.'
Overjoyed, he did not eat and forgot hunger as before.
The Buddha, leading five hundred monks, entered the royal kingdom ahead.
The king's name was Zhīwéi.
He personally went to welcome the Buddha.
The king descended from his carriage, removed the five royal insignia,
paid respects, inquired, took a seat, and listened to the sutra. After finishing, he said:
'I pray, Lord of Gods,
with all the monks, condescend to partake of our humble food.'
The Buddha silently consented.
When the feast was fully prepared, he sent an envoy to respectfully welcome them.
The king personally poured water for washing, served the meal, made offerings, and after the ceremony, sat before the Buddha.
The Buddha told the king:
"Your Majesty, having long revered the Three Jewels, now receives the blessings from the past.
You were born into the human realm, transformed from a woman into a man, and attained a high worldly position.
The way of a king should be to govern his mind with the teachings of the sages.
Extend compassion to yourself and nurture the people.
Deceptive words are a fire that burns a kingdom.
Your Majesty must be cautious of this."
The king bowed his head and accepted the instruction. The king then entreated the Buddha to stay.
For three months, he offered the Seven Treasures: beds, tables, canopies, cushions, medicines, and exhausted the nation's treasures in his provisions.
The Buddha did not consent.
The king thought to himself:
"In offerings, who could surpass me?"
The Buddha, knowing the king's mind had thoughts of arrogance,
immediately said to the king:
"There is one who surpasses the king; his generosity is immeasurable."
The king said:
"I wish to hear his name."
The Buddha said:
"In Wéilíng County, there is a son of utmost filial piety.
His name is Huānyù.
He reveres the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and receives my clear teachings.
He extends compassion to himself and regards others equally, nurturing all beings.
Pure and chaste, he guards the truth, his hands never holding treasures.
Together with various sharp blades and utensils, he sells them to support his parents.
He does not haggle over prices, endures insults, and is kind and generous.
He takes the right path as his heart.
He delights in the sacred scriptures.
He dares not take a wife,
fearing it would show disrespect to his parents, considering it unfilial.
Whenever he goes to the Buddha's place, he listens to the Dharma with a sincere heart.
For his parents, he describes the suffering of losing sight, unable to see the Buddha clearly.
Speaking of it, he sheds tears.
The Buddha takes his food and removes the tiles from his roof, yet the entire household bears no resentment.
He forgets hunger in joy for fifteen days.
His utmost benevolence and filial piety, his virtue is difficult to fully describe.
I must travel around to teach and transform the world, and cannot accept Your Majesty's invitation."
The king felt displeased and argued.
The Buddha said:
"Judging by merit and virtue,
his benevolence, purity, chastity, faith, and filial conduct are difficult to match.
In daily life and interactions, he has never been unfilial.
His benevolent virtue and thoughts for his parents—such conduct is hard to equal.
It is not something one can easily attain."
The king said: "Excellent!
Huānyù's utmost filial piety is praised by the Buddha.
The praise of his virtue reaches even this.
I shall offer tribute to assist in supporting his parents."
When Kāshyapa Buddha finished preaching the sutra,
he traveled to teach and transform beings.
The king dispatched an envoy,
heavily loading five hundred carts,
with non-glutinous rice, sesame oil, ghee, rock sugar, various goods, and precious treasures.
Humbly and respectfully,
the envoy arrived and said:
"O Heavenly One,
you greatly praise the worthy one's utmost filial piety and universal compassion.
The great king is delighted and joyful, sending me to convey his reverence.
I hope you will accept this tribute,
to support his parents and also make offerings to the Buddha."
Huānyù replied:
"The great king is kind and generous to assist me.
Return to the palace and fully convey this intention."
In the same county, a Brahmin's son named Huājié,
was a close childhood friend of Huānyù.
For many kalpas they had been relatives, their paths of transformation mutually accomplished.
Over time, their bond grew even stronger.
Together, they bathed in deep water.
From afar, they saw a great tree.
Huānyù pointed and said:
"Kāshyapa Tathāgata, the sage, is here.
We must first go to pay homage.
The Buddha's path is hard to forget; how dare I hope for it?"
Huānyù said sorrowfully:
"A Buddha's appearance in the world is hard to encounter, like the udumbara flower.
Sometimes, it takes many kalpas for one to appear.
How can we miss this opportunity?"
He tugged at his sleeve, forcefully pulling him along to where the Buddha was. Huānyù bowed his head; Huājié did not bow.
They exchanged courtesies and sat down.
Huānyù addressed the Buddha:
"This Huājié is my close childhood friend.
He is deluded and has not yet awakened.
I wish to dispel his ignorance."
Kāshyapa Tathāgata expounded the Dharma according to his affliction.
His mind immediately opened and understood, and he revered and believed in the Three Jewels.
The two rejoiced, bowed their heads, and withdrew together.
Huājié, along the way, said:
"How fortunate the world has a Buddha, yet home is a foul den.
Why don't you become a śramaṇa?"
He replied:
"My parents are advanced in years,
and both have lost their sight; they depend on me for their lives, so I cannot leave home."
Huājié said:
"I shall become a śramaṇa."
Huānyù then reported the matter to the Buddha, who then conferred the precepts upon him.
After a hundred million years,
he was born in the fourth Tuṣita Heaven.
Descending from heaven, he attained Buddhahood by himself.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Huājié at that time was my former self.
Huānyù was Ānanda.
Ānanda was my good friend.
He forcefully pulled me to where the Buddha was to listen to the sutra, enabling me to attain Buddhahood.
The analogy of a worthy friend is the foundation of ten thousand blessings.
In the present life, it avoids the king's prison;
after death, it blocks the gates to the three wretched paths.
Ascending to heaven and attaining the Way are all aided by worthy friends."
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Since I attained Buddhahood,
over thirty years have passed.
Now, in this assembly,
who can uphold the twelve divisions of the scriptures for me,
attend to my needs on the left and right,
ensuring nothing is lost and benefiting himself with good?"
The five hundred arhats all said:
"I can."
The Buddha said: "Not sufficient."
Maudgalyāyana observed the Tathāgata,
whose mind was on Ānanda.
Maudgalyāyana repeatedly urged Ānanda.
Ānanda said:
"I am defiled and weak, unfit to serve.
If the Buddha grants me three wishes,
I will follow the Sangha's command.
First, if the Tathāgata bestows used robes,
allow me not to accept them.
Second, if I receive a separate invitation from a donor,
allow me not to comply.
Third, allow me to come and go without restriction of time."
Mañjuśrī said: "Excellent!
Foreseeing criticism and suspicion."
Ānanda served me
for over twenty years,
possessing eight kinds of inconceivable qualities:
First, he does not accept separate invitation meals.
Second, he does not accept used clothing.
Third, he does not come at inappropriate times.
Fourth, though initially possessing afflictions,
accompanying me in and out of the homes of kings and nobles,
upon seeing women, he does not generate desire.
Fifth, regarding the twelve divisions of scriptures,
once heard, he never asks again,
like pouring from one bottle into another.
Sixth, he knows others' minds like the Buddha entering samādhi.
Seventh, though not having attained the wisdom of vows, he can fully understand
those presently attaining the four fruits and those who will later attain them.
Eighth, secret words he can fully comprehend.
Therefore, I often praise his extensive learning.
Ānanda, possessing these eight qualities,
is capable of upholding the twelve divisions of scriptures.
First, his faith is firm and solid.
Second, his mind is courageous and advancing.
Third, his body is free from illness and suffering.
Fourth, he is constantly diligent and vigorous.
Fifth, he possesses a mindful heart.
Sixth, his mind is free from arrogance and conceit.
Seventh, he has achieved concentrated mind.
Eighth, he possesses wisdom born from hearing."
The Buddha was at the Jeta Grove.
Ānanda dreamed of seven things in another place.
Immediately, his hair stood on end in alarm.
Last night, I dreamed and saw seven things in total.
First, rivers, streams, and seas were all ablaze with fire.
Second, the sun was about to set, and Jambudvīpa became dark.
I saw myself carrying Mount Sumeru on my head.
Third, bhikṣus were writhing in filth.
I also saw a person stepping on a bhikṣu’s head to cross over to clean ground.
Fourth, I saw bhikṣus whose Dharma robes were incomplete, wearing only a kāṣāya tied together.
Holding torches, they joyfully entered wrong paths.
Amidst thorns and brambles, their robes were torn.
Fifth, I saw a sandalwood tree, very large and flourishing.
A pig emerged from filth and rubbed against the sandalwood tree.
Sixth, I saw three grades of young elephants.
They butted, gored, bit, and charged at the great elephants.
They trampled good grass and muddied clear water.
The great elephants, troubled by this, fled and went away.
They went to great clear waters and good grass.
The young elephants frolicked, completely unaware.
Thus, in their original place, water and grass were exhausted.
Suffering extreme hunger and thirst, they gnawed at trees and eventually all starved to death.
Seventh, I saw a dead lion king.
Named Qǐsà.
White hair grew on its head, as if tied and adorned.
Flying birds and a hundred beasts dared not approach or touch it.
Worms emerged from within the lion’s body and ate its flesh.
Because of these dream causes, in the morning, he went to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
Dreaming of water ablaze with fire means:
In the future, bhikṣus will violate the Buddha’s teachings.
They will use offerings gained through wrongdoing and breaking precepts.
Moreover, they will stir up disputes and conflicts.
Dreaming of the sun about to go dark and carrying Mount Sumeru on the head means:
The World-Honored One will, after ninety days,
attain parinirvāṇa.
Afterwards, the multitude of bhikṣus, devas, nāgas, and people
will follow Ānanda to receive and uphold the sutra teachings.
Dreaming of bhikṣus wearing Dharma robes not according to the usual rule,
only a kāṣāya tied together, writhing in filth,
and someone stepping on their heads to emerge and dwell on clean ground means:
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the Dharma is about to end,
there will be bhikṣus gathering in great assemblies to expound sutras.
At that time, they will not uphold the Buddha’s profound Dharma.
They will associate closely with laypeople, pursuing wealth and sensual pleasures.
Lay devotees will admonish and reprove them, but they will not believe or follow.
The bhikṣus will suffer calamity, and the lay devotees will gain merit.
Dreaming of bhikṣus wearing a tied kāṣāya,
holding torches, joyfully entering wrong paths,
amidst thorns and brambles, tearing their robes means:
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there will be bhikṣus
without Dharma robes, wearing laypeople’s clothes,
only a single kāṣāya tied under the armpit.
They will abandon precepts, delight in worldly life, and raise wives and children.
For alms and provisions, if they have them, they are joyful; if not, they are sorrowful.
Dreaming of a sandalwood tree, very large and flourishing,
and a pig emerging from filth rubbing against the tree means:
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there will be bhikṣus
who do not follow the rules, drink alcohol, become confused and disordered, and eat without moderation.
Wise and intelligent people with good intentions will instruct and explain,
but they will instead slander and revile arhats.
Dreaming of three grades of young elephants butting and charging at great elephants,
trampling good grass and muddling clear water,
the great elephants, troubled, flee and go away,
going to clear water and fine grass,
while the young elephants frolic, completely unaware,
and water and grass become exhausted, leading to starvation means:
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there will be elder bhikṣus versed in sutras
who instruct and admonish the young, showing them the consequences of wrongdoing and merit.
The young will not accept or follow, and after death, they will fall into hell.
Dreaming of a dead lion king named Qǐsà,
with white hair growing on its head as if tied and adorned,
insects, birds, and beasts dare not invade or eat it,
but worms emerge from within its body and devour its flesh means:
While the Buddha is in the world, he extensively expounds the Dharma.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, no external path will be able to destroy this Dharma.
But it will be the disciples themselves who will destroy my Dharma.
Your dreams merely foretell these strange events of the future.
Ānanda, while walking on the road, became parched with thirst.
There was a Caṇḍāla woman named Pójítí drawing water.
Ānanda approached her to beg for water.
The woman replied to Ānanda:
I am of the Màodéngjiā caste.
Ānanda said:
I am not asking about that; just give me water.
The woman said:
Your mother’s caste is accomplished.
You are the foremost disciple of the ascetic Gótama.
Revered by King Prasenajit.
Preceptor to Queen Màolì.
I am lowly and base.
I dare not give you water.
Ānanda said again:
I am not asking about that.
Just give me water.
The woman agreed.
At that time, the woman first scooped water and poured it on Ānanda’s feet.
She scooped water again and poured it on Ānanda’s hands.
Then she gave rise to lustful thoughts.
Ānanda drank and then left.
Pójítí returned and told her parents:
Mother, I wish to have the ascetic Ānanda as my husband.
The mother said:
He is the son of a wheel-turning king,
of the kṣatriya Śākya clan, a noble master of the holy teacher’s lineage.
Devas and humans revere and serve him.
How can our lowly family caste obtain him as a husband?
The daughter said:
If I cannot, I will drink poison, stab myself with a knife,
or hang myself to death.
The mother said:
There is the Màodéngjiā deity’s mantra and spell.
It can move the sun and moon to fall to the ground.
It can also summon Indra and Brahmā devas to descend.
How much more can it not obtain a śramaṇa?
It can make Ānanda come, whether dead or alive, and if not capable of lust,
if protected by Gótama,
I cannot obtain him.
Other than that, all can be obtained.
The daughter then arose, bathed, adorned her body,
put on white garments and ornaments, spread out various bedding,
and gazed from afar.
The mother smeared the ground with cow dung,
tied threads of five colors into cords,
filled four vessels with water,
filled four bowls with gruel,
placed four large knives upright in the cow dung,
four arrows at the four corners,
lit eight bright lamps,
took four human skulls,
anointed them with various perfumes,
scattered flowers on the ground,
held an iron, burned incense,
circumambulated three times, knelt facing east,
and recited the Màodéngjiā spell.
At that time, Ānanda was in the Jeta Grove forest,
his mind became dazed and bound by the spell,
like a fish or elephant hooked.
Following the spell, he arrived at the Caṇḍāla’s house.
The mother then said to her daughter:
Ānanda has arrived.
At that time, the daughter went forward and embraced Ānanda,
seated him on the bed,
pulled and restrained his robe,
pinched and pressed Ānanda.
It was like a strong man grasping a long-haired
lamb with his hand.
Ānanda saw all ten directions become completely dark,
as if the sun and moon were eclipsed by Rāhu.
Ānanda had great man’s strength,
equal to the strength of ten mighty men.
Yet he could not move.
Ānanda, with the power of the holy truth of the Path, mindful, regained awareness.
I am now in distress; the World-Honored One is greatly compassionate; does he not pity me?
The Buddha immediately knew.
Then he recited a Buddha-word verse, saying:
Ānán, having grasped the true meaning,
was liberated in the house of the Caṇḍāla.
Just as he finished reciting the verse,
within the Caṇḍāla's house,
the ritual implements, knives, and arrows were shattered,
jars and pots were broken,
lamps were extinguished, and skulls burst apart.
A black wind arose, and they could no longer see each other.
The Caṇḍāla's spells lost their power.
The mother then said to her daughter,
"This must be the divine power of the Śramaṇa Gautama.
All objects are shattered and scattered, and the spells no longer work."
Ānán thought,
"This is the power of the World-Honored One's grace."
Ānán was liberated,
like a great elephant king, sixty years old, fierce and violent,
with a massive body and long tusks,
freed from iron shackles,
running from the city to an open, empty place.
Ānán was likewise.
The World-Honored One recited the Buddha's words,
and Ānán was liberated from the Caṇḍāla's house.
He returned to the Jetavana.
At that time, this woman
followed Ānán to the gate of the Jetavana,
repeatedly saying,
"Ānán is my husband, Ānán is my husband."
She followed Ānán without leaving him for a moment.
Ānán reported all this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"Among all dharmas, I have never seen such delusion.
This woman's mind is bound by lust."
Ānán, at dawn, put on his robes and took his bowl,
entering Śrāvastī to seek alms.
And this woman also followed behind him,
telling the elders,
"Ānán is my husband, Ānán is my husband."
Ānán returned to where the Buddha was,
and again reported to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"Go and speak to her
as if she were your sister.
Why?
This woman should become a bhikṣuṇī."
The woman said to the Buddha,
"I only wish, World-Honored One,
that you return my husband to me."
The Buddha said,
"If you want Ānán,
become a bhikṣuṇī in my Dharma,
and I will give him to you."
The woman was delighted and returned to bid farewell
to her parents, who were also joyful. Having previously planted good roots,
each should attain the Way.
The parents and their daughter together went to see the Buddha.
The World-Honored One extensively expounded the Dharma for them,
using countless skillful means to reveal the meanings of the dharmas:
the meaning of gentleness, the meaning of dāna, the meaning of śīla,
the impurity of lust,
the meaning of increasing and generating the roots of the fetters,
the meaning of leaving home, the meaning of the factors of the path,
and also explained the Four Noble Truths.
At that time, this woman, right on her seat, understood the Four Noble Truths.
The parents attained the Anāgāmin path,
and the daughter attained the Srotaāpanna path.
It was like a pure white cloth, easily dyed.
At that time, the parents took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha,
and were accepted as upāsakas by the Buddha.
Ānán repented of his foolish offense,
and requested that she become a bhikṣuṇī,
so she could rely on the World-Honored One to cultivate the holy life.
The Buddha told Ānán,
"Take two bhikṣuṇīs and this woman
to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī,
and have her ordained with the full precepts for the path."
Mahāprajāpatī asked Ānán,
"How is it, Ānán?
Has the World-Honored One
permitted this Caṇḍāla woman to enter the path?"
Ānán replied to Gautamī,
"Yes," and then she was tonsured and received the precepts.
She attained Arhatship.
The Buddha was in Śrāvastī.
At that time, he suffered from a wind illness.
He called Ānán
to go to a brāhmaṇa's house to beg for cow's milk.
Ānán immediately went as instructed to request it.
The brāhmaṇa said,
"The cow is over there; go and milk it yourself."
Ānán then went to where the cow was.
The cow often liked to butt and trample people, so no one could approach it.
Ānán thought to himself,
"According to the Dharma of the teacher I serve,
I cannot milk the cow myself."
Śakra, the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, then descended,
transformed into a brāhmaṇa dressed in robes, and stood beside the cow.
Ānán requested that he milk the cow.
The brāhmaṇa said, "Yes,"
and with his right hand, he touched the cow's udder and said,
"The Buddha has a slight wind illness.
Give me your milk
so the Buddha may drink it.
If the Buddha recovers, the merit you gain will be immeasurable."
The cow said,
"What good or pleasure is there in this hand touching my udder?
Take both my udders,
remove both udders,
and leave them for my calf.
My calf has not eaten or drunk since this morning."
The calf was beside its mother.
Hearing the mention of the Buddha's name, it said,
"Take my share and give it all to the Buddha.
The Buddha is the great teacher of humans in heaven and on earth.
He is very difficult to encounter.
I will eat grass and drink water.
When I was a human, I followed evil companions,
did not believe in the Buddha's sutras,
and thus became an ox or horse for sixteen kalpas.
Only now have I been able to hear the Buddha's name.
Take the milk I drink
and give it all to the Buddha.
Fill the vessel and go.
May I, in future lives, attain wisdom and achieve Buddhahood."
Ānán took the milk and returned.
The Buddha asked him,
"What did the cow and calf say?"
Ānán answered according to what happened.
The Buddha said,
"The mother cow, in the time of Maitreya Buddha,
will become a śramaṇa and attain the path of Arhatship.
The calf, after death, will be reborn as a human,
and will make offerings of banners, scatter flowers, burn incense,
uphold the sutras and precepts for twenty kalpas, and thereafter
will become an Arhat.
The Buddha liberates all the people of the world."
In Śrāvastī, there was a famine year.
The bhikṣus each wanted to disperse,
considering it the end of the year.
Ānán said,
"If the bhikṣus go to other countries for the year's end,
these countless people will lose the foundation of virtue.
If the Tathāgata remains here,
Śrāvastī will have much peace and stability."
King Prasenajit heard this
and invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha for a three-month offering.
The Buddha said,
"In a past world,
in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a king
named Brahmadatta, who had great majesty and virtue,
and his fame spread far and wide.
At that time, the country was in famine, and there were many beggars.
The king delighted in giving,
and they gathered from all directions like clouds.
Heaven had not rained for a long time,
grain became increasingly expensive, and the people were hungry and distressed.
The number of beggars grew daily, and the granaries were empty and exhausted.
The ministers requested that he stop.
The king said,
'If so, it would go against my original intention.
How could I bear to oppose them?'
At that time, the officials who understood the law announced to the four directions,
'Anyone who dares to beg will be abandoned in the city.'
The beggars were sorrowful. The king asked,
and the ministers replied,
'There are those who have come from afar.'
A brāhmaṇa then entered.
The king asked,
'Who sent you?' The brāhmaṇa answered,
'My belly sent me.'
At that time, the king, moved with compassion, replied with a verse:
'I give a thousand red calves and all their calves.'
That brāhmaṇa was Ānán."
Ānán and two bhikkhus
arrived in the kingdom of King Āyù.
In the mountains, a bhikkhu named Shānxiàng
was on a pine tree.
Fragrant flowers came to him of their own accord.
Bells rang as if speaking.
The bhikkhu Shānxiàng
did not know the reason.
He came out and paid respects in all four directions.
Returning to the fasting hall, he recited scriptures.
Ānán and the two bhikkhus
transformed into beggars.
They also brought three hundred beggars to beg for food.
The bhikkhu Shānxiàng prepared food and served them.
He asked for clothes and lent them his own garments.
The three hundred beggars refused to leave.
So he provided for the beggars day and night until they all fell ill.
The bhikkhu Shānxiàng then burned incense day and night, praying for blessings and preparing medicine.
The three hundred beggars all died.
The bhikkhu Shānxiàng then went out to beg, bathed them, and prepared coffins for burial.
King Āyù ordered people to bury them.
A few days later,
Ānán,
along with the two bhikkhus, transformed into three scholars.
Their clothes were clean and neat.
They went to the pine tree.
The bhikkhu Shānxiàng came down from the lecture hall to greet them.
He set up seats and invited them to sit.
The three scholars said to the bhikkhu Shānxiàng,
"What do you seek by serving the Buddha?"
The bhikkhu Shānxiàng replied,
"The Buddha's path is a divine path.
Between heaven and earth, only the Buddha's path is divine.
I serve the Buddha
because I wish for the Buddha's path to liberate humans and non-humans.
I seek nothing else."
The three scholars said,
"The Buddha's path is not divine.
It is merely empty and void.
Few people engage in such matters.
Why are you so foolish and deluded,
chasing after people to serve the Buddha?"
The bhikkhu Shānxiàng said,
"What you say is not in accordance with the Dharma.
The Buddha's path is the most divine, unseen by ordinary people.
Its transformations are unpredictable, unknown to ordinary people.
Ordinary people are foolish and deluded, unaware of this.
Speaking such empty words only increases your sins."
The three scholars became angry.
"You serve the Buddha but do not oppose people's wishes.
Will you willingly become our slave?"
The bhikkhu Shānxiàng said,
"Yes."
The three scholars said,
"You are not fit to be a good slave.
We will make you carry excrement.
You must gather one hundred shi of manure.
If you fail to gather one hundred shi of manure,
we will cut off your head."
The bhikkhu Shānxiàng went to carry excrement.
Unable to gather much, he returned and apologized to the scholars, saying his strength was exhausted and he could not gather more.
He begged for forgiveness for his failure.
The three scholars became furious.
They seized and bound him.
They whipped him three hundred times painfully.
Suddenly, they left on their own.
Ānán then transformed into an upāsaka.
He went and said to the bhikkhu Shānxiàng,
"The actions of the three scholars are unrighteous.
Shouldn't you report them to the king to punish them?"
The bhikkhu Shānxiàng said,
"This is due to my own faults, hence this outcome.
Those who serve the Buddha have nothing to cherish.
If they seek my head, I give my head; if they seek my body, I give my body.
I merely carried excrement and was whipped—what suffering is there in this?"
Ānán and the two bhikkhus
then transformed into King Āyù.
They went and said to the bhikkhu Shānxiàng,
"Serving the Buddha is certainly of no benefit.
It is merely empty toil.
Human life in this world is fleeting, and death comes soon.
Why toil alone in upholding these scriptures?
I now wish to discuss something with you.
It would be best if you follow me.
If you do not follow me,
you, monk, will surely die."
The bhikkhu Shānxiàng said,
"What does the king wish to discuss?"
The king said, "I have a noble daughter.
Her talents and virtues are unparalleled.
Her face is beautiful.
Her hands are like bees.
I admire you, monk, for your gentle and kind nature.
I wish to give her to you, hence I came to convey my intention.
You must certainly comply."
The bhikkhu Shānxiàng said,
"I know the king's generous intention.
I have upheld the Buddha's teachings for many years.
My merits and virtues are not yet accomplished; how could I covet the king's daughter?
To disgrace the Buddha's path is no small sin.
If the king wishes to kill me, I will accept it."
The king then ordered people to take the bhikkhu Shānxiàng to the market to be beheaded.
The bhikkhu Shānxiàng paid respects to the Buddha and left.
He turned and thanked the king.
It was then Ānán.
The bhikkhu Shānxiàng stepped forward, paid respects, and touched his head to the ground.
Ānán rose and supported him.
He made him sit again, and they recognized each other.
Ānán said to the bhikkhu Shānxiàng,
"Your merits and virtues are accomplished.
You shall attain the Way.
I deliberately tested you,
to observe your resolve."
The bhikkhu Shānxiàng knelt and said,
"I am ignorant, yet I have received the Buddha's grace.
I am within the Dharma but unable to do good.
I have troubled divine beings to worry about me."
Ānán bestowed the Way upon the bhikkhu Shānxiàng.
Together they went upstairs to recite scriptures and explain their meanings.
They rejoiced in harmony and joy.
King Āyù paid respects and knelt.
Ānán asked the king,
"How many volumes of Buddhist scriptures are there?"
The king replied,
"Buddhist scriptures are numerous beyond count.
The scriptures currently existing comprise twelve divisions,
with eighty-four thousand volumes."
Ānán asked the king,
"How many volumes has the king already upheld?"
The king replied,
"I have recited twelve thousand volumes of the Samādhi Sūtra,
and twelve thousand volumes of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra."
Ānán asked the king,
"The king has seen many scriptures.
Do you know how many miles apart heaven and earth are?"
The king replied,
"The Great Samādhi Sūtra states
that heaven and earth are eight hundred and ten thousand miles apart."
Ānán asked the king,
"How many categories does the earth have?"
The king replied,
"The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra states
that the earth has eighty-one cities.
Each city has its own people.
People in the northern city are ten zhang tall.
People in the central city are eight chi tall.
People in the southern city are three chi tall."
Ānán asked the king,
"Does the king know who you were originally?"
The king replied,
"I do not know the distant past, only the recent.
I have once been in hell,
I have once been in heaven,
I have once endured toil and suffering,
I have once been a slave,
I have once been among the six kinds of livestock,
I have once been in fire,
I have once been a virtuous person.
From being a virtuous person,
I became a king.
Having witnessed the hardships of life,
I dare not commit evil again."
Ānán said,
"The king was originally a bhikkhu of Buddha Tíhèjié,
named Títóuluó.
The bhikkhu Shānxiàng was Śākyamuni Buddha's
bhikkhu Xūbá.
Since the Buddha departed,
we have been isolated and impoverished, upholding the Dharma unsteadily,
leading to sins and faults.
Over the years,
we no longer recognized each other.
In the past, I and the bhikkhu Shānxiàng
were born into a humble family; I was the elder brother, and the bhikkhu Shānxiàng was the younger brother.
We always cherished each other and followed each other everywhere.
Initially, we did not recognize each other.
Later, I became a king.
The bhikkhu Shānxiàng was reborn, and I still did not recognize him.
The world is ever-changing, beings are reborn in mutual dependence,
beyond count.
Now I know I have escaped the cycle of birth and death."
He then bestowed upon King Āyù the path of an arhat.
The arhat Mòtiándì
received Ānán's entrustment of the Dharma treasury.
He was sent to the kingdom of Jìbīn.
First, he subdued the dragon there.
He entered samādhi,
causing the land of that kingdom to shake in six ways.
The dragon became uneasy.
It went to where Mòtiándì was.
Mòtiándì entered the samādhi of compassion.
The dragon king raised a wind to blow at him,
but the corner of his kasaya did not move.
The dragon then raised thunder, lightning, weapons,
and a volcanic mountain to crush him.
Mòtiándì used his divine power to transform them into heavenly flowers.
Then a verse was heard in the sky.
After receiving Ānán's entrustment, Shènàpósī
went to the country of Mótóuluó.
Along the way, there was a monastery
named Píntuópónà.
Shènàpósī stayed at the monastery for one night.
In the monastery, there were two elderly bhikṣus
discussing and reciting verses.
These bhikṣus said to Shènàpósī:
Shènàpósī spoke,
"The meaning you speak of is not what I speak of.
Venerable ones,
in the past, in Vārāṇasī, there was a merchant leader
who, with five hundred merchants, intended to enter the great sea.
He saw a Pratyekabuddha who was ill.
The merchant leader personally provided medical treatment.
The illness gradually improved.
The merchant leader took a śāṇa garment, washed and softened it, and offered it to the Pratyekabuddha.
The Pratyekabuddha received the garment, performed eighteen transformations, and then entered Nirvāṇa.
That merchant leader was I.
Therefore, I now encounter the most supreme teacher,
enabling me to attain the path."
Shènàpósī gradually traveled to the Yōuliúmàntuó Mountain in the country of Mótóuluó.
There were two nāga kings, brothers, with five hundred small nāgas.
Shènàpósī thought,
"If I do not subdue them, I cannot teach and transform them."
He then used his divine power to shake the mountain.
The two nāga kings became angry,
raising fierce wind and rain,
and emitting fire.
Shènàpósī entered the samādhi of loving-kindness.
The wind, rain, and fire could not approach his body,
and all transformed into flowers,
such as utpala flowers, etc.,
which all fell to the ground.
They then raised thunder, lightning, and various weapons,
but he also used his divine power to transform them into heavenly flowers.
At that moment, a verse was spoken in the sky:
Thereupon, the two nāga kings
went to Shènàpósī and said,
"Holy one, what do you wish to do?"
He replied,
"I wish to build a monastery here.
You must permit me."
The nāgas replied,
"It cannot be done."
The elder said,
"The World-Honored One has already said,
'After my Nirvāṇa, within a hundred years,
in the most excellent place of the great Dàtíhú Mountain, a monastery shall be built,
named Nàduōpóduō.'"
The nāga kings said again,
"Did the World-Honored One truly say this?"
The elder replied,
"Yes."
The nāga kings said,
"If the World-Honored One said so, then I shall comply as you wish."
Shènàpósī.
Built a monastery on Mount Dàtíhú.
There was a merchant dealing in incense,
named Jíduō.
Shènàpósī,
through skillful means,
taught and guided the incense merchant,
urging him to be diligent.
At that time, Shènàpósī went alone to his home.
