Jíduō asked,
"Why does the sage have no disciples?
I enjoy living at home and indulging in the pleasures of the five senses,
and cannot leave home to become a monk.
If I have a son, I will let him follow you, Elder."
Later, Jíduō had a son,
named Ābōjíduō. When he grew up,
Shènàpósī went to Jíduō's place
and said,
"You previously made a vow:
'If I have a son, I will give him to the Elder.'
Now that you have a son, you should allow him to follow me and leave home."
Jíduō said,
"I now have only one son.
If a second son is born,
I will give him to the Elder."
Later, a second son was born,
named Tuónàjíduō. Again, he was asked but not given.
A third son, Yōubōjíduō, was also requested.
Jíduō replied,
"I will make a vow:
Let Yōubōjíduō engage in business.
If he prospers or fails, he cannot leave home.
Only if he neither prospers nor fails will he be allowed to leave home."
At that time, the demon king
caused all the people in the country of Mótóuluó
to buy his goods, enabling him to make a profit.
At that time, Yōubōjíduō was selling incense.
Elder Shènàpósī said to him,
"What is the nature of your mind and mental states?
What is good, and what is evil?"
He replied, "I do not know."
The Elder said,
"If the mind and mental states
are associated with greed, hatred, and delusion,
that is called evil.
If they are associated with non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion,
that is called good."
At that time, the Elder made pellets of black soil and white soil
and said to him,
"If a black thought arises, take a black pellet.
If a white thought arises, take a white pellet."
Yōubōjíduō
followed his instructions.
His mind did not produce good thoughts,
so he only obtained one white pellet.
Gradually progressing,
he took two parts black pellets and one part white pellet.
Further contemplating,
he took half black pellets and half white pellets.
Subsequently, thinking of good, he ceased to produce evil and took only white pellets.
At that time, in the country of Mótóuluó,
there was a courtesan named Pósuōdá, who had a maid.
The maid went to Yōubōjíduō to buy incense and obtained a large amount.
Her mistress asked,
"Where did you get so much incense?
Did you steal it?"
The maid said,
"There is a merchant named Yōubōjíduō,
handsome in appearance and eloquent in speech,
who sells goods in accordance with the Dharma."
Upon hearing this, her mistress developed lustful thoughts
and sent her maid again to Yōubōjíduō,
saying, "Tell him I wish to enjoy myself with him."
Yōubōjíduō replied,
"It is not yet time to meet."
Despite repeated attempts,
he still refused.
At that time, she summoned the son of an elder to come to her place.
A merchant from northern India
brought five hundred horses and various goods
to the country of Mótóuluó.
Upon arrival, he asked the people of Mótóuluó,
"Where in this country is the most beautiful woman?"
The people replied,
"There is a woman
of exceptional beauty,
named Pósuō Pódáduō."
The merchant said,
"I now wish to take five hundred silver coins and various goods to her place."
At that time, the courtesan,
greedy for his possessions, killed the elder's son,
took his body and placed it in an unclean place,
and enjoyed herself with the merchant.
A close friend of the elder's son
found the body in the unclean place
and reported it to the king.
The king said,
"You may take that Pósuō Pódáduō,
cut off her hands, feet, ears, and nose,
and scatter them in the wilderness."
It was done as the king commanded.
At that time, Yōubōjíduō thought to himself,
"Previously, I had no desire to see her and indulge in the pleasures of the five senses.
Now I wish to see her hands, feet, ears, and nose."
He went to see her
and recited a verse.
Pósuō Pódáduō,
upon hearing his words, deeply feared the cycle of birth and death.
Hearing of the Buddha's virtues, she changed her mind and aspired to Nirvana.
She then recited a verse in reply to Yōubōjíduō.
Yōubōjíduō explained the Four Noble Truths to her.
Further observing her body, she became disgusted with the desire realm
and attained the Anāgāmi fruit.
Pósuō Pódáduō attained the Sotāpanna fruit.
Not long after Yōubōjíduō left,
Pósuō Pódáduō passed away and was reborn in heaven.
At that time, Elder Shènàpósī
went to Jíduō and said,
"You should allow Yōubōjíduō to follow me and leave home."
Jíduō replied,
"I previously made a vow: let him engage in business.
Only if he neither prospers nor fails will he be allowed to leave home."
Shènàpósī then used his supernatural power
to make his business neither prosper nor fail.
At that time, Yōubōjíduō thought to himself,
"Calculating and weighing, it is neither profitable nor unprofitable."
Shènàpósī
went again to Jíduō
and said to him,
"This son of yours is prophesied by the Buddha.
A hundred years after my Nirvana, he will carry out the Buddha's work.
You should allow him to follow me and leave home."
Jíduō agreed.
Shènàpósī took Yōubōjíduō to the Nàjí Monastery and ordained him.
During the fourth Karma of the full ordination,
he eliminated all defilements and attained Arhatship.
At that time, Shènàpósī said to Yōubōjíduō,
"Good man,
as prophesied by the Buddha,
a hundred years after my Nirvana,
there will be a monk named Yōubōjíduō
who will carry out the Buddha's work.
He will later become a Buddha
named Wúxiàng.
Thus, he taught the Dharma.
At that time, the demon king
rained pearls upon the assembly
to disturb people's minds.
Due to the disturbance, no one could perceive the truth.
Realizing it was the demon king,
he thought to himself.
On the second day, twice as many people came.
The demon king rained gold and again disturbed the minds of the assembly.
On the third day, even more people came.
The demon rained pearls and gold and created heavenly music.
At that time, the people had not yet abandoned desire.
Seeing the colors and hearing the sounds, their minds were agitated, and they no longer listened to the Dharma.
At that time, the demon king
placed a floral garland on Yōubōjíduō's head.
When Yōubōjíduō thought about it,
wondering who had done this,
he realized it was the demon.
Yōubōjíduō then thought,
"Why did the World-Honored One not subdue him?"
He then reflected, "It is my duty to subdue him.
The Buddha prophesied about me
as the Buddha Wúxiàng,
to teach and guide people."
Yōubōjíduō took three corpses:
one of a dead snake,
one of a dead dog,
and one of a dead human.
Using his supernatural power, he transformed the three corpses
into a floral garland
and went to the demon king to place it around his neck.
At that time, the demon king went to Maheśvara,
Śakra, and the other thirty-three gods and the Four Heavenly Kings,
seeking to remove the dead corpses,
but could not do so.
He then went to the Great Brahma Heaven.
Great Brahma said,
"Good man,
this is the work of the supernatural power of the disciple of the Ten-Powered One.
No one can remove it.
Just as the water of the great sea cannot be split,
so it is with this."
The demon king said,
"What should I do?
To whom should I now turn for refuge?"
Great Brahma said,
"You should now quickly go and take refuge in Yōubōjíduō.
Just as a person who falls on the ground
gets up from the same place."
At that time, the demon king finally understood the great supernatural power of the Buddha's son.
In Southern India, there was a man.
He constantly visited another man's home to commit adultery with his wife.
His mother tried to stop him.
He then killed his mother.
He went to another country but could not fulfill his five desires.
Deeply troubled and distressed,
he then renounced the world to follow the Buddha's teachings.
He mastered the Three Baskets and became widely learned.
Surrounded by his disciples, he went to the Natapata Temple in Mathurā, to where Upagupta was.
Upagupta, seeing that he had killed his mother,
did not attain the fruit of the path and did not offer him comfort or inquiry.
At that time, that bhikṣu felt ashamed in his heart.
He went even farther away.
Upagupta's disciples who had not yet attained the path
thought thus:
"Our teacher has little wisdom.
He preaches the Dharma to old bhikṣus whose minds are dull and dim.
Yet this bhikṣu is intelligent and wise,
skillfully versed in the Three Baskets, with followers accompanying him—
he does not preach the Dharma to him."
At that time, Upagupta, seeing his disciples' thoughts, became angry with them.
He also saw their capacity and response,
thinking, "They should be taught and subdued by my teacher, Śāṇavāsin."
At that time, Śāṇavāsin resided in the country of Kāśmīra.
He also observed what Buddha-work Upagupta was doing.
Seeing his disciples harboring anger and resentment,
and observing that these people should receive my guidance,
he immediately used his supernatural power to come and enter this temple.
His beard and hair were long, and his robes were coarse and worn.
The five hundred disciples all said this:
"Where did this ignorant old man come from?"
He sat on the sleeping place of Upagupta.
The disciples tried to pull him out by hand,
but could not move him, as if he were Mount Sumeru.
They wanted to scold him, but their voices would not come out.
They then reported to Upagupta, saying,
He replied:
"Except for my teacher, no one can sit on my bed."
Upagupta returned to the temple.
With the utmost reverence, he made offerings to his teacher.
He himself took a small seat and sat beside his teacher.
The disciples thought:
"If this bhikṣu
is our teacher's teacher,
then his wisdom must still be inferior to our teacher's."
At that time, Śāṇavāsin, seeing their thoughts,
raised his right arm and produced cow's milk.
He said to Upagupta:
"What is this samādhi?"
Upagupta replied, "I do not know it."
"I wish to hear its name."
The teacher said:
"It is called the Dragon's Sigh Samādhi."
Then he successively entered various other samādhis.
Upagupta said each time:
"I do not know it."
He also said:
"When I enter Nirvāṇa, all these samādhi methods will be lost."
Upagupta's disciples, hearing these words,
immediately thought:
"This bhikṣu's wisdom surpasses our teacher's."
They then eliminated their arrogance.
Śāṇavāsin taught and preached the Dharma to them.
All those disciples attained the fruit of Arhatship.
When Upagupta was about to enter Nirvāṇa,
he entrusted the Dharma treasury to his last disciple to be converted, Dhītika,
saying:
"Good man,
the World-Honored One's Dharma treasury was entrusted to Mahākāśyapa.
Kāśyapa entrusted it to Ānanda.
Ānanda entrusted it to Madhyāntika.
Madhyāntika entrusted it to my teacher Śāṇavāsin.
Śāṇavāsin entrusted it to me.
I now, entering Nirvāṇa, entrust it to you."
He announced it throughout Jambudvīpa.
One hundred thousand Arhats gathered at once.
Countless ordinary bhikṣus
then displayed supernatural powers, performing the eighteen transformations.
After these matters were completed, he entered Nirvāṇa.
Among the disciples he had converted who attained the four fruits of the path,
all took tallies and placed them in a stone chamber.
They then cremated his body with the tallies.
They even erected a stūpa.
At that time, there were also one thousand Arhats
who entered Nirvāṇa together.
Dhītika guarded the Dharma treasury.
From Upagupta, twenty-eight people attained the four fruits.
At that time, there was an Arhat
named Upagupta,
who resided at the Natapata Temple on Mount Mahāmandā in Mathurā.
Not far from the temple,
there was a tigress who gave birth to cubs.
Unable to find food, they starved to death.
Upagupta,
through the power of compassion, gave food to the tiger cubs.
He had five hundred disciples
who had not yet attained the path, who said:
"Why do you give food to such difficult beings?"
He replied:
"For the cause of liberation."
At that time, the tiger cubs' lifespans were short.
As they were about to die,
Upagupta said to the tiger cubs:
"All conditioned things are impermanent.
All dharmas are without self.
Nirvāṇa is tranquility.
You should develop faith in me.
You should feel aversion to the animal realm."
At that time, the tiger cubs, toward Upagupta,
developed faith and reverence in their hearts.
They then died.
They were reborn as humans in Mathurā.
When they reached the age of seven,
Upagupta taught and guided them to renounce the world.
Within seven years, they attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Using their supernatural powers, they gathered various flowers
to make offerings to Upagupta, surrounding his side.
The five hundred disciples who had not yet attained the path said:
"These fellow practitioners are still young in years.
How have they already attained supernatural powers and virtues?"
Upagupta replied:
"They are all the former tiger cubs."
Upagupta preached the Dharma.
The five hundred disciples felt deep shame.
They cut off afflictions and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
The Buddha was at Jīzú Shān.
At that time, a Brahmin had a son.
He had a physiognomist examine him.
The master said,
"This child has no auspicious features; he should be named Ābǎo."
Upon hearing this, his parents,
though they raised him, from the beginning showed him no affection or pity.
By the age of twelve, he was able to support himself.
His parents then drove him away, telling him not to return.
The child did not dare to stay and went out to beg for food.
He then arrived at Qíhuán.
The Buddha, with great compassion, took note of his hardship.
He immediately had Ānán call him and ask,
"Can you leave home?"
The boy was overjoyed and wished to become a śramaṇa.
The Buddha then stroked his head with his hand.
His hair immediately fell out, and a kāṣāya robe appeared on his body.
The Buddha gave him the name Luóxún Yú.
At that time, the monks of the five divisions would go out to seek alms.
But wherever Luóxún Yú went with a division, they would return with empty bowls.
The Buddha instructed the bhikṣus to share their alms with him.
This happened not just once.
Mùlián thought to himself,
"This bhikṣu cannot obtain food on his own.
Why do the others also return empty-handed?
If I go with him, perhaps he will get something."
The Buddha knew his intention and went with Shèlìfú.
He had Mùlián go with Luóxún Yú.
They each formed a separate group.
The Buddha told Mùlián,
"Where I am, you must not go."
Mùlián then went with Luóxún Yú.
Wherever they intended to go, they would immediately see the Buddha
and Shèlìfú at the gate.
Thus, they passed through hundreds of millions of countries,
but still obtained no food.
Mùlián thought,
"Today, I certainly will not get any food.
Luóxún Yú
was extremely hungry and stopped by the Héngshuǐ River.
Mùjiànlián
then returned to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the Buddha still had some leftover food in his bowl.
He gave it to Mùlián.
Mùlián thought,
"I am very hungry now.
Even if I swallowed Mount Sumeru, I would still not be full.
How can this little bit of food be enough?"
The Buddha told Mùlián,
"Just eat this food; do not worry about it being insufficient."
Mùlián then ate the food.
After eating, he was full, yet the bowl was not empty.
Only Shèlìfú then thought,
"Luóxún Yú
has not yet obtained food.
He must be suffering greatly from hunger."
He then said to the Buddha,
"I wish to beg for the leftover food to give to Luóxún Yú."
The Buddha immediately said,
"I do not begrudge the food.
But due to Luóxún Yú's past actions and karmic retribution, he should not receive it.
If you doubt this,
you may give it to him."
Shèlìfú then gave the food to him.
Luóxún Yú, upon receiving it, was about to take the food
when the bowl sank a hundred fathoms into the ground.
Shèlìfú, using his spiritual power,
reached for the bowl with his hand and retrieved it for Luóxún Yú.
Just as he was about to eat it,
he accidentally overturned the bowl, spilling it.
The food scattered into the water.
Luóxún Yú sat down and concentrated his mind.
He reflected to himself,
"Whenever I go with the other bhikṣus,
I never obtain anything and return with an empty bowl.
Now Shèlìfú gives me the Buddha's leftover food,
and it is immediately overturned and lost.
This is all due to my karmic retribution, which I must endure."
He then contemplated deeply,
untied his bonds, removed his defilements, and attained Arhatship.
He then ate earth and attained parinirvāṇa.
If you wish to know about Luóxún Yú:
During the time of the Buddha Wéiwèi,
he was an ordinary person
who was always miserly and unwilling to give alms.
When it was time to eat, he would spread his clothes on the ground, fearing that grains of rice would fall.
A śramaṇa came by seeking alms.
Luóxún Yú saw him and said,
"What should I give you?"
He then scooped up a handful of dirt and gave it to the śramaṇa.
The śramaṇa then made a vow, saying,
"Because of your foolishness,
may you soon attain liberation."
From that distant time, through successive rebirths,
up to the present, wherever he went, he could not obtain food.
Now, having attained the Way, he ate earth and attained parinirvāṇa.
The śramaṇa to whom Luóxún Yú gave dirt was Shèlìfú.
The retribution of sin and merit: even though he has now attained the Way, he still suffers from past karma.
People in the world are foolish and ignorant,
thinking that committing evil brings no retribution.
Luóxún Yú is proof of this.
During the Buddha's time, the monks' robes
were only made of pure, discarded cloth and worn-out silk from the dead.
Afterward, the bhikṣu Luóxún Yú arose,
and whenever he went seeking alms, he would return hungry and empty-handed.
The Buddha knew his past actions
and divided the monastic community into five divisions.
The robe colors were also of five kinds.
He instructed that each day, they should follow one division in their activities.
Thus, regulations were established,
each highlighting their strengths and naming their robe colors.
The Sàhéduō Division,
broadly learned and insightful, guiding with the Dharma,
should wear black kāṣāya robes.
The Jiāyèwéi Division,
diligent, vigorous, and protecting sentient beings,
should wear magnolia-colored kāṣāya robes.
The Míshāsāi Division,
deep in meditation, penetrating the profound and mysterious,
should wear blue kāṣāya robes.
The Móhēsēngqí Division,
diligently studying the scriptures and expounding their meanings,
should wear yellow kāṣāya robes.
From then on, he was able to obtain ample food.
Why?
It was because Luóxún Yú
had no virtue in his past life.
Ānán asked the Buddha,
"Luóxún Yú had no virtue in his past life.
How could he become a śramaṇa?"
The Buddha said,
"This Luóxún Yú, in a past life, was the son of a virtuous man.
He was envious and jealous.
When he saw śramaṇas coming to seek alms,
he would immediately close the door and say,
'The master is not home.'
When the śramaṇas went to other homes,
he would also go and close their doors,
saying,
'The master is not home.'
That is why now, when seeking alms, he cannot obtain any.
When he saw others joyfully giving food and holding gatherings,
he would think, 'I also wish to become a śramaṇa.'
That is why he is now so destitute.
The Buddha resided in Shèwèi City.
At that time, there were two sisters in the city
who were pregnant and had not yet given birth but left home to follow the path.
When the bhikṣuṇīs saw their pregnant bellies,
they immediately drove them out.
Because of this matter,
they went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One replied,
"If one is pregnant while a layperson, it is permissible and without fault.
These bhikṣuṇīs later gave birth to a son,
named Tóngzǐ Jiāyè.
By the age of eight,
he left home to follow the path and became an Arhat.
Together with a group of sixteen bhikṣus,
each holding a water pot, they went to the Āqíluó River.
They bathed, entered the water, floated on their backs and stomachs, playing.
They crossed the river, splashing water and bathing.
At that time, King Bōsīnì
was watching from a high tower, looking in all directions.
The king did not yet believe in the Buddha's teachings.
Seeing this, his disbelief doubled.
He said to Lady Mòlì, "The field of merit that your family serves, these great beings,
you deeply believe in without doubt. Why don't you take a look?"
She immediately replied to the king,
"Perhaps they are young and newly ordained,
having just received full precepts and not yet knowing the monastic rules,
or perhaps the World-Honored One has not yet established this precept, hence this behavior."
Tóngzǐ Jiāyè,
with his divine ear, heard the king's words.
He then said to his companions,
"The king's disbelief has doubled, and Lady Mòlì is displeased.
We should now make them feel joyful."
They all said, "Excellent!"
Each took their water pot, filled it with water, and placed it in front of them.
They sat in lotus posture, forming an orderly row,
and soared through the air, passing over the king's palace in the sky.
Lady Mòlì was sitting in an open area.
Seeing their shadows, she looked up.
She saw an orderly row of figures sitting in lotus posture, with water pots in front, flying through the air like a flock of geese led by their king.
Seeing this, her heart was filled with great joy.
She said to the king,
"Look, the spiritual virtue of the field of merit my family serves is like this!"
The king, seeing this, was also filled with great joy.
He said these words:
"Excellent, excellent!
I have obtained great benefit.
May the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the community of bhikṣus
remain in this country for their entire lives as a field of merit."
The Buddha heard of this matter
and immediately established a precept, forbidding such behavior thereafter.
In the kingdom of Jìbīn, the rice had just begun to form ears.
The dragon king, Āluópólóu,
poured down a great deluge, and the rice was submerged and died.
At that time, the great virtuous monk Mòchǎntí and four other bhikkhus
from the country of Bōzhàlìfú
soared through the empty sky to the edge of the Snowy Mountains,
to the pond of Āluópólóu.
They then walked, stood, sat, and lay upon the water.
The dragon king's retinue entered and reported to the dragon king.
The dragon king, in anger, exerted various supernatural powers:
violent winds, torrential rain, thunder, lightning, and thunderbolts;
cliffs collapsed and trees were broken;
his body emitted smoke and fire, and he rained down large stones,
intending to frighten the great virtuous Mòchǎntí.
He further summoned troops, yet still could not subdue him.
Mòchǎntí said,
"Even if you had all the gods and every person in the world come to frighten me, not a single hair of mine would stir.
If you were to take Mount Sumeru and all the smaller mountains
and cast them upon me, I would still not stir."
Gradually, he taught and converted them with the flavor of the Dharma, causing them to rejoice and submit.
Hearing the Dharma, the dragon king immediately took refuge and received the precepts.
Together with his retinue, they all became disciples.
The ghosts, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kumbhāṇḍa ghosts of the Snowy Mountains, hearing this, all believed and submitted, also becoming disciples.
All saw the path.
Mòchǎntí addressed the dragons and ghosts:
"From now on, do not give rise to anger and hatred, do not harm people or damage the rice crops.
Give rise to compassionate minds and enable them to live in peace and happiness."
They all bowed their heads and respectfully received the teaching and precepts.
They offered a jeweled seat for Mòchǎntí to sit upon.
The dragon king stood in attendance, fanning him with a fan.
The people of the country of Jìbīn Qiántuó Lèchā,
seeing these events, greatly gave rise to reverence.
They all came to listen to the Dharma, and many attained the fruit of the path.
During the time of King Āyù,
the Buddha had already attained parinirvāṇa
for over two hundred years.
At that time, the bhikkhu Móxīntuó
arrived on the island of Shīzi.
At that time, the king was about to go hunting.
There was a tree deity
who wished for the king to see Móxīntuó.
The tree deity transformed into a deer,
not far from the king, appearing to graze on grass and then slowly walking away.
Seeing the transformed deer, the king immediately strung his bow, nocked an arrow, and drew the bow to shoot.
The king then thought to himself,
"I should aim carefully to shoot this deer."
The deer then turned and ran towards the road to Shépótuóluó.
The king immediately pursued it.
He arrived at Shépótuóluó,
and the deer vanished not far from Móxīntuó.
At that time, Móxīntuó, seeing the king had drawn near,
had this thought:
"Now, using supernatural power, I will cause the king to see only me and not see the others."
The great virtuous Móxīntuó then called the king by name:
"Dìxū, come here."
Hearing himself called, the king
then thought to himself,
"Who in this country dares to call me by name?
What kind of person is this?
Wearing red robes, cut and sewn together,
calling my name."
He gave rise to a suspicious mind:
"What is this?
Is it a human?
Or is it a ghost or spirit?"
Móxīntuó replied,
"A śramaṇa, a descendant of the Śākya clan, a child of the Dharma,
out of compassion for the king,
from the land of Yánfúlì,
has purposely come here."
At that time, King Tiān'ài Dìxū
had correspondence with King Āyù;
they knew each other from afar and exchanged precious treasures,
repaying each other.
The Dharma master then said,
"I have the Three Jewels to offer to the king,
not comparable to those worldly treasures of King Tiān'ài."
He then explained to the king the Dharma of taking refuge in the Three Jewels.
The king took refuge in the Three Jewels and became an upāsaka.
He further reported the Śākya Dharma,
showing it to King Tiān'ài Dìxū.
In the hunting grounds,
he then recalled again:
In King Āyù's letter, there was mention of a descendant of the Śākya clan.
He immediately laid down his bow and arrows and warmly inquired after him.
The Dharma master expounded a sūtra for him and he received the Three Refuges.
He then sent Móxīntuó
to call the śrāmaṇera Xiūmónà:
"Now you should preach the Dharma.
You may proclaim the turning of the Dharma wheel."
Xiūmónà said,
"If I proclaim it now, how far should the sound reach?"
He answered,
"Let the sound fill the land of Shīzi."
At that time, Xiūmónà entered the fourth dhyāna.
Emerging from meditative concentration, he proclaimed the turning of the Dharma wheel.
The people of the land of Shīzi all heard it.
The various gods and devas in the empty sky all assembled.
After proclaiming it three times,
Móxīntuó then preached the Dharma for them.
Countless humans and devas all attained the path.
There was the country of Nàlì, near the southern seashore.
Its people made their living by gathering pearls and sandalwood.
This was their regular occupation.
In the country, there was a family with two brothers.
Their parents passed away, and they wished to divide the household.
The family had one slave named Fēnnà,
young, intelligent, and skilled in trade.
He went to sea to make a living; there was nothing he did not know.
The household's wealth and property were divided into one share,
and the slave Fēnnà was counted as another share.
The brothers drew lots, and the younger brother got Fēnnà.
Taking his wife and children, he left the house empty-handed.
At that time, the world was suffering from famine. Although he had obtained Fēnnà, he feared they could not survive and was filled with worry.
The slave Fēnnà addressed his master, saying,
"Master, please do not worry. Fēnnà has a plan.
Within a month, I will make you surpass the elder master's household."
The master said,
"If you can truly do this, I will set you free as a commoner."
The master's wife had some private pearls and valuables,
which she gave to Fēnnà as capital.
At that time, the sea tide came in.
The people of the city went to the water's edge to gather firewood.
Fēnnà took the pearls and valuables outside the city.
He saw a beggar carrying firewood.
In the firewood was some ox-head sandalwood,
which could cure serious illnesses.
One liang was worth a thousand liang of gold.
At that time, it was something rarely obtained.
Fēnnà recognized it.
He bought it with two gold coins and took it back.
He broke it into several tens of pieces.
At that time, there was an elder who had a serious illness.
He needed two liang of this ox-head sandalwood to compound medicine.
He sought it but could not obtain it.
Fēnnà took it to him and immediately obtained two thousand liang of gold.
In this way, he sold it all, and the wealth he obtained was ten times that of the elder brother's household. The master was deeply moved.
Fēnnà had not broken his word and oath.
He was set free as a commoner to follow his own wishes.
Fēnnà took his leave to pursue the path.
He went to Shèwèi country and paid respects to the Buddha.
Kneeling with folded hands, he addressed the Buddha:
"I am of lowly birth, but my mind delights in the path and virtue.
I only wish the World-Honored One would bestow compassion and save me."
The Buddha said, "Welcome."
Fēnnà's hair immediately fell out, and the Dharma robes clothed his body.
He immediately became a śramaṇa.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he quickly attained the path of an arhat.
Sitting, he reflected to himself:
"Now I have attained the six supernatural powers and freedom over life and death.
All this is due to my master's kindness.
I should now go to convert him and also convert the people of that country."
At that time, the Venerable Fēnnà went to his original country and arrived at his master's house.
The master was joyful, invited him to sit, and prepared food.
After eating, they washed their hands.
He then soared into the empty sky,
divided his body and scattered his forms,
his body emitted water and fire,
light shone everywhere, and he descended from above.
He addressed his master, saying,
"These divine powers are all due to the merit of my master setting me free.
Going to where the Buddha is, this is what I have learned."
The master replied,
"The divine transformations are subtle and wonderful.
I wish to see the World-Honored One and receive his teachings."
Fēnnà replied,
"Just sincerely prepare offerings and food.
The Buddha, with his triple knowledge, will surely come of his own accord."
They then prepared the offerings, and by the next morning, everything was ready.
Facing Shèwèi country, they bowed with folded hands, knelt, burned incense, and invited the Buddha:
"We only wish the Honored One would condescend to come and broadly save all beings."
The Buddha knew their intention.
He then, with five hundred arhats,
each using supernatural power, went to their house.
The king and people were all awed and respectful.
They came before the Buddha, prostrated themselves with five limbs touching the ground.
Then they sat in the king's seat.
After the meal, they washed up.
The Buddha, for the master and the king's officials and retinue,
broadly expounded the clear Dharma.
They all received the five precepts and became disciples of the Buddha.
Rising, they stood before the Buddha.
Praising Fēnnà, they said,
"At home, diligent and earnest; leaving home, he attained the path.
His divine powers are lofty and far-reaching; his family and country received salvation.
How should we repay his kindness?"
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised Fēnnà
and spoke a verse:
The master and the king were even more joyful.
They made offerings for seven days.
They attained the path of the stream-enterer.
The Buddha was dwelling in the Āmrapālī Grove in the Āmrapālī settlement.
He was together with a multitude of bhikṣus.
At that time, there was an elder named Zhìduōluó.
He addressed the senior monks, saying,
"I humbly request all you venerable ones
to accept my invitation for a meal in this grove."
The senior monks remained silent.
The senior monks put on their robes and took their alms bowls.
They went to the elder's house, took their seats, and sat down.
The elder personally served them with various kinds of food and drink.
After washing their hands and rinsing their mouths, they listened to the Dharma.
The senior monks expounded the Dharma for the elder.
They instructed, taught, benefited, and gladdened him.
The senior monks ate their fill of ghee, curds, and honey.
It was the latter part of spring, the day was hot, and the journey had been strenuous.
There was a junior monk
named Móhējiā.
He addressed the senior monks,
"Today is very hot; I wish to make clouds arise, bring rain, and stir a gentle breeze."
The senior monks replied,
"If you can do so, that would be excellent."
Then Móhējiā entered samādhi.
As he properly attained it,
clouds immediately arose, a fine rain gently fell,
and a cool breeze, wafting gently, came from the four directions to the gate of the vihāra.
He then ceased his supernatural power and returned to his own room.
At that time, the elder thought to himself,
"The most junior monk possesses such great supernatural power;
how much more so the middle and senior ones?"
He paid homage to the bhikṣus
and followed Móhējiā to his dwelling place.
Bowing at his feet, he said,
"Venerable one, I wish to see a display of supernatural feet."
Móhējiā said,
"Elder, there is no need to see this."
He refused three requests.
The elder still repeatedly entreated him.
Móhējiā said to the elder,
"Go outside and gather some dry grass,
then cover it with a cloth."
The elder did as instructed, gathering firewood into a pile.
He came and reported to the venerable one.
Móhējiā then entered the fire-light samādhi.
From the hole of the door latch, flames emerged,
their light burning the entire pile of firewood to ashes.
Only the white cloth remained unburned.
He said to the elder,
"Do you see now?"
The elder replied,
"I have seen.
It is truly extraordinary."
Móhējiā said to the elder,
"You should know that all this is based on heedfulness.
Because of heedfulness, one attains anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi
and the other factors of the path."
The elder said,
"Venerable one,
Móhējiā,
I wish you to permanently dwell in this grove.
I will provide the four requisites for the rest of my life."
Móhējiā, due to his practice and conditions, did not accept his invitation.
After hearing the Dharma, the elder paid homage and departed.
Yuànzú was an arhat
who constantly taught and transformed hungry ghosts.
He saw a hungry ghost whose form was ugly and repulsive.
Those who saw it had their hair stand on end, and none were not terrified.
Its body emitted blazing flames like a great mass of fire.
Maggots flowed from its mouth, and pus and blood streamed forth.
The stench permeated far and wide, making it impossible to approach.
Sometimes it spewed flames from its mouth, tens of zhang long.
Sometimes from its ears, nose, eyes, body, and limbs,
it emitted various flames, tens of zhang long.
Its lips hung down, inverted like those of a wild boar.
Its body measured one yojana in length and breadth.
It scratched itself with its own hands, wailing loudly as it ran east and west.
At that time, Yuànzú asked the hungry ghost,
"What past offense did you commit to now suffer this torment?"
The hungry ghost replied,
"In a past life, I practiced as a śramaṇa.
I was attached to my dwelling, miserly and unwilling to relinquish it.
I maintained a dignified outward demeanor but uttered foul words.
If I saw bhikṣus who upheld precepts and were diligent,
I would immediately revile and insult them, glaring at them with a biased and malicious eye.
Relying on my powerful clan, I thought myself immortal.
I created immeasurable unwholesome roots.
I would rather cut out my own tongue with a sharp knife
and willingly suffer thus from kalpa to kalpa
than slander a diligent bhikṣu for even a single day.
If I return to the Jambudvīpa continent,
let my form serve as a warning to all bhikṣus:
Guard well against verbal transgressions; do not speak recklessly.
If you see bhikṣus of pure conduct who uphold precepts,
proclaim their virtues.
Since receiving this hungry ghost form,
for many hundreds of thousands of years,
I have endured this suffering.
After my life ends here, I will fall into hell.
Having said this, the hungry ghost
let out a loud wail and threw itself to the ground,
like Mount Tài collapsing, heaven and earth turning upside down.
This all came about due to verbal transgressions.
Those who can guard against verbal transgressions receive boundless blessings.
Furthermore, when Kāśyapa Buddha appeared in the world,
he spread the teaching of the Dharma, and his教化 was complete.
He attained parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.
After his nirvāṇa, there was a Tripitaka bhikṣu
named Huángyán.
The saṅgha instructed him,
"All miscellaneous duties are not for you to undertake.
Only expound the wonderful Dharma for the later learners."
At that time, the Tripitaka bhikṣu inwardly felt contempt but could not refuse the saṅgha's order.
So he expounded the meaning of the scriptures for the later learners.
Calling the one receiving the teaching, he said,
"Come quickly, elephant-head!"
Calling the second one,
he again said, "Horse-head!"
Next, "Camel-head!"
Next, "Donkey-head!"
Next, "Pig-head!"
Next, he called, "Sheep-head!"
"Ram-head!"
Next, he called, "Lion-head!"
Next, "Tiger-head!"
Next, "Bird-head!"
Next, "Bear-head!"
Thus he called them by the names of various beasts and creatures,
too numerous to count.
Tripitaka Huángyán
uttered such immeasurably evil words.
Although he taught the meaning of the scriptures, he could not avoid the offense.
His body perished, his life ended, and he fell into hell.
For many tens of millions of kalpas, he suffered immeasurable torment.
His remaining offense not yet exhausted, he emerged from hell
and was born in the great sea, receiving an aquatic form.
He had one body with a hundred heads, his form extremely large.
Other creatures, seeing him, all fled.
The Buddha was in the kingdom of Shèwèi.
At that time, in the kingdom of Xūyé, there was a poor man.
He hired a boy to shave his head, agreeing to pay one hú of wheat at harvest time.
On the way, he met an old friend who wanted to drink with him.
Upon returning, he sought the wheat payment but could not find it anywhere.
He then gave rise to a malicious thought.
He vowed that after his life ended, he would become a great divine dragon.
He would then submerge this kingdom.
After his life ended, he indeed became a great dragon.
For years, the kingdom suffered from untimely wind and rain.
The Buddha, concerned about the famine, sent the monk Shāhè to convert that dragon.
Upon seeing the monk, the dragon immediately conceived evil intentions.
He wanted to kill the people of the kingdom and Shāhè himself.
Shāhè transformed his alms bowl to cover the entire kingdom.
The dragon then caused rain to fall, thinking the kingdom was already submerged.
The monk, through the Buddha’s majestic power, made the dragon see the people safe and secure as before.
The dragon again became enraged.
He caused heavy snow to fall.
The monk caught it in his bowl, swept it with his hand, and placed it in one spot.
He then entered the dragon’s chamber.
The dragon immediately came out.
The monk came out again.
The dragon went in, and the monk went in again.
This went on repeatedly until the dragon was exhausted and stopped.
He knelt and asked,
"What kind of deity are you,
to trouble me like this?"
The monk said,
"I am a disciple of the Buddha."
The dragon said,
"I wish to submit myself."
He then followed him.
The monk Shāhè
placed this dragon inside a bamboo box.
When people saw the monk capture the dragon like this, they were all greatly delighted.
They asked,
"What kind of deity is this monk, who has subdued the kingdom’s calamity?"
He replied,
"I am a disciple of the Buddha."
The people asked,
"Can the Buddha be seen?"
He answered, "He can be seen."
"When I return, it will be around midday."
On the way, he passed by to collect alms.
Some people gave him rice, others gave him wine.
The monk accepted it and sat under a tree.
He became drunk and lay down.
The dragon, his bowl, and his robe were each in a separate place.
At that moment, the Buddha smiled, and a five-colored light emerged.
Ānanda inquired about it.
The Buddha answered accordingly.
He also spoke of four matters:
First, an arhat who does not enter samādhi cannot know.
Second, one cannot casually see supernatural powers.
Third, one should not forcefully urge others to give alms.
Fourth, the body still contains worms.
An arhat is inferior to the Buddha due to these four matters.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva who was inclined toward the śrāvaka path.
Upon seeing this event, his mind became steadfast.
The Buddha sent Mùjiànlián to where the monk Shāhè was.
He commanded him to bring the dragon.
He explained its past lives to it.
The dragon’s mind was then liberated.
It received the five precepts.
It practiced the ten good deeds.
It attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Ānanda asked the Buddha about the causes and conditions of this event.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"An arhat no longer experiences hunger or thirst.
He appeared drunk and lying down due to three reasons:
First, the Buddha wished to open and transform the minds of bodhisattvas.
Second, he did not wish to go against the intentions of the donors.
Third, he feared that disciples who had not yet attained the Way might drink wine and commit many errors.
Therefore, he manifested this event to examine and uphold the precepts.
Although the monk Shāhè drank wine,
he was not actually drunk."
The arhat traveled to the kingdom of Mótóuluó and went to Yōulóumàntuó Mountain.
He sat on a rope-bed.
There were two dragon kings, brothers,
with five hundred followers.
Shènàpósī contemplated
and wished to subdue them.
Using his supernatural power,
he shook the mountain valley.
The two dragon kings became angry.
They went to Pósī’s place, raising fierce winds, rain, thunder, lightning, weapons, and raging fire.
At that time, Pósī entered the samādhi of loving-kindness.
He caused the wind, rain, fire, and such not to approach his body.
He transformed into the precepts, like utpala, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka.
In the country of Shèwèi, there was a man named Lì.
His family was extremely wealthy.
He was already old and advanced in years, yet he had absolutely no heir.
He performed prayers and sacrifices to the sun, moon, and heavenly deities, leaving nothing undone.
In the end, he still could not obtain one.
He thought to himself that his supplications were futile.
His precious wealth was dissipating, and his estate was not being maintained.
Illnesses followed one after another, and disasters came one after the other.
His servants and slaves died, and his six domestic animals did not multiply.
He was deluded by sorcerers and spirit-mediums.
They said he would have blessings, yet heavy misfortunes arrived instead.
It was like a blind man swallowing poison, thinking it good medicine.
Hoping for recovery and relief, he instead lost his life.
Since I have killed living beings for sacrificial rites, I should enter hell.
Yet I hope for heavenly blessings—isn't that delusion?
In the world, there is the Buddha's path, the lofty and pure way of the sages.
Those who study and attain immortality are called Arhats.
Pure as lapis lazuli, diligent in practice and contemplation, one may then see them.
Those who follow this path only maintain tranquility and solitude.
Without desire, without seeking, they take this as joy.
In the present life, they attain peace, and after death, they are born in heaven.
I will establish a constant offering to the Three Jewels of the Buddha.
After a year had passed, his wife gave birth to a boy.
They named him Fódà.
Later, she bore another boy.
They named him Sēngdà.
Lì instructed his two sons.
He showed them the holy path.
Sēngdà, by nature, was compassionate, filial, and benevolent, loving all beings.
He upheld the Buddha's precepts and drew close to monks.
Pure, content, and knowing satisfaction, both parents loved him.
Lì lay ill upon his bed.
He then called his elder son and, weeping, admonished him:
"All that lives must die. Those who uphold the precepts are safe; those who violate them are in peril.
Sēngdà is still young, benevolent, filial, pure, and upright.
I entrust him to you." Having finished speaking, he then passed away.
Afterwards, Sēngdà frequently pleaded with his elder brother, wishing to become a monk.
According to the laws of their country, one must first take a wife.
He said he wished to become a monk.
Fódà then arranged a marriage for him.
He sought a virtuous family's daughter named Kuàijiàn.
Her brilliance was radiant, her beauty peerless among her peers.
When the bride entered the hall, the elder brother gathered the guests, and the nine clans were joyful.
The elder brother, before the crowd, said to his younger brother:
"On this very day, are you still willing to become a monk?"
Sēngdà replied:
"It is truly my long-held wish."
The elder brother teased him, saying:
"You may follow your aspiration."
The younger brother, his heart joyful, bowed to his elder brother and immediately went into the mountains.
He saw a monk.
Young and handsome, dwelling alone beneath a tree.
He asked:
"Virtuous one, for what reason have you come to practice as a monk?"
This person had already attained the path of an Arhat.
He knew beforehand past and future events of countless eons.
He said to Sēngdà:
"The Buddha said that people who are fond of licentiousness and debauchery
are like one holding a torch walking against the wind.
The flame blows back; if one does not let go of the torch, the fire will burn one's hand.
It is also like a crow carrying meat.
Hawks and falcons pursue to snatch it away.
If the crow does not drop the meat, disaster will reach its body and life.
It is for this reason that I practice as a monk.
Again, it is like honey smeared on a sharp blade.
A child, greedy for sweetness, licks it with its tongue.
There is the danger of having its tongue cut off.
Those who are licentious and debauched, merely seeking to gratify their foolish hearts,
do not consider the consequences.
There is the harm of burning their bodies.
Like a moth, greedy for the fire's color, throws itself into the lamp.
Its body is seen being burned and boiled—what can it possibly gain?
Those deluded by lust do not distinguish good from evil.
They distance themselves from the wise and draw close to the foolish, daily sinking into darkness.
They bring ruin to states and destruction to multitudes; after death, they enter hell.
Evil deeds accumulate, sins are accomplished; when regret comes, how can it reach them? Such are these analogies."
Sēngdà bowed his head to the ground at his feet.
"I wish to leave the turbid world and tread the pure path.
I will uphold the monk's precepts, considering them glory and blessing."
The master said: "Wait a little."
Sēngdà said:
"My intention is to enter the mountains for meditation and solitude."
The master said:
"Those who dwell in mountains and marshes should learn the constellations.
Clearly know the seasons; always store and prepare water, fire, and honey.
The reason for this is:
When bandits seek water, fire, or honey,
from midnight until dawn,
if asked, you should explain.
Provide what the bandits desire; if you oppose their wishes,
the bandits will kill people."
Sēngdà said: "Yes.
I respectfully follow your compassionate teaching."
He then retreated and entered the mountains.
His elder brother thought:
"My younger brother has become a monk; he will never keep a wife.
Kuàijiàn is beautiful; my heart is very pleased with her."
He rose, took a zither from Kuàijiàn, and played it.
He sang a licentious and debauched song, saying:
"Brilliant are the tulips, growing in the wild.
If not plucked in season, the flowers are cast aside.
Lush and abundant, their color ever fresh.
Rejoice with me."
Kuàijiàn perceived his desire was to cause disorder.
She answered with a song, saying:
"Lofty is my teacher, honored by gods and men.
His disciples are pure and clean, called monks.
To contemplate truth is sagehood; lust is the way of beasts.
I have received strict precepts; I do not serve two lords.
I will never engage in licentious acts; I would rather be cut to pieces."
Fódà sang a song of passionate sorrow, with soft and seductive words.
"My longstanding heart has favored you; therefore, through a good matchmaker, I asked your name.
I visited the master for divination and a favorable time.
Anxious and fearful,
I feared you would not come.
Having seen your face, my heart is joyful.
If we do not unite now, is it not all in vain?
This vow is settled; virtuous lady, why doubt?"
Kuàijiàn was alarmed and agitated.
She answered with a song, saying:
"The Buddha established rituals; respect and humility have their order.
A younger brother's wife is like a daughter.
A sister's husband is like a father.
I personally uphold the precepts; each day my practice grows.
Truth aligns with sainthood; lust aligns with
worms and rats.
Alas, elder brother!
Why speak such words?"
The elder brother's heart was greedy and deluded.
Kuàijiàn knew his intention was utterly unchangeable.
Kuàijiàn again sang:
"A person living in the world should avoid two things: unfiliality and licentious disorder; actions that violate the Buddha's precepts.
Heaven and the virtuous
will record their own distinctions."
Fódà sang:
"Your countenance and beauty shine brilliantly.
Under heaven, among beautiful women, who has a face like yours?
My heart delights in you; therefore, I crossed the great mountains."
Kuàijiàn thought to herself:
"This man wants me to commit a perverse and wild transgression.
It will lead to great calamity.
I shall speak of the foul impurities within the body.
Then you will retreat."
Kuàijiàn said again:
"You covet my body; what is good about the body?
The head has nine bones joined to form the skull."
Thus she fully described all the impurities.
Fódà thought to himself:
"You are mindful of your husband; how would you listen to me?
If I kill my younger brother, then you will follow me."
He then went to recruit men known to be bandits.
He went before them and said:
"Do you know that in my household, a slave boy of the sixth generation ran away to become a monk and is now in the mountains?"
The bandits said: "We know him."
Fódà then brought out gold and silver and gave it to them.
"You kill that slave boy, quickly take his head,
along with the clothes on his body and the monastic robe he holds,
the sandals on his feet—bring them all back.
I will again heavily reward you with gold and silver."
The bandits were greatly pleased and said:
"Follow us to get what you need." They then went into the mountains.
Arriving at the younger brother's place, they called out:
"Monk! Come out quickly!"
His younger brother came out and said:
"Gentlemen, what do you seek?
I have water, fire, and honey for you to consume.
The night is already half gone."
The bandits said:
"We do not seek water or fire.
We do not ask for honey.
At this time, we want your head to take away."
His younger brother, hearing this,
was greatly terrified and wept, saying:
"I am not a slave; I am the son of a nobleman.
I left the secular life to follow the path; I have no contention with the world.
My study of the path is still shallow; I have not yet attained the fruit of Stream-Entry. What benefit is there in killing me?"
The bandits said:
"We have come for your head."
His younger brother said to the bandits:
"If you want treasure, I will write a letter to my elder brother to bestow treasure upon you."
The bandits said:
"Your elder brother sent us here now to kill you."
The younger brother said: "Now I will die.
It is because of this woman.
The master previously warned me:
'To associate with the licentious
is like holding a torch walking against the wind.
If you do not let it go, the fire will burn your hand.'
Now, as the day grows dark, it is just as the master warned." He wept.
He begged the bandits for one year of life.
The bandits said:
"We must quickly take your head and go."
His younger brother said again:
"I wish you would not kill me immediately.
First cut off one of my thighs and place it before me."
The bandits cut off one thigh and placed it before him.
The younger brother, suffering this pain,
a deity came to his side and said:
"Be careful, do not be terrified.
Firmly hold your mind."
In your previous life, you entered the animal realm.
People slaughtered, cut up, and sold your flesh—this was not for just one lifetime.
You have passed through both hell and the hungry ghosts.
Suffering and pain have come to you not only now.
Sēngdà said to the heavens,
“Please inform my teacher.”
The heavens then spoke to the teacher, saying,
“Bandits wish to kill him.
Your disciple, out of compassion for others, weeps and pleads for mercy, wishing to see you.”
The teacher immediately flew there and preached the Dharma to him, saying:
“Even heaven and earth, and Mount Sumeru, will perish.
The seas will dry up, and the seven suns will be destroyed.
In the world, there is a wind named Wéilán.
When the Wéilán wind arises, mountain strikes against mountain, and this wind too will cease.
How much more so your small body—what is it worth counting?
Simply contemplate the Buddha.
The Buddha himself often said:
‘Prosperity must decline, meetings must part, glory and status are hard to preserve.
The body is also like this.’”
Sēngdà then attained the path of Stream-enterer.
Again, one thigh was cut off.
He deeply remembered his teacher’s precepts.
Again, he attained the path of Once-returner.
The bandits cut off his left hand; again he remembered his teacher’s precepts.
He attained the path of Non-returner.
The bandits cut off his right hand.
Again, he remembered his teacher’s precepts and attained the path of Arhat.
He then no longer feared the three evil paths.
He was free in life and death, with nothing more to fear.
Sēngdà said,
“Bring tree bark.”
They immediately stripped tree bark and gave it to him.
Sēngdà took a branch to use as a brush.
He pierced his own body for blood and wrote on the tree bark:
“Elder brother, may you live in peace and well-being according to the times.
While our parents were alive, they entrusted me to you.
You did not accept this, violating and abandoning their loving instruction.
For the sake of a woman, you have brought harm between flesh and blood.
To violate the compassionate teaching of our parents is unfilial.
To cruelly kill a human life is unkind.
Killing even one animal brings no small sin.
How much more killing an Arhat—this sin does not cease in five lifetimes.
Now I happily wander in solitude, parting from this world forever.
Strive, strive, and may you revere the true path.”
He stretched out his neck, two feet long.
He said to the bandits:
“If you cut off my head,
it is like cutting off a head of mud.
I fear you will fall into hell.”
The bandits came forward and cut off his head.
They took his robe, staff, sandals, and bowl.
They brought them to his brother, who richly rewarded the bandits with gold and silver.
The brother took his younger brother’s head and made a false body.
He placed the head on top and clothed it with robes.
The staff, bowl, and sandals were all placed beside it.
He said to Kuàijiàn:
“Your husband has returned; you may go and greet him.”
Kuàijiàn was overjoyed and ran to where he was.
Seeing him with lowered eyes, sitting, she thought he was contemplating the Way.
The wife did not dare to call him, but prepared fine food.
“When he finishes contemplating the Way and awakens, I will feed him.”
By midday, he had not awakened.
The wife then approached and said, “It is now midday; I fear the time has passed.”
She found it strange that he did not respond.
She tugged at his robe; the head fell off, and the body scattered apart.
The wife stamped her feet and cried out:
“You have caused me to sit here and see this cruel banditry!”
Grieving and indignant, she cried out to heaven; her liver and heart broke.
Blood came from her mouth, and she suddenly died.
His precept practice was pure and unstained, like empty space.
His mind was a sage’s model, unmovable like the earth.
His true purity and conduct were lofty, unreachable like heaven.
Before his life ended, the heavens sighed in admiration.
They welcomed his spirit to dwell in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Enduring for a mere moment,
he attained the boundless glory of the heavens.
The elder brother entered the meditation room.
Seeing his younger brother’s head and body scattered,
and his wife dead from vomiting blood,
he cried out:
“Alas, alas!
I have acted against heaven; my cruelty has led to this.”
He immediately went to where the bandits were and asked,
“Did my younger brother have any last words before his death?”
The bandits showed him the writing.
The words were mournful and pitiful; after reading them, his innards choked, and tears flowed across his face.
“I violated the compassionate teaching of my revered parents at their death.
I brought harm between flesh and blood.
I also killed an Arhat.
Grief-stricken, I will die.
After death, I will enter hell.”
The king and his subjects all wept.
They sighed and recounted his pure virtue, and buried his younger brother.
Four carriages were set up, and a stūpa was erected.
Dragons, gods, and spirits filled the sky.
Scattering flowers and burning incense, all choked with sobs.
And when parting with Dà Kuàijiàn,
the people of the country mourned and grieved.
They sang and praised his virtue.
In Śrāvastī, there was an elder.
His household was very wealthy.
He had a son.
The boy’s body was golden in color.
A physiognomist examined him and saw his extraordinary features.
He then gave him a name:
named Xiūyuènàtípó. On the day of his birth,
a well of water naturally appeared in his home.
It was eight feet across.
Drawing water from it could fulfill people’s wishes.
Whatever was needed would appear as desired.
As the boy grew older, he became learned and skilled in many arts.
The elder loved him.
He did not dare to oppose his wishes.
And he thought thus:
“My son is handsome, with a peerless appearance.
I must seek and select a renowned girl.
One with golden beauty and a wonderful form,
like my son—I should go and seek her.”
He then recruited merchants to search everywhere.
At that time, in the country of Yánpó, there was a great elder.
He had just had a daughter.
Named Xiūbánà Bōpósū, she was exceptionally beautiful, with a golden body.
On the day of her birth,
there was also a natural eight-foot well of water.
What came from that well fulfilled people’s wishes.
At that time, that elder
also thought to himself:
“My daughter is beautiful.
I must find a worthy man.
Only one like my daughter will I marry her to.”
At that time, the girl’s fame spread far to Śrāvastī.
Jīntiān’s reputation also reached the girl’s family.
Then the two elders each felt joy.
They sought a marriage alliance.
After the marriage was completed,
they returned to Śrāvastī.
At that time, Jīntiān’s family prepared a superior offering.
They invited the Buddha and the monks to receive offerings.
One day, the Buddha accepted their invitation.
For the elder and Jīntiān and his wife,
he extensively proclaimed the wonderful Dharma.
All attained the fruit of Stream-enterer.
The Buddha returned to the vihāra.
Jīntiān and his wife
told their parents they wished to leave home.
Their parents consented.
They both went to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
“Welcome, bhikṣus.” Their beards and hair fell off by themselves, the Dharma robes covered their bodies, and they became śramaṇas.
Gradually taught, they all became Arhats.
The Buddha said:
“After the past Buddha Vipaśyin entered parinirvāṇa,
his teachings remained in the world.
There were bhikṣus who traveled to teach and came to a village.
There were people, wealthy and virtuous elders,
who, seeing the monks arrive, each vied to make offerings.
At that time, there was a husband and wife.
They were poor, hungry, and destitute.
They often thought to themselves:
‘When our fathers were alive, wealth and treasures were abundant.
Now we ourselves are extremely poor.
How bitter it is!’
At that time, though wealthy, they did not encounter such a community of holy monks.
Now that they have met them, they have no money to make offerings.’
They wept in sorrow.
The wife, seeing her husband weep, said to him:
‘Now you can go to our former house.
Search in the old storeroom for money and treasures to use for offerings.’
The husband did as his wife said.
In the old storeroom, he found one gold coin.
At that time, his wife had a bright mirror.
Together they wholeheartedly used these to make an offering.
They bought a new jar, filled it with clean water,
placed this gold coin in the water of the jar,
and put the mirror on top.
They brought it to where the monks were.
With utmost sincerity, they made the offering.
At that time, the monks accepted it.
Each took water to wash their bowls.
Some also took water to drink.
At that time, that husband and wife,
joyful and delighted, fell ill and died.
They were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Those poor people
were this Jīntiān and his wife.”
There was a merchant leader named Tiānhù.
He went to the country of Lùqiúnà.
He always delighted in almsgiving.
He had faith in the Buddha.
He wished first to go to sea.
If he returned safely,
he would hold a great assembly for five years within the Buddha's Dharma.
Throughout the heavens and the human realm, none did not hear of it.
At that time, there was an Arhat bhikṣuṇī.
She also went to that country.
Contemplating and observing,
she knew Tiānhù would return safely and hold the five-year great assembly.
He invited eighteen thousand bhikṣus.
All were Arhats.
Learners were twice as many.
Ordinary people were countless.
She then saw the senior monk named Āsuōtuó.
He was an ordinary person but very diligent.
Entering the saṅghārāma, she paid respects in order.
She said to the senior monk:
"Venerable one, you are very unadorned."
The senior monk thought to himself:
"Why does she say I am unadorned?"
He then observed his body and saw his beard and hair were long.
He immediately called a youth to shave his beard and hair.
The bhikṣuṇī still said he was unadorned.
The senior monk again called a youth to wash and dye his robes.
The bhikṣuṇī again came to the saṅghārāma.
She still said he was unadorned.
The senior monk angrily said:
"I have already shaved my beard and hair and washed and dyed my robes.
Why do you say I am unadorned?"
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"In the Buddha's Dharma, attaining the four fruits is adornment.
Venerable one, have you heard that the merchant leader Tiānhù made a lion's roar for the five-year great assembly?"
He replied, "I have heard."
"Venerable one, you are an ordinary person, the foremost senior monk.
Among the assembly of Arhats, you receive offerings first.
Is this adornment?"
The senior monk then realized and wept with regret.
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"Why do you weep?"
He replied:
"Sister,
I am now old and incapable."
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"The Tathāgata's Dharma can be seen; there is no fixed time.
Venerable one, you can go to the Nàduōpóduō Monastery.
Approach the bhikṣu Upagupta.
This bhikṣu was predicted by the Buddha.
'Among my disciples, he is foremost in teaching.'"
At that time, the elder bhikṣu arrived.
Upagupta came out to welcome him and said:
"Venerable one,
wash your feet and rest."
He replied:
"I have not washed my feet.
I wish to see Upagupta."
At that time, Upagupta's disciple said:
"Venerable one,
this is Upagupta.
He has come to welcome you."
He was greatly joyful and then washed his feet.
Upagupta then taught him.
He sought a donor for him.
Bathing, food, drink, and various offerings were provided.
He said to the karmadāna:
"Now there is a bhikṣu who has attained two liberations entering the meditation place."
Up to eighteen thousand Arhats all entered the meditation place.
At that time, the bhikṣu entered the first dhyāna seat and sat.
Then Upagupta entered the fire-light samādhi.
Thus, eighteen thousand Arhats
all entered the fire-light samādhi.
The bhikṣu saw this and his mind produced joy.
Upagupta taught and expounded the Dharma.
The bhikṣu diligently contemplated and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
He returned to his own country.
The Arhat bhikṣuṇī
went to the saṅghārāma, paid respects, and said:
"Today the venerable one is adorned."
He replied:
"It is due to the sister's power."
At the five-year great assembly,
Tiānhù asked the senior monk:
"The World-Honored One expounded various Dharmas.
What the senior monk says is no different."
The senior monk replied:
"In a past life ninety-one kalpas ago,
we were merchant leaders who went to sea to seek treasure.
We vowed to fill the ship.
Returning to Jambudvīpa,
we encountered a great wind that blew the ship onto a sand sea.
We made a sand stūpa for Vipaśyin Buddha
and offered precious treasures to it.
At that time, devas showed us the path, saying:
'After seven days, a great flood will come.
It will float your ship to Jambudvīpa.'
When the seven days arrived,
it was as the devas said.
Due to this sand stūpa cause,
for ninety-one kalpas we did not fall into evil destinies.
Now we have attained the fruit of Arhatship.
You are now able to make offerings
to so many people in the presence of the Three Jewels.
I pronounce an aspiration: the suffering of birth and death is endless.
You should now leave home."
Tiānhù followed the instruction and became a śramaṇa.
He attained the path of Arhatship.
In the country of Pāṭaliputra, there was a merchant leader
named Sudāna.
A being in the intermediate state entered his mother's womb.
It caused his mother to become upright and gentle,
without any evil thoughts.
The husband asked a teacher.
The teacher replied:
"She is carrying a good child."
Later, she gave birth to a son,
named Surata.
As he gradually grew up,
he sought to leave home.
His parents permitted it.
Diligently practicing,
he realized the fruit of Arhatship.
The bhikṣu Kṣema had a severe illness.
He suffered great pain.
The bhikṣu Dāsa was the attendant.
The senior monks instructed Bhikṣu Dāsa
to explain the five aggregates to the sick one.
He went back and forth twice.
Bhikṣu Kṣema said to Bhikṣu Dāsa:
"Why trouble you to run back and forth?
Bring a staff; I will support myself with it
and go to those senior monks."
Those senior monks saw from afar Kṣema coming with a staff.
They spread a seat themselves and invited him to sit.
They further explained ancient discussions in detail.
Bhikṣu Kṣema then expounded the Dharma.
At that time, those senior monks
became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Bhikṣu Kṣema did not give rise to any outflows;
his mind attained liberation.
Once, when the Buddha was in Śrāvastī,
the disciple Kaundinya
regressed from the fruit of Arhatship six times.
On the seventh occasion,
he himself realized he had attained it.
Fearing regression again,
he sought a sharp sword and took his own life.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas
sought where the bhikṣu's spirit was reborn.
But he could not know.
He went to ask the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said:
"Bhikṣu Kaundinya has already attained parinirvāṇa.
His consciousness is in space, united with space as one body."
Hearing this, the evil Māra's heart swelled with poisonous resentment.
He threw himself into a blue lotus pond to bathe.
The pond water boiled and all aquatic creatures perished.
Due to this cause, all the bhikṣus
diligently practiced, fearing they might regress.
Once there was a country.
It was named Duōmóluó.
Seven lǐ from the city was a vihāra.
Five hundred śramaṇas constantly resided there.
They recited scriptures and practiced the Way.
There was one elder bhikṣu.
Named Móhēlú.
He was dull and obtuse by nature.
The five hundred monks together took turns teaching him.
Yet over several years, he could not master a single verse.
The assembly all looked down on him.
They did not include him in gatherings, and he always stayed guarding the vihāra.
They ordered him to do sweeping and cleaning.
Later, the king invited the monks.
To enter the palace to receive offerings.
The bhikṣu Móhēlú thought to himself:
"I was born into this world so dull and obtuse.
I do not know a single verse; people despise and belittle me.
What is the use of living like this?"
He then took a rope to a large tree in the rear garden.
Intending to hang himself.
The Buddha, with his divine eye, saw this from afar.
He transformed into a tree deity, appearing as half a human body.
And rebuked him, saying:
"Hey, bhikṣu!
Why are you doing this?"
Móhēlú then fully recounted his hardships.
The transformed deity admonished him:
"Do not do this.
Just listen to my words.
In the time of the Buddha Kāśyapa,
you were a Tripitaka śramaṇa.
You had five hundred disciples.
Considering yourself highly knowledgeable, you looked down upon others with arrogance.
You were stingy with the meaning of the scriptures and never instructed or taught them.
Therefore, in life after life, your faculties have been dull and obtuse.
You should only blame yourself; why demean yourself?"
Then the World-Honored One manifested his radiant form and spoke a wonderful verse for him.
At that time, Móhēlú bowed his head at the Buddha's feet.
Contemplating the meaning of the verse, he immediately entered meditative concentration.
Soon, before the Buddha, he attained the path of an arhat.
He himself remembered countless past lives and events.
The Tripitaka and all the scriptures were instantly mastered in his mind.
The Buddha said to Móhēlú:
"Put on your robe, take your bowl, and go to the king's palace for the meal.
Take the seat of honor above the five hundred monks."
"These monks were your five hundred disciples in a past life.
Now explain the Dharma to them so they may attain the path."
And also make the king clearly believe in sin and merit.
He then accepted the instruction.
Entered the king's palace.
And sat in the seat of honor.
The minds of the assembly were resentful, wondering why this was so.
Each, out of respect for the king's intention, dared not call out or send him away.
They thought him foolish and dull, not understanding the dedication of merit.
Their minds were weary because of it.
The king then served the food, personally ladling it out.
Móhēlú then performed the dedication of merit.
His voice was like thunder, his clear words falling like rain.
The seated monks were astonished and fearful, repenting on their own.
They all attained arhatship.
He expounded the Dharma for the king, and none failed to understand and awaken.
The assembled ministers and officials.
All attained the stage of srotāpanna.
Zhūlí Pántè's elder brother said:
"If you cannot uphold the precepts, return to being a layman."
Pántè went to the gate of the Jetavana and wept.
The Buddha asked him:
"Why are you sad?"
He answered with his brother's words.
The Buddha said:
"Do not fear.
I have attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
It is not due to your brother."
Taking Pántè by the hand.
He led him to a quiet room, taught him to hold a broom, and had him recite.
Pántè, reciting "sweep," forgot "broom"; reciting "broom," forgot "sweep."
After several days, "sweep broom" was again named "remove defilement."
Pántè contemplated:
"Dust, earth, tiles, and stones—if removed, then it is pure.
Bondage is defilement.
Wisdom can remove it.
I now use the broom of wisdom to sweep.
Remove all knots and bondages."
The Buddha was in Śrāvastī.
There was a bhikṣu named Pántè.
Newly ordained, his innate nature was dull and obtuse.
The Buddha had five hundred arhats teach him daily.
Yet in three years, he could not master a single verse.
The four groups in the country knew of his foolishness and dullness.
The Buddha took pity on him.
Summoned him to the front.
And bestowed upon him a verse:
"Guard the mouth, restrain the mind, let the body commit no offense.
One who practices thus may cross over the world."
Pántè, moved by the Buddha's compassionate kindness.
With a joyful and open heart, recited the verse until it came fluently to his lips.
The Buddha said to him:
"You are now old and have only just obtained one verse.
Everyone knows it.
It is not enough to be considered remarkable.
Now I shall explain its meaning for you.
The body's one, the mouth's four, the mind's three—their origins.
Observe their arising, discern their cessation.
The three realms and five destinies revolve without cease.
Through this one ascends to heaven.
Through this one falls into the abyss; through this one attains the Way.
Nirvāṇa is spontaneous.
He separately expounded for him immeasurable wonderful Dharmas.
Suddenly his mind opened, and he attained the path of an arhat.
At that time, there were five hundred bhikṣuṇīs.
They had a separate vihāra.
The Buddha said to send a bhikṣu to expound the sutras and Dharma for them.
The next day, it was Pántè's turn to go.
The nuns heard this.
They all smiled in anticipation.
"Tomorrow when he comes, we will recite the verse to him first.
To make him ashamed, without a single word to say."
The next day, Pántè went.
All the nuns, young and old, came out to pay respects, looking at each other and laughing.
After sitting, food was served.
After eating, they rinsed their mouths.
Then requested him to expound the Dharma.
Pántè then ascended the high seat.
Ashamed of his own lowliness, he said:
"Of meager virtue and inferior talent,
I am hardly a śramaṇa.
Stubborn and dull by nature,
What I have learned is not much.
I know only one verse.
Roughly understand its meaning.
I shall expound it for you.
May you all listen quietly."
The young bhikṣuṇīs intended to recite the verse to him first.
But their mouths could not open.
Astonished and fearful, they blamed themselves, bowed their heads, and repented their faults.
Pántè then, as the Buddha had explained.
Expounded each point separately.
The origins of body and mind.
Sin and merit, internal and external, ascending to heaven, attaining the Way.
The method of concentrating the spirit, cutting off thoughts, entering meditation.
Immediately, the nuns heard his exposition.
Greatly marveling at its wonder, with one-pointed joyful minds.
They all attained the path of an arhat.
Later, King Prasenajit.
Invited the Buddha and the saṅgha to an assembly in the main hall.
The Buddha wished to display Pántè's majestic spiritual power.
Gave him a bowl to hold and follow behind.
The gatekeeper recognized him and stopped him, not allowing him to enter.
"You are a śramaṇa who cannot even manage one verse.
What is the use of your receiving an invitation?
I am a layman.
Yet I still know verses.
How much more should a śramaṇa?
You have no wisdom.
Offering to you is of no benefit.
You need not enter the gate."
Pántè then stood outside the gate.
The Buddha was seated in the hall.
After the water for hand-washing was passed around.
Pántè lifted the bowl, extended his arm, and from afar handed it to the Buddha.
The king, his assembled ministers, the queen, the crown prince.
The assembly of the four groups.
Saw an arm come in but not its form; astonished, they asked the Buddha:
"Whose arm is this?"
The Buddha said:
"It is the arm of the worthy one, the bhikṣu Pántè."
The king said, "He has attained the Way?
I earlier had him carry the bowl.
The gatekeeper did not allow him to enter.
Therefore he extended his arm to hand me the bowl."
He was then invited in, his majestic spiritual power doubled as usual.
The king addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I heard that the Venerable Pántè was originally foolish and dull by nature.
He only recently knew one verse.
How did he attain the Way?"
The Buddha told the king:
"Learning need not be many; practice is paramount.
The worthy one Pántè understood the meaning of one verse.
With refined principle entering the spirit.
Body, mouth, and mind tranquil, pure as celestial gold.
Though a person may learn much, if they do not practice, they merely waste perception and thought.
What benefit is there?"
Then the World-Honored One.
Spoke a verse, saying:
Hearing this verse together.
Two hundred bhikṣus attained the path of an arhat.
The king, his assembled ministers, the queen, the crown prince.
None failed to rejoice.
The Bhagavān
was in Śrāvastī,
in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.
At that time, many bhikṣus,
at the proper time, donned their robes and took their bowls,
and entered Śrāvastī to beg for alms.
They heard that outside the palace gate of King Prasenajit, there were many people
holding hands, weeping, and crying out.
They were saying this:
"In this country, there is a great evil bandit,
named Aṅgulimāla,
who kills people, is violent and merciless.
Villages and settlements find no peace.
He kills people and takes a finger from each to make a garland.
For this reason, he is called Aṅgulimāla (Finger-Garland).
We wish the king would subdue this man."
After the bhikṣus had eaten,
they went to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and reported the above matter in full.
The Buddha then went to that place.
At that time, there were people
carrying firewood and grass,
and farmers,
and travelers.
They came upon the World-Honored One
and said to him:
"Śramaṇa, do not go by this road.
The reason is this:
On this road is Aṅgulimāla,
who kills people and has no compassionate heart.
People in cities, towns, and villages are all harmed by that man.
After he kills people,
he makes a garland from their fingers.
We fear he will harass the World-Honored One."
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, proceeded further ahead.
Then Aṅgulimāla saw the World-Honored One coming from afar.
Upon seeing him, he thought this:
"Now this śramaṇa comes alone, without companions.
I shall kill him."
Then Aṅgulimāla
immediately drew the sword at his waist and went to where the Buddha was.
The World-Honored One, seeing him from afar, turned back on the path.
Then Aṅgulimāla ran after the World-Honored One.
He exerted all his strength and speed trying to catch up to the World-Honored One,
but he could not.
Then Aṅgulimāla thought this:
"My running can overtake an elephant,
can also overtake a horse,
can also overtake a chariot, can also overtake a fierce bull,
can also overtake a man.
Yet this śramaṇa's walking is not fast.
Yet even with all my strength and speed, I cannot catch up to him."
Then Aṅgulimāla called out from afar to the World-Honored One, saying:
"Stop, stop, śramaṇa!"
The World-Honored One replied:
"I have long been stopped.
But you have not stopped."
Then Aṅgulimāla thought this:
"I have committed evil deeds."
He immediately discarded the sword at his waist.
Prostrating with his five limbs touching the ground,
he sought to become a śramaṇa and receive the full precepts.
The Buddha said:
"Come, bhikṣu."
His beard and hair fell off by themselves as if shaved.
The clothes he was wearing transformed into a monastic robe.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to him, and he became an Arhat.
At that time, King Prasenajit gathered an army of four divisions,
left Śrāvastī,
and intended to go and kill that bandit Aṅgulimāla.
He first passed by the World-Honored One and reported the matter fully to the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said:
"If the king now sees Aṅgulimāla
with his beard and hair shaved off, wearing the three Dharma robes,
having left home to train on the path with firm faith,
what would the king do with him?"
The king replied, saying:
"If I were to take him, I would inquire after him, pay respects, and have no harmful intent.
However, that man is fierce and evil, with no compassionate heart.
How could he possibly practice the conduct of a śramaṇa?"
At that time, Aṅgulimāla was not far from the Buddha,
sitting cross-legged, his body upright, his mind correctly focused, with mindfulness established before him.
Then the Buddha raised his hand and pointed to where Aṅgulimāla was.
When Prasenajit saw Aṅgulimāla,
he was filled with terror, and the hairs on his body stood on end.
The Buddha said, "Do not be afraid.
Go to him yourself; he will speak with the king."
Then King Prasenajit
went to where Aṅgulimāla was.
Upon arriving, he bowed with his head at his feet and stood to one side.
Then King Prasenajit asked Aṅgulimāla:
"Venerable Aṅgulimāla,
what is your name now?"
