Aṅgulimāla replied:
"Great King, my name is Gāgu.
My mother's name is Maṇṭāyanī."
The king replied, saying:
"You should strive well yourself.
I now, for the rest of my life,
will make offerings to the Venerable Gāgu.
Robes, food and drink, medicine for illness, bedding and seats—I will be unstinting.
I shall always protect and support you with the Dharma."
Then King Prasenajit
bowed with his head at his feet, circumambulated three times,
went to the World-Honored One, and said:
"World-Honored One, you subdue those whom others cannot subdue.
There are those who, although they have cut off all afflictions,
still have the appearance of afflictions in body and speech.
Ordinary people, upon seeing or hearing them, give rise to impure thoughts.
For example, the Arhat Míg Póhézhà
spent five hundred lifetimes among monkeys.
Now, although he has attained the Way, he still leaps and jumps among trees.
Foolish people, seeing this, give rise to contempt and disrespect.
Also, the Arhat Bìlíngjiāpócuō
was born into a Brahmin family for five hundred lifetimes,
cultivating a habit of contemptuousness.
Now, although he has attained the Way,
he still speaks to the spirit of the Ganges River, saying:
'Little slave girl, stop the flow.'
The Ganges spirit became angry,
went to the Buddha to complain.
The Buddha instructed him to repent,
yet he still called her 'little slave girl.'
The Buddha has no such matters.
Once, a Brahmin spoke harshly,
at one time reviling the Buddha with five hundred things; the Buddha showed no sign of anger.
The Brahmin's mind then became joyful.
Then again, at one time, he praised the Buddha with five hundred good things;
the Buddha also showed no sign of pleasure.
One should know that the Buddha's habitual tendencies of afflictions are exhausted,
therefore good and bad are no different to him."
The Buddha was in the Bamboo Grove at Rājagṛha.
At that time, there were four brothers from a great family.
Their parents had died early, and they were disputing over the family property.
Seeing Śāriputra, they joyfully asked him,
"We wish you to explain this so that we will no longer quarrel."
Śāriputra said,
"Excellent.
I have a great teacher, the Buddha, who is the most revered in the three realms.
You all follow me.
Return with me to where the Buddha is.
You will certainly gain understanding."
They followed Śāriputra back.
The Buddha, seeing the four from afar, smiled and emitted light of five colors.
The four paid homage to the Buddha and said,
"We are foolish and ignorant.
We beseech the Buddha to explain,
so that we may cease quarreling."
Long ago, there was a king
named Wéilóu.
He had an illness in his body.
He summoned a physician to come and examine him.
To prepare the medicine, lion's milk was required.
The king then offered a reward:
whoever could obtain it would be granted land and enfeoffed,
and also married to his youngest daughter.
At that time, a poor man declared,
"I can obtain it." The king then gave his permission.
That man, clever and cunning, first sought out where the lion was.
Then he killed a sheep and prepared several hu of grape wine.
He went to that mountain.
Waiting for the lion to go out,
he then killed the sheep,
and placed the grape wine at its dwelling place.
The lion, seeing the wine and meat, immediately ate and drank, became greatly intoxicated, and lay down.
He went forward, seized the milk, and joyfully returned.
Before reaching his own country,
he stayed overnight at a settlement.
There was an Arhat staying there.
Together with this man, he pursued the lion.
They traversed dangerous paths.
His body extremely tired, he lay down to sleep.
He was completely unaware.
The monk observed the six consciousnesses in his body,
each contending for merit.
The foot deity said,
"It is because of my walking that we arrived here and obtained the milk."
The hand deity then said,
"It is because of my hand seizing it."
The eye deity then said,
"It is because of my seeing it."
The ear deity then said,
"It is because of my hearing the king seek milk that I brought you all here."
The tongue deity then said,
"You all contend in vain.
This merit is mine.
Now, to kill or let live is up to me."
This man brought the milk to the king's place.
He said,
"Now I have obtained lion's milk; it is outside."
The king said,
"Is it or not? Just bring it in."
As soon as the king saw the milk,
the tongue immediately said,
"This is not lion's milk.
It is merely donkey milk."
Hearing this, the king was greatly angered and said,
"I sent you to fetch lion's milk.
Yet you bring donkey milk."
He immediately wanted to kill him.
At that time, the monk who had stayed with him
immediately used his supernatural power
to come before the king and reported,
"This truly is lion's milk.
At that time, I stayed with this man in the settlement.
I saw within his body,
the six parts contending over their diligent merit.
The tongue said,
'I will turn against you all.'
Now indeed it is so.
Your Majesty, just use the milk to prepare the medicine.
Your illness will certainly be cured."
The king then believed the Arhat's words.
He used the milk to prepare the medicine and married his daughter to him,
and enfeoffed him as originally promised.
The monk told the king,
"Even within one person's body and consciousness, there is mutual opposition and contradiction,
how much more so among others?"
At that time, the one who obtained the milk,
grateful for the monk's kindness,
requested to become a śramaṇa.
With understanding of the mind, he attained the path of Arhatship.
At that time, the king also joyfully received the five precepts
and attained the path of Srotaāpanna.
The four, hearing this, gained understanding.
They then followed the Buddha, begging to become bhikṣus.
The Buddha silently placed his hand on their heads.
Their hair fell off, and the robes adhered to their bodies.
Their knots were untied, and defilements were removed.
Ānanda asked,
"What merit did these four originally have,
that now, upon hearing the scripture, they understood
and quickly attained Arhatship?"
The Buddha said,
"In the time of the Buddha Kāśyapa,
Śāriputra was a bhikṣu.
These four were merchants.
Together they offered a robe to Śāriputra.
Śāriputra made an aspiration,
'May you all in later lives quickly attain liberation.'
Now, from Śāriputra, they have attained liberation."
There was a man
who left home under the true Dharma.
He was able to serve.
Wherever he went to monasteries, the various bhikṣus, etc.,
had him serve.
Later, he became extremely weary.
He thought to himself,
"Who can teach me the Dharma and guide me?"
He heard that in the country of Mathurā,
there was Upagupta,
who was predicted by the Buddha
to be foremost among later disciples.
He went, paid homage, joined his palms, and said,
"Venerable One,
please perform the Buddha's work and teach me the Dharma."
Upagupta said,
"If you can follow my instruction, I will teach you the Dharma."
He replied, "I can."
He asked,
"How many monastics are there in the Nàduōpóduō Monastery?
You further serve the monastic community."
He replied,
"There are eighteen thousand Arhats,
twice as many learners,
and countless diligent ordinary people."
At that time, that bhikṣu
then served all the monastics,
enabling all the monastics to devote themselves to cultivating the path.
At that time, the serving bhikṣu rose early,
put on his robe, took his bowl, and entered Mathurā.
A wealthy elder, going out in the morning, met him.
The elder thought,
"I have never seen him before,
but now I see him." He bowed with his head at his feet
and asked,
"Venerable One,
from far or near, what matter brings you here?"
He replied,
"I come from the eastern country.
I came to Upagupta's place
to hear the Dharma.
But Upagupta instructed me to serve the monastics.
I now do not know who among the people of Mathurā is diligent and who is not."
The elder said,
"You now need not ponder this matter.
I will take your place in serving the monastic community with all food, clothing, and medicine.
I will provide everything." The bhikṣu and the elder
together took food and other necessities
to make offerings to the monastic community.
During the three-month summer retreat, the bhikṣu, through these offerings, cultivated and attained the fruit of the path.
In Mathurā,
there was a man
who requested his parents to allow him to leave home.
He went to Upagupta's place,
respectfully paid homage, and said,
"Venerable One,
may I become a bhikṣu?"
Upagupta saw that he was bound by attachment to his body.
He said, "Welcome.
I will grant you ordination."
Joyfully, he bowed at his feet
and begged to first briefly return home.
On the road, he thought,
"If I reach home,
there might be obstacles."
In the evening, he stayed overnight at a shrine along the way. Upagupta created two rākṣasas:
one holding a corpse,
the other empty-handed.
Both entered the shrine.
Each said, "I got it,"
and contended without resolution.
They asked this man,
"Who brought the corpse?"
This man thought,
"I must not speak falsely.
I will speak truthfully."
The empty-handed ghost then grabbed his arm, bringing it to its mouth to eat.
The corpse-carrying ghost helped him break free.
Barely, he escaped.
This continued for a long time until sunrise.
After two days, he returned to Upagupta's place.
He left home to follow the path,
diligently and earnestly cultivated,
and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Long ago, there were many people.
They lived beside a river.
They were harmed by the water.
The people had no fixed limits.
Among them, only one in ten thousand attained liberation.
A person who attained liberation from the deep water
went to the Buddha's place.
He sought to become a śramaṇa.
The Buddha then consented, allowing him to join the path.
Internally, he did not contemplate, thinking he had escaped hardship.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to him, urging him to practice the path.
At that time, that bhikṣu felt ashamed within.
He understood that all things are impermanent.
His mind opened, his thoughts resolved, serene and free from attachments.
Then, before the Buddha,
he became an arhat.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha,
there were two brothers.
Both were śramaṇas.
The elder brother upheld precepts, practiced meditation, and single-mindedly sought the path,
but did not practice generosity.
The younger brother practiced generosity and cultivated merit,
but delighted in breaking precepts.
The elder brother, under Śākyamuni, left home and attained the path of an arhat,
but his robes were insufficient, and he was often not full from food.
The younger brother was born as an elephant.
As an elephant, he was very strong,
able to repel enemies.
He was beloved by the king,
adorned with gold, silver, jewels, and precious ornaments,
granted a fief of several hundred households,
which provided for this elephant
according to his needs.
At that time, the elder brother bhikṣu encountered a great famine in the world.
Traveling to beg for food, for seven days he obtained nothing.
Finally, he obtained a little coarse food,
barely enough to survive.
Knowing beforehand that this elephant was his younger brother from a past life,
he went to the elephant,
grasped the elephant's ear with his hand,
and said to him,
"In the past, both you and I had faults."
The elephant pondered the bhikṣu's words,
immediately recognized his past lives,
saw the causes and conditions from previous existences,
became sorrowful and stopped eating.
The elephant keeper was frightened
and went to report to the king,
"The elephant is not eating or drinking,
we do not know why."
The king asked the elephant keeper,
"Previously, was there anyone who offended this elephant?"
The elephant keeper replied,
"There was no one else,
only a śramaṇa came to the elephant's side,
stayed a moment, and then left."
The king immediately sent someone to find the śramaṇa.
He asked him,
"What did you say when you came to my elephant's side?"
The śramaṇa replied,
"I said to the elephant,
'Both you and I have faults.'"
The śramaṇa explained everything to the king as above.
The king's mind then awakened,
and he released the śramaṇa,
allowing him to return to his dwelling.
In the country of Vaiśālī,
there were five hundred blind people.
They begged for alms to sustain themselves.
At that time, they heard that the Buddha had appeared in the world,
and those who saw him
had all kinds of disabilities and illnesses cured,
the poor were given clothing and food,
sorrows, worries, and sufferings
were all relieved.
The blind people discussed together,
"Our accumulated sins and sufferings are especially severe.
If we meet the Buddha, he will surely save us."
So they went begging together,
each person obtaining one gold coin,
to hire someone to take them there.
After begging for some time, each obtained one coin.
They called out to people around, "Who will take us to Śrāvastī?
We have five hundred gold coins to hire you for your labor."
Then a man came,
they agreed and gave him the money.
He said to the blind people,
"Hold each other's hands in a chain,
I will lead in front."
He took them to Magadha,
abandoned the blind people,
leaving them in an empty marsh.
The blind people did not know which country they were in.
Holding each other's hands, they trampled through others' fields,
damaging and crushing the seedlings and grains.
The field owner saw this and became very angry.
He scolded them and beat them.
The beggars pleaded for mercy, explaining everything that had happened.
The elder took pity on them,
sent a servant to take them to Śrāvastī.
Just as they reached that country,
they heard that the World-Honored One had already gone to Magadha.
The servant took them toward Magadha.
The blind people revered the Buddha, their hearts longing to see him.
Although their physical eyes were closed, their mind's eye had already seen.
Joyful and inspired, they did not feel fatigue.
When they reached Magadha,
they heard that the World-Honored One had returned to Śrāvastī.
Thus chasing after him, they went back and forth seven times in total.
At that time, the Tathāgata observed that the blind people's good roots had matured.
He then stopped and waited for them.
The Buddha's light touched their bodies,
and immediately their two eyes opened and became clear.
They saw the Tathāgata surrounded by the fourfold assembly,
his body shining brightly like a purple-gold mountain.
They went before the Buddha, prostrated themselves with five limbs touching the ground,
paid homage to the Buddha,
and with different mouths but the same voice,
together addressed the Buddha, saying,
"We beseech your compassion,
allow us to join the path."
The Buddha said,
"Welcome, bhikṣus."
Their beards and hair fell off by themselves, and the Dharma robes appeared on their bodies.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to them again,
and they attained arhatship.
In the city of Shèwèi,
there was a Caṇḍāla boy who made a living by removing dung.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the city to beg for alms.
He arrived at that house in turn.
The dung-remover immediately avoided him by going to another lane.
The Tathāgata went to meet him.
The man thought to himself,
"I carry dung, which is impure.
How can I meet the World-Honored One today?"
He then went to a marsh.
The Buddha called to him from afar,
"I have come for you."
The man replied,
"I dare not approach.
I do not know what teachings the World-Honored One has to give,
that you would show such compassion as to speak with a sinner."
The World-Honored One said,
"I wish to ordain you as a śramaṇa."
The man said to the Buddha,
"Can even those destined for hell or the animal realm attain the Path?"
The Buddha said,
"I have appeared in this world
precisely for the sake of sinners and the suffering."
He took the man by the hand
and ascended into the sky.
They arrived at the banks of the Héng River,
where he bathed his body.
Then they went to the Jetavana,
where the Buddha commanded the bhikṣus,
"Ordain him as a śramaṇa."
The man diligently exerted himself and made daily progress.
Before ten days had passed, he attained the fruit of Stream-Entry.
He then reached the fruit of Arhatship,
with the six supernormal powers pure and clear, able to emerge and submerge at will.
He went to a large square stone, sat in its center, and mended his old robes.
The king heard that the Buddha had ordained the Caṇḍāla boy.
Reflecting that the Buddha came from the noble Śākya clan,
and that his disciples all came from the four castes,
he would enter palaces
to receive offerings and alms.
The king would prostrate himself with his five limbs
and worship by touching the Buddha's feet.
"Now I hear that the Tathāgata has ordained a Caṇḍāla.
How can I pay him reverence?
I shall now go and reprimand the Tathāgata."
Before he arrived,
he saw the aforementioned bhikṣu sitting on the large square stone,
surrounded and worshiped by five hundred pure abode gods.
The king approached and said,
"Please inform the World-Honored One
that King Prasenajit wishes to see him."
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu submerged into the stone.
He emerged from the vihāra and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "The time is right."
The bhikṣu returned and emerged from the stone.
He said to the king,
"The Tathāgata has a command:
First ask this bhikṣu how he can enter this hard stone
and emerge and submerge at will."
The king then went to the Buddha, bowed his head at his feet,
and sat to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
"That bhikṣu from earlier—
what is his name?
How does he possess such spiritual power?"
The Buddha told the king,
"This is the dung-remover."
At that time, the World-Honored One, due to this circumstance, spoke two verses:
"Just as from filth and impurity,
from fields, ditches, and deep pits,
fragrant, pure lotuses grow.
O great king, would a person with eyes
take these flowers or not?"
The king said,
"World-Honored One,
the flowers are extremely fragrant and pure.
One should take them to adorn the filth.
Observe the mother's womb: from that womb, a flower of virtue is born."
Then the king said to the Buddha,
"That man has quickly obtained great benefit,
inconceivable.
From now on,
I invite this bhikṣu
to receive the four requisites."
Once, when the Buddha was in the country of Mójié,
in the Gānlí Garden,
in a stone cave chamber north of the city,
there were many hunters
who went into the mountains to hunt.
They widely set traps and nets,
killing countless deer.
They then returned up the mountain.
At that time, a deer
fell into one of the pits.
It cried out loudly.
The hunters heard it
and each ran swiftly,
only to fall into pits themselves.
They injured many people,
too numerous to count.
Although they did not die, their wounds were extremely severe,
and the pain was indescribable.
Supporting one another,
they barely made it home.
They sought various ointments
to apply to their wounds.
Their families and relatives each received the corpses
and returned to cremate them.
Among those who were wounded,
knowing their wounds would heal,
they grew weary of hunting.
Due to past conditions ripe for liberation,
they planted various wholesome roots,
left home to study the Path, and became śramaṇas.
At that time, the World-Honored One,
surrounded by countless hundreds of thousands of beings
before and behind,
preached the Dharma to them.
At that time, the World-Honored One,
for the sake of those beings,
wishing to uproot their defilements and establish merit,
demonstrated teachings and precepts
to forever leave birth and death and dwell constantly in the hall of blessings.
In the midst of the great assembly,
he spoke this verse.
At that time, those hunters, though they had become śramaṇas,
did not realize
that the Tathāgata today
was bearing witness to them,
confirming they were hunters.
They felt ashamed within,
reflected on their past faults,
and in quiet places,
contemplated cessation and insight,
focusing their minds without distraction.
Therefore, these sons of good families shaved their heads and beards, donned the three robes,
left home to study the Path, and cultivated the unsurpassed Brahma-conduct.
They realized it themselves and found joy in it.
Birth and death were exhausted, the Brahma-conduct was established,
what was to be done was done, and they would no longer undergo birth and death.
They knew this as it truly is.
At that time, all the bhikṣus
attained Arhatship,
with the six supernormal powers pure and clear,
unobstructed.
Therefore, this verse was spoken.
In the country of Shèwèi, there was a wealthy elder.
His wealth was immeasurable.
Yet he had no children and was always distressed about it.
He prayed and made offerings, seeking earnestly and with sincere devotion.
His wife gave birth to a boy, handsome and rare.
Parents and relatives,
taking advantage of a festive occasion, gathered together.
They went to the great riverbank to eat, drink, and enjoy themselves.
The parents brought their son to the gathering place.
Out of affection for this child, they took turns holding him and dancing.
After the father finished dancing,
the mother took him and danced.
They were joyful and happy.
When they reached the riverside, their attention suddenly became distracted.
Not holding him firmly, they lost their grip and the child fell into the water.
Immediately they tried to grab him but could not.
The parents, filled with pity, love, and sorrow, grieved deeply.
Due to the child’s merit and virtue, he did not die.
Floating and sinking with the water, he was swallowed by a fish.
Though inside the fish’s belly, he still did not die.
Downstream in a village, there was another wealthy family.
They also had no son.
They had tried various means to obtain one but were unable.
That wealthy family always employed a slave to catch live creatures as his trade.
He happened to catch the fish that had swallowed the child.
Cutting open the fish, he found the child.
He presented him to the master.
The master examined him.
And joyfully declared:
"Our family has long prayed and made offerings to the gods,
seeking offspring with sincere devotion, and this is the response.
Thus Heaven has given him to me."
He then wiped him clean, nursed him, and raised him.
The parents from the upstream village heard that the elder downstream had obtained a child from a fish’s belly.
They immediately went to his place.
Demanding and saying:
"This is our child.
We lost this child at that river.
Now you have found him.
We hope you will return him."
At that time, the elder replied to them:
"Our family has long prayed and made offerings seeking a son.
Now the gods have responded and granted me this child.
Where, then, is your lost child?"
They argued back and forth without resolution, so they went to the king to seek judgment.
Thus both families presented their reasons.
The child’s parents said he was their child,
that they had lost him in the river at a certain time.
And that elder also stated:
"I obtained him from a fish’s belly in the river.
This is truly my child, not yours."
The king, hearing their arguments, did not know what to do.
He then arbitrated the matter for the two families:
"You two elders both claim this child.
Now if I give him to one, it would not be fair.
Instead, you shall both raise him together.
When the child grows up,
each of you shall arrange a wife for him.
Establish households and livelihoods.
He shall reside separately in two places.
The children born to the wife here shall belong to this family.
The children born to the wife there
shall belong to that family."
At that time, both elders followed the king’s instruction.
When the child grew up, both arranged wives for him.
They provided all necessities without any shortage.
The son addressed both sets of parents:
"Since my birth, I have encountered many hardships.
I fell into the water, was swallowed by a fish, and narrowly escaped death.
Now my intention is to leave home and become a monastic.
I only hope that my parents will permit me."
At that time, both sets of parents loved this child dearly.
They could not refuse him.
So they permitted him.
He went to the Buddha’s place,
seeking to enter the path.
The Buddha said:
"Welcome."
His hair fell off by itself, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
He was named Chóngxìng.
The Buddha taught him the Dharma.
He exhausted all suffering and became an arhat.
The Buddha said:
"Long ago in the past, there was a Buddha, the World-Honored One,
named Pípóshī.
He assembled the great multitude and taught the wonderful Dharma.
At that time, an elder came to the assembly.
Hearing the great Dharma about the merit of giving and precepts,
he gave rise to faith and reverence.
He took refuge in the Three Jewels and received the precept of not killing.
He also gave one coin as an offering to that Buddha.
For generations, he received blessings, and wealth and treasures were never lacking.
That elder’s son is now the bhikṣu Chóngxìng.
Because he offered one coin to the Buddha,
for ninety-one kalpas he was always wealthy with money.
Up to the present life, both sets of parents provided all his needs.
Because he received the precept of not killing, even when he fell into the water and was swallowed by a fish, he did not die.
Because he took refuge in the Three Jewels, he attained arhatship.
The Buddha was at the side of Léishēng Pond in the country of Zhànbō.
The Venerable Èrshí Ěryì was in a quiet place,
practicing the Dharma fundamentals without abandoning the dhūta practices.
He practiced walking meditation day and night.
The places where he walked were marked with footprints like flowing blood.
He constantly disciplined and exerted himself.
Yet his mind with outflows was not liberated.
At that time, Èrshí Ěryì thought:
"In ascetic practice and diligence, I am second to none.
Yet my mind with outflows is not liberated.
Moreover, my family estate is rich with abundant treasures.
I should discard my robes and return to lay life.
I will use my wealth for extensive giving."
The Buddha, knowing his mind, went to that place.
The Buddha said to Èrshí Ěryì:
"You were skilled at playing the lute when you were a layperson.
If the lute strings are too tight, will the sound be harmonious and pleasant to hear?"
"No, World-Honored One."
The Buddha said: "If the lute strings are too loose, will it be pleasant to hear?"
"No, World-Honored One."
The Buddha said:
"If neither too tight nor too loose, will the sound be pleasant to hear?"
"Yes, World-Honored One."
The Buddha said:
"Excessive diligence is like overstraining.
If one is lax, this falls into wrong views.
If one can abide in the middle way,
this is the superior practice.
In this way, before long,
you will attain the state without outflows."
Èrshí Ěryì, hearing these words,
returned to the side of Léiyīn Pond.
Contemplating the Buddha’s teaching,
he became an arhat.
Làizhāpó, a Brahmin,
sought to leave home under the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"First bid farewell to your parents."
His parents did not consent.
Làizhā lay on the ground for many days without eating.
His parents tried to comfort and persuade him.
He remained silent to the end.
Seeing his determination,
they finally consented.
He left home, received full ordination, and became an arhat.
After ten years, he returned to his village.
Going in order to beg for alms,
his father saw him but did not recognize him, scolded him, and gave him nothing.
A maidservant took his bowl, filled it with spoiled food, and gave it to him.
She then reported to the master:
"Làizhā has returned."
His father immediately went out to see.
He asked:
"Since you returned, why did you not come to my door?"
He replied:
"I did come, and was scolded."
His father led him into the house.
Prepared various delicious foods.
Had elephants carry gold and silver into the courtyard,
piling it higher than a person.
There was countless money and goods.
"You should return to lay life."
His mother had the new wife dress up and go to where Làizhā was.
Relatives together tried to persuade him.
Làizhā said he wished to give alms food to them.
Why trouble him like this?
In the city of Shèwèi, there was a great elder.
His wife gave birth to a son.
He was named Jīncái.
He was exceptionally handsome and outstanding.
This child’s hands were clenched.
His parents were alarmed and frightened.
They then opened his two hands.
They saw two gold coins.
In the child’s hands.
Delighted, they took them, and they immediately grew again.
Thus, diligently taking them, the treasury was filled inexhaustibly.
As the child grew older,
he told his parents, requesting to leave home.
They then permitted him.
He went to the Buddha, shaved off his hair and beard, and donned monastic robes.
When he came of age, he received the precepts.
At the ordination platform, before the assembly of monks,
he paid respects in order.
Wherever he bowed in respect,
each time he pressed both hands to the ground,
there were two gold coins.
After receiving the precepts,
he diligently practiced and attained the path of an arhat.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“This bhikṣu Jīncái,
what merit did he previously create, that he holds gold coins in his hands?”
The Buddha said:
“Ninety-one kalpas ago,
there was a Buddha named Pípóshī,
who appeared in the world.
He traveled through the kingdoms with the assembly of monks.
At that time, various elders
made offerings to the Buddha and his disciples.
Then a poor man gathered firewood and sold it.
At that time, he obtained two coins.
Seeing the Buddha, he rejoiced.
Then he offered the two coins to the Buddha and the sangha.
Because the poor man
offered two coins to the Buddha and the sangha,
for ninety-one kalpas he always held gold coins,
and wealth and treasures came naturally.
That poor man of that time
is this bhikṣu Jīncái.
In the kingdom of Shèwèi, there was a wealthy elder.
He had a son.
His face and head were handsome.
Heavenly flowers rained down, filling the house.
They then named this child
Fúbǎtí. As the child grew older,
he went to the Buddha.
In his heart he thought:
“In my lifetime, I have encountered the Holy One.”
He then approached and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I only wish that the World-Honored One and the assembly of monks
would condescend tomorrow to come to my humble home,
to accept a modest vegetarian meal.”
The Buddha accepted the invitation.
Huātiān returned home.
He transformed into precious seats throughout his house.
Just as they were being properly adorned,
the Buddha and the assembly of monks sat on the seats.
Through Huātiān’s merit, the food prepared itself.
After the Buddha and monks had eaten,
he extensively expounded the essential teachings to Huātiān.
Huātiān and his entire family attained the fruit of stream-enterer.
Huātiān then took leave of his parents,
requesting to leave the household life.
His parents permitted him.
The Buddha said, “Welcome.”
His hair and beard fell off by themselves, and monastic robes clothed his body.
He diligently practiced the Buddha’s teachings and attained arhatship.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“What merit did Huātiān have,
that he obtained such [results]?”
The Buddha said:
“In the past, there was a Buddha,
named Pípóshī,
who appeared in the world to liberate beings.
At that time, various wealthy clans all made offerings.
There was a poor man.
Seeing the sangha, he rejoiced.
Then in the wild marshes,
he gathered various grasses and flowers to scatter over the great assembly.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
‘That poor man of that time,
is now this bhikṣu Huātiān.
Due to the merit of scattering flowers,
for ninety-one kalpas his body was handsome,
and whatever he desired in mind,
came to him as he wished.’
In the kingdom of Shèwèi, there was an elder.
He had a son.
At that very time,
heavenly jewels rained down,
filling his household.
A physiognomist observed this
and said to the elder:
‘The child’s features are extraordinary.
At his birth there were auspicious signs.
He should be named Lènàtípó.’ As the child grew older,
he became broadly learned in arts and skills.
Hearing of the Buddha’s divine sageliness,
his heart held deep reverence.
He took leave of his parents and went to the Buddha.
And addressed the Buddha, saying:
‘I wish to leave home.’
The Buddha said, ‘Welcome.’
His hair and beard fell off by themselves, and the dharma robes clothed his body.
The Buddha preached the dharma to him.
He immediately attained arhatship.
When the Buddha Pípóshī appeared in the world,
there were householders
who together invited the assembly of monks,
making various offerings.
At that time, there was a poor man.
Although he had a joyful heart, he had no means to make offerings.
With a handful of white stones resembling pearls,
he scattered them over the assembly of monks.
He made a great vow.
That poor man is now this bhikṣu Bǎotiān.
For up to ninety-one kalpas, he received immeasurable blessings,
abundant wealth and treasures, with food and clothing coming naturally.
Now, encountering my era,
he attained the fruit of the path.
At that time, in Southern India, there was a man.
He left home within the true dharma.
He had few desires, was content, and did not delight in glory or prominence.
He did not anoint his body with ghee or oil,
nor did he bathe with hot water.
He did not eat ghee or oil.
He constantly feared birth and death; the four elements were weak.
He had not attained the sage’s path.
Then he thought in his heart:
“Only Upagupta
can preach the dharma to me.”
He then went to the kingdom of Mótóuluó.
With palms joined, he paid respects
to Upagupta.
Upagupta saw that in his later life,
he feared birth and death,
constantly disliked coarseness and harshness,
and did not desire glory or splendor.
Upagupta said to him:
“Just follow my instruction,
and I will explain to you.”
He replied, “Yes.”
Upagupta
had the donors prepare various foods and bathe the assembly of monks.
He also told a young śrāmaṇera:
“You may bathe this bhikṣu with hot water,
anoint his body with ghee and oil,
and give him various delicious foods.”
This bhikṣu, after eating for several days, gained physical strength.
Upon hearing the wonderful dharma spoken by Upagupta,
he diligently contemplated and attained the fruit of arhatship.
There was a man.
He left home to become a monk in the Buddha's Dharma.
He was skilled in craftsmanship.
Wherever he went,
he would have all the monks
build monasteries and dwellings without ceasing day after day.
He grew greatly weary and exhausted.
He then thought to himself,
"I should sit in meditation and contemplate.
When the Buddha was in the world,
he said that all bhikṣus should sit in meditation and cultivate the Way.
They must not be indulgent."
He then went to where Upagupta was,
bowed, joined his palms, and said,
"The Buddha has already entered parinirvāṇa.
Venerable One, you now perform the Buddha's work.
I wish you would preach the Dharma for me."
At that time, Upagupta saw that the conditions for his later life to fear the suffering of birth and death were not yet complete.
He had him engage in craftsmanship again.
Again, he saw him weary and exhausted,
unable to continue the work.
Upagupta said to him,
"If you follow my instruction,
I will preach the Dharma for you."
He replied, "So be it."
Upagupta said,
"If there is land where a monastery has not yet been built,
you should build a monastery there.
The Buddha said in the past that this yields the merit of Brahmā."
He replied,
"Venerable One,
in the country of Mathurā,
I do not know who is diligent and who is not diligent."
Upagupta said,
"Can you rise early, put on your robes, take your bowl, and enter the country?"
He replied,
"I can rise early and enter the country."
He encountered an elder coming out,
whom he had never seen before.
This bhikṣu now saw him.
The elder immediately paid respects and asked,
"Venerable One,
have you come from far or near?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"I have come from the eastern country."
He asked further, "For what matter?"
He replied as such.
The elder said,
"Venerable One,
you need not contemplate now.
It is I who should provide for the bhikṣu
all kinds of necessities."
At that time, the bhikṣu together with the elder
took the measuring cord and ink to survey a site.
Before the cord touched the ground,
he thought to himself,
"The merit I have made
removes all afflictions,
and I attain the fruit of Arhatship."
The Buddha was in Śrāvastī.
At that time, in the country of Kośala,
King Prasenajit ordered the jailer:
"All thieves and robbers whose crimes warrant punishment according to the law shall be taken to the market and executed."
At that time, there was a thief among the crowd
who escaped by stealth.
Outwardly, he donned the Dharma robes,
privately becoming a śramaṇa.
However, inwardly he did not contemplate,
thinking he had permanently escaped the calamity of hardship and peril,
and no longer feared harm.
In a quiet place,
he did not contemplate the Way and virtue,
nor did he study the sūtras and precepts,
the path of vinaya, meditation, and recitation.
Yet he had not attained the fruit of realization,
nor did he diligently seek to attain it.
The Buddha told that person,
"You have escaped the calamity of the thieves and bandits of birth and death,
but there remains other fear.
The body of the five aggregates revolves through the five destinies,
with no end to liberation.
Harassed by the bonds and defilements,
you will fall into the paths of hungry ghosts and animals."
At that time, that bhikṣu,
in a quiet place,
contemplated and reflected,
inwardly reproaching himself earnestly.
He understood that all things are impermanent,
life does not last long,
and all ends in extinction.
The changes of rise and decline
have been coming for a long time.
He then, before the Buddha,
repented his faults and blamed himself,
and attained the path of Arhatship.
At that time, in the country of Mathurā, there was a man
who, under Upagupta,
left home to become a monk.
Due to greed for food, he could not attain the Way.
Upagupta said to him,
"Tomorrow I will give you food."
At the time, he placed before him one vessel filled with a bowl of gruel
and another empty vessel.
He then said to him,
"You may take the food and empty this vessel."
He also said,
"Wait until it cools and then eat it gradually."
But this bhikṣu had a heavy and strong greedy mind.
He blew on it to cool it,
and said to the upādhyāya,
"It has cooled, so I will eat it all at once."
Upagupta said,
"Although the milk gruel is cold,
your mind is still hot.
You should cool it further.
Use the contemplation of impurity as water
to remove this heat of mind.
When you see food and drink, regard it as taking medicine."
The bhikṣu, after eating,
immediately vomited it out,
filling the empty vessel.
Upagupta said,
"You may eat it again."
The bhikṣu said,
"How can one eat filth again?"
He also said,
"You should regard all dharmas as like snot and vomit."
Thereupon, he preached the Dharma for him.
The bhikṣu diligently contemplated and observed,
and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Prince Jeta sent a message
inviting the Buddha and the monks to eat the next day.
Only the beggar monks were not invited.
The beggar monks, having come well, all followed the Buddha and the monks into the palace to eat.
The beggar monks,
using their supernatural powers, went north to Uttarakuru,
took naturally grown rice,
each maintaining their dignified demeanor, descended through the sky,
entered the prince's palace, and sat in order.
The prince saw this and marveled at what he had never seen before.
He asked the Buddha,
"Where have these worthy sages come from?"
The Buddha said,
"They are the five hundred beggars who became śramaṇas."
The prince was deeply ashamed.
The Buddha was at the Śrāvastī Monastery.
Four bhikṣus were sitting beneath a tree.
They asked each other,
"Of all things in the world, what is the most painful?"
One said,
"In all the world, nothing is more painful than lustful desire."
Another said,
"In the world, nothing is more painful than hunger and thirst."
Another said,
"In the world, nothing is more painful than anger and hatred."
Another said,
"In all the world, nothing is more painful than fear and terror."
They argued over the meaning of suffering, unable to reach an agreement.
The Buddha, knowing their discussion,
went to where they were
and asked what they were debating.
They reported the matter to the Buddha, who said,
"Your discussion does not get to the root of suffering.
In all the world, nothing is more painful than having a body.
Hunger, thirst, cold, heat, anger, hatred, fear, terror, lust, enmity, and calamity—all arise from the body.
The body is the basis of all suffering and the vessel of affliction and calamity.
It toils the mind, exhausts thought, and brings endless worries and fears.
All sentient beings in the three realms harm and devour one another.
Bound by attachment to self, they cycle endlessly through birth and death.
All this arises from the body.
To escape the suffering of the world, one must seek extinction.
Restrain the mind, uphold righteousness, and dwell in serene thoughtlessness.
Then one may attain nirvāṇa.
This is the greatest joy."
The Buddha then spoke a verse to the bhikṣus:
"Long ago, countless ages past,
there was a bhikṣu with the five supernatural powers,
named Jīngjìnlì.
He dwelled in solitude beneath a mountain tree, seeking the Way.
At that time, four creatures relied on him and often found peace and safety:
one was a dove,
one was a crow,
one was a poisonous snake,
and one was a deer.
These four creatures
would go out by day to seek food
and return to rest at night.
One night, the four creatures
asked each other,
'Of the sufferings in the world, which is the most severe?'
The crow said,
'When hungry and thirsty, the body grows weak, the eyes grow dim, and the spirit becomes restless.
One throws oneself into nets and traps, heedless of sharp blades.
Our loss of life is always due to this.
Thus it can be said
that hunger and thirst are the most painful.'
The dove said,
'When lust burns fiercely, one becomes heedless of all else.
Endangering the body and destroying life—all arise from this.'
The poisonous snake said,
'Once anger arises, one does not distinguish between kin and stranger.
It can kill others and also kill oneself.'
The deer said,
'I dwell in the forests and wilds, my heart constantly trembling with fear,
afraid of hunters, tigers, and wolves.
At the faintest sound, I flee and plunge into pits and cliffs.
Mothers and children are separated, their livers and gallbladders trembling with terror.
Thus it can be said
that fear and terror are the most painful.'
Then Jīngjìnlì replied,
'What you have discussed is not yet complete.
You have not reached the root of suffering.
The greatest suffering in the world is none other than conditioned existence.
It is the vessel of suffering, bringing endless worries and fears.
It is for this reason that I left the secular life to study the Way,
extinguishing thoughts and cutting off imaginings,
not coveting the four elements.
I seek to cut off the source of suffering and aspire to nirvāṇa.
The path of nirvāṇa is extinction and formlessness.
All worries and afflictions end forever.
Only then is there great peace.'
The four creatures, hearing this,
immediately understood and were liberated in mind.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus,
'That bhikṣu with the five supernatural powers was I in a past life.
The four creatures are the four of you now.
You already heard the meaning of the root of suffering in a past life.
Why do you now speak in such a way again?'
The bhikṣus, hearing this, felt ashamed and blamed themselves.
Then, in the presence of the Buddha, they attained arhatship.
The Buddha was at the Śrāvastī Monastery.
At that time, there were four newly ordained bhikṣus
who went to sit in meditation and cultivate the Way beneath a pear tree.
The pear blossoms were luxuriant, beautiful, and fragrant.
They said to each other,
'Of all things in the world, what is most enjoyable?'
One said,
'In mid-spring, when all plants bloom gloriously,
roaming the fields and plains—this is the most enjoyable.'
Another said,
'Gatherings of kin and auspicious meetings, with cups of wine passed back and forth,
music, singing, and dancing—this is the most enjoyable.'
Another said,
'Amassing great wealth and treasures, obtaining whatever one desires,
carriages, horses, clothing, and ornaments different from others,
going out and coming in with splendor, attracting the attention of passersby—
this is the most enjoyable.'
Another said,
'Having beautiful wives and concubines, dressed in bright silks,
perfumed and fragrant, indulging in desires and passions—
this is the most enjoyable.'
The Buddha, knowing they could be transformed,
went and proclaimed to them,
'These are the most painful.'
He said, 'Long ago, there was a king
named Pǔ'ān.
He was close friends with the kings of four neighboring countries.
He invited these four kings to feast for a month,
with food, drink, and entertainment.
On the day of parting,
King Pǔ'ān asked,
"In the human world,
what is most enjoyable?"
The answers of the four kings
were no different from yours.'
At that time, King Pǔ'ān expounded the truth for them.
The four kings, hearing this, rejoiced and believed with understanding.
That King Pǔ'ān was I in a past life.
Those four kings are the four of you now.
You already discussed this before, yet now you still do not understand.
How can the cycle of birth and death ever cease?'
Then the four bhikṣus,
hearing this teaching again, felt ashamed and repented of their faults.
Their minds opened in understanding, and they attained arhatship.
Long ago, there was a man
who left his family to study the Way and attained the state of an arhat.
He sought to repay all who had shown him kindness.
He saw that his mother was in the hells,
and he sought extensively for a means to free her from suffering.
He saw that in a border region, there was a king who had killed his father and usurped the throne.
He had only seven days left to live.
The place of his punishment was the same as that of the arhat's mother.
At night, the arhat went to the king's place
and manifested half his body through the wall.
The king saw him and was terrified.
He drew his sword and struck the arhat's neck.
The neck fell to the ground,
but the arhat remained unmoved.
Only then did the king understand.
He bowed his head and apologized.
The arhat said to the king,
"Did you kill your father and usurp the throne?"
The king replied,
"Indeed, I did."
The arhat said, "You have only seven days left to live,
and then you will fall into hell.
I have come especially to tell you this."
The king then begged for mercy.
The arhat said,
"Even if you perform great meritorious deeds, I fear it may be too late.
But if you simply recite 'Námó Fó'
without ceasing for seven days, you may be spared punishment."
The king then single-mindedly recited 'Námó Fó'
without slackening for seven days.
When his life ended, his spirit still remembered and, as he entered the gates of hell,
he continued to recite 'Námó Fó'.
The hell immediately grew cold.
All the people in that city were able to escape.
The arhat then preached the Dharma to them.
The arhat's mother, the king,
and all the people in the hells were liberated.
In the southern land of Tiānzhú, there was a man.
He had left home under the Buddha's Dharma.
His body was bound by craving.
He would anoint his body with ghee and oil.
He would also bathe with hot water.
He partook of various kinds of food and drink.
Bound by craving for the body, he could not attain the holy path.
He went to the country of Mótóuluó, to where Yōubōjíduō was.
He bowed at his feet and said,
"I wish to hear the essential Dharma, Yōubōjíduō."
Yōubōjíduō, seeing that his mind was later bound by craving,
spoke, saying,
"Man,
if you can accept my instruction, I will teach you."
He replied, "I can."
Yōubōjíduō led him into the mountains.
Using his supernatural power, he transformed and created a large tree.
He said,
"You must climb this large tree."
At that time, the bhikṣu then climbed the tree.
He also transformed and created a large pit beneath the tree.
It was a thousand cubits deep and wide.
He spoke again,
"Let go with your two feet."
He immediately let go with his feet.
He then told him to let go with one hand.
He let go with one hand.
"Now let go with the other hand."
The bhikṣu replied,
"If I let go with the other hand, I will fall into the pit and die."
Yōubōjíduō said,
"We previously agreed that you would accept all instruction.
Why do you not accept this?"
At that moment, craving for the body ceased.
He let go and fell.
He did not see the tree or the pit.
Jíduō preached the Dharma.
Through diligent contemplation, he attained the fruit of Arhatship.
In the country of Mótóuluó, there was a man.
He left home under Yōubōjíduō.
He heard teachings on the contemplation of impurity and so forth.
Using the contemplation of impurity, he subdued the afflictions.
He thought he had done what was to be done.
Jíduō said,
"You should be diligent; do not think of slacking."
He replied,
saying, "I have already attained Arhatship."
Jíduō said,
"Have you seen the wine-selling woman in the country of Qiántuóluó?
This woman
claims to have attained the Way,
no different from you.
The afflictions are not yet severed, yet she claims they are severed.
This is overestimation.
Now, observe this woman: has she attained the Way or not?"
He replied,
"I have not yet seen her.
I wish to go to that country."
The teacher then permitted him.
At that time, the bhikṣu
went to the country of Qiántuóluó.
He settled in a stone monastery below, resting.
Rising early, he donned his robes, took his bowl, and entered the village to beg for food.
At that time, the wine-selling woman took food intending to give it.
The bhikṣu saw the woman.
Lustful craving arose, and he himself took curdled milk from his bowl
and gave it to this woman.
The woman saw this.
Lust also transformed her mind; she bared her teeth and smiled.
The bhikṣu then entered the contemplation of impurity.
He even contemplated the body as a skeleton.
From this contemplation, he attained the fruit of Arhatship.
The Buddha was in the country of Shèwèi.
He dwelled for the summer retreat for three months.
When the new year arrived,
he told Ānán,
"You strike the ghaṇṭā."
The sound of the ghaṇṭā pervaded one Buddha-land.
All the suffering of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals—all illness and pain—
upon hearing the sound, were entirely removed, and all attained peace and comfort.
At that time, the Buddha said,
"Bhikṣus, you should rise and perform the śalākā count.
Face each other, repent of faults, and blame yourselves.
Apologize for the multitude of faults and violations of the Dharma committed.
Each endure, be harmonious, and purify body, speech, and mind,
so that no defilement remains."
At that time, the bhikṣus accepted the Buddha's instruction.
When the matter was concluded, they returned to their seats.
At that time, the Buddha, out of compassion,
rose from his seat.
Facing the bhikṣus,
he joined his palms and said,
"Although the Supreme Honored One, the Ultimate Truth, is without fault,
it is fitting to practice this as instruction."
At that time, the Buddha delayed, repenting and apologizing to the holy assembly.
Out of pity for all, he returned to his grass mat.
The Buddha had just sat down again, and the holy assembly did likewise.
Each returned to his former place.
At that time, ten thousand bhikṣus attained the path-fruit.
Eight thousand bhikṣus attained Arhatship.
The Buddha was in the Jīshù Jīngshè.
The bhikṣus
diligently cultivated the path and abandoned the hindrances.
There was one bhikṣu
who, after eating his fill, entered his cell, closed the door, and slept peacefully.
He enjoyed the pleasure of the body, not contemplating impermanence.
He no longer distinguished day and night.
After seven days, his life was about to end.
The Buddha, pitying and sorrowing for him,
entered his cell and snapped his fingers to awaken him.
He spoke a wonderful verse for him.
Startled awake, he bowed his head in reverence.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu, "In your past life,
at the time of Buddha Wéiwèi, you once left home.
Greedy for bodily benefits and offerings, you did not heed the sūtras and precepts.
You ate your fill and then slept, not contemplating impermanence.
When your life ended, your spirit was born among wēng insects.
For fifty thousand years you accumulated [life there].
When that lifespan ended, you again became a snail-clam insect, a tree-boring insect.
Each for fifty thousand years.
These four kinds of insects
grew in darkness, greedy for the body and attached to life.
They delighted in dwelling in hidden, dark places as homes, disliking light.
One sleep would last a hundred years before awakening.
Entangled in the net, they did not seek liberation.
Now your offenses have finally ended.
You have become a śramaṇa.
How can you sleep, not knowing satiety?"
The bhikṣu, hearing this, was ashamed, fearful, and blamed himself.
The five hindrances were immediately removed.
He became an Arhat.
In the country of Mótóuluó,
there was a man.
He left home under Yōubōjíduō.
He was always fond of sleeping.
Sometimes when the Dharma was preached, he slept and did not hear.
Instructed to meditate under a tree, he also slept.
Jíduō, using his supernatural power,
transformed and created a deep pit around him, a thousand cubits deep.
At that time, the bhikṣu awoke from sleep.
He was immediately terrified.
At that time, Yōubōjíduō again transformed and created a path,
allowing him to walk.
At that time, this bhikṣu
followed the path and came out.
He went to where Yōubōjíduō was.
Yōubōjíduō told him to go back again.
The bhikṣu replied,
"There is a deep pit there."
Yōubōjíduō said,
"This deep pit is small. The great deep pit
is called birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress.
If a person does not know the Four Truths,
he will fall into it."
The bhikṣu, hearing this,
went again under the tree and sat cross-legged.
His mind constantly contemplated, fearing to fall into the deep pit.
He no longer slept.
Because of this fear, he contemplated diligently.
He removed all afflictions.
He attained the fruit of Arhatship.
There was a female elephant
named Mótú.
She carried the Buddha's relics to the country of Jìbīn.
Because of this good root, she died and was born among humans.
She left home and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Because she ate one hú of rice, she then attained parinirvāṇa.
She told the bhikṣuṇīs, "You all assemble.
I will myself speak of the supreme Dharma I have attained."
The bhikṣuṇīs did not believe her words.
She again said to the nuns,
"Do not give rise to disbelief.
In a past life, I was a female elephant.
Abandoning that elephant body, I immediately obtained this body.
I could eat one hú and five dǒu of rice.
Yet I ate one hú."
And so on, extensively explained.
Such as this, although eating much,
it was easily satisfied.
It has been heard that King Pōsīnì
ate two hú of rice.
Because of his meritorious causes and conditions,
due to one stalk of rice
and one stalk of sugarcane,
they grew daily.
Because of eating that much rice, his body became large and fat.
With this large body, he went to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha asked,
"Great King,
your body is large and fat; are you not weary?"
At that time, Pōsīnì felt ashamed in his heart.
He fully explained to the Buddha. The World-Honored One spoke a verse.
At that time, King Pōsīnì,
hearing what the Buddha said,
gradually reduced his eating.
Until later times, he ate only one hú.
The Buddha was in Shèwèiguó.
There was an elder
who invited the Buddha and the monks.
At that time, the monks went,
but the Tathāgata did not go.
He sent a messenger to fetch food.
There were two reasons for this:
first, he wished to preach the Dharma to the devas;
second, he intended to visit the sick.
At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed the monks
and saw that they had all accepted invitations.
He then took the master key and opened a room door.
He saw a monk
who was gravely ill, lying in his own filth, unable to turn over.
The World-Honored One asked:
"What is your ailment?"
The monk replied:
"I am by nature dull and constantly indulged in laziness.
I never encouraged others to care for anyone else,
so today no one comes to see me.
Now I am truly alone and destitute, with no one to rely on."
At that time, the World-Honored One,
filled with compassion, personally lifted him,
removed the filth,
washed the sitting mat,
cleansed his body with water,
changed his clothes,
spread a new sitting mat,
and placed him back in the room.
He personally massaged him
and said to the monk:
"If you do not strive diligently for the supreme Dharma,
after death you will suffer even greater torment."
Gradually, he preached the Dharma to him, urging him to be courageous.
Then he addressed the monks:
"You monks
have no parents or brothers,
nor sisters or clan relatives.
Not caring for one another is not appropriate.
My Dharma is impartial and harmonious, with superiors and inferiors in accord.
From this day forward,
disciples shall serve their teachers as they would their parents,
never abandoning them even unto death.
Teachers shall care for their disciples as their own children,
nurturing them at all times, never abandoning them even unto death.
Teachers and disciples shall be compassionate toward each other, extending this through endless kalpas.
All belongings shall be distributed equally.
If there are no belongings, one should widely seek alms.
Those who care for the sick are caring for me.
The merit gained will be no different."
At that time, the sick monk reflected
and soon relinquished his life,
attaining the state of no remainder.
At that time, in Mótóuluóguó,
there was a man
who left home under Upagupta.
He was fond of sleep.
Upagupta transformed into a ghost
with seven heads,
holding a tree branch, suspended in midair.
When the monk saw this, he was startled awake
and greatly terrified.
He returned to his original place.
Upagupta said to him:
"Go back to your meditation spot."
The monk replied:
"Venerable teacher, in that forest there is a ghost
with seven heads right in front of me,
holding a tree branch, suspended in midair.
It is extremely terrifying."
Upagupta said:
"That ghost is not to be feared.
Sleep is the most fearsome.
If a monk is killed by that ghost,
he will certainly not fall into birth and death.
But if he is killed by sleep,
then birth and death will be endless."
The monk then returned to his meditation spot.
Again, he saw that ghost.
Fearing the ghost, he dared not sleep.
At that time, the monk diligently contemplated
and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
The Buddha dwelt in Shèwèiguó.
There was another monk
in the region of Jūsuòluó,
staying in a forest.
The monk frolicked with the wife of an elder,
giving rise to an evil reputation.
The monk thought to himself:
"I shall now kill myself."
In the forest, a deva
transformed into the form of the elder's wife
and said to the monk:
"The people in the world, for my sake and yours,
falsely spread evil words,
saying that you and I were intimate
and engaged in improper conduct.
Since there is already an evil reputation,
why not draw close, return to lay life, and enjoy ourselves together?"
The monk replied:
"Because of this reputation,
I shall now kill myself."
The deva resumed its heavenly form
and spoke a verse:
There was a person on the road.
He had killed his own mother.
He stopped and stood beneath a tree.
Wailing in anguish and distress,
he cried out, "What can I do?"
He blamed himself for his wickedness in committing such a great transgression.
"Having killed my own mother, I shall surely fall into hell."
Although he was in such a state, he should cultivate disciplined conduct.
The Bodhisattva Pǔshǒu,
seeing that he was presently fit to be saved,
transformed into a different person.
Taking along his parents, he went to the place where the mother-killer was.
Not far away, he stopped midway on the road.
The parents said to their son, "This is the right path."
The son said it was not right.
Thus they argued and disputed.
The son, displaying anger, killed the transformed parents.
Then he wailed bitterly, overwhelmed with sorrow and unable to control himself.
He went to the place of the mother-killer.
He said,
"I have killed my parents; I shall fall into hell."
He wept, saying, "What can I do?"
"What plan should I devise?"
The mother-killer then thought to himself,
"Now this person who has come has killed both his parents.
I only endangered my mother.
That person is foolish and ignorant; his sin is even greater.
My transgression is still less than his.
Knowing that he will suffer punishment, I still feel my burden is lighter."
That person, in sorrow and bitter anguish, declared aloud,
"I should go to the Buddha Néngrén.
For those without salvation, the Buddha provides salvation.
For those who are fearful and anxious, the Buddha can comfort and remove it.
I shall follow and uphold the teachings of the Buddha."
At that time, the transformed person, weeping, proceeded on the road, walking ahead.
This mother-killer then followed behind him.
"Just as he repents, I too shall do likewise.
My sin is slight; that person's is very heavy."
The transformed person approached the Buddha, bowed his head to the ground,
and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"O World-Honored One,
I have committed a great transgression by killing both my parents.
I have committed this grave sin."
The Buddha said to the transformed person,
"Excellent, excellent.
You are utterly sincere and without deceit; your words and actions correspond, coming before the Tathāgata.
You speak with utmost sincerity.
Your words are not duplicitous.
Nor do you harm yourself.
You should observe and examine the nature of the mind.
With what kind of mind
did you endanger your two parents?
Was it with the past mind, the future mind,
or the present mind?
The past mind has already ceased.
The present mind has already departed elsewhere.
It has no fixed location.
Nor does it have a direction.
One does not know where it abides.
As for the future mind,
it has not yet arrived.
There is no place where it gathers.
It is not seen to revolve or return.
Nor does it come and go.
You should know this:
The mind does not reside within the body.
Nor does it come from outside; it has no realm.
It does not dwell between the two, nor does it rest in the middle." The transformed person sighed and said,
"Unprecedented!
The Tathāgata has attained perfect enlightenment.
He fully understands the Dharma realm, where there is no doer,
nor any experiencer, nor any being born,
nor any entering nirvana.
There is nothing to rely upon.
I wish to leave home.
Through the Buddha, the World-Honored One, may I become a śramaṇa.
May I receive the full precepts."
The Buddha said,
"Bhikṣu, come well."
At that time, the transformed person became a śramaṇa.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying,
"O World-Honored One,
I have attained spiritual powers and now wish to enter nirvana."
Through the Buddha's majestic power, that transformed person rose forty-nine feet above the ground.
In the empty space, he attained nirvana.
Fire issued from his body,
and consumed his own form.
The unfilial son saw this
and thought to himself,
"That person became a śramaṇa and then attained nirvana.
I shall emulate this person.
I shall go to the Buddha."
He bowed his head at the sage's feet
and said, "I too have committed a transgression,
endangering my mother's life."
The Buddha said,
"Excellent.
You are utterly sincere and without deceit.
Your words and actions correspond."
Then, hell-fire issued from the pores of the unfilial person's body.
The pain was extremely severe,
and there was no one to rescue him.
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I am now being burned.
O God among gods, please save and relieve me."
The World-Honored One extended his golden-colored arm
and placed it upon the man's head.
The fire immediately ceased.
He beheld the Tathāgata's body,
with its numerous excellent marks.
The pain in his body subsided,
and he attained peace and comfort.
He again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I wish to become a śramaṇa."
The Buddha immediately permitted him.
He then left home.
The Buddha expounded the Four Noble Truths.
Hearing this,
he became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma eye.
Cultivating the Dharma teachings,
he attained liberation,
realizing arhatship.
He again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I wish to enter parinirvāṇa."
The Buddha said, "As you wish."
At that time, the bhikṣu leaped into the empty space,
forty-nine feet above the ground.
Fire issued from his body,
and consumed his own form.
Hundreds of thousands of devas and humans in the empty space
came to make offerings.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"The compassionate teaching of the Tathāgata's Vinaya
can even save transgressors.
Only the Tathāgata
and the great bodhisattvas can perceive the roots of all beings
and save them accordingly.
This is not within the realm of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
The Buddha said, "So it is."
In the kingdom of Śrāvastī,
there was an old man who was extremely poor.
He was over two hundred years old.
His eyebrows had grown long and elegant hairs, and his ears were large and prominent on his head.
His teeth were as even as shells.
His hands hung down past his knees.
In appearance, he seemed to possess auspicious features.
Yet he was poor and suffered hardship.
His clothes did not cover his body, and his limbs were exposed.
His stomach was always empty and hungry as he walked.
He could barely move, showing only faint signs of life.
He wished to go see the Buddha.
Śakra and Brahmā, guarding the gate, ordered that he not be admitted.
The old man cried out loudly,
saying:
"Although I am poor,
the lowliest among the people,
it is a rare fortune after a thousand years
that I now have the chance to meet the Buddha.
I wish to ask about sin and merit,
seeking to escape all sufferings.
I have heard that the World-Honored One's compassion reaches all universally.
None fail to receive his grace.
Yet to exclude me alone would also contradict the sage's intent."
The Buddha called him forward.
Crawling inch by inch,
he paid homage to the Buddha.
Tears of sorrow and joy flowed together.
He described his poverty and suffering,
saying he had wished for an audience for ten years before finally succeeding.
His strength was already failing,
with no way to advance or retreat.
He only feared that his life would end, defiling the sacred gate,
and further increasing his sins.
He begged the Heavenly Honored One to take pity and not deny his original wish.
If he were to die like this, he would have no further regrets.
He only wished for a swift end and hoped for the Buddha's compassionate aid.
The Buddha said:
"The circumstances of a person's birth are mostly due to causes and conditions.
I will explain it to you.
In your previous life,
you were born into a powerful and wealthy great kingdom, in the royal family of a wise and intelligent king.
At that time, you were the crown prince,
arrogant and noble beyond compare.
Above, you were treasured by your parents;
below, you were revered by ministers and people.
Because of this, you acted willfully, looking down upon and oppressing others.
You gazed haughtily with lofty eyes, proud and aloof.
Your wealth and treasures, amounting to billions, were all taken from the people's possessions.
The common people were impoverished and distressed, all due to levies and exactions.
You only knew how to amass wealth and never practiced charity.
At that time, there was a humble and austere śramaṇa
named Jìngzhì.
He came from a distant country
and purposely went to you to make a request—not for much,
only for a Dharma robe.
Yet you completely refused to receive him,
treating him very badly.
Not only did you not give him the robe he begged for,
you also did not give him food.
You left him sitting there empty-handed, and when he tried to leave, you would not allow it.
For seven days and nights,
he was deprived of even water.
Only when he showed faint signs of life
did you become greatly delighted,
gathering a crowd to watch him,
considering it great amusement.
A minister advised, saying:
'This śramaṇa is compassionate and respectful,
his virtue and wisdom complete within.
He does not feel cold even when frozen,
nor hunger even when starved.
The reason he comes begging is to seek merit for you.
Since you will not give alms,
how can you torment him to such an extent?
It would be fortunate to send him away,
lest you incur sin.'
The crown prince then said:
'What kind of person is this, falsely claiming virtue and wisdom?
Let us test him with a little hardship.
Just keep him barely alive,
and then we will let him go.
There is nothing to worry about.'
Only then was he sent away,
driven out of the country.
After going more than ten miles beyond the border,
he encountered starving bandits
who wanted to kill and eat him.
The śramaṇa said:
'I am a poor, freezing śramaṇa,
emaciated to the bone, with little flesh, rank and foul, unfit to eat.
You would kill me for nothing, with no gain.'
The starving bandits replied:
'We have been starving for days and will eat even dirt.
Although you are thin, you are still flesh.
We will not let you go; you must face death.'
After much back and forth for a long time,
the crown prince learned of this and rushed there, saying:
'Since I could not give him food or clothing,
how could I let bandits kill him?'
The bandits, seeing the crown prince, all kowtowed and apologized for their offense,
releasing the śramaṇa.
That śramaṇa was Maitreya.
Therefore, you now suffer this poverty as retribution
for your stinginess and greed.
Your long life is due to saving the śramaṇa's life. Sin and merit each bring their consequences, like shadow following form and echo following sound."
The old man said:
"Past events are as they were.
I wish to end it now.
I beg, like a life on the verge of extinction,
to become a śramaṇa,
so that in future lives, I may always serve by the Buddha's side."
The Buddha said: "Excellent."
Immediately, the old man's
beard and hair fell to the ground.
The Dharma robe covered his body.
His physical vitality became robust again.
His ears and eyes became clear and sharp.
He immediately attained superior resolve,
entered the samādhi gate,
praised the Buddha with verses,
paid homage, and withdrew.
In the country of Mathurā, there was a man
who left home under Upagupta.
Upagupta taught the Dharma.
The bhikṣu diligently practiced contemplation.
He attained the fruit of Stream-enterer.
Due to heedfulness, he was freed from the fear of the evil paths.
He would be reborn seven times in the heavens
and seven times among humans,
enjoying the pleasures of gods and humans,
and would then enter Nirvāṇa.
Upagupta, knowing his disposition,
went with him into Mathurā.
Begging for alms in order, they came to a caṇḍāla's house.
There was a caṇḍāla's son
who had attained the fruit of Stream-enterer.
He had a severe illness;
his entire body was being eaten by worms.
His breath was foul and putrid.
Upagupta said to his disciple:
"Look at this child.
He has attained Stream-entry,
yet suffers such pain."
The bhikṣu asked what cause
led him to attain Stream-entry
yet suffer this pain.
Upagupta answered:
"In a previous life, he left home.
When the saṅgha was sitting in meditation, he was the karmadāna.
There was an arhat
who had this severe illness.
Scratching and scraping, he made noise.
The karmadāna said:
'Evil insects are eating you,
and you make such noise.'
He then pulled him by the arm and said,
'Go into the caṇḍāla's room.'
The arhat said to the karmadāna:
'You should practice diligently;
do not go into saṃsāra to suffer.'
That karmadāna then repented to him.
After repenting, he attained the fruit of Stream-enterer.
But he did not continue diligently.
Now this child is he.
For dragging the arhat out,
he is now born in a caṇḍāla family,
receiving this retribution."
The bhikṣu, terrified, diligently practiced,
and immediately attained the fruit of arhat.
Once there were two bhikṣus.
Their observance of precepts and wisdom were equal.
Both attained the path of Stream-entry.
One bhikṣu only went begging
to use [the alms] for charity,
feeding the saṅgha of bhikṣus and the poor.
The other bhikṣu only sat in meditation, guarding himself.
He said to the one who went begging and practiced charity:
"Why do you not sit in meditation,
guarding yourself, instead of toiling in vain?"
The other bhikṣu replied:
"Virtuous one,
the Buddha said:
'A bhikṣu should also practice charity;
otherwise, in future lives, he will be poor.'"
Later, both bhikṣus attained arhatship.
The son of a householder became a śramaṇa.
In a previous life, he had begged,
so now he could guard himself and support others.
He provided his own food and clothing and gave them daily.
The other bhikṣu, in a previous life, only guarded himself.
Now he was the son of a slave woman,
becoming a śramaṇa who begged
with no one giving to him,
always greatly hungry and thirsty. Therefore, one should uphold precepts and practice charity;
one should not only guard oneself.
When the Buddha was in the world,
there was a practitioner
who cultivated the Way under a tree by a river.
He could not rid himself of greedy thoughts.
His mind wandered and scattered, dwelling only on the six desires.
Though his body was still, his thoughts roamed, never finding peace or rest.
For twelve years, he could not attain the Way.
The Buddha, knowing he could be saved,
transformed into a śramaṇa
and went to where he was.
They stayed together under the tree.
After a while, the moon shone brightly.
A turtle emerged from the river
and came to the tree.
Then a hungry otter came searching for food.
It encountered the turtle
and wanted to eat it.
The turtle retracted its head, tail, and four legs,
hiding within its shell, so the otter could not eat it.
When the otter went a short distance away,
the turtle extended its head and legs again and walked as before.
Thus it managed to escape.
Then the transformed śramaṇa said to the bhikṣu,
"I consider that people in the world are not like this turtle,
which has a protective armor for its life,
enabling it to prevent the otter from taking advantage.
People in the world lack wisdom and indulge their six senses.
The heavenly demon Māra finds an opening, kills the body, destroys the spirit, and it departs.
Birth and death have no end, revolving through the five destinies.
There are hundreds and thousands of sufferings."
He then spoke a verse to encourage and exhort him.
The bhikṣu, hearing the verse, cut off greed and stopped longing.
He attained the path of an arhat.
He realized the transformed śramaṇa was the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
He respectfully straightened his robes and bowed his head at the Buddha's feet.
There was a śramaṇa
who performed mopali (alms-gathering).
He offered food to a bhikṣu.
He divided some cheese and put it on his hand,
then smeared it on a pillar with his hand.
The pillar immediately cracked.
There was a śramaṇa
who, without snapping his fingers, came to urinate,
splashing the face of a ghost in a clear stream.
The fierce ghost became greatly angry
and wanted to kill the śramaṇa.
The śramaṇa upheld the precepts.
The fierce ghost followed him,
seeking to find his faults.
It could not find an opening.
Later, the śramaṇa performed mopali.
Someone offered something to this monk.
Immediately upon his seat,
he attained the path of an arhat.
There was a śramaṇa who had previously studied the Way together
and lived in the same hall with another.
One śramaṇa said,
"This śramaṇa has a bad nature; I cannot live with him."
He left and went to another country.
Returning, he passed by to see him,
wondering if he had attained the Way yet.
He arrived at his dwelling at night.
The śramaṇa unlocked the door, called him in, and invited him to sit.
He raised his five fingers, and fire came forth from outside.
The visiting śramaṇa was greatly astonished
and sighed in admiration of his attainment of the Way.
In the past, there was a man of the fourth caste,
named Yīlìshā.
He had immeasurable wealth
but was miserly with food and clothing.
There was an old poor man
who lived nearby.
He indulged himself daily,
eating fish and meat,
with guests never ceasing.
The fourth-caste man thought to himself,
"I have immeasurable wealth, yet I am not like this old man."
So he killed a chicken
and cooked a liter of white rice.
He placed it in his cart and went to a deserted place.
Getting off the cart, he was about to eat
when the god Śakra transformed into a dog and came.
It looked up and down at him.
He said to the dog,
"If you hang upside down in the air,
I will give it to you, okay?"
The dog immediately hung upside down in the air.
The fourth-caste man, greatly frightened, said,
"If your eyes fall to the ground, I will give it to you, okay?"
The dog's two eyes fell to the ground.
The fourth-caste man then fled.
Śakra transformed into the form of the fourth-caste man,
rode the cart home, and ordered,
"If any outsider falsely claims to be the fourth-caste man,
drive him away and beat him."
When the real fourth-caste man returned late,
the gatekeepers scolded him and made him leave.
Śakra took all the wealth and distributed it widely in charity.
The fourth-caste man could not return home either.
With his wealth completely gone, he went mad with grief.
Śakra transformed into a man and asked,
"Why are you so distressed?" He said,
"All my wealth is completely gone."
Śakra said,
"Having treasures causes people much worry.
The five claimants are unpredictable; accumulating wealth without giving
leads to rebirth as a hungry ghost after death,
constantly lacking food and clothing.
If one escapes to become human again,
one often falls into low and base status.
You did not realize impermanence.
You were wealthy yet miserly,
greedy and stingy, not eating—
what were you hoping for?"
Śakra explained the Four Noble Truths to him.
The fourth-caste man understood the meaning.
Śakra's transformation vanished.
The fourth-caste man returned home.
He repented his former thoughts,
devoted his mind to giving, and when his wealth was exhausted, he attained the Way.
In the past, near the Jetavana,
there was a poor family
that wished to make offerings to the World-Honored One and his disciples.
Living in poverty and destitution, they had nothing to arrange.
So they went to sweep the Buddha's vihāra.
They did so with utmost sincerity, without weariness.
Next to the poor virtuous one's dwelling was a wealthy elder.
While walking and observing,
he saw in a great marsh several tens of seven-treasure halls.
Seeing them from afar, he went and asked someone,
"Who built these palace halls?
They are so exquisite and marvelous."
That person replied,
"There is a poor virtuous one
who sweeps the Buddha's vihāra.
The merit from this will cause him to be born here.
These palace halls are prepared and waiting for him."
The elder joyfully said,
"I must plan for this."
He went to the poor man's house and said to him,
"Give me that excellent thing,
and I will give you five hundred taels of gold."
The poor man said, "I have always been poor;
how could I have any excellent thing?"
The elder said,
"Just promise it to me."
He said, "Alright."
The elder then gave him five hundred taels of gold. The virtuous one obtained the gold
and widely performed charitable giving.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to him,
and he immediately attained the path.
The Buddha was in Vaiśālī.
At mealtime, he put on his robe and took his bowl.
Taking Ānanda with him, he entered the city to beg for food.
At that time, in the city of Vaiśālī,
there was a householder named Viroṣaṇa.
He had ordered his guests to be dismissed
and for seven days indulged himself in the five desires for amusement.
He told the gatekeeper not to allow anyone from outside to enter.
