At that time, the Buddha was begging for food
and gradually approached Viroṣaṇa’s house.
Hearing the sound of music,
he then told his attendant Ānanda.
Ānanda reported the matter accordingly.
The Buddha said:
"Now this elder,
after seven days have passed, will die.
After death, he will be reborn in the Weeping Hell.
The reason for this is:
he previously cultivated wholesome roots, but here they are cut off;
he creates no new ones.
Therefore, at death he will be reborn in hell."
Ānanda said:
"Is there any means
to prevent this householder from dying after these seven days?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"There is no means to prevent death.
But there is a means to avoid hell.
If that elder
shaves off his hair and beard, dons the three Dharma robes,
and with firm faith leaves home to practice the path,
then the elder will not fall into hell."
Ānanda said:
"I shall now urge him to leave home."
At that time, all the Śākya clansmen in Vaiśālī
had made an agreement with Ānanda, saying:
"When Ānanda speaks of coming to our homes,
if in those households
there are people sleeping,
or any other matters,
all allow Ānanda to have people enter directly.
The reason for this is:
his speech is gentle and does not harm others."
Then Ānanda said to the gatekeeper:
"You may go and inform him."
The gatekeeper immediately entered
and fully reported this matter.
The elder then abandoned his music, quickly came out, and bowed at Ānanda’s feet.
He said to Ānanda:
"Please enter my home and bring blessings to my sons and daughters."
Ānanda replied:
"That Tathāgata knows the time and does not speak falsely.
He predicts that you, elder, will die in seven days.
After death, you will be reborn in the Weeping Hell."
Hearing this, the elder was terrified and wept sorrowfully.
He said to Ānanda:
"Is there any means to prevent my death?"
Ānanda replied:
"There is no means to avoid death.
But there is a means to avoid hell."
The elder asked why.
Ānanda replied:
"If you leave home, you will avoid hell."
At that time, this elder thought of entrusting his household affairs,
and later went to the Buddha to leave home and practice the path.
He then said:
"Seven days is still far off.
Today I will indulge in the five desires for amusement.
At dawn tomorrow I will go."
Ānanda arrived at the time.
Putting on his robe and taking his bowl, he entered the city to beg for food.
Coming to the householder’s house, he said to the householder:
"Now one day has passed; six days remain.
You should leave home now."
The elder replied:
"I will go later."
Again he said:
"I wish to enjoy myself further;
I will go the day after tomorrow."
Thus he postponed and could not bring himself to do it.
Ānanda went daily to urge him.
When the sixth day was completed,
on the morning of the seventh day,
Ānanda spoke again.
Then he entrusted his household affairs,
bade farewell to his family,
and went to the Buddha.
The World-Honored One instructed Ānanda
to confer the full precepts on him.
After receiving the precepts,
on the last watch of the night of the seventh day, he died.
He was reborn in the Heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings.
Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"Where has he been reborn?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The bhikṣu Viroṣaṇa
has died and been reborn in the Heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings.
After dying there,
he will be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.
Thus he will transmigrate among humans and gods,
passing through nine kalpas.
In heaven and among humans, he will alternately take rebirth until his final body,
when he will again come among humans,
shave off his hair and beard,
and with firm faith,
leave home to practice the path,
and become a pratyekabuddha
named Viroṣaṇa.
The reason for this is:
this bhikṣu Viroṣaṇa,
having received the full precepts, diligently practiced until death."
Ānanda’s pure conduct bore fruit;
he received blessings wherever he was reborn.
The Buddha was staying at the Wilds Monastery in Rājagṛha.
There were five hundred bhikṣus
who all begged for materials to build dwellings.
When merchants saw bhikṣus coming,
they would close their shops and return home to avoid them.
The bhikṣus would intercept them by other paths and meet them,
then speak of karmic retribution,
teaching them to generate faith,
even grabbing their heads by hand,
forcibly urging them to give alms.
The reason for this was:
"To enable you to gain beauty, strength, and long life,
increase merit, and attain the fruit of nectar."
Hearing this, the merchants generated faith
and gave a little alms.
Later, they saw Śāriputra
and fully reported this matter to Śāriputra.
Śāriputra, having heard it,
taught the Dharma to make them joyful,
then fully reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus in charge of construction:
"In a past age,
there was a bhikṣu
named Bhadra
who dwelled in a forest.
At that time, Śakunta birds
also nested in this forest.
Morning and evening they cried noisily, disturbing Bhadra.
Bhadra went to the World-Honored One,
bowed at the Buddha’s feet,
and stood to one side.
The World-Honored One inquired:
'Are you slightly ill, slightly troubled, dwelling happily in the forest?'
The bhikṣu replied:
'I am slightly ill, slightly troubled, dwelling happily therein.
But the Śakunta birds
cry and clamor, disturbing me so that I cannot contemplate.'
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
'Do you wish these birds not to come at all?'
He replied:
'I wish so.'
The Buddha said: 'Bhikṣu,
when these birds come,
you should beg each bird for one feather.'
The bhikṣu followed the instruction and begged for feathers.
Each bird dropped one feather.
Every morning when they left, he again begged.
Then the birds moved to another place for a night,
but could not dwell peacefully and soon returned.
Then the bhikṣu again begged for feathers,
and they each gave one.
The birds said to each other:
'The śramaṇa begs for feathers incessantly.
I fear we will soon lose all our feathers
and be unable to fly.'
They further discussed together, saying:
'This bhikṣu constantly dwells in the forest.
We should leave
and seek another dwelling.'"
The bhikṣus fully reported this to the Buddha, saying:
"The bhikṣu in the forest is timid and weak,
fond of disturbance yet afraid of the evil bird sounds."
The Buddha said:
"Not only today is he timid and weak.
In a past age, there was a great elephant
dwelling in a forest.
A great wind suddenly arose,
breaking trees.
The elephant heard the sound of breaking,
became frightened, and ran.
When his fear slightly subsided,
he took shade under another tree.
That tree also broke,
so he ran again.
Then a deva, seeing the elephant, thought:
'This elephant is running wildly for no reason.'
He then spoke a verse."
The Buddha said:
The elephant at that time
is the monk in the forest.
The Buddha further told the monks:
In a past age,
there were five hundred sages
living in the Snowy Mountains.
At that time, one sage
dwelled in a separate place.
There was a fine spring,
with abundant flowers and fruits.
Not far from there,
was the Sàluó River,
in which lived a dragon.
The dragon, seeing the sage's dignified and composed demeanor,
felt affection in its heart and came to visit the sage.
It happened that the sage was seated in full lotus posture.
The dragon coiled around the sage seven times,
placed its head over his crown, and remained there.
This happened every day,
only not coming during mealtimes.
Because the dragon coiled around his body,
the sage sat upright day and night without rest.
His body grew emaciated and sores developed.
At that time, there were people living nearby
who made offerings to the sage.
They came to the sage’s place
and saw his emaciated state and sores.
They asked:
Why is it like this?
The sage explained the above matter in detail.
They asked further:
Do you wish for the dragon not to come again?
He replied: Yes.
They then said to the sage:
This dragon has a jeweled necklace on its throat.
You may ask the dragon for the jewel.
Dragons are by nature miserly and will never give it.
When the dragon comes, ask for the jewel.
The dragon, hearing this request,
became displeased and slowly left.
The next day, when the dragon came, it recited a verse from afar, saying:
The dragon replied with a verse:
At that time, a heavenly being
in the sky
recited a verse:
The Buddha told the monks in charge of affairs:
Dragons and elephants are beasts,
yet they detest excessive demands.
How much more so for humans?
You monks,
do not engage in many affairs or seek extensively without satisfaction,
causing those faithful Brahmins and householders
to suffer and relinquish their wealth.
At that time, the Buddha and five hundred bhikṣus
arrived in the country of Vṛji.
They stayed in the city of Vaiśālī.
The people were suffering from famine, and the five grains did not ripen.
The dead lay scattered everywhere, and it was difficult to obtain alms.
In the city, there was an elder named Yèshè.
Yèshè had left home, but it was difficult to obtain alms.
He often returned home to seek food.
His mother told him,
"You are suffering greatly.
Our family's wealth is not small.
You may use it as you wish.
Your wife is still here.
You should live together.
You may freely give alms and make offerings to the Three Jewels."
She said this up to three times.
Yèshè did not comply.
His mother again told him,
"If you do not enjoy the five desires,
at least beg me for a seed to continue the lineage,
so that after my death, the family wealth will not be confiscated by the state."
Yèshè replied,
"If you wish me to leave a seed,
I will now obey this command."
His mother quickly went in and told
his wife, "Good.
Adorn yourself and meet him once."
The wife then became pregnant.
Later, she gave birth to a boy, who was therefore named Xùzhǒng.
People called him
and even the family wealth "Xùzhǒng."
When Yèshè heard this,
he felt greatly ashamed.
He then reported it to Śāriputra.
Śāriputra reported it to the World-Honored One.
Yèshè and Śāriputra together went to the Buddha.
They fully reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"Bhikṣu Yèshè,
such a thing has never occurred in the Saṅgha.
You foolish man,
you have opened the door to great offenses."
The Buddha said,
"Not only today has he caused such disgrace in my Dharma.
In a past life,
he was born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
When this world was first formed,
there was a person
who was frivolous and greedy.
He was the first to eat the earth's essence.
The other beings followed his example.
Their minds became attached,
their bodies grew heavy, and desires arose.
They lost their supernatural powers, and their light vanished.
From then on, the sun and moon came into being.
That frivolous being was Yèshè.
His mother not only today
deceived and misled her son.
In the past, I have already told the bhikṣus:
There was a country named Kāśī,
a city named Bōluónài.
The prince was named Dàmíngchēng.
He practiced generosity and morality, guiding the world with the Way.
The chief queen observed the stars
and saw a golden deer king
coming from the south, soaring through the sky and heading north.
The queen thought,
'If I could obtain this skin to make a mat, I would die without regret.
If I cannot obtain it, what use is it to be the king's queen?'
She then removed her jewels, put on dirty clothes,
and entered the chamber of sorrow.
The king, noticing something was wrong, went to look for her.
He asked the attendants,
and the attendants replied,
'The queen has entered the chamber of sorrow and is staying there.'
The king went and asked, 'Who has offended you?'
She remained silent and did not answer.
The king sent someone to ask her,
but again she did not answer.
He then ordered an old maidservant,
skilled in various methods, to persuade her in many ways.
She answered,
'No one has offended me.
I am thinking of something else, so I do not speak.'
She then described seeing the golden deer
and wishing to obtain its skin to make a mat.
The maidservant reported to the king.
The king asked his ministers,
'Who can obtain it?'
He then gathered the hunters and ordered,
'Search urgently.'
The hunters all said,
'We have never even heard of it,
let alone seen it.'
The king ordered them imprisoned.
At that time, there was a hunter
named Nàizhé.
He was brave, strong, and could run as fast as a galloping beast.
He could shoot flying birds with his bow, never missing.
He thought to himself, 'I am innocent, yet I am imprisoned.'
He devised a plan and asked,
'Has anyone seen or heard of it?'
The king said,
'You may ask the queen yourself.'
The queen answered,
'I saw it from the tower,
coming from the south, soaring through the sky and heading north.'
The hunter was skilled in tracking animals.
He knew that the deer rested in the south and fed in the north.
He searched for it in the feeding area.
The hunter, carrying his bow and arrows, gradually traveled north.
He arrived at the Snowy Mountains.
There were immortals there.
He hid his hunting tools
and went to the immortals.
He bowed and greeted them.
They invited him to sit and offered him fruit and drinks.
The hunter asked,
'How long have you lived here?'
The immortal answered,
'For many years.'
The hunter asked,
'Have you ever seen anything unusual?' The immortal answered,
'To the south of this mountain, there is a tree
named Nyagrodha.
A golden deer king often
flies here and eats its leaves.'
The immortal showed him the way.
He went to the tree and saw
its lush, spreading leaves.
Soon, he saw the deer,
like a king of geese, soaring through the sky and arriving.
It stopped on the tree and ate the leaves.
After eating its fill, it flew away.
The hunter returned and reported to the king,
'It is beyond the reach of nets and arrows.
There is no way to capture it.
You may go and report to the queen yourself.'
The queen said to the hunter,
'You can smear honey on the leaves
and set up nets and traps below.
The deer will follow the scent of honey
and eat the leaves, gradually
descending to where the traps are.
It will be caught by the traps.
You can then capture it alive.'
The immortal saw from afar and said,
'Alas, what a cruel misfortune!
Although it can soar through the sky,
it cannot escape the hands of evil people.'
The immortal spoke a verse:
'The hunter smeared honey on the tree leaves,
and the deer ate them and was captured.'
When the king heard the deer had arrived,
he burned incense to welcome it.
The queen saw it,
went forward, and embraced the deer king.
Due to her heavy defilement and attachment,
the golden color of the deer king immediately vanished.
The king said to the queen,
'The golden color of this deer has suddenly disappeared.
What should we do?'
The queen said,
'This gold is a thing of no use.
Release it and let it go.'
The golden deer was Yèshè.
The queen was Yèshè's mother.
The Buddha was in Shèwèi City.
There was a bhikṣu named Nándí.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, his mind was constantly abiding in concentration.
After seven years had passed, he lost his meditative concentration.
Again, he relied on a tree and practiced proper absorption, seeking to regain his original concentration.
Māra, seizing his opportunity, transformed into a woman of incomparable beauty.
She stood before him and said,
"Bhikṣu, come and engage in sexual intercourse with me."
Nándí said,
"Evil one, perish quickly.
Evil one, perish quickly."
Although he spoke with his mouth, his eyes did not look.
The second and third times were also like this.
The heavenly maiden then removed her clothes, exposed her form, and stood before Nándí.
Nándí saw her form and appearance, and his mind became tainted with desire.
At that time, the heavenly maiden gradually retreated.
Nándí called out, saying,
"You may stay a while."
The heavenly maiden swiftly arrived at the moat of the Jīyuán Garden.
In the moat was a dead horse.
The heavenly maiden concealed her form here and disappeared.
Nándí's desire blazed fiercely.
He then engaged in intercourse with this dead horse.
After his desire subsided, he thought to himself that this was unwholesome.
He then removed his Dharma robe and went to the Jīyuán Garden.
He said to the bhikṣus,
"I have committed a grave offense."
The bhikṣus then inquired about the cause.
Nándí explained in detail.
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha ordered him to be expelled.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
"Nándí has long cultivated the pure practice.
How was he deluded by a woman?"
The Buddha said,
"Nándí was not only deluded by a woman now;
in the past it was also so.
In a past world, in the southern country of Āpántí, there was a member of the Jiāyè clan.
He had left home as an ascetic, was intelligent and widely learned.
He assisted the king in governing the country.
The king upheld the laws of the state, investigating and punishing treacherous criminals.
The ascetic thought,
'I have already left home.
How can I participate with the king in deliberating and judging these matters?'
He then said to the king,
'I wish to leave home.' The king said,
'Master, you have already left home.
Why do you now say you wish to leave home?'
He replied,
'I am now involved in these various penal laws.
How can this be called leaving home?
I now wish to leave home according to the method of the ṛṣis.'
The king said, 'So be it.'
He then built a vihāra on Bǎiyán Mountain.
He practiced the method of the ṛṣis and attained the five supernatural powers.
Suddenly, due to a minor excretion, impurity flowed out.
At that time, there was a doe.
She drank this urine and licked his genital area.
She then became pregnant and gave birth to a child.
The ṛṣi went and saw the deer giving birth to a child.
Astonished, he thought,
'How can a beast give birth to a human?'
He entered concentration and contemplated it.
Knowing it was his son, he took and raised him.
Because he was born from a mother, his body was spotted like a deer's.
Therefore, he was named Lùbān (Deer-Spot).
The ṛṣi thought,
'Nothing corrupts righteousness and destroys virtue more than women.'
Thereupon, he taught him meditation.
He transformed him with the five supernatural powers.
He spoke a verse to him, saying:
At that time, the ṛṣi then passed away.
Thereupon, this youth purely cultivated the holy practice.
He attained the five supernatural powers.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas,
riding a white dragon-elephant, inspected the world,
asking who was filial to their parents, who made offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas,
and who could also practice giving, uphold precepts, and cultivate the pure practice.
While inspecting the world, he saw this ṛṣi youth.
The Deva Lord thought,
"If this youth
wishes to seek the position of Śakra or Brahmā, he will be able to attain it.
He should be corrupted early."
He then devised a skillful means and struck the Dharma drum.
Hundreds of thousands of devas all assembled.
Śakra announced,
"In Jambudvīpa, there is a ṛṣi youth,
named Lùbān.
He possesses great merit.
I wish to corrupt him."
When the devas heard this, they were displeased.
They thought to themselves,
"If this person is corrupted,
it will diminish the hosts of devas
and increase the asuras."
One deva then proclaimed, saying,
"Who should act?"
At that time, there was one who replied, saying,
"A heavenly maiden should act."
He then summoned her.
Immediately, hundreds of thousands of heavenly maidens all assembled.
There was one heavenly maiden,
named Ālánfú.
Her hair was variegated, having four colors:
blue, yellow, red, and white; therefore, it was called variegated.
He dispatched this heavenly maiden to Jambudvīpa
to corrupt the youth Lùbān.
At that time, that heavenly maiden said to Śakra,
"Since ancient times,
I have repeatedly corrupted people's pure practice,
causing them to lose their supernatural powers.
I wish you would send another heavenly maiden, one of beautiful and pleasing appearance that people would delight in."
At that time, Śakra again, among the assembly, spoke various verses to exhort and instruct the heavenly maiden.
Thereupon, the heavenly maiden corrupted the ṛṣi youth.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus,
"Was that ṛṣi youth someone else?
He is none other than the present Chán Nándí.
The heavenly maiden Ālánfú
is this present heavenly maiden."
The Buddha was residing in the country of Kuśāmbi.
At that time, the elder Chǎntuó
was of a wicked nature and difficult to speak to.
The bhikṣus even admonished him three times in the assembly,
yet he still did not cease.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
In the past, there was a householder’s son
who had a servant named Āmóyóu.
He was by nature fierce and wicked.
At that time, the householder’s son was playing in a garden grove with the sons of brahmins.
All their attendants were waiting outside the garden gate.
Then Āmóyóu, outside the garden gate, struck the attendants.
Those attendants who were beaten
each reported it to their masters.
Then all the brahmin sons came out and rebuked him.
At that time, Āmóyóu did not accept their words.
He replied to the brahmin sons, saying:
"I will not follow your words.
Only when my own master’s son comes and rebukes me will I accept his words."
And he continued beating without stopping.
They then came and reported to Āmóyóu’s master.
Āmóyóu’s master was born with the divine eye.
Observing that place of conflict,
he saw that below it was a hidden treasure of gold and silver.
Because the ground was inauspicious, it caused them to fight.
He immediately went and rebuked him.
Then the servant stopped.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
Was that householder’s son someone else?
It was I myself.
That Āmóyóu at that time
is now the bhikṣu Chǎntuó. Furthermore, in a past age,
there was a great learned brahmin, Fúlúxī,
who served as the king’s teacher and often instructed youths.
At that time, a servant was born in the brahmin’s household,
named Jiāluóhē.
He was often made to serve the youths.
This servant was sharp-witted; having heard the teachings spoken, he could remember and retain them all.
Once, this servant harbored a slight resentment toward the youths,
so he fled to another country.
Falsely claiming,
"I am the son of the brahmin Fúlúxī,
named Yéruòdáduō,"
he said to the brahmin who was the teacher of that country:
"I am the son of Fúlúxī, the king’s teacher of Bālónài,
and have come here
wishing to join the great master to study the brahmin teachings."
The teacher replied, "Very well."
This servant was intelligent; having already heard them before,
now hearing them again, he could retain all he heard.
His teacher was greatly pleased.
He then instructed him to teach the five hundred disciple youths, saying:
"You shall teach in my place.
I will go to and from the king’s palace."
This teacher brahmin had no sons,
only one daughter.
He then thought:
"Now I can give my daughter in marriage to Yéruòdáduō.
He will then be in my household like a son to me."
He then told him:
"Yéruòdáduō, do not return to that country.
I now give my daughter to you as your wife."
He replied:
"I obey your instruction."
He then stayed at home with the daughter,
like a son, sharing in the household work.
The household gradually became prosperous.
This Yéruòdáduō, if the food and drink were not to his liking,
would immediately become greatly angry.
His wife respected him greatly.
She sought that person but had not yet been able to find him.
At that time, that Fúlúxī brahmin fully heard that his servant was there.
He thought:
"My servant Jiāluóhē
has fled to another country.
I should go and seize him.
Perhaps I can obtain the servant’s price." So he went to that country.
At that time, Yéruòdáduō
was going with his disciples to a garden grove for amusement.
On the road, he encountered his original master.
Immediately frightened, he secretly told his disciples:
"You youths,
return now.
Each of you go and recite your lessons."
After the disciples had left,
he went before his master,
bowed his head at his feet, and said to his master:
"I came to this country.
The teacher said, ‘Great master, this is my father.’
So I joined the great learned brahmin, the teacher of this country, as his disciple.
Because of the great learning scriptures,
the teacher brahmin gave me his daughter as a wife.
I beg you, honored one, do not expose my affair today.
I will present to you the servant’s price."
The master brahmin, well-versed in worldly affairs,
immediately replied: "You are indeed my son.
What more need be said?
Only devise a means
to send me off early." He then took him home.
He announced to the household:
"My relative has come."
His wife was joyful
and prepared various kinds of food and drink.
After offering the meal,
during a brief moment of leisure,
she bowed at the feet of the guest brahmin
and asked him:
"I serve my husband Yéruòdáduō,
providing food and drink, but it is often not to his satisfaction.
I wish you would instruct me now: what did he eat
when he was originally at home? I will prepare food according to the former method."
The guest brahmin immediately became angry
and thought:
"Such a son, such a son!
He causes hardship to another’s daughter."
He said to this woman:
"Just quickly send me off.
When I am about to leave,
I will teach you a verse.
If you recite this verse,
it will make your husband speechless."
After sending off the guest brahmin,
just as he was about to depart,
he recited a verse for her, saying:
"Now I give you this verse.
If he becomes angry and complains the food is bad,
then by his side, facing away, softly recite it,
letting him hear it."
Having given this instruction,
he returned to his own country.
This Yéruòdáduō,
after seeing off his master,
whenever it was mealtime,
would again become angry.
The wife, by her husband’s side, tried reciting the verse.
When the husband heard this verse, his mind immediately became displeased.
He then thought:
"Alas, this old creature
has exposed my disgraceful affair."
From then on, he always spoke gently,
fearing his wife would tell others his private matters.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
Was that Fúlúxī brahmin of the city of Bālónài
someone else?
It was I myself.
That servant Jiāluóhē at that time
is now the bhikṣu Chǎntuó.
At that time,
he already relied on me to bully others.
Now again it is so:
he relies on my influence
to bully others.
In the city of Shèwèi, there were two Mahallakas.
Both had abandoned their wives and children to leave home and follow the Path.
Having wandered among people for a long time,
they both returned to Shèwèi.
They shared a single room.
Each thought to himself,
wishing to temporarily return home to see his wife and children.
They went to their original homes.
Upon seeing him, the wife angrily said,
"You, with your meager virtue and poor appearance, abandoned home to study the Path.
Our daughter has grown up and cannot be married off.
Now I will use this to break your legs."
At that time, the younger Mahallaka,
returned to the room, sorrowful and unhappy.
At that time, the elder Mahallaka was also driven out.
They returned together to the room.
The elder asked his younger companion,
"Why are you so distressed?"
He replied,
"Why bother asking?"
The elder asked again,
"We two,
share a single room.
If we don't know each other's good and bad affairs,
and you don't tell me,
who else should you speak to?"
So he told him everything.
At that time, the elder Mahallaka said,
"Why is this worth worrying about?
My family is the same.
Your son and my daughter could be a match."
He replied, "That would be fine."
At that time, the younger Mahallaka went back and told his wife,
"I have found a husband for our daughter."
The wife replied, "Excellent."
The elder one also returned home.
He reported to his wife,
"I have found a wife for our son."
She asked, "Who is it?"
He replied, "So-and-so's daughter."
At that time, the two Mahallakas arranged the marriage.
Each was as joyful as a poor man finding treasure.
They loved and respected each other even more.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus,
"These two Mahallakas not only did such things today.
In the past, in the country of Jiāshī,
there was a Brahmin
who had old, stored mung beans.
They could not be cooked soft.
He could not sell them.
There was another family that raised a stubborn donkey.
It also could not be sold.
The bean owner thought,
'Now I will exchange these beans for that donkey.'
He went and spoke to him.
The donkey owner also thought,
'I will use this stubborn donkey to exchange for those beans.'
He replied, "That would be fine."
Both were happy.
The bean owner recited a verse:
At that time, the donkey owner,
also recited a verse:
At that time, the bean owner,
again recited a verse:
At that time, the donkey said to its owner,
and recited another verse:
The bean owner again said to the donkey,
reciting a verse:
The donkey replied again:
At that time, the bean owner,
knowing it was stubborn and could not be spoken to harshly,
then praised it, reciting a verse:
The donkey, hearing these gentle, loving words,
again recited a verse:
The Buddha said,
"Those two men
are today's two Mahallakas.
The donkey at that time
is today's Mahallaka's son.
They had already deceived each other, causing the Brahmin householder distress and loss of wealth."
The Buddha told Śāriputra,
"In the past, there was a Buddha
named Jìnshèng.
There were two bhikṣus,
one named Wúshèng,
the other named Chánghuān.
The bhikṣu Wúshèng possessed the six supernatural powers and spiritual feet.
The bhikṣu Chánghuān had not yet eliminated his defilements.
There was an elder,
named Dà'ài.
His wife was named Shànhuàn.
She was incomparably beautiful.
These two bhikṣus were their patrons.
The wife Shànhuàn provided for Wúshèng,
lacking nothing in her care and arrangements.
Chánghuān received very meager provisions.
Chánghuān, arising with jealousy, slandered, saying:
'The bhikṣu Wúshèng is having an affair with Shànhuàn.
It is because of their intimate affection that he receives such provisions.'
The Buddha told Śāriputra,
"Do you know who Chánghuān was?
It was I myself.
The wife Shànhuàn
was the Brahmin woman named Zhānshā.
At that time, slandering the arhat Wúshèng,
for countless thousands of years I was in hell.
Now, although I have attained Buddhahood, due to the remaining retribution,
a young girl with a loose tongue, dancing with a pestle and with a swollen belly,
came before me and said:
'Śramaṇa, why don't you speak of household affairs?
Instead you speak of other matters.
You are now enjoying yourself alone, not knowing my suffering.
You previously had relations with me and I became pregnant.
The time of delivery is near and I need ghee and oil,
to nourish the child.
You must give me all of it.'
At that time, the entire assembly bowed their heads in silence.
Śakra Devānām Indra, standing behind fanning the Buddha,
transformed into a mouse,
entered her clothing,
gnawed the pestle, and it fell to the ground.
At that time, the fourfold assembly of disciples and the six teachers,
raising their voices in celebration, laughed immeasurably and all together cursed, saying:
'You creature deserving death!
You raise slander against the unsurpassed, truly enlightened one!
This earth is ignorant,
that it can bear and carry such an evil creature!'
The earth immediately split open, and fierce flames burst forth.
The woman then fell into the great Niraya hell.
The great assembly witnessed this.
King Ajātaśatru was startled, his hair standing on end.
He immediately rose and said,
'Where is this woman now?'
The Buddha answered,
'Great King,
where this woman fell
is named the Avīci Niraya.'
The King asked the Buddha again,
'This woman did not kill, steal, or directly lie.
Why did she fall into Avīci?'
The Buddha told the King,
'In the Dharma I teach,
there are superior, middling, and inferior actions of body, speech, and mind.
The King asked the Buddha again,
'Which are the heaviest?
Which are middling?
Which are inferior?'
The Buddha told King Ajātaśatru,
'Actions of mind are the heaviest.
Actions of speech are middling.
Actions of body are inferior.'
In the country of Jiāosàluó, there were two bhikṣus.
One violated the precepts.
One upheld the precepts.
They wished to go together to see the Buddha.
On the road, they encountered water with insects.
The precept-violator said to the precept-upholder,
'We can both drink this water.'
The precept-upholder said,
'There are insects in the water.
How can we drink it?'
The precept-violator said,
'If I do not drink, I will die.
I will not be able to see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, or see the Sangha.'
The precept-upholder would not drink even unto death.
At that time, the precept-violator drank.
The precept-upholder, not drinking, died.
He was immediately reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
Obtaining a heavenly body in full,
he first arrived at the Buddha's place, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet,
and stood to one side.
The Buddha expounded various teachings to him, and he attained the pure Dharma-eye.
He immediately bowed at the Buddha's feet and said,
'I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, I take refuge in the Sangha.
For the rest of my life, I will be an upāsaka.'
The Buddha expounded further teachings to him and then fell silent.
At that time, the deva, having bowed to the Buddha,
suddenly vanished.
At that time, the one who drank the water later arrived at the Buddha's place.
The Buddha was surrounded by an immeasurable multitude, expounding the Dharma. The Buddha saw the bhikṣu arriving.
The Buddha then parted his uttarāsaṅga robe,
revealing his golden-colored arm,
and said, 'You foolish man, you wish to see my physical body.
Is it not inferior to the precept-upholder
who first saw my Dharma-body?'
The Buddha spoke a verse:
After the Buddha spoke this verse,
he addressed the bhikṣus,
'From now on, not carrying a water filter is not permitted for travel.
If one does not carry it, it is an offense.
It is not an offense if there is clear flowing water,
or a great river, or a spring.
From this monastery to that monastery,
within twenty yojanas, it is not an offense.'
In the country of Jiāluó.
At that time, there was a hungry ghost.
Standing leaning against the city gate.
The monk Mǎnyuàn asked the hungry ghost, saying:
"What are you seeking here now?"
The ghost said:
"Do you see me now?"
The monk said: "I see you."
The ghost said:
"My husband entered the city and has not yet returned."
"Therefore, I stand here waiting for my husband to come out."
The monk asked:
"Why did your husband enter the city?"
At that time, the ghost replied:
"Now, in this city, there is a great elder."
"He suffers from an abscess that has accumulated for a long time."
"Today it will rupture."
"Pus and blood will flow out."
"My husband will bring it."
"The two of us will eat it together to sustain our lives."
The monk asked again:
"How long has your husband been in the city?"
"The city walls are close to rivers."
Raising a hand and pointing at the city,
she said to the monk:
"Since this city was built on this bank and the other bank,"
"Now it is the seventh."
"My husband has been in the city for that long."
"The lifespan of a hungry ghost cannot be measured, nor is there any limit."
"In the past, there were five hundred monks."
"Traveling through a great marsh, they encountered robbers."
"The robbers took their clothes."
"Tied up the monks,"
"Made them all sit on the ground,"
"Gathered fresh grass and bundled it,"
"Tied their hands and then left."
"These monks, just as they were about to break the grass and rise, would violate the Buddha's precepts."
"Each thought to themselves,"
"Rather than destroy themselves,"
"They would never violate the precepts."
"They endured for four days."
"The king went out hunting."
"He saw the monks,"
"Sitting in the wilderness."
"He dismounted, paid respects, and asked the reason."
"They immediately explained in detail."
"He untied the monks and took them back to provide for them."
"In the mountains, there was a Buddhist temple."
"There was a separate room."
"Inside was an evil ghost."
"It liked to come and torment people."
"The monks abandoned it."
"A visiting monk came."
"The temple manager assigned him to stay in this room."
"And said to him:"
"This room has a ghost that likes to come and torment people."
"The visiting monk, relying on the power of his precepts,"
"Replied:"
"What can a little ghost do?"
"I can subdue it."
"He then entered the room to stay."
"As the day was about to end,"
"Another monk came seeking a place to stay."
"The temple manager also told him to stay in this room."
"Also mentioning there was a ghost."
"That person also said:"
"I will subdue it."
"The one who entered first,"
"Closed the door and sat upright, waiting for the ghost, but it did not come."
"The later arrival,"
"Knocked on the door at night, asking to enter."
"The one inside thought it was the ghost,"
"And did not open the door."
"The one outside knocked with all his might."
"The monk inside resisted with force."
"The one outside prevailed,"
"Pushed open the door and entered."
"The one inside hit him."
"The one outside also fought back with all his might."
"By morning, when they saw each other,"
"They were old classmates."
"The monks each felt ashamed and apologized."
"Everyone gathered, laughing and finding it strange."
"The Buddha was in Śrāvastī."
"There was a monk."
"In a earthen chamber among the rocks in Cān country."
"With long hair, beard, and nails, wearing tattered clothes."
"At that time, King Udayana,"
"Wanted to go on an excursion and had the roads cleared."
"The king, along with his beauties, arrived at the foot of the mountain."
"One beauty glanced and saw the earthen chamber."
"There was a monk,"
"With long beard, hair, and nails, clothes torn and tattered,"
"Looking like a ghost."
"She then cried out loudly:"
"Your Majesty,"
"There is a ghost here."
"The king then asked from afar:"
"Where is it now?"
"The beauty said:"
"Nearby, in the earthen chamber among the rocks."
"The king immediately drew his sword and went there."
"Seeing the monk like this,"
"He asked: 'What kind of person are you?'"
"He replied:"
"I am a śramaṇa."
"The king asked:"
"What kind of śramaṇa are you?"
"He said:"
"I am a Śākya śramaṇa."
"The king said:"
"Are you an arhat?"
"He said: 'No.'"
"Do you have the fourth dhyāna?"
"Again he said: 'No.'"
"Do you have the third dhyāna, the second dhyāna?"
"Again he said: 'I do not.'"
"Have you reached even the first dhyāna?"
"He replied:"
"To tell the truth, I practice the first dhyāna."
"The king then became angry and did not understand."
"Turning to his attendants,"
"He said: 'This eunuch, with such lustful thoughts,'"
"'Now this śramaṇa is an ordinary person without true practice.'"
"'How dare he see my beauty?'"
"He then ordered his attendants to quickly take him and execute him."
"The attendants then went."
"The mountain deity thought:"
"This monk is without fault."
"Now he is about to die in fear."
"I can protect him and help him escape this calamity."
"He then transformed into a large pig,"
"Slowly walking near the king."
"The attendant immediately reported to the king:"
"A large pig is near Your Majesty."
"The king then left the monk,"
"Drew his sword and chased the pig."
"The monk, seeing the king was already far away,"
"Immediately ran out."
"There was a monk,"
"Who recited the Amitābha Sūtra"
"And the Mahāprajñāpāramitā."
"When this person was about to die, he said to his disciples:"
"Amitābha Buddha and his great assembly have all come."
"He moved his body, paid homage, and shortly after passed away."
"After his death, his disciples cremated him."
"The next day, when collecting the ashes, they saw his tongue was not burned."
In the kingdom of Jiāosàluó.
There was a bhikṣu.
Dwelling alone deep in the mountains.
In the forest was a non-human female.
She spoke to the bhikṣu, asking him to engage in sexual desire together.
The bhikṣu said.
Do not speak such words.
I am one who has severed sexual desire.
The female said.
If you do not come.
I will ruin your offerings and bring you decline and distress.
The bhikṣu said, As you wish.
At midnight, the bhikṣu was lying down.
The female ghost took the bhikṣu with a rag robe.
Placed him lying beside the queen in the royal palace.
The king awoke and asked.
Who are you?
The bhikṣu said.
I am a śramaṇa.
What kind of śramaṇa?
He replied.
I am a śramaṇa of the Śākya clan.
The king said.
Why have you come here now?
The bhikṣu fully explained to the king.
The king said.
What use is it for you to be in the deep mountain forests?
Thus you are harassed by evil ghosts.
Get out.
Because I know the Buddha's Dharma, I will not question you further.
The bhikṣu, having escaped, fully recounted the incident.
The Buddha therefore established a rule.
Do not enter deep mountain forests.
Also in the kingdom of Jiāosàluó.
There was a bhikṣu.
Dwelling in an araṇya (secluded) place.
There was a piśāca ghost female.
Who came and said to the bhikṣu.
Come, let us engage in sexual desire.
The bhikṣu said.
Do not speak such words.
I am one who has severed sexual desire.
The ghost female said.
If you do not do it.
I will ruin your offerings and bring you decline and distress.
The bhikṣu said.
As you wish.
The bhikṣu lay down at night.
The ghost female wrapped him in a rag robe and carried him.
Placed him inside a wine jar in a wine shop.
The wine shop family the next day saw the bhikṣu inside the wine jar.
Asked.
Who are you?
He replied.
I am a śramaṇa.
What kind of śramaṇa?
He replied.
A śramaṇa of the Śākya clan.
They asked.
Why are you in here?
The bhikṣu fully explained the matter.
The wine shop people said.
You may leave.
Because of this, the Buddha said.
Bhikṣus must not dwell in deep mountain forests, empty places, fearful places, or uninhabited places.
There was a bhikṣu.
Routinely going for alms.
By chance entered a brothel.
The courtesan, seeing him enter, was delighted and overjoyed.
Immediately welcomed him, bowed at his feet.
Invited him to come out and sit.
And asked the bhikṣu.
Venerable one, from where have you come?
The bhikṣu replied.
I have come begging for alms as my duty.
She then prepared a feast of various delicacies.
Filled a bowl to the brim and offered it to him.
The bhikṣu accepted it and left.
Having obtained such delicious food.
His heart was filled with joy he could not contain.
He went there repeatedly.
At that time, the woman thought.
Considering this bhikṣu.
His observance of precepts is hard to match; frequently I prepare for him.
Sweet, crisp, rich, and delicious food.
And give it to him.
He comes and goes without ceasing.
His learning is not yet clear.
His practice is not yet accomplished.
He has not yet subdued his faculties.
Seeing the woman's exquisite beauty, lustful thoughts arose.
His mouth uttered soft, tender words of affection.
His heart harbored thoughts of intimacy.
The bhikṣu, hearing and seeing, became confused and disordered by lust.
Unaware of himself.
At that time, the World-Honored One said.
Although one may see women.
The elder ones like a mother.
The middle-aged like an elder sister.
The younger ones like a younger sister.
Like a daughter.
One should inwardly contemplate the body.
Reflecting that it is all foul and impure, with nothing lovable.
Externally, it is like a painted vase filled with filth.
Contemplate these four great elements conditionally combined.
Originally having no inherent existence. At that time, that bhikṣu did not understand the contemplation of emptiness.
But only practiced contemplation of form.
His mind disordered by lustful desire.
He spoke a verse to the woman.
The courtesan spoke a verse.
At that time, she drove out the bhikṣu.
He fled to the Jeta Grove.
Asked the other bhikṣus.
Then came to the Buddha.
Reported to the World-Honored One.
Fully explained the beginning and end.
The Buddha said.
This bhikṣu.
In a past life, was once a water turtle.
The woman was a monkey.
They also felt affection and attraction, but their wishes did not bear fruit.
Returning to self-inflicted deception, not entering the right teaching.
Increasing distress and suffering.
Now it is again like this.
His wishes not following his heart.
Encountering opposition and humiliation.
Ashamed, he left.
The Buddha said.
In a past age, there was a turtle.
By the riverbank, the trees were lush.
Among those thick trees was a monkey.
Who dwelled in that tree.
The turtle came out from the water.
From afar, seeing the tree with the monkey.
And conversed with it.
Approached to become close.
Daily it was like this.
Gazing without weariness.
Then arose a defiled mind.
Spoke verses back and forth, cursed, and avoided. At that time, the monkey is now the courtesan.
The turtle is the alms-seeking bhikṣu.
In the past, there was a devout layman.
His name was Yōuduōluó.
He revered the Buddha, delighted in the Dharma, and drew near to the assembly of sages.
On the six fasting days each month, he observed the eight precepts, cut off calamities, and practiced benevolence.
He protected the lives of all living beings.
He was called Zhēnzhòng.
Wealth and glory could not turn his heart.
Beautiful women and national treasures could not disturb his resolve.
His chaste faith was difficult to sway.
Wine never passed his lips.
Filial piety was his foremost duty.
He did not eat outside the proper time.
With an empty mind, he received the Way.
Incense, flowers, rouge, and powder never touched his body.
Weapons and instruments of violence were not used to destroy virtue.
He avoided fools and drew near to the wise.
He used the spiritual transformations of the Buddha to enlighten his mother's heart.
His mother believed in heresy and held inverted views.
She was stingy and ungenerous.
After her life ended,
her son became a śramaṇa.
His mind, defiled, entered into extinction.
He sat upright beneath a tree.
Observing the ten directions,
he often thought to himself:
"My mother has been dead for over twenty years.
Let me try to find where she is,
wishing to repay the kindness of her bearing and raising me."
In a moment, there appeared a hungry ghost,
ugly and black, repulsive,
with hair long and tangled around its body,
wrapped around its feet, dragging on the ground, staggering forward and back, wailing with no one to save it.
It came to the śramaṇa and said:
"I allied with a crowd of foolish, evil people,
did not believe in the Buddha's teaching,
indulged my mouth's desires.
Now I am a hungry ghost.
For twenty-five years I have not seen a śramaṇa.
Today I have met one.
Upon death, I became hungry and thirsty.
I wish for heavenly moisture,
grant me water and grain,
to sustain my slight life."
The śramaṇa replied:
"Is the clear water of the great sea not enough to drink?"
The ghost said:
"Just as I approach to drink,
the water turns into pus,
foul-smelling beyond measure.
If I obtain rice,
when I eat it, it turns into burning charcoal,
scorching my mouth and burning through below.
Evil ghosts also fasten an iron chain around my neck.
An iron rod, glowing red,
randomly beats my body.
How grave are my sins,
that I have come to this?"
The śramaṇa said:
"When you were a human in the past,
you opposed the Buddha's teaching,
allied with the deaf and blind,
chased after folly and delusion yourself,
taking misfortune for fortune.
You clung to stinginess and did not give,
greedily took what was not your portion."
The ghost wept tears and said:
"Truly it is so.
Moreover, when I was in the world,
as a human, I had a son.
He upheld the Buddha's five precepts,
devotedly maintained the ten good deeds,
was a devout layman.
The six fasting days and eight precepts he never neglected.
He served his parents with filial piety,
served the sages with wisdom.
Seeking the traces of lofty, pure śramaṇas,
like following a shadow to find the form,
he urged me to give alms,
to make offerings to the assembly of sages.
But I, lacking correct and true wisdom,
believed in wild, foolish, demonic words.
Now I reap this calamity,
the bitter pain is hard to describe."
Weeping, he said:
"Śramaṇa, pity me, save me."
The śramaṇa said:
"Now facing this transgression,
by what virtue can I avert the calamity?"
The ghost said:
"Take a bottle and fill it with water,
place a willow branch inside,
cover it with a Dharma robe,
offer it to the bhikṣu saṅgha.
Have a meal prepared and offered.
Mention my name and dedicate the merit.
Then I may obtain clothing and food.
It will not be long.
For those whose lives end
among the hungry ghosts,
when a śramaṇa dedicates merit,
they all obtain it in due time."
The śramaṇa did as he said:
placed water and a willow branch in a bottle,
offered a meal to the bhikṣu saṅgha,
presented the Dharma robe to the saṅgha,
mentioned his name and dedicated the merit.
Immediately, a great pond appeared, with lotuses growing in the water,
their fragrance wafting, touching the body.
Fruit trees provided cool shade.
His wishes were fulfilled according to his heart.
His five hundred companions
wondered, saying:
"This fellow alone—what meritorious aid does he have,
that he is early spared heavy blame,
and his wishes are immediately fulfilled according to his heart?"
In the past, there was a śramaṇa
who traveled across the sea with merchants.
Midway, the ship turned back,
unable to proceed further.
Everyone said together:
"There must be someone impure on the ship."
They drew lots to expel him.
The monk drew the lot three times.
He threw himself into the sea.
The dragon king immediately received him on a seven-jeweled lotus flower and took him into the sea.
He then reached the dragon palace,
saw towers, jeweled houses, and halls.
The dragon king invited him in,
bowed his head to the ground at his feet, and said:
"I have had a headache
for over six hundred years, seeking a monk.
Now I have finally found one.
The monk must cure my illness."
The monk said:
"I do not know medicine;
how can I treat you?"
The dragon king said:
"In this sea of mine, there are many divine medicines,
but they do not cure my illness.
Only the Dharma medicine is lacking."
The monk expounded the Dharma for a short while.
The dragon king himself felt cured.
The dragon was greatly delighted,
made offerings to the monk for ninety days,
and said to the monk:
"You have long been troubled and constrained; I imagine you are also weary and distressed.
The former ship has just arrived; now I shall send you back."
The dragon king selected three maṇi jewels:
one to offer to the Buddha,
one to give to the saṅgha,
and one for the monk.
He sent a deity to escort him.
Suddenly, he arrived at the ship.
The shipmates were surprised and joyful.
Together they returned to their homeland.
Everyone followed the monk to see the Buddha.
The Buddha expounded the Dharma for them.
They all aroused the mind for the Way.
Those he saved were beyond measure.
In the past, concerning Ānanda's report of events,
there was a śramaṇa who attained the fruit of Anāgāmin.
On a mountain, he boiled grass to dye his robes.
At that time, someone who had lost an ox searched everywhere.
Seeing smoke, he went there.
Looking into the pot, he saw the grass had all turned into ox bones.
The alms bowl had turned into an ox head.
The monastic robe had turned into ox hide.
The man then tied the bones to his head
and paraded through the country.
Everyone saw him together.
The śrāmaṇera,
seeing the sun already at noon,
beat the clapper but did not see his teacher arrive.
He entered the room and pondered deeply.
He saw his teacher being humiliated by people.
He then went, placed his head at his feet, and said:
"When did you say such a thing?
It was a sin from a distant time long ago."
The śrāmaṇera said:
"You may return briefly to eat."
The two men then released him.
With supernatural feet, they left together.
The śrāmaṇera had not yet attained the Way,
and still had anger not yet removed.
Looking back at the devout layman and the people of the country,
he thought, "They treated my teacher like this.
Let a dragon rain down sand and stones, shake this country,
and make them terrified."
As soon as he thought this,
sand rained from all four sides.
City walls, houses, and buildings were all destroyed.
The teacher said:
"In my past life, for one lifetime, my occupation was butchering oxen.
Therefore, I received this retribution.
For what reason do you create sin?"
"You should leave; there is no need to follow me further."
The teacher said:
"Sin and blessing are like this.
Can one not be cautious?"
In a foreign land, there was a śramaṇa.
He went begging for alms to the house of a pearl merchant.
The host prepared a meal for him.
There was a large pearl worth hundreds of millions.
The host had someone bring it back.
He placed it beside the śramaṇa.
At that time, there was a parrot.
It came out and swallowed it.
The host did not see this.
He then questioned the śramaṇa.
The śramaṇa replied,
"I did not take it."
The host asked again,
"Was there someone else?"
He replied, "There was no one."
The host angrily said,
"I just brought the pearl here.
Since there is no one else,
only the śramaṇa is present,
yet you say you did not take it.
Where is the pearl now?"
He then beat the śramaṇa.
Blood flowed onto the ground.
The śramaṇa still said,
"I am not hiding the pearl."
After a moment, the parrot came out to drink the blood on the ground.
It encountered the beating stick.
The parrot immediately died.
The host was about to raise his hand to beat the śramaṇa again.
The śramaṇa said,
"Stop, listen to me.
The parrot swallowed it."
They then cut open the parrot and retrieved the pearl.
The host said to the śramaṇa,
"Why didn't you say so earlier?
That it would come to this?"
The śramaṇa said,
"I uphold the Buddha's precepts and must not kill living beings.
I wanted to speak earlier,
but I feared the parrot would be killed.
Now that the parrot is dead,
I can speak of it.
If the parrot were alive,
even if you beat me to death,
I would never have spoken."
The host then reproached himself and repented of his wrongdoing.
He apologized to him.
The śramaṇa was not angry.
His countenance did not change.
There was a śramaṇa
who practiced the Way in the mountains.
There was a ghost
that transformed into a headless man and walked about.
The śramaṇa said,
"Ah, how wonderful to be without a head!
Then one would not know headaches,
and without eyes or ears, one would not perceive sounds."
The ghost then transformed into a man without a torso.
The śramaṇa said,
"Ah, how wonderful to be without a head!
One would not know pain or itch,
and without the five viscera, one would not fall ill."
The ghost then transformed into a man without hands or feet.
The śramaṇa said,
"Ah, how wonderful to be without hands or feet! One cannot walk,
nor can one take others' belongings."
The ghost realized the śramaṇa was steadfast in his resolve.
It then vanished and left.
In a foreign land, a śramaṇa was practicing the Way
when he encountered a man-eating ghost.
The ghost urgently embraced him.
The śramaṇa said,
"Today, I happen to meet you.
Your mind and mine are as far apart as heaven and earth.
Your mind delights in killing,
while my mind delights in preserving life.
You are contrary to the Way."
The ghost then released the śramaṇa
and dared not embrace him again.
It immediately retreated and apologized, saying,
"I am foolish and ignorant, and cannot compare."
In the past, there was a practitioner of the Way
who practiced day and night,
never slacking or resting.
However, there was the urgent need of the body and mouth,
requiring food and drink.
He thus went out to beg for alms.
Suddenly, he came to a hunter's side to beg.
The hunter, lacking virtue,
became greatly angry.
He wanted to shoot the practitioner.
The practitioner said,
"Stop, stop.
Do not shoot me elsewhere.
Shoot me right in the abdomen."
He then opened his robe and exposed his abdomen,
calling for the hunter to shoot him.
The hunter immediately lowered his bow and set aside his arrow.
He approached and asked the practitioner,
"People in this world
all fear death.
Why then did you, practitioner, ask me to shoot your abdomen?"
The practitioner said,
"This abdomen desires food.
Because of this,
it does not avoid danger.
Therefore, shoot it."
The hunter immediately understood.
"I traverse mountains and ridges,
not avoiding tigers and wolves,
also for the sake of this abdomen."
Due to past blessings arriving,
he suddenly gained insight.
The practitioner explained to him the sufferings of the three wretched paths and the bliss of Nirvāṇa.
The hunter realized for himself the gravity of his sins from killing and hunting.
He then received the precepts from him
and aroused the mind of Bodhi.
The Buddha was residing in Shèwèi City.
There was an elder.
His name was Nántí.
He had renounced household life to become a monk; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,
his mind was constantly abiding in concentration.
He was called Chán Nántí (Meditation Nántí).
At that time, Nántí built a grass hut in the Open-Eyed Forest.
There, practicing his own vocation during the early, middle, and later parts of the night, he attained worldly meditative absorption.
After seven years had passed,
he regressed from his meditative concentration.
Again, he relied on a tree, seeking to regain his original concentration.
At that time, the retinue of Māra constantly sought an opportunity, looking for a chance.
They transformed into a woman of unparalleled beauty.
Adorned with flowers, incense, and necklaces,
she stood before Nántí and said,
"Bhikkhu,
let us amuse ourselves together and engage in sexual intercourse."
Nántí then said,
"Evil one, perish quickly!
Evil one, perish quickly!"
Though his mouth spoke these words, his eyes did not look.
The heavenly maiden repeated this a second and third time, speaking as before.
Nántí responded the same way the second and third time.
As she spoke, the heavenly maiden then removed her necklace-adorned garments, exposing her body.
She stood before Nántí.
She said to Nántí,
"Let us engage in intercourse."
When Nántí saw her form and appearance,
he gave rise to lustful thoughts and replied, "Alright."
At that moment, the heavenly maiden gradually retreated, walking backward.
Nántí called out, saying,
"You can stay a little; let us amuse ourselves together."
Nántí went to approach her.
The heavenly maiden swiftly departed.
Nántí pursued her until they reached the moat of the Jīhúan Garden.
There was a dead horse belonging to the royal family.
The heavenly maiden reached the horse, concealed her form, and became invisible.
At that time, Nántí's lustful thoughts blazed intensely, and he immediately had intercourse with the dead horse.
After his lustful thoughts subsided, he then thought thus:
"I have acted very unwholesomely, contrary to the Dharma of a śramaṇa.
Having gone forth out of faith, I have committed a pārājika offense.
What use is it for me to wear the Dharma robes and eat the faithful offerings of people?"
He then removed his Dharma robes, held them in his right hand,
covered his form with his left hand, and hurried to the Jīhúan Garden.
He said to the bhikkhus,
"Venerable ones, I have committed a pārājika offense."
At that time, the bhikkhus were walking in meditation between the gates of the Jīhúan Garden.
They said to each other,
"This is the seated meditation practitioner Nántí, a cultivator of pure conduct.
He should not have committed a pārājika offense."
Nántí said again,
"Venerable ones, it is not so.
I have truly committed a pārājika offense."
The bhikkhus asked him the reason.
Nántí then fully explained it.
The bhikkhus fully reported this matter to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikkhus:
"This good man Nántí has confessed his grave offense himself. He should be expelled and driven out."
At that time, the bhikkhus, following the instruction, expelled him.
The bhikkhus said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One,
how is it that the Venerable Nántí, having long cultivated pure conduct,
was deceived and confused by this heavenly maiden?"
The Buddha told the bhikkhus:
"This Nántí was not only today confused by a heavenly maiden and regressed from pure conduct;
in a past life, he was also confused by her and lost his pure conduct.
In a past life,
in the southern country of Āpántí, there was a member of the Jiāyè clan,
a non-Buddhist renunciant, intelligent and widely learned.
He was comprehensively versed in the classics and texts, with nothing he did not understand.
That non-Buddhist assisted the king in governing the country.
At that time, the king of that country apprehended wicked criminals,
punishing them with various penalties, cutting off ears and noses, inflicting severe suffering.
That non-Buddhist deeply reflected thus:
'I have already renounced household life.
How can I participate in such matters with the king?'
He then addressed the king, saying:
'Allow me to go forth.'
The king immediately replied:
'Master, you have already gone forth.
Why do you now say you wish to go forth?'
He answered:
'Great King,
I am now involved in these various punishments,
causing suffering to living beings. How can this be called going forth?'
The king then asked:
'Master, where do you now wish to go forth?'
He replied:
'Great King,
I wish to go forth like the sages.'
The king said: 'Very well.
Go forth as you wish.'
Not far from the city was Bǎiyán Mountain.
There were flowing springs, jade pools, with flowers and fruits flourishing.
He then went to that mountain and established a quiet dwelling.
He practiced non-Buddhist paths in the mountains,
attained worldly concentration, and aroused the five supernormal powers.
One day in late spring, after eating various fruits and melons, his four elements became imbalanced.
Due to a minor excretion, impurity flowed out.
At that time, a doe, thirsty and exhausted, sought water and drank this urine.
The impurity touched her tongue, which then licked her birth canal.
The karmic retribution of living beings' actions is inconceivable.
Because of this, she conceived.
She constantly stayed by the hut, eating grass and drinking water.
When her months were full, she gave birth to a small child.
At that time, the sage went out to gather grass.
The doe, having difficulty giving birth, let out a great cry of distress.
The sage heard the doe's urgent cry,
thinking she was harmed by a vicious creature.
Wishing to rescue her, he saw she had given birth to a small child.
The sage, seeing this, found it strange and thought:
'How can a beast give birth to a human?'
He immediately entered concentration to contemplate and saw the original cause: it was his own child.
Toward that small child, he then gave rise to affectionate thoughts.
Wrapping it in a leather garment, he carried it back to raise it.
The sage held and lifted it; the doe nursed it.
Because it was born from a doe mother, its body had spots resembling a deer.
Therefore, he gave it the name
Lùbān (Deer-Spot).
Gradually he grew up until the age of seven.
He was benevolent, loving, filial, and kind, gathering fruits and fetching water to make offerings to the sage.
At that time, the sage thought:
'In the world, nothing is more fearsome than women.'
He then instructed and admonished his son, saying:
'Nothing is more fearsome than women.
They ruin righteousness and destroy virtue; there is nothing not caused by them.'
Thereupon, he taught him meditation concentration,
transformed him with the five supernormal powers,
and spoke a verse to him, saying:
Humans have seven repositories.
The first is called the wind repository.
The second is the repository of generation.
The third is the repository of maturation.
The fourth is the cold repository.
The fifth is the heat repository.
The sixth is the repository of views.
The seventh is the repository of desire.
Among these various repositories,
the repository of desire is the most tenacious.
It is based on phlegm and saliva,
bile, pus, and blood,
sinews, bones, skin, and flesh,
the heart, liver, and five viscera,
intestines, stomach, feces, and urine.
At that time, there was a layman in the assembly,
named Xuǎnzé.
His wife was named Miàosè,
with a dignified and beautiful face,
and an outstanding, graceful appearance.
The layman was deeply attached, his afflictions blazing fiercely.
Hearing the Buddha speak this,
he immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
do not speak thus.
How could desire arise from feces and urine?
My wife is dignified and beautiful, without any foulness or filth."
The Buddha then magically transformed a woman,
dignified, beautiful, and pure, resembling Miàosè,
who, composed, walked slowly into the midst of the assembly.
The layman asked her:
"Why have you come?"
She replied:
"I wish to listen to the Dharma."
The layman immediately pulled her to sit on his robe.
Through the Buddha's spiritual power,
this woman defiled his robe with feces.
Causing this layman to be unable to bear the stench,
he covered his nose with his hand,
looked around, and asked those beside him:
"Who did this?"
Bá Nàntuó, unable to bear it,
said to the layman:
"Why are you covering your nose and looking at me?"
He replied:
"It is extremely foul and stinking."
Through the Buddha's spiritual power,
Bá Nàntuó and the entire assembly
saw this woman defiling the layman's robe.
Then Bá Nàntuó said to the layman:
"Just look at the foul stench caused by your wife."
The layman replied:
"My wife is clean and pure,
her body free from all filth.
If you have doubts, you should see for yourself."
He said to Bá Nàntuó:
"I thought you were the source of this filth."
Bá Nàntuó became greatly angry,
rose from his seat and said:
"You should now be called Layman Shit!
When your wife sat, feces came out onto your robe,
smeared with shit,
yet you feel no shame,
and instead wish to slander others.
Furthermore, he proclaimed:
'This Layman Shit should be expelled from the assembly!'"
He then took him by the hand and led him outside the assembly.
The layman said to his wife:
"Out of respect for you,
I had you sit on my robe.
As a grown person,
is this the proper way?"
His wife immediately replied:
"You approached a shit-sack; it is only natural."
At that moment, the layman felt disgust,
wanting to remove the soiled robe,
but it further fouled his body.
He said to Bá Nàntuó:
"By what means can I be rid of this filth?"
Bá Nàntuó said:
"Not only has this feces polluted your body,
but there are other degradations
that are your lot.
If you wish to be free, you should stay far from this.
It is because of your wife's feces
that this entire assembly has headaches and feels distressed."
The layman replied:
"All the Śākya sons are full of compassion.
Your speech is extremely harsh;
how can you be like this?"
Bá Nàntuó said:
"How can you, as you are now, be pitied?
Look at yourself now—are you clean and pure?
And yet you wish to slander me."
Then the layman said to his wife:
"You may return home."
Having sent her away,
he said to Bá Nàntuó:
"I now clearly see that women are deceitful and crooked,
full of many faults and transgressions,
filled with impurity.
My mind feels disgust and detachment,
and I wish to leave home for the Dharma and practice the path."
Bá Nàntuó said:
"Your body is now so foul and stinking;
if you were to apply fragrance for years,
only then might you be fit to leave home."
The layman replied:
"If I apply fragrance for years,
perhaps my body will have perished,
or the Buddha will have entered parinirvāṇa,
ruining my cause and condition for leaving home and seeking the path.
If I may now, with difficulty, be permitted to leave home,
I will not dwell in cities, towns, villages, monastic dwellings, or vihāras.
I will practice as a forest-dweller, begging for food and wearing rag-robes,
in an empty, quiet place.
Who will smell my stench there?"
The Buddha, hearing this, called to him, saying: "Ehi!"
"You are a śramaṇa,
cultivate the holy life."
The layman's hair and beard fell off by themselves,
the monastic robe covered his body,
he took up the alms bowl,
appearing like a bhikṣu.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to him:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Free from dust, detached from defilement,
he attained the pure Dharma-eye,
becoming a Srotāpanna.
The Buddha further preached the Dharma to him until he attained Anāgāmin.
After that night,
taking his robe and bowl,
he went to Rājagṛha.
Proceeding in turn to beg for food,
he eventually reached his former home,
and stood outside the gate.
At that time, his wife Miàosè saw her husband
with shaven head, in Dharma robes, having left home for the path.
She immediately said to him:
"Is it proper to abandon me and become a śramaṇa?"
Xuǎnzé replied:
"Was it proper for you yesterday,
to discard impurity on my robe and defile my body?"
Miàosè replied:
"As a bhikṣu, should you slander others?
I came from my father's house to your home;
I have not even seen the outer gate,
let alone gone to the Bamboo Grove."
At that time, there was an evil Māra
who said to the layman:
"What you saw yesterday was not Miàosè at all;
it was a magical transformation,
deceiving and confusing your mind.
Now you can still enjoy yourself with the five desires.
The śramaṇa Gautama has deceived you.
You are now false, not a true bhikṣu.
The śramaṇa Gautama
often uses tricks to delude many people,
making them leave home,
just as he has deceived you now."
Bhikṣu Xuǎnzé, having realized the true Dharma,
immediately perceived that this was Māra.
He said:
"Evil one, you are also a transformation;
I am also a transformation; this elder sister Miàosè
is also a transformation.
All dharmas spoken by the Buddha are empty, like transformations."
At that time, Miàosè, hearing this Dharma,
became free from dust, detached from defilement, and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
She eliminated doubt and regret, not following others' words,
and attained the fearless Dharma within the Buddha's teaching.
She said to Xuǎnzé:
"What you have done is excellent.
Being able, within the Buddha's Dharma,
to joyfully cultivate the holy life,
I too shall leave home for the Dharma and practice the path."
In the past, there was a man given to lust and indulgence.
His mind was fixated on women.
His thoughts could not be separated from them.
He desired to converse and communicate with them even in his dreams.
At that time, his wife fell ill.
Her bones wasted away and her flesh diminished.
A learned monk who was acquainted with the family came and went.
The wife said to the monk,
"The illness I suffer from now causes me to grow weaker day and night.
For the sake of his intentions, I wish to express my feelings.
May I do so?"
The monk replied,
"Speak freely, without worry.
If there are hidden matters,
I will conceal them and not let them be exposed."
The woman said,
"My husband has many desires.
Day and night he harasses me, allowing no rest for eating or sleeping.
Because of this, I have fallen ill and fear I may not recover."
The monk said,
"If your husband approaches you,
tell him these words:
'The Dharma of a Stream-enterer—
is it proper to act like this?'"
The wife then told her husband.
The husband felt deeply ashamed.
Reflecting inwardly, he thought,
"I am a Stream-enterer.
I should not continue with such intentions."
In a quiet place, he contemplated the fruit of Non-returner.
Knowing he had attained the path,
he no longer engaged with women.
The wife asked her husband,
"Why have you now permanently ceased your desires?"
The husband said,
"I have truly seen you.
How could I continue to associate with you?"
The wife said to her husband,
"You say you have truly seen me.
What fault do I have?
I have always been chaste and pure,
never violating the propriety of a woman.
Why do you insult me
to such an extent?"
The woman then gathered her five kinds of relatives and clan members.
She told them,
"Now my husband's regard for me has grown distant and cold.
He has permanently ceased affection and even insults me,
claiming he has seen me.
Now, before everyone, he can explain himself."
The husband said,
"Wait, allow me to present evidence to clarify myself."
The husband returned home.
He painted a beautiful vase,
filled it with filth,
tightly sealed its mouth,
and perfumed it with fragrant flowers.
He returned to the gathering.
He said to his wife,
"Do you truly love me?
If you love me, you can embrace and play with this vase
as you would my body."
The wife followed his words,
embracing and fondling the vase, unwilling to part with it.
Seeing his wife attached to the vase,
the husband immediately broke it.
Foul filth overflowed, and maggots appeared.
He then said to his wife,
"Can you still embrace this broken vase now?"
She replied,
"I would rather die than go near this.
I would rather enter a pit of fire,
throw myself into deep water,
jump from a high mountain,
with head and feet separated,
than ever go near it."
The husband said, "You now see correctly.
I regard your body as worse than this vase.
From head to foot,
analyze and contemplate:
the thirty-six impure substances—
what is there to crave?"
He further recited a verse:
There was a bhikṣu
who attained the cessation of perception and feeling.
When going for alms,
he put on his robe and went to the dining hall.
That day, the monastery struck the ghaṇṭā
late. That bhikṣu,
diligent and earnest, thought:
"Why should I waste this time
without contemplating the future?
When will the ghaṇṭā be struck?"
He then made a vow:
"I will enter the cessation of perception and feeling,
and arise only when the ghaṇṭā is struck."
At that time, a calamity arose in that saṅghārāma.
The bhikṣus
abandoned the saṅghārāma and left.
After three months,
the calamity was resolved.
The bhikṣus then reassembled and struck the ghaṇṭā.
That bhikṣu arose from his samādhi and immediately died.
Later, there was an alms-seeking bhikṣu
who attained the cessation of perception and feeling.
In the early part of the day,
he intended to go for alms.
At that time, heavy rain fell.
He thought:
"If I enter the village, my robe will be soiled.
If I do not go, why return empty-handed?"
Without contemplating the future at that moment, he made a vow and entered samādhi:
"I will arise only when the rain stops."
Some say
the rain lasted half a month;
others say it lasted a month.
When the rain finally stopped, that bhikṣu arose from samādhi and immediately died.
In the country of Mathurā,
in the Nyagrodha Garden,
there was a bhikṣu
meditating in a quiet place.
There was also a poisonous snake
coiled beneath his seat.
The bhikṣu was asleep,
his head sometimes lowered, sometimes raised.
The poisonous snake thought:
"If this person sees me, he will surely try to kill me."
It then threw its whole body at him.
The bhikṣu died and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Heavenly maidens came to attend to him.
The devaputra said,
"Sisters, do not come near me.
If you come near, I will certainly violate the precepts."
The maidens thought:
"This devaputra must have been a śramaṇa in his previous life,
thus reborn here to enjoy heavenly blessings."
The heavenly maidens each held up a mirror to show the devaputra his face.
Seeing his heavenly attire and crown,
he realized he had been reborn in heaven.
He immediately rose from his seat,
saw his attendants,
walked to the garden,
sat under a tree,
and sat upright contemplating, seeking samādhi.
In a pond, there were birds of different kinds
facing each other, crying mournfully.
Their sorrowful calls harmonized.
He desired to attain the path,
but could not accomplish it.
At that time, the devaputra
descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Jambudvīpa,
came to the World-Honored One,
and said,
"When my heavenly blessings are exhausted,
I will fall into the hells of Mount Tài.
Thus, I will revolve endlessly.
Please have compassion and save me, enabling me to cross over."
The Buddha preached the Dharma to him.
Right there on his seat, his defilements were exhausted, and he attained the pure Dharma-eye.
According to the usual internal rules,
those entering a monastery to listen to the Dharma or pay respects to the Buddha
should all remove their head coverings.
At that time, there was a king
who naturally had little hair
and moreover had sores.
He also wore leather sandals.
Relying on his noble status,
he wrapped his head with layered cloth
and entered the hall to listen to the sutra.
The king said to the bhikṣu,
"Preach the Dharma for me."
The bhikṣu said,
"The Tathāgata has a teaching:
Do not preach the Dharma for those wearing leather sandals."
Hearing this, the king became angry.
He immediately removed his leather sandals and said to the bhikṣu,
"You, quickly preach the Dharma to satisfy my wishes.
If you go against my original intention, I will behead you."
The bhikṣu told the king,
"Also, the Tathāgata's precepts prohibit preaching the Dharma for those with covered heads."
The king, enraged, exerted his heavenly authority and said,
"You wish to humiliate me.
Now I have removed my head covering.
Listen as you preach the Dharma.
If you do not resolve my deluded knots,
I will have your body divided into three parts."
The bhikṣu recited a verse.
The king felt ashamed and remorseful.
He immediately rose from his seat.
Prostrated himself with five limbs touching the ground.
He repented and sought to eradicate the faults of body, speech, and mind.
Kneeling with hands clasped, he addressed the bhikṣu, saying:
"I wonder if this verse
came from the divine mouth of the Tathāgata,
or if the venerable one, knowing my thoughts, spoke it?"
The bhikṣu replied to the king:
"This verse was spoken by the Tathāgata.
It has been passed down for a long time."
The king reflected to himself:
"Excellent, O Great Sage!
With your threefold wisdom, nothing is beyond your understanding.
You knew that in the future, someone like me
would harbor harmful thoughts.
Now I deeply repent and vow not to create new offenses."
The bhikṣu expounded the Dharma.
The king, seated there, saw all defilements vanish and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
The Buddha was in Śrāvastī.
There was a certain bhikṣu
who daily traveled to a desolate path among graves outside the city.
He had to cross another's field to reach that place.
The field owner, seeing him, became angry:
"What kind of ascetic is this?
Daily coming and going without cultivating virtue."
He then questioned the ascetic:
"What kind of mendicant are you,
wandering back and forth in my field,
trampling it into paths?"
The ascetic replied:
"I have a dispute and am seeking witnesses."
At that time, the field owner,
due to past karmic connections, was destined to attain liberation.
He followed the ascetic,
secretly trailing behind.
They arrived at the gravesite,
where corpses lay scattered.
Swollen and foul-smelling,
birds and beasts devoured them,
scattering remains everywhere.
Some were partially eaten, others not.
Some resembled gray pigeons.
Maggots wriggled and swarmed.
The stench was unbearable.
Crows, foxes, dogs,
old vultures, owls,
feasted on the dead bodies.
The bhikṣu raised his hand
and said to the man:
"These birds and beasts
are my witnesses."
The man asked:
"How can these birds and beasts
be witnesses?
With whom are you disputing, O bhikṣu?"
The bhikṣu replied:
"The mind is afflicted,
full of defilements and suffering.
I observe these corpses,
contemplating their foul impurities.
Then I return to my dwelling
and examine my own body,
from head to toe,
finding no difference from them.
Yet this mind
races in countless directions,
chasing illusions and deceptions,
the objects of sight, sound, smell, taste, and touch.
I now wish to understand the mind's true nature.
Your mind should now give rise to this thought:
'Do not let it lead me into hell or the realm of hungry ghosts.'
I am still an ordinary person, not free from all bonds.
Yet this mind, like a thief, does not obey.
For this reason, I come daily to the wilderness
to practice contemplation on foulness and impurity.
I also reflect on the mind itself,
this agitated, confused, and unstable mind.
Now I must change and not create conditions for evil."
At that time, the field owner,
hearing the ascetic's teaching,
wiped away tears with his hand,
choked with emotion, unable to speak.
Indeed, that field owner,
