during the ten thousand years of Kāśyapa Buddha,
had practiced contemplation on impurity.
Immediately, he discerned
the thirty-six impure substances of the body,
foul and unclean.
Then, both the bhikṣu and the field owner,
right there in the desolate, fearsome graveyard, attained the path of Stream-enterer.
There was a blind bhikṣu
who could not see.
While sewing his robe by hand,
the needle came unthreaded.
He said:
"Who loves merit?
Please thread this needle for me."
At that moment, the Buddha came to him.
He said to the bhikṣu:
"I am one who loves merit.
I have come to thread it for you."
The bhikṣu recognized the Buddha's voice,
quickly rose and bowed.
He addressed the Buddha:
"The Buddha's merit is already complete.
Why do you say you love merit?"
The Buddha replied:
"Although my merit is complete,
I deeply understand the causes and effects of merit.
Among all beings,
I am foremost in this.
Because of this merit,
I, as a bhikṣu, praise merit."
He then expounded the Dharma for him.
At that time, this bhikṣu attained the pure Dharma-eye,
and his physical eyes regained sight.
A Tripiṭaka bhikṣu from Jìbīn,
practicing the method of dwelling in the forest,
came to a royal temple
where a great assembly was being held.
The gatekeeper, seeing his coarse and worn clothes, barred him from entering.
This happened repeatedly.
Because of his poor clothing, he was always prevented from entering.
He then devised a plan:
he borrowed fine clothes and came again.
The gatekeeper did not stop him.
Once seated at the assembly,
he received various fine foods.
He first offered them to the clothes.
People asked him:
"Why are you doing this?"
He replied:
"I, a bhikṣu, came many times but was never allowed to enter.
Now, because of these clothes, I can sit here
and receive various fine foods.
Therefore, I first offer them to the clothes."
There was a man of noble family
who abandoned his home, left his wife, and forsook all relatives
to become a śramaṇa.
His wife was beautiful and charming.
Seeing her husband leave home,
she remarried.
The nobleman heard of this,
and thoughts arose in his mind:
memories of amusement and intimacy with his wife.
He became sorrowful and troubled,
no longer able to joyfully cultivate pure brahmacarya.
He decided to return home.
The other bhikṣus heard of this
and went to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha summoned him to dispel the defilements of delusion and desire, to calm his thoughts.
The nobleman immediately realized the holy Dharma.
The bhikṣus then addressed the World-Honored One:
"If not for the Tathāgata, who could have accomplished this?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣu
not only in this life has his mind constantly dwelling on desire.
In the distant past,
there was a king
named Fāngjì.
His palace had countless concubines,
who were licentious, quarrelsome, and refused to live in harmony.
After quarreling,
they would leave the palace.
Fāngjì searched for them but did not know where they went.
He became sorrowful and unhappy, unable to free himself.
At that time, there was a sage
endowed with the five supernatural powers,
able to fly with his spiritual feet, of immense power and majesty.
His name was Wúlè.
Flying in the sky,
he suddenly descended
to expound on the difficulty of abandoning desire and the virtue of renunciation,
to leave home and practice the path,
cultivating the four Brahmā practices.
After his life ended,
he was reborn in the Brahmā heaven."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The king Fāngjì of that time
is this bhikṣu.
The sage Wúlè
is myself."
In the past, a family of the Caṇḍāla caste gave birth to seven sons.
The six elder brothers attained the path of Stream-enterer.
The youngest remained an ordinary person.
The mother, a woman of the Caṇḍāla caste, attained the path of Non-returner.
All seven brothers received the five precepts.
According to the customary practice of that country,
the Caṇḍālas carried out executions.
Men and women of the kingdom
who committed murder, theft, adultery, and other grave offenses
were all executed by the Caṇḍālas.
At that time, the king summoned the eldest son and said,
"There are criminals deserving death.
You shall carry out their execution."
The son bowed and pleaded on his own behalf,
earnestly hoping for leniency and forgiveness:
"I have received the five precepts
and guard my conduct with utmost caution.
I dare not even kill an ant.
I cannot commit wrongdoing.
I would rather take my own life
than dare to violate the precepts."
The king, enraged,
ordered his execution in the marketplace.
The son again addressed the king:
"My body belongs to the king as a subject,
but my mind is my own treasure.
If you wish to kill me, then kill me.
I cannot comply with your command."
The king immediately ordered him beheaded.
He then summoned the younger brothers in turn.
All six declared:
"Having received the precepts, we dare not carry out executions."
The king's wrath blazed fiercely,
and he had them all killed.
He then summoned the youngest son.
Both mother and son came.
Seeing the mother arrive, the king's anger doubled.
"When I executed the six elder sons,
you did not accompany them.
Now that I summon the youngest,
why have you come?"
The mother replied:
"I beg you to hear my humble words to explain my reasoning.
As for the previous six sons,
they had all attained the path of Stream-enterer.
Even if Your Majesty were to grind their bodies to dust,
they would not give rise to a single hair's worth of malice.
But this youngest one,
remains an ordinary person.
Although he cultivates goodness in body,
he has not yet attained the Dharma of the path.
Therefore, I am concerned for my son.
Since he has not yet attained the path,
he might lose his resolve.
Fearing the king's command,
and cherishing his own life and form,
he might break the precepts and carry out killings.
Upon the destruction of his body and the end of his life,
he would fall into the great mountain hell.
Out of pity and concern for my son,
I have therefore accompanied him."
The king asked the mother further:
"Did the six sons who died earlier
all attain the path of Stream-enterer?"
She answered:
"They all attained it."
The king asked the mother again:
"What path have you, mother, attained?"
The mother replied:
"I have attained the path of Non-returner."
Hearing these words,
the king threw himself to the ground,
lamenting the injustice and blaming himself:
"I have created roots of sin.
With deliberate intent, I killed six Stream-enterers."
His body and mind troubled, he could not sit still. He immediately prepared fragrant oil and ghee, and firewood.
He took the six corpses and cremated them.
He erected six stūpas and made offerings to atone for the killings.
Three times a day he repented,
wishing to eradicate his sins.
Gradually, they became less severe.
He also gave wealth and goods
to that old mother.
On observance days,
he repeatedly repented,
hoping his offenses would lessen,
and he might avoid hell.
At that time, Devadatta,
with a mind full of poison, slandered the Tathāgata.
He claimed to possess the Way himself.
People reproached him.
Devas, dragons, spirits, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings
all together made him understand:
"You wish to destroy the Buddha—
it is like raising your hand to strike the sun and moon."
Devadatta heard this,
but his mind remained unchanged.
At that time, the bhikṣus
fully reported this to the Buddha:
"What grave grievance does Devadatta hold, harboring such enmity?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Devadatta is not only like this in this life;
he has been so for countless lifetimes.
In a past age,
there was a brāhmaṇa maiden,
of outstanding beauty, with features of the highest order.
According to brāhmaṇa custom, a maiden was to be given to one learned in the scriptures.
They invited five hundred fellow students,
provided for them for three months, and observed their knowledge.
Among those five hundred,
one was profoundly learned,
but he was aged, with an ugly face and greenish eyes.
Her parents were distressed,
and the maiden was also troubled.
"How can I become this man's wife?
It would be like marrying a resentful ghost.
What can be done about it?"
At that time, from a distant land, there was a brāhmaṇa
who was young in years,
with exceptionally handsome features,
intelligent and wise.
Hearing that those brāhmaṇas had invited fellow students intending to bestow the maiden,
he immediately went there.
He posed challenging questions to the assembled brāhmaṇas.
All were exhausted and had no reply.
The wisdom of the five hundred could not match his.
The maiden's parents and the maiden herself,
upon seeing him, were greatly delighted.
"In seeking a son-in-law, today we have finally attained our wish."
The elderly brāhmaṇa said:
"I am already old, and it was long promised to me
that the maiden would be my wife.
Moreover, all the offerings I have received
I will give to you.
Pity my advanced age;
do not disgrace me."
The young man replied:
"One cannot transgress the Dharma to follow human sentiment.
I should accept her."
When the three months concluded,
they gave the maiden to the young man.
The elderly one,
harboring poisonous malice in his heart,
thought: "They have disgraced me and taken my wife."
"Wherever we are reborn, I will be your enemy.
I will never let this go."
The young brāhmaṇa constantly practiced a mind of kindness.
He alone harbored harm.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"That elderly brāhmaṇa of that time
is now Devadatta.
The young brāhmaṇa
is myself.
That maiden is Gopī."
Tiáodá and King Āshèshì
conspired to destroy the Buddha and his disciples.
The king ordered the people of the country not to honor the Buddha.
At that time, Shèlìfú and others,
along with Bhikṣuṇī Póhétí and others,
each took their disciples and left for other countries.
Only the Buddha and five hundred arhats
remained in the Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain.
Tiáodá went to the king and said,
"The Buddha's disciples have now scattered.
There are still five hundred disciples by the Buddha's side.
I hope Your Majesty will invite the Buddha into the city tomorrow.
I will make five hundred elephants drink
until they are drunk and have them trample him to death.
I will then become the Buddha and teach the world."
The king heard this and was delighted.
He immediately went to invite the Buddha.
The Buddha knew of their plot
and replied,
"Excellent."
The king withdrew and left,
returning to report to Tiáodá.
The next day at mealtime,
the Buddha and the arhats entered the city gate together.
The drunken elephants trumpeted and charged forward,
crashing into walls,
breaking trees, and causing the entire city to tremble in fear.
The five hundred arhats flew up into the air.
Only the Venerable Ānán remained by the side.
The drunken elephants, heads lowered, charged straight toward the Buddha.
The Buddha raised his five fingers, transforming them into five lions,
which roared in unison,
shaking heaven and earth.
The drunken elephants fell to the ground, not daring to lift their heads.
Sobering up, they shed tears and repented of their wrongdoing.
The king and his subjects were all filled with awe and reverence.
The World-Honored One slowly proceeded to the king's palace,
and after eating with the arhats, he gave a blessing.
The king said to the Buddha,
"My nature is unenlightened,
and I believed those slanderous words,
committing such wicked deeds.
I beseech you to extend your great compassion
and forgive my delusion and foolishness."
The Buddha told Āshèshì and the great assembly,
"There are eight things in the world
that give rise to slander,
all stemming from reputation, leading to great offenses.
What are these eight?
Gain and loss, defamation and praise, acclaim and criticism, suffering and pleasure.
From ancient times to the present, few have not been deluded by them."
The Buddha then spoke a verse, saying:
"Long ago, there was a king
who loved to eat goose meat.
He often sent hunters
to set nets and catch geese.
Each day, one goose was sent
to supply the king's meals.
At that time, there was a goose king
leading five hundred geese flying down to search for food.
The goose king fell into the net and was caught by the hunter.
The other geese, startled, flew away but hovered nearby, unwilling to leave.
At that time, one goose repeatedly circled and followed,
unafraid of bows and arrows, crying mournfully until it coughed up blood,
not resting day or night.
The hunter saw this
and was moved by its loyalty.
He then released the goose king, allowing it to rejoin the flock.
The flock of geese, overjoyed to have their king back, circled around him.
At that time, the hunter
reported everything to the king.
The king, moved by their loyalty,
ordered that geese no longer be hunted.
The goose king at that time
was myself.
The one goose was Ānán.
The flock of five hundred geese
are now the five hundred arhats.
The king who ate goose meat
is now Your Majesty.
The hunter at that time
was Tiáodá. From past lives until now,
he has always sought to harm me.
Through the power of my great compassion,
I have been saved each time.
Not harboring resentment or malice,
I have attained Buddhahood.
The king and his ministers
were all filled with joy.
Once there was a bhikṣu.
His name was Tiáodá.
He was intelligent and widely learned.
For twelve years he sat in meditation, entered samādhi, and his mind did not waver or change.
For twelve years he practiced the dhūta austerities without any deficiency or reduction.
He cultivated the contemplation of impurity.
He thoroughly understood the incoming and outgoing breath.
The foremost worldly dharmas,
even up to the summit dharmas, he analyzed one by one.
The Buddhist sūtras he had recited numbered sixty thousand,
so many that elephants could not carry them.
Later, his mind turned regressive and gradually gave rise to evil thoughts.
He hoped for people's offerings and became attached to worldly gain and support.
He went to the World-Honored One, bowed his head at his feet,
stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O World-Honored One, I pray you explain the path of supernatural powers.
Having heard this, I will diligently cultivate it.
Once I attain supernatural powers,
I will travel to other regions, teaching and transforming beings everywhere."
The World-Honored One told him:
"For now, set aside supernatural powers.
Why not study the four
meanings of impermanence,
suffering, emptiness, and non-self?"
At that time, the bhikṣu Tiáodá
then thought this:
"The reason the Tathāgata does not speak to me of supernatural powers
is that he fears I might surpass him and he would be shamed by inferiority."
Tiáodá then left the Tathāgata
and went to Śāriputra,
seeking the path of supernatural powers.
Śāriputra then said to Tiáodá:
"For now, set this aside.
Why not cultivate the four impermanences?"
Tiáodá considered:
"This Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom.
But as I see it, he is like a firefly compared to the sun and moon.
No one equals me in recitation and study.
Even I do not yet understand the path of supernatural powers;
how could Śāriputra possibly understand it?"
He immediately left
and went to Maudgalyāyana,
seeking the path of supernatural powers.
Maudgalyāyana said:
"Enough, enough, Tiáodá.
One who is just beginning should first study the four impermanences.
Then one should diligently cultivate the four dhyānas.
Only then can one attain the path of supernatural powers."
Tiáodá became angry:
"This Maudgalyāyana boasts of his supernatural powers, claiming no one equals him.
The reason he does not give them to me
is that he fears he is not my equal.
If I obtained them, he would have no fame.
Now I have sought the path of supernatural powers everywhere,
and no one teaches me.
My younger brother Ānanda is widely learned and erudite,
complete with all virtues. I shall now go and ask him."
He said to Ānanda:
"I have heard you are skilled in understanding the path of supernatural powers.
Please explain it to me.
Once I attain supernatural powers, I will travel to other regions,
teaching and transforming beings everywhere."
Ānanda then explained it to him.
After Tiáodá heard it,
he went to a quiet place, concentrated his mind single-pointedly,
moving from coarse to subtle, and again from subtle arising back to coarse.
He lifted his body with his mind and lifted his mind with his body.
Body and mind joined together, gradually leaving the ground.
At first like a sesame seed, then turning like a walnut,
he gradually left the ground, from ground to bed,
from bed to roof, from roof to the sky.
In empty space, he performed eighteen transformations,
appearing and disappearing at will.
He transformed into an infant child,
with upright form and appearance,
with five places on his head and a face like a peach blossom.
He sat on the knee of Prince Ajātaśatru,
sometimes laughing, sometimes crying, displaying infantile mannerisms.
However, the prince knew it was Tiáodá's body,
and played with him all day without tiring or being satisfied.
Sometimes he would suckle saliva,
or lift his body and pass him from hand to hand.
The prince thought:
"Tiáodá's supernatural powers surpass those of Gautama.
He can perform countless transformations."
Ajātaśatru daily provided five hundred pots of food,
offering them in a timely manner without allowing any lack.
At that time, many bhikṣus
saw Ajātaśatru providing for Tiáodá
and fully reported it to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Do not covet Tiáodá's offerings.
Tiáodá ensnares himself and also ensnares others.
Both fall into transgression.
It is like a banana tree:
a foolish person seeks fruit but cannot obtain it.
So too with bamboo and reeds.
A mule carrying a foal causes both lives to perish.
Once there was a flock of vultures, each hatching and nursing its young.
A vulture told its chick:
'If you learn to fly and hover in empty space,
see the ground as a plate and be careful not to fly too high.
There is the Suìlán wind that will harm you,
scattering your head, brain, limbs, and joints in different places.'
At that time, the chick did not follow its father's teaching,
flew beyond the limit, was blown by the wind, and perished in a different place.
You bhikṣus, do not give rise to such thoughts.
Bhikṣus should know it is like a group of turtles
who told their young:
'Protect yourselves and do not go to a certain place.
There are hunters there who will capture you and divide your bodies into five parts.'
At that time, the young turtles did not heed their words,
went to that place and enjoyed themselves together,
and were captured by hunters.
Some returned safely and securely.
The turtle asked its young: 'Where have you come from?'
The young replied to their parents:
'We went together to observe that place.
We did not see hunters,
only saw long threads chasing after us.'
The turtle told its young:
'These threads have pursued you for a long time.
Ancestors, grandparents, all perished because of these threads.'
Bhikṣus should know:
It is like a fox day and night seeking excrement.
Having eaten the feces of livestock and beasts,
it then defecates itself.
The bhikṣu Tiáodá,
greedy for offerings, is also like this.
Once in the great country of Yuèzhī,
the customary practice was to feed pigs with fried wheat in butter.
At that time, a young palace horse said to its mother:
'We exert effort for the king regardless of distance,
all responding to his command.
Yet we eat grass and fodder,
and drink muddy water.'
The horse told its young:
'Do not give rise to this thought, envying that fried wheat in butter.
Before long, the proof will manifest itself.'
As the festival time approached and the new year was about to arrive,
every household tied up pigs and threw them into boiling cauldrons.
They cried out loudly.
The mother horse told her young:
'Do you still remember the fried wheat in butter?
If you wish to know the proof, go and observe.'
The young horses, knowing this was indeed so,
then understood the true nature of the fried delicacy.
When eating grass, if they encountered wheat,
they guarded against it and did not eat.
The Buddha spoke a verse, saying:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Tiáodá is dangerous and harmful.
He and others praise each other falsely.
The bhikṣu Jūjiālì praises Tiáodá.
Tiáodá also praises Jūjiālì.
Those two have no righteousness, no principle."
The bhikṣus heard this and said:
"O Great Sage,
observe the bhikṣu Jūjiālì:
for a long time he has relied on the orthodox canon, the teachings of the Dharma and Vinaya.
He left home out of faith.
Yet he falsely praises Tiáodá.
Tiáodá praises Jūjiālì.
Both take the non-virtuous as virtuous
and the virtuous as non-virtuous."
The Buddha said:
"These foolish and dull-witted ones
were also like this in a past life.
In the past,
a eunuch died and was discarded among paper mulberry trees.
At that time, a fox and a crow came together to eat the flesh.
They praised each other.
The crow said:
The fox praised, saying:
Thus they went back and forth.
At that time, a great ṛṣi said:
'Falsely praising each other, their words empty and without truth.'
The fox was Tiáodá.
The crow was Jūjiālì.
The ṛṣi was the Bodhisattva."
Tiáodá
went to the place of the World-Honored One.
He bowed with his head at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I observe the Tathāgata:
his complexion has changed, his faculties are entirely mature,
he has passed the prime of youth and is approaching decrepit old age.
I only wish, World-Honored One,
that you would retire to a quiet chamber and enjoy meditation and concentration.
As for the fourfold assembly, I hope you will entrust them to me.
I will instruct and discipline them no differently than the Buddha.
I will provide for them at all times, ensuring the four necessities are never lacking.”
The Buddha said:
“Shame on you, foolish man!
You give no thought to the calamity that will follow.
Even the bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana
I have not yet entrusted;
how much less could I entrust the noble assembly to you, a lazy and wicked man?”
Tiáodá inwardly stirred with jealousy.
Hearing the World-Honored One’s words,
his anger doubled.
“Today the Tathāgata praises the bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana,
but looks down on this humble disciple.
I must find a way to destroy both master and disciples,
so that the beings in this realm will neither see their forms nor hear their voices.”
Then the bhikṣu Tiáodá
rose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew.
Everywhere he went, he schemed and used clever, deceitful words
to delude ordinary people, enticing several tens to follow him.
In every place, he urged and encouraged them together.
To put it briefly:
When the Buddha was surrounded by the great assembly, teaching the Dharma,
Tiáodá said to his own disciples:
“Do not listen to what Gautama says; it does not accord with the true Dharma.
I have profound sūtras and excellent meanings,
which I will teach you.
He only sought expedient means to ruin the noble assembly.”
The Buddha said: “Enough, enough.
Tiáodá,
be careful not to give rise to the intention to disrupt and ruin the noble assembly.
Later you will suffer retribution, the pain of which will be unbearable.”
Tiáodá stubbornly persisted and would not change, knowing his own intention was correct.
The Buddha, observing past causes and conditions and karmic debts, knew it could not be turned back.
Tiáodá led five hundred disciples,
and the Tathāgata also led five hundred disciples.
Together they traveled beside Mount Bǎo Jī.
The Bodhisattva’s disciples were broad-minded, benevolent, gentle, and harmonious.
He taught them the true Dharma.
They upheld the precepts, and in all their comings and goings, advances and halts, they did not transgress the proper order.
Tiáodá’s followers spoke coarsely.
Their words often gave rise to anger.
When speaking with his disciples, it was like quarreling and disputing with enemies.
The disciples grew weary and distressed, and all abandoned him.
They went to the Bodhisattva
and each declared:
“I have a thousand disciples,
fully endowed with virtues,
unparalleled in the world—who can match them?”
Tiáodá grew angry
and immediately made a vow:
“This man today
has enticed my disciples and ruined my following.
Even if he becomes a Buddha, I will ruin his disciples,
just as now.”
The Tathāgata observed and knew that Tiáodá
would certainly ruin the noble assembly; there was no doubt.
The Tathāgata then rose from his seat
and left the assembly.
There are five things
by which one knows the assembly of monks cannot be disrupted:
First, when the Tathāgata is present,
due to the Tathāgata’s awesome spiritual power and not abandoning his original vow.
Second, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa,
if someone says,
‘I have now attained Buddhahood, achieved supreme perfect enlightenment,’
one should ask him,
‘Where were you when Śākyamuni Buddha was in the world?’
Third, when there has never been an evil time.
Fourth, when the bhikṣus do not compete for offerings.
Fifth, when the wise and spiritually powerful disciples are harmonious.
The Tathāgata, using his knowledge of past lives, observed
and knew for certain that Tiáodá would disrupt and ruin the assembly of monks.
The Tathāgata then left and departed.
Tiáodá, remaining behind, taught the Dharma to the assembly:
“If there are beings
who regard me as their master and receive my teachings and precepts,
they should practice five dharmas. Any bhikṣu who cultivates these five dharmas
will quickly attain liberation, exhaust all outflows, and become free from outflows.
Why rely on Gautama’s eightfold right path?”
He said to Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana:
“I have gained great benefit, becoming the honored one of the three realms, resembling the Tathāgata.”
The Buddha said to Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana:
“I have a backache and wish to rest a little.
You two should teach the Dharma to the noble assembly.”
Tiáodá lay down on his right side, wanting to sleep.
A heavenly being forced Tiáodá to lie on his left side; the heavenly being again loathed his deceit. There was speech, snoring sounds appeared outwardly, and foul odors spread far.
Maudgalyāyana, using his spiritual power,
soared into the sky, performing eighteen transformations.
He sat, lay down, walked, and meditated, emerging and submerging freely.
Śāriputra addressed the assembly:
“The Tathāgata’s body and spiritual virtues are immeasurable.
He is fully endowed with all-knowledge.
He penetrates the infinite past and the boundless future.
The Tathāgata’s Dharma
yields visible results in this life, happiness, and the unconditioned.
It is what the wise cultivate and learn,
not what the foolish practice.
The Tathāgata’s noble assembly
has fully accomplished the fivefold Dharma body.
They are worthy of respect, honor, service, and offerings.
They are a field of merit, a good refuge for beings.”
Then each of the bhikṣus thought:
“We are foolish and deluded, not recognizing what is true and genuine.
We abandoned the substance for the flower, discarded the root for the branch.
Now, observing what these two worthies say is rare in the world.
Should we not abandon this Tiáodá and join the Tathāgata’s assembly?
Would that not be joyful?”
Śāriputra knew their thoughts.
He immediately rose from his seat,
and five hundred bhikṣus all followed him.
Maudgalyāyana followed behind, chasing after them.
The bhikṣu Jūbōlí
kicked Tiáodá with his right foot, saying:
“Wicked Tiáodá, why are you sleeping so soundly?
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana
have taken all your disciples away.”
Tiáodá woke from sleep, deeply distressed and sorrowful.
In ancient times,
there was a young brāhmaṇa who recited Kṣatriya texts in a mountain cave.
A wild fox came to his side
and intently listened to the recitation, understanding something in his mind.
He thought:
“If I understand these texts,
I am fit to become king among the beasts.”
He then set out wandering.
He met a thin, weak wild fox
and wanted to kill him.
The other said: “Why do you want to kill me?”
He replied:
“I am the king of beasts.
You do not submit to me.”
The other said:
“I beg you not to kill me.
I will follow you.”
So the two foxes traveled together.
They met another fox,
and the question and answer were as above.
Thus, one after another, they subdued all foxes.
Then with the group of foxes, they subdued all elephants.
Next, with the multitude of elephants, they subdued all tigers.
Then with the multitude of tigers, they subdued all lions.
Thus, he temporarily became king among the beasts.
He again thought:
“I am the king of beasts.
I should not take a beast as my wife.”
So he mounted a white elephant
and had all the beasts surround the country of Jiāyí
in hundreds of thousands of circles.
The king sent an envoy to ask:
“Why are you doing this?”
The wild fox replied:
“I am the king of beasts.
I should marry your daughter.
If you do not give her to me, I will destroy your country.”
The envoy returned and reported to the king.
The king assembled his ministers for discussion.
Except for one minister,
all said she should be given.
“What the state relies on is only elephants and horses.
We have elephants and horses; they have lions.
When elephants and horses smell their scent, they will be terrified and lie on the ground.
In battle, we will certainly not prevail.
Why begrudge one daughter and lose a whole country?”
At that time, one great minister, wise and far-sighted,
said to the king:
“Your servant observes that, from ancient times to the present, it has never been heard or seen that a king’s daughter is given to a lowly beast.
Although your servant is weak and ignorant,
I will certainly kill this fox, and the beasts will scatter and flee.”
The king then asked him how.
The minister replied:
“Your Majesty need only send an envoy to set a date for battle
and ask for one condition:
that the lions fight first and roar afterward.
He, thinking we are afraid, will certainly order the lions to roar first and fight later.
On the day of battle,
Your Majesty should order everyone in the city to plug their ears.
The king followed his advice and then sent out the army.
As the armies were about to engage,
the wild fox indeed ordered the lions to roar first.
When the wild fox heard it, his heart broke into seven pieces.
He fell from the elephant to the ground.
The beasts scattered and fled.”
The Buddha spoke a verse:
He told the bhikṣus:
“At that time, the king of Jiāyí was I.
The wise and far-sighted minister was Śāriputra.
The wild fox king was Tiáodá.”
Tiáodá was in the city of Rājagṛha.
He harbored a mind to harm.
Later, the matter was exposed.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru
said to Tiáodá:
"You should leave the country and not stay here."
The sixteen great kingdoms have all heard of this.
Tiáodá committed evil deeds against the Tathāgata.
Upon hearing this, Tiáodá was inwardly filled with sorrow and distress.
He then returned to his homeland, entangled by resentment.
He rashly intruded into the palace of the Bodhisattva.
He said to Gūyí:
"I wish to make you my first consort.
I wonder if the holy maiden would consent to this?"
Gūyí replied:
"First, give me your right hand so I may hold it."
Tiáodá extended his hand for her to grasp.
His wrist bones shattered, and blood flowed from his five fingers.
At that moment, he fainted and remained unconscious for a long time before reviving.
At that time, Tiáodá proceeded further into the palace.
He sat on the Bodhisattva's bed.
The palace attendants saw him, seized him, and threw him off the bed.
He injured his left hip and was unable to walk.
He was carried back to his own residence.
All the Śākyas were displeased and came to tell him:
"You should now go to the Buddha and repent."
Tiáodá heard this.
He secretly devised a cunning scheme.
He secretly made iron claws.
He coated them with poison.
Outwardly gentle, inwardly he harbored hatred.
At that time, Tiáodá recalled what the Buddha had said:
"The Śākyamuni ascetic always says this:
'If the body has no sores, poison cannot harm it.
Poison can do nothing to sores.
Without evil, nothing is created.'
I will now go pretending to repent.
I will use the claws to scratch his feet.
The poison will flow, and he will surely die."
People carried him on a litter to the World-Honored One.
When they were twenty-one ren away, he said to the people around him:
"Put me down, I wish to walk there."
They immediately set him down.
At that moment, fierce flames erupted and enveloped his body.
He was taken to hell.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, Dípódáduō
wished to break the harmony of the Sangha.
The bhikkhus admonished him three times, but he did not stop.
The Buddha said:
"In a past age,
in the country of Bālínà,
there was a Brahmin
who built a charitable well in the wilderness
to provide for travelers.
As the day drew toward evening,
a pack of wild foxes came to drink the leftover water.
There was a fox king who would not drink water from the ground.
Instead, he would put his head into the jar to drink water.
After drinking, he would lift the jar high and smash it.
The other foxes advised him with good intentions, but he would not listen.
Not just once, he broke fourteen jars.
The Brahmin, observing the fox,
then made a wooden jar that was sturdy and hard to break.
It was easy to enter but hard to exit, and he placed it by the well.
He took a stick and waited.
The pack of foxes gathered.
The king, as before, drank his fill.
He threw it to the ground but could not break it.
The Brahmin then came out with his stick.
He beat the fox to death.
That fox king
is now Dípódáduō.
The pack of foxes
are now the bhikkhus who admonished Dípódáduō."
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikkhus
performed the act of suspension against Dípódáduō.
The six groups of bhikkhus sided with Dípódáduō, sharing his words and views.
The Buddha told the bhikkhus:
"In a past age,
in a secluded place,
there were five hundred monkeys roaming in the forest.
They came to a Nyagrodha tree.
Under the tree was a well with the moon's reflection in it.
The monkey king saw this reflection of the moon.
He said to his companions:
'The moon has now died and fallen into the well.
We must pull it out so that the world is not plunged into long darkness.'
They discussed together: 'How can we pull it out?'
The monkey king said:
'I know how to pull it out.
I will hold onto a branch, and you hold onto my tail.
Linking one after another, we can pull it out.'
The monkeys then did as the king said.
They linked together, but before reaching the water,
the weight of the monkeys broke the weak branch, and all the monkeys fell into the well.
That monkey king
is now Dípódáduō.
The other monkeys at that time
are now the six groups of bhikkhus."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If any being gives rise to a single evil thought
toward the Buddhas of the three times,
or toward Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, and those wearing dyed robes—the various ascetics—
they will incur immeasurable offenses.
Why is this?
Because dyed robes are the emblem of the sages.
If one can generate a mind of reverence toward those wearing dyed robes,
they will obtain immeasurable merit.
It is because of my reverent faith in them that I attained Buddhahood."
Ānanda said:
"How did you show reverence in the past?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In ancient times, countless kalpas ago,
in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great king named Típílǐng, who ruled over eighty-four thousand minor kings.
The world had no Buddha-Dharma.
There was a Pratyekabuddha
who practiced meditation and the path in the mountains.
At that time, various wild animals came to be close to him.
There was a lion
named Jiāluópíqū, whose body was golden and radiant.
He ate fruits and grass and did not harm living beings.
At that time, there was a hunter.
He shaved his head and wore a kasaya.
Carrying a bow and arrows inside, he walked through the marshes.

Seeing the lion asleep, he shot it with a poisoned arrow. The lion, startled awake, was about to charge and harm him, but upon seeing the kasaya, he thought: 'This wearer of dyed robes is a mark of a good person.
If I harm him,
it would be an evil thought toward the sages.'
After this reflection, he restrained himself.
The arrow poison spread internally, and his life was soon to end.
He then spoke a verse: 'Yé luó pó shē shā pó hē.'
As he spoke these words,
the earth and heavens shook greatly, and blood rained from the sky without clouds.
The devas were alarmed.
Using their divine eye, they observed
that the hunter had killed the lion.
They rained heavenly flowers to make offerings to his body.
At that time, the hunter skinned the lion.
He presented it to King Típílǐng.
The king thought:
'The scriptures say:
If an animal is golden, it must be a Bodhisattva.'
He asked the hunter:
'What auspicious signs occurred when the lion died?'
The hunter replied as above.
Hearing this, the king
was filled with both sorrow and joy, and his faith grew even stronger.
He summoned his ministers, elders, and wise men
to explain the meaning.
In an empty forest, there was a sage named Shēmó.
He explained to the king:
'Yé luó means:
"Those who shave their heads and wear dyed robes
will quickly attain liberation from birth and death."
Pó shē shā means:
"They are all close to the sages and near to Nirvana."
Pó hē means:
"They will be revered and looked up to by all devas and people of the world."'
After the sage explained these words,
Típílǐng was overjoyed.
He summoned all the kings to gather at this place.
They made a seven-jeweled chariot and displayed the lion skin,
showing reverence from all.
They burned incense and scattered flowers as offerings.
Later, they also made a golden coffin
to enshrine the lion skin and built a stupa.
That lion,
because he gave rise to a good mind toward the wearer of dyed robes,
for ten billion kalpas became a wheel-turning sage king."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"That lion
was my former self.
That king is now Maitreya.
That sage is now Śāriputra.
That hunter is now Dípódáduō."
The Bhagavān was in Śrāvastī,
at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four great hells.
The first is the great hell of Tiśya.
Flames issue from his body, extending twenty cubits.
The second is the great hell of Gopālī.
Flames issue from his body, extending thirty cubits.
The third is the great hell of Devadatta.
Flames issue from his body, extending forty cubits.
The fourth is the great hell of Mòqiēlí.
Flames issue from his body, extending sixty cubits.
If there are people who wish to seek peace and safety,
to obtain relief for him,
even if twenty great oceans of water were poured over his body,
that ocean water would be exhausted, yet the fire would still not be extinguished.
It is like molten copper.
If someone were to take twenty drops of ocean water
and sprinkle them onto molten copper, the water drops would vanish instantly.
So too, the flames of the bhikṣu Tiśya are not extinguished.
If again there were someone who wished to seek peace and safety, to obtain relief for him,
and again poured twenty great oceans of water
over his body, that water would quickly be exhausted.
The bhikṣu Tiśya, a foolish man,
obstructed the community of bhikṣus, causing them to go without food for a day.
This caused the bhikṣu Tiśya to fall into the great hell.
As for the bhikṣu Gopālī,
if someone wished to bring him peace and safety, to obtain relief for him,
and poured great ocean water over his body,
that ocean water would quickly be exhausted.
It is like copper melted by two suns.
If there were a person
who took thirty drops of ocean water
and put them into the molten copper, they would be consumed and vanish.
The bhikṣu Gopālī, a foolish man,
if someone arose wishing to bring him peace and safety, to obtain relief,
and poured thirty great oceans of water
over his body,
the great ocean water would quickly be exhausted.
The bhikṣu Gopālī, a foolish man,
slandered the bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
His body perished, his life ended, and he was reborn among the three evil destinies,
falling into the Padma Hell.
The bhikṣu Gopālī entered the great hell.
As for the great hell of Devadatta,
if again there were someone who wished to bring him peace and safety, to obtain relief,
and again poured forty great oceans of water
over his body,
that great ocean would quickly be exhausted, yet that fire would not be extinguished.
It is like copper melted by three suns.
If someone were to take forty drops of water
and put them into the molten copper,
they would instantly vanish without remainder.
Devadatta, a foolish man,
if someone arose wishing to bring him peace and safety, to obtain relief,
and poured forty great oceans of water over his body,
that great ocean would quickly be exhausted, yet that fire would not be extinguished.
The reason for this is
that Devadatta, a foolish man,
sought to harm the Tathāgata, killed an arhat bhikṣuṇī,
and disrupted the community of bhikṣus.
His body perished, his life ended, and he was reborn among the three evil destinies, in the Avīci Hell.
The bhikṣu Devadatta entered the great hell.
Flames issue from his body, extending forty cubits.
As for the bhikṣus,
that great hell of Mòqiēlí—
if there were a person wishing to bring him peace and safety,
and poured sixty great oceans of water over his body,
the ocean water would quickly be exhausted, yet that fire would not be extinguished.
It is like copper melted by four suns.
If someone were to take sixty drops of water
and put them into the molten copper, they would instantly vanish.
So too is it with Mòqiēlí.
If sixty great oceans of water were poured over his body,
the great ocean water would quickly be exhausted, yet this fire would not be extinguished.
This Mòqiēlí, a foolish man,
taught and led a hundred koṭis of people
to practice wrong views."
The Buddha said:
At one time,
I was staying in Rājagṛha.
The bhikṣu Shànxīng served as my attendant.
In the first watch of the night,
I was explaining the essentials of the Dharma to Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
According to the disciples' rule, one should retire after one's teacher.
At that time, Shànxīng,
because I sat for a long time, gave rise to an evil thought.
In Rājagṛha, when young boys and girls
cried incessantly, their parents would say to them,
'If you do not stop,
we will hand you over to the Bó Jūluó ghost.'
At that moment, Shànxīng, being constrained,
said to me,
'Quickly enter the meditation chamber, the Bó Jūluó is coming!'
Śakra said,
'World-Honored One,
can such a person
also enter the Buddha's Dharma?'
I said,
'He also possesses Buddha-nature.
He will attain unsurpassed bodhi.'
Although I expounded the Dharma for this Shànxīng,
he had not a single thought of faith or acceptance.
I was in the city of Śīvapura in the country of Kāśī.
Shànxīng served as my attendant.
I entered the city to beg for food.
Immeasurable beings, with humble hearts and eager reverence, wished to see my footprints.
Shànxīng followed behind, destroying them.
Since he could not destroy them,
he caused the beings to give rise to unwholesome thoughts.
After I entered the city,
in a tavern I saw a Nirgrantha
crouching on the ground with a hunched back, eating distillers' grains.
Shànxīng said,
'If there are arhats in the world,
this man is the most supreme.
Why?
Because this man teaches non-causality and non-result.'
I said, 'Foolish man,
have you not constantly heard that
arhats do not drink alcohol, do not harm others, do not deceive, do not steal, and are free from sexual desire?
Such a person
kills his parents and eats distillers' grains—
how can you say he is an arhat?
When this man abandons his body,
he will certainly fall into the Avīci hell.
An arhat
has eternally severed the three evils.
How can you say he is an arhat?'
Shànxīng then said,
'The nature of the four great elements can still be transformed.
To claim that this man must fall into Avīci—
there is no such possibility.'
I said, 'Foolish man,
have you not constantly heard that the Tathāgatas' words of truth are without duplicity?
Although I expounded the Dharma for him,
he had not a single thought of faith or acceptance.
Good man,
when I and Shànxīng were staying in Rājagṛha,
there was a Nirgrantha
named Kǔdé,
who constantly said this:
'The afflictions of beings have no cause or condition.
The liberation of beings also has no cause or condition.'
Shànxīng said,
'If there are arhats in the world,
Kǔdé is the foremost.'
I said,
'Foolish man, the Nirgrantha Kǔdé
is truly not an arhat.
He cannot comprehend the path of an arhat.'
Shànxīng again said,
'Why does an arhat
feel jealousy toward another arhat?'
I said, 'Foolish man,
I do not feel jealousy toward arhats.
Rather, you yourself give rise to evil and wrong views.
If you say Kǔdé is an arhat,
then after seven days,
he will suffer from indigestion, die of abdominal pain,
and be reborn among the vomiting ghosts.
His fellow students will carry his corpse
and place it in the charnel ground.' Shànxīng then went to the Nirgrantha and said,
'Elder,
consider well and employ skillful means
to cause the World-Honored One to fall into false speech.'
Kǔdé abstained from food.
From the first day until the sixth day,
when the seventh day was complete, he then ate black honey,
drank cold water, and died of abdominal pain.
His fellow students carried his corpse and placed it in the charnel ground.
Immediately, he manifested the form of a vomiting hungry ghost
beside his corpse.
Shànxīng went to the charnel ground
and saw Kǔdé's body.
Shànxīng said to him,
'Venerable, have you died?'
Kǔdé replied,
'I have already died.'
'How did you die?'
He answered,
'I died of abdominal pain.'
'Who carried out your corpse?'
He answered,
'My fellow students.'
'Where did they place it?'
He answered, 'Foolish man,
do you not recognize this as the charnel ground?'
'What kind of body have you obtained?'
He answered,
'I have obtained the body of a vomiting ghost.'
Shànxīng said,
'World-Honored One,
the Nirgrantha Kǔdé has been reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.'
I said, 'Foolish man,
an arhat has no place of rebirth.
How can you say
Kǔdé has been reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven?'
The Tathāgata and Kāśyapa
went to where Shànxīng was.
Shànxīng saw them from afar and gave rise to an evil, wrong thought.
His living body sank into the ground and fell into the Avīci hell.
It is like a person who has fallen into a latrine.
A good friend reaches in with his hand to search for him.
If he finds even a hair of his head, he wishes to pull him out.
Searching for a long time without finding it,
he then gives up the intention.
I am also like this.
Seeking for even a minute wholesome root of Shànxīng,
I wished to pull him out and save him.
I sought for him all day long,
yet could not find even a hair's worth.
Therefore, I could not pull him out from that hell.
In the kingdom of Śràvastī,
there was a mountain village.
It had fifty or sixty households.
It was five hundred *lǐ* from the capital.
In the village, there was a poor family.
The wife, after ten months of pregnancy, gave birth to twin boys.
They were extremely handsome and incomparable.
Their parents loved them dearly.
They gave the children names.
The first was named Shuāng Dé,
the second Shuāng Fú.
When they were fifty or sixty days old,
their father was resting on the bed after herding cattle,
and their mother had gone to gather firewood and had not yet returned.
These two children began to reproach and question each other.
One said, "In a previous time, we were on the verge of attaining the Way.
But due to our foolish thoughts, we believed life could be permanent.
We fell back into the cycle of birth and death for incalculable eons.
Now we are born into this poor family.
We wear garments of straw and coarse cloth.
We eat coarse food, barely enough to sustain life.
How can we endure such hardship for long?
All this is because in our past lives we were attached to wealth and honor.
We indulged our bodies and scattered our minds, seeking momentary pleasure.
From that time until now, we have suffered greatly along the long path.
Now, in our distress, upon whom can we rely?"
The other replied,
"At that time, we faced a minor difficulty and, due to a moment of laziness, did not persevere in our diligent practice.
And so, for many lifetimes, we have encountered various misfortunes and sufferings.
This is our own doing, not our parents' fault.
We must bear it together; what more is there to say?"
Their father heard this and found it strange, thinking they were ghosts.
"While they are still small and not yet grown, we should kill them."
The father, alarmed, went to the fields.
He gathered firewood, intending to burn them to death.
When the mother returned, she asked her husband,
"What are you going to do with this firewood?"
The husband explained the situation.
Upon hearing this, the mother was bewildered.
The next day, both parents went out and secretly listened.
The two children were reproaching each other as before.
So they gathered firewood together, secretly planning to burn them.
The Buddha, with his divine eye, saw this.
He went to the village, radiating light everywhere.
Heaven and earth shook greatly.
Mountains, rivers, and trees all turned golden.
He arrived at the home of the twin children.
The two children saw the Buddha's radiance.
They leaped for joy, immeasurably delighted.
Their parents, again alarmed, each picked up a child.
They brought them before the Buddha and asked the World-Honored One,
"These children, only forty or fifty days old,
speak like this. We find it very strange.
Fearing they might bring calamity, we wanted to burn them with fire.
We do not know what kind of ghosts or demons they are.
We beseech you to explain."
The children, upon seeing the Buddha, leaped and danced with joy.
The Buddha, seeing the children, laughed heartily.
From his mouth issued forth five-colored light.
It illuminated heaven and earth everywhere.
The Buddha declared,
"These two children are not ghosts or demons.
They are children of blessed virtue.
In the time of the past Buddha Kāśyapa, they were *śramaṇas*.
From a young age, they were friends.
With shared resolve, they left home to cultivate, each diligently advancing.
Just as they were about to attain the Way, suddenly evil thoughts arose.
They discouraged and hindered each other, delighting in worldly glory and splendor.
Relying on their accumulated merit, they were reborn in the heavens.
Later, they descended as marquises, kings, rulers, or elders.
Suddenly, these thoughts arose, and they regressed on their own.
They failed to attain Nirvāṇa and continued in this cycle of birth and death.
For countless years, they have been bound together.
They are always reborn as twins, encountering my era now.
Only now have they been born.
Because they once made offerings to a Buddha, their residual merit should lead them to liberation.
They remember their past lives, and now I have come to liberate them.
If I did not liberate them, they would unjustly be burned by fire."
Then he spoke a verse:
The Buddha said,
"These children, upon seeing the Buddha,
their bodies leaped and grew to the size of eight-year-olds.
They immediately became *śrāmaṇeras* and attained the path of Arhatship.
The villagers, young and old, saw the Buddha's radiant form.
They also saw the children's forms change and leap to grow larger.
All were greatly delighted and attained the path of Srotāpanna.
The parents' doubts were resolved, and they also attained the Dharma-eye.
There was a king.
His name was Zhāntuóyuè.
He served the Brahmin way.
He governed the country justly and also employed them.
The king favored a young consort.
The other consorts hated and were jealous.
They gave gold to the Brahmins to slander her to the king.
Saying that if she bore a son, he would surely bring calamity to the kingdom.
The king heard this and was displeased.
He asked the Brahmins,
"What should be done?"
They replied,
"Only by killing them both."
The king said,
"Human life is precious; how can they be killed?"
They reported,
"If you do not kill them, you will surely lose the kingdom and your life."
The king then unjustly killed the child.
Later, it was born from the tomb.
Its mother's upper body did not decay.
The child drank her milk.
Milk is breast milk.
For up to three years,
the tomb collapsed and sank.
The child was able to emerge.
He played with the birds and beasts.
At dusk, he returned to the tomb.
When he reached six years old,
the Buddha, mindful of his hardship living among birds and beasts,
transformed into a śramaṇa.
He went and called to him, asking,
"Whose child are you?"
"Where do you live?"
The child joyfully replied,
"I have no home."
"I only dwell and sleep in this tomb."
He begged to follow the ascetic.
The Buddha said,
"What do you wish to do?"
The child replied,
"Now, whether good or bad, I will follow the ascetic."
The Buddha then took him to the Jetavana.
Seeing the dignified conduct and rules of the bhikṣus,
he was very pleased.
He then said to the Buddha,
"I wish to beg to become a bhikṣu."
The Buddha immediately consented.
He stroked his head with his hand.
His hair fell off by itself, and the kāṣāya robes clothed his body.
He was named Sudā.
He upheld the precepts diligently, his mind never slacking.
After seven days, he attained the path of an arhat.
The Buddha told Sudā,
"You should go convert King Zhāntuóyuè."
Sudā went and arrived.
The king said,
"My heart is greatly troubled; what should I do?"
The ascetic said,
"What troubles you?"
The king said,
"I am already old."
"Past my time, I have no heir; this troubles me."
Hearing the king's words,
the ascetic at first did not respond, only laughed.
The king became angry and said,
"I am speaking to the ascetic."
"He does not answer me at first."
"Instead, he laughs alone."
He then wanted to kill him.
Sudā knew his intention.
He lightly rose, flew up, and stayed in the air.
Dividing his body and scattering his form, he moved in and out without hindrance.
Seeing this divine transformation, the king repented and said,
"I am truly foolish and ignorant, unable to distinguish truth from falsehood."
"I only wish, Great Divine One, that you would return once."
"So that I may submit myself."
Sudā then descended from the air and stood before the king.
He said to the king,
"If you can submit yourself, that is excellent."
"You should submit yourself to the Buddha."
"The Buddha is my teacher."
"The honored one of the three realms, who liberates sentient beings."
Sudā then, in the time it takes to stretch an arm,
took the king and his people,
and together arrived at the Buddha's place.
They submitted to the Three Jewels, begged to receive the Five Precepts, and became upāsakas.
The Buddha fully explained.
Sudā was the king's son.
Hearing the Buddha's words,
the king became even more terrified, unable to control himself.
The Buddha said,
"In the past, during the time of Buddha Krakucchanda,
there was a king named Fúshědá."
"The people of the country all made offerings to the Three Jewels."
"At that time, there was an ordinary man who was poor and without livelihood."
"He was often employed by the wealthy and noble of the country,"
"hired to herd and tend several hundred head of cattle."
"Seeing the king and the people making offerings to the bhikṣu saṅgha,"
"he then asked,"
"What are you all doing?"
"The people replied,"
"We are making offerings to the Three Jewels."
"So that in the future we may always dwell in peace and happiness, honored and noble, without hardship."
"He then thought to himself,"
"I am poor; I should only boil the cows' milk to make cheese and ghee."
"And with a pure heart offer it to the bhikṣus."
"The bhikṣu saṅgha chanted blessings, saying,"
"May you attain blessings for life after life."
"From then on, through successive rebirths and deaths,"
"he always received those blessings."
"Sometimes born above as one of the devas,"
"sometimes below as a king or noble."
"When he was a king or noble, he once went out hunting."
"He saw a good pregnant cow and killed it."
"His consort said to the king,"
"Do not kill its calf."
"At that time, the cow's owner took the calf and raised it."
"Its owner angrily said,"
"May the king become like this cow!"
"Afterward, his spirit became the king's son."
"At that time, before he was born,"
"his mother was killed by the king; this is Sudā."
"Sudā's mother was the king's consort at that time."
"The Brahmin was the cow's owner."
"Sudā was born from the tomb."
"His mother's upper body did not decay."
"He was able to drink her milk."
"And thereby grew up."
"This was due to his past life offering cheese and ghee to the bhikṣu saṅgha."
"Hearing this, the king's mind was liberated."
"He attained the fruit of Srotāpanna."
"The Buddha was in Śrāvastī."
"At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra,"
"with his divine eye, observed three times day and night,"
"who should be converted, and then went to convert them."
"At that time, there were merchants about to go to another country; the various merchants together took a dog along the way."
"The merchants stopped to rest, and the dog stole meat."
"Then the people together beat the dog."
"And broke its leg, abandoning it in the wilderness, leaving it behind and departing."
"At that time, Śāriputra, with his divine eye, saw the dog,"
"crippled on the ground, starving and near death."
"He flew to the dog and gave it food."
"The dog's life was saved, and it was very joyful."
"At that time, Śāriputra,"
"then expounded the subtle Dharma for this dog."
"The dog then died."
"It was reborn in a Brahmin family in Śrāvastī."
"At that time, Śāriputra,"
"was walking alone begging for alms."
"The Brahmin saw him and asked,"
"Venerable One, walking alone, do you not have a śrāmaṇera?"
"Śāriputra said,"
"I have no śrāmaṇera."
"I hear you have a son."
"You should give him to me."
"The Brahmin said,"
"I have a son."
"His name is Jūntí."
"He is still a young child."
"Not yet fit for service."
"When he grows a bit older, I will give him to you."
"At that time, Śāriputra,"
"kept this in mind."
"When he reached seven years old, he came again to ask for him."
"At that time, the Brahmin had his son leave home."
"Śāriputra took him to the Jetavana."
"Gradually expounded the Dharma to him."
"His mind opened in understanding, and he attained arhatship. The śrāmaṇera Jūntí, having just attained the path,"
"with his own wisdom power, contemplated his past lives."
"He saw that in a previous life he had been a starving dog."
"Receiving the master's kindness, he now obtained a human body."
"And also attained the fruit of the path."
"Joy arose within him."
"And he thought to himself,"
"I received my teacher's kindness and was able to escape all sufferings."
"Now I should devote my whole life to supplying his needs, forever being a śrāmaṇera."
"Going back to the past, during the time of Buddha Kāśyapa,"
"there were bhikṣus gathered in one place."
"At that time, a young bhikṣu had a clear and elegant voice."
"He was skilled in chanting hymns."
"There was one bhikṣu,"
"old and aged, his voice coarse and dull."
"Unable to chant hymns."
"He often voiced sounds to amuse himself."
"The old bhikṣu had already attained arhatship."
"At that time, the young bhikṣu scolded him, saying,"
"Now you, Elder, your voice is like a dog barking."
"Then the old bhikṣu,"
"called to the young one,"
"Do you recognize me?"
"The young one replied,"
"I recognize you well."
"You are the senior bhikṣu from the time of Buddha Kāśyapa."
"He replied,"
"I have now attained arhatship."
"The young one was alarmed and terrified, blaming himself and repenting."
"For five hundred lifetimes, he was always reborn as a dog."
"Because he had left home and upheld pure precepts,"
"he now met me and obtained liberation."
In the past, there was a small kingdom.
Not far from the city was a fine forest.
Five ascetics practiced the Way there.
One of the bhikṣus had attained the six supernatural powers.
There was a śrāmaṇera who was just eight years old.
They dwelled together in the mountains.
Each sat facing a direction, contemplating the scriptures and the Way.
The master knew the śrāmaṇera had only seven days left to live.
If he died here, his parents would say of me,
"He did not watch over him well, causing his life to end."
They would harbor resentment.
So he told the śrāmaṇera,
"Your parents miss you.
You may return home and come back early on the eighth day."
The śrāmaṇera joyfully bowed and left.
On the way, he encountered heavy rain with torrential flooding.
There was an ant hole on the ground, and the flowing water was about to enter it.
The śrāmaṇera thought,
"I am a disciple of the Buddha.
First, to have a compassionate heart.
Second, to preserve life."
He immediately used earth to block the breach and diverted the water away.
The śrāmaṇera returned home without any mishap.
On the morning of the eighth day, he returned.
The master saw him from afar.
He wondered why this was so.
He should have died in seven days.
Now, what was the cause?
Could it be that ghosts or spirits had transformed and come?
He immediately entered samādhi.
He saw that by saving the ants, his present life's lifespan had been extended.
The śrāmaṇera arrived.
He bowed and paid respects, then sat to one side.
The master said to him,
"You performed a great meritorious deed.
Are you aware of it?"
The śrāmaṇera said,
"I was at home for seven days and performed no other meritorious deeds."
The master said,
"Your life was due to end.
Yesterday, because you saved the ants,
your present life's lifespan increased by over eighty years."
The śrāmaṇera was delighted, believing that good deeds bring reward.
He then diligently cultivated with vigor and without slackening.
He attained Arhatship.
In Śrāvastī, there was an old man.
He lost his wife early.
He lived alone with his son.
Impoverished and without wealth,
he realized the impermanence of the world.
He left home to follow the Buddha.
His son was still young.
He also became a śrāmaṇera.
He begged for food together with his father.
As dusk approached, they were to return.
The father walked slowly.
The son feared poisonous beasts.
He urgently supported his father, pushing him along the road.
He did not hold him firmly.
He pushed his father, who fell to the ground and died instantly.
He went alone to where the Buddha was.
Then the bhikṣus reproached the śrāmaṇera.
They reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha told them,
"Although this master died, it was not with malicious intent."
He then asked the śrāmaṇera,
"Did you kill your master?"
He replied,
"I indeed pushed him.
It was not with malicious intent."
The Buddha said,
"I know your mind had no malicious intent.
In a past life, it was also like this.
There was no malicious intent, yet they killed each other.
In the past, a father and son lived together in one place.
At that time, the father was gravely ill.
He was then sleeping.
Many flies came repeatedly to annoy and disturb him.
The father told his son to keep the flies away,
hoping to sleep peacefully.
At that time, the son urgently tried to keep the flies away, but they kept coming.
The son then became angry.
He took a large stick and waited to kill the flies when they gathered on his father's forehead.
He struck with the stick, and his father died instantly.
The father then is this śrāmaṇera.
The son then is the dead bhikṣu.
Because there was no evil mind, no malicious intent,
it was also not intentional killing.
The śrāmaṇera diligently cultivated without slackening.
He then attained the Way of Arhatship.
The Buddha traveled to Śrāvastī, the Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.
At that time, a different bhikṣu
had a disciple whose nature was gentle and elegant, whose thoughts and actions were benevolent and virtuous.
He constantly attended to his upādhyāya with sincerity, diligence, and vigor.
He respectfully followed the teachings of the Dharma and did not disobey his master's instructions.
His lifespan was short; he died young.
He was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and looked upon the heavenly realm.
But he saw only a great fire.
His original aspirations and wishes could not be fulfilled.
He could not stay with his good friends.
Now he had left his good teacher and followed evil companions.
Thus, he was far away from the most venerable upādhyāya,
and the Ācārya assembly,
and all those who practiced brahmacarya.
The fourfold assembly of disciples,
the one with omniscience,
called the Tathāgata—
now he was far from all of them.
For countless kalpas, difficult to encounter, difficult to see,
the Buddha arises in the world, expounding the scriptures, subtle, profound, and abstruse, never before spoken.
He peacefully guides and transforms, explaining all conditioned origins.
Each understands clearly the causes from which things arise.
What had not been seen or heard for countless kalpas
was all resolved for him.
He encountered this sūtra and vinaya.
He left home to practice the Way.
What should have been accomplished was not completed.
Now, instead, he was indulgent and negligent.
He first approached the World-Honored One and bowed at his feet.
The Buddha saw his mind,
truly devoted to the Way, purely focused on the Dharma.
He explained the truths of suffering, its origin, cessation, and the path.
He immediately realized the truth.
The upādhyāya sorrowfully thought of him, weeping tears like rain.
The Buddha called and asked him,
"Why are you distressed?"
He replied,
"My disciple has passed away."
The Buddha said,
"Why do you grieve?"
He replied,
"My śrāmaṇera disciple was very virtuous and excellent.
He had not completed his practice and died young.
Therefore, I am sorrowful and cannot console myself."
The Buddha said,
"Do not grieve; he has already attained completion.
He has been reborn in heaven.
Today, in the middle of the night, he discerned the noble truths."
The bhikṣu no longer wept.
Śāriputra had a novice monk.
His name was Chúntóu.
At the age of eight, he attained the six supernatural powers.
He soared through the empty sky and arrived at the Anòu Spring.
There was a Brahmin with the five supernatural powers.
His name was Xūbá.
He also arrived at that spring.
At that time, above the spring,
there was a green-clothed ghost guarding the spring.
It drove away the Brahmin with the five powers,
hurling tiles and stones at him, not allowing him to approach the divine spring.
The novice monk Chúntóu arrived through the empty sky.
Those green-clothed ghosts, hundreds in number, all came forward to welcome him.
Some came forward to gather his robes,
some held pure water to wash his hands and feet,
some used clean towels to wipe his head and face,
and some bathed his body with fragrant water.
The Brahmin Xūbá cried out loudly, saying:
"I have now attained the five supernatural powers and immeasurable divine virtue.
My strength can move mountains and stop flowing waters,
turn heaven and earth around like turning a bead in the palm.
Since I began studying the path, over one hundred and twenty years have passed.
I have toiled my body and suffered, exhausting both form and spirit.
Sometimes I practiced the five sciences,
lit fires in four places,
with sunlight shining from above,
or I lay on ashes and dung,
or lay on thorns and in perilous difficulties.
There is no path I have not studied.
Yet I am still driven away and cannot reach the spring.
But this little boy in black robes,
only seven or eight years old,
not yet weaned from the breast,
his body foul and stinking, receives excessive respect and reverence.
For what reason?"
Then the green-clothed ghost said to the Brahmin:
"Now this student,
though young in form and years, his conduct surpasses the three realms.
He has attained the noble eightfold path of the sages.
You now lack this, therefore you do not receive reverence."
There was a Brahmin.
His name was Yuèchā.
He established a monastery.
It was also named Yuèchā.
He constantly supplied ghee and oil to the monastery for lighting lamps.
At that time, a Brahmin from afar
came to that monastery.
He also heard that the Brahmin Yuèchā was of high talent, bright virtue,
exclusively believed in the Buddha's teachings, and had established a divine temple, and wished to meet him.
At that time, a novice monk
came to fetch the ghee and oil
to supply the monastery for lighting lamps.
Many Brahmins
said to the Brahmin Yuèchā:
"Do you truly bow to this person in colored robes?"
Before the words were finished, the novice monk had arrived.
He immediately bowed to him again.
Many Brahmins
said to this Brahmin:
"You come from the four castes, your talents surpass others.
Astronomy and geography, there is nothing you have not studied and mastered.
Divine incantations evoke spirits, there is nothing you cannot accomplish.
Now this person in colored robes
comes from many surnames,
his lineage is not pure.
Why do you violate our fundamental law and bow respectfully to him?
Moreover, you, Brahmin, practice purity,
cultivate the inner treasury of charts, prophecies, and secret records yourself.
Practicing the path brings blessings, what wish cannot be accomplished?
Writing, seals, there is nothing you do not know thoroughly.
The Buddha's conduct is meager and insignificant, what is there to value?
Abandoning the fundamental for the trivial is what I detest.
I have heard that śramaṇas are lowly and base,
cunning and deceitful, numerous and flourishing, deluding worldly people.
Their conduct is short-lived, bringing glory only to this one body.
They cannot extend and bring about Brahminic blessings.
Even if you meet them, you should at most raise your joined palms.
Why prostrate yourself with the five limbs touching the ground, reverently and respectfully bowing?
We personally witness this and find it very strange.
Moreover, the elders who studied before,
how could they forgive you for this offense?"
Yuèchā replied to the many Brahmins:
"Everyone, be silent and listen to what I say.
One who attains can ultimately reach
Srotaāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin,
can cut off the bonds of the desire realm, all entanglements, aggregates, and sense bases.
Therefore it is said: 'One who attains can exhaust the source of Māra.'
Those who enter concentration and sit in meditation,
delight in quiet places, their will reveres single-mindedness.
They contemplate the incoming and outgoing breath, their mindfulness is firm and solid.
They can cut off the bonds of Māra,
and bind Māra himself.
One who enters concentration
can command ghosts and spirits, and they arrive according to his will.
One should seek expedient means to cut off the strong bonds of Māra.
In the past, there was a little boy.
He was just seven years old.
He greatly loved the Buddha's path and became a novice monk.
He followed his Arhat teacher to study in the mountains.
He was diligent and unrelenting.
When he reached eight years old,
he then attained the four supernatural powers.
First, the divine eye of penetrating vision.
Second, the divine ear of penetrating hearing.
Third, flying and transformations.
Fourth, knowing his own past lives and where he came from.
Sitting, he reflected on himself.
He then saw his previous existences and past lives.
He had been a son to five mothers.
He then laughed to himself.
His teacher asked why he laughed.
The novice monk said:
"How dare I laugh at my teacher?
I look at this one body and it had five mothers.
Day and night they wept and wailed, grieving, sorrowful, and pained.
They constantly said:
'I think of my son, never forgetting for a moment.'
I reflect:
This one body's sorrow and pain was shared by five families.
That is why I laugh.
When I was the son of the first mother,
a neighbor had a child born at the same time as me.
After I died, the one born on the same day went out and came in, walking about.
My mother saw him and then said:
'If my son were alive, he would also be going out and coming in, walking about like this.'
She then grieved, felt pain, and thought of me.
Again, I was the son of the second mother.
I died again not long after birth.
My mother saw people nursing their children,
then felt pain and thought of me.
She grieved and wept.
I was again the son of the third mother.
I died again not long after.
My mother, when about to eat, shed tears thinking of me, saying:
'If my son were here, he would eat with me.
He abandoned me and died.'
I was again the son of the fourth mother.
I died again not long after.
At that time, my peers were getting engaged and married.
My mother again thought of me, saying:
'If my son had not died, he would also be taking a wife now.'
I was the son of the fifth mother, and now I am still alive.
I left home to study the path.
My mother wept daily, saying:
'I have lost my son.
I do not know where he is.
Hungry, cold, life and death, we will not see each other again.'
All were filled with grief and sorrow, lamenting and mourning.
Now if the five mothers were to meet together,
each speaking of their lost son, facing each other,
weeping and thinking of me, this one person,
that is why I laugh.
People in the world do not know there is life after death,
they only speak of death.
People doing good receive blessings, doing evil receive calamities.
People in the world, good and evil, fear for themselves.
They have nothing to fear about evil, but later suffer pain.
Entering the evil paths, regret is of no avail.
I, weary of the world, therefore left my relatives to seek the path.
I look upon the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, and poverty,
and feel terror on their behalf.
I received my teacher's kindness, accepted the Buddha's scriptures and precepts.
Now I am liberated.
I think of the five mothers,
unable to attain liberation,
instead repeatedly worrying about me."
There was a monk.
He had few desires and was content.
At that time, in the land of Āntuó, there was an upāsaka.
He revered and believed in the Three Jewels, providing lifelong support.
Every day he sent offerings.
In that land, there was an elder.
He had a son.
Wishing for him to leave home, he sought a good teacher.
He went to tell the monk, saying:
"I have this one son; I wish to have him leave home.
I only pray that the Great Virtuous One, in his compassion, will accept and guide him."
At that time, the monk, with his spiritual eye, observed.
This person, upon leaving home, would be able to uphold pure precepts.
He accepted him as a śrāmaṇera. At that time, the upāsaka had a close and good lay friend.
The next day, there was a guest gathering.
In the morning, he thought:
"Now I must attend the gathering; who will stay behind to guard the house?"
His daughter then said to her father:
"I only pray that my parents and all the servants
go to answer the invitation; I am capable of staying behind to guard."
Her father said: "Very good."
The entire family all went.
The daughter then closed the door and stayed alone inside the house.
That day, the upāsaka was in a hurry and forgot to send food.
At that time, the Venerable One thought to himself:
"The day is growing late.
Laypeople have many affairs.
He then sent the śrāmaṇera to go fetch it.
Maintain dignified conduct as the Buddha taught."
The śrāmaṇera knocked on the door.
The girl asked who it was.
He replied:
"A śrāmaṇera, coming for food for his teacher."
She then opened the door for him.
This girl was beautiful, with a lovely appearance.
She was just sixteen, burning with lustful desire.
Before the śrāmaṇera,
she acted seductively, deeply displaying signs of desire.
The śrāmaṇera, seeing this, thought:
"Does this girl have a wind-sickness?
Or is she driven by lustful thoughts, wanting to ruin my pure practice?"
He firmly maintained his dignified conduct, his expression unchanged.
The girl then prostrated herself on the ground and said to the śrāmaṇera:
"What I have always wished for, I wish to state.
In this house of mine are treasures and storehouses,
like the treasure troves of Vaiśravaṇa's heavenly palace.
Yet they have no master.
You could condescend to be the master of this house.
I will be your servant girl, serving and obeying to fulfill my wish."
The śrāmaṇera thought:
"I would rather give up my life than violate the precepts.
In the past, a monk went to a prostitute's house.
He would rather throw himself into a pit of fire than commit a lustful act.
Also, monks were robbed by bandits and bound with grass.
Wind blew, sun scorched, and insects bit them.
To protect the precepts, they did not break the grass and leave.
Like a bird swallowing a pearl,
a monk saw it,
but to uphold the precepts, despite extreme suffering, he did not speak.
Like a sea ship wrecking,
a junior monk,
to keep the precepts, gave the plank to a senior monk and drowned in the sea.
Such people are truly the Buddha's disciples, able to uphold the prohibitive precepts.
If I am not a disciple, I cannot uphold them.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is solely their teacher, not mine.
He skillfully said:
'Firmly close the doors; I will enter a room to do what should be done.
Then we can be together.'
The girl then closed the door.
The śrāmaṇera entered the room and bolted the door.
He found a razor.
He removed his clothes and placed them on a stand.
With palms joined, he knelt facing the city of Kuśinagara, where the Buddha attained parinirvāṇa.
He made a vow:
'I now do not abandon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Nor do I abandon the precepts; precisely to uphold the precepts,
I give up this body and life. I vow that wherever I am reborn,
I will leave home, practice purely, exhaust defilements, and achieve enlightenment.'
He then cut his throat and died.
At that time, the girl, wondering at the delay, hurried to the door to look.
Seeing he was already dead, she lost her original composure.
Her lustful desire immediately ceased; shame, regret, and distress arose; she wailed mournfully and fainted.
Her father returned from the gathering and, seeing his daughter thus, asked what had happened.
She truthfully explained everything.
Her father then entered the room and saw the śrāmaṇera.
His body, stained with blood, was red like sandalwood.
He bowed and praised, saying:
"Upholding the Buddha's precepts, able to give up body and life."
At that time, according to the laws of that land,
if a śramaṇa or white-clad layperson died in a house,
a fine of gold coins was to be imposed.
The upāsaka then placed a thousand gold coins on a bronze tray and carried it to the king's palace.
He said:
"Great King,
I have incurred a penalty.
It should be paid to the king.
I pray you accept it."
The king said:
"In my kingdom, you revere and believe in the Three Jewels; your words and deeds are without fault.
You are the only one; what fault could you have
that you pay a penalty?"
The upāsaka then fully recounted the above events.
He condemned his own daughter and praised the śrāmaṇera.
The king, hearing this, was awed and said to him:
"The śrāmaṇera protected the precepts and gave up his own life.
You are without guilt or fault.
Just take it back to your house.
I now personally wish to go to your house to make offerings to the śrāmaṇera."
The king went and saw him.
He went forward and bowed.
With various treasures adorning a high carriage, he carried the dead śrāmaṇera to a flat ground.
He piled fragrant wood and cremated him with offerings.
He adorned that girl with the utmost worldly splendor.
He placed her in a high, conspicuous place so that all present at the gathering could see.
He said to the crowd:
"This girl is exceptionally beautiful, with such radiant appearance.
Who among those not free from desire would not have a defiled mind?
Yet this śrāmaṇera, though not yet attained the Way,
with his samsaric body, upheld the precepts and gave up his life—extremely rare and extraordinary."
The king then sent someone to invite his teacher.
He extensively expounded the subtle Dharma for the great assembly.
At that time, all present, seeing and hearing this event,
some sought to leave home,
some aroused the mind of unsurpassed bodhi.
In the past, there was an arhat.
