He and a śrāmaṇera were practicing the path in the mountains.
The śrāmaṇera went daily to people's homes to beg for food and drink.
He passed along an embankment.
The path was rugged and dangerous; his foot slipped and he fell to the ground.
The food was soiled with mud; the śrāmaṇera took the unsoiled food
and put it in his teacher's bowl.
The soiled food he washed and ate himself.
This happened not just one day.
The teacher said:
"Why do you wash and discard the taste of the food?"
He replied:
"When going to beg, it was clear;
when returning from begging, it rained.
On the embankment, I fell and the food was covered."
The teacher silently pondered this.
Knowing it was a dragon harassing the śrāmaṇera, he went to the embankment.
Holding a staff, he knocked and struck the thicket.
The dragon transformed into an old man.
He came out, head and face to the ground.
The śramaṇa said:
"Why do you harass my śrāmaṇera?"
He replied:
"I truly love his appearance."
"From today onward, come daily to my dwelling to eat."
The śramaṇa accepted the invitation and went daily to eat.
Later, the śrāmaṇera saw in his teacher's bowl
two or three grains of rice that were not of this world.
He asked his upādhyāya:
The teacher silently did not respond.
The śrāmaṇera then went under the bed, hands grasping the bed legs.
When the upādhyāya finished meditation, he followed along,
and both flew to the dragon's palace.
The dragon and the women all bowed to the śramaṇa and also bowed to the śrāmaṇera.
The teacher then noticed him.
He called him out and said:
"These are not palace women;
they are animals.
You are a śrāmaṇera.
Though not yet attained the Way,
you will certainly be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven,
surpassing that a hundredfold.
Do not have defiled thoughts."
The śrāmaṇera said:
"This dragon's dwelling is rare in the world."
The teacher said:
"He has three sufferings:
First, though having food of a hundred flavors, upon entering the mouth it turns into toads.
Second, the palace women are incomparably beautiful,
but when wishing to be husband and wife, two snakes intertwine.
Third, on the dragon's back are reverse scales,
sand and stones grow among them,
the pain reaches the heart and chest.
This is great suffering.
Why would you follow him?
You have not attained the Way;
you cannot be allowed to see the ghost path or the inner affairs of kings."
The śrāmaṇera did not respond.
Day and night he thought,
yearning for that, he did not eat, fell ill, and died.
His spirit was reborn as a dragon's son.
There was once a novice monk.
His mind was constantly attached to curd, and when lay devotees offered curd to the monks,
this novice would always receive the leftover portion.
His heart clung to this pleasure and took delight in it, never letting go.
After his life ended, he was reborn inside a jar of leftover curd.
His teacher had attained Arhatship.
When the monks were distributing curd,
he said, "Slowly, slowly.
Do not harm this curd-loving novice."
The others asked,
"Why do you call him the curd-loving novice?"
He replied,
"This was originally my novice.
But because he was greedy and attached to leftover curd,
he was reborn in this jar."
When the teacher received his portion of curd,
a worm came out from within it.
The teacher said,
"Curd-lover, why have you come?"
And he immediately gave the curd to it.
The Bhagavān was in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā
left the bhikṣuṇīs' garden and sat under a tree.
Sitting upright, concentrating her mind, she recollected her past lives and then smiled.
The other bhikṣuṇīs saw this and asked her,
and Bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā said,
"I recollect my past lives.
Ninety-one kalpas ago,
there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin
who appeared in the world.
There was a youth
named Bhadramadeva,
who possessed abundant wealth and treasures, immeasurably rich.
The youth, holding a jeweled canopy, left his house.
There was an elder's wife,
incomparably beautiful,
who also passed by that place.
Many people were all looking at her.
Then the youth thought to himself,
'Today I am holding a jeweled canopy,
made of various jewels, passing along this road,
yet no one is looking at me.
This elder's wife—
I shall now devise a means to make people look at me.'
Then the youth, holding the jeweled canopy,
left that area
and went to where the Buddha Vipaśyin was.
He stood behind the Tathāgata, holding up the jeweled canopy
for seven days and seven nights,
making this vow:
'By the merit of my offering to the World-Honored One,
may I become a woman of incomparable beauty,
so that whoever sees me will be infatuated and fall to the ground.'
When the youth's life ended,
he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven as a goddess,
excelling in five things:
What are the five?
Heavenly lifespan, heavenly beauty, heavenly pleasures, heavenly supernatural powers, and heavenly superior virtues.
The gods, seeing this goddess, all cherished hopes of being with her.
Then the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven all quarreled with each other.
When the goddess's life ended, she was reborn in the human world as the daughter of the brāhmaṇa Guòdáduō.
She was exceptionally beautiful.
Moving between the human and heavenly realms, she always obtained beauty.
She encountered many Buddhas, all of whom she served and made offerings to,
seeking to become a woman.
Later, she was reborn in the human world in a lowly brāhmaṇa family,
becoming a servant girl for the youth Yuèguāng.
Her name was Jīluó.
The youth Yuèguāng's wife was named Mónúhēluó,
and she was incomparably beautiful.
Then the lady Yuèguāng said to that servant girl,
'Go outside the house.
If you see any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, bring them here,
for I wish to make offerings.'
Then the servant girl went out of the house.
There was a Pratyekabuddha
begging for food at the threshold of the gate.
Then the servant girl Jīluó said, 'Please come in,
for I wish to make an offering to you.'
When the lady saw that his appearance was not dignified,
she said to Jīluó,
'Send that śramaṇa away; I will not make an offering.'
The servant girl said,
'I beg you, open your mind and do not dislike the śramaṇa's appearance.
The merit of making offerings is immeasurable.'
Then the lady replied,
'Quickly drive this śramaṇa out.
I cannot bear to make an offering.'
The servant girl replied,
'If you, noble one, will not make an offering to this śramaṇa,
then I beg you not to begrudge me the portion of food that is due to me today.'
Then the lady immediately gave the food to the servant girl.
Then the servant girl Jīluó
immediately placed her portion of food into the Pratyekabuddha's bowl.
After eating, his body rose into the sky.
When the servant girl saw this, she was overjoyed and unable to contain herself.
She then made a vow:
'By this merit, may I not fall into the evil destinies.
May I, for a long time to come, always encounter such a sage,
who will preach the Dharma to me and enable me to quickly attain liberation.'
At that time, King Brahmadatta of Vārāṇasī
saw that Pratyekabuddha rising into the sky
and said to his ministers,
'That offering was made—'
At that time, the elder Yuèguāng
had gathered five hundred merchants in a great assembly hall.
From afar, they saw the Pratyekabuddha holding his bowl and rising into the sky.
Some merchants said,
'This holy one must have received food from my house.'
Then the great lady Yuèguāng,
seeing this, said to the servant girl Jīluó,
'The merit you have gained,
give it to me.
This then is my offering.'
'I will now give you more food.'
The servant girl said, 'I will not give it.'
She said again,
'I will now give you two portions of food.'
The servant girl replied,
'I do not need it.'
The lady said again,
'I will give you three portions, five portions, ten portions, twenty portions, even up to a hundred portions, a thousand portions.'
The servant girl Jīluó said,
'I will not give it to you.'
The lady replied,
'If you do not give it to me,
I will cut off your ears, nose, and hands.'
The servant girl Jīluó said,
'I will not give it.'
Then the elder's wife
beat the servant girl with a stick.
After beating her,
the elder Yuèguāng returned.
Seeing the servant girl Jīluó
with her head broken, clothes torn, weeping and shedding tears,
he asked her for the whole story.
She told him everything that had happened.
Then the youth Yuèguāng
took that wife and made her a servant girl,
and made the servant girl Jīluó his chief wife.
Five hundred court ladies surrounded her,
and she was adorned with hundreds of thousands of jewels.
At that time, King Brahmadatta,
hearing that the servant girl of Yuèguāng had offered food to that Pratyekabuddha,
then King Brahmadatta
sent hundreds of thousands of taels of jewels as a gift to the wife of Elder Yuèguāng.
He also bestowed estates as a gift to Elder Yuèguāng.
That King Brahmadatta
is now Kapilamaśaila.
The elder Yuèguāng is Mahākāśyapa.
The servant girl Jīluó is myself.
Now I have encountered the Buddha and attained Arhatship.
At that time, in the Shèwèi Kingdom, there was an elder’s wife.
She gave birth to a daughter.
She was exceptionally beautiful, unmatched in the world.
When she was first born,
she was wrapped in a fine, soft white cloth and came out.
Her parents found it strange.
After examining her, they deemed it very auspicious.
Therefore, they gave her a name,
calling her Shūlí. As Shūlí grew up,
the cloth grew with her.
This girl was outstandingly noble.
People from near and far within the kingdom competed to seek her hand in marriage.
The girl said to her parents,
“I wish to leave home and become a monastic.”
Her parents, out of love and affection, did not oppose her wish.
Soon, they brought out the cloth
intending to make the five monastic robes.
The girl said to her parents,
“What I am wearing is already fully sufficient.
There is no need to make more.
I only ask that you allow me to go to the Buddha from time to time.”
She went to the Buddha, paid homage, and requested to leave home.
The Buddha said, “Welcome.”
Her hair fell off by itself.
The white cloth she was wearing immediately transformed into the five monastic robes.
She was entrusted to Mahāprajāpatī to become a bhikṣuṇī.
Diligent and advancing, she soon attained the path of an arhat.
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“What virtue did Shūlí cultivate in the past,
that she was born with the cloth and, upon leaving home, attained the path?”
The Buddha said,
“In the past, there was a Buddha
named Vipaśyin.
At that time, the king, ministers, and people made many offerings.
There was a woman
named Tánnìjī,
who was extremely poor.
The husband and wife together owned only one cloth.
If the husband went out, he would wear it and go.
The wife would then stay naked.
If the wife wore the cloth,
the husband would sit naked.
There was a bhikṣu who encouraged and transformed others.
He came to their home
and saw this woman.
He then encouraged her, saying,
‘It is difficult to encounter a Buddha in the world, and it is difficult to obtain a human body.
You should listen to the Dharma and you should give alms.’
The woman went back and told her husband,
‘There is a śramaṇa outside
who encourages me to see the Buddha, listen to the Dharma, and give alms.’
The husband replied, saying,
‘Our family is poor and destitute.
Although we may have the intention, what can we use to give?’
The wife said,
‘I intend to give this cloth as alms.’
The husband said, ‘You and I
share this one cloth.
We go out and seek to make a living.
If we use it now for almsgiving, we will both surely die.’
The wife said,
‘All humans are born and die; whether we give or not, we will die.
If we give and die, there is hope for the afterlife.
If we die without giving, the afterlife will surely be worse.’
The husband joyfully said,
‘Even if it means death, let us use it for almsgiving.’
The wife then went back out
and said to the bhikṣu,
‘Venerable, please write down
my name.’
The bhikṣu replied, saying,
‘If you wish to give, you should give it in person.
I will chant blessings for you.’
Shūlí said,
‘I only have this cloth; I have no other clothes inside.
The female body is unclean and unsightly; it is not appropriate to undress here.’
She then went back inside,
and from a distance, below, she removed the cloth from her body
and handed it to the bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu chanted blessings and brought it to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
‘Bhikṣu, bring this cloth here.’
The bhikṣu handed it to the Buddha.
The Buddha received it with his own hands.
This cloth was dirty.
At that time, the king and the assembly
secretly felt disdain that the Buddha accepted this dirty cloth.
The Buddha, knowing the minds of the assembly, told them,
‘I observe this assembly.
Among pure and great offerings, none surpasses this one.’
Those who gave the cloth
heard this, and the entire assembly could not help but feel awe.
The queen was delighted.
She immediately removed the exquisite ornaments, jeweled necklaces, and precious clothes she was wearing
and sent them to Tuónìjī.
The king was also pleased.
He removed the clothes he was wearing and sent them to her husband, ordering him to come to the assembly.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
‘You should know that the poor woman Tuónìjī of that time
is now the bhikṣuṇī Shūlí.
Because at that time she gave the cloth with a pure mind,
for ninety-one kalpas, in the places she was born,
she was always born with cloth,
never lacking anything.’
In the Kośala Kingdom,
King Prasenajit
heard that Báduójiāpíluó had left home.
He then invited her into the palace,
where they stayed together in one place for the summer retreat of four months.
The king went to the garden
and said to the gatekeeper,
‘Guard the gate well.
Do not let this bhikṣuṇī leave.’
The gatekeeper thought to himself,
‘This bhikṣuṇī is content to stay and will not leave.’
At that time, the gatekeeper had other matters to attend to.
The bhikṣuṇī put on the queen’s clothes and left through the gate.
She went far away to the Jetavana Monastery,
to listen to the Buddha’s teachings.
The Buddha saw her from afar and said,
‘Welcome, Báduójiāpíluó.’
Immediately, the queen’s clothes disappeared,
her hair fell off by itself, and monastic robes appeared on her body, making her a bhikṣuṇī.
She went to the Buddha, bowed with her head at his feet, and paid homage.
The Buddha taught her the four bases of spiritual power.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī attained the power of spiritual feet.
When the king heard that Báduójiāpíluó had left,
he led troops to surround the assembly of bhikṣus
and also surrounded the bhikṣuṇī quarters.
This bhikṣuṇī then flew into the sky.
The king looked up
and immediately felt remorse.
‘How could I have defiled an arhat bhikṣuṇī?’
Distressed, he prostrated on the ground and repented to the bhikṣuṇī.
The bhikṣuṇīs in the monastery drove her out,
saying,
‘I have no desire for love.’
The other bhikṣuṇīs said,
‘You stayed with the king in the palace for four months during the summer.
How can you say you have no love?’
They reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, knowing the truth, asked,
‘This bhikṣuṇī,
did you actually experience sensual pleasure?’
She replied, saying,
‘World-Honored One, how could I have experienced it?
To me, such sensual pleasure feels like hot iron entering the body.’
The Buddha said,
‘If you had no mind to experience sensual pleasure, you are without fault.’
The Buddha was in Shèwèi City.
At that time, in Yōushànnà Town,
there was a young householder.
While traveling for amusement,
he saw a woman
named Liánhuāsè.
Her beauty was like that of a peach or plum.
She possessed all the marks of a woman.
Feeling affection and respect for her,
he immediately took her as his wife.
Not long after, the wife became pregnant.
He sent her back to her family home.
When the month was full, she gave birth to a daughter.
Because his wife was in childbirth, he no longer approached her.
He then secretly had relations with her mother.
When Liánhuāsè found out, she left.
The marital bond was broken, and fearing she would burden her parents,
yet pitying the infant, she swallowed her shame and humiliation,
and returned to her husband's home.
She raised the daughter for eight years and then left.
She reached Bōluónài.
Hungry, thirsty, and utterly exhausted,
she sat by the water's edge.
At that time, an elder
was traveling for sightseeing.
Seeing her, he felt love and respect and asked,
"Where do you reside? Who are your parents and clan? To whom do you belong now,
that you are alone here?"
Liánhuāsè said,
"I am the daughter of such-and-such clan.
Now I belong to no one."
The elder asked again,
"If you belong to no one,
can you become my principal wife?"
She replied, "Since I am a woman without a husband,
why not?"
He then took her in his carriage, brought her home, and honored her as his principal wife.
Liánhuāsè managed his household,
harmoniously pleasing all, young and old.
Husband and wife respected each other for eight years.
Then the elder said to his wife,
"I have outstanding debts in
Yōushànnà Town that I have not collected for
eight years now.
Calculating the interest, the amount has grown to hundreds of millions.
I will go to collect them and will be parted from you for a while."
The wife said,
"The customs of that town are such that women are wanton.
If you go now, you might lose your husbandly virtue."
He replied,
"Though I am of shallow wisdom, I would not sink to such disorder."
The wife said again,
"If you must go,
I wish to hear a vow."
He replied,
"Very well.
If I give rise to an improper heart, may I perish together with that thought."
Thus he departed.
Arriving at that town,
he spent a year collecting the many debts.
His longing for home gradually deepened.
"If I commit adultery, I would betray my original vow.
But taking another wife would not violate my pledge."
So he inquired and met a girl,
elegant and lovely in appearance, her gaze not improper.
He felt great affection for her.
He then went to seek her hand in marriage.
Her father, considering the elder talented, wise, and very wealthy,
gladly gave her to him.
After collecting the debts, he prepared to return to his own country.
He settled her in a separate residence,
and only then returned home.
He left in the morning and returned in the evening, different from before.
Liánhuāsè found this strange.
She secretly asked his attendants.
An attendant answered,
"There is a young wife.
Her husband returns in the evening."
Liánhuāsè asked,
"You have a new wife.
Why hide her and not let me see her?"
He replied,
"I feared you would resent her, so I kept her outside."
The wife said,
"I bear no jealousy.
The deities bear witness.
You may summon her here
to help you manage affairs."
He then brought her back.
It was her own daughter.
Mother and daughter met but did not recognize each other.
Later, while washing her hair, she carefully observed her features,
and suspected it was her daughter.
She asked about her homeland, parents, and clan.
The girl answered in detail.
Only then did she know.
The mother exclaimed in shock and sorrow,
"I once shared a husband with my mother,
and now I share a husband with my daughter.
How confused and disordered life and death are, that it has come to this!
If I do not cut off love and desire and leave home to study the path,
how can such perverse delusion ever cease?"
She then abandoned everything and left.
She reached the gate of Qíyuán.
Hungry, thirsty, and utterly exhausted, she sat under a tree.
At that time, the World-Honored One,
surrounded by a great assembly, was expounding the Dharma.
Liánhuāsè, seeing the large crowd,
thought it was a festival gathering.
"There must be food and drink," she thought.
She entered the monastery.
She saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, expounding the Dharma for the assembly.
Hearing the Dharma, her understanding opened, and her hunger and thirst vanished.
Then the World-Honored One,
surveyed the assembly to see who should be liberated.
Only Liánhuāsè was ready to attain the fruit of the path.
He then taught the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Right there on her seat, she became free from dust and defilement and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Having attained the fruit,
she single-mindedly placed her palms together and stood facing the Buddha.
When the Buddha finished teaching,
the assembly each departed.
Then Liánhuāsè approached, bowed at the Buddha's feet, knelt with palms together, and said,
"In the Buddha's Dharma, I wish to leave home."
The Buddha immediately permitted it.
He addressed the bhikṣuṇī Póshépótí:
"You may now ordain this woman into the path."
She was then ordained, received the full precepts,
diligently practiced with vigor, and attained arhatship.
She possessed the eight liberations.
Her countenance glowed, surpassing even her former beauty.
Entering the city to beg for food,
a brāhmaṇa saw her and felt defiled delight.
He thought to himself,
"This bhikṣuṇī cannot be had now.
I should find her dwelling and devise a means."
Later, when she went again to beg for food,
that brāhmaṇa sneaked in afterward and hid under her bed.
That day, the bhikṣuṇīs
had discoursed on the Dharma all night and were exhausted.
Returning to her room, she lay on her back and fell into deep sleep.
Then the brāhmaṇa came out from under the bed
and committed an impure act.
At that moment, the bhikṣuṇī leapt into the sky.
The brāhmaṇa then fell alive into hell from the bed.
The Buddha was at Ráoyuèqí, Qíshéjué Mountain.
There was a courtesan
named Liánhuá.
A good heart spontaneously arose in her, and she abandoned worldly affairs
to become a bhikṣuṇī.
She went to the mountains and walked to where the Buddha was.
Before reaching halfway, there was a flowing spring.
The woman drank water, washed her hands, and looked at herself.
Seeing her own face, peerlessly beautiful,
she immediately thought,
"Why should I abandon myself to become a śramaṇī?
I should indulge my private passions a little longer."
She then returned home.
The Buddha knew Liánhuá should be liberated.
He transformed into a woman of peerless beauty,
surpassing Liánhuá.
She came along the path.
Liánhuá saw her
and felt great affection and respect.
She asked the transformed woman,
"Where have you come from?
Where are your husband and relatives?
Why do you travel alone without attendants?"
The transformed woman replied,
"I came from the city and wish to return home.
Though we are not acquainted, let us go together to that spring."
Liánhuá said, "Good."
The two went together to the spring.
They conversed intimately.
The transformed woman lay down to sleep,
resting her head on Liánhuá's lap.
In a moment, she suddenly died.
Her body swelled, stank, rotted, and worms emerged from her belly.
Her teeth fell out, her hair dropped off, and her body decomposed.
Liánhuá saw this and was greatly terrified.
"How can a lovely person suddenly become impermanent?
If this person is thus, how can I last long?
In fear, I should go to the Buddha, be diligent, and study the path."
She immediately went to the Buddha's place.
Prostrating with her five limbs touching the ground, she paid homage and explained herself.
The Buddha told Liánhuá,
"A woman has four things
she cannot rely on:
First, youth—she will inevitably grow old.
Second, health—she will inevitably die.
Third, the joy of relatives—they will inevitably part.
Fourth, accumulated wealth and treasures—they will inevitably disperse."
Liánhuá, hearing the Dharma, joyfully understood
and attained arhatship.
In the sea southeast of the kingdom of Shèwèi, there was a terrace.
Upon it grew fragrant flowers and trees, pure and clean.
There were five hundred Brahmin women.
They served heterodox paths with sincere diligence, unaware of the Buddha.
At that time, the women said to one another:
"We are born with this form as women.
From youth to old age, we are constrained by three matters and lack freedom.
Our lives are short, our forms illusory, and we will surely face death.
It would be better for us all to go to the Fragrant Flower Terrace.
There we shall gather fragrant flowers, practice diligently, and observe fasting.
We shall beseech Brahmā and seek his favor.
May we be reborn in the Brahmā heaven, with long life and no death.
There we shall attain autonomy, free from constraints and jealousy.
We shall be rid of all offenses and adversities, with no more worries or troubles."
They then took offerings and went to the terrace.
Gathering flowers and incense, they served Brahmā.
With single-minded devotion, they fasted, hoping the noble deity would descend.
The Buddha, seeing their hearts were ready for transformation,
together with the great assembly, soared into the sky.
He went to the terrace and sat beneath a tree.
The women joyfully said,
"This is Brahmā!" and congratulated one another, thinking their wish fulfilled.
Then a heavenly being said to the women:
"This is not Brahmā.
This is the most revered in the three realms,
named the Buddha.
He saves countless beings."
The women addressed the Buddha:
"We are deeply defiled, now born as women.
We seek to escape constraints and wish to be reborn in the Brahmā heaven."
The Buddha said:
"It is good fortune that you women have made this aspiration.
In the world, two matters yield clear retribution:
Doing good brings blessings; doing evil brings calamity.
The suffering of the world, the joy of the heavens;
The troubles of conditioned existence, the tranquility of the unconditioned.
Who can discern and seek the true path?
Excellent, you women,
that you have such noble resolve."
Then the World-Honored One
spoke a verse.
Hearing the verse, the women
wished to learn the true path and become bhikṣuṇīs.
Their hair fell out by itself, and their monastic robes were complete.
Contemplating in serene concentration,
they attained arhatship.
Udāyin
went to the kingdom of Kośala.
He stayed in the Āmra garden of the Brahmin woman Bhāradvājī.
The nun's disciples went out to gather firewood.
Coming to the Āmra garden,
they saw Udāyin sitting under a tree, handsome in appearance, his faculties serene.
His mind was peaceful and concentrated, perfected in supreme discipline.
They approached him, greeted him, and sat to one side.
Then Udāyin expounded various teachings to the young women.
After exhorting them, he fell silent.
Those young women, hearing the Dharma, rejoiced.
Carrying their bundles of firewood, they returned to the nun.
They said, "Reverend teacher,
in the garden there is a śramaṇa
of the Gautama clan,
who is extremely skilled in teaching the Dharma."
The nun said to her disciples,
"You may go and invite him for tomorrow's meal."
The disciples, receiving the instruction, went to invite him.
The Venerable One remained silent.
They returned and reported to the teacher,
"The Venerable One has accepted the invitation."
When the night had passed, Udāyin
donned his robes, took his bowl, and went to the nun's dwelling.
The nun saw him coming from afar,
spread a seat, and invited him to sit.
She set out various foods and drinks,
personally serving him with abundant and excellent offerings.
After washing his hands, rinsing his mouth, and cleaning his bowl, he returned to his seat.
The Brahmin woman put on fine leather sandals,
covered her head with her robe, and sat on a high seat,
displaying an arrogant demeanor.
She said to Udāyin,
"I wish to ask something.
Do you have leisure to answer or not?"
He replied,
"Sister, now is not the time."
The next day, the disciples
again went to the garden to gather firewood and listen to the Dharma.
They returned and reported to the teacher.
The nun again sent an invitation for a meal, as before, three times.
Even when requesting the Dharma,
he replied, "It is not the time."
The disciples said,
"The teacher sat disrespectfully;
how could he speak?"
The teacher said,
"If that is so, invite him again for me."
Receiving the instruction, they invited him again.
The offering was as before.
Then the teacher,
knowing the meal was finished,
removed her leather sandals and upper garment, sat on a low seat,
and respectfully said,
"I wish to ask something.
Will you answer?"
He replied,
"Just ask, and I shall explain for you."
She then asked,
"Some say pleasure and pain are self-made;
others say they are made by another;
others say they are made by both self and another;
and others say they are made by neither self nor another."
He replied,
"Sister, the Arhat says
pleasure and pain arise differently."
She asked further,
"What does that mean?"
He replied,
"From causes and conditions arise all pleasures and pains."
She said,
"Now I ask you,
answer as you wish.
Is there the eye?"
He answered, "Yes."
"Are there forms?"
He answered, "Yes."
"Is there eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and from the condition of contact arises feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither pleasant nor painful?"
He answered, "It is so."
Udāyin said,
"This is what the Arhat says:
From such causes and conditions arise pleasure and pain."
When the Venerable One taught this Dharma,
the Brahmin woman's dust and defilements were removed, and she attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Rising from her seat, she straightened her clothes,
respectfully joined her palms, and said to the Venerable One,
"Today I have crossed over and entered certainty.
From this day forth, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
For the rest of my life, I rely on the Three Jewels."
Formerly, in the city of Shèwèi,
also called the kingdom of Kośala,
there were groups of heedless and licentious people
devoted to wickedness.
At that time, in the country, the bhikṣuṇīs
practiced diligently under trees, contemplating the true path without abandoning their resolve.
Among the bhikṣuṇīs, the foremost in wisdom
was named Kṣemā;
the foremost in supernatural powers
was named Padmāvatī.
Each had virtuous conduct and majestic spiritual power.
One day, when it was slightly hot, they went together to bathe.
They went to a flowing stream.
The wicked crowd saw them from afar and conceived evil thoughts.
Lust arose strongly, and they wished to violate them.
Waiting until the bhikṣuṇīs
had just removed their robes and entered the water to bathe,
they rushed forward, seized their robes, and placed them far away,
intending to drag and violate them.
Then the bhikṣuṇīs, filled with compassion,
plucked out both their eyes and placed them in their palms,
showing them to the offenders:
"What you love about us
is merely our facial appearance.
Now blind and eyeless,
what is there to desire?"
They further showed their stomachs and intestines,
the various parts of their bodies—the five viscera, hands, and feet—
cast aside separately.
They said to the wicked crowd:
"Where is the beauty now?"
The offenders, seeing this,
were suddenly terrified.
They realized the world is impermanent, the three realms like a temporary lodging.
Their bodies would turn into bones and blood, impure,
with nothing to cling to.
They immediately returned the robes,
bowed their heads in repentance for their wrongful actions.
"We have acted contrary and without righteousness; may our transgressions be forgiven."
Kneeling with joined palms, they each received the five precepts.
They were brought before the Buddha,
bowed their heads to the ground,
and confessed their offenses.
The elder Sudatta had an old maidservant.
Named Vidiṛa.
She was diligent and conscientious in managing the household affairs, overseeing the treasury, and everything was entrusted to her.
The elder Sudatta
invited the Buddha and the monks, providing all their needs.
The monks who cared for the sick made many requests.
The old maidservant was miserly and greedy, and she despised the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
She spoke thus:
"My master is foolish and deluded.
He has fallen under the spell of the śramaṇas, who beg without ever being satisfied—what kind of path is this?"
After saying this, she further made an evil vow:
"When will I be able to no longer hear the names of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha?"
Queen Mǎlì heard of this.
And said:
"How is it that Sudatta, like a beautiful lotus flower,
has four poisonous snakes standing beside him?"
She then commanded Sudatta:
"Send your wife to me."
When his wife arrived,
the queen said to her:
"That old maidservant in your household
speaks evil and slanders—why not drive her away?"
The wife replied:
"The Buddha's appearance brings great benefit and enrichment.
How much more so for an old maidservant?"
Upon hearing this, the queen was greatly delighted.
"I wish to invite the Buddha.
You send the maidservant to me."
The next day, when the Buddha arrived,
the elder sent the maidservant,
carrying a full vase of gold and mani pearls with a canopy,
to assist the royal household in making offerings to the assembly of monks.
As the Buddha entered the gate,
the old maidservant saw him and felt displeasure in her heart.
She immediately tried to retreat and leave through a dog hole.
But the dog hole and all the narrow alleys in all four directions were suddenly blocked.
Only the main path remained open.
The old maidservant covered her face with a fan.
The Buddha stood before her,
causing the fan to become like a mirror, offering no obstruction.
Turning her head to look in all directions, she saw the Buddha everywhere.
When she lowered her head to the ground, even her ten fingers transformed into Buddhas.
The old maidservant saw the Buddha and all these similes.
Eighty trillion
Although she did not yet give rise to faith, she was still able to dispel the sins of birth and death.
The Buddha saw her body transformed.
The maidservant fled back home and hid inside a wooden cage.
She wrapped her head in white cotton cloth, fearing she would see the Buddha again.
The Buddha said:
"This maidservant's sins are heavy, and she has no connection with me.
Ráhula has a great connection with her.
He shall convert her."
At that time, Ráhula, relying on the Buddha's majestic power,
entered the samādhi of as one wishes.
He transformed his body into that of a wheel-turning sage king.
The 1,250 bhikṣus transformed into a thousand sons.
Ānanda became the treasurer minister.
Nanda became the commander of the army.
The seven treasures and the fourfold army were all fully present.
At that time, the golden wheel treasure was in the sky,
riding on a lotus platform,
and went directly to the great elder Sudatta's house.
A yakṣa proclaimed:
"A sage king has appeared in the world.
He expels all evil people.
And proclaims the good Dharma."
Hearing this, the old maidservant was greatly delighted.
"When a sage king appears, he possesses a wish-fulfilling pearl.
There is nothing to seek or ask for—this is truly worth speaking of."
At that time, the sage king struck bells and beat drums, riding in a great jeweled carriage,
and arrived at Sudatta's house.
When the old maidservant saw him, she was extremely delighted.
"The appearance of a sage king brings great benefit and enrichment; he distinguishes good from evil and certainly will not be
deluded by śramaṇas." She emerged from the wooden cage.
And paid homage to the sage king.
The sage king then sent the minister in charge of the treasure treasury
to go to the woman and announce:
"Sister, you have past blessings and should
have the appearance of a king. The sage king
now wishes to make you the jewel woman treasure."
The old maidservant said:
"My body is lowly and base, like filth.
That the sage king would inquire after me brings immeasurable joy.
How could I be worthy of being the jewel woman treasure?
If you think of me,
command my master
to release me and set me free.
That would already be a great gift."
At that time, the sage king
said to Sudatta:
"The old woman in your household has majestic features.
I now wish to make her the jewel woman treasure."
Sudatta replied:
"I obey your command.
I offer her to the great king."
Hearing she was to be freed, the old maidservant was overjoyed beyond measure.
The sage king then used the wish-fulfilling pearl to illuminate the woman's face, allowing her to see herself
as the jewel woman treasure.
She was doubly delighted
and said:
"Those śramaṇas and others speak loftily and boastfully,
claiming they have the Way, yet not a single one shows any proof.
The appearance of a sage king brings vast benefits.
He has made this old and decrepit me into a jewel woman treasure."
After saying this, she prostrated herself on the ground, paying homage to the sage king.
At that time, the treasurer minister
proclaimed the king's excellent decree,
expounding the ten good Dharmas.
Hearing the ten good Dharmas, the woman was greatly delighted.
She then said:
"What the sage king says
is all good and without fault."
She paid homage to the king, repented her faults, and blamed herself.
Her mind was thus tamed.
At that time, Ráhula returned to his original form.
The old maidservant raised her head
and saw the 1,250 bhikṣus.
She then said: "The Buddha's Dharma is pure and does not abandon sentient beings.
Even someone as base and evil as me is still transformed and saved."
After saying this,
she requested to receive the five precepts.
At that time, Ráhula
explained the three refuges and the method of receiving the five precepts.
Upon hearing this Dharma,
before she could even raise her head, she became a Srota-āpanna.
At that time, Ráhula
led this old maidservant to the Jeta Grove.
Upon arrival, she saw the Buddha,
joyfully joined her palms, paid homage, and repented.
She requested the Buddha to allow her to leave home.
The Buddha told Ráhula: "Take this woman to Gautamī."
Before they arrived,
Ráhula
explained to her the Dharma of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.
Upon hearing this, the old maidservant
had her hair fall out naturally and became a bhikṣuṇī.
She attained the three insights, the six supernatural powers, and possessed the eight liberations.
King Prasenajit
and Queen Mǎlì
were greatly delighted and said:
"World-Honored One,
what past sins did this old maidservant have,
and what blessings
allowed her to attain the path of an arhat?"
The Buddha replied:
"Great King,
in a past kalpa,
there was a Buddha, the World-Honored One,
named Ratnacchatra-dīpa-rāja.
After that Buddha's parinirvāṇa, during the period of the semblance Dharma,
there was a king named Vicitra-ratna-puṣpa-prabha.
That king had a son
named Sukha-darśana.
He sought to leave home.
His father permitted it.
The prince went to the saṅgha's dwelling
and requested to leave home.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu
who was intelligent and wise, deeply understanding the true reality.
He accepted him as a disciple.
There was another bhikṣu
named Guṇa-puṣpa-prabha,
who skillfully expounded the essential Dharma, guiding and advancing beginners.
Although the prince-bhikṣu had left home,
he still harbored arrogance.
His upādhyāya explained to him the profound and wonderful Dharma of Prajñāpāramitā and the meaning of great emptiness.
Upon hearing this, the prince misunderstood and held wrong views.
After the bhikṣu's parinirvāṇa, he said:
'My great upādhyāya is empty of wisdom.
He only praises empty and虚无 matters.
May I in future lives not delight in seeing him.
My ācārya has wisdom and eloquence; may he in this life be a good spiritual friend.'
After the prince-bhikṣu said this,
he taught what is not Dharma as Dharma and what is Dharma as not Dharma.
He instructed his disciples
to all practice wrong views.
Although he upheld the precepts and did not lack dignified conduct,
due to his misunderstanding, after his life ended,
in the time it takes to shoot an arrow, he fell into the Avīci hell.
For eighty billion kalpas, he constantly suffered great torment.
Afterward, he was reborn as a poor and lowly person,
deaf, foolish, and blind,
working as a maidservant.
At that time, the upādhyāya was myself.
The ācārya at that time was Ráhula.
The prince-bhikṣu is this old maidservant."
There was a woman, a Brahmin named Sìzhàpó.
She had six sons.
One after another, they passed away; thinking of her sons, she went mad.
Naked, with disheveled hair, she wandered along the road.
From afar, she saw the World-Honored One and immediately regained her senses.
Ashamed and embarrassed, she gathered herself and crouched down.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"Take your uttarāsaṅga robe and give it to her to wear while listening to the Dharma."
Ānanda gave her the robe to wear.
She came before the Buddha, bowed her head, and paid homage to the Buddha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for her, instructing and benefiting her, bringing her joy.
She took refuge in the Three Jewels and became a lay disciple.
Joyfully, she departed.
Later, her seventh son also passed away.
She did not weep at all.
Her husband asked her in verse, saying:
The wife said:
The husband said:
The wife said:
The husband said:
The wife said:
The husband went to see the Buddha.
The Buddha spoke in verse, saying:
Hearing the Dharma, he understood its meaning and left home to follow the Buddha.
Dwelling in solitude and contemplation, he became an Arhat.
His wife and granddaughter, Sūntuópánlí,
also left home and ultimately reached the end of suffering.
Shèwèi City.
There was a solitary widow.
She gave birth to a daughter.
The girl was just seventeen years old.
Her face and appearance were dignified and proper, but her clothes could not cover her form.
The mother begged for food to support herself.
The daughter was chaste, virtuous, intelligent, and perceptive.
She widely read the scriptures, guarded her chastity, and did not leave the house.
She lived near the king's road and in her heart wished to marry the king.
She also wished to serve the gods like the Buddha.
The king traveled within the country.
He saw a crow cawing on the poor girl's door.
The king then raised his bow and shot at the crow.
The crow, holding the king's arrow, flew into the girl's house.
The king's attendants chased the crow into the dwelling.
The girl did not show her face.
She only pulled out the arrow, released the crow, and threw the arrow outside.
The king's men saw her finger and knew she was no ordinary person.
Later that year.
The king's first wife passed away.
He sought to marry a new wife.
No one suitable was found.
He extensively searched among the people.
His attendants reported, saying:
"The poor solitary mother and daughter from the time when you shot the crow.
The daughter is sixteen or seventeen; although we did not see her face,
observing her hand and hearing her voice, she seems like a noble person."
The king then went to see and called for her to come.
He sent a physiognomist to examine her; the envoy went to the girl's door and entered directly inside.
The girl's mother was not there; only the girl was present.
The envoy called for the girl to come out; he called three times, but she did not respond.
The envoy said:
"Poor girl, come out."
The girl replied:
"Whether capable or not, each is a child of a family.
Who are you to intrude into my home?
Quickly go outside."
The envoy said:
"The king has sent me to call you.
How dare you, a lowly girl, act like this?"
The girl said:
"For what reason has the king sent you here?
If he seeks me to be a maidservant,
my family has not violated the king's laws.
If he seeks me to be his wife,
then you all are my servants.
How dare you lightly insult a poor household?
Taking advantage of your position to intrude and threaten a woman.
Although I am lowly,
I have my own destiny and will not submit to intimidation.
You all report to the king."
The envoy dared to respond.
He fully reported to the king.
The king then ordered all officials.
To prepare the carriage and complete the rituals.
He went to welcome her with five hundred court ladies.
The envoy carried gifts of respect: oxen, sheep, pigs, wine, and betrothal offerings.
The envoy rode in a black-canopied carriage.
Drawn by five horses to welcome the girl.
In front, a vanguard of a hundred thousand elite soldiers.
Following, a thousand carriages.
Ten thousand fine horses.
Scattered followers numbering one hundred twenty thousand.
Bells rang and drums beat, the sound shaking heaven and earth.
Countless onlookers went to the girl's door.
The envoy descended from the carriage and presented the gifts of respect.
The girl respectfully ordered, saying:
"Thank the envoy and all the officials, officers, and people.
Great and small, you have toiled on the road.
This solitary and poor girl is lowly and unworthy, not to be forgotten.
Distantly troubling the officials and attendants.
Wrongfully humiliating the king's heavy command.
The girl, due to her humble and lowly status, mistakenly relying on past blessings,
should be at the king's steps and hall, aware of her own ugliness.
In virtue, lacking the demeanor of a woman.
In appearance, lacking the color of peach blossoms or the udumbara flower.
In voice, lacking the pleasing sound of strings and pipes.
In wisdom, lacking the clarity of divine sages and great men.
In knowledge, lacking the vision of sages that spans ten thousand li.
In body, lacking the luster of purple gold's radiance.
In aura, lacking the fragrance of sandalwood or musk.
In speech, lacking the beauty of loyalty, harmony, benevolence, and goodness.
In conduct, lacking the propriety of advance and retreat, high and low.
Wrongly receiving the king's command, only toil the onlookers."
The envoy and all officials could not help but sigh.
She spoke to the court ladies:
"You all, with little fortune, have fallen into this lowly service.
From now on, working together,
you should each correct your minds, cultivate goodness in your actions.
Do not violate the king's decorum."
The five hundred court ladies all responded with assent.
She also called the two thousand five hundred maidservants.
Speaking to them, she said:
"People have no inherent nobility or baseness; those who possess the Way are honored.
You all are children of good people.
In the changes of ancient and modern times, you find yourselves in lowly positions.
Do not belittle yourselves; you should strive to do good."
They all said: "We obey your teaching."
The officials presented the king's gifts.
One thousand jīn of gold.
Two thousand jīn of silver.
Flowery auspicious necklaces, crystal, and lapis lazuli.
Bright moon divine pearls, coral, and amber.
One thousand bolts of plain white silk, one thousand bolts of imperial fine silk.
Patterned silks, damasks, brocades, red embroidery, purple and green.
Plain, yellow, red, white gauze and crepe garments.
Sandalwood incense, various kinds, one thousand bolts.
The officials presented one hundred sets of clothing and the lady's ornaments.
The girl then accepted them; after dressing solemnly,
she came out to pay respects to the higher position.
The officials saw her and all rejoiced.
They all exclaimed "Long live the king," and that the country would surely be greatly peaceful.
"We have gained the mother of our hundred surnames and ten thousand people."
The court ladies and maidservants drew close and attached to her like children finding a mother.
She arranged her clothes and boarded the carriage; the carriage became steady and peaceful.
The horses were well-controlled; the sky became clear and bright.
White elephants gathered like clouds, following and mournfully trumpeting.
The officials, ministers, and people all said:
"A heavenly being has descended; the country will surely be safe and secure."
Upon reaching the palace gate, it naturally opened.
Five hundred attendants entered the palace and descended from the carriage.
The palace naturally emitted light of five colors.
The hall shone brilliantly, illuminating inside and out.
She entered the hall and bowed to the king.
The king saw her and was startled, not knowing what to do.
He descended from his seat to respond to her.
The great lady bowed to the king.
She bowed a hundred times, kneeling like flowing water.
She knelt and rose by herself, a hundred bows before stopping.
The king knelt long to respond to her.
She instructed within the palace:
"Be gentle, kind, and benevolent; do not hurt others' feelings."
The king loved and respected her.
She spoke slowly and little, but her words always matched righteousness.
Inside and outside, all respected and submitted to her.
For seven days and seven nights after entering the palace, she did not sleep or rest.
She amused herself together with the various ladies and court ladies.
The king wished to see her.
The lady's intention was chaste and pure, not dwelling in turbidity and filth.
Her original intention was pure; she did not speak with the king.
Nor did they meet.
The king said:
"The principle of the household, the distinction between husband and wife,
is based on affection and love as closeness.
The lady has entered the palace for seven days and seven nights,
yet we have not met.
What is her intention?
Does she consider this the rule?"
The lady had the court ladies reply to the king, saying:
"I originally had two vows.
Now I have obtained one.
I have not obtained the other.
Therefore, we have not met."
The king said:
"What have you obtained?
What have you not obtained?"
The lady replied:
"Since I was young, I made a vow:
To have a husband like the king and to serve the gods like the Buddha.
The king said:
"We can meet once,
and afterward I will go to call the Buddha."
The lady said: "No.
Until I see the Buddha,
I will ultimately not meet with the king."
The king became greatly angry and said:
"You were originally lowly and poor, of beggar stock.
How dare you defy the intention of the ruler of ten thousand chariots?"
The lady said:
"A woman's fate is tied to her husband.
East or west, I follow his command.
But I have an old vow that cannot be betrayed."
"Although the king is honored,
he should not wrongfully question an innocent person."
The king said:
"I am the ruler of ten thousand chariots.
Those who offend are executed.
Why ask about right or wrong?"
The lady said:
"The king is the parent of the hundred surnames.
Judgment and punishment should follow reason.
How can you act on personal joy or anger?
What ordinary people do not do,
how much less should the king?"
The king said:
"Those who follow my heart are pardoned.
Those who do not are executed."
The lady said:
"A woman also has a humble heart.
If my heart is followed, then we can meet.
If my heart is not followed,
we will ultimately not meet."
The king said:
"How then should I invite him?"
The lady said:
"The Buddha is in our country; if invited, he will surely come."
The king said:
"I fear the officials will laugh at me."
The lady said:
"If the king invites the Buddha into the palace."
When the king ascended the hall, all the officials naturally rejoiced.
Generation after generation would receive blessings, and he would not be mocked as a foolish king.
The king said,
"Excellent."
That very day, he ordered the kitchens to prepare food for a hundred thousand people.
He sent a maidservant to inform the queen, saying,
"The food for a hundred thousand people to invite the Buddha is ready.
You may go and invite the Buddha."
The queen said,
"A woman follows orders.
As for the propriety of inviting the Buddha, Your Majesty should personally go in your carriage.
Temporarily go to meet the Buddha and deeply revere him."
The king said,
"If I invite him, I will go myself.
If you invite him, you go yourself.
I will not go."
The queen said,
"The king is noble and is my husband.
A woman's strength is not as slight as the king's words.
The king, wielding his authority, should temporarily go to meet the Buddha.
If not, you are not a member of the great king's family.
There is no righteousness of husband and wife or household.
Thus, you are merely another person."
The king said,
"If husband and wife are not yet established, then there is no shared duty; it lies in your intention."
The queen fell silent and did not speak.
Her radiance was dazzling, her appearance extraordinary.
The king suspected the queen might intend to kill herself.
Or perhaps she might suddenly leave.
He ordered the internal and external patrols and guards
to prepare defenses with officers and soldiers, closing the palace gates.
Guards stood in rows, connected so tightly that even a flying bird could not pass through.
The palace maids were arranged in succession, making it impossible for a needle to drop between them.
The queen knew the king's mind was set against going to invite the Buddha,
and that he did not trust her.
The queen then vanished through transformation in the hall.
Her body completely disappeared without a trace.
A thousand maids and seventy-one consorts
were all startled, looking at each other, scattering to search.
Inside and outside, the search was thorough, but nothing was seen.
The king was greatly ashamed and frightened, weeping as he rose.
The king said,
"What to do, what to do?
My stubbornness has caused this; I regret it deeply.
By what means can I make her return?"
The second consort said to the king,
"The great queen
is not among our ordinary, lowly kind.
Your Majesty should have complied with her wishes.
Yet you suddenly rejected and opposed her, treating her with angry words.
She is a heavenly being.
If the king has caused the great queen to leave,
what shall we seventy-one depend on?"
The maids and attendants all wept.
It was as if someone had died.
The nobles, men and women, also grieved and lamented.
"Now in our country, whom shall we rely on?"
Birds cried out, heaven and earth greatly stirred.
The king, moved to the extreme, wished to die.
He sighed toward heaven, tears falling like rain.
The people ceased their work, markets and streets empty and abandoned.
In groups of ten or five, they followed each other in sorrow.
For seven days and seven nights, the king lay still, fasting and not eating.
The second consort said,
"You should temporarily go to see the Buddha,
and invite him to come together."
The king went to where the Buddha was, bowed with his head at the Buddha's feet,
and said to the Buddha,
"I am King Héjiādáliú of Āqíluónài Country.
Thus, three times he bowed in reverence.
"I am occupied with state affairs day and night without rest."
The Buddha said,
"State affairs are laborious and troublesome, truly taxing to the spirit.
Are the officials, people, and borders peaceful?"
The king said,
"All receive the Buddha's grace.
I only wish to trouble you to
temporarily come to my humble abode."
The Buddha remained silent.
In a moment, the Buddha arrived at the hall.
The great queen,
along with the various consorts and maids, three thousand five hundred and seventy-one in total, bowed to the Buddha.
The king initially did not see the queen.
The maids also did not see her.
Only the Buddha saw her.
The king, having bowed to the Buddha, was sad and unhappy.
The Buddha said to the king,
"The great queen you seek
is precisely this person."
The king saw her and rejoiced.
All the officials, consorts, maids, great and small, also rejoiced.
The king set out food and drink.
After the meal, the Buddha gave a great blessing,
each seeking what they desired in their hearts.
The king said to the Buddha,
"My great queen
was originally the daughter of a poor, lowly, and orphaned mother.
Now she is the great queen.
Moreover, she can vanish and transform like this.
What karma led to this?
She is honored above all others,
becoming the mother of the people.
She is benevolent, virtuous, wise, kind, her words gentle and not hurting others.
She remained invisible for seven days; humans, spirits, dragons did not know her whereabouts."
The Buddha said,
"The great queen
in the past was a great householder
with immeasurable wealth but was stingy and unwilling to give.
Therefore, she is now poor.
That householder was fond of licentiousness and pleasure,
enjoying affairs with women.
Therefore, she now falls among women.
Also, she enjoyed associating with learned Daoist masters,
thus she now has wisdom.
She has already seen five hundred Buddhas,
and now encounters me.
In the past, she and the king were good friends,
therefore they became husband and wife.
The great queen served five hundred Buddhas in previous lives,
but her mind was not steadfast.
She troubled worldly people, therefore she fell among women.
The great queen, after thirty-nine kalpas,
will attain Buddhahood.
The king will also be reborn seven times in heaven
and seven times in the human world.
When the king is born in heaven,
the great queen will be a heavenly maiden,
attending the king,
always pleasing him.
The king and the great queen vowed to die together,
following each other life after life, both seeking liberation."
The king, due to his pride and indulgence, controlled his emotions of joy and anger.
All would not see such things again.
The king's heart was greatly joyful,
and he immediately attained the irreversible path.
Then he was given the Five Precepts.
The queen, maids, great and small, nobles, officials, and all the people of the country all received the Five Precepts.
The great queen previously received the Ten Precepts,
observing three annual fasts
and six monthly fasts.
Together with the后宫 consorts and maids, three thousand five hundred and seventy-one in total,
they engaged in practices, leading each other in goodness.
The king's righteous rule was broad and magnanimous, the country achieved great peace.
They built stūpas and monasteries, all with the seven treasures.
They respected each other, inside and outside without thoughts of separation.
When people died, they all ended their lives naturally.
The great queen awakened, contemplating the impermanence of the world.
People day and night engage in licentiousness, affection, ignorance, and impurity.
In life, they have no virtuous reputation;
in death, they become impure ghosts.
She then sighed deeply, changed her clothes, disheveled her appearance and hair,
and said to the king,
"All things under heaven are impermanent and must return to death.
The reason the king covets me
is because I am young, with smooth skin, fragrant and pure breath.
These are all impermanent and must return to death.
The union of husband and wife is nothing extraordinary; it is all impure.
Affection here will face old age and sickness.
When they come, there is no set time; who can ward them off for me?
I am now sorrowful and fearful; disasters may come suddenly and cannot be escaped.
All, noble and lowly, because of this one matter,
will all swell, become foul, impure places.
Vainly cherishing them—what benefit is there?"
The king pondered,
"What is extraordinary about the union of man and woman?
My words are true, not irrelevant."
The king said,
"You are of heavenly descent;
what you say is not false.
All attain the essence of the matter; there is nothing unacceptable.
The men, women, great and small of the country all rely on you.
Only please consider and stay."
The great queen said,
"I am a woman
and cannot decide for myself; therefore, I inform the king.
Great king, you may send me forth to fulfill the original vow of past lives."
The king said,
"I am growing old.
Although there are various consorts, maids, and children,
not one pleases me.
You should complete my remaining years.
After my eventual death, I will entrust the later affairs to you.
The crown prince is still young.
How can you think of abandoning me and leaving?
To where would you go?"
The queen said,
"My birth and death are impermanent; I am weary of these changes.
I wish to follow the Buddha and become a śramaṇā."
The king said,
"You are the mother of the country, the foremost queen.
The consorts of various countries, the palace maids, great and small, all rely on you.
How can you suddenly plan this?
When scholars near and far hear of it, will they not mock that such a śramaṇā life is not what a queen of your lineage should aspire to? Consider this again."
The queen said,
"All Buddhas of the ten directions come from among the śramaṇas.
King Fójiāshā
abandoned ninety-nine minor countries, consorts, and maids, eight or nine thousand in total,
to seek to become a śramaṇa.
Before and after, many men and women have sought to become śramaṇas."
It is not only I who am a woman.
The king, out of affection, greed, desire, and beauty, cherishes my body.
My body is entirely of pus, blood, foul discharge, and impurity.
It is difficult to engage with women.
Those who engage with women invariably fall into sin.
A woman’s body is hotter than boiling water or fire.
It scorches people, causing them to fall into grave sins.
For a thousand kalpas they will not escape.
In my previous life, I was also a man.
But because I engaged with women,
due to excessive affection, I lost my male form and became a woman.
Women are fearsome.
The king is simply unaware of it.
If the king’s mind cannot be separated from women,
the queen, concubines, and maidens—over three thousand in total—are sufficient for amusement.
The king should send them away to avoid sorrow and distress.
I will become a śramaṇā, and even death will not stop me.
The king should persuade, not hinder me.
The king said:
"If you are like this, what use is the kingdom to me?"
The queen said:
"If the king can understand impermanence, that is the king’s highest aspiration.
The kingdom, throne, officials, concubines, maidens, treasures, and palace—none of these belong to the king.
The king has a body, bones, skull, brain, and five viscera.
All will scatter and disperse.
What is there to cherish?"
The king said:
"Today, I will listen only to you.
But I fear my queen, concubines, and maidens will follow and leave together."
The queen said:
"Each has their own karmic destiny and blessings.
It is not something people can stop.
Even if you threaten them with knives and clubs,
it will ultimately be futile.
I only hope that I alone am sent away.
The king should comfort them with affection and compassion.
They will naturally draw close and rely on the king."
The king said:
"These people admire and delight in your virtue.
How can I, a single man, extend goodwill to all of them?
I rely solely on you to be my proper consort.
If you abandon me now,
these women will wield knives to kill me, and only then will they fear me."
The queen said:
"No.
Women regard men as their proper masters.
If the king pays attention and draws near to them, they will naturally be at peace."
The king said:
"It is up to you."
The queen then called the three thousand women—queen, concubines, and maidens.
She advised them, saying:
"You women,
draw close to the great king with respect and dignity, and do not be disrespectful.
I now bid farewell to all of you.
Each of you must strive diligently, morning and evening,
devotedly uphold the sutras and Dharma, and increase your diligence.
May I soon attain Buddhahood.
I will return to deliver you."
The queen, concubines, and maidens then raised their voices and wept loudly.
It was heard in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
Śakra then descended and bestowed upon her a monastic robe.
It naturally clothed her body, and her hair fell to the ground.
He conferred the five hundred precepts, making her a bhikṣuṇī.
The queen, concubines, and maidens all rejoiced greatly.
Śakra also bestowed a monastic robe and alms bowl, making her a śramaṇā.
The king, having attained contentment, remained calm and unangered.
He laughed joyfully and said:
"The merits and virtues of you noble ones are lofty and majestic—is this not delightful?"
He then attained the path and returned to the palace.
His mind was greatly bewildered.
He went out and summoned the crown prince, entrusting the kingdom to him.
The king then made a vow, saying:
"I now wish to become a śramaṇā—who knows of me?"
Śakra then shaved the king’s head.
A monastic robe clothed his body, and an alms bowl appeared of itself.
He then followed the Buddha.
Twelve minor kings
also relinquished their kingdoms, entrusting them to their crown princes,
and followed the king to become śramaṇās.
Together, they attained the path of arhatship.
Ājiādálíu is myself.
The great queen is Jūyí.
The Buddha resided in Vaiśālī.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"I have heard that among the nuns, the one with the foremost merit and virtue
is Shīlìmó.
At that time, there was a famine, and alms were difficult to obtain.
Then, the bhikṣuṇī Shīlìmó entered the city to beg for alms.
Seeing a bhikṣu, she asked:
'Venerable one, have you obtained food?'
The bhikṣu showed her his empty alms bowl.
She then gave him the food from her own bowl.
The bhikṣu, having obtained the food, returned to the monastery.
He called other bhikṣus to share the meal.
The bhikṣus asked:
'Elder, where did you obtain such fine food?'
He replied:
'I obtained it from the bhikṣuṇī Shīlìmó.'
Hearing this, the bhikṣus each went to request alms.
Thus, in succession, up to five hundred bhikṣus
all obtained food.
Only then did she seek for herself.
The time had passed,
and having missed the meal, she returned to the monastery.
The next morning,
the bhikṣus again donned their robes and took their alms bowls,
standing at the gate of the bhikṣuṇīs’ monastery.
Seeing them, the bhikṣuṇīs entered
and said to Shīlìmó:
'The bhikṣus are now waiting outside the gate.'
Hearing this, Shīlìmó said to her disciples:
'Bring my robe and bowl.
I will beg for alms for these venerable ones.'
Thus, in succession, she provided for five hundred people, and only then sought for herself.
Again, the time passed, and she missed the meal, returning empty-handed.
On the third day, it was also thus.
Up to the point of providing for five hundred people in succession,
only one person had not received food.
This bhikṣu followed Shīlìmó into a household.
Because he had missed meals for the past three days,
his body was weak and exhausted, and he fainted, falling to the ground.
There was a bhikṣuṇī named Bàozhì
who, harboring evil faith, slandered the Buddha and defamed the saṅgha.
The Buddha said:
"Not only in this life,
but in past countless kalpas,
a monkey king lived in a forest, eating fruits and drinking water.
At that time, he thought of all crawling, breathing beings, humans, and creatures,
wishing to deliver them all to the state of non-action.
At that time, there was a turtle who became his close friend.
The turtle often went to visit the monkey.
They ate, drank, conversed, and discussed righteous principles.
His wife saw this
and suspected there was illicit intimacy. She asked:
'Husband, where have you been going?'
He replied:
'I have formed a close friendship with a monkey.
He is very intelligent and wise, and also understands righteous principles.'
The wife still did not believe.
She then pretended to be ill,
lying weakly on the ground, and refused to recover.
She said to her husband:
'My illness is severe.
Only if I obtain the liver of that monkey you are close to
will I survive.'
The husband replied:
'He entrusts his life to me.
How can I take his life to save you?'
The wife said:
'Husband and wife share one body. If you do not think of helping me,
instead favoring the monkey...' The husband, respecting his wife,
went to invite the monkey to share a meal.
The monkey replied:
'My home is on land.
Yours is in water.
How can I follow you?'
The turtle said:
'I will carry you on my back.'
The monkey agreed. Carrying him midway, the turtle said to the monkey:
'My wife is ill and needs your liver.'
The monkey said:
'Why didn’t you say so earlier?
My liver is hanging on a tree; I did not bring it with me.
Let me return to fetch it, and then I will accompany you.'
He then returned to the tree, leaping about joyfully.
The turtle asked:
'You should have fetched your liver.
Why, instead of going to my home,
are you leaping about?'
The monkey replied:
'Under heaven, none is more foolish than you.
We are close friends, entrusting our lives to each other,
yet you seek to endanger me.'
The turtle’s wife is Bàozhì.
The turtle is Tiáodá.
The monkey king is myself."
The Buddha traveled to the kingdom of Shèwèiqí.
King Pōsīnì
invited the Buddha and his monks.
He prepared a meal in the palace.
As they were about to go to the king's palace,
there was a bhikṣuṇī
named Bàozhì.
She tied a wooden bowl to her abdomen, pretending to be pregnant.
Then she demanded the Buddha's robe,
saying, "You are my husband; from you I have conceived this child.
You do not provide me with food or clothing—what is the meaning of this?"
At that time, all the great assemblies—humans, devas, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, various devas, spirits, and ghosts,
as well as the people of the kingdom—were all shocked and alarmed.
The Buddha is the most revered in all the three realms.
His mind is purer than a mani jewel.
The brilliance of his wisdom surpasses that of the sun and moon.
He stands alone across the three periods of time, with none able to match him.
He subdues all heresies;
the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths all submit to him.
His virtue is lofty and immeasurable, beyond description.
The sky is formless and cannot be defiled.
The Buddha's mind surpasses even that, with no equal.
This bhikṣuṇī, being a disciple of the Buddha,
how could she harbor evil intentions and seek to slander the Tathāgata?
The Buddha, seeing the minds of the assembly and wishing to resolve their doubts, looked up toward the heavens.
At that moment, Śakra, lord of the devas, immediately descended.
He transformed into a rat that gnawed through the rope tying the bowl.
The bowl then fell to the ground.
The assembly witnessed this.
Anger and joy arose together, and they wondered about the reason for this.
At that time, the king was angry,
saying, "This bhikṣuṇī abandoned her home and distant pursuits to become a disciple of the Buddha.
Not only could she not praise the immeasurable virtues of the Tathāgata,
but she instead harbored jealousy and slandered him." Then the great king
immediately ordered his attendants,
"Dig a pit in the ground to bury her upside down."
At that time, the Buddha explained and advised, "Do not do this.
This is my past karma, not solely her fault.
In the distant past, long ago,
there was a merchant
selling many fine genuine pearls.
They were round, bright, and beautiful.
At that time, there was a woman who wanted to buy them all.
Just as they were about to complete the transaction,
a man
came and doubled the price, taking the pearls away alone.
The woman, unable to obtain them, harbored anger and resentment in her heart.
She then begged him for them, but he again refused to give them.
Her anger grew intense,
and she thought, 'I was about to buy the pearls,
and he came and snatched them away.
I begged him for them, and again he refused to give them.
You have humiliated me.
In whatever life I am born, I will repay you for this grievance.'
The man who bought the pearls was me in a past life.
The woman was Bàozhì in a past life.
This is due to past causes,
not just the present life."
When the kalpa was about to form,
the water calamity arose, destroying the second dhyāna heaven.
The wind calamity blew and coalesced, forming the world.
The devas of Ābhāsvara, their merit and lifespan exhausted,
were reborn as humans, taking joy as their food.
Their bodies emitted light, illuminating themselves, and they could fly with supernatural powers.
There were no distinctions of male and female, noble and lowly.
Thus it is said that sentient beings naturally had the earth's essence,
like clarified butter.
Its color was like fresh butter,
and its taste was sweeter than honey.
Taking it by hand to taste,
they became attached to its flavor.
Those who ate more had coarse and haggard complexions;
those who ate less had radiant skin and appearance.
Thus, superiority and inferiority arose, and they began to dispute among themselves.
The earth's essence then vanished.
Next, an earth crust appeared,
resembling thin pastry.
Its color, taste, and fragrance were delightful, and they all ate it together.
Mutual contempt arose, and the earth crust also vanished.
Then an earth skin appeared, and depending on how much they ate, various evil dharmas arose.
The earth produced non-glutinous rice, and they all ate it.
Male and female forms appeared, and eventually kings were established. The world was prosperous and joyful. The earth produced green grass,
like a peacock's tail, gradually spreading out.
There were eighty thousand countries,
with settlements of people so close that the crowing of roosters could be heard from one to another.
The world was free from illness, extreme heat, and extreme cold.
They ruled the country with Dharma, practicing the ten good deeds.
They cared for all beings like parents.
Human lifespans were long.
Later, the kings' virtue gradually declined, and lifespans shortened.
Down to ten thousand years,
and now to one hundred years.
When a king passed away, his successor
was named Zhēnbǎo.
The wheel-turning sage king
obtained the golden wheel because
Śakra often commanded the Four Heavenly Kings
to inspect the world on the sixth day of each month,
observing people's good and evil deeds.
The Four Heavenly Kings and the messengers of the crown prince
saw that a great king ruled the world with the ten good deeds and the four immeasurables,
diligently caring for the people, his heart surpassing even a compassionate father.
They reported this matter to Śakra, lord of the devas.
Śakra, hearing this,
rejoiced at his ability.
He then commanded Viśvakarman
to bestow upon him the golden wheel.
It was brought out and entrusted to Vaiśravaṇa, the heavenly king.
Vaiśravaṇa, the heavenly king, entrusted it to a flying yakṣa.
The flying yakṣa brought it to the great king.
Vaiśravaṇa, the heavenly king, commanded this yakṣa,
"You shall always hold this golden wheel for the king,
above his head, for the duration of his lifespan.
You must not abandon it midway."
This yakṣa always held it for him,
moving, stopping, coming, and going according to the sage king's wishes, until the end of his lifespan.
Then it was returned to Vaiśravaṇa, the heavenly king.
Vaiśravaṇa, the heavenly king, returned it to Viśvakarman.
Viśvakarman placed it back into the treasure vault. The king of the nature of the Way, with firm virtue, rode the golden wheel, ruling over the four continents.
The king of the nature of the lineage rode the silver wheel, ruling over three continents.
The king of the nature of practice rode the copper wheel, ruling over two continents.
Those who attained kingship through the ten good deeds
rode the iron wheel, ruling over one continent.
The Wheel-Turning Sage King.
He possesses the seven treasures.
And has four divine virtues.
First, the golden wheel treasure.
Second, the white elephant treasure.
Third, the dark blue horse treasure.
Fourth, the divine pearl treasure.
Fifth, the jade maiden treasure.
Sixth, the householder treasure.
Seventh, the commander-in-chief treasure.
When the Wheel-Turning King appears in Jambudvīpa,
the kṣatriyas pour water over the king's head, and at the time of the full moon, he bathes in fragrant water.
He ascends to a high hall and gathers musicians.
Suddenly, the heavenly golden wheel treasure appears before him.
The wheel has a thousand spokes, complete in radiance and color.
It is made of heavenly gold, not of this world.
The wheel's diameter is fourteen feet.
Seeing it, the king thinks to himself:
"From ancient times I have heard of this; now this wheel appears—could this be it?"
"Now I should test this wheel treasure."
The king then summons the fourfold army,
faces the golden wheel treasure,
uncovers his right shoulder, places his right knee on the ground,
and with his right hand touches the golden wheel, saying:
"You should turn to the east according to the Dharma, without violating the constant rule."
The wheel immediately turns eastward.
The king leads the fourfold army, following behind it.
Four deities guide the wheel to where it stops.
The king then halts his chariot.
The small kingdoms of the east bring silver millet in golden bowls,
and golden millet in silver bowls,
coming before the king,
bowing their heads and saying:
"Excellent, great king!
Now this eastern land is rich and joyful, abundant with treasures, and the people are prosperous.
We wish the great king to remain here to govern and transform."
The great king replies:
"You should only govern the people with righteous Dharma.
Do not allow injustice, nor let there be unlawful conduct within your countries.
Do not kill yourselves,
and teach others not to kill, steal, engage in sexual misconduct, slander, harsh speech, false speech,
frivolous talk, greed, wrong views, or jealousy.
This is what is called my governance."
Then the various small kings
follow the great king on his tour of the countries,
to the east, south, west, and north.
Wherever the wheel goes,
the various kings all offer their lands, the flat and open areas.
The wheel then travels around, marking boundaries and measuring.
East to west, twelve yojanas.
North to south, seven yojanas.
Heavenly deities build the city walls,
the city having seven layers,
seven layers of railings, seven layers of nets,
seven layers of rows of trees, adorned all around,
made of the seven treasures, and even countless birds singing in harmony.
Furthermore, within the city, palaces are built.
The palace walls have seven layers, made of the seven treasures.
Then the golden wheel treasure stays in the air above the palace.
The king sits in the main hall in the early morning.
Suddenly, the natural elephant treasure appears before him.
Its hair is pure white, with seven places level.
It has the power to fly, and its head is variegated in color.
Its six tusks are delicate and filled with genuine gold.
Seeing it, the king thinks:
"This elephant is virtuous.
If well-trained, it could be ridden."
He then tests and trains it, and it masters all skills.
Then the Wheel-Turning King wishes to test the elephant himself.
He mounts it,
leaves the city in the early morning, travels around the four seas,
and returns by mealtime.
Then the king sits in the main hall in the early morning.
Suddenly, the natural horse treasure appears before him.
It is dark blue in color, with a red mane and tail,
its head held high like a horse, with the power to fly.
Seeing it, the king thinks:
"This horse treasure is excellent.
If well-trained, it could be ridden."
He then tests and trains it, and it masters all skills.
The king wishes to test the horse.
He mounts it himself, leaves the city in the early morning,
travels around the four seas, and returns by mealtime.
Then the king is in the main hall in the early morning.
Suddenly, the natural divine pearl appears before him.
Its substance is clear and pure, without flaw or impurity.
Seeing it, the king thinks:
"This pearl is exquisite.
If it has light, it could illuminate the palace."
The king wishes to test the pearl.
He summons the fourfold army,
places this treasure pearl on a high banner,
and in the dark of night, carries the banner out of the city.
The pearl's light illuminates one yojana.
People in the city see it and rise to work,
thinking it is daytime.
The jade maiden treasure suddenly appears on her own.
Her complexion is calm, her face端正.
Not tall, not short, not coarse, not fine.
Not white, not black, not hard, not soft.
In winter, her body is warm; in summer, her body is cool.
From all the pores of her body emits the fragrance of sandalwood.
From her mouth emits the fragrance of utpala flowers.
Her speech is gentle, her movements serene.
She rises first and sits later, never violating proper decorum.
At that time, the king has no attachment, not even a momentary thought,
let alone any intimacy.
The householder treasure suddenly appears on his own.
Within the treasure store, wealth is immeasurable.
The householder, due to past merits, has eyes that can see through things.
Hidden treasures underground, whether they have owners or not,
he can see and know them all.
Those with owners, he can protect for them.
Those without owners, he takes for the king's use.
Then the householder treasure goes to tell the king:
"Great king,
if there is anything you need to give, do not worry.
I can manage it myself."
Then the king wishes to test this householder treasure.
