He orders a ship to be prepared for play on the water.
He tells the householder:
"I need gold and treasures; quickly give them to me."
The householder replies:
"Great king,
wait a moment until I reach the shore."
The king presses him, saying:
"I need them now."
The householder treasure places his right hand into the water.
A treasure vase from the water comes out with his hand,
like a worm climbing a tree.
Seeing this, the king
says to the householder:
"Enough, enough! I have no need.
I was just testing you."
Immediately, he returns the treasures to the water.
The commander-in-chief treasure
suddenly appears.
He is wise and brave, with outstanding strategies and decisive judgment.
He goes before the king and says:
"Great king, if there is any punishment or campaign, do not worry.
I can manage it myself."
Then the king, wishing to test the commander-in-chief treasure,
gathers the fourfold army and tells him:
"Now, with the troops,
those not yet assembled, assemble them;
those already assembled, dismiss them;
those not yet prepared, prepare them;
those already prepared, release them;
those not yet departed, have them depart;
those already stationed, have them stay."
Then the commander-in-chief treasure does exactly as the king says.
Seeing this, the king leaps for joy, saying:
"Now I am truly the Wheel-Turning Sage King!"
First, long life, not dying young, unmatched by others.
Second, a strong body, free from illness, unmatched by others.
Third, a handsome appearance, unmatched by others.
Fourth, a treasure store overflowing, unmatched by others.
These are the four virtues possessed by the Sage King.
Beyond the great sea,
there is also the Padma Pond,
the Kumuda Pond,
and the Pundarīka Pond.
Beyond this land is empty space.
In that empty space, there is a great sea of water,
named Uttāna.
Below this water is the path of the Wheel-Turning Sage King.
It is twelve yojanas wide.
Along both sides of the path are seven layers of walls, seven layers of railings, seven layers of nets, and seven layers of rows of trees.
They are made of the seven treasures.
When the Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world in Jambudvīpa,
the water naturally recedes, and the path becomes level and straight.
The Wheel-Turning Sage King
then orders his chariot to go out to the rear garden for an excursion.
He tells the charioteer:
"You should drive carefully.
The reason is, I wish to observe carefully
whether the country's people are joyful and free from suffering."
Then the people of the country,
watching by the roadside,
also say to their attendants: 'You should go slowly.
I wish to observe carefully the majestic appearance of the Sage King.'"
At that time, the king compassionately nurtures the people and creatures like a father loves his children.
The people admire the king like children look up to their father.
All rare and precious things they offer to the king,
hoping he will accept them.
Then the king replies:
"Enough, people.
I have my own treasures; you may use them yourselves."
When the king governs this Jambudvīpa,
the land is level and even,
without thorns, pits, mounds, or hills.
There are also no mosquitoes, gadflies, bees, flies, snakes, vipers, or harmful insects.
Stones, sand, tiles, and gravel naturally sink.
Gold, silver, and precious jade appear on the ground.
The four seasons are harmonious, neither cold nor hot.
The land is soft and smooth, without dust or filth.
Like oil smeared on the ground, it is clean, bright, and glossy.
The ground produces flowing springs, clear and inexhaustible.
Trees are lush, flowers and fruits abundant.
The ground grows tender grass, green in winter and summer, like the feathers of a peacock.
Naturally, the polished rice had no husks or chaff, and all flavors were fully present.
At that time, there were fragrant trees with abundant flowers and fruits.
When the fruits ripened, they naturally split open, emitting a pervasive and fragrant aroma.
There were also clothing trees with abundant flowers and fruits.
When the fruits ripened, their skins and shells naturally split open, producing various garments.
There were also adornment trees.
When the fruits ripened, they produced various adornments.
There were also garland trees.
When the fruits ripened, they produced various garlands.
There were also utensil trees.
When the fruits ripened, they produced various utensils.
There were also fruit trees.
With abundant flowers and fruits, when the fruits ripened, their skins and shells naturally split open, producing various fruits.
There were also musical instrument trees.
When the fruits ripened, they produced numerous musical instruments.
When the Wheel-Turning Sage King ruled the world,
the dragon king Anàodá,
after midnight,
raised a great dense cloud that filled the world,
and poured down heavy rain like a cow urinating.
The eight-flavored water moistened and saturated everywhere.
The ground had no stagnant water nor mud.
The moisture thoroughly soaked the earth.
After midnight, the sky was clear and bright,
pure and without clouds or haze.
The sea produced a cool breeze, pure, gentle, and soft, bringing physical pleasure.
The Sage King governed the country with righteousness, without injustice, and cultivated the ten virtuous deeds.
At that time, the people also upheld correct views and were endowed with the ten virtuous actions.
After a long time, the king, like a musician eating, felt slightly unwell,
and then passed away, being reborn in the Brahmā heaven.
At that time, the golden wheel, the white elephant, the dark-blue horse, and the bright pearl all vanished.
The jewel of women, the jewel of the householder, and the jewel of the general,
along with the country's officials and people,
performed music and washed the king's body with fragrant water.
They wrapped it with five hundred sheets of karpāsa cloth,
then wrapped it again as before.
They lifted the king's body and placed it in a golden coffin,
pouring fragrant oil over it.
They placed it in an iron coffin,
then wrapped it with a wooden outer coffin, covering it with layers of fragrant firewood and garments on top.
They cremated it.
At the crossroads, they erected a seven-jeweled stupa,
measuring one yojana in length and width.
It was variegated and interwoven, made of the seven jewels.
The jewel of women, the jewel of the householder, the jewel of the general, and all the country's officials and people
came to make offerings to this stupa.
They gave to the poor and needy,
providing food to those who needed food and clothing to those who needed clothing.
Elephants, horses, and precious carriages
were given to the masses as needed, according to their wishes.
In the past, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable kalpas ago,
this world was called Rìyuèléi.
There was also a five-turbidity era.
At that time, I was a Wheel-Turning King,
ruling over Jambudvīpa,
named Dēngguāngmíng.
I taught countless people to abide in wholesome dharmas.
I saw a person bound with ropes,
and I asked,
"What offense has he committed?"
The minister replied,
"From farming grains and wheat, one-sixth goes to the government.
This person did not comply with the king's law, so he was bound."
I ordered him released.
The minister replied,
"Now, the king's sons, the harem attendants, and all their expenses are forcibly taken from others.
Not one person gives with a pure heart."
The king was greatly distressed.
He divided this land into five hundred parts,
equally distributing them among his sons.
Then he renounced the world
and went to the Yùtóumó forest by the southern sea,
eating various fruits.
Gradually, through cultivation and study, he attained the five supernatural powers.
At that time, in Jambudvīpa, there were five hundred merchants
who went to sea to gather treasures.
There was one merchant leader,
named Mǎnyuè,
who obtained what he desired.
He then prepared to return.
A dragon, harboring anger, sought to harm the merchants.
There was another dragon king,
named Mǎjiān,
who was a great bodhisattva.
Due to his original vow, he was born among dragons.
He aroused a compassionate mind to save the merchants,
enabling them to safely cross the great sea to the other shore.
The dragon king then returned to his original abode.
At that time, there was a great evil rākṣasa
following the merchants like a shadow,
intending to harm them.
This evil rākṣasa
on that very day raised a great evil wind.
The merchants became confused, lost their way,
felt great terror, and cried out in distress,
calling upon the devas, Maheśvara, water gods, earth gods, fire gods, and wind gods.
They also called upon their parents, wives, children, and relatives,
pleading, "Save us!"
Good man,
at that time,
with my pure divine ear, I heard their voices.
I immediately went to their location
and comforted them with a gentle voice,
saying, "Do not be afraid; I will show you the way,
enabling you to safely return to Jambudvīpa."
Good man,
at that time,
I wrapped my arm with white cloth, poured oil on it,
and used it as a wick, making a true declaration:
"Previously, in the Yùtóumó forest,
for thirty years, I diligently cultivated the four immeasurable minds.
For the sake of all beings, I ate fruits
and urged eighty-four thousand dragons, yakṣas, and gods
not to regress from anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
With this wholesome root, I now burn this arm
to show the way,
enabling these merchants to safely return to Jambudvīpa."
I burned my arm for seven days and seven nights.
These merchants
then safely returned to Jambudvīpa.
Good man,
at that time,
I made another wholesome vow:
"If Jambudvīpa lacks various treasures,
and if I am certain to attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi,
having attained my own benefit, I will become a merchant leader,
raining treasures seven times in each world,
and entering the great sea to obtain wish-fulfilling pearls.
In each world, I will rain various mixed treasures.
In this way, successively throughout this world,
and even in the ten directions, in immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable worlds, it will be likewise."
Good man,
in the past, all the vows I made were fulfilled.
For kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
I constantly served as the supreme leader of merchants,
in kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, in the five-turbidity evil world, raining various treasures,
seven times in a single day,
enabling satisfaction.
Then I urged and taught them to abide in the three vehicles.
In the past, in Jambudvīpa,
there were four rivers and two great kings.
One was named Brāhmaṇadeva, who alone controlled three rivers.
His people were numerous and prosperous, yet also weak and timid.
The other king was named Faquejianti, who only obtained one river.
His people were few, but all in his kingdom were brave and strong.
At that time, Vajrasena was in the main hall.
The king thought:
"My troops are brave and fierce, yet we have obtained little water.
That kingdom is weak and timid, yet alone dominates three rivers.
Now I should send an envoy to demand one river.
If they give it to me, we shall become close and friendly.
If either country has fine goods, we shall present them to each other.
If there are difficulties, we shall come to each other's aid.
If they do not give it, then I shall seize it by force."
He immediately sent an envoy to the Brahmā Kingdom.
The envoy fully conveyed the king's intention.
The Brahmā King said:
"My kingdom is abundant and prosperous, and the people are also many.
Moreover, this kingdom's territory was my father's possession.
He transferred it and bestowed it upon me.
As for contending by force, I am not inferior to him."
The envoy replied:
"This kingdom was also bestowed upon me by my father.
My strength is not diminished.
If you wish to settle it by force,
I am not afraid."
The envoy returned and fully reported to the king.
The king then assembled his army and attacked the Brahmā Kingdom.
After one engagement, the Brahmā army was defeated.
Taking advantage of this, they pursued them straight to the city walls.
The people were terrified and shrank back, not daring to come out again.
The various ministers gathered together and went to where the Brahmā King was.
They addressed the great king, saying:
"The other kingdom's soldiers are strong; our kingdom is weak and timid.
We begrudged one river, and now this defeat has come about.
If things continue like this, we fear we will soon lose the kingdom.
We only hope you will be open-minded and give one river to them.
Becoming close and friendly will be sufficient to ensure safety."
The king sent an envoy to give one river.
He also promised his daughter to be his wife.
If either country had rare goods, they would present them to each other.
In times of urgent difficulty and danger, they would come to each other's aid.
At that time, Vajrasena welcomed his daughter and honored her as his wife.
They each made peace and the army returned to their country.
After several days, the king's wife realized she was pregnant.
After becoming pregnant,
there was always a spontaneously appearing great canopy of the seven treasures
covering her body.
Whether sitting, lying, walking, or standing, it never left her.
When ten full months had passed, she gave birth to a boy.
His body was purple-gold in color, his hair dark blue.
His radiant appearance was dazzling, rarely matched in the world.
When the child was born, the canopy was above him.
They summoned various physiognomists to examine this child.
The physiognomists addressed the king:
"The prince's virtuous appearance is rare in the world."
The king and his ministers were overjoyed.
They then gave him a name.
He was named Chàluójiālì. When he reached adulthood,
his parents passed away and he became a minor king.
The ministers and people together established him to handle affairs.
After governing for several years, he went out on an excursion.
He saw the people toiling hard at plowing and sowing.
He asked his attendants:
"What are these people doing?"
They replied:
"The state takes the people as its foundation; the people take grain as their life.
If it is not so, the people's lives cannot be sustained.
If the people's lives are not sustained, the state will perish."
The king then said:
"If my fortune and appearance are fit for a king,
may my people obtain grain spontaneously."
As soon as he finished speaking,
the people's granaries and baskets were filled with various grains, all as they wished.
Later, he went out on another excursion.
He saw people drawing water, pounding grain, grinding, and laboring.
He again asked his ministers:
"Why are these people like this?"
The ministers addressed the king:
"Thanks to the king's grace, we have obtained spontaneous grain.
But it needs to be processed.
Therefore, the common people prepare and cook food."
The king again said:
"If my virtuous fortune is fit for a king,
may all the people in my kingdom have spontaneous food."
As soon as he finished speaking,
the entire realm obtained spontaneous food.
Later, he went out on another excursion.
He saw people weaving and preparing clothing materials.
He asked:
"Why are these people engaged in this work?"
The ministers said:
"To prepare clothing."
The king said:
"If my virtuous fortune is fit for a king,
may all the trees in my kingdom produce spontaneous clothing."
As soon as he uttered these words,
the various trees in the kingdom all produced exquisite clothing.
It was extremely fine and soft, in blue, yellow, red, and white, according to each person's preference.
Later, he went out on another excursion.
He saw the people vying to make musical instruments.
The king again asked his ministers:
"Why is this so?"
The ministers said:
"To make musical instruments."
The king said:
"If I have fortune and am fit to be king,
may the trees in my kingdom grow musical instruments, all as desired."
After a short while,
various kings, ministers, and people all came to pay their respects and offer congratulations.
It happened to be the king's mealtime, so he kept them to eat and drink.
At that time, the various ministers
obtained the king's food and drink, which was complete with a hundred flavors.
They all addressed the king together:
"The food and drink in our homes is bland and meager.
Now, having the king's food, the delicious flavor is extraordinary."
The king told them:
"You, my ministers and people,
if you wish to always obtain food like mine,
if you eat at my mealtime,
you will all obtain such food."
He then commanded the officer in charge:
"When my mealtime arrives, always beat a great drum,
so that all the people may hear and know.
By eating at my time, they shall obtain the supreme offering of a hundred flavors."
From then on, when eating, they would beat the drum.
All the people, upon hearing the sound, would think of eating,
and the supreme delicacies of a hundred flavors would spontaneously appear before them.
The people were at ease and happy.
At that time, King Brahmā sent an envoy
to come to King Gàishì's kingdom.
He said to Gàishì:
"When your father was alive,
I gave the river water to your father.
Now that your father has passed away, you should return it to me."
At that time, King Gàishì replied to that envoy:
"My territory and the river water now
were not obtained by my force taking them from you.
However, as king, I do not labor the people or their goods.
Please wait, and later I will meet with your king."
The envoy returned and reported to the king.
The king agreed to his intention.
They set a date for a mutual meeting.
The two kings both advanced, surrounded by their troops.
Each set up a great camp on one side of the river.
The two kings rode in boats and met in the middle of the river.
When King Brahmā first saw Gàishì,
his body color was radiant like a purple-gold mountain.
His hair was glossy like dark lapis lazuli.
His eyes were wide and long, rarely seen among men.
A feeling of reverence arose within him, and he thought it was Brahmā.
They approached, greeted each other, and sat facing each other in one place.
They discussed the two countries' territories and the matter of demanding the river.
Gàishì replied:
"In my country, whatever the people desire appears spontaneously.
There is also no taxation or labor service for the king."
Before he finished speaking, mealtime arrived.
King Gàishì's army beat the drum, intending to eat.
Brahmā, thinking they intended to kill him, rose in terror and apologized for his offense.
He spread out a sheepskin and prostrated himself, striking the ground before him with his belly.
Gàishì himself rose and pulled him up to sit again.
He again said to him:
"Great King, why are you so terrified?
My army always beats the drum at mealtime.
The reason for this is:
By eating at my time, they all obtain the supreme offering of a hundred flavors."
Brahmā rose again and addressed Gàishì:
"I only wish, Great King,
that you would universally extend your care to cover me and my people.
We all wish to submit.
May all the common people receive your grace."
Thereupon, Gàishì ruled over Jambudvīpa.
All the people obtained peace and happiness.
After ascending the throne, he was in the main hall.
The assembled officials and hundred officers stood guard and attended.
At sunrise, a golden wheel treasure came from the east.
Thus, the seven treasures arrived in succession, and he ruled over the four continents.
All living beings, benefiting from the king's virtuous grace, obtained whatever they desired at will.
The king taught and commanded them all to practice the ten good deeds.
After their lives ended, they were all reborn in the heavens.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"King Chàluójiālì was my former self.
King Faquejianti is now my father.
The mother is now Māyā."
At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King,
in his quest for the Dharma, inquired throughout Jambudvīpa:
"Who understands the Buddha Dharma?
The great Wheel-Turning King wishes to study and practice it."
Then all said:
"In a small borderland country,
there is a Brahmin
who understands the Buddha Dharma."
The king immediately invited him into the palace,
saying, "Explain it for me."
The Brahmin said:
"Great King, you are most foolish!
I have studied the Buddha Dharma for a long time, enduring hardship and toil, and only then achieved mastery.
Now how can you simply wish to hear it?"
The king addressed the teacher, saying:
"What do you require?"
The Brahmin said:
"Give me offerings."
The king said:
"What offerings do you require?"
The Brahmin said:
"If you can carve a thousand wounds on your own body,
fill them with oil, place wicks in them, and offer them as lamps,
then I will explain the Buddha Dharma to you."
Before the king could reply, the Brahmin descended from his high seat.
At that time, the great king
immediately stepped forward, embraced him, and replied:
"Please wait a moment, consider carefully, and I will make the offering."
Then the great king
entered the palace and informed all his consorts:
"Now I bid you farewell.
I intend to carve my body to make a thousand lamps as an offering to the great teacher."
The consorts said:
"Nothing in the world is more precious than one's own body.
Why destroy and harm it?"
The king said:
"I seek the Buddha Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings,
to light the lamp of wisdom in the great dark chamber,
illuminating the darkness of ignorance in your cycle of birth and death,
cutting off all fetters and attaining Nirvāṇa.
All of you,
why now do you oppose my will?"
Then all the consorts fell silent,
their hearts sorrowful and choked with grief.
The king bid farewell to everyone, both inside and outside the palace.
He returned to the hall and went to the great teacher.
Removing his jeweled ornaments, he sat upright
and addressed the crowd, saying:
"Who can carve a thousand wounds on my body?"
All replied together:
"We would rather gouge out our own eyes
than dare to raise a hand to carve the king's body."
There was a Caṇḍāla of wicked nature,
who, hearing this, approached and said to the princes:
"Do not grieve; I have a method
to ensure the great king's endeavor does not succeed,
and he will rule the kingdom as before, unchanged."
The princes heard this and rejoiced.
Then the Caṇḍāla said:
"If you wish to carve the body, I can do it."
The king said:
"You are now my supreme companion on the path."
Then the Caṇḍāla,
holding an ox-tongue knife, approached the king's body
and swiftly carved until the number reached a thousand wounds.
Thinking the king would relent, he threw down the knife and fled.
They filled the wounds with oil and used fine cotton for wicks.
Then the Brahmin addressed the king, saying:
"Such diligence is difficult to achieve, yet you have achieved it.
You practice this asceticism
to hear the Buddha Dharma."
He then spoke half a verse.
The king said:
"Those who have compassion for me
should remember and uphold this Dharma."
Throughout the lands, wherever there were people, the king's command was proclaimed:
"All people should know
that the great Wheel-Turning King,
seeing sentient beings submerged in the sea of suffering,
unable to escape, gave rise to great compassion,
carved a thousand lamps on his body to seek this half-verse.
All people should now copy this verse,
recite, study, contemplate its meaning, and practice as taught."
All people, with one voice, praised the great king, saying:
"Excellent, great king!
Truly a compassionate father,
practicing such asceticism for the sake of sentient beings.
We should quickly go and copy it,
whether on paper or silk, or on stone,
or on trees, tiles, rubble, grass, or leaves,
on paths, main roads, and places where many people pass—everywhere it should be copied."
Those who saw or heard it all gave rise to the mind of enlightenment.
The king lit the thousand lamps as an offering to the great teacher.
Their light shone far, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.
From within the lamplight, a voice also emerged, speaking this half-verse.
Those who heard the Dharma
all gave rise to the mind of enlightenment.
The light shone upward to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
obscuring the heavenly light.
The Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven thought:
"For what reason is there such light?"
He then observed the world with his divine eye
and saw the Wheel-Turning King, his heart purified by great compassion,
carving a thousand lamps on his body for the sake of sentient beings,
making offerings to the great teacher to deliver sentient beings.
He thought, "We should go to encourage, admonish, and assist him."
He then descended to the world, transforming into an ordinary person,
went to the king, and asked:
"Carving a thousand lamps on your body, practicing such asceticism—
for the sake of half a verse, what do you seek to accomplish?"
The king replied:
"Good man,
I do this for sentient beings, to enable them to give rise to the mind of enlightenment."
Then the transformed person revealed his true form as Śakra.
He said:
"Making such offerings,
do you seek to become a heavenly king, a demon king, or a Brahmā king?"
The king said:
"I do not seek these.
I solely seek Bodhi for the sake of sentient beings,
to bring peace to the unsettled,
liberation to the unliberated,
deliverance to the undelivered,
and to enable those who have not attained the path to attain it."
Śakra, the heavenly king, said:
"Great King,
are you not foolish now?
Those who seek Bodhi
must endure long hardship and toil before they can achieve it.

The king replied to Śakra:

"If I do not truly seek the threefold Bodhi,

Śakra, the heavenly king, said:

When you attain Bodhi, you must deliver me first."

God-Emperor Śakra was Kāśyapa Buddha.
The wheel-turning sage king was myself.
In the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, the king’s clan name was Peacock.
His name was Bimbisāra, and he had a son
named Aśoka, whose body was rough and coarse, so his father did not cherish him.
Later on,
the king had a skilled physiognomist examine
which of his sons was fit to be king.
He summoned Aśoka’s mother and secretly informed her:
“You should take your turn.”
Aśoka addressed his mother:
“The king, my father, does not favor me.”
His mother said, “Just go.”
The minister Cheng Hù asked,
“Where are you going now?”
He answered truthfully.
Cheng Hù harnessed the finest elephant
and provided it for him to ride.
When food was set out for all the princes, all the vessels were of precious material,
but Aśoka was not given any.
His mother privately prepared a meal for him, and both the vessels and the food were superior.
The physiognomist said:
“Aśoka is the most outstanding; he is fit to be king.”
The great king said:
“He is not esteemed by me.
He will surely be killed; you must investigate further.”
The physiognomist again said:
“Now, the one with the best mount, the best food, and the best vessels—
this one is fit to be king, and there is none superior to him.”
Later, a small state within the realm,
named Takṣaśilā,
intended to rebel.
The king commanded Aśoka:
“You gather the fourfold army and seize that country.
Weapons, equipment, and supplies will not be provided to you.”
Aśoka accepted the command.
He then thought to himself:
“If I have merit and virtue and am destined to be king,
may vessels and food spontaneously emerge from the ground.” The earth immediately quaked and split open, and countless vessels and food appeared.
The country of Takṣaśilā heard that Aśoka was coming.
They adorned the roads and, sensing his approach, came forth to welcome him.
All the people vied to make offerings.
Initially, there was no resentment.
Secondly, he sent messengers to the country of Kāśī
to seek two strong men capable of toppling mountains and overturning peaks.
At that time, the devas spoke out,
addressing the two men, saying:
“This is the fourth part of the cakravartin king,
who rules Jambudvīpa; he cannot be opposed.”
All the heroes and worthies paid him homage without exception.
The devas placed a heavenly jeweled crown upon his head.
The great king heard of this.
He immediately dispatched his eldest son, Susīma,
to raise a great army, but in the end he was unable to punish him.
The great king
personally encountered a severe illness and became even more enraged.
Again hearing that he had not been subdued,
he vomited hot blood and then passed away.
Aśoka then ascended the great throne.
He appointed Cheng Hù as the chief minister
to govern the affairs of the state.
Susīma and others heard that their father had died and that Aśoka had been established as king behind their backs.
Their hearts could not bear it.
They immediately gathered troops to attack Aśoka.
The two mighty men and Cheng Hù each guarded one gate.
The king stationed himself at the eastern gate.
He had a great fire pit dug and covered it with materials,
so that there was no smoke or flame visible.
He made mechanical wooden men.
The king rode a large wooden elephant,
moving slowly to show weakness.
Susīma led his elite troops,
intending to kill Aśoka.
Seeing the wooden men moving clumsily,
he urged his army straight forward and fell into the great fire pit, where he was burned to death.
For twenty-eight thousand li, all submitted to him.
The dragons on land and the yakṣas were all subdued.
Only one dragon remained in the place where it dwelled,
an area over three hundred li wide,
where the first stūpa was built with the Buddha’s relics.
It was in the village of Rāma.
This dragon had great merit and virtue,
and alone did not submit to conversion.
Aśoka therefore recruited a caṇḍāla agent,
named Jīlika,
who was capable of carrying out killings.
He then established a prison to deal with those who did not submit.
He adorned the prison gate, making it extremely splendid,
so that those who saw it would be delighted to enter but unable to leave.
At that time, a monk from Kukkuṭārāma Monastery was reciting a sūtra.
The sūtra described the affairs of hell.
Jīlika heard it
and subsequently created cauldrons of boiling water, furnaces of charcoal, mountains of knives, and forests of swords, and so forth.
There was a monk named Hǎiyì,
who rose early, put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the city to beg for alms.
He happened to enter the gate of hell.
Jīlika seized him.
The monk wept and said to him:
“Human birth is difficult to obtain; leaving home is difficult to encounter.
I have already attained both.
I beg for a one-month extension.”
The reply was:
“I have received the king’s command;
it cannot be granted.”
He was allowed up to seven days.
The monk practiced diligently day and night.
He also saw the prince
speaking with a palace woman.
There was an order to deliver him to prison.
Jīlika immediately crushed him with an iron mortar and pestle.
The monk’s heart grew even more terrified.
On the seventh night, through contemplation, he attained the fruit of arhatship.
The next day, Jīlika
placed the monk in an iron cauldron,
filled with boiling excrement, urine, mixed filth, pus, and blood,
and boiled it over a fierce fire for a long time, but the monk was not harmed.
The monk sat alone on a lotus flower.
The king heard of this and went with all the people to see it.
The monk then, using his spiritual power, rose into the empty sky,
manifesting eighteen transformations.
The king was greatly delighted and said:
“Your body is the same as a human body,
but your power surpasses human power.
You should let me know:
are you performing spiritual feats?”
He answered:
“The king, heed the Buddha’s words, extensively build stūpas and temples, and make offerings to the relics.
For the benefit of the Dharma, after the Buddha’s extinction, the various corruptions—
compassion without equal, the most supreme discourse— the heterodox teachers,
I am a disciple.
The Buddha prophesied that a cakravartin king
would take my relics and erect eighty-four thousand stūpas,
extensively performing all Buddha deeds.
The king previously established hells and so forth, killing and harming countless beings.
You should eliminate all sinful karma and bestow fearlessness.”
The king then joined his palms
and, facing this monk, confessed his transgressions.
He then personally entered the hell and brought him out.
Jīlika said:
“I previously received the command that there is no exemption; those who enter cannot leave.”
The king said:
“Do you wish to kill me?”
He answered, “Yes.”
The king asked:
“When this prison was first established, who was the first to enter?”
The answer was:
“Jīlika entered first.”
The king said to the jailers:
“Place Jīlika inside the glue house and burn him with fire.”
Then he destroyed the hell and left.
Then, for the saṅgha of the five groups,
with thousands of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli jars,
filled with fragrant water,
and various kinds of food, incense, flowers, and other offerings, he made offerings.
After receiving the eight precepts,
he held a censer
and ascended a high tower, inviting monks from the four directions,
saying:
“Disciples of the World-Honored One in the four directions,
for the sake of accepting me, should all come here.”
And he spoke a verse:
There were three hundred thousand bhikkhus.
One hundred thousand arhats.
Two hundred thousand learners.
Countless ordinary people.
In the foremost seat, one place.
There was no one sitting.
The king asked Yéshè, saying:
"Why is the first seat empty?"
He replied, saying:
"The Buddha said:
Among the disciples, there is one capable of a lion's roar,
named Bīntóulú.
He is the foremost senior seat."
The king heard this and his hair stood on end.
Like a Kadamba flower. He also said:
"Is there anyone who saw the Tathāgata enter Nirvāṇa,
and is still present now?"
He replied, saying:
"That is precisely Bīntóulú."
He asked again:
"Can I see this person now?"
He replied, saying:
"He should come now."
Hearing this, the king was filled with great joy.
He then recited a verse of praise.
Joining his palms, he looked up into the sky.
His gaze did not waver.
At that time, Bīntóulú,
followed and surrounded by countless arhats,
descended from the sky and sat in the first seat.
The entire assembly rose.
Seeing Bīntóulú,
his hair and temples white as snow, his forehead skin and eyebrows
all joined together covering his face like a Pratyekabuddha's body.
He prostrated himself, touching the ground with his five limbs, paying homage to Bīntóulú.
He licked his feet with his tongue, weeping and reciting a verse.
Praising Bīntóulú.
He lifted his eyebrows with both hands and sighed to Āyù, saying:
"I have seen the Tathāgata many times," and thus praised the Buddha's virtues.
Āyù asked again:
"Where did you see the Buddha?"
He replied:
"The Buddha, together with five hundred arhats,
went to Rājagṛha for the rainy season retreat.
I was among the assembly then.
Also in Śrāvastī,
to overcome heretics, he displayed various supernatural powers.
Also in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, during the rainy season retreat,
after finishing preaching the Dharma to his mother, he descended.
He also went to the country of Asaṃkhyeyaśā.
Also, the solitary woman Xiūmótuóqié
invited the Buddha and five hundred arhats.
The Buddha, using his supernatural power, went to the country of Pindavardhana.
I, using my supernatural power, lifted a mountain
and also went to that country through the sky.
At that time, the Tathāgata commanded, saying:
'You shall not enter Nirvāṇa.
Preside over my Dharma's abiding.'"
Āyù asked again:
"Venerable Bīntóulú,
how many followers do you have?"
He replied with a verse:
"After the Saṅgha has finished eating,
we shall speak further with the king."
He agreed.
Various ones wishing to leave,
he provided for them all.
At that time, the king said to a bhikkhu
named Yīqièzhī:
"I shall give the Saṅgha one hundred thousand gold pieces and one thousand silver and lapis lazuli jars.
In the great assembly, proclaim my name for the offering."
Āyù's son, named Jiūnàluó,
went to his father's side.
Fearing his father, he dared not speak.
He raised two fingers to indicate
that the bhikkhu's merit-making would double his father's.
The assembly burst into laughter.
The king, seeing the assembly laugh,
said to his minister Chénghù:
"What you did was not right, so people laugh."
Chénghù replied:
"Many people wish to make merit,
they must wish to double it."
Āyù replied:
"I shall give three hundred thousand gold pieces to provide for the Saṅgha.
And three thousand jars filled with fragrant water."
The king also said:
"Venerable ones, I now make a treasury of the seven treasures.
All the great land's officials, ministers,
and together with my own body and Jiūnàluó,
I give entirely to the Saṅgha."
In the past, there was a king of Jambudvīpa,
named Qiánzhénípólí,
ruling over eighty-four thousand settlements.
Compassionate to all, grains and rice were abundant and cheap.
Each attained peace and happiness, yet my heart was not fully satisfied.
I must seek the wonderful Dharma to benefit all.
He proclaimed to all: 'Who has a wonderful Dharma,
to preach for me, shall obtain whatever he desires.'
There was a brāhmaṇa
named Láodùchā,
who said: 'I have a Dharma.'
The king welcomed and honored him, saying:
'I wish the great master to expound the Dharma for me to hear.'
Láodùchā said:
'Great King,
if today you can bore a thousand lamps in your body to make an offering,
then I shall preach for you.'
The king proclaimed to Jambudvīpa:
'After seven days, I shall bore my body and light lamps.'
The people, filled with sorrow, came to the king's place.
Their lives depended on the king as infants depend on their mother.
If the king perishes, on whom shall we rely?
Why for the sake of one brāhmaṇa abandon all?'
'You all must not obstruct my supreme bodhicitta.
I do this vowing to seek Buddhahood.
Later, when I attain Buddhahood, I shall certainly first liberate you.'
The people wept, prostrated on the ground, and lamented.
He then bored his body and placed the fat wicks.
He said to the great master:
'Take pity and preach the Dharma,
then light the lamps.
If my life ends, I will not hear it.'
Láodùchā said:
The king was immeasurably joyful.
He then ordered the lamps lit.
The Dharma he sought was to attain Buddhahood.
He would use the light of wisdom to illuminate and awaken all beings.
When he made this vow, heaven and earth greatly shook.
Up to the Pure Abodes, all also trembled.
Seeing this great being disregard his body and life,
they all descended together, filling the sky.
Weeping and shedding tears like heavy rain.
The heavenly emperor said:
'With such pain and torment, does your heart not regret?'
He replied: 'No regret.'
Thereupon he made a vow:
'If from beginning to end my heart does not regret,
may [my body] be restored completely.' It was restored as he wished.
That king was precisely the Buddha's former body.
In the past, in Jambudvīpa,
there was a great king
named Pílèngjiélí.
His heart loved the wonderful Dharma.
There was a brāhmaṇa
named Láodùchā,
who came to the palace gate, saying:
'I can preach the Dharma.
If you can have a thousand nails driven into your body,
then I shall preach.'
The king said:
'In the cycle of birth and death, I have killed my body countless times.
Sometimes for the three poisons, the accumulated white bones are higher than Sumeru, the blood shed exceeds the five lakes, the tears wept are more than the great ocean.
In vain I discarded body and life, never for the Dharma.
Now I pierce with nails seeking the Way.
Later, when I attain Buddhahood,
with the sword of wisdom I shall cut your bonds.
Do not obstruct my supreme bodhicitta.'
The great assembly was silent.
At that time, Láodùchā then recited a verse himself.
He then drove the nails into his body.
Thereupon he made a vow, saying:
'If I never regret,
may [my body] be restored as before.'
His body then became as it was originally.
In the past, there was a kingdom.
It was named Bōluónài.
The king was named Dà Guāngmíng.
His heart was compassionate towards all, never opposing others' wishes.
There was a minor king who constantly harbored wickedness and rebellion.
On the monthly fasting days, the great king
had five hundred elephants carry treasures, clothing, and food,
placing them in the great marketplace and outside the four city gates,
to give alms to all.
At that time, an enemy state's adversary heard
that the king gave alms according to people's wishes.
He became envious and jealous,
immediately gathering his ministers,
asking, "Who can beg for Dà Guāngmíng King's head?
I will reward them with a thousand catties of gold."
A Brahmin said, "I can."
The king then provided him with supplies.
The Brahmin went to the border,
where the earth shook in six ways.
Birds and beasts scattered in all directions; the sun and moon lost their brilliance, and the stars lost their proper courses.
Red, black, and white rainbows appeared day and night; meteors fell.
In that kingdom, all springs and bathing pools dried up.
The Brahmin went to the city gate.
At that time, the gate-guarding deity said to the gatekeeper,
"This man is greatly evil.
He has come from afar to beg for the great king's head.
Do not allow him to enter."
At that time, the Brahmin was delayed for one week and could not proceed.
He said to the gatekeeper,
"I have come from afar to see the great king."
The gatekeeper then entered and reported to the king.
Upon hearing this, the king came out to welcome him,
like a son seeing his father, bowing before him and asking where he had come from.
"You have braved the long journey; are you not weary?"
The Brahmin said,
"I heard from another land
that the king gives alms without opposing others' wishes.
Your fame has spread far, reaching the heavens above and the underworld below.
Therefore, I have come from afar to seek something."
The king said,
"I give everything; whatever you seek, do not hesitate or doubt."
The Brahmin said,
"Is this truly so?
I do not want anything else.
Now I wish to perform a great sacrifice.
I beg for the king's head."
The king thought to himself,
"From beginningless time, I have never acted for the Dharma,
vainly undergoing birth and death, exhausting my spirit.
Now I have this body, seeking Bodhi, vowing to benefit all beings.
If I do not give now, I would contradict my original intention.
How then could I attain unsurpassed Bodhi?"
The king said, "Excellent.
Allow me to settle affairs, entrusting the kingdom to my queen and crown prince.
After seven days, I will give it to you."
At that time, the great king
entered the palace and told his queens,
"A Brahmin
wishes to beg for my head, and I have already agreed."
When the queens and crown prince heard this,
they fell to the ground, wailing loudly, tearing their hair and ripping their clothes.
They said,
"Great king, nothing in the world is more precious than one's own body.
Why would you give it away today?"
At that time, five hundred ministers said to the Brahmin,
"What use do you have for this foul, rotten, pus-filled head?"
The Brahmin said,
"I am begging for it; why do you question me?"
The ministers said,
"You have entered our kingdom; we should question you, and you should answer us."
At that time, the Brahmin
was about to answer truthfully but feared for his life, afraid they would kill him.
The ministers said,
"We now grant you safety, for the king's sake.
Poor Brahmin, what use is this head to you?
We five hundred
will each make a head of the seven treasures,
to trade with you and give you whatever you need."
The Brahmin said,
"I do not want them."
At that time, the ministers failed in their wish.
They wailed sorrowfully and appealed to the great king,
"How can you bear to abandon the kingdom, your queens, and crown prince,
for the sake of one Brahmin, forever forsaking and leaving them orphaned?"
The king said,
"Now, for the sake of all, I give up this body."
When the chief minister heard the king's firm words,
he thought to himself,
"How can I now witness the king giving up his life?"
He entered a quiet room and killed himself with a knife.
At that time, the great king
went to the rear garden and called the Brahmin to come.
"You have begged for my head.
Out of compassion for you, I will not oppose your wish.
May I in future lives obtain a head of wisdom to give to you all."
After saying this, he joined his palms,
bowed to the Buddhas of the ten directions, and said,
"May the Buddhas of the ten directions and all noble Bodhisattvas protect and assist me with their spiritual power, so that this matter may be accomplished."
He told the Brahmin, "Take it as you wish."
At that time, the Brahmin said,
"The king has the strength of a warrior; if at the moment of pain you regret and change your mind, you might harm me instead.
If the king is truly willing, why not tie your own hair to a tree branch?"
Hearing this, the king felt compassion,
thinking, "This Brahmin is old and weak; if he cannot cut off my head, he will lose great benefit."
He followed his words and tied his hair to a tree.
He told the Brahmin,
"Cut off my head and place it in my hands.
I will then hand it to you."
At that time, the Brahmin took a knife and approached.
Then the tree deity struck the Brahmin with his hand, causing him to fall unconscious.
At that time, Dà Guāngmíng King said to the tree deity,
"You do not help me but instead create obstacles."
Hearing this, the tree deity felt great sorrow,
and cried out, "Alas!"
In the sky, without clouds, it rained blood.
Heaven and earth shook greatly; the sun lost its brilliance.
At that time, the Brahmin cut off the king's head and took it back to his own country.
Then the five hundred crown princes and all the ministers
collected the king's remaining bones, built a stupa, and made offerings.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"At that time, the chief minister, unable to bear hearing that Dà Guāngmíng King gave his head in almsgiving,
and who then gave up his own life, is now Śāriputra.
At that time, Dà Guāngmíng King is now Śākyamuni.
The king was greatly diligent,
regarding all beings as a mother loves her child.
In the world, there was no Buddha.
Śakro Devānām Indra, when his life was about to end, thought to himself,
'Where is there an omniscient one?'
He asked everywhere but could not resolve his doubts; he sat down sorrowfully.
A skillful transformation master named Pishou Jiemó Tiān
asked,
'Heavenly Lord,
why are you sorrowful?'
He replied,
'I seek an omniscient one but cannot find one; therefore I am sorrowful.'
Pishou Jiemó said,
'There is a Bodhisattva practicing giving, morality, meditation, and wisdom who will soon become a Buddha.'
Indra asked who.
He replied,
'It is Yōushīnàzhǒng Shīpí King.'
Śakro Devānām Indra said to Pishou Jiemó,
'Let us test him.'
Pishou Jiemó transformed into a red-eyed, red-footed pigeon.
Śakro Devānām Indra transformed into a hawk.
Swiftly flying, chasing the pigeon, it came directly under the king's arm.
Its whole body trembled in fear, eyes darting, voice urgent.
At that time, many people spoke among themselves,
'This king is compassionate and benevolent; all should be protected.
Like this small pigeon, it seeks refuge as a person enters a house.'
At that time, the hawk was on a nearby tree.
It said to Shīpí King,
'Return my pigeon to me; it is my prey.'
The king then said to the hawk,
'I accepted it first; it is not your prey.
When I first aroused the mind, I accepted all beings, wishing to save them all.'
The hawk said,
'The king wishes to save all beings.
Am I not one of all?
Why do you not pity me alone and take my food?'
The king replied,
'What food do you need?
I have made a vow that any being who comes to me for refuge, I will surely protect.
What food you need, I will also provide.'
The hawk said,
'I need freshly killed, warm meat.'
The king thought,
'This is difficult to obtain; unless I kill a living being, I cannot get it.
How can I kill one to give to another?'
After thinking it over, he decided,
'Having thought thus,'
he called for someone to bring a knife, cut flesh from his own thigh, and gave it to the hawk.
The hawk said to the king,
'Although the king gives me warm meat,
you must do so fairly, making the meat equal in weight to the pigeon.'
The king said,
'Bring a scale to weigh the meat against the pigeon.'
They cut the king's flesh until it equaled the pigeon.
He admonished himself,
'You must be firm; do not become confused or faint.
All beings are falling into a great sea of suffering; I vow to save them.
Why be weary or faint? This suffering is very little; the suffering of hell is much greater.
I have wisdom, diligence, morality, and meditation, yet I still suffer this pain.
How much more so for those in hell without wisdom?'
When his mind became firm, heaven and earth shook in six ways.
The ocean waves surged; withered trees bloomed with flowers.
Heaven rained fragrant rain and scattered famous flowers.
Heavenly maidens sang praises, saying he would surely become a Buddha.
Indra said to the king,
'You cut your flesh painfully; is your mind not troubled or faint?'
The king said,
'My mind is joyful, not troubled or faint.'
Indra said,
'Who will believe you?'
Then the king made a vow,
'If, as I cut my flesh and blood flows, I feel no anger, no trouble, with a single-minded, unfainting heart seeking Buddhahood,
may my body immediately be restored as before.'
Instantly, it was as before.
In the country of Shèwèi, there was a separate dwelling place.
The ground was very level and broad.
At that time, the Buddha went and sat there.
Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings,
the human kings such as King Bīngshā,
each addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We wish to set up a high seat for the World-Honored One."
The Buddha said:
"Stop. I know the time myself."
At that time, there were householders who had faith in non-Buddhist teachings;
each set up a seat worth a hundred thousand.
There were also those who had faith and joy in making offerings to the Buddha.
From the first day of the month to the fifteenth day,
the kings of Mójié and Bīngshā took turns setting up offerings.
In the center of the seats, a lion throne of the seven treasures naturally appeared.
The Tathāgata sat upon it.
At that time, all took their seats.
There was a donor
who, on the following day, made an offering and presented a tooth-cleaning twig to the Buddha.
The World-Honored One chewed it and then discarded it behind his back.
It immediately became a great tree, with roots, trunk, branches, and leaves spreading out luxuriantly.
At that time, the great assembly, witnessing the Buddha's spiritual power, rejoiced, praised, and experienced something unprecedented.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
through countless skillful means and various teachings, caused them to attain joy.
At that time, countless hundreds of thousands of people on the seats, far removed from dust and defilement, attained the pure Dharma-eye.
In this way, manifestations of spiritual transformations occurred until the fifteenth day, each different.
The great assembly, seeing the Buddha's spiritual power and transformations, all greatly rejoiced.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they attained the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, King Bīngshā of Mójié,
on the fifteenth day, offered food to the Buddha and the Sangha, along with King Bōluóshūtí,
King Yōutuóyán, King Fànshī,
King Pòsīnì, Lady Mòlì,
the elder Líshīdáduō, Fùluónà, and the entire great assembly,
all made offerings. When the meal was finished, they set aside their bowls and passed water.
King Bīngshā took a low seat and sat before the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One,
breaking his cross-legged posture, stretched his feet onto a footstool.
At that moment, the earth shook six times in eighteen different ways.
At that time, from the soles of the Buddha's feet, wheel marks appeared, each wheel having a thousand spokes, with rims fully formed and the characteristics of spokes complete.
Their light shone brilliantly, illuminating three thousand lands.
At that time, the King of Mójié,
upon seeing this, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, and said:
"World-Honored One,
what merit did you cultivate in the past to attain such marks of excellence?"
The Buddha told Bīngshā:
"In a past world, in the land of Jambudvīpa,
there was a king named Lìzhòngshēng.
At that time, the country was prosperous and the people were numerous.
He ruled over eighty-four thousand cities and fifty-five billion settlements.
The king's capital city was named Huìguāng.
The king's chief queen was named Huìshì.
Initially, she had no children.
In order to seek an heir, she made offerings to the various gods, mountains, rivers, and spirits, praying everywhere.
Later, she became pregnant.
She informed the king, saying:
'I am now with child.'
The king doubled her provisions of food, drink, clothing, and medicine.
Later, she gave birth to a son, handsome and upright in appearance.
On the day the child was born,
eighty-four thousand treasures naturally welled up, each according to its kind.
The king said to his mother:
'Name the child Huìdēng.'
Later, the king passed away.
The crown prince was eight or nine years old.
His mother had him taught skills, writing, arithmetic, and riding.
When he reached the age of fifteen,
the ministers addressed him, saying:
'The great king has passed away; it is your turn to ascend the throne.'
The crown prince replied:
'In a past life, I was a king for six years.
Afterwards, I fell into hell for sixty thousand years.
For this reason, I cannot become king.'
The ministers said:
'Is there any means by which you could become king?'
He replied:
'If all the people of Jambudvīpa, men and women, all who can speak, practice the ten good deeds, then I will become king.'
At that time, the ministers and people, hearing the prince's command,
immediately proclaimed it in all directions:
'All people of Jambudvīpa must practice the ten good deeds, beginning with not killing.'
The ministers fully reported to the crown prince:
'Now you may ascend the throne.'
The crown prince then ascended the throne himself.
The ministers addressed the king, saying:
'When the king was first born,
eighty-four thousand treasures naturally welled up.
Now they may be taken into the royal treasury.'
The king said:
'There is no need to put them in the treasury.'
He then ordered that at each place where they appeared, at the crossroads,
they be distributed to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, orphans, and the aged.
At that time, the great ministers, following the king's command,
according to where the treasures were located,
at the crossroads of the eighty-four thousand city gates,
distributed them as alms.
At that time, Śakra, lord of gods, transformed into a man and said to himself:
'The king instructs me to practice the ten evils.'
The ministers reported to the king:
'Is there such a command?'
The king replied:
'My previous command
was that all speaking beings within Jambudvīpa
should practice the ten good deeds. I never said such a thing.'
He immediately mounted a jeweled elephant and went to that place.
The king asked:
'Do you say that Huìdēng instructed you to practice the ten evils?'
The transformed man replied: 'Indeed.'
The king asked again:
'Can you practice the ten good deeds?'
He replied:
'If one wishes to accomplish the bodhisattva path,
I will eat his flesh raw and drink his blood raw,
and then I will personally practice the ten good deeds.'
The king thought to himself:
'Since beginningless time, I have undergone many sufferings,
revolving in the five paths, experiencing slaughter repeatedly.'
He then took a knife, cut flesh from his own thigh, placed it in a vessel with his blood, and gave it to him, saying:
'Man, you may eat the flesh and drink the blood.
Practice the ten good deeds.'
At that, the transformed man disappeared and was no longer seen.
He reappeared in the form of Śakra and asked him:
'Is your giving for the sake of one world or for the four worlds?'
The king said: 'It is for seeking the unsurpassed path, to liberate those who are not yet liberated.'
Śakra poured heavenly nectar on his wound, and it was immediately healed, bringing benefit to living beings.
The father king at that time is my present father king.
The chief queen is my present mother.
King Huìdēng is myself.
In the past, there was a king
named Dàlì.
He had great roots of goodness.
He held a great offering assembly, granting whatever was desired.
If someone needed food, he gave food; even elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, fields, land, and property—he gave them all.
At that time, Mùlián said:
'You are a great giver.'
At that time, Śakra transformed into a brāhmaṇa
and went to the king, saying:
'King, you are such a great giver.
I now need a part of your body.'
The king thought to himself:
'This brāhmaṇa does not need wealth or goods.
He has come now simply to break my great giving.
If I do not give him a part of my body,
then I will have broken my own great offering assembly.'
Having thought this, he said to the brāhmaṇa:
'I give you a part of my body. Cut it off and take it away.
But now there are many beggars who have gathered from all directions.
I should satisfy them all.'
The brāhmaṇa said:
'I alone am not yet satisfied now.
How much less others?'
The king then took a knife and cut off his own arm,
giving it to the brāhmaṇa without any regret.
With single-minded giving, relinquishing all things, his arm was restored.
Since Śakra created an obstacle,
his heavenly blessings were exhausted, and he fell into the Avīci hell.
King Dàlì was myself.
Śakra was Tiáodá.
The Buddha was in the country of Shèwèi.
At that time, Ānán,
after the midday meal, was meditating in the forest.
He thought: 'Since the Tathāgata appeared in the world, all kinds of beings have attained peace and happiness.
And what good roots did Jiāochénrú and the others plant,
that when the Dharma gate first opened, they were the first to enter?'
He reported his thoughts to the Buddha.
The Buddha told him:
'Jiāochénrú and the others—
in a distant past kalpa, in this Jambudvīpa,
there was a great king named Míluó. He had twenty thousand consorts and ten thousand ministers.
The king possessed the four immeasurables and never grew weary.
He taught the people the ten good deeds; all directions admired him, and the country was peaceful and happy.
There were plague demons who constantly drank human blood.
At that time, the people guarded their body, speech, and mind, diligently practicing the ten good deeds.
The evil plagues did not dare invade, but they were hungry, emaciated, and in distress.
At that time, five yakṣas came to the king's place.
They said: 'We depend on human blood and energy to sustain our lives.
Due to the king's teaching, all practice the ten good deeds.
We are hungry and thirsty, with no way to survive.
Great king, with your compassion, will you not take pity on us?'
The king, filled with sorrow,
immediately opened his veins and pierced his body in five places.
At that time, the five yakṣas received the blood and drank it, rejoicing immensely.
The king said:
'You remember to cultivate the ten good deeds. I now use my body's blood to relieve your hunger and thirst.
When I attain Buddhahood in the future, I will use the Dharma-body's blood of precepts, concentration, and wisdom to remove your three poisons and establish you in the peace of Nirvāṇa.'
The compassionate king at that time is my present self.
The five yakṣas are now Jiāochénrú and the others.
I have vowed life after life that I shall liberate them first.'
In the past, there was a king named Xūtuóxūmó.
This king was diligent and upheld the precepts.
He always adhered to truthfulness.
One morning, he rode in a carriage with his court ladies to the garden for amusement.
As they were leaving the city gate, a Brahmin came to beg.
The king said, "Agreed."
He respectfully complied as requested.
"Wait for me to return after bathing and playing in the garden."
At that time, there was a winged king named Lùzú.
Flying through the air, he seized the king from among the court ladies and carried him away.
The ladies wept and wailed, causing the entire city and its surroundings to be thrown into turmoil, grief, and panic.
Lùzú carried the king through the air to the mountain where he resided.
He placed him among ninety-nine other kings.
King Xūtuóxūmó wept tears like rain.
Lùzú said to him,
"Great Kshatriya king,
why do you weep like a child?
Life entails death, and meetings inevitably lead to partings."
King Xūtuóxūmó replied,
"I do not fear death; I regret breaking my promise.
Since my birth, I have never spoken falsely.
This morning when I left the gate,
a Brahmin came to beg from me.
I promised him that I would give alms upon my return.
I did not anticipate impermanence, and now I have betrayed his trust.
I have brought upon myself the sin of deceit; that is why I weep."
King Lùzú said,
"If you fear false speech,
I permit you to return.
Within seven days, give alms to the Brahmin and then come back.
If you exceed seven days and do not return, with my winged power, capturing you will not be difficult."
King Xūtuóxūmó
returned to his own country and gave alms freely.
He installed the crown prince as king.
Gathering the people, he confessed and apologized, saying,
"My wisdom is insufficient to govern all things, and my rule is not in accordance with the Dharma; I ask for your loyalty and forgiveness.
As for me today, my body is no longer my own, and I must now return."
All the people of the country and his relatives kowtowed to detain him.
"We beg Your Majesty to stay and protect this country; do not worry about the ghost king Lùzú.
We will set up iron chambers and deploy extraordinary troops.
Even if Lùzú is divine, we do not fear him."
The king said,
"That will not do."
And he spoke a verse:
After such contemplation,
the king immediately departed and went to King Lùzú's place.
Seeing him from afar, Lùzú joyfully said,
"You are a truthful person who does not break promises.
Yet all people cherish their lives.
Having escaped death, you still return to fulfill your promise; you are a great man."
At that time, King Xūtuóxūmó praised truthfulness:
"Truthfulness makes one human.
Without truthfulness, one is not human."
In this way, he variously praised truthfulness and condemned false speech.
Hearing this, Lùzú's faith became pure.
He said to King Xūtuóxūmó,
"Now I release you, and the ninety-nine other kings may also return to their own countries."
This is the perfection of Śīla Pāramitā.
In the past, there was a king
named Sàhuòtán, who never refused anyone's requests.
His name spread far and wide across the eight directions.
Mañjuśrī wished to test him.
He transformed into a young Brahmin from a foreign country and went to the king's palace gate.
The king was very pleased.
He immediately came out to welcome him and asked, "Venerable sir, where have you come from?"
The Brahmin said,
"Having heard of Your Majesty's virtues, I have come to see you. Now I wish to beg."
The king said, "Excellent.
Whatever you desire, do not hesitate."
The Brahmin said,
"I wish to have Your Majesty's person to serve as my slave,
and Your Majesty's queen to serve as my maidservant."
The king was very delighted.
He replied, "Excellent.
As for my person, it is certainly available.
I wish to belong to the venerable sir and serve him.
As for my queen, she is the daughter of a great king.
I must go and ask her."
The king then entered and said to the queen,
At that time, the queen immediately followed the king out.
She said to the venerable sir herself,
"I wish to offer my person to serve the venerable sir."
The Brahmin said,
"You shall follow me.
You must both go barefoot, without wearing shoes,
as is the way of slaves."
They both said, "Yes, we obey our master's instructions."
He then took the slaves and set off on the road.
He transformed people to take the place of the king and queen,
managing state affairs as before.
The queen had long lived in the deep palace, unaccustomed to hardship.
Moreover, she was pregnant, several months along.
Walking behind her master, her whole body ached, and the soles of her feet were injured and torn.
Unable to go on, exhausted, she lagged behind.
The Brahmin turned back and scolded her,
"You are now a slave; you must act like a slave.
You cannot behave as you did in your former status."
The queen knelt and said, "I dare not be negligent.
I am just slightly exhausted and need to rest a moment."
He called out, "Come quickly!"
Urging her to follow closely behind, they arrived at the market of a country.
He sold the slaves separately, each to a different master.
They were several miles apart.
At that time, an elder bought this male slave and had him guard a house.
Whenever there were burials of the dead, he was to collect taxes and not levy them arbitrarily.
As for the female slave, her master
was a very jealous woman who made her work day and night without rest.
Several months later,
the slave woman gave birth to a baby boy.
The mistress angrily said,
"You are a slave; how can you have this child?"
She seized and killed it.
Obeying her mistress's order, she killed her child,
carried it away, and buried it.
She went to where the male slave was so they could meet.
They did not speak of their hardships and harbored no resentment toward each other.
Such were their words.
In an instant, it was as if in a dream—
they were back in their own country, sitting on the main throne as before, unchanged.
All the ministers, court ladies, and palace women were as before.
The child they had given birth to was also naturally alive.
The king and queen wondered in their hearts how this had come about.
Mañjuśrī,
sitting on a precious lotus in the sky, revealed his form and praised them, saying,
"Excellent!
Now your giving is so sincere."
The king and queen leaped for joy.
They stepped forward and bowed.
Mañjuśrī expounded the Dharma to them.
Three thousand worlds trembled.
Covering the entire country, all the people resolved to attain the unsurpassed true path.
The king and queen immediately attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"The king at that time was myself.
The queen at that time is now Jūyí.
The crown prince at that time is now Luóyún."
In the past, in Jambudvīpa, there was a great king
named Qúlóupó.
He ruled over eighty-four thousand small countries,
nurturing the people.
He thought to himself,
"I only provide material goods to support everyone;
ultimately, I have no Dharma teaching to offer. This is truly my fault."
He proclaimed throughout the country: "Whoever has the Dharma to teach me, I will supply all their needs."
Vaiśravaṇa transformed into a yakṣa and came to the palace gate,
saying, "Who wishes to hear the Dharma? I will teach it."
The king personally came out to welcome him and bowed.
He assembled his officials and requested to hear the true Dharma.
The yakṣa said,
"Learning the Dharma is difficult.
I require the king's beloved wife and children
for me to eat."
The king immediately ordered his queen and crown prince to be given to the yakṣa to eat.
All the ministers wept.
The king's resolve did not waver.
After the yakṣa had eaten his fill,
he spoke a verse:
The king's heart was joyful and without regret. He displayed it to gods and humans, having all recite and uphold it.
Vaiśravaṇa returned to his original form.
The queen and crown prince were intact as before.
They praised the king's extraordinary deed.
The Buddha said,
"The king at that time is now myself."
Long ago, there was a man-eating demon.
He became a king among men.
He constantly ate human flesh, using it as his kitchen provisions.
A neighboring country waged war and captured ninety-nine kings.
These ninety-nine kings said to the Rākṣasa King:
"In the neighboring country, there is a king,
named Shànsù,
who is fond of practicing generosity and cultivating the virtues of a Bodhisattva. He never refuses anyone who asks him for something.
Great King, if you can capture him, we will willingly accept death without regret."
At that time, the Rākṣasa King raised an army of demons
and went to wait for an opportunity.
It happened that Shànsù was traveling outside, viewing the bathing pool in his outer garden.
There was a Brahmin who had left home to study abroad.
According to the Brahmin custom, when leaving home,
he said to his parents:
"I am now leaving home to pursue learning with companions.
The date of my return is uncertain.
If I become impoverished and lack resources, I will borrow from the king.
I will repay it when I return."
That man completed his studies and achieved success.
He returned home only to find an empty house, with no one there.
He then asked his neighbors:
"Where have my parents, brothers, and sisters gone?"
The neighbors replied:
"After you left to study, they borrowed wealth from the king and had no means to repay it.
They were imprisoned by the king and are now in jail."
The man thought to himself:
"My family is poor and our affairs are limited; we have no treasures.
If I go to the prison to see my parents, I will also be detained.
We would suffer together and not escape the king's law.
It is better for me to stay outside, change my appearance and clothes, and secretly seek
to fully repay the official debt before I can emerge."
The man further thought:
"In the neighboring country, there is a king,
named Shànsù,
who cultivates virtue and morality and never ceases in his generosity.
I should go to him and sincerely make my request.
He will surely not refuse and I will be able to repay the king's debt."
He then went to that king and begged from him.
The king said, "Excellent.
I shall provide for you.
Wait until I have finished bathing,
and then I will bestow alms.
Wait a little while; do not worry, I will not break my promise."
The king went to the bathing pool and was captured by the demon army.
The king looked back, weeping sorrowfully.
The demon king asked:
"We have heard that the king is benevolent, kind, and universally charitable.
Although you are in distress, why are you weeping?"
The king replied to the demon:
"In my life, I have practiced generosity without ever regretting it.
Just now, a Brahmin came begging from me.
I promised but have not yet given.
That is why I am sorrowful."
The demon king said to the king:
"The king keeps his promises and has never changed.
I will now release you. After you have given alms, return at the appointed time, and then I will know your true heart."
The king returned to his palace,
opened his treasury, and gave generously, satisfying the man's wishes.
He then returned to keep his promise and went to the demon king.
The demon king said to him:
"Are you not afraid of me?
Why have you come to accept death?"
Shànsù replied with a verse.
Hearing this, the demon king felt ashamed within.
He changed his mind and conduct, thinking to cultivate goodness.
He then said to King Shànsù:
"Now hearing your words, I realize they are rare among men.
I now release the ninety-nine kings.
I relinquish this position.
I wish for the king to take charge and rule with law. I will lead the demon hosts back to our lair.
If we both follow the precepts, I will naturally visit often."
They then parted and each returned to his own place.
The people celebrated, and the country was peaceful and prosperous.
All practiced the ten good deeds and did not engage in evil.
Shànsù accumulated practices without ceasing.
Later, he attained Buddhahood.
Under the Bodhi tree, he again spoke the previous verse.
Long ago, there was a king
named Héhēi.
He resided in a border region and had not witnessed the holy teachings.
He served heretical paths, and the whole country held false beliefs.
They killed living beings for sacrifices. The king's mother fell ill.
They sought various medical deities for years,
but she was not cured.
They further summoned two hundred Brahmins from the country
and told them:
"My great queen has been seriously ill for a long time; I do not know the reason."
The Brahmins said:
"The stars are disordered; yin and yang are not in harmony, hence this has happened."
The king said:
"What method should be used to cure her?"
The Brahmins said:
"Outside the city, in a clean, level place,
sacrifice to the four mountains, the sun, moon, and stars.
You must obtain a hundred heads of various kinds of animals and one small child, kill them, and sacrifice to heaven.
The king himself must lead his mother to kneel and pray for her life; then she will be cured."
The king then followed the order.
They drove men, elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, and a hundred kinds of creatures.
Along the way, they cried mournfully, shaking heaven and earth.
They exited the east gate to go to the sacrificial altar to be killed and offered to heaven.
The Buddha, with great compassion, pitied the king's obstinate ignorance.
He led his disciples and went to that country.
The king saw the Buddha from afar,
like the sun at dawn, like the moon at its fullest, his radiant light shining brightly.
The people who saw him all loved and respected him.
The sacrificial victims all wished for liberation.
The king paid homage to the Buddha, joined his palms, knelt, and inquired, saying:
"My mother has been ill for a long time; skilled doctors and deities have all been consulted.
Now I am about to perform rites to appease the stars, the four mountains, and the five peaks,
to beg for my mother's life, hoping she will be cured."
The Buddha said:
"If you want grain to eat, you must plow and sow.
If you want great wealth, you must practice generosity.
If you want long life, you must practice great compassion.
If you want wisdom, you must pursue learning.
Practice these four things, and according to what you sow, you will reap the fruit.
Sacrificial rites and licentiousness take the wrong as right.
Killing living beings to seek life is far from the path of life."
He then spoke a verse.
The Buddha emitted brilliant light, illuminating heaven and earth.
The three wretched paths and eight difficulties all rejoiced.
The king, hearing the Dharma and seeing the light, immediately attained the path.
His mother, hearing it, felt joy in her heart, and her illness was eliminated.
The two hundred Brahmins felt ashamed, repented, and all became monks. The king thereafter loved his people like his own children.
The five grains were abundant, and the country was free from disasters and poisons.
People lived for eighty thousand years, compassionately protecting all beings like the god Śakra.
They believed in and revered the Three Jewels, constantly practiced the ten good deeds, and led all the people of the four regions in transformation.
At that time, there was a poor man who stole another's property.
The owner caught him.
The king asked why he stole.
He replied:
"I am poor and cannot support myself; I have violated the holy law."
The king sighed and said:
"When the people are hungry, it is I who am hungry.
When they are cold, it is I who am naked.
My power should ensure that there are no poor in the country.
The suffering and joy of the people depend on me alone."
He then proclaimed a great amnesty throughout the country.
He brought out the treasures of the treasury to give to the hungry and cold.
Carriages, horses, medicines, they could take as they wished.
Birds, beasts, down to insects and fish, the king gave to them.
Afterward, the country was prosperous and the people wealthy, all following the Way.
There was no reputation for the ten evils.
The spirits and gods rejoiced and protected the country.
The five grains were abundant, and every household had surplus wealth.
They then obtained the five blessings:
first, long life;
second, a better complexion;
third, virtue moving in all directions;
fourth, freedom from illness and increased strength;
fifth, peace and security within the borders, with hearts always joyful.
In the past, there was a king.
He offered a kasaya robe to the Buddha.
Thereby, he aroused the intention of supreme, impartial salvation.
When the Buddha entered Parinirvana and cremated himself,
the kasaya robe did not burn.
He collected the Buddha's relics and built a stupa.
After the stupa was destroyed, the kasaya robe remained.
Later, the stupa was no longer there for offerings.
The kasaya robe accumulated many years.
No longer did they hear the Buddha's teachings.
Every fasting day,
the king, ministers, and countless people
would offer incense, flowers, banners, and canopies to the kasaya robe.
They passed this tradition down, emulating each other, never abandoning it.
Later, there was a king
who thought:
"My predecessors and I have reverently served this robe.
What blessings will we receive?
What kind of robe is this?"
No one knew.
A merchant from the Buddha's country came for trade and livelihood.
He said to the king:
"In my country, there is a king
named Shuddhodana.
He had a holy son named Siddhārtha.
He left home to cultivate the path and is called the Buddha.
His body bears the thirty-two marks.
He wears exactly this robe."
The king heard this and rejoiced.
He sent an envoy to invite the Buddha.
The merchant said:
"If you wish to invite the Buddha, simply burn incense and respectfully invite him from afar."
So he burned incense and invited the Buddha.
He wished the Buddha
to condescend and exert his spirit.
The incense smoke traveled to the Buddha, circling him seven times.
It then transformed into a flower canopy in the sky.
At that moment, the Buddha smiled.
The light from his breath illuminated countless realms.
It ascended into the sky and merged with the incense.
Together, they formed a flower canopy and returned into the crown of his head.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"Where does this incense smoke come from?"
The Buddha fully informed Ānanda.
Immediately, the three-thousandfold great-thousand world system trembled greatly.
The gates of that country's city all turned to gold.
Lutes and musical instruments played by themselves without being struck.
Women's pearl rings all made sounds.
Hundred-year-old withered trees sprouted anew.
The king was greatly terrified and called out, asking people:
"What calamity is this?
Why is my country shaking?"
The merchant said to the king:
"Wherever the World-Honored One goes, auspicious signs appear first.
This is all due to Your Majesty's merit."
The king then leaped for joy.
He announced to his ministers and people:
"Burn incense to welcome the Buddha!"
The king wished in his heart:
"May I become like the World-Honored One's attendant, an Arhat."
The king offered the kasaya robe to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha could not lift it.
It sank into the ground, reaching down to countless Buddha realms below.
It hung suspended in midair.
Bodhisattvas in the lower realms addressed their Buddha:
"Where does this kasaya robe come from?
It does not fall to the ground."
The Buddha said:
"In a moment, there will be a response."
Śākyamuni Buddha
instructed Maudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, and five hundred disciples to go and retrieve the kasaya robe.
Each exhausted his supernatural powers but could not obtain it.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī to go and fetch it, but he also could not lift it.
The Buddha said:
"This kasaya robe
was offered by people of the past to a previous Buddha.
They aroused the intention for the Great Path.
After countless lifetimes,
it returned to belong to the king.
Now he offers it to me again.
In between, he sought attainment,
wishing to be a Śrāvaka.
Therefore, the kasaya robe cannot be lifted.
Why is this?
Because the former intention was reverent, so the kasaya robe was light.
The later aspiration was small, so the kasaya robe is heavy."
The king, hearing the Buddha's teaching, immediately repented.
"I am the king.
I do not wish for anyone in the country to aspire to my position.
If anyone has such an intention,
I consider it rebellious.
The Buddha is the World-Honored One.
Therefore, I dare not aspire to Buddhahood."
The king and his ministers and people all aroused the intention of supreme, impartial salvation.
The kasaya robe naturally emerged from the ground.
The king lifted the kasaya robe
and raised it to offer to the Buddha.
