He wished that for all sentient beings in the ten directions,
the Buddha would accept this kasaya robe.
Then the Buddha preached a sutra for them.
The king and his ministers all attained the irreversible stage.
In a past kalpa, there was a great king named Sàhédá, who gave to all śramaṇas and everyone without opposing their wishes.
In another country, a Brahmin's son lost his father young.
He lived alone with his mother, elder sister, and younger brother, in great poverty.
His mother said:
"Now we are destitute and cannot support ourselves.
You should go to King Sàhédá to beg."
The son replied to his mother:
"I am still ignorant now.
I should first study, then go."
The mother did not allow it.
The son first borrowed one tael of gold.
It could provide food for one year.
Then he left home to study for a year and returned.
His mother met him and asked:
"Did you go to King Sàhédá?"
The son again replied to his mother:
"My studies are not yet complete; I must study more."
The mother said:
"The previous gold is already spent."
He went again to the previous lender's house.
He borrowed one tael of gold.
The lender said to the son:
"You previously took gold and have not repaid me.
If you want to borrow again,
you must pledge your mother and elder sister as security.
If you do not repay on time, they will become slaves."
So he made a contract, took the gold, and gave it to his mother.
Again, he left home to study.
After another year,
his knowledge was roughly sufficient, and he intended to return
to go to King Sàhédá.
On the way, he was seized by the creditor.
His mother, elder sister, and younger brother were taken and imprisoned.
The Brahmin's son said to the creditor:
"Imprisoning me all year will be of no benefit.
Better to release me to go to King Sàhédá.
I can beg for goods to repay you."
The creditor let him go.
At that time, another country raised troops
to capture King Sàhédá.
The king heard and thought to himself:
"Human life is short; all must face impermanence.
Since youth, I have enjoyed giving,
being compassionate and patient, causing no harm. I do not wish to resist that country.
Why?
There is no need for preparation.
Do not be afraid.
Just solemnly go out to welcome them, show respect, serve them,
and accept their commands, letting them surpass me."
The ministers said to the king:
"Another country has entered our borders; why not prepare?"
The king remained silent and did not respond.
This happened three times.
The king said:
"There is no need to resist.
As I said before."
The ministers obeyed the order.
The king said: "Excellent.
Each of you, return home peacefully; do not cause disturbance."
That night, the king removed his seal and silently fled.
That other king entered the country and assumed the throne.
He then offered a reward for Sàhédá.
The reward was very heavy.
The king traveled over five hundred li out of the country when he saw a Brahmin's son from afar.
The two met.
The king asked:
"Where are you going now?"
He replied:
"I wish to go to Sàhédá.
I lost my father young.
My family is very poor.
I pledged my mother and elder sister
as security for debt.
I wish to beg to redeem them
and also support myself."
The king said:
"I am Sàhédá.
Another king wants my country.
I do not wish to cause harm, so I avoided him."
The Brahmin's son fell to the ground, weeping bitterly,
unable to control himself.
The king advised and comforted him, telling him to rise and not cry.
"Whatever you seek, I will give it to you now."
The Brahmin's son said:
"Your Majesty has lost your country.
What can you use to help me beg?"
The king then replied:
"That king has offered a heavy reward for me.
You can now cut off my head and take it to him.
Whatever you seek, you can obtain."
Then the Brahmin's son spoke a verse:
King Sàhédá.
Again spoke to the Brahmin's son, saying:
"If you do not wish to take my head,
then you may cut off my nose or ears and send them.
It will no longer be the king's concern."
The Brahmin's son said:
"That too is unbearable."
The king said:
"Binding and sending me would also be acceptable."
The Brahmin's son said:
"I know that the other king means no harm."
Thereupon, the king and the Brahmin's son went together to return.
When they were about twenty li from the kingdom,
the king said:
"You may bind me."
The Brahmin's son then bound the king.
All the people of the kingdom, men and women, young and old, wept and collapsed in grief,
more intensely than mourning their own parents, and they went before the palace gates.
The ministers then entered
and reported to that king, saying:
"The one who previously sought Sàhédá has been bound and sent by the Brahmin's son.
He is now at the palace gates."
That king immediately said:
"Quickly, bring him before me."
All the ministers and people, upon seeing King Sàhédá,
without exception fell to the ground weeping.
That usurping king also shed tears.
And he asked the ministers:
"Why are all of you weeping?"
The ministers replied, saying:
"We see King Sàhédá
abandoning his kingdom for the king,
and further offering his body to the Brahmin's son.
What he has done he does not regret, and that is why we weep."
That usurping king, hearing each of the ministers and people say this,
immediately fell to the ground and wept bitterly, unable to control himself.
He then asked the Brahmin's son:
"How did you originally come to have this king?"
The Brahmin's son answered the king, saying:
"I am truly poor.
I used my mother, elder sister, and younger brother as collateral for a debt.
Hearing that this King Sàhédá was greatly generous in almsgiving,
I came from afar to beg for alms to redeem my mother, elder sister, and younger brother, so they could survive.
On the road, I met him, and we exchanged greetings.
King Sàhédá then said to me:
'I have now abandoned my kingdom and given it to another king.
I have nothing to give you as alms.'
At that time, I was deeply sorrowful, distressed, and helpless.
Then King Sàhédá
instructed me to cut off his head and bring it to the king.
At that time, I did not dare.
He then told me to cut off his nose or ears and send them.
I again refused.
So we came together, and he had me bind and send him.
The whole story of what was asked is truly like this."
As for that usurping king,
hearing what the Brahmin's son said,
he again fell to the ground in tears.
And he said:
"Command the ministers:
Quickly untie the king's bonds, bathe him, clothe him, and return his seal and ribbons, reinstating him as king."
He then ascended the throne and ruled the kingdom as before.
Thereupon, that king knelt with hands clasped in praise,
and spoke a verse:
The Buddha said:
"The king Sàhédá at that time was I.
That other king was Shèlìfú.
The Brahmin's son was Tiáodá.
He fulfilled my six pāramitās,
the thirty-two marks, the ten powers, and all meritorious virtues.
All are due to Tiáodá's grace.
Tiáodá is my good friend,
and also a good teacher."
In the past, in the country of Mótiānluó,
there was a king named Rì Nán.
His learning reached the divine and spiritual; there was nothing obscure he did not perceive.
Awakening to the impermanence of the world, he said:
"My body will decay, becoming the world's waste and ruin.
What kingdom can I preserve?
He renounced glory, abandoned pleasures, donned the robes of the highest Dharma,
and was content with a single bowl of food.
Upholding the precepts of a śramaṇa, he dwelt in the mountains and forests for thirty years.
Beside a tree, there was a pit thirty zhang deep.
At that time, a hunter, galloping in pursuit of a deer, fell into the pit. At that moment, there was also a crow and a snake.
Both were startled and fell, their bodies injured.
Looking up to heaven, they wailed mournfully, their cries filled with loneliness and desperation.
The ascetic, filled with compassion, lit a torch to see them,
tears and mucus streaming down his neck.
Approaching the pit, he declared:
"Do not worry; I will rescue you."
He immediately lowered a long rope, and they either grasped it with their mouths or held it,
thus saving their lives.
Together, they thanked him, saying:
"We have received the ascetic's boundless kindness and grace.
We have seen the light of day again.
We wish to devote our lives to providing for whatever you lack."
The ascetic said:
"I was a king.
My kingdom was vast, with many people, palaces, treasures, and maidens, surpassing all other countries.
My wishes were instantly fulfilled; what could I not obtain?
Yet I regarded the kingdom as an enemy; the six dusts were like six swords,
constantly cutting my body,
six arrows piercing my flesh.
Because of these six evils,
I would transmigrate into the three wretched paths.
The suffering is severe and unbearable; I deeply detest it.
Therefore, I renounced the kingdom to become a śramaṇa,
hoping to attain Buddhahood, to teach and transform all beings, enabling them to return to their original source.
How could this be merely for the sake of your three lives?
Return each to your former dwellings, see your loved ones,
and have them take the Three Refugees, not transgressing the Buddha's teachings."
The hunter said:
"I have lived in the world for many years and have seen good people,
but none compare to the Buddha's disciples.
They forgive themselves and aid the masses, concealing their deeds without seeking fame.
If the ascetic lacks anything, I hope you will come to my home to beg for modest offerings."
The crow said:
"My name is Bō.
If the ascetic encounters difficulty, please call my name.
I will swiftly come to you."
The snake said:
"My name is Cháng.
If the ascetic faces calamity,
please call my name; I will surely come to repay your kindness."
After bidding farewell, each departed.
Another day, the ascetic went to the hunter's home.
The hunter saw him approaching from afar
and told his wife:
"That inauspicious person is coming.
I command you:
prepare food slowly.
He will not eat after midday."
The wife saw the ascetic,
feigned a pleasant expression, deceitfully delayed setting out the food, engaged in empty talk until past midday.
The ascetic left and returned to the mountains.
Seeing a crow, he called out: "Bō!"
The crow asked:
"Where have you come from?"
He replied: "From the hunter's place."
The crow said: "Have you eaten?"
He said: "He had not prepared the food; the sun had passed midday, so I did not wait and left."
The crow said:
"Ominous beings are difficult to aid with compassion.
Those who violate benevolence and betray kindness are wicked and rebellious people.
I have no food or drink to offer you.
But please sit and stay awhile.
I will fly shortly to the country of Bānzhē.
I saw the king's consort sleeping among her head ornaments; there was a bright moon pearl.
The crow took it in its beak and returned, presenting it to the ascetic.
The consort awoke and sought it but could not find it.
She immediately reported it to the king.
The king commanded his ministers and people:
"Whoever obtains it
will be rewarded with a thousand jin each of gold and silver, and a thousand head each of oxen and horses.
If found and not presented, the crime will extend to the extermination of the clan."
The ascetic gave it to the hunter.
The hunter was bound and interrogated, and he confessed to the king.
The king said:
"How did you obtain this?"
The ascetic pondered deeply:
"If I reveal the true owner, all the crows in the country will die.
This is not the way of a Buddha's disciple."
He silently endured the interrogation and was beaten a thousand times with rods.
He did not resent the king nor bear a grudge against the hunter.
He made a compassionate vow, saying:
"May I attain Buddhahood and deliver all beings from suffering."
The king buried the ascetic, leaving only his head exposed, intending to execute him the next day.
The ascetic then called the snake: "Cháng!"
The snake said: "No one in the world knows my name,
except the ascetic.
If he calls my name aloud, there must be a reason."
It swiftly went to see the ascetic.
It asked:
"How did you come to this?"
The ascetic then explained the reason.
The snake shed tears and said:
"The ascetic is benevolent and compassionate; even between heaven and earth, he still encounters misfortune.
How much more so for those without the Way—who will protect them?
I will enter the palace and bite the crown prince to death."
The snake gave the ascetic a divine medicine to apply, and he was immediately healed.
The snake entered the palace at night, bit the crown prince, and he died instantly.
The body was kept for three days, and a decree was issued:
"Whoever can revive the crown prince
will share the kingdom and rule jointly."
They carried the body through the mountains, passing by the ascetic.
The ascetic said:
"I can revive him."
The king heard and was overjoyed.
The ascetic applied the medicine to the crown prince's body.
Suddenly, he spoke:
"Why am I here?"
The attendants explained the situation in detail.
The crown prince returned to the palace; all, great and small, rejoiced and danced. The king offered to share the kingdom with the ascetic.
The ascetic accepted nothing.
The king realized and said:
"He refuses to share the kingdom—could he possibly be a thief?"
He asked how he had obtained the pearl.
"His conduct is so lofty; how did he suddenly escape this calamity?"
The ascetic explained everything from beginning to end.
The king's face streamed with tears.
He addressed the hunter:
"You have merit for the country.
Summon all your nine classes of relatives to come.
I wish to reward them generously."
Relatives, great and small, all gathered at the palace gate.
The king said:
"The unkind, the ungrateful, the chief of evil—kill them all."
The ascetic entered the mountains to study the Way, diligent and tireless.
After death, he was reborn in heaven.
The ascetic at that time was myself.
The crow was Qiūlùzǐ.
The snake was Ānán.
The hunter was Tiáodá.
The wife was the woman Huái Bàn.
This is so.
In the past, in Jambudvīpa, there was a great king
named Xiānyù.
He cherished and esteemed the Mahāyāna; his heart was pure and good.
He had no coarseness, malice, jealousy, or stinginess.
His mouth constantly proclaimed loving and kind words.
His body constantly protected the poor, orphaned, and lonely.
He practiced giving and diligence without cease.
At that time, there was no Buddha, Śrāvaka, or Pratyekabuddha in the world.
The king loved and delighted in the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras.
For twelve years, he served brāhmaṇas,
providing all their needs. After twelve years,
when the offerings were completed,
he spoke thus:
"Teachers, you should now arouse the mind of supreme enlightenment."
The brāhmaṇas said:
"Great King,
the nature of enlightenment is non-existent.
The Mahāyāna sūtras are also like this.
Great King,
how can you want people to be like empty space?"
The king, hearing the brāhmaṇas slander the Vaipulya,
immediately took their lives.
Because of this cause, he did not fall into hell,
but protected and upheld the Mahāyāna sūtras.
Such is their power.
In the past, the king of the country of Tiānluó had a crown prince
who wished to ascend the throne.
His name was Bānzú.
He received the teachings of a non-Buddhist teacher named Luótuó:
"You should take the heads of a thousand kings to sacrifice to the tomb deity, and then ascend the throne."
He had already obtained nine hundred and ninety-nine kings.
He lacked one more king.
He traveled north ten thousand li and obtained King Pǔmíng.
Pǔmíng said to Bānzú:
"Please allow me one day to feed śramaṇas and pay homage to the Three Jewels."
Bānzú permitted it.
Pǔmíng then followed the method of the past seven Buddhas.
In one day, during two periods, he finished expounding the eight thousand gāthās of the Prajñāpāramitā.
The first Dharma master spoke a gāthā for the king.
At that time, King Pǔmíng,
together with his retinue, attained the Dharma-eye of emptiness.
The king himself realized the samādhi of equality with space and, upon hearing the Dharma, gained understanding.
He returned to the kingdom of Tiānluó, where King Bānzú was,
and addressed the nine hundred and ninety-nine kings, saying:
"The time of facing death has arrived; each person should recite the verses on the Prajñāpāramitā of the Benevolent Kings of the Past Seven Buddhas."
Bānzú asked:
"What Dharma should be recited?"
King Pǔmíng then replied to the king with the verses above.
Upon hearing this Dharma, the king attained the samādhi of emptiness.
The nine hundred and ninety-nine kings also, having heard the Dharma,
all realized the samādhi of the three gates of liberation.
At that time, King Bānzú was filled with great joy.
He addressed the kings, saying:
"I was misled by heretical teachers of external paths;
it was not your fault.
Return each to your own kingdoms,
and each invite Dharma masters
to expound on the names, meanings, phrases, and assemblies of the Prajñāpāramitā."
At that time, King Bānzú entrusted the kingdom to his younger brother,
left home to cultivate the Way, and realized the patient endurance of the non-arising of dharmas,
as described in the Ten Stages of the Bodhisattva.
King Ajātaśatru addressed Mañjuśrī, saying, "I sincerely hope you will bestow your grace and condescend to come to my palace for a meal tomorrow morning."
Mañjuśrī replied, "What you have is sufficient as an offering."
Moreover, the Dharma is not about food and clothing.
The king said,
"How then should I make offerings?"
Mañjuśrī replied,
"If one deeply enters the subtle and profound, the matter is truly discerned.
There is no defilement, nor is there any attachment.
There is also no doubt.
Nor is there any fear or difficulty.
Furthermore, contemplate all dharmas without contemplating existence or non-existence, without contemplating past, future, or present, ultimately.
Also, one should not contemplate that all that is visible can receive compassion."
The king said,
"As you have said, it is entirely in accordance with the Dharma, without any difference.
Only for the sake of the body, please bestow compassion and accept the invitation."
Mañjuśrī said,
"Stop.
The Way is not for such reasons.
Whether drinking or eating,
if the king does not contemplate self, life, or person,
by contemplating this, compassion is attained." The king was greatly delighted and asked,
"How many people are there?"
Śāriputra said,
"Five hundred people.
They can all be invited to eat at the palace."
Returning to the city, the king ordered the preparation of a hundred flavors of food and arranged the hall.
He set up banners, curtains, and canopies.
He spread flowers on the ground and perfumed everything with incense.
He set up five hundred high seats.
The palace, city, and streets were all cleaned.
Flowers and incense were spread, and the people came to welcome them.
Mañjuśrī, in the time it takes to stretch out an arm, arrived in the east.
Passing through eighty-two thousand Buddha lands,
he reached a Buddha named Cháng Míng Wén.
That Buddha's name is Wéi Jìng Shǒu.
He is presently in the world.
There are many bodhisattvas, with no other paths.
In that land, the irreversible Dharma wheel constantly turns.
The land constantly emits the sound of the Three Jewels.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha,
"I wish to bring all
the bodhisattvas to the Śāha land,
to Ajātaśatru's place for the meal."
The Buddha said,
"Those who wish to go, may go." The king heard
that Mañjuśrī was coming with twenty-two thousand five hundred bodhisattvas.
There were also five hundred bhikṣus. The king thought to himself,
"I have only prepared for five hundred people. How can I provide for them?"
At that moment, a heavenly king named Xiū Xí Xīn,
together with a respected yakṣa named Jīn Pí,
came to see the king and said,
"Do not fear, do not panic, do not consider it difficult."
The king said, "How is it not difficult?"
They replied,
"Mañjuśrī possesses upāya-kauśalya and limitless wisdom.
He comes fully endowed with merit and light.
He can take a single meal and share it with Mañjuśrī and others.
Even if all the people of the three thousand great thousand worlds
requested food, they could all be satisfied, and the food would not be exhausted.
What concern is there for these twenty-two thousand people?"
Mañjuśrī's merit
is extremely profound and inexhaustible.
The king was overjoyed and elated.
He led musicians and personally went out to welcome them, and they all entered the palace together.
There was a bodhisattva
named Pǔ Shì Xī Jiàn.
Mañjuśrī instructed Sāmādhi Ālóu Tuó
to prepare the place to accommodate the arrivals.
The bodhisattva received the instruction.
Looking around and assessing, he immediately prepared everything.
Another bodhisattva,
named Fǎ Lái Zé Dé,
was instructed to prepare seats.
In the snap of a finger, twenty-two thousand seats appeared, adorned in various ways.
The bodhisattvas and śrāvakas all took their seats.
The king addressed Mañjuśrī,
"The offerings I have prepared are very few.
I hope you will bear with me a little longer while I prepare more."
Mañjuśrī replied,
"What has been prepared is sufficient. Do not trouble yourself further."
The heavenly king Vaiśravaṇa,
along with his family, servants, and attendants, all came to pay respects.
They respectfully attended to everyone.
Śakra Devānām Indra,
together with his great consort,
named Shǒu Yē,
and celestial maidens,
all held famous incense as offerings.
They scattered it over Mañjuśrī, the bodhisattvas, and the bhikṣu saṅgha.
The bodhisattvas and others were not moved by the flowers and incense.
Brahmā,
transforming himself into a young brāhmaṇa,
handsome and upright,
stood to Mañjuśrī's right, fanning him.
All the Brahmā deities
fanned the bodhisattvas and bhikṣus.
The dragon king Anavatapta,
invisible in the sky,
held strings of pearls hanging like banners.
Water with eight flavors of perfume flowed down from the strings.
Before each person, a string of pearls hung,
and water flowed from them, providing all that was needed.
The king thought, "The attendees have not brought bowls. What will they eat from?"
At that moment, Mañjuśrī said,
"Bodhisattvas do not carry bowls when they travel.
Wherever they eat, bowls come into their hands of their own accord."
The bodhisattvas thought of bowls,
and the bowls flew over in rows and arrived.
King Anavatapta
personally cleaned them and filled them with water.
The dragon maidens
each held twenty-two thousand bowls
and presented them to the bodhisattvas, one in each hand.
Mañjuśrī said to the king,
"You may distribute the food. It will be enough for all and not diminish."
Mañjuśrī said,
"Is it finished now?"
The king replied, "It is not finished."
"The reason it is not finished is because there is doubt."
When the bodhisattvas finished eating,
they tossed their bowls into the sky, where they remained in rows.
They did not fall to the ground nor sway.
The king asked again,
"How do the bowls remain? What do they rely on?"
Mañjuśrī said,
"The bowls remain just as the king's doubts remain." The king said again,
"These bowls have no place to remain.
They are not on the ground.
They have no reliance,
nor any location."
Mañjuśrī said,
"Just as the king's doubts have no abode,
all dharmas are like the bowls, having no abode and no falling."
After the meal was finished,
the king took a seat
and addressed Mañjuśrī, saying,
"Please resolve my doubts."
Mañjuśrī replied,
"Even Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges could not explain the king's doubts."
The king was terrified at that moment.
He fell from his seat like a great tree collapsing.
Mahākāśyapa said to the king,
"Do not fear, do not be afraid.
Why?
Mañjuśrī has entered profound upāya-kauśalya.
Ask slowly."
The king said,
"Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges cannot explain my doubts."
Mañjuśrī said,
"Do you think they can be seen through mental conditions?"
The king said,
"It is not because of the mind's production that the Buddha can be seen.
Neither birth and death nor liberation—these two matters make a Buddha.
My doubts cannot be explained by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Why?
If someone says,
'Can dust defile empty space? Can it be done?'
If someone says,
'Can one remove the defilement of empty space? Can it be removed?'"
The king said, "It cannot."
Mañjuśrī said,
"The Buddha knows that all dharmas are like empty space.
Why?
Because they are free from origin.
Nor does one see any dharma as having an origin.
If there were someone to explain it, the king's doubts could not be explained by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
At that moment, the king attained faith and patience.
Overjoyed and elated, he said,
"Excellent, excellent!
You have resolved my doubts."
Mañjuśrī said,
"This is a great doubt pertaining to the Dharma. Since there is no origin, from where does doubt arise?"
The king said,
"Having received this great kindness, I have attained some relief.
Now, when my life ends, I do not worry about not reaching Nirvāṇa."
Mañjuśrī said,
"What the king hopes for has no origin.
Why?
Because the origin of all dharmas is Nirvāṇa, thus there is no production."
The king then rose from his seat,
took a fine cloth worth billions and hundreds of thousands, and wrapped it around Mañjuśrī's body.
Mañjuśrī's body became invisible.
The cloth remained in the air.
Only the sound of speech was heard; his form was not seen. Hearing the speech was like seeing him.
The king saw his own doubts and saw all dharmas as he saw them.
A voice in the air addressed the king's vision,
and gave the cloth to him.
The next bodhisattva in the seat was named Dé Shàng Yuàn.
The king again took the cloth, intending to offer it to him.
Dé Shàng Yuàn said,
"Those who seek liberation and Nirvāṇa—
I do not receive anything from them.
Nor do I receive anything from ordinary people.
Why?
Ordinary people
are said to have worldly affairs, so I do not receive from them.
Nor do I receive from those who seek arhatship or pratyekabuddhahood.
Those who give
have no dual mind; those who receive
also have no dual mind."
Therefore it is said that what is received surpasses liberation.
The king then took his robe intending to place it upon the Bodhisattva.
Suddenly, he vanished and his whereabouts were no longer known.
Only his voice was heard; his form was not seen.
He spoke, saying:
"To the one who manifests his body, give the robe."
Thus, in sequence, each one was given a robe, and each one vanished.
Even the beds, stools, and seats all vanished as well.
Only their voices were heard.
Saying: "To the one who manifests, give the robe."
Even the five hundred Śrāvakas also did not accept it.
The king pondered deeply:
"All the Bodhisattvas and Bhikṣus have vanished.
To whom shall I give my robe?"
He intended to give it to his chief queen in the inner palace.
At that moment, the queen also vanished.
The king then attained samādhi.
He saw no forms.
He saw neither women.
Nor men.
Even walls, trees, dwellings, houses, cities, and ramparts—
He still had a remaining thought, believing:
"There is my body, forms, and consciousness."
All ceased.
Again, he heard a voice:
"As with all things seen, one should doubt one's own seeing.
As with the doubt in what is seen, seeing all dharmas is also like this."
He then took his robe back, intending to wear it himself.
He did not see his body or mind. Mañjuśrī said:
"Have you heard the Buddha say that those who commit grave offenses will fall into the great hell?"
The king said: "I have heard."
"Do you know yourself that you will fall into hell?"
The king said:
"Is there a dharma by which one attains Buddhahood, ascends to heaven, or falls into hell?
Is there a dharma of peace that leads to Nirvāṇa?"
Mañjuśrī said: "No." The king said:
"I know all dharmas are empty.
Why is this?
Hell, heaven, and peace are also all empty.
All dharmas cannot be destroyed.
Therefore, one enters the Dharmakāya.
In the Dharmakāya, there is neither heaven, the human world, hell, animals, hungry ghosts, nor the like."
The king, through purification of all grave offenses, attained this forbearance.
The king said:
"All dharmas are entirely pure, without any defilement."
When he spoke these words, he swiftly attained the faith-forbearance.
Ānanda knew what the assembly was thinking.
He came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One,
from what cause did you first arouse the mind of enlightenment?"
The Buddha said:
"In a past distant kalpa,
in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great king
named Dà Guāngmíng.
He was virtuous, fortunate, and intelligent.
At that time, a king of a neighboring country was on close terms with him.
They exchanged gifts of their countries' treasures.
That king hunted and obtained two elephants,
white as crystal, with seven limbs touching the ground,
adorned with various jewels, the rarest treasures in the world.
He sent someone to deliver them.
When King Guāngmíng saw the elephants, his heart was delighted.
He entrusted them to the elephant trainer Sàn Zhé.
Sàn Zhé received the command.
Before long, he tamed them.
He went to inform the king, saying:
'The elephants are now tamed.
I wish the king would observe and test them.'
The king assembled his ministers and ordered the testing of the elephants.
After the great assembly had gathered,
the king first mounted an elephant and went out of the city for amusement.
The elephant's spirit was fierce and strong.
Seeing a herd of elephants at a lotus pond,
it chased after a female elephant and entered a deep forest.
At that time, the king's body was torn and bleeding.
He thought to himself that he would surely die.
Grabbing a tree branch, the elephant left, and the king remained.
Descending from the tree and sitting on the ground, he felt great distress.
The elephant trainer kowtowed and said:
'May the king not worry or suffer.
When the elephant's lustful mind ceases, disgusted with foul grass and longing for fine food and drink, it will return on its own.'
The king then said:
'I no longer have any use for it.'
Later, the elephant indeed returned.
The elephant trainer informed the king:
'The elephant has now returned.'
The king said:
'I have no need for you, nor for the elephant.'
Sàn Zhé addressed the king:
'If the king has no need,
I only wish the king to observe my method of taming elephants.'
The king consented.
Immediately, the trainer made seven iron balls and heated them until extremely red.
After making them, he thought:
'If the elephant swallows these balls, it will certainly die.'
Later, the king might regret it, so he said:
'Great King,
this white elephant treasure is only obtained by a Cakravartin king.
Now, for a minor fault, it should not be lost.'
The king's anger was intense, and he declared:
'Away with you!'
The elephant trainer told the elephant:
'Swallow these iron balls.
If you do not swallow them, I will use an iron hook to split your brain.'
The elephant knew his mind.
'I would rather swallow these hot balls and die.'
Kneeling towards the king, shedding tears, it looked to him for rescue.
The king, angered, slowly looked at Sàn Zhé and said to the elephant: 'Why do you not swallow the balls?'
Then the elephant took the balls, placed them in its mouth, and swallowed them.
Entering its belly, they scorched and burned, passing straight through, and it died.
The balls fell to the ground, still red.
The king saw this and then regretted it.
He said to Sàn Zhé:
'You tame elephants like this?
Why then, in the forest, could you not control it?'
At that time, the devas of the Pure Abode knew that King Guāngmíng should arouse the mind of enlightenment.
They caused the elephant trainer to kneel and reply to the king, saying:
'I can only tame the body, not the mind.
Only the Buddha can tame the mind.'
The king said:
'What kind is the Buddha?
From what lineage is he born?'
He replied: 'Born from two lineages.
One is wisdom.
The other is great compassion.
Diligently practicing the six deeds,
namely the six pāramitās.
When merit, virtue, and wisdom are fully complete,
he is called Buddha.'
Hearing this, the king leaped for joy.
He immediately arose, bathed, put on new clothes, and bowed in the four directions.
Towards all sentient beings, he aroused great compassion, burned incense, and made a vow:
'May all my merit and virtue be dedicated to the Buddha Way.
I will tame my own mind and also tame all sentient beings.
If there is benefit for those in hell, I will enter that hell.
I will never abandon the mind of enlightenment.'
After making this vow,
the six kinds of tremors occurred.
In the mountains, great seas, and empty space, music naturally sounded.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
'At that time, the white elephant that swallowed the iron balls was Nanda.
The elephant trainer at that time was Śāriputra.
King Guāngmíng was myself.
At that time, seeing the elephant tamed and subdued, I first aroused the mind of enlightenment.'
In the past, there was a king
named Duō Fú.
His crown prince was named Zēng Fú.
The king served the six teachers.
His son served the Buddha.
In the world, there were no śramaṇas;
only a white-robed layman was the leading teacher.
Five hundred non-Buddhists were jealous of his fame and virtue.
They addressed the king, saying:
'The affairs of the state follow two laws, causing the mind to be not unified.
We wish to compete with the Buddha's teacher, each displaying extraordinary virtue.
The one who loses shall be enslaved.'
The king consented.
The non-Buddhists and the teacher set a date and made an agreement.
Before the king, each would test their skills.
The Brahmin was skilled in archery and went into the mountains.
The five hundred men each shot a great deer,
all piercing the left eye, and brought them back to display their skills.
The virtuous one entered the mountains, concentrated his thoughts, and recollected the Buddha,
seeking divine assistance to manifest the great Way.
A five-colored deer leaped forth from the ground.
Joyfully, he took it back.
The non-Buddhists learned of this.
Waiting for the virtuous one to leave,
they went and said to his wife:
'Your husband has left home to become a śramaṇa.
It is only because of this deer that
your family's law is broken.'
The wife, hearing this, became angry and gave the deer to them.
When the virtuous one returned, he did not see the deer.
He immediately asked where it was.
The wife said:
'This inauspicious thing is now lost.'
The husband was very worried and sorrowful.
He returned to the mountains and sincerely repented his fault.
Then a bright moon divine pearl suddenly emerged from the ground.
Taking this pearl, he observed the Brahmin going out,
went to his door, and displayed the rare object for sale.
The Brahmin's wife said:
'My family also has a rare object that can compare.'
She brought out the five-colored deer.
The virtuous one then said:
'The king sent me to present this deer.
You have now stolen it; your crime is immeasurable.'
The wife hastily returned it.
On the day of the test,
the Brahmins each presented deer, all injured in the left eye, both filthy and foul-smelling.
The king was very displeased.
The virtuous one came and offered the divine deer, presenting the bright moon divine pearl in the king's palace hall.
The two objects flew and soared, playing together like flowing stars and flashing lightning.
The entire palace praised the wonder.
The five hundred Brahmins,
knowing their skills were inferior,
were enslaved.
Their wives became maidservants.
The virtuous one guided and taught them the scriptures, making them his disciples.
The king of Bōluónài.
During the summer heat, he resided in a high tower.
Seated on a bed of seven treasures, he had maidservants massage him.
His body was anointed with gośīrṣa sandalwood.
The maidservants wore many bracelets on their arms while massaging the king.
The sound of the bracelets filled his ears, greatly troubling the king.
He ordered them to remove the bracelets one by one.
When only one bracelet remained, it was completely silent.
The king then realized:
“The affairs and troubles of the state, its ministers, people, and concubines are just like this.”
Immediately, he renounced desires, dwelled alone in contemplation, and attained Pratyekabuddhahood.
His hair and beard fell off naturally, and he was clothed in garments that appeared of their own accord.
He left the tower and, by his own supernatural power, renounced the world and entered the mountains.
Such is the cause and condition of a middling Pratyekabuddha.
There are those who vow to become Pratyekabuddhas.
They plant such wholesome roots.
When the world is without a Buddha,
and their merit ripens,
they renounce the world out of weariness and attain the path.
They are called Pratyekabuddhas.
The king of Yuèzhī,
seeking the Buddha Way, built thirty-two stūpas.
He constructed them one by one for offerings, reaching thirty-one.
At that time, an evil person offended the king.
The king’s mind regressed.
“How can such an evil person be saved?”
He immediately turned his mind, abandoning saṃsāra and turning toward nirvāṇa.
He built the thirty-second stūpa to seek liberation.
Through this cause and condition, he attained the path of an arhat.
Therefore, this monastery is named Pōluótí Mùchā. Since then, less than two hundred years have passed.
This monastery still exists.
I have also seen it.
The king of Shèwèi was named Pōsīnì.
At that time, there was a kingdom to the south,
named Jīndì.
Its king was named Jiébīnníng.
The crown prince was named Móhē Jiébīnníng.
When his father passed away, the crown prince ascended the throne.
He was intelligent and valiant by nature.
He ruled over thirty-six thousand small states.
His might was far-reaching, and none could withstand him.
However, he had no contact with the central lands.
Later, merchants traveled to Jīndì.
They presented four bolts of fine cloth to that king.
The king asked the merchants:
“This item is excellent. Where does it come from?”
They replied:
“It comes from the central lands.”
The king asked again:
“What is the name of that central land?”
They answered:
“It is called Luóyuèqí,
also known as Shèwèi.”
The king asked again:
“Why has the king of the central lands not come to offer tribute to me?”
They replied again:
“Each rules his own territory, and their might and fame are equal.
Therefore, he does not come.”
The king thought to himself:
“Now I must exert my might to make him submit.”
He asked the merchants again:
“Among the kings of the central lands, which is the greatest?”
They said:
“The king of Shèwèi is the greatest.”
He immediately dispatched an envoy to Shèwèi,
carrying a letter with detailed instructions to inform its king,
Pōsīnì, saying:
“My might extends throughout Jambudvīpa.
By what authority do you cut off diplomatic missions?
Now I send an envoy to communicate with you.
After seven days, meet with me.
If you do not comply, I will raise an army and destroy your borders.”
Pōsīnì heard this and was deeply alarmed.
He went to the Buddha and fully reported the matter.
The Buddha told the king:
“Return and tell the envoy:
‘I am not the greatest; there is a greater king.’”
The king, following the Buddha’s teaching,
said to the envoy:
“There is a sage king in the world,
near here.
You may go to him and convey your king’s message.”
The envoy then went to the Jetavana.
At that time, the World-Honored One
transformed himself into a cakravartin king,
with the seven treasures fully present as attendants.
The envoy entered the transformed city.
Upon seeing the great king, he was greatly awestruck and presented the letter.
The transformed king received the letter and stepped on it with his foot,
saying to the envoy:
“I am the great king ruling over the four continents.
Your king is stubborn and deluded, daring to defy me.
Return quickly to your country and convey my command.
Upon receiving this message, he must rush to pay homage.
If he hears it while lying down, he must rise;
if he hears it while sitting, he must stand.
He must comply within seven days without delay.
If he dares violate this decree, the punishment will be severe.”
The envoy returned to his country and fully reported what he had seen and heard to the king of Jīndì.
The king, upon receiving this inquiry, deeply blamed himself.
He gathered all the minor kings under his rule to pay homage to the great king but did not set out immediately.
First, he sent an envoy to inform the great king:
“The thirty-six thousand kings under my rule—
should they all come,
or only half?”
The great king replied:
“Let half remain; bring only half.”
At that time, the king of Jīndì brought eighteen thousand minor kings and arrived together.
Upon seeing the transformed king and paying homage,
he thought to himself:
“Although the great king’s appearance surpasses mine,
his strength may not.”
The transformed king then
ordered his minister of arms to give a bow to him.
The king of Jīndì could not lift it with his hand.
The transformed king took it back, drew the bow with his finger,
and handed it to him, ordering him to draw it.
The king of Jīndì could not draw it at all.
The transformed king took it again and plucked the string,
causing the three-thousandfold world to tremble.
Next, he took an arrow, bent the bow, and shot.
After leaving his hand, the arrow transformed into five.
The tips of the arrows emitted light,
and at the tip of each light was a lotus flower as large as a chariot wheel.
On each lotus flower, there was a cakravartin king,
complete with the seven treasures, radiating light
that universally illuminated the three-thousandfold great thousand worlds.
The beings in the five paths all benefited.
The heavenly realms, seeing this light and hearing the Dharma,
purified their bodies and minds, some arousing the mind of unsurpassed true enlightenment,
others attaining the irreversible stage.
Among human beings, some attained the first, second, or third fruit,
some aroused the mind of unsurpassed true enlightenment,
and those attaining the irreversible stage were beyond count.
Beings in the three wretched paths were freed from suffering, reborn in the human or heavenly realms.
At that time, King Móhē Jiébīnníng
and the minor kings of Jīndì,
witnessing this supernatural transformation, believed and submitted.
They were freed from defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
All eighteen thousand minor kings attained the same in an instant.
In a moment, the Buddha withdrew his supernatural power and returned to his original form,
surrounded by bhikṣus before and after.
The kings of Jīndì sought to renounce the world.
Their hair and beards fell off naturally, and robes appeared on their bodies.
Contemplating the wondrous Dharma, they all became arhats.
In a distant past kalpa,
in this city of Jūshī, a Buddha appeared in the world,
named Huānxǐ Zēngyì.
He dwelled in the world for immeasurable time, saving beings,
and then entered parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the remaining Dharma dwelled in the world for immeasurable billions of years.
In the last forty years before the Dharma’s extinction,
there was a precept-holding bhikṣu
named Juédé.
He had many disciples and followers surrounding him and could roar like a lion, extensively expounding the scriptures.
He prohibited bhikṣus from keeping slaves, cattle, sheep, or other improper things.
At that time, many precept-breaking bhikṣus
hearing this teaching harbored ill will.
They took up knives and staves, threatening this Dharma master.
At that time, the king,
named Yǒudé,
hearing of this matter,
went to the place of the Dharma speaker to protect the Dharma.
He fiercely fought
with these precept-breaking evil bhikṣus,
enabling the Dharma speaker to escape harm.
The king was wounded all over his body.
Juédé immediately praised the king:
“Excellent, excellent!
Now you are truly a protector of the true Dharma.
In future lives, this body will become an immeasurable vessel of the Dharma.”
The king, hearing the Dharma at that time,
was greatly joyful and soon passed away.
He was reborn in the land of Buddha Akṣobhya as his foremost disciple.
The king’s followers, people, and retinue—
those who fought,
and those who rejoiced—
all did not regress from the bodhi mind.
After death, they were all reborn in the land of Buddha Akṣobhya.
Bhikṣu Juédé, after his lifespan ended,
also went to be reborn in the land of Buddha Akṣobhya,
becoming the second disciple among the śrāvaka assembly.
If, when the true Dharma is about to perish,
one should uphold and protect it in this way.
The king at that time was myself,
and the Dharma-teaching bhikṣu was Buddha Kāśyapa.
At that time, King Gōngdé Zhuāngyán,
having heard the verses from the Buddha and witnessed the divine transformations,
strengthened and solidified his resolve for Bodhi.
He bowed at the Buddha’s feet and addressed him, saying:
“I beseech the World-Honored One,
along with the bodhisattvas, disciples, and the great assembly,
to accept my invitation for eighty-four thousand years.
May the Tathāgata Pǔmíng Wáng
allow me to provide clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all necessities of service.
That Buddha and the great assembly then accepted his invitation.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted his invitation,
the king rejoiced and departed.
The prince Shīzǐ Jìn, along with twenty thousand princes, renounced worldly glory and status,
shaved off their hair and beards, left home, and cultivated the path in the Dharma.
They diligently practiced vigor and delighted in seeking wholesome dharmas.
At that time, Shīzǐ Jìn attained the five supernatural powers and became steadfast and unretreating.
That Buddha empowered him with majestic spiritual power, and he constantly expounded wondrous Dharma for sentient beings,
performing Buddha-deeds throughout the three-thousand-great-thousandfold world.
Immeasurable sentient beings became steadfast and unretreating in the supreme Great Vehicle.
For eighty-four thousand years, King Gōngdé Zhuāngyán
offered all kinds of delightful provisions to the World-Honored One and the great assembly.
Together with all his ministers, he led the retinue before and after, forming an audience to listen to the Dharma.
And he thought to himself:
“My sons have shaved off their hair and beards, left home, and cultivated the path.
They constantly receive offerings but cannot themselves practice giving.
Nor have I seen them attain any surpassing Dharma.
It would be better to return home, give up wealth to practice charity, and cultivate all meritorious deeds,
just as I have planted various wholesome roots.”
At that time, the Tathāgata Pǔ Guāngmíng Wáng
immediately knew what King Gōngdé Zhuāngyán was thinking in his heart.
He addressed the Bodhisattva Shīzǐ Jìn, saying:
“Good man,
manifest now your autonomous meritorious and spiritual powers.
Through the transformations of a great bodhisattva, let this great assembly universally see and hear,
turning back their erroneous minds and enabling them to attain right view.”
The Bodhisattva Shīzǐ Jìn immediately entered samādhi and manifested such signs as these:
The great thousandfold world trembled and quaked.
In the sky above rained down flowers, incense, canopies, banners, music, fine food and drink, necklaces,
clothing, and various precious jewels,
descending profusely and filling the great thousandfold world.
Sentient beings experienced what they had never experienced before and all rejoiced greatly.
At that time, from the earth deities up through the heavens to Akaniṣṭha,
all proclaimed these words:
“This great bodhisattva may be named Xūkōng Zàng (Ākāśagarbha).
The reason is this:
From empty space, he can rain down jewels and treasures, satisfying all.”
The Buddha then confirmed this.
Seeing this, the king leaped for joy, experiencing what he had never experienced before, and abandoned his arrogant mind.
He joined his palms toward the Buddha
and spoke these words:
“How rare, World-Honored One!
The merit and wisdom of a bodhisattva can indeed be like this.
World-Honored One,
the benefits of giving by householders are few.
But those who have left home, through spiritual powers, give without limit.
The giving of householders does not match their intentions;
even when giving, they are stingy and regard it as suffering.
Those who have left home are not stingy and do not produce suffering.”
The king abdicated his throne
and gave it to his son, Jíyì.
With genuine faith, he shaved off his hair and beard
and left home to cultivate the path in the Dharma.
He increased wholesome dharmas, constantly practiced diligence and vigor, and attained the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, and the five supernatural powers.
At that time, King Jíyì
ruled according to the Dharma, and there were no resentful people in the kingdom.
He practiced vigor without weariness and made offerings to the World-Honored One.
King Gōngdé Zhuāngyán
was the Tathāgata Krakucchanda.
The Bodhisattva Shīzǐ Jìn
is the Bodhisattva Xūkōng Zàng (Ākāśagarbha).
King Jíyì
is Maitreya.
In Shèwèi, there was a king.
His name was Lándá.
The land was fertile and the people were honest and faithful.
Rulers and subjects, fathers and sons, all followed the Way together.
Later, a new king ascended the throne.
Laws and customs deteriorated, and governance became unjust.
He oppressed the people and executed the innocent without cause.
Disorder brought calamity; rain did not fall in its season.
The five grains did not ripen, and monsters appeared everywhere.
This led to famine and ruin, and they feared destruction.
They served heretical paths, over five hundred people.
They also worshipped demonic gods; high and low learned from each other.
Like the wind bending the grass.
The common people delighted in chaos, competing in wickedness and crime.
The strong bullied the weak, injuring and killing each other.
They robbed people of their wealth, disregarding all reason.
They violated others' wives and daughters; ruler and ministers were lost in drunkenness.
Delusion grew daily; the drought lasted over three years.
Despite repeated prayers and supplications, still no rain fell.
The various masters told the king.
"Now we must hold a great sacrifice.
We must use seven young boys, ten white oxen, and ten white horses, burn them to sacrifice to Heaven.
Only then can we obtain rain."
The king immediately prepared the items.
The whole country was in turmoil, all disturbed and agitated.
The Buddha told Mùlián.
"The land of King Lándá is desolate, the people suffer hardship.
Three hundred million people should attain liberation through you.
You should go and enlighten them."
Mùlián went and preached the Dharma to enlighten their minds.
At first, none of the people in the country accepted it.
Mùlián.
Transformed into the body of a great demon-god.
Dozens of *zhàng* tall.
He sat before the city gate.
In a thunderous voice, he called for the king and his close ministers to come out.
The ruler and ministers were terrified, fearing for their lives.
The king immediately led his close ministers, kowtowed, and pleaded.
"We only beg for our lives."
The demon-god said to the king.
"Quickly bring me ministers who are disloyal and sons who are unfilial.
I wish to eat them."
The king immediately inquired.
The reply was: "There are none."
The demon-god said to the king again.
"Quickly bring me thieves.
The licentious.
Those who slander and speak harshly.
I wish to eat them."
The king immediately inquired.
Again, the reply was: "There are none."
The demon-god said to the king again.
"Quickly bring me those who drink alcohol.
I wish to eat them."
The king immediately inquired.
Again, the reply was: "There are none."
Then Mùlián resumed his true form.
He went and spoke with the demon-god.
The king saw Mùlián.
He kowtowed and earnestly requested him to explain things to the great demon-god.
Mùlián said to the king.
"What does this demon-god seek?"
The king said.
"He wishes to eat wicked people."
Mùlián asked.
"Are there truly such people in your country?"
The king replied, "No."
He earnestly requested him to send the demon-god away.
"I will devote my life to following the Dharma master."
Mùlián said to the great demon-god.
"Among the people of this country, there are none of the kind you seek.
You should pardon their offenses.
If there are offenders in the future,
you may come again to eat them."
The demon-god then heeded his words.
And suddenly departed.
The king and his ministers and people.
All together kowtowed, expressed gratitude, and begged to take refuge.
Mùlián told them.
"If the king wishes to take refuge,
you should first take refuge in the Buddha."
The king asked about the Buddha's virtues.
Mùlián explained that the Buddha is the sole honored one in the Three Realms, and the Dharma he teaches is heard by three thousand *śrāvakas*.
The king said.
"I am fortunate today to hear such extraordinary teachings."
He then addressed Mùlián.
"I wish to invite the Buddha to receive our reverence and teachings, which we will uphold for life."
Mùlián told the king.
"If you can truly believe thus,
your merit will be immeasurable.
Only maintain a pure mind and remember the Buddha."
The king then received the teaching, bathed, observed fasting, and purified himself.
Facing the Buddha's land from afar, he bowed his head in reverence.
Saying, "Due to my ignorance, I mistakenly ruled over the people.
I could not cleanse my heart and guide them rightly.
That the country became empty and desolate is my fault.
I only pray that the Heavenly Honored One will shine his light and descend.
To universally grant the common people boundless blessings."
The Buddha and the bhikṣus.
When still a hundred *lǐ* away, proceeded through the air in advance.
Five-colored lotus flowers supported their feet.
Deva beings flanked them, with precious canopies and parasols welcoming them along the road.
Various celestial music filled the sky.
Beholding the Buddha's majestic spiritual power, his light illuminated heaven and earth.
The king and his ministers bowed at his feet.
At the crossroads, they widely spread canopies and awnings, sweeping and cleaning until spotless.
The Buddha sat on a naturally-formed lion throne.
All spread with heavenly silks and fine cloth.
The king personally served food and drink and poured water for washing.
When the blessings and prayers were finished.
The Buddha then expounded the essentials of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and the Four Noble Truths.
The king was overjoyed and begged to receive the Five Precepts.
His bonds were loosened, his defilements removed.
He attained the fruit of Srota-āpanna.
At that time, the five hundred heretics the king had served begged to become bhikṣus.
The Buddha immediately consented.
He placed his hand on their heads; their hair fell away and monastic robes appeared on their bodies.
After seven days, they all attained Arhatship.
The assembled people attained Srota-āpanna.
Some received the Five Precepts and diligently practiced the Ten Wholesome Deeds.
They took refuge in the Three Jewels.
Observing the six monthly fast days.
And the three annual fasts.
They guided each other, making this the constant practice.
Ānanda asked the Buddha.
"This king and his people,
what past connection did they have with Mùlián?"
The Buddha said.
"In the time of Buddha Wéiwèi.
Mùlián was an upāsaka.
He lived in poverty but upheld the precepts, guarding his mind without transgression.
Gathering flowers in the mountains, he saw a *xūwén* tree.
Just as he was about to climb the tree to pick flowers,
he did not know there was a beehive ahead.
A swarm of several thousand bees, startled, scattered and pursued him.
He then thought to himself.
'If I attain the Way, I shall liberate you all.'
Those who attained the Way today were all the bees of that time."
Once there were five kings.
Their kingdoms bordered each other, and they were close friends who frequently visited one another.
The eldest among them was named Pǔ'ān.
He practiced the Bodhisattva path.
The other four minor kings often engaged in unwholesome conduct.
The great king, taking pity on them,
summoned them to his palace to enjoy themselves together.
They stayed for up to seven days,
day and night until the seven days were completed.
Then the minor kings addressed the great king, saying,
"Our state affairs are many; we request to return home."
The great king escorted them,
and when they reached the road, he spoke to the minor kings:
"Each of you, speak of what brings you joy."
One king replied,
"In the sunny spring of the third month, when trees flourish and bloom, to roam the fields and plains."
Another king answered,
"I wish to always remain a king,
with saddled horses, fine attire, officials, and people surrounding me left and right.
Resplendent and glorious, with bells struck and drums sounded when I come and go, while passersby gaze in admiration."
Yet another king said,
"I wish for my wife and children to be peerless in beauty,
and to enjoy ourselves together, indulging in utmost pleasure and delight."
Another king replied,
"I wish for my parents to always be present,
with friends, brothers, wife, and children gathered around.
Fine clothes and delicious food to satisfy body and mouth,
playing the plain qin in dark robes, enjoying ourselves together."
They all then asked the great king, "What brings you joy?"
The great king answered,
"I rejoice in being free from birth and death, from suffering and affliction, from hunger and thirst, from cold and heat, and in having mastery over existence and cessation."
The four kings said together,
"For such joy, there must be a wise teacher."
The great king replied,
"My teacher is called the Buddha.
He resides nearby at the Qíhuán Monastery."
The kings rejoiced and together went to see the World-Honored One.
The great king addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Now that we have obtained human birth, we are dull and without wisdom, deeply attached to the world.
We take pleasure without knowing sin and merit.
We beseech the Buddha to explain to us disciples the Truth of Suffering."
The Buddha said,
"Listen well, all of you.
I shall explain it to you.
Human life in this world is beset by numerous sufferings.
Briefly stated, there are eight sufferings.
First, the suffering of birth.
When a person dies, the spirit does not know which path it will take.
Before obtaining a place of rebirth, it universally receives an intermediate body.
After up to twenty-one days,
when the parents unite, it comes to receive a womb.
In the first week, it is like thin curds.
In the second week, like thick curds.
In the third week, like solidified butter.
In the fourth week, like a morsel of meat.
In the fifth week, the womb is fully formed, and a skillful wind enters the abdomen,
blowing through the body, opening the six senses.
In the mother's womb, it lies below the living organs and above the digested organs.
When the mother eats a single morsel of hot food,
it scalds the body like boiling water.
When the mother drinks a cup of cold water,
it feels like icy cold cutting through the body.
When the mother is full,
the body is compressed, and the pain is indescribable.
When the mother is hungry,
the abdomen feels empty and upside down, suffering immeasurably.
When the full term arrives and birth is imminent,
the head turns toward the birth canal.
The pain is extreme, as if crushed between two mountains; born and falling onto the grass,
the body is tender and soft, and the grass touching it feels like treading on swords. Suddenly, it loses its voice and cries out loudly.
Is this suffering?"
They all said it is suffering.
Second, the suffering of old age.
Parents nurture and raise one until adulthood.
When hungry, one is extremely hungry; when full, one is extremely full,
without moderation.
Gradually reaching old age, the hair turns white and teeth fall out.
Eyesight becomes dim, hearing becomes unclear.
Vigor departs, decline arrives; skin slackens, face wrinkles.
Every joint aches, walking becomes extremely painful.
Sitting or rising, one groans, sorrowful and distressed.
Consciousness fades, and one soon passes away.
Life dwindles day by day; speaking brings tears, and sitting or rising requires assistance.
Is this suffering?"
They answered, "Truly suffering."
Third, the suffering of sickness.
The body is formed by the combination of earth, water, fire, and wind.
When one element is imbalanced, one hundred and one illnesses arise.
When the four elements are imbalanced, four hundred and four illnesses occur simultaneously.
When the earth element is imbalanced, the whole body aches.
When the water element is imbalanced, the whole body swells.
When the fire element is imbalanced, the whole body feels hot and painful.
When the wind element is imbalanced, the whole body becomes stiff, every joint in pain as if beaten with a rod.
The four elements conflict, hands and feet become useless.
Strength is exhausted, sitting or rising requires assistance.
Mouth is parched, lips cracked, tendons severed, nose broken.
Eyes cannot see colors, ears cannot hear sounds.
Impurities flow out, and one lies upon them.
The heart is filled with distress, and speech is mournful.
Relatives are by one's side, watching day and night without rest.
Delicious food and drink taste bitter when entering the mouth.
Is this suffering?"
They answered, "Truly suffering."
Fourth, the suffering of death.
When a person dies, four hundred and four illnesses occur simultaneously.
The four elements are about to disperse, the soul is unsettled.
At the moment of death, a cutting wind disintegrates the body, causing pain everywhere.
Cold sweat flows out, hands grope in the air.
Family members, inside and outside, gather around.
They weep in sorrow, the pain piercing to the marrow, unbearable.
The wind departs, breath scatters, fire extinguishes, the body turns cold, and the soul leaves.
The body lies stiff, no longer aware.
Within ten days, flesh decays, blood flows, swelling, rotting, and stench become unbearable to approach.
Discarded in the wilderness, birds devour the flesh until only bones remain dry, skulls separated.
Is this suffering?"
They answered, "Truly suffering."
Fifth, the suffering of parting from loved ones.
Within the household, brothers, wife, and children
are deeply attached to one another, yet one day they are torn apart.
Plundered by others, each is scattered—father east, son west, mother south, daughter north, not in one place.
Enslaved by others, each grieves in heart.
Calls from within are cut off, in darkness and obscurity, with no hope of meeting again.
Is this suffering?"
They answered, "Truly suffering."
Sixth, the suffering of not obtaining what is sought.
One uses family wealth to seek office,
hoping for wealth and honor, striving incessantly.
If by chance one obtains it, one is appointed to a remote post.
Not long after, one greedily takes the people's possessions.
When accused by others, one day trouble arises.
Carted in a prison wagon, sorrow and suffering are immeasurable, not knowing whether one will live or die, or when.
Is this suffering?"
They answered, "Truly suffering."
Seventh, the suffering of encountering the hated.
People in this shallow world, dwelling in desire and love, quarrel over trivial matters.
Mutual killing leads to great enmity.
Each avoids the other, hiding with no place to go.
Each sharpens knives and arrows, carries bows and staffs.
Meeting on a narrow path, they draw bows and set arrows.
Blades face each other, not knowing who will prevail.
At that moment, fear is immeasurable.
Is this suffering?"
They answered, "Truly suffering."
Eighth, the suffering of sorrow, grief, and distress.
Human life in this world—
the longest is a hundred years, the shortest ends in the womb, all are subject to injury.
Even if one lives a hundred years, nights consume half, leaving
fifty years.
Drunkenness and illness make it hard to live as a human.
In youth, foolish and ignorant, for fifteen years one knows no etiquette.
Past eighty years old, aged and dull, without wisdom.
Deaf ears, dim eyes, no longer following rules.
When the world is about to fall into chaos, drought, fire, and heavy frost cause crops to fail.
Within the household, many illnesses and pains arise.
In livelihood, losses are frequent; the government imposes numerous levies, imprisonment in jail with no known release date.
Brothers and sons travel far and have not returned.
The home is poor and cold, without clothes or food.
Neighbors and villages cannot perform communal rites.
Family members die, with no means for burial.
In spring planting, there are no plows or oxen.
On festive days when all gather, one should rejoice, yet all face each other in sorrow.
Is this suffering?"
They answered, "Truly suffering."
At that time, the five kings and the assembled ministers, numbering tens of thousands,
hearing the explanation of the Truth of Suffering, opened their minds and attained understanding.
They immediately attained the fruit of Stream-Entry.
Now looking upon their palaces, they saw them as filthy latrines, with nothing enjoyable.
They then abdicated their thrones to their younger brothers and left home to follow the path,
cultivating all merits tirelessly day by day.
In the country of Duōmèi,
there was a Brahmin king.
He abandoned his royal duties and engaged in many heterodox practices.
One day, the king suddenly conceived a virtuous intention to perform a great act of almsgiving.
Following the Brahmin method,
he amassed treasures into a mountain-like pile, allowing those who came to beg to take as they wished.
Each person could take one handful with their hand, and after several days, the pile remained undiminished.
The Buddha, knowing that this king possessed past merit and was ready for salvation,
transformed into a Brahmin ascetic
and went to his country.
The king came out to meet him.
After greeting and inquiring about his well-being, he said,
"What do you seek? Do not hesitate." The Brahmin ascetic replied,
"I have come from afar to beg for precious jewels to build a house."
The king said, "Excellent.
Take one handful yourself."
The Brahmin ascetic took one handful and walked away.
After seven steps, he returned and placed it back in its original spot.
The king asked,
"Why did you not take it?"
The Brahmin ascetic replied,
"This is only enough to build a small hut.
Moreover, I must also take a wife, and it is still insufficient, so I did not take it."
The king said,
"Take three handfuls more."
The Brahmin ascetic then took them.
After walking seven steps, he again returned and placed them back.
The king asked the Brahmin ascetic,
"Why have you done this again?"
He replied,
"This is enough to take a wife,
but there is still no land, servants, cattle, or horses.
Considering this, it remains insufficient.
Therefore, I have given up the idea."
The king said,
"Take seven handfuls more."
The Brahmin ascetic then took them.
After walking seven steps, he again returned and placed them back.
The king said,
"What is the reason this time?"
The Brahmin ascetic replied,
"If I have sons and daughters,
they will need to marry, with expenses for both auspicious and inauspicious occasions.
Considering this, it is still insufficient, so I did not take it."
The king said,
"Take all the piled treasures; I offer them to you."
The Brahmin ascetic accepted them but then abandoned them and left.
The king was greatly astonished.
He pressed for an explanation.
The Brahmin ascetic replied,
"Originally, I came begging to sustain my livelihood.
But upon deep reflection, I realized that human life is brief in this world.
All things are impermanent, difficult to preserve even for a day.
Due to heavy karmic ties, sorrow and suffering deepen daily; amassing treasures like a mountain benefits oneself not at all.
Greedy desires and scheming are but futile toil.
It is better to relinquish such intentions and seek the path of non-action.
Therefore, I did not take them."
The king's mind opened with understanding.
He vowed to follow the enlightened teaching.
Thereupon, the Brahmin ascetic
revealed the Buddha's radiant form, rising into the air,
and spoke a verse:
The king saw
the Buddha's light shining afar, illuminating heaven and earth.
Hearing this verse, he leaped for joy.
The king and his ministers then received the Five Precepts
and attained the fruit of Stream-enterer.
There was a king
named Módá.
He led an army on a campaign, conscripting millions of people.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had attained Arhatship.
He entered the country to beg for alms
but was captured and brought before the king's palace.
The king ordered him to tend the royal horses.
After toiling for seven days,
the king came to inspect.
The bhikṣu, seeing the king,
lightly rose, flew up, and hovered in the air, displaying his spiritual power.
The king became terrified, kowtowed, and repented his error, saying,
"I am truly foolish and ignorant, unable to distinguish truth from falsehood.
I will investigate both inside and outside to find out who made this holy man do such a thing.
Now, I shall punish and execute them."
The bhikṣu told the king,
"It is not the fault of the king or the people.
In my past life, while practicing the path, I often served my teacher.
At that time, I prepared a drink for my teacher.
My teacher said to me,
'First wash your hands, then you may drink.'
In my foolish mind, I thought,
'My teacher does not tend royal horses either.
Why did he not wash his hands beforehand?'
My teacher then said to me,
'You now think this is trivial, but later the consequences will be heavy. What then?'
Hearing these words, I became sorrowful.
The teacher, knowing my thoughts,
then thought,
'I will soon attain Nirvāṇa.
Why cause distress to others?'
That very night, at the third watch,
the teacher entered Parinirvāṇa.
Through long ages, each underwent birth and death anew.
Now, because of that, I am receiving my past retribution,
tending horses for seven days.
Indeed, good and evil deeds invariably bring retribution or blessing, like a shadow following the body."
The king, hearing the bhikṣu speak of sin and blessing,
understood with joy and begged to submit himself to the holy man.
The bhikṣu told him,
"You should submit yourself to the Buddha.
The Buddha is the teacher of the Three Realms."
The king and the people of the country
all followed the bhikṣu out to where the Buddha was.
They bowed their heads in reverence and received the Five Precepts.
Becoming upāsakas,
the Buddha then manifested for the king and the people
his majestic form and radiant spiritual light, illuminating heaven and earth.
He further expounded on impermanence, suffering, and emptiness.
At that time, the king attained the fruit of Stream-enterer.
The people of the country all received the Five Precepts and Ten Virtues.
They submitted to the Three Jewels, observing monthly fasting and precepts
as a constant practice.
At that time, there was a king
named Jiàntuó.
He served Brahmins who lived in the mountains.
They grew many fruit trees, and woodcutters damaged the trees.
The Brahmins
brought them before the king, reporting their misconduct,
saying they had ruined the fruit trees and requesting the king to punish and execute them. The king, revering the Brahmins,
had them executed.
Not long after,
an ox ate someone's rice.
Its owner then beat the ox, breaking one of its horns.
Blood covered its face, and the pain was unbearable.
The ox went straight to the king and said,
"I was indeed at fault for eating a little of the man's rice.
Now he has beaten me and broken my horn."
The king understood the speech of birds and beasts.
He told the ox,
"I shall punish and execute him for you."
The ox said,
"Even if you kill this man, it will not stop my pain.
Just instruct him not to harm others in the future."
The king was deeply moved and reflected,
"I serve the Brahmins,
yet over fruit trees, I had people killed.
I am not as good as this ox."
He then summoned the Brahmins and asked,
"What blessings come from following this path?"
The Brahmins replied,
"One can avert disasters, attract blessings, and attain wealth, honor, and longevity."
The king asked further,
"Can one escape birth and death?"
They replied,
"One cannot avoid birth and death."
The king went to where the Buddha was.
Prostrating himself with five limbs touching the ground, he paid homage to the Buddha and said,
"I have heard that the Buddha's path is supreme,
teaching and transforming the world, saving countless beings.
I wish to receive the Dharma teachings to reform myself."
The Buddha then bestowed upon the king the Five Precepts and Ten Virtues.
He explained that all beings in heaven, earth, and among humans—none are born without dying.
Giving alms and upholding precepts bring blessings in the present life.
Those who practice forbearance, diligence, and cultivate wisdom with their minds—their virtue is immeasurable.
In future lives, they may be reborn in heaven or become Cakravartin kings.
They may attain the path of non-action and liberation from the world."
The Buddha manifested his majestic form and radiant spiritual light.
The king rejoiced and understood.
He attained the fruit of Stream-enterer.
The ox died seven days later,
and was reborn in heaven.
There was a king of Fūyán country.
His name was Pǔdá.
He personally served the Buddha's Dharma, never deviating or being unjust.
He always had compassion.
The ignorant people in his country did not know of the Three Jewels.
Whenever he observed the precepts, he would ascend a high place to look out.
Upon returning, he would always bow his head and face to the ground in prostration as a gesture of respect.
The ministers and people in the country found the king's behavior strange.
They discussed among themselves, saying:
"The king occupies the position of honor over ten thousand people.
Those near and far respect and submit to him; when he ascends, they call for people to follow.
What request or desire does he have that he would demean his dignity, placing his head and face on the ground?"
The ministers wished to remonstrate but did not dare.
Together with several thousand officials and people, they left the palace, but not far out, they saw a monk.
The king descended from his carriage, removed his canopy, and stopped.
His entourage paid respects to the monk.
He then followed the monk and returned.
He arranged for a meal, and thus the journey did not proceed.
The ministers remonstrated, saying:
"Great King, you are of the utmost honor.
Why should you, on the road, bow your head and face to the ground for this begging monk?
In all the world, the most honorable thing is the head and face.
Moreover, as the king of a country, you are not the same as others."
The king ordered his ministers:
"Find a dead person's head and the heads of six kinds of livestock."
The ministers searched everywhere and only obtained them after many days.
The king said:
"Sell them in the market."
The ministers sold them.
The heads of oxen, horses, pigs, and sheep were all sold.
But the human head was not sold.
The king said:
"Sell it at a high or low price; if it still does not sell,
give it to beggars." Thus, after many days, it still did not sell.
Beggars would not take it; the heads all became swollen and foul-smelling.
The king then became greatly angry.
He said to his ministers:
"You said
that a human head is most honorable and must not be demeaned.
Now, why is it that no beggar will take a human head?"
He then ordered the carriage prepared and went out to the open wilderness, intending to ask something.
The ministers, trembling with fear, went out to outside the city walls.
He told the ministers:
"Do you recognize the young boy who always held the canopy during my late father's time?"
The ministers replied: "We truly recognize him."
The king said:
"Where is this boy now?"
They replied:
"He died seventeen years ago."
The king said:
"What was this boy's character like, good or evil?"
They replied:
"We often saw him serving the late king.
He observed the precepts respectfully and solemnly, was sincere and trustworthy, guarded himself, and did not speak of improper things."
The king told the ministers:
"If you now saw the clothes this boy wore during his lifetime,
would you recognize them?"
The ministers replied:
"Although it has been a long time, we would still recognize them."
The king had someone bring the clothes of the deceased boy.
He said:
"Are these they?"
The ministers replied: "Yes."
The king said:
"If you now saw the boy's body, would you recognize it?"
The ministers were silent for a long while.
They replied:
"We fear our own obscurity and ignorance; suddenly seeing it, we might not distinguish it."
The monk they had seen before arrived.
The king was greatly delighted.
He also said to the monk: "I had the heads sold, but beggars would not take them.
Now I wish to show the beginning and end of this matter.
It is fortunate that we have met.
I wish you to enlighten us."
The monk then explained to the ministers:
"The king was originally the young boy who held the canopy during the late king's time.
He always followed the late king.
He observed the precepts, practiced the true Dharma, purified his mind, guarded his thoughts, and did not commit any evils.
Afterwards, when he passed away, he was reborn as a prince.
Now he has attained honor and nobility, all due to his past practice of observing the precepts."
All the ministers, great and small, unanimously said:
"We are fortunate to have encountered and seen the monk.
We beg you, pity our ignorant and dim minds, and allow us to become your disciples."
The monk told the officials and people:
"I have a great teacher.
You should follow him and receive instruction."
The officials replied:
"We wish to devote our entire lives to receiving the Dharma's words."
The monk said:
"My teacher's name is Buddha.
His body can fly; there is light on his head.
He can divide his body and scatter it, transforming in ten thousand ways.
He walks alone in the Three Realms, with none who can equal him.
His disciples are pure and clean, all being śramaṇas.
His teachings liberate without fail."
The ministers then asked the monk:
"Can we see the Buddha?
How far is he from here?"
The monk replied:
"Very well.
I shall inform the World-Honored One.
It is over six thousand lǐ away."
The monk then flew to Śrāvastī.
He fully reported to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Tomorrow I shall go to Fūyán country. When I arrive, I will manifest my majestic spiritual power."
The king and his ministers, holding flowers and incense, went out of the city to welcome the Buddha.
Seeing the Buddha's majestic spiritual power, they felt both joy and fear, prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, bowing their heads in respect.
They addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We have troubled the World-Honored One,
along with the assembly of monks, to come far to this land."
The king wholeheartedly provided offerings,
personally serving and pouring water for washing.
After the dedication of merits was completed,
the Buddha smiled, and light of five colors issued from his mouth.
Ānanda said:
"The Buddha does not smile without reason."
He replied:
"In the time of the Buddha Mahāvipaśyin,
the king was the son of a great family.
His father made offerings to the Three Jewels.
The father ordered the son to pass the incense.
At that time, there was a servant
who in his mind looked down upon him and did not give him the incense.
Karmic retribution responds accordingly; he temporarily received the retribution of servitude.
But because he served the Dharma without fail, he now has become a king.
If I attain the Way, I shall liberate this person."
Understanding the beginning and end of the matter, he immediately attained the fruit of Stream-enterer.
The people of the country
all received the Five Precepts and practiced the Ten Wholesome Deeds.
Long ago, King Píngshā
had a chief minister
who committed an offense and was exiled to the Southern Mountains, a thousand li from the kingdom.
Since ancient times, no one there had cultivated the five grains.
