When the chief minister arrived,
springs flowed freely and the five grains flourished abundantly.
People from all directions and various kingdoms who suffered from hunger and cold came to this place.
Within a few years, three to four thousand households had gathered.
Newcomers were given fields and land so they could make a living.
Among them, the elders and senior leaders of old
discussed together that the land lacked a ruler.
Just as a body lacks a head, they went together to the chief minister’s place
and raised him up as king.
The chief minister replied to the elders,
"If you make me king,
it must be according to the laws of the kings of other kingdoms.
There must be ministers on the left and right, civil and military generals and officers.
There must be court tributes from above and below, selection of women to open the palace, and taxes of grain and silk, all according to the people’s customs."
The various elders said,
"So be it, we accept your command.
Everything will follow the king’s law."
Thus he was established as king.
He appointed his ministers,
civil and military officials high and low, and levied the people.
They built walls, constructed dwellings, palaces, towers, and pavilions.
The people, suffering bitterly, could no longer endure it.
They all conceived thoughts and plotted against the king.
The treacherous ministers took the king out hunting.
Thirty or forty li from the city,
in the wild marshes, they sought to kill the king.
The king asked those around him,
"Why do you kill me?"
They all said,
"The people admired prosperity and happiness and served the king with ritual.
Now the people are distressed and think of rebellion, ruining their homes to plot against the state."
The king told them,
"You yourselves did this; it was not my original doing.
If you wrongfully kill me, the spirits and deities will know.
Allow me to utter one vow before I die, and I will have no regret."
Immediately he vowed,
"I originally opened the wasteland, brought forth the soil, and nourished the people.
All who came here were given life, wealth, and happiness without limit.
You yourselves raised me as king.
Following the pattern of other kingdoms, you together created this, and now you turn to kill me.
I truly have done no evil to these people.
If I die, may I become a rākṣasa.
May I return into my former body and repay this grievance."
Thereupon they strangled him, discarded the corpse, and left.
Three days later, the king’s spirit returned into his body.
He named himself Āluóbō.
He rose and entered the palace,
killing the new king along with the rear palace ladies, attendants, and treacherous ministers.
He wished to kill all the people.
The three elders of the kingdom came with grass ropes binding themselves.
They presented themselves to the rākṣasa and confessed,
"This was the doing of treacherous ministers.
It was not something the common people could have known.
We beg for your forgiveness and wish you to return and govern the kingdom."
He said, "I am a rākṣasa.
When dealing with humans, eating and drinking, I must have human flesh."
The rākṣasa was fierce by nature, wrathful and heedless of difficulty.
The three elders said,
"The kingdom is what the king permits, so it should be as before.
For your food and drink needs, we will arrange it in turns."
The elders of the kingdom together issued a proclamation to the people:
"From now on, take turns.
Each household shall give one small child.
They shall be used as food while alive."
Thus the rākṣasa king ate from three to four thousand households.
There was exactly one household that were disciples of the Buddha.
The family diligently upheld the Buddha’s five precepts.
The virtuous ones, young and old, were distressed and wept.
From afar, they bowed toward Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, paying homage to the Buddha.
They repented and blamed themselves.
The Buddha, with his divine eye, saw their hardship.
He then said to himself,
"Through this child, I shall deliver countless people."
He alone flew to the rākṣasa’s gate.
Manifesting his radiant form, he illuminated the palace interior.
The rākṣasa, seeing the light, suspected it was a stranger.
He came out, saw the Buddha, and immediately conceived a malicious thought.
He wished to advance and bite the Buddha, but the light pierced his eyes.
He lifted mountains and spewed fire, but all turned to dust.
After a long time, exhausted, he then submitted and was transformed.
He invited the Buddha to enter and sit, bowed his head and face in homage.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to him; he listened with single-minded attention.
He then received the five precepts and became an upāsaka.
The village officer came to催促 the food, seized the child, and brought him back.
The family wailed and cried, following along the road.
Countless onlookers felt sorrow for them.
The officer held the child, lifted the food, and placed it before the rākṣasa.
The rākṣasa lifted the child with his hand.
Kneeling upright, he addressed the Buddha,
"The people of the kingdom take turns offering children as food.
Now that I have received the Buddha’s five precepts, I can no longer eat humans.
I ask to give this child as an offering to the Buddha,
to serve the Buddha."
The Buddha accepted him.
He preached the Dharma and uttered a blessing.
The rākṣasa rejoiced and attained the path of srotāpanna.
The Buddha placed the child in his alms bowl.
Carrying it out of the palace gate, he returned him to his parents.
And told them,
"Quickly raise the child; do not grieve anymore."
The people, seeing the Buddha, were all astonished.
"What kind of deity is this? What merit did this child have
that he alone was saved?
The rākṣasa’s food was taken and returned to his parents."
The Buddha then spoke a verse:
"Those who see the Buddha’s luminous form all become disciples of the Buddha."
Hearing the verse, they rejoiced and all attained the trace of the path.
In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there were two merchants.
One of them thought to himself:
"The Buddha's body is sixteen feet tall, with a radiant purple-gold complexion.
On his head is a fleshy protuberance, and from his neck and back emanates a brilliant light—so majestic it is beyond words.
The Buddha is like an emperor, and the monks are like loyal ministers.
The Buddha expounds the clear Dharma, and the monks recite and proclaim it. This shows the king's wisdom.
I know the Buddha is worthy of reverence."
The Buddha, aware of his thoughts, gazed intently at him.
That man's heart was filled with joy, as if he had obtained a treasure.
The other one thought:
"The Buddha is like an ox, and his disciples are like a cart.
That ox pulls the cart east, west, north, and south.
The Buddha is just the same."
The Buddha knew that he had evil thoughts and would surely suffer misfortune, and he felt sorrowful pity for him.
That man harbored malice, and the two of them departed together.
After traveling thirty li, they reached a pavilion to stay overnight and bought wine to drink.
They argued and quarreled over trivial matters.
The one with good thoughts—
the Four Heavenly Kings dispatched benevolent spirits to protect him.
The one with poisonous thoughts—
the ghosts and spirits of Mount Tài caused the wine to enter his belly,
as if his body were burning with fire.
He went out of the pavilion, lay down exposed, tossed and turned, and fell into a wagon rut.
In the morning, a merchant's convoy of five hundred carts passed over him.
His companion saw this and said:
"Now I am in a dire situation.
If I return to the country, I will be suspected of taking his belongings and fleeing, which would be called unrighteous."
So he abandoned his possessions and left alone.
Traveling far and wide, he went tens of thousands of li away from Śrāvastī.
There was a kingdom.
The king had died without an heir.
A prophetic text stated:
"In the central kingdom, there is a humble man who shall become king of this land."
The officials deliberated and said:
"A kingdom without a ruler is like a body without a head.
It cannot long endure."
The former king had a horse that always paid respects to the king.
If someone were fit to be king, the horse would surely kneel.
They all said, "Excellent!"
Immediately, they prepared a grand carriage and placed the king's seal and ribbon on the carriage.
People and horses filled the road, and all who watched could not help but shed tears.
At that time, that merchant also came out to watch.
The Grand Astrologer of the kingdom said:
"Above him is a canopy of yellow clouds—this is the aura of a king."
The divine horse went straight forward, knelt, and licked his feet.
The ministers rejoiced, bathed him with fragrant water,
and proclaimed him king of the country.
All acknowledged him as their ruler.
The king said:
"I am originally a merchant.
I have no virtue toward the people and am not fit for this heavenly position."
The officials said:
"Heaven bestows it upon the virtuous; the divine horse knelt.
Thereupon, he took residence in the royal palace.
He heard and decided on state affairs.
Deep in thought, he reflected:
"I have no slight virtue; how did I obtain this?
It must be due to the Buddha's grace that this has come to pass."
In the morning, seated on the throne, he praised the Buddha's supreme holiness.
Leading all the officials of the land toward Śrāvastī,
he bowed and said:
"This humble man, moistened by the World-Honored One's grace, has become a ruler.
In this land, through generations, they have not known of the Buddha.
The common texts also have no record of him.
I wish to use the great illumination to open the ears and eyes of the people of this country.
Tomorrow, I hope that you, together with the Arhats and the holy assembly,
will kindly consider staying here for three months."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Command all the bhikṣus:
Tomorrow, that king has invited us.
All should follow, manifesting transformations to display divine dignity and virtue,
so that all the people of that country may witness it."
The devas, hearing that the Buddha would go there to teach,
led one another in procession, making music and singing praises of his virtue.
Precious canopies, banners, and flowers descended in profusion, their radiant colors dazzling the eyes.
The Buddha and the Arhats all sat in the main hall.
The king personally served them until the meal was finished.
Then, taking a small seat, he sat before the Buddha.
The Buddha expounded the Dharma extensively.
The king said:
"I was originally a humble man.
I had no joyful virtue in my karma; how did I obtain this?"
The Buddha told the king:
"In the past, when that king offered food to the Buddha,
the king thought to himself:
'The Buddha's mind is like a king's,
and the monks are like ministers.'
The king planted this seed, and now he reaps the fruit.
That other man said:
'The Buddha is like an ox, and the disciples are like a cart.'
That man himself planted the seed of being run over by a cart.
Now he is in Mount Tài, being crushed by a fiery cart.
He himself reaps the fruit of his actions.
It is not due to the king's valor that this came about.
Doing good, fortune follows; committing evil, calamity pursues.
Like an echo responding to a sound, good and evil are like the sound itself.
It is not bestowed by devas, dragons, or spirits,
nor is it the doing of ancestors.
It is the mind that creates,
and the body and speech that accomplish."
The Buddha then spoke a verse:
The World-Honored One further told the king:
"Among the evils and offenses, the gravest are five.
Being unfilial, disloyal, killing relatives, killing the ruler, destroying families, and throwing the country into chaos—
this is the first grave offense.
The conduct of an Arhat attains the emptiness, wishlessness, and signless samādhis.
They share the Buddha's intent to save and aid all beings.
Yet foolishly harming them—
this is the second grave offense.
The Buddha, in whom all offenses have ended and glorious blessings have come to fruition,
with his marks and powers, guides all beings.
His compassion, loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, and equanimity surpass even a loving mother's heart.
Yet foolishly slandering him with evil—this is the third grave offense.
Pure monks, with tranquil minds and lofty conduct,
embrace the sūtras and Dharma, aiding the Buddha in transforming the foolish.
The Buddhas succeed one another; all beings attain liberation through the Saṅgha.
Slanderous and deceitful strife leads to discord.
Because of discord, the true Dharma is destroyed.
When the true Dharma is destroyed, the people run wild.
When the people run wild, the three evil paths flourish.
Harassing the community of bhikṣus—
this is the fourth grave offense.
The Buddha's revered temples, precious objects, water, and land—
beings offer them with sincere hearts to the Three Jewels.
Foolish people may destroy or steal them—
this is the fifth grave offense.
Those who commit these five offenses have no means of appeal for their sins.
It is called killing oneself, destroying one's own clan, and throwing oneself into the fires of Mount Tài.
The gravity of these five offenses is heavier than Mount Sumeru; be careful not to commit them."
When the Buddha finished speaking the sūtra,
the king and all his ministers attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
They received the Five Precepts and became pure lay devotees.
Among the citizens, some became monks,
and those who upheld the precepts became pure lay devotees.
Thereupon, they made the Five Precepts and Ten Good Deeds the state's governance.
The devas protected and aided them, and the country prospered.
King Prasenajit,
having planted roots of virtue in past lives, had blessings naturally respond.
In his rear garden, a sugarcane tree grew naturally,
flowing with sweet juice day and night without cease.
Also, a stalk of rice grew,
bearing hundreds of ears; taking from it was endless.
The king enjoyed this fortune, eating without restraint.
His body became heavy and fat, breathing with great difficulty, unable to turn over.
He went to where the Buddha was, bowed humbly,
and sat to one side.
The Buddha then spoke a verse:
The king rejoiced and leaped with joy.
He rose from his seat, bid farewell to the Buddha, and returned to the palace.
He commanded the food servers: "Before I eat,
first recite this verse as a constant practice."
The king gradually reduced his food intake,
his body became lighter,
and he moved about without trouble.
King Pòsīnì.
While sleeping at night, he had ten kinds of dreams.
First, a small tree blossomed.
Second, he saw a small tree bearing fruit.
Third, he saw a cow seeking milk from her calf.
Fourth, he saw a person cutting up a sheep and eating it as he followed.
Fifth, he saw ten cauldrons arranged in layers, with the top cauldron boiling over and pouring into the bottom cauldron.
Sixth, he saw a horse with two heads on one body eating wheat.
Seventh, he saw blood flowing to form a channel.
Eighth, he saw clear water, pure at the edges but turbid in the center.
Ninth, he saw a dog urinating in a golden vessel.
Tenth, he saw four oxen coming from the four directions to butt heads, then scattering and returning.
The king was terrified, and the hairs on his body stood on end.
Immediately upon waking from sleep, he thought to himself:
"Am I about to die and lose this kingship?"
He then went to ask the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Great King, do not harbor terror.
It is not because of these dreams that you will lose your kingship.
The dream of a small tree blossoming means:
In the future, beings will act with unrighteous desires.
They will constantly harbor greed and jealousy, corresponding to unrighteous dharmas.
At that time, people will not be filial to their parents.
They will not serve śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
Yet they will receive offerings.
It is like those who are filial to their parents and make offerings to śramaṇas today.
The small tree bearing fruit means:
In the future, beings will act with unrighteous desires.
They will constantly harbor greed and jealousy, corresponding to unrighteous dharmas.
At that time, people will marry and, not long after,
return to their parents' home carrying a child, feeling no shame.
The cow seeking milk from her calf means:
In the future, beings will act with unrighteous desires.
They will constantly harbor greed and jealousy, corresponding to unrighteous dharmas.
Mothers will guard the door while their daughters engage in illicit relations to sustain themselves.
The person cutting up a sheep and eating it as he follows means:
In the future, beings will act with unrighteous desires.
They will constantly harbor greed and jealousy, corresponding to unrighteous dharmas.
They will use their own wealth and treasures to engage in affairs with outsiders.
The dream of ten cauldrons arranged in layers, with the top cauldron boiling over and pouring into the bottom cauldron, means:
In the future, beings will act with unrighteous desires.
They will correspond to unrighteous dharmas.
Children will say to their parents:
'Quickly leave this home and go to the mountains, wilderness, or marshes.
I wish to live in this village.'
The horse with two heads on one body eating wheat means:
In the future, beings will act with unrighteous desires.
They will constantly harbor greed and jealousy, corresponding to unrighteous dharmas.
Some, relying on the king, will plunder brāhmaṇas and elders;
or, relying on brāhmaṇas and elders, will plunder the king's treasury.
The dream of blood flowing to form a channel means:
In the future, there will be kings who are dissatisfied with their own realms.
They will gather the fourfold army to invade and seize others' territories.
They will be uncontrollable and not follow the teachings of the Dharma.
At that time, many people will die.
The dream of clear water, pure at the edges but turbid in the center, means:
In the future, beings will act with unrighteous desires.
They will constantly harbor greed and jealousy, corresponding to unrighteous dharmas.
Beings in the central kingdom will delight in conflict and disorder,
while people in the borderlands will have no disputes or lawsuits.
The dream of a dog urinating in a golden vessel means:
In the future, beings will act with unrighteous desires.
They will constantly harbor greed and jealousy, corresponding to unrighteous dharmas.
The Dharma treasures I have accumulated through arduous efforts over three asaṃkhyeya kalpas
will all be slandered.
They will strike my śrāvakas with knives, sticks, tiles, and stones,
saying, 'These śramaṇas teach unrighteous dharmas.
They are fond of composing songs and praises.'
The dream of four oxen coming from the four directions to butt heads, then scattering and returning, means:
In the future, beings will act with unrighteous desires.
They will constantly harbor greed and jealousy, corresponding to unrighteous dharmas.
At that time, great clouds will arise from the four directions,
with thunder, lightning, and peals, but they will disperse without rain.
These are the ten dreams and their corresponding meanings.
Great King, these ten dreams
have these ten correspondences.
For this reason, the king should not harbor terror, nor will he die or lose his kingship.
All these are signs of the future Dharma in the degenerate age.
Great King, you should learn thus."
The king was greatly delighted.
King Pòsīnì
had a daughter named Pótuó who passed away.
He loved her dearly.
He had never taken his eyes off her.
After the funeral and burial were completed,
he personally visited the Tathāgata, bowed with his head at the feet, and sat to one side.
The Buddha said:
"Why is the king's clothing dusty and his sorrow so great?"
The king said:
"I had a daughter who just passed away; I loved her dearly.
After her funeral, I wished to use elephants to redeem her life,
even chariots, horses, and hidden treasures.
Sorrow, worry, and suffering all arise from affection and love.
The reason is this:
In ancient times, great king,
in this city of Shèwèi,
there was a person whose daughter passed away.
Because of his love for his daughter, he never took his eyes off her.
He became confused and unaware,
wandering everywhere and asking people:
'Who has seen my daughter?'
Great King, you should know by this example
that sorrow, worry, and suffering all arise from affection and love.
Great King, do not harbor sorrow.
All affection and love must eventually separate.
All that is born must inevitably decay.
Thus, he extensively expounded the Dharma.
The king received the teaching and departed.
At that time in the city of Shèwèi,
there was a great Brahmin household named Yēruòdá.
He was extremely wealthy and possessed abundant treasures.
He had a maidservant named Huángtóu,
who was often assigned to guard the Mòluó garden.
This maidservant was constantly sorrowful, thinking to herself,
"When will I ever be freed from being a maidservant?"
One morning, after the maidservant had eaten,
she took her portion of dried rice and went to the garden.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the city to beg for alms.
From afar, the maidservant Huángtóu saw the Tathāgata.
She thought to herself,
"I should now offer this rice to that ascetic.
Perhaps I can thereby escape this servitude."
She then presented the rice as an offering to the Buddha.
The World-Honored One, out of compassion, accepted it and returned to the monastery.
The maidservant Huángtóu then proceeded to enter the Mòluó garden.
King Pòsīnì,
with his fourfold army arrayed in splendor, went out hunting.
His attendants scattered, chasing herds of deer.
The weather was extremely hot, and from afar he saw the Mòlì garden.
He turned his chariot and went on foot into the garden.
Huángtóu saw King Pòsīnì approaching from a distance.
His gait and demeanor were not those of an ordinary person.
She went forward to greet him, saying,
"Welcome, great one. Please sit here."
She then removed one of her garments and spread it for the king to sit on.
Huángtóu asked,
"Might you need water to wash your feet?"
The king said, "Very well."
She then fetched water for the king
and washed his feet for him.
She asked again,
"Would you like to wash your face?"
She then brought more water for the king to wash his face.
She asked further,
"Would you like a drink?"
She then went to the pond, washed her hands again,
took a fine lotus leaf, filled it with water, and offered it to the king.
She asked once more,
"Might you wish to rest lying down?"
She then removed another garment and spread it for the king.
Seeing the king lying down, she knelt before him
and massaged his feet and other limbs,
alleviating the king's fatigue.
Huángtóu's body was like that of a heavenly being, delicate, soft, and exquisite.
The king, feeling her gentle touch,
thought to himself,
"Never before have I seen a woman so intelligent.
She does things without being instructed."
The king then asked,
"Whose daughter are you?"
She replied,
"I am a maidservant of Yēruòdá's household.
I was assigned to guard this garden."
As they were speaking,
the king's ministers,
following the tracks of the king's chariot, arrived at the garden.
They knelt and bowed at the king's feet, then stood to one side.
The king commanded one of them,
"Summon the Brahmin Yēruòdá here."
The Brahmin came to where the king was.
The king asked,
"Is this woman your maidservant?"
He replied, "Yes."
The king said,
"I now wish to take her as my wife.
What is your opinion?"
He replied,
"This is a maidservant. How can she be a wife?"
The king said,
"Do not worry.
Just state her price."
The Brahmin said,
"If we are to discuss her price,
it would be a hundred thousand taels of gold.
But how could I accept payment from the king?
I now offer her to you."
The king said,
"No.
I am taking her as my wife.
How can I not pay the price?"
He then took out a hundred thousand taels of gold
and gave it to the Brahmin.
He then welcomed her into his carriage and brought her into the palace,
with his ministers guarding and following.
Because she came from the Mòlì garden, she was henceforth named Lady Mòlì.
The king loved and respected her greatly.
On another occasion later,
the king, among five hundred women,
established her as his chief consort.
While in the high palace, she thought to herself,
"By what karmic cause and condition was I freed from being a maidservant and now enjoy such happiness?"
She further thought,
"It must be because I previously offered the portion of dried rice mixed with honey to the ascetic.
Because of this cause and condition, I am now freed from servitude
and enjoy such happiness."
In ancient times, there was a Buddha named Shǐwú.
At that time, there was a king named Hàoxìn,
who delighted in the Buddha's teachings and never tired of gazing upon the Buddha.
He planted a Níjùlèi tree
and beneath it spread a sandalwood seat for the Buddha.
The Buddha sat upon it,
and King Hàoxìn listened to the sutras.
After the Buddha's parinirvāṇa,
the king, no longer able to see the Buddha,
then called the Níjùlèi tree the Buddha Tree.
Seeing it was like seeing the Buddha.
He went daily to sit beneath the tree,
and at the place where he always sat, he contemplated and heard the teachings and precepts.
The king had a maidservant named Jūlù,
who constantly attended by the king's side.
The queen, out of jealousy, hired a Brahmin to cast a spell to kill the Buddha Tree.
That Brahmin,
on the seventh night of the fourth month, took the brain of a great poisonous snake from the southern mountains and smeared it on the tree.
The tree immediately withered and died.
The king then wept bitterly, unable to control himself.
On the eighth night of the fourth month, at midnight when the bright star appeared, he took five-colored fragrant water, gathered flowers, and used them to bathe the tree.
It then revived and grew again.
The king then made a vow, saying,
"May all Buddhas of the ten directions be born on this day,
attain enlightenment on this day,
and enter parinirvāṇa also on this day."
From that time onward, whenever Buddhas arose in the world,
it was on this day.
Therefore, the eighth day of the fourth month is used for bathing the Buddha.
The physician king Qíyù
invited the Buddha and the saṅgha,
excluding only Pántè.
Pántè, throughout the fourth month,
recited the name 'broom' but could never succeed.
The Tathāgata and the saṅgha went to sit in Qíyù's house.
When pure water was offered, the Tathāgata did not accept it.
Qíyù addressed the Buddha,
"I do not understand for what reason the Tathāgata does not accept the water."
The Buddha told Qíyù,
"In this assembly, there is no bhikṣu Pántè.
Therefore, I do not accept it."
Qíyù said to the Buddha,
"This Pántè is foolish and dull.
Even cowherds and shepherds surpass him."
The Buddha told Qíyù,
"If you do not invite Pántè, I will not accept the pure water."
Then Qíyù, following the Buddha's instruction, immediately sent someone to summon Pántè.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"Give the bowl to Pántè.
Have him not rise from his seat but pass it to me from afar."
Qíyù, witnessing this supernatural power, then regretted and blamed himself,
exclaiming, "Alas! What a great mistake to slander and insult a sage!
Today I realize I have committed a grave verbal transgression."
He then developed a reverent mind toward the bhikṣu Pántè,
surpassing even that toward the five hundred monks.
The World-Honored One extensively explained:
In a past life, Qíyù was a horse trader who traveled about buying and selling.
Once, he drove a thousand horses to another country.
On the way, one of the horses gave birth to a foal.
He gave the foal to someone and proceeded to the other country.
He met with the king of that country.
The king said to the horse trader,
"Sir, these thousand horses are all ordinary horses.
One horse whinnied mournfully; its sound was unusual. It must have given birth to a foal.
When that foal grows up, its value will equal a thousand horses.
If you obtain this foal, I will buy all the horses. If not, there is no need."
The horse trader went back to where he had given away the foal.
The foal, not yet ten days old, could already speak human language.
It said to its owner,
"If the horse trader comes seeking me,
if he offers five hundred horses, you may give me to him."
The horse trader sought to redeem it with one ordinary horse.
That person replied,
"I did not force you to give it to me.
I have worked hard to raise and keep it alive.
If you now want it,
redeem it with five hundred horses, and I will return it to you."
He then agreed.
Previously, the horse foal was despised and considered worthless;
now Pántè was left behind.
Later, both became highly valued.
The causes and conditions involving Pántè are of long standing,
not only from today.
In the past, King Bīngshā's ancestors.
Governed criminals by law.
If someone committed theft, they would pat the thief's head.
The thief would feel great shame, no different from death.
Afterward, they would not commit theft again.
By the time of his father's reign, the governance was:
If someone committed theft, they would be driven out of the city as a strict punishment.
The thieves would all feel shame, no different from death.
Afterward, they would not commit theft again.
When Bīngshā succeeded to the throne.
If someone committed theft, they would be driven out of the country.
At that time, there was a thief who was driven out seven times.
Yet he still returned to rob and kill in villages and cities.
Finally, he was captured and brought before the king.
The king said.
"Take him away and cut off his little finger."
At that time, the official hurriedly cut it off, fearing the king might regret it.
The king tried biting his own finger and found the pain unbearable, so he immediately ordered them not to cut it off.
The minister replied to the king.
"It has already been cut off."
The king was deeply troubled and regretful.
He then thought to himself.
"I am the last of the righteous kings.
Yet I have become the beginning of unrighteousness.
A king should care for his people.
But I have cut off a man's finger."
He then ordered his carriage.
And went to the Buddha, saying.
"From my ancestors to my father.
They all governed the people by law.
But when it came to me.
Evil has increased daily, and righteous governance has gradually declined.
I have mistakenly become a king who injures and mutilates people's bodies.
I reflect on my lack of virtue and feel deep shame and fear."
The Buddha told the king.
"The laws of governing a country.
For theft, how much money warrants the death penalty? How much warrants exile?
And at what point should punishment be applied?"
The king said.
"World-Honored One.
Nineteen ancient coins make one Jìlìshāpán.
One Jìlìshāpán is divided into four parts.
If someone steals one part, the crime warrants death."
The Buddha preached the Dharma to him.
The king paid respects to the Buddha and left.
At that time, the bhikṣus said.
"Why is King Bīngshā so afraid of committing a crime?"
The Buddha said.
"He is not only afraid of committing a crime in this life.
In the past, there was a country named Jiāshī.
The king was called Chēngchēng.
At that time, the people of the country.
Were skilled in crafts and arts, all able to make a living for themselves.
Those without skills were called foolish.
Those who committed theft were also called foolish.
At that time, there was a thief who was captured and brought before the king.
The king said.
"Stop, stop.
That person lost property, and this person committed theft.
What use is it for me to join in doing evil?"
He thought.
"Since ancient times, there has only been one foolish person.
If the number of foolish people does not reach a thousand, I should die."
He then handed the foolish person over to his minister, saying.
"I need a thousand foolish people for a grand assembly.
Gather them until the number is full, then inform me."
The minister detained the foolish person and confined him in one place.
The king then thought.
"This foolish person might suffer."
So he told the minister.
"Take good care of this person, do not let him become emaciated.
Place him in my Wúyōu Garden.
Provide him with the five desires, entertainment, and music."
The minister followed the order.
Wanting to please the king, he treated the person with extra care.
Not long after, the number reached a thousand.
The minister reported that it had reached a thousand.
"What else is needed? I will quickly prepare it."
When the king heard this.
He became deeply troubled and sorrowful.
"Since ancient times, there has only been one person.
How has it now suddenly reached a thousand?
This must be the end of an era, with evil laws increasing."
The king ordered his ministers.
"Sweep and clean the garden, burn incense, and hang silk banners.
Prepare various delicacies and food."
The king, along with his ministers and the eighteen groups, went to the Wúyōu Garden.
He ordered the foolish people to be presented. Seeing their clothes torn, dirty, nails long, and hair disheveled.
He ordered them to be bathed, their hair cut, and their nails trimmed.
He gave them new clothes.
Then he brought them forward and gave each various foods and treasures.
Allowing them to take whatever they needed.
He told them to return home and support their parents.
To diligently engage in productive work and not commit theft again.
The foolish people, hearing the order, joyfully followed it.
At that time, the king handed over the throne to his crown prince.
And went into the mountains to practice the way of the immortals.
That king was Bīngshā.
He always feared retribution for his crimes.
The Buddha said.
"King Bīngshā.
Not only in this life did he order a finger to be cut off and immediately regret it.
In a past life, there was a brāhmaṇa.
Who had no wealth and lived by begging.
This brāhmaṇa's wife bore no sons.
The household originally had a Nàjùluó insect.
Which then gave birth to a child.
The brāhmaṇa regarded it as his own son.
The Nàjùluó child also regarded the brāhmaṇa as its father.
Later, the wife gave birth to a son.
When going out to beg for food, the brāhmaṇa told his wife.
'If you go out, take the child with you.'
The wife, after feeding the child, went to the neighboring house to grind grain.
The child had the fragrance of butter and cheese.
A poisonous snake opened its mouth and spat venom, intending to kill the child.
The Nàjùluó insect then thought.
'My parents are not here.
How can this poisonous snake try to kill my younger brother?'
It immediately killed the poisonous snake, cutting it into seven pieces.
It smeared blood on its mouth and stood at the door.
Hoping its parents would see it and rejoice.
At that time, the brāhmaṇa.
Had just returned from outside and saw his wife outside the house from afar.
He became angry and said.
'I told you to take the child with you when you go out.
Why did you go alone?'
The father, upon entering the door, saw the Nàjùluó with blood on its lips.
He then thought.
'My wife and I were not here.
Did the Nàjùluó kill and eat my child?'
He struck and killed the Nàjùluó with a stick.
Entering the house, he saw his child.
Sitting in the courtyard, playing with his fingers.
He also saw the poisonous snake cut into seven pieces and became deeply troubled and regretful.
'This Nàjùluó saved my child's life.
I did not observe carefully and hastily killed it. How painful and pitiable!'
He then fainted and fell to the ground.
At that time, a deity in the sky.
Spoke a verse.
'The brāhmaṇa at that time.
Is now King Bīngshā.'
King Bīngshā asked Mùlián.
"Which heaven has good food?"
Mùlián sighed and said.
"The Heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings."
Bīngshā should be reborn in Tuṣita.
He then thought to first be born in this heaven.
And later be born in Tuṣita.
After his death, he became the son of Vaiśravaṇa.
Named Zuìshèngzǐ.
As Mùlián explained.
The first humans, who acted on impulse, were called Mahoraga.
Those born with three hands were called elephants.
Question.
"Why are they called humans?
Some are Mahoraga.
Some are elephants."
Answer.
At that time, they were born among animals.
But their form was like that of humans.
Their food, evil intentions, and cunning increased.
So the human form gradually disappeared, and they became animals.
Their form was like that of a toad."
At that time, in the Rājagṛha kingdom, there was a king
named Bimbisāra.
When he was young as crown prince, he often sought five wishes:
first, that I become king while still young;
second, that there be a Buddha in my kingdom;
third, that I may always come and go [to see the Buddha];
fourth, that I may always listen to the sutras being preached;
fifth, that upon hearing them swiftly I may understand and attain Stream-Entry.
The king obtained them all.
At that time, the king of Rājagṛha traveled north to a different kingdom,
named Takṣaśilā,
whose king was named Puṣkarasārin.
He was extremely arrogant and aloof.
He had previously met the Buddha and received the Buddha’s teachings,
studying the scripture on the six elements within the body,
namely earth, water, fire, wind, emptiness, and consciousness.
Now King Bimbisāra
and King Puṣkarasārin had never met in person,
yet from afar they loved and respected each other like brothers.
They often exchanged letters and sent each other gifts.
In King Puṣkarasārin’s kingdom, a lotus flower bloomed
with a thousand petals, all golden in color.
He sent it as a gift to King Bimbisāra.
King Bimbisāra,
upon seeing the flower, was greatly delighted and said,
"King Puṣkarasārin
has sent me something extremely rare and extraordinary."
King Bimbisāra
then wrote a letter to King Puṣkarasārin, saying:
"In my country there is much gold, silver, and precious jewels,
but I do not consider them treasures.
Now in my country has appeared a human flower,
named the Buddha,
with a body of purple-golden hue, possessing the thirty-two marks.
King Puṣkarasārin,
hearing of the Buddha, rejoiced and leapt with joy.
He wrote a letter to King Bimbisāra,
asking him to fully inform him of the Buddha’s precepts and practices.
King Puṣkarasārin,
a few days later, thought to himself:
"Human life is uncertain, lasting only a breath;
I cannot wait any longer for Bimbisāra’s reply."
He ordered the minor kings and his ministers
to prepare carriages and set out, intending to go to where the Buddha was.
On the way, he encountered King Bimbisāra’s letter,
which stated:
"The Buddha teaches people to abandon their homes, forsake wives and children, and cut off desires.
They must shave their heads and beards, don monastic robes, and become śramaṇas."
It also explained the twelve links of dependent origination
and sent it to King Puṣkarasārin.
King Puṣkarasārin,
after reading the letter, pondered to himself.
Late at night, when all the ministers and officials were asleep,
he quietly rose and slipped away.
Entering a burial ground, he shaved his own head,
put on monastic robes, and became a śramaṇa.
The Buddha, with his divine eye, saw Puṣkarasārin
arrive at Rājagṛha and stay at a potter’s house.
The Buddha thought:
"King Puṣkarasārin’s life will end tomorrow."
He then flew to the potter’s house and asked to stay for one night.
The potter replied:
"You may stay."
The Buddha sat upright in one spot
and thought to himself:
"This Puṣkarasārin is calm and serene."
He went before Puṣkarasārin
and asked:
"Under whose teaching have you become a śramaṇa?"
He replied:
"I have heard there is a Buddha, and now I take him as my teacher."
The Buddha thought:
"This worthy one became a śramaṇa because of me;
I should teach him the scripture I knew from past lives,
then he will understand."
The Buddha said:
"I will explain the scripture to you;
listen well."
Puṣkarasārin said, "Very well."
The Buddha taught him the Dharma,
and he attained the third fruit of Non-Returner.
Only then did he realize it was the Buddha.
He immediately rose and paid homage to the Buddha.
The next day, not far after entering the city,
a young horned cow gored Puṣkarasārin.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"Yesterday at the potter’s house, you taught the scripture to that śramaṇa,
and he was killed by a charging cow.
Where will he be reborn?"
The Buddha said:
"After I taught him the scripture, he attained the Non-Returner stage,
and will be reborn in the sixteen heavens, where he will attain Arhatship."
He then instructed the bhikṣus to together retrieve Puṣkarasārin’s body,
bury it properly,
and build a stūpa over it.
At that time, there was a deity named Red Horse,
of exceedingly fine appearance.
In the later part of the night, he came to where the Buddha was
and said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One,
is there anyone who can travel beyond the edge of the world
to the place where there is no birth, no aging, and no death?"
The Buddha told Red Horse:
"There is no one who can reach it."
The Red Horse deity again said to the Buddha:
"How marvelous, World-Honored One!
You have well explained this meaning.
As the World-Honored One says,
why is that?
I recall a past life
when I was named Red Horse,
a non-Buddhist ascetic
who attained supernatural powers and was free from all desires.
At that time, I thought:
'I have such swift supernatural feet;
like a strong man shooting a sharp arrow sideways
in the time it takes to pass the shadow of a tāla tree,
I can ascend Mount Sumeru,
reach one Sumeru,
step from the Eastern Sea and leap to the Western Sea.'
Thinking of my swift supernatural power, I now sought the edge of the world.
So I set off,
only pausing for food, rest, and necessities,
reducing sleep, constantly traveling for a hundred years.
On the way, I died without ever reaching it."
Then he vanished and was gone.
In a foreign land, there was a poisonous rain.
If it fell into rivers, lakes, wells, or ponds,
anyone who drank it would go mad and intoxicated for seven days.
There was a king
who was wise and knew how to recognize the poisonous rain by observing the clouds.
He had a well covered so the rain could not enter.
At that time, the officials and ministers drank the poisoned rainwater,
and the entire court went mad.
They stripped naked, smeared mud on their heads, and sat in the king’s hall.
Only the king alone remained sane.
All the ministers did not realize they were mad;
instead, they thought the king was mad.
"Why is he wearing clothes, different from everyone else?"
They all said to each other:
"This is no small matter; we should discuss it together."
The king, fearing the ministers might rebel, became frightened and anxious.
He said to the ministers:
"I have good medicine that can cure my illness.
Please wait a moment while I take it."
The king then went inside, took off his clothes, and came out looking like them.
All the ministers saw this and were greatly pleased.
After seven days, the ministers sobered up and felt deeply ashamed.
They put on their clothes and caps and came to court.
The king, as before, sat naked.
The ministers were shocked and asked:
"Your Majesty has always been wise;
why are you like this?"
The king replied to his ministers:
"My mind has always been steady and unchanged.
Because you were mad, you instead thought I was mad.
That was not my true mind."
In the past, the king of Kāśī
ruled with righteous law,
and the people were peaceful and happy, free from all troubles.
At that time, the king had no son.
Suddenly, the queen became pregnant.
After ten months, she gave birth to a child without eyes or nose.
Seven days after birth, a great assembly was held, gathering all the ministers.
Diviners and priests were to give the child a name.
According to the customs of that country,
names were given based on auspicious features, astrological signs, or parents’ wishes.
A brāhmaṇa asked:
"What distinctive features does the prince’s body have?"
Those beside him replied:
"This prince’s face is perfectly flat, with no eyes or nose."
The brāhmaṇa said:
"He should be named Mirror-Face."
Four wet nurses were provided to care for and raise him:
one to bathe and wash him,
one to remove impurities,
one to hold him,
and one to breastfeed him.
These four wet nurses attended to him day and night.
Like a lotus flower, he grew day by day.
When he came of age, his father the king passed away,
and Mirror-Face was enthroned as king.
Now, this prince had planted roots of virtue in past lives;
although born without eyes, he possessed divine sight.
He was fit to be king.
His merit and virtue were great.
The people of the country, hearing that Prince Mirror-Face had become king, were all astonished.
At that time, a minister wanted to test him,
but found no opportunity.
When the king issued an order
commanding the ministers
to build a new palace,
carved, engraved, and painted with various colors,
the minister tested the king.
He took a monkey, dressed it in clothes, put it in a leather bag,
carried it on his shoulder, and brought it before the king, saying:
"The skilled craftsman has arrived; may Your Majesty give instructions."
The king knew he was being tested.
He then spoke a verse:
At that time, King Jìngmiàn.
That is now me.
King Bùlíxiānní.
Lay down at night and dreamed of ten things.
First, he dreamed of three jars, with the two side jars full and steam coming out, passing back and forth between them.
It did not enter the central empty jar.
Second, he dreamed of a horse eating with its mouth and also eating with its rear.
Third, he dreamed of a small tree blooming with flowers.
Fourth, he dreamed of a small tree bearing fruit.
Fifth, he dreamed of a person seeking a rope.
Behind the person was a goat.
The goat ate the rope.
Sixth, he dreamed of a fox eating from a golden vessel on a golden bed.
Seventh, he dreamed of a large cow returning to drink milk from its calf.
Eighth, he dreamed of four cows coming from four directions, bellowing as they approached, about to fight.
Just as they were about to meet, the cows disappeared.
Ninth, he dreamed of a large pond with turbid water in the center and clear water around the edges.
Tenth, he dreamed of a great stream flowing with bright red water.
The king awoke in great terror.
Fearing the loss of his kingdom and his life.
He immediately summoned his ministers and various Daoists who understood dreams to ask them.
There was a Brahmin.
Who said none of these were auspicious signs.
He should take his most beloved consort and crown prince.
Along with his close attendants and servants.
And kill them all to sacrifice to the heavenly king.
All bedding and personal treasures and fine items.
Should be burned to sacrifice to heaven.
Only by doing so could the king avoid disaster.
The king was displeased upon hearing this.
The consort asked the king.
Why are you worried and sorrowful?
The king explained.
Last night I dreamed of ten things.
I fear the loss of my kingdom and my life.
There is a Brahmin.
Who interpreted the dreams as all inauspicious.
The consort said.
Do not worry, my king.
The Buddha is now nearby in the monastery.
Not far from the kingdom.
Why not go and ask about the meaning of the dreams?
According to the Buddha's interpretation.
The king should follow it.
The king then went to where the Buddha was.
Bowed his head to the ground at the Buddha's feet and fully explained to the Buddha.
Fearing the loss of his kingdom, his life, and his wife and children.
He wished to hear instruction and precepts.
The Buddha said.
Do not fear.
The king's dreams.
Concern people in later ages who will not fear laws and prohibitions.
They will be greedy, lustful, envious, and never satisfied.
Lacking righteousness and compassion, without shame or remorse.
The first dream: the noble and powerful will only associate with each other.
Ignoring the poor and lowly.
The second dream: seeing the horse eating with two ends.
In later ages, emperors and ministers.
Will receive salaries and also exploit the common people, never satisfied.
The third dream: the small tree blooming.
In later ages, people under thirty.
Will have white hair.
Greedy and lustful, with many desires, young in age but prematurely aged.
The fourth dream: the small tree bearing fruit.
In later ages, people under fifteen.
Will marry and return carrying children.
Without shame or remorse.
The fifth dream: a person seeking a rope, with a goat behind.
The goat eating the rope.
In later ages, when husbands travel.
Wives will commit adultery and consume their wealth.
The sixth dream: the fox eating from a golden vessel on a golden bed.
In later ages, the lowly will become noble.
Possessing wealth, revered and feared by all.
The descendants of dukes and marquises will become poor and lowly.
Sitting in low positions, eating and drinking last.
The seventh dream: the large cow returning to drink milk from its calf.
In later ages, there will be no propriety or righteousness.
Mothers will act as matchmakers for their daughters, seducing other men.
To have relations with their daughters, seeking wealth for them.
To enrich themselves, without shame or remorse.
The eighth dream: four cows coming from four directions, bellowing as they approached, about to fight, just as they were about to meet, the cows disappeared.
In later ages, emperors, officials, and the people.
Will all lack sincerity.
Deceiving each other, foolish, ignorant, and angry.
Not revering heaven and earth, and because of this, rain will not fall in season.
Officials and people will pray for rain.
Heaven will bring forth clouds from four directions, with thunder and lightning.
Officials and people will all say.
Rain should come, but in a moment, the clouds will disperse and the rain will cease, not falling.
Why is this?
Because emperors, officials, and the people lack loyalty, integrity, benevolence, and compassion.
The ninth dream: the large pond with turbid water in the center and clear water around the edges.
In later ages, the central kingdom will be disturbed, governance unjust.
People will not be filial to parents, nor respect elders.
The border regions will be peaceful and orderly.
People will live harmoniously, filial and obedient to both parents.
The tenth dream: the great stream flowing with bright red water.
In later ages, various kingdoms will quarrel, raise armies, gather crowds, and attack each other.
They will use chariots, infantry, and cavalry.
Fighting and killing each other, casualties beyond count.
The dead on the roads, blood flowing bright red.
The king knelt and said.
Having received the Buddha's instruction and precepts, my heart is joyful.
He paid respects to the Buddha and returned to the palace.
He honored his rightful consort even more.
And confiscated the salaries of all ministers.
No longer believing in heterodox paths and Brahmins.
In the Yuèzhī kingdom, there was a king.
Named King Èshào.
Under heaven, none did not submit to him.
His mother instructed the king, saying.
If faced with mortal danger, be careful not to circle a Buddhist temple to the left.
Remember to circle to the right, and do not disobey this teaching of mine.
At that time, King Èshào.
Led a great army to attack the city of Chúnxuè.
Personally wielding a sword, he killed three hundred million people.
Later, the battle turned against him.
He fled on an elephant, looking back at the Buddhist stupa.
Remembering his mother's instruction, he turned the elephant to the right.
The enemy state saw this and scattered in submission.
The king saw the enemy retreat and pursued them.
Recaptured his original city and captured the enemy king.
Then he remembered the Buddha's words.
Those who take refuge in the Buddha are the most honored and supreme, with none surpassing them.
If I had not turned to the right, how could I have defeated this enemy?
The Buddha was in the kingdom of Shèwèi.
There was a king of the kingdom of Nán.
His name was Fēnhétán.
He greatly loved virtue and the Way.
He daily fed over a thousand ascetics.
The king himself claimed
to have unparalleled wisdom, and he bound his abdomen with iron
because he constantly feared that his wisdom would burst forth sideways.
He wished to arrange a marriage for his son.
He asked his ministers:
"Is there anyone under heaven as wise as I?
If there is such a person,
I wish to take his daughter for my son."
There was none within the kingdom.
The king dispatched envoys to seek elsewhere.
They arrived in the kingdom of Shèwèi and asked the people there about the Buddha.
The envoys said:
"Does the Buddha have a daughter?"
They replied:
"The ascetic has no daughter."
The envoys said:
"Who is next?"
They replied:
"Ānánbīndī is virtuous, good, and loves the Way. He has a daughter who is foremost."
The envoys said:
"Why is she considered foremost?"
They replied:
"He once disputed over gardens and fields with Prince Zhī and offered them to the Buddha.
Elephants carried gold amounting to tens of millions and billions, yet he did not covet such heavy treasures, but only aspired to do good."
The envoys then went to Ānánbīndī's residence.
They returned and reported to the king.
The king immediately galloped to see him.
The king of Nán had no clothes on his body at all.
He was naked, dark, and ugly, resembling a ghost.
Ānánbīndī asked:
"What do you seek?"
The king said:
"I have heard that you are virtuous, good, and love the Way, and have a foremost daughter.
Therefore, I have come to request your daughter for my son."
Ānánbīndī called him forward to sit and said:
"I must inform the Buddha."
He fully reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "Give her to him."
Ānánbīndī said:
"My daughter would be terrified to death."
The Buddha said: "No."
So he gave her.
The daughter's name was Sānmójié.
She would liberate eighty thousand people in the kingdom of Nán.
Ānánbīndī dared to ask the Buddha again:
"My heart truly harbors resentment."
He then returned and said to the king of Nán:
"The daughter shall be given to you."
The king then performed rites, betrothed her, and brought her back to his kingdom.
The prince went at night to Sānmójié's place.
Sānmójié kicked the prince and knocked him to the ground.
This happened four or five times.
The prince dared not go again.
The king's wife asked him:
"Why do you not go?"
The prince remained silent.
The wife then went to Sānmójié's place.
"I married a wife for my son; now she should serve him.
Why does my son suffer humiliation?"
Sānmójié said:
"Madam, the prince, and the people of this kingdom,
all have forms like dogs, no different from animals."
The wife reported to the king:
"The king, with unparalleled wisdom, sought a daughter-in-law from afar.
Without any fear or difficulty, she humiliates my son.
She also insults me to my face."
The king heard this.
He immediately went to Sānmójié's place.
Sānmójié did not come out to bow in greeting.
The king said:
"I married a new daughter-in-law from afar.
Is it acceptable for her to insult my wife to her face and humiliate my son?"
Sānmójié said: "Yes.
The people of the king's kingdom are all like dogs and animals."
The king was greatly astonished and said:
"I constantly fear that my wisdom will burst forth sideways from my abdomen,
so I bind it with iron.
I daily feed over a thousand ascetics.
Who can compare to me?
Yet I am instead insulted."
Sānmójié said:
"Men and women, old and young, face each other naked.
Even if you cultivate blessings, you are still despicable and lowly."
The king went to his teacher's gate and fully recounted the above events.
The teacher said:
"Go again and question her.
Be careful not to be angry."
The king then returned and asked:
"How are the people of your kingdom superior?"
Sānmójié said:
"In my kingdom, men and women all have clothing.
The noble and the lowly have different positions and do not see each other's bodies.
There is a great man named the Buddha.
He teaches and transforms tens of thousands, hundreds of millions of people, enabling them all to attain the Way.
He enters fire without burning, enters water without drowning.
He can govern three thousand suns and moons, twelve thousand heavens and earths.
He knows the affairs of the three times.
His body has the thirty-two marks and eighty excellent characteristics.
His virtue and the Way are comprehensive, and all the heavens revere and pay homage to him."
The king said:
"Can the Buddha be seen?"
Sānmójié said:
"If invited from afar, he can be summoned."
The king said:
"Excellent.
How should we invite him?"
Sānmójié said:
"Just burn incense yourself, and the king follow behind me.
The queen and the prince all follow me."
Sānmójié then ascended a high platform and requested:
"The king of Nán has just heard the name of the Tathāgata.
May the Buddha accept the king's food offering tomorrow."
The Buddha told Mùlián:
"Command all the bhikkhus:
Tomorrow, all go to the kingdom of Nán."
Sānmójié
instructed the king, queen, and prince to observe fasting, burn incense, spread mats, and set up food utensils.
They prepared to serve one thousand two hundred and fifty people.
Sānmójié,
together with the king, queen, and prince, went to the central courtyard.
She said: "When the arhats come, they will arrive first, and the Buddha will come last.
Do not be alarmed; follow my actions."
The Buddha and the bhikkhus each transformed themselves.
Shèlìfú manifested as a pair of white elephants.
Mùlián transformed into a lion.
The great bhikkhus each changed their bodies,
displaying various forms.
Some were geese, all different, descending from above.
The people of the kingdom of Nán were greatly astonished.
Sānmójié said:
"Do not be afraid."
The Buddha came last, his body emitting water and fire.
Sānmójié stepped forward and bowed to the Buddha.
The king, queen, and prince also bowed.
The arhats took their seats in order of seniority.
Sānmójié, the king, queen, and prince
then proceeded to offer water for washing and the food utensils.
The people of the kingdom wondered why the king had closed the gates.
They became very angry and took axes to chop the palace gates.
The Buddha said:
"I wish to make all people do good."
He then caused the palace walls to transform into crystal,
so that inside and outside could see each other. The people then stopped and dared not chop further.
At that time, Bīntóulú was sitting on a mountain.
He suddenly left and went to the kingdom of Nán.
He pierced the ground with a needle,
with thread connected to his robe.
He traveled by supernatural power to the kingdom of Nán.
The mountain followed behind him.
A woman in the kingdom was pregnant and, seeing the mountain coming, feared it would fall.
Terrified, she miscarried.
The Buddha ordered Mùlián to ask Bīntóulú:
"What is that behind you?"
Bīntóulú looked back.
He threw the mountain back to its former place, eight thousand li away.
The Buddha said:
"I taught you to liberate people.
Now you missed the time and also killed one person.
The gravity of human life is something I do not favor.
From now on, you shall not follow me for even a meal's duration.
Only when Maitreya Buddha appears will you attain parinirvāṇa."
Bīntóulú remained silent, sorrowful and distressed.
The king said to the Buddha:
"Could we compete in spiritual power?
The one who is inferior shall throw himself into a well."
The Buddha said: "Excellent."
He asked three times: "The one who is inferior shall throw himself into a well."
The king said: "Agreed."
The Buddha asked:
"When you recite scriptures, how is it?"
The king said:
"When I recite scriptures,
I crawl on all fours, and at the extreme, I prostrate on the ground."
The Buddha said:
"When I recite scriptures, I sit; when sitting is extreme, I walk mindfully.
If you crawl while reciting scriptures, that is the behavior of a dog."
The king was inferior.
The king wanted to throw himself into the well but placed his hands on the ground and refused to enter.
The Buddha said: "Let it be."
The king then returned to his kingdom and practiced the Buddha's teachings.
Sānmójié
then served the king, queen, and prince.
In the kingdom of Nán, she taught and transformed eighty thousand people.
All attained the four fruits of śrāvaka.
At that time, there was a king.
His name was Āzhì.
The territory he ruled extended for a hundred thousand li in circumference.
The people were prosperous and numerous.
The king was greatly valiant and fierce, never deviating from his own methods.
He invaded and attacked neighboring countries, oppressing and tormenting the good and virtuous.
The neighboring countries all suffered under him.
The Buddha, together with his great assembly, went to his country.
Āzhì heard of this.
Together with his thirty-two sons, all of them brave and strong, he harbored malicious intent and raised an army.
He gathered a multitude of people, numbering in the millions.
They positioned themselves on the main road, intending to block and resist the Buddha.
The Buddha spoke to Ānán.
"King Āzhì and his sons
tomorrow will harbor malicious intent toward me and the great assembly.
How will you all subdue them?"
The great beings, heavenly beings, and humans laughed, shaking heaven and earth.
The Buddha asked, "Why are you laughing?"
Ānán said,
"We are laughing at King Āzhì."
The Buddha said,
"Āzhì is foolish and ignorant, giving rise to this malicious intent.
He causes his people to incur guilt.
Having already raised a great army, he relies on the strength of men and horses.
Even if they filled the entire fourfold world, they could not move a single hair of mine.
How much less just a few million people?"
The Buddha told Ānán,
"Command all the enlightened ones to take their alms bowls and go forth.
Tomorrow, they shall receive food from within the army of King Āzhì."
The king, his sons, and their troops were extremely numerous, startling ghosts and spirits.
At that moment, the Buddha's body went ahead, emitting a great radiance.
He passed through the midst of the army and crossed into King Āzhì's country.
The king's drums no longer sounded.
Bows and crossbows were not drawn, swords and weapons were not unsheathed.
Elephants and horses toppled over, foot soldiers suffered cramps.
Heaven and earth grew dark and gloomy, the sun and moon lost their light.
The king and his sons
all became confused, lost their breath, fell prostrate, and fled.
The Buddha's great assembly halted and all received food, filling their bowls.
They proceeded to the king's capital.
The city gates opened by themselves.
The Buddha advanced to the king's palace, entered the hall, and sat down.
All was silent and still.
Eight hundred and eleven thousand heavenly beings each took their seats.
The palace expanded naturally, with high seats appearing, jeweled canopies interwoven, and the five tones playing of themselves.
The king and his sons said to each other,
"The power of a king is not equal to the power of the Way and virtue."
The soldiers were terrified.
The princes said,
"Now we hear that the Buddha has entered and is already within the palace.
We should return and meet the Buddha."
The king said,
"What face do I have to meet the Buddha?
Above, I am ashamed before the spirits; below, I have failed the people."
The sons said,
"Since the Buddha is compassionate and benevolent, he does not harm people's feelings."
The king then gathered his troops and calmly, slowly returned to the palace.
He met the Buddha.
He placed his head and face on the ground, made obeisance to the Buddha, and apologized before him.
The Buddha said, "Lowly, ignorant, and uncultured, having studied little, not knowing ritual and righteousness, comparable to wolves and beasts.
Foolish and deluded, offending against heavenly beings and humans.
The great sage does not disregard even a small border country.
Now we have troubled the World-Honored One to come from afar to this humble land, where ruler and ministers have acted rebelliously.
We only pray that the Heavenly Honored One pities this lack of wisdom."
"Having already bestowed great kindness, instructing and transforming the people,
the king again placed his head and face on the ground, joined his palms, and stepped back to stand."
The king's thirty-two sons, the ministers and officials, and all the officials and people
all repented of their faults, blamed themselves, and turned their minds single-heartedly toward the Buddha.
The king saw the eight hundred and eleven thousand divine beings and humans all seated in rows on lion thrones.
Within the interwoven canopies, music played naturally.
He understood the Buddha's divine wonder.
The king commanded the ladies and maidens of the rear palace
all to come out and pay respects to the Buddha.
The king prepared a feast of a hundred flavors.
Together with his ladies and thirty-two sons,
he moved forward on his knees, offered water for washing, and personally served.
The food was distributed to all, high and low were reverent and solemn, single-minded and joyful. When the meal was finished,
the king came forward, bowed his head, and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I have received the grace of the Heaven of Heavens.
Due to the depth of my past merit and the aid of my ancestors, I have attained a position above the common people.
Heavenly Honored One, great sage,
please pity the people of my country. I beg for precepts to uphold for life.
In governing the people with correctness and fairness, by what method should I proceed?
I should form alliances with neighboring countries, abandoning evil and drawing near to good.
I pray the Buddha will give this his attention."
The Buddha said,
"The king's invasions and attacks are neither righteous nor sought for
the sake of long life and securing the altars of grain and soil.

The king should practice kindness, trustworthiness, benevolence, righteousness, compassion, filial piety, chastity, purity, magnanimity, gentleness, forbearance, humility, charity, nurturing the people, covering their faults, and forgiving oneself.
If you practice these things,
you can long preserve the altars of grain and soil.
If you lack these nine, the altars of grain and soil are difficult to preserve."
The king said, "How should I do this?
I pray you bestow compassionate instruction."
The Buddha said,
"Sentient beings are pitiable; human life is precious.
The treasures of the country and land are not to be relied upon.
The king should cherish human life as parents pity their children.
The people are closer to the king than to their parents.
All the myriad countries under heaven can be preserved.
Not just one country alone.
Although the king has millions of troops, chariots, cavalry, and infantry,
they are only sufficient to resist a small enemy.
When I was practicing the bodhisattva path, sitting in meditation under a tree,
the demon king, together with ghost and spirit troops numbering one hundred and eighty million,
all transformed their shapes into various beasts and animal bodies, intending to destroy my mind.
I, with my spiritual power, pressed the earth with my right hand.
And heaven and earth greatly shook, and they all fell down.
They could not return to their original forms.
The demon king submitted.
Compared to the power of hundreds of millions of ghosts and spirits,
what is the power of the king's millions of people?"
The king said,
"Truly, it is because I was foolish and ignorant, knowing nothing."
The king then knocked his head on the ground, confessed his faults, and begged to reform and exert himself.
The Buddha said,
"With great compassion, I think of and liberate all people of the ten directions, causing them all to attain liberation,
to soon attain Buddhahood, liberating those not yet liberated.
It is not only for the king and his sons.
The king again repented and blamed himself,
"I pray the Buddha pities me further and grants me instruction and precepts to uphold for life,
so that the people of the country may be peaceful and secure."
The Buddha said,

"The king should lighten punishments, reduce taxes, broaden kindness and trustworthiness, provide for the orphaned and solitary, frequently pardon prisoners, rescue the destitute, enrich the poor, and feed the hungry.
If the king acts thus, he can preserve his beginning and end."
The king, having aroused the mind for the Way, said to the ministers at his side,
"Fetch the stored treasures to offer to the World-Honored One."
The Buddha finished his blessing.
He bestowed them all upon the king's attendants, and they all became wealthy.
The king's thirty-two sons said to each other,
"To live as unrighteous men,
to die as unrighteous ghosts—
it is not as good as we brothers seeking to become śramaṇas."
They all said, "Excellent!"
They immediately went together to the Buddha and fully expressed their thoughts.
The Buddha knew their intention, which deeply entered the wisdom of the Way.
The god Śakra shaved their heads and beards, and they all became śramaṇas.
The ladies and maidens of the rear palace, three thousand in number,
the ministers and officials, and all the people
all received the five precepts and observed the six monthly fast days.
The country became prosperous and abundant.
Neighboring countries heard of this and revered and admired from afar.
From that time on, the king
governed the country with magnanimity and benevolence; there were no thieves or bandits.
Men and women respected each other, without covetous desire; all were harmonious and good.
The king made a great monastery with the seven treasures.
The people of the country all practiced the ten good deeds.
When their lives ended, they were reborn in heaven; none fell into the evil paths.
The Buddha said,
"I seek the Way for the sake of people, only to cause liberation.
It is not something that heavenly dragons, ghosts, or spirits can shake.
You all, practicing the Way,
should be like me."
At that time, King Yōutián
addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How many qualities must a king possess,
World-Honored One,
so that he does not soon perish in this world with external enemies contending fiercely,
and, having failed to cultivate practice, dies and falls into the evil destinies?"
The Buddha said: "Ten qualities.
What are these ten?
First, his mind is not single-pointed in all undertakings.
Second, he greedily craves for food like a starving tiger.
Third, he greedily indulges in wine and meat, neglecting state affairs.
Fourth, he is prone to anger and harbors many worries and sorrows.
Fifth, he constantly practices foolishness and does not accept others' admonitions.
Sixth, he relies solely on his own strength, thinking he can accomplish everything.
Seventh, he often delights in killing and oppresses the weak.
Eighth, he frequently dispatches troops to invade other countries' borders.
Ninth, he speaks much but his words lack true substance.
Tenth, he is not compassionate toward people.
If he possesses these qualities, he will not long remain in this world, and external enemies will contend fiercely.
After his life ends, he will go to the three evil destinies, and his evil reputation will spread far and wide."
The king said:
"How many qualities must a king possess to long remain in this world without external enemies contending fiercely,
and after his life ends, be reborn in a heavenly realm of goodness?"
The Buddha said: "Ten qualities.
He will long remain in this world without external enemies contending fiercely,
and after his life ends, be reborn in a heavenly realm of goodness.
What are these ten?
First, his mind is not confused in all actions and undertakings.
He treats all equally, abandons wrong conduct, and draws near to good deeds.
Second, the king is not greedy for food.
He sustains his life equally, distinguishes the precepts, and cultivates them.
Third, he is not greedy for flavors or addicted to wine.
He sees faults and knows that liberation is joy.
Fourth, he is not stingy but delights in generosity, observing all actions.
Fifth, he has wisdom, understands its meaning, and constantly cultivates goodness,
abandoning unwholesomeness.
Sixth, he does not rely on his own strength or follow his own ideas.
Whenever there are śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, ministers, or people who are intelligent and wise,
he asks them about meanings, and they all explain clearly, and he follows their teachings.
Seventh, he is not cruel or murderous toward the people.
He observes their actions and then imposes punishments accordingly.
Eighth, he does not frequently dispatch troops to invade other countries' borders.
He constantly maintains harmony with other kings.
Ninth, what he says is true and essential, without redundancy.
He considers the other's words before speaking.
Tenth, he constantly harbors compassion for his ministers and people, always overseeing state affairs.
Possessing these ten qualities, he will long remain in this world without external enemies contending fiercely.
When his body perishes and life ends, he will be reborn in a good destination, in heaven.
After his life ends, his good name will spread far and wide, transmitted among gods and humans.
Rule with equal Dharma, not with unrighteousness."
Then the king replied:
"To rule the people with equal Dharma
leads to rebirth in a good heaven after the body perishes and life ends.
Those who act unrighteously
will, after the body perishes and life ends, go to the three evil destinies, with their evil reputation spreading far and wide."
The people of the country presented a beautiful woman to King Yōutián.
The king was greatly delighted.
He appointed the woman's father as Grand Tutor.
He built a palace for the woman.
A thousand musicians and attendants served her.
The king's chief queen, who served the Tathāgata as her teacher, had attained the path of Stream-Entry.
Later, the king, having been slandered against the queen,
shot a hundred arrows at the queen.
The queen, seeing this, was not afraid and harbored no anger at all.
With single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha and compassionate thoughts toward the king,
the arrows all circled the queen three times and then returned to stand before the king.
All hundred arrows did likewise.
The king, startled and fearful,
immediately mounted a white elephant and golden chariot and hastened to where the Buddha was.
Bowing his head at the Buddha's feet, he confessed:
"I have committed grave offenses in the presence of the Three Jewels.
I indulged in lust and gave rise to perversity.
I harbored poisonous, evil thoughts toward the Buddha's holy assembly.
Even a white-robed disciple possesses such compassionate power.
How much more so the Tathāgata!
I now confess my faults and take refuge in the Three Jewels.
I only wish for your great compassion to forgive my offenses."
Long ago, in the country of Píhuántí,
there was a king named Dànnà.
In the country, there was to be a great flood.
After the flood subsided,
suddenly a great snake encircled the city once, its head resting on the city gate.
There were over three hundred million inhabitants in the city.
For days, they could not go out.
Many began to starve.
The snake, however, harbored no anger.
If anyone came out, it would devour them.
All the people in the country were terrified.
At that time, in the mountains of the king's realm, there were two ascetics who practiced the path purely.
One was named Móhē Tiáo,
the other Shāhē Tiáo.
Sitting in meditation, they thought:
"A snake is a venomous creature.
Now it has encircled the city, endangering people's lives."
Immediately, they went together.
Entering the country, they met the king.
The king, seeing the two ascetics, said:
"Due to my improper governance, this calamity has occurred.
The whole country is distressed and desolate, losing heart."
The two ascetics then told the king:
"We shall now devise a means to remove it for the king."
The king and his ministers all bowed their heads and earnestly requested:
"If we receive the grace of the two ascetics,
the people of this country will be as if reborn."
Shāhē Tiáo then transformed into a large toad.
It passed before the snake. The snake, unbearably hungry,
chased after the toad.
Móhē Tiáo transformed into a qíunài (a type of mythical bird or creature).
and pursued from behind.
The snake, seeing the qíunài, fled in terror into the deep mountains.
After the snake left, the people were safe.
The king and his ministers then sought out the two ascetics at their dwelling.
Bowing their heads, they expressed gratitude, saying:
"The two ascetics have been nearby all along.
I was truly foolish and ignorant, not serving you earlier.
Only when disaster struck did the ascetics come to rescue us.
We only wish the ascetics would return to dwell in the palace.
