There was a king of a neighboring country.
He raised an army to attack his enemy country.
The ministers of the enemy country informed their king, saying:
"A certain country has raised an army and is now approaching closely.
We hope Your Majesty will prepare yourself and join us in resisting the attack."
The king said to his ministers:
"This is a trivial matter; why must I be involved?"
The bandits attacked the city gate.
The ministers informed the king:
"The bandits are now outside."
The king told his ministers:
"Although the bandits are outside, there is no need for distant concern.
Just attend to your private affairs; why worry about public duties?"
At that time, the bandits grew increasingly violent and advanced into the city.
His attendants reported:
"The bandits have entered the city."
The king told his ministers:
"This matter is insignificant; why is it worth reporting?"
The king of the neighboring country advanced further and reached the palace hall.
The ministers reported:
"The king of the neighboring country is now in the hall.
We do not know what considerations Your Sacred Majesty has."
The king replied:
"I now dwell in a world where change never ceases.
What rises must decline.
Meetings inevitably lead to partings.
It is difficult to maintain constancy.
I shall change my appearance like a mendicant.
I will retreat and go deep into the mountains.
Contemplating the Way and virtue can bring me joy.
If this violent king wishes to harm my body, I will not evade the blame.
The reason for this is:
The loss of a country and its territory all stem from one person.
If I now accept death, the myriad people will be free from calamity.
Would this not be greatly fortunate for me?"
The king of that enemy country marveled at what he had never seen before.
Raising his voice, he exclaimed:
"Excellent, great king!
From ancient times until now, there has been none like you.
Although I have gained victory, I am not equal to you, O king.
You open your heart to the great Way, disregarding worldly glory.
From now on, I will return your great kingdom to you.
Rise as king and complete your transformation.
Let us receive each other and become close and intimate."
Once there was a king.
He selected the wisest person in the country
to serve as his chief minister.
At that time, the king
employed skillful means and immeasurable wisdom.
He selected one person
who was intelligent, broadly learned, with lofty aspirations and refined character,
dignified yet not violent, possessing both fame and virtue in full measure.
The king wished to test him.
Therefore, he imposed a heavy penalty: he filled a bowl to the brim with oil and made him carry it for twenty lǐ.
If even a single drop fell, he would be executed without further consultation.
The ministers carried out the order.
Spectators filled the road.
It was like water being still but wind blowing it, causing waves to rise.
His mind was unsettled and uneasy.
The man thought to himself, "I am certainly going to die now.
If I can carry the bowl without letting the oil fall until I reach that country, then I may survive."
He focused solely on the oil bowl, walking calmly and slowly.
At that time, all the ministers, soldiers, parents, relatives, and countrymen gathered
and followed to watch.
They also encountered a great drunken elephant charging into the road, roaring violently,
like the sound of thunder.
It trampled to death elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, pigs, calves, and the like on the road.
It smashed various carriages, scattering them in disarray.
People saw this and were terrified, fleeing east and west,
like clouds blown by the wind.
There were also people shooting arrows.
But the man carrying the bowl
initially did not know the elephant had come.
He also did not notice the elephant leaving.
A fire broke out in the city, burning various palaces.
Also, wasps released poison and stung people, while officers and soldiers tried to extinguish the fire.
Five-colored clouds arose, and the sky thundered loudly.
A chaotic wind blew dust, sand, tiles, and gravel, blocking the king's road.
It uprooted trees, broke branches, and scattered flowers and fruits.
Lightning flashed, thunder rumbled, peacocks all cried out, and heavenly disasters and hailstones fell.
Despite these changes, the man noticed and heard none of them.
Carrying the full bowl of oil, he reached that country,
without spilling a single drop.
The king was delighted and appointed him as chief minister.
Once there was a king
with a human body and a donkey's head.
The Buddha told the king:
"In the Snowy Mountains, there is a medicine
called 'Supreme Flavor.'
If the king goes and eats it, he can regain a human head."
The king went to the Snowy Mountains, selected the medicine, and ate it.
But his head remained unchanged.
The king returned and said to the Buddha:
"Why did you speak falsely?"
The Buddha said to the king:
"Do not pick and choose the medicinal herbs to regain a human head."
The king went back to the mountain.
All that grew on the mountain could cure his illness.
He no longer picked and chose.
He ate one mouthful of grass and immediately regained a human head.
Once there was a king
who could not sleep day or night.
If any of his attendants on duty fell asleep, he would kill them.
He had killed four hundred and ninety-nine people in total.
There was an elder's son who was due to take his turn on duty.
His family wept as they sent him off.
A young man asked:
"Why are you weeping?"
They answered truthfully.
"If you can hire me,
I can take your place."
The elder was overjoyed.
He gave him a thousand liǎng of gold and sent him to take duty.
The king said:
"Why have you come?"
He said, "I am replacing the elder's son on duty."
The king said:
"Be careful not to sleep, or I will kill you."
At that time, the young man fell asleep.
The king wanted to kill him.
He said, "Why did you sleep?"
He said, "I did not sleep; I was thinking about something."
The king said:
"What were you thinking?"
He said, "Making a one-shēng container that can hold two shēng of material.
Filling it with one shēng of sand and then adding one shēng of water."
The king tested it and found it to be true.
He fell asleep again, rolling on the ground.
The king again wanted to kill him.
He said, "I was thinking about something."
The king said, "What were you thinking?"
He said, "Digging a one-chǐ hole and then filling it with soil, but it does not reach eight cùn."
The king again had someone do it and found it to be true.
He fell asleep again, lying face down on the ground.
The king again wanted to kill him.
He asked, "Why did you fall asleep again?"
He said, "I was thinking about something.
If Your Majesty pardons my offense, I will tell you."
The king said, "Speak then."
The young man said:
"Your Majesty is exactly like a ghost."
Having said this, he left.
The king thought:
"Why did this person call me a ghost?"
He then asked his mother.
His mother said:
"You truly are a ghost.
When I was pregnant with you, I dreamed at night of a ghost
who had relations with me, and then you were born."
The king then awoke to the truth.
He changed his ways, stopped killing people, repented of his wrongs, and turned to goodness.
He then began to study the Way.
The king at that time was myself.
The four hundred and ninety-nine people are now the five hundred chief disciples.
The young man who awakened me
was Wénshū Shīlì.
In the past, King Aśoka,
before he understood the Buddha’s teachings,
created various hells.
Those who entered were inevitably punished,
cruelly, with all kinds of poisons.
Later, he gained faith,
and therefore abandoned all wrongdoings and devoted himself to the True Enlightened One.
When an epidemic struck the people,
the king ordered the inside and outside to be cut off, not allowing communication,
fearing the illness would reach the palace.
He sent a message to the Saṅgha,
begging them to recite blessings from afar.
“Could you send a bhikṣu into the palace,
to bestow blessings so that the world may be at peace and the epidemic eliminated?”
The Saṅgha accepted the request,
and wished to inform him.
At that time, the Saṅgha sent a śrāmaṇera, eight years old,
named Miàoyán,
who had already attained arhatship and possessed complete supernatural powers.
He flew to the king’s palace and spoke to the queen and the palace ladies,
explaining what was lacking and demonstrating the Dharma, showing that the Buddha is the most venerable, let alone his disciples.
Miàoyán accepted the instruction,
flew into the king’s palace, and stood before the queen.
The queen bowed and raised her hands, intending to embrace him,
saying, “Son Miàoyán, how could you humble yourself to display your supernatural powers?”
Miàoyán said to the queen,
“Step back, step back.
It is not appropriate to be physically close to a śrāmaṇera.”
The queen replied,
“You are young, only eight years old.
My heart feels affection for you as if you were my own son.
Even if I were physically close to you, what harm could there be?”
The śrāmaṇera replied,
“Considering affection, as the queen says,
affection arises from subtle beginnings.
Like a spark from a grain of millet that can burn a wilderness of ten thousand li,
or a drop of water that can wear through jade and stone and also fill a vessel.
All things progress gradually,
from little to much,
from small to great.
Therefore, the wise avoid suspicion and doubt,
to prevent what has not yet occurred.”
The śrāmaṇera and the queen debated back and forth, their voices rising,
until the sound reached the main hall.
The king asked those beside him,
“Whose voices are these, as if they are arguing?”
The attendant officials replied,
“The śrāmaṇera Miàoyán has come to the palace,
and is speaking with the queen.
Their voices are so loud that they can be heard here.”
The king immediately rose and went to see them,
bowed and inquired, “What is the argument about?”
The śrāmaṇera replied,
“The noble queen, seeing me, showed compassion and affection,
and wished to approach me, but the Dharma does not permit it.
Therefore, I resisted.”
King Aśoka said,
“You are still young, like my own son.
Loving and embracing you—what suspicion could there be?
Why use such strong words to refute?”
The śrāmaṇera replied,
“It is not as the king says.
The ancient sages established rules to prevent what has not yet sprouted, and to admonish from beginning to end.
A girl of seven does not play on her father’s mat;
a boy of eight does not sit on his mother’s bed.
One does not touch the head under a fruit tree;
one does not touch the feet in a melon field.
The reason for this is
to avoid suspicion and doubt, to stop things at their inception and eliminate sprouts.
To instruct the future is to prevent what has not yet occurred.
My mind is already pure, without even a trace of defilement.
It is like a lotus flower, untainted by mud and water,
or like a vessel of crystal or glass.
Truly, as the Tathāgata said,
it is equal to the relationship between mother and child, so there is no difference.
Although I know there is no flaw, I must act for those who are not yet capable.”
The king and queen, hearing his words, were astonished and admired him.
As Miàoyán said,
though only eight years old, he still considered the multitude of difficulties;
how much more so for those who are older and have not yet extinguished the three poisons?
Then the śrāmaṇera expounded the Dharma for them.
The queen, palace ladies, and over five hundred others all attained the path.
And the queen, attendant officials, and crown prince all generated the intention for the path.
Immediately, they attained the irreversible stage.
In the past, the queen of the kingdom of Bālínà was pregnant.
This queen knew she was pregnant,
and said to the king,
and the king provided for her care, ensuring everything was well-arranged.
When the month was full, she gave birth to a piece of flesh,
red like hibiscus flowers.
The other queens gave birth to beautiful children,
but I gave birth to a piece of flesh without hands or feet.
My heart felt shame.
If the king saw it, he would surely despise it.
She placed it in a vessel, hammered gold into thin sheets, and wrote on it with cinnabar,
“This is what the queen of the kingdom of Bālínà gave birth to.”
She covered the mouth of the vessel and sealed it with the king’s seal,
attached the gold sheet to the outside of the vessel,
and sent it floating on the river.
After the person abandoned it,
various spirits protected it, so there were no winds or waves.
At that time, a Daoist,
living by the river with cowherds,
was bathing early in the morning when he saw this vessel from afar.
He picked it up and saw the gold sheet with writing,
and also saw the king’s seal on it.
He opened the vessel and saw only a piece of flesh.
He thought to himself,
“If this were dead flesh, it would have rotted and stunk long ago.
There must be something extraordinary.”
He took it back to his dwelling and carefully placed it in one spot.
After half a month, it split into two pieces.
From then on, after another half month,
each of the two pieces grew five protrusions.
After another half month,
one piece became a boy,
and the other became a girl.
The boy’s complexion was like gold,
and the girl’s like silver.
The Daoist saw them,
and his heart felt deep affection as if they were his own children.
Milk naturally flowed from his two thumbs,
one thumb feeding the boy,
and the other feeding the girl.
The milk entered the children’s bellies like clear water or a mani pearl, transparent inside and out.
The Daoist named the boy
Líjūzǐ. The Daoist raised these two children with great difficulty.
He would go into the village to beg for food in the morning,
and also for the two children, returning late in the day.
At that time, the cowherds,
seeing the Daoist toiling so hard for these two children,
said,
“Venerable one,
a renunciant should be practicing the path.
Why let these two children hinder your spiritual practice?
You can give them to us, and we will raise them.”
The Daoist said, “Excellent.”
The cowherds each returned home,
and the next day, with their companions, leveled the roads,
erected banners, scattered various flowers,
beat drums, and came to welcome the two children to the Daoist’s place.
They said to the Daoist,
“Now it is time for these two children to go.”
The Daoist entrusted them,
“These two children have great merit and virtue,
beyond measure.
You must take good care of them.
You should nourish them with milk, yogurt, fresh butter, clarified butter, and the five kinds of offerings.
When these two children grow up, let them marry each other.
Find a flat, broad place for them to settle,
and appoint the boy as king and the girl as queen.”
The cowherds accepted the instruction and left.
When the two children reached the age of sixteen,
on a flat, broad area measuring one hundred yojanas in length and breadth,
a residence was built in the center.
The girl was married to the boy,
and they became husband and wife.
Later, they gave birth to two children, a boy and a girl.
This happened sixteen times,
and the cowherds, seeing the royal children increasing in number,
expanded the residences and built gardens and lands.
There were thirty-two residences in total.
Thus, after three expansions, it was named Vaiśālī.
The Buddha, accompanied by twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus,
traveled to the country of Jūlánní and stayed at the Měiyīn Monastery.
As his foot stepped upon the threshold, heaven and earth shook.
Pearls, jades, and musical instruments sounded of their own accord without being struck.
Poisons and hidden evils vanished, auspicious signs appeared, and harmony and purity prevailed.
All the people within the realm yearned and looked up to him.
There was a king named Yōutián.
He was violent, oppressive, and aggressive; he listened to flattering words and indulged excessively in women and music.
He established two queens on his left and right.
Their appearances were exquisitely beautiful.
The one on the left was named Zhàotáng.
She was arrogant, haughty, slanderous, and jealous.
The one on the right was named Jiǎnróng.
She constantly practiced benevolence and compassion.
The king treasured her virtue and privately favored her in all matters.
Jiǎnróng had an elderly maidservant
named Dùshèng.
She constantly practiced giving and offering incense.
She saved and gathered
food to offer to the Buddha and the saṅgha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to her.
She listened with her whole heart and did not forget.
After making the offering, she returned to the palace.
She carried the incense she had offered.
Due to this merit,
the fragrance from her past actions followed her, spreading far and wide.
The incense became twice as fragrant in weight.
Jiǎnróng questioned her,
and she first confessed to having saved money on incense
to offer food to the Buddha and the saṅgha.
The Dharma is profound and its meaning wondrous, not heard of in the world.
When Jiǎnróng heard about the Buddha,
joy arose in her heart.
She thought to herself that she had no means to hear the true Dharma.
She then replied to Dùshèng,
"You must explain it to me."
Dùshèng said,
"My body is lowly and my mouth impure; I dare not casually proclaim the venerable words of the Tathāgata.
I beg to go to the Buddha, receive his instruction, and then return."
She was then sent out of the palace.
Jiǎnróng further instructed her,
"Receive the complete ritual procedures."
Before Dùshèng returned,
the lady and her maidservants filled the central courtyard.
The Buddha told Dùshèng,
"When you return to preach the Dharma, many will be liberated."
"The ritual for preaching the Dharma first requires setting up a high seat."
Dùshèng fully conveyed the holy instruction.
Jiǎnróng was delighted.
She opened her chest and took out clothes, piling them up to make a high seat.
Relying on the Buddha's majestic power, she preached the Dharma accordingly.
Lady Jiǎnróng and the various maidservants, through resolving their doubts, attained the Way.
Dùshèng attained total retention (dhāraṇī).
Zhàotáng, out of jealousy, reproached and slandered her repeatedly.
The king would not comply.
Later, she spoke of it again.
The king's mind then became confused.
Waiting for the time of her fasting, she urged the king to have music played
and requested to summon the lady.
The king then summoned everyone broadly, and all who were commanded assembled.
Jiǎnróng, observing the fast, alone did not respond to the summons.
Though summoned three times repeatedly, she held to her precept and did not move.
The king's anger blazed fiercely; he had her bound and dragged before the hall.
He was about to shoot and kill her.
Jiǎnróng, with her whole heart, took refuge in the Buddha.
The king shot two arrows himself, but both turned back toward him.
The king, terrified, released her.
He asked,
"What art do you possess that has caused this?"
She replied,
"I only serve the Tathāgata and take refuge in the Three Jewels.
I observe the Buddhist fast in the morning and do not eat after noon.
Additionally, I practice the eight precepts, maintaining purity and not approaching [defilement].
It must be the World-Honored One who, out of compassion, has shown such mercy."
The king said,
"Excellent!
How can this be spoken of lightly?
I must go to the monastery to pay homage to the World-Honored One."
At that time, an enemy state raised troops and invaded the border.
The king went forth to battle himself and entrusted the governance of the state to a brāhmaṇa
named Jíxīng.
He temporarily administered the affairs of state.
Zhàotáng joyfully said,
"My father is in charge; he will surely kill my son."
The woman plotted with her father and then burned and killed Jiǎnróng and the various maidservants.
They falsely claimed it was an accidental fire, thinking they could cover it up.
Afterward, the matter was exposed.
The king was greatly enraged.
He banished Jíxīng far away, casting him out beyond the borders.
Zhàotáng and her like were imprisoned in an underground dungeon.
He suppressed and expelled the heretical paths
and widely propagated the Buddha's teachings.
The Buddha was in the country of Shèwèi.
The king and his ministers all revered and looked up to him.
At that time, there was a merchant
named Bōlì.
He, along with five hundred merchants, entered the sea to seek treasure.
Then a sea deity emerged, holding up water in his hands,
and asked Bōlì,
"Is the seawater greater,
or the water in my hands greater?"
Bōlì replied,
"The water in your hands is greater.
Although the seawater is vast, it cannot save those who are hungry and thirsty.
Although the water in your hands is little, it can save the lives of those who are thirsty and in need.
The blessings received through lifetimes are immeasurable."
The sea deity was delighted.
He then took off the eight kinds of fragrant necklaces from his body
and adorned them with the seven treasures, giving them to Bōlì.
Bōlì returned to his country
and presented these fragrant necklaces to King Bōsīnì.
The king found them extremely rare and precious.
He then assembled all his consorts,
saying that he would give the fragrant necklaces to the most excellent one.
Sixty thousand consorts, all adorned and dressed up, came forth.
The king asked,
"Why has Consort Mòlì not come out?"
The attendant replied,
"Today is the fifteenth day; she is observing the Buddhist fast and is plainly dressed, not adorned."
The king said,
"Does observing the fast now mean she should disobey the king's command?"
This was repeated three times.
Consort Mòlì came out in plain clothes.
Among the crowd, she shone like the sun and moon, twice as beautiful as usual.
The king was awed and, with increased respect, asked,
"What virtuous practice causes such radiant distinction?"
The consort said to the king,
"I reflect that I have little merit, born into this female form.
Defilements of emotion and condition pile up like mountains day and night.
Human life is brief and short; I fear falling into the three wretched paths.
Therefore, on certain days of the month, I observe the Buddhist fast.
Renouncing attachment to follow the Way brings blessings through lifetimes."
The king heard this and rejoiced.
He then gave the fragrant necklaces to her.
The consort declined, saying,
"I am now observing the fast and should not wear these.
You may give them to someone else."
The king said,
"My original intention was to give them to the most excellent.
You are now the most excellent.
Moreover, you observe the Dharma fast; your aspiration for the Way is especially lofty.
Therefore, I give them to you.
If you do not accept them, where shall I place them?"
The consort replied,
"Great King, do not worry.
I wish Your Majesty would condescend to go together to where the Buddha is.
Present these fragrant necklaces to the World-Honored One,
and also receive his holy instruction, accumulating blessings for countless eons."
The king then agreed.
He ordered the carriages prepared and went to where the Buddha was.
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
"These fragrant necklaces from the sea deity were presented by Bōlì.
Sixty thousand consorts all desired to obtain them.
Consort Mòlì, when offered, did not take them.
Observing the Buddhist fast, her mind was free from greed and desire.
Reverently, I present them to the Buddha.
May you condescend to accept them.
The disciples of the World-Honored One have minds difficult to equal.
Is there truly such blessing in straightforward faith like this?"
Then the World-Honored One accepted the fragrant necklaces
and spoke a verse, saying:
In the kingdom of Pántí, there was a king named Yōudá.
During the time of Kāshyapa Buddha, he left home to cultivate the Way.
He encountered Shakyamuni and all attained the path of enlightenment.
His kingdom was prosperous and the people were flourishing.
The king had twenty thousand consorts.
The foremost consort,
named Yuèmíng,
was dignified and beautiful, and the king loved and respected her deeply.
Before half a year had passed, signs of her impending death appeared.
The king was greatly distressed.
Yuèmíng asked him about it.
The king said,
"Your life is about to end.
The sorrow of parting from one you love is why I am grieving."
Yuèmíng replied,
"Birth leads to death;
this is the constant way of the world.
Why grieve alone?
If you truly care for me, just allow me to leave home.
If you permit me to enter the path,
even if I do not attain the Way, I will surely be reborn in heaven.
If I am reborn in heaven, I will return to you."
The king allowed her to leave home.
Yuèmíng then made her vow.
She summoned the bhikshunis.
She immediately renounced the five desires.
Many came to inquire, pay respects, and make offerings, which hindered her spiritual practice.
Therefore, she traveled to various kingdoms.
From the day she left home, after six months had passed,
she maintained pure precepts and grew weary of the worldly life.
She attained the stage of Anāgāmin.
She passed away in a village and was reborn in the realm of form.
Reflecting on her past connection, she remembered her promise to the king.
Wishing to fulfill her original vow,
she observed that the king was submerged in the five desires, stubborn and difficult to transform.
Going to him directly would not inspire him.
It was appropriate to use fear to subdue him.
She then transformed herself into a great rākshasa.
Her hair stood on end, and she held a five-foot-long knife.
While the king was sleeping at night, she hovered in the air not far from him.
The king was terrified.
She then said to the king,
"Though you have thousands of troops,
now you belong to me alone and are not free.
Your time of death has come; how will you save yourself?"
The king replied,
"I have no other reliance except the good deeds I have performed,
cultivating a pure mind to be reborn in a good place after death."
The heavenly being said,
"This is the most reliable; there is no other principle."
The king then asked,
"What kind of spirit are you, making me so afraid?"
The heavenly being answered,
"I am Consort Yuèmíng.
You allowed me to leave home; I contemplated renunciation and was reborn in the realm of form.
Now I have come to fulfill my promise."
The king said,
"Even though you say this, I still do not believe it.
Return to your original form, then I will believe."
The heavenly being then transformed back into her former appearance.
Her clothes and ornaments were exactly as before as she stood there.
The king's desire arose, and he rushed to seize her.
Yuèmíng then ascended into the sky and preached the Dharma to the king, saying:
"This body is impermanent, not lasting even a snap of the fingers.
It is like morning dew, vanishing at sunrise.
Not only is it impermanent, but you are also attached to this body of mine.
Do you not see, O King,
that youthful beauty is devoured by old age?
The faculties decay and wither.
The eyes grow dim,
the ears become hard of hearing.
The body deteriorates and rots, no longer capable of anything.
It is like fermenting wine: once the pure flavor is extracted, the dregs are worthless.
This body, once old, holds no pleasure to cling to.
Only death remains.
Since the body is born, death and impermanence accompany it.
Do you not see, O King,
that the unborn, infants, youths, and adults all die?
This body is fragile and perilous; the thief of death constantly follows.
Body and mind burn like fire, filled with nothing but suffering.
The mind has the three poisons; the body experiences cold, heat, hunger, and thirst.
Yet you do not grow weary, clinging to this body of mine.
Palace women, entertainers, beauty, and the five desires—
the kingdom's wealth, wife, and children—none of these are truly mine.
When death comes, not one follows.
Even the body is abandoned, let alone other things.
Deluded and submerged in the five desires, drifting in the cycle of birth and death, unaware of the way out.
You are a wise man; why not grow weary and renounce the world to seek the Way?"
The king's mind turned toward goodness, and he agreed to leave home.
Yuèmíng further transformed him, saying:
"I shall leave home to seek the wondrous Dharma, receive it, practice it, and diligently advance day and night without slackening."
After saying this, she suddenly vanished.
The king then abdicated the throne to the crown prince.
He renounced the five desires
and went to Kātyāyana to leave home and follow the Way.
At that time, people, because he had abandoned great glory and profit
to seek the true path,
many officials and commoners came to make offerings, pay respects, and inquire, hindering his spiritual practice.
Therefore, he traveled to the kingdom of Mójié.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to him, and he attained Arhatship.
Holding an earthen bowl, he entered the city of Rājagriha.
He begged for leftover food and returned to the forest to sit and eat.
King Bimbisāra went out to the forest.
He inquired, saying:
"You were once a king, coming and going with honor and retinue.
Now you are a beggar, walking alone to beg for food.
Can this be enjoyable?
Return and renounce the path; I will give you half the kingdom to rule."
The monk replied,
"I was a great king with many territories.
Why should I now abandon the great for the small? It is not fitting for me."
King Bimbisāra said,
"You used to eat exquisite food served in precious vessels.
Now you hold an earthen bowl and beg for leftover food—is this not difficult?
You used to be a king with brave warriors guarding you.
Today you are alone—is this not frightening?
You once lived in deep palaces, with beautiful consorts and entertainers pleasing your eyes and ears.
You sat on jeweled beds spread with fine mats.
Today you sleep alone in the wilderness, resting on grass—is this not suffering?"
He replied,
"Now I am content and free from greed and attachment."
King Bimbisāra said,
"You are pitiable now."
He answered,
"You are pitiable, not I."
"Why is that?"
"You are entangled by the five desires, driven by affection and love, and not free.
I am now joyful, with a mind unhindered."
Bimbisāra, hearing this, then departed.
Once there was a man
who saw a Buddhist temple
and wished to build one.
But he lacked sufficient money and silk.
He vowed to go to sea to acquire gold and treasures.
"I shall build a temple, the foremost in the kingdom."
After obtaining gold and silver, he pondered deeply again:
"Who can share my intention to build the temple together?"
The king often said,
"I wish to build a temple and pagoda."
"He has not yet begun.
I should present the jewels and treasures to the king."
The king was delighted and asked,
"Where did you obtain these?"
The virtuous man said,
"I wished to build a temple but could not do it alone.
I went to sea to obtain treasures to build the temple.
Now I have returned safely—this is my first benefit.
Having obtained gold and treasures—this is my second benefit.
My mind is free from greed, and I will erect a temple—this is my third benefit.
Relying on these three beneficial merits, I now wish to build a temple,
but I lack manpower and labor.
Therefore, I inform the king."
The king said,
"I also have three benefits:
I wish to build a temple and pagoda; I have become king, the highest among men—this is my first benefit.
Abundant wealth, treasures, and soldiers—this is my second benefit.
All four directions submit to me—this is my third benefit.
I shall build the temple together with you."
The king summoned his five hundred consorts and gave them the jewels.
The five hundred consorts all adorned themselves, each wishing to obtain the jewels.
Only the chief consort did not adorn herself.
The king asked why.
She replied that she also had three benefits:
"Therefore, I became the king's consort.
Respected throughout the palace—this is my first benefit.
Giving birth to a son who is the crown prince—this is my second benefit.
Constantly delighting in the scriptures and the Way, wishing to build a Buddhist temple—this is my third benefit."
The king said, "Excellent!"
He gave her the jewels.
The chief consort contributed a hundred thousand taels of gold to assist the king in building the temple.
The king, together with the virtuous people of the kingdom, built a temple a thousand paces wide.
It was all adorned with gold, silver, and carvings.
The king said,
"Only we three have such merit.
Do the people of my kingdom not share in this?"
He sent messengers to the streets to proclaim:
"Whoever can give generously with good intention will obtain immeasurable merit."
There was a poor woman who had only a small hut and begged for food and clothing.
Hearing this, she reproached herself:
"In past lives, I did not practice charity, leading to my current poverty."
She took off her cloth skirt and threw it to the messenger, offering the skirt to assist the king.
"My body is now exposed, with no clothes to wear."
The king, hearing of this, was astonished that such a good heart existed.
He immediately ordered her to be brought.
The messenger said,
"This woman has no clothes to wear."
The king ordered the five hundred consorts
each to take a garment and give it to her.
"Quickly go and bring her."
The king then saw her and made her his second consort.
He ordered her to instruct the palace women.
In the kingdom of Qiántuóshīlì, the crown prince
disliked worldly glory and lived in seclusion among mountains and marshes.
At that time, deep in a valley, there was a starving tigress.
She had just given birth to seven cubs when heavy snow fell from the sky.
The tigress, holding her cubs, had already gone three days without finding food.
Fearing her cubs would freeze to death, she endured hunger to protect them as the snow fell incessantly.
Mother and cubs, starving and exhausted, were near death.
Driven by hunger, the mother was about to devour her own cubs.
Then the various ascetics said:
"Who can sacrifice his body to save them?"
The prince said:
"Excellent! My wish shall be fulfilled."
He went to the cliff's edge and looked down.
Seeing the tigress and her cubs covered by snow, he felt great compassion.
Standing on the mountain peak, he entered serene meditation.
Immediately he attained the pure patience of the unborn.
He perceived past events of countless kalpas and future ones as well.
Then he returned and told his teacher and five hundred fellow students:
"I now sacrifice my body. May you all rejoice."
The teacher said: "Your learning is still shallow, your insight not yet broad.
Why suddenly resolve to sacrifice your beloved body?"
The prince replied:
"I made a vow long ago to sacrifice a thousand bodies.
Previously, I have already sacrificed nine hundred and ninety-nine bodies.
Today's sacrifice completes the thousand. Therefore, I sacrifice it.
I ask my teacher to rejoice."
The teacher said:
"Your aspiration is lofty and sublime. You will surely attain the Way first. Do not forget us."
The prince bid farewell to his teacher and departed.
The teacher and five hundred ascetics, eyes filled with tears, escorted the prince to the cliff's edge.
At that time, there was an elder named Fùlán.
Leading five hundred men and women, he brought offerings up the mountain.
Seeing the prince sacrifice himself, he wept in sorrow.
He too followed the prince to the cliff's edge.
Before the crowd, the prince made a great vow:
"I now sacrifice my body to save living beings.
May all merit swiftly lead to bodhi.
May I attain the vajra body, eternal bliss, self, purity, and the unconditioned dharmakāya.
May those not yet liberated be liberated, those not yet awakened be awakened, those not yet at peace be at peace.
This body of mine is impermanent, suffering, and a gathering of poisons.
This body is impure, with nine orifices flowing filth, bitten and stung by the four great poisonous snakes.
The five sword-wielding thieves pursue, wound, and cut it.
Such a body, unreliable, is nourished with fine delicacies and the pleasures of the five desires.
After this body's life ends, it brings no good reward or gratitude.
Instead, it falls into hell, enduring immeasurable suffering.
This human body should only be made to suffer, not given pleasure."
He further made a vow:
"Now I use my flesh and blood to save that starving tigress.
As for my remaining śarīra bones,
my parents will later certainly build a stūpa for them.
May all beings whose illnesses and sufferings arise from past karmic causes, and whom medicines, acupuncture, and moxibustion cannot cure,
come to my stūpa and make sincere offerings.
According to the severity of their illness, within a hundred days, they will surely be healed.
If this is truly not false, may the devas rain down fragrant flowers."
Immediately, maṇḍārava flowers rained down, and the earth shook.
The prince then removed his deerskin robe and wrapped it around his head.
He threw himself down before the tigress.
The tigress ate the bodhisattva's flesh,
and both mother and cubs survived.
Those on the cliff, seeing the prince
devoured by the tiger, his bones and flesh scattered,
wailed loudly, their cries shaking the mountains.
Some beat their chests, threw themselves down, writhing on the ground.
Some meditated.
Some bowed their heads in repentance.
The Śuddhāvāsa devas, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, and others,
along with countless devas of the sun and moon,
all aroused the mind of unsurpassed bodhi.
They made music, burned incense, scattered flowers, and made offerings to the prince,
singing these words:
"Excellent, Mahāsattva!
From now, not long hence, you shall sit at the place of enlightenment."
The five hundred ascetics all aroused the intention for unsurpassed true enlightenment.
The ascetic master attained the patience of the unborn.
The queen sent messengers with food.
They only saw his clothes, umbrella, bowl, staff, bottles, and jars in the stone chamber.
They asked the ascetics everywhere.
In groups of ten or five, they faced each other weeping.
They went to the master's place.
They only saw the master, cheek resting on his hand, eyes filled with tears, groaning as he sat.
They questioned all around, but no one would answer.
The messengers were terrified.
They gave the food to the ascetics and hurried back to report everything to the queen.
The queen said:
"Disaster! My son is dead."
She beat her chest, cried out, and ran to the king.
The king heard and fainted.
Ministers advised the king:
"The prince is in the mountains.
May Your Majesty rest a little."
The king, queen, consorts, court ladies, officials, and common people rushed up the mountain.
Elder Fùlán came to meet the king and told him:
"Yesterday, the prince threw himself from the cliff, offering his flesh to feed the tiger.
Now only his bones remain, scattered on the ground." They went together to the corpse.
The king, queen, consorts, court ladies, ministers, officials, and people cried out in grief, shaking the valleys.
The king and queen fell upon their son's body, hearts broken, fainting unconscious.
A consort came forward, cradled his head, and smoothed the prince's hair, saying:
"Rather let my body be shattered to dust than let my lord perish suddenly like this."
Then the ministers addressed the king:
"The prince practiced giving, vowing to save all beings.
He was not seized by the impermanent killing demon.
Before his body decays, we should make offerings."
They collected his bones and brought them out of the valley mouth.
On level ground, they piled sandalwood and fragrant wood,
and fragrant oil, and cremated him.
They collected the śarīra and built a seven-jeweled stūpa.
That prince was I myself.
The king was my present father, Shūtóután.
The queen was my mother, Móyé.
The consort was present-day Qúyí.
The one who cremated him was Ānán.
The mountain ascetic master was Maitreya.
Long ago in Jambudvīpa, there was a king named Fàntiān.
The king had a son named Tánmógàn.
He deeply delighted in the true Dharma.
Śakra transformed into a brāhmaṇa and said:
"I can expound the Dharma."
The prince bowed at his feet, reverently requesting to hear it.
The brāhmaṇa said:
"I have studied for a long time.
How can you wish to hear it just like that?
If you can spare neither body and life nor wife and children,
and enter a great fire pit as an offering,
then I will give you the Dharma."
The prince did exactly as he said.
He made a great fire pit.
The king, queen, and court ladies
went to the palace to persuade the brāhmaṇa,
begging him to take the kingdom, city, wife, and children as servants,
and not let the prince throw himself into the fire.
The brāhmaṇa said:
"I do not force him; it is according to his will.
But if it is like this, I will not expound it."
The king proclaimed throughout the land that in seven days the prince would burn himself.
Those who wished to see should come early that day.
The entire country, noble and common, gathered at once.
They pleaded sorrowfully, firmly requesting as before.
The prince said to the crowd:
"For long ages in the cycle of birth and death, I have lost countless bodies.
Among humans, out of greed, they kill each other.
In heaven, when life ends, they lose their desires and suffer sorrow.
In hell, they are burned, boiled, cut, sliced, in ash rivers and sword trees, pain piercing heart and marrow.
Among hungry ghosts, a hundred poisons bore through their bodies.
In the animal realm, their bodies feed many mouths, they eat grass and bear heavy burdens.
Enduring all these sufferings, this body's life is empty.
Never with a good mind for the Dharma.
Now I abandon this foul, filthy form to seek purity and excellence.
Why do you wish to hinder me?
When I attain Buddhahood, I will give you the fivefold dharmakāya."
The prince then stood at the edge of the fire pit.
The brāhmaṇa said:
Hearing this, the prince was about to jump into the fire.
Then Śakra and Brahmā took hold of one of his hands
and challenged him, saying:
"All living beings in Jambudvīpa
rely on the prince's grace; none fail to find their place.
If you throw yourself into the fire now, the world loses its father. Why drown yourself alone, abandoning all?"
The prince declined, saying:
"Do not obstruct my mind for the unsurpassed Way."
He threw his body into the fire pit.
Heaven and earth greatly shook.
Devas in the sky wept together, tears like heavy rain.
Then the fierce fire pit turned into a pool of flowers.
The prince sat on a lotus throne.
Devas rained flowers up to his knees.
King Brahmā is present-day King Jìngfàn.
The mother is present-day Queen Móyé.
The prince is present-day the World-Honored One.
During the time of the Buddha Vipaśyin,
the king of Bālànà was intelligent, benevolent, and virtuous, but had no children.
He served a mountain deity for twelve years, praying tirelessly.
Later, his first consort gave birth to a son.
His nature was kind and free from anger, and he possessed all the marks of a great man.
The king summoned his ministers to divine the child's fortune.
They named him Rěnrǔ (Endurance).
As he grew older, he greatly enjoyed practicing generosity.
He treated all beings with equal compassion.
The state had six ministers.
Treacherous, deceitful, flattering, and wicked, they were lawless and hated by all, and they envied and resented the crown prince.
At that time, the king fell gravely ill, and his life was hanging by a thread.
Prince Rěnrǔ asked the king's ministers,
"The king is critically ill; what should we do now?"
The ministers replied,
"A rare medicine is needed, but it is hard to obtain. His life is not long for this world." The prince, grief-stricken and distressed, fell to the ground.
The wicked ministers devised a plan to eliminate the prince.
They addressed the prince, saying,
"The king's illness requires a medicine that is difficult to obtain."
The prince asked,
"What is it?"
They answered,
"It is the eyes and marrow of a person who has never felt anger.
If we can obtain this medicine, the king's life will surely be saved."
The prince said,
"I seem to be such a person."
He then bid farewell to his mother
and gathered the kings of the smaller states,
proclaiming to the assembly,
"I now take leave of you all with this body."
He then summoned a caṇḍāla to break his bones, extract the marrow, and gouge out his two eyes.
The ministers pounded and mixed these into a medicine and presented it to the king.
The king took it, and his illness was cured.
He asked his ministers,
"This medicine is extraordinary; it has relieved my suffering.
Who prepared it?"
The ministers replied,
"This medicine was prepared by the crown prince."
The king asked,
"Where is he now?"
They answered,
"He is outside, his body injured and broken, and his life is not long for this world."
The king wept in great sorrow.
He went to his son, but the prince had already passed away.
His mother, overwhelmed with grief, threw herself upon the corpse, lamenting,
"I must have committed grave sins in a past life, deserving to be crushed to dust,
that I should cause my son to lose his life."
They cremated his body with gośīrṣa sandalwood
and built a seven-jeweled stūpa from his bones.
In the past, there was a king of Jambudvīpa named Zhìlì,
who constantly protected the Buddha's teachings with deep sincerity.
A bhikṣu was related to the king
and was highly respected by the king and beloved by the people.
The king never tired of seeing him.
The bhikṣu developed a severe sore on his thigh,
and no medicine in the kingdom could cure it.
The king and his twenty thousand consorts were all deeply concerned.
One night, the king dreamed
that a heavenly being came and told him,
"If you wish to cure this bhikṣu,
you must feed him the flesh and blood of a living person, and then he will recover."
The king awoke, troubled.
He thought, "The bhikṣu's illness is severe, and this medicine is required."
He ordered his ministers,
"Where can we obtain the flesh and blood of a living person?"
At that time, the crown prince, named Zhìzhǐ,
addressed the king,
"Do not worry, Your Majesty.
Human flesh and blood are the lowliest of things.
What the world values does not contradict the Way."
The king said, "Excellent."
The prince remained silent.
He then returned to his quarters, took a knife, cut flesh from his thigh,
and sent the flesh and blood to the bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu consumed it, and the sore was cured; his body became peaceful and at ease.
When the king heard that the bhikṣu had recovered,
he was overjoyed and could not contain his happiness.
The prince's wound naturally healed.
The king bestowed all the treasures of the kingdom upon the prince.
The one with such sincere intent at that time was the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.
King Zhìlì was Maitreya.
Prince Zhìzhǐ was myself.
There was also Prince Yuèguāng,
who went out for an excursion.
A leper saw him and stopped his chariot, saying,
"I am gravely ill, suffering and distressed.
While you, Prince, amuse yourself, enjoying happiness alone,
please take pity with great compassion and save me."
The prince, upon hearing this, asked the physicians,
who said, "We need the blood and marrow of a person who has never felt anger from birth to adulthood. Applying and consuming these will cure him."
The prince thought to himself,
"Even if such a person exists, who clings to life and cherishes longevity, how could we obtain it?
Apart from myself, there is no one else."
He then summoned a caṇḍāla,
ordering him to cut the flesh from his body, break his bones, extract the marrow to apply to the patient, and give his blood to drink.
Such acts of giving, even giving away one's wife and children, were done without reluctance,
as if discarding grass and wood, viewing the objects given as arising from conditions,
seeking their true essence and finding nothing obtainable,
all purified like the nature of nirvāṇa,
until attaining the patience of the birthless dharmas.
This is the practice of dāna-pāramitā with a body bound by karma.
During the time of the Vipaśyin Buddha’s Dharma.
In the kingdom of Bālànài.
There was a king named Luóshé.
He had only three sons.
Each was appointed to govern a small state.
At that time, the king was wise and governed with the true Dharma, never wronging the people.
The king possessed virtuous power, so wind and rain came in due season, and the five grains were abundant.
The king had a chief minister named Luóhóuluó.
He harbored evil rebellion and suddenly raised an army to attack the kingdom of Bālànài.
He ended the great king’s life.
Then he attacked the first and second princes.
Next, he pursued the third.
The third prince was tall and imposing, upright and exceptionally handsome, gentle and kind by nature.
He always spoke with a smile, bringing benefit and never hurting others’ feelings.
He governed the people with the true Dharma, and the land was prosperous and joyful.
The state’s resources were abundant, and all quarters praised him.
The deities in the sky and all spirits and ghosts also revered and loved him.
He had a prince named Xūchántí.
He was intelligent, compassionate, and fond of giving alms.
His body was golden in color, with seven places full and smooth, possessing all the marks of a great man.
He was only seven years old, and his father loved and cherished him, never parting from him even for a moment.
At that time, the palace guardian spirit spoke to the king, saying:
“Luóhóu has rebelled with evil intent, plotting to seize the throne and intending to kill your father, the king.
He has raised troops and captured your two elder brothers, already ending their lives.
His army and horses will soon arrive here.”
When the king heard these words,
he was filled with sorrow and distress, unable to control himself.
His heart and liver felt as if bursting, and he fell to the ground, writhing.
After a long while, he regained consciousness.
In a faint voice, he addressed the voice in the sky:
“Who are you?
I only hear your voice,
but do not see your form.
Is what you just said truly so?”
The voice replied to the king:
“I am the palace guardian spirit. Because you are wise and upright and do not wrong the people, I have come to inform you.
You should leave quickly; he will arrive soon.”
The king considered fleeing to a neighboring country, and there were two routes.
One route took seven days, the other fourteen days.
He immediately prepared a seven-day supply of food for one person.
Entering the palace, he called Xūchántí and held him on his lap.
The queen came forward and asked:
“Great King, you seem to be in a state of fear.”
The king said:
“This is not for you to know.”
The queen replied:
“My body and yours are like the two wings of a bird.
How can you say it does not concern me?”
The king then told her what had happened.
He immediately took the prince and set out on the road.
The queen followed behind, but in confusion and distress, she mistakenly took the fourteen-day route.
The road was treacherous, with no water or grass.
After traveling for several days, the food supply for the three of them was exhausted.
The road ahead was still long.
The king and queen cried out loudly, weeping.
“How strange! How bitter! From birth until now, we have never heard of such suffering.
How is it that today we personally experience it?”
They deeply regretted and blamed themselves.
Pressed by hunger and thirst, their lives hung by a thread.
They thought of a plan.
Not wanting all three to die together, they considered killing the queen to save themselves and the child.
Xūchántí saw the king’s unusual expression.
He stepped forward, took his father’s hand, and asked:
“What are you planning to do?”
The father, with tears filling his eyes, said to his son in a faint voice:
“I intend to kill your mother, take her flesh and blood to sustain your life.”
Xūchántí, holding back tears, said to his father:
“Where is there a son who eats his mother’s flesh?
If I do not eat the flesh, both mother and son will die.
I wish you would kill me instead to save my parents’ lives.”
When the king heard his son’s words,
he fainted on the spot. In a faint voice, he said to his son:
“You are like my own eyes. Where is there a person who gouges out his own eyes and then eats them?
I would rather lose my life than kill you and eat your flesh.”
Xūchántí said again:
“If you die, your flesh and blood will rot and stink.
Before many days pass, I have a wish.
If you go against it, you are not compassionate parents.”
At that time, the king said to the prince:
“I will not go against your wish.”
Xūchántí said:
“I only wish that every day you cut three catties of flesh from my body.
Two parts to offer to my parents,
and one part for me to eat to sustain my life.”
The parents wept and agreed.
They proceeded on the road, but after two more days, the flesh on his body was nearly exhausted, only his joints, bones, and sinews remained connected, and his life was not yet ended.
The parents held him and cried out loudly: “We are heartless.
We have recklessly eaten your flesh, causing you such pain.
The road ahead is still far, and we have not yet reached our destination.
Now your flesh is exhausted; let us die together and gather our corpses in one place.”
At that time, Xūchántí said in a faint voice, advising them:
“You have eaten my flesh and come this far on the road.
Parents, do not act like ordinary people now.
Do not refuse me out of pity because we are dying together.
You may cut the remaining clean flesh from between the joints of my body.
Use it to sustain yourselves and reach your destination.”
The parents followed his words, and after eating, they wept and parted.
Xūchántí stood up and watched his parents.
The parents wept loudly as they continued on the road.
When the parents had gone far and could no longer see Xūchántí,
the prince longed for his parents, not taking his eyes off them for a moment.
After a long while, he fell to the ground. The fresh flesh and blood on his body emitted a fragrance in all ten directions.
Mosquitoes and horseflies,
smelling the fragrance of flesh and blood, came and covered his body.
They swarmed all over him, biting and eating, causing unbearable pain and suffering.
His life not yet ended, he made a vow aloud:
“May the evils and misfortunes from past lives be completely eradicated from now on.
From this day forward, I will never commit them again.
Now I offer this body to nourish my parents.
May my parents always receive ten times the remaining blessings.
May the remaining flesh and blood be given to these mosquitoes and horseflies, so they may all be satisfied.”
When he made this vow,
heaven and earth shook in six ways.
The sun lost its brilliance, and birds and beasts scattered and fled.
The great sea surged, and Mount Sumeru rose and sank.
The deities of the six desire heavens were all frightened and descended to Jambudvīpa.
They transformed into lions, tigers, wolves, and the like.
With eyes wide open, bristling whiskers, roaring and leaping on the ground, they rushed forward as if to pounce and bite.
At that time, Xūchántí saw these beasts making such fierce displays.
In a faint voice, he said:
“If you wish to eat me, take as you please. Why do you frighten me?”
At that moment, the heavenly king Śakra resumed his heavenly form.
When the prince saw him, he was immeasurably joyful.
Śakra then asked the prince:
“You are able to give up what is difficult to give up.
With such merit, do you wish to be reborn in heaven as a Māra king or a Brahma king?”
The prince replied:
“I wish to attain unsurpassed enlightenment.”
Śakra said:
“Empty words; who will believe you?”
The prince vowed:
“If I am deceitful, may the wounds on my body never heal.
If not, may I be restored to wholeness.”
Immediately, his blood turned into milk, and his body was restored, more upright and handsome than before.
At that time, the heavenly king Śakra bowed at his feet and exclaimed: “Excellent!
I am not your equal.
You are diligent and courageous; you will attain enlightenment. Please liberate me first.”
At that time, the heavenly king Śakra
disappeared into the sky and was no longer seen.
At that time, the king and queen reached the neighboring country.
When the neighboring king heard of it,
he came out to welcome them from afar. After meeting, they recounted the events in detail.
He provided for all their needs, fulfilling their wishes.
The neighboring king was moved by
the prince’s compassion and filial piety.
He immediately raised an army and returned with that king.
They marched against Luóhóu and returned along the same road.
When they reached the place where they had parted from the prince,
they intended to collect his remains. Looking ahead, they wept in sorrow.
As they drew nearer, they saw from afar that the prince’s body was restored to wholeness.
They went forward, embraced him, and were filled with both sorrow and joy.
At that time, Xūchántí recounted all that had happened to his parents.
The parents rejoiced.
They mounted a great elephant together and returned to their own country.
The prince’s blessings were profound, and they were able to return to their homeland.
They immediately established the prince as the great king.
The king at that time is now King Śuddhodana.
The mother at that time is now Queen Māyā.
Xūchántí is now the Buddha himself.
The heavenly king Śakra at that time is Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya.
In the past, there was a king of Yèbō Country named Shīsuí.
His crown prince was named Xūdànà.
He universally protected all with the four immeasurables, and his words did not harm others.
He constantly vowed to practice charity to save and aid all living beings.
So that in my future lives I may receive boundless blessings.
Foolish people do not see the impermanence of change and say things can be preserved.
The wise perceive the five threats to wealth.
If one desired food, clothing, gold, silver, various treasures, carriages, horses, fields, or houses, there was nothing he would not give.
His radiance and reputation spread far, praised throughout the four seas.
The king, his father, had a white elephant.
Its majestic and fierce martial power could match sixty; when hostile countries came to fight, this elephant would always win.
The kings [of those hostile states] deliberated together.
They sent eight Brahmins to beg for the white elephant.
The prince joyfully asked what they sought, and they replied:
"We wish to beg for the white elephant that walks upon lotuses."
The elephant was named Luóshéhétán.
The prince said, "Excellent."
Gold, silver, and assorted treasures, take whatever your hearts desire.
He immediately commanded his attendants:
"Quickly, saddle the white elephant with a golden and silver harness and bridle."
Holding the elephant's bridle in his left hand,
and a golden vessel in his right,
he washed the Brahmins' hands.
With compassionate joy, he gave them the elephant.
The Brahmins were overjoyed.
They finished chanting blessings, mounted the elephant, and left.
The prime minister and all the officials were deeply dismayed.
They all said:
"This elephant's strength is fierce; in battle it always prevails.
Now you have given it to an enemy country.
What shall we rely on?"
They reported this in full to the king.
The king heard this and was grief-stricken. After a long time, he said:
"The prince greatly delights in the Buddha's path.
His practice is to aid the poor and destitute, to compassionately nurture; there is no way to stop him.
Even if we were to detain and punish him,
that would be unrighteous."
All the officials said:
"The teaching of mutual admonition and correction is surely not mistaken.
Detention and punishment are cruel.
We dare not hear of it.
Banish him from the country, place him in the wilderness.
For ten years, let him reflect and repent.
This is our wish."
The king then dispatched a messenger,
instructing him to say:
"The elephant is a national treasure; how could you give it to an enemy?
I cannot bear to punish you harshly; leave the country quickly."
The messenger, following orders, proclaimed this as instructed.
The prince replied:
"I dare not disobey the heavenly command.
I wish to use my personal wealth for seven more days of almsgiving, not daring to encroach upon the state's [resources]."
The messenger reported this.
The king then permitted it.
The prince joyfully gave great alms to the destitute.
He announced: "Come quickly, take whatever you desire."
When the seven days were completed, the poor had all become wealthy.
His wife was named Màndí.
She was originally a princess.
Her face was radiant and graceful, unmatched in the land.
From head to foot, she wore jeweled necklaces of the seven treasures.
He said to his wife:
"Rise and listen to my words.
The great king is banishing me to the Dántè Mountains for twelve years as the term. Do you know this?"
His wife looked at the prince in shock, shedding tears, and said:
"For what crime are you banished, abandoning the honor of the kingdom to dwell in deep mountains?"
He replied:
"I used the kingdom's famous elephant to give to an enemy king.
The king and his ministers, angered, are banishing me."
His wife then made a vow:
"May the kingdom be prosperous, the king, ministers, and millions of people enjoy boundless wealth and longevity.
I shall only establish my resolve in the mountains and wilderness, vowing to achieve the Way."
The prince said:
"But those mountains and wilds are places of terror.
Tigers, wolves, and harmful beasts make it difficult to dwell there.
There are also poisonous creatures, specters, demons, and hungry ghosts.
Thunder, lightning, fierce winds, rain, clouds, and fog are most terrifying.
Extreme heat and cold, trees difficult to rely on, thorns and sharp stones unfit for treading.
You are a king's daughter.
Born into glory and pleasure, raised in the palace.
Your clothes are fine and soft, your food and drink sweet and delicious.
You sleep within curtains and canopies, with various music sounding in your ears.
Your wishes are immediately gratified.
Now dwelling in the mountains and wilds,
sleeping on grass mats, eating fruits and vegetables—this is not what humans can endure.
How can you bear it?"
His wife said:
"Fine silks, various treasures, canopies, sweet delicacies—
what benefit are they to me if I am parted from you, my prince?
A king uses his banner as his mark.
Fire uses smoke as its mark.
A woman uses her husband as her mark.
I rely on you, my prince, as I rely on my two parents.
When you were in the country, giving alms to the four directions, I always shared your vow.
Now that you must traverse dangers, should I remain behind clinging to glory? Is that the way of benevolence?
If beggars come and do not see my husband, the sorrow in my heart would surely knot, and I would die without doubt."
The prince said:
"If people from distant lands come to beg for my wife and children, I have no mind to refuse.
If you, bound by affection, were to violate the path of generosity, you would cut off the great flow and ruin my important duty."
His wife said:
"Your almsgiving, my prince, is rare in the world. You must fulfill your great vow; be careful not to grow weary.
For a hundred thousand, a million ages, no one like you has undertaken the Buddha's important task. I dare not disobey."
The prince said, "Excellent."
He then took his wife and children to bid farewell to his mother.
Bowing his head to the ground, he sorrowfully took his leave, saying:
"I pray you relinquish heavy thoughts and preserve your jade-like body in peace.
State affairs are burdensome; frequently advise with compassion.
Do not, acting freely, wrong those heaven-sent people.
Endure what cannot be endured."
His mother said:
"Before I had a child, I made vows seeking an heir.
During the pregnancy, it was like a tree holding a flower, daily awaiting its maturity.
Heaven did not thwart my wish, granting me a son.
I nurtured and raised him to adulthood, and now we must part in life.
The consorts and concubines will no longer respect me."
The prince, his wife, and children bowed in farewell and withdrew.
Everyone in the palace, great and small, choked with sobs.
Going out, he sorrowfully parted from all the officials and left the city together [with his family].
All secretly said:
"The prince is the country's sacred spirit, the most precious treasure.
What heart do his two parents have to banish him?"
The prince sat outside the city, thanking those who had escorted him, and sent them back to their homes.
The millions of people bowed low, all raising cries of sorrow.
Some stamped their feet, called to heaven, the sound shaking the country.
Having gone far from the country, they sat under a tree.
A Brahmin came from afar, begging for his personal jewels, fine clothes, and his wife and children.
Pearls and gems he gave entirely as alms.
He had his wife and children mount the carriage and, taking the reins, they departed.
Just as he was about to set out on the road,
he again met a Brahmin begging for the horse.
He gave the horse to him.
He himself pulled the carriage from the shafts to proceed on the road.
Again he met a Brahmin who came to beg for the carriage.
He immediately gave the carriage away.
The prince's carriage, horses, clothes, personal jewels, and miscellaneous possessions were all completely exhausted, with nothing left.
He had his wife carry the girl, while he himself carried the boy.
After twenty-one days, they finally reached the mountains.
The prince beheld the mountain: trees lush and flourishing, flowing springs of sweet water, delicious fruits abundant.
Wild ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks sported among them.
The prince said to his wife:
"The trees reach the heavens, with few broken or injured.
Flocks of birds sing mournfully; springs and fruits are plentiful.
Sufficient for food and drink, we must only attend to the Way."
The mountain-dwelling ascetics all upheld discipline and loved learning.
There was one ascetic named Āzhūtuó.
He had long dwelt in the mountains and possessed excellent virtue.
The prince then went with his wife and children to see him.
Bowing his head, he said:
"I have brought my wife and children here to study the Way.
I pray you bestow your great compassion and instruct me to fulfill my aspiration."
The ascetic instructed him.
The prince then built a hut with firewood and grass, tied his hair with rushes, ate fruits, and drank from springs.
The boy was named Yēlì.
He wore small grass garments and followed his father in and out.
The girl was named Jìnúyán.
She wore deerskin clothes and followed her mother in and out.
After one night in the mountains, heaven increased the springs and caused medicinal trees to grow anew.
Later, there was an old, poor Brahmin named Jiūliúsūn.

Having traveled far, I am weary and exhausted.
He replied,
"I have come from there, my whole body aching and in pain.
I am also very hungry and thirsty."
The prince offered fruit juice.
"Now, in my dire straits, I hope to prolong my humble life."
The prince, moved with compassion, said,
"I do not regret exhausting my wealth."
The Brahmin said,
"You could give me your two children to support me in my old age."
He answered,
"My heart does not refuse."
The prince called his children.
The brothers were afraid.
They also said to each other,
"Our father is calling for us.
He must intend to give us to this demon.
To disobey his command would be unfitting."
The prince knew they were hiding in the cave.
He removed the firewood and saw them.
The children came out, embraced their father, trembling and weeping, saying,
"This is a demon, not a Brahmin.
We have seen Brahmins many times; none have looked like this.
Do not use us as food for a demon.
Why is our mother so late in returning with fruit?
Today we are certain to die, devoured by a demon.
When our mother returns seeking us,
like a cow seeking her calf,
she will run wild, weeping in grief.
Father will surely regret it."
The prince said,
"In my life of giving, I have never felt the slightest regret.
I have promised; you must not disobey."
The Brahmin said,
"I am old and weak; if the children run away to their mother, great prince, in your vast generosity, bind them and hand them over."
The prince held the children and had the Brahmin bind them, taking the end of the rope himself.
The two children threw themselves down, writhing before their father, wailing and calling for their mother, saying,
"Heavenly gods, earth spirits, mountain and tree deities, please tell our mother,
'Your two children have been given away; come see them once.'"
Their grief moved heaven and earth; the mountain spirits roared as if with thunder.
At that time, the mother, while picking fruit, felt her heart [beating anxiously].
She looked up at the blue sky but saw no clouds or rain.
Her right eye twitched, her left foot itched, and milk flowed from her breasts.
The mother thought,
"This is a very great omen; I must return to see my children."
She abandoned the fruit and hurried back, frantic as if mad.
Indra thought,
"The Bodhisattva's resolve is lofty; he wishes to accomplish a great task.
If his wife arrives, it may ruin his noble intention."
He transformed into a lion and crouched blocking the path.
The woman said,
"You are the king of beasts.
I am the daughter of a king among men; we both dwell in this mountain.
I have two children, both still very young.
They have not eaten since morning and are waiting for me."
The lion moved aside, and the woman proceeded on the path.
Returning again ahead, he transformed into a white wolf.
The woman spoke as before, and the wolf also moved aside.
He then transformed into a tiger; considering the Brahmin was far away, he finally withdrew.
The woman saw the prince sitting alone and said in distress and fear,
"Where have my children gone, that you sit alone now?
The children always come running to meet me when I return.
They jump for joy, laughing happily, saying, 'Mother is back!'
Now their playthings—clay elephants, clay oxen, clay horses, clay pigs, and various clever objects—are scattered on the ground.
Seeing this, my heart is stricken; I shall go mad.
Have they been devoured by tigers, wolves, demons, or thieves?
Quickly release me from this anguish; I shall surely die."
The prince, after a long silence, said,
"A Brahmin came and asked for the two children.
He said,
'My years are spent, my life is frail; I wish to sustain myself.' I gave them to him."
When the wife heard these words, she was struck, fell to the ground, writhing in grief and weeping, saying through tears,
"It is exactly as in a dream I had last night.
I dreamed I saw an old, poor Brahmin
cut off my two breasts and seize them, running swiftly away.
It was precisely for this moment."
Wailing and calling to heaven, she shook the entire mountain region.
The prince saw his wife's intense grief.
It was extreme.
He said to her,
"I originally feared that your deep filial piety and reverence would lead you to seek nothing that was not given, and our vow was very clear.
But now your grief disturbs my heart."
The wife said,
"Prince, your pursuit of the Way—how exceedingly arduous it is!"
Indra and the various gods all deliberated, saying,
"The prince's Way is vast; he gives universally without end. Let us test him by asking for his wife."
Indra transformed into a Brahmin and said,
"You possess the benevolence of heaven and earth.
You universally aid all living beings, giving without refusal; therefore I come to submit to you.
Your wife is virtuous and chaste, her virtue fragrant and far-known; therefore I come to beg for her."
He answered, "Very well."
Heaven and earth suddenly shook greatly; gods, humans, and spirits all sighed in admiration.
The Brahmin said,
"I am the Lord of Heaven, not an ordinary man of the world.
I came to test you.
Your Buddha-wisdom and exemplary conduct are difficult to match.
Now, what wish do you have? Ask freely, and it shall be granted."
The prince said,
"I wish to attain great wealth, to always delight in giving, without greed surpassing this.
Now, my royal father and the country's ministers and people—I long to see them again."
The Lord of Heaven said,
"So be it." Then he vanished instantly.
The Brahmin joyfully obtained his [children].
Walking, he felt no fatigue, leading the two children continuously as if having regained lost servants.
The children, grandsons of a king, accustomed to glory and freedom,
taken from their parents, bound by ropes,
the tied places all wounded, wailing and calling for their mother.
He whipped them to make them walk; their blood stained the ground red.
Heavenly spirits, taking pity, loosened their bonds and healed their wounds.
They caused sweet fruits to grow and made the ground soft.
The brothers picked fruit and fed each other, saying,
"Sweet as the fruit in the garden."
"The ground is as soft as the felt mats by the king's side."
The brothers supported each other, looked up to heaven, and called for their mother.
Weeping, tears streaming down, they arrived at his house. He laughed and said,
"I have obtained two slaves for you; use them as you wish."
The wife looked at the children and said,
"They are not fit to be slaves.
These children are handsome, their hands and feet delicate; they are not suited for labor.
Let us take them to sell, then buy suitable servants."
They also intended to go to another country.
Heaven confused their path, so they went to their native land instead.
The multitude recognized them and all said,
"These are the royal grandsons!"
They reported it to the king.
The king summoned them to the palace.
Everyone in the palace, great and small, could not help but sigh and weep.
The king wanted to embrace the two children, but they would not approach.
The king said, "Why?"
The children said,
"Formerly we were royal grandsons; now we are lowly slaves.
What right have we to sit on the king's knee?"
The king asked the Brahmin,
"How did you obtain these children?"
He answered truthfully.
The king said, "For how much are you selling the children?"
The Brahmin did not answer.
The grandson [the boy] said sharply,
"A boy is worth a thousand silver coins and
a hundred head each of oxen and cows.
A girl is worth a thousand gold coins and two hundred head each of oxen and cows."
The king said,
"The boy is older but cheap, the girl younger but expensive—why is that?"
He replied,
"The crown prince is both sage and benevolent, relied upon by all.
Yet he was banished far away; thus I know the boy is cheap.
A commoner's daughter, if she possesses beauty, may dwell in the deep palace;
thus I know the girl is expensive."
The king said,
"An eight-year-old child yet speaks the words of a lofty scholar!
How much more so his father!"
Everyone in the palace, great and small, hearing his indirect admonition, could not help but weep.
The king paid the full amount as stated, and the Brahmin departed.
The king embraced his two grandchildren and sat them on his knee, saying,
"Earlier you would not come to be embraced; why do you come so quickly now?"
They replied,
"Earlier we were slaves; now we are royal grandsons."
He said, "What does your father eat to sustain himself in the mountains?"
Both children said,
"He eats vegetables and tree fruit to sustain himself."
Daily he finds amusement with birds and beasts, and also has no sorrow in his heart."
The king sent messengers to summon him.
The messengers set out on the road.
The trees in the mountains bowed and stretched as if performing the rituals of kneeling and rising.
Hundreds of birds sang mournfully, stirring human emotions with grief.
The prince said,
"What auspicious sign is this?"
His wife, lying on the ground, said,
"The king's anger has dissolved; messengers are coming to welcome you. The spirits are aiding goodness, hence this auspicious sign arises."
The wife, since losing her children, had lain on the ground.
When the messengers arrived, she then rose and bowed to receive the king's command.
The messengers said,
"The king and the queen have reduced their food, weeping incessantly; their health declines daily, longing to see the crown prince."
The prince looked around, longing for the mountain trees and flowing springs, wiped his tears, and mounted the carriage.
From the moment the messengers departed, the whole country rejoiced.
They repaired the roads, swept clean, prepared tents and canopies in advance.
They burned incense, scattered flowers, with music, banners, and parasols.
The whole country hastened respectfully, offering endless congratulations.
The prince entered the city, bowed his head to apologize for his fault, then withdrew to inquire after their well-being.
The king again entrusted the entire state treasury of jewels to the crown prince, urging him to give alms.
Impoverished people from neighboring countries came like rivers flowing to the sea.
Old enemies, seeing him, came and bowed, declaring themselves subjects.
Tribute arrived continuously; bandits and robbers esteemed benevolence, thieves competed in giving, weapons were stored away, prisons were abolished.
All beings enjoyed eternal happiness; all directions celebrated goodness, accumulating virtue without cease.
Though he first suffered hardship as an infant, now he is the honored one of the boundless.
After the prince's life ended, he was born in the Tuṣita Heaven.
From heaven he descended, born in the palace of King Śuddhodana.
That is my present self.
The father king is Ānanda.
The wife is Gopī.
The son is Rāhula.
The daughter is the mother of the Arhat Jūjī.
The Lord of Heaven Indra is Maitreya.
The hunter is Udāyana.
The swineherd is Mahākāśyapa.
The Brahmin who bought the children is Devadatta.
Thus is the Bodhisattva's compassionate giving.
In the past, in the country of Vaiśālī,
a plum tree grew in the king's garden.
Its branches and leaves were luxuriant and had an extraordinary luster, fragrance, and beauty.
The king treasured it greatly.
None but the noble and esteemed within the palace were allowed to taste its fruit.
At that time, there was a Brahmin.
His household was wealthy beyond compare in the entire country, and he was intelligent, erudite, and exceptionally talented.
The king appointed him as a high minister.
When the king hosted a feast and served plums, he gave one plum to the Brahmin.
Seeing the plum's extraordinary fragrance and beauty, the Brahmin asked:
"Could I perhaps request a small sapling from this plum tree?"
The king said:
"If you wish, I will give you a sapling."
The Brahmin planted it.
He watered it morning and night, and the branches grew lush and beautiful. After three years, it bore fruit.
Its brilliance and size were like those of the king's tree.
The Brahmin was overjoyed and thought to himself:
"My wealth is countless, no less than the king's.
Only I lacked this plum. Now that I have it, I lack nothing."
He then took and ate it, but it was extremely bitter and astringent.
He then reflected:
"It must be that the soil is not fertile enough."
He then took milk and fed it to one cow, then successively to a hundred cows, and boiled it into clarified butter.
He watered the tree with it every day until the next year.
The fruit then became sweet and delicious.
But a knot grew beside the tree.
It was as large as a clenched fist.
As days and months passed, it grew larger, and he feared it would hinder the fruit.
He was about to chop it off.
But he feared it would injure the tree.
He hesitated and could not decide.
The knot then grew a branch.
It was thick, straight, well-shaped, and rose above the tree's crown.
It was seventy feet above the ground.
Its twigs produced many branches, shaped like a canopy.
Its flowers and leaves were lush and beautiful, surpassing the main tree.
He then built a scaffold and climbed up to look.
He saw that within the canopy there was a pool of water.
It was clear and fragrant, with many bright flowers.
Parting the flowers to look beneath them,
he saw a girl in the pool of water.
The Brahmin picked her up and took her home to raise.
He named her Nǚnǚ.
By the age of fifteen, her appearance was端正, unparalleled in the world, and her fame spread to distant countries.
There were seven kings.
