They all came simultaneously to the Brahmin to seek Nǚnǚ's hand in marriage as their夫人.
The Brahmin did not know whom to give her to.
In his garden, he built a tall tower and placed Nǚnǚ atop it.
He said to the kings:
"This girl was not born to me.
She emerged from the plum tree herself.
Now seven kings all seek her.
If I give her to one, the other six will surely be angered.
I dare not be partial.
The girl is now in the tower in the garden.
Let the kings deliberate among yourselves.
Whoever should obtain her may take her; it is not for me to decide."
The seven kings argued among themselves,纷纭 without resolution.
That night, King Bǐngshā entered through a hidden channel, climbed the tower, and spent the night with her.
In the morning, as he was about to leave,
Nǚnǚ said:
"Your Majesty has graciously bestowed your noble presence upon me.
If I bear a child, it will be of royal lineage. To whom should I entrust it?"
The king said:
"If it is a boy, return him to me; if a girl, keep her with you."
The king then removed his gold ring seal and gave it to Nǚnǚ, saying:
"Take this as a token."
He went out and told his ministers:
"I have obtained Nǚnǚ and spent one night with her."
Bǐngshā's soldiers all shouted "Long live the king!" and said:
"Our king has obtained Nǚnǚ."
The other six kings heard this and each returned to their own countries.
Nǚnǚ gave birth to a boy.
At birth, he held a needle and medicine pouch in his hand.
The Brahmin said:
"This is the king's son, yet he holds medical instruments; he must be a physician king."
He was named Qíyù. By the age of eight,
he was intelligent and learned, surpassing his peers in writing and scholarship.
When playing with neighboring children, he often looked down on them.
The children scolded him:
"You fatherless son, born of a promiscuous woman! How dare you look down on us?"
Qíyù was startled and silent, not answering.
He returned home and asked his mother:
"I see that all the children are inferior to me,
yet they scold me, calling me a fatherless son.
Where is my father now?"
His mother said:
"Your father is King Bǐngshā."
Qíyù said:
"King Bǐngshā is in the country of Ràoyuèqí,
five hundred miles from here.
How then was I born?"
He took the ring and went to the country of Ràoyuèqí.
He entered the palace gate directly and went before the king.
He bowed to the king, knelt, and said:
"I am the prince, born of Nǚnǚ.
This year I am eight years old and have only now learned that I am of Your Majesty's lineage.
Therefore, I bring the finger ring seal as proof and have come from afar to return home."
The king saw the seal imprint.
Recalling his past vow, he knew this was his son.
Moved with compassion, he made him crown prince.
After two years had passed, it happened that Prince Āshéshì was born.
Qíyù then said to the king:
"When I was born, I held a needle and medicine pouch in my hand.
I am destined to be a physician king.
Although you have made me crown prince, it is not what I desire.
Your Majesty now has a legitimate son born.
He should inherit the noble succession.
I wish to go and study medicine."
The king then permitted it.
He ordered all the country's foremost physicians to teach him.
But Qíyù played and never attended the lessons.
The teachers reproached him, saying:
"Medicine is a humble craft, truly not something for a crown prince of such尊贵 to study.
However, the king's command cannot be disobeyed or neglected.
Since receiving the order, much time has passed.
Yet the crown prince has not learned a single word from us.
If the king asks us,
how shall we answer?"
Qíyù said:
"I was born with evidence of medicine in my hand.
Therefore, I requested the king to abandon荣耀 and seek medical learning. How could I be懈怠?
It is simply that what the teachers have to offer is not worth learning."
He then took the本草,药方,针脉, and various classics and questioned the teachers extensively.
The teachers could not answer.
Instead, they bowed to him and said: "The crown prince is divine and sage, beyond our reach.
Generations of疑难义理, please explain them, crown prince."
He then explained their meanings.
The physicians were delighted, bowed, and respectfully followed his teachings.
Qíyù then began to treat patients.
Those he treated were always cured, and his fame spread to distant countries.
Returning to the palace gate, he encountered a child carrying firewood. Looking at him, he saw the child's五脏 clearly and distinctly.
Qíyù thought to himself:
"The本草经 says:
There is a medicine king tree that illuminates the inside from the outside.
This child's firewood contains the medicine king tree."
He then asked:
"How much does this firewood sell for?"
The child said: "Ten coins."
He paid the ten coins as agreed.
The child set the firewood on the ground.
Then it became dark, and he could no longer see inside the child's abdomen.
Qíyù thought:
"I do not know which piece in the bundle is the medicine king wood."
He untied the two bundles and gathered the pieces one by one, placing them on the child's abdomen.
None illuminated the inside. He did this until both bundles of firewood were exhausted.
Finally, a small twig illuminated the inside of the abdomen.
Qíyù was overjoyed.
He knew this small twig must be the medicine king.
He returned all the firewood to the child.
The child happily left.
At that time, in the country, there was a girl from the Jiāluóyuè family, aged fifteen.
On the day she was to be married, she suddenly died of a headache.
Qíyù heard of this and went to her home to inquire.
"What illness did the girl usually have that led to her premature death?"
Her father said:
"The girl had a slight headache illness that grew worse daily; it struck this morning and caused her death."
Qíyù used the medicine king to illuminate the girl's head.
He saw sharp worms.
Large and small, they bred from one another, numbering in the hundreds,钻食 the brain. When the brain was consumed, she died.
He then used a gold knife to剖破 her head.
He removed all the worms and sealed them in a jar.
He applied three kinds of divine ointment to the wound.
One kind repaired the injury to the bone where the worms had eaten.
One kind regenerated the brain.
One kind treated the external knife wound.
He told the girl's father:
"Keep her well and quiet; be careful not to startle her.
In seven days she will recover.
On that day, I will return." As soon as Qíyù left,
the girl's mother began to weep again, saying:
"My child has died a second time!
How can someone with a broken head and凿脑 possibly come back to life?"
Her father stopped her, saying:
"Qíyù was born holding针药.
He abandoned his尊位 to become a physician.
He does so solely to protect and treat human lives for all.
This天医王 would never act recklessly.
He instructed you to be careful not to startle her.
Yet you now weep and startle her instead.
Do you wish this child not to come back to life?"
The mother, hearing this, stopped crying and cared for her protectively.
For seven days it was tranquil.
The girl then exhaled and awoke as if from sleep.
She said:
"I now have no headache at all.
My body is entirely at ease. Who cared for me, enabling me to be like this?"
Her father said:
"You had already died.
The physician king Qíyù came specifically to care for you.
He broke open your head, removed the worms, and thus you have been revived."
He then opened the jar and showed her the worms.
Seeing them, the girl was greatly startled and astonished.
Deeply feeling侥幸, she said:
"Qíyù is indeed divine.
How can I repay his恩?"
Shortly after, Qíyù arrived.
The girl was overjoyed.
She went out the door to welcome him, bowed, knelt, and said:
"I wish to be your婢 for life to repay the恩 of rebirth."
Jīyù said,
"I am a physician who travels around treating illnesses and have no fixed residence; what use would I have for a maidservant?
If you must repay my kindness, give me five hundred taels of gold.
I will not use it for myself but will give it to my teacher as thanks.
Although my teacher had nothing to teach me,
I once considered myself his disciple.
Now that I have received your gold, I should give it to him."
The woman then presented five hundred taels of gold.
Jīyù accepted it and gave it to his teacher.
He then informed the king that he would temporarily return to visit his mother.
He arrived in the country of Vaiśālī.
There was a son of a wealthy household
who loved learning and made a wooden horse over seven feet tall.
While learning to mount it, he initially succeeded in getting on the horse.
But later he lost his balance, fell to the ground, and died.
Jīyù heard of this
and went to examine him with the Medicine King's illumination.
He saw that the liver had turned backward, causing the qi to stagnate and become blocked, which led to his death.
He then used a golden knife to open the abdomen, reached in with his hand to adjust and treat it,
returning the liver to its forward position.
Afterward, he applied three kinds of divine ointment.
One kind repaired the places his hands had held and protected.
One kind promoted the smooth flow of qi and breath.
One kind was for closing knife wounds.
He instructed the father, saying,
"Be careful not to startle him; he will recover in three days."
The father followed the instruction, keeping quiet and caring for him until the third day.
The boy then exhaled and awoke, as if waking from sleep.
He immediately sat up.
Soon after, Jīyù arrived.
The boy came out to greet him and said,
"I wish to serve as your slave for life, providing for you to repay the kindness of saving my life."
Jīyù said,
"I am a physician who travels around treating illnesses.
The families of the sick compete to serve me; why would I need a slave?
My mother raised me with great toil and hardship.
I have not yet provided for her.
If you wish to thank me,
give me five hundred taels of gold
to repay my mother's kindness."
He took the gold and gave it to Nàinǚ.
He then returned to the country of Rājagṛha.
After Jīyù revived these two people, his fame spread throughout the world, and everyone heard of him.
To the south, there was a great country eight thousand li away from Rājagṛha.
Bimbisāra and the various small countries were all subject to it.
Its king had been ill for many years without recovery.
He constantly suffered from anger and resentment, glaring and killing people.
If people looked directly at him, he would kill them.
If they lowered their heads and did not look up, he would kill them.
If messengers walked too slowly, he would kill them.
If they ran too fast, he would kill them.
The attendants around him did not know how to act.
When physicians prepared medicine, he would suspect it was poisoned and kill them as well.
The number of courtiers, palace maids, and physicians he had killed before and after was incalculable.
His illness grew daily, and the poisonous qi attacked his heart.
He was troubled, full of discomfort, short of breath, and felt as if his body were burning.
Hearing of Jīyù's fame, he sent a letter
ordering King Bimbisāra to summon Jīyù.
Jīyù heard that this king had killed many physicians, and everyone, young and old, was terrified.
Bimbisāra also pitied Jīyù for his youth and feared he would be killed.
He wanted not to send him but feared being attacked.
Father and son stayed together, worrying day and night.
They then took Jīyù to ask the Buddha.
The Buddha told Jīyù,
"In your past life, you made a vow with me to save and heal the sick people of the world.
I treat internal illnesses, and you treat external illnesses.
Now that I have attained Buddhahood, you have appeared before me as originally vowed.
This king is gravely ill and has come from afar to welcome you; how can you not go?
Go quickly to protect him.
Find a skillful means to ensure his illness is cured.
He will not kill you."
Jīyù then relied on the Buddha's majestic power
and went to the king's place.
He examined the king's pulse and condition
and used the Medicine King's illumination to inspect him.
He saw that within the king's five viscera and hundred vessels,
the blood and qi were in turmoil, all visible.
It was the poison of snakes and scorpions, surrounding his entire body.
Jīyù said to the king,
"Your Majesty's illness can be treated.
If treated, it will surely be cured.
However, I must see the queen mother to discuss preparing the medicine.
If I do not see the queen mother, the medicine will not be completed."
When the king heard this, he did not understand the reason
and was very angry.
But suffering from his illness
and having long heard of Jīyù's fame, he had welcomed him from afar.
Hoping he would surely be beneficial, and seeing he was a child, he knew there was no deceit, so he endured and listened.
He then sent a eunuch to take him to see the queen mother.
Jīyù said to the queen mother,
"The king's illness can be treated, and now I must prepare the medicine.
The formula should be kept secret and not revealed.
I wish for the attendants to be dismissed."
The queen mother then sent the eunuch out.
Jīyù then asked the queen mother,
"Earlier, when I examined the king's illness,
I saw that the blood vessels in his body were all filled with the poison of snakes and scorpions, as if he were not human.
Whose son is the king really?
Tell me the truth, Queen Mother.
I can treat him.
If you do not tell me,
I will not know how to treat him."
The queen mother said,
"Once, in the Golden Pillar Hall, I was lying down during the day.
Suddenly, something came and rubbed against me.
At that time, I was in a daze and dreamed of having intimate relations.
Suddenly, I awoke.
I saw a large scorpion over three zhang long leaving me, and then I realized I was pregnant.
The king is truly the son of this scorpion.
I have been ashamed of this and have never spoken of it.
Now, young man, you have discovered it; how divine and marvelous!
If the illness can be treated,
I entrust the king's life to you, young man.
Now, what medicine should be used to treat him?"
Jīyù said,
"Only ghee."
The queen mother said,
"Hush, young man, be careful not to say that.
This king greatly hates the smell of ghee.
He also hates hearing its name.
Previously, thousands of people were killed for mentioning ghee.
If you mention it now, he will surely kill you.
If you give this to the king to drink, he will never swallow it.
Please use another medicine."
Jīyù said,
"Ghee treats poisonous illnesses.
His hatred of ghee is precisely why.
If the king's illness were mild or caused by another poison, there would be other medicines to cure it.
But the scorpion poison is severe
and has already spread throughout his body.
If not for ghee, it will never be eliminated.
Now, I must boil and refine it until it turns into water."
He then went out to see the king and said,
"Earlier, I went to see the queen mother
and have obtained the medicine formula; now I must prepare it.
It will take fifteen days to complete.
Now, I have five wishes.
If Your Majesty grants them, your illness can be cured immediately.
If you do not grant them, your illness will not be cured."
The king asked what the five wishes were.
Jīyù said,
"First, I wish to have a new garment from Your Majesty's treasury, one that has never been worn, for me to wear.
Second, I wish to be allowed to enter and leave the palace gate alone without being stopped or questioned.
Third, I wish to be allowed to enter alone daily to see the queen mother and the queen without being stopped or questioned.
Fourth, when Your Majesty drinks the medicine, you must drink it all in one gulp without pausing in between.
Fifth, I wish to have Your Majesty's eight-thousand-li white elephant for me to ride."
When the king heard this, he became furious and said,
"How dare a child ask for such five wishes?
Explain them one by one.
If you cannot explain, I will have you killed now."
Jīyù said,
"Preparing medicine requires purity and fasting.
But I have been traveling for a long time,
and my clothes are covered in dust and dirt, so I wish to wear Your Majesty's garment to prepare the medicine.
Also, Your Majesty has previously sent many physicians, all of whom were suspected and not trusted.
Moreover, you killed them because they did not take the medicine.
All the courtiers, great and small, say that Your Majesty will kill me again.
But Your Majesty's illness is already severe.
I fear that outsiders may have rebellious thoughts and cause chaos.
If I am allowed to come and go alone without being stopped or questioned,
then everyone, great and small, will know that Your Majesty trusts me without doubt.
They will surely take my medicine, and the illness will surely be cured.
Then they will not dare to have rebellious thoughts.
Also, it is said that you have killed many people before.
All the courtiers, great and small, are filled with terror.
None of them wish for Your Majesty's safety and peace.
There is no one to be trusted.
Now, when we prepare the medicine together,
I fear that in the moment I turn my gaze,
they might put poison into the medicine.
If I do not notice, it will not be a small matter. I have thought about it,
and in the world, those who can be trusted are those whose affection never wanes.
Only a mother and a wife.
Therefore, I wish to enter to see the queen mother and prepare the medicine together, which must be boiled.
It will take fifteen days to complete, so I wish to enter daily to tend to the fire and adjust it.
Also, the medicine has a specific composition, and its flavor and qi should be consistent.
If you pause in the middle, the qi will not connect.
Moreover, in the southern mountains, there is a divine and marvelous medicinal herb.
It is four thousand li from here.
After Your Majesty takes the medicine, you should immediately obtain this herb
and take it again, so I wish to ride this elephant to go and gather it.
I will leave in the morning and return in the evening, so the flavor of the medicine will be consistent."
The king's mind was greatly relieved.
He granted all of them.
Then Jīyù boiled and refined the ghee for fifteen days until it turned into clear water.
He obtained five sheng in total and brought it with the queen mother and the queen,
presenting the medicine and saying it could be taken.
He requested that the white elephant be brought to the front of the hall.
The king agreed.
The king saw that the medicine was like clear water and drank it all in one gulp.
Jīyù then mounted the elephant and went straight back to his own country.
After traveling three thousand li, being young and weak, he could not endure the rapid pace, became dizzy and exhausted, and rested on a mountain.
After noon, the king belched and emitted the smell of ghee.
He angrily said,
"That little child dared to give me ghee!
No wonder the little child asked for my white elephant;
he just wanted to rebel and leave!"
The king had a warrior
named Wū,
who had divine speed and could travel swiftly.
He immediately ordered the child to be pursued and brought back.
I will beat him to death before my eyes.
The crow caught up with him and said.
Why did you give the ghee to the king?
And said it was medicine? The king has ordered me to chase after you and call you back.
You must quickly follow me back to confess and surrender, hoping to be spared.
If you still try to flee, I will certainly kill you today; you will not escape.
Jīyù thought to himself: Although I used skillful means to obtain this white elephant,
I still could not escape.
Now I must again use skillful means; how can I follow him back?
So he said to the crow:
I have not eaten since morning; if I return, I will surely die.
Would you allow me a moment in the mountains
to eat some fruit and drink water before meeting my death?
The crow saw that the child Jīyù, fearing death, spoke with such distress.
Taking pity, he listened and said:
Eat quickly and then we must go; you cannot stay long.
Jīyù then took a pear, ate half of it,
put poison under his fingernail, and divided the remaining half, placing it on the ground.
He also took a bowl of water, drank half of it,
then secretly put poison into the remaining water with his fingernail and placed it on the ground.
Then he sighed and said:
This water and pear are both divine medicines.
Fragrant and delicious.
Those who consume them will find their bodies at peace,
all illnesses cured, and their strength doubled.
It is a pity they are not in the capital city,
where the people could all share them.
Instead, they are deep in the mountains, unknown to anyone.
Then he went further into the mountains to search for other fruits.
The crow, being greedy by nature, could not resist food and drink.
Hearing Jīyù praise them as divine medicines,
and seeing that Jīyù had already consumed them,
he thought they must be harmless.
So he ate the remaining pear and drank the remaining water.
Immediately, he began to suffer from diarrhea.
The diarrhea flowed like pouring water.
He collapsed to the ground and lay there.
Whenever he tried to get up, he would become dizzy and fall.
Unable to move again.
Jīyù went over and said to him:
The king, having taken my medicine, will surely recover from his illness.
But now the medicine's effect has not yet taken hold, and the remaining poison has not dissipated.
If I go now, he will certainly kill me.
You know nothing.
Eager to capture me to absolve yourself, you have caused yourself to fall ill.
The illness itself is not severe; be careful not to move, and in three days you will recover.
If you try to get up and chase me now, you will undoubtedly die.
Then he mounted the elephant and left.
Passing by a village, he told the village head:
This is an envoy of the great king.
He has suddenly fallen ill.
You must quickly go and carry him back,
take him home, and care for him well.
Provide him with a thick mattress and give him thin porridge; be careful not to let him die.
If he dies, the king will destroy your village.
After saying this, he left and returned to his own country.
The village head, following the order,
welcomed and cared for him. After three days, the poison subsided,
and the diarrhea stopped, so he returned.
Seeing the king, he kowtowed and confessed:
I was truly foolish and ignorant, violating the king's command.
I believed Jīyù's words and consumed
the remaining fruit and water.
I was poisoned and suffered diarrhea for three days; only now have I begun to recover. I know I deserve death.
By the time the crow returned, within those three days, the king's illness had already been cured.
The king regretted sending the crow.
Seeing the crow return,
he felt both joy and sorrow, saying:
Fortunately, you did not bring the child back immediately.
When I was angry, I would certainly have beaten him to death.
I owe him my life for his kindness,
yet I would have killed him instead—such perverse cruelty is unbearable to contemplate.
All those wrongly killed before and after, I will have them buried with greater honors,
restore their families, and bestow wealth upon them.
I long to see Jīyù and repay his kindness.
So he immediately sent an envoy to respectfully invite Jīyù.
Although Jīyù knew the king's illness had already
been cured, he still felt fear and did not wish to go again.
The Buddha told Jīyù:
In your past lives, you have already made great vows to achieve merit.
How can you stop now? You should go again.
You have cured his external illness; I will also cure his internal illness.
Jīyù then followed the envoy.
The king saw Jīyù and was greatly delighted.
He led him to sit together, held his arm, and said:
Thanks to your kindness, I have been reborn.
How can I repay you? I will divide my kingdom and give half to you.
The palace maidens, treasury treasures—all will be divided in half.
Jīyù said:
I was originally a crown prince.
Although it was a small country, it still had people
and abundant treasures.
I did not enjoy governing a country, so I sought to become a physician and practice healing.
What use would land, maidens, or treasures be to me? I have no need for them.
Previously, the king granted me five wishes,
and your external illness was cured.
Now, if you grant me one more wish,
your internal illness will also be eliminated.
The king said:
I will listen to your benevolent teaching.
Please tell me what it is.
Jīyù said:
I wish for the king to invite the Buddha to receive the bright Dharma.
He explained the Buddha's virtues to the king.
The king, hearing this, was overjoyed and said:
Now I wish to send the crow minister with a white elephant to welcome the Buddha. Can he be brought here?
Jīyù said:
There is no need for a white elephant.
The Buddha knows thoughts from afar.
Simply observe purity and fasting, prepare various offerings, burn incense, bow from afar, kneel and invite the Buddha—the Buddha will surely come of his own accord.
The king did as he said.
The Buddha came with 1,250 bhikkhus. After the meal was finished,
he preached the sutra to the king.
The king immediately understood and gave rise to the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.
The entire country, great and small, all upheld the five precepts.
When Nǚshēng was born, there were already extraordinary signs.
As she grew, she was intelligent and learned from her father,
widely knowledgeable in scriptures, astrology, and various arts, surpassing her father.
Moreover, she excelled in music, her voice like that of Brahmā.
Five hundred daughters from Kṣatriya and Brahmin families all went to study under her as their great teacher.
Nǚshēng often led her five hundred disciples, teaching scriptures and arts.
Sometimes they would play together in gardens and ponds or make music.
The people of the country did not understand the reason for this,
so they slandered her, calling her a licentious woman.
Her five hundred disciples were all called the licentious faction.
When Nǚshēng was born,
two other girls were also born in the country.
One was Xūmàn Nǚ,
the second was Bōtán Nǚ.
Xūmàn Nǚ was born in a Kṣatriya household that often pressed
Xūmàn to make fragrant ointment.
While pressing ointment by a stone, a tumor-like knot suddenly formed.
It was as large as a pellet,
and as long as a rolled-up hand.
The stone then cracked open,
and inside the stone knot, something shone like a firefly's light.
It shot out, fell to the ground, and after three days, Xūmàn grew.
After another three days, it became a flower,
inside which was a small girl.
The Kṣatriya took her and raised her,
naming her Xūmàn Nǚ.
When she grew up, her talent, intelligence, and wisdom were second only to Nǚshēng.
Bōtán Nǚ was from a Brahmin family.
In their bathing pool, a blue lotus grew.
It grew larger each day, like a five-sheng bottle.
When the flower opened, a small girl was seen inside.
The Brahmin raised her and named her Bōtán Nǚ.
When she grew up, her talent, wisdom, and understanding were like Xūmàn Nǚ's.
The kings of various countries heard that these two girls had peerless beauty,
and they came one after another to seek their hands in marriage.
The two girls said:
We were not born from a womb,
but emerged from grass and flowers.
We are different from ordinary people.
How could we follow worldly customs and marry?
We have heard that Nǚshēng is intelligent, unmatched in the world.
Moreover, she shares the same nature as us.
So they bid farewell to their parents and went to serve Nǚshēng, seeking to become her disciples.
Their wisdom and broad knowledge surpassed that of the five hundred others.
At that time, the Buddha arrived in the country of Vaiśālī.
Nǚshēng led her disciples out of the city to respectfully welcome him. Kneeling, she said:
I wish for the Buddha to dine in my garden tomorrow.
The Buddha silently accepted.
The king came out of the palace to welcome him,
and also invited him to dine in the palace the next day.
The Buddha said:
Nǚshēng invited me first; you are later.
The king said:
I am the ruler of the country and sincerely invite the Buddha. I earnestly hope you will compassionately agree.
Nǚshēng is merely a licentious woman.
Every day, she leads five hundred disciples in improper conduct.
Why would the Buddha forsake me and accept her invitation?
The Buddha said:
This woman is not licentious.
In her past lives, she had great merit, having already made offerings to three hundred million Buddhas.
In the past, she was also often together with Xūmàn and Bōtán as sisters.
Nǚshēng was the eldest, Xūmàn the second,
and Bōtán the youngest, born into a great family.
Their wealth and treasures were abundant. The sisters learned from each other and together made offerings to five hundred bhikkhunīs.
They provided food, drink, and clothing, supplying whatever was lacking, and supported them throughout their lives.
The three made a vow:
May we in future lives encounter a Buddha, be born spontaneously,
not from a womb, and be far removed from filth and impurity.
Now, as per their original vow, they were born and encountered me.
Although they had made offerings to five hundred bhikkhunīs in the past,
being born into wealth and nobility, their speech was frivolous and arrogant.
At times, they teased the nuns, saying:
You reverend ones, having long been repressed, must surely wish to marry.
It is only because you are constrained by our support that you cannot indulge your desires.
Therefore, they now suffer this residual retribution.
Although they expound the scriptures and the path, they are falsely slandered as licentious.
These five hundred disciples, at that time, were united in heart and mind; now they are born again to follow one another.
At that time, Jīyù was a poor child. Nǚshēng saw his intention to make offerings and greatly admired his devotion, but he had no wealth.
So he often cleaned for the bhikkhunīs, and after finishing,
he would think to himself:
May I be able to cure the illnesses of all people in the world.
Nǚshēng pitied his poverty,
and appreciating his diligence, often called him her son.
Among those bhikkhunīs, there were those who fell ill.
He often sent Jīyù to welcome physicians and prepare decoctions and medicines.
Everyone said,
"May you and I together attain such blessings in future lives."
All those treated by the physicians welcomed by Jīyù were cured.
He then vowed,
"May I in a future life become a great king of physicians, always curing all diseases of the four great elements in people's bodies, and may all I treat be healed."
The king, hearing the Buddha's words,
repented of his own faults.
He postponed the date to later.
The Buddha, the next day, went with the bhikkhus to the garden of Nàinǚ.
He fully explained the merits of his original vow.
Hearing the sutra, the three women all gained understanding.
And the five hundred disciples all attained the path of Arhatship.
Śākyamuni Buddha in a previous life was a great physician king.
He cured all illnesses.
He sought neither fame nor profit, doing so out of compassion for sentient beings.
The sick were many, and his strength was insufficient to save them all.
He worried about all beings, but his will could not be fully realized.
He died in distress and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
He thought to himself:
"Now that I am born in heaven, I merely enjoy the fruits of my blessings without gaining any real benefit."
He then, by his own means, ended his life.
He abandoned this heavenly lifespan.
He was reborn in the palace of the Nāga King Pāgata.
He became the nāga prince.
His body grew large, and his parents loved and cherished him dearly.
He wished to end his own life by going to the Garuḍa king.
The bird then seized this nāga prince, swallowed him on a Śamali tree.
His parents wailed and cried in anguish.
After the nāga prince died, he was reborn in Jambudvīpa.
He became the crown prince of a great king.
His name was Nengshī (Able to Give).
He could speak from birth.
He asked his attendants:
"What things are there in this kingdom now?
Bring them all here for me to give away in charity."
The people, astonished and afraid, all abandoned him and fled.
His mother, pitying and loving him, alone stayed to watch over him.
He said to his mother:
"I am not a rākṣasa; why did the people run away?
In my past lives, I always delighted in giving alms.
I am the dānapati (benefactor) for all people."
His mother, hearing his words, told the people.
The people then returned.
His mother raised him well, and when he grew up, he had exhausted all his own possessions.
He went to his father the king to ask for things to give away.
His father gave him his share, and he again gave it all away.
Seeing the people of Jambudvīpa poor and suffering, he thought to provide for them.
But his wealth was insufficient, so he wept himself.
He asked the people:
"What means can we employ to ensure everyone has sufficient wealth?"
Some elders said:
"We have heard it said
there is a wish-fulfilling jewel.
If one obtains this jewel, then whatever one desires, one will obtain without fail."
He told his parents he wished to enter the great sea to seek the wish-fulfilling jewel on the head of the nāga king.
His parents replied:
"We have only you, our one son.
If you enter the great sea, the many dangers are hard to overcome.
If we lose you, what use is living for us?
We still have things in our treasury to give you."
The son said:
"The treasury is limited, but my aspiration is boundless.
I wish to fill everything, leaving nothing lacking.
I beg you to allow me to fulfill my original intent.
So that the people of Jambudvīpa may all be fully provided for."
His parents, knowing his great resolve, dared not stop him and so let him go.
At that time, five hundred merchants were all willing to follow him.
Knowing the day of his departure, they gathered at the seaport.
The prince asked the crowd:
"Who knows the way to that nāga palace?"
There was a blind man named Tuóshè,
who had already entered the great sea seven times and knew the sea routes well.
The Bodhisattva then asked him to go together.
He replied:
"I am already old, and both my eyes are blind.
Although I have entered several times before, now I cannot go."
The Bodhisattva said:
"My journey now is not for my own sake.
It is universally for all beings, seeking the wish-fulfilling jewel.
I wish to provide sufficiently for sentient beings, so they lack nothing physically.
Afterwards, I will teach them through the causes and conditions of the Dharma.
You are a wise man; how can you refuse?
If my wish is achieved, will it not be due to your strength?"
Tuóshè, with sincere thoughts, replied:
"If I enter the sea now, my life will certainly not be safe.
Place my corpse on the golden sand island.
The ship sped away.
They reached the Isle of Many Jewels.
The merchants vied to load jewels until they had enough.
They asked the prince:
"Why do you not take any?"
He replied:
"What I seek is the wish-fulfilling jewel.
These are exhaustible things; I do not need them.
You all should know contentment and know your limits, lest the ship becomes too heavy and you cannot save yourselves."
At that time, the merchants said to the Bodhisattva:
"O Virtuous One, please chant blessings so we may return safely."
Then they bid farewell and left.
Tuóshè then said to the Bodhisattva:
"Keep a small boat separate; we will take a different route.
Wait for the wind for seven days, then sail south along the coast to a dangerous place.
There will be a sheer cliff with jujube trees whose branches all hang over the water.
A great wind will blow, and the ship will be wrecked.
You should reach up and grab the jujube branches to save yourself.
I have no eyes; I will die there.
Past this narrow shore, there will be a golden sand island.
You can place my body in this sand.
The golden sand is pure; this is my wish."
It was as he said; the wind came and they departed.
Reaching the sheer cliff, it was as Tuóshè had described.
The Bodhisattva reached up and grabbed the jujube branches, thereby saving himself.
He placed Tuóshè's corpse, laying it to rest on the golden ground.
Then he went on alone.
Following the previous instructions,
he floated in deep water for seven days.
He walked in water up to his neck for seven days.
He walked in water up to his waist for seven days.
He walked in mud for seven days.
He saw beautiful lotuses, fresh, clean, and soft.
He thought to himself:
"These flowers are soft and fragile; I should enter the emptiness samādhi."
He made his body light and walked on the lotuses for seven days. Then he saw many poisonous snakes.
He thought:
"Poisonous creatures are truly fearsome."
He then entered the loving-kindness samādhi.
He walked on the heads of the poisonous snakes for seven days.
The snakes all raised their heads, offering them to the Bodhisattva to step on and pass over.
Having passed this difficulty,
he saw a seven-jeweled city with seven moats.
The moats were all filled with poisonous snakes.
There were two great nāgas guarding the gate.
The nāgas saw the Bodhisattva's handsome appearance, dignified bearing, and excellent marks, and that he could overcome many difficulties to come here.
They thought:
"This is no ordinary man.
He must be a Bodhisattva, a man of great merit."
They then allowed him to proceed, and he directly entered the palace.
The nāga king and his wife had lost their son not long ago and were still grieving.
Seeing the Bodhisattva arrive, the nāga, with his supernatural knowledge, knew this was his son.
Milk flowed from both her breasts.
She bade him sit.
And asked him, saying:
"You are my son.
After you left me and died, where were you reborn?"
The Bodhisattva also knew his past lives and recognized them as his parents.
He answered his mother:
"I was born in Jambudvīpa.
I became the crown prince of a great king.
Pitying the poor people, their hunger, cold, toil, and suffering, and their lack of freedom, I came here for this reason.
I wish to seek the wish-fulfilling jewel."
His mother said:
"Your father has this jewel on his head as an ornament; it is hard to obtain.
I will certainly take you into the various treasuries; whatever you desire, I will surely give you.
You should then say:
'I do not need the other miscellaneous jewels.
I only wish to obtain the great king's head jewel.
If you pity me, I beg you to give it to me.'
In this way, you may obtain it."
He then went to see his father.
His father was greatly joyful and delighted beyond measure.
He pitied his son for traversing such hardships to come here.
He pointed out the wonderful jewels: "Take whatever you wish according to your desire."
The Bodhisattva said:
"I have come from afar, wishing to see the great king to seek the wish-fulfilling jewel on your head.
If you pity me, you should give it to me.
If you do not give it, I need no other thing."
The nāga king replied:
"I have only this one jewel, always worn as an ornament.
The people of Jambudvīpa have little merit and are lowly; they do not deserve to see it."
The Bodhisattva said:
"It is precisely for this reason that I traversed hardships, braving death to come from afar.
It is because the people of Jambudvīpa have little merit and are poor and lowly.
I wish to use the wish-fulfilling jewel to fulfill their desires.
Afterwards, I will teach them through the causes and conditions of the Buddha Path."
The nāga king gave him the jewel but stipulated, saying:
"Now I give this jewel to you.
After you pass away, you must return it to me."
He answered:
"I respectfully agree to your words."
The Bodhisattva obtained the jewel.
Soaring through the sky, in the time it takes to bend and stretch an arm, he reached Jambudvīpa.
His human king parents saw their son return safely.
Overjoyed and leaping, they embraced him and asked:
"What did you obtain?"
He replied:
"I obtained the wish-fulfilling jewel."
They asked:
"Where is it now?"
He said:
"It is here inside the corner of my garment."
His parents said:
"How can it be so small?"
He replied:
"Its power lies in its spiritual virtue, not in its size."
He said to his parents:
"Command that inside and outside the city be swept clean, incense burned, silk banners and canopies hung, and that people observe fasting and precepts.
Tomorrow at dawn, erect a tall wooden pole and place the jewel on top."
The Bodhisattva then made this vow:
"If I am to achieve Buddhahood and liberate all beings,
then may this jewel, according to my wish, produce all kinds of precious things.
Whatever people need, may it all be fully provided."
At that time, dark clouds spread widely, raining down various precious things, clothing, food, drink, bedding, and medicines.
Whatever people said they needed, everything was fully provided.
Until the end of their lives, it continued unceasingly.
Such deeds are called the Bodhisattva's practice of giving, generating the pāramitā of vigor.
In the past, in Jambudvīpa,
there were two kings at one time.
The king of Lìshībá country was named Yuè,
and the king of Bōluónà country was named Yuègài.
They were of one mind and interacted without any suspicion or grudge.
They made an agreement together:
If they had sons, they would arrange a marriage alliance between them.
King Yuègài had neither sons nor daughters.
In order to seek a son,
he made offerings to the water deity and even to various ghosts and spirits.
By the Āxiūluózhà River, there were two ascetics with the five supernatural powers.
The river deity said to the king,
"If the two ascetics are willing to be reborn in the king's household, the king will have a son."
The king went to the ascetics and said,
"If you are born into my family, you will enjoy the five desires freely, with happiness and no lack."
The ascetics replied,
"So be it."
Seven days later, one of the ascetics passed away and entered the womb of the first consort.
After another seven days, the other ascetic also passed away
and entered the womb of the second consort.
The first consort, after a full nine months,
gave birth to a boy with a handsome and dignified appearance.
On the day of his birth, five hundred merchants returned from the sea,
five hundred hidden treasures were spontaneously unearthed,
and five hundred prisoners sentenced to death were released from prison.
When the second consort gave birth,
there were many strange omens: jackals howled,
Asuras seized the sun,
and five hundred people who deserved death willingly went to their deaths. The king was very pleased.
He immediately summoned diviners to determine the auspiciousness and inauspiciousness and to give them names.
The diviners asked,
"What auspicious signs appeared when this child was born?"
The reply was,
"The mother of the first crown prince was originally jealous, arrogant, and conceited.
But since conceiving the child, her nature has become gentle and kind, her face pleasant, her speech joyful, and she has shown compassion for all beings."
The diviners replied,
"This is due to the child's virtue and merit."
They named him Shànyǒu.
Regarding the one born to the second consort, they asked about the auspicious signs.
The reply was,
"His mother was originally gentle and kind, and her words pleased everyone.
But since becoming pregnant, her nature has suddenly become violent, and her speech coarse and harsh."
The diviners replied,
"It is the child's actions that have caused his mother to be like this."
They named him Èyǒu. When they reached the age of fourteen,
Crown Prince Shànyǒu was intelligent, compassionate, benevolent, and fond of giving alms.
His parents doted on him, regarding him as their very eyes.
Èyǒu was violent and wicked, despised by his parents, who did not like to see him.
He was jealous of his elder brother and constantly sought to harm and destroy him.
He was disobedient in all matters, contrary and rebellious.
The crown prince, with his retinue preceding and following, accompanied by musicians and performers,
surrounded by a great crowd, went out of the city to observe.
He saw farmers plowing the soil, bringing out worms that birds followed and pecked at; he felt pity and sorrow for them.
He asked his attendants,
"What is this thing that causes mutual harm and destruction?"
They replied,
"The state depends on the people, the people depend on food and drink, and food depends on farming."
The crown prince said,
"How bitter, how bitter!"
Proceeding further, he saw men and women spinning and weaving.
He asked again,
"What is this thing?"
They replied,
"Spinning and weaving to make clothes to cover shame and conceal the five bodily forms."
The crown prince said,
"This too is laborious, and not just one kind."
Going further, he saw people slaughtering oxen and skinning sheep.
He asked again,
"What is this again?"
They replied,
"Slaughtering to sell meat to provide for clothing and food."
The crown prince said,
"How strange, how bitter!"
"The strong and the weak harm each other, creating calamities that accumulate over kalpas."
Going further, he saw nets catching birds and bait catching fish.
He asked again.
They answered again.
"Setting nets to catch birds and fishing."
The crown prince's eyes filled with tears of sorrow.
"The beings of the world create the roots of all evils, suffering endlessly, sorrowful and unhappy." He then turned his carriage and returned to the palace.
The king asked,
"Why are you sorrowful?"
The crown prince answered in detail as above.
The king said,
"Such things have always existed; why should you be troubled?"
The crown prince said,
"Now I wish to ask the king for a favor.
I wish to obtain the treasures of the state treasury to give to all."
The king said, "As you wish."
The crown prince then ordered his ministers to open the king's treasury.
Using five hundred elephants to carry the treasures, they went out through the four city gates,
proclaiming throughout the land that everyone could take whatever they desired according to their wishes.
The fame of Crown Prince Shànyǒu spread in all eight directions, and everyone gathered.
Not long after, one-third had been used.
The treasurer reported to the king,
"Your Majesty should consider this."
The king said,
"I do not wish to oppose him."
After a little more time had passed,
the ministers discussed together,
"The state depends on the treasury; if the treasury is exhausted, the state will also be empty."
They went again to report to the king,
"Two-thirds of all the treasures have been used.
Your Majesty should deeply consider this."
The king said,
"I do not wish to oppose him.
You may delay a little, but do not let him have his way completely."
When the crown prince wished to open the treasury,
the treasurer happened to be away on business.
He was urgently pursued but missed due to a mix-up.
The crown prince said,
"How dare a petty man disobey my wishes?
It must be my father the king's instruction.
A filial son should not deplete his parents' treasury.
I should now seek wealth myself to provide sufficiently for all beings.
If I cannot provide all beings with clothing, bedding, food, and drink as they wish,
how can I be called a great king?"
The crown prince then gathered all the ministers and officials to discuss, saying,
"In seeking wealth and profit, what occupation is the best?"
Some said farming, others said animal husbandry.
One minister said,
"In this world, for seeking profit, nothing surpasses going to sea to gather wonderful treasures.
If one obtains the maṇi jewel, one can then satisfy all beings as they wish."
The crown prince said,
"Indeed." He then reported this to the king.
The king heard this and was speechless.
Later, he said to the crown prince,
"The state is yours.
The treasures of the treasury are for you to use as you wish; why go to sea?
You are my son, raised in the deep palace.
You sleep with curtains and canopies, and eat as you please.
Now, traveling far on the roads, who will know of your hunger, thirst, cold, and heat?
In the great sea, there are many dangers, not just one.
There may be evil ghosts, poisonous dragons, fierce winds, waves, mountains of water, and the great makara fish.
Of those who go, thousands and tens of thousands, only one or two reach their destination.
How can you now think of entering the great sea?"
The crown prince immediately prostrated himself with his five limbs on the ground, spreading his four limbs, and said this:
"If my parents do not permit me, I will abandon my life and never rise again."
The king and queen came forward to persuade and admonish him, but he did not eat or drink until the sixth day.
His parents were worried and afraid, fearing he would not survive.
On the seventh day, they took his hand and gently persuaded him.
The crown prince said,
"If my parents do not permit me, I will surely die here."
The first consort said to the king,
"Our son's mind is difficult to sway; we cannot oppose his determination.
How can we bear to see him abandon his life here?
I beg Your Majesty to have compassion and allow him to go to sea.
Thus, there is a ten-thousandth hope.
If we do not permit him now, he will surely die here."
The king then gave his permission.
The crown prince was overjoyed and bowed to the king, touching his head to the ground.
The great king proclaimed, "Who wishes to go to sea?"
When the people heard this, they joyfully gathered.
Five hundred of them said,
"Great King, we now wish to follow the crown prince."
There was a sea pilot who had gone to sea many times before.
He was well-versed in the conditions of the routes, whether passable or blocked.
But he was eighty years old and both his eyes were dim and blind.
The king said to the guide,
"I have only one son who has never ventured out before.
I trouble you, Great Master, to follow him into the sea.
I hope you will accompany him."
The guide then said,
"The sea is full of hardships and dangers, not just one.
Of those who go, thousands and tens of thousands, only one or two reach their destination.
Great King, how can you let the crown prince travel far on such a dangerous path?"
The king told the guide,
"Out of compassion, please follow and permit him."
The guide said,
"I dare not disobey."
The crown prince prepared five hundred people with travel supplies and proceeded to the seashore.
Èyǒu thought to himself,
"Shànyǒu is favored and loved by our parents.
Now he is going to sea to gather wonderful treasures.
If he returns, our parents will abandon me."
He said to his parents,
"I wish to follow Shànyǒu to sea to gather treasures."
His parents replied,
"As you wish. On the difficult road, brothers should accompany each other and surely rescue one another."
When they reached the sea, they secured the ship with seven iron chains.
The ship remained anchored for seven days.
At sunrise, the crown prince beat the drum and proclaimed,
"You people, who wishes to go to sea?
Those who wish to go, remain silent.
If you are attached to your loved ones, you may return now.
In the great sea, there are many hardships, not just one."
The crowd remained silent.
They then cut one chain and placed it on the ship.
Each day they proclaimed until the seventh day.
They then cut the seventh chain, raised the sails to catch the wind.
Due to the crown prince's compassionate heart and the power of his virtue, they encountered no hardships.
They reached the sea island and arrived at the mountain of precious treasures.
The crown prince beat the drum and proclaimed,
"The road is long and distant; quickly load the treasures.
Stop at most for seven days."
He also said this:
"These treasures are very heavy.
Even in Jambudvīpa, they are not of such value.
Do not overload the ship, lest it sink and not reach its destination.
Do not take too little, for the road is long and distant, and it will not compensate for the labor."
Having finished his preparations, he bid farewell to the others.
And spoke these words:
"You all should now return safely and peacefully.
I wish to press forward to seek the Mani jewel."
The prince and the blind guide
then proceeded further ahead.
After traveling for one week, the water reached their knees.
After advancing another week, the water reached their necks.
After yet another week, they floated across and finally reached the treasure site.
The guide asked:
"What kind of ground is this?"
The prince replied:
"The ground here is entirely white silver sand."
The guide said:
"Looking around, there should be a white mountain. Have you seen it?"
The prince said:
"To the southeast, there is a white silver mountain. We have reached its foot."
The guide said:
"Next, we should reach golden sand."
The guide, exhausted and fainting, collapsed to the ground and said to the prince:
"My life will not last long; I will surely die here."
The prince then traveled east for one week, where there should be a golden mountain.
From the mountain, proceed another week further, where there are pure blue lotus flowers.
Advance another week, and the ground is entirely red lotus flowers.
After passing another week, there is a great treasure city.
It is entirely adorned with the seven treasures and is the dwelling place of the dragon king.
In the dragon king's ear, there is a Mani wish-fulfilling jewel.
Go and request it from him.
If you obtain the jewel, it can fill Jambudvīpa with rain, producing the seven treasures, clothing, food, drink, medicine, music, and entertainment as desired.
It is called the wish-fulfilling jewel."
After speaking, the guide breathed his last and died.
The prince embraced him, raised his voice, and wept bitterly.
"How unfortunate, that I should lose you in this life."
He then buried him in the ground.
Covered him with golden sand.
Circumambulated him seven times to the right, paid homage, and departed.
Proceeding ahead, he passed the golden mountain and saw blue lotus flowers.
Beneath them were blue snakes.
These snakes possess three types of poison:
namely, bite poison, touch poison, and breath poison.
These poisonous snakes coiled their bodies around the lotus flowers.
They opened their eyes, panted, and stared at the prince.
The prince then entered the samādhi of loving-kindness.
Rising, he advanced along the path, stepping on the lotus leaves.
At that time, the poisonous snakes neither harmed nor injured him, and he reached the dwelling place of the dragon king.
Seven layers of moats were filled with poisonous dragons, coiled together, raising their heads and intertwining their necks, guarding the city gates.
The prince arrived outside the city gate.
Seeing the poisonous dragons, he immediately felt loving-kindness.
He thought of all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa.
"If my body is harmed by these poisonous dragons now,
all of you sentient beings will lose great benefit."
He then raised his right hand and addressed the poisonous dragons:
"You should know
that I have come for the sake of all sentient beings to see the dragon king."
The poisonous dragons cleared the way, allowing the prince to enter.
He saw two jade maidens spinning crystal thread.
The prince asked:
"Who are you?"
They replied:
"We are the dragon king's maidservants guarding the outer gate."
Entering to the middle gate, he saw four jade maidens spinning silver thread.
The prince asked again:
"Are you the dragon king's consorts?"
They replied, "No.
We are the dragon king's maidservants guarding the middle gate."
The prince entered the inner gate and saw eight jade maidens spinning golden thread.
The prince said:
"Who are you?"
They replied:
"We are the dragon king's maidservants guarding the gate."
The prince said:
"Inform the great sea dragon king for me:
Shànyǒu, crown prince of King Bōluónà of Jambudvīpa, wishes to meet him and is now at the gate."
The gatekeepers then reported to the king.
The king was greatly puzzled and surprised.
"Unless he is a man of pure virtue and goodness, he could not have traveled such a perilous path from afar."
He then invited him into the palace, and the king came out to welcome him.
The ground was made of dark blue lapis lazuli, and the seven treasures emitted various lights, dazzling to the eyes.
The prince expounded the Dharma, teaching and delighting him with its benefits.
He praised and explained the discourses on generosity, precepts, and the paths of humans and gods.
The dragon king was pleased.
"You have traveled a long and arduous journey. What do you need?"
The prince said:
"Great King,
all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa suffer endlessly for lack of clothing and food.
Now I wish to request from you the Mani jewel in your left ear."
The dragon king said:
"Accept my humble hospitality for one week, and I will present it to you."
The prince accepted the dragon king's invitation.
After seven days, he took the jewel and returned to Jambudvīpa. The dragon king sent dragon spirits to escort him through the air.
They reached the shore.
He saw his younger brother Èyǒu and asked:
"Where are your companions now?"
He replied:
"The ship sank, and all perished.
Only I alone survived by clinging to a corpse.
All the wealth is now lost."
Shànyǒu said:
"In all the world, no treasure is greater than one's own life."
The younger brother said, "Not so.
People would rather die rich than live poor.
How do I know this?
I once went to a cemetery and heard the dead ghosts discussing thus."
Shànyǒu, honest and sincere, spoke truthfully to his brother:
"Although you lost the treasure, it is of little consequence.
I have now obtained the dragon king's wish-fulfilling jewel."
The younger brother said:
"Where is it now?"
Shànyǒu said:
"It is now in my hair knot."
Upon hearing this, the younger brother grew jealous and said to Shànyǒu:
"Excellent! Very good!
Having obtained this jewel, you should guard it carefully."
Shànyǒu removed the jewel and gave it to his brother, admonishing him:
"If you are tired and lie down, I will guard it.
If I sleep, you should guard it."
At that time, it was Èyǒu's turn to guard the jewel.
His elder brother was fast asleep.
He rose, took two dry bamboo sticks, pierced his brother's eyes, seized the jewel, and left.
Shànyǒu called out to Èyǒu:
"There is a thief! He pierced my eyes and took the jewel away!"
Èyǒu did not respond.
The elder brother then became distressed, fearing he might be killed by the thief.
He cried out loudly for a long time, but there was no response.
A tree deity spoke:
"Your younger brother Èyǒu is your evil thief.
He pierced your eyes and took the jewel away."
The prince was disheartened, angry, and tormented.
Èyǒu brought the jewel back to the kingdom and said to his parents:
"By my own virtue and fortune, I alone survived.
Shànyǒu and his companions drowned and perished."
His parents wailed loudly, fainted, and collapsed to the ground.
They said to Èyǒu:
"How can you show your face like this?"
Hearing this, Èyǒu felt remorse in his heart.
He then buried the jewel in the ground.
Shànyǒu, pierced by the bamboo sticks, had no one to remove them.
He wandered aimlessly, not knowing where to go.
At that time, tormented by great suffering, hunger, and thirst,
he could neither live nor die.
Gradually, he made his way to the kingdom of Lìshībá.
The king had a daughter
who had previously been betrothed to Prince Shànyǒu of Bōluónà.
There was a cowherd who tended five hundred cattle for the king, following water and grass.
The prince sat in the middle of the road.
The herd of cattle approached closely.
The lead bull stepped over the prince, allowing the other cattle to pass.
Then it moved its foot, turned right, looked back, bent its neck, stuck out its tongue, licked the prince's eyes, and pulled out the bamboo sticks.
The cowherd saw this and asked:
"Who are you?"
Shànyǒu did not reveal his origins.
He replied:
"I am a blind beggar."
The cowherd observed him closely.
Seeing he was no ordinary person, he said:
"My home is nearby.
I will provide for you."
He then took him home and gave him various kinds of food and drink.
He instructed his family:
"Treat him as you would treat me."
After more than a month, the family grew weary of him.
Shànyǒu, feeling disheartened, said to his host the next morning:
"I wish to leave now."
The host said:
"Is something unsatisfactory?"
Shànyǒu said:
"The relationship between guest and host cannot last forever."
Shànyǒu said:
"If you care for me,
please give me a zither and send me to a populated village."
The host then provided as requested and sent him to the city of Lìshībá, a place with many people.
Shànyǒu played the zither.
Its sound was harmonious and elegant, pleasing to all.
All the people provided him with food and drink.
The king had an orchard.
The orchard was lush but often troubled by birds.
The orchard keeper said to Shànyǒu:
"Guard against the birds for me,
and I will provide for you.
I will tie ropes to the treetops and attach bronze bells.
You sit under the tree, and when you hear the birds, pull the rope ends."
Shànyǒu said:
"Very well.
I can stay under the tree and also play the zither for my own amusement."
At that time, the daughter of the king of Lìshībá entered the garden with her attendants.
Seeing the blind man, she went to him and asked:
"Who are you?"
He replied:
"A blind beggar."
The king's daughter felt affection for him and could not bear to leave.
The king sent messengers to summon her back.
She said, "I will not go. Send food for me
to provide for this blind man." After the meal,
she said to the king:
"If you now give me to this blind man, it would suit my wish perfectly."
The king said:
"A demon must have possessed you, driving you mad and confusing your mind. How can you wish to live with a blind man?
Your parents previously betrothed you to Prince Shànyǒu of Bōluónà.
Shànyǒu went to sea and has not returned.
How can you now become the wife of a beggar?"
The woman said, "Even so, I would rather give up my life than abandon you."
Upon hearing these words, the king could not refuse.
He immediately sent messengers to bring the blind man and confined him in a quiet chamber.
The king's daughter said to the blind man,
"I now wish to become your wife."
Shànyǒu replied,
"Whose daughter are you, that you wish to be my wife?"
She answered,
"I am the daughter of King Lìshībá."
Shànyǒu replied,
"You are a king's daughter,
while I am a beggar. How can we respect each other?"
The woman said,
"I will serve you with all my heart."
Later, the wife went out without informing her husband and returned after a long while.
Shànyǒu reproached her, saying, "You went out secretly without telling me. Where did you go?"
The woman said,
"I did not go out secretly."
The husband said, "Whether you went secretly or not, who would know?"
The woman made a solemn vow:
"If I went out secretly, may your eyes never heal.
If not, may one of your eyes be restored as before."
After making this vow, his eye became perfectly whole again, clear and radiant.
The woman said,
"Do you believe me now?"
Shànyǒu smiled.
The woman said,
"You are ungrateful.
I am the daughter of a great king,
while you are a lowly person, yet I serve you with all my heart.
And you still do not trust me."
The husband said,
"Do you know who I am?"
She replied, "I know you are a beggar."
The husband said, "No.
I am Prince Shànyǒu, son of the king of Bōluónà."
The woman said,
"You are a great fool! How can you say such a thing?
Prince Shànyǒu of Bōluónà went to sea and has not returned.
Now you speak falsely—I do not believe you."
Shànyǒu said, "Since I was born, I have never spoken falsely."
The woman said,
"Whether it is false or true, who would believe it?"
The husband said,
"If I am deceiving you, may my other eye never heal.
If I am speaking the truth, may my other eye be restored as before, so that you may see."
Immediately, as he vowed, his eye became radiant and moved as before, no different.
Prince Shànyǒu's eyes were both restored, his face and head were upright, and his appearance was extraordinarily beautiful.
When the woman saw this, she was overjoyed.
As if encountering a sage, she gazed at his entire body without taking her eyes off him.
She then entered the palace and said to her father, the king,
"My husband is none other than Prince Shànyǒu."
The king said, "Foolish one!
Shànyǒu has not returned. How can you call a beggar the prince?"
The daughter said, "No.
If you do not believe me, go and see for yourself."
The king went to look.
He recognized Shànyǒu.
Filled with terror, he said,
"The king of Bōluónà
will surely hold a great grudge against me if he hears of this."
He then approached and apologized to Prince Shànyǒu, saying, "I truly did not know."
The prince said,
"Do not worry. Please provide for
and reward this cowherd."
The king then gave gold, silver, jewels, clothing, food, and drink,
along with the five hundred cows that had been released.
The man was overjoyed and praised him endlessly.
"And I have not yet repaid the little kindness I received."
Thus, I loudly proclaimed,
"Hidden acts of charity bring visible rewards, vast and immeasurable."
Upon hearing this, the multitude all developed a charitable heart.
Before Shànyǒu went to sea, he had raised a white goose.
They shared clothing, food, and drink, and were always together, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
The queen said to this goose,
"When the prince was here, he was always with you.
Now his fate is unknown, yet you do not grieve for him."
The goose then cried mournfully, its voice trembling with tears, and replied,
"I wish to find the prince."
The queen personally wrote a letter and tied it to the goose's neck.
The goose rose into the sky and flew away.
It flew to the great sea but could not find him.
It then flew in succession to the kingdom of Lìshībá.
From afar, it saw Shànyǒu in front of the palace.
The goose approached him, crying mournfully yet joyfully.
The prince took the letter from his mother, placed it on his head in reverence, opened it, and read it.
He learned that his parents wept day and night, longing for him.
The prince's eyes were blind.
The prince wrote a letter detailing everything that had happened, tied it to the goose's neck, and sent it back to Bōluónà.
When his parents received the letter, they were overjoyed and praised him endlessly.
They learned in detail how the prince had suffered at the hands of Èyǒu, who had stolen the precious pearl.
His parents shackled Èyǒu and imprisoned him.
They sent messengers to inform King Lìshībá,
"Why have you detained the prince, causing us such sorrow?"
King Lìshībá was filled with terror.
He immediately prepared a grand escort for the prince and sent him to the border.
He sent messengers to announce,
"I have given my daughter in marriage to him and am sending him back to his country."
His parents rode on a great elephant,
with musicians playing, the ground swept and incense burned, banners and canopies hung, and went far to welcome the prince.
The people of the kingdom, men and women, husbands and wives, hearing of the prince's return, all came out to welcome him.
The prince approached and bowed to his parents.
His parents, blind, could not see the prince.
They touched him with their hands and said, "Are you Shànyǒu? We have missed you and grieved for you so much."
The prince inquired about his parents' well-being.
The prince said to his father, the king,
"Where is Èyǒu?"
The king said,
"He is now in prison."
The prince said,
"I wish for Èyǒu to be released so that I may see him." He repeated this three times.
The king could not bear to refuse and ordered him released.
The prince approached, embraced him, and spoke kindly, persuading and comforting him with gentle words.
"You have endured great hardship. Where is the precious pearl you took from me?"
He repeated this three times.
Only then did Èyǒu reply,
"It is buried in the ground."
The prince retrieved the precious pearl.
He went before his parents, knelt, burned fine incense, and made a solemn vow:
"If this pearl is the wish-fulfilling jewel,
may my parents' eyes become clear and bright as before."
Immediately, their eyes were restored, and they saw their son with joy.
On the fifteenth day of the month, at dawn,
the prince purified himself by bathing, put on fresh, clean clothes, and burned fine incense.
On a high tower, holding an incense burner, he bowed his head in reverence to the Maṇi pearl.
He made a vow, saying,
"For the sake of all beings in Jambudvīpa,
I endured this great suffering to seek this precious pearl."
At that moment, a great wind arose from the east,
blowing away the clouds and mist, making everything clear and bright.
All the filth, excrement, urine, dust, and weeds in Jambudvīpa were swept away by the pure wind, leaving everything clean.
Through the power of the pearl,
over Jambudvīpa,
rained fully ripened, natural rice,
fragrant, sweet, soft, and fine, with perfect color and flavor.
Ditches and canals were filled to the knees.
Next rained clothing, pearls, rings, bracelets, and hairpins.
Next rained the seven treasures and wonderful music.
All that the beings needed was fully provided.
Later, when King Yuègài passed away, he succeeded to the throne.
Èyǒu pleaded,
"I beg for food to sustain myself."
The king said,
"Guard my neck, and I will give you food."
The king fell asleep again.
Èyǒu drew his sword to cut off the king's head, but the head fell off by itself.
The king awoke and asked,
He replied,
"Heaven brought about this karma."
The father at that time is now Shuddhodana.
The mother at that time is now Queen Māyā.
Èyǒu is now Devadatta.
The daughter of King Yuè is now Gopī.
Shànyǒu is now me.
Once there was a bodhisattva.
He was a great king.
His name was Chángshòu.
The king had a crown prince.
Named Chángshēng.
The king governed with righteousness, and the suffering of weapons and staffs did not befall his officials or people.
Wind and rain came in their seasons, and the five grains were abundant.
There was a neighboring king.
Who established cruel and harmful practices, did not cultivate proper governance, and his people were impoverished.
He said to his ministers:
"I hear that King Chángshòu is very wealthy and prosperous, with no military preparations. I wish to seize his kingdom."
The ministers said: "Excellent."
They raised troops to attack.
King Chángshòu told his assembled ministers:
"He covets my wealth.
If we engage in battle, it will certainly harm my people.
To contend for a kingdom and kill its people—I cannot bear it."
The ministers did not obey.
They dispatched troops beyond the border to meet and resist them.
The king and the crown prince crossed the city walls and went into seclusion.
The greedy king entered the kingdom and offered a reward for Chángshòu: a thousand catties of gold and ten million coins.
Later, the king came out by the roadside under a tree.
He encountered a Brahmin and asked where he had come from.
He replied:
"I am a poor ascetic.
I heard that King Chángshòu is fond of giving alms, so I came from afar to beg."
The king thought silently:
"He has met me after I lost my kingdom."
Shedding tears, he said:
"I am that king.
Meeting me in such a state, I have nothing to give you."
The two wept.
The king said:
"I hear the new king seeks me with a heavy reward.
If you take my head to him, you will certainly receive a rich reward."
The Brahmin said:
"I have little merit; I dare not accept this command."
The king said:
"You came from afar and met me in my destitution.
All men must die.
I wish to bestow this upon you; why decline?"
He replied:
"How could I bear to kill you?
If you truly wish to bestow alms, I hope you will accompany me back to the kingdom."
Thus they returned together, and upon reaching the city gate,
the king had him bind him and report to the greedy king.
The greedy king immediately rewarded him with gold and coins and sent him away.
At the crossroads of the four streets, he intended to burn and kill Chángshòu.
Throughout the city suburbs and wilderness, none did not cry out to heaven.
The crown prince heard of it.
He went out before his father, his heart filled with grief and pain.
The father, fearing his son would seek revenge,
looked up to heaven, sighed, and said:
"This death is what I delight in.
If you wish to be supremely filial, ensure your father dies without regret; do not seek revenge."
Chángshēng could not bear to see his father die and returned to the mountains.
After the king died, Chángshēng thought:
"My father was deeply benevolent and righteous, unwavering even unto death.
The greedy king is without principle, unable to distinguish good from evil.
He wrongfully killed my father; I cannot endure it.
If I do not kill him, I will not live in dishonor."
He then went out to hire himself as a laborer to a high minister, tending his vegetable garden, and the vegetables grew well.
The minister asked the garden overseer.
The overseer replied:
"I borrowed a man who is very diligent and capable."
The minister summoned Chángshēng and asked:
"Can you prepare food and drink?"
He replied: "I can."
Later, he then prepared food and drink for the king, which was delicious.
The king asked who made it.
He replied: "The laborer."
The king then summoned him to the palace to prepare food and drink.
The king later asked:
"Can you learn military tactics?"
He replied: "Most suitable."
The king had him serve by his side.
He told him:
"I have an enemy; I constantly fear encountering him.
Now I rely on you; assist me in preparing for him."
He replied: "Yes.
I will exert my strength and devote my life for the king."
Another day, the king asked:
"Do you enjoy hunting?"
He replied:
"Your subject enjoyed hunting since youth."
The king then ordered the outside to prepare the carriage and went out hunting with Chángshēng.
Just as they entered the mountain forest, they saw running beasts.
The king and Chángshēng galloped after them.
They turned into the deep mountains, lost their way for three days.
Then they became hungry and exhausted.
The king then dismounted, took off his sword, and handed it to Chángshēng, saying:
"I am very weary. Sit down; I wish to rest my head on your knee."
Chángshēng drew the sword, intending to kill the greedy king.
Remembering his father's command, he sheathed the sword and stopped.
This happened three times.
The king then awoke with a start and asked Chángshēng:
"I dreamed that the son of King Chángshòu wanted to come and harm me."
Chángshēng said:
"That is a fierce ghost coming to frighten you."
Finally, he said: "I originally intended to kill you."
Chángshēng said:
"I am indeed the crown prince of King Chángshòu, who came intending to kill you, great king.
My father, on the verge of death, earnestly enjoined me not to repay the king's enmity.
Thinking of my father's teaching, I threw the sword to the ground, obeying my father's command.
Even so, I fear that in the future I may become confused and lose my resolve.
I beg you, great king, to kill me now."
The king then repented, saying:
"I have been cruel and rebellious.
I did not distinguish good from evil.
The father and son of the virtuous one practiced benevolence, pure and steadfast, unwavering even unto death.
Yet I, greedy and cruel, was initially unaware.
Today, my life belongs to your hands.
You, however, cherish benevolence.
Remembering only your father's words,
how could you harm me?
I am sincerely moved by your great kindness.
Now I wish to return to my kingdom; which way should we go?"
Chángshēng said:
"I know the way. Previously, I deliberately misled you, intending to avenge my father's enmity."
Then they both left the forest and saw their troops.
The king returned to his own kingdom and returned this kingdom to the crown prince. They swore brotherhood, vowing not to invade or seize from each other.
They exchanged tributes and assisted each other in times of urgent difficulty.
King Chángshòu was myself.
The crown prince was Ānán.
The greedy king was Tiáodá.
In the past, the king of the kingdom of Zhēluó
had a queen but no heir.
The king was deeply grieved by this.
He commanded:
"You must return to your clan to seek a method for obtaining an heir."
The queen wept and took her leave, withdrawing.
She vowed to sacrifice herself and threw herself into the perilous mountains and dense forests.
The god Śakra was moved and said:
"This queen was my elder sister in a past life.
Now, because she has no heir, she sacrifices her body in the mountain dangers.
I am sorrowful and pity her."
Suddenly, he descended.
He gave her a vessel filled with fruit, saying:
"Sister, if you swallow this fruit, you will surely have a holy heir,
who will become a hero of the world.
If the king has doubts, show him this vessel.
This is a divine vessel of the heavenly king, the highest form of clear proof."
The queen looked up to the sky, swallowed the fruit, and suddenly he was no longer visible; she then felt her body
heavier. She returned and saw the king, reporting everything truthfully.
When the month was full, she gave birth to a boy.
His appearance was frail and ugly, rare in the world.
In his childhood years, he was intelligent, broadly knowledgeable, and his wisdom and strategies were unmatched.
His strength could cripple an elephant, catch a flying eagle, and his voice thundered like a lion's roar.
His fame spread far and wide, and all directions sighed in admiration.
The king arranged for him to marry a daughter from a neighboring kingdom,
named Yuèguāng, who was upright, elegant, and possessed all the virtues admired by the world.
She also had seven younger brothers,
who were also handsome and good.
The queen feared that Yuèguāng would despise the crown prince's appearance,
so she deceitfully said:
"Our country's old custom is that husband and wife do not see each other during the day.
This is to show respect.
Do not fail in proper conduct, my lady."
Yuèguāng replied:
"I respectfully obey.
I dare not neglect your esteemed instruction."
From then on, the crown prince came and went without ever showing a different expression.
Deeply considering that his own country was at odds with seven other kingdoms, locked in constant strife with no peace, and the people sighed in distress,
he thought, "I must use strategy to pacify them."
He pondered to himself:
"My body is extremely ugly; if my consort sees it, she will surely flee."
He asked his mother if he might once see his consort's appearance.
The queen said:
"Your appearance is ugly; your consort's beauty is radiant.
The crown prince insisted again.
The queen pitied him and took the consort to see him.
The crown prince pretended to be a herdsman.
The consort saw him and said:
"Is the herdsman ugly?"
The queen said:
"This was the late king's herdsman."
Later, they went to see the elephants.
The consort saw him again.
Suspicious, she said:
"Wherever I go, I keep seeing this man. Could he be the crown prince?"
The consort said:
"I wish to see the crown prince's glorious appearance."
The queen then devised a plan, having his younger brothers go out on an excursion,
with the crown prince's officials and attendants escorting them.
The consort saw this and felt a slight joy in her heart.
Later, they entered the garden again.
The crown prince climbed a tree and dropped a fruit onto her back.
The consort said:
"This must be the crown prince."
At night, while he slept, she silently shone a light to see his form and appearance; frightened, she fled back home.
The queen was angry and said:
"Why did you make the consort return?"
He replied:
"If the consort flees, it will be the foundation for the world's peace, and the people will finally have peace with their kin."
He bowed and took his leave, searching for her until he reached her kingdom.
He pretended to be a potter, hiring himself out to make pottery.
Then he entered the city and hired himself out as a dyer.
Then he hired himself out to a high official to tend horses and fatten them.
Then he became the chief steward, overseeing various delicacies, and entered the palace with soup.
The king had eight daughters, and all were pleased with these matters, but Yuèguāng paid no attention.
The god Śakra sighed and said:
"The Bodhisattva worries about and aids all beings, even to this extent.
I must use strategy to help him."
He provoked the seven enemy kingdoms, transforming into Yuèguāng's father's handwriting,
promising Yuèguāng in marriage to them.
