The seven kingdoms prepared ceremonies and came to the kingdom to personally welcome her.
They all said:
"We have been promised the king's daughter named Yuèguāng."
Disputes arose in confusion.
Each produced the handwritten letter.
Their grievances united as they said:
"We will destroy your lineage.
This is without doubt."
They sent back letters, all demanding together:
"Because of your one daughter, you have made seven kingdoms resentful.
Our combined armies are strong and numerous; consider your kingdom lost as of today."
The king heard this and feared, saying:
"This disaster is coming because of past actions."
He said to Yuèguāng:
"You are someone's consort.
Whether your husband is wise or foolish, fortunate or unfortunate, handsome or ugly, it is due to past karma; who can avert it?
Yet you were not chaste and devoted, failing to serve with respect; with shallow wisdom, you returned to your kingdom, bringing disaster to this point.
I will now cut your body into seven parts to apologize to the seven kings."
Yuèguāng wept and said:
"I beg you to spare my life for a brief moment.
I will recruit wise men; surely there is one who can repel the threat of the seven kingdoms."
The king then announced a recruitment:
"Whoever can avert this disaster,
I will give Yuèguāng in marriage and bestow great blessings."
The crown prince said:
"Quickly build a high tower; I can repel them."
The tower was completed.
The crown prince pretended to be ill, staggering and stumbling on the ground.
"Only if Yuèguāng carries me on her back can I repel the enemy."
Yuèguāng, terrified of being slaughtered, supported him and climbed the tower.
The crown prince shouted loudly:
"Kings of the seven kingdoms, your voices thunder afar,
like a lion's roar. I explain that the Buddha's teaching is great.
Governing the people should be with benevolence.
But now you raise great anger, and disaster will surely follow.
Disaster follows, and you will lose your lives and your kingdoms.
Is it because of fame and form?"
The heroic masters of the seven kingdoms all fell prostrate.
After a short while, they revived and wished to return to their own lands.
The crown prince addressed the king: "In matters of marriage, none are better than kings.
Why not give your seven daughters to the seven princes?
They will be sons-in-law acting as protective screens, and the king will have great peace.
The ministers and people will rest.
Kin will be cared for."
The king said:
"Excellent! This brings great joy."
He then commanded the seven kings to take his daughters as wives.
The eight sons-in-law paid their respects, and ruler and ministers were joyful.
The king and his ministers and people then realized that the crown prince was Yuèguāng's original husband.
He selected good assistants and warriors to escort each back to their kingdom.
Nine kingdoms were harmonious and peaceful, and the people danced with joy.
All sighed and said:
"Heaven sent a holy strategist, not an ordinary illumination; virtue gathered, merit accomplished, peacefully without blame."
After returning to his country for some years, the great king passed away.
The crown prince ascended the throne and granted a great amnesty for all crimes.
He taught the people with the five precepts, the six pāramitās, the eight precepts, and the ten good deeds.
Disasters and evils all ceased; the country prospered, the people were secure, and the great teaching spread widely; all revered the Three Jewels.
Virtue flourished, blessings returned, and all illnesses were eliminated.
The reason for this is:
In a past life, the Bodhisattva was at home plowing together with his wife, and he told his wife to fetch food.
He watched for his wife's return and saw her walking with a Pratyekabuddha, hiding in the mountain cliffs.
After a long time, she did not arrive, and doubt arose in his mind.
Angered, he took his hoe, intending to go and beat her.
Upon arriving, he saw his wife offering the food she had brought to the monk.
She stepped back and stood with hands clasped.
After the monk finished eating, he raised his bowl into the sky; light shone brilliantly, and he flew away.
The husband felt regret and shame, thinking his wife had virtue.
"She has brought about such reverence.
I have grave foolishness and will suffer its calamity."
He then said to his wife:
"The merit from your offering, I should share it.
Let us eat the remaining rice together; do not refuse."
At the end of their lives, each was born into a royal family.
The wife had pure and compassionate virtue,
so she was born beautiful.
The husband first had anger and later compassion, so he was first ugly and later handsome.
The crown prince was my former self.
The wife was Jùyí.
The father king was King Śuddhodana.
The mother was my mother, Shěmiào.
The god Śakra was Maitreya.
The enlightened being, in life after life, worries about and saves all beings from suffering and distress.
At that time, in the kingdom of Bōluónài, the king's crown prince,
named Mùpò,
was exceptionally handsome, unmatched in appearance.
He knew his past lives from countless kalpas.
All the good and evil, long and short lives, beauty and ugliness he had experienced were fully known and seen by him.
At the age of thirteen, he sealed his lips and did not speak.
The king had only this one son, beloved and esteemed by the entire kingdom, destined to inherit the throne.
He did not speak of hunger or cold, serene and simple in nature, his mind like withered wood.
Though he had eyes and ears, he did not use them to see or hear.
Though his wisdom and thoughts were profound, it was as if he had no mind or will.
Like one blind and deaf, he did not speak of east or west.
His demeanor was like that of a dull fool, unlike other people.
His father was deeply worried and troubled by this.
Greatly ashamed before neighboring kingdoms, fearing ridicule and scorn,
he summoned the brāhmaṇas of the kingdom and asked them,
"Why is this child unable to speak?"
The brāhmaṇas said,
"Though this child's face is handsome, he harbors inauspiciousness within.
He wishes to harm his parents, endanger the kingdom, and destroy the clan; this will come to pass soon.
If you no longer bear children, it will all be hindered by this evil son. He should be buried alive.
Only then can Your Majesty preserve yourself, secure the kingdom, and protect the clan.
Afterward, you may again beget noble sons.
Otherwise, it is extremely dangerous."
The king, believing their foolish madness, thought it to be true and thus became sorrowful.
He could not sit or rise in peace, took no pleasure in music, and found no enjoyment in fine clothing or food.
He then consulted with the elders and ministers, some suggesting to abandon him deep in the mountains,
others to cast him into deep waters.
One minister said,
"Simply dig a deep pit.
Carve a side chamber like a room.
Provide him with provisions and assign five servants to attend him.
Place him alive inside and let him do as he pleases."
The king followed this advice.
The crown prince grieved, saddened by their foolish delusion.
His mother, pitying and loving him, was heartbroken and said,
"My son's fate is so bitter, to encounter such calamity."
Weeping and sorrowful, with no other choice, she reluctantly let him go.
She gathered all the prince's clothes, necklaces, jewels, and treasures and sent them with him.
The servants were outside.
Together they dug the pit, but before it was finished,
Mùpò, alone in the carriage, deeply contemplated.
His heart spoke to his mouth:
"The king and the people all believe I am truly mute and foolish.
The reason I do not speak is to renounce worldly ties, find peace for my body, avoid troubles, save my spirit, and leave suffering behind.
Now, instead, I am endangered by this madness and deceit.
Once my life is lost, I will fall into the hands of those people.
He then silently took his necklaces, jewels, and treasures and left.
The pit-diggers did not notice.
Mùpò took the items and departed.
At that time, Mùpò went to the water's edge.
He bathed himself clean and anointed his body with fragrant oils.
He put on all his clothes and adorned himself with necklaces.
He went to the pit-digging site and asked,
"For what purpose are you digging this pit?"
The servants replied,
"The king has a crown prince named Mùpò.
Mute, deaf, and foolish, thirteen years old and unable to speak.
We are digging this pit to bury him alive."
The crown prince answered,
"I am Mùpò."
The workers were terrified and ran to look in the carriage, but he was not there.
Returning to the pit site, they carefully observed and listened; his speech was extraordinary, unlike any other voice.
His radiance was like the moon, rare in the world to hear.
Those around him were moved: travelers halted, those seated rose.
Birds in flight and beasts on the ground all gathered, prostrating before the crown prince to listen to his words.
He also said,
"Look at my hands and feet, observe my appearance.
How can the multitude believe this madness and deceit, seeing me buried alive and abandoned?"
His speech formed into eloquent phrases, astonishing those around him.
They all bowed, kowtowed, and begged for mercy and forgiveness.
The crown prince said,
"Now that I have been cast away, it is not fitting for me to return."
The servants immediately rushed to report to the king.
The king heard and felt both sorrow and joy.
He and the queen rode in a carriage to welcome him back.
Before the king arrived, Mùpò thought to himself,
"I should pursue the path of learning and practice."
Indra transformed into a garden tree of unparalleled joy.
The king saw from afar the crown prince sitting beneath the tree.
Mùpò saw the king and rose to greet him.
The king paid his respects, and Mùpò then addressed the king, inviting him to sit.
When the king heard the crown prince's voice and speech,
its majestic power was immeasurable, shaking heaven and earth, utterly without equal.
The king was overjoyed.
He then circled Mùpò, and together they returned to the kingdom.
"Take the throne and govern the kingdom; I shall step aside."
Mùpò said,
"No.
I am ashamed and weary of the hardships and manifold sorrows of hell.
I once was a king,
named Qǐngniàn.
I governed the kingdom with laws and upheld all good deeds.
For twenty-five years, no whips or canes were used, no weapons deployed, and no prisoners were held in jail.
I bestowed benevolence and love, spreading kindness widely, aiding the poor and distressed without greed or stinginess.
Despite such conduct, I still committed minor offenses and ultimately fell into hell for over sixty thousand years.
There, I was boiled, skinned, and torn apart; the pain was excruciating and unbearable.
I sought death but could not die; life held no solace.
At that time, my parents were wealthy and noble, living in boundless joy.
Could they have known I was suffering such severe torment in that hell?
Could they have come to share my suffering?
The reason for my fall into sin was that in a past life, I was a king ruling over small states.
My nature was very compassionate, my moral discipline strict, but my laws were not severe.
The kings of the small states all looked down on me and conspired together,
saying, 'This great king
is both kind and weak; his authority cannot control, his virtue cannot manage the great kingdom. He should be punished and deposed.'
They then raised armies to attack the great kingdom.
At that time, King Qǐngniàn sent them precious treasures and wealth as gifts.
He also bestowed high offices and generous salaries to appease and comfort them, pacifying them.
They then returned to their own kingdoms.
Not long after, they attacked again, repeatedly and not just once.
The ministers of the great kingdom addressed the king,
'These petty kings are foolish, ignorant, and without righteousness.
They do not consider their crimes, repeatedly acting with arrogance and insolence.
They plot murder and rebellion, offending Your Majesty.
They cause the people alarm and unrest, forcing constant vigilance. They should be executed to eliminate the bandit threat.'
The king said,
'As parents to the people, we must focus on benevolent transformation.
Forgive others, nurture beings, risk our lives to save the multitude.
They are like infants; pity their ignorance and gradually guide them. I cannot bear to harm them.'
The king loved all lives and never executed or punished anyone.
The great kingdom's ministers could not bear the repeated offenses.
The subordinate small states, looking down on them, grew angry and disregarded the difficulties.
They raised armies to attack, slaughtering the people.
The great king shed tears.
He mourned for the dead people of those states as if for his own children, with boundless compassion.
The petty kings, seeing the great king's compassionate heart and pity for the people,
all surrendered and came to submit.
The great king prepared a grand feast, requiring the slaughter of cattle, sheep, and livestock to provide various delicacies.
They first sought the king's permission.
Though the king's heart was compassionate, circumstances left no choice.
He nodded in agreement, and thus incurred guilt, suffering such hardships.
Each time I recall this, my heart trembles, my body grows cold and sweaty, remembering past lives' fortunes and misfortunes, safety and danger, success and failure.
Fearing to encounter such again, I hoped through silence
to escape flaws and impurities, transcend worldly toils,
permanently leave secular life, and avoid calamitous encounters.
But then, thinking to remain silent, I was nearly buried alive by the king.
I feared the king might later incur such calamity and fall into hell with no chance of escape.
I did not wish the king to incur guilt, so I spoke again.
Guard the mind, be non-active, and take no pleasure in being king.
The people and the world are fleeting like a dream.
Family joys are but momentary.
Considering life's brevity, worries and fears extend long.
Pleasures are few, sufferings many, with countless troubles.
Therefore, the wise
see the kingdom's wealth and treasures, love and affection as burdens.
All desires are dust.
If I were to become king, I would again grow arrogant, indulgent, greedy for pleasure,
causing the people worry and distress.
This is the great affliction of the world.
Now I wish to renounce it,
reverse the flow, exhaust the source, and save those not yet liberated.
Life in the world is like a sojourn; nothing can be relied upon.
I do not covet wealth or honor, nor treasure jewels.
I abandon worldly glory and contemplate the great path.
Transcendent and far-reaching, I extricate myself from the world."
The father king said,
"You are a wise man; you cannot simply do this."
Mùpò said,
"How can it be that father and son, once born, abandon each other?
Flesh and bone already separated, such conduct is deeply wrong.
To insist on welcoming me back only adds to the toil and trouble."
The father saw his determination was firm.
At a loss, with no words to reply,
he then said,
"You, as in your past life as a king, upheld all good deeds.
With only minor faults, not even remembered or known,
you still suffered such severe punishment and hardship.
Now I govern the kingdom without upholding the law and governance.
Having no minor good deeds, instead full of faults and wrongs,
purely engaging in peril, how immeasurable will my sins be?"
He then released the crown prince, allowing him to pursue the path of learning.
The crown prince then renounced the kingdom, abandoned kingship, and disregarded human affairs.
With single-minded focus, he contemplated the path, cultivated virtue, accumulated merits and achievements, leading to the present.
Mùpò is myself.
The father king is Shuddhodana.
The mother is Māyā.
The diviner is Devadatta.
The attending servants were Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya and the other five.
In the past, there was a king named Móhēluótuó.
He cultivated virtuous conduct, and his kingdom had no enemies.
The king had three sons.
The eldest was named Móhēbōnàluó.
The second was named Móhētífó.
The youngest was named Móhēsàduǒ.
They went out together for an excursion and came to a bamboo grove, where they rested and stopped.
Proceeding further, they saw a tigress.
She had given birth seven days ago, with seven cubs surrounding her.
She was starving, emaciated, and weak, on the verge of death.
The first prince said,
"How strange! This tigress cannot find food.
Driven by hunger, she will surely eat her own cubs."
The third prince said,
"What does this tigress usually eat?"
The first prince said,
"Fresh, warm flesh and blood."
The third prince said,
"Who can give food to this tigress?"
The second prince said,
"Her remaining life is short; even if someone sought to help, it would be too late.
Who would be willing to spare not their own life?"
The first prince said,
"Nothing is harder to give up than one's own body."
The third prince said,
"Those with little wisdom are deeply attached and miserly.
They cannot give up their bodies and are terrified at the mere thought.
Only great beings, with hearts full of compassion,
find it not difficult to give up their lives for the benefit of others."
They all felt sorrowful, gazed intently, and then left.
The third prince thought to himself,
"The time has come for me to give up my body.
Since ancient times, I have wasted this body to no purpose.
I have constantly protected this house-like body, clothing it,
feeding it, and nurturing it in every way so that it lacks nothing.
It knows no gratitude or affection, but instead breeds resentment and harm.
In the end, it is impermanent and brings no benefit.
It is as detestable as a thief and as foul as a latrine.
Now, this body of mine shall serve as a great bridge across the sea of birth and death.
It is filled with countless sores, ulcers, diseases, and hundreds of thousands of fears.
Urine, feces, sinews, blood, skin, and marrow are all interconnected.
I shall now give it up to seek the quiescence of supreme Nirvāṇa.
I shall attain immeasurable meditative concentration, wisdom, and meritorious virtues,
fully accomplishing the subtle Dharma-body,
and bringing the joy of Dharma to all sentient beings."
Fearing that his two elder brothers might hinder him,
he immediately said to them,
"You may return ahead with the retinue to where we stopped."
Sàduǒ returned to where the tigress was.
He removed his garments and hung them on the bamboo.
"For the sake of Bodhi-wisdom, I shall forever leave the three realms of existence."
He then threw himself down in front of the starving tigress.
The tigress could not eat him.
He pierced his neck with a dry bamboo stick.
Throwing himself down from a height, the earth shook, and the sun lost its brilliance.
Heavenly flowers of various kinds and wondrous fragrances rained down.
A voice praised from the sky, saying,
"This is unprecedented!"
The tigress licked the blood and gradually was able to eat the flesh.
She regained her strength to eat.
Only bones remained.
In a past age,
when the people of Jambudvīpa
were afflicted by a plague, all were suffering from illness.
At that time, the king of Jambudvīpa,
named Móxīsīnà,
ruled over eighty-four thousand great cities.
His power and authority were supreme.
His chief consort, from the time she became pregnant,
could heal any sick person she touched with her hand.
When the month was full, she gave birth to a son.
As soon as he was born, he said,
"I can cure illnesses."
Also, at the time of his birth,
all the gods and spirits in Jambudvīpa proclaimed together,
"The child born to the king now is the human medicine."
Because this sound was heard everywhere, he was named Rényào (Human Medicine).
Sick people were then brought before this prince.
When the sick came,
if the prince touched them with his hand or body, they were all cured.
They became safe, secure, and happy.
Prince Rényào healed illnesses in this way for a thousand years.
Later, he passed away.
When the sick came and heard he had died,
they wept in sorrow, asking, "Who will now relieve us of our sickness and suffering?"
The sick said,
"Where was Prince Rényào's body cremated?"
They asked to know the location and went to the cremation site.
They took out his bones, ground them into powder, applied it to their bodies, and were all cured.
After the bones were exhausted, even going to the cremation site cured their illnesses.
Prince Rényào was I in a past life.
There was a prince who wished to know his past lives.
He then asked the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"It is better not to know, for it will bring you sorrow."
The prince still wished to know.
He asked three times like this.
The Buddha then gave him the precept, allowing him to know his past lives.
Thereupon, the prince saw his own affairs.
He was fated to die at fifteen, and his sorrow was beyond words.
When he reached fifteen, he died.
The royal family buried him and planted a cypress tree, which grew tall.
Its roots went deep into the earth, right where his heart was.
His consciousness remained in the body, and he saw the cypress root grow,
piercing right through his heart. As it grew, it pierced his heart.
Then, he emerged from the root among the cypress leaves and saw a goat coming.
He thought to himself,
"This goat will eat the cypress and harm me again."
Sure enough, the goat came and ate.
He was inside the goat's belly.
He came out with the goat's dung and clung to it.
A gardener collected the dung to fertilize the chives.
He was among the chive leaves.
It happened that the queen craved chives.
She ordered some to be sent from outside.
The gardener took a knife to cut the chives.
Fearing the knife would harm him,
he was filled with endless worry and sorrow.
The gardener cut the chives, bundled them, and sent them to the royal palace.
He was in the bundle of chives.
The palace received the chives, and the queen ate them.
He entered her belly with the chives and became her child.
When the month was full, he was born.
As he grew up, he again remembered his past lives.
He went to the Buddha and said,
"I no longer wish to know my past lives.
It brings me sorrow.
I now return the knowledge of past lives to you."
The Buddha said to the prince,
"I did not want to give it to you then.
You insisted on having it.
Now that you regret it, it is acceptable."
In the city of Rājagṛha, there was a young maiden.
Her name was Bālāvatī.
The king ordered a brothel to be established for her.
Anyone who stayed overnight with her would pay two hundred gold coins per day and night.
People from all directions gathered to gaze upon her, finding her extremely beautiful.
At that time, Prince Wúwèi, son of King Bimbisāra,
stayed with this courtesan and she consequently became pregnant.
The courtesan then instructed the gatekeeper, saying,
"If anyone asks to see me, tell them I am ill."
Later, when the months were fulfilled, she gave birth to a baby boy.
His features were handsome and proper.
At that time, the courtesan
immediately wrapped the child in white cloth, ordered a maidservant, and abandoned him in an alley.
Prince Wúwèi saw this and asked a bystander,
"What is this?"
The person replied,
"This is a child."
He asked,
"Alive or dead?"
The reply was,
"Still alive."
He had someone carry the child back to his residence and gave him to a wet nurse to raise.
He then gave him a name, calling him the youth Jīpó.
Later, as he gradually grew up,
the prince, who loved him, called him and said,
"If you wish to remain long in the royal household,
without any talent or skill,
you cannot idly consume the king's provisions.
You should learn a craft."
He replied, "Yes."
He then went to study under a physician in the country of Takṣaśilā,
of the Ācārya clan,
named Piṅgala.
After seven years of study, he said to his teacher,
"How long must I study before I am finished?"
The teacher then gave him a basket and digging tools,
saying, "You may go within one yojana around Takṣaśilā
to seek out various plants.
Bring back any that are not medicinal."
At that time, the youth Jīpó
did as his teacher instructed but ultimately could not find any that were not medicinal.
Every plant, tree, and all things he saw,
he could expertly distinguish and know their uses—there was nothing that was not medicinal.
He returned and reported this to his teacher.
The teacher replied,
"You may go now. Your medical training is complete.
I am the foremost in Jambudvīpa.
After my death, you will be next."
He returned to the city of Vārāṇasī.
The wife of a great elder in the city
had suffered from a headache for twelve years.
Many physicians treated her but could not cure her.
Jīpó heard of this
and went to her house, telling the gatekeeper,
"Inform your elder
that a physician is at the gate."
The gatekeeper reported this to the elder.
The elder's wife asked,
"What does the physician look like?"
The reply was,
"He is young."
She thought to herself,
"Even the old, experienced physicians could not cure me,
let alone a young one.
If there is no harm, let him in."
Jīpó then went to see the elder's wife.
He took good medicine and fried it with ghee.
He poured it into the elder's wife's nose and mouth.
Both ghee and saliva came out.
He had someone hold a vessel to catch it.
The ghee was collected and kept,
while the saliva was separately discarded.
Jīpó then said,
"You are so stingy as to save even this small amount of unclean ghee.
How then could you repay me?"
The elder's wife replied,
"Managing a household is not easy.
What good would discarding it do?
It can be used to fuel a fire, hence I collect it.
You just treat the illness; why worry about such things?"
Later, her illness was cured.
The elder's wife
gave him four hundred thousand gold coins,
along with slaves, cattle, and horses.
Jīpó returned to Rājagṛha and went to Prince Wúwèi's gate.
The prince summoned him in.
Jīpó recounted the previous events in detail to the prince.
He offered all that he had received to the prince. The prince said,
"This is the youth Jīpó's first medical treatment."
There was a king
named Brahmadatta.
He made offerings to the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
Every fasting day,
the king would lead his retinue to where the Buddha was.
Whenever the Buddha taught the Dharma,
the king would joyfully and reverently listen to the sutras.
His son was named Kṣudrapanthaka.
With utmost sincerity and diligence, he realized the impermanence of the world.
He understood that there is no life without death and did not covet worldly glory.
He said to the king,
"The Buddha is hard to encounter, and the Dharma is hard to hear.
I beg to become a śramaṇa." The king permitted him.
Kṣudrapanthaka then bid farewell to the king and went to where the Buddha was.
He requested to become a bhikṣu.
The Buddha then touched his head with his hand.
His hair fell off by itself, and the monastic robes appeared on his body.
He upheld the heavy precepts, diligently cultivated,
and tirelessly practiced day and night for three months.
He then attained Arhatship.
The king did not yet know that he had attained the path.
Seeing him toiling hard, eating coarse vegetables,
he often went to make offerings to him, treating him differently from the other monks.
His mind was not the same.
He would say to him,
"In my kingdom, there are all kinds of rare treasures, delicious food, and delicacies—nothing is lacking.
Why do you delight in being a śramaṇa?"
Kṣudrapanthaka then lightly rose and stayed in mid-air.
He flew, transformed, divided his body, and moved in and out without hindrance.
When the king saw this,
he was filled with both sorrow and joy, prostrated himself with his five limbs on the ground, and paid homage to Kṣudrapanthaka.
The Buddha instructed Kṣudrapanthaka to explain to the king the Dharma of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and the Four Noble Truths.
The king then understood the meaning.
He attained the path of Srotāpanna.
When King Aśoka first ascended the throne,
he appointed his younger brother Tissa as crown prince.
And he said to him,
"You should develop good faith and confidence in the Buddha's Dharma."
Later, while hunting, the younger brother entered a forest.
He saw an ascetic scorching his body with five fires.
He immediately developed deep faith.
He bowed with his head at the ascetic's feet and asked,
"How long have you lived here? What do you eat and wear?
How do you rest and arise, and how do you deal with lustful desires?"
The ascetic replied,
"For twelve years, I have always eaten tree fruits and roots.
I make clothes from woven grass.
I spread grass to sleep on.
When I see deer mating, lustful thoughts arise in me."
Tissa doubted,
"Even this ascetic, practicing such austerities, still gives rise to lustful thoughts.
The disciples of the Buddha live comfortably and enjoyably.
How can they see desire and not give rise to thoughts?
If lustful thoughts arise, how can they attain dispassion?"
He then spoke a verse:
Tissa further said,
"The disciples of Śākyamuni deceive the king into making merit."
The king heard this and told his ministers,
"My younger brother has developed faith in heretics.
We must use skillful means to lead him to correct understanding.
I wish to bathe
and should enter the bathhouse.
You should adorn my younger brother with a crown and royal garments,
and have him ascend my throne."
When the king went to bathe,
the ministers urged Tissa.
Tissa complied.
The king saw this and said,
"I am not yet dead.
You have already assumed kingship."
He then ordered him killed.
Many men with weapons surrounded him.
The ministers said to the king,
"This is the king's younger brother.
We beg the king to be forbearing and not give rise to anger."
The king replied,
"I will be forbearing.
For seven days, I will temporarily give him the kingdom to rule as king.
All kinds of music and court ladies will be provided for him.
All ministers and people will go to pay their respects.
Executioners will stand at the door with swords.
Each day, they will report to the king until the seventh day."
Adorned as king, Aśoka's ministers and others took Vitāśoka to pay respects to Aśoka's ministers.
The king then asked,
"You have been king for seven days.
Did you enjoy the various music and sights?"
He replied with a verse:
The king spoke to his younger brother again.
Throughout your life, contemplate the suffering of death.
Even if you obtain the finest five desires, do not develop attachment.
A bhikṣu who has left home contemplates the twelve āyatanas.
He contemplates the immeasurable cycles of birth and death and the sufferings of the three evil destinies.
He also contemplates how, whether among humans or in the heavens, pursuing the four directions ultimately ends in decay and ruin.
It is like an empty village with no inhabitants.
The fire of impermanence burns all worlds.
The Buddha's disciples constantly make this contemplation.
How then could they give rise to afflictions?
The king, using skillful means and the Buddha's Dharma, taught and transformed him.
Píduōshūkē said,
"I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."
The king embraced his younger brother's neck with both hands.
And said to him,
"I did not abandon you; it was to make you have faith in the Buddha's Dharma.
Therefore, I manifested this skillful means."
At that time, Píduōshūkē made offerings of various flowers, incense, and musical performances to the Buddha's stūpa.
He made offerings of various foods and drinks to the assembly of monks. On another day, he went out again for hunting.
He arrived at a secluded forest dwelling.
He saw a bhikṣu's seat.
His name was Tánwúdé.
A *[text missing/corrupt]* broke off a tree branch and from a distance brushed it towards the bhikṣu.

The king's nephew, a brāhmaṇa named Āshì, had one son leave home. The feudal lords, officials, slaves, and servants all upheld the five precepts, observed the six fasting days each month, and fully practiced the eightfold path.
Because of this, many kṣatriyas left home, and the Buddha's Dharma flourished.
The non-Buddhists declined and were extinguished, all losing their support; going everywhere to beg for food, they could not obtain it.
They deceitfully entered the Buddha's Dharma and became śramaṇas.
Yet they still held to their original doctrines and taught the people.
The virtuous bhikṣus did not associate with them.
At that time, Mùliánzǐ Dìxū entrusted his disciples to Móxīntuó.
He secluded himself in the tranquil Āxiūhé Mountain.
The non-Buddhist bhikṣus wanted to mix their scriptures with the Buddha's Dharma.
This then became defiled and turbid.
Some were fire-worshippers.
Some scorched their bodies with five heats.
Some entered water in extreme cold.
Some destroyed the Buddha's Dharma.
This went on and on until for seven years they could not recite the precepts.
Āyù sent a great minister into the king's saṅghārāma.
He said to the senior monk,
"The king orders the community of monks to be harmonious and recite the precepts."
The senior monk replied,
"The virtuous bhikṣus do not perform the poṣadha together with the non-Buddhist bhikṣus."
The minister, proceeding in order, beheaded them, reaching even Dìxū.
The minister asked,
"Who are you?"
He answered,
"I am the king's uterine brother."
Only then did he stop.
The minister then reported to the king.
The king heard and was shocked and alarmed; distress arose in his mind.
He immediately went to the monastery and asked,
"Among the bhikṣus, who has incurred offense?"
One bhikṣu said,
"Both have incurred offense."
Another bhikṣu said,
"There was no intent to kill.
The king himself has no offense."
Doubt arose in the king's mind.
He asked the bhikṣus,
"Is there anyone who can resolve my doubt?
If my doubtful mind is resolved, I will re-establish the Buddha's Dharma."
The bhikṣus said,
"Dìxū can resolve it."
He sent a messenger to invite Dìxū.
The envoy conveyed the king's message, saying,
"Now the Buddha's Dharma has perished.
We respectfully implore you, Great Virtuous One,
to come and together re-establish it."
Dìxū replied,
"I left home precisely for the Buddha's Dharma; now the time has come."
The king dreamed at night of a white elephant rubbing the king's head with its trunk and grasping the king's right hand.
The next morning he asked an astrologer.
The astrologer replied,
"The one grasping the king's hand is the image of a śramaṇa."
He then asked the messenger,
"Has Dìxū arrived now?"
The king went out to welcome him.
Dìxū grasped the king's hand; the king's attendants drew their swords intending to harm him.
The king saw the reflection of the swords in the water and said,
"Previously I ordered you to go to the monastery and have the community of monks harmoniously recite the precepts.
You misinterpreted my intention and killed the bhikṣus.
Now you want to kill me again?"
The king led Dìxū into the garden.
With his own hands, he washed his feet and anointed them with oil.
He requested, saying,
"I wish to see the Great Virtuous One's spiritual power."
Dìxū went around the four directions, each for one yojana, and stretched a cord to mark a boundary.
In the east he placed chariots, in the south horses, in the west people, and in the north copper.
He placed a basin of water and had them each ride on the boundary line; the area outside the boundary shook.
The feet outside all swayed, but the feet inside did not move.
The king was delighted and said,
"My previous doubt is gone.
Within the Buddha's Dharma, the evil dharmas can be extinguished."
Dìxū then explained the Jātaka Sūtra, saying,
The Buddha told the bhikṣus,
"First consider the mind, then undertake actions.
All karma arises from the mind." Later he attained Arhatship and experienced the joy of liberation.
Remembering the king's previous stipulation,
"After leaving home, always come to see the king,"
he thought, "I should now fulfill the original agreement."
And so, proceeding in order, he traveled to the country of Bōzhàlìfúduō.
In the morning, he put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the country to beg for food.
Proceeding in order, he reached the royal city and said to the gatekeeper,
"You go in and inform the king, saying,
'Píduōshūkē is now outside the gate and wishes to see the great king.'"
At that time, the gatekeeper immediately informed the king.
The king said, "Bring him in."
He immediately rose and paid respects, like a great tree falling.
He rose and joined his palms, gazing at him without tiring.
Weeping sorrowfully, he said,
"Great Minister Shànhù, look!
Píduōshūkē wears rag-robes, holds an earthenware bowl, and begs for food in order, accepting both coarse and fine without discrimination in his mind."
He then said to the king,
"Píduōshūkē has few desires and knows contentment; what needed to be done has been done."
At that time, the king respectfully placed him on a fine seat.
He personally offered him various foods and drinks with his own hands.
After eating, he washed the bowl and set it aside.
He expounded the Dharma for the king.
His body ascended into the empty sky, and all the people saw it.
The king and the great assembly joined their palms and gazed at him.
Without taking their eyes off him for a moment, they asked the king,
Píduōshūkē went to the border region.
Upon arriving, he fell ill.
Because the illness was severe, sores broke out all over his head.
When the king heard of this,
he immediately dispatched attendants and physicians to treat him with medicine.
Later, he recovered slightly.
The physicians and attendants were all sent back.
The only nourishment for his body was cow's milk.
To beg for food, he went to a place with many cows.
There was another country named Fènnàpótuónà, where everyone believed in non-Buddhist teachings.
A Buddhist disciple saw this and reported it to the king.
The king ordered a yaksha, and in the span of a single thought,
he brought the non-Buddhist disciples and their painted images.
The king became greatly enraged.
Regarding all the non-Buddhists in the country of Fènnàpótuónà,
he had them all killed.
In a single day, one hundred and eight thousand non-Buddhists were killed.
There was another disciple of the non-Buddhists,
who loved the non-Buddhist practices and worshipped a naked deity.
He painted an image of the Tathāgata and paid respects to the deity's feet.
When the king heard of this matter again,
he ordered others
to seize this person and his relatives,
place them in a house, and burn them with fire.
At that time, the king issued a decree:
"If anyone can obtain the head of a Nirgrantha,
I will give them a gold coin."
Píduōshūkē entered a cow-herding place, having been ill for many days.
His hair, beard, and nails had all grown long and sharp.
His clothes were worn and tattered, lacking any shine or color.
At that time, a cow-herding woman secretly thought to herself:
"Now this Nirgrantha has come into my dwelling."
She then said to her husband,
"You should kill this Nirgrantha, take his head to the king,
and you will surely receive a gold reward."
The husband drew his knife and went.
Píduōshūkē then reflected to himself,
seeing his karmic retribution with no means of escape.
He thus accepted death.
The husband took the head to the king, seeking to obtain gold.
The king, suspicious, immediately questioned his physicians and attendants, saying,
They replied, "This is the head of Píduōshūkē."
The king fainted and remained unconscious for a long time.
A minister addressed the king,
"Even one without outflows cannot avoid such suffering.
Great King, you should grant fearlessness to all beings."
The king followed his words and proclaimed an order that no one should kill Nirgranthas anymore.
The bhikṣus became doubtful
and asked Upagupta,
"What karma did Píduōshūkē create in the past that he now receives this retribution?"
He replied,
"In a past life, there was a hunter who killed many deer.
In a great forest, there was a spring.
At that time, this hunter set up nets and snares by the water's edge, killing many deer.
At that time, the Buddha had not yet appeared in the world.
There was a pratyekabuddha who ate by the water.
After eating, he washed and returned to sit under a tree.
At that time, the herd of deer, smelling the scent of the pratyekabuddha, did not go to the water's edge.
The hunter, sitting there, saw that no deer came.
He then followed their tracks to where the pratyekabuddha was.
He thought to himself,
'Because this person is sitting here, the deer do not come.'
He then killed the pratyekabuddha with a knife.
That hunter of the past was Píduōshūkē.
Because he killed many deer, he now suffers from many illnesses.
Moreover, because he killed a pratyekabuddha, for countless years he constantly fell into hell,
enduring various sufferings and torments for five hundred lifetimes.
In the human realm, in every life, he was always killed by others.
Now is the final retribution:
although he attained arhatship, he was still harmed by others.
He went forth under the Dharma of Kāśyapa Buddha,
delighted in practicing generosity,
and constantly encouraged others to make offerings to the saṅgha.
There was a stūpa containing the Buddha's hair and nails.
He made offerings to it with incense, flowers, banners, canopies, and various musical performances.
Due to this karmic retribution, he was born into a great clan.
For one hundred thousand years, he constantly practiced brahmacarya.
He also made a vow,
and due to this karmic condition, he attained arhatship."
Prince Jeta said to the Buddha,
"In the past, I received the five precepts.
The precept against alcohol is difficult to uphold; I fear breaking it and incurring offense.
Now I wish to abandon the five precepts and receive the ten wholesome practices."
The Buddha said,
"When you drink alcohol, what evil arises?"
He replied,
"In the country, the powerful and influential from time to time gather together,
bringing wine and food to enjoy themselves together,
leading to joy and without any other evil.
Even when obtaining wine, I remember the precept and do not commit evil."
The Buddha said,
"If people can be like you, what evil is there in drinking alcohol for a lifetime?
For one who acts thus, merit should arise, and there is no offense.
People's practice of good is of two kinds:
one is with outflows,
the other is without outflows.
Good with outflows leads to the bliss of humans and devas.
Good without outflows leads beyond the suffering of birth and death,
to the fruition of nirvāṇa.
If a person drinks alcohol without giving rise to evil karma,
due to the condition of a wholesome mind, they receive wholesome karmic retribution.
What fault is there in your upholding the five precepts?"
In Śrāvastī, there were powerful clans, kṣatriyas, nobles, and lords.
Due to minor disputes, they developed great enmity.
Each formed plans and raised troops to attack one another.
Both families were among the country's most outstanding,
and were also relatives, so they could not be arrested.
The conflict and fighting were chaotic, and they would not heed reasoned advice.
The king was deeply troubled by this.
He further reflected to himself,
"In the past, there was a senior minister of the former king named Tíwéiluó.
Relying on his clan's wealth, nobility, and power,
he was disrespectful, ridiculing and mocking me.
At that time, in my anger, I truly wished to have him executed.
I reported the matter to my father,
but my father would not permit it.
I harbored poison and resentment, not knowing what to do.
I was distressed, sorrowful, and unable to eat or drink.
The queen mother saw my worry and suffering,
and tried with various means to advise and enlighten me, but my mind remained unsettled.
She then sought fine wine and urged me to drink.
At that time, I said to my mother,
'Our ancestors for generations have served the god Nārāyaṇa.
If I drink wine now, I fear the god will surely be angry,
and the brāhmaṇas will reprimand and punish me.'
My mother, in the quiet of the night,
secretly opened the palace gates without anyone knowing,
and pressed me repeatedly until I reluctantly complied.
After drinking the wine, I forgot my sorrow and resentment.
I gathered palace maidens for singing and musical performances for twenty-one days,
and from this, I found peace.
Reflecting on this,
I then ordered a loyal minister
to prepare fine wine and various sweet delicacies,
and summoned all the ministers to assemble in the king's hall.
The loyal minister prepared crystal bowls,
each holding three liters.
The king first filled one bowl,
and each person was given a bowl of the sweet dew, a wonderful elixir.
Afterwards, they discussed state affairs and also had various entertainers perform.
The people, having obtained the wine and hearing the music, felt joy in their hearts, forgot their hatred and enmity, and were carefree and without worry.
The king again raised his bowl and addressed the lords, saying,
'Noble men cultivate virtue, passed down through generations.
They follow and uphold the holy teachings and should not deviate.
Why do you, my lords, because of minor matters, quarrel and contend like this?
If you cannot endure, I fear the destruction of the state and its ancestral temples.
Therefore, I earnestly advise you; it is fortunate that you yourselves should cease.'
The ministers addressed the king,
'We respectfully obey your weighty command and dare not disobey.'
Thus, peace was achieved—this was the merit of wine."
King Aśoka had a consort
named Bómópódǐ, who gave birth to a son.
His form and complexion were upright, and his eyes were the finest.
No one who saw him failed to love and delight in him.
The palace attendants informed the king,
"The consort has given birth to a son."
The king was greatly joyful.
Therefore, he named this child Dharmavardhana, and they brought the child to show King Aśoka.
At that time, when the king saw him, he joyfully spoke a verse.
When Kunāla grew up, a consort was taken for him.
The consort was named Yúzhēnàmóluó. At that time, King Aśoka
took Kunāla to the Kukkuṭārāma monastery.
In the monastery was a senior monk, an arhat with the six superknowledges,
named Yaśas.
At that time, Yaśas saw Kunāla
and knew that before long, he would lose his eyes.
He then said to the king,
"Therefore, do not let Kunāla create his own karma."
At that time, King Aśoka said to Kunāla,
"The Venerable One is mindful of your actions.
You should follow him."
At that time, Kunāla paid respects at Yaśas's feet
and said,
"Venerable One, instruct me on what to do."
Yaśas replied,
"The eye is impermanent; you should contemplate this."
He then spoke a verse.
At that time, Kunāla, in a quiet place in the palace, sat alone and contemplated,
"The eye and other sense bases are suffering and impermanent."
At that time, King Aśoka's chief consort,
named Wēishāluòqǐduō,
went to where Kunāla was and saw him sitting alone.
Gazing at his eyes, she gave rise to lustful thoughts.
She embraced him with her hands
and spoke a verse.
Kunāla covered his ears
and spoke a verse.
The mother became angry and resentful.
She again spoke a verse.
Kunāla said,
"Wēishāluòqǐduō
constantly watched for his faults and wished to kill him.
To the north, there was a country
named Takṣaśilā.
It was disobedient to the king.
King Aśoka commanded Kunāla,
'You go to that country.'
The king replied, 'Yes.'"
The king was troubled in his heart.
Therefore, he had the roads adorned and repaired with extra care.
Old age, sickness, death, and such were all to be kept out of sight.
At that time, the king and Jùnàluó rode together in one chariot to see him off.
As they approached the road where they were to part,
he embraced his son by the neck.
Seeing Jùnàluó's eyes,
he wept and said,
"The physiognomist, upon seeing the king,
only observed the child's eyes and paid no attention to anything else."
He then spoke a verse:
...and so Jùnàluó
proceeded in order to the country of Tèchāshīluó.
The people of that country, hearing of his arrival, went out half a yojana to adorn the various roads.
At every place they set out water to await the coming multitude.
At that time, the people then spoke a verse:
When the king arrived,
the people joined their palms and spoke thus:
"We welcome the king,
not for strife nor to oppose him,
O great king, nor do we bear you any grudge.
But the minister dispatched by the king to reside in our country
governs without principle.
We wish to depose him."
At that time, the people
with various offerings made offerings to King Jùnàluó and welcomed him into the country.
At that time, King Āyù fell gravely ill.
Feces came from his mouth, and all sorts of impure fluids issued from his pores.
All skilled physicians were unable to cure him.
The king then said to his ministers,
"Summon Jùnàluó to return.
I shall perform the abhiṣeka and confer upon him the kingship.
As for me now, I do not cling to life or body."
At that time, Wēishāluòqǐduō said to the king,
"I can cause the king's illness to be cured."
The king accepted his words and dismissed all the physicians.
Wēishāluòqǐduō said to the physicians,
"If there are men or women outside who are ill like the king, bring them in."
At that time, in the country of Āpíluó, there was a man whose illness was no different from the king's.
At that time, the sick man's wife sought a physician.
The physician replied,
"Bring him here; I wish to see him.
I shall then prescribe medicine."
The wife sent him to the physician.
The physician sent him to the king's consort.
At that time, the king's consort placed this sick man in a deserted place.
She had his belly cut open, revealing the raw and cooked entrails.
There was a large worm.
If the worm moved upward, feces came from the mouth.
If the worm moved downward, then it came from below.
If it moved left or right, it came from the pores.
At that time, the king's consort placed málízhē beside the worm.
But the worm did not die.
Again, she placed bìbō beside the worm.
The worm also did not die.
Again, she placed dried ginger beside the worm.
The worm also did not die.
...until she placed garlic beside the worm.
The worm then died.
At that time, the king's consort fully reported this matter to the king.
"The king should now eat garlic.
The illness will then be cured."
The king replied,
"I am a kṣatriya; I may not eat garlic."
The consort said again,
"For the sake of life and body, consider it medicine and eat it."
The king then ate it; the worm died and the illness was cured.
His bowel movements returned to normal.
The king bathed and purified himself and said to his consort,
"What do you desire now? I shall grant it to you as you wish."
The consort said to the king,
"I wish the king to allow me to be king for seven days."
The king said to the consort, "If you become king, you will surely kill me."
The consort said again,
"After seven days have passed, I shall return the kingship to you."
At that time, the king permitted it.
The consort, pretending to be king,
wrote to the people of Tèchāshīluó,
ordering them to take Jùnàluó's eyes. Having finished writing the letter,
it needed to be sealed with the tooth seal.
The king was asleep.
The consort, wishing to seal the letter, approached the king's side.
The king immediately awoke with a start.
The consort said to the king,
"Why are you startled?"
The king said,
"I dreamed that a vulture wanted to take Jùnàluó's eyes."
The consort replied,
"The child Jùnàluó is now very safe and secure."
A second time he dreamed.
The king started up again, "I have dreamed again."
The consort asked,
"What was the dream about?"
The king replied,
"I saw Jùnàluó's head, beard, hair, and nails all grown long and sharp."
But he could not speak.
The consort replied,
"He is safe and secure now; I pray, do not worry."
The king slept again.
The consort secretly sealed it with the great king's tooth.
She dispatched a messenger to deliver it to the people of Tèchāshīluó.
The king again dreamed that all his own teeth fell out.
At dawn the next morning, after bathing and washing were completed,
he summoned the physiognomist and told him the dream.
The physiognomist replied,
"If a person has such a dream,
his son will lose his eyes.
It is no different from losing the son."
When the king heard this,
he immediately stood up and joined his palms,
facing the western gods and made a vow, saying:
The messenger, holding the letter, arrived in the country of Tèchāshīluó.
At that time, the people there, seeing this letter arrive,
out of concern for Jùnàluó, together concealed this letter and did not give it to him.
Those people further considered,
"King Āyù is greatly to be feared; his heart is not reverent or faithful.
Towards his own son he still wishes to take his eyes;
how much more towards us would he not harbor malice?"
They gave the letter to Jùnàluó.
Jùnàluó, having received the letter,
said to the people,
"If you are to take my eyes, now do as you wish."
At that time, the people summoned a caṇḍāla,
"You shall gouge out Jùnàluó's eyes."
The caṇḍāla joined his palms and said,
"I cannot do this now."
At that time, Jùnàluó,
took off his jeweled crown and said to the caṇḍāla,
"You gouge out my eyes; I shall give it to you."
There was another man of repulsive appearance,
ugly in eighteen ways,
who said to Jùnàluó,
"I can gouge out the eyes."
At that time, Jùnàluó suddenly remembered what the great virtuous Yéshě had said.
He then spoke a verse:
He said to the ugly man,
"You shall take one of my eyes and place it in my hand; I
wish to look at it."
At that time, this ugly man, about to take his eye,
countless people together angrily cursed and
spoke a verse:
These countless people wailed and wept.
At that time, the ugly man took out his eye and placed it in Jùnàluó's hand.
At that time, Jùnàluó received it with his hand and, facing the eye, spoke a verse.
Contemplating that all dharmas are impermanent,
he attained the fruit of Stream-Entry.
He again said to the ugly man,
"Take the remaining eye as you wish."
At that time, that ugly man again gouged it out
and placed it in Jùnàluó's hand.
Having lost the fleshly eye, he gained the wisdom eye.
He again spoke a verse:
Jùnàluó knew that the one who took his eyes was Wēishāluòqǐduō.
And he spoke a verse:
Jùnàluó's wife, hearing that her husband had lost his eyes,
fainted upon seeing him and was revived only when water was sprinkled.
Weeping, she spoke a verse:
Jùnàluó said to his wife,
"Do not weep.
I myself created the karma; I myself receive this retribution."
He again spoke a verse:
Jùnàluó together with his wife
returned from the country of Tèchāshīluó to where King Āyù was.
The two had never walked on the ground since birth.
Their bodies were weak and soft, unfit for labor.
Jùnàluó was skilled at playing the lute.
He could also sing and play wind instruments.
Following their original road, they begged for food to sustain their lives.
Gradually traveling, they reached their native country.
Wishing to enter the palace gate,
the gatekeeper at that time
would not allow them to proceed.
Being unable to proceed, they turned back again.
They went out and stayed in the stable for chariots and horses.
In the latter part of the night, he played the lute and sang.
The song said:
"My eyes are already lost.
The Four Truths I have seen."
He again spoke a verse:
The king, hearing the song,
was greatly delighted in his heart.
He then spoke a verse:
The king ordered a person to listen,
"It sounds like Jùnàluó's voice.
Clear, wonderful, sorrowful, and fine, it troubles my heart.
Like an elephant that has lost its calf, restless and uneasy.
You may go and see.
If it is he, bring him here."
The messenger saw he had no eyes.
His skin exposed, he was no longer recognizable.
He returned and reported to the great king,
"It is a lonely blind man together with his wife staying in the stable for chariots and horses."
At that time, the king, hearing this, was troubled and pondered.
And he spoke a verse:
The messenger, receiving the instruction, went again to where he was.
He said to Jùnàluó,
"Whose son are you? What is your name and surname?"
Jùnàluó again replied with a verse.
He had someone bring Kūṇāla and his wife to the palace.
At that time, the king saw Kūṇāla.
Exposed to wind and sun, wearing clothes patched together with grass and coarse cloth.
His appearance was altered and no longer recognizable.
The king, his heart filled with doubt, spoke to him, saying:
"Are you Kūṇāla?"
He replied, "Yes."
The king fainted and fell to the ground.
Those beside him saw the king.
And spoke a verse:
The attendants sprinkled water on the king, and only then did he awaken.
He returned to his seat.
Embracing Kūṇāla, he placed him on his lap.
Again embracing his neck, he wept and shed tears.
Stroking his head and face, he recalled his former appearance.
And spoke a verse:
At that time, Kūṇāla.
Answered with a verse:
The king again spoke a verse.
At that time, the king knew it was the work of Miśrakā.
He summoned Miśrakā.
And spoke a verse:
The king's anger blazed like fire.
His heart seeing Miśrakā.
He again spoke a verse:
The king spoke of these matters.
Wishing to punish Miśrakā's deeds.
Kūṇāla heard this.
Deeply feeling compassion.
Again spoke a verse:
At that time, the king did not accept his son's words.
He had Miśrakā.
Placed in a thatched hut and burned with fire.
He also ordered the killing of the people of Takṣaśilā.
At that time, the bhikṣus had doubts.
They asked the Venerable Upagupta, saying:
"What karma did Kūṇāla create in the past that he now receives this retribution?"
He replied:
"Long ago, in the country of Bārāṇasī, there was a hunter.
He went to the Himālaya mountains and killed many herds of deer.
Again going to the Himālaya, he encountered thunder and lightning.
There were five hundred deer.
Out of fear, they entered a rocky cave.
The hunter captured them all.
If he killed them all, the meat would rot and spoil.
He had no other choice.
So he gouged out the eyes of all of them, leaving them alive but unable to see and go away.
Later, he gradually killed them.
That former hunter was Kūṇāla.
For countless years, he constantly fell into hell.
After emerging from hell, he was born among humans.
For five hundred lifetimes, his eyes were constantly gouged out.
Now is the final remnant of that karmic retribution.
The bhikṣus asked further:
"Due to what cause was he born into a great family with handsome eyes?"
He replied:
"In the distant past, when human lifespan was forty thousand years.
A Buddha named Krakucchanda.
Appeared in the world and entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, there was a king.
Named Suprabha, who built a four-jeweled stūpa for the Buddha.
Later, that king passed away.
His younger brother did not believe in the Buddha.
He dug up and took all the treasures from beneath the stūpa, leaving only earth and wood.
All the people saw the stūpa destroyed.
They lamented and cried out.
At that time, the sons of elders asked:
'Why are those people lamenting?'
The people replied:
'The World-Honored One's stūpa originally had four jewels.
Who would have thought that now they are all destroyed?'
At that time, the sons of the elders restored the four jewels to adorn it as before.
They also made it taller and broader, surpassing its original state.
Moreover, they erected a golden image and placed it inside the stūpa.
After completing their work.
They again made a vow, saying:
'The Buddha Krakucchanda was originally the teacher of the world.
May our future teacher also be like today.'
Bhikṣus, you should know.
Those sons of elders in the past were Kūṇāla.
Because he repaired the stūpa of the Tathāgata Krakucchanda, he was born into a great family.
Because he made an image of the Tathāgata, he now obtained a body of foremost handsomeness.
Because he made a vow to encounter a good teacher, he now met Śākyamuni.
And saw the Four Noble Truths.
Long ago, when the Buddha was in the Deer Park at Bārāṇasī.
He preached the Dharma to the assembly.
At that time, the crown prince of a great king, along with the sons of minor kings, over five hundred people.
Went to where the Buddha was.
Paid homage to the Buddha and sat to one side.
And listened to the Dharma being preached.
The princes then said to the Buddha:
'The Buddha's path is pure, wonderful, profound, and far-reaching, difficult to reach.
Since ancient times.
Have there ever been crown princes, ministers, or sons of elders.
Who renounced their kingdoms, officials, people, affections, honors, and pleasures to become śramaṇas?'
The Buddha said:
'The honors, pleasures, and affections of the worldly kingdoms.
Are known to be like illusions, dreams, echoes.
Suddenly coming, suddenly going, cannot be permanently maintained.'
He also said:
'Crown princes cannot attain the path due to three matters.
What are the three matters?
First, being arrogant and self-indulgent, not mindful of studying the wonderful meanings of the Buddha's scriptures to aid their spiritual foundation.
Second, being greedy and acquisitive, not mindful of giving to the poor and those in distress.
The wealth and treasures of all the ministers and generals.
Are not shared with the people to cultivate the foundation of wealth.
Third, being unable to distance themselves from matters of sensual desire and pleasures.
Abandoning the worries and vexations of the prison-like [world].
To become śramaṇas and extinguish all sufferings and difficulties to cultivate their bodily foundation.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva, when born as a king.
Removes these three matters and thereby attains Buddhahood.
There are also three matters.
First, in youth, studying and learning, governing the country.
Leading and transforming the common people, making them practice the ten good deeds.
Second, in middle age, giving wealth to the poor, orphans, and widows, sharing joy with ministers, warriors, and the people.
Third, constantly contemplating impermanence, that life does not last long.
One should renounce the household life and become a śramaṇa.
Severing the causes of suffering, not continuing in birth and death.
If these three matters are not carried out, one obtains only ordinary death.'
The World-Honored One said:
'Long ago, in my past life, I was a Cakravartin king.
Named King Nánwáng Huángdì, with the seven treasures leading the procession.
I thought to myself:
Human life is short, impermanent, difficult to maintain.
One should only create merit to seek the true path.
I was constantly mindful of giving.
All the wealth and possessions of the world's people.
I shared with the people, having already planted the field of merit.
I only needed to renounce the household life and become a śramaṇa.
Severing greed and desire, only then could I extinguish suffering.
Combing my hair, white hairs were pulled out and placed on the table.
The king wept and said:
"The first messenger has suddenly arrived again.
I should renounce the household life and become a śramaṇa, seeking the natural path."
Holding the hairs in his palm.
He spoke a verse himself:
He became a śramaṇa, entered the mountains to cultivate the path.
At the end of his human lifespan, he was born in the second heaven.
Becoming the crown prince of Śakra, lord of the gods.
Later, governing the world was also like that of a great king.
Again seeing white hairs, he became a śramaṇa.
They were father and son.
Above, as lord of the gods.
Below, as a sage king.
In the middle, as crown prince.
Each thirty-six times.
For millions of years, ending and beginning again.
Practicing these three matters, he thereby attained Buddhahood.
That father at that time is now my body.
The crown prince is Śāriputra.
The grandson king is Ānanda.
They were reborn following one another, successively becoming kings to transform the world.
At that time, the crown prince and all the people.
Were greatly joyful.
They received the Buddha's five precepts and became upāsakas.
Attaining the path of Srotāpanna.
Long ago, King Prasenajit.
Had two consorts.
The first consort's son was named Virūḍhaka.
The second consort's son was named Jī.
On the day Jī was born.
Treasures were presented from the four directions, all arriving at once.
The king said:
'None of my other sons' births were like this.
He can be named Jī.'
When he grew up and studied, there was no scripture he did not master.
The king separately built a residence for him, made of the seven treasures, with golden and silver male and female attendants at the left and right of the gate.
Holding jeweled bowls filled with the seven treasures.
Day and night, if taken away, they would become full again as before.
The crown prince was jealous and sent soldiers to seize them.
At that time, there were over five hundred heavenly cavalry.
Guarding Jī's residence.
Virūḍhaka's army saw them, became frightened, retreated, and returned.
The crown prince was angry.
Jī came and asked:
'I sent soldiers at night to console you.
Did you hide soldiers inside, intending to rebel?'
Jī said:
'I dare not, I do not keep military men.
Inside, there is not an inch of weaponry.'
Virūḍhaka sent someone to inspect inside and outside, and there was none.
Virūḍhaka's mind was relieved, and he fully reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
'Jī planted virtue, encountering a firm cause.
Therefore, it cannot be taken away.'
At the time of Buddha Vipaśyin.
Someone went to a monastery, offered food to the saṅgha, and then gave a male slave and a female slave to sweep the temple.
From then on, in heaven and among humans, he received immeasurable blessings.
That is Jī.'
In the kingdom of Bōluónài, the king’s consort gave birth to a daughter.
Her body was the color of gold,
and her hair was dark blue.
At the age of sixteen,
her parents, seeing that she had grown up,
wished to seek a husband for her.
The daughter said,
"I do not need a husband.
If you wish to seek a husband for me,
he must have a body the color of gold and hair dark blue.
Only such a man would be suitable."
Her parents then sought for such a man,
but were completely unable to find one.
At that time, the Buddha was in the kingdom of Shèwèi.
There was a man from Shèwèi
who traveled as a merchant to Bōluónài.
The king immediately invited the merchant to meet and converse with him.
He showed him his daughter and said,
"I am seeking a husband for this daughter.
Is there any good man in the world?"
The merchant replied,
"In my country, there is a man
who surpasses even this daughter."
Hearing this, the king was delighted
and ordered the merchant to invite the Buddha.
The merchant then wrote a letter to the Buddha,
saying in the letter that this daughter was extremely beautiful and incomparable,
and that he wished to arrange for the Buddha to take her.
The Buddha was in the Jīyuán Garden,
preaching the sutras to several thousand bhikṣus.
The messenger carrying the letter went straight to the Buddha’s presence.
The Buddha, knowing in advance what was written in the letter,
immediately tore it to pieces.
He then wrote a reply to the golden-bodied daughter, saying:
"All suffering of sentient beings arises from attachment and affection.
Birth leads to old age,
old age leads to sickness,
sickness leads to death,
and death leads to sorrow and weeping.
All suffering in the world arises from attachment and affection."
Upon receiving the letter, the daughter reflected on it
and immediately attained the five supernatural powers:
first, the ability to see through all things;
second, the ability to hear through all things;
third, the ability to know the thoughts of others;
fourth, the ability to know past lives;
fifth, the ability to fly.
She then bid farewell to her parents and flew to the Buddha’s presence.
The Buddha immediately smiled,
and a five-colored light emerged from his mouth.
Ānanda stepped forward and asked,
and the Buddha said,
"Ānanda,
do you see how determined this daughter is?
If you wish to know,
during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha,
this golden-bodied daughter
was the wife of a poor family.
Her husband’s hands and feet were crippled, and he could not walk.
At that time, there was a king named Jīlì
who had a daughter,
beautiful
and adorned with gold and silver ornaments.
She went directly to Kāśyapa Buddha to receive the precepts.
At that time, the poor man’s wife
was only clothed in a single coarse cloth.
She also followed along to the Buddha’s presence,
but outsiders would not allow her to approach.
The poor man’s wife thought to herself,
"Why am I alone not allowed to approach?
Only the king’s daughter is allowed to approach."
The Buddha immediately knew this
and had someone call her forward.
The wife then bowed and said,
"Why is this king’s daughter alone so noble and wealthy?
Why am I alone so poor?"
The Buddha said to the wife,
"This king’s daughter,
in a past life, delighted in reading sutras and gave robes to śramaṇas.
Therefore, in this life, she attained nobility, wealth, dignity, and beauty.
You, in a past life, did not delight in the Dharma,
were stingy and unwilling to give alms,
and did not serve śramaṇas when you saw them.
This is why you are so poor in this life."
The poor wife said,
"May the Buddha have compassion for my ignorance and teach me the Dharma."
Kāśyapa Buddha then taught her.
She read sutras under a tree,
sat and reflected,
and then took tree leaves to sew together as a garment
to cover her body.
She wished to offer the coarse cloth she was wearing to the Buddha.
The heavenly king Śakra saw her sincere heart
and gave her heavenly robes, gold coins, and food.
The wife, upon receiving the robes, used the cloth to make offerings.
After her life ended, she was reborn in heaven.
When her heavenly life ended, she was reborn in the human world
as the daughter of a king.
Because she delighted in reading sutras and giving alms,
her body became the color of gold and her hair dark blue."
The Buddha was in the country of Shèwèi.
At that time, King Pòsīnì’s chief consort,
named Mòlì,
gave birth to a daughter.
Her name was Bōshéluó, but her face was ugly and her skin coarse and rough,
like camel hide;
her hair was like horsehair. The king, seeing this daughter, felt no joy in his heart.
He then ordered the palace,
“Guard her diligently; do not let outsiders see her.”
As the girl grew older and reached marriageable age,
the king told his officials,
“You may seek out a noble but impoverished man and bring him here.”
The official followed the command
and found a poor man of noble lineage.
He brought him before the king.
The king said to that man,
“I have a daughter whose face is extremely ugly,
and she has no match.
I will provide for her,
and I trust you will not refuse.
You should accept her.”
The elder’s son knelt and replied,
“I will obey the king’s command.”
The king then gave his daughter in marriage to that poor man.
He built a palace with seven layers of gates and towers.
The king ordered the husband,
“Take the door latch yourself.
When you wish to go out, close it yourself.
Do not let anyone see my daughter’s appearance.”
The king provided for his son-in-law so that he lacked nothing.
He also appointed him as a high minister.
This man, now wealthy,
held gatherings with other noble families.
Each month, when it was time for the gatherings,
he and his wife would attend, and others would come to the gatherings.
Everyone brought their wives,
but that minister always went alone.
The people wondered and found it strange:
“Perhaps his wife is beautiful,
or perhaps extremely ugly.
That is why he never brings her.”
They secretly agreed among themselves
to get him drunk, take the door latch,
and open the door.
At that time, the woman was distressed and blamed herself for her sins:
“What sin have I committed to be despised by my husband?
I am always confined and never see anyone.”
She then thought to herself,
“The Buddha is now in the world,
benefiting all beings, relieving their suffering and distress.”
She then sincerely paid respects to the World-Honored One from afar,
wishing only for his compassion,
to come before me and teach me briefly.”
The woman’s sincerity was profound, and the Buddha knew her thoughts.
He immediately went to her home.
Before the woman,
he emerged from the ground.
When the woman saw the Buddha, her heart was filled with joy.
Her ugly appearance vanished,
and her body became graceful and dignified,
like a heavenly maiden.
Her extraordinary beauty surpassed the world.
Out of compassion for the woman, the Buddha taught her the wonderful Dharma.
She then eradicated all evils and attained the path of the Stream-Enterer.
At that time, those five men
opened the door and entered, seeing the woman’s beauty.
They wondered why she had not been brought out before.
They closed the door again,
tied the key to its original belt,
and left. The husband, sobering up after the gathering, returned home.
Seeing his wife’s appearance, rare among humans,
he joyfully asked,
“Who are you?”
The woman replied to her husband,
“I am your wife.”
The husband said,
“You were extremely ugly before; now you are beautiful.”
The woman explained everything that had happened.
Her husband then went to inform the king,
“Now, by the Buddha’s divine grace,
she has become beautiful,
no different from a heavenly maiden.”
The king ordered her to be brought, and she was welcomed into the palace.
The king saw her and rejoiced.
The king, the queen,
the daughter, and her husband
all went to the Buddha, paid respects, and asked,
“We do not know what merit this woman
cultivated in the past to be born into a noble family yet receive an ugly form.”
The Buddha told the king,
“In a past life,
there was a country named Bōluónài.
There was a great elder
with immeasurable wealth.
His entire family always made offerings to a Pratyekabuddha.
The Pratyekabuddha’s body was coarse and his appearance ugly.
At that time, the elder had a young daughter
who saw that Pratyekabuddha
and, with a malicious heart, scorned and reviled him, saying,
‘His face is ugly, his skin coarse and rough—how detestable!’
This Pratyekabuddha,
having received their offerings, was about to enter Nirvana.
For his benefactor, he performed eighteen transformations,
then descended from the sky and returned to their home.
The elder was doubly joyful.
The daughter then repented,
saying, ‘I only hope the Venerable One will forgive me.’
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha accepted her repentance.
The Buddha told the king,
‘That daughter at that time is now your daughter.
Because she slandered this sage, she received an ugly form.
Later, seeing his divine transformations,
she repented and thus regained her beauty.
Because she made offerings to the Buddha, she enjoyed wealth and nobility life after life and attained liberation.’”
The Buddha went to the home of Jiāluóyuè to eat.
He entered without closing the door.
Afterward, all who followed were given food until they were full.
The younger brother harbored malicious thoughts:
“I will not let them enter.
If I have my way, when the monks come, I will break their legs.”
The two brothers then went their separate ways.
Both slept under trees.
The younger brother, with his malicious thoughts,
was trampled by a startled ox, breaking his leg.
The elder brother, with his good thoughts,
slept under a tree where the shade remained even in the afternoon.
King Pòsīnì’s son-in-law died.
The king deeply loved him.
For his daughter, he summoned a Brahmin
to seek a fortunate man as a son-in-law.
The Brahmin went out and saw a man sleeping under a tree.
In the afternoon, the tree’s shade still covered him.
The Brahmin said,
“This is a fortunate man.”
He then reported to the king.
The king said,
“How do you know? Explain the details.”
He summoned the man, bathed him, and dressed him in fine clothes.
He then gave his daughter in marriage to him.
In a foreign land, there was a city.
It was named Tóujiāluó.
Within it lived a layman.
Every day, he invited a śramaṇa to his home for a meal.
The śramaṇa was an arhat.
While the śramaṇa was sitting for his meal, there was a dog inside.
When the śramaṇa ate, he would often scoop some rice and share it with the dog.
The dog, having received the rice to eat, developed a good heart towards the śramaṇa.
The śramaṇa went daily, and the dog became accustomed to waiting for him.
When the śramaṇa ate, the dog longed to see him.
When the śramaṇa came, he would again take a scoop of rice and give it to the dog.
The dog had a good heart towards the śramaṇa.
After many years, its life ended.
It was then reborn as the daughter of the King of Ānxīguó.
From birth, she knew her past life, understanding she had been a dog.
She said, "I have cast off the body of a dog and obtained the body of a king's daughter."
In that kingdom, there were no Buddhist monasteries or śramaṇas.
At that time, the King of Yuèzhī sent an envoy to the king.
Seeing the envoy was virtuous and wise, the king intended to give his daughter to him as a wife.
The envoy took the girl away.
The girl, upon seeing śramaṇas, was greatly delighted.
She recalled previously being a dog; the śramaṇa gave her rice, and she had a good heart towards the śramaṇa.
Now she had obtained a human body.
Now she should greatly make offerings to śramaṇas.
In Yuèzhīguó, there were many śramaṇas.
The wife often fed three to five hundred people daily.
She personally served them, not letting guests serve themselves.
When the meal was just finished,
she personally swept the ground.
The women and servants in the household all developed good hearts, saying,
"This wife is a king's daughter.
She has come here.
She constantly sweeps and makes offerings to śramaṇas.
We too should apply our minds."
The servants then hid the brooms.
Wanting to sweep the ground herself,
the mistress searched but could not find them.
She then took the clothes she first wore upon arrival from a trunk, rolled them up, and used them to sweep the ground.
Her husband saw his wife using new clothes to sweep the ground.
He then said,
"Although you revere the Buddha-Dharma, why must you use new clothes to sweep the ground?
You should look for a broom."
The wife said,
"I merely had a good heart towards one śramaṇa.
For two years, I obtained these clothes.
Precisely using these clothes to sweep, what hardship is there?
In my previous life, initially,
I had nothing to use for giving.
I merely had a good heart and faith in the Buddha-Dharma, hence I obtained this fortune.
I also did not engage in livelihood to obtain these clothes."
The husband said to his wife,
"Although you have faith in the Buddha-Dharma and make offerings to śramaṇas,
I have never seen a śramaṇa give you a single coin or two coins.
These clothes are all obtained through my physical strength."
The wife then told her husband about her past life, saying,
"In my previous life,
I was born as a dog.
The master often invited śramaṇas.
A śramaṇa scooped rice and gave it to me.
Because I had a good heart towards the śramaṇa,
I left that dog's body and was born as a king's daughter."
The husband heard this and rejoiced.
He said to his wife,
"You merely had a good heart towards one śramaṇa,
and obtained blessings like this."
The husband was previously stingy and greedy.
Hearing what his wife said, he immediately practiced great generosity.
He was without miserliness or reluctance.
He observed precepts, purified conduct, diligently progressed, and established Buddhist monasteries.
The husband thought to himself,
"Merely by having a good heart, one obtains such merit."
The wife then replied, saying,
"The mind can enable one to attain Buddhahood, be reborn in the heavens, become a Pratyekabuddha, or become an Arhat.
All are due to the power of the mind.
If the mind thinks evil,
it causes one to fall into hell."
In Bōluónàiguó, at the bodhimaṇḍa,
from the ground upwards, all was golden in color.
Fish scales and turtle shells were layered one upon another in succession.
Buddhas of ancient times all sat upon it.
There was a king named Zhīxúnní.
He became an upāsaka.
He was learned in the scriptures and the Path.
He built a vihāra for the Buddha.
It was extremely grand and magnificent.
The king had seven daughters, all of upright appearance.
