They all upheld the Five Precepts, maintained their vows, and did not marry.
The first daughter was named Shūtiáo.
The second was named Yìmiào.
The third was named Chútān.
The fourth was named Qīngshǒu.
The fifth was named Xīxīn.
The sixth was named Jìngyǒu.
The seventh was named Sēngbì.
Constantly on the eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, twenty-third, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth days of the month,
they diligently received the Eight Precepts and observed the correct Dharma fast.
They cultivated their faith, upheld precepts, practiced generosity, and were renowned for their wisdom.
When the seven daughters finished their fast,
they requested to go outside the city to the charnel grounds to wander and observe.
The king told the seven daughters,
"The charnel grounds are detestable; there are only dead people there.
Skeletons are scattered in disorder; foxes, owls, and other birds and beasts eat their flesh.
Those who weep and wail fill the place.
What is there to observe?
In my palace, there are gardens, parks, and bathing pools.
Within them are five-colored lotus flowers.
Jacanas, mandarin ducks, and flocks of birds gather and soar there.
Rows of dazzlingly bright grasses grow.
Fine trees provide shade and coolness; sweet fruits are freely enjoyed.
You may go there to play."
The seven daughters replied, saying,
"Great King, what benefit are sweet fruits and all these beauties to us?
We see that people in the world have little lifespan.
Life daily hastens towards death; the body is an illusory transformation.
None can endure long.
We have avoided husbands and young children.
We are not deluded by sweetness and beauty.
We merely wish to observe the impermanent Dharma.
We wish to dispel greedy thoughts.
We beg the King to compassionately permit us."
The king then allowed them.
The seven daughters all went outside the city.
They went to the charnel grounds, a place of great stench.
Hearing the sounds of weeping,
they shuddered, their hair standing on end.
Thereupon, they went straight forward together to observe the various dead people.
They saw some with severed heads, severed arms, hands and feet in different places.
Some were stiff corpses covered by grass or wrapped in mats.
Some were criminals bound to frames on the ground.
Among them were those not yet dead, bound with fresh grass.
Their families wept, seeking their release.
There were also those carrying dead people on their shoulders, coming out from the city.
The seven daughters looked around into the distance.
They saw the dead were very many.
Various flying birds and running beasts fought to eat their flesh.
Some dragged corpses out from the soil.
They were swollen, maggots born within; the stench was difficult to approach.
Thereupon, the seven daughters circled them once.
They said to each other,
"Our bodies, too, will soon be like this."
Each spoke a verse.
The first daughter said:
The second daughter said:
The third daughter said:
The fourth daughter said:
The fifth daughter said:
The sixth daughter said:
The seventh daughter said:
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, heard this and praised them,
"Excellent, excellent!
What do you wish?
I shall now grant it to you."
The seven daughters asked,
"Are you Brahmā?
Or are you an earth deity?
Could you be Śakra?"
He replied, "Indeed.
I am Śakra, Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
The first daughter said,
"I wish to obtain a tree without root, without branches, without leaves.
To be born within it—
that would be bliss."
The second daughter said,
"I wish for the place where I am born
to be pure, without desire, without yin and yang.
Tranquil, with nothing to cling to."
The third daughter said,
"I wish to be like the echo of a call in the mountains.
Not going, not returning.
Naturally without form."
The fourth daughter said,
"I wish to be like empty space, without beginning, without end, without anything being born, penetratingly connected with the Path."
Śakra said,
"Enough, enough. The wishes of you maidens are very profound.
If you wish to become kings among suns and moons, that can be attained.
But as for the formless, the thoughtless—that is not within my power to grant."
The seven daughters said,
"Heavenly Lord,
your divine virtue is lofty and great; why can you not bring this about?
The Buddha said those who feed on blessings, when their blessings are exhausted, cannot avoid fear.
It is like an old ox that cannot be of use to people.
What benefit is that to us?"
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said,
"You maidens cultivate precepts and fasting; I too revere the Buddha.
We should be Dharma brothers.
How wonderful are your profound wishes!"
Having spoken, he vanished.
King Prasenajit
had a widowed daughter
named Jīngāng.
Splendidly adorned, she returned home.
The king, pitying her,
separately built a palace for her
and provided five hundred female entertainers to amuse her.
There was an elderly maidservant
named Dùshèng,
who constantly went to the market to buy cosmetics, incense, and flowers.
Suddenly, she saw countless men and women, a great crowd, each carrying incense and flowers, leaving the city.
She immediately asked,
"Where are you going?"
The crowd replied,
"We wish to pay our respects to the Buddha.
The Buddha has appeared in the world, the honored one of the three realms,
to liberate
all beings, enabling them to attain Nirvana."
Hearing this, Dùshèng
felt joyful and delighted in her heart.
She then thought to herself,
"Meeting the Buddha in my old age is a blessing from past lives."
So she divided the money for incense and used it to buy fine incense and flowers,
following the crowd to where the Buddha was.
After paying her respects, she stepped back and stood,
scattered flowers, burned incense, and with single-minded devotion listened to the Dharma.
Passing through the market, she took a fragrant item because listening to the Dharma,
through the merit of past actions, the fragrance she obtained
was twice as fragrant as before.
They blamed her for being late and questioned her together.
Dùshèng said,
"In the world, there is a holy teacher, the honored one of the three realms,
who expounds the supreme Dharma.
I followed others to listen and receive it.
That is why I was delayed."
Jīngāng heard this with joy
and sighed to herself,
"What fault have we committed to be isolated and not hear of this?"
She then replied to Dùshèng,
"Try to explain it to me."
Dùshèng accepted the command
and first went out to fully receive the proper procedure.
Before Dùshèng returned,
Jīngāng's maidservants waited anxiously in the courtyard,
like children awaiting their mother.
The Buddha told Dùshèng,
"When you return to explain the Dharma, the procedure
is to first spread a high seat."
Dùshèng received the instruction
and fully conveyed the holy message. All were greatly joyful.
Each took off one garment and piled them up to make a high seat.
Dùshèng bathed,
relying on the Buddha's majestic power,
and expounded the Dharma as appropriate.
Jīngāng and over five hundred others
resolved their doubts, eradicated evil, and attained the path of Stream-enterer.
The Dharma exposition was so wonderful that they did not notice a fire breaking out.
They were all burned to death at once and were immediately reborn in the heavens.
The king provided coffins, had them encoffined and buried, and after the funeral,
went to visit the Buddha.
The Buddha asked,
"Where has the king come from?"
The king said,
"Jīngāng unfortunately did not notice a fire breaking out.
All, young and old, were completely burned. I have just returned from the encoffining.
I do not understand what offense they committed to encounter this fire disaster.
I only wish the World-Honored One would reveal what I have not heard."
The Buddha told the king,
"In a past age, there was a city
named Vārāṇasī.
There was an elder's wife
who led five hundred maidens
to a great sacrificial ceremony outside the city.
Their rule was difficult to violate:
people of other clans were not allowed near.
Without distinguishing between relatives or strangers,
those who came were thrown into the fire.
At that time, there was a Pratyekabuddha
named Jiāluó.
He dwelled in the mountains and came in the morning to seek alms,
returning to the mountains in the evening.
Jiāluó came seeking alms and approached the suburban sacrifice.
The elder's wife saw him
and suddenly became angry.
Together they seized Jiāluó and threw him into the fire.
His entire body was scorched and blistered.
Then he displayed his supernatural powers,
flying up into the sky.
The women were terrified, wept tears of regret, and repented.
Kneeling and raising their heads, they declared,
'We women are foolish and ignorant, not recognizing the ultimate truth.
Our multitude of evil deeds, foolish and wild, have insulted the divine spirit.
We reflect that our offenses pile up like mountains.
We beg you to descend with your honored virtue to eliminate this heavy calamity.'
Following their voices, he descended and entered Parinirvana.
The women built a stūpa and made offerings to his relics."
The Buddha then spoke a verse to the king:
The Buddha told the king,
"The elder's wife of that time
is now your daughter Jīngāng.
The five hundred maidens
are now Dùshèng and the five hundred maidservants.
In the past, there was a king's daughter
whom the king loved dearly and never took his eyes off.
At that time, rain fell from the sky, and bubbles formed on the water.
The girl saw the water bubbles and felt great affection and admiration for them.
The girl said to the king,
'I want to have the bubbles on the water made into a floral garland for my head.'
The king told the girl,
'Now, the bubbles on the water cannot be grasped or held.
How can they be taken to make a floral garland?'
The girl said,
'If I cannot get them, I will kill myself.'
Hearing the girl's words, the king
told the skilled craftsmen,
'You are exceptionally skilled and there is nothing you cannot do.
Quickly take the water bubbles and make a garland for my daughter.
If not, I will behead you all.'
They replied,
'We are incapable of taking bubbles to make a garland.'
There was an old craftsman who said,
'I can take the bubbles.'
The king was very pleased.
He then told the girl,
'Now there is one person capable of making the garland.
You may go yourself and personally oversee it.'
The girl followed the king's words and went outside to watch.
Then that old craftsman said to the king's daughter,
'I have never distinguished between beautiful and ugly water bubbles.
I beg the king's daughter to personally take the bubbles, and I will make the garland.'
The girl then tried to take the bubbles, but they broke as soon as she touched them, and she could not get any.
Thus, after a whole day, she still could not obtain any bubbles.
The girl grew tired and weary and gave up, leaving.
The girl said to the king,
'Water bubbles are illusory and cannot last long.
I wish the king would make me a purple-gold garland instead,
which will not wither day or night.'
The bubbles on the water deceive people's eyes.
Though they have form and substance, they are born and immediately perish.
The blazing heat and the mirage are also like this.
Thirsty craving and weariness cause one to lose one's life.
The human body is illusory, with little joy and much suffering.
The nature of things is to wear out and cannot last long.
They change and transform, and in this world, they do not endure.'"
In the past, there was a king.
His name was Jìnmèi.
He had a daughter.
She wore a natural golden flower garland.
She was called Mólíní.
The king summoned five hundred girls born on the same day from across the country.
To serve as her attendants.
When Mólíní grew older,
she made offerings to five hundred Brahmins every day without fail.
At that time, Kāshyapa Buddha resided in a garden.
She often went out for excursions and came to the garden where the Buddha stayed.
The charioteer would not enter.
The girl asked,
"There is no garden I do not enter; why do you avoid this one?"
He replied,
"In this garden, there is only a bald-headed śramaṇa.
His name is Kāshyapa.
It is not suitable for you to see him.
That is why we do not enter."
The girl said,
"We may enter."
Upon seeing the Buddha's golden complexion, her heart was greatly delighted.
She bowed her head to the ground in reverence; the Buddha preached the wonderful Dharma, and she received the Three Refuges and Five Precepts, then paid her respects and departed.
The girl reflected to herself,
"Brahmins are not a good field of merit.
They should not receive offerings.
I will instead make offerings to the Buddha."
When the Brahmins heard that Mólíní had become a disciple of Kāshyapa,
they brought even finer food to offer her.
Their hearts became jealous.
Jìnmèi, in the middle of the night,
had eleven kinds of dreams.
In the morning, he assembled his ministers and recounted his dreams.
The ministers ordered him to consult a Brahmin diviner.
The Brahmin said,
"These dreams are inauspicious.
You may lose your kingdom or even your life."
The king said,
"Can it be avoided?"
The diviner replied,
"You must sacrifice various cattle, sheep, elephants, and horses,
along with your daughter Mólíní,
and her five hundred attendants.
Seven days from now, at the crossroads, kill them as a sacrifice to the heavens.
Then this disaster can be averted."
Upon hearing the order,
the king prepared accordingly and summoned Mólíní to inform her of the matter.
"Within six days, you may have whatever you desire."
She replied,
"I do not particularly regret dying.
I wish that on the first day, all the men and women of the city may go together to where Kāshyapa Buddha is,
and all receive the Three Refuges and Five Precepts."
The king agreed to this.
"I wish that on the second day, I may go with the king's ministers to where the Buddha is.
I wish that on the third day, I may go with the princes to where the Buddha is.
I wish that on the fourth day, I may go with the princesses to where the Buddha is.
I wish that on the fifth day, I may go with the king's consorts and palace ladies to where the Buddha is.
I wish that on the sixth day, I may go with the king to where the Buddha is."
The king granted all these requests.
Together with the multitude, they went to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to them, and they attained fruition.
They all received the Three Refuges and Five Precepts.
The king told Kāshyapa Buddha about the eleven dreams.
The Buddha said,
"These dreams pertain to the future, not the present.
Dreaming of a small tree blooming means
that in the future, there will be a Buddha named Shakyamuni.
At that time, people will have white hair at the age of twenty and will already have children.
Dreaming of a calf plowing means ten-year-old children will manage household affairs.
Parents will have no freedom.
Dreaming of three pots cooking side by side, with the rice from the side pots jumping into each other but not falling into the central one, means
the wealthy will exchange gifts with each other, while the poor will receive nothing.
Dreaming of a camel eating grass with two heads means
ministers will consume the king's salary and also take the people's possessions.
Dreaming of a mare drinking her foal's milk means
mothers will marry off their daughters and then demand sustenance from them.
Dreaming of a golden bowl floating in the sky means
rain will not fall in season. Dreaming of a wild fox urinating in a golden bowl means
people will marry for wealth, disregarding clan and family.
Dreaming of a monkey sitting on a bed means
kings will rule unlawfully, with tyranny and unrighteousness.
Dreaming of an ox head wearing a sandalwood turban being of the same value as rotten grass means
the Shakya clan will be greedy for profit and teach the Dharma for personal gain.
Dreaming of muddy water in the center and clear water at the edges means
the Dharma will decline in the central lands but flourish in the border countries.
For you personally, there is no inauspiciousness."
The king then commanded his ministers from his seat, saying,
"The sacrificial animals for the heavens are now all safe.
From now on, I would rather lose my own life
than intentionally kill any living being, let alone kill people."
There was a king who had a daughter.
Her name was Gǒutóu.
There was a fisherman.
Named Shùpójiā.
He was walking along the road.
From afar, he saw the king's daughter in a high tower.
Seeing her face through the window, he became infatuated and obsessed.
His heart could not rest even for a moment; as days and months passed, he could not eat or drink.
His mother asked him the reason.
He truthfully answered his mother.
"I saw the king's daughter and cannot forget her."
His mother tried to dissuade him, saying,
"You are a commoner; the king's daughter is noble.
It is impossible."
The son said,
"My heart desires her and cannot forget her even for a moment.
If I do not get my wish, I cannot live."
For her son's sake, the mother entered the king's palace.
She often sent fat fish and meat
as gifts to the king's daughter, without asking for payment.
The king's daughter found it strange and asked,
"What do you seek?"
The mother said to the king's daughter, "Please dismiss your attendants, and I will tell you the truth.
I have only one son.
He admires the king's daughter; his feelings have made him ill, and his life will not last long.
I beg for your compassion to grant him his life."
The king's daughter said,
"On the fifteenth day of the month, wait behind the deity's image in such-and-such a temple."
The mother returned and told her son,
"Your wish has been granted."
She informed him as above.
He bathed, put on new clothes, and waited behind the deity's image.
When the time came, the king's daughter said to her father the king,
"I have had inauspicious signs and must go to the temple to seek good fortune."
The king said, "Very well."
He prepared five hundred carriages and went out to the temple.
Upon arrival,
she commanded her attendants,
"Stay outside the gate."
She entered the temple alone.
The deity thought to himself,
"This should not be so.
The king is a donor; I cannot let this commoner defile the king's daughter."
He immediately caused this man to fall into a deep sleep, unaware.
When the king's daughter entered,
she saw him sleeping soundly and could not wake him no matter how she pushed.
She then left a necklace worth a hundred thousand taels of gold for him and departed.
After she left, the man awoke.
He saw the necklace.
He asked the people and learned that the king's daughter had come.
His desire unfulfilled,
he was filled with sorrow, regret, and frustration; the fire of lust burned within him, and he died consumed by it.
This serves as proof that
a woman's heart does not distinguish between noble and lowly.
She only follows her desires.
Furthermore, in the past, there was a king's daughter
who pursued a Chandāla and engaged in impurity with him.
There was also a sage's daughter
who followed a lion.
In the city of Bōluónài, there was an elder.
His name was Ājùlìzǐ.
His style was Shétuó, and he was twenty-four years old.
He was born with glass shoes on his feet.
His parents considered him extraordinary.
They named him Shétuó.
They built a separate house for him.
He moved between cool and warm places as the seasons changed, with female entertainers amusing him, never leaving his side.
In the middle of the night, Bǎochēng suddenly saw all the female entertainers as if dead.
Pus and blood flowed, limbs were broken and ruined; the house and all its furnishings resembled a tomb.
The door opened by itself; heaven and earth were plunged into great darkness.
He only saw a small light heading toward the eastern city gate.
The gate also opened by itself, illuminating the Deer Park.
Following the light, he saw the Buddha and beheld his auspicious marks.
His fear ceased, his confusion dissolved, and he exclaimed aloud,
"Long have I been in the prison of craving, bound by the shackles of name and form.
Now I approach the Divine Honored One; may I be liberated?"
The Buddha said,
"Welcome, youth; you have awakened.
Here there is no sorrow; all actions are ultimately extinguished."
He bowed at the Buddha's feet.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to him, and he attained the undefiled Dharma-eye.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I wish to become your disciple."
The Buddha said,
"Welcome, bhikshu," and he became a śramaṇa.
The next morning, the women searched everywhere in panic.
The household was alarmed and did not know where he was.
The elder sent out horses in all directions to search.
The father rode in his son's carriage and went east to seek him.
On the way, he encountered a river.
The river was named Bōluónài.
Crossing the river, he saw his son's glass shoes left on the bank.
He followed the footprints straight to the Deer Park.
The Buddha, using skillful means, caused father and son not to see each other.
The elder asked the Buddha,
"My son Bǎochēng's footprints lead here.
Have you seen him, Gautama?"
The Buddha told the elder,
"If your son is here, why worry about not seeing him?"
The Buddha preached the Dharma to him, and he entered the stream of Srotāpanna.
Bǎochēng's mind was liberated, and he attained Arhatship.
Father and son met; their affection had grown faint.
The elder said to the Buddha,
"Today my heart is joyful for two reasons.
First, the joy of encountering the Buddha and understanding.
Second, the joy of liberation from attachment."
At that time, Bǎochēng had four close relatives.
The first was named Fùnòu.
The second was named Wéimóluó.
The third was named Qiáoyánbō.
The fourth was named Xūtuó.
They heard that Bǎochēng had already become a śramaṇa.
Startled and overjoyed, their hair stood on end, and they said:
"Let us go together to see the Buddha and also visit Bǎochēng."
They then set out together.
Seeing the Buddha's shadow, they acted according to their original vows.
They paid homage and addressed the Buddha:
"We have long thirsted for the teachings of the Way with humble hearts.
Do not despise our lowliness; we wish to become your disciples."
The Buddha said:
"Welcome, bhikṣus!" and they all became śramaṇas.
He expounded to them that the mind is originally pure; hearing this teaching, their minds understood.
They then attained arhatship.
Those who heard of this set out to seek [the Dharma],
and all attained the fruits of the Way.
In the city of Zhānpó, there was the son of a great elder.
His name was Shǒulóngnà.
His parents had only this son,
and they cherished him deeply.
Since birth, he had been accustomed to pleasure and had never stepped on the ground; hair grew on the soles of his feet.
At that time, the king of Mójiéguó heard of the son of the great elder in Zhānpó city and wished to see him.
He then ordered the city lord:
"Have all the elders bring their sons to me."
At that time, the lord of Zhānpó city received the order
and went to the king of Mójié.
He stood to one side.
The king ordered that cloth be spread on the ground,
and [Shǒulóngnà] went to where the king was.
The king saw the hair on his feet
and was greatly pleased.
He then said:
"You should go see the Buddha, pay homage, and inquire after him.
It will bring you benefit in future lives."
At that time, the lord of Zhānpó city and the various elders
went together to Qíshéjué Mountain.
At that time, there was an elder named Pójiétuó
who served the Buddha; he was sitting on a flat rock.
The lord of Zhānpó city
went to Elder Pójiétuó and said:
"We wish to see the Tathāgata."
At that time, Pójiétuó sank into the rock and emerged before the Buddha.
He addressed [the Buddha]:
"The elders of Zhānpó wish to see the World-Honored One."
The Buddha said:
"Go and spread a seat in the shade of the hut;
I will go and sit there."
At that time, Pójiétuó spread the seat and returned to where the Buddha was.
He addressed the World-Honored One:
"The seat has been spread."
After the World-Honored One sat down,
he said to Pójiétuó:
"Tell the elders to come."
At that time, Pójiétuó sank before the Buddha and emerged on the rock.
The various elders marveled at this unprecedented sight, thinking, "The disciples of the World-Honored One possess such spiritual powers,
how much more so the Tathāgata!"
Pójiétuó said:
"Elders, you should know."
At that time, the lord of Zhānpó city came to where the Buddha was.
The World-Honored One at that time
then expounded the Dharma to the sons of the various elders and the lord of Zhānpó city, exhorting and transforming them.
They immediately attained the pure Dharma-eye while seated.
They addressed the World-Honored One:
"Great Virtuous One,
from now on we take refuge in the Three Jewels
and become upāsakas."
At that time, Shǒulóngnà later left home
and went to the bank of the Wēnshuǐ River, in the Śītā Forest.
He diligently practiced with vigor.
The place where he walked in meditation was stained with blood,
as if painted with blood.
At that time, Shǒulóngnà reflected in solitude:
"Among the Buddha's disciples, none surpasses me in diligent practice and vigor.
Why then have I not yet attained the undefiled [state]?
I should abandon the precepts, return home, indulge in the five desires, and practice giving and merit-making."
The Buddha knew his thoughts
and went to where Shǒulóngnà was.
"I now ask you;
answer me as you wish.
When you were at home, you played the lute.
If the strings were too loose or too tight, was the sound good?
Only when neither too loose nor too tight did it produce a good sound."
The Buddha said:
"It is the same for a bhikṣu.
Neither too lax nor too tense, the mind then attains the Way."
Following this teaching, he practiced and eventually became an arhat.
In the past, within the city of Shèwèi,
there was an elder
named Zuìshèng.
There was another elder,
named Nánjiàng.
These two were the most miserly in the country.
They possessed abundant wealth and treasures beyond measure.
Each had seven gates at their homes and ordered the gatekeepers:
"Do not allow beggars to enter my house."
Iron nets covered their courtyards to keep out flying birds.
Iron walls on all sides prevented rats from burrowing and gnawing their possessions.
At that time, the five great śrāvakas each in turn went to teach them.
Emerging from the ground, they taught the Dharma of giving.
The two elders heard them but each refused to be transformed.
Later, the Buddha himself went, sitting and lying in empty space, emitting great light.
The Buddha expounded the subtle Dharma to the elders.
Although the elders heard it, their minds still did not comprehend.
They thought to themselves:
"The Buddha has come; we cannot let him return to the monastery empty-handed.
We should enter the treasury and take one white woolen cloth to give to the Tathāgata."
They then rose and entered the treasury.
[Zuìshèng] selected a poor-quality one but instead got a good one.
He put it aside and took another, but got an even better one.
His mind was conflicted, unable to decide.
On that very day, the asuras and the Trāyastriṃśa gods were fighting.
Sometimes the gods prevailed and the asuras were defeated,
and sometimes the asuras prevailed and the gods were defeated.
At that time, the World-Honored One, with his divine eye, observed the elder's mind:
sometimes the miserly mind prevailed and the giving mind was defeated,
and sometimes the giving mind prevailed and the miserly mind was defeated.
At that time, the World-Honored One then spoke this verse.
Hearing it from afar, the elder felt ashamed within.
"What the Tathāgata said precisely refers to me."
He then took out a good woolen cloth and offered it as a gift.
Elder Nánjiàng
took out five hundred taels of gold to give as alms.
Their minds opened and understood, and each saw the traces of the Way.
If one releases men and women, or releases slaves and servants.
If one allows people, or even one's own body,
to leave home and enter the path, the merit is immeasurable.
The reward of giving is rebirth among the six heavens and the human realm for ten lifetimes.
The merit of leaving home is boundless and immeasurable.
It surpasses building a seven-jeweled stupa reaching up to the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.
Because a greedy person can destroy it.
The virtue of leaving home cannot be destroyed.
It is higher than Sumeru,
deeper than the great ocean, and vaster than empty space.
If one creates obstacles for those leaving home,
their sin is extremely grave.
They will enter the deep hells, dark and without eyes.
There was an elder,
named Shìlì Bìtí, one hundred years old, who sought to leave home.
All his family, young and old, considered him useless.
Shìlì Bìtí went to the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove,
and sought to leave home from Shèlìfú.
Being old, he could not leave home.
He asked all five hundred arhats, and all gave the same answer.
Shèlìfú left the bamboo grove gate,
and cried out loudly, weeping.
"Yōubōlí is a lowly barber,
Nítí is a filthy dung-cleaner,
Yāngjué Móluó killed countless people,
and Tuósāijī is a great thief and evil man.
Such people as these were still able to leave home.
What crime have I committed that I alone cannot?"
The Buddha immediately manifested,
and asked Fúzēng,
"Why are you crying?"
Hearing the Buddha's Brahma-like voice, his heart rejoiced and he paid homage.
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
"All those evil sinners were able to leave home.
What crime have I that I am not allowed to leave home?
My family considers me useless.
If I cannot leave home within the Buddha's Dharma,
and if I return home, I will certainly not be welcomed.
Where should I go?
Today I will surely abandon my life here."
The Buddha consoled him, saying,
"Do not grieve or distress yourself.
I permit you to leave home."
He instructed Dà Mùlián,
"Allow him to leave home."
Thus he was able to leave home.
He received the full precepts.
Day and night, diligently practicing, studying, reciting, and widely mastering the scriptural treasury.
Because of his old age, he could not at all times respectfully welcome, see off, bow to, or inquire after the senior monks.
The young bhikkhus, all senior to him, often harshly criticized him.
He then thought to himself,
"I would rather die now.
I will go to the great river bank, remove my kasaya and place it on a tree branch."
Weeping, he made a vow,
"I do not abandon the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
I only wish to abandon my life.
May this body of mine, through giving, upholding precepts, diligence, and reciting sutras,
if there is retribution,
may I, after abandoning this body, be reborn in a wealthy and happy family.
May my family be harmonious and compliant.
May they not create obstacles for my wholesome practices.
May I constantly encounter the Three Jewels and meet virtuous teachers.
May they show me the realization of Nirvana." Then he threw himself into the swirling waters.
Before reaching the water, Mùlián placed him on the bank.
Having him grasp the corner of his robe, he soared up into empty space.
Like a fierce eagle carrying a small bird,
in the time it takes to bend and stretch an arm, they reached a great sea island.
By the seashore was a newly dead person,
a woman's form complete.
He saw a worm emerge from her mouth, re-enter through her nose, then emerge from her eye and enter again through her ear.
Bìtí asked,
"What woman is this?"
He replied,
"When the time comes, I will tell you."
Proceeding further, he saw another woman.
Carrying a bronze cauldron herself, she lit a fire and blew on it until it boiled.
Removing her clothes, she entered the cauldron herself.
Her hair and nails fell off first, her flesh cooked and separated from the bones, the boiling blew the bones out.
Outside, the wind blew and they quickly reformed into a person.
She took her own flesh and ate it.
Next, proceeding further, he saw a great tree.
Many worms surrounded it, gnawing at its body, even the branches and leaves.
There was not an empty space even the size of a needle tip.
It cried out loudly, shaking like the sounds of hell.
Next, he saw a man.
Surrounded by beast-headed evil spirits,
holding bows and crossbows, they shot three poisoned arrows, their tips all aflame.
They competed in shooting him.
His body was completely scorched.
He also saw a great mountain.
Below were placed swords and blades; he saw a person
jump down from above onto the spears, swords, and halberds, which pierced his body.
He then pulled them out himself and placed them back in their original positions.
He went back and forth without rest.
Ahead, he saw a mountain of bones,
seven hundred yojanas high.
Mùlián, by the mountain, explained:
"The wife of the great merchant in Shèwèi City,
her husband loved her dearly.
He wished to enter the great sea but could not bear to part from his wife.
So he took her into the sea.
The wife held up a mirror to look at her face.
Seeing her own beauty,
she became arrogant and deeply attached.
At that time, they encountered a great turtle which capsized the ship, sinking it into the sea.
All died.
All five hundred merchants died.
The sea did not accept the corpses.
Yakshas and rakshasas brought them out and placed them on the shore.
According to their attachments in life, after death they were reborn as worms.
After abandoning this worm body, they will fall into the great hells.
In Shèwèi Kingdom, a upāsikā's maidservant; the upāsikā invited a bhikkhu
for the ninety days of summer to make offerings and provide support.
She had the maidservant deliver the food.
The maidservant, in a secluded place, selected the good food and ate it herself.
The remainder she gave to the bhikkhu.
The mistress found out and questioned her.
The maidservant replied,
'If I ate first, may I for generations eat my own flesh.'
Now she first receives the flower-retribution, later she will fall into hell.
The many worms gnawing the tree, emitting great evil cries,
this is the steward bhikkhu Làilìzhā.
Using the Sangha's property, flowers, fruits, and food,
he gave them to laypeople.
He receives this flower-retribution.
Later he will fall into hell.
The worms gnawing the tree
are the people who received the things.
The one crying out loudly, shot by many arrows,
this person in a previous life was a great hunter.
He killed many birds and beasts; because of this sin, he receives this bitter poison.
After this life ends, he will fall into the great hells.
The one on the great mountain throwing himself onto swords and blades,
this is the great fierce general of Wángshè City.
Because of his ferocious bravery, he was at the front line.
Or because he used swords, spears, and shields to wound and kill living beings, he receives this retribution.
There was a king named Tánmó Bìtí.
He practiced giving, upheld precepts, was compassionate and did not harm living beings.
He governed the country with righteous rule for twenty years.
Once, playing a game with someone,
at that time a person killed someone.
The ministers reported to the king.
He replied,
'Deal with it according to the national law.'
So they applied the law and executed him.
After the king finished his game, he asked,
'Where is the criminal?'
The ministers said, 'Already executed.'
The king heard and wept, saying,
'The seven treasures all remain, I alone will enter hell.'
He then abdicated the throne and entered the mountains to guard himself.
After death, he became a makara fish.
Its body was seven hundred yojanas long.
The king's ministers, relying on their power, oppressed the people.
After death, they also became great makara fish.
Body worms causing itching, they rubbed against the crystal mountain.
Crushing and killing the worms, the blood flowed for a hundred li, all red.
They should fall into the great hells.
At that time, the fish slept for a hundred years before awakening.
Awakening, greatly hungry and thirsty,
it immediately opened its mouth; seawater flowed in like a great river.
There were five hundred merchants entering the sea to seek treasure.
They encountered it; their ship headed toward the fish's mouth.
The merchants called out, 'Namo Buddha!'
The fish heard and closed its mouth.
The merchants survived.
The fish, starving, died and was reborn in Wángshè City.
A yaksha brought the body and placed it by this seashore.
That king is you yourself.
The killer became a fish."
Bìtí, hearing this, understood impermanence and became weary of the world.
He exhausted his defilements and attained the fruit of arhatship.
In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a great elder.
His name was Sudatta, and he often gave alms to orphans and beggars.
People thus called him by this epithet.
Previously, he had fields and estates in Rājagṛha.
Each year, when traveling there, he would stay at the home of the elder Hùmí.
One night, he rose to sweep and tidy the house and prepare food.
Sudatta asked him about this.
He replied:
"In the city of Kapilavastu, there is a descendant of the Śākya clan.
His name is Siddhārtha,
of the Gautama lineage.
Shortly after his birth, physiognomists predicted of him
that he would certainly become a wheel-turning king.
But his heart did not delight in this.
He renounced it and left home.
Without a teacher, he attained Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi by his own realization.
Because his mind is equal toward all beings, he is called the Buddha.
Tomorrow he has accepted my invitation."
Sudatta asked further:
"Where is he now?"
He replied:
"He is at the Kalandaka Veṇuvana Vihāra." Sudatta single-mindedly contemplated all the virtues of the Buddha.
Suddenly, a great light appeared.
Following the light, he went out and reached the gate of Śrāvastī.
By the Buddha's spiritual power, it opened of its own accord. Outside the gate, there was a shrine to the celestial beings.
Sudatta paid his respects, but then the light vanished and it became dark again.
His mind became fearful and alarmed.
He wanted to turn back to the city gate.
Then a great celestial deity
said to Sudatta:
"Benevolent one, seeing the Buddha will bring you excellent benefit.
All the merit one could gain throughout Jambudvīpa
is not equal to the resolve to take a single step toward the Tathāgata's abode."
Sudatta asked:
"Who are you?"
He replied:
"I am the Brahmin Xìnxiàng's son, your good friend from past lives.
Because in a past life I saw Śāriputra and Mahā-Maudgalyāyana and bowed to them with joy,
I relinquished that body and was reborn as the son of Vaiśravaṇa, the Northern Heavenly King.
I am specially assigned to guard this city. How much more so if one sees the Tathāgata, bows, and makes offerings?"
Sudatta paid homage to the Buddha.
The Buddha expounded the Dharma to him appropriately.
He attained the path of Stream-enterer.
Elder Sudatta had experienced poverty seven times, and this last poverty was the most severe.
From a dung heap, he found a wooden peck measure.
It was actually made of sandalwood.
He took it to the market to sell it.
He obtained four pecks of rice.
He said to his wife: "Cook one peck for now.
I will go look for vegetables."
At that time, the Buddha thought:
"I should liberate Sudatta and cause his fortune to be renewed."
Just as the rice finished cooking,
Śāriputra arrived.
The wife saw him and was delighted.
She put the entire peck of cooked rice into his bowl.
She cooked another peck.
Maudgalyāyana then arrived.
Again she joyfully gave it to him.
She cooked yet another peck.
Mahākāśyapa then arrived.
She also gave it to him.
There was exactly one peck left.
Soon it was cooked as well.
The Tathāgata himself came.
The wife thought to herself:
"Our provisions for the day
—there is nothing left.
But now we have this rice.
The Tathāgata himself has come.
Could it be that our transgressions are ended and fortune is arising?"
She gave the entire peck of cooked rice to the Tathāgata.
The Buddha uttered a blessing:
"Transgressions are extinguished, fortune arises—from this day forth."
Sudatta soon returned.
His wife, fearing he would be angry,
asked him:
"Now, if the Buddha, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana,
and Kāśyapa all came seeking food,
should we give it?"
He replied: "We should give.
Fields of merit are hard to encounter.
If they come seeking, that is a rare meeting."
His wife said:
"Earlier, I used all four pecks of rice in offering."
Her husband was greatly delighted.
There was some rice water left, and the couple drank it together.
In a short while, as they wandered about,
all the rooms were naturally filled with treasures, storehouses, grain, and silks.
They became completely full,
as in his former wealth.
Sudatta leaped for joy,
knowing the Buddha had compassionately thought of him.
He further invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha and made offerings until everything was exhausted.
The Buddha expounded the Dharma for them, and they all attained the path.
The most excellent elder, hearing the wondrous Dharma expounded,
right there on his seat, had all defilements extinguished and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
He took the Three Refuges and became an upāsaka,
vowing not to kill for the rest of his life.
Not long after the Buddha departed,
the evil Māra Pāpīyas transformed into the Buddha's form, complete with marks and characteristics,
and came to the elder's home.
The elder thought:
"The Tathāgata just left—how could he return so quickly?"
The false Buddha said to him:
"I thought you, elder, were of high talent and broad wisdom, able to discern and critique principles.
But upon careful consideration, elder,
you are foolish, deluded, and without wisdom.
What I expounded earlier regarding the Four Truths was actually not the true truth.
That is inverted,
the practice of outsiders."
The elder immediately realized the truth himself.
He then replied to him:
"Enough, enough, do not speak.
I have obtained the eye of wisdom and abide in firm ground.
Even if you were to transform into hundreds of millions of bodies,
I would not regress.
How can the light of a firefly compete with the sun?
How can a farmer's ash pile compare to Mount Sumeru?
Owls, vultures, crows, and magpies flying alongside the golden-winged garuḍa?"
Pāpīyas felt ashamed and withdrew, restoring his own form.
At that time, the king resided in the country.
There was a wealthy elder of the four surnames.
His name was Shēn Rì.
His property was extremely abundant.
Gold, silver, and precious treasures were countless.
Shēn Rì served other ascetics,
but did not serve the Buddha.
The various heterodox ascetics were all jealous.
They discussed together with Shēn Rì, saying:
"Now the Buddha is revered by the king, his ministers, elders, officials, and the people.
Yet we alone are not respected.
The Buddha often says of himself:
'I know matters of the past, future, and present.
I know the thoughts of others.'
Now we should test him,
to see if it is truly so or not."
Shēn Rì said:
"How shall we test him?"
The heterodox ascetics said:
"Invite the Buddha and place poison in his food.
Dig a pit five zhang deep inside the gate.
Place fire in it and thinly cover it over.
Have the Buddha come from above.
If he knows, he will not accept the invitation.
If he accepts the invitation, then he does not know."
Shēn Rì said: "Agreed."
He then went to invite the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "Excellent."
The heterodox ascetics said:
"He already knows nothing.
We should just dig the ground."
Shēn Rì had a son,
named Zhānluófǎ,
sixteen years old.
He had attained knowledge of past lives, excelled in studying the Buddha's path, and could know matters of the past, future, and present.
He addressed his father, saying:
"The Buddha already knows.
Do not use the words of evil men to cast yourself into boiling water and fire."
Shēn Rì did not believe him.
He dug the pit, lit the fire, and placed poison in the food.
He announced to the bhikkhus:
"Follow behind me."
As the Buddha was just heading toward the road,
he emitted a radiant light, causing Shēn Rì's house to become entirely golden.
Then Zhānluófǎ said to his father:
"Now the Buddha has arisen and is heading toward the road.
All ten directions are bright as the sun."
When the Buddha reached the city gate,
his foot stepped upon the threshold.
Immediately the great city shook greatly.
The sick were instantly healed.
Musical instruments like konghous played by themselves without being struck.
When the Buddha reached Shēn Rì's gate,
the five-zhang fire pit transformed into a bathing pool.
Lotus flowers grew in it.
Each flower had a thousand petals.
Wherever the disciples stepped,
lotus flowers produced a hundred flowers.
All walked upon the flowers.
Shēn Rì saw the fire become a water pool with lotus flowers growing in it,
and was greatly terrified.
He prostrated himself with his head and face to the ground and confessed sincerely:
"Now I have prepared food for the Buddha, all with poison placed in it.
I beg to cook it again."
The Buddha said:
"There is no need to cook again.
Bring the poisoned food for me to eat."
He commanded the bhikkhus:
"Do not eat yet.
Wait for my instruction before eating."
The Buddha then chanted:
"In the world, there are generally three poisons.
First, greed and lust.
Second, anger and hatred.
Third, ignorance and delusion.
The Buddha does not have these three poisons, so they do not operate.
For those of utmost sincerity who possess the Dharma,
the poison also does not operate."
The poison in the food all dissipated of itself.
The Buddha said: "All may eat."
Shēn Rì prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, saying:
"I have been greatly at fault.
I used the words of evil men.
I wish to follow the World-Honored One, seeking compassion and repenting my transgressions."
The Buddha preached the sutra to him.
He attained the path of Stream-Entry.
In the country of Shèwèi, there was an elder's son,
named Biànyì.
Hearing the Buddha expound the fifty essential matters,
he attained the Dharma-patience.
Five hundred elders' sons attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Biànyì said:
"I only wish the World-Honored One and the great assembly
would deign to come to my house for a meal tomorrow at noon."
The Buddha and the great assembly went to his house to eat.
Before the blessing was chanted,
there was a beggar
who went around the seats begging.
No one dared to give to him; he went everywhere and obtained nothing.
He left in anger and hatred.
Then he gave rise to an evil thought:
"These śramaṇas
are unrestrained, foolish, and deluded.
What path do they have?
When the poor beg from them, they have no mind to give.
If I become king,
I will use iron-rimmed chariots to crush off their heads."
Having said this, he left.
After the Buddha finished the blessing,
another beggar came.
He begged for food from the assembly.
Each gave to him.
He obtained much food and left joyfully.
He then gave rise to the thought:
"These śramaṇas have compassionate hearts.
If I become king, I will make offerings to the Buddha and the saṅgha,
even for seven days,
to repay today's kindness in relieving my hunger and thirst."
Having said this, he left.
The two beggars wandered about begging,
reaching another country and lying in deep grass by the roadside.
At that time, the king of that country suddenly died without an heir.
The diviners judged and said:
"According to the records, a lowly person should become king."
The ministers, officials, and a thousand chariots and ten thousand horsemen patrolled the country's borders.
They saw clouds and a radiant canopy above the grass.
The diviners said:
"There is a divine person within."
They then found the beggar.
The ministers paid homage to him.
The beggar was startled and said of himself:
"I am lowly, not of royal lineage."
They all said:
"You should bathe in fragrant water,
don royal garments,
adorned with glorious majesty, and be escorted into the country."
The beggar with the evil thought
was lying asleep in the deep grass, unaware.
A chariot crushed off his head.
Long ago, there was an elder
named Tánmó Liúzhī who came to inquire.
The Buddha said:
"Tánmó Liúzhī,
it has been a very long time since we parted, and now we meet again."
Someone asked about this.
The Buddha replied:
"In a past asaṃkhyeya kalpa,
there was a Buddha in the world
named Dìngguāng.
At that time, I was a brahmin
named Chāoshù.
At that time, Dìngguāng Buddha
was about to enter the city.
I met him on the road.
I loosened my hair and spread it on the mud for the Buddha to tread upon.
The Buddha then predicted:
'You are so courageous.
After an asaṃkhyeya kalpa, you will attain Buddhahood.'
You at that time gave rise to an angry thought, saying:
'This person is no different from an animal,
treading on another's hair to pass by.'
From the time that thought arose for an asaṃkhyeya kalpa,
you constantly fell into the animal realm.
Again, in the great sea,
you became a makara fish,
its body seven thousand yojanas long.
At that time, there were five hundred merchants
who sailed into the sea to seek treasure.
They encountered this great fish, which swallowed the ship, nearly taking it into its mouth.
Then the five hundred people each called upon what they practiced.
The chief merchant said to the crowd:
'Now in the world, there is a Buddha named Shìjiāwén.
There is none better than he at saving people from peril and distress.
Let us call his name, hoping to be delivered.'
They then called out in unison.
The fish heard the Buddha's name, and its original consciousness remained.
It then thought to itself:
'Shìjiāwén Buddha has already appeared in the world.
Why is my body still in the form of a fish?'
It then submerged into the water.
The five hundred merchants returned safely.
Then the fish threw its body onto a sandbank.
Without drinking or eating, after two weeks it died.
It was reborn in an elder's household as a son,
named Tánmó Liúzhī.
Now he has come to meet me.
That is why I said it has been a long time."
Liúzhī, hearing this whole story,
went to the seashore to seek his former corpse.
He saw the bones of the great fish, its flesh already gone, walking upon its rib bones.
He thought:
"This is my former corpse."
He then scattered flowers upon the former corpse.
Contemplating this, he proceeded,
and suddenly attained the path.
In the past, there was a man who was very wealthy but miserly.
His wife was fond of the Dharma and wished to give alms, but did not dare.
Her husband was about to go to sea.
He first surrounded the house with three layers of iron caltrops.
His wife was obstructed and could not get out.
She wholeheartedly recited the Buddha's name.
All the iron barriers turned into goose feathers.
She took a bolt of silk, entrusted it to someone, and offered it to the Buddha.
The Buddha accepted it and gave a blessing.
Her husband and five hundred companions were together at sea.
They were devoured by demons.
Only her husband was left.
The demons said to each other,
"This man's wife serves the Buddha.
We cannot approach him."
His companions all died, but he alone returned with treasure.
He asked his wife what she had done.
His wife told him everything.
The two were overjoyed.
They immediately invited the Buddha and the Sangha to a feast and attained the Way.
In the past, when the Buddha was in the world, there was a great elder.
His name was Xiūluótuó, and he had immeasurable wealth and faith in the Dharma.
He made a vow:
He would always invite the Buddha and the Sangha on the eighth day of the twelfth month.
This practice continued throughout his life, and his descendants carried it on without ceasing.
When the elder died,
he instructed his son not to abandon it.
His son's name was Píluótuó.
Later, they gradually became poor.
When the time came, they had nothing to prepare and were distressed and unhappy.
The Buddha sent Mùlián to ask him,
"Your father's offering day is approaching; what plan do you have?"
He replied,
"I only hope the World-Honored One
will not abandon us.
As the eighth day approaches,
I will take my wife to her parents' home
to pawn a hundred taels of gold,
and then return to prepare the offerings."
The Buddha, along with 1,250 monks, went to his house and sat down.
Water was offered, food was served, and after the pure meal, they returned.
That night, all the old storehouses were filled with treasures.
The husband and wife saw this
and were both joyful and fearful,
afraid that officials would inquire.
They immediately went to tell the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"Be at ease and use it freely; do not have doubts.
You kept your faith and did not disobey your father's teaching.
Hearing of giving, wisdom, and the Way, the seven treasures are fully satisfied."
The Buddha was in the country of Luóyuèzhī.
There was a wealthy elder
named Shīlìzhì,
who was extremely rich.
His wife gave birth to a son, whose appearance was extraordinarily handsome.
They invited a teacher to divine and prognosticate, and he praised the boy's blessings and virtue.
He asked,
"Since conceiving this child, what auspicious signs have there been?"
The elder said,
"His mother was originally slow of speech and dull in expression.
But after conceiving this child, her speech became clever and eloquent."
They named him Póshìzhì.
When he grew up and went out to stroll and observe,
he saw a girl from a Nàluó performer family
and his heart became attached; he desired to marry her.
He returned and told his parents, hoping they would seek her hand.
His parents told him,
"The families are not of equal status; how can we arrange a marriage?"
The son insisted, saying,
"Do not ask about family status, only consider the person herself.
Please seek her for me; if I do not get my wish, I will end my own life."
His parents complied.
They arranged the marriage together.
The son, infatuated with her beauty, was not ashamed of lowly work.
He went to her family's home
and learned performing arts, mastering them all.
At that time, the king gathered many Nàluó performers for various entertainments.
The elder's son was next to perform, walking on a tightrope.
The king did not see it clearly.
He ordered him to go up again.
His strength gradually waned, and midway he was about to fall.
His heart was terrified, with nowhere to turn.
Mùlián, soaring through the air, said to him,
"On this day, would you rather preserve your life and leave home to learn the Way,
or fall and marry that girl?"
He replied,
"I wish to save myself; I do not want the girl."
Mùlián immediately transformed the ground into level land, and he landed safely.
Overjoyed,
he followed Mùlián
to visit the World-Honored One, paying respects and making offerings.
The Buddha then extensively expounded the wonderful Dharma.
His mind opened in understanding, and he attained the first fruit.
He then requested to leave home, and the World-Honored One permitted it.
His hair and beard fell off by themselves, and the Dharma robe was upon his body.
He concentrated on meditation and became an Arhat.
The Buddha said,
"In a past life, in the country of Bōluónài,
there was a great elder.
He first had a son, incomparably handsome.
Someone came from across the sea, bringing a bird's egg to offer to the elder.
The elder accepted it.
After a short time,
the egg hatched, and a bird chick emerged.
Its feathers were glossy.
The elder gave it to his son to play with.
The son rode on the bird's back, flying around to observe.
He heard that the king of another country was holding Nàluó performances.
He rode the bird there.
The bird perched in a tree.
By chance, he saw the king's daughter and became infatuated with love.
He sent a message to convey his feelings.
The girl then had relations with him.
The king found out.
He had him captured, bound, and was about to execute him.
The elder's son said,
"Why trouble yourselves to kill me?
Let me climb the tree and jump to my death."
The people agreed.
He then climbed the tree, mounted the bird, and soared into the sky, flying away.
Thus, his life was prolonged.
That elder's son is now Póshìzhì.
The king's daughter is now the performer's girl.
The bird at that time is now Mùlián.
In a past life, infatuation with beauty led to danger, and he was saved by the bird.
Now, on the verge of death,
he was saved by Mùlián, thus attaining safety."
In the country of Shèwèi, there was a great elder.
He had a son
whose appearance was handsome and who could speak at birth.
He asked his parents,
"Are the World-Honored One, Shèlìfó, Ānán, and others still in the world?"
His parents replied that they were.
Seeing that he could speak, they thought he was not human.
They went to ask the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"This child has auspicious signs."
The parents were joyful.
The child also said,
"I only hope you will invite the Buddha and the Sangha."
They replied,
"We have nothing to offer on short notice."
The child said again,
"Just sweep and clean the hall, arrange the seats solemnly,
set up three high seats,
and a hundred-flavored feast will naturally fill the hall."
Moreover, his mother from a previous life still existed,
living in the country of Bōluónài.
He wished to repay her.
His parents sent a messenger riding an elephant to fetch her.
They prepared three high seats:
one for the Tathāgata,
one for his father,
and one for his mother from the previous life.
The Buddha and the assembly of monks entered their house.
Sweet and delicious food naturally descended, abundant in variety.
The Buddha expounded the Dharma for them.
The entire family, young and old, all attained the first fruit.
In the city of Shèwèi, there was Ānàbīndǐ.
He had seven sons whose hearts lacked sincere faith.
Toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, they did not uphold the five precepts.
The elder Ānàbīndǐ said,
"I shall grant each of you a thousand taels of gold.
You must take refuge in the Three Jewels and receive the five precepts."
Hearing this,
the seven sons wished to take refuge in the Three Jewels and receive and uphold the five precepts.
Their father granted each a thousand taels of gold.
Together they went to the World-Honored One,
and fully reported this to the Buddha.
"What do you think, World-Honored One?
Do those seven sons possess any merit, virtue, or good deeds?"
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, elder!
You have greatly benefited beings, bringing peace and security to gods and humans.
Those seven sons, because of these various good deeds and merits, are fully endowed.
The rewards they will obtain, I shall now explain.
In the north, there is a country.
Its city is named Shíshì.
The land is fertile and abundant, the people prosperous and flourishing.
There is the Īrapatrā treasure trove,
countless hundreds and thousands of gold, silver, and precious jewels.
Among the seven treasuries of the people of the Jiàntuó lài country,
they may use as they desire,
without any decrease, including this great Īrapatrā treasure trove.
Those seven thousand taels of gold, a hundredfold, a thousandfold, countlessfold—
all are not equal to the merit your seven sons will obtain."
The World-Honored One spoke subtle Dharma to Ānàbīndǐ.
He then rose from his seat and addressed the World-Honored One, saying,
"I beg you to accept my invitation,
along with the community of bhikṣus.
I wish to offer nectar-like food and drink
for the sake of my seven sons."
The World-Honored One silently accepted.
Knowing the appropriate time,
the World-Honored One, surrounded by the community of bhikṣus, entered the city of Shèwèi.
They went to Ānàbīndǐ's home and all took their seats.
The elder and his sons paid homage to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One spoke the Dharma, and they immediately attained equal insight.
He declared thus:
"Elder, your seven sons have offered sweet delicacies, food, and drink,
serving the Buddha and the bhikṣus.
After the meal, the bowls were cleared.
The Buddha spoke Dharma to the seven sons.
Each, while seated, exhausted all defilements;
without stain or impurity, the Dharma-eye arose.
They had seen the Dharma,
without doubt or hesitation."
The Elder's Son Flowing Water.
In the kingdom of King Tiānzìzàiguāng.
He treated all beings of their boundless suffering and afflictions.
Causing their bodies to be restored to health.
Because their illnesses were removed, he performed many meritorious deeds.
They spoke thus:
Excellent, Elder.
You can benefit beings with boundless lifespans.
You must be a Bodhisattva who understands all medicines.
At that time, the elder, together with his two sons, Shuǐkōng and Shuǐcáng.
Took his two sons and traveled in succession through cities, towns, and villages.
Finally arriving at a great empty marsh.
They saw all the tigers, wolves, dogs, birds, and beasts.
All uniformly running swiftly away.
The elder pursued them to observe and saw there was a pond.
Its water had dried up.
Within that pond were many fish.
Seeing these fish, he gave rise to a great compassionate mind.
At that time, a tree deity manifested half its body.
And spoke thus:
Great virtuous man.
These fish are pitiable; you can give them water.
Therefore, you are named Flowing Water.
You should now live up to your name in reality.
At that time, the elder's son asked the tree deity:
How many fish are there in number?
The tree deity replied:
Fully ten thousand.
His compassionate mind increased.
At that time, this empty pond was scorched by the sun.
Only a little water remained.
These ten thousand fish.
Were about to enter the gate of death, writhing in all directions.
Seeing this elder, their minds gave rise to reliance.
Following the direction the elder went.
They followed and gazed, their eyes never leaving him.
Then the elder swiftly ran in the four directions.
Seeking and searching for water but could not find any.
Seeing a large tree, he quickly took its branches and leaves.
Returned to the pond and made shade for them.
He further sought to find from where the water in this pond originally came.
Immediately he went out to the four directions, searching all around.
He did not know the location of the water.
He ran swiftly again and saw a great river.
Named Shuǐshēng.
There were evil men who, to catch these fish, at a steep, dangerous place upstream.
Had diverted the water, not letting it flow down.
The elder went to the king and explained the circumstances.
I only wish, Great King, to borrow twenty great elephants.
To have them carry water to save the lives of those fish.
Just as I give life to the various sick people.
The king commanded his ministers to quickly provide them.
You may now go to the elephant stables and freely select them to benefit beings.
At that time, Flowing Water and his two sons.
Took the twenty elephants and borrowed leather bags.
Hastened to the river, filled them with water, and had the elephants carry them.
The water then became full again, restored as before.
At that time, the elder's son walked around the four sides of the pond.
The fish also followed, circling along the bank.
Then the elder's son again thought thus:
These fish must be tormented by the fire of hunger.
They also wish to seek food and drink from me.
I shall now give it to them.
At that time, the elder's son told his sons:
You take the elephant with the greatest strength.
Quickly go to the house.
All edible things there.
Which are the portions for parents to eat and drink.
And the portions for wife, children, and servants.
Gather everything and load it upon the elephant.
Hasten back quickly.
At that time, the two sons went to the house.
Told their grandfather the matter as above.
Collected all edible things in the house.
Loaded them on the elephant's back, hastily returned to their father, and arrived at the empty marsh pond.
When the elder's son saw his sons return.
His mind gave rise to joy, leaping with boundless happiness.
He took the food and drink from his sons.
Scattered it into the pond and gave it to the fish to eat.
Then he himself contemplated:
I have now been able to give these fish food.
Causing them to be full.
In future lifetimes, I shall bestow the food of Dharma.
I once heard that in a past empty, quiet place, there was a bhikṣu who recited the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras.
In those sūtras it is said:
If there are beings approaching the end of life.
Who hear the name of the Tathāgata Bǎoshèng.
They will be born in the heavens.
I shall now for these ten thousand fish.
Explain the profound twelve links of dependent origination.
And also proclaim the name of the Buddha Bǎoshèng.
Immediately he entered the water.
And spoke thus:
Homage to the past Tathāgata Bǎoshèng.
Who in times past practiced the Bodhisattva path.
Made this vow:
If there are beings in the ten directions.
Who, approaching the end of life, hear my name.
I shall cause these beings to immediately ascend and be born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
He further explained to these fish such profound and wonderful Dharma.
Namely, the twelve links of dependent origination.
Having explained this Dharma.
He then returned home together with them.
This elder's son again at a later time.
At a gathering of guests, lay drunk and asleep.
At that time, the ground suddenly greatly quaked.
Then the ten thousand fish on the same day ended their lives and were born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Having been born in the heaven, they thought thus:
By what good karma have we been born in this heaven?
They further said to each other:
We previously within Jambudvīpa.
Fell into the animal realm, receiving fish bodies.
The Elder Flowing Water gave us water and also food and drink.
Explained to us the twelve links of dependent origination.
And proclaimed the name of the Tathāgata Bǎoshèng.
Because of these conditions, he caused us to be born in this heaven.
We should now repay his kindness and make offerings.
At that time, the elder's son was sleeping exposed on the upper floor of the house.
These ten thousand devas.
Placed ten thousand pearl heavenly marvelous necklaces by his head.
And another ten thousand by his feet.
And another ten thousand by his right side.
And another ten thousand by his left side.
Rained down Māndārava flowers, Mahā-Māndārava flowers, piling up to the knees.
Various heavenly music emitted wonderful sounds.
In Jambudvīpa, those who were sleeping all awoke.
The Elder's Son Flowing Water also awoke from sleep.
These ten thousand devas in the sky above flew and roamed about.
In the kingdom of King Tiānzìzàiguāng, everywhere rained down heavenly marvelous lotus flowers.
These devas further went to their original place, the empty marsh pond.
And again rained down heavenly flowers.
Then from there they disappeared and returned to the Trāyastriṃśa palace.
Freely enjoying the five heavenly desires.
After that night passed.
King Tiānzìzàiguāng.
Asked his various ministers:
Last night, for what reason did such pure and wonderful auspicious signs appear?
The ministers replied:
Great King, you should know.
The various devas of Trāyastriṃśa at the house of the Elder's Son Flowing Water.
Rained down forty thousand pearl necklaces and immeasurable Māndārava flowers.
The king then told his ministers:
You may go to that elder's house and summon him to come.
They immediately went to his house and proclaimed the king's command.
At that time, the elder soon arrived at the king's place.
The king asked the elder:
For what reason did such auspicious signs appear?
The elder's son said:
I certainly know.
That those ten thousand fish have ended their lives.
At that time, the great king said:
Now we can send someone to verify this matter.
At that time, Flowing Water immediately sent his sons to that pond.
To see whether those fish were dead or alive, to verify it.
At that time, his sons went to that pond.
Saw that in the pond were many Mahā-Māndārava flowers.
Accumulated into a heap within it.
The various fish had all ended their lives.
They returned and told their father:
Those various fish have all ended their lives.
At that time, Flowing Water again went to the king's place.
Those ten thousand fish have all ended their lives.
The king heard this and rejoiced.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Virtuous Goddess:
The Elder's Son Flowing Water at that time is now my body.
The eldest son, Shuǐkōng, is Rāhula.
The second son, Shuǐcáng, is now Ānanda.
The ten thousand fish at that time are now the ten thousand devas.
Therefore, I now give them a prediction.
The tree deity who manifested half its body at that time is now your body.
Once there was an elder.
His name was Shùtíjiā.
His storehouses were overflowing, and he had a complete abundance of gold and silver.
Servants and maidservants were lined up in rows, and he lacked nothing.
There was a white cotton hand towel that was hung by the pondside.
It encountered a heavenly wind that blew it before the king's palace hall.
The assembled ministers deliberated and divined to find out the reason.
All the ministers said,
"The state is about to prosper; Heaven has bestowed this white cotton cloth."
Minister Shùtíjiā remained silent, saying nothing.
The king asked,
"Why do you not speak?"
Tíjiā replied,
"I dare not deceive Your Majesty.
This is my household's towel for wiping the body.
It was hung by the pondside.
It encountered a heavenly wind and was blown before the hall."
A few days later,
a nine-colored flower as large as a cartwheel
again encountered a heavenly wind and was blown before the king's palace hall.
The king once more deliberated and divined with his assembled ministers.
Tíjiā replied, saying,
"This is a withered, fallen flower from my household garden, blown here by the wind."
The king asked Tíjiā,
"Your household is like this?
I wish to lead two hundred thousand troops to your household to see."
Tíjiā replied, saying,
"I wish Your Majesty would follow me there at once."
The king then led two hundred thousand troops
to Shùtíjiā's home.
Entering straight through the south gate,
there were thirty youths with handsome, upright faces.
The king asked Shùtíjiā,
"Are these your sons and grandsons?"
He replied, saying,
"They are my household's gate-keeping servants."
Proceeding to the central pavilion,
there were twenty maidens with beautiful, upright faces.
The king asked,
"Are these your household's women?"
Tíjiā replied, saying,
"They are my household's pavilion-keeping maidservants."
Proceeding to the inner chamber,
the walls were of silver and the floor of crystal.
The king saw flowing water and doubted he could enter.
Shùtíjiā then guided the king through the front door of the chamber.
There was a bed of gold and a table of white jade.
Shùtíjiā's wife had one hundred and twenty layers of gold and silver curtains; her beauty was matchless.
She paid respects to the king, tears flowing from her eyes.
The king asked,
"Why, upon seeing me, does your wife have something... tears flow from her eyes?"
He replied, saying,
"The smoke from Your Majesty's clothing is the reason for the tears."
The king said,
"Commoners burn fat,
feudal lords burn wax,
and the Son of Heaven burns lacquer.
None of these produce smoke.
How can tears flow?"
Shùtíjiā replied, saying,
"In my household, there is
a Bright Moon Divine Pearl
hung in the hall.
Day and night are no different; no firelight is needed.
Your Majesty is the king among smoke,
that is why the smell is noticed."
In front of Shùtíjiā's household hall,
there was a twelve-story high tower.
He took the king to the top.
Looking east, he forgot west;
looking south, he forgot north.
All was silent and still.
The king thought it was a brief moment and could be endured a little longer.
They went to the rear garden's flowing spring and bathing pool.
Eating various fruits and melons, the taste was naturally sweet and delicious.
It was extremely delightful, so much so that a month passed.
The great minister informed the king,
"It is time to return to the state."
Shùtíjiā then bestowed gold, silver, precious gems, damasks, silks, and colored fabrics.
The two hundred thousand troops, horses, and chariots all returned to the state at once.
The king then assembled his ministers, finding the situation strange.
"Shùtíjiā is my minister.
His women and residence surpass mine.
I wish to attack him.
Can he be captured or not?"
All the ministers said,
"He should indeed be captured."
The king then led four hundred thousand troops, striking bells and beating drums, surrounding Tíjiā's residence.
They destroyed one hundred layers of walls.
At Tíjiā's gate, there was a mighty warrior.
In his hand, he held a golden staff, which he pointed at the four hundred thousand troops.
All at once, they fell to the ground, lying down and unable to rise.
Tíjiā rode a flying cloud-wheeled chariot in the empty sky and asked,
"You people, what was your intention in coming here, lying on the ground unable to rise?"
The people replied as above.
Shùtíjiā asked,
"Do you wish to rise?"
They all said they wished to.
Shùtíjiā opened his great divine eyes and looked once.
The four hundred thousand troops all rose at once.
They returned to their own state.
The king then sent an envoy to summon Shùtíjiā.
Together they went to where the Buddha was. The king asked, saying,
"World-Honored One,
Shùtíjiā is my minister.
What meritorious deeds did he perform in a past life,
that his women and residence surpass mine?"
The Buddha replied, saying,
"Shùtíjiā's meritorious deeds of giving.
He saw the joys of heaven and desired them.
Five hundred caravan leaders, leading various merchants,
carrying heavy treasures, fled to an empty mountain.
They encountered a sick ascetic.
They provided him with a grass hut, thickly spread bedding,
provided water, broth, rice, and grain,
provided him with lamps and candles.
At that time, they begged for the offerings of heaven.
Now they receive such a karmic reward.
The Buddha said,
"Those who gave at that time
are now Shùtíjiā and his wife.
The sick ascetic at that time
is now my own body.
The five hundred merchants all attained the path of Arhat."
In the past, in the kingdom of King Āyù,
there was a Kālodayin.
He made offerings to twenty thousand bhikṣus.
He invited them for a full year.
His fame reached the king.
The king summoned him for an audience.
"I have heard you are greatly wealthy.
What do you possess in full?"
He replied,
"In truth, I possess nothing."
The king did not believe him.
He detained Kālodayin and sent someone to see his home.
They saw that at his gate were seven layers of houses and halls.
All were made of the seven treasures.
They surpassed the king's palace.
The women also surpassed [the king's].
But there was no grain, cloth, or money.
They returned and reported to the king; the king's mind gradually understood.
Kālodayin immediately laughed.
The king asked, "What are you laughing at?"
He replied, saying,
"Your Majesty did not believe me, that is all."
Kālodayin pointed with his finger to the east.
Immediately it was filled with the seven treasures.
Pointing to the south was also thus.
The king then sent him back.
And the monks' vihāra was not far from the palace.
The king then went to the vihāra.
He saw the bhikṣu saṅgha.
He paid respects reverently and asked the senior monk,
"That Kālodayin, what blessings from past lives cause precious gems to appear naturally when he thinks of them?"
The senior bhikṣu entered samādhi.
He saw things within four hundred yojanas with his mind.
He saw that this elder,
during the time of Buddha Vipaśyin, had four people together build a stūpa and monastery.
Among them, one person was diligent and earnest in his intention.
After the stūpa and monastery were completed, he took gold, silver, the seven treasures, and various fine flowers, mixed them together,
went up to the top three stories of the stūpa,
and scattered them in all directions,
vowing that future enjoyment of blessings would never cease.
Now, the one who obtains natural treasures
is this one person.
The king heard this and greatly cultivated meritorious deeds.
In the past, there was an elder Kālodayin.
He was intelligent, learned, and wealthy beyond measure.
He lived near the seashore.
He planted many trees, flourishing and reaching to the sky.
At that time, on the sea islets, there were many precious gems,
worth thousands of koṭis, but people could not get near.
Only birds came and went.
They only ate the Bright Moon Pearls.
They entered in the morning and emerged at dusk,
roosting and resting in the elder's grove.
The elder, being very wise, devised a skillful means to obtain them.
He prepared food of a hundred flavors
and gave it to the birds.
The birds, eating until full, then spat out pearls covering the ground.
The elder obtained them
and thus became greatly wealthy.
In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a householder.
He lost his fields and home, his family members were convicted and died, and all were gone.
Only one son remained, with no one else to rely on.
The son heard people say:
"Those who offer food to the Buddha and the Saṅgha will be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
He then wished to offer food to the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
He could only work as a hired laborer to fulfill this wish.
There was a householder who owned many fields and homes.
Although this boy was young, he possessed many skills and talents.
He sought to be hired.
The householder asked:
"What are you capable of?"
He replied:
"I can write, calculate, understand texts and meanings, distinguish gold, silver, pearls, shells, coins, and treasures, oversee fields,
and manage a shop—there is nothing I cannot do."
The householder asked:
"How much do you ask for per year?"
He replied:
"One thousand gold coins per year."
The householder said:
"Nowadays, with famine, I will hire you for five hundred.
When the year is full, I will pay it all." The boy said:
"My talent is not worth this, but my need is urgent.
I will work for you now."
He was immediately set to manage the shop.
After just one month,
the accounts showed that the profits had already tripled.
He ate only one meal a day, saving the other portion.
He was then put in charge of the fields, and by winter, the harvest had tripled again.
When the year was full, he asked for his gold and food.
The householder, worried he would leave, repeatedly claimed he was not available.
Later, he said to him:
"Why are you in such a hurry to leave?"
The boy said:
"I wish to offer food to the Buddha and the Saṅgha."
When the householder heard this, he immediately felt faith.
He asked further:
"Where do you wish to do this?"
He replied:
"I wish to go to the Jetavana."
The householder said:
"Just stay at my gate; I will provide the utensils and help."
The boy addressed the Buddha:
"I wish for you to accept my food tomorrow."
The Buddha and the Saṅgha remained silent, as it happened to be a festival day.
Many laypeople sent pork, dried cakes, and various kinds of food.
The monks accepted them and said to one another:
"Today, a poor boy is exerting all his effort to hold this feast.
Each of us should eat sparingly for his sake."
When they arrived at the householder's home,
he personally served the food.
They all said: "Give us less."
Thus, the food was not reduced.
The poor boy asked the monks:
"Is the food coarse and unpalatable, or do you pity my poverty?"
They replied:
"Today is a festival day.
Early in the morning, people sent food.
At first, we took little,
but as the households were many,
we became full."
The poor boy grew worried, fearing his wish would not be fulfilled.
Weeping, he asked the Buddha.
The Buddha explained the Dharma to him, assuring him he would certainly be reborn in heaven.
"You should return quickly."
The poor boy rejoiced.
He again served the monks' food, letting them take as they wished.
"I exerted all my strength to provide this offering in time.
Now, even if you venerable ones cannot eat it,
please take it as you wish."
At that time, five hundred merchants
came from the country of Udyāna, arriving in the afternoon.
The road was long and distant,
and they had been without food for three days.
They entered the city to buy food.
At that time, there was famine, and the weather was extremely hot, so they found nothing.
The merchant leader sighed:
"The sea does not lack, but in this great city, there is no food.
We should search everywhere for whatever we need."
The poor boy was weeping before the Buddha.
Many people saw him and told the merchants:
