"There is food at a certain house."
They went to the householder's home
and said to the boy:
"We need food."
The boy asked:
"How many are you?"
They replied:
"There are five hundred."
"You may all come.
There is no need to discuss the price."
When they arrived, food was set out, and all were fully satisfied.
There was a large copper bowl.
One merchant leader
untied a pearl from the corner of his garment,
worth one hundred thousand gold coins,
and placed it in the bowl.
The other merchants also untied pearls
and threw them into the bowl.
The boy said:
"I am not selling food.
Why are you suddenly leaving pearls?"
"Stay a little while; let me ask the Buddha."
The Buddha said:
"Take them; it will not hinder your rebirth in heaven.
This is the flower reward; the fruit reward will come later.
You may accept the treasures."
The merchants asked further:
"Householder, in this city, there was formerly a certain person. Where is he now?"
He replied:
"He has passed away."
They asked again:
"Does he have descendants?"
He replied:
"The donor you just met is his son."
The merchants said to the boy:
"Your father was our teacher."
They also gave him one hundred thousand taels of gold to renew the old friendship.
At that time, the householder had no sons,
only one daughter, beautiful and graceful.
He sought to marry her to the boy
and sent one hundred thousand taels of gold.
After the householder died,
King Prasenajit asked:
"Does he have a son?
Who will manage his affairs?"
He replied:
"He only has a son-in-law.
At that time, there was a great elder in the kingdom of Shèwèi.
He possessed immeasurable wealth but had no sons.
He only had five daughters, who were all beautiful, intelligent, and accomplished.
His wife was pregnant when the elder passed away.
According to the law of the kingdom, if there were no sons, the property would revert to the king.
The king dispatched a minister to seize and record his wealth.
His daughters thought to themselves:
"Our mother is pregnant, but we do not know whether it will be a boy or a girl.
If it is another girl, the wealth should belong to the king.
But if it is a boy, he should be the master of the wealth."
They went to inform the king.
At that time, King Pòsīnì governed with impartial laws and just administration.
He approved their petition.
Not long after, their mother's pregnancy reached full term and she gave birth to a child.
Its body was formless, lacking eyes and ears.
It had a mouth but no tongue, and no hands or feet.
It only possessed male genitalia.
They named the child Màncí Pílí.
At that time, the daughters
went to inquire of the king about this matter in detail.
The king told the daughters:
"The wealth belongs to your brother.
I will not take it."
At that time, the eldest daughter
went to marry into another family and served her husband.
She was humble, respectful, and diligent, like a maidservant.
The elder of her husband's household, seeing her like this,
found it strange and asked her:
The woman replied:
"When my father passed away, he left immeasurable family wealth.
Although he had five daughters, it would still have reverted to the king.
But then my mother became pregnant and gave birth to a brother of mine.
He lacks all human features but possesses male genitalia.
Thus he became the master of the wealth.
Although there were many daughters, they are not equal to one son."
After hearing this, the elder
immediately went with the woman to the Buddha's place.
He said:
"World-Honored One,
what causes and conditions led to that elder's son being like this?"
The Buddha said:
"In the past, there were two elder brothers.
The elder brother was named Tánruò Shìzhì.
The younger brother was named Shīluó Shìzhì.
The elder brother, from a young age,
was loyal, trustworthy, sincere, and always fond of giving alms, praised by the entire kingdom.
The king appointed this man as the kingdom's impartial arbitrator.
According to the kingdom's law, for loans and transactions without written contracts, all parties would go to the impartial arbitrator.
At that time, a merchant borrowed a large sum of money from the younger brother Shīluó Shìzhì.
At that time, the younger elder
had only one son, who was still young.
He took his son and the money to be loaned
to the impartial arbitrator's place.
He said:
'Elder brother,
this merchant's son is borrowing money from me.
When he returns from the sea, he should repay this amount.
If I pass away, please ensure that he receives it.'
The impartial arbitrator agreed.
Not long after, the younger elder passed away.
The merchant went to sea, encountered a storm, and lost his goods.
The merchant survived.
When the elder's son heard that he returned empty-handed,
he thought to himself:
'Although he owes me, how can I obtain repayment?
I must wait until he is able to repay.'
This merchant borrowed money again elsewhere,
then went to sea once more and obtained great treasures.
He returned safely.
He thought to himself:
'That elder's son previously did not demand repayment of the loan from me,
perhaps because he was young and might not remember,
or perhaps because he saw I was poor before and thus did not press me?
Now I should test him.'
He then adorned a fine horse with numerous treasures and ornaments.
When the elder's son saw this, he immediately sent someone to say:
'You owe me money; now you should repay.'
The merchant replied: 'Very well.'
The merchant thought to himself:
'The loan is large, and with accumulated interest,
I cannot repay it all.
I must devise a plan to settle it.'
He took a precious pearl to the wife of the impartial arbitrator.
He said:
'Madam,
I originally borrowed money from Shīluó Shìzhì.
His son is now demanding repayment.
I present this pearl, worth one hundred thousand.
If he demands repayment from me, please ask the impartial arbitrator to intervene.'
The woman replied:
'The elder is honest and trustworthy; he certainly would not agree to this.
But I will try to speak to him.'
She accepted the pearl. When the impartial arbitrator returned in the evening,
the woman explained the situation in detail.
The elder replied:
'How could such a thing be?
Because of my loyalty, trustworthiness, and never speaking falsely, the king appointed me as the kingdom's impartial arbitrator.
If I speak one false word, this matter cannot be done.'
The next day, when the merchant came, he was fully informed of the situation.
The pearl was returned to him.
At that time, the merchant's son offered another pearl worth two hundred thousand,
hoping she would persuade him.
'This is a small matter;
just say one word and gain three hundred thousand.'
At that time, the woman, coveting the precious pearl, accepted it.
In the evening, she again told her husband:
'Regarding what I mentioned yesterday, I hope you will agree.'
The elder replied:
'Absolutely not.'
At that time, the elder had one son.
His wife wept and said:
'If you do not comply, I will first kill our son and then kill myself.'
When the elder heard this,
it was as if he were choking.
He thought to himself:
'I have only one son.
If he dies, the wealth will have no one to inherit.
But if I comply with her words, people will not trust me,
and I will suffer in the future.' Tormented and distressed,
he eventually agreed.
The woman told the merchant:
'The elder has agreed.'
The merchant was overjoyed.
He adorned a great elephant with numerous treasures and ornaments, dressed in magnificent robes, and rode the elephant into the market.
When the elder's son saw him, he went and said:
'The money you owe me should now be repaid.'
The merchant feigned surprise and said:
'I do not recall ever owing you anything.'
They went together to the impartial arbitrator.
The elder's son said:
'This man previously borrowed a certain amount of money from my father.
Uncle, as the impartial arbitrator at that time, were you aware of this or not?'
He replied: 'I do not know.'
His nephew exclaimed in shock:
'Uncle, at that time, did you truly not see or hear?'
He again replied: 'No.'
The nephew said angrily:
'Because of your loyalty and integrity,
the king appointed you as impartial arbitrator.
The people of the kingdom trust you.
If even my own nephew is treated unjustly like this,
how many outsiders must have been wronged?
The truth of this matter will be known in future lives.'
The Buddha told the elder:
'Know that the impartial arbitrator elder of that time
is now Màncí Pílí.
Because he spoke one false word at that time, he fell into the great hell and suffered many torments.
After emerging from hell, for five hundred lifetimes he constantly received this body.
Because he planted good roots through almsgiving,
he was often born into wealthy families and became a master of wealth.'
There was an elder named Yīnyuè.
He possessed immeasurable wealth but was old and childless.
He considered this a cause for sorrow.
However, due to past blessings pursuing him,
his reward manifested in four ways.
First, his wife gave birth to a son.
Second, five hundred white horses simultaneously gave birth to foals.
Third, the king sent an envoy to confer upon him a golden seal.
Fourth, five hundred treasure-laden ships arrived together at the same time.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In a previous life, the elder Yīnyuè
sent five hundred men on a ship to sea.
They obtained many treasures and returned home safely.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says these four blessings gathered together simultaneously."
The elder thought to himself:
"Heaven has bestowed blessings and fortune upon my household.
I should prepare a feast and celebrate with my family."
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra, Brahmā, various gods, dragons, spirits, ghost kings, asuras, and others,
each with their retinues, filled the sky.
The Tathāgata, with his divine insight, knew this elder was joyful and elated.
Because of his joy, he went to praise him.
If he could understand, he could plant blessings indeed.
He then chanted the auspicious eight-toned hymn.
The elder, overjoyed, addressed Gautama:
"Truly divine and marvelous!
You know the immeasurable auspiciousness of my household.
I trouble your venerable divinity to come and praise me."
He offered fine white cotton cloth worth ten million taels of gold
to the Tathāgata, and the Buddha accepted it.
The Buddha told the elder:
"Wealth has five calamities.
If you can act now, you will surely receive a shadowy reward.
Wherever you are born, blessings will naturally return to you."
The elder asked the Buddha:
"What are the five calamities?"
The Buddha said:
"First, destruction by fire.
Second, loss by water.
Third, confiscation by officials.
Fourth, wasteful spending by wicked sons.
Fifth, theft by bandits—these five things,
once they arrive, cannot be restrained."
Hearing this, the elder became even more elated.
Then the Tathāgata suddenly returned to Vulture Peak.
At that time, in the country, there was a Nirgrantha heretic
named Bùlánjiāyè.
He heard that the Tathāgata had gone to the elder's house, chanted one verse,
and received ten million taels of gold from the elder.
"Even a śramaṇa can obtain gold;
surely if I go to beg, I will get some too."
He also thought to himself:
"I should go and ask the śramaṇa Gautama for the verse he chanted.
Then I will go begging and surely obtain treasures.
My praise should surpass Gautama's."
Bùlánjiāyè,
harboring this foolish, envious, and jealous thought,
went to ask the Buddha:
"It is said, Gautama,
you went to the elder's house, chanted a verse, and greatly obtained treasures.
Could you, out of compassion, bestow upon me the verse you chanted,
so that I may recite it, hoping to obtain treasures?"
The Tathāgata, with his triple insight, knew that later, this elder's wealth would scatter.
Bùlánjiāyè did not know the appropriate time.
To go to a household facing calamity and speak auspicious words
would surely cause the elder to inflict upon him immeasurable beatings and pain.
The Tathāgata told him:
"I do not begrudge this verse, but you do not know the time.
If you recite this verse, you will surely receive severe pain.
Therefore, I oppose you.
If you still wish to have timely words and supremely wonderful verses,
I will give them to you.
This will allow the elder to hear true words
and also spare you the pain of beating."
Bùlánjiāyè thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama does not want me to go begging for treasures.
That is why he is stingy and unwilling to give it to me."
He then asked again:
"Just give it to me; how do you know about other matters?"
The Tathāgata, out of compassion, admonished him three times, but he still did not believe or understand.
The Buddha also foreknew that due to Bùlánjiāyè's past karma, he should receive this pain.
The Tathāgata also said:
"Sin cannot be admonished."
The Buddha then recited the auspicious verse for him.
The Nirgrantha recited it for a year before mastering it.
Then the elder's house caught fire, burning down, and all his rare treasures were completely destroyed.
The five hundred foals were simultaneously burned to death.
The wonderful son he had just borne suddenly died.
The king sent an envoy to seize back the golden seal.
Later, he again took a ship to sea to gather treasures and returned safely.
But upon reaching shore, his five hundred treasure ships were suddenly lost to the waves.
His entire household, young and old, was filled with sorrow and bitterness.
Bùlánjiāyè went to his gate
and chanted the Tathāgata's auspicious verse as mentioned above.
Hearing this, the elder and his entire household became furious.
"Under heaven, no misfortune surpasses mine.
How dare this shameless, naked man
come here with his sorcery,
speaking auspicious words to me, only increasing my worries and troubles?"
They immediately came out and beat him,
from head to foot, and he crawled back home.
The leaders of the six heretical teachers met him and asked what happened.
He replied:
"This misfortune is precisely because of Gautama."
Unable to restrain himself internally, he instead blamed the World-Honored One.
The Buddha addressed the assembly:
"Bùlánjiāyè previously came to the Tathāgata to request a verse,
wishing to go to the elder's house, chant it, and seek treasures.
The Tathāgata admonished him,
but he did not believe it.
Now he has already suffered severe pain there."
Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"What karma exists between Bùlánjiāyè and this elder that he suffered this calamity?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the distant past, countless kalpas ago,
there was a king also named Yīnyuè.
There was also a bird
named Yīngwǔ (parrot).
It perched on the king's palace, singing with a harmonious and pleasant voice.
The king was napping during the day when he heard the bird's song and woke with a start.
He asked his attendants:
'What bird is this, singing so wonderfully?'
The attendants replied:
'There is a marvelous bird,
radiant with five colors, that was just on the palace; it sang and then left.'
The king sent foot soldiers and cavalry to pursue and find it.
After a long search, they captured it and brought it to the king.
The king adorned it with a seven-jeweled necklace and always kept it by his side.
Day and night he watched over it, never leaving it.
Shortly after, there was another bird
named Túxiāo (owl).
It came to the palace
and saw the parrot alone receiving such favor and宠爱.
It asked the parrot:
'How did you achieve this?'
The parrot replied:
'I came to the palace and sang mournfully yet beautifully.
The king loved and respected me, took me, and always keeps me by his side.'
The owl heard this
and harbored jealousy.
It thought to itself:
'I will also sing, making my song surpass yours.
The king will surely love and宠爱 me too.'
When the king was sleeping, the owl began to cry.
The king immediately woke with a start,
trembling, his hair standing on end as if terrified.
The king asked his attendants:
'What sound is this, startling and frightening me?'
The attendants replied:
'There is an evil-sounding bird named Túxiāo (owl).'
The king sent a large force to search everywhere.
They captured it and brought it to the king.
The king ordered his attendants to pluck its feathers alive.
Its whole body in great pain, it walked away.
The other birds asked:
'How did you come to this?'
The owl, angry and resentful, replied to the birds:
'It is precisely because of the parrot that I suffered this calamity.'
The Buddha said:
'A good voice attracts fortune; an evil voice brings disaster.
The retribution for sin comes from oneself, yet he blamed the parrot.'
The king of old is now Yīnyuè.
The parrot is now myself.
The owl is now Bùlánjiāyè.
Once there was an elder named Jiūliú.
He did not believe in the retribution for good and evil in this life or the next.
He traveled with five hundred men to make a living.
Before reaching another country, they ran out of food for three days.
Ahead, they saw a grove from afar,
thinking it was a dwelling.
Upon arriving, they saw a tree spirit.
They immediately paid their respects.
The men were starving and exhausted.
The spirit raised its hand,
and from the tips of its five fingers naturally emerged food, drink, and sweet water, giving them to Jiūliú until he was full. He then began to wail loudly.
The spirit asked why.
He replied:
'My five hundred companions are all greatly hungry and thirsty.'
The spirit told him to call them.
It again provided food and drink.
Both men and horses had their fill.
Jiūliú asked the spirit:
'What blessings did you originally have to attain such a state?'
The spirit said:
'In the time of Buddha Kāśyapa, I was a poor man.
I constantly polished mirrors at the city gate.
When śramaṇas came and went,
I always gladly pointed out places for alms
and Buddhist temples and monasteries.
I did this not just once.
After my life ended, I was born here,
naturally receiving blessings without any lack or shortage.'
The elder's mind awakened, and he greatly cultivated generosity.
He fed eight thousand people daily.
The water from washing rice flowed out of the city gate,
enough to float boats.
Later, he was reborn in the second heaven,
becoming a flower-scattering deva."
In the past, in the country of Bālónài, there was an elder.
His name was Rìnán.
He was extremely wealthy and possessed rare treasures.
He was miserly and envious.
Before the sun set, he would often order the gatekeeper:
"Do not allow any beggars to pass."
Rìnán's son, Zhāntán,
was also miserly and greedy.
After Rìnán's life ended, he was reborn in the same country.
He became the son of a blind woman.
Her husband said to the woman:
"You are seriously ill and now you are pregnant again.
I have no food or clothing; you should leave on your own."
The woman went out and found a large pile of straw.
She settled there.
After nine months, she gave birth to a son, and both his eyes were blind.
She begged for food to raise him.
When he was seven years old, his mother lamented:
"Now if only someone would give me a little rice to ease my hunger like rain for the thirsty."
The child heard his mother's words and went to beg for food, arriving at his former son's house.
At that time, the gatekeeper had briefly stepped out, and he entered the central courtyard.
Zhāntán heard the commotion.
He called the gatekeeper to question him.
The gatekeeper, fearing punishment,
immediately seized the blind child and threw him outside the gate, injuring his head and breaking his arm.
The mother heard and rushed over, asking, "Who is so heartless?"
At that moment, the deity at the gate said to her:
"The pain you suffer now is still minor.
Greater suffering awaits.
You endure this hardship because in your previous life you had wealth but did not give alms.
Death brings even greater pain." Those who heard the commotion,
the Buddha asked Ānán:
"What is that sound?"
Ānán explained in detail.
"May the Buddha have compassion.
Go to this child's place and share your leftover rice." After doing so,
he went to see the blind child and touched his head with his hand.
His eyes immediately opened and became clear.
His broken injuries were healed.
He then remembered his past lives.
The Buddha asked:
"Were you not the elder named Rìnán in your previous life?"
He replied, "Yes, I was."
The Buddha told Ānàn:
"People in this world suffer greatly due to ignorance and delusion.
Father and son for a lifetime do not recognize or know each other."
At that time, the Buddha preached a sutra to dispel their confusion.
In the past, there was an elder.
He aspired to the bodhisattva path.
He gathered poor people, about five hundred in total.
He provided them with clothing and provisions.
They went to sea to seek treasure and stayed overnight on a large mountain.
The others were dull and drowsy, but the elder sat alone.
He was observing everything.
At night, he saw a person emerge from the mountainside.
His radiance was extraordinary, and his face was handsome.
But his mouth resembled a pig's snout, and he amused himself with music.
He circled around the mountain.
The elder asked:
"Who are you?"
Hearing the voice, he was startled and said:
"I am a person who receives blessings and dwells here."
The elder asked:
"Your body and face are handsome, but why is your mouth like this?"
He replied:
"It is because I committed faults with my mouth, often enjoying gossip and idle talk."
The celestial being asked:
"Who are you?"
He replied:
"I am an elder from the country.
I am concerned about the poverty and hardship of the people and wish to bring them peace, so I led everyone to sea to seek treasure.
I also wish to transport the treasure to benefit Jambudvīpa."
The celestial being said:
"Are you not a bodhisattva?"
The elder said:
"I have aspired to the bodhisattva path.
To save all from the illnesses of desire, anger, and ignorance.
Those who have not yet been liberated, I will liberate them."
The celestial being said:
"Excellent!"
He then guided them to the treasure site, and they returned heavily laden.
In the past, in the country of Jìbīn, there was an elder.
He was originally very wealthy.
After his parents passed away,
he often provided for several monks.
After several years, his household became impoverished.
He had nothing left to give.
He grieved deeply, thinking of making merit for his parents.
His wife said to her husband:
"Better to endure hardship for one lifetime and later attain liberation.
So that our parents may receive immeasurable blessings."
The elder agreed.
"Take the two of us as collateral and borrow a hundred taels of gold.
Agree to work off the debt once the gold is spent.
Use the gold for almsgiving, and when it is exhausted, go to work."
She sent her husband to plow the fields while she cooked in the kitchen.
While plowing, he found a large stone like a millstone lid.
He lifted it and saw a thousand ding of gold.
He covered it back up and did not return to eat.
The elder sent his wife to bring food to her husband.
The husband then carried the gold back home.
The next day, they weighed the gold to repay the debt.
The master and his wife returned home.
They again used it for almsgiving for their parents of seven past lives.
It lasted them their entire lives.
In the past, there was a king.
He was greedy for sensual pleasures and acted without virtue.
Whenever he heard of a beautiful woman, he would go and seize her.
The entire country suffered because of this.
There was an elder.
He possessed immense wealth and was highly talented and learned.
His wife was beautiful and dignified.
The ministers informed the king.
The king's heart was stirred, and he sent envoys to forcibly seize her.
Her husband was distressed and grieved.
He abandoned his home and became a monk.
Fragrance emanated from his mouth, spreading for forty miles.
His entire body was permeated with the scent of sandalwood.
The king saw this man.
Since he had no descendants,
all his family wealth was confiscated.
The king established his wife as the principal queen.
In the country, beautiful lotus flowers bloomed.
Blue, yellow, red, and white, they were large, fragrant, and pure.
The king, honoring his queen, first presented them to her.
The queen, upon receiving the flowers, became even more sorrowful.
The king asked:
"You are now the mother of the country.
We respect each other and do not fail each other.
Is there something unsatisfactory?
Why are you so unhappy?"
The queen said:
"I dare not be unhappy.
But I remember my former husband, whose body and mouth were more fragrant than these flowers.
Secretly thinking of my old affection, I cannot help but grieve."
The king did not believe her words and sent for him.
The former husband had already attained arhatship.
He possessed supernatural powers, could fly, and his body emitted a fragrance that filled the entire country.
The king had him bathed and scrubbed repeatedly.
The fragrance of his body became even stronger.
The king tried asking the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"In the past, there was a poor boy.
He was destitute and had no livelihood, so he sold firewood to survive.
Once, while gathering firewood, before he could reach the city gate,
the gate had already closed.
Outside the gate, there was a temple where monks chanted sutras at night.
He stayed there overnight and sat listening to the sutras.
He burned incense and praised until dawn.
Because of this, for five hundred lifetimes, he did not fall into evil realms.
He was always reborn in the heavens, with his body and mouth fragrant and pure."
In the past, there was an elder.
His wife became pregnant.
Fragrance emanated from her mouth, filling the entire country.
King Ajātaśatru
sent envoys to search, and they found the elder's household.
They questioned the elder.
The elder explained in detail.
The envoys reported to the king.
The king was greatly pleased and summoned the elder, saying:
"If you give birth to a son, you must give him to me." Later, she gave birth to a daughter.
A golden-threaded robe naturally clothed her body.
Her mother found it strange and removed it.
But as soon as she did, another identical robe appeared on her body.
She went to ask the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"In the past, there was a poor family.
The wife went out and encountered rain.
She saw an old monk who was a pratyekabuddha.
He had slipped and fallen in the mud, injuring his knee, which was bleeding.
She immediately helped the monk up and washed away the mud.
She tore her own clothes to bandage his injured knee.
Although the woman had not yet fully embraced the Dharma,
she often praised the Buddha's path.
After death, she was reborn in the heavens.
After her heavenly life ended, she was reborn below.
Therefore, she had a naturally appearing robe.
And fragrance emanated from her mouth."
In the city of Śrāvastī, there was a wealthy elder.
He died without children.
All his money and property were confiscated by the state.
During his lifetime, the elder ate coarse food, wore thin and shabby clothes, and used leaves as a cover.
The Buddha said:
"Although he obtained a noble position, he did not care for his own body.
Nor did he care for his children, provide for his parents,
associate with friends, or give alms to monks.
Today, after his death, he has entered the weeping hell."
The Buddha said:
"In the past, he gave food to a pratyekabuddha.
After giving, he regretted it, thinking:
'I should not have given it to a shaven-headed monk,
but to my servants instead.'
Because of this good deed,
he was reborn in the heavens seven times and as a human seven times, always attaining nobility and wealth.
But because of his regret, this karmic result
caused him not to eat good food, not wear good clothes,
and not crave the five desires."
King Prasenajit,
you must diligently practice vigor and eliminate laziness.
There was an elder who wished to build a pagoda and temple.
All the timber was prepared.
Only one stone was missing.
There was nothing to serve as the pillar base.
There was another elder.
Although he did not venerate the Buddha, he still knew about merit.
He then donated a stone from his home used for pounding clothes.
Thus the temple was completed.
When the life of the donor of the stone ended,
he was immediately reborn in the second heaven, in a palace of the seven treasures.
Jade maidens attended and guarded him; food and clothing appeared spontaneously.
After a long time like this, his country perished.
No one maintained the temple, and it all fell into ruin.
Only one stone remained, buried in the ground.
When people plowed the land, the stone hindered their plow.
They conceived the intention to dig it up.
The heavenly being who was the stone's owner felt a disturbance in his heart.
With his divine eye, he observed people digging up the stone.
He thought to himself:
"Because of this stone, merit brought me rebirth in heaven.
Now if people take it away, will my merit not be exhausted?"
He then descended and transformed into an ordinary person, standing before the man digging the stone.
He asked:
"Do you intend to take this stone away?"
The man replied:
"I wish to plow this land, but the stone hinders the plow, so I want to remove it."
The heavenly being asked:
"Suppose you plow this land, you might harvest several tens of hu of grain."
The heavenly being said:
"Do not take this stone.
I will give you five hundred taels of gold."
The man asked:
"Are you not a deity?"
He replied:
"I am a heavenly being."
He immediately resumed his heavenly form and said to the man:
"I was originally a person of this land.
In a previous life, I gave this stone to a monk to establish a temple.
Because of this merit, I was reborn in heaven, receiving natural enjoyment.
Just now, my heavenly palace trembled; I wondered why.
Observing, I saw it was because of you, so I have come.
This stone is the root of my merit.
Please do not take it."
Hearing this, the man said:
"I did not know originally.
This is a sacred pagoda and temple,
the field of merit for heavenly beings; I dare not violate it." The heavenly being returned to heaven. The man pondered:
"This heavenly being merely donated this stone and gained such merit.
I should also establish a pagoda and temple."
He then immediately undertook the work and restored the pagoda as before.
In the past, the householder Gúdú had three sons.
All turned their backs on the right and followed the wrong, indulging in wine and women.
They galloped hunting and engaged in gambling and games.
Leaving light for darkness, daily becoming wild and foolish.
Their father pitied and grieved for them.
With compassion and sorrow, he instructed and admonished them, pointing out misfortune and fortune, never missing a day.
The sons alone did not change; their dissipation grew daily worse.
The father then clothed them in straw garments and fed them beans and wheat.
In destitution, they repented.
The father said:
"You did evil; in this present life you receive such severe hardship.
How much more the pain of hell's burning and boiling—who will save you then?"
The sons bowed their heads and said:
"Evil friends led us; we were deluded and practiced it.
Like pigs in a sty, we did not know the stench.
From now on, we restrain ourselves and revere the Three Jewels."
The father said: "Excellent.
If you cleanse your hearts, revere the Buddha, and observe the Five Precepts for life without transgression,
I will give you fifty million in gold each year."
"Threefold Refuge" [means] thirty million.
The sons replied:
"We will." Having received the venerable teaching,
he immediately had them bathe and brought them before the Buddha.
They bowed and received the precepts, then withdrew to cultivate virtue.
They purified their aspirations, aiding the poor and relieving the needy.
Their kindness reached all beings; the country's scholars praised their virtue.
Their fame equaled that of ancient worthies.
In the past, in the city of Rājagṛha,
there was an elder
named Xūtán.
He was very wealthy with abundant riches.
His son was named Xūmóti.
When his father passed away,
his younger brother was named Xiūyēshè. Xūmóti
devised a plan not to share with his brother.
He thought to kill him.
The elder brother said to the younger:
"Let us go together to Vulture Peak Mountain to discuss something."
He then took his brother's hand and led him to a sheer cliff.
He pushed him to the bottom and piled stones on him.
He thus died.
Xūtán was King Śuddhodana.
At that time, Xūmóti was myself.
Xiūyēshè was the present Devadatta.
King Prasenajit
had a minister
named Líqímí.
For his seventh son to take a wife,
he married the beautiful daughter of King Prasenajit's younger brother, Tánmóhē.
This woman was intelligent, sharp-witted, and skilled in many virtues and arts.
She conceived for ten months and gave birth to thirty eggs.
From the eggs emerged boys.
Their forms were outstanding, brave and strong, unmatched.
The strength of one surpassed a thousand men.
Their parents loved them, and the whole country revered and feared them.
There was a wealthy elder
who had a foolish and dull son.
He boarded a ship for trade, carrying only aloeswood.
The incense was fine and expensive.
Buyers were few.
It remained unsold for a long time.
His companions returned home; he alone could not afford to leave.
Fearing to lose his companions,
he observed the market and saw that charcoal sold fastest.
He then burned the incense to make charcoal, hoping for a quick sale.
People saw this
and all reproached and laughed at him:
"Great madman! Selling incense, though slow, would fetch no small price.
Now burning it into charcoal, what gain is there?"
In the country of Āshīmójiā Āpándì.
There was a settlement king.
Named Sàbó.
Within it was a wealthy householder.
His wealth and treasures were abundant, only he lacked a son.
Praying to various deities, he could not obtain one.
When the time for a son arrived, his wife realized she was pregnant.
This woman was sharp-witted and possessed four unique knowledges.
First, knowing when a man loves.
Second, knowing when a man does not love.
Third, knowing the time of pregnancy.
Fourth, knowing from whom it was obtained.
She told the householder.
The householder was overjoyed.
When the month was full, she gave birth to a boy with golden rings in his ears.
This child was handsome, and those who saw him were delighted.
He assembled the Brahmins.
They examined him and said.
This child truly possesses virtuous power and might.
They gave him two names.
In a past life, he left home.
So he was named Shāmén Ěrhuán.
Not of this world, he was worth a hundred million.
His name was Shāmén Yì'ěr.
He was cared for by five kinds of mothers.
First, the mother who tended his body.
Second, the mother who cleansed him.
Third, the wet nurse.
Fourth, the auspicious mother.
Fifth, the playful mother.
This child, due to his virtuous power, grew up quickly.
He was then taught writing, arithmetic, and seals.
He excelled at knowing the prices and values of various goods.
This king's settlement was a gathering place for merchants.
At that time, people from all directions came to the settlement.
They asked, saying.
Who here is virtuous and can be entrusted with words to show me profit and harm?
The people pointed out Shāmén Yì'ěr.
These merchants then went to him.
He received them as host.
These merchants saw his great power.
They thought thus.
If he becomes the Sàbó and leads many people to sea, they will surely return safely.
The people said.
Shāmén Yì'ěr.
Why do you not enter the great sea?
He replied.
What would I do entering the great sea?
There are many terrors within it.
Of hundreds and thousands who go, only one returns.
These merchants urged and encouraged him, saying.
What kind of person relies on others for survival?
Shāmén Yì'ěr, believing and accepting, desired to go.
He went to his parents to bid farewell, wishing to enter the sea.
At that time, his parents described various frightening things, hoping to make him change his mind and restrain him to stay.
At that time, he did not follow his parents' words.
His parents told the nobles to help them keep Yì'ěr.
At that time, the great officials, elders, and householders all helped to keep him.
He ultimately did not comply.
His parents, knowing his resolve was firm, then allowed him to go.
Thereupon, riding an elephant and shaking bells, he announced throughout the settlement, saying.
Shāmén Yì'ěr wishes to enter the great sea.
I will be the Sàbó; who wishes to go together?
Due to this man's virtue, five hundred merchants all gladly followed.
They prepared the ship, launched it, and cut one rope each day.
On the seventh day, they got the Īlè wind and cut the seventh rope.
The ship sped faster than an arrow, straight to the treasure isle.
He told the merchants, saying.
Take treasures to fill the ship, but do not make it too heavy.
They got the Īlè wind, and at that time the ship departed, faster than an arrow.
Returning to Jambudvīpa, heading toward the Sàbó king's settlement.
There were two routes.
Shāmén Yì'ěr said to the merchants.
Which route do you wish to take?
The people all said.
The land route is good.
They stayed overnight in an empty wilderness.
He said to the merchants.
I have heard that bandits come to rob merchants.
If they first kill the Sàbó.
Then the merchants will be unable to accomplish anything.
If they do not kill the Sàbó.
Then with the power of money and goods, or one's own strength.
Or with the strength of others, they can surely capture the bandits.
I will stay elsewhere.
When leaving, call me.
The people said yes.
Yì'ěr drove the donkey to stay elsewhere.
These merchants departed at midnight.
Each person woke the other, but ultimately did not call Yì'ěr.
Later that night, there was a great wind and rain.
Yì'ěr woke and called, but no one answered.
Immediately he galloped after them; the road had much sand and soil.
Wind and rain flowed and spread; he looked up and the donkey sniffed the tracks and went forward.
Yì'ěr, extremely hungry, went forward and saw a city.
Thinking of obtaining food, he stood at the city gate.
Following his thoughts, he cried out without thinking.
Food, food.
At that time, countless hundreds of thousands of hungry ghosts came out.
All said.
What food? Who gives it? Yì'ěr said.
No food.
I am traveling, extremely hungry, thinking of obtaining food.
Because of this, I uttered these words; I have no food.
The hungry ghosts said.
This is the city of hungry ghosts.
For hundreds of thousands of years, today we finally hear the cry for food.
We did not give alms.
Due to much miserliness and stinginess, we fell into the realm of hungry ghosts.
Where do you wish to go?
Yì'ěr said.
I wish to go to the Sàbó king's settlement.
The ghosts said.
Take this road.
Thereupon, going forward, he again saw a city.
Following his thoughts, he cried for water; the situation was as before.
Going forward not long after, he again saw a tree.
Named Bōluó.
At night, he stayed beneath it.
Shaking the tree, leaves fell; the fine ones he ate himself, the coarse ones he gave to the donkey.
Thus, as dusk fell.
Immediately a bed appeared, with a man and woman.
Their appearance handsome, wearing heavenly jeweled crowns, amusing each other.
He thought thus.
I should not be like this, watching them.
Private matters.
At that time, night passed and day came.
Immediately the bed vanished, and dogs came to devour this man's flesh until only bones remained.
Yì'ěr thought, saying.
What deeds did this person do previously to now receive this retribution?
Good at night, evil by day.
I will wait and ask him.
When night came again, there was a fine bed.
The man and woman amused themselves.
He then went and asked him.
The man said.
Do you know in Āshīmójiā Āpándì, in the Sàbó king's settlement, a certain butcher?
There is the elder Jiāzhānyán.
He often comes to my house.
I constantly provided him with food, drink, clothing, and medicine.
He often told me, saying.
Do not do evil deeds; later you will receive great suffering.
I then replied, saying.
Since past generations, this has been my livelihood.
If I do not do it now, how can I survive?
Zhānyán again said.
When you do this evil, is it more by day or by night?
I said more by day.
He then told me, saying.
You can receive the five precepts at night to obtain a little good.
I then accepted them from him.
Now I receive this retribution.
Going forward not long after, he again saw two trees.
Named Bōluó.
Staying beneath them to rest, he ate leaves as before.
A man and woman came by day to amuse themselves.
At dusk, the bed and woman both vanished.
A centipede came out and devoured this man's flesh.
Until only bones remained.
Yì'ěr asked, saying.
What deeds did you do to now receive this retribution?
The man said.
In the country of Āshīmójiā Āpándì.
In the Sàbó king's settlement.
A certain man committed adultery with another's wife.
There is the elder Jiāzhānyán who comes to my house.
He taught me, saying.
Do not do evil deeds; later you will receive bitter retribution.
I replied, saying.
I cannot restrain myself; what can be done?
He again said to me.
In this matter, when do you do it more?
I said more at night.
Jiāzhānyán then told me, saying.
Receive the five precepts by day to obtain a little good.
I followed his words, therefore I receive this retribution.
Again he saw a grove with a pond of clear, pure water.
Yì'ěr bathed in it and watered the donkey.
By this pond was a hall, adorned with various treasures.
Yì'ěr looked up.
He then thought thus.
I am dying of hunger and thirst; where should I go?
Immediately he went up to the hall.
He recited a Buddhist verse.
He saw a woman sitting on an ivory bed.
Two hungry ghosts were tied to the bedposts.
This woman recognized Yì’ěr.
She then greeted him, saying,
“Monk Yì’ěr, was your journey not exhausting? Are you not thirsty or hungry?”
Yì’ěr replied,
“Noble lady, please give me some food.”
The woman said, “I will share with you,
but do not give any to these two hungry ghosts.”
The woman then gave him water to wash his hands and provided him with food.
To let Yì’ěr understand this karmic cause, the woman briefly stepped outside the hall.
At that moment, the two hungry ghosts stretched out their hands and said,
“Give me a mouthful,”
“Give me half a mouthful.”
“My stomach is so hungry it feels like it’s burning.”
Yì’ěr, being generous, gave each of them a mouthful.
The food turned into pus and blood; they swallowed much of it but then vomited it out, filling the place with a foul stench.
The woman said,
“I told you not to give them any.
Why did you give it to them?”
Yì’ěr said,
“Sister,
I did not know, so I gave it to them.”
At that time, another woman came and said,
“Noble lady,
give me some food.”
The woman said,
“Eat your usual food.”
As soon as she said this,
three strange cauldrons appeared, with boiling water and fire.
This woman took off her clothes and entered the cauldron; her skin and flesh completely rotted away,
leaving only her bones. A cold wind blew, and she emerged from the cauldron, alive again.
She put on her clothes and ate her own rotten flesh.
After eating, she left.
Yet another woman came and said,
“Noble one,
give me some food.”
The woman said,
“Eat your usual food.”
As soon as she said this,
the woman turned into a black goat and ate grass.
Yì’ěr asked the woman,
“What is all this?”
The woman said,
“Do you know the settlement of King Sàbó in the country of Āshīmójiā Āpándì?”
Yì’ěr said he did.
“The ghost tied to the bedpost near my head
is my husband, a certain householder.
The one tied to the bedpost near my feet
is my son.
There was an elder, Kāzhāyán, who used to come to my house
and receive my offerings of food, clothing, medicine, and other necessities.
These two became angry with me, saying,
‘We work hard to earn a living,
yet you give it all away to others, exhausting yourself for nothing.’
Because of their stinginess and unwillingness to give alms, they fell into the realm of hungry ghosts.
Due to their evil speech, the food given to them turns into pus and blood.”
Yì’ěr asked,
“Why does that woman eat her own flesh?”
The woman said,
“She is my daughter-in-law.
I gave her things to store,
but she either ate them herself or gave them to others.
When I asked about them,
she replied,
‘I did not eat them, nor did I give them to anyone.’
She said, ‘If I ate them myself or gave them to others,
may I eat my own flesh in the future.’ That is why she now eats her own flesh.”
“The second woman is my maid.
I had her pound grain and grind flour,
but she either ate it herself or gave it to others.
When I asked her, she said,
‘I did not eat it myself, nor did I give it to anyone.’
She said, ‘If I ate it myself or gave it to others, may I be reborn as a goat eating grass.’
Because of this karmic cause, she is now a black goat eating grass.”
Yì’ěr asked,
“What deeds have you done?”
The woman said,
“I committed minor offenses, so I was reborn here.
But I will not stay here long; I will be reborn in the Heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings.
Can you go to the settlement of King Sàbó for me
and tell my daughter:
‘I have seen your parents, brother’s wife, and maid.
Only your mother is receiving blessings,
while the others are suffering.’
Your mother, through me, tells you:
‘Do not commit evil deeds, or you will suffer greatly in future lives.’
If you do not believe your mother’s words,
there is a hidden treasure in a certain place, containing much wealth.
Take it and make merit for me,
making offerings to the monastic community and to Kāzhāyán.
Whatever remains, you may use to support yourself.’”
She asked Yì’ěr,
“Do you wish to go?”
He replied, “I do.”
The woman said,
“Close your eyes and sleep.”
In an instant, he arrived at the settlement of King Sàbó.
The merchants had arrived earlier.
People asked them,
“Have you seen Monk Yì’ěr?”
They replied,
“We lost him at sea.”
The entire settlement wept as if mourning their own parents.
Yì’ěr heard this and thought,
“If they see me now, it will surely cause a commotion. There is no need for me to return.”
He gradually made his way to the woman’s house.
After exchanging greetings,
he relayed her mother’s words to the daughter.
The daughter said,
“You foolish man,
you are insane!
My parents gave alms and performed meritorious deeds; they must have been reborn in heaven after death.
How could they be among hungry ghosts?”
Yì’ěr then said to the daughter,
“Your mother said,
‘There is a hidden treasure in a certain place, containing much wealth.
Have you retrieve it to make offerings.’”
The daughter, hearing this, opened the hidden treasure and obtained great wealth,
and thus came to believe.
Following her mother’s instructions,
she invited Kāzhāyán to expound the Dharma.
Right there on his seat, she attained the pure, undefiled Dharma-eye and gained fearlessness.
She bowed to Kāzhāyán and said,
“Venerable One,
I take refuge in the Three Jewels and become a lay follower.
I wish to renounce the household life in this excellent Dharma and receive full ordination.”
Kāzhāyán said,
“Have your parents given you permission to renounce?”
She replied, “Not yet.”
Kāzhāyán said,
“In our Dharma, without parental permission, one cannot renounce the household life and receive full ordination.”
She then returned home and bowed to her parents.
Previously, due to grief, they had both lost their eyesight.
Hearing that Yì’ěr had returned safely from the sea,
they wept tears of sorrow and joy, and their eyesight was restored.
After five or six days,
she said to her parents,
“Please allow me to renounce the household life.”
Her parents said,
“We wholeheartedly prayed and wished for you.
When we heard news of your death at sea, we grieved so much that we went blind.
Now that you have returned, our great joy has restored our sight.
It is as if you have been reborn to us.
If you heed our words, that will be your offering to us.
How much longer can we live?
If you can stay until the end of our lives
and not renounce, we will die without regret.”
Yì’ěr replied, “Agreed.”
In the past, there was an upāsaka (lay Buddhist).
He was residing in the Śrāvastī Kingdom.
His wife’s appearance was upright and beautiful, known throughout the country.
When friends wished to see her, he would never consent to show her.
Someone reported this to the king.
The king thought of wanting to see her but did not know how.
One minister advised, saying:
“This couple both uphold the Five Precepts and support Daoist priests, personally serving them.
Your Majesty could disguise yourself as a Daoist priest, take a bowl, and go to their door.
You will certainly get to see her.”
Following the minister’s words,
he temporarily changed his appearance and attire and secretly went to their home.
The wife, seeing the Daoist priest, bowed her head to the ground in respect.
After the king observed her, he returned and told his ministers,
“This woman is truly beautiful; she has entered my heart.
I do not know how to obtain her.”
The many ministers said,
“Although he is a resident alien, he should pay homage to the king.
His arrogance and refusal to come can be considered a crime.
Over a thousand li away from Śrāvastī City,
in a large pond, grow five-colored lotus flowers.
It is said there are three dangers:
vipers, ghosts, and fierce beasts.
Those sentenced to death should be sent to fetch the flowers.
They will invariably perish there.”
The king then summoned and asked him, saying,
“What kind of person are you?” He bowed twice and replied, “I am Your Majesty’s subject.”
The king said,
“Why have you not come?”
He replied,
“Due to my foolish ignorance, I did not realize I should.”
He acknowledged his offense.
The king said,
“I sentence you to go to the pond to fetch the flowers; you must return in seven days.
If you violate the deadline, I will severely punish you.”
Receiving the command, he took his leave and withdrew.
Returning home, he fully informed his wife.
The wife said to her husband,
“Your offense now is due to my beauty.
You understand the Buddha’s clear teachings: the three realms offer no refuge; only the precepts can be relied upon.
On your journey, keep the Three Jewels in mind, recite the Ten Virtues with your mouth, and do not forget them for a moment.
If you do not return, I will renounce the household life and take joy in the precepts, never remarrying.
She provided her husband with provisions.
Bidding farewell, he set out on the road. Halfway there,
a man-eating ghost asked,
“What kind of person are you?” He replied,
“I am a disciple of the Buddha.”
The ghost said,
“Those who commit crimes are sent to us.
They falsely claim to fetch flowers.
You, virtuous one, have truly committed a crime?”
“I have been slandered by evil people.”
He replied to the ghost,
“Human life is hard to obtain; it is entirely up to the great deity.”
The ghost said,
“You are a disciple of the Buddha and also without crime.
I will not harm you.
There are two more dangers; I fear you will not escape them. What should be done?”
The ghost further said,
“I will fetch the flowers on your behalf to save you.
May I attain immeasurable merit throughout the long night.
You, quickly wait here.” The ghost then left.
In a short while, he returned,
bringing five-colored beautiful flowers and giving them to the virtuous one.
The virtuous one, unable to lift them due to their weight,
the ghost then took the flowers and also supported the virtuous one.
In the time it takes to bend and stretch an arm, they arrived at the palace gate.
Bidding farewell, he departed.
The virtuous one approached the gate and announced himself.
The king was surprised at his speedy return.
He inquired fully about the whole story.
He truthfully recounted it himself.
The king was greatly astonished and ashamed, saying,
“Ghosts lack human righteousness and harm living beings.
Now one has aided a good person, while I have been unrighteous.
Not distinguishing good from evil, I am inferior to a ghost.
He then reproached himself for his fault, bowed his head to the ground, and took refuge.
Wishing to become a disciple,
he received and upheld the Five Precepts and widely practiced the Six Pāramitās.
The country achieved great peace.
The virtuous couple both increased their diligence,
attaining non-retrogression.
A hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
the king of a country served heavenly deities,
conducting great sacrifices using oxen, sheep, pigs, dogs, chickens, etc., one hundred of each.
All were made to be killed by kitchen workers.
At that time, a kitchen worker said,
“I have received the Buddha’s precepts and must not kill living beings.”
The kitchen supervisor was greatly angry and reported to the king to punish him.
The king said,
“Those who disobey the command shall die.”
The kitchen worker replied,
“I am a disciple of the Buddha, upholding the Five Precepts.
I would rather kill myself than violate the Buddha’s teaching by killing living beings.
If I obey the king’s command and commit killing,
after death I will fall into hell; only after the punishment ends will I emerge, and I will always have a short life.
If I die upholding the precepts,
I will be reborn in heaven immediately; heavenly blessings and happiness, all wishes will be naturally fulfilled.
Even if I were to die, transforming from this human body, I would receive a heavenly form.
For this reason, I would rather die than kill.”
The king said,
“I give you a seven-day period.
I will have elephants trample you to death.
If you do not die,
your words will be proven true.”
Seven days later, the king saw that this upāsaka’s body was like the Buddha’s body.
He drove five hundred elephants to go trample him to death.
The upāsaka, following the Buddha’s Dharma, raised his five fingers.
They transformed into five mountains.
Between each mountain, a lion emerged.
The elephants, seeing the lions, were terrified and prostrated on the ground.
It was as if the Buddha were present.
The king then believed in the Buddha.
He abolished the sacrifices,
and immediately received the Buddha’s Five Precepts from this man.
Officials and people, inside and outside, all also received the Dharma.
He thus became the state preceptor.
There was an upāsaka
who, together with many merchants, traveled far to conduct business.
They encountered cold weather and snow.
Traveling at night, he lost his companions and stayed in a stone chamber.
At that time, a mountain deity transformed into a female form
to test him, saying:
“White snow covers heaven and earth; birds and beasts are all hidden.
I alone have no one to rely on.
I only wish for your compassion and pity.”
The upāsaka covered his ears with both hands and said,
“Shameless, vile person, speaking such impure words.
May water wash away, fire burn away; I do not wish to see or hear you.
Having a wife, my heart does not desire,
how much less to commit illicit sexual conduct?
The pleasure of desire is shallow and thin; great suffering is deeply fearsome.”
The mountain deity, hearing this,
lifted him with both hands and delivered him to his companions.
An upāsaka married his daughter to a worldly man.
When sending off his daughter,
the parents wanted to make her abandon her precepts.
The daughter said,
“Why abandon the precepts?”
The parents said,
“According to custom, marrying a daughter to a worldly person
is like throwing gold into cow dung.
What use are the precepts then?”
The daughter said,
“It is like a person traveling far through a great empty wilderness with no people.
One should increase provisions and food.
Our family serves ghosts; I fear ghosts might take advantage of me.
I should increase my upholding of precepts to make my resolve firm.
Gold in cow dung,
after washing, can still be used.
How could it then be the same as cow dung?”
The parents were moved by her words.
They gave her a Buddha image.
The daughter placed it respectfully in a vessel.
Morning and evening, she bowed toward the vessel.
Her husband asked,
The wife replied,
“This is the Buddha; he can prevent the head from turning white and keep one’s complexion always good.”
The husband also made offerings.
Later, they were reborn together in heaven, not returning to the three wretched paths.
In the past, there was a pure-faith layman.
When he first received the precepts, his diligence was unmatched.
Later, as he aged and grew weak, he distanced himself from the virtuous community.
Dwelling alone in a mountain recess, his will further declined.
He neglected his fields and gardens, forgot the Buddha, and abandoned the Dharma.
He became an ordinary person again.
In that mountain, there was a Brahmin ascetic.
Thirsty, he sought a drink.
The farmer was busy with work and gave him nothing.
The Brahmin, bearing a grudge, thus left resentfully.
The Brahmin could raise the dead and also command ghosts and spirits.
He then summoned a killing ghost and commanded it, saying:
“That person insulted me; you go and kill him.”
In the mountain, there was an arhat who knew of this and went to the farmer’s home.
The farmer, seeing the śramaṇa, joyfully bowed his head to the ground.
He prepared a meal for him.
The śramaṇa said,
“From this evening onward, light a lamp early, diligently take the Three Refuges, recite the verse ‘Guard the mouth, restrain the mind.’
With compassionate thoughts for living beings, you can long be safe and secure.”
After the śramaṇa left, the master of the house followed the teaching.
Throughout the night, he mindfully recited the Buddha’s name and recited the precepts without ceasing.
The killing ghost arrived at dawn, waiting for a slight opportunity to kill him.
Observing his compassionate mind, it found no opening to kill him.
According to the law of ghosts and spirits, if one orders them to kill, and they are unable to kill,
but the intended victim possesses virtue that makes him unkillable,
by law, the one who ordered the killing should be killed instead.
The killing ghost then became angry and wanted to harm the Brahmin.
The arhat used his spiritual power to conceal him,
causing the ghost not to see him.
The farmer awakened to the Way.
The Brahmin’s life was spared.
The ghost thus avoided the sin of killing a living being.
The farmer, at that time, received the Three Refuges,
recited the Buddha’s name unremittingly,
and saved the lives of his entire household.
There was a lay devotee.
He upheld the precepts diligently and tirelessly.
There was a monk who had already cast off the heavy burden,
having forever ended birth and death and attained supernatural powers.
He was close friends with the lay devotee.
At that time, the lay devotee suddenly fell seriously ill.
Medicine could not cure him, and his wife was deeply sorrowful and distressed.
She said to her husband:
"We are husband and wife, yet you alone suffer.
How can I share your illness to make it lighter?
If you pass away, what will I rely on?
Our child will be orphaned—what support will they have?"
Hearing this, the husband felt even more attached and affectionate.
As his life was about to end, he died at that moment.
His spirit immediately returned and entered his wife's nose,
transforming into a worm.
The wife wept bitterly, unable to stop herself.
At that time, the monk went to see the wife.
He intended to advise and console her, urging her to abandon her grief and sorrow.
When the wife saw the monk coming, she became even more sorrowful and wept.
"What can I do, Venerable? My husband has already died."
Suddenly, the worm fell from her nasal mucus to the ground.
The wife, feeling ashamed, was about to step on it.
The monk said:
"Stop, stop! Do not kill it.
This is your husband transformed into this worm."
The wife said, "Venerable,
my husband revered the scriptures, upheld the precepts, and was diligent beyond compare.
Why, after his life ended, did he transform into this?"
The monk replied:
"The fault arose from attachment and affection, leading to rebirth as a worm."
The monk then preached the scriptures to the worm:
"You diligently revered the scriptures and upheld the precepts; your merit should have led to rebirth in heaven to see the Buddhas.
But because of thoughts of affection and attachment,
you fell into this worm's body.
You should feel ashamed."
Hearing this, the worm understood.
It then reproached itself.
Soon after, its life ended,
and it was reborn in heaven.
Once there was a man
who had only one son,
named Bó Jū Luó.
He was just seven years old
when his mother passed away, and his father took another wife.
The stepmother hated the son of the former wife and steamed buns in a steamer.
The child asked his stepmother for some.
The stepmother picked him up and placed him in the steamer,
covering it with a jar to make the child die.
But the child ate the buns in the steamer and did not die.
Later, she placed him on a hot iron plate.
He ate buns on the plate and suffered no harm.
Later, she went to the riverbank to wash clothes
and threw him into deep water, where he was swallowed by a fish.
After seven days,
the father invited monks to hold a great assembly.
He bought a fish, loaded it onto a cart, and brought it home.
When he was about to cut open the fish's belly,
the child said:
"Slowly, do not injure the child's head."
This child had previously received the precept of not killing,
and now he attained five kinds of non-death.
Once there were five brothers.
Their father taught them to uphold the precepts.
The eldest son alone refused to uphold them.
He took five coins to a fortune-teller to seek a divination.
The fortune-teller said:
"You may live to a hundred years old and attain great wealth and honor."
Then he said it was definitely bad,
and again said it was not good.
He predicted that after thirteen days,
you would die.
The man was greatly terrified and said:
"This is not something an ordinary worldly teacher can cure.
Only the Buddha can foresee the future.
He is nearby in the Qí Shé Jué Mountain.
I can go and ask him."
So he went to ask the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"You have a karmic debt from a past life, and your enemy is coming to take you.
If you wish to escape,
you must uphold the five precepts to be freed.
Return home, prepare more oil and candles, burn them, and pass the thirteen days.
Then receive the refuge and precepts, keep the lamps burning continuously,
and recite scriptures and verses day and night,
saying 'Námó Fó,'
taking refuge in the Buddha, and do not rest."
After thirteen days, he would be freed.
That night, two ghosts came to kill him together.
One ghost stayed a hundred paces away,
sending the other ghost to kill him.
Seeing the light of the lamps,
he only heard the sounds of "Námó Fó, taking refuge in the Buddha."
He dared not go forward and said to the other ghost:
"This person cannot be taken.
He only calls 'Námó Fó, taking refuge in the Buddha.'
I hate hearing this sound—it gives me a headache."
So the two ghosts held each other and left, never coming near him again.
From then on, he lived in peace and security.
Once in Jiā Luó Nài Country,
there was a Brahmin's son
named Zhí Chí.
He received the Buddha's precepts and did not violate them.
After a long time, Zhí Chí went to another country.
Seeing people kill, steal, and commit adultery, he became greedy and attached to such acts.
Seeing people's good and evil deeds, he would discuss and judge them.
Seeing people drink alcohol, he desired to join them.
He had no stability at any time.
He then thought to himself:
"I regret receiving the precepts. I should return them to the Buddha."
He went to the Buddha and said:
"Previously, I received the five precepts, which imposed many restrictions, preventing me from following my desires.
The Buddha's teachings are profound and not something an ordinary person like me can respectfully serve.
May I renounce them?"
The Buddha remained silent and did not respond.
Before his words had even finished,
from his mouth emerged natural ghosts and spirits.
One ghost held an iron mallet and struck Zhí Chí's head.
Another ghost stripped off his clothes and hooked his tongue.
A licentious female ghost cut his genitals with a knife.
A ghost poured molten copper into his mouth.
All around him were ghosts and spirits
competing to tear apart his flesh and blood
and devour it.
There was also a natural fire burning his body.
He could not seek life nor seek death.
The ghosts held him tightly, not allowing him to move.
The Buddha saw him and asked:
"How are you now, Zhí Chí?" He was speechless, unable to speak.
He only beat himself with his hands.
The Buddha used his majestic power to rescue the elder.
The ghost kings saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
and each stood to one side.
Then Zhí Chí regained consciousness.
He rose, kowtowed, and said to the Buddha:
"My body has five thieves
dragging me into the three evil paths.
Because of my desires, I committed sins and violated what I had received.
May the Buddha have compassion for me.
From now on, I will reform, cultivate for the future, and respectfully receive the precepts.
I will uphold the six monthly fasts and the three annual long fasts,
burn incense, scatter flowers, hang various banners and canopies,
and serve the Three Jewels, never daring to violate them again."
The Buddha said:
"What you say now is very good.
If you see with your own eyes, you create your own sins—they are not bestowed by heaven."
Once, a person did not believe in sin and merit.
He was already fifty years old.
He dreamed of a killing ghost coming to take him.
Waking in terror, he sought a master to interpret his dream.
The master performed a divination and said:
"There is a killing ghost determined to harm you within ten days.
If you wish to avert this,
from now on, within the next ten days,
receive the Buddha's five precepts, burn incense, light lamps, hang silk banners and canopies,
and have faith in the Three Jewels. Then you can avoid this death."
He followed this method, wholeheartedly placing his faith in it.
When the killing ghost arrived at his door and saw him performing meritorious deeds, it could not harm him.
The ghost then left.
Because of this, the person lived to a hundred years old
and was reborn in heaven after death.
Once there was a very wealthy family
with six family members and servants.
Their gold, silver, and treasures were beyond measure.
The Buddha and Ānán went begging in the streets.
When the Buddha arrived at their door,
the parents, sons, wives, and grandchildren
leaped for joy and invited the Buddha inside to sit.
They spread woolen carpets on the ground, and the eating utensils were all made of gold and silver.
The Buddha said:
"In a past life, during a time of famine,
this family was poor and destitute.
They only gathered vegetables to sustain themselves.
Just as they finished cooking a soup,
a monk came begging outside, and they saw the monk.
The parents said:
'I will share with him.'
The sons and grandchildren each shared their portions with him.
They urged their mother to eat.
All six of them, at the same time, resolved to fast for one day each.
They only regretted their family's poverty and lack of good offerings. Because of this merit, they were reborn in heaven and among humans,
always enjoying peace, security, and abundant wealth.
Because they made the same resolve,
they formed karmic connections life after life.
Now they meet again.
The parents, sons, and all family members, young and old, all received the five precepts at the same time.
After death, they were reborn in heaven, receiving immeasurable blessings.
Now, having encountered the Buddha, they all attained Arhatship."
Someone was walking on the road.
He saw a dead person by the roadside.
A ghost was whipping it with a staff.
The traveler asked,
"This person is already dead; why are you whipping him?"
The ghost replied,
"This was my former body.
While alive, he was unfilial to his parents and disloyal in serving his lord.
He did not revere the Three Jewels.
He did not follow his teacher's words.
Now he makes me follow my sins.
The pain is indescribable.
Out of anger, I whip him."
Walking a little further ahead,
he saw another dead person.
A heavenly being descended,
scattered flowers over the corpse, and caressed it with his hand.
The traveler asked,
"You appear to be a heavenly being.
Why are you caressing this dead person?"
He replied,
"This was my former body.
While alive, he was filial to his parents,
loyal and faithful in serving his lord,
revered the Three Jewels,
and accepted his teacher's teachings.
He enabled my spirit to be reborn in heaven.
All this is due to the grace of my former body.
Therefore, I have come to repay him."
Walking a little further ahead,
he saw another heavenly being.
His clothes were fresh, fine, proper, fragrant, and clean.
By the roadside, he was picking and eating sour jujubes.
The traveler asked,
"You appear to be a heavenly being.
Why are you eating sour jujubes?"
The heavenly being replied,
"While I was in the world, I was filial to my parents,
loyal and faithful in serving my lord, and revered the Three Jewels.
I performed various meritorious deeds.
Only, I did not enjoy offering food and drink to guests.
Now, as a heavenly being, I am constantly underfed.
That is why I eat sour jujubes."
The traveler saw these three transformations in one day.
He then returned to uphold the Five Precepts and cultivate the Ten Good Deeds.
He was filial to his parents and loyal and faithful in serving his lord.
He showed and told later generations that sin and blessing pursue people.
There was an upāsaka who formerly served non-Buddhist paths, weary of the hardships of their sacrifices.
He abandoned them, entered the Dharma, upheld the precepts diligently,
earnestly recited scriptures, was fond of giving alms and admonishing,
his mind was patient and forbearing, and he always had a compassionate heart.
He fell seriously ill and passed away; when he was about to die, he instructed his parents,
"If my illness proves fatal, do not bury me for seven days."
Suddenly, as if dead, his corpse was kept for eight days.
His relatives all said,
"We should quickly prepare for burial."
His parents said,
"He does not stink; we wish to keep him until ten days."
As they spoke these words, they saw his eyes open.
He could not yet move.
His parents were overjoyed and guarded him until ten days.
Then he sat up by himself and was able to speak well.
They asked where he had come from and all that he had seen.
He replied,
"Officers and soldiers came and took me to a great city.
In the city, there was a prison.
The prison was pitch black, with iron walls on all four sides.
The prison gates were all made of burning iron, glowing red.
People imprisoned there sat in fire,
burned through from top to bottom, with blue smoke rising.
Some had their flesh cut with knives and eaten.
The prison king asked me,
'What kind of person are you?
What crime have you committed to come here?
Here we punish the five heinous crimes: being unfilial to parents and disloyal in serving one's lord.'
I replied,
'In my youth, I was misled by evil people,
served non-Buddhist paths out of foolishness,
also drank alcohol, killed living beings, and sacrificed to heaven and earth.
Moreover, in the markets and neighborhoods, I took wealth and profit,
using false measures to enrich myself.
Later, I met a good teacher,
who led me into the Buddha's path.
I saw śramaṇa practitioners,
who gave me the Five Precepts to uphold and the Ten Good Deeds to practice.
From that time until today,
I have not committed evil again.
I beg Your Majesty to pity my ignorance.'
I then kowtowed.
The king immediately stood up, joined his palms, and said to me,
'Enough, enough.
A pure-faith person should not be treated like this.'
He then gave me a seat.
He called the officers and asked them,
'This is a disciple of the Supreme True One.
You all should attain liberation through such a person.
Only when his lifespan naturally ends
should he die.
The soul is pursued after death.
If reborn in heaven, heavenly beings welcome him.
If reborn among humans, humans welcome him.
How could you bring this person here,
into this place of the five heinous crimes?'
The officer replied to the king,
'In the world, there are many such people.
They do not fear the king's law,
do not fear the four seasons,
are not bound by the five phases,
and roam the world recklessly, defying heaven, earth, ghosts, and spirits.
They cannot go unpunished.
There are teachers named śramaṇas.
They shave their heads and wear simple clothes,
yet are arrogant because of this.
They lead many disciples east, west, south, and north.
Moreover, they are even more extreme; they should be punished.'
The king said,
'Enough, enough. Those who wear the Dharma robes are honored and revered by people, feared and avoided by others.
The Śakra, Brahmā, sun, moon, and kings,
down to emperors, ministers, and common people,
all revere such people and gain immeasurable blessings.
Those who slight them seek suffering and sin for themselves.
Quickly check the records to see if his lifespan should have ended.'
The officer said,
'It should not have ended yet.
He still has twenty years remaining.
Because he previously committed crimes, we took him
to make his companions humble themselves a little.'
The king said,
'A Buddha's disciple who upholds precepts diligently is honored by heavenly beings.
The Buddha, with great compassion, saves and protects all flying and crawling creatures.
Heavenly beings, earth spirits, ghosts, dragons, and others all honor and revere him.
How can he be bound by kings, phases, four seasons, or five phases?'
The Buddha's grace is like the four seas, immeasurable and limitless.'
The officer said, 'Great King,
do you uphold the Buddha's precepts?'
The king said,
'Because I did not uphold the Buddha's teachings, I was punished and made the king of this prison.
If someone has entered the true Dharma
and later regrets it, returning to non-Buddhist paths,
even if he lives a thousand years, he will encounter nine untimely deaths.
If a precept-holding bhikṣu or any disciple
diligently practices the six pāramitās, cuts off the six defilements, and contemplates the Buddha's virtues, they are like a vast ocean, unsurpassable.'
The officer said,
'Truly, as the king says.
We did not distinguish true from false.
Quickly send him away, apologize, and let him go.'
I fell from a height, suddenly awoke,
and went with my parents to the Jetavana.
Reflecting and restraining myself,
I received and upheld the Five Precepts and cultivated the Ten Good Deeds.
In the country of Píniǔqián.
Many hold heretical views.
There is no Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha.
There was a woman.
Named Yōubōsīnà, who had some business that took her to the country of Shèwèi.
After finishing her business with King Pòsīnì.
She heard about the Buddha's virtues from some devout upāsakas.
Wishing to see the Buddha.
She went to the Jíhuán Grove.
Encountering the Buddha preaching the Five Precepts to the great assembly.
Yōubōsīnà requested to receive them from the Buddha.
And immediately obtained the Five Precepts.
The Buddha also gave her the Dharmapada to recite.
At midnight, while reciting the Dharmapada.
There was the heavenly king Vaiśravaṇa.
With several thousand yakṣas, intending to go south to Virūḍhaka.
Hearing the sound of scripture recitation, they all stopped to listen.
Praising, saying:
"Excellent, sister, you well expound the essentials of the Dharma."
Yōubōsīnà then asked:
"Who are you?
I only hear a voice from the sky, not seeing any form."
He replied:
"I am the ghost king Vaiśravaṇa.
For the sake of listening to the Dharma, I remain in the air."
She asked further:
"You are a deva, I am a human.
Why then do you address me as sister?"
He answered:
"The Buddha is the Dharma King and also the father of humans and devas.
Sharing the same flavor of the Dharma, hence I say sister."
At that time, Yōubōsīnà was greatly joyful.
She often sent people into the forest to gather firewood.
Later, at dawn, climbing a tree.
From afar, she saw Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and five hundred bhikṣus diligently practicing meditation and recitation in this forest.
The servant returned and reported to the mistress.
Yōubōsīnà, immeasurably joyful, took off two gold rings to reward the messenger.
The messenger further said:
"The World-Honored One has good words to send to the mistress."
Fully explaining the five kinds of giving.
She again removed her necklace and bestowed it upon him.
The messenger said:
"Quickly rise, wash your hands, and prepare food and drink.
I have already taken the liberty of conveying the mistress's words.
Inviting the two venerable ones and the five hundred disciples.
To come for a meal today."
She then dismissed the messenger along with the jewels.
Informed all her household and neighbors.
To set up offerings.
The venerable ones and the bhikṣus, donning their robes and holding their bowls, took their seats.
After paying respects, she personally served water and various foods.
The flavors and aromas were complete.
She said to Śāriputra:
"This house has a deity who is close and friendly with me.
When I make offerings, it tells me:
'This one is an arhat.
This one is a sage, this one ordinary.
This one upholds the precepts, this one violates them.
This one is wise, this one foolish.'"
She told Śāriputra:
"I have four sons and a husband.
All hold evil heretical views.
If I make offerings to the Three Jewels or give to the poor.
They become jealous and angry.
Yet I cultivate good deeds and give alms, never retreating, and have attained the fruit of Stream-enterer."
Śāriputra said:
"This is extremely rare."
"The World-Honored One this evening.
Will come to the Píqiánchí Forest.
Now returning to where they stay."
After the Sangha left.
She prepared what was needed and went to where the Buddha was.
Observing the places where the monks stayed overnight.
She saw a sick monk lying in a grass hut.
Asked what afflicted him and what he desired.
He replied:
"The four elements are imbalanced, causing great suffering.
The physician prescribed fresh meat broth." Sīnà said:
"Seek nothing else.
I will send it tomorrow."
The next day was the fifteenth, a national day of no killing.
She searched everywhere but could not obtain it.
So she sent the attendants away.
Bathed herself in a quiet room, cut flesh from her thigh.
Wrapped it in woolen cloth, mixed it with various herbs.
Cooked it into a broth and sent it to the sick bhikṣu.
After the bhikṣu ate it, his illness was immediately cured.
Her husband soon returned and saw his wife's complexion changed.
He then asked:
"Why are you so haggard?"
She replied:
"I am ill."
He immediately summoned a physician who could not diagnose it.
Pressing the household servants, they told him everything.
The husband went to the streets and loudly cried out:
"The Śākya monks eat human flesh like King Jùnzú!"
The Buddha therefore established a rule:
"All bhikṣus.
Should not eat any impure meat."
The upāsikā said:
"Because of me, meat-eating was prohibited."
She then said to her husband:
"If you can invite the Buddha and the Sangha here for a meal, that would be excellent.
If you cannot, I will give up my life."
For his wife's sake, the husband went into the forest to invite the Buddha.
The next day, for the meal offering.
The Buddha and the assembly of monks took their seats.
Asked where Sīnà was.
He replied she was ill.
The Buddha said: "Summon her."
The husband said:
"Your teacher calls for you."
She replied:
"The illness is too severe, I cannot rise."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Go and tell her to rise."
Ānanda went and conveyed the Buddha's call.
They carried her on a bed to the Buddha's presence.
Encountering the Buddha's light, her suffering illness was immediately cured, restored as before, and she rose to pay homage to the Buddha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to her, and she attained the fruit of Anāgāmin.
Her husband and household abandoned their heretical views.
Received the Five Precepts and became disciples of the Buddha.
In the city of Wéiyélí.
There was a woman.
Named Āfánhélì.
Hearing the Buddha had come traveling, she was immeasurably joyful.
With five hundred women, she went to where the Buddha was.
