Hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, her mind opened in understanding.
Invited the Buddha for a meal.
At that time, in the city, there were also five hundred elders' sons.
Who also invited the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"I have already accepted Āfánhélì's invitation for tomorrow."
Then the elders' sons.
Said to Hélì:
"The supremely honored Buddha has come to transform our country.
We should offer the meal first.
You should postpone your offering."
The woman said:
"Do not use your powerful status to oppress a weak woman.
If you can grant me four wishes, I will yield to you.
First, that my mind remains steadfast in goodness.
Second, that my life remains secure and does not perish.
Third, that my wealth and possessions do not diminish.
Fourth, that the Buddha long abides in this country."
The elders said: "Well said.
You are now able to comprehend impermanence.
All these hopes and wishes are beyond our ability to fulfill.
We permit you to offer the meal to the Buddha first."
Among them was a youth ashamed to be after her.
Stubbornly persisted.
Then ordered the market officials to halt all trade.
Hélì sent people to seek various goods.
Could obtain nothing.
Yet the storehouse of provisions naturally became full.
Only lacking firewood and charcoal.
Used oil-soaked white woolen cloth as substitutes.
Also, the inner city gates were ordered shut, not allowing exit.
She entreated the Buddha.
Who then sent a parrot to announce the meal was ready.
The elders shot at it.
By the Buddha's spiritual power, the arrows turned into flowers.
It reached the Buddha's presence.
Flying and calling, it announced to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the Sangha.
As the Buddha's foot touched the city gate, heaven and earth shook.
The five hundred elders.
Āfánhélì and the women.
Seeing and hearing this, attained the Dharma-eye and received and upheld the Five Precepts.
In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was an elder named Sudatta.
He had a youngest daughter,
named Sūmàn.
Her face and head were most exquisite.
Her father cherished and loved her.
He took her to where the Buddha was.
When the girl saw the Buddha, her joy and excitement doubled.
She wished to obtain fine incense to anoint the Buddha's dwelling.
This girl had a bīngpóluò in her hand.
The Buddha asked the girl for it.
She then gave it to the Buddha.
He wrote the word 'incense' on it and returned it to her.
The girl and her father returned to the city to search and buy [incense],
and as the Buddha required, they brought it to the Jetavana.
She personally pounded and ground it.
She did this every day.
At that time, the king of the Takṣaśilā country
sent one of his sons as an envoy to Śrāvastī to travel widely and observe.
He also came to the monastery and saw the girl Sūmàn.
He then took her as his wife.
Later, she became pregnant and gave birth to ten eggs.
The eggs later opened, revealing ten boys.
Their forms and appearances were handsome and excellent, brave and strong beyond the ordinary.
However, they delighted in hunting.
Their mother taught them not to do so.
The sons said to their mother,
"Archery and hunting are the greatest joy."
The mother said, restraining them, thinking they would be disliked.
The mother further told them,
"It is because I love you all that I restrain you.
If I were to dislike you, I would never say such words.
The sin of killing leads to falling into hell.
For countless kalpas, how could one find liberation?"
The sons said to their mother,
"Did this come from your own mind, or did you hear it from another?"
The mother replied again,
"I heard it from the Buddha."
The sons again asked their mother,
"Who is the Buddha?
We earnestly wish you to explain fully."
The mother told her sons,
"The son of King Śuddhodana of Kapilavastu,
weary of old age, sickness, and death, left home to practice the path and attained the unsurpassed fruit.
His great body is sixteen feet tall; he possesses the three insights and six supernatural powers, his far-reaching vision encompassing all without exception."
The sons entreated their mother, asking to go see the Buddha.
The mother then permitted them.
They went to the Jetavana and paid homage to the Tathāgata.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to them.
All ten simultaneously attained the pure Dharma-eye.
They then requested to leave home.
The Buddha allowed them to follow the path.
Their beards and hair fell off by themselves, and the Dharma robes were upon their bodies.
Diligently pursuing the great task,
they all attained Arhatship, exhausting all suffering.
Ninety-one kalpas ago, there was the Buddha Vipaśyin.
After his parinirvāṇa, his relics were distributed and countless stūpas were erected.
At that time, there was one stūpa that was old and dilapidated, collapsing in ruin.
There was an old woman who repaired and restored it.
There were ten young men who happened to pass by and see it.
Joyfully, they assisted, and the task was completed.
They vowed to be mother and sons.
From that time onward, for ninety-one kalpas,
in the heavens and among humans, they were always born together, receiving blessings and happiness.
That old woman is now the girl Sūmàn.
Those ten young men at that time are now the ten Arhats.
The Buddha was in Śrāvastī, at the Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.
There was a bereaved mother who had lost a son.
Grieving, distressed, and confused, she embraced the corpse, weeping and wandering.
She was like a mad person.
She went out to the Jetavana.
Hearing that the Buddha was a great sage, revered by gods and humans,
who proclaimed the sutras and path, forgetting sorrow and removing afflictions,
the bereaved mother saw the Buddha, made obeisance, and knelt.
Wishing to release her bonds of sorrow.
The Buddha told the bereaved mother,
"Quickly enter the city, go through all the streets and alleys,
and if there is a household where no one has died, beg for fire and bring it back."
The bereaved mother searched but could not find one.
She returned empty-handed.
The Buddha told the bereaved mother,
"People in the world have four conditions that cannot long be preserved.
First, what is constant must become impermanent.
Second, wealth and honor must become poverty and lowliness.
Third, gatherings must end in separation.
Fourth, strength and health must end in death.
Why do you now [grieve so]?
Do not trouble yourself.
Why not practice extensive giving, uphold precepts, observe the six fasting days each month, and according to your ability, give to the orphaned and destitute?"
The bereaved mother said to the Buddha,
"I love my son to the marrow of my bones.
How could I begrudge my own body and life?"
At that time, the Buddha wished to transform her so she might gain awakening.
He immediately manifested four great pits of fire surrounding the bereaved mother.
The heat of the flames pressed upon her body, and she used her child as a shield.
The Buddha said to the bereaved mother,
"You yourself said your love for your child is deep, to the marrow of your bones.
You would rather lose your own life than let your child die.
Now the heat of the flames presses upon you, the pain is hard to bear.
Should you endure it yourself, or use your child as a shield?
The small fires of the human world are hardly worth mentioning.
The fires of hell burn with immeasurable agony.
Animals bear the suffering of stupidity.
Hungry ghosts suffer hunger and thirst.
Those who can benefit themselves should cultivate giving, uphold precepts, and practice forbearance.
Then they will not be born in hell or among hungry ghosts and the like.
They will receive the blessings of gods and humans, gradually approaching Nirvāṇa."
At that time, that bereaved mother inwardly reproached herself, growing weary of and averse to affection.
Right before the Buddha, she exhausted all defilements.
She became a Stream-enterer.
In India, there was a man.
He went to the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
His wife had borne two sons.
The eldest son was seven years old.
The younger son was still in arms.
The mother was again pregnant.
She was about to give birth.
According to Indian custom,
when women are near their month, they return to their parents' home.
At that time, this husband and wife rode together in one cart, taking their two sons,
heading to the city of Śrāvastī.
On the road, they let the ox graze.
At that time, a poisonous snake coiled around the ox's leg.
The ox then broke free from the yoke.
The husband went to fetch the ox; the snake then left the ox and killed the husband.
The wife saw this and was terrified, crying out.
The sun was about to set.
They were not far from home,
but separated by a river.
In the darkness, fearing bandits,
she abandoned the cart and took her two sons,
arriving at the riverbank.
She left the elder son by the water's edge,
and carrying the younger one, began to cross the river. Halfway across,
a wolf devoured her son, who cried out for his mother.
The mother heard his voice, turned to look, and saw it.
Startled and frightened, unconsciously she dropped the child she was holding into the river.
It drifted away with the current.
The mother became even more anguished, confused, and lost her senses.
Stumbling in the water, she miscarried the child she was carrying.
She then crossed the river and asked a traveler on the road,
"Are my parents at home safe and well?"
The answer was,
"Yesterday there was a fire; they were all burned to death."
She asked another traveler,
"Have you heard if my husband's family, my in-laws, are safe and well?"
The answer was,
"They encountered bandits; your in-laws were both killed."
Grief-stricken, distressed, and bewildered, she could not tell east from west.
Naked, she ran madly.
Travelers who saw her found it strange.
They thought she had a demonic illness.
She ran and saw the Buddha.
The Buddha was holding a great assembly, preaching the Dharma.
When the woman saw the Buddha, her mind immediately became settled.
She was no longer sorrowful or anxious.
Looking at herself naked, she felt ashamed and prostrated on the ground.
The Buddha called Ānanda to fetch a robe and give it to her.
The woman put on the robe and paid homage.
The Buddha then preached a sutra, revealing to her karma and its results.
She then aroused the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment.
She attained the stage of non-retrogression.
Her sorrow and anxiety dispersed like clouds clearing to reveal the sun.
She aroused the unsurpassed mind.
In the country of Pèishànshé.
There was a woman.
Named Tíwéi.
Of the Brahmin caste.
Her family was very wealthy, but she had lost her husband and had no sons.
She lived in lonely widowhood, with no one to rely on.
According to Brahmin law,
if one is dissatisfied, one may burn oneself alive.
Various Brahmins came to instruct and persuade her,
urging her to wish for rebirth in the heaven of Nàluóyán.
She invited one hundred Brahmins,
arranged a great assembly, and after the meal,
each was given a milch cow.
Along with their calves, and all the possessions in her household,
all her belongings,
she gave to the five hundred Brahmins.
By the banks of the Héng River, she piled up firewood to burn herself.
The Brahmins would chant blessings for her,
saying, "May all your grave and minor sins be extinguished at once.
In future lives, may your six kinds of relatives and dependents have immeasurable lifespans and endless joy."
Tíwéi followed their advice.
She then gathered firewood,
intending to burn herself.
In the country, there was a śramaṇa named Bōdǐpó.
Diligent in practice, upholding precepts, widely learned, and wise.
He always taught the world with a compassionate heart,
urging people to turn from wrong to right, abandon evil, and cultivate goodness.
He went and asked Tíwéi, "What is the firewood for?"
She replied,
"I wish to burn myself to eliminate calamities and sins."
Biàncái said,
"The sins of past lives follow the spirit,
not the body.
Burning oneself in vain—how can that eliminate sin? Misfortune arises from the mind.
If the mind thinks good thoughts, the retribution will be good.
If the mind thinks evil thoughts, the retribution will be evil.
The remaining retributions are likewise.
How can one, in the midst of suffering,
seek to eliminate sins and hope for good retribution?
Fortunately, you need not do this; it is unreasonable.
It is like a sick person tormented by pain,
who is then scolded and beaten by a wicked person.
At that time, would this sick person have a good mind, free from anger and distress?"
Tíwéi said,
"Only anger and distress would arise."
Biàncái said,
"You are like this now.
Due to sins from past lives, if you burn yourself now,
when fierce flames arise, your body will be scorched and charred, but before your breath ceases,
because your mind is not yet destroyed,
at that time, your body and mind will be boiled.
Since your consciousness has not yet departed, you will suffer torment, distress, and mental anguish.
After dying from this, you will be born in hell,
where suffering is hundreds of millions of times more intense.
It is also like an ox weary of pulling a cart,
wishing the cart to break. If the front cart breaks, the rear cart still bears the yoke.
If your sinful karma is not exhausted, even if you burn and destroy
hundreds of millions of bodies, the causes and conditions of sinful karma will continue uninterrupted.
It is like in Avīci hell, where one dies eighty thousand times and is reborn eighty thousand times in a single day.
Only after passing through a kalpa will the sin be exhausted.
How much less can you, by burning yourself once, hope to eliminate sin?"
She asked,
"I wish to hear the method for eliminating sin."
Biàncái replied,
"The mind that previously did evil is like clouds covering the moon.
The mind that later gives rise to goodness is like a torch dispelling darkness.
The source of arising sins lies in the actions of body, speech, and mind.
Now you should wholeheartedly and sincerely repent, turn from wrong to right.
Through successive lives, until you attain Buddhahood."
Biàncái taught her the ten good precepts.
Tíwéi rejoiced.
She prepared various foods and treasures,
and invited him to stay and teach.
Biàncái said,
"You have received the ten good dharmas; you are now a vessel for the Dharma.
Moreover, by teaching others, you will repay the kindness.
You have already been saved.
It is not fitting for me to stay.
I must go elsewhere to teach."
He accepted none of the offerings.
And so he departed.
There was a woman.
Pregnant for several months,
she saw the Buddha and the monks.
She vowed, "May the child I bear later leave home and become a śramaṇa."
After giving birth, her love and attachment grew strong, and she could not fulfill her earlier wish.
When the child was seven years old, she suddenly remembered her vow and prepared food for two and three monastic robes.
Taking a water bottle and leading her child, she went to where the Buddha was.
She said to the Buddha,
"Please have pity on my child and let him become a śramaṇa.
May he later attain the Way and have a form like the Buddha."
The Buddha immediately consented.
The mother poured water from the bottle to wash her child.
Instantly, nine dragons emerged from the bottle,
spouting water to bathe the child.
After bathing, the remaining water scattered on the child's head.
Above his head, it transformed into a canopy of flowers,
a jeweled curtain interwoven,
and a lion throne with various Buddhas upon it.
The Buddha smiled at that time.
Emitting five-colored light that illuminated ten billion lands,
it circled back around the Buddha's body and entered the child's crown.
The mother then stepped forward and offered food to the Buddha and fed her child.
The child aroused the mind of supreme, impartial enlightenment.
Ten billion Buddha lands shook in six ways.
All the Buddhas in those lands spontaneously appeared.
The Buddha, with the mother's portion of food, satisfied that many.
The Buddha and all the bhikṣus were equally satiated.
Yet the food remained as before.
The mother rejoiced greatly.
She and various devas attained the stage of non-retrogression.
At that time, the child's hair fell out, and he became a śramaṇa.
He stood firm in non-retrogression.
That was my former self.
The Buddha was staying at the Jetavana monastery.
King Pòsīnì offered alms to the Buddha and the great assembly of followers.
The Jetavana measured one hundred and sixty li in length and breadth.
King Pòsīnì lit lamps everywhere, and the people vied to see.
A poor woman named Nántuó had no house to live in.
Asking passersby, she learned
that King Pòsīnì had used a thousand hu of oil to light lamps for the Buddha.
Nántuó reproached herself,
"Why am I alone so poor?"
She then entered the streets,
begging from house to house, obtaining a little mixed rice.
She thought to herself,
"I will sell this to get money for lamp oil."
She sold it for one coin and went to an oil seller.
The oil seller asked the woman, "With one coin's worth of oil, what merit do you seek?"
Nántuó replied,
"I wish to light a lamp for the Buddha."
Hearing this,
the oil seller, sharing her joy, gave her a lamp's worth of oil.
He gave it to her.
The poor woman joyfully received it and went to the Jetavana.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"There is a great elder who has aroused supreme merit.
He cannot come himself; open the gate and let him approach."
King Pòsīnì, hearing the Buddha's words,
pondered to himself,
"I am the sovereign of the country of Shèwèi.
Who could surpass me in making offerings to the Way?
Why then does the Buddha
not praise me but instead speak of an elder?"
Shortly after, the poor woman arrived where the Buddha was.
She lit the lamp she had brought before the Buddha.
She then made a great vow:
"For the sake of all beings,
I seek the Buddha's knowledge and insight.
May this light penetrate the ten directions,
and may the dark, evil paths all cease."
Having said this, she withdrew. The next morning,
the Venerable Mùlián inspected all the lamps.
The lamp lit by Nántuó alone still burned brightly.
Mùlián blew on it,
but could not extinguish it.
He then used his supernatural power, taking water from five Ganges rivers to pour on it, but still it did not go out.
He blew with the great wind of Suílán, but it could not be extinguished.
Exhausting his supernatural powers, he still could not put it out.
He felt fear in his heart.
The Buddha told Mùlián,
"The one who lit this lamp had a sincere and earnest heart.
Because of this, the lamp remains constantly bright.
Even if arhats like Shèlìfú and others, or pratyekabuddhas,
with all their supernatural transformations and merits, tried together to extinguish this lamp, they could not.
Even if the golden-winged king stirred the ocean waters,
or the lion king roared and charged to extinguish this lamp,
the lamp could not be extinguished."
At sunrise, the woman Nántuó
went herself to check the lamp she had lit the previous night.
The lamp was still not extinguished.
Its light was undiminished.
She was greatly delighted and bowed at the Buddha's feet.
The Buddha knew her mind sought supreme enlightenment.
He emitted five-colored light from his mouth.
Whenever the Buddha expounded the Dharma, for the three vehicles' practices, for śrāvakas, the light
entered from the crown.
For pratyekabuddhas, the light
entered from between the eyebrows.
For bodhisattvas, the light entered from the mouth.
The Buddha's great light rose to the Heaven of the Thirty-Three,
penetrating everywhere.
Then it returned,
circled the Buddha three times, and entered his mouth.
Then Ānanda rose and asked,
The Buddha said,
"Ānanda,
did you see the woman who lit the lamp last night?
This woman, after her life ends, due to this merit,
will transform from a woman's body and become a man.
For twenty kalpas thereafter, she will not fall into evil paths.
She will be born among the devas and as a golden-wheel-turning king.
After twenty kalpas,
she will attain Buddhahood,
named Sānmàntuó Yōuhē."
The Buddha was in the country of Shèwèi.
At that time, there was an elder’s daughter.
Her name was Shànxìn.
She was just fifteen years old.
She was compassionate and filial by nature.
Wise and broadly learned.
From a young age, she had always held a great aspiration.
She took no pleasure in worldly affairs.
Sitting alone, she reflected:
"All things are impermanent and must return to death.
Even a lifespan of ten thousand years will also end in death.
Heaven and earth will decay and perish, how much more so the human body.
Thinking that I must undergo such blame and retribution,
the pain and suffering are beyond words.
After death, the spirit will enter the evil paths.
The cruel poison and intense suffering I alone must bear.
From where did this originally arise?
Suddenly there is anger, fear, sorrow, and worry.
Or sometimes joy.
These are the affairs of impermanence.
I do not see from where they come,
nor to where they go.
These things come and go without cease or rest.
I think of my parents, my various family brothers, and relatives of the five kinds, inside and outside.
They do not know sin and merit, their greed and desire are insatiable.
I am fifteen and have been promised to another man.
My various family brothers have received food, wine, meat, and bolts of silk.
I think that my body must go and undergo hardship and difficulty.
Bound and fettered, I cannot be free.
What should I do?
Rather than wait for this birth, old age, and sickness to reach me,
today, while pure, I should arouse the supreme aspiration.
I should seek a peaceful, secure, and eternally joyful palace where I can delight myself.
It is not fitting to sink into the turbid mire, submerged in the three wretched paths.
Not seeing the light, forever accompanied by suffering."
Then she focused her mind and made a vow:
"I dedicate my body and life.
If there are spirits, if there are divine beings, know my sincere heart."
At that time, a heavenly deity appeared in the empty sky.
He said to Shànxìn: "If you wish to dedicate yourself, go to the peaceful, secure, and pure Dharma land in the West.
First, you should bow in worship to the ten directions.
With a compassionate mind and reverent intention, your thoughts will surely reach."
Having spoken, he vanished.
Then Shànxìn, leaping with joy,
bathed herself, burned incense, scattered flowers, and bowed with hands joined to the ten directions.
She reflected alone:
"For all people, there is a heavenly deity who speaks from the sky:
'You should turn your mind correctly toward the West.'
Recite this verse,
to praise Āmítuófó."
Shànxìn then turned toward the West.
As the deity had instructed,
heaven and earth greatly shook.
All those in distress and hardship were liberated.
Illnesses were cured, poison and pain were pacified, sorrow turned to joy.
The blind and deaf were healed, the mute could speak.
The unwholesome became wholesome, the faithless gained faith.
Humans and non-humans alike each attained their wishes.
Shànxìn burned incense, scattered flowers, and recited a verse:
"With a correct mind, close the eyes, count the breaths, and contemplate the affairs of the body."
Indra transformed into a handsome young man,
eighteen or nineteen years old,
holding gold in his hand, stood before Shànxìn.
He teased her with a verse.
Shànxìn, with a correct mind, replied with a proper verse,
admonishing the faults of men and women.
Indra, leaping with joy, joined his hands and praised her:
"What do you seek?
Your virtue is unparalleled in the world, vast and immeasurable.
Please tell me."
Then Shànxìn, hearing Indra's praise,
was filled with joyful faith, and the earth greatly shook.
She then spoke a verse:
"I wish to serve the Buddha's Dharma."
Indra was greatly delighted.
He then transformed and vanished.
Shànxìn burned incense and dedicated herself to all Buddhas.
The Buddha, together with the great assembly, flew and arrived at Shànxìn's home.
Her parents and brothers saw the Buddha flying through the air,
and all were overjoyed.
Shànxìn approached, bowed, and circumambulated the Buddha a hundred times.
The Buddha then smiled, and countless rays of light emerged.
He spoke the precepts to her.
The light circled her body a hundred times and re-entered through the crown of her head.
He then conferred the twenty-four precepts.
The Buddha said:
"These are my upāsikā's high practice, the three eights making twenty-four precepts."
Shànxìn, joyful, attained the seventh stage.
Then, before the Buddha, she transformed her body into that of a man.
Her parents and brothers all received the five precepts.
The Buddha said to Wénshū:
"Do you wish to hear about the establishment of worldly, external paths?
In a past age, there was a Buddha,
named Jūsūntuóbátuóluó,
who appeared in the world.
At that time, in that world, there were no gravels,
no names of external paths.
There was only the Great Vehicle.
After the Buddha's nirvana, when the Dharma was about to perish,
there was a forest-dwelling bhikṣu,
named Fóhuì.
A virtuous person offered him a priceless robe.
The bhikṣu accepted it.
Some hunters conceived a thieving mind.
At night, they took the bhikṣu to a deep mountain,
destroyed his body, stripped him naked, hung him by the neck, and tied him to a tree.
Then a flower-gathering Brahmin came to the forest dwelling.
Seeing a tiger, terrified, he fled toward the mountain.
He saw that bhikṣu,
body destroyed, naked, hung by the neck and tied to a tree.
He exclaimed in astonishment:
"The śramaṇa formerly wore a kasaya robe,
but now he is naked.
He must know that the kasaya is not the cause of liberation.
Hanging himself and practicing austerities is the true way of learning the path."
"Would that person abandon wholesome dharmas?
One should clearly know
that this is the cause of the path of liberation, destroying the true Dharma."
He then discarded his clothes, pulled out his hair, and became a naked śramaṇa.
The naked external path arose from this.
At that time, the bhikṣu freed himself from the bonds.
He then took tree bark,
stained it with red ochre,
to cover himself.
He made a grass whisk to drive away mosquitoes.
Another flower-gathering Brahmin saw him.
He thought:
"This bhikṣu has abandoned his former fine robe,
wears such clothes,
holds such a whisk.
Would he abandon wholesome dharmas?
One should clearly know
that this is the path of liberation."
He then learned this method.
The出家婆羅門出家 Brahmin path arose from this.
At that time, that bhikṣu entered the water to bathe in the evening.
While washing a sore on his head,
he took a water plant to cover the sore.
He took a worn-out cloth discarded by cowherds to cover his body.
Then a certain person saw him and thought:
"This bhikṣu formerly wore a kasaya,
but now he has completely abandoned it.
He must know that the kasaya is not the cause of liberation.
Therefore, he lets his hair hang loose, wears ragged clothes, bathes three times day and night, and practices austerities.
Would he abandon wholesome dharmas?
One should clearly know
that this is the path of liberation."
He then learned that method.
The苦行婆羅門苦行 Brahmin path arose from this.
After bathing, the bhikṣu's body had many sores; flies and bees bit and ate at them.
He then smeared white ash on the sores everywhere.
He covered his body with water plants.
Someone who saw him said:
"This is the path," and learned that method.
The灰塗婆羅門 ash-smeared Brahmin path arose from this.
The bhikṣu lit a fire to cauterize his sores.
The sores became more painful; he could not bear it.
He threw himself off a cliff to kill himself.
Someone who saw him said:
"This bhikṣu formerly wore fine clothes,
but now he is like this.
Would he abandon wholesome dharmas?
He correctly knew that throwing himself off a cliff is the path of liberation."
The投巖事火 cliff-jumping and fire-worship paths arose from this.
Thus, successively, ninety-six kinds
all arose because of this bhikṣu's various forms and appearances,
giving rise to all sorts of false thoughts.
Each generated their own views.
It is like a country where people look at one another
and give rise to coarse thoughts.
Once coarse thoughts arise,
they kill one another.
The arising of external paths' differences is also like this.
In the past, the six teachers were in the world.
Greedy for offerings, they each claimed to be supreme.
Hearing that the Buddha had appeared in the world, with divine virtues surpassing others,
they gathered and made a pact together.
"We should unite our minds and deliberate together.
If our words do not contradict each other, we can then overcome him."
They immediately sent one person to observe the Tathāgata,
to see if he was like other people or not.
He gazed without growing weary.
Returning, he reported to the six teachers:
"The appearance of Gautama is rare in the world; his majestic divine radiance surpasses the sun and moon.
From what I have seen, there is nothing to compare it to."
The six men thought again:
"That man comes from a royal lineage,
so it is natural that he is handsome.
What is there to be surprised about?
Now let us send another person to observe him—
whether he is composed or agitated."
He returned and told the six teachers:
"Gautama among the multitude is like the king among beasts,
fearless and unperturbed."
The six men thought again:
"Foolish people are easily impressed by new things.
They are captivated by his radiance.
This is a common occurrence.
What is there to be surprised about?
He came from a royal palace with sixty thousand court ladies, day and night amusing himself, without having studied under a teacher.
Send someone again to listen—
does he have any principles, or is he like an ordinary person?"
They immediately sent a wise and discerning person to observe what the Buddha said.
He returned and reported to the six men:
"What he expounds reaches ancient times and knows the present.
He foresees the limitless past and beholds the endless future.
He judges meanings and analyzes principles without redundancy."
The six teachers again thought:
"There are many people in the world with quick and clever speech that pleases people's hearts.
Yet the principles are not there and cannot be investigated."
They sent someone again to observe:
"When the multitude hears his teachings, do they listen quietly and accept, or are they confused?"
He returned and reported to the six teachers:
"What Gautama reveals is as sweet as nectar.
The multitude thirsts for it and listens without growing weary."
The six men thought again:
"When people gather at first, they will eventually disperse after a long time.
Send another superior person to observe—
are his principles profound or shallow?"
He returned and reported to the six teachers:
"What Gautama reveals is like the sea without shores.
What we have seen is like water in a cow's hoofprint.
Now I, this one person,
wish to go to him and seek to become his disciple."
The messengers, one after another, went together to where the Tathāgata was.
There were also countless beings competing to arrive.
The Buddha spoke a verse:
The disciples of the six teachers, hearing the Buddha speak the verse,
those with steadfast minds immediately sought the Path.
Those with hesitant minds returned and reported to their teachers, saying:
"The sole honored one of the three realms, ruling over the ten directions,
truly has no equal.
We should each disperse and seek our own peace."
There was a king named Duōfú,
and a crown prince named Zēngfú.
The king served the six teachers,
while the son served the Buddha's Path.
What they followed was different.
At that time, there were no śramaṇas in the world,
only a layperson as the head teacher.
Five hundred followers of other paths envied the teacher's reputation and virtue.
They immediately said to the king:
"Having two doctrines in the state causes people to not be single-minded.
We wish to have the teacher of the Buddha's Path and us each display extraordinary virtues.
Whichever is inferior shall be enslaved."
The king agreed to this.
The followers of other paths set a date with this teacher,
making an agreement
to test their skills before the king, each acknowledging the other.
The Brahmins were all skilled in archery and charioteering.
They went into the mountains.
Five hundred people each shot a deer,
all piercing the left eye, displaying their skills.
The virtuous one also entered the mountains, concentrating his thoughts on the Buddha, seeking divine assistance to manifest the great Path.
Immediately, a five-colored fawn suddenly emerged from the ground.
He joyfully took it back.
The followers of other paths learned of this.
Waiting for the virtuous one to go out,
they went to his home.
Deceitfully, they said to his wife:
"Your husband wishes to leave home and become a practitioner.
It is only because of this deer that your household will be ruined."
The wife heard this and became angry.
She gave the deer to them.
When the virtuous one returned, he did not see the deer.
He asked his wife:
"That inauspicious thing is now lost."
The husband was very worried.
He returned to the mountains and sincerely repented.
Immediately, a bright moon-like divine pearl suddenly emerged from the ground.
He took this pearl to present to the Brahmins.
Arriving at their door, he went to sell this extraordinary object.
The Brahmin's wife said:
"Our household also has a rare object; we can compare them."
She brought out the fawn.
The virtuous one then reported to the king:
"I was entrusted with this fawn.
You have now stolen it; your crime is immeasurable."
The wife, ashamed, returned it.
When it came time for the test,
the Brahmins each presented dead deer, all wounded in the left eye, both filthy and foul-smelling.
The king was greatly disgusted.
The virtuous one came forward, leading the divine deer,
and presenting the bright pearl, he ascended the king's hall.
The two objects flew and frolicked, streaming like stars and flashing like lightning.
The entire palace marveled at them.
The five hundred Brahmins, knowing their skills could not compete,
were immediately enslaved.
Their wives all became maidservants.
In Southern India, there was a debating teacher.
He bound his abdomen with a copper band,
and lit a fire on his head.
He came to Śrāvastī.
People at the time asked him:
"Why are you like this?"
He replied:
"I have so much wisdom that I fear my abdomen will split.
I light a fire to illuminate the darkness."
People at the time said:
"Foolish Brahmin,
the sun shines upon the world; why do you speak of darkness?"
He replied:
"You do not know.
There are two kinds of darkness:
one is without sun, moon, or torchlight;
the other is foolishness without the light of wisdom."
The people also said:
"You have not seen the bhikṣu Hēduō of the Śākya clan.
How dare you speak like this?"
"If I were to meet and speak with him, it would be like seeing the sun rise in the dark night."
The people in the city then summoned the bhikṣu Hēduō of the Śākya clan,
wanting them to debate.
When Hēduō heard this,
he was worried and entered the city.
On the way, he saw two rams fighting.
He immediately took it as an omen:
one ram is the Brahmin,
the other ram is me.
I am inferior.
He became even more worried.
Going forward, he again saw two bulls fighting.
He again thought:
one bull is the Brahmin,
the other bull is me.
Again, I am inferior.
He then reached the front gate.
Again, he saw two people wrestling.
He again thought:
again, I am inferior.
As he was about to enter the debating place,
he saw a person carrying a full water jar.
The water jar broke.
He again thought:
"I have seen many inauspicious signs.
I have no choice but to enter the house."
He saw the Brahmin,
and from his eyes and mouth, he knew he was inferior.
After sitting for a moment,
the people said:
"You may now debate."
He replied:
"I am not feeling well now.
I must wait until tomorrow." He then returned to his lodging.
In a past age,
there was a great kingdom
in the northern borderlands,
named Zhìhuàn.
The people of Zhìhuàn brought crows
to the country of Bōzhēlí.
In that country, there were no such crows,
nor any other marvelous birds of different kinds.
When the people saw the crows,
they rejoiced and leaped for joy,
making offerings and serving them with food, fruits, and melons.
And they spread the news.
Crows from distant places all gathered in countless numbers.
The entire country universally served and revered them without measure.
Later, at another time, a merchant brought peacocks from another country.
The multitude saw their extraordinary feathers and majestic, elegant gait, which they had never seen before.
Hearing their voices, their hearts leaped with joy.
They all abandoned the crows and loved the peacocks.
The offerings previously made to the crows were all given to the peacocks.
They revered and submitted to them.
All the crows vanished, and no one knew where they went.
At that time, a heavenly verse said:
Ānanda recited a verse:
"The peacock is my body.
The crows are the various external heterodox teachers.
The heavenly one is Ānanda."
In the past, in the kingdom of Shèwèi, there was a Brahmin teacher.
His name was Fùlánjiāyè.
He was followed by five hundred disciples.
The king and the people all served him.
When the Buddha first attained enlightenment,
he traveled with his disciples from Luóyuèqí to Shèwèi.
His majestic form was radiant, and his teachings were pure and beautiful.
The king, his palace, and all the people revered him.
Jiāyè, out of jealousy, sought to slander the World-Honored One.
He said to King Pòsīnì,
"We elders are the kingdom's former teachers,
while the ascetic Qútán
came later, seeking the Way, yet he possesses no divine power.
But the king has abandoned us. Now I wish to compete with the Buddha.
Whose virtue and teachings prevail, the king shall serve."
The king said, "Excellent."
The king informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Very well."
They set a date for seven days later to compete in transformations.
The king prepared a broad, level ground east of the city.
Two high platforms were erected.
The king, his ministers, and a great assembly gathered like clouds.
They wished to witness the two men compete in the Way.
Jiāyè and his disciples arrived first at the platform and climbed the ladder to ascend.
The divine king Bānshī,
seeing their falsehood and jealousy,
immediately raised a great wind,
overturning their seats and banners,
scattering sand and gravel like rain,
so that none could see.
The World-Honored One's high platform remained steadfast and unmoved.
The Buddha and the great assembly proceeded in orderly fashion.
Facing the high platform, they suddenly ascended.
All the monks sat silently in order.
The king and his ministers, with increased reverence, bowed and said,
"We pray that you will manifest your divine power to subdue false views,
and enable the people of the kingdom to clearly believe in the true and genuine."
The World-Honored One, from his seat, suddenly vanished,
then rose into the sky, radiating great light.
He disappeared in the east and appeared in the west, and likewise in all four directions.
His body emitted water and fire, alternating above and below.
He sat, lay, and moved through the air, performing twelve transformations.
He vanished from sight and returned to his seat.
Heavenly dragons, spirits, and ghosts offered flowers and incense in worship.
The sound of praise shook heaven and earth.
Fùlánjiāyè, knowing he had no power,
lowered his head in shame and fear, not daring to raise his eyes.
The Vajra-wielding guardian raised his vajra pestle,
and fire emerged from its tip, aimed at Jiāyè.
He asked, "Why do you not manifest transformations?"
Jiāyè, terrified, jumped down and fled.
His five hundred disciples scattered in panic.
The World-Honored One's majestic countenance showed neither joy nor sorrow.
He returned to the Jìyuán Garden.
The king and his ministers rejoiced and withdrew.
Thus, Jiāyè and his disciples, humiliated, departed.
On the road, they encountered an old laywoman,
named Móní.
She confronted them, saying,
"You foolish crowd, without self-reflection,
dared to compete with the Buddha in the arts of the Way.
Arrogant, foolish, deceitful, and shameless—
you should not show your faces in this world."
Jiāyè, ashamed before his disciples,
went to the riverbank and deceived them, saying,
"I will now throw myself into the water and surely be reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
If I do not return, then there is bliss."
His disciples waited, but he did not return.
They discussed among themselves,
"Our master must have ascended to heaven.
Why should we remain here?"
One by one, they threw themselves into the water, hoping to follow their master.
Unaware that their sins would drag them down, they all fell into hell.
Later, the king heard of this
and was greatly astonished. He went to the Buddha and said,
"Master Jiāyè and his disciples—what caused this?"
The Buddha told the king,
"Master Jiāyè and his disciples committed two grave sins:
First, their three poisons burned fiercely, yet they claimed to have attained the Way.
Second, they slandered the Tathāgata, desiring reverence for themselves.
For these two sins, they should fall into hell.
Their retribution hastened them, driving them into the river.
Their bodies died, their spirits departed, and they suffer immeasurably.
In the past, there were two monkey kings,
each ruling five hundred monkeys.
One king grew jealous
and sought to kill the other, planning to rule alone.
He went to fight him,
but was repeatedly defeated.
Ashamed, he retreated.
He came to the seashore, at a bend in the sea,
where there was a great accumulation of foam.
The wind had piled it up hundreds of feet high.
The foolish monkey king thought it was a snow mountain.
He said to his followers,
"I have long heard that in the sea there is a snow mountain,
where there is happiness and sweet fruits to enjoy freely.
Today I see it. I shall go first to see.
If it is truly joyful, I will not return.
If it is not joyful, I will return and tell you."
So he climbed a tree, leaped with all his strength,
and plunged into the foam, drowning in the sea's depths.
The others wondered why he did not emerge,
thinking it must be greatly joyful.
One by one, they jumped in, the whole group drowning to death.
The jealous monkey king was Fùlánjiāyè.
The group were the five hundred disciples of Fùlán today.
The ascetic Chǎntí was in a great forest,
cultivating patience and compassion.
At that time, King Jiālì brought his court ladies into the forest to play.
After they had eaten,
the king took a short nap.
The court ladies gathered flowers in the forest
and saw this ascetic.
They paid him respects and stood to one side.
The ascetic then explained compassion and patience to the court ladies.
His words were beautiful, and the listeners never tired.
They stayed a long time without leaving.
King Jiālì awoke and did not see the court ladies.
Drawing his sword, he followed their traces
and saw them before the ascetic.
Blinded by pride and jealousy, he glared and brandished his sword,
asking the ascetic,
"What are you doing?"
The ascetic replied,
"I am here cultivating patience and compassion."
The king said,
"I will test you now.
I shall cut off your ears, nose, hands, and feet with a sharp sword.
If you feel no anger, I will know you cultivate patience."
The ascetic said, "As you wish."
The king then drew his sword, cut off his ears and nose, and severed his hands and feet.
He asked,
"Is your mind disturbed?"
He replied,
"I cultivate compassion and patience; my mind is undisturbed."
The king said,
"You are alone here, without any power.
Though you say your mind is undisturbed, who will believe it?"
Then the ascetic made a vow,
"If I truly cultivate compassion and patience,
may my blood turn to milk."
Immediately, his blood turned to milk.
The king was greatly astonished and pleased,
and led the women away.
At that time, the dragon spirits of the forest, for this ascetic's sake, thundered and struck with lightning.
The king was poisoned and perished, never returning to his palace.
In the past, there was an ascetic
named Luówén, diligent and pure in practice.
Yet he lived at home, without observing brahmacarya.
Some said,
"Like that Luówén, he has pure conduct,
yet living at home, he is not fully pure."
Luówén wrote scriptures
that wind and rain could not destroy.
Living in the world, he cultivated brahmacarya,
like an Anāgāmin.
Surrounded by family at home,
is this not pure conduct?"
The realm of spiritual powers is inconceivable.
The Buddha was in Luóyuèzhī.
He was expounding the true Dharma.
The various Nirgranthas and others were all distressed and troubled in their hearts.
On Líyí Mountain, there were five hundred ascetics.
The Nirgranthas sent a messenger, saying:
"Here there is a Buddha,
who claims to have attained the Way and to be foremost in spiritual transformations.
He is not equal to us, yet he exalts himself.
We hope that you great masters
will condescend to come and assist us,
to debate the essential points of the Way and destroy his doctrine,
thus causing the fame and merit of you masters to become even more illustrious."
They replied, "Excellent!
We shall first send four men to go and challenge Jiātán."
The Nirgranthas proclaimed throughout the country:
"After seven days, four Buddhas will enter the country to deliver people."
When the day arrived,
the four men displayed their spiritual transformations.
They came from the sky, each entering from one side of the city.
The multitude saw this and believed them to be true Buddhas.
The Nirgranthas sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"You may come to debate the Way."
The Buddha said:
"I will go at mealtime."
The Nirgranthas rejoiced, saying:
"Jiātán is afraid he is no match;
he falsely does not come forward."
The crowd all thought so.
The Buddha caused fire to arise in the sky,
coming from the west.
The four men flew south, but the fire also came south.
Heat surrounded them on all sides, and the four men were terrified.
They fell prostrate on the ground.
The Buddha appeared in a cool place.
Immediately, seeking coolness, they came before the Buddha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to them.
They all became śramaṇas and attained the path of arhatship.
The Buddha entered the city.
The people in the city said:
"Just now there were four Buddhas in the empty sky."
The Buddha said:
and pointed to his left and right,
"These four arhats are they."
Like the ascetic Yùtuóluójiā,
who attained the five supernatural powers,
flew to the king's palace to eat.
The king's chief consort, according to the custom of that country,
bowed, touching his feet.
When the consort's hand touched him, he immediately lost his supernatural powers.
He asked the king for a chariot,
rode out, and returned to his original place.
Entering among the trees in the forest, he sought again the five supernatural powers.
With single-minded concentration, he was on the verge of attaining them,
but birds in the tree cried urgently, disturbing his mind.
He left the tree and went to the water's edge to seek concentration.
Again he heard the sound of fish fighting and stirring the water.
This man, unable to attain meditation,
immediately gave rise to anger.
"I shall kill all the fish and birds."
After a long time, this man, through contemplation, attained concentration.
He was reborn in the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception.
When his lifespan there ended,
he descended and was reborn as a flying fox,
killing many fish and birds,
committing immeasurable offenses and falling into the evil paths.
King Yōutuóyán,
leading his palace women and court ladies,
went to the Yùdúbōtuó mountain forest.
He dismissed the men and, purely with women, amused himself with the five pleasures.
The music was clear and wonderful, and they burned various fine incenses.
At that time, among the court ladies,
some danced naked.
At that time, five hundred ascetics were passing by that place.
When those ascetics saw the forms, heard the sounds, and smelled the fragrances, they immediately lost their supernatural powers.
Like wingless birds, they fell into that forest.
The king asked:
"Who are you?"
The ascetics replied:
"We are ascetics."
The king asked again:
"Have you attained the concentration of neither perception nor non-perception?"
They replied, "We have not."
He asked again:
"Have you attained the first dhyāna?"
They replied:
"We once had, but now we have lost it."
Then the king angrily said:
"It is not fitting for men with desires to see my palace women."
He then drew his sharp sword and cut off the hands and feet of the five hundred ascetics.
Yōutuóluómózǐ,
there was a king
who regularly offered him food.
When mealtime arrived,
he would fly through the empty sky with his supernatural power to go to the king's palace.
The king would then welcome him, embrace him, and seat him on a golden couch.
He would offer him the food that ascetics eat.
When that ascetic had finished his meal,
he would clear the utensils, rinse his mouth, recite verses and blessings, and fly away through the sky.
Later, that king,
due to affairs of state, had to go elsewhere.
There was no one to serve the ascetic.
The ascetic had a volatile nature.
"If he becomes angry and curses me,
I may lose my throne or my life."
He then asked his daughter:
"If the ascetic comes, can you make offerings according to my usual practice?"
The daughter replied, "I can."
The king then strictly instructed his daughter to serve him wholeheartedly.
Only then did he depart.
He attended to state affairs.
On a later day at mealtime, the ascetic flew in.
The king's daughter, following the king's practice,
personally welcomed him, embraced him, and seated him on the golden couch.
The king's daughter's body was soft and delicate.
When the ascetic touched the girl, he lost his supernatural powers.
After eating and drinking,
he cleared the utensils, rinsed his mouth, and recited verses and blessings.
He wished to fly but could not.
At that time, there was a rear garden in the king's palace.
He entered it, wishing to cultivate supernatural powers.
He heard the sounds of elephants, horses, and chariots and could not cultivate.
The people in the city constantly thought thus:
"If we could have the great ascetic walk on the ground,
we could then personally approach and bow at his feet."
The ascetic was intelligent, clever, and skilled in expedient means.
He said to the king's daughter:
"You now announce to the people of the city:
'Today the great ascetic will walk out from the king's palace.'
You people should do whatever is appropriate."
Then that king's daughter, as instructed,
immediately announced it.
The streets were clean, without tiles, gravel, or filth.
Banners were hung, incense burned, and various flowers scattered.
Everything was adorned, fresh, and clean.
The ascetic walked out; not far from the city,
he entered among the trees in the forest, wishing to cultivate supernatural powers.
He heard the sounds of many birds and could not cultivate.
He left the forest and trees and went again to the riverbank.
Using his original method, he wished to cultivate supernatural powers.
Again he heard the sounds of fish and turtles turning in the water,
and could not cultivate.
He then went up the mountain and thought thus:
"The reason I have now lost my wholesome dharmas is all because of sentient beings.
All the wholesome dharmas and pure practices I have—
may I become such a being
that can harm all ground-walking, flying, and water-dwelling beings seen in the world,
with none escaping me."
He made this evil vow and wished to see it fulfilled.
He left the desire of the eight stages and was born in the summit existence of neither perception nor non-perception.
He opened the gate of ambrosia, the tranquil garden.
For eighty thousand kalpas, he dwelt in quiet, serene bliss.
When the retribution of his karma ended, he returned here.
In the Dápō forest, at the Tánmó'ālánruò place,
he became a winged fox,
with a body fifty yojanas wide.
Each of its two wings was fifty yojanas wide.
The size of its body was one hundred fifty yojanas.
With this great body, it killed sky-going, water, and land beings,
with none escaping.
When its body perished and life ended, it was born in the Avīci hell.
Before the Buddha appeared in the world,
the god Śakra often went to the ascetic Tíbōyánnuó to listen to the Dharma.
Later, once, riding in a jewel-adorned chariot, he wished to go to the ascetic.
But Shèzhī thought:
"Now Śakra is abandoning me to go to other court ladies."
She hid her form and got onto the chariot.
Śakra did not know; as they were about to reach the ascetic's place,
he looked back and saw her.
He asked:
"Why have you come?"
The ascetic does not wish to see women with his eyes.
You should return to the palace."
Shèzhī did not wish to go.
Śakra struck her with a lotus stem.
Shèzhī, with a woman's soft, beautiful voice, apologized to Śakra.
The ascetic heard it,
and gave rise to desire and attachment.
His coiled hair immediately fell off, and his divine ear-knowledge retreated.
In the past, there was an immortal on Snow Mountain.
His name was Bájiāpó.
He ate fruits and grass roots, cultivating a mind of compassion.
Yet he could not eliminate all the bonds of afflictions.
At that time, residing in that place was a female tiger.
She mated with him and thus became pregnant.
When the months and days were fulfilled, she came to the immortal's place and gave birth to twelve offspring.
The immortal, feeling pity, took them, bathed them, and nurtured them.
The tiger mother, with loving care, nursed them in due time.
The immortal gave each a name.
The first was named Jiégā.
The second, Bówóqié.
The third was named Tiger.
The fourth, Lion.
The fifth, Heavy Burden.
The sixth, Póluóduòshé.
The seventh, Walker.
The eighth, Póluónú.
The ninth, Strong Eater.
The tenth, Evil Nature.
The eleventh, Lion's Burden.
The twelfth, Strong Walker.
At the age of seven, they could eat roots, flowers, and fruits.
Both parents died, and the children's hearts were filled with sorrow and distress.
They cried out to the heavens, weeping with no one to rely on.
The tree spirit said,
"Do not cry out.
You should bathe yourselves in purity six times day and night, bow respectfully toward the sky, and sincerely worship, seeking mercy from Brahma.
Brahma will hear you.
He will come to your place, dispel your ignorance and darkness,
bestow upon you the light of wisdom, and will surely provide for you."
Following these teachings, they practiced for twelve years.
Then Brahma, Lord Śakra, and the Thirty-Three Gods,
along with countless attendants, all came to provide for them.
They said to the children,
"For what reason have you diligently practiced austerities for twelve years,
providing for us? What do you seek?"
They all replied,
"We only wish, O Great Being, that you bestow wisdom upon us,
so that we may know the deeds of good and evil, and the matters of suffering and happiness."
In a distant past age,
there was an immortal.
His name was Bōjié.
He attained the five supernatural powers.
At that time, he was served by a king.
With his supernatural feet, he flew back and forth to the king's palace.
The king provided for him with all comforts and security.
The king personally spread his hair for the immortal to walk upon,
and personally served him a hundred kinds of food and drink.
This continued for many years.
Then the king had official duties.
The king had a daughter,
beautiful and lovely, rare in the world.
The king held her in great esteem.
The daughter had not yet left home.
The king told his daughter,
"I serve the immortal and dare not displease him.
Now I must travel far; you must provide for him.
Act as if I were present."
Then that immortal flew down from the sky to the palace.
When the king's daughter saw him arrive,
she lifted him with her hands and seated him on a throne.
Touching the girl's soft body, he immediately arose with lustful thoughts.
As desire flourished, he soon lost his supernatural powers.
Though he contemplated and practiced walking meditation to regain his supernatural powers, he could not obtain them.
He walked out of the palace.
At that time, countless people gathered to watch.
When the king finished his journey and returned, he heard that the immortal had fallen into affection and could no longer fly.
The king went to the palace at night, going alone in secret.
He went to see the immortal, bowing at his feet.
He spoke in verse:
Bōjié replied:
The king said:
Bōjié replied:
The immortal felt ashamed and remorseful, blaming himself earnestly.
He diligently practiced day and night and regained his supernatural powers.
That immortal is now Śāriputra.
That king is now myself.
At that time, in the mountains of the kingdom of Bōluónài, there was an immortal.
In the mid-autumn month,
he urinated into a bathing basin.
Seeing deer mating, lustful thoughts immediately arose.
His semen flowed into the basin, and a deer drank it.
She immediately became pregnant.
After a full month, she gave birth to a child, largely human-like,
with a single horn on its head and feet resembling those of a deer.
When the deer was about to give birth, she went to the immortal's dwelling and gave birth in front of it,
entrusting the child to the immortal before leaving.
When the immortal came out, he saw this deer-child.
Reflecting on the original circumstances, he knew it was his own child.
He took it and raised it.
When it grew older,
he diligently taught and instructed it.
It mastered eighteen great scriptures.
It also learned meditation.
Practicing the four immeasurable minds, it attained the five supernatural powers.
Once, while going up the mountain,
it encountered heavy rain and slippery mud.
Its feet were inconvenient, and it stumbled, injuring its foot.
It became greatly angry.
It cursed, commanding no rain to fall.
Due to the immortal's virtue, all dragons, spirits, and ghosts caused no rain to fall.
Because there was no rain, grains and fruits did not grow.
The people became impoverished, with no means of livelihood.
The king of Bōluónài was worried and distressed.
He ordered his high officials to gather and discuss the matter of rain.
The wise ones discussed and said,
"We have heard of a one-horned immortal.
He went up the mountain, injured his foot, and in anger cursed that there be no rain for twelve years."
The king then opened a recruitment,
saying, "If anyone can cause the immortal to lose his five supernatural powers and become my subject,
I will share half the kingdom with them to govern."
In that kingdom of Bōluónài, there was a courtesan.
Her name was Shàntuó.
Beautiful and immensely wealthy,
she came to answer the king's recruitment.
The courtesan said,
"If it is this person, I can ruin him." After saying this,
she took a golden tray filled with fine treasures.
She told the king,
"I will ride this immortal back."
The courtesan immediately requested five hundred carriages,
carrying five hundred beautiful women.
Five hundred deer carriages carried various欢喜丸,
all mixed with medicinal herbs.
And they brought various strong and fine wines.
Wearing tree-bark garments, they traveled among the forests and trees,
imitating immortals.
They built a grass hut to dwell near the immortal's dwelling.
The one-horned immortal, while wandering, saw them.
The women all came out, offering fine flowers and wonderful incense to provide for the immortal.
The immortal was delighted.
The women addressed the immortal with sweet words and respectful greetings.
They led him into a room, seated him on a fine bed and mat,
and gave him fine pure wine, presenting it as pure water.
They gave him欢喜丸, presenting them as fruits and melons.
After eating and drinking his fill,
he said to the women,
"Since my birth, I have never obtained such fruits and water."
The women said,
"Because I practice goodness with a single mind, heaven granted my wish, giving me these fruits and water."
The immortal asked the women,
"Why is your skin so lustrous and plump?"
They replied,
"I always eat these fine fruits and drink this fine water."
The immortal said,
"Why don't you stay here?"
They replied,
"We could stay."
The women called him to bathe together.
The women's hands were soft to the touch.
His heart stirred, and lustful desire arose.
He immediately lost his supernatural powers.
Heaven sent heavy rain for seven days and seven nights.
They enjoyed欢乐 and饮食 for seven days.
When the wine and food were exhausted,
they continued with water, wood, and fruits,
but their flavor was not good.
He asked for the previous items.
They replied they were finished.
"Now we should go together to get more.
Not far from here is a place where we can obtain them."
The immortal said,
"As you wish."
They went out together, not far from the city.
The woman then lay on the ground, saying,
"I am extremely tired and can no longer walk."
The immortal said,
"If you cannot walk, ride on my neck.
I will carry you."
The woman first sent a message to report to the king,
"Your Majesty may come out briefly to observe my wisdom and ability."
The king saw and asked,
"How did you manage this?"
The woman said, "By skillful means, he is no longer capable."
She had him stay in the city, well provided for and respected.
He was given all he desired and appointed as a high official.
After staying in the city for a few days, his body became emaciated.
Recalling his meditative mind, he grew weary of worldly desires.
The king asked the immortal,
"Why are you not happy?"
He replied,
"Although I have the five desires, I constantly think of the forest."
The king said,
"Originally, we sought to eliminate the drought disaster. Why force him against his will?"
He then sent him away.
After returning to the mountains, through diligent practice, he soon regained the five supernatural powers.
The one-horned immortal is now myself.
The courtesan is now Yēshūtuóluó.
In the past, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara appeared.
In the country of Padma,
there were countless assemblies of the fourfold community.
They all came to make offerings and provide for his needs.
At that time, there was a Brahmin
named Yéruòdá.
He lived on the side of the Snowy Mountains.
He studied all the secret prophecies, astronomy, and geography, mastering them thoroughly.
He was also fully knowledgeable in writing and literature.
The Brahmin Yéruòdá had a disciple,
named Léiyún,
who was intelligent and widely learned, proficient in all matters.
He was constantly cherished and taught by Yéruòdá, never leaving his side for a moment.
The Brahmin Léiyún thought to himself:
"All that I should learn, I have now mastered.
I should repay my teacher's kindness.
However, I am poor and destitute.
I should go to the borders of the country to seek what I need."
His teacher thought:
"He is my beloved disciple.
Even if I were to die, I could not bear to part with him,
how much more so now that he wishes to leave me?"
He composed five hundred verses for him to recite.
Within a few days, he had mastered them fluently.
At that time, the Brahmin Yéruòdá
addressed his five hundred disciples, saying:
"This Brahmin Léiyún is proficient in all arts and skills.
Therefore, I shall give him a name:
Chāoshù (Superior Skill)."
After a few more days, the Brahmin Chāoshù
again said to his teacher:
"What I have learned is now known.
However, according to the scriptures, one who surpasses in learning should repay the teacher's kindness."
The teacher said:
"You know this, you know."
Chāoshù bowed and departed.
At that time, in the country of Padma,
not far from the city, there were many Brahmins
gathered in one household to perform a great sacrifice,
and also to engage in debate.
Eighty-four thousand Brahmins assembled.
The foremost elder recited writings and texts, and there was nothing he did not know.
Five hundred taels of gold, a golden staff, a golden water vessel, and a thousand head of cattle
were offered to the teacher.
They first tested the skills of the foremost elder.
Whoever surpassed him would receive these offerings.
The Brahmin Chāoshù thought to himself:
"Why should I go from house to house begging?
It would be better to go to that great assembly and compete in skills."
Chāoshù went.
From afar, the many Brahmins called out:
"Excellent! The host of the sacrifice now gains great benefit,
for even Brahmā has descended in person."
At that time, the eighty-four thousand Brahmins
all rose together to welcome him,
speaking in unison with one voice:
"Welcome, great Brahmā, divine god!"
The Brahmin Chāoshù said:
"I am not Brahmā.
Stop, stop, O virtuous ones.
Have you not heard
that north of the Snowy Mountains, there is a great Brahmin, the teacher of many,
named Yéruòdá?
I am his disciple,
named Chāoshù."
Then he addressed the foremost elder:
"If you know any skills, speak them before me."
At that time, the foremost elder of that assembly
recited the three baskets of skills without any omission.
Then Chāoshù said to the elder:
"One verse of five hundred words—
can you recite it now?"
The elder said:
"I do not understand it."
Chāoshù then recited the three baskets and the one verse of five hundred words on the marks of a great being.
At that time, the eighty-four thousand Brahmins
exclaimed that this was unprecedented, most extraordinary and rare:
"We have never before heard of the marks of a great being.
Now, O venerable one, you should take the foremost seat."
Chāoshù moved to the foremost seat and thus became first.
At that time, the elder of that assembly harbored extreme anger
and made this vow:
"Now this person has taken my seat.
In whatever place this person is born and whatever he seeks to accomplish,
I will always ruin his achievements."
At that time, the donor made the offering according to the rules for the foremost seat.
Chāoshù addressed the host:
"I now return the gold and silver coins as an offering.
I will only take five hundred coins each.
I will use the golden vessel to make offerings to women,
and the thousand head of cattle I return to the host.
I do not indulge in desires, nor do I accumulate wealth."
Having done so, he went to the country of Padma.
Its king was named Guāngmíng.
At the eastern gate of the city, he saw five hundred elderly Brahmins of virtuous repute.
At that time, the king of that country invited the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, and under the sun's heat and fire's blaze,
he gave each of the five hundred Brahmins one coin and to the community of monks,
provided food, clothing, and offerings, sweeping and cleaning to make it pure.
He ensured there were no entertainers, dirt, sand, or impurities.
He hung silk banners and canopies, sprinkled fragrant water on the ground.
There were countless musical performances.
He saw a woman,
named Shànwèi,
holding seven stems of flowers and fetching water with a vase.
He asked this woman:
"I wish to buy flowers."
The woman said:
"I am taking them to offer to the Buddha."
He then offered five hundred silver coins for five stems of flowers.
The woman, coveting the silver coins, gave him five stems.
After walking several tens of steps, the woman thought to herself:
"This man's appearance is upright, and he does not spare silver coins."
She called after the man, asking what he intended to do with them.
He replied: "To offer to the Buddha."
The woman said:
"Please take two more stems of flowers and also offer them to the Buddha.
May we be husband and wife in future lives."
Chāoshù said:
"A bodhisattva has no attachments.
If you were to become my wife, it would surely disturb my mind."
The Brahmin woman said:
"I will never disturb you.
Even if you were to give me away,
I would endure and comply."
The Buddha Dīpaṃkara said:
"A bodhisattva's practice involves no attachments."
The Brahmin replied with a verse.
He then spoke a verse:
"O young man,"
he again replied with a verse.
He then loosened his hair and spread it on the ground,
speaking a verse:
The Buddha again replied with a verse.
The Buddha stepped on the hair and passed over.
With his spiritual power, he received the five stems of flowers,
and I myself was lifted into the air.
The remaining two flowers rested on the Buddha's two shoulders.
Since breaking the Brahmin's sacrifice to the heavenly emperor and fire,
practicing right view and the method of equality,
I have never again fallen into the three evil paths or the eight difficulties.
At that time, Chāoshù was I,
and the flower-selling woman, Jūyí, was she.
There was a Brahmin named Bǎohǎi.
He addressed the Buddha,
"May the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus
accept my offerings of the four necessities for a full seven years."
The Tathāgata granted permission.
Later, the Brahmin thought thus:
"I have now caused hundreds of thousands, billions, nayutas of beings to develop the mind of bodhi.
Yet I do not know what kind of aspiration the Cakravartin King has—whether his aspiration is
for human kingship, heavenly kingship, the Śrāvaka vehicle, or the Pratyekabuddha vehicle,
or whether he seeks unsurpassed bodhi.
If I am destined to attain Buddhahood in a future life,
then while I sleep at night, various heavenly Māras, Brahmās, and Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, should manifest dreams for me."
While asleep, he saw a bright light.
He then saw the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions.
Each, from afar, bestowed a lotus flower upon him.
The flowers were exquisite, and on each lotus pedestal, he saw an image of a sun disc.
Upon each sun disc was a seven-jeweled canopy.
From each sun disc emanated six billion rays of light.
All entered the Brahmin's mouth.
He saw his own light filling an area of a thousand yojanas,
pure as a bright mirror, and saw within his abdomen
sixty billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas,
seated on lotus flowers in full lotus posture, absorbed in samādhi.
He further saw sun rays encircling his body.
From the flowers emerged various musical instruments playing music.
He also saw that king,
bleeding, defiling his body, running wildly in all directions,
his face resembling a pig's, eating various insects.
He was sitting under an Elan tree.
Innumerable beings came to devour his body,
leaving only his bones.
Repeatedly receiving bodies, it was also thus.
He further saw the princes,
some with faces of pigs, elephants, water buffaloes, lions, foxes, wolves, tigers, leopards, monkeys, and so forth,
their bodies stained with blood, all eating beings.
They were sitting under Elan trees.
Again, innumerable beings
came to devour their bodies.
Their bones were already scattered.
Repeatedly receiving bodies, it was also thus.
He also saw a prince
wearing a garland of Sumana flowers,
riding in a small, shabby cart drawn by a water buffalo,
speeding southward on an improper path.
He further saw the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra, and Mahābrahmā arriving at his place.
They said to the Brahmin,
"All the lotus flowers around you now—
you should first take one flower and give it to the Cakravartin King.
Give one flower to each prince.
Give the remaining flowers to the various minor kings.
Next, give them to your sons,
and also to others." He then distributed them all.
Suddenly, he awoke.
Recalling the various things seen in the dream,
he understood that the holy king's aspiration was lowly, delighting in saṃsāra.
He further understood that the princes had developed minds
seeking the Śrāvaka vehicle; therefore, I dreamed of them wearing garlands of Sumana flowers,
riding in water buffalo carts, speeding southward on an improper path.
For what reason did I dream of this?
The Buddhas, World-Honored Ones,
because I first taught and urged immeasurable beings within Jambudvīpa
to all abide in the three bases of merit and develop the mind of bodhi,
invited the Buddha and the saṅgha
to accept offerings for a full seven years, providing all comforts."
In Śrāvastī, there was a Brahmin
who extensively cultivated fields among the Jeta Grove.
Going to inspect them, he was delighted,
thinking he had attained his wish.
That very night, however, heaven rained large hailstones,
and all the crops died.
His daughter also passed away.
Distraught, worried, and troubled, he wept uncontrollably.
At that time, the bhikṣus entered the city to seek alms.
Seeing his two misfortunes, they returned and fully reported to the Buddha.
Shortly after, the Brahmin personally came to the Buddha's place.
After paying homage with his head at the Buddha's feet,
the Buddha, knowing his thoughts,
said to the Brahmin,
"There are five things in the world that cannot be avoided or escaped:
first, diminishment;
second, loss and abandonment;
third, sickness and emaciation;
fourth, aging and decay;
fifth, death.
Only the truth of the path can bring liberation.
Practice generosity and uphold precepts."
The Brahmin's mind softened, and he then perceived the four truths.
From that day onward, he took refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha,
becoming a lay devotee.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha,
"World-Honored One,
explain the Brahmin's intention; he left joyfully and laughing."
The Buddha said,
"It is not only now that he has resolved his sorrow.
In the past, in the land of Jambudvīpa, there were five kings.
One king was named Jiétān (Greedy Tyrant).
He ruled the country unjustly.
The ministers and people
took up arms, raised white banners, and all came before the king.
Together they said to the king,
'Do you not know yourself? You greedily harm the myriad people.
Leave the country immediately.
Otherwise, we will harm you.'
The king trembled with great fear
and left the country with his chariots and cavalry.
He wove grass mats to sell for his livelihood.
The ministers and people then enthroned the king's younger brother as king.
He ruled without oppressing the people.
The former king sent a letter stating his case,
begging the king for a single village to support himself.
The king gave it to him.
Having obtained one village, he governed it justly.
He then begged for two villages,
up to half the country.
The king gave them all to him.
After a long time,
Jiétān thought,
'I will raise an army from half the country to attack my brother.' He was victorious and regained his former kingdom.
He then raised an army from one country to attack the second,
and successively doubled his troops to attack the fifth country.
He was repeatedly victorious.
At that time, all within the four seas became subject to him, and he changed his title to Dàshèng (Great Victor).
Śakra tested him to see
if he knew contentment.
He transformed into a young Brahmin boy,
of the Jūyí clan,
with disheveled hair, holding a golden staff and a golden vase, and stood at the palace gate to seek an audience with the king.
The king came forward, sat down, and after exchanging greetings,
the boy said to the king,
'I have come from the seashore.
I saw a great country there,
with a prosperous population and abundant treasures.
You could go and attack it.
I wonder if you are already satisfied
and still desire this?'
The king said he desired it.
The heavenly king said,
'Then prepare more ships and raise an army to wait.
After seven days, I will lead you there.' Having said this, he vanished.
On the appointed day, the king raised an army and prepared ships.
The Brahmin did not come, and the king became worried and unhappy.
At that time, the people of the country all turned and sat facing the king.
When the king wept, they wept;
when the king was worried, they were worried.
The king then had an idea and declared,
'Whoever can resolve this will be rewarded one thousand gold coins.'
There was a youth named Yùduō
who said he could resolve it and asked for seven days to respond.
On the seventh day, he said to his mother,
'I wish to resolve the king's worry.'
The mother said to her son,
'Son, stop.
Do not go.
Matters concerning emperors are difficult.'
The son said,
'I have the ability to handle it.'
He went to the king and said,
'I have come now to respond.'
He then recited a verse.
King Dàshèng then bestowed one thousand gold coins upon him.
That Dàshèng was none other than the Brahmin of various kinds.
That youth Yùduō was myself.
In the past, the Brahmin Móyīntí
had a daughter of beautiful appearance.
Kings, princes, ministers, and elders came to seek her hand but could not obtain her.
Seeing the Buddha's golden complexion and thirty-two marks,
he thought to himself,
'Such a man is a match for my daughter; I will give her to him.'
Returning home, he said to his wife,
'Now I have found a son-in-law superior to our daughter.'
He then adorned his daughter with various precious necklaces
and led her out of the city.
The mother saw the Buddha's footprints, with the wheel marks clearly visible.
She said to the father,
'You should know that we are going in vain; we will ultimately not get a son-in-law.'
The wife recited a verse.
The father said,
'Foolish woman, you are creating trouble for our daughter.'
He then led his daughter to the Buddha's place.
Holding her arm with his left hand and a vase with his right hand,
he addressed the Buddha, saying,
'Now I offer this daughter to be your wife.'
The daughter, seeing the Buddha's form, became attached with lustful thoughts.
Her heart burned with fire.
The Buddha then recited a verse.
In the past, there was a Brahmin who left home to study while young.
By the age of sixty, he had not attained enlightenment.
According to the rules, he had to return home.
He took a wife and became a lay devotee.
They had a son.
He was handsome and lovely.
At the age of seven, he suddenly fell seriously ill.
One night, he passed away. The Brahmin grieved for him.
He lay over the corpse and fainted, then revived.
His relatives advised and persuaded him, forcibly taking the body for burial outside the city.
The Brahmin thought to himself:
"My weeping now is of no avail.
It would be better to go to King Yámǎluówáng and beg for my son's life."
He bathed, observed fasting, and brought flowers and incense.
He left his home and departed.
Wherever he went, he asked people:
"Where is the place ruled by King Yámǎluówáng?"
He traveled several thousand li forward, reaching deep into the mountains.
He saw other Brahmins and asked them as before.
They replied:
"Why do you ask about the place ruled by King Yámǎluówáng? What do you seek?"
He answered:
"I had a son who recently died.
I wish to go to King Yámǎluówáng to beg for my son's life."
The Brahmins pitied his foolishness.
They told him:
"The place ruled by King Yámǎluówáng is not reachable by the living.
But I will show you the way.
Go west from here for over four hundred li.
There is a great river, and within it lies a city.
This is a city where heavenly deities rest while inspecting the world.
King Yámǎluówáng always passes through this city on the fourth day of each month while inspecting. If you observe fasting and go, you will surely see him."
He joyfully departed.
Reaching the river, he saw a fine city with palaces and buildings.
Like those in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
The Brahmin approached the gate.
He burned incense, raised his feet, and chanted prayers, seeking his son.
King Yámǎluówáng ordered the gatekeeper to see him.
The Brahmin pleaded:
"Late in life, I had a son to rely on in old age.
I raised him for seven years, and recently he passed away.
I beg Your Majesty to bestow grace and charity, returning my son's life to me."
The king said: "Very well.
Your son is now playing in the eastern garden.
Go and take him yourself."
He went and saw his son.
Playing with other children.
He went forward, embraced him, and wept, saying:
"I think of you day and night, unable to eat or sleep in peace.
Do you not remember your parents' hardships?"
The child rebuked him, scolding:
"Foolish old man, you do not understand the principle.
I was merely a temporary lodger, called your son.
Do not speak nonsense.
Better leave early.
Here, I have my own parents now."
The Brahmin was disheartened, wept, and left.
He thought to himself:
"I have heard that the ascetic Gautama knows the way of the soul's transformations.
