I should go and ask him."
He returned to the Buddha, bowed, and paid homage.
He recounted the whole story to the Buddha.
"He was indeed my son, but he refuses to return.
He calls me a foolish old man.
Saying he was merely a temporary lodger, called someone else's son.
There is no lasting bond between father and son.
Why is this so?"
The Buddha told the Brahmin:
"You are truly foolish.
When a person dies, the spirit departs and takes on another form.
Parents, wives, and children come together due to causes and conditions.
Like a temporary guest who leaves when the time comes.
Hearing this, the Brahmin suddenly understood, bowed, and submitted.
He wished to become an ascetic.
The Buddha said: "Excellent."
His hair and beard fell off, and the Dharma robe appeared on his body.
He became a bhikṣu.
Right on his seat, he attained Arhatship.
In the past, there was a Brahmin.
Wealthy and learned, he did not believe in the true path.
He often debated with ascetics but was not their equal.
Whenever he heard that ascetics ate alms given by believers but did not practice diligently,
he thought that after death they would become oxen or horses to repay the donors.
So he secretly planned to set out food.
To obtain them in the next life.
To make them work for him.
By nature stingy, he suddenly went to the monastery.
There were five hundred monks in the monastery, and he invited them all.
He showed respect, set out food, richer and better than others.
He thought he would surely obtain five hundred oxen and horses.
The senior monk, one who had attained the four fruits of Arhatship,
knew his thoughts.
He called the overseer and instructed the bhikṣus:
"All should concentrate. When each person recites a verse, all should show respect together."
The senior monk said:
"The debt has already been repaid.
You will not get oxen or horses."
The Brahmin was shocked and said:
"The monk is divine, knowing my thoughts in advance."
The senior monk then fully informed the bhikṣus.
"After you have eaten,
with a compassionate mind, think of the path and recite a Dharma saying.
Even Mount Sumeru could be digested,
let alone this small meal."
The Brahmin was greatly ashamed.
The monk then expounded the Dharma for him, broadly presenting the essential meaning.
His mind opened, he accepted the path, and immediately realized the trace of the path.
In the past, there was a Brahmin.
He vowed not to see the Buddha and secretly entered another's house.
The Great Sage pitied him and appeared before him.
He tried to avoid and flee but could not.
He came to the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One
expounded the sutra and Dharma for him, and joy arose in his heart.
He took refuge in the Dharma and Saṅgha, received the precepts, circumambulated the Buddha, and left.
He then took a bowl, filled it with honey,
and held it with both hands, wishing to offer it to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Take this bowl of honey and distribute it among the assembly."
At that time, one bowl of honey satisfied the Buddha and the entire assembly.
The bowl remained full as before.
It was then offered again to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the Brahmin:
"Pour it into a great river of immeasurable flow."
The Brahmin asked why.
The Buddha said:
"So that all water creatures, insects, turtles, fish, and shellfish may partake of its flavor."
The Brahmin accepted the instruction.
The World-Honored One smiled joyfully, emitting five-colored light.
It rose to the Brahma heaven, illuminating the five paths everywhere.
It circled his body three times.
When bestowing the prediction of Bodhisattvahood, the light entered from the crown.
When bestowing the prediction of Pratyekabuddhahood, the light entered from the mouth.
When bestowing the prediction of Śrāvakahood, the light entered from the arm.
When speaking of heavenly blessings, the light entered from the navel.
When speaking of bestowing human birth, the light entered from the knees.
When speaking of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, the light entered from the feet.
Ānanda rose from his seat, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
"The Buddha does not smile without reason.
There must be meaning in this smile."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Did you see the Brahmin offering honey to the Buddha?"
He replied: "Yes."
"This Brahmin, in future lives,
will pass through twenty kalpas without falling into evil realms.
After twenty kalpas, he will attain Pratyekabuddhahood.
He will be named Mìjù.
The bhikṣus said:
"This Brahmin, with one bowl of honey, greatly benefited and will attain Pratyekabuddhahood."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This Brahmin not only in this life,
but in past lives was also like this.
In the past, there was a Brahmin living in solitude.
He saw an immortal.
Someone said:
'This immortal is auspicious and hard to reach.
You should go and receive instruction.'
Someone else said:
'What use is seeing this body-nourishing kind?'
There was a sage with five supernatural powers.
He saw what was in his mind.
He then leaped from among the trees,
hovering in the air before him.
Seeing him, the Brahmin rejoiced and leaped.
He filled a bowl with honey and offered it to him.
The sage accepted it and flew into the sky.
Due to this act of giving, he later became a king.
Named Mìjù.
He ruled the country with righteous law, and after his life ended, he was reborn in heaven.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Know that the sage with five supernatural powers at that time
was myself.
The Brahmin at that time is the present Brahmin.
The offering of honey at that time brought heavenly blessings.
Due to that, in this life he also offered to the Buddha.
Leading later to Pratyekabuddhahood."
There was a Brahmin.
In Rājagṛha.
He heard that in Śrāvastī, people were mostly filial, respectful, upheld the scriptures, cultivated the Way, and served the Three Jewels.
Wishing to gain learning, he went there to inquire and receive instruction.
Not far from the country,
he saw a father and son plowing the land and sowing seeds.
At that time, a poisonous snake came out and bit and killed the son.
The father continued plowing without stopping and did not even look.
The Brahmin asked him.
The plower also asked.
"Where have you come from?"
The Brahmin replied,
"I have come from Rājagṛha.
I heard that the people of this country are mostly filial and serve the Three Jewels, so I came to learn."
"Who was that just now?"
He said, "My son."
"If he is your son, why are you not grieving, but instead continue plowing?"
The man replied,
"In life there is death; when things are complete, there is decay.
It is not something that sorrow, worry, or weeping can change.
Even if I did not eat or drink, what benefit would it bring to the dead?
When you enter the city, please pass by my house and tell them:
'My son has died.
Do not bring food for two people anymore.'"
The Brahmin thought to himself,
"This man has no human feeling.
His son lies dead on the ground.
He is calm, not grieving, and instead asks for food."
He entered Śrāvastī city and went to the plower's house.
He saw the dead boy's mother and said,
"Your son has died.
His father says,
'Just bring food for one person.'"
The boy's mother said,
"Like a guest coming to lodge,
coming is not difficult, leaving does not linger.
This child is like that.
Birth is by itself; death is also gone alone.
It is not within my power to advance or retreat it.
It follows its own past actions, pursuing life according to its destiny."
He also spoke to the sister.
The sister also spoke of the metaphor of impermanence.
The Brahmin said to the wife,
"Your husband has died."
The wife gave the Brahmin a parable.
He also spoke to the slave boy.
"The master has died."
The slave boy also gave a parable.
Hearing this,
the Brahmin felt distressed in his heart, his eyes darkened, and he did not know east from west.
"I heard that in this country people are filial and serve the Three Jewels, so I came to learn.
I have not found good intentions.
I have seen five people with no human feeling, vainly toiling body and mind."
He asked a passerby, "Where is the Buddha?"
The person replied,
"Nearby, in the Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park."
The Brahmin then went to where the Buddha was.
He bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, stepped back, and sat to one side.
He was sorrowful and unhappy.
He lowered his head silently, saying nothing.
The Buddha knew his thoughts.
He said to the Brahmin,
"Why are you unhappy?"
The Brahmin replied,
"It goes against my original wish, so I am sorrowful."
The Buddha asked again,
"How so?"
He fully recounted the matter in reply.
The Buddha said, "Not so.
It is not as you say.
These five people have the most human feeling.
They know that life is impermanent and cannot be changed by sorrow.
They return to their own composure, therefore they have no sorrow.
Ordinary people do not recognize impermanence.
They are distressed, weep, and cannot cut themselves off from it.
It is like a person's body contracting a feverish illness.
Unaware, they become confused and speak deliriously.
A good physician gives them medicine.
The fever then subsides and they no longer speak deliriously.
Ordinary people's sorrow is like the intoxication and fever of foolish ignorance; they cannot free themselves.
If they themselves understand impermanence, they will no longer be sorrowful.
It is like recovering from a fever.
These five people can all attain the Way and realization."
Hearing the Buddha's words, the Brahmin immediately reproached himself.
"I am foolish and ignorant, not knowing the great meaning.
Now hearing the Buddha's words,
it is like the blind gaining sight, seeing light in darkness."
He then received the Five Precepts, bowed, and withdrew.
The Brahmin had four brothers.
Each had attained the five supernatural powers.
After seven days, they would all meet their end.
They discussed among themselves,
"With the power of the five supernatural abilities, we can overturn heaven and earth.
We can touch the sun and moon with our hands, move mountains, stop rivers.
There is nothing we cannot do.
How could we not avoid this confrontation with death?"
One said,
"I will enter the great sea.
I will not surface above nor reach the bottom below.
I will position myself exactly in the middle.
How will the ghost of impermanence and death know my whereabouts?"
One said,
"I will enter Mount Sumeru.
I will close up its surface so that no gap appears.
How will the ghost of impermanence and death know my whereabouts?"
One said,
"I will lightly rise and hide in empty space.
How will the ghost of impermanence and death know my whereabouts?"
One said,
"I will hide in the midst of a great marketplace.
The ghost of impermanence and death, if it gets one person, why must it seek me?"
The four finished their discussion.
Together they went to bid farewell to the king.
"Our remaining lifespan is seven days.
Now we wish to flee for our lives.
We hope to escape and then return to visit you.
We only wish you to advance in virtue."
Thereupon they departed.
When the seven days were fulfilled, each one met his end.
Like ripe fruit falling.
The market overseer reported to the king,
"A Brahmin has suddenly died in the marketplace."
The king then realized and said,
"Four men avoided confrontation; one has died.
How could the remaining three alone escape?"
The king immediately prepared his carriage and went to where the Buddha was.
He paid respects, stepped back, sat down, and said,
"Recently there were Brahmins,
four brothers, each possessing the five supernatural powers.
Knowing their lives were ending, they all sought to avoid it together.
I do not know whether now they were able to escape or not."
The Buddha told the great king,
"There are four things from which people cannot be separated.
First, in the intermediate state, one cannot avoid receiving birth.
Second, having been born, one cannot avoid receiving old age.
Third, having grown old, one cannot avoid receiving sickness.
Fourth, having become sick, one cannot avoid receiving death."
There was a devout layman.
His wife was dignified and beautiful, with unparalleled virtue.
Eloquent and articulate, she was respected by all.
Yet her husband did not value her, nor did he enjoy seeing her.
Instead, he loved a servant girl.
The wife, seeing her husband's heart,
said to her husband:
"You do not love me.
I wish to be allowed to leave home."
The husband then permitted it.
Immediately, she left home and became a bhikṣuṇī.
Day and night, she diligently practiced,
and before long, she attained the state of an arhat.
Afterward, the woman whom the devout layman respected died.
The devout layman called for the bhikṣuṇī to return.
The nun firmly refused.
The bhikṣuṇī reported to the Buddha,
recounting the whole story.
The Buddha said:
"This devout layman had already insulted this virtuous person in a past life.
This woman had exceptional determination.
This man constantly sought to disrupt her.
Having entered the great path, he again sought to destroy her,
but could not succeed."
The Buddha said:
"In a past life, there was a Brahmin's wife
named Liánhuā,
of unparalleled beauty.
The Brahmin did not love her.
What he loved was a maidservant.
Following the maidservant's words,
he abandoned his wife in the mountains.
He climbed an udumbara tree to pick ripe fruits,
discarding the unripe ones and giving them to his wife.
The wife asked:
'Why do you alone eat the ripe fruits,
while discarding the unripe ones for others?'
The husband said:
'You may climb the tree.'
The wife then climbed the tree.
The husband took thorns and brambles to surround the tree on all sides,
intending to prevent her from descending, so she would die.
At that time, the king was out hunting.
Seeing the woman's beauty,
he asked her:
'Who are you?'
The woman recounted her story in detail.
The king thought of the Brahmin,
foolish and ignorant, not a true man.
He immediately removed the thorns and brambles,
took her by carriage back to the palace, and made her his queen.
She possessed many skills and arts, with unparalleled wisdom and eloquence.
She was also skilled at dice games.
Women from near and far came to play dice with her,
but the queen always won, and no one could match her.
The Brahmin was skilled at gambling and chess.
Hearing from afar that the queen was winning,
he thought:
'This is my former wife, not someone else.'
He then wished to go before the king to display his skills.
The queen, hearing of a Brahmin with a certain appearance, knew it was her former husband.
She informed the king and had him appear.
From a distance, they tested each other in a dice game.
The queen replied with a verse.
The Brahmin felt ashamed and resentful,
immediately blaming himself, regretting it to no avail.
That Brahmin is now the devout layman.
That wife is now the wife.
That king is now myself."
There was a Brahmin with immeasurable wealth.
He had only one son, just twenty years old,
who had recently taken a wife.
Before seven days had passed,
in the early spring of the third month,
the husband and wife went together to the rear garden to play.
There was a tall and beautiful apple tree in full bloom.
The wife wanted a flower, but there was no one to pick it for her.
The husband, knowing his wife's wish, immediately climbed the tree.
Just as he picked one flower,
she wanted another.
The tree branch broke, and he fell to the ground and died.
The family rushed to where the son was,
crying out to heaven, wailing until they fainted and revived.
Countless relatives all shared in the grief.
Hearing it was heartbreaking, seeing it was sorrowful.
The parents blamed heaven, saying it did not protect them.
After the coffin was prepared and the funeral completed,
they returned home, weeping uncontrollably.
Then the World-Honored One,
pitying their foolishness, went to inquire and comfort them.
The family, seeing the Buddha,
expressed their sorrow and recounted their suffering.
The Buddha said to the elder:
"Cease and listen to the Dharma: all things are impermanent and cannot be preserved for long.
Where there is life, there is death; karma and blessings follow one another.
This son is being wept for in three places.
The grief and anguish are also unbearable.
After all, whose son is he?
Who are his true relatives?"
Then the World-Honored One spoke a verse:
The elder, hearing the verse, understood and forgot his sorrow.
Kneeling respectfully, he said to the Buddha:
"What offense did this son commit in a past life,
that such a flourishing life was cut short?
I only wish for an explanation of the offenses he committed."
The Buddha said:
"Long ago, there was a young boy
who took a bow and arrows into a sacred tree to play.
Nearby, three people were watching a sparrow in the tree.
The boy wanted to shoot it.
The three encouraged him, saying:
'If you can hit it, the world will call you a strong boy.'
The boy, pleased with the idea, drew his bow and shot,
hitting the sparrow, which died immediately.
The three laughed together, rejoicing with him, and then each went their own way.
Through countless kalpas of birth and death,
they encountered each other and met to suffer together.
Of those three, one had blessings and is now in heaven.
One was born in the sea as a nāga king born by transformation.
One is now the elder.
That young boy was first born in heaven as a son of the gods.
After his life ended, he descended to become the elder's son.
Falling from the tree and dying, he was immediately born in the sea as a nāga prince born by transformation.
On the very day he was born, the garuḍa king took him and ate him.
Today, the three places weep and grieve—how can this be spoken of?
Because in their past life, they rejoiced and encouraged him,
these three are now repaid with weeping."
In Śrāvastī, the king, ministers, and people
revered the World-Honored One and made offerings of the four necessities.
They abandoned the Brahmins.
The Brahmins plotted together:
"We should find a beautiful woman, kill her, and bury her among the trees,
so that Gautama's followers will be widely defamed.
Those who treat us well—
they together coerced and instructed a woman named Hǎoshǒu, saying:
'From now on, go morning and evening to the Buddha, so that all the people will see and know.'
The young woman followed the instruction,
then killed her and buried her among the trees.
The Brahmins then gathered at the palace gate,
crying out in complaint:
'In our school, there was a woman
who alone was the most beautiful,
with unparalleled beauty, and now we do not know whether she is alive or dead.'
The king said:
'Where did she usually go?'
They replied:
'She went to Gautama.'
The king said:
'You should search there.'
Messengers went to the Jeta Grove,
dug up the woman's corpse, and placed it on a bed.
Throughout the streets, they cried out in complaint:
'The śramaṇa Gautama always claims to have broad and unsurpassed virtue in precepts.
How could he secretly have an affair with a woman,
then kill and hide her?
What kind of precepts are these?'
At that time, the bhikṣus entered the city to beg for food.
The people cursed them, saying:
'These śramaṇas have committed such offenses.
How can they receive food and clothing?'
The bhikṣus returned with empty bowls, leaving the city.
They reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
'This slander against me will not last more than seven days.'
At that time, a woman named Wéiyán in the city heard
that the bhikṣus were begging for food and returning with empty bowls.
She went to the Buddha, bowed with her head at his feet,
joined her palms, and said to the Buddha:
'May the Buddha and the Sangha accept meals from my house for seven days.'
The Buddha silently accepted.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
'You and the Sangha should go into the city's streets and alleys,
and recite this verse:'
Wéiyán then provided meals for the Buddha and the Sangha.
Within the city of Shèwèi.
There was a Brahmin named Bīntóulúduǒshé.
His wife was ugly and hideous, with two eyes that were deep blue.
They had seven daughters but no sons.
He himself was poor, his wife was destitute and fond of scolding.
When his daughters came seeking necessities, he would glare at them with tears streaming down.
In his field, there was ripe grain, so he borrowed an ox from someone else.
He took it to trample the grain but lost it in the marsh.
At that time, the Brahmin sat and thought to himself:
"What sin have I committed?
I am tormented by my wife and daughters, and now I have lost another man's ox."
Exhausted from searching, he happened to arrive in a forest.
There he encountered the Tathāgata.
Upon seeing him, a thought arose:
"The ascetic Gautama is now the most at ease.
He has none of my troubles."
The Buddha knew his thoughts.
And said to him:
"As you have thought,
the Buddha told him:
'Do you wish to leave home?'
He immediately replied to the Buddha:
'World-Honored One,
if you permit it, it would fulfill my humble wish.' The Buddha said:
'Come, bhikṣu.'
His beard and hair fell off by themselves.
The clothes he was wearing transformed into a monastic robe.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to him.
And he became an arhat.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the past, there was a king
named Ābōluótídìmùqū.
He governed with the Way.
At that time, there was a Brahmin
named Tánnìjī.
His home was empty and poor, with a small amount of ripe grain.
He borrowed an ox to trample and process it, then drove it back to its owner.
But he forgot to inform him.
Although the ox owner saw it, he thought it was not yet finished being used.
So he did not take it back, and both households abandoned it.
The ox owner took Tánnìjī to the king for a judgment.
As they left, they encountered the king's horse running loose.
He called to Tánnìjī, 'Stop the horse for me.'
Picking up a stone he found, he threw it.
It hit the horse's leg and broke it.
Next, they came to a river and did not know where to cross.
They encountered a woodcutter.
With an adze in his mouth, he lifted his clothes and was about to cross.
Tánnìjī asked that man:
'Where can we cross?'
As he answered,
his mouth opened and the adze fell into the water.
Pressed by his creditors and also hungry and thirsty,
he went to a wine seller and begged for a little white wine.
He got onto the bed to drink it.
Unknowingly, there was a small child lying beneath the covers.
He pressed on the child's stomach, and it ruptured.
He went to a wall,
thinking and fearing punishment.
He leaped over the wall himself.
Below, there was a weaver.
He fell on him and killed him.
The weaver's son then caught him.
And together with the crowd, took him to the king.
'You killed my father.'
At that time, the creditors brought him before the king.
Then the ox owner stepped forward and said to the king:
'This man borrowed an ox from me.
He did not return it to me.
He lost it and will not compensate.'
The king asked why.
Tánnìjī said:
'I did borrow the ox, and after using it, I drove it back.
The owner also saw it.
Although I did not verbally hand it over, the ox was at his gate.'
The king said to that man:
'Both are at fault.
Because Tánnìjī did not verbally hand it over to you,
his tongue should be cut out.
Because you saw the ox but did not take it back,
your eyes should be gouged out.'
That man said to the king:
'I beg to abandon this ox; I do not wish to have my eyes gouged or his tongue cut out.'
So he allowed them to reconcile.
The horse handler then said:
'That man acted without principle and broke my horse's leg.'
The king then asked:
'This is the king's horse; how dare you break its leg?'
Kneeling, he said to the king:
'The creditors were bringing me along the road.
That man called to me to stop the king's horse.
Picking up a stone, I threw it.
And accidentally broke the horse's leg.'
The king said:
'Because you called him, your tongue should be cut out.
Because he struck the horse, his hand should be cut off.'
The horse handler said to the king:
'I beg for each to reconcile.'
The woodcutter stepped forward and said:
'Tánnìjī lost my adze.'
The king said to the woodcutter:
'Because he called you, his tongue should be cut out.
The proper way to carry something is with the hands.
Because you carried it in your mouth,
two of your teeth should be broken.'
The woodcutter said to the king:
'I would rather abandon the adze than have this punishment carried out.'
Then the wine seller's mother came forward and said to the king, 'He wrongfully killed my son.'
Kneeling, he said to the king:
'I was driven by hunger and thirst.
I begged for a little wine to drink.
Unknowingly, there was a small child lying beneath the covers.
May the king investigate.'
The king said to the woman:
'Your house sells wine, and there are many customers.
Why did you place the child in a seating area?
Both are at fault.
Your son is already dead.
Let Tánnìjī become your son-in-law.
When he gives you a grandson, then he may go free.'
The woman kowtowed and said:
'Allow us to reconcile.
I do not need a husband.'
Then the weaver's son came forward:
'This man is violent and trampled my father to death.'
The king asked:
'Did you kill his father?'
Tánnìjī said:
'The crowd was pressing and accusing me.
In panic, I leaped over the wall and accidentally fell on him.
It was truly not my intention.'
The king said to that man:
'Both are at fault.
Your father is already dead.
Let Tánnìjī become your father.'
That man said to the king:
'My father is now dead.
I certainly do not want this Brahmin as my father.
Allow us to reconcile.'
The king then permitted it.
At that time, Tánnìjī's matters were all settled, so he remained before the king.
He saw two women arguing over a child.
The king was wise and clever, using his wisdom to devise a plan.
'Now there is only one child,
and two mothers are fighting over him.
I will let each of you two pull one of his hands.
Whoever can take him,
the one who is not the mother has no compassion for the child and will pull with all her strength.
The birth mother, out of deep compassion for the child,
cannot bear to pull hard.'
The king discerned the truth.
He questioned the impostor who forcibly seized another's child.
She then confessed to the king, and the child was returned to his mother.
Each was then sent away.
At that time, Tánnìjī said to the king:
'Earlier, on the roadside,
I encountered a poisonous snake who asked me to tell the king:
"I do not know why, when I leave my hole, I am soft and flexible,
but when I return to my hole, I suffer obstruction and pain."'
The king replied:
'When leaving the hole, there are no disturbances,
so the mind is calm and gentle, and the body is likewise.
Outside, birds, beasts, and various things provoke and annoy,
causing anger to swell and the body to become coarse and large.
You can tell it:
If it maintains a mind free from anger, it will not have this problem.'
Next, he saw a woman.
She asked me to tell the king:
"When I am at my husband's home, I miss my parents' house.
When I am at my parents' house, I miss my husband's home."'
The king said:
'You can tell her:
Because of your improper thoughts,
while at your parents' house, you took a lover.
When at your husband's home, you think of that lover.
When with him and slightly displeased, you think of your proper husband again.
That is why it is so.
If she maintains a mind free from improper thoughts, she will not have this problem.'
Next, in a tree, he saw a pheasant.
It asked me to tell the king:
"When I am in other trees, my song is not good.
But when I am in this tree, my song is mournful and harmonious.
I do not know why."'
The king told that man:
'Because under that tree, there is a large pot of gold.
That is why, when perched above it, its song is mournful and good.
Other places have no gold,
so the sound is not good.'
The king told Tánnìjī:
'You have many faults, but I have pardoned you.
You are poor and suffering; take the pot of gold under the tree.
I give it to you.'
He received the king's instruction, dug up the ground, and took the gold.
He traded for what he needed and lived happily without want.
At that time, the great king was I.
As for Tánnìjī,
he is now the Brahmin Bīntóulúduǒshé.'
In the country of Pāṭaliputra, there was a Brahmin.
His name was Āgnidatta.
He was well-versed in the scriptures and treatises.
After taking a wife, she soon became pregnant.
During her pregnancy, she greatly desired to engage in debate.
Her husband consulted a fortune-teller.
The fortune-teller replied,
"The child in the womb is skilled in debate."
When the months were fulfilled, she gave birth to a son.
He mastered all the scriptures and treatises.
He became a teacher of the Brahmins.
He also taught people the art of medicine.
At that time, the people of Rājagṛha,
according to their clans, invited the Buddha and the monastic community.
At that time, the Brahmins
gathered from all directions and set their own rule:
each would contribute one hundred coins for the Buddha and the monastic community.
At that time, the Brahmin Jītou knew that Yì was poor and had no money,
and could not obtain anything to offer to the assembly.
The people said,
"You have no money."
Jītou then returned to his wife and said,
"The people have driven me out of the assembly
because I have no money."
His wife replied,
"You may go into the city and borrow one hundred coins."
He searched everywhere but could not obtain them.
He returned and told his wife.
His wife again said,
"Go to the house of the elder Fúshémìduōluó,
and borrow from him."
He went and pleaded, promising to repay in seven days.
"If I do not repay, my wife and I will become your slaves."
The elder then lent him one hundred gold coins, and he returned to tell his wife.
His wife said,
"Take them to the assembly and say,
'I have obtained the money; allow me to join the ranks.'"
The assembly said to Jītou,
"It is already settled; we do not need your money."
Jītou then returned.
The husband and wife went to the World-Honored One.
They exchanged greetings.
At that time, Jītou's wife bowed at the feet of the World-Honored One.
She fully explained everything to the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Jītou,
"You may then invite the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus."
At that time, Jītou's wife said to her husband,
"Follow the Buddha's teaching."
At that time, Jītou rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder,
joined his palms, and said to the Buddha,
"May the World-Honored One accept my invitation,
along with the community of bhikṣus."
The World-Honored One remained silent.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King,
"Koubiluo, assist this Brahmin
in preparing the third meal."
He replied, "I accept your command."
At that time, Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King, concealed his form,
transformed into a human body, and commanded five hundred rākṣasas,
"Quickly go to the sandalwood forest,
and bring fragrant firewood.
We will offer a meal to the Buddha and the monastic community in the Bamboo Grove.
Transform into an iron kitchen."
The five hundred rākṣasas each carried ox-head sandalwood fragrant firewood into the iron kitchen.
At that time, Jītou used the iron kitchen to cook the food.
The fragrance spread for twelve yojanas, and all could smell it.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to the deva Viśvakarmā,
"You may transform into a spacious and lofty lecture hall,
so that the Buddha and the monastic community may sit and eat."
He replied, "I accept your command."
In the time it takes a strong man to bend and stretch his arm,
he descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to the Bamboo Grove.
Beside the iron kitchen, he transformed into a lecture hall,
made of the seven treasures.
He created one thousand two hundred and fifty seats,
adorned with embroidered patterns.
Holding incense burners, he burned various precious incenses.
He made the tāla trees adorned with the seven treasures.
A gentle breeze stirred, and the sound of bells could be heard from afar.
At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha heard of this.
He asked his ministers,
and the ministers replied,
"It is the Brahmin Jītou,
who is cooking food for the Buddha and the monastic community in an iron kitchen using ox-head sandalwood.
This is the source of the fragrance."
The king then went to the Buddha's place.
He said to his ministers,
"In ancient times, there was no such lecture hall.
Who created it?"
The ministers said to the king,
"We do not know."
The World-Honored One explained everything to the king as above.
The king shed tears, unable to contain himself.
He thought, "Sentient beings have little merit and short lives,
and do not even know the names of these treasures, let alone see them.
Now, by the Buddha's grace, I have seen this lecture hall,
which has never appeared before."
The World-Honored One said,
"In the future, sentient beings will not even hear of the seven treasures,
let alone see them with their own eyes.
Now, by the Buddha's grace, they witness such things."
The World-Honored One expounded the subtle Dharma for the king,
bringing joy to his heart.
The king said,
"The Brahmin Jītou has obtained great benefit."
The king said,
"I wish to return to the palace."
The Buddha said,
"Now is the time."
The Buddha said to Jītou,
"You may invite the king to offer a day's meal."
He replied, "So be it."
He then went to the king, raised his right hand,
and said to the king,
"May the Heavenly King
accept my invitation tomorrow and gather in this lecture hall."
The king remained silent.
The next day, at dawn, Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King, bathed.
Jītou was given fine clothes,
held an incense burner,
and went to the World-Honored One.
He prostrated with his head to the ground and thought,
"Now is the time.
The meal is prepared.
May you graciously come."
The Buddha, surrounded by the monastic community, went to the lecture hall.
He took his seat, and the monks sat in order.
At that time, the king, adorned and surrounded by ministers, went to Jītou's place.
Delicious food of a hundred varieties was served.
They assisted Jītou in offering the meal to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered Śrāvastī.
There was another Brahmin,
old and mature in years,
who held a staff and a bowl, begging from house to house.
The World-Honored One asked him,
"Why are you like this?"
He replied,
"Gautama,
I have given all my wealth to my son,
arranged a marriage for him, and then renounced everything,
holding a bowl to beg for food."
The Buddha again said to him,
"Can you receive and recite a verse from my Dharma,
and then teach it to your son?"
He replied to the Buddha, "I can receive it."
At that time, the World-Honored One recited a verse.
The Brahmin received the verse from the Buddha.
Returning home, upon reaching the door,
he first addressed the assembly,
"Listen to what I say."
Then he recited the verse as above.
His son felt ashamed and fearful,
immediately embraced his father, and brought him back into the house.
He rubbed his body, bathed him, and covered him with clothes and blankets.
He reinstated him as the head of the household.
At that time, the Brahmin thought,
"I have now gained victory over my clan; this is the grace of the śramaṇa.
According to my scriptures,
one should make offerings to a teacher as to a teacher.
I now take this exquisite robe
to the World-Honored One, bow before him, and say,
'May you accept this robe,
out of compassion for me.'"
The World-Honored One accepted it.
He further expounded various Dharmas,
instructing, teaching, illuminating, and delighting him.
In a past age,
there was a young Brahmin
named Sànruò.
He went to an archery master to learn archery.
The master said, "You may learn."
For seven years, Sànruò constantly practiced this craft.
Later, he asked his master,
"When may I stop?"
The master replied,
"Take your bow and nock an arrow.
I will briefly enter the village; wait until I return before you release it."
The master then entered the village.
Sànruò waited for his master for a long time, but he did not return.
He shot at a large tree ahead, and the arrow accidentally wounded a snake.
When the master returned, he asked,
"Have you not yet released the arrow?"
Sànruò replied, "I already have."
The master said,
"If you had not released it,
you would have become the foremost master in Jambudvīpa.
But since you have already released the arrow,
after my death, you shall be next."
The master then adorned his daughter
and gave her, along with five hundred arrows and a horse-drawn carriage, to Sànruò.
Sànruò accepted them.
While crossing a wilderness,
there were five hundred bandits
eating in the wilderness.
Sànruò sent his wife to beg for food from the bandits.
The bandits said,
"Judging by his messenger, he is no ordinary man.
It is fitting to give him food."
One bandit said,
"Should we, while still alive, allow this man to take his wife and carriage away?"
Sànruò shot at them,
and each fell dead with a single arrow.
As they rose, he shot them, and none survived.
Only the bandit leader remained, and he said to the wife,
"Take off your clothes and place them on the ground."
She immediately removed her clothes.
Seeing this, Sànruò shot him, and he fell dead with the arrow.
The five hundred bandits were the five hundred bhikṣus,
and Sànruò was Śāriputra.
The Buddha entered Śrāvastī to seek alms.
His robe had a small tear.
A Brahmin
saw the Buddha's torn robe
and immediately brought a small piece of white cloth from his home.
He offered it to the Buddha,
saying, "May the Tathāgata use this cloth to mend his robe."
The Buddha accepted it.
The Buddha then bestowed a prediction upon him,
saying that in a future world,
after two asaṃkhyeyas and one hundred kalpas, he would attain Buddhahood.
The Brahmin joyfully departed.
The wealthy elders and householders in the country said,
"Why does the World-Honored One give such a great reward for a small offering?"
Each then offered fine cloth to the Buddha to make various robes.
In the past, there was a Buddha
named Vipaśyin.
At that time, there was a king named Paṇḍu.
A minister
invited the Buddha and his saṅgha for a three-month offering.
The Buddha accepted.
King Paṇḍu then said to the Buddha,
"I desire to offer to the Buddha and his saṅgha for three months."
The Buddha told Paṇḍu,
"I have already accepted the minister's invitation."
The king told the minister,
"The Buddha is in my kingdom.
Since you have already invited him, please yield to me."
The minister replied to the king,
"If Your Majesty can guarantee my life,
and also guarantee that the Tathāgata will remain here forever,
and that the kingdom will always be peaceful, then I will relent."
The king further explained,
"You invite for one day, and I will invite for the next."
The minister agreed.
Thus, both fulfilled their wishes.
The king prepared three robes for the Buddha
and also made seven-piece robes for ninety thousand bhikṣus.
The minister offered food and clothing to the Buddha and his saṅgha.
That minister was I.
There was a Brahmin
who asked his wife,
"Do we have any food at home?
I do not wish to accompany others in offering to the ascetic Gautama."
The wife said, "We do."
He then took it and went.
Encountering the king, ministers, kṣatriyas, Brahmins, and eighteen great village chiefs seated there,
the Brahmin dared not approach.
He thought to himself,
"The Buddha is omniscient; he should know my mind."
The Buddha called him from afar and asked,
"What is in your vessel?"
He replied, "It is flatbread."
The Buddha said,
"Distribute it among the saṅgha."
He replied, "It is too little to go around."
The Buddha said,
"Just distribute it."
After one round, the bread remained undiminished.
Even after three rounds, it still did not decrease.
The Buddha, knowing his mind,
expounded the Dharma accordingly, and he attained the path of stream-enterer.
In the past, there was a nāga king
named Bádi.
His nature was violent and cruel.
He frequently caused storms, thunder, lightning, and hail, killing people,
birds, beasts, and creeping creatures without number.
Ten thousand venerable arhats gathered to discuss,
"If one kills a single person, they fall into hell for a kalpa, and the sin is still not exhausted.
Now, this nāga has harmed countless beings
without cease.
We fear he will be difficult to subdue.
Let us go together to admonish him."
At that time, the Buddha knew of this
and praised them, saying, "Excellent!"
The ten thousand arhats then went together.
The nāga released storms, rain, thunder, lightning, and hail.
The ten thousand arhats were terrified and immediately returned, prostrating themselves.
At that time, the Buddha was on Vulture Peak,
and together with ten thousand bodhisattvas and ten thousand arhats, he went to the nāga's abode.
The nāga became enraged
and unleashed violent winds, torrential rain, thunder, hail, and lightning.
He released a hailstone, making it as large as a wall,
forty zhang in size.
If it reached the ground, it would sink four feet deep.
He intended to harm the Buddha and the bodhisattva saṅgha.
When the arhats saw the nāga's calamitous transformations,
each filled with terror, they drew near to the Buddha.
The nāga himself saw the hailstones transform into a canopy of flowers.
He then thought to himself,
"I will coil my body tightly to a length of forty zhang
and hurl myself upon the Buddha and the saṅgha."
Immediately, he hurled himself but could not strike anyone.
Raising his head and opening his eyes, he gazed intently at the Buddha.
Suspecting this was a supremely wondrous and divine being,
the smaller nāgas also hurled themselves but could not move him.
The nāga king then ended his life and was reborn as a deva.
The other smaller nāgas also ended their lives and became devas.
They all descended and stood by the Buddha's side.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"Do you know from where these devas were reborn?"
Ānanda replied, "I do not know."
The Buddha said,
"These are the nāgas who earlier harbored evil intentions.
They hurled themselves to the ground, gave rise to a single good thought, and recognized the Buddha as supreme.
They ended their lives and became devas; these are they."
Hearing the Buddha's words,
the deva and the other devas all gave rise to the intention for unsurpassed, impartial liberation.
The Buddha said,
"In the past, the nāga king Bádi and Śākyamuni Buddha were both Brahmins.
Bádi had
ten thousand disciples at that time.
They abandoned their master to follow Śākyamuni.
Bádi, harboring resentment, became a nāga.
The Buddha, having attained enlightenment, saved many beings.
The ten thousand disciples all became arhats.
The nāga, filled with venomous malice, sought to harm them.
Though the ten thousand were accomplished in the four paths,
they still suffered his humiliation.
But if one is a bodhisattva, the nāga dares not harm them."
In the past, there was a Brahmin
who disliked worldly affairs.
He secluded himself in the mountains, single-mindedly contemplating the Way.
He entered meditative concentration for over three hundred years.
Dust and earth buried his body, and plants grew upon him.
At the foot of the mountain, there were several hundred Brahmins who kept wives and children.
Young and old together gathered firewood, climbing trees,
breaking off dry branches and roots.
The tree connected to the Brahmin's forehead shook as it was disturbed.
The Brahmin awoke from his meditation and emerged from the ground.
Seeing the firewood gatherers, he asked them,
"Who are you?"
They replied,
"We are Brahmins."
"Who are the others?"
They replied,
"Our wives and children."
The Brahmin laughed and said,
"I have been in meditation for over three hundred years,
and I still dare not call myself a Brahmin.
How can you bear to call yourselves Brahmins?"
In the past, east of Shèwèi City,
there was a very wealthy Brahmin.
His son took a wife,
who came from a Buddhist family.
She upheld the Five Precepts and observed the Six Fasting Days,
and was always fond of giving alms to śramaṇas and ascetics.
She urged her husband to cultivate generosity.
Her husband then understood and was enlightened.
He informed his parents,
who became greatly enraged,
saying it would ruin their family.
The wife gave money and silk to her husband,
who gave it to the maid guarding the inner gate.
The maid gave it to the slave guarding the main gate,
who took it to the Buddhist monastery,
to give alms to the śramaṇas, burn incense, and light lamps.
The husband and wife together made a vow:
"Even if this act of giving brings no merit for ourselves,
or if it does bring merit,
may all people under heaven witness it together."
At that time, it was the national custom on the third day of the third month
for all the people of the country to go to the waterside to make music, sing, and play games.
Then, from the southeast corner, a deva appeared,
riding a white horse and passing through the sky.
The crowd looked up and asked what divine spirit this was.
He replied,
"Ask the one who comes later."
After a short while, there appeared a hall of seven treasures,
with a jade maiden sitting alone atop it,
borne aloft by four great devas.
The crowd asked again,
"What merit do you possess?"
The jade maiden also
said, "Ask the one who comes later."
Soon after, there came a four-pillared treasure hall,
with a deva and a jade maiden sitting together inside it,
surrounded by musicians on all four sides,
borne aloft by twelve devas.
The crowd asked again,
"What merit do you possess?"
They also answered,
"Ask the one who comes later."
After a short while, there appeared two hungry ghosts,
their bodies three zhang tall,
black, emaciated, ugly, suffering from hunger and thirst,
their bodies burning,
each holding a large club and beating each other.
The crowd asked again,
and they replied,
"Have you all heard of the very wealthy Brahmin east of Shèwèi City?
The one riding the white horse is the slave guarding the main gate.
The jade maiden in the small hall is the maid guarding the inner gate.
The two in the great hall are my son and my daughter-in-law.
The two ghosts are the Brahmin couple.
In their previous life, they were foolish and deluded, not believing in the true Dharma.
Now they face calamity and misfortune—what can be done?"
The Buddha traveled to the city of the Brahmins.
The Brahmin kings,
knowing the Tathāgata's divine virtue could move the hearts of the multitude,
feared that once they received his teachings, who would listen to their words?
Therefore, they together established a rule:
Anyone who gives food to the Buddha or listens to the Buddha's words shall be fined five hundred gold coins.
When the Buddha entered the city to beg for food,
people all closed their doors, and he left with an empty bowl.
There was a servant woman
who took a broken earthenware vessel containing foul fermented rice water and went out to discard it.
Seeing the Buddha with an empty bowl, her faith was pure,
and she wished to make an offering but had no means to fulfill her wish.
She said, "If this poor food is needed, you may take it."
The Buddha, knowing her intention, accepted her offering and said,
"This woman, through offering food, shall for fifteen kalpas
enjoy happiness and blessings in the heavens and among humans, not falling into evil paths.
Later, she will be reborn as a man, leave home to study the path, and become a pratyekabuddha."
A Brahmin nearby
spoke in verse, accusing the Buddha of lying for the sake of food,
saying, "How can such foul food bring such a heavy reward?"
The Buddha then extended his tongue, covering his face up to his hairline,
and said to the Brahmin,
"Have you ever seen in the scriptures a tongue like this that speaks falsehood?"
The Brahmin said,
"With such a tongue, one certainly does not speak falsely.
But I do not understand how such a small offering can bring such a great reward."
The Buddha said,
"Have you ever seen the Nyagrodha tree, whose shade can cover five hundred merchant carts and still not be exhausted?"
He replied, "I have seen it."
The Buddha asked again,
"How large is the seed of this tree?"
He replied,
"Like one-third of a mustard seed."
The Buddha asked again,
"Who would believe this?"
He replied,
"It is seen with one's own eyes."
The Buddha said,
"I am also like this.
This old woman obtained a great fruit of reward
because the field of merit of the Tathāgata is excellent and virtuous."
Then the Brahmin's mind opened and understood; he prostrated himself with his five limbs on the ground and repented before the Buddha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to him, and he attained the first fruit of the path.
He then cried out loudly to the crowd,
"The gate of ambrosia is open—why do you not come out?"
The Brahmins begged to pay the fine,
welcomed the Buddha, and made offerings.
The Brahmin kings, along with their ministers and people, took refuge in the Buddha's Dharma.
All the men and women in the city attained pure faith.
In the past, there was an elder named Xūdá,
who invited the Buddha and the saṅgha to a grand assembly.
On the way, he met a person carrying a bottle of yogurt.
Seeing a Brahmin, he asked him to carry it back.
When they arrived and saw the Buddha and the saṅgha, he was overjoyed and stayed,
listened to the sutras, observed the fasting, and only returned in the evening.
His wife at home found this very strange.
She also did not eat until evening, then urged him to eat.
He did not complete the fasting observance, and after his life ended,
his spirit became a great tree spirit in a marsh in the land of Uttarakuru.
At that time, there were five hundred scholars
who wished to go to the Three Shrine God's pool to bathe, hoping to become immortals.
Their provisions were exhausted, and they had no water or drink,
so they became distressed and weary.
Seeing the tree from afar, they thought it was a spring,
but when they reached the tree, there was no spring at all.
They were on the verge of great distress
when they cried out together, begging the tree spirit to save their lives.
The tree spirit then manifested half its body,
raised its right hand, and from its fingertip
naturally flowed food of a hundred flavors,
and it offered honeyed drink and all kinds of provisions,
so that they were all fully satisfied.
Then the five hundred people discussed among themselves,
"We wished to go to the divine pool to bathe, hoping to become immortals.
But compared to this lofty path of immortality, how could that surpass it?"
They asked the tree spirit again,
"What merit did you cultivate to possess such sacred virtue?"
The tree spirit replied,
"In the past, I saw the Buddha at the vihāra in Shèwèi,
and observed the Eight Precepts Fasting.
But I was disrupted by my wife and did not complete the fasting observance.
My spirit should have been reborn in heaven.
Then the five hundred people together upheld the fasting observance and precepts,
and later attained the path of the stream-enterer.
In the past, there was a Brahmin couple
who had no children
but possessed immeasurable wealth.
As they approached the end of their lives, they said to each other,
'Let us each swallow coins to serve as provisions.'
According to the customs of their country,
the dead were not buried but placed under trees.
Each swallowed fifty gold coins and died.
When their bodies decayed, the coins came out.
A wise man in the country saw this while walking,
and shed tears of pity, grieving at their stinginess and greed.
He arranged blessings for them,
inviting the Buddha and the saṅgha and preparing offerings with all his heart.
Holding food before the Buddha, he invoked their names and made a vow.
Then the stingy couple,
suffering the torments of hungry ghosts, were reborn in heaven.
He arranged blessings widely, inviting the four assemblies.
Those reborn in heaven, having attained the divine eye, knew that blessings were being made for them.
They descended from heaven, transformed into youths, and assisted the donor.
The Buddha said,
"These youths in the kitchen are the true donors."
When they arrived, he preached the Dharma, and they attained the path.
The wise man also attained the path.
The assembly rejoiced, and all were reborn in heaven.
When the Buddha was in the world, there was a Brahmin
who had two daughters, both of beautiful appearance.
He deliberately hung gold
and for ninety days sought someone who could criticize the girls' ugliness.
If they could, he would give them the gold.
No one came forward to take up the challenge.
He brought them to the Buddha,
and the Buddha criticized them, saying,
"These girls are both ugly; there is not one good thing about them."
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
"These girls are beautiful, yet the Buddha says they are ugly.
What is not good about them?"
The Buddha said,
"Eyes that do not look at forms are good.
The ears, nose, and mouth are also like this.
A body that does not crave fine and smooth sensations is good.
Hands that do not steal others' wealth are good hands.
Not committing these acts is what is truly good.
Eyes that look at forms, ears that listen to sounds, a nose that smells fragrances,
a body that delights in fine and smooth sensations,
hands that delight in stealing others' wealth—
such things are not good."
In the past, there was the city of Duōshòuyì.
There was a Brahmin
who served as the Grand Historian for the king.
He was the foremost in the kingdom.
He had a son.
On his head was a natural flame-like tuft of hair,
and because of this, he was named accordingly.
His appearance was upright and handsome, possessing thirty marks.
There was a potter's son,
named Nántí Póluó,
who from childhood was a close friend of Huǒmán, and they held mutual respect and affection in their hearts.
The potter's son was diligent, courageous, compassionate, benevolent, filial, and obedient.
Both his parents were blind, yet he provided for them without lack.
Although he was a potter, his hands never dug the earth.
He only took broken walls, collapsed banks, and rat burrows, mixing them to make vessels.
If there were buyers,
he would place grain, wheat, hemp, or beans on the ground and take the vessels.
He never haggled over prices from the start.
He also did not accept gold, silver, wealth, or silk.
He only took grain and rice to provide sustenance.
The vihāra where Kāśyapa Tathāgata resided
was not far from Duōshòuyì.
He was with twenty thousand great bhikṣus,
all of whom were arhats.
Hùxǐ said to Huǒmán:
"Let us go together to see Kāśyapa Tathāgata."
Huǒmán replied:
"What use is seeing this ascetic?
He is merely a shaven-headed man.
What Way does he possess?"
The Buddha's Way is difficult to attain.
Thus it went up to three times.
Hùxǐ again said to Huǒmán:
"Shall we go together to bathe in the water?"
Huǒmán replied, "Very well."
Then they went together to the water to bathe.
Hùxǐ raised his right hand and pointed into the distance, saying:
"Kāśyapa's vihāra is not far from here.
We can go together for a brief visit."
Huǒmán replied:
"What use is seeing this?"
Hùxǐ then grabbed Huǒmán's clothing and pulled.
Huǒmán took off his clothes and ran away.
Hùxǐ then seized his head and pulled, saying:
"Just this once, come with me to see the Buddha."
The custom of the kingdom forbade seizing a person's head; the penalty for such an act was beheading.
Huǒmán, alarmed and fearful, thought to himself:
"Is the potter's son determined to die by seizing my head?"
Hùxǐ said:
"Even if I die,
I will not let go until death.
I must make you see the Buddha."
Huǒmán thought to himself:
"There must surely be something good about this.
Otherwise, why would this man be so determined to die by seizing me?"
Huǒmán said:
"Release my head, and I will go with you."
Then he tied up his hair, put on his clothes,
and followed him to see Kāśyapa Buddha.
Hùxǐ addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This Huǒmán is my childhood friend.
However, he does not recognize or have faith in the Three Jewels.
I wish the World-Honored One would enlighten him."
The youth Huǒmán beheld the Buddha's excellent marks.
He thought to himself:
"All the marks recorded in the texts are present,
except for two things."
At that time, Kāśyapa Tathāgata
then extended his broad, long tongue to cover his face,
and his uṣṇīṣa, also covering both ears seven times.
He licked his head and retracted his tongue into his mouth.
Light and color emanated, illuminating the great thousandfold world,
obscuring the light of the sun and moon, reaching even up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
The light then circled his body seven times and entered from the top of his head.
Through his supernatural power, he manifested the hidden horse's member,
causing Huǒmán alone to see it,
while others did not behold it.
The youth Huǒmán fully saw the Buddha's thirty-two marks.
He leaped for joy, unable to contain himself.
Kāśyapa Tathāgata
explained to the youth Huǒmán the merits of the bodhisattva's abandonment.
What are the merits of the bodhisattva's abandonment?
The body should not act, yet it acts;
the mouth should not speak, yet it speaks;
the mind should not think, yet it thinks.
These are the three evil actions of a bodhisattva.
Thereupon, Huǒmán approached, bowed at the Buddha's feet, and said:
"I now repent and wish the Buddha to accept it.
From now on, I dare not transgress again."
Thus he said up to three times.
Kāśyapa Tathāgata silently accepted it.
The youth Huǒmán and the youth Hùxǐ
both bowed at the Buddha's feet, took their leave, and returned.
Huǒmán said:
"You have suffered loss, not gained benefit.
I do not delight in seeing your face.
I do not delight in hearing your name."
Hùxǐ replied:
"Why is it so?"
Huǒmán said:
"You heard the profound Dharma from the Buddha long ago.
How can you remain a householder?"
Hùxǐ replied:
"My parents are old and both are blind.
How can I leave home while providing for my two parents?
If I leave home, my parents will die.
That is why I cannot leave home."
Huǒmán said to Hùxǐ:
"I heard from Kāśyapa Buddha about the bodhisattva's practice and the three evil conditions.
I no longer delight in being a householder.
I wish to return from here to the Buddha and seek to become a bhikṣu."
Hùxǐ replied:
"Excellent, Huǒmán.
Have you attained the power of contemplation?
Then you should return now.
The reason is that encountering a Buddha in the world is difficult."
The youth Huǒmán then embraced Hùxǐ,
circled him three times, joined his palms, and apologized, saying:
"If I have any faults of body, speech, or mind toward you,
I hope you will forgive me.
For you have pointed out the true and right Great Way."
Thereupon, Huǒmán spoke a verse in praise, saying:
After speaking this verse,
he circled Hùxǐ three times and returned to the vihāra.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"May I enter the Path and receive the full precepts?"
Then he ordained Huǒmán and conferred upon him the full precepts.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"The youth Huǒmán at that time was my own body.
Huǒmán's father is now King Śuddhodana.
Hùxǐ, who repeatedly urged me to leave home,
was then my good spiritual friend.
I previously spoke evil words to Hùxǐ, saying:
'Kāśyapa Buddha is a bald-headed śramaṇa; what Way does he possess?'
Therefore, for six years I endured eating one sesame seed, one grain of rice, one large bean, and one small bean each day.
In the past, there was a Brahmin
who served non-Buddhist paths.
His wife served the Buddha.
She said to her husband:
'Allow me to become a servant for the Buddha,
hanging banners and canopies, burning incense, and lighting lamps.'
Her husband did not permit it.
So she made a banner and hung it inside the house.
Morning and evening she bowed toward it.
Her husband killed oxen and sheep and called a master to perform rituals.
When the master arrived at their door, he said:
'Your house has a Buddha banner and canopy.
I dare not enter.'
The husband then went in and asked his wife.
Searching, he found the banner.
The husband, angry, beat his wife.
The wife then threw herself into the river.
Her sincere heart moved the spirits, and the river water dried up.
Naturally, a seven-jeweled canopy appeared above her.
Seeing this marvel, the husband knew the Buddha was worthy of reverence.
He then abandoned the non-Buddhist paths and served the Great Dharma.
In the city of Bátíchéng, there was a great householder,
named Wéntú, who was extremely wealthy in jewels and treasures and possessed great power.
He gave to people according to their wishes.
In his granary was a hole as large as a cart axle,
from which grain and rice spontaneously emerged.
His wife used eight dou to make rice,
feeding four armies and people from all directions who came.
The food never ran out.
His son gave a thousand taels of gold to the four armies and beggars from all directions.
According to their wishes, it never ran out.
His daughter-in-law used one bundle of incense to anoint,
the four armies and beggars from all directions who came, satisfying them according to their wishes.
The incense never ran out.
Their male servant plowed seven furrows in one day with one plow,
producing abundant rice.
Their female servant used eight dou of grain
to feed the horses of the four armies.
The horses' food never ran out.
The family members argued among themselves, each saying:
"It is my merit and power."
Wéntú went to the Buddha, bowed with his head at the Buddha's feet.
He asked,
"Whose power is this?"
The Buddha said,
"It belongs to all of you together.
In the past, in the city of Wángshèchéng, there was a weaver.
The weaver had a wife and also a son, and the son also had a wife.
They had one male servant and one female servant.
One time, they were eating together.
A Pratyekabuddha came to beg for food.
Each of them wanted to give up their own portion to offer.
The Pratyekabuddha said,
'You all have already given with good hearts.
Each of you may reduce your portion a little.
It will not be too little for you.
For me, it will be enough.'
They all followed his suggestion.
After the Pratyekabuddha ate, he displayed various supernatural transformations in the sky.
Then he departed.
The weaver's family members, after their lifespans ended,
were reborn in the Heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings, up to the Heaven of Free Enjoyment of Others' Transformations.
After transmigrating through seven rebirths, their remaining merit led to this birth here."
Míntú heard this.
He then invited the Buddha and the monastic community to receive unlimited offerings.
"Whatever is needed, whenever and however much, all may be taken from me."
The bhikṣus did not dare to accept.
They reported to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"Allow them to accept as they wish."
Later, when the bhikṣus traveled and requested provisions,
he sent messengers carrying gold and silver to follow them wherever they went.
Much of what was given was brought back to the elder.
The elder said,
'I have already given it away; it should not be brought back.'
Yùqié was drunk, surrounded by courtesans,
in the great grove of Píshělí.
From afar, he saw the World-Honored One sitting among the trees.
Upright and extraordinarily wonderful, his faculties and mind were settled in concentration.
His radiance was like a pile of gold.
Upon seeing him, his drunkenness dissipated.
He went to the World-Honored One, sat to one side, and withdrew.
The Buddha expounded the Four Noble Truths to him.
He attained the fearless Dharma.
He bowed with his head at the Buddha's feet.
'I take refuge in the Three Jewels.
I will be an upāsaka, receiving and upholding the five precepts.'
Returning to his original place, he announced to his household,
'You should now know
that I have received precepts from the World-Honored One.
If you wish to enjoy yourselves, practice giving and make merit.
If you are not pleased, each of you may return to your relatives.
I will set you free.'
At that time, the chief wife said,
'My lord has received precepts from the World-Honored One for life.
There is a certain man who should take me as his wife.'
At that moment, the householder summoned that man.
Holding the chief wife's hand with his left hand,
and holding a golden water vessel in his right hand, he said to that man,
'I give this chief wife to you as your wife.'
That man was terrified, his hair standing on end.
He said to Yùqié,
'Householder, do you not wish to kill me?'
He replied, 'No.
I have undertaken the pure life from the Buddha for life.
Therefore, I give my chief wife to you.
I will never change or regret this.'
In the past, there was a great clan
that always delighted in generosity.
Later, they gave birth to a son.
He had no hands or feet.
His body resembled a fish.
He was named Yúshēn (Fish-body).
When his parents passed away, he inherited and managed the family estate.
He lay in his bedroom, and no one saw him.
At that time, there was a strongman
who relied on the king's kitchen for food.
He constantly suffered from hunger and deprivation.
Alone, he pulled sixteen cartloads of firewood,
selling them to support himself.
Yet he was often not provided for.
He went to this man of the fourth caste to seek what he lacked.
Yúshēn requested to meet him.
He showed him his body.
The strongman thought to himself,
'With my strength like this,
I am inferior to a man without hands and feet.'
He went to the Buddha and asked about his doubt.
The Buddha said,
'In the time of Buddha Kāśyapa,
Yúshēn and this king were offering food to the Buddha.
You were poor then and assisted in the tasks.
Yúshēn prepared what the king offered.
But he said to the king,
"Today I have duties and cannot go together.
If I go, it would be no different than cutting off my hands and feet."
The one who went then is the present king.
The one who did not go and spoke thus is Yúshēn.
The one who assisted then is you.'
The strongman understood.
He immediately became a śramaṇa.
He attained the path of an arhat.
In the past, within the city of Shíshìchéng, there were three householders.
The first was named Shélì,
the second was named Pūtuómǎn,
and the third was named Póbōnà.
These three were close brothers.
They had abundant wealth, treasures, elephants, horses, and the seven jewels.
There was a brāhmaṇa
who observed the fast of the dragon Yílubō,
hoping for wealth and honor.
The dragon appeared and said to the brāhmaṇa,
'Why are you toiling so hard now,
fasting, cutting off grains, and eliminating flavors here?
What are you seeking?'
The brāhmaṇa said,
'I hope for great wealth.'
The dragon said,
'I have two names.
One is Yílubō,
the other is Cáiwúyàn (Wealth-Insatiable).
Since I am called Insatiable,
how can you seek from me?'
The brāhmaṇa said,
'If you do not bestow, I will die.'
The dragon brought out purple-polished fine gold to repay him.
At the city gate, there was a wealthy elder
from India.
'Take this gold and seek goods from him.'
The elder saw it and told him,
'Hide it; do not let others see.'
He informed his five relatives.
They feasted and enjoyed themselves, hiding the gold in the treasury.
All the miscellaneous items in the treasury sank into the ground.
They returned to that dragon's treasury.
The wealth of the seven households on the left and right was like this.
The three householders heard of this.
They said to each other,
'Our three households obtained wealth through the Dharma, not unjustly.
Unlike the five households who seized it.'
The people of the country heard this and thought it was boastful talk.
They gathered at the three households.
They asked the householders,
'You claim to have obtained wealth through the Dharma without wrongful loss.
What proof do you have?'
At that time, the three householders each took out ten catties of gold.
They divided it into six portions.
Taking the people and the owners of the lost goods from the seven households,
they went to the dragon spring and threw the gold into the water.
The water all boiled and surged like a cauldron of hot water.
The dragon king was alarmed and frightened.
He immediately sent a dragon maiden to bring out the gold and return it.
He apologized and sent them back.
Those who obtain through the Dharma accomplish things according to principle.
They are never encroached upon by the five households.
Those who hoard wealth unlawfully are like those seven households.'
Once there was a kingdom.
It was named Huānlè Wúyōu (Joy Without Sorrow).
The king was titled Guǎngcí'āi (Vast Compassion and Pity).
In the kingdom lived a householder.
His name was Móhētán (Mahādanā).
His wife was named Zhāntuó (Candā).
They had a son.
His appearance was upright and handsome, peerless in the world.
Upon falling to the ground, he could speak.
He uttered a vow, saying:
"I shall give alms to all under heaven and save the people, especially those who are orphaned, alone, poor, and destitute.
I shall provide for and protect them, enabling them to attain peace and security."
His parents therefore named him Dàyì (Great Intention).
Seeing his extraordinary appearance, unlike other people,
they feared he was a heavenly dragon, ghost, or spirit.
They wished to consult a diviner to inquire.
Dàyì knew of this.
He then replied, saying:
"I am truly a human, not a heavenly dragon, ghost, or spirit.
I merely think of the people of the world who are poor and in distress,
and wish to protect and care for them."
Having expressed this intention,
he then spoke no more.
When he reached the age of seventeen, he told his parents:
"I wish to give alms to suffering people, enabling them to attain peace and security."
His parents thought to themselves:
"When our son was first born, he already had this vow."
They then told their son:
"Our wealth is immeasurable; give freely as you wish, we will not restrict you."
Dàyì replied:
"Although my parents' wealth and goods are plentiful, they are still insufficient for my use.
I must only go to sea to gather treasures in order to provide alms for the people of the world."
He repeated this several times.
His parents then consented.
On his way to sea, Dàyì passed through another country.
In that country was a Brahmin.
His wealth was immeasurable.
Seeing Dàyì's radiant countenance and upright appearance,
he was greatly pleased and delighted by him and said:
"I respect and honor you.
Now I have a young daughter and wish to offer her to you.
I hope you will stay here."
Dàyì replied:
"I have left home to go to sea, wishing to gather the seven treasures.
I dare not promise you this.
Please wait until I return."
He then proceeded to gather treasures.
He immediately sent people to take the treasures back to his own country.
He then went again to the seashore to seek rare objects.
Suddenly he saw a great tree.
It was eighty yojanas high and broad.
Dàyì then climbed the tree and from afar saw a silver city.
Its palaces, towers, halls, and dwellings were all of white silver.
Heavenly maidens attended at his side, and music arose spontaneously.
There was a poisonous snake coiled three times around the city.
Seeing Dàyì, it raised its head. Dàyì thought to himself:
"People are harmed by poison all because they lack good intention."
He then sat down and concentrated his mind.
After a short while, the snake lowered its head and slept.
Dàyì wished to enter the city.
The gatekeeper then entered and reported to the king, saying:
"Outside there is a virtuous one who wishes to see Your Majesty."
The king personally came out to welcome him.
Joyfully, he said:
"I only hope the benevolent one will stay here.
For a period of three months, allow me to offer provisions."
He replied: "I am traveling to gather treasures; it is not suitable for me to stay long."
The king replied, saying:
"I pay no heed to affairs of state.
I only hope you will stay."
Dàyì then stopped.
The king immediately provided clothing, food, drink, music,
and bedding furnishings.
When ninety days had passed,
Dàyì took his leave from the king, wishing to depart.
The king then took rare and precious seven treasures, wishing to give them to him.
Dàyì said:
"I do not have much use for these seven treasures.
I have heard that Your Majesty possesses a bright moon pearl.
I wish to request it."
The king said:
"I do not begrudge this pearl.
But I fear the road is arduous and perilous, making it difficult to carry with you."
Dàyì said:
"When fortune accompanies a person, they do not fear arduous and perilous paths."
The king said:
"This pearl has treasures following it for twenty leagues. I vow
that I may become your disciple and be able to provide offerings,
surpassing those of today."
Dàyì then accepted the pearl and departed.
Thereupon, Dàyì traveled onward and saw a golden city.
Its palaces, towers, halls, and dwellings were all of gold.
Trees of the seven treasures produced music spontaneously.
The heavenly maidens in attendance were twice as many as before.
There was also a poisonous snake coiled six times around the city.
The snake saw Dàyì and raised its head to look at him.
Again he sat and concentrated his mind.
The snake again lowered its head and slept.
Dàyì wished to enter the city.
The gatekeeper immediately entered and reported to the king.
The king immediately came out to meet him and invited him forward.
He spoke, asking him to stay
for a period of three months to allow for offerings.
Dàyì then stopped.
The king treated him as before.
After sixty days had passed, he took his leave to depart.
He said to the king:
"I have heard that Your Majesty possesses a bright moon pearl.
I hope you will bestow it upon me."
The king answered as before.
"Treasures follow it for forty leagues.
I now offer it to you.
When the benevolent one later attains the Way,
may I become your disciple.
With supernatural powers unmatched,
I may then offer provisions surpassing those of today."
He accepted the pearl and departed.
Dàyì traveled onward again.
He saw a crystal city.
Its palaces, towers, halls, dwellings, and everything were as before.
There was also a poisonous snake.
It was coiled nine times around the city, its head lowered in sleep.
The king came out to welcome him.
He hoped he would stay for three months.
Dàyì then stayed.
The king again wholeheartedly provided offerings,
setting out food, drink, clothing, and music.
When forty days had passed, he took his leave to depart.
He said to the king:
"I have heard
that Your Majesty possesses a bright moon pearl.
I hope you will bestow it upon me."
The king then replied, saying:
"This pearl has treasures following it for sixty leagues,
spontaneously pursuing it.
I now offer it to you.
If the benevolent one later attains the Way,
may I become your disciple.
With wisdom unmatched,
I shall again offer provisions surpassing those of today."
He then accepted the pearl and departed.
Traveling onward, he again saw a lapis lazuli city.
He also saw a poisonous snake.
It was coiled twelve times around the city, its head lowered in sleep.
The king welcomed him and begged him to stay for three months.
Dàyì then stayed.
The king personally provided offerings of food, drink, clothing, and music to delight him.
When twenty days had passed, he took his leave to depart.
He said to the king:
"I have heard that Your Majesty possesses a bright moon pearl.
May you bestow it upon me."
The king said:
"This pearl has rare treasures following it for eighty leagues.
I now offer it to you.
When the benevolent one later attains the Way,
may I become your disciple.
With pure intention, I shall offer provisions surpassing those of today,
enabling me to long attain wisdom."
Dàyì accepted the pearl and departed.
He thought to himself:
"I originally came to seek treasures.
Now my wish has been fulfilled; I should return from here."
He then sought the old road, wishing to return to his own country.
While traversing the great sea,
the various divine kings of the sea consulted together, saying:
"Although our sea has many rare and famous treasures,
none compare to these pearls."
They then commanded a sea god to intercept and seize his pearls.
The god then transformed into a human and met Dàyì.
He asked, saying:
"I have heard you have obtained wondrous and rare objects.
Might I borrow them to look at?"
Dàyì opened his hand and showed him the four pearls.
The sea god then shook his hand, causing the pearls to fall into the water.
Dàyì thought to himself:
"The kings told me that these pearls are difficult to safeguard. I was fortunate to have obtained them.
Now they have been taken by this fellow; this is not my purpose."
He immediately said to the sea god:
"I myself toiled diligently, traversing perilous obstacles to obtain these pearls.
You instead seize them from me.
If you do not return them now,
I shall drain the sea dry." The sea god, hearing this, asked, saying:
"Your aspiration is extraordinarily lofty.
The sea is three million three hundred and sixty thousand yojanas deep.
Its breadth is boundless.
How can you drain it?
It is like the sun, which will never fall to earth.
It is like a great wind, which cannot be bundled up.
Even the sun could be made to fall to earth,
even the wind could be bundled up,
but the waters of the great sea cannot be drained to make it dry."
Dàyì laughed and replied, saying:
"I myself reflect:
In my previous and later existences, through birth, death, decay, and destruction,
the accumulated bones surpass Mount Sumeru.
The blood that has flowed could fill five rivers.
The four seas are not enough to serve as a metaphor.
I still wish to sever this root of birth and death.
How could this small sea be insufficient for me to drain?
In the past, I made offerings to all the Buddhas and vowed, saying:
This makes my will and actions courageous in the Way, decisive in direction, without difficulty.
Even if I must move Mount Sumeru and drain the great ocean’s waters, I will never retreat.
With firm resolve, he single‑mindedly used a vessel to bale the seawater.
Moved by his utter sincerity,
the Four Heavenly Kings came to assist Dàyì.
Two‑thirds of the water had already been baled out.
Thereupon the various divine kings of the sea
were all greatly shaken and terrified, and together they deliberated, saying:
“If we do not return his pearl now, it will not be a trivial matter.
Once the water is exhausted and the mud appears, our palaces will be ruined.”
The sea‑god then brought forth a multitude of treasures to give to Dàyì.
Dàyì did not accept them.
He declared:
“I have no use for such things.
I only wish to recover my pearl.
Return my pearl to me, and I will not persist further.”
Knowing his determination was fierce, the sea‑god then brought out the pearl and returned it to him.
Having obtained the pearl, Dàyì crossed over and married a Brāhmaṇa’s daughter.
Returning to his own country, he gave generously in great almsgiving.
From that time onward, within his realm there were no longer any who suffered hunger, cold, poverty, or want.
People from all four directions left their former lands
and, carrying their infants on their backs, turned toward his benevolence.
In this way he practiced charity for many years, his kindness reaching far and wide.
Every creature that flies, crawls, or wriggles received his beneficence.
After his life ended, he was reborn above as Śakra, Lord of the Devas,
or below as a Cakravartin king who travels through the air.
Accumulating merit and virtue, he thereby attained Buddhahood.
His supreme status in the three realms was all due to his past actions;
it was not accidental.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Dàyì was my former self.
The householder Mahādāna of that time is present‑day Śuddhodana.
The mother Candā of that time is present‑day Lady Māyā.
The king of the Joyful‑and‑Carefree Kingdom of that time is Mahākāśyapa.
The Brāhmaṇa maiden of that time is Gopikā.
The maiden’s father of that time is Maitreya.
The king of the Silver City of that time is Ānanda.
The king of the Golden City of that time is Maudgalyāyana.
The king of the Crystal City of that time is Śāriputra.
The king of the Lapis Lazuli City of that time is Sudatta.
The Fourth Heavenly King who assisted Dàyì in baling the seawater is Udāyī.
The one who stole his pearl is Devadatta.
The guards of the four city gates are Subhadra, Pāṇḍaka, Svāgata, and Kālodāyin.
