The poisonous snakes encircling the four cities are the four ministers Cātura, Śāṇḍa, Udraka, and Rāṣṭrapāla.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“By what merit did he obtain the four bright moon‑pearls, with treasures following him?”
The Buddha said:
“In the time of the Buddha Vipaśyin,
Dàyì once used four jewels to build a stūpa for the Buddha.
He made offerings to the Three Jewels and observed the eight precepts for seven days.
At that time there were five hundred people
who together built a monastery.
Some hung silk banners and lit lamps;
some burned incense and scattered flowers;
some made offerings to the community of bhikṣus;
some recited sūtras and expounded the Dharma.
All of them have now come to this assembly.
Once there was a merchant
named Bōlì.
Together with five hundred men he entered the sea in search of treasure.
The sea‑god then scooped up a handful of water
and asked Bōlì:
‘Is the seawater greater, or is this handful of water greater?’
Bōlì replied:
‘The handful of water is greater.
Why is that?
Although the seawater is vast, it is of no timely use;
it cannot save those who are hungry and thirsty.
Though a handful of water is little, if one meets a thirsty person and gives it to him to drink, it can sustain his life.
The blessings received from this act over countless lifetimes are immeasurable.’
The sea‑god rejoiced and praised him, saying, ‘Excellent!’
He then removed from his body eight kinds of fragrant necklaces adorned with the seven treasures
and gave them to Bōlì.
The sea‑god escorted him,
and he returned safely to Śrāvastī.
He presented these fragrant necklaces to King Prasenajit,
fully relating their origin and hoping the king would accept them.
The king, receiving the fragrant necklaces, considered them extraordinarily precious.
He summoned all his consorts to line up before him,
intending to give the necklaces to the most excellent one.
Sixty thousand consorts, all finely adorned, came forth.
The king asked:
‘Why has Consort Mallikā not come out?’
An attendant replied:
‘Today is the fifteenth, and she is observing the Buddhist fasting day; she is plainly dressed and not adorned, therefore she has not come out.’
The king became angry and sent someone to summon her, saying:
‘Even if she is observing the fast, she should not disregard the king’s command.’
This was repeated three times.
Mallikā then came out in plain attire.
Amid the crowd she shone like the sun and moon,
even more beautiful than usual.
The king, awestruck, regarded her with increased respect and asked:
‘What virtuous practice makes you so radiant and extraordinary?’
Consort Mallikā replied to the king:
‘Reflecting on my meager merit,
I have been born in a female form, with its inherent defilements and impurities.
Day and night my offenses pile up like a mountain, human life is brief,
and I fear falling into the three wretched destinies.
Therefore, each month I observe the Buddhist fasting day,
renouncing attachments to follow the Path, so that I may receive blessings life after life.’
Hearing this, the king was delighted
and offered her the fragrant necklaces.
Mallikā replied:
‘As I am now observing the fast, I should not wear these.
You may give them to someone else.’
The king said:
‘My original intention was to give them to the most excellent.
You are now the most excellent,
and moreover you uphold the Dharma fast, your aspiration is especially lofty.
Therefore I give them to you.
If you do not accept them, where shall I place them?’
Mallikā replied:
‘Do not worry, Great King.
I wish you would condescend to go with me to where the Buddha is.
Offer these fragrant necklaces to the World‑Honored One,
and receive the holy teaching besides.
This will bring blessings for countless kalpas.’
The king agreed.
He ordered the carriage prepared and went to where the Buddha was.
Bowing his head to the ground, he then took his seat as king
and addressed the Buddha:
‘These fragrant necklaces from the sea‑god were presented by Bōlì.
None of my sixty thousand consorts failed to covet them.
Consort Mallikā, however, when offered them, did not accept them.
Observing the Buddhist fast, her mind is free from greed and desire.
Respectfully I offer them to the Buddha.
May you condescend to accept them.
It is difficult for your disciples to maintain such a mind—
such straightforward faith.
Could there be any blessing greater than this?
I only pray that the World‑Honored One will accept these fragrant necklaces.’
The Buddha then spoke a verse:
In the past, in Jambudvīpa,
there was a country named Bōluónài.
At that time, there was a merchant,
named Móhēyèyí.
His wife became pregnant,
naturally kind-hearted, with a gentle and amiable disposition.
When the month was full, she gave birth to a boy,
with a dignified and handsome appearance.
His parents loved and cherished him,
prepared a sumptuous feast,
invited relatives,
and together with various fortune-tellers, they all enjoyed themselves.
They held the child to show the crowd and gave him a name.
The fortune-teller asked,
"What auspicious signs occurred when this child was conceived?"
The father replied,
"When he was conceived, his mother naturally became kind and gentle."
The fortune-teller named him Shànqiú.
He was nursed and grew up, fond of accumulating virtues and showing compassion to all beings.
Later, she became pregnant again.
When the term was fulfilled, she gave birth to a boy,
with an ugly and unsightly appearance.
The fortune-teller asked,
"What signs occurred when this child was conceived?"
The reply was,
"When she was pregnant with this child, the mother herself became wicked and malicious."
The fortune-teller named him Èqiú.
He was nursed and grew up, fond of doing evil deeds,
constantly harboring greed and feelings of jealousy.
As they each grew older,
they traveled together to the sea to seek treasures.
Each had five hundred attendants.
The journey was long and arduous, and midway they ran out of provisions.
After seven days, they were on the verge of death.
At that time, Shànqiú and the other merchants
all sincerely prayed to various deities, hoping to be saved from starvation and danger.
In the vast wilderness, they saw a tree in the distance,
with lush and dense branches.
They immediately headed toward it.
There was a spring of water.
Shànqiú and the crowd all pleaded together.
The tree deity appeared and spoke to them,
"Chop off one branch, and what you need will emerge."
Everyone was overjoyed.
They chopped off one branch, and delicious drinks flowed out.
They chopped off a second branch, and various foods emerged, complete with a hundred flavors.
They all received them and were fully satisfied.
They chopped off a third branch, and exquisite garments of all kinds appeared, fully equipped.
They chopped off a fourth branch, and various treasures all appeared in abundance.
Their loads were fully packed, and all their needs were met.
Èqiú arrived later.
The crowd, as before, obtained everything they needed.
He then thought to himself,
"Now this tree branch can produce such various good things.
How much more its roots?
Now I should cut it down.
I will surely obtain extremely wonderful and excellent things."
He ordered people to cut it down.
Shànqiú said to Èqiú,
"We were starving and exhausted, and by the grace of this tree, we were able to save our lives.
Why do you want to cut it down?"
Èqiú then dug up its roots.
Shànqiú, feeling sorrowful and unable to bear seeing it,
led the crowd back home.
After the tree was cut down,
five hundred rākṣasas seized Èqiú and all the merchants and devoured them.
Their wealth and possessions were lost.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"Shànqiú is now my present self.
The father is now King Jìngfàn.
The mother is now Móyé.
Èqiú is now Dípódáduō.
In the past, I often encountered him and constantly taught him good dharma.
But he did not accept it.
Instead, he regarded me as an enemy."
In the land of Jambudvīpa, there were many merchants.
They joined together and went to sea to gather treasure.
They encountered a swirling, fierce wind that wrecked their great ship.
There were also other people.
Riding on damaged, broken ships, they were blown by the wind and fell into the realm of the rākṣasas.
The rākṣasī women, with beautiful and upright appearances, came forward to greet the merchants, saying:
"Here there is much treasure.
Pearls of priceless value—take them freely as you wish.
We have no husbands, and you have no wives or concubines.
You may stay here and enjoy yourselves together.
Later, when favorable winds and good companions come, you can return home."
Gentlemen, you should know:
If you see a path
on the left side,
do not follow it.
At that time, among the merchants, there was one wise man who said:
"What these women say cannot be followed."
He then proceeded along the left path for several miles.
Along the way, he heard a city where tens of millions of people were crying out in lamentation and wailing.
"Why did we abandon Jambudvīpa to come here and meet our end?"
The merchant approached the city's perimeter and carefully observed it.
He saw that the city was enclosed by iron walls, with no gates or places to enter or exit.
Not far from the city was a śirīṣa tree.
He went and climbed the tree, seeing tens of millions of people inside the city.
He called out from afar to the people in the city, asking:
"Why
are you crying out for your parents and brothers?"
The people in the city replied:
"We went to sea to gather treasure but were blown off course by the wind.
We were deceived by the rākṣasī women and shut inside this prison city.
Five hundred people were here before, but they were gradually taken and killed.
Now only two hundred and fifty remain.
Do not call these women human beings.
They are all rākṣasa demons."
The man descended from the tree and told his companions.
He urged them to return home and seek a good plan.
"What do you all intend to do today?"
The others replied:
"Why did you not ask more thoroughly last night?
Did those people have any expedient plan?
Could we and our companions return home safely or not?"
The wise man replied:
"I will rise tonight and go ask them again."
When the women were asleep, he secretly rose and climbed the tree.
He asked the people in the city if they had any plan.
"Could you all, and I as well,
return to the land of Jambudvīpa?"
The people in the city answered:
"We long to return.
But this iron city transforms into multiple layers, impossible to breach.
People die day by day, with no way to escape.
Only you outsiders have some expedient means.
You can cross over and return to your homeland.
On the fifteenth day, at dawn, there will be a horse-king.
He will come from Uttarakuru to this realm.
He will dwell atop a high mountain peak.
The king himself will call out:
'Who wishes to return to the land of Jambudvīpa?'
If you hear the horse's voice,
all go and pay respects, seeking to return to your homeland."
The man reported the situation in detail to his companions.
The others said:
"Can we go now?"
He replied:
"We must wait until the fifteenth day when the horse-king
arrives; only then can we leave."
Not many days passed before the horse-king arrived.
The merchants, hearing this, went to where the horse-king was.
They addressed him:
"We all wish to return to our homeland.
We hope you will take us with you."
The horse-king told them:
"Listen carefully to what I say with wise minds.
Those who wish to return home to their homeland—
if your minds are single-pointed and upright, you will be able to return home.
If your minds are not single-pointed and upright, you will not be able to return.
These women
will carry their children and chase after you, wailing and crying.
If any among you give rise to attachment,
even if you are on my back, you will not be able to leave.
If you can abandon affection and love,
with upright minds, single-pointed and unattached,
and wholeheartedly grasp a single hair of mine, you will be able to return home."
At that time, the women each said to their husbands:
"You may abandon my humble self,
but why abandon the children?"
First, they taught the children to go embrace their fathers' necks,
weeping and crying out:
"Why are you abandoning us? Where are you going?"
Those whose minds were attached could not return.
Only the greatly wise Shīzǐ alone
returned safely.
At that time, the rākṣasī women,
carrying their children, went chasing after Shīzǐ.
They told the villages:
"Shīzǐ is my husband.
We bore children together.
He abandoned me and fled; I don't know where he went."
The people, hearing this, asked Shīzǐ:
"Looking at your wife,
her nature and appearance are outstanding among humans.
The children are pitiable; why abandon them?"
Shīzǐ replied:
"She is not human; she is a rākṣasa demon.
On the sea isles, she has killed and devoured countless merchants.
My several hundred companions are shut in the iron city.
Only I alone was fortunate to escape.
Now this demon woman is chasing after me again,
planning to harm me; I fear I may not escape."
He continued forward.
He returned to his native country.
The demon still chased after him to his country's land.
The demon went and told the king:
"I and Shīzǐ were husband and wife.
We bore these children.
I hoped for support, not expecting to be abandoned forever today."
The king summoned Shīzǐ to ask about the truth of the matter.
Shīzǐ reported the above events in detail to the king.
The king told Shīzǐ:
"If you don't want her, you can give her to me."
Shīzǐ replied:
"She truly is not human; she is a rākṣasa demon.
She harbors faults; later, do not blame me."
He also said to the ministers on the left and right:
"This demon coming here will certainly cause harm.
If the king does not believe and wishes to take her into the inner palace,
before long, the king and the inner palace will all be reduced to ashes."
The king again became angry and said to Shīzǐ:
"This woman's beauty is like that of a heavenly jade maiden.
Why do you still call her a rākṣasa demon?
Quickly leave; I will observe for myself."
The king took the demon woman into the palace for one night.
The next day at mealtime, the palace gates did not open.
The ministers discussed together:
"The king has taken a new wife; he is likely indulging in pleasure, so the gates are not open."
Shīzǐ said:
"It is not as you discuss.
The king, his wife, and all the palace maidens
must have been devoured by the rākṣasa; that is why the gates are not open."
They immediately set up a tall ladder, climbed over the wall, and entered inside.
They saw dead people's bones filling several rooms.
The ministers reproached Shīzǐ:
"It is precisely because of you that the rākṣasa demon was brought here,
killing the king, destroying the state, and annihilating the palace.
What do you intend to do?"
Shīzǐ replied:
"I previously made an agreement; later, do not blame me.
Why are you reproaching me now?"
The ministers and people came forward and said to Shīzǐ:
"The king is now dead, with no heir.
We hope Shīzǐ will ascend the throne and govern the people."
Shīzǐ told them:
"If you wish to make me king,
you must follow my teachings." They all responded in unison, saying it was good.
The king told the ministers:
"We must gather troops and go to sea to attack,
killing all the rākṣasa men and women, leaving none behind.
Then break open the iron city and free the people inside."
The local customary law was:
If a person did not serve the Buddha, they would be sent to the western mountains and given to demons to devour.
From then on, the Buddha's teachings flourished greatly, and countless attained the Way.
Therefore it is said:
All who have faith in the Buddha—these beings were able to return safely all because of the horse-king.
Also, that country's constant practice was:
When the king had sons,
whether ten, a hundred, or countless,
they all went forth to practice the Way, studying and reciting the Buddhist scriptures.
They fully mastered the Three Baskets.
Then they returned to lay life
and ascended the throne.
In general, those who did not master the scriptures and were not learned could not ascend the throne.
In the past, there were five hundred merchants.
One was named Mí Lián.
He was the most respected elder.
The five hundred men boarded a ship together and entered the sea.
A makara fish struck and broke their ship.
All five hundred perished.
Mí Lián, riding on a plank, survived.
He arrived at the land of Bímó.
To guard against fish, he walked east and west.
He saw a small path.
Entering, he saw a silver city.
Its trees reached the sky.
In between were bathing pools.
The city was square and upright, with water channels encircling the land.
Four women came out from the city.
Their appearance was upright and like jade.
The women together welcomed Mí Lián, saying,
"You have labored alone and suffered greatly.
We greatly rejoice at your arrival.
We have long desired to meet you.
We shall serve you, benevolent one.
Now this silver city is yours, benevolent one.
Within the city are joyful trees reaching the sky.
There are water channels, bathing pools, places for amusement, and dwellings.
In the city is a hall of seven treasures.
Its name is Luómàn.
It is made of gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and chēqú for the hall.
We four shall provide and serve you.
Retiring late, rising early, our minds mindful of your instructions.
You may stay here.
There is no need to go to another place."
Mí Lián then entered the city with the four women.
He ascended the hall of seven treasures and daily indulged to his utmost desire.
He remained in this city for over a thousand years.
Later, Mí Lián thought to himself,
"These four women do not wish me to leave and go to another place.
What is the meaning of this?"
Mí Lián waited until the four women were asleep.
He secretly arose, descended from the hall, left the city, and proceeded forward.
In the distance, he saw a golden city.
Its trees and bathing pools, everything was as before.
There were eight women.
Their upright appearance and pleasing words were all as before.
Mí Lián delighted with the eight women, indulging to his utmost desire for several thousand years.
Later, Mí Lián pondered,
suspecting that these eight women
did not wish him to go further to another place.
What is the meaning of this?
Mí Lián waited until the eight women were sleeping during the day.
He secretly arose and proceeded forward.
In the distance, he saw a crystal city.
Its trees and bathing pools, everything was as before.
Sixteen women came out from the city to welcome him, their words and speech as before.
Mí Lián then
delighted together with the sixteen women, indulging to his utmost desire for several thousand years.
Mí Lián left again and then saw a lapis lazuli city.
Everything was also as before.
Thirty-two women came out from the city to welcome him.
Mí Lián delighted with the women together, indulging to his utmost desire for several thousand years.
Later, he left the city and proceeded forward.
In the distance, he saw an iron city.
Within, there was no one at all to welcome him.
Mí Lián entered the city gate.
A ghost asked him,
"Mí Lián, for the path you have walked,
within the city, you will see a man with your own eyes.
His name is Jù Yǐn.
A burning iron wheel runs over his head.
Because he entered various cities and sat without becoming satiated,
therefore, he is made to have a burning iron wheel run over my head."
Mí Lián thought,
"The Luómàn Hall, the Xièmò Hall, the Luómó Hall, the Fànyùdān Hall."
Tears flowed as he said,
"For what reason have I entered this place?"
Mí Lián said to the ghost pouring the iron city,
"When the burning iron wheel enters and runs over my head, when will I be freed?"
The ghost replied, saying,
"When someone like you comes, then you will be freed."
The Buddha said,
"The iron wheel ran over Mí Lián's head.
After sixty billion years, he was then freed.
Mí Lián is my former self.
Before seeking the Way,
foolish and ignorant, I bathed, put on new clothes, and stepped on my mother's head.
Therefore, my head was burned for one day.
For four months of observing the eight precepts of fasting, my mind was still joyful.
Therefore, I obtained the four treasure cities of gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli.
My lifespan was tens of millions of years.
Therefore, people in the world, until death, are not satiated with the five desires.
Those who think of desired people,
who are not filial to parents and teachers,
a wheel will trample them.
They shall be like Mí Lián."
In the country of Luóyuèzhī, there were merchants.
Two brothers lived together in one place.
The elder brother sought the daughter of an elder, wishing to take her as his wife.
The girl was young and not yet fit for marriage.
The elder brother traveled far to another country with many merchants.
After many years, he was delayed and did not return in time.
The girl's age approached maturity, and she said to his younger brother,
"Your elder brother traveled far and perished there, not returning.
You should now take my daughter."
His younger brother replied, saying,
"How could such a thing be?"
The elder repeatedly urged.
His younger brother's mind was firm and never turned. The elder deceitfully wrote a distant letter.
Entrusting it to various merchants, he said the elder brother had died.
He again told him, saying,
"Your elder brother is already dead.
What will you do?"
The younger brother married the girl. After some time had passed,
the girl became pregnant.
The elder brother returned from afar.
The younger brother, his heart filled with fear, fled to Shèwèi.
Thus,辗转 he came before the Buddha.
He sought to leave home.
The Buddha then permitted it.
He then became a śramaṇa named Yōu Bōsī.
Upholding the precepts and practices, he attained Arhatship.
The elder brother, knowing this, was resentful and hateful.
Wishing to kill him, he came to the country of Shèwèi.
He then offered a heavy reward of five hundred taels of gold.
Those who responded to the recruitment went together.
Seeing his younger brother sitting in meditation, suddenly a thought of compassion arose.
"How can I kill this bhikṣu?
If I do not kill him, he will surely take my gold."
Wishing to shoot the bhikṣu, he instead hit his elder brother.
His elder brother, harboring anger and resentment, suddenly died.
He received the form of a poisonous snake.
Born within the door pivot of this ascetic's dwelling.
The door was frequently opened and closed.
His body was crushed and he died.
He again vowed to become a small poisonous insect.
He dwelled in the ascetic's house.
From the house, he fell onto the bhikṣu's head.
The virulent poison fiercely flared up, and he immediately died.
(The Buddha) told Śāriputra,
"In the past, there was a Pratyekabuddha.
He appeared in the world, dwelling in mountain forests.
At that time, there was a hunter who constantly captured birds and beasts.
He set up schemes, hoping to catch them by any means.
The Pratyekabuddha startled his birds and beasts, so he could not catch them.
He then harbored anger and, with a poisoned arrow,
shot the Pratyekabuddha.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha,
his mind compassionate towards this person, wishing to make him repent,
manifested supernatural powers.
At that time, the hunter's heart was filled with reverence.
Terrified, he reproached himself and sincerely confessed his fault.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha accepted his repentance.
The poison attacked and he died.
That person, after death, then fell into hell.
After leaving hell,
for five hundred lifetimes, he was always killed by poison.
Until today, having attained the path of Arhatship,
he was still stung by a poisonous insect and died."
In the past, in Jambudvīpa,
five hundred merchants
traveled together through the wilderness, passing along a perilous road.
Within a large mountain cave, it was extremely dark.
At that time, the merchants were confused, distressed, and sorrowful.
Fearing the loss of their wealth and goods,
and this place having many bandits, they were again terrified.
All together with one mind,
they turned towards heaven and earth, the sun and moon, mountains and seas, all deities and spirits,
weeping and seeking mercy.
At that time, Sàbó,
compassionate towards the merchants,
told them, "Do not be afraid.
I shall make a great light to illuminate for you."
At that time, Sàbó then wrapped his own two arms with white cotton cloth.
He poured clarified butter on them.
Then used them as torches.
Leading the various merchants,
after seven days, they passed through this darkness.
At that time, the various merchants, grateful for his kindness, revered and respected him immeasurably.
Each attained safety and security, their joy beyond measure.
At that time, Sàbó was my former self.
The various merchants are now the five hundred bhikṣus.
In the past, there was a merchant.
He heard that in foreign lands there were even more extraordinary treasures.
He wished to go and trade.
But between the two countries lay a difficulty of Rākṣasas.
It was impossible to pass through.
The merchant, while wandering, saw at the western gate of the market,
a Daoist sitting on an empty bed, saying he was selling the Five Precepts.
The merchant asked, "What are the Five Precepts?"
He replied:
"They have no form or price.
One receives them by mouth and upholds them in the heart.
Later, one may be reborn in heaven.
In this present life, they can ward off the difficulty of Rākṣasa demons."
The merchant wished to buy them.
He asked how much money was required.
The reply was one thousand gold coins.
He then approached, gave the payment, and received the Five Precepts.
The Daoist said to him:
"When you go to the foreign land and reach the border,
if the Rākṣasas come, you just say:
'I am a disciple of Śākyamuni who upholds the Five Precepts.'"
After a short while, the merchant arrived between the two countries.
He saw a Rākṣasa.
Its body was ten feet three inches tall.
Its head was yellow like a rush mat.
Its eyes were like red nails.
Its entire body was covered in scales.
It alternately opened its mouth like a fish puffing its gills.
It caught flying swallows by looking up and sank into the ground up to its knees when stepping.
Its mouth was hot and blood flowed.
A crowd of several thousand came straight to seize the merchant.
He said:
"I am a disciple of Śākyamuni who upholds the Five Precepts."
Upon hearing this, the Rākṣasa would not let him go.
The merchant casually struck it with both fists.
His fists sank into the scales and could not be pulled out.
He then stepped on its head with his foot.
He pushed and pulled but still could not free them.
His five limbs were submerged in the scales.
Only his back could still move.
The Rākṣasa said:
"The merchant's will is still firm."
He said to the Rākṣasa:
The Rākṣasa also said to the merchant:
The merchant, in his rashness, wished to curse in anger.
He thought to himself:
"This body cycles through the three realms.
I have never begged from anyone.
Now I shall beg
to make this Rākṣasa have a full meal at once."
He then said:
The Rākṣasa was intelligent.
It understood the merchant's words.
It then felt ashamed.
It released the merchant.
Kneeling with palms together, it apologized to him, saying:
The Rākṣasa repented of its faults.
It finally escorted the merchant to the foreign land.
He obtained great treasures.
It also escorted him back home.
He greatly cultivated merit.
Thus he attained the path.
Animals and humans, all four kinds of birth,
Question:
How do we know that among humans there are those born from eggs?
Answer:
As it is said:
In Jambudvīpa,
there were many merchants who went to sea to seek treasures.
They obtained two swans.
As they wished, they transformed, losing one, one remained.
They played together with it.
They slept in one room and united with it.
Then two eggs were born.
The eggs gradually warmed and hatched.
Then two children were born.
Later, they grew up, left home to study the path,
and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
One was named Śīpíluó,
the other was named Yōubōshīpóluó.
Question:
How do we know that among humans there are those born from moisture?
Answer:
As the scriptures say:
There was King Dǐngshēng,
the Venerable Zhēluó,
the Venerable Yōupózhē,
and the Rākṣasī woman.
Question:
How do we know that among humans there are those born by transformation?
Answer:
Those at the beginning of the kalpa are such.
Those who have attained the holy Dharma are no longer born from eggs or moisture.
Question:
Why are they no longer born from eggs or moisture?
Answer:
Birth from eggs and moisture belong to the animal realm.
In the past, there was a guide.
He traveled with five hundred merchants to trade.
They reached a great wilderness where there was absolutely no water.
They were extremely hungry and thirsty, searching in all directions.
Climbing high and looking far, they saw trees.
Thinking there must be water,
they all hurried there together.
Upon arriving, they saw under the trees,
grass growing all around, and the ground was clean.
They all dug together.
At that time, a heavenly being saw the guide from afar.
In the time it takes to stretch an arm, he arrived at their location.
Staying in the tree, he stretched out his right hand.
From between his five fingers flowed the eight-flavored sweet and delicious water.
And it was inexhaustible.
They all became fully satisfied.
The Buddha was dwelling in the great grove near the city of Shèwèi.
A merchant was driving eight oxen
to the northern country of Jùduō.
There was another merchant
who was grazing cattle together with him in the marshes.
At that time, a Licchavi caught a dragon maiden
and pierced her nose to lead her away.
Seeing this, the merchant
immediately felt compassion.
He asked the Licchavi,
"What are you going to do with this creature you are leading?"
The Licchavi replied,
"I intend to kill and eat her."
The merchant said, "Do not kill her.
I will give you one ox
in exchange to free her." The captor refused.
Eventually, up to eight oxen,
he finally said,
"Now for your sake, I shall release her."
He then took the eight oxen and released the dragon maiden.
At that moment, the merchant thought again,
"This is an evil man; I fear he may pursue and recapture her."
So he followed to see where she would go.
They arrived at the edge of a pond.
The dragon transformed into a human form
and said to the merchant,
"You, heavenly one, have spared my life; now I wish to repay your kindness.
Please come with me into my palace;
I shall repay your heavenly grace."
The merchant replied,
"You dragons have violent natures, prone to sudden wrath and unpredictable anger.
You might kill me."
She answered,
"That man earlier bound me;
I had the power to kill him.
But because he observed the Posadha precepts,
he harbored no intention to kill.
How much more so, now that you, heavenly one, have granted me life,
would I harm you?
Stay here a while;
I will first go in and prepare."
At the dragon gate, he saw two dragons bound together.
He asked,
"What have you done?"
They replied,
"This dragon maiden observes the fasting precepts for three days every half-month.
We brothers were guarding this dragon maiden,
but we were not vigilant, and she was captured by the Licchavi.
For this reason, we have been bound.
We beseech your heavenly compassion to speak for our release."
"If this dragon maiden asks what food you desire to eat,
request food from the human world of Jambudvīpa."
After the dragon maiden had prepared,
she called him to enter.
He sat upon a jeweled couch.
The dragon maiden addressed him,
"Heavenly one, what food do you wish to eat now?"
He replied,
"I desire food from the human world of Jambudvīpa."
She then served various foods.
He asked the dragon maiden,
"Why are these beings bound?"
The dragon maiden said,
"They have committed offenses; I intend to kill them."
The merchant said,
"Do not kill them."
"If not, I must kill them."
The merchant said,
"If you release them, then I will eat."
She said,
"I cannot release them just like that.
They must be punished by being banished to the human world for six months."
The merchant asked,
"With such splendid adornments, why do you observe the Posadha precepts?"
She replied,
"We dragons suffer five kinds of distress.
What are the five?
When born as dragons,
when sleeping as dragons,
when engaged in intercourse as dragons,
when angry as dragons,
and three times a day,
our skin and flesh fall to the ground, and hot sand scorches our bodies."
He asked further,
"What do you seek?"
She replied,
"I seek to be born in the human path."
He asked, "Having obtained a human body, what should one seek?"
She replied,
"It is difficult to attain renunciation."
He asked again,
"Under whom should one renounce?"
She replied,
"The Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is now in the city of Shèwèi.
He liberates those not yet liberated.
You may go to him for renunciation."
He then said,
"I wish to return home."
The dragon maiden gave him eight gold ingots and said,
"This is dragon gold.
It will suffice for your parents
and relatives for their entire lives." She said,
"Close your eyes."
Then, through supernatural power, she transported him back to his own country.
His traveling companions had arrived earlier
and told his family,
"He has entered the dragon palace."
His parents thought their son had died.
Relatives and clan members gathered together, weeping and wailing in grief.
At that time, the herdsmen and those gathering firewood and grass
saw him and returned first to tell his family,
"So-and-so has returned."
Hearing this, his family was overjoyed.
They went out to welcome him home and held a celebration for his survival.
During the celebration, he gave the eight gold ingots to his parents.
"This is dragon gold.
If cut, it regenerates.
You may use it for your entire lives."
There was a caravan leader
who led merchants into a perilous place.
They encountered a rākṣasa demon.
It blocked their way with its hand and said,
"Stop, do not move; I will not let you pass."
The caravan leader struck it with his right fist.
His fist stuck to the demon and could not be pulled free.
He struck it with his left fist.
It also stuck fast.
He kicked it with his right foot.
Again, it was the same.
He butted it with his head.
His head also stuck fast.
The demon asked,
"What do you intend to do now?
Has your mind ceased its striving?"
He replied, "Although five parts of my body are bound,
my mind will never cease.
I will strive with diligent effort to contend with you."
The demon then thought,
"This man's courage and strength are immense."
It said,
"Your diligent effort is great; you will certainly not cease.
I release you now."
There was a caravan leader
named Jílì.
He went to sea to obtain great treasures
and returned safely.
In all, he had eight billion maṇi pearls,
each worth a hundred billion taels of gold.
He gave many treasures to a beggar,
then, without entering his home, returned to the sea
to gather more treasures.
After entering the sea, he obtained twice as many treasures.
After eighty years, he returned to his own country.
As he was about to enter the city, he saw a criminal
being bound, beaten, and led with loud drumbeats,
proclaimed through the streets and alleys, to the execution ground
for punishment and death.
At that moment, the condemned man, upon seeing Jílì,
said these words:
"Caravan leader,
save me from death.
Grant me life.
You are a great benefactor, a virtuous and good man."
Hearing this, Jílì said to the condemned man,
"Alas, man,
I now grant you fearlessness.
I will save you from death."
He went to the executioners
and gave each a maṇi pearl worth a hundred million taels of gold.
"Wait a moment now;
I will go to the king and return."
At that time, Jílì hurried to the king
and said,
"Great King,
I wish to buy this man's life with fine treasures."
The king replied,
"Jílì,
this man's crime cannot be pardoned; it cannot be bought. If you insist on buying it,
you must give me all that you possess,
and even substitute your own life for his, only then can he be freed."
Jílì was joyful.
"I gain great benefit; my wish is fulfilled.
I can save this man and fulfill my intention."
He then took all the wealth from his household and the treasures obtained from the sea,
countless thousands of billions of gold, silver, and precious objects,
and presented them to the king, saying,
"Release this man.
All that I possess is here now."
He said to the executioners,
"Execute Jílì."
So they bound Jílì and led him to the execution ground.
The executioner raised his sword with his right hand to strike Jílì,
but his hand would not descend.
Astonished and terrified, he reported to the king.
"See for yourself."
Hearing this, the king
personally took up a sword to kill Jílì.
As he raised the sword, both his hands fell to the ground; he suffered great distress, cried out, and died.
At that time, Jílì was myself.
The king at that time was Devadatta.
Innumerable, countless kalpas ago,
there were two groups of merchants, each with five hundred men.
In Bōluónài,
they gathered their capital and goods, prepared a ship, and crossed the sea.
They untied the moorings, raised the sails, and rode the wind straight ahead.
They soon reached the Treasure Isle.
There were exquisite women and nothing was lacking.
The leader of the first group of merchants said,
"We have toiled hard to come here for the sake of wealth.
We should stay and enjoy ourselves."
The second Sàbó said,
"Although this place abounds with treasures, we should not stay long."
At that time, a heavenly maiden, compassionate toward these men,
spoke to the crowd from the sky:
"Although this place is pleasant, it is not fit for long residence.
After seven days, this land will sink."
Having spoken, she vanished.
Then there was a demon maiden who wanted the merchants to perish here.
She announced from the sky:
"You all need not prepare to depart.
This land has no water; if there were water,
how could these treasures, women, and five pleasures exist?
What the previous heavenly being said is all false."
Having spoken, she vanished.
The first Sàbó commanded his followers:
"Do not leave; do not believe the previous heavenly being."
The second Sàbó returned and told his followers:
"Do not be greedy; quickly prepare the ship.
What the previous heavenly being said is utterly true, not false.
If the water does not come, we can enjoy ourselves here and then return slowly.
If the water truly comes, we will have prepared and departed."
The Buddha said to Shèlìfú,
"After seven days, as the previous heavenly being said,
the water flooded the land.
The second Sàbó led his followers and immediately boarded the ship.
The first Sàbó had not prepared beforehand.
When the water arrived that day, they donned armor and weapons and fought each other.
The second Sàbó, from the ship, pierced the foot of the first Sàbó with a spear.
It went straight through, and he immediately died.
The Buddha said to Shèlìfú,
"Do you know who the first Sàbó was? It was Típódádōu.
The second Sàbó was myself.
The five hundred men of the first merchant group are now the five hundred disciples of Típódádōu.
The five hundred men of the second merchant group are now the five hundred Arhats.
The first heavenly maiden at that time was Shèlìfú.
The second heavenly maiden at that time is now the disciple of the Brahmin monk named Mǎnyuè."
At the time of Dìngguāng Buddha,
there were five hundred merchants who went to sea seeking treasure.
One with evil thoughts considered:
"I will now kill all the merchants and take the treasures alone."
At that time, in Jambudvīpa, there was a great guide
named Dà'āi.
In his sleep, the sea god spoke to him:
"Among the merchants, there is a thief
who wants to kill his five hundred companions and take the treasures alone.
If this deed is done, he will fall into hell.
Now, benevolent guide, you should employ skillful means
so that the merchants do not die and the thief does not incur guilt."
The guide pondered for seven days.
There was no other expedient.
He could only kill this wicked man.
If he told the merchants, they would surely become angry and kill him together,
and all would fall into evil destinies.
If he killed him alone,
he would bear the sin.
He would rather endure suffering for hundreds of thousands of kalpas himself
than let the merchants be universally endangered
and cause one thief to fall into hell.
First, he preached the Dharma to him,
making his heart joyful and exuberant, then he lay down to sleep.
The Buddha said,
"The great guide Dà'āi, out of great compassion for the merchants, used skillful means to kill this one thief.
After his life ended, he was reborn in the twelfth Light-Sound Heaven.
That Dà'āi was myself.
By this expedient, he transcended a thousand kalpas of birth and death.
The five hundred merchants on the same ship
are those among whom the five hundred Buddhas of the present auspicious kalpa will arise."
Once there were five hundred merchants
who boarded a ship and went to sea.
They encountered a makara fish raising its head and opening its mouth, wanting to devour living beings.
At that time, there was little wind, yet the ship sped like an arrow.
The Sàbó leader said to the crowd:
"The ship is going too fast; we should lower the sails."
As he said, they lowered them,
but the ship went even faster and could not be stopped.
The Sàbó leader asked the man in the crow's nest:
"What do you see?"
"I see two suns above,
a white mountain below,
and a black mountain in between."
The Sàbó leader exclaimed in alarm:
"This is a great fish! What shall we do?
We are now in dire straits.
If we enter this fish's belly, there is no chance of survival.
Each of you, according to what you worship, pray with one mind."
Thereupon, each person, according to their devotion,
prayed with one mind, seeking deliverance from this calamity.
The more fervent their prayers, the faster the ship went.
In a moment, if it did not stop, they would enter the fish's mouth.
Then the Sàbó leader told everyone:
"I have a great deity called Buddha.
Each of you, abandon the gods you originally worship and invoke him with one mind."
At that time, the five hundred people together raised their voices and called, "Námó Fó!"
The fish, hearing the Buddha's name,
thought to itself:
"Today in the world, there is again a Buddha.
How can I bear to harm living beings?"
It immediately closed its mouth.
The water reversed its flow, and they moved far from the fish.
The five hundred merchants gave rise to wholesome minds.
They all attained liberation.
There was a county.
All its inhabitants practiced the Five Precepts and Ten Virtuous Deeds.
Within the county borders, there were no brewers of alcohol.
Among them was the son of a prominent family.
He wished to travel far for trade.
As he was about to depart, his parents told him:
"Diligently uphold the Five Precepts and practice the Ten Virtuous Deeds.
Be careful not to drink alcohol and violate the Buddha's important precept."
He traveled to another country and met an old classmate.
Overjoyed, the classmate returned home and brought out grape wine, wishing to drink together.
The son declined, saying:
"In my country, we revere the Buddha's precepts; none dare violate them.
Moreover, I bid farewell to my parents, who also admonished me. Though we have been parted long and reunite with shared joy,
it is not fitting to make me break the precept and disobey my parents' teaching."
The host said:
"You and I share the same teacher; in gratitude we are like brothers.
My parents are thus your parents.
If parents offer a drink, how can you refuse?
If I were at your home, I would certainly follow your parents."
Having no alternative, he then drank with him.
After the matter concluded, he returned home and fully reported it to his parents.
His parents replied:
"You disobeyed our teaching and furthermore broke the precept.
This is the beginning of undermining the Dharma; you are not a filial son.
Do not speak of this."
They then took the goods he had obtained and expelled him from the country.
The son, having broken the precept and been driven out by his parents,
went to another country and stayed at an inn.
The innkeeper served three demonic spirits.
They could take human form.
They faced people, ate and drank, and spoke with people.
He served them for years until his wealth was completely exhausted.
Moreover, his family suffered from illness, death, and continuous misfortunes.
Privately, they discussed it.
The demons knew people's thoughts.
The demons discussed among themselves, saying:
"This man's property is exhausted.
It is precisely for our sake, yet we have never benefited him.
Now he is weary and troubled.
We should seek precious treasures to give him."
They then went and stole fine treasures from the treasury of another country's king, accumulating them in the garden.
They reported:
"You have served us for years, toiling very long.
Now we wish to bless you, to make you wealthy."
The innkeeper said:
"I receive the great spirits' grace."
The demons said:
"In your garden there is gold and silver; you may go and take it."
The innkeeper joyfully
entered the garden, saw the items, carried them back to his house.
He expressed gratitude for the grace received.
The next day, he wished to prepare a meal.
"I hope you will condescend to come."
All preparations were made.
The demonic spirits arrived at the gate.
Seeing a man from Shèwèi country in the innkeeper's house,
they immediately turned and fled.
The innkeeper chased and called out:
"Since you have already condescended to come,
why abandon and leave?"
The spirits said:
"Your house has a venerable guest; how could we approach?"
Again, they fled in alarm.
The innkeeper pondered:
"In my dwelling, there are no unusual people.
There is only this man."
He then went out and spoke, the respectful preparations already complete.
He then asked him:
"What meritorious virtues do you possess, that the spirits I serve fear you and flee?"
The guest fully explained the Buddha's merits, the Five Precepts and Ten Virtuous Deeds.
"I truly violated the alcohol precept and was driven out by my parents.
I still retain the other four precepts, hence I am protected by heavenly spirits.
Your spirits dare not face me."
The innkeeper said:
"I wish to uphold the Five Precepts."
He then received from the guest the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.
With single-minded diligence, he did not dare be negligent.
He asked: "Where is the Buddha? Can he be seen?"
The guest said:
"In Shèwèi country, at the Jìgūdú Garden."
The innkeeper, with single-mindedness, set out for that place. Passing through a pavilion,
there was a woman inside.
She was precisely the wife of a man-eating demon.
The road was long and far, the time pressing towards dusk.
He asked the woman for lodging.
The woman immediately replied:
"Be careful not to stay here.
You should hurry forward."
The man asked:
"For what reason? Do you have some intention?"
The woman replied:
"I have already told you; why ask further?"
The man thought to himself:
"Previously, the man from Shèwèi country, complete in the Buddha's four precepts, even my spirits feared him.
I have already received the Three Refuges and Five Precepts.
My mind is not negligent.
What is there to fear?"
He then stayed overnight himself.
At that time, the man-eating demon, seeing the awe-inspiring spirits protecting the precepts, stayed forty miles away from the pavilion.
For one night it did not return.
The next day, advancing, he saw the human bones and skeletons devoured by the demon, scattered in disorder.
His heart was terrified, and he regretted, turning back.
He thought to himself:
"In my own country, clothing and food were sufficient.
Vainly I was influenced by that man,
who said the Buddha is in Shèwèi country.
I have not witnessed any wondrous marvels, but instead see skeletons strewn about.
It would be better to take this woman and return to my homeland, living together as before."
He immediately turned back.
He then asked the woman again to let him stay overnight.
The woman said to the man:
"Why have you returned?"
He replied:
"My travel plans did not succeed, hence I returned."
He asked to lodge for another night.
The woman said: "You will die.
My husband is a man-eating demon.
He will come soon.
You must leave here quickly."
The man did not believe and thus stopped, not leaving.
He then became confused, and lustful thoughts arose again.
He no longer believed in the Buddha's Three Refuges and Five Precepts.
The heavenly spirits immediately left, and the demon was able to return.
The woman, fearing the demon would eat this man,
hid him in a jar.
The demon smelled human scent and said to his wife:
"Have you obtained meat?
I wish to eat it."
The wife said:
"I have not gone out; from where would I get meat?"
The wife asked the demon:
"Why did you not return yesterday?"
The demon said:
"Because of what you did, having a venerable guest lodge here,
causing me to be driven out."
The man in the jar became increasingly terrified.
He no longer remembered the Three Refuges.
The wife said:
"Why could you not obtain meat?"
The demon said:
"Precisely because you hosted a disciple of the Buddha.
Heavenly spirits drove me out forty miles away.
I slept in the open, trembling in fear; to this day I am unsettled, hence I could not obtain meat."
The wife then asked her husband:
"What are the Buddha's precepts like?"
The demon said:
"I am extremely hungry; quickly bring meat, no need to ask this.
This is the unsurpassed, truly right precept;
it is not something I dare speak of."
The wife said:
"Explain them.
I will then give you meat."
Demonic kinds are greedy, cruel, and their desire to eat is insatiable.
The wife pressed him with questions.
He then explained the Three Refuges and Five Precepts.
When the demon first explained the first precept, the wife immediately received it.
By the fifth precept, her mind grasped it and her mouth recited it.
The man in the jar recognized the Five Precepts and accordingly received them.
The God-Emperor Shì knew these two people's minds had taken refuge in the Buddha.
He immediately sent fifty good spirits to protect the two people.
The demon then fled away.
The next day,
the woman asked the man:
"Were you afraid?"
He replied: "Very afraid.
I received your benevolent grace.
My mind awakened and recognized the Buddha."
The woman said to the man:
"Why did you return yesterday?"
He replied:
"I saw the skeletons of newly and long-dead people strewn about, and was afraid, hence I returned."
The woman said:
"The bones are what I discarded.
I was originally a daughter of a good family.
I was seized by the demon, who took me as his wife.
In sorrow and desperation, I had no plan.
Now, receiving your benevolent grace,
I am able to hear the Buddha's precepts and leave this demon."
She also said:
"Virtuous one, where do you wish to go?"
The man replied:
"I wish to go to Shèwèi country to see the Buddha."
The woman said: "Excellent.
I will follow the virtuous one to see the Buddha."
They then proceeded forward together and encountered four hundred and ninety-eight people.
They exchanged greetings.
"Virtuous ones, from where have you come, and where do you wish to go?"
They replied:
"We have come from where the Buddha is."
They asked:
"You have already seen the Buddha; why are you leaving again?"
They replied:
"The Buddha spoke the sutra with his mouth, but our minds were bewildered, hence we still did not understand, and were told to return to our own country."
The two virtuous ones fully explained the whole story.
Because the demon feared those of high conduct who upheld the precepts,
their minds then opened in understanding, and they all returned to see the Buddha.
The Buddha, seeing them from afar, smiled.
From his mouth, five-colored light emerged.
Ānán knelt with reverence.
The Buddha does not smile without reason; he will have something to say.
The Buddha said to Ānán,
"Do you see that these four hundred and ninety-eight people have returned?"
"These people have now found their original teacher."
"Those who come to see the Buddha will all attain the Way."
At that time, five hundred people came to where the Buddha was and listened to the sutra with one mind.
Their minds opened and their thoughts were liberated, and they all became śramaṇas.
They attained the path of Arhatship.
However, these two people were the former teachers of the four hundred and ninety-eight people.
When people seek the essential path,
they should find their original teacher and good friends.
Only then will they understand."
In the city of Rājagṛha,
there was a magician.
His name was Bátuó.
He was well-versed in the classics, skilled in arts and techniques, clever and capable, and his fame and reputation were high and far-reaching.
The people of Magadha were all inferior to him.
People of all ages in the country studied under him.
Bátuó encountered the World-Honored One and saw his majestic and wonderful physical appearance.
He thought to test him.
He then invited the Buddha.
"If he knows my intention, he will not accept the invitation."
"If he does not know, he will undoubtedly accept."
The Buddha knew his intention and intended to liberate him.
He silently accepted.
Bátuó thought,
"The Buddha has no supernatural wisdom and does not see my intention."
He entered Rājagṛha.
In a clean place, he transformed a lecture hall.
He hung silk canopies and flowered canopies.
Under each tree,
he laid lion seats for the bhikṣus.
In the lecture hall,
he specially set up a lion seat for the Tathāgata.
It was forty-nine feet high.
He prepared a feast of a hundred flavors.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings and Śakra, Lord of the Devas,
along with thirty-two thousand devas, said to Rénxián,
"You have truly obtained great benefit."
"You have invited the Tathāgata to the lecture hall to make offerings."
"We will assist in providing what is lacking."
They immediately transformed a palace hall like the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The Buddha, along with the bodhisattvas and bhikṣus, went to his lecture hall.
He saw the Buddha sitting on the seat he had created.
Śakra also saw the Tathāgata sitting on the majestic seat he had created.
Rénxián listened to what the Buddha said.
He eliminated his arrogance and bowed his head at the Buddha's feet.
He said to the Buddha,
"I only wish that the Tathāgata would forgive my offenses."
He wanted to dispel his transformations.
The Buddha commanded them not to change.
He further explained that all dharmas are like illusions and transformations.
Ānán Bīntí
lived at the foot of Mount Ěrlián.
He was extremely wealthy with treasures.
Merchants from far and wide came to borrow money.
Beggars who went to him never left empty-handed.
At that time, there were five hundred merchants.
Their ship was wrecked at sea, and all their treasures were lost.
Many died, but some survived by clinging to planks.
They all went to Ānán Bīntí.
The host prepared food.
The host drew water from a well and obtained a treasure chest.
Each had a label with their name.
After the merchants ate, they all grieved.
The host asked the reason.
They replied,
"We, five hundred companions,
traveled together on the sea, but our ship capsized and sank."
"Many died."
"We clung to small planks and barely survived."
"We lost our treasures and grieve for our companions."
They happened to see the treasure chest obtained from the well.
"These are all ours, but we don't know how this happened."
The host said,
"You all engage in trade and business."
"If you are sincere, you will not lose anything."
"It is only because you are not sincere that you lose things."
"For countless kalpas,
I have never been insincere and have never deceived or encroached."
"All those who lost treasures come to my well."
"You should each take yours according to your names."
In the past, there was a man named Xiánzhí.
He had participated in the eight precepts three times and heard sutras being recited.
His heavenly eye never blinked, and he recited and remembered without forgetting.
However, this Xiánzhí
was good at stealing others' things right before their eyes without them noticing.
The king lost a pearl.
He summoned his ministers to discuss.
A minister replied to the king,
"I have heard that Xiánzhí is extremely capable of stealing."
The king ordered him arrested and interrogated, hoping he would confess to not stealing.
Since the king was righteous, how could he wrong someone?
He summoned the ministers again to discuss.
A minister said,
"We should devise a skillful means to make him confess."
"We should heavily shackle him, parade him through the market announcing his execution."
"Give him wine to get him drunk, then remove the shackles and place him in a hall with courtesans performing music."
The king commanded the courtesans,
"When Xiánzhí is drunk, ask him,
'You should answer,
'This is heaven, and I am a heavenly maiden.'"
"'You should serve by his side.'"
"'In your previous life, you stole the king's pearl, so you are reborn here.'"
The king followed this plan.
Xiánzhí heard this and silently thought to himself,
"I have heard in the sutras,
'Heavenly eyes do not blink,' but these women all blink."
"Moreover, if I stole the pearl, I should go to hell."
"Is the king not trying to trick me into confessing?"
He then spoke,
"I was reborn in heaven because I did not steal the pearl."
The courtesans reported to the king,
saying that Xiánzhí said,
The king then laughed heartily.
"This fellow definitely did not steal my pearl."
He immediately released him.
He bestowed gold and treasures upon him.
He actually stole the pearl.
By reciting one verse, he avoided punishment and received rewards.
In the past, there was a man named Cíluó.
He saw someone selling a turtle and pitied it in his heart.
He wept towards the turtle.
The turtle seller said,
"Why are you crying towards the turtle?"
Cíluó replied,
"I cannot bear to see it."
The poor turtle seller laughed loudly.
"You are crazy."
He replied,
"I think of this turtle and ask to buy it from you."
The seller said,
"The turtle is worth a million."
Cíluó then took it home.
He gathered all his savings, which amounted to eight hundred thousand.
Cíluó said,
"This is all my money; I have nowhere to borrow more."
The turtle seller said,
"Since your money is insufficient, you can work as a laborer to pay off the debt."
Cíluó agreed.
He loaded the turtle onto a cart and released it into a pond.
The turtle was then able to speak.
"When there is a great flood, you should climb a tree and call for me."
Later, a great flood arose, and the people all died.
Cíluó climbed a tree and called for the turtle.
The turtle then came.
Cíluó sat on the turtle's back.
After traveling several miles,
he saw a woman on a drifting log, exhausted and about to die.
She begged Cíluó to take her aboard.
Cíluó asked the turtle,
"This person is pitiful; please let her come aboard."
The turtle said,
"Go ahead and take her."
After traveling ten miles,
he saw the turtle seller on a drifting log.
He begged Cíluó to take him aboard.
The turtle said, "I am already heavy."
"I am afraid I will be too tired and cannot cross by myself."
"Be careful not to take him."
Cíluó said,
"He is pitiful; we should take him."
Cíluó took him aboard.
After traveling several tens of miles,
he saw several sheng of ants on a drifting log.
Cíluó again asked the turtle to take them aboard.
They arrived at the country of Nàjié.
The woman then gave gold to thank Cíluó.
The turtle seller said,
"This turtle was originally sold by me."
"The gold you received should be given to me."
Cíluó refused.
The turtle seller then went to the king of Nàjié and said,
"Cíluó stole someone's wife and is trafficking her."
"He has brought gold and silver to this country."
The king of Nàjié immediately summoned Cíluó and ordered an official to execute him.
The official began to write down the matter, but
ants swarmed the brush, making it impossible to write.
The king heard of this and asked Cíluó,
"What meritorious deeds have you performed?"
Cíluó explained in detail.
The king executed the turtle seller.
In the city of Fójiāluó in Dàyuèzhī.
There was a painter.
Named Qiānnà.
He traveled to the eastern country of Duōchà Shīluó.
Working as a guest painter for twelve years.
He earned thirty taels of gold and took it back to his home country.
He encountered a community of monks whose faith was pure and serene.
He then asked the Karmadāna (monastic administrator).
"How much is needed to provide a day's meal for this assembly?"
The answer was.
"Thirty taels of gold can be used."
The painter gave it all to the Karmadāna.
Begging him to arrange a single meal.
"I will come tomorrow."
He returned home empty-handed.
His wife asked.
"What have you gained from twelve years of work?"
He replied.
"I gained thirty taels of gold."
"I have already planted it in the field of merit."
"Given it to the monks for a feast."
The wife bound her husband and delivered him to the authorities.
She fully presented the above matter.
The official asked.
"You did not provide for your wife and children but instead gave it to others?"
The painter answered.
"In my previous life, lacking merit, I was poor and constantly suffered."
"Encountering this community of monks is a fine field of merit."
"If I do not plant good seeds again, in later lives I will be poor again."
"Poverty and suffering will continue with no time of escape."
"Therefore, I gave it all to the monastic community."
The judge was an upāsaka (lay devotee).
He immediately removed his jeweled necklace and gave it, along with the horse he rode and a village, to the painter.
He said to him.
"You gave to the monastic community."
"The monks have not yet eaten."
"This is like grain seeds not yet planted, yet sprouts have already appeared."
"And the great fruit is yet to come."
In the past, there was a man.
After death, his spirit returned to stroke his old bones.
Someone asked him.
"You are already dead."
"Why then do you stroke these dry bones?"
The spirit said.
"This was my former body."

"It did not kill living beings, did not steal, did not commit adultery, did not engage in divisive speech, harsh speech, false speech, or frivolous speech, was not jealous, not hateful, not ignorant."
"After death, it was reborn in heaven."
"All wishes were naturally fulfilled, with limitless happiness."
"Therefore, I cherish and value it."
In the past, in North India.
There was a skilled craftsman.
He made a wooden woman.
Beautiful beyond compare, with clothes and adornments no different from a woman of the world.
She could come and go, serve wine, and attend to guests.
Only she could not speak.
At that time, in South India, there was a painter.
Also very skilled in painting.
The craftsman heard of him.
Prepared fine food and drink and invited the painter.
Then had the wooden woman serve wine and hold food.
From morning until night.
The painter did not know she was not real and thought she was a real woman.
His desire grew extremely strong, he could not forget her.
As the day grew late.
The woodworker went to sleep.
Let the painter stay.
With this wooden woman standing by his side to attend him.
Then said to the guest.
"I purposely leave this woman here, you may stay with her."
The host had gone in.
The wooden woman stood by the lamp.
The guest called to her.
But the woman did not come.
The guest then went forward to pull her.
Only then did he know she was wood.
He felt ashamed.
"The host deceived me."
"I should repay him."
Thereupon, the painter also devised a scheme.
He painted his own likeness on the wall.
The clothes painted were no different from what he wore.
With a rope tied around the neck, appearing as if hanged to death, he painted the rope image covering his mouth.
After finishing, he closed the door and hid himself under the bed.
At daybreak, the host came out and saw the door unopened.
He looked inside.
Only saw the image on the wall of the guest hanged dead.
The host was greatly frightened and thought he had really died.
He broke the door open and cut the rope with a knife.
Thereupon, the painter came out from under the bed.
The woodworker was greatly ashamed.
The painter then said.
"You could deceive me."
"I could deceive you."
"Guest and host are even, neither owes the other."
The two men, convinced of their own folly and delusion.
Each abandoned their loved ones and left home to cultivate the path.
There was a king.
Who contracted a serious illness.
For twelve years it did not improve.
All the great physicians were unable to cure it.
At that time, a small border country was subordinate to the great king.
There was a physician skilled in treating illness.
The king summoned him and ordered him to cure his own illness.
Not long after, he was relieved and recovered.
The king then thought of repaying this physician's kindness.
He ordered an envoy to proclaim to that country.
"This physician has cured me, he should be rewarded."
"Elephants, horses, carriages, cattle, sheep, fields, houses, servants, attendants, and fine adornments shall all be given to him."
That small country's king received and proclaimed the superior command.
The physician was by the king's side and no one spoke of it.
The physician then thought.
"I cured the king's illness with great effort."
"I do not know if the king will repay me or not."
After several more days, the king gradually recovered fully.
The physician requested to take leave and return to his home country.
The king then permitted it.
He gave him a weak horse and the riding gear was also shabby.
The physician laughed greatly, resentful that he had cured the king's illness.
With great effort.
Yet the king did not recognize the kindness.
Did not arrange anything.
"Making me go back empty-handed."
Along the way he sorrowfully sighed, considering it an eternal regret.
Just as he reached his home country, he saw a herd of elephants.
He asked the elephant keeper.
"Whose elephants are these?"
The elephant keeper answered.
"These are the elephants of a certain master."
He asked the elephant keeper again.
"How did a certain master obtain these elephants?"
The answer was.
"A certain master cured the great king's illness and he recovered."
"They are the reward for his merit."
He went a little further ahead.
Saw herds of horses, cattle, and sheep.
Asked.
"Whose possessions are these?"
The shepherd answered.
"They belong to a certain master."
He went a little further ahead.
Saw his original house, now with tall halls and multi-storied pavilions, vastly different from his former dwelling.
He asked the gatekeeper.
"Whose house is this?"
The gatekeeper answered.
"This is the house of a certain master."
He then entered the inner chamber.
Saw his wife, her appearance radiant and joyful, her body clad in precious robes.
Astonished, he asked.
"Whose wife is this?"
An attendant answered.
"This is the wife of a certain master."
From seeing the elephants and horses.
To entering the house.
He then knew all were rewards obtained for the merit of curing the king's illness.
He then regretted his original thoughts.
That he had considered his effort in curing the king's illness small.
In the past, there was a Kālavat (a wealthy householder).
Who set up a great altar and invited the Buddha and the monastic community.
At that time, there was a man selling yogurt.
The host kept him to eat.
Urged him to keep the fast and listen to the sutra.
He did not return until dusk.
His wife said to him.
"I have not eaten since morning, waiting for you until now."
"You have broken your fast."
"The merit of half a fast still results in rebirth in heaven for seven lifetimes."
"Born among humans, one constantly attains natural provisions."
"One day of keeping the fast yields six hundred thousand years of natural sustenance."
"Furthermore, there are five blessings."
"First, little illness."
"Second, body and mind are peaceful and secure."
"Third, little lust."
"Fourth, little sleep."
"Fifth, after life ends, the spirit is reborn in heaven, always knowing past lives."
Once there was a man working in the fields.
The sun was already past noon.
The meal from home had not yet arrived.
A mendicant monk, having lost his way, came to his field.
He begged for a midday meal.
The farmer said, "Alright.
Please wait a little while.
The meal from home is late."
The monk said,
"Since the food has not yet come, I would like to rinse my mouth."
The farmer untied his belt and gave him a myrobalan fruit.
The monk accepted it and ate it.
He also gave a coin as an offering to the monk.
The monk said,
"If your heart is truly sincere, I have nothing to repay you with.
I wish to bestow upon you the Five Precepts.
Can you accept them?"
He replied,
"As a layman, it is difficult for me to fully observe all Five Precepts.
I will only accept the precept against killing."
When the farmer's life ended, he was reborn in the womb of the queen of a kingdom.
The queen, with her retinue, went to the riverside.
Singing, dancing, and making merry, she held the child near the water.
She accidentally dropped the child into the water, and a fish immediately swallowed him.
For seven days inside the fish's belly, he felt neither hunger nor thirst.
Carried downstream, he traveled over a thousand li.
Entering the territory of a lower kingdom, people caught the fish and sold it in the market.
At that time, the king of the lower kingdom sent someone to buy fish.
When they brought it back to the city and were cutting the fish with a knife,
the child inside the belly cried out,
"Slowly, do not harm me!"
They then cut open the fish's belly and saw a small child.
Handsome and peerless, the entire kingdom rejoiced.
The king of the upper kingdom heard of this and said,
"This must be my child."
He sent a message demanding the child.
The king of the lower kingdom replied,
"Heaven bestowed this child from the fish's belly.
I will not give him up."
The two kingdoms disputed, and the matter reached a great kingdom.
The great king judged, saying,
"If the upper kingdom had not given birth to this child and he had not fallen into the water, how could the lower kingdom have obtained him?
If the lower kingdom had not obtained this child,
where would the upper kingdom seek to find him?
Both have a connection.
You two kingdoms,
in between, build a palace and jointly care for this child.
He shall be called the Crown Prince of Two Kingdoms."
Following this decree, he was placed there.
According to the ceremonial laws for a crown prince.
The Buddha told his disciples,
"The farmer of old,
with one fruit and one coin given as alms to the monk,
thus became the Crown Prince of Two Kingdoms.
Once there was a lame mendicant monk.
Upholding the precepts and begging for food, he came upon a household.
The family, long devoted to the great Dharma, saw his afflicted foot.
Their hearts filled with compassion, and they provided for him for a year.
When the monk prepared to leave,
the host said,
'I hope you will visit us often.'
At the moment of parting, both guest and host shed sad tears.
After the monk departed,
the host lifted the bed and found only gold and treasures.
Thus he became wealthy.
A neighboring family, seeing his great wealth,
asked how it came about.
The man truthfully answered.
The neighbor, with an evil thought hoping to find treasures,
sought a lame person to provide for.
Searching everywhere, he found none.
He happened upon a monk whose body was whole and intact.
He bound him, broke his leg, and provided for him for a short time.
Then he forcibly drove him away.
After he left, the neighbor lifted the bed.
Summoned by his evil mind,
poisonous snakes, wasps, and scorpions came and stung his entire family.
This was the evil retribution in the present life; afterward, they fell into hell.
The one who obtained treasures had a sincere and virtuous heart.
Those stung by poison had hearts lacking benevolence.
In the past, there was a brother and sister.
The sister had a son.
Both the uncle and nephew worked for the government.
They wove gold-threaded brocade, silks, and other exquisite, rare garments, storing them in the treasury along with precious treasures.
They then discussed together, saying:
"We weave diligently and tirelessly.
We know the quality and quantity of all the items in the treasury.
Why not take some for ourselves to alleviate our poverty?"
At night, they dug a hole in the ground and tunneled in to steal the items.
The next day, the treasury guards noticed that items were missing.
They reported the matter to the king.
The king ordered them not to publicize it widely.
He said, "Let the thieves think the king is too busy to notice.
In the future, they will surely come again.
Tighten the guard and capture them when they come; do not let them escape."
The treasury guards accepted the order.
They increased their vigilance.
After a long time, the thieves indeed returned to steal.
The nephew instructed his uncle:
"You are older, frail, and weak.
If the guards catch you, you won't be able to escape.
Go back through the tunnel and enter from the other end.
If they catch you,
I am strong and will surely rescue you."
The uncle entered the tunnel and was caught by the guards.
The guards shouted.
The nephew, fearing he would be recognized,
cut off his uncle's head and fled.
At dawn, the treasury guards reported the incident in detail.
The king again ordered:
"Take the body and place it at a crossroads for public display.
Whoever comes to mourn and take the corpse will be the thief."
Several days passed like this.
A merchant from afar arrived.
His horses and men crowded the road, bustling and pushing.
The merchant loaded two carts with firewood and placed them on the corpse.
The guards reported this to the king.
The king ordered:
"If anyone sets it on fire, capture and bring them to me."
The nephew then instructed some children to hold torches and play games.
A crowd gathered, and they threw the torches onto the firewood.
The fire blazed fiercely.
The guards did not notice.
They reported it to the king.
The king again ordered:
"Increase the guards.
Watch the bones closely."
The nephew then brewed pure wine,
making it especially strong.
He went to the guards
and secretly sold it to them.
The guards had been hungry and thirsty for days.
Seeing the wine, they drank together.
They drank too much and all fell into a drunken slumber.
The nephew then used a wine jar to collect the bones
and left.
The guards did not notice.
The next day, they reported to the king.
The king again ordered:
"Despite all the vigilance, we still haven't caught the thief.
This thief is cunning; we must devise another plan."
The king then adorned his daughter with jewels and precious ornaments,
and placed her in a room by a large body of water.
Many people stood guard, watching carefully for any suspicious activity.
"Surely someone greedy for beauty will come for the girl," he thought.
He instructed the girl to grab and hold anyone who approached and call for the guards to capture them.
On another night, the nephew came to steal again.
He released a log into the water, letting it float downstream.
He shouted and then hid.
The guards were alarmed and rushed over, thinking someone was there.
But they only saw a log.
This happened repeatedly for several nights without change.
The guards grew weary and fell asleep.
The nephew then rode the log to the girl's room.
The girl grabbed his clothes.
The nephew said to the girl:
"Grab my arm instead."
The nephew had prepared a dead man's arm and gave it to her.
The girl let go of his clothes, grabbed the arm, and screamed.
The guards woke up, but the nephew had already escaped.
The next day, they reported to the king.
The king again ordered:
"This man's cleverness is unmatched.
We have long failed to capture him.
What can we do?"
The girl became pregnant.
After ten months, she gave birth to a boy.
He was very handsome.
The king had a wet nurse carry the child around the entire country.
"If anyone kisses the child, capture and bring them here," he ordered.
The child was carried all day.
The nephew, working as a baker, stayed under his bakery oven.
The child cried from hunger.
The wet nurse carried the child to the bakery oven.
She bought a cake to feed the child.
The nephew saw the child and kissed him.
The wet nurse then reported to the king:
"The child was carried all day, and no one came near.
When he was hungry near the bakery oven,
the baker gave him a cake and kissed him."
The king ordered:
"Why didn't you capture him?"
The wet nurse replied:
"The child was crying from hunger, and the baker gave him a cake and kissed him. He shouldn't be the thief."
The king ordered the wet nurse to carry the child out again, along with all the watchers.
"If anyone comes near the child, capture and bring them here," he said.
The nephew bought fine wine.
He invited the wet nurse and the watchers to a tavern and urged them to drink.
They got drunk and fell asleep, and he stole the child away.
When they woke up, the child was gone.
They reported it to the king.
The king again ordered:
"You fools! Greedy for wine, you not only failed to catch the thief but also lost the child."
The nephew took the child and fled to another country.
He went before the king.
He paid his respects, answered questions, and expounded on scriptures and their meanings.
The king was greatly pleased.
He bestowed an official position upon him, making him a high minister.
And said to him:
"In my entire kingdom, no one matches your wisdom and ingenuity.
I wish to marry you to my daughter or any woman of your choice."
He replied, "I dare not.
But if Your Majesty pities me, I wish to marry the daughter of a certain king."
The king said, "Excellent.
Follow your wish."
The king treated him as a son.
He sent an envoy to seek the hand of that king's daughter.
That king agreed.
But then he thought to himself:
"This might be that cunning thief from before."
He sent an envoy,
saying he would send his daughter,
but also dispatched his crown prince with five hundred cavalry, all in full array.
The nephew was afraid.
He feared that upon arriving in that country,
the king would capture him.
He then said to his king:
"If Your Majesty sends me,
I must have five hundred cavalry with identical clothing and saddles.
Only then can I go to fetch the bride."
The king agreed.
So he went to fetch the bride.
The other king had his daughter serve food and drink to the guests.
Two hundred fifty cavalry rode in front,
and two hundred fifty rode behind.
The nephew was among them, riding his horse without dismounting.
The girl's father walked among the cavalry.
He grabbed the nephew and said:
"Are you the one who, with such ingenuity, could not be captured before?
Is it you or not?"
The nephew bowed his head and replied:
"It is I."
The king said:
"Your intelligence is unmatched under heaven.
As you wish, I give you my daughter in marriage."
The nephew is me.
The girl's father, the king, is Śāriputra.
The uncle is Devadatta.
The king, the father, is Śuddhodana.
The mother is Māyā.
The wife is Gopikā.
The son is Rāhula.
In ancient times, there was the country of Qíshéjué.
There was a young woman.
Her appearance was beautiful and her intelligence was unparalleled.
Her temperament was broad and gentle, and she never became angry.
All nine clans of her family and all relatives, near and far, loved and respected her.
From various countries, thousands of people sought her hand.
Yet she remained unmarried.
At that time, in the country of Luóyuè, there was a young man.
He was naturally handsome and outstanding, with lofty aspirations.
All the people of the country feared and respected him.
Although he had concubines and wives, he never favored or approached them.
He often thought:
"In the country of Qíshéjué, there is a woman.
She is truly my match.
I have not yet reached her."
That very day,
he thought: "The entire hall is filled with those gained through power and influence, not my true partner."
