Immediately, he dismissed them all, leaving the place empty and quiet.
Then, riding a white elephant and accompanied by two servants, he set out for that country.
Crossing mountains and traversing grasslands, he traveled thousands of miles.
It took five years to arrive.
The woman, residing deep in the palace, felt her heart stir for no reason.
She went out to stroll.
Trying to peek outside the pavilion,
she suddenly saw this man.
Both sorrowful and joyful, she could not suppress her feelings.
"This is my husband.
All those who sought me before were not my destined match."
She then personally approached him, and their affection grew deep.
The woman's parents were worried and distressed, with no plan, saying:
"We raised our daughter to adulthood, never expecting this."
They urgently increased precautions, preventing any communication.
The woman was distressed, not knowing what to do.
The man was sorrowful and anxious, sharing the same melancholy.
Thereupon, the woman diligently practiced austerity, observed fasting, and cultivated the path day and night.
She abandoned and distributed her wealth, making offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha.
Her heart wearied and her body withered, passing through five years.
No news could be exchanged, yet both cherished their feelings.
Still, nothing moved them.
Then, on the eighth day of the fourth month,
she personally bound herself and went to the Buddha's stupa.
Burning incense and paying homage, she made this vow:
"I will cut my flesh to make offerings to the World-Honored One.
I dare not cherish myself.
I only wish that this aspiration may bear fruit."
The Buddha instructed a bhikṣuṇī to act as their matchmaker.
Thus, they were united as a couple.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Why is this so?
It is because since countless kalpas ago,
they have long made vows and agreements, hence this outcome."
In the past, there was a husband and wife.
They shared three fruits to eat.
Each took one.
The remaining one they intended to split.
The wife said:
"Do not split it.
Let us bet with you.
Each will remain silent.
The one who speaks first loses.
The one who speaks later gains it."
Thus, they kept silent until midnight.
A thief sneaked in.
Seeing the two sitting without speaking,
he thought they were greatly afraid and dared not make a sound.
He gathered their belongings, carried them, and was about to leave the house.
The wife loudly shouted:
"You are a man, how can you let the things be taken away?"
The husband said:
"I win, I win!
Now I get the big fruit."
Everyone scolded and laughed, calling them utterly foolish.
In the past, there was a man.
Seeing another woman's nose was well-shaped,
he thought to himself:
"My wife's face is the best,
only her nose is ugly.
I will take this nose to replace my wife's nose."
He then led the woman to a secluded place.
Cut off her nose and took it back.
Then cut off his wife's nose and attached the other woman's nose.
Both lost their noses, and neither could be attached properly.
Everyone found it strange and cursed him, calling him truly mad.
In the past, there was an extremely poor man.
He was skilled at understanding bird language.
He worked as a porter for a merchant.
Passing by the water's edge to drink,
a crow cawed.
The merchant was frightened.
The porter instead laughed.
Upon reaching home, the merchant asked:
"When I was drinking there,
I heard the crow caw.
I was greatly frightened, but you instead laughed. Why?"
He replied:
"The crow said to me:
'The merchant has a fine white pearl on him.
You can kill him and take the pearl.
I want to eat his flesh.'
That is why I laughed."
The merchant said: "Why didn't you kill me?"
He replied:
"Because in my past life, I coveted others' wealth and possessions, hence I am poor and work as a porter.
If I kill someone and take their belongings, I will suffer in future lives.
When will it ever end?
I would rather die than do such a thing."
A great flood suddenly submerged the land.
All living beings relied on hills to avoid it.
As the water was about to cover them completely,
suddenly, a phoenix arrived.
It went to where the wise man was, and he clung to its wings.
Thus, he ascended to the high plain and escaped the water disaster.
Those who did not leave,
seeing a cormorant, entrusted themselves to its feathers.
But this cormorant
entered deep water, and they all drowned at once.
In the past, there was a man.
Poor and without means,
he made a living by going to sea to gather treasures and returned to his country.
He met a knowledgeable friend who said:
"I have always been poor, now I have these things.
They are enough for me to be content.
If my mother is not pleased,
I intend to leave my mother and live apart.
If my wife is not pleased,
I intend to seek another."
The knowledgeable friend replied:
"Near here, in the city, there are many great wise people.
You can go and buy wisdom from them.
It will not cost more than a thousand taels of gold.
They will surely tell you the method of wisdom."
The man followed his words.
He entered a Buddhist settlement.
He asked people in detail.
They replied:
"Regarding matters you doubt,
take seven steps forward, then seven steps back.
Repeat this three times, and wisdom will arise by itself."
That night, the man returned home.
He saw his mother sleeping beside his wife.
Thinking it was another man,
he drew his knife, intending to kill.
His mind was unsettled.
Then, lighting a large lamp, he illuminated from afar and pondered:
"This morning, I bought wisdom."
Thus, he went forward and back three times.
His mother then awoke.
The man sighed and said:
"This is truly wisdom.
How can it be worth only a thousand taels of gold?"
He then gave three thousand taels of gold.
In the past, a man was walking in the mountains.
He encountered a man-eating ghost.
The ghost seized him, intending to eat him.
The man pleaded for mercy,
asking for a moment to inquire about one thing.
Then he would be eaten without regret.
The ghost believed the man, thinking it sincere,
and allowed him his wish.
The man then asked the ghost:
"Why is your face white, your knees and belly white,
while the rest of your body is completely black?"
The ghost replied:
"I, as a creature, am averse to sunlight.
I can walk with my back to the sun, but not facing it.
That is the reason."
The man then ran toward the sun.
The ghost could only hate in vain, unable to catch him.
In the past, there was a man with two wives.
He went to the younger wife.
The younger wife said:
"I am young.
My husband is old.
I do not enjoy living here.
You should go to the elder wife's place to live."
The husband plucked out his white hairs.
He went to the elder wife's place.
The elder wife said:
"I am old, my head is already white.
My husband's head is black, you should leave."
Thereupon, he plucked out his black hairs, making them white.
Continuing like this without stop,
his head eventually became completely bald.
Both wives despised him.
They each abandoned him and left.
He sat in sorrow until he died.
In a past life, he was a dog in a temple.
There was a temple east of the water and a temple west of the water.
Hearing the sounding of the gong, the dog would go and get food.
Later, one day, both temples sounded their gongs simultaneously.
The dog swam, wanting to cross the water.
Just about to reach the west, he feared the east temple's food was better.
Turning east, he feared the west temple's food was better.
Hesitating like this, he drowned in the water.
Once there was a man.
He heard that in a foreign land there was immortal water, and whoever drank it would become an immortal.
So he traveled to that foreign land and sought lodging.
The host asked the guest,
"Where do you intend to go?"
The guest replied, "To learn immortality."
The host harbored ill intentions.
He said to the guest,
"I have an immortal tree.
If you can labor for me for one year,
I will grant you immortality. Why trouble yourself to go far away?"
The guest said, "Excellent."
For a year he toiled without ever showing resentment.
When the year was completed,
the host, who had originally intended to deceive him,
had no immortal tree.
He took him to the mountains and pointed to a tree at the edge of a cliff, saying it was the immortal tree.
"Climb to the top of it,"
"and when I call out 'Fly!', you must respond and leap."
The guest, with utmost sincerity,
immediately ascended the tree and soared into the sky.
Thus he attained the Way of Immortality.
The host thought, "I meant for him to die.
How did he instead become an immortal?"
He deeply revered this tree, believing it to be sacred.
After a short time,
he and his son went together to the tree.
He yielded to his father to go first.
The son then called out, "Father, you may fly!"
The father immediately tried to fly,
but fell onto the rocks below,
his body shattered to pieces.
Once there was a man
who sold a Píyé guǐ at the market.
A prospective buyer asked how much it cost.
The owner of the guǐ said,
"Two hundred taels of gold."
The buyer asked,
"What is so extraordinary about this guǐ
that you demand such a price?"
He replied,
"This guǐ can do anything; there is nothing it cannot accomplish.
It is estimated that its work in one day equals that of a hundred men.
It has only one flaw,
which you must guard against beforehand."
The buyer asked what kind of flaw it was.
He said,
"When you set this guǐ to work,
you must keep it working day and night,
never letting it rest.
If there is no work for it to do, it will turn and harm its master."
The master, considering the gold, took it home
and set it to work farming.
When the farming was done, he set it to carpentry.
When the carpentry was done, he set it to leveling the ground,
building houses, pounding grain, and cooking—never allowing it a moment's rest.
Within a few years, he became immensely wealthy.
The master had some business to attend to and went away as a guest,
but forgot to give instructions, and the guǐ, wanting to work, had no order of tasks.
It took the master's son and put him in a cauldron, lighting a fire to boil him.
By the time the master returned, his son was already cooked to a pulp.
Grieved and remorseful, what more could he say?
Once there was a wealthy man.
The king ordered him to itemize his possessions.
He then listed:
In such-and-such a year, he used so many tens of millions to build a Buddha statue;
so many to hold vegetarian feasts and copy scriptures;
and so many to aid and support the poor and elderly.
Now he currently had eighty-nine million.
He presented the list to the king.
The king was greatly enraged and asked,
"Why have you listed your current possessions as already used?"
The wealthy man replied,
"What has already been used is the most precious treasure,
nourishing one's spirit. That is why I presented it.
Wealth not yet used is shared by the five families,
not mine alone.
That is why I dared to list it."
The king then became enlightened,
realizing that merit and virtue are reliable.
Once there was a man who committed a crime against the king.
The king was greatly angry,
and ordered someone to cut five catties of flesh from his back.
It was placed in a lower room.
This man, in pain, cried out so loudly that the king heard.
The king asked why he was making such a fuss.
He replied,
"Truly, it is not my crime."
The king reflected and felt ashamed.
He ordered a hundred catties of meat to be given to him.
But the man still groaned and cried out.
The king said,
"I have given you a hundred catties at once. Why are you still crying out so loudly?"
The ministers replied,
"We have never seen such a method.
What good does a thousand catties do for his pain?
If a man's child has died,
and another gives him a hundred children,
can this man not still mourn his own child?"
There were two men who were close friends.
Their wives were both pregnant.
They made a vow,
that if one gave birth to a boy and the other to a girl, they would marry them to each other.
After parting, one family had a boy and the other a girl.
The boy's father died early, and the boy grew up without marrying.
He traveled selling sundries and happened to arrive at the girl's home.
The girl's father asked the young man where he came from,
where he lived, and the names of his parents.
The young man answered in detail.
The father was greatly surprised.
He then said to the young man,
"When your father was alive, we made a prenatal marriage agreement.
I have often searched for you but did not know where you were.
My daughter has not dared to marry."
The young man said,
"I knew nothing of this."
The father said,
"You may ask your close relatives."
The young man returned and asked his wet nurse, and it was indeed true.
The young man went to the girl's home.
On the way, he saw ditch water flowing
into a skull, yet it never filled.
Fearing to go forward, he then saw a tree with ripe fruit.
He wanted to pick and eat it.
The fruit then said,
"Take me, take me."
The young man was greatly terrified and ran swiftly, stumbling to the ground.
He arrived at the girl's home.
A dog came forward, knelt on its hind legs, and licked his feet.
Puppies in the dog's belly barked and came forward,
wanting to bite and injure him.
He fell to the ground again and lay unconscious for a long time before reviving.
The girl's father came out, and the young man recounted everything.
The father found it very strange and went in to tell his daughter.
The daughter replied to her father, "Seeing ditch water flowing into a skull without ever filling means
that in later generations, there will be those who gather the wealth and treasures of the world
to supply one person, yet it will never be enough.
Seeing ripe fruit on a tree and wanting to pick and eat it,
and the fruit saying 'Take me, take me' means
that in later generations, when men seek a great wife,
the lesser wife will say,
'Why not choose me? Why not choose me?'
The dog kneeling on its hind legs and licking his feet,
and the puppies in its belly barking and coming forward to bite him means
that in later generations, when people speak to each other,
their mouths are like sweet ointment, but their hearts are like awls and knives.
Outwardly they appear satisfied, but inwardly they plot and scheme.
All this is for later generations, not for the present."
He then married his daughter to the young man,
fulfilling their original intention.
Once, a great family had two sons.
Each was given two million to go trading.
The elder son spent it all on gambling.
His clothes worn out, he returned and reported to his father.
His father said,
"I am glad to have you back.
What use is wealth?"
He provided him with clothes, food, and drink,
comforting him kindly.
The younger son returned and reported to his father,
"I have gained two million in profit."
His father said,
"Bring the account book."
They checked the accounts together, and it was short by several thousand.
So he bound and beat him.
This happened three times.
He collected six million in profit,
but each time he returned, he was beaten.
The elder son lost six million over three ventures.
He stayed in another country and did not return.
He fell in with a scoundrel.
He said to that man,
"My father has a chest each of gold, silver, and white pearls
at the head of his large bed.
You go back and tell my father
that I am not foolish for losing wealth,
but I dare not return.
If you get the chance, kill my father, take the things, and bring them here.
We can share them."
This man went to his home and met his father.
He recounted his son's words.
The father, hearing this, wept and said,
"What use are material possessions?
Why does my son not come back?"
He ate and rested, grieving and sobbing.
The guest said,
"Your son is unfilial; he used money to do evil
and spent it all at once.
He sent me to kill you and take your gold and silver.
But seeing how you miss your son and have treated me so kindly,
my heart is moved."
The father said,
"My son is still foolish. Please go and bring him back."
He said to his son,
"You lost the money, so come back early.
Why speak such foolish words?"
He gave him more clothes and bedding.
The Master said,
"The younger son repays debts;
the elder son demands debts."
Once there were three men who went on a trading journey together.
Each received over five million.
There was one coin that they wanted to give to one person.
But this would be unfair.
They considered breaking it to share.
Yet that was not feasible.
At that time, a monk was seeking alms.
The three men agreed to make an offering to the monk, each saying it was excellent.
Together they handed it over.
The monk chanted blessings,
wishing that in this life and the next, they would all receive blessings.
They were reborn together in Ràyuèguó, each becoming wealthy and powerful.
One was in charge of mining gold in the mountains.
One was in charge of farming the land to obtain gold.
One was in charge of drawing gold from the water.
This was due to the blessings from their previous life's offering.
The king heard of this.
Thinking that all people and things in his kingdom belonged to him,
he led soldiers to the mountains to mine it.
The gold turned into stone.
He then went to the farmland of one family.
When they tried to farm for gold,
the gold turned into soil.
He then went to the well of another family to draw gold.
The gold turned into tiles.
He could not obtain any of it.
The king asked the Buddha,
"The gold of these three men should belong to me.
But when I went to take it, it all transformed and I could not get the gold.
What merit did these people accumulate in their previous life to attain such blessings now?"
The Buddha explained in detail.
"This is not the king's property.
The king should not take it."
Once there was a poor family who supported a monk.
After a year, the monk left.
Using a copper bottle, he begged the master of the house, saying,
"This bottle is divine.
Whatever you ask for from the mouth of this bottle, you will receive.
Do not invite the king."
After he left, they struck the bottle.
The family became immensely wealthy.
They forgot the monk's warning.
They invited the king.
The king asked about the source of their wealth.
They truthfully answered the king.
The king then seized the bottle.
The family became poor and destitute again.
Only then did they remember the monk and went out in all directions to find him.
They truthfully told him.
The monk said,
"You still need this bottle.
I ask you for a pot filled with forest stones.
Take it to the king's gate and demand the bottle."
They went straight to the king's gate and loudly demanded the bottle.
The king heard and was furious.
He sent dozens of men to capture them.
They opened the pot, and the forest stones were blown by the wind, flying through the air.
The king's men were struck by these wood and stones, breaking their heads and foreheads; in an instant, a thousand men emerged.
The force of the wind broke them, and dead bodies blocked the gate.
The king was terrified.
He begged to return the bottle.
The man got the bottle back.
His family became immensely wealthy again.
They extensively performed meritorious deeds.
After death, they were reborn in heaven.
The Buddha and Ānán entered Rājagṛha.
At that time, heavy rain fell.
Water washed away the soil, revealing hidden treasures.
The Buddha said, "Poisonous snakes."
Ānán said, "Vicious poisonous snakes."
A man cutting wheat at the foot of the mountain heard this and thought,
"I have never seen a monk's poisonous snake."
He went to see the objects.
Using a cart and clothing sacks, he took them home.
He displayed signs of wealth and built a new large house.
An envious person reported to the king,
"Previously, there was a poor, lowly man who suddenly appeared wealthy.
This man must have obtained a great treasure."
The king summoned and questioned him.
He replied that he had not obtained anything.
The king ordered him to be tortured.
The man remembered the Buddha and Ānán calling it a vicious poisonous snake.
Who would obtain treasure and not speak of it?
With single-minded devotion, he thought of the Buddha.
The king said such words.
The Buddha said, "Poisonous snakes."
Ānán said, "Vicious poisonous snakes."
The king summoned and questioned him.
The man replied,
"Great King,
if you grant me safety, I will tell the truth."
The king agreed.
He recounted the above events in detail.
"Now, what can you do to me?
You will surely devour my life."
The king rewarded him with five hundred gold coins,
for being able to quote the Buddha's words and Ānán's words in a moment of crisis.
Once there was a poor, cold, lonely old man.
He had no property of his own.
He came across an axe in the market.
It was the essence of many treasures,
but he did not recognize it.
He used it to chop firewood to sell for a meager living.
The axe was nearly worn out.
He happened to meet a foreign merchant named Sàbó,
who was a great trader.
Seeing the axe, he recognized it.
He asked the old man,
"Are you selling this axe?"
The old man said,
"I rely on this axe to live; I will not sell it."
Sàbó said again,
"I will give you a hundred bolts of silk; why not sell it?"
The old man did not respond.
Sàbó said again,
"I will give you two hundred bolts."
The old man became distressed and unhappy.
Sàbó said again,
"If it's too little, I will increase it.
Why are you unhappy?
I will give you five hundred bolts."
The old man began to weep loudly.
Sàbó said again,
"If the silk is too little, I will increase it.
Why are you crying?"
The old man said,
"I do not regret the small amount of silk; I regret my own foolishness.
This axe was originally one and a half feet long.
It has been worn down until only five inches remain.
Yet it is still worth five hundred bolts of silk.
This is what I regret."
Sàbó said again,
"Do not have any regrets.
Now I will give you a thousand bolts of silk."
He immediately broke the contract and took it away.
When burned with firewood, it all turned into precious treasures.
The World-Honored One entered Śrāvastī in the morning.
The Venerable Ānán followed.
There were two old men and women.
Aged and decrepit, their backs bent like hooks.
They went to the head of an alley where rubbish was burned.
Both crouched toward the fire like old crows.
They looked at each other with desire.
The Buddha said to Ānán,
"Do you see that couple?"
Ānán said,
"Yes."
The Buddha said,
"These two old people,
if in their youth and prime,
had diligently sought wealth, they would have become the wealthiest in Śrāvastī.
If they had left home to study the Way and diligently practiced, they would have attained Arhatship.
In the second half of their prime,
if they had diligently sought wealth, they would have become the second wealthiest in Śrāvastī.
If they had left home to study the Way, they would have attained the Anāgāmi fruit.
In middle age, if they had diligently sought wealth,
they would have become the third wealthiest in Śrāvastī.
If they had left home to study the Way, they would have attained the Sakṛdāgāmi fruit.
But now, aged and decrepit,
they have no money and no means.
They are no longer capable
of toiling for money.
Nor can they attain superior human qualities.
He then spoke a verse:
In the country of Yéyélí, there was a Kālāyue.
After making offerings to the Buddha and completing the incantations and vows,
he requested to hear the meaning of the Dharma.
The Buddha smiled, and a light from his mouth circled his body three times before returning and entering through the top of his head.
Ānán asked the reason.
The Buddha said:
"In that country, there were five hundred men
who went to sea to gather treasures, loaded them onto a ship, and returned on foot.
They passed through deep mountains and stopped to rest at dusk.
They prepared to depart early in the morning.
Four hundred and ninety-nine of them left,
but one man was sleeping soundly
and missed the group.
Then it began to rain and snow.
He lost the path.
Stranded and desperate in the mountains, he cried out to heaven.
There was a sandalwood tree spirit
who said to the poor man:
'You may stay here.
I will provide you with food and clothing.
You can leave when spring comes.'
The poor man stayed until the third month.
He addressed the tree spirit:
'I have received your kindness and preserved my life,
but I have not yet made even a small repayment.
However, I have two parents now in my homeland,
and I truly wish to see them.
I hope you will allow me to depart.'
The tree spirit said: 'Very well.
I will give you a gold ingot.
Not far from here,
you will reach a city,
and from there you can return to your hometown.'
As the poor man was about to leave, he asked the tree spirit:
'This tree is fragrant and pure, rare in the world.
Now that I am about to go far away, I wish to know its name.'
The spirit said:
'There is no need to ask.'
The poor man said again:
'I have relied on the shade of this tree for three months.
Now that I am about to go far away, my heart is filled with regret.
If I reach my homeland, I will proclaim the tree's kindness.'
The spirit then said:
'The tree is called sandalwood.
Its roots, stems, branches, and leaves can cure a hundred illnesses.
Its fragrance is known from afar, and people covet it. There is no need to speak of it.'
The poor man reached the country.
His relatives, both near and far, rejoiced and congratulated him.
Later, the king of the country fell ill with a headache.
Prayers and sacrifices to heaven, earth, mountains, rivers, and various spirits could not cure it.
Famous physicians examined him and said that only sandalwood incense could cure the illness.
The king then sought it among the people but found none.
So he proclaimed throughout the country:
'Whoever obtains sandalwood incense
will be enfeoffed as a marquis and married to my youngest daughter.'
When the poor man heard of the heavy reward,
he said:
'I know where sandalwood incense can be found.'
The king then ordered a close minister to take the poor man and go to cut it down.
They went straight to the tree.
The envoy saw that the tree was tall and straight,
with lush branches, brilliant flowers, and fruits,
a rare sight that made him reluctant to cut it down.
If he did not cut it down, he would disobey the king's order,
and the illness would not be cured.
If he cut it down, his heart would ache.
He hesitated, not knowing what to do.
The tree spirit spoke from the air:
'Cut it down.
But leave the roots.
After cutting, smear it with human blood,
and cover it with liver and intestines.
The tree will then grow again
and return to its former state.'
Hearing the spirit's words,
the envoy ordered people to cut it down.
The poor man stood by the tree,
and the tree's falling branch struck and killed him.
The envoys discussed it
and butchered the poor man, taking his liver and blood.
As the spirit had commanded, the tree grew again.
They loaded the cut tree onto a cart and returned to the country.
The physician then administered the medicine,
and the king's illness was cured.
The whole country rejoiced.
The king ordered the people of the country:
'All who are ill should come to the palace gate.
The king will distribute the fragrant medicine to them.'
All illnesses were cured.
The king's health was restored, and the common people were free from illness.
The whole country celebrated joyfully, and peace prevailed.
Once, a man was walking in an empty marsh
and saw a black elephant.
The man thought:
'This elephant will surely harm me.
I should kill it.'
The elephant also thought:
'The man will surely kill me.
I should attack him.'
The man then fled.
The elephant chased after him.
After running several miles forward, he fell into a deep valley.
The valley was bottomless.
He grabbed a tree root on the edge,
which was as thin as a finger.
He followed the root downward
and hung on the edge.
The elephant above the valley tried to reach him with its trunk,
but could not.
Looking down, he saw only bronze and iron at the bottom, and two rats gnawing at the tree root.
Three black snakes also emerged, intending to bite.
Mosquitoes and horseflies came to sting his eyes.
The man thought:
'Today I will die.'
He looked up to heaven and cried for help,
his voice sorrowful and his feelings sincere.
Heaven sent down sweet dew, dripping into his mouth.
With one drop, the two rats left.
With two drops, the poisonous snakes abandoned him.
With three drops, the black elephant returned on its own.
With four drops, the mosquitoes and horseflies were removed.
With five drops, the deep valley leveled itself, and he emerged on flat ground.
Heaven guided him and brought him back to the heavens.
Five hundred young children formed a group
and played together every day, going to the river.
They piled sand to build pagodas, each saying their pagoda was the best.
Although they had good hearts, their past-life blessings were thin.
Suddenly, it rained, the river swelled violently, and they were swept away and drowned.
The Buddha told the crowd:
'The five hundred children were reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.
They all resolved to practice the bodhisattva path.'
The Buddha emitted light, allowing their parents to see where their children were.
The Buddha called from afar: 'Five hundred children, come.'
Immediately, they all arrived and stood in the air.
They scattered flowers before the Buddha, bowed, and said:
'Through the World-Honored One's kindness,
although our bodies perished, we can see Maitreya.'
The Buddha said: 'Excellent.
You have firmly resolved to know the ultimate truth and built pagodas and temples.
Because of this, you were reborn in heaven and saw Maitreya, receiving his teachings.'
The Buddha preached the sutra to them, and they all rejoiced, establishing unwavering resolve.
Each told their parents: 'Do not grieve anymore.
Strive diligently and cultivate yourselves with the Dharma.'
The parents all developed the intention for enlightenment.
They bowed at the Buddha's feet and circled him three times.
Suddenly, they vanished and returned to the Tuṣita Heaven.
Once, several children
were playing on the road when they encountered the Buddha.
One child bowed
and offered five beans to the Buddha from his hand.
Four beans fell into the alms bowl, but one fell to the ground.
The Buddha said:
'May you receive blessings for many lifetimes.'
After the child died, he was reborn in heaven.
For eighty lifetimes afterward, he became a wheel-turning king.
A hundred years after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa,
the mountains, fields, and marshes were lush with vegetation.
Not far outside the mountains was a village, and cattle and horses entered a pond,
giving rise to five-colored lotus flowers.
A cowherd boy entered the pond to gather them,
filled a vessel with lotus flowers, and took them out of the mountains to offer to the Buddha.
Before reaching the temple,
he encountered a herd of cattle on the road, which trampled and killed the boy.
His spirit was immediately reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
A natural palace with five-colored lotus flowers appeared.
Upon being reborn in heaven, he thought to himself:
'My palace alone has lotus flowers of unusual colors.'
But according to heavenly law,
one first observes past-life causes and conditions before enjoying blessings.
He then saw his previous life.
The other heavens said to each other: 'This heaven-dweller is new. We should entertain him together. Why is he so anxious and unsettled?'
They went to ask him.
He replied:
'I was originally a cowherd boy.
I gathered lotus flowers to scatter at the Buddha's pagoda.
I died unexpectedly along the way.
Because of this merit, I was reborn here.
That is why I now pick flowers again, wishing to go to the former pagoda to scatter them before the Buddha, bow in worship, and fulfill my original vow.'
At that time, five hundred heavenly beings took hold of lotus flowers
and followed him to scatter them at the Buddha's pagoda.
Because of this merit, when Maitreya descends, they will all attain enlightenment together.
Once there was a man.
He made an offering of three coins.
He prayed for three wishes.
First, that in the future he would become a king.
Second, that he would understand the speech of all living beings.
Third, that he would possess great wisdom.
After his life ended, he was reborn into a commoner's family.
His appearance was upright and handsome.
The king recruited him to serve by his side.
This youth joined the recruitment and gained the position of attending the king.
He saw swallows in their nest.
He looked up and laughed.
The king asked why he was laughing.
He replied,
"The swallow says,
'I have obtained a dragon maiden's hair, ten zhang long, and I call my companion to look at it.'"
The king said,
"If this is true, it is good.
If not, you will be killed."
He sent someone to look, and it was indeed obtained.
The king wanted to take the maiden as his wife.
He said to the youth,
"Since you understand bird speech, you must have many strategies.
I will provide you with provisions.
Seek out this woman.
If you succeed, you will be greatly rewarded.
If you fail, I will kill you and your family."
The youth risked death and went to the eastern seashore.
He saw two men arguing over an invisible hat, water-walking boots, and a life-and-death staff.
The youth said,
"Why must you argue?
I will shoot an arrow, and you two chase after it.
The one who reaches it first gets the three items."
They replied, "Good."
He drew his bow and shot the arrow.
The two men raced after it.
The youth took the hat, put on the boots, and grasped the staff.
He went straight into the sea and reached the dragon's abode.
He removed the invisible hat so the dragon maiden could see him.
Women have many desires.
So she went with the youth, taking a box of gold, and returned to a foreign country.
The king sent someone to welcome them.
He ordered the maiden to enter alone.
The maiden then went forward.
The youth put on the invisible hat and followed her in.
The maiden saw the king was ugly.
She threw gold at the king, breaking his forehead and killing him.
The youth removed his hat.
Together with the maiden, he ascended the hall.
He loudly proclaimed,
"I should be king, and the maiden should be queen."
He ruled the kingdom.
Once there were many merchants.
They passed through a dangerous road and encountered robbers.
They lost many clothes and goods.
Among them was one garment.
It was made of deer fetus hair, fine, soft, smooth, and glossy, woven into clothing.
Its value was a hundredfold.
But its color was purplish-black and not pleasing to the eye.
The robbers did not appreciate it and used it as a cloth wrapper.
They used it to hold coarse clothes and divided them elsewhere.
Each took miscellaneous items, thinking they were wonderful.
Only this one cloth wrapper remained unopened and undivided.
Among the robber band was a weak and poor man.
He alone was not given a share.
He pleaded bitterly, and they gave him the cloth wrapper as alms.
He then sold it himself.
At that time, a great nobleman knew it was a good item.
He paid the price according to its worth.
Compared to the shares the other robbers received, it was equal.
When the robbers heard this, they felt great shame and annoyance.
Once there was a maiden.
She was upright, with dark blue hair as long as her body.
The king's consort offered a thousand taels of gold for her hair, but she refused to give it.
Seeing the Buddha, she rejoiced and wished to make an offering.
She asked her parents to invite him.
Her parents said,
"Our family is poor and has nothing to feed him."
The maiden said,
"Take the value of my hair to use for the offering."
Her parents told the Buddha, wishing the Buddha to briefly visit for a humble meal the next day.
The maiden cut her hair and gave it to the king's consort.
The consort, knowing her urgent need, only gave five hundred taels of gold.
The maiden took the gold to buy food, rejoicing immeasurably.
She regretted her past stinginess and present poverty.
She wished that in the future she would not encounter such suffering.
The maiden saw the World-Honored One.
Golden light of five colors illuminated inside her door.
She placed her head and face on the ground and circumambulated the Buddha three times.
Her hair was restored as before.
The Buddha said,
"In her past life, this maiden was poor and had nothing to give.
She often placed her head and face on the ground in reverence.
For eighty-one kalpas thereafter, she was always born among humans.
That merit exhausted, she was born into a poor family in this life.
Yet she recognized merit and virtue, rejoiced upon seeing me, and her blessings were immeasurable.
After her life ends, she will be born in the second heaven of Trāyastriṃśa.
When her heavenly
blessings and lifespan end, she will arouse the mind of the bodhisattva path."
The maiden's parents and brothers all rejoiced, and after their lives ended, they were born in heaven.
Once there was a lone mother.
She was hired to guard gardens and fields.
The master had matters and sent food past mealtime.
When the food arrived and she was about to eat,
a śramaṇa came begging.
She put all her portion of food into his bowl.
She also offered a single lotus stem.
The ascetic then displayed supernatural powers.
The mother joyfully exclaimed,
"Truly a sage!
May I in a future life have a hundred sons like this."
After the mother died, she became the offspring of a Brahmin.
Her spirit gathered at the place where the Brahmin urinated.
A deer licked the urine and thus conceived.
When the time was full, a daughter was born.
The Brahmin raised her.
When she reached over ten years of age,
she was tasked with guarding the dwelling and the fire.
The girl played with the deer and unknowingly let the fire go out.
Her father ordered her to fetch fire.
The girl went to a human settlement, and with each step, a lotus bloomed.
The fire owner said,
"You must circle my dwelling three times, and I will give you fire."
The girl complied.
Lotuses grew on the land, surrounding the house in three layers.
The king heard of this.
He summoned and asked an astrologer.
The astrologer said,
"There must be a holy offspring who will spread transformation endlessly."
The king ordered his virtuous ministers
to propose marriage and bring her back to the palace.
She became pregnant, and when the month was full, she gave birth to a hundred eggs.
The queen, consorts, and concubines were all jealous.
They put the eggs in a bag, secretly sealed its opening,
and threw it into the river's flow.
The god Śakra descended and sealed the opening with his seal.
Various gods protected it with wings, and it stopped as it flowed.
It drifted to a downstream country where a pillar was planted.
The king of that country, from his tower, saw from afar in the water
a bag flowing down.
It shone brightly, as if containing divine spirit.
He took it and looked.
Seeing Śakra's seal,
he opened it and found a hundred eggs, which he kept warm and nurtured.
When the time was full, their bodies formed, and a hundred boys were born.
They were born with sagely wisdom, understanding without being taught.
Their features were rare, and their strength equaled a hundred men's.
The king provided a hundred white elephants for the holy offspring.
They campaigned against neighboring countries, and none did not submit.
They also campaigned against the country of their birth father.
The king said,
"Who can repel this enemy?"
Their mother said,
"Great King, do not fear.
I will subdue them for you."
She then ascended a tower and loudly declared to them,
"There are three great acts of rebellion:
First, not distancing from evil crowds, bringing suffering in two lifetimes.
Second, being born not recognizing kin and opposing filial conduct.
Third, relying on power to kill kin, poisoning the Three Jewels.
Those who harbor these three rebellions, their evil is endless.
Now, open your mouths and see the proof."
The mother then rotated her breasts.
By heavenly mandate, milk shot into the mouths of all hundred sons.
Moved by sincere feeling, they drank the milk with sorrowful emotion.
Together they said,
"This is our mother!"
They bowed their heads in repentance.
Kin and offspring met, and none were not sorrowful and pained.
The two countries harmonized, and none did not praise this as good.
The sons, seeing the impermanence of the world,
bid farewell to their kin to study the path, distancing from worldly defilements.
Ninety-nine sons all became pratyekabuddhas.
One son governed the country; when his father passed away, he became king.
He granted great amnesty for all crimes, opened the treasuries to give alms.
The people lacked nothing.
He transformed them with the ten good deeds, governing the country with correct goodness.
He established stūpas and monasteries, making offerings to śramaṇas.
He recited sūtras, discussed the path, and his speech was free from the four evils.
The god Śakra protected him because he nurtured his kin's children.
The one who remained as king is myself.
The father is now King Śuddhodana.
The mother is Śākyamuni."
There was a woman who had been pregnant for several months.
Upon seeing the Buddha and his monks, she thought to herself,
"If I give birth to a son like this,
I will make him a śramaṇa and a disciple of the Buddha."
When the month was full, she gave birth to a boy, exceptionally handsome and different from the crowd.
By the age of seven,
the family was poor, so they prepared only two portions of food and three monastic robes.
Holding a water bottle, she took her son to the Buddha and said,
"I beg you to have pity on my son and make him a śramaṇa."
The Buddha immediately consented.
He instructed her to wash the boy's hands with the bottle.
Instantly, nine dragons emerged from the mouth of the bottle,
spouting water to bathe the boy.
The remaining water scattered over the boy's head,
transforming into a jeweled canopy.
Within it was a lion throne,
upon which sat a Buddha.
The Buddha smiled, emitting light of five colors,
illuminating billions of Buddha lands.
The light then circled the Buddha's body and entered through the boy's crown.
The mother offered food to the Buddha,
and her son also ate.
They aroused the mind of supreme enlightenment.
Billions of Buddha lands shook six times,
and all Buddhas manifested themselves.
The mother's food offering was distributed to all those Buddhas and the community of bhikṣus,
satisfying them all without diminishing.
The boy's hair fell out on its own, and he became a śramaṇa.
He immediately attained the irreversible stage.
In the past, east of Rājagṛha, there was an old woman
who was stingy, greedy, and faithless.
Her maidservant was diligent, constantly practicing compassion.
She kept two things in mind to benefit living beings:
first, not pouring hot water on the ground;
second, always giving the leftover grains from washing utensils to others.
The old woman fell ill and was on the verge of death.
Her soul was taken to hell,
where she saw fiery chariots, burning coals, boiling cauldrons, mountains of knives, forests of swords, and countless other torments.
The old woman saw and asked, "What is this place?"
The hell guards replied,
"This is hell.
East of Rājagṛha, there is a stingy, greedy old woman
who should enter here."
The old woman, realizing it was herself, trembled with fear and distress.
She walked a little further
and saw a palace of seven treasures, with hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens and all kinds of rare jewels.
She asked, "What is this place?"
They answered,
"A heavenly palace.
East of Rājagṛha, the stingy, greedy old woman has a diligent maidservant who, after her life ends, will be reborn here."
The old woman suddenly revived, clearly remembering what had happened.
She said to her maidservant,
"You are to be reborn in heaven.
You are my maidservant;
how can you enjoy it alone? You must share it with me."
The maidservant replied,
"If it were possible, I would gladly obey.
But I fear that good and evil follow one's own form and cannot be shared."
The old woman then gave up her stinginess and greed
and performed many meritorious deeds.
In the past, during the time of Buddha Vipaśyin,
accompanied by sixty-two thousand bhikṣus,
he first came out of the mountains and returned to his father's kingdom.
The king allotted land outside the city to establish a monastery.
Each bhikṣu received a plot of land.
One bhikṣu spoke to the neighboring household,
wishing to request them to build a hut.
The man of the house refused.
The old woman of the household built the hut with her own hands.
All ten of her fingers were pierced.
The bhikṣu sat inside in meditation,
and upon entering the samādhi of fire-light, the hut appeared to be engulfed in a great fire.
The old woman saw it from afar
and thought, "The hut I built has been burned down so quickly. How unfortunate I am!"
She entered and found the hut still intact.
But within the fire-light, she saw the bhikṣu
and was greatly delighted.
After her life ended, she was reborn in heaven.
When Śākyamuni became a Buddha, her heavenly life had not yet ended.
She descended and said to the Buddha,
"Tomorrow, I will offer food to the Buddha and the holy assembly."
The Buddha silently accepted.
King Prasenajit also sent an invitation to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"I have already accepted a heavenly invitation."
The king said,
"I have never seen a heavenly being come down to make an offering.
How could this happen?"
The next day, he sent people to wait, but they saw no preparations.
Even by mid-morning, it was still quiet.
The king ordered food to be prepared,
saying, "If no one else does it, I will provide it."
At noon, the heavenly being arrived but brought no food.
She only brought celestial maidens
and played various musical instruments, paying homage to the Buddha and standing there.
She announced, "The time has come."
Then she raised her hand towel, and everything was prepared.
After water was offered for washing,
she raised her hand again,
and a hundred flavors of sweet dew emerged from the kitchen and were placed on the ground.
She personally served, satisfying the entire assembly.
The king saw this and was amazed and joyful.
After the washing was completed, he said to the Buddha,
"I wonder what merit this heavenly being
accumulated in the past that her hand can produce a hundred flavors, and her merit is so great."
The Buddha explained to the king,
"In a previous life, she built a hut for a bhikṣu with her own hands.
From that, she was reborn in heaven for ninety-one kalpas.
The merit of her hand producing various things has not yet ended."
A mother had two sons.
One did not know how to swim
and drowned.
The mother did not cry at all.
The other knew how to swim but also drowned.
The mother wept bitterly for him.
People asked,
"You did not cry for the first son,
but you cry for the second son. Why?"
The mother said,
"The first did not know how to swim, so it was fitting.
The latter was skilled at swimming, so his death was unjust."
In the past, there was a man who had no faith.
His wife, however, devoutly served the Buddha.
The wife said to her husband,
"Human life is impermanent; you should cultivate merit."
The husband was indifferent and lazy.
The wife feared he would fall into hell in the future.
She again said to her husband,
"I wish to hang a bell on the door.
When you go in or out,
ring the bell and say, 'Námó Fó.'"
The husband said, "Very well."
This went on for a long time.
Eventually, the husband died.
Hell guards seized him and threw him into a boiling cauldron.
As he was tossed, the cauldron made a sound.
Thinking it was the bell,
he said, "Námó Fó."
The hell official heard this
and said, "This man served the Buddha."
He released him and sent him out,
and he was reborn among humans.
The people of Zhānpó country served the six teachers.
They had never before heard the names of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
They committed extremely evil deeds.
At that time, the Buddha, for the sake of sentient beings, went to the city of Zhānpó.
At that time, in that city, there was a great elder.
He had no heir.
Together, they served the six teachers to seek offspring.
Not long after, his wife became pregnant.
The elder, knowing this, went to the six teachers.
Joyfully he asked,
"Will it be a boy or a girl?"
The six teachers replied,
"It will certainly be a girl."
The elder became distressed.
Then a friend came and said to the elder,
"Have you not heard of the brothers Uruvilvā Kāśyapa?
Whose disciples are they?
If the six teachers are omniscient,
why did Kāśyapa abandon them and follow the Buddha?
Also, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others,
and kings such as King Bimbisāra and his queens,
Queen Mallikā,
elders of various countries such as Sudatta,
all these people are disciples of the Buddha.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has unobstructed knowledge and vision of all dharmas,
therefore he is called Buddha.
The Tathāgata is now residing nearby.
If you wish to know the truth, you should go to the Buddha."
At that time, the elder came to me.
He asked me about the matter.
The Buddha said, "Elder,
your wife is pregnant with a boy, without doubt.
His blessings and virtue are incomparable."
The elder was overjoyed.
The six teachers, envious in their hearts, took an āmra fruit, mixed it with poison, and gave it to the elder,
saying, "Excellent, Gautama has well described the signs.
When your wife is due, she can take this medicine.
The child will then be handsome, and the birth will be without trouble."
The elder accepted it and gave it to his wife to take.
After taking it, she died immediately.
The six teachers were delighted.
They went throughout the city proclaiming,
"The śramaṇa Gautama predicted
that the elder's wife would give birth to a boy.
Now the child is not yet born, and the mother has already died."
At that time, the elder again lost faith in me.
He then prepared the body, placed it in a coffin, and cremated it.
Seeing this, I turned and instructed Ānanda,
"Bring my robe; I wish to go there to destroy their wrong views."
At that time, the six teachers saw the Buddha coming from afar and said to each other,
"The śramaṇa Gautama is coming to this cemetery to eat flesh?"
Those upāsakas who had not yet attained the Dharma-eye were each filled with shame and fear.
They said to the Buddha,
"That woman has already died; please do not go."
At that time, Ānanda said to the people,
"Wait a moment.
The Tathāgata will soon extensively expound the realms of the Buddhas."
When the Buddha arrived,
the elder challenged him, saying,
"Your words are not contradictory?
The child's mother has already died; how can she give birth to a child?"
I said, "Elder,
at that time you did not ask about the length of the mother's life,
but only asked whether what she was carrying was a boy or a girl.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, speak without contradiction.
Therefore, you should know that you will certainly have a son."
At that time, the corpse's belly split open in the fire, and a child emerged from within.
Sitting upright in the fire like a lotus flower on a pedestal.
The six teachers saw this and said it was an illusion.
The elder saw it and his heart was again filled with joy.
He rebuked the six teachers,
"If you say it is an illusion, why don't you perform one?"
At that time, I immediately told Jīvaka,
"Go into the fire and bring that child here."
Jīvaka went forward into the fire as if entering a cool, great river.
He held the child and returned to me.
He handed the child to me.
After receiving the child, I said to the elder,
"The lifespan of all sentient beings is uncertain,
like bubbles on water.
If sentient beings have heavy karmic retribution,
fire and poison cannot harm them.
This is not my doing."
The elder said,
"Excellent, World-Honored One.
If this child can live out his natural lifespan,
I only wish the Tathāgata would give him a name."
The Buddha said,
"Elder,
this child was born in a fierce fire.
Fire is called Jvāla.
Therefore, his name is Jvāla."
The Buddha was in Śrāvastī.
An innumerable multitude was gathered to listen to the essential teachings of the Dharma.
At that time, there was a female disciple of the heretics named Manākhī.
Due to deep past offenses, she carried a wooden pestle hidden under her clothes.
She left Śrāvastī and went to the Jetavana monastery.
From afar, she saw the World-Honored One teaching the Dharma to an innumerable multitude.
She was overjoyed and could not contain herself.
"Today, I must disgrace Gautama in this assembly,
so that my teacher may receive offerings."
She then went into the assembly and spoke a verse:
"This preacher of the Dharma has made my body pregnant with a child."
At that time, in the great assembly, there were many heretics and naked ascetics.
Those who believed in the Buddha were few; those who practiced heresy were many.
Hearing this woman's words, they all believed and accepted them.
Those who believed in the Buddha thought to themselves,
"In the past, the Buddha was in the palace.
He abandoned his royal position and left behind his court ladies.
He left home to practice the path and attained perfect enlightenment.
How could he possibly have relations with this filthy and ugly woman?"
At that time, Śakra, the lord of the devas, was behind the Tathāgata, holding a fan and fanning him. He thought to himself,
"How could this vile Brahmin woman dare to have such thoughts and slander the Buddha?"
He transformed into a white rat.
It gnawed through the string of the wooden pestle; the sound was loud,
and all in the assembly saw it.
Those who were not firmly faithful were startled,
"What is this sound that shakes the four directions?"
Those who believed in the Buddha heard this sound and were overjoyed and elated.
They were all pleased together.
Immediately, one person rose from his seat,
picked up the wooden pestle, and said to the woman,
"Is this your child?"
At that moment, the ground split open, and her whole body fell into the Avīci hell.
The woman's relatives mourned and wept, unable to let go.
Those who did not believe in the Buddha immediately repented.
Those who believed said to each other,
"The retribution for slander is such a crime.
The proof is evident here;
how can one speak of a later life?"
There was a great householder
with immeasurable wealth.
His son was handsome, intelligent, and greatly fond of the scriptures and the path.
He left home to follow a teacher and practiced the scriptural teachings.
The teacher first sent him to seek alms for seven days.
In the country, there was a household of licentious women.
They called him to enter.
Upon entering, they closed the door and pulled the śramaṇa forward.
The śramaṇa did not comply.
The woman became very angry.
She called her maidservants to dig a fire pit one zhang deep.
She had four maidservants quickly seize him so he could not move.
They held him over the fire pit.
The śramaṇa said,
"Stop!
I must consider this."
The śramaṇa thought to himself,
"If I enter the fire, it is just one death.
Dying while upholding the precepts, I can be reborn in heaven.
If I die violating the precepts, I will fall into hell with no time of escape." He then entered the pit.
The fire turned into water, reaching up to the śramaṇa's waist.
He calmly and slowly emerged.
In the past, there was an elder named Shànshī.
He had an unmarried daughter at home.
While at home, she was warming herself by the fire.
The warmth entered her body, and she became pregnant.
Her parents were shocked and questioned her about the circumstances.
The girl truthfully replied that she did not know how it happened.
Her parents questioned her again,
and even beat her, but her story did not change.
They reported it to the king.
The king also questioned her, and her words remained unchanged.
He sentenced her to death.
The girl then cried out in grievance,
"How can there be an unrighteous king in the world who wrongfully kills the innocent?
If I am immoral, you can test me.
To be wronged like this!"
The king then examined and tested her.
As the girl said, there was nothing added or subtracted.
He said to her parents,
"I wish to take her."
The mother replied,
"Take her as you wish.
What use is this dead girl?"
The king then took her into the palace.
He cared for her as time passed, and the months were fulfilled.
She gave birth to a boy, handsome and wonderful.
As he grew up,
he left home to study the path, intelligent and learned.
Diligent and not long after, he attained the fruit of Arhatship.
He then liberated his parents.
Once there was a monk who was diligent and upheld the Dharma.
He observed the precepts strictly and never violated them from the start.
What he recited was the Prajñāpāramitā.
All who heard this monk’s voice rejoiced.
There was a young boy, seven years old, herding cattle outside the city. From afar he heard the monk reciting the sutra.
He then went to the monastery, paid homage to the monk,
and listened to the sutra’s words.
At that time, the teaching was on the emptiness of form.
As soon as he heard it, he understood.
The boy was greatly delighted.
He then asked the monk
questions, but the monk’s answers did not satisfy the boy.
At that moment, the boy instead explained the meaning to the monk.
The monk rejoiced at what he had never heard before.
He marveled that this boy’s wisdom was extraordinary.
The boy then left and returned to where the cattle were.
The calves he was herding had scattered and run into the mountains.
The boy followed their tracks, chasing and searching for them.
At that time, he encountered a tiger that killed the boy.
The boy died and was reborn into a wealthy household.
The lady of the house became pregnant.
From her mouth she could speak the Prajñāpāramitā.
From morning till night, she never ceased.
The wealthy household found it strange.
They thought the lady was speaking nonsense, calling it a ghostly affliction.
They consulted diviners and sought to exorcise the evil, but no one could understand it.
At that time, the monk entered the city to beg for alms and came to the wealthy man’s door.
From afar, he heard the voice and was greatly pleased.
He asked the wealthy man,
“Who inside is speaking this profound sutra?”
The wealthy man replied,
“My wife has a ghostly affliction; day and night she speaks nonsense without ceasing.”
The monk replied,
“This is not a ghostly affliction.
She is speaking the revered sutra, the great path of the Buddha.
I wish to enter and meet her.”
The wealthy man said, “Very well.”
He then went to his wife’s quarters.
The monk posed difficult questions, and she responded with thorough explanations.
The wealthy man then invited the monk to stay and prepared food for him.
Word spread among them:
The lady, while pregnant, recites the revered sutra.
Her voice is wonderfully pleasing.
Later, the wealthy man again invited the monk,
asking all the monks to come to his house, where he prepared food and offerings.
The lady came out, paid homage to the assembled monks, and again expounded the Dharma.
All the doubts and difficulties that the others could not resolve, she explained fully.
The monastic community rejoiced.
When the months were fulfilled, she gave birth to a son.
As soon as he was born, he joined his palms, knelt, and spoke the Prajñāpāramitā.
After giving birth, the lady returned to her original state.
The wealthy man asked,
“What is this?”
The monk answered,
“He is a true disciple of the Buddha. Take good care of him.
When this child grows up, he will become a teacher for all people.
We will all receive instruction from him.”
When the child was seven years old, he was fully accomplished in the Dharma.
He surpassed the entire assembly, his wisdom and insight boundless.
If there were errors or omissions in the sutras,
or anything lacking,
he would revise and supplement what was missing.
Wherever the child’s mother went, she would teach and transform people.
The wealthy man’s household, inside and out, all five hundred people, followed the child’s teachings.
Those he inspired numbered eighty-four thousand.
All of them aroused the mind for the unsurpassed, true, and right enlightenment.
The five hundred monks, hearing the child’s teachings, were freed from defilements, their minds liberated, aspiring to the Great Vehicle, and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
That child was I myself.
The monk was Kāśyapa Buddha.
There was a couple who had no children.
They made offerings to the heavenly gods, praying for offspring.
The god granted their wish.
The wife then became pregnant.
She gave birth to four kinds of objects:
first, a sandalwood peck-measure filled with rice;
second, a vase of ambrosia;
third, a treasure pouch;
fourth, a seven-jointed divine staff.
The man sighed and said,
“I sought a son, but instead gave birth to other things.”
He went to the god’s shrine and again made his request.
The god then said,
“What benefit do you seek in having a son?”
He replied,
“A son should serve and support us.”
The god said,
“Now, this peck-measure of rice will never be exhausted in use.
The vase of ambrosia will never diminish when eaten.
It cures a hundred illnesses. The pouch of treasures will never decrease when seen.
The seven-jointed divine staff protects against violence and calamity.
Could a son accomplish such things?”
The man was greatly pleased.
He returned home and tested them, finding the words true.
He then became immensely wealthy beyond measure.
The king heard of this.
He dispatched troops to attack and seize them.
The man raised the staff, flew about, struck the enemy, and defeated them.
The strong forces all retreated and scattered.
The man rejoiced, free from further worries.
Understand that those who are licentious and unrestrained
would rather lose their relatives
than cease their lustful activities.
Outside the city of Śrāvastī, there was a woman
carrying her child and a pitcher, going to the well to draw water.
There was a man with a handsome appearance,
sitting to the right of the well, playing the lute for his own amusement.
The woman, filled with desire, became infatuated with the man.
The man also desired the woman. The woman, deluded and unrestrained,
tied a rope around the child’s neck and hung him in the well.
She then quickly pulled him out,
but the child was already dead.
Overwhelmed with grief and sorrow, she cried out to heaven, shedding tears,
and spoke a verse:
The Buddha assembled the great multitude and addressed the monks:
“The fire of lust is fierce; it can burn away wholesome roots.
Those who are licentious and unrestrained do not recognize good and evil, do not distinguish purity from impurity, and do not understand bondage and liberation.
Such people have no shame or remorse.
They would rather lose their relatives and suffer punishment and disgrace.
Some, because of adultery and lust, kill their parents, siblings, and relatives.
They are executed by the king and suffer evil retribution after death,
rebirth after rebirth without end.
Once there was a man
who was deeply addicted to adultery and lust.
His parents had only this one son.
One night, at an ungodly hour,
when the sky was dark with thunder and lightning, he took a knife and arrows, intending to go to the village of prostitutes.
His mother became aware of this.
She stopped him and tried to persuade him:
‘The night is dark; you might be harmed by others.
I have little virtue and only have one son.
If you encounter evil, I will have no one to rely on.’
The son replied to his mother,
‘I must go; I cannot stay.’
The mother knew his mind was set.
She then went to where her son was.
He drew his knife and killed his mother.
He then knocked on the prostitute’s door.
The woman responded,
‘Who are you?’ The man answered with a verse:
The woman replied with a verse:
The man again said to the woman,
‘For your sake, I killed my mother, committing boundless sin.
Please show a little mercy.
Open the door so we may talk briefly,
and then I will return home.’
The woman replied,
‘The man returned home.
On the way, he encountered evil bandits and was killed by them.
He fell into the Avīci Hell to suffer retribution.’
Once there was a wealthy man with limitless riches.
He had only one sister, who married a poor husband.
The brother repeatedly gave her provisions.
Gradually, he grew tired of his sister’s visits.
She came to borrow flour from her brother.
The brother said,
‘Go and take it yourself.’
The sister then pressed and took it,
carrying it away.
The brother did not notice, and this happened repeatedly.
After the sister died, she was reborn as a calf in her brother’s household.
The brother loved it dearly, feeding it until it grew fat,
intending to kill it for a sacrificial offering.
At that time, five hundred merchants wanted to borrow money from the master at high interest.
Outside, they discussed among themselves,
‘How much will you borrow?’ Each stated the amount.
The last one said,
‘Just take more.
Later, if we don’t repay, what does the amount matter?’
The calf was nearby.
It spoke in human language:
‘Why do you people harbor such thoughts?
I am the master’s sister.
Because I deceived my brother when borrowing flour,
I am now in the form of a cow, repaying my brother’s debt.’
When the five hundred merchants
heard these words, they all trembled.
None of them borrowed money and they left.
A Pratyekabuddha came to the wealthy man’s house to beg for food.
The lady of the house saw his handsome appearance.
She said to the Pratyekabuddha,
‘If you comply with my desires, I will make offerings to you.’
The Pratyekabuddha said,
‘I cannot.’
Since the Pratyekabuddha did not comply with her wishes,
she felt ashamed and angry, sending him away.
A maidservant of the wealthy man disapproved of the lady’s words.
‘Why did you propose something improper to him?’
She took her own portion of food and gave it to the Pratyekabuddha.
After eating, she returned to her room to rest. When she awoke,
her dark, coarse skin naturally fell away.
Her face and appearance became extraordinarily beautiful, surpassing ordinary people,
like a heavenly jade maiden.
The wealthy man was astonished and asked her about what had happened.
He then honored her as his principal wife.
Within the city of Shèwèi.
There was a wealthy elder.
Named Chénjū.
In his household, there was a maidservant.
Named Fúníchí.
She had a large head, bald hair, and eyes that were a piercing blue.
Her mouth and nose were twisted and distorted, barely resembling a human.
She was often assigned to outdoor tasks, gathering firewood and cutting grass.
Several lǐ from the home, there was a spring.
It was both fragrant and sweet.
The maidservant took a bottle to fetch water.
At that time, a woman from a neighboring house.
Was hanging herself from a tree, her shadow falling into the spring.
The maidservant saw the reflection and thought it was her own form.
She immediately flew into a rage and cursed.
"I am so beautiful and proper.
Yet I am driven to toil in the fields and gardens, suffering such hardship."
She then smashed the bottle and returned home, ascending to the main hall.
She sat upon the mistress's throne of seven treasures, within the curtains adorned with tassels.
The household was greatly astonished, thinking the maidservant had gone mad.
They asked her what she was doing.
She replied:
"I saw my own proper beauty in the water.
The mistress does not recognize it, only treating me with contempt."
They then gave her a mirror to look into.
Only then did she see her ugly form, yet still she refused to believe it.
They took her to the water's edge to see the shadow of the dead woman.
The maidservant's mind was finally cleared, and she felt ashamed, recognizing her own error.
The great Asura King, named Luóhē.
Dwelled at the bottom of the great sea north of Mount Sumeru.
Water hung above his palace, held by the four winds; his city walls extended eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
Within and without were seven layers, three thousand yojanas high, with golden walls and silver gates; the gardens and ponds were cool and clear, with many birds singing in harmony.
It was ten thousand yojanas from Mount Sumeru.
His body was twenty-eight thousand lǐ long; he also ate ordinary food, and bathing and clothing served as his delicate sustenance.
On the fifteenth day of the month.
He entered the center of the sea.
Transforming his physical form.
Placing water upon his navel, he covered Mount Sumeru, pointing and obscuring the sun and moon.
The sun and moon devas.
Seeing his ugly form, were greatly terrified.
They lost their light.
When he roamed and gazed, a natural wind arose.
It blew the gates open and shut, swept the ground clean.
It scattered the flowers.
He had five great ministers.
The first named Zhuōchí.
The second named Xiónglì.
The third named Wǔyí.
The fourth named Tóushǒu.
The fifth named Cuīfú.
They guarded and attended to his left and right.
Suddenly, he thought to himself:
"I possess such majestic virtue and divine power.
Yet I allow the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and the sun and moon devas to move above my head.
I vow to seize the sun and moon to wear as my earrings."
Gradually growing more furious, he desired to strike them.
He then thought of.
The two Asura Kings, Shèmólí and Pímózhìduō.
And all the great ministers, each preparing weapons to go and battle the devas.
At that time, the two great dragon kings, Nàntuó and Bánàntuó.
Coiled around Mount Sumeru, encircling it seven times.
The mountain shook, clouds gathered, and they struck the water with their tails.
The great sea surged with waves, cresting over Mount Sumeru.
The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven said:
"The Asuras wish to fight."
The various dragons in the sea, the Garuḍa spirits, and the ghosts who always held flowers in joy.
These two types of spirits and others each took up arms and engaged in battle one after another.
If they were not victorious, they all fled.
The palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings prepared their chariots for attack.
They first informed Śakra Devānām Indra.
Śakra informed the higher devas.
At that time, from the Yāma Heaven upward, reaching as far as the Parinirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
Countless hosts of devas, along with various dragons and spirits, surrounded them front and back.
Śakra commanded:
"If our army is victorious, bind him with five bonds.
Bind Pímózhìduō.
And bring him back to the Hall of Good Dharma.
I wish to see him."
The Asura also said:
"If my host is victorious, bind him with five bonds.
Bind Śakra and bring him back to the Seven-Leaf Hall.
I wish to see him."
A great battle ensued at once; weapons clashed, but neither side could harm the other.
Only upon touching the body did pain arise.
Śakra manifested his form, now with a thousand eyes.
Wielding a vajra pestle, flames and smoke issued from its head.
Seeing this, the Asura host retreated and was defeated.
They then captured Pímózhìduō, bound him, and brought him back.
From afar, seeing Śakra, he spewed vile words.
Śakra replied:
"I wish to discuss the principles of the Dharma with you."
The lifespan of devas is a thousand years, but few reach it, most dying earlier.
Though they harbor malicious thoughts and love to fight, they do not break the precepts.
Because they greatly practiced generosity, they received this body.
As for Pímózhìduō.
In the beginning of the kalpa.
The devas entered the water, and their bodies experienced the pleasure of touch.
Their essence flowed within, naturally forming an egg.
The egg gave birth to a girl, her form blue-black.
She entered the great sea, slapping the water for her own amusement.
Water essence entered her body, and she immediately felt she was with child.
She then gave birth to a boy.
With nine heads, each head having a thousand eyes, and fire issuing from his mouth.
He had nine hundred and ninety-nine hands and eight feet.
He crouched in the sea, eating mud, algae, and lotus roots.
He took a Gandharva goddess from the Fragrant Mountain as his wife.
Her appearance was exquisitely beautiful, her complexion surpassing white jade.
Later, she gave birth to a daughter.
Upright and outstanding, unparalleled between heaven and earth.
Jiāoshījiā sent an envoy to seek her hand.
The Asura said:
"If you can make me ride in a palace of seven treasures, I will give her to you."
Śakra then removed his jeweled crown, dedicating the merit of the ten good deeds.
So that the Asura could sit in a victorious hall.
Riding a six-jeweled platform, he went to welcome her.
Placing her in the Hall of Good Dharma.
He further gave her the name Yuèyì.
All the deva ministers were overjoyed.
Later, Śakra was wandering in the Garden of Joy.
Together with his celestial maidens, he entered a pond to play.
Yuèyì became jealous.
She sent five yakṣas back to inform her father.
Her father was greatly enraged.
Raising four kinds of troops, he went to attack Śakra.
Standing in the great sea, he crouched atop Mount Sumeru.
His nine hundred and ninety-nine hands all moved simultaneously.
Shaking the City of Joyful Sight, he made Mount Sumeru tremble.
The waters of the four great seas surged with waves all at once.
Śakra was terrified and alarmed, not knowing where to turn.
At that time, there was a spirit in the palace.
Who addressed the Heavenly King:
"The Buddha of the past said:
The king of mantras, the Prajñāpāramitā, should be recited and upheld.
The ghostly troops will then be shattered of themselves."
Then the Lord of Devas, in the Hall of Good Dharma, gathered the multitude, burned fine incense, and made a great vow.
"The Prajñāpāramitā is the great bright mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, the unequalled mantra; it is true and not false.
I uphold this Dharma and shall attain Buddhahood.
May the Asuras naturally retreat and scatter."
As he spoke these words.
In the empty sky, four great blade-wheels.
Naturally descended upon the Asuras.
Their ears, noses, hands, and feet all fell off at once.
Making the waters of the great sea red like crimson pearls.
Then the Asuras were greatly terrified.
Fleeing with nowhere to hide, they entered the holes of lotus roots.
In the past, the Asuras.
Raised troops and fought with the Lord of Devas.
Śakra was not victorious.
Riding in his thousand-spoked jeweled chariot, he retreated in fear.
On the way, he saw a śāla tree.
With a bird's nest containing two chicks.
He immediately commanded his charioteer:
"There are two birds in this tree.
You must turn the chariot to avoid them.
Better that harm come to me.
Than that these be injured."
They immediately turned the chariot.
The Asura, seeing from afar, said to each other:
"Śakra has turned his chariot; he must be returning to fight.
We cannot withstand him."
They then retreated and scattered, and the devas were victorious. The Asuras surpass Jambudvīpa in three things:
First, their palaces are lofty and vast.
Second, their palaces are adorned and majestic.
Third, their palaces are pure and clean.
In a past age,
there was an Asura king
named Luóhóuluó.
He had a daughter
of extraordinary beauty and grace.
She possessed all sixty-four feminine virtues,
leaving none unfulfilled.
Her breath, when she spoke, was like the fragrance of the Utpala flower;
her body emitted the scent of gośīrṣa sandalwood.
Her complexion was rosy and fair, and all who saw her loved her.
At that time, Śakro Devānām Indraḥ thought to himself:
"There are many beautiful women in my palace,
but none compare to this daughter of the Asuras.
Now I shall gather my troops, go to war, seize her, and make her serve me."
He immediately summoned the gods and explained the matter.
The gods advised him, saying:
"You may send the Gandharva musicians.
Let them take the ninety-one-stringed lapis lazuli lute and sing of the bliss and happiness enjoyed by us gods and men.
He then commanded the Gandharva deities, such as Pañcaśikha,
to prepare their instruments and go before Pṛthivī to play the lute.
They conveyed his intent, saying:
"He desires Pṛthivī to serve him.
If she is not given, he will take her by force."
The Asura was greatly enraged.
"I too have power enough to oppose him!"
Pañcaśikha and the others reported back to Indra.
At that time, the Asura gathered his troops and arrived at the side of Mount Sumeru.
He destroyed the palace of the Khaḍgāṅga deities,
then destroyed the palaces of the wind deities, the horse deities, the Vyūha deities, and others,
reaching even the four gates.
Indra, recalling an incantation he had learned in the past, chanted it.
The Asura troops gradually retreated.
They led their fourfold army into the hollow of a lotus stem in the Kuśīra pond.
A man saw this
and thought to himself:
"I must be mad, out of my senses, to be seeing such strange things."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This is true.
At that time, Śakro Devānām Indraḥ assembled the host of gods and went out from the four gates.
They saw only swords, armor, bows, and arrows lying on the ground,
but did not see the Asura host.
Advancing further, they went straight into the palace of the Asuras.
They saw Pṛthivī and her attendants, numbering in the tens of millions,
but did not see the Asuras.
They took the women and returned to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
Then the Asuras pleaded for mercy and submitted,
saying to Śakro Devānām Indraḥ:
"We were foolish and deluded, not recognizing the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha's disciples.
Our ancestors faithfully served the Tathāgata.
We heard that the Buddha has a precept against taking what is not given.
Now the heavenly king Indra has taken all our dependents to fill his heavenly palace.
This is not conduct befitting a disciple of the Buddha."
When Indra heard this, he was troubled and displeased.
"I would rather uphold the precepts and not violate the prohibition against stealing."
He immediately returned the women.
Then the Asura king offered his most beloved daughter to the heavenly king Indra.
Indra, in return, gave him amṛta.
The Asuras and the gods made peace
and together upheld the Three Refuges and the Eight Precepts of the Tathāgata.
In a previous life, the Asura
had been a poor man
living near a river, often crossing it to gather firewood.
At that time, the river was deep and its current swift.
This man was often swept away by the water.
He would lose what he carried,
and his body would sink and drown.
Carried by the current, nearly dying, he would manage to escape.
At that time, there was a Pratyekabuddha
who, in the form of a śramaṇa, came to his house to beg for food.
The poor man joyfully offered him food.
After eating, the Pratyekabuddha threw his bowl into the air and flew away.
Seeing this, the poor man made a vow:
"May I in a future life have an enormous body,
so that no deep water will reach above my knees."
Because of this cause and condition, he obtained an extremely large body.
The waters of the four great oceans could not reach above his knees.
Standing in the great ocean, his body surpassed Mount Sumeru.
Placing his hands on the mountaintop, he looked down upon the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
The Gandharva king
dwells in a city
named Vaiśālī, to the right of the Snowy Mountains.
When the world was first formed, a wind circle arose,
named Vyūha.
It created this palace city.
North of the city are seven black mountains.
North of those mountains is the Fragrant Mountain.
Between the ten precious mountains,
the sound of music is constant. The mountain has two caves:
one named Day,
the other named Good Day.
They are made of the seven treasures, soft, fragrant, and clean,
like heavenly garments.
The Gandharva king,
with five hundred Gandharvas, dwells within them.
The Buddha was on Mount Vipula.
Śakro Devānām Indraḥ instructed the Gandharva musician
Pañcaśikha to take the lapis lazuli lute and sing before the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"You are able to use the lute and song to praise the Tathāgata.
The sorrow and harmony, the mournful beauty, move people's hearts.
Within this sound, you say:
'Desire binds the pure-conduct śramaṇa; Nirvāṇa contains all meanings.'"
Indra turned and said to him:
"You shall succeed your father's position.
