Among your kind, you shall be the foremost.
I give you my daughter in marriage."
The Kiṃnaras dwell north of Mount Sumeru.
Beyond the small Iron Ring Mountains is a great black mountain.
It is also among the ten precious mountains.
There is no Buddha-Dharma, sun, moon, or stars there.
Due to the power of past giving,
they now dwell in palaces of the seven treasures.
Their lifespans are very long.
This king was originally among humans,
where a great elder was building a Buddha stūpa.
This Kiṃnara donated a flagpole pillar, completing the temple.
He also gave pure food to the craftsmen.
After his life ended, he became a chest deity,
dwelling between two mountains.
Previously, among humans, he was a great elder of immeasurable wealth.
A śramaṇa came begging for food.
His wife took food and offered it to him.
He became greatly angry, saying:
"Who is this beggar, looking at my wife?
May this man's hands and feet be broken and ruined!"
After his life ended, he received this ugly form.
For eighty-four kalpas, he constantly had no hands or feet.
When the gods hold feasts, they all take turns with the Gandharvas, alternating above and below.
When the gods wish to perform music,
filth flows from their armpits,
so they ascend to heaven themselves.
There was a Kiṃnara
named Droṇamukha.
He played the lute and sang of the true nature of all dharmas to praise the World-Honored One.
At that time, Mount Sumeru and all the forests and trees trembled and shook.
Mahākāśyapa, seated there, could not remain still.
The minds of five hundred ṛṣis became wildly intoxicated;
they lost their spiritual powers and all fell to the ground at once.
There are four great divine beings: first, earth;
second, water;
third, wind;
fourth, fire.
The earth deity thought to himself:
"Earth has no water, fire, or wind."
The Buddha said:
"Within earth, there are water, fire, and wind.
But because earth is predominant, it is named thus."
The water, fire, and wind deities each thought similarly.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to them.
They all received the five precepts and became upāsikās.
All the dwellings where people live
have spirits and deities; none are empty.
Streets, lanes, crossroads, slaughterhouses, marketplaces, and various mountain graves—
all have spirits and deities; no place is empty.
All such spirits and deities are named according to what they rely upon. When a person is first born, there are spirits and deities that follow and protect them.
When a person is about to die, spirits collect their vital energy.
For a person who commits the ten evils, perhaps a hundred or a thousand share one protective deity,
just as a king has a hundred or a thousand people guarding a single minister.
If there are beings born among the hungry ghosts,
due to constant hunger and thirst, their eyes sink in, their hair grows long,
and they wander aimlessly east and west. They may eat vomit, fat, flesh, pus, blood, feces, urine, mucus, saliva, or leftover wash water.
Their lifespans are immeasurable, hundreds of thousands, millions of years.
They have never even heard the name of broth or water.
If by chance they see it and hurry toward it,
it turns into fierce fire or pus and blood.
Sometimes it does not change, but many people holding weapons prevent them from approaching.
Or when summer rain falls, it turns to fire upon their bodies; this is called the evil retribution.
By the banks of the Gaṅgā River, there are hungry ghosts,
five hundred in number.
For immeasurable years, they have never seen water.
Even when they reach the riverbank, they see only flowing fire.
Driven by hunger and thirst, they cry out and wail.
The hungry ghosts said to the Buddha:
"We are hungry and thirsty; our lives will not last long."
The Buddha said:
"The Gaṅgā River flows with water."
The ghosts said:
"The Tathāgata sees water, but we always see fire."
The Buddha said:
"I will remove your inversion and enable you to see water."
He extensively explained the faults of miserliness.
The ghosts said:
"We have been thirsty for so long that even hearing the Dharma words, they do not enter our minds.
First, let us enter the river and drink to our heart's content."
By the Buddha's power, they were able to drink water.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to them, and they all aroused the bodhi mind,
abandoning their ghost forms.
Some hungry ghosts are constantly burned by fire,
like when the mountains emit fire at the end of a kalpa.
Some are emaciated, running wildly, with disheveled hair covering their bodies.
Some stand by latrines, waiting to seek filth.
Some constantly seek afterbirth blood to drink.
Their forms are like burned trees, their throats like needles.
If given water to drink, they would not be full for a thousand years.
Some break their own heads and lick the brains.
Some have forms like black mountains, with iron chains locking their necks.
They kowtow, pleading for mercy and submitting to the jailers.
Some, due to past evil speech, liking to use harsh words against others, were hated by all who saw them like enemies.
Because of this sin, they fell among the hungry ghosts.
Such are the retributions of sin, suffering immeasurable pain.
There was a man who made a living by selling wine.
A ghost appeared to drink wine without paying.
And told the host,
"Tomorrow, there will be a man holding flowers, wearing white clothes with a green belt.
In the belt, there will be a thousand catties of gold and silver.
He will bathe in the lake and suddenly die without coming out.
You should go and take the gold and silver, and you will have no worries afterward."
The next day, the host waited.
He saw a man come, enter the water to bathe, come ashore to put on his clothes, wash his feet, and then fall to the ground and die.
The wine seller went and obtained the gold and silver as described.
Later, the ghost came.
The host prepared food and brought out wine, saying to the spirit,
"I saw the man put on his clothes and was about to leave before he died.
Why didn't you kill him in the water and let him come ashore?"
The ghost said,
"I cannot kill people who are sick.
I only know when a person's lifespan is declining."
The host said,
"In heaven and on earth, ghosts and spirits
know when a person's lifespan, sins, or blessings are about to arrive or not yet arrived.
They cannot make people live, nor can they kill people.
They cannot make people rich, noble, poor, or lowly.
They only want people to commit evil deeds and kill.
They take advantage of people's decline to disturb them.
They speak of fortune and misfortune to make people worship them and offer sacrifices."
The king of Jiāyí Kingdom was named Fànmódá.
Once, he went out hunting in the wilderness.
He saw a house and went toward it.
Inside was a woman.
He asked for food and drink, and she gave him everything he requested.
The king asked to meet her.
The woman was completely naked.
The king took off his clothes and gave them to her, and as soon as she put them on, they vanished.
This happened three times.
The king asked the woman about it.
The woman replied,
"I was once your wife.
You offered food to monks and also gave them clothes.
At that time, I advised you,
'Just give food, no need for clothes,' so I am suffering this punishment.
If you want me to be able to wear clothes,
make clothes for me and first give them to monks and those who understand the scriptures."
The king sought monks but could not find any.
He could give to those who uphold the five precepts and virtuous people.
A virtuous person chanted a blessing, saying,
"May the woman on the golden bed receive immeasurable blessings and be able to wear the king's clothes."
The king asked the woman,
"What kind of spirit are you?"
She replied,
"I am superior to humans,
but slightly inferior to gods.
Therefore, I am in the realm of ghosts and spirits.
After leaving this life, I will be reborn in the highest heaven."
Once, a man traveled far and stayed alone in an empty house.
At night, a ghost carried a dead man and placed him in front of him.
Another ghost followed, angrily shouting,
"The dead man is mine! Why did you suddenly carry him away?"
The first ghost said,
"He is mine, I carried him here." The second ghost said,
"This dead man was actually carried by me."
The two ghosts each grabbed one foot and one hand, arguing over him.
The first ghost said,
"There is a person here we can ask."
The second ghost then asked,
"Who carried this dead man here?"
The man thought to himself,
"These two ghosts are very powerful.
Whether I speak truthfully or falsely, I will not escape death."
He said,
"The first ghost carried him here."
The second ghost became very angry.
He grabbed the man's hand and pulled it off, throwing it to the ground.
The first ghost took an arm from the dead man and attached it to him.
It attached just like that.
Both arms, both legs, head, torso—his entire body was replaced.
Then the two ghosts ate the replaced human body together.
They wiped their mouths and left.
The man thought to himself,
"My body was born from my parents.
I saw with my own eyes the two ghosts eat it all.
Now this body of mine is entirely made of others' flesh.
Do I truly have a body now, or do I not?"
He went to a Buddhist stupa and asked the monks.
He recounted the above events in detail.
The monks said,
"From the beginning, there has never been a self.
It is only due to the combination of the four elements that we consider it as our body.
Your original body and your current one
are no different."
The monks ordained him into the monastic life.
He attained Arhatship.
There was a ghost spirit
with an extremely large body and golden hands.
From its five fingers constantly flowed sweet dew.
If there were travelers in need,
whether food, drink, or necessities for living,
everything would come from its fingers, given freely.
Mùlián asked,
"What kind of god are you?
Your blessings and merits are so extraordinary."
"I am not a heavenly king or Brahmā king.
I am a ghost spirit.
I reside near a great city in a certain kingdom.
I came here to wander and observe."
Mùlián asked,
"What good deeds did you perform to receive such a reward?"
The spirit replied,
"That great city in the kingdom is called Luólóu.
In the past, I was a poor woman there.
I wove woolen bags and sold them to make a living.
My livelihood grew poorer, and my house fell into ruin.
I ended up at the roadside,
near the house of a wealthy and generous elder, weaving wool to survive.
Around noon,
if there were monks or Brahmins
holding bowls to beg for food,
they would ask me,
'Where is the elder's house?'
With a sincere heart, free from falsehood,
I joyfully raised my hand and pointed to his house, saying,
'Go there.
The time is passing; do not seek elsewhere.'"
In the kingdom of Vṛji, there was a demon.
Named Piśāca, he was extremely fierce and violent.
He killed countless people.
Daily, he would kill dozens of people.
The people all gathered together and said this:
"We should flee this kingdom and go far away to another land."
The demon, knowing their thoughts, then said to those people:
"Do not leave this place for another country.
You will not escape my grasp in the end.
If you offer me one person daily as a sacrifice, I will not trouble you."
At that time, the people of Vṛji took one person daily as a sacrifice.
That evil demon,
this demon devoured people until bones filled the valleys.
At that time, there was an elder's son named Shànjué.
He lived there, wealthy and possessing many treasures.
His son was named Nàyōuluó.
He had only this one son.
Under this restriction,
the son Nàyōuluó was to be sacrificed to this demon.
The parents bathed this young child, and when finished,
dressed him in fine clothes and took him to where the demon was.
They wept and cried out beyond measure.
And they said this:
"All demons and earth deities, bear witness together.
I have this one son; I wish to protect this child, that he may be saved."
Śakra Devānām Indra and Brahmā,
all Tathāgata's disciples, Arhats free from outflows, and Pratyekabuddhas,
even the Tathāgata, the most venerable, supreme, excellent field of merit,
none surpass the Tathāgata.
May they observe this.
I wish the Tathāgata would illuminate this sincere heart."
They handed the child over to the demon and then withdrew and left.
At that time, the World-Honored One, with his divine eye and ear, clearly heard and saw.
With his supernatural power, he went to the north of the Snowy Mountains.
He entered the demon's dwelling place and sat down cross-legged.
At that time, the young child arrived at the demon's dwelling.
From afar, he saw the Tathāgata, his radiance shining brightly,
adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty excellent characteristics.
He felt joyful and turned toward the Tathāgata.
Thinking it was the evil demon who would eat him at will.
At that time, the World-Honored One said:
"Nàyōuluó, as you have said,
I am now the Tathāgata, the perfectly enlightened one.
Therefore, I have come to save you and subdue this demon."
Nàyōuluó, overjoyed, bowed with his head at the feet.
At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the profound meaning to him.
Right there on the seat, his defilements were exhausted, and he attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Having seen the Dharma, he took refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha and received the five precepts.
The evil demon returned to his place and from afar saw the World-Honored One sitting upright and unmoving.
He then became enraged.
He rained down thunder, lightning, and thunderbolts, or rained down swords and blades.
Before they could fall to the ground,
the Tathāgata transformed them into utpala lotuses.
Again, he rained down various supernatural powers, and the Tathāgata accordingly subdued them.
"The śramaṇa's robe and hair remain unmoved. I shall now go and ask him profound meanings.
If he cannot answer me, I will take you by both feet and throw you into the southern sea."
The Buddha said:
"Whether human or non-human, none can take me by both feet and throw me into the southern sea.
If you wish to ask, then ask."
At that time, the demon asked:
"What are old actions, new actions, and the cessation of actions?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"You should know the eye is old action.
What was created in the past, conditioned by illness, becomes action.
Ear, nose, mouth, body, mind—these are old actions.
What is created by the present body—three by body, four by speech, three by mind—these are new actions. You should know old actions cease.
They do not arise again, and no further actions are created.
One who can grasp this action will never again be born, completely ended without remainder.
This is called the cessation of actions."
The demon said to the Buddha:
"I am now extremely hungry; return my little child to me."
The World-Honored One replied:
"In the past, when I was a Bodhisattva,
a dove sought refuge with me, and I did not spare my own life to save that dove from calamity.
How much more now that I have become the Tathāgata,
could I abandon this child to let you devour him?
During the time of Buddha Kāśyapa, you once were a śramaṇa.
You cultivated pure conduct but later broke the precepts.
Thus, you were reborn as this evil demon."
At that time, the evil demon, empowered by the Buddha's majestic spirit,
then remembered the various actions he had created in the past.
He went to where the World-Honored One was,
bowed with his head at the feet,
and said, "I am now foolish and confused, unable to distinguish true from false.
I even harbored such thoughts toward the Tathāgata.
I only wish the World-Honored One would accept my repentance."
Thus, three or four times.
The World-Honored One said:
"I allow your repentance."
He expounded the profound Dharma to him.
At that time, that evil demon took up several thousand taels of gold and offered them to the World-Honored One.
"I now give this mountain valley
as a donation to the Saṅgha.
I only wish the World-Honored One would accept it for me."
The World-Honored One then accepted it.
He then spoke this verse:
The demon said, "What further instructions are there?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"Abandon your original form, don the three robes, and become a śramaṇa.
Enter the city of Vṛji and everywhere teach the command:
'The Tathāgata has appeared in the world; those not yet saved shall be saved,
enabling them to attain liberation.
The most venerable, supreme, excellent field of merit,
now saves the young child Nàyōuluó,
and subdues the evil demon Piśāca.
You all should go there to receive transformation.'"
At that time, the demon Piśāca, in the kingdom of Vṛji,
proclaimed thus:
At that time, the elder Shànjué,
hearing these words, was overjoyed and unable to contain himself.
Leading a crowd of eighty-four thousand people,
he went to where the World-Honored One was.
Once there was a woman.
She had many children.
Her nature was wicked and without compassion.
She delighted in stealing other people's children, killing and eating them.
The families who lost their children did not know who had taken them.
They wept and wailed in the streets, and this happened not just once.
Ānán, going out, would always see them weeping.
Returning, he discussed it with the others.
They grieved for the families who had lost children.
The Buddha, knowing, asked on purpose:
"What are you all discussing?"
Ānán said to the Buddha:
"Just now, going out for alms, I saw people weeping.
Asking them, they all said:
'Our children have been lost; we do not know where their bodies are.'"
The Buddha then explained to Ānán:
"The one in this country who steals people's children is no ordinary person.
She is the ghost-mother Hārītī.
Born now as a human, she delights in stealing people's children.
This mother has a thousand sons.
Five hundred sons are in the heavens.
Five hundred sons are in the human world.
The thousand sons are all ghost-kings.
Each king commands tens of thousands of ghosts.
Thus, five hundred ghost-kings in the heavens harass the gods.
Five hundred ghost-kings in the world harass kings, rulers, and people.
Even the heavens can do nothing about these five hundred ghost-kings."
Ānán said:
"Since Hārītī is in this country,
is it possible to command her to stop stealing people's children?"
The Buddha said: "Excellent."
Ānán said:
"By what means?"
The Buddha told Ānán:
"Go to that mother's place, wait until she goes out,
gather up her children and place them in the monastery."
He immediately went, waited, gathered over ten children, and hid them in the monastery.
The mother returned, did not see them, and then abandoned stealing other children, not daring to kill anymore.
She searched everywhere for her children but could not find them.
Walking the roads, she wept for ten days like this.
The mother then beat her breast, threw herself down, looked up to heaven and cried out, and stopped eating and drinking.
The Buddha sent a monk to ask her.
She immediately replied to the monk:
"I weep because I have lost many children."
The monk also said:
"Do you want to get your children back?"
She replied: "I want to."
The monk said:
"If you truly want to get them, you can go ask the Buddha; you can get your children back."
The mother, hearing these words,
was joyful and relieved, and went to the Buddha.
She paid homage to the Buddha.
The Buddha immediately asked the mother:
"Why are you weeping?"
The mother replied:
"Because I have lost my children."
The Buddha asked:
"When you abandoned your children,
where did you go that you lost your children?"
The mother then fell silent.
This happened three times.
The mother realized that stealing people's children was evil.
She then rose and paid homage, saying:
"It is because of my foolishness."
The Buddha asked again:
"You have children; do you love them?" The mother said:
"I have children; whether sitting or rising, they always want to be by my side."
The Buddha asked again:
"You have children and know to love them.
Why then do you daily steal other people's children?
Other people have children whom they love just as you do.
The families who lose children also weep on the roads just like you.
Yet you, on the contrary, steal people's children, kill and eat them.
After death, you will fall into the great mountain hell.
Do you still want to get your children back?"
The mother then placed her head and face on the ground, saying:
"May the Buddha have pity on me."
The Buddha said:
"If your children were here, could you repent?"
"If you can repent, I will return your children to you."
The mother said:
"I can repent."
The Buddha said:
"If you can repent, what kind of repentance will you make?"
The mother said:
"I will listen to the Buddha's precepts and follow the Buddha's words."
"The Buddha will return my children to me." The Buddha said:
"If it is truly as you say,
I will give you the five precepts.
You have a thousand sons; I will give names to them all.
Five hundred sons are in the heavens.
Five hundred sons are in the world.
They harass gods and humans.
Your sons are ghost-kings, commanding tens of thousands of ghosts.
They are innumerable like this.
Some falsely claim to be tree spirits, earth spirits, water spirits, and spirits of boats and carts.
Spirits of houses, of darkness, of dreams and waking, of terror and strange occurrences, all kinds of spirits.
Thus falsely claiming, they cause people to make sacrifices to them.
They cook, kill, eat, and drink, unable to protect and save human lives.
They only increase their sins.
These foolish people do not know that by sitting and thinking, they become poor."
Hārītī, hearing the Buddha's explanation,
with single-mindedness repented.
She immediately attained the fruit of Stream-Entry.
Kneeling, she said to the Buddha:
"May the Buddha have pity on me.
I wish to dwell beside the Buddha's monastery.
I wish to call my thousand sons.
I wish to have them make a pact with the Buddha.
I wish to repay the kindness of the people in the heavens and the world."
The Buddha said: "Excellent.
If you have such an intention, it is very good."
The Buddha said:
"Then dwell beside the Buddha's monastery.
The people in this country who have no children,
when they come seeking children, you shall give them children according to their wishes.
I will command your sons to go and protect people.
They must not recklessly harass them anymore.
Those who wish to seek blessings from Hārītī,
her name is Pútúo Móníbō.
Her elder sister is named Zhìnì.
The ghosts of the heavens and the world are under Móníbō's command.
Within the four seas, boats, carts, livelihoods, and property all belong to Móníbō.
Móníbō made a pact with the Buddha and received the precepts.
She protects people's wealth and property.
Zhìnì protects people; if there is childbirth, she goes to assist."
At that time, the yakkha Qūmó
came to the Buddha, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, and stood to one side.
Then the yakkha Qūmó said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One,
now I invite the World-Honored One and the great assembly
to stay here overnight."
The World-Honored One remained silent.
At that time, Qūmó transformed five hundred multi-storied pavilions, dwellings, bedding, sitting mats, and low couches.
All had mattresses and pillows, five hundred sets each.
He also transformed five hundred lamps.
They had no smoke or flame.
At that time, Mùlián was walking in meditation at night.
The evil demon Māra transformed himself into a penetrating shadow and entered Mùlián's abdomen.
Mùlián entered samādhi and observed its origin.
He immediately said to the evil demon:
"Come out, come out!
Do not harass the Buddha's disciple.
You will suffer for a long night."
Māra thought to himself:
"Now this monk has never seen me before.
He is arbitrarily making false statements.
Even his teacher does not yet know me,
let alone his disciple."
Mùlián replied:
"I also know what you are thinking in your heart."
Māra then became afraid, thinking: "He has already perceived me!"
He then transformed his penetrating body and came out, standing before him.
Mùlián told Māra:
"In a past age, at the time of Buddha Krakucchanda,
I was once a demon
named Mínghèn.
I had an elder sister
named Yǎnhēi.
You were her son.
Therefore I know you are my sister's son."
At that time, when the Buddha appeared in the world,
he had two disciples.
One was named Hóngyīn,
the second was named Zhīxiǎng.
Why was he named Hóngyīn?
Dwelling in the Brahma heaven, the sound of his clearing his throat
was heard throughout the three thousand worlds.
As for Zhīxiǎng, he dwelled alone in solitude, sitting under a mountain tree.
In samādhi, absorbed in right concentration, cowherds and shepherds carrying firewood and grass
said to each other:
"He has already passed away; let us cremate him together."
Zhīxiǎng arose from samādhi and entered the city for alms.
There was once a woman
possessed by a hungry ghost.
He used a spell and asked the ghost:
"Why are you tormenting this woman?"
The ghost replied:
"This woman is my enemy.
For five hundred lifetimes she has constantly killed me.
I also, for five hundred lifetimes,
have cut off her life root.
If she can abandon her old hatred,
I can also abandon mine."
At that time, the woman said thus:
"I now abandon my hatred."
The ghost observed that although the woman spoke of abandoning,
her heart did not let go.
He then cut off her life.
The demon set out a feast.
He transformed into forty thousand bhikṣus.
They wore soiled, tattered robes and held broken bowls.
Their chests and backs were exposed, their faces ugly and repulsive.
They were lame, hunchbacked, and their hearts were filled with anxiety and fear.
They received various foods.
Mañjuśrī caused the bowls of these transformed beings to be constantly full.
When they scooped food into their mouths, it became blocked and they could not swallow.
Their bodies became uneasy and they naturally fell to the ground. They asked the demon,
"Why do the bhikṣus not eat?"
The demon said,
"They are about to die."
Mañjuśrī said,
"Can one who is without poison still act with the filth of poison?"
"One who has lust, anger, and delusion—this is poison."
He then expounded the Dharma for them: "I have no such poison."
Five hundred devas who had come with the demon
aroused the mind of bodhi.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana went to the banks of the Gaṅgā River.
He saw five hundred hungry ghosts coming in a crowd toward the water. There was a water-guarding ghost
driving them away with an iron staff, not allowing them to approach.
Thereupon, the ghosts went directly to Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
They bowed at Mahāmaudgalyāyana's feet and each asked about their offenses.
One ghost said,
"Since receiving this body, I constantly suffer from heat and thirst.
Previously, I heard that the water of the Gaṅgā was clear and cool.
I joyfully approached it, but it was boiling hot and destroyed my body.
I tried to drink a mouthful,
but my five viscera were scorched and rotten, the stench unbearable.
For what cause and condition do I receive such suffering?"
Mahāmaudgalyāyana said,
"In your previous life, you were a fortune-teller.
You told people's fortunes, good and bad.
You spoke little truth and much falsehood.
Sometimes you slandered, sometimes you praised.
You claimed your words were accurate and true to sway people's minds.
You deceived and tricked people to seek wealth and profit.
You confused sentient beings, causing them to lose what they desired.
Another ghost said,
"A large dog with sharp, red-white teeth constantly comes to devour my flesh, leaving only bones behind.
When the wind blows,
the flesh regrows.
The dog comes again to devour it.
For what cause is this suffering?"
Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied,
"In your previous life, you were the head of a deva temple.
You often taught people to kill sheep and use their blood to sacrifice to the devas.
You yourself ate the meat.
Therefore, today you repay it with your flesh."
Another ghost said,
"Excrement constantly covers my entire body.
I also eat it.
For what offense is this?"
Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied,
"In your previous life, you were a brāhmaṇa.
You were wicked, heretical, and faithless.
When a Dharma practitioner begged for food, you took a bowl, filled it with excrement, placed rice on top, and gave it to the practitioner.
The practitioner took it back and ate the rice with his hands.
The excrement soiled his hands.
Therefore, today you receive such suffering."
Another ghost said,
"My belly is extremely large like a jar.
My throat, hands, and feet are as thin as needles.
I cannot eat or drink.
For what cause is this suffering?"
Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied,
"In your previous life, you were a village head.
You relied on your wealth and status.
You ate and drank recklessly and looked down upon others.
You seized their food and drink, causing sentient beings to starve and suffer."
Another ghost said,
"I constantly go to the latrine wanting to eat excrement.
But a large crowd of ghosts with sticks drives me away, not allowing me near the toilet.
I am putrid, stinking, starving, and helpless.
For what cause is this?"
Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied,
"In your previous life, you were in charge of a Buddhist temple.
There were laypeople who made offerings to the saṅgha and prepared food and utensils.
You served coarse food to the visiting monks
and kept the fine food for yourself."
Another ghost said,
"Tongues grow all over my body.
An axe comes to chop the tongues.
They are cut off but regrow, and this never ceases.
For what cause is this?"
Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied,
"In your previous life, you were a Dharma practitioner.
The saṅgha assigned you to make honey syrup.
The lumps of rock sugar were large and hard to dissolve.
You chopped them with an axe.
With a thieving mind, you ate a mouthful.
Because of this cause and condition, your tongue is now chopped."
Another ghost said,
"Seven hot iron balls constantly fly directly into my mouth.
They enter my belly and scorch my five viscera.
They come out and then enter again.
For what cause do I receive this punishment?"
Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied,
"In your previous life, you were a śrāmaṇera.
You carried melon seeds to your teacher.
Out of respect for your teacher, you were partial and gave him seven extra real ones."
Another ghost said,
"There are always two hot iron wheels
under my armpits.
They turn, scorching my body.
For what cause is this?"
Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied,
"In your previous life,
you made cakes for the saṅgha.
With a thieving mind, you took two cakes and hid them under your armpits."
Another hungry ghost said,
"My testicles are extremely large like jars.
When walking, I carry them on my shoulders.
When standing still, I sit on them. Moving or stopping, I suffer.
For what cause is this?"
Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied,
"In your previous life, you were a market overseer.
You often used light scales and small measures when giving,
and heavy scales and large measures when taking.
You constantly sought great profit for yourself, encroaching upon and exploiting others."
Another ghost said,
"I always have eyes on my two shoulders.
I have a mouth and nose on my chest.
I constantly have no head.
For what cause is this?"
Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied,
"In your previous life, you were always an executioner.
When your disciples killed criminals,
you always felt joy.
You tied ropes into knots and pulled them."
Another ghost said,
"Hot iron needles constantly
enter and exit my body. I suffer unbearably.
For what cause is this?"
Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied,
"In your previous life, you were a horse trainer.
Or you trained elephants.
When a horse was difficult to control,
you pierced its feet with iron needles.
Also, when an ox was slow, you likewise pierced it with needles."
Another ghost said,
"Fire constantly emerges from my body, burning and tormenting me.
For what cause is this?"
Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied,
"In your previous life, you were a king's consort.
There was another consort whom the king greatly favored and loved.
You constantly felt jealous and watched for an opportunity to harm her.
Once, when the king had gotten up and left,
the beloved consort was still asleep and had not yet dressed.
You immediately conceived an evil thought. It happened that cakes were being made.
There was hot sesame oil, which you poured into her belly.
Her belly rotted and she died immediately."
Another ghost said,
"A whirlwind constantly swirls around my body.
I have no freedom to go east or west as I wish.
My mind is constantly tormented and distressed.
For what cause is this?"
Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied,
"In your previous life, you were often a diviner.
Sometimes you spoke truth, sometimes falsehood.
You confused people's minds, not allowing them to follow their wishes."
Another ghost said,
"My body is constantly like a lump of flesh.
It has no feet, eyes, ears, nose, etc.
It is constantly eaten by insects and birds.
The suffering of this offense is hard to endure.
For what cause and condition?"
He replied,
"In your previous life, you often gave medicine to others to abort their children."
Another ghost said,
"There is always a hot iron cage
enveloping my body.
It scorches and torments me.
For what cause do I receive this?"
Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied,
"In your previous life, you often used nets to catch fish and birds."
Another ghost said,
"I cover my head with something,
and I constantly fear that people will come to kill me.
My mind is constantly terrified and I cannot bear it.
For what cause is this?"
He replied,
"In your previous life, you committed adultery with other women and constantly feared being seen.
You either feared her husband catching, binding, and beating you to death,
or feared the government laws executing you in the marketplace.
This terror was continuous."
Another ghost asked,
"In this body I receive,
on my shoulders I always carry a bronze bottle filled with molten copper.
Holding a ladle, I take it and pour it over my own head.
My entire body becomes scorched and rotten.
I suffer such torment countless, immeasurable times.
What crime did I commit?"
The answer came:
"In your previous life, you left home to follow the path,
and were in charge of the monks' food and drink.
You privately hid a bottle of ghee elsewhere.
When visiting monks came, you did not give it to them.
After they left, you took out the ghee and distributed it among the old monks.
This ghee was the property of the saṅgha, to be shared by all.
You hid it and distributed it unfairly.
Because of this, you now suffer this punishment."
Śakra Devānām Indra was in the Pǔjí Lecture Hall,
amusing himself with jade maidens.
At that time, a deva said to Śakra,
"Know this, O Śakra:
There is now an evil ghost on your honored seat."
The Thirty-Three Heavens were filled with great anger, but the ghost transformed, becoming more handsome and radiant than usual.
Śakra Devānām Indra then thought,
"This ghost must be a wondrous spirit."
He went to where the ghost was, not far away,
and announced his name, saying,
"I am Śakra Devānām Indra, lord of the devas."
The evil ghost then turned ugly and repulsive,
gradually diminishing.
In the past, in a foreign land, a person died,
and his soul returned to whip his own corpse.
Someone nearby asked,
"This person is already dead; why whip him again?"
He replied,
"This is my former body.
It committed evil deeds for me:
seeing scriptures and precepts but not reading them,
stealing, deceiving, and violating others' wives and daughters,
being unfilial to parents and siblings,
clinging to wealth and unwilling to give alms.
Now that I am dead, it has caused me to fall into the evil paths.
The hardship, pain, and torment are beyond words.
That is why I have come to whip it."
In a past age, there was a lion king
living in a deep mountain cave.
He often thought,
"I am the king of all beasts.
With my strength, I can protect all animals."
In the mountains lived two macaques
who had given birth to two offspring.
The two macaques then asked the lion king,
"If you, O King, can protect all beasts,
we now entrust our two children to you.
We wish to go elsewhere to seek food."
The lion king then agreed.
The macaques left their two children in his care and departed.
At that time, in the mountains, there was a vulture king
named Lìjiàn.
While the lion king was asleep,
he seized the two macaque children and perched in a dangerous place.
The lion king awoke
and said to the vulture,
The vulture king replied,
The lion king then said,
After speaking this verse,
he went to a high place, intending to sacrifice himself.
The vulture king then said,
The lion king was born and dwelled in deep
mountain valleys.
He had a broad jaw, massive bones, and a body full of flesh.
His head was large, his eyes long, his eyebrows high and wide.
His mouth and nose were deep and square, his teeth even and sharp.
He could extend a red and white tongue, and his ears stood tall.
His spine was long, his waist slender, his belly not protruding.
He had six tusks, a long tail, and glossy, smooth fur.
He knew his own strength, the sharpness of his teeth and claws.
With four paws planted on the ground, he dwelled securely in a rocky cave, shaking his tail and emitting sounds.
If one can possess such marks,
know that he is a true lion king.
At dawn, he would emerge from his cave, stretching and yawning,
looking around in all directions and roaring with a thunderous voice,
for eleven purposes:
First, to destroy those who falsely pretend to be lions.
Second, to test his own strength.
Third, to purify his dwelling place.
Fourth, to let his cubs know his location.
Fifth, so that his companions would have no fear.
Sixth, to awaken those who are sleeping.
Seventh, so that other beasts would not be negligent.
Eighth, so that other beasts would come to rely on him.
Ninth, to tame the great fragrant elephants.
Tenth, to instruct his offspring.
Eleventh, to adorn his retinue.
Whenever the lion's roar is heard,
aquatic creatures dive deep,
land animals hide in their burrows,
birds in flight fall to the ground,
and fragrant elephants in stables break their chains in terror, losing control and fleeing in panic,
like jackals.
Even if a jackal imitates a lion for a hundred thousand years,
it can never produce a lion's roar.
But a lion cub, even at just three years old, can roar mightily.
On the paths of the Fragrant Mountain, where lions dwell,
birds and beasts dare not tread or even peek.
Among all animals,
the lion is supreme.
The Buddha told Mùlián,
"The Bodhisattva Yǒngzhì,
in the time of the Buddha Guāngmíng, was a lion king.
I was a Brahmin cultivating pure conduct.
At that time, the lion king would stand firm at dawn in eight places without moving,
shake his body vigorously, and then let out a great thunderous roar.
Running beasts would crouch in fear, and flying ones would fall.
Only then would he rise.
He would patrol the wilderness, mountains, and marshes, inspecting his territory and seeking herds of beasts.
He encountered an elephant king, killed it, and ate it.
A bone stuck in his throat, and he died and revived. At that time, he told a woodpecker,
'Pull out this bone for me.
If I find food later, I will repay your kindness.'
The woodpecker heard this, put its beak in, exerted all its strength, pulled out the bone, and then left.
Later, the lion king went hunting, killing many beasts.
The woodpecker was nearby and asked for a small reward, but the lion did not repay him.
The Buddha told Mùlián,
"At that time, the lion king
replied to the woodpecker with this verse:"
At that time, the woodpecker
also replied with this verse,
saying to the lion:
The lion king ultimately did not repay the kindness,
and left him.
The woodpecker thought to himself,
"My kindness was immense, yet I am treated with contempt.
Now I shall follow him and wait for an opportunity.
One who does not repay kindness should not remain in the world.
Wherever he goes, I will not leave him."
Later, the lion king again killed a herd of beasts and ate his fill.
Satiated, he fell asleep without any fear.
Then the woodpecker flew to the lion,
landed on his forehead, and with all its strength pecked out one of his eyes.
The lion awoke in alarm, looked left and right, but saw no other beast,
only the woodpecker perched alone on a tree.
The lion king then said to the woodpecker,
"Why have you now destroyed my eye?"
At that time, the woodpecker replied with a verse:
The lion king of that time is now the Bodhisattva Yǒngzhì.
The woodpecker of that time is now Mùjiānlián.
In the past, there were two bhikṣus in the mountains.
Living in seclusion and practicing the Way, they attained supernatural powers.
Not far away, there was a lioness.
She gave birth to two cubs and raised them until they grew a bit older.
She needed to go out to search for food.
So she entrusted her cubs to the two ascetics.
She went to seek food near the cave.
Sometimes she would return to see them every five days.
The cubs became close and attached to the ascetics.
Eventually, she left them and went away.
As time passed,
one day, the ascetics were each away, not present.
A hunter came across them and intended to shoot them.
The lioness fled into the forest.
The hunter thought to himself:
"These cubs are often attached to the ascetics.
If I dress in the robes of an ascetic,
then I can capture them."
In the rock cave, there were left-behind kasāya robes and Dharma garments.
The hunter put them on and went to where the lion cubs were.
The lion cubs thought he was an ascetic.
They happily approached him.
The hunter struck and killed them, skinned them, and made fur coats to sell.
When the ascetics returned, they did not see the lion cubs and searched for them but could not find them.
They concentrated their minds and observed, knowing they had been killed by a hunter.
They used their supernatural powers to pursue and seize the skins.
They used them as sitting mats, constantly stroking them and reciting vows, wishing to liberate them.
Not long after, they sat in meditation again.
Observing to see which path they had taken,
they found they had been reborn as twin sons in the household of a great elder in the Middle Kingdom.
Just entering the womb, their mother was not yet aware.
The ascetics asked:
"What does the elder lack?"
He said, "My family is very wealthy, but we lack sons."
The ascetics told him:
"I can enable you to have sons."
The elder was overjoyed and said, "Then I will be greatly indebted."
The ascetics said:
"If you must have sons, how will you repay the kindness?"
He said, "When they grow up, they will become disciples of the ascetics."
The ascetics recited vows and left.
From then on, she became aware of being pregnant.
Later, she gave birth to two boys, as alike as one.
When they turned eight years old, the ascetics came again to their home.
The boys, due to past connections, naturally loved and respected them.
The ascetics said to the elder:
"Do you remember the previous agreement?"
The elder, bound by his original vow, had no choice.
So he offered both boys to the ascetics.
The ascetics made them śrāmaṇeras.
Diligent and advancing, before long, they also attained the Way.
They also often sat on the skins themselves, trying to meditate together.
Observing that these skins were born from divine beings,
they realized they were their own former skins.
Reflecting back and forth, they went together before their teacher.
Bowing at his feet, they thanked him, saying:
"We have truly received great kindness."
In a past life near the Snowy Mountains,
there was a lion, king of beasts.
He was the lord of five hundred lions.
This lion king later grew old, sick, thin, and his eyes dim.
While walking ahead of the lions, he fell into an empty well.
The five hundred lions all abandoned him and left.
At that time, there was a jackal who saw the lion king.
He thought to himself:
"The reason I can live in this forest peacefully and eat my fill of meat is because of the lion king.
Now he has fallen into a desperate situation; how should I repay him?"
At that time, there was a flowing stream beside the well.
The jackal immediately said:
"Use your feet to channel the water."
Water filled the well, and the lion floated out.
At that time, the forest deity spoke:
A verse:
The Buddha said: "The lion king was I myself.
The five hundred lions were the bhikṣus.
The jackal was Ānanda."
In a past life at the Snowy Mountains, there were two beasts.
One was named Fine-Fur Lion,
the other was named Fine-Tooth Tiger.
They became good friends, closing their eyes and licking each other.
These two beasts always got moist, good meat to eat.
Not far away, there was a two-tongued jackal.
He thought:
"I will go to the two beasts and say,
'Let me be your third companion.'
You allow me to join."
The lion and tiger said:
"As you wish." The two-tongued jackal ate the leftover meat of the two beasts and grew fat.
He thought:
"This Fine-Fur Lion and Fine-Tooth Tiger,
being good friends, are very affectionate with each other.
Closing their eyes and licking each other, they always eat good meat.
If sometimes they don't get any, they will surely eat me.
I must first devise a means to make them turn against each other."
He said to the lion:
"The tiger has evil intentions toward you, lion.
All the food you eat is due to my efforts."
The lion said:
"How do you know?"
The two-tongued jackal replied:
"When the tiger sees you tomorrow, if he closes his eyes and licks your fur, you will know it is an evil sign."
He went and said to the tiger:
"The lion has evil intentions toward you, saying,
'All the food we eat is due to my efforts.'"
The tiger said:
"How do you know?"
He replied:
"When the lion sees you tomorrow, if he closes his eyes and licks your fur, you will know it is an evil sign."
Between these two friends,
the tiger grew fearful.
So he went first to the lion and said:
"Do you have evil intentions toward me?"
The lion said:
"Who said such a thing?"
He replied:
"The two-tongued jackal."
Fine-Fur then asked:
"Do you also have evil intentions toward me?"
The tiger said, "No."
The tiger said to the lion:
"If you have such evil words, we cannot remain good friends."
Fine-Fur said:
"It was the two-tongued jackal who said such things.
Why are you unwilling to stay with me?"
He then spoke a verse:
The tiger and lion, having verified the facts,
together caught the jackal and tore him into two parts.
East of Jambudvīpa, in the sea,
there is a glass mountain called Tide.
Twenty yojanas high, adorned with various treasures.
On the mountain, there is a cave named Various Colors.
It was the former dwelling place of a bodhisattva.
One yojana in length and width, six yojanas high.
Inside, a poisonous snake dwells, cultivating śrāvaka-kindness.
There is another cave named Deathless.
Its height and width are the same.
It was the former dwelling place of a bodhisattva.
Inside, a horse cultivates śrāvaka-kindness.
There is another cave named Well-Dwelling.
Its height and width are the same.
Formerly, a bodhisattva dwelled inside.
Inside, a goat cultivates śrāvaka-kindness.
The mountain tree deity is named Invincible.
There is a rākṣasī named Good Conduct.
Each has five hundred attendants surrounding them; these two women often together make offerings to these three animals.
South of Jambudvīpa, in the sea,
there is a crystal mountain, twenty yojanas high.
There is a cave named Superior Color.
Its length, width, height, and depth are also thus.
It was also the former dwelling place of a bodhisattva.
Inside, a monkey cultivates śrāvaka-kindness.
There is another cave named Vow.
Its height and width are the same.
Formerly, a bodhisattva dwelled inside.
Inside, a chicken cultivates śrāvaka-kindness.
There is another cave named Dharma Grove.
Its height and width are the same.
Formerly, a bodhisattva dwelled inside.
Inside, a dog cultivates śrāvaka-kindness.
Inside, there is a fire deity.
There is a rākṣasī named Eye-Seeing.
Each has five hundred attendants surrounding them.
These two women often together make offerings to these three birds and beasts.
West of Jambudvīpa, in the sea,
there is a silver mountain named Bodhi Moon.
Twenty yojanas high.
Inside, there is a cave named Vajra.
Its height and width are the same.
Formerly, a bodhisattva dwelled inside.
Inside, a pig cultivates śrāvaka-kindness.
There is another cave named Fragrant Merit.
Its height and width are the same.
Formerly, a bodhisattva dwelled inside.
Inside, a rat cultivates śrāvaka-kindness.
There is another cave named High Merit.
Its height and width are the same.
Formerly, a bodhisattva dwelled inside.
Inside, an ox cultivates śrāvaka-kindness.
On the mountain, there is a wind deity named Moving Wind.
There is a rākṣasī named Unprotected.
Each has five hundred attendants surrounding them.
These two women often together make offerings to these three animals.
North of Jambudvīpa, in the sea,
there is a golden mountain named Gōngdé Xiàng.
It is twenty yojanas high.
Within it is a cave named Míngxīng,
one yojana wide
and six yojanas high.
In the past, a bodhisattva dwelled there.
There was a lion cultivating the śrāvaka-kindness.
There is another cave named Jìngdào,
with the same height and width.
In the past, a bodhisattva dwelled there.
There was a rabbit cultivating the śrāvaka-kindness.
There is another cave named Xǐlè,
with the same height and width.
In the past, a bodhisattva dwelled there.
There was a dragon cultivating the śrāvaka-kindness.
The mountain has a water deity named Shuǐtiān.
There is a rākṣasī named Xiū Cánkuì.
Each has five hundred attendants.
These two women constantly make offerings to these three animals.
These twelve animals constantly traverse Jambudvīpa day and night.
They are revered by humans and devas, and their merit is accomplished.
They have already made profound vows before the Buddhas.
Day and night, they always have one animal travel to teach and transform,
while the remaining eleven animals abide peacefully, cultivating kindness.
This cycle repeats continuously.
On the first day of the seventh month, the rat begins its travels,
using the Śrāvakayāna to teach and transform all beings in rat form,
causing them to abandon evil deeds and urging them to cultivate good deeds.
Thus, in sequence, until the thirteenth day,
the rat travels again.
And so on throughout the twelve months and twelve years, it is also like this.
Therefore, this land has much merit.
Even animals are able to teach and transform.
Therefore, bodhisattvas from other lands
should always revere this Buddha-world.
If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās
who wish to see these twelve animals,
who wish to attain great wisdom, great concentration, and great supernatural powers,
who wish to receive all scriptures,
who wish to increase good dharmas,
such a person should make a mountain from white earth,
seven feet in length and width, and twelve feet high.
Adorn it with various fragrant pastes and gold leaf.
Surround it on all sides for twenty feet.
Scatter Campaka flowers, which should be held in a copper vessel.
Place various untimely juices on all four sides.
Maintain purity, uphold precepts, and bathe three times a day.
Revere and have faith in the Three Jewels.
Stand facing due east, three zhang away from the mountain.
Recite this mantra for fifteen days.
Then, on the mountain, you will see the image of the first moon.
At that time, you will know you have seen the twelve animals.
Having seen them, your wishes will be fulfilled as desired.
If you can cultivate ascetic practices, you will attain it.
You will see with your eyes these twelve animals and the various bodhisattvas,
who may appear in the form of devas, ghosts, birds, or beasts,
traveling through Jambudvīpa to teach and transform such various beings.
If it is to tame beings among humans and devas,
that is not difficult.
But if it is to tame beings among animals, that is truly difficult.
The Buddha traveled alone, seeking tranquility,
and arrived at the country of Jiāosàluó, beneath the precious tree in the Bōlìluóyé Sālā Grove, where he stayed.
At that time, there was a herd of five hundred elephants.
The elephant king was always at the rear.
He always got muddy water and leftover grass.
Disgusted with the herd, he came alone to the tree.
From afar, he saw the Buddha.
With his trunk, he pulled out grass and trampled the ground to make it level.
With his trunk, he carried water to sprinkle the dust, spread grass to make a seat,
bent his knees, and invited the Buddha to sit.
For three months, he made offerings.
The Buddha knew the elephant's intention.
He accepted his invitation.
And spoke a verse:
At that time, the elephant king
took good lotus roots, washed them clean,
and offered them to the World-Honored One.
Thus for three months.
There was an elephant king named Shànzhù,
his body pure white, with seven places level,
able to fly with his strength.
His head was red, his body hair variegated,
with six delicate tusks.
He had eight thousand elephant kings as his attendants.
He dwelled beneath a sāla tree on the Fragrant Mountain.
The sāla tree king had eight thousand bathing pools,
fifty yojanas in length and width.
The water was cool and clear, with seven treasures as the embankment.
Variegated flowers of five colors gathered within the pools.
When the elephant king thought of entering a pool, eight thousand elephants responded to his thought and arrived.
Some held canopies and fans,
some sang praises and led the way,
some washed the elephant king's tail, back, thighs, and feet,
some pulled up flower roots and gave them to the king to eat,
some picked flowers and scattered them over the king.
The eight thousand elephants also bathed and enjoyed themselves together.
When they relieved themselves,
the yakṣa ghosts
moved it outside the mountain forest. The lowest elephant ridden by Śakra,
when ridden by a wheel-turning sage king, is called the elephant treasure.
In the Golden Wall Mountain, there are eighty thousand rocky caves,
where eighty thousand elephants rest.
Their bodies are pure white,
their heads variegated in color,
their mouths have large tusks,
with gold filling between their teeth.
In a past age,
there was a solitary elephant living in seclusion.
It gave birth to a calf.
Not long after it fell to the ground,
its mother died.
Not far from there was a place where immortals dwelled.
There was one with great power,
full of merit and virtue, whose heart held great compassion.
From afar, he saw the elephant calf,
its mother having just died, barely able to lift its feet,
wandering east and west, unable to sustain itself.
Immediately, he brought it back to his dwelling,
feeding it with fruits.
That elephant calf
was benevolent, gentle, virtuous, and excellent in merit,
delighting in righteousness and principle.
Having attained peace and security, without worries or troubles,
it then dwelled with the immortal, sleeping and rising together.
Its body gradually grew, its fur fresh and glossy.
It then used water and juice to make offerings to the immortal, along with fine fruits and melons,
before eating itself.
The immortal, compassionate, observed its conduct, loving it like a son, never tiring of looking at it.
At that time, Śakra, lord of the devas, immediately had a thought:
"Now this immortal's heart is set on the elephant calf, attached without weariness.
Now I should cause him sorrow and distress."
Then Śakra manifested to test him, transforming to make the elephant calf suddenly fall dead, its blood flowing.
The immortal, seeing the elephant calf dead, grieved and wept.
Other immortals heard and came to advise and console him,
but they could not remove his sorrow.
At that time, Śakra, lord of the devas, abiding in empty space,
spoke a verse to the immortal.
Then Śakra, lord of the devas, revived the elephant calf.
The immortal was greatly joyful.
The immortal was the Elder,
the dead elephant calf was the disciple,
and Śakra, lord of the devas, was myself.
In a past age, there were three friends:
an elephant, a monkey, and a dove, dwelling together relying on one nyagrodha tree.
They said to each other:
"Since we rely on this same tree, we should respect each other."
The monkey and dove together asked the elephant:
"How far back do you remember?"
The elephant said:
"I remember when I was small, walking past this tree, it reached my belly."
The elephant and dove asked the monkey.
The monkey answered:
"I remember when I was small, this tree reached my raised hand and head." The elephant said to the monkey:
"You were born many years before me."
The elephant and monkey together asked the dove.
The dove said:
"I remember on the right side of the Snowy Mountains, there was a great nyagrodha tree.
I ate its fruit, came here, and then turned, and this tree grew."
They said to each other:
"The dove was born many years before."
The elephant placed the monkey on its head, and the monkey
placed the dove on its shoulder.
Together they traveled among humans,
from village to village,
from town to town,
constantly reciting a verse:
At that time, the dove spoke such a Dharma.
People all followed its Dharma teaching, and it spread.
You all, having left home in my Dharma,
should further respect each other.
Thus will the Buddha-Dharma spread.
From now on, I permit following seniority in respect, bowing, welcoming, and inquiring after each other."
When the bhikṣus heard the Buddha's teaching,
the bhikṣus, according to seniority, respected and bowed to each other.
There is a horse king named Póluóxī.
His palace is located on a great sea island, on the Moonlight Mountain.
He has eight thousand horses as his attendants.
If a wheel-turning sage king appears in the world,
he takes the smallest as the horse treasure,
to serve as the king's mount.
There were people from a distant land.
They brought a large ox.
It was plump, vigorous, and powerful.
They sold it to a man in the city of Shèwèi.
The city man bought it intending to kill it.
At the city gate, he encountered the Buddha.
The ox saw the Buddha from afar.
In its heart, it felt sorrow and joy.
It broke its bonds and galloped away; no one could restrain it.
It went straight to the Tathāgata, bent its front legs,
and cried out with tears, speaking on its own:
"Great Sage, you are hard to encounter, appearing once in a billion ages.
I only beg for your great compassion to see and save me."
The Buddha said, "Very well.
In a distant past age, there was a wheel-turning king.
The king ruled the four continents, had a thousand sons and the seven treasures,
and governed with righteous law, bringing peace and security to the people.
He also possessed four virtues.
He regarded the people as his children, and the people revered him as a father.
Monks, Brahmins, elders, and common people never fell ill.
His virtue spread throughout the four regions, reaching the ten directions.
The king traveled to the four directions and was returning to his palace.
He encountered an old acquaintance who had been detained by a creditor, who said,
'He owes fifty taels of gold,' and had him bound to a tree.
The king, with his seven treasures and attendants, stopped and did not proceed.
Wondering why,
he was told:
'Release him and let him go; I will repay you double, a hundred taels.'
He was immediately released and returned home.
That person repeatedly went to the king's palace gate to ask for the gold but could not obtain it.
The creditor had already fled, and his whereabouts were unknown.
Thus, in the cycle of birth and death,
they wandered through countless kalpas.
The debt remained unpaid until this present life,
when he fell into this ox form.
The creditor sold him for thousands of taels of gold.
The wheel-turning king at that time was my own body.
The creditor is this ox.
The Buddha, as the sage king, guaranteed repayment for him.
In the end, he did not give it, so he came to seek help."
The Buddha told the ox owner,
"The Buddha will beg alms on your behalf and repay double the ox's value."
The ox owner refused and still wanted the ox.
The Buddha again told him,
"I will weigh the ox's body in catties and taels and give you a certain amount of gold."
But he still refused to give it.
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and Brahmā all descended.
They addressed the Buddha,
"Ten thousand, a thousand, a hundred million taels—we will provide them."
They took the ox to the Jetavana Grove.
After seven days, its life ended, and it was suddenly reborn in heaven.
It immediately recalled and remembered the Buddha's merit.
It returned to the human world, scattered flowers as an offering, and repaid the Buddha's kindness.
The Buddha preached a sutra for it.
It immediately attained the stage of non-retrogression and the patience of the unborn dharmas.
Then it returned to heaven.
In a past age, there was a different wilderness.
A water buffalo king settled there.
It wandered about, eating grass and drinking spring water.
At that time, the water buffalo king and its retinue
went wherever they gathered, with the king alone in front.
Its appearance was majestic and splendid, its dignity lofty, its virtue extraordinary, patient, humble, gentle, and its conduct calm and composed.
There was a monkey living by the roadside.
Seeing the water buffalo king with its retinue,
it felt angry and envious.
It then stirred up dust and threw tiles and stones,
hurling them in contempt and insult.
The water buffalo silently endured it and did not retaliate.
Not long after they passed,
another herd of water buffaloes came following behind.
The monkey saw them and also cursed them, stirring dust and throwing things.
The later herd,
seeing the earlier buffalo king silently endure, imitated it,
practicing patience and not harboring resentment.
These retinues passed by.
Not long after, there was a water buffalo calf
following behind,
trailing the herd.
Then the monkey chased it, cursing, insulting, and belittling it.
The calf felt resentful and displeased.
Seeing the earlier ones endure without resentment,
it also learned to imitate them.
Not far from the road, in a large grove of trees,
there was a tree deity dwelling there.
It asked the water buffalo king,
"Why do you all, seeing this monkey vilely curse you,
instead endure silently and not respond?"
The water buffalo replied,
"All water buffaloes, in the past,
not long ago, there were Brahmins,
great assemblies, groups of sages, and others who came along the road.
At that time, that monkey also insulted them.
The Brahmins and others
immediately caught it and trampled it to death."
Then the tree deity recited a verse:
The Buddha said,
"The water buffalo king was me.
When I was a bodhisattva, I fell into wrongdoing and became a king among water buffaloes.
I constantly practiced patience and cultivated the four immeasurables:
compassion, loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, and thus attained Buddhahood."
In the past, there was a person who had a black ox.
Another ox owner, for the sake of wealth, proclaimed,
"Whose ox is stronger than mine?
If it wins, I will give you goods.
If it loses, you give me goods."
The black ox owner replied, "Agreed."
At that time, they loaded heavy goods and tied the ox cart to the left.
They mocked and laughed, saying,
"Black crooked horn,"
and hit it with a stick, urging the ox to pull the cart away.
The ox, hearing this, immediately lost its color and strength and could not pull the heavy load up the slope.
At that time, the black ox owner lost a great deal of wealth.
The winner later proclaimed again,
The black ox, hearing the sound, said to its owner,
"You can agree."
The owner said, "I cannot.
The reason is:
Your wretched black ox caused me to lose a great deal of goods.
If we do it again, I will lose everything." The ox said to its owner,
"Earlier, in front of everyone, you mocked and belittled me.
Hearing the bad name, I immediately lost my color and strength.
That is why I could not pull the heavy load up the slope.
Now, listen to my words: do not speak harshly.
When in front of others, say to me,
'You are a good, big black ox, born auspicious, with broad and straight horns.'"
The owner accepted the ox's words.
He immediately washed and brushed it, adorned its horns with fine garlands,
tied the cart to the right, and spoke gently and lovingly:
"Great auspicious black ox, with broad horns and great strength,
pull this cart away."
The ox, hearing these gentle and loving words, immediately regained its color and strength.
It pulled the heavy load up the slope.
At that time, the black ox owner recovered what he had lost, and gained three times more.
The ox owner, having gained great profit, was very joyful.
He then spoke a verse:
The Buddha told the bhikkhus,
"Even animals, hearing words of form and appearance,
lose their color and strength.
How much more so humans?"
In the past, a great householder made a living by lending money.
Two people borrowed ten thousand coins.
When the time came, they repaid it.
Later, the two said to each other,
"Let us each borrow a hundred thousand more.
Later, we will not repay it."
There was an ox tied in a pen.
It said to the two,
"In my previous life, I owed my master a thousand coins and did not repay the debt.
Three times I was reborn as an ox, and still it is not settled.
How much more for you, wanting to take a hundred thousand? The sin will never end."
The two were astonished; by then, dawn had broken.
The master came out.
The two told him what the ox said.
The master immediately released it into the herd and no longer used it.
He made a vow:
"May this ox, from now on, never again take this animal form.
If there is any leftover money, use it all for charity."
The ox later passed away and was reborn as a human.
In the past, a person had a donkey used for pulling carts.
It traveled several hundred li a day.
He said to his younger brother,
"Do not let the donkey meet other donkeys."
The younger brother found it strange and thought to himself,
"When wise ones meet, they rejoice.
When flatterers meet, they also rejoice.
When creatures of the same kind meet, they all rejoice."
The younger brother deliberately let the donkey meet others.
It did not bray or sniff; it did not eat.
Later, when the elder brother harnessed it, it lay down and would not move.
The elder brother became very angry and cut off its hair and ears.
The donkey, suffering pain, again moved as before.
The donkey said to its master,
"Your younger brother let me meet bad companions.
I asked, 'Why are you so fat?'
They replied,
'We carry earth for the potter's master.
When we reach a bad road, we lie down and do not move.
The master then carries the earth on foot.
He lets us eat by the roadside.
We get good grass to eat and return to hay and grain.
That is why we are fat.'
I asked, 'Why are you so thin?'
They replied,
'We pull carts, traveling five hundred li a day.
Our food and drink are rough; that is why we are thin.'
I, being thin, thought that by being released I would become fat.
Instead, I was shorn and did not dare lie down again.
I beg to live."
The master took pity on it and released it to freedom.
The herd of oxen were gentle and well-tempered by nature.
Wherever they went,
they would choose soft, fine grass to eat.
They selected cool, clear water to drink.
At that time, there was a donkey.
It then thought to itself:
"I will also imitate their eating and drinking."
It immediately entered the herd of oxen.
It pawed the ground with its front hooves, disturbing those oxen.
It imitated their lowing and bellowing but could not change its own voice.
With its own voice, it declared, "I am also an ox."
The oxen gored it to death with their horns, left it, and went away.
The Buddha was in Shèwèiguó.
In a past life, there was a dog.
It left its own home and went to another's house to beg for food.
When entering the other's house, its body was inside the door, but its tail remained outside.
At that time, the master of the house, a householder, beat it and did not give it food.
The dog went to the officials and said:
"This householder,
I went to his house to beg for food.
Not only did he not give me food, but he also beat me.
I did not break the dog's code."
The officials asked, "What code does a dog have?"
It replied:
"In my own home, I sit and lie down as I please.
When going to another's house, my body enters inside the door, but my tail remains outside the door."
The officials said:
"Summon the householder here."
They asked him:
"Did you really beat the dog and not give it food?"
He replied that it was indeed so.
The officials asked the dog:
"How should this man be dealt with?"
The dog said:
"Give him the position of a great householder in this city of Shèwèi."
"Why do you answer thus?"
"I formerly was a great householder in this city of Shèwèi.
Because I committed evil with body and speech, I received this dog's body.
This man's evil is greater than mine. If this man is given power and influence,
he will certainly commit great evil, causing him to fall into hell,
where he will suffer extreme torment."
Long ago, there was a country.
Grain and rice became extremely expensive, and the people were starving.
At that time, a śramaṇa entered the city to seek alms.
He obtained nothing at all.
Next, he came to the gate of a wealthy elder, a man of great riches and high status.
He received coarse, poor-quality rice.
As he was about to leave the city,
he encountered a butcher carrying a puppy, taking it home to kill.
Seeing the śramaṇa, the butcher joyfully approached and paid his respects.
The śramaṇa gave a blessing.
Knowing there was a puppy
that the man intended to kill,
he deliberately asked the man what he was carrying.
The man replied, "I am walking empty-handed."
He asked again:
"I have seen it. Please show it to me.
I will trade my food for the puppy, to save its life."
The man replied:
"I cannot give it to you."
Thus, up to three times, he earnestly entreated and persuaded him.
The man was obstinate and unwilling to comply.
He said again, "Please at least show it to me."
The man then brought it out to show the śramaṇa.
He offered the rice to the puppy, stroked it, and gave a blessing.
Tears flowed from the puppy's eyes.
"Your own offenses have brought this upon you; you are not free.
May you, through successive lifetimes, have your offenses extinguished and blessings arise.
May you leave this puppy's body and be reborn as a human.
May you encounter the Three Jewels."
The puppy, having received the food, gave rise to a wholesome mind.
After its life ended, it was immediately reborn into the family of a wealthy, noble elder.
From birth, it had a compassionate mind.
At that time, that śramaṇa next came to the elder's gate to seek alms.
The elder's son was then seven years old.
Seeing that śramaṇa, he remembered his past cause.
He immediately approached, bowed his head to the śramaṇa's feet, and invited him forward to make offerings.
Returning, he told his parents:
"Now I wish to follow this great monk, to receive and uphold the sūtras and precepts,
to become his disciple."
His parents, loving and cherishing him, would not consent.
The child wept and cried, refusing to eat or drink.
"If you do not allow me to go, I will die."
His parents then consented.
He followed his teacher to study the path.
He shaved off his hair and beard, donned the three Dharma robes,
and attained samādhi, establishing himself in non-retrogression.
He opened up and transformed all beings, arousing in them the mind for the great path.
The Buddha went to Shèwèi city to wander and seek alms.
At that time, he arrived at the house of Yīngwǔ Móláo Dōuluózi.
He happened to be away from home.
There was a white dog named Jù.
It sat on a fine mat, eating polished rice and meat from a golden bowl.
The white dog saw the World-Honored One coming from afar.
Upon seeing him, it began to bark.
The World-Honored One said:
"Stop, white dog.
There is no need to make such a sound.
You were originally chanting, and thus became a white dog."
The white dog became extremely angry.
It got down from the bed-mat, went to the threshold of the door, lay down quietly, and remained there.
Later, Móláo Dōuluó returned and asked those nearby:
"Who upset my dog, causing it such distress?"
"Today, the śramaṇa Gáutamá came to your house to beg for food.
The dog barked at him.
Gáutamá said:
'Stop, white dog.
You should not make such a sound.
You were originally chanting.'
The dog became displeased and unhappy."
Yīngwǔ Móláo Dōuluózi reviled the World-Honored One from afar,
slandering him in anger, and went to the Jìyuán Garden.
From afar, he saw Yīngwǔ Móláo Dōuluózi coming.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"This man, due to his anger, upon the breaking up of his body, will be born in the Niraya hell."
At that time, Yīngwǔ Móláo Dōuluózi said to the World-Honored One:
"Śramaṇa Gáutamá, today you came to my house to beg for food.
What fault did the white dog have with you that you caused it unhappiness?"
The Buddha said:
"The white dog saw me and barked.
I said:
'White dog, you should not make such a sound.
You were originally chanting.'
And the white dog became angry."
"Gáutamá, what relative of mine was this white dog originally?"
The Buddha stopped Móláo, saying, "Do not ask.
You might become distressed and unhappy."
Thus, up to three times.
The World-Honored One said:
"This Móláo, the white dog in a previous life
was your father, named Dōuluó."
His anger doubled.
"My father Dōuluó
constantly practiced giving and always served the sacred fire.
Upon the breaking up of his body after death, he was born in the Brahmā heaven.
Why would he be born as a dog?"
"This Móláo, because of your conceit,
my father Dōuluó later also became thus,
born as a wretched, evil dog."
And he spoke a verse:
The Buddha said:
"If you do not believe what I say,
then go back home and say to the white dog:
'If you were originally my father Dōuluó in a past life,
then return to the bed-mat and eat polished rice and meat from the golden bowl.
Show me my father's hidden wealth.
You originally hid and stored it in a place I do not know.'"
Then Yīngwǔ Móláo Dōuluózi, hearing what the World-Honored One said,
thought well and reflected.
Returning home, he fully related it to the white dog.
At that time, the white dog then returned to the bed-mat and sat.
It ate polished rice and meat from the golden bowl.
It went to the place under the four legs of the bed where it originally slept.
With its mouth and paws, it dug at the ground.
Then Yīngwǔ Móláo Dōuluózi obtained a great amount of money and wealth.
A mind of joy arose.
With his right knee on the ground, facing the Jìshù Garden,
he declared his name,
"The true śramaṇa speaks truth, without falsehood."
After declaring it three times himself,
he left Shèwèi city and went to the Jìshù Garden.
The World-Honored One saw him from afar and addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you see that Yīngwǔ Móláo Dōuluózi coming?"
"Yes, World-Honored One."
"If at this time
Dōuluózi's life were to end, he would be born in a good place,
because he has a wholesome mind toward me.
Beings, because of a wholesome mind,
upon the breaking up of the body at death, are born in a good place, in heaven."
At that time, Yīngwǔ Móláo Dōuluózi went to where the World-Honored One was.
After exchanging greetings face to face, he said...
The Buddha said, "There is no difference."
There was an elder with immeasurable wealth.
He had a vicious dog that often delighted in biting people.
No one could casually enter his gate.
There was a bhikṣu.
He was intelligent, wise, sagely, and profound, difficult to match.
He entered his gate to beg for alms.
It happened that the dog had gone out to lie down and was unaware when he entered.
The elder prepared food, and only then did the dog notice and see him.
The dog thought, "I went out to lie down and was unaware, allowing the śramaṇa to enter.
Now that he is already seated, what can be done?
If he eats alone, I will certainly bite him to death when he leaves.
I will devour the delicious food in his stomach.
Only if he shares his food with me will I spare him."
The śramaṇa knew his thoughts.
He ate one handful himself and gave the dog one handful.
The dog developed good will and kindness toward the śramaṇa.
It came forward and licked his feet.
Then it went out the door and lay down.
Someone who had been bitten by it before struck its head with a sword.
That dog was then reborn in the womb of the elder's wife.
After birth, it died young, passing away soon after.
It was reborn again in that country, in the home of another elder.
At over ten years old,
he saw a śramaṇa, went forward to greet him, and paid his respects.
He informed his parents, requesting, "Let him be my teacher."
They arranged offerings, and he soon received the scriptures and precepts.
He further converted everyone in the household, young and old, to recite scriptures and contemplate the Way.
In repayment to his parents, he sought to become a śramaṇa.
He did not receive full ordination.
He served his preceptor day and night without negligence.
After his preceptor passed away, he then received the precepts and virtues.
In the past, there were deer, several hundred in a herd.
They followed the lush grass, encroaching near human settlements.
The king went out hunting, and they scattered in all directions.
There was a mother deer.
Pregnant, she wandered alone and was pursued.
Hungry, exhausted, and separated from her companions,
she gave birth to two fawns and left them to seek food.
Anxious and confused, she lost her way and fell into a hunting trap.
She cried mournfully, wanting to escape but unable to break free.
The hunter heard the sound and went to look.
Seeing the deer, his heart was gladdened, and he approached intending to kill her.
The deer then kowtowed, pleading for mercy and explaining herself:
"I have just given birth to two fawns, still young and ignorant.
They have just opened their eyes, still dim and unaware of east or west.
I beg for a brief respite to temporarily return and see my children.
I will show them water and grass so they may live.
I will then return to face death, not breaking my sincere vow."
The hunter was astonished.
He immediately replied to the deer:
"All people in the world lack utmost sincerity.
How much more a deer? Having escaped death, how could there be a return?"
The deer replied again, saying:
"If you let me go, my children will live.
If you keep me, my children will die."
She then spoke a verse:
The hunter found this extremely strange and extraordinary.
Yet his mind was still filled with greed.
He again answered the deer:
"Crafty deception lacks truth; treachery and fraud are hard to trust.
Empty appearances are myriad; cunning and guile are not one.
Cherishing one's body and fearing death, few can sacrifice their lives.
Human lack of goodness shows how difficult it is to expect such a promise.
How much more for a wild animal? Once gone, how could it return?
I will certainly not release you."
The deer again shed tears.
She replied with a verse:
The hunter, hearing the deer's words again,
felt increasingly awed in his heart.
He then stepped back and sighed:
"Only I, living in this world, was born as a human.
Yet I am foolish, deluded, ignorant, turning my back on kindness and belittling righteousness.
I harm living beings, making killing and hunting my livelihood.
Deceitful and fraudulent, I seek gain recklessly, greedy and insatiable.
I do not know impermanence, nor do I recognize the Three Jewels.
The deer's words surpass those of humans.
Her sincere vow and kowtow show utmost loyalty in her feelings.
He then stepped forward, released the trap, and let her go.
Thereupon, the deer returned to where her fawns were.
Lowering her head, she murmured and licked her children's bodies.
With both sorrow and joy,
she spoke a verse together:
Thereupon, the mother deer led her two fawns.
She showed them good water and grass.
Tears streamed down.
She spoke a verse of farewell:
After the mother deer finished speaking, she then left them and departed.
The two fawns wailed mournfully, shedding tears of longing and attachment.
