They pursued from behind, stumbling and rising again.
The mother looked back and commanded:
"Go back, do not come.
Do not let mother and child both die together.
My death, I accept willingly, though it pains me.
You do not yet understand that in this world, all things are impermanent and there is separation.
My own fate is meager; your birth lacks blessings.
Why grieve and sorrow, only increasing worry and suffering?
Just establish your resolve and fulfill your lives."
Thereupon, the mother again spoke this verse to her children:
The fawns still grieved and longed, crying and wailing.
They searched for her until they reached the trap.
Seeking east and west,
they then saw the hunter lying under a tree.
The mother deer stood still.
She spoke a verse to awaken him:
The hunter then suddenly awoke and rose in alarm.
The deer again knelt toward him.
She repeated the verse:
The hunter saw the deer's deep sincerity and commitment to die for righteousness.
Her will and integrity were red with sincerity; her compassionate actions manifested loyalty.
Releasing her should be verified; she abandoned life to fulfill her vow.
Mother and child, grieving and attached, had searched for each other and arrived.
Moved by compassion and pity,
he bowed his head and apologized, saying:
The hunter then released the deer and let her go.
Mother and child, with sorrow and joy, cried with gentle calls.
They thanked the hunter with a verse:
The hunter reported all this to the king.
The people of the country all came to know.
Universally moved by compassion and sincerity,
they saw that the deer's humane conduct surpassed righteousness.
None failed to respectfully sigh.
They ceased killing and hunting.
The deer returned, called their herd, gathered their companions, and roamed, each resting in their place.
The Buddha said:
"The deer at that time was my own body.
The two fawns were Rāhula and Cūlā's mother.
The king at that time was Śāriputra.
The hunter was Ānanda."
In the past, a king went on a hunting excursion.
He made a trapping ground with pits to capture herds of deer.
At that time, there was a deer king leading hundreds of millions of deer.
They successively ate the lush grass and entered his trapping ground.
The guards closed the gate.
They went to report to the king.
The king was greatly delighted.
The deer king immediately knew.
He thought to himself:
"The reason the herd came here is because of me alone.
I must devise a plan to save the multitude's lives."
He then used his own body to lie horizontally over the pit.
He let the herd of deer tread on his back to get out.
Their hooves injured his back; the flesh was completely gone.
Only bones remained.
Enduring the pain, he saved them; all had already gotten out.
With his last strength, he climbed onto the bank and looked around in all directions.
There was only one deer who did not know to seek escape.
The deer king called to it, and only then did it come out.
Thereupon, the deer king's life ended, and he fell into the pit.
The Buddha was at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak.
He suffered from a wind ailment.
The royal physician Jīvaka prepared a medicinal paste for him,
using thirty-two ingredients.
Each day, he took thirty-two liǎng of it.
At that time, Devadatta was always filled with jealousy.
His heart was arrogant, hoping to equal the Buddha.
Imitating the Buddha, he also took the medicine, applying it to his pulse channels.
His body weakened, and he groaned in pain and distress.
The World-Honored One, out of compassion, stroked his head with his hand.
The medicine dissipated, and the illness was cured. Recognizing the Buddha's hand,
he said,
"Siddhartha, the other arts are not accepted in the world, so he has studied medicine instead."
The Buddha said,
"Devadatta harbors an unwholesome mind, not only today.
In the past, in Jambudvīpa, there was a city named Vārāṇasī.
Its king was named Brahmadatta.
He was cruel and without compassion.
He dreamed of a beast,
with golden fur, the tips of its hair glowing with golden light.
He then summoned the hunters,
and told them his dream in detail.
'You all must seek and capture it.
If you obtain its skin, I will reward you heavily.
If you fail, I will exterminate your clans.'
The hunters were worried and distressed, gathering to discuss a plan.
Together they recruited one man, ordering him to go and search for it.
'If you meet misfortune, we will still provide for your wife and children.'
The man thought to himself,
'If I must abandon my life, I will go.'
He journeyed through perilous terrain.
After a long time, his body grew weary.
The weather was hot and sultry, and he was near death.
In sorrow and despair, he said,
'Who has compassion to save my life?'
There was a wild beast named Mṛga,
with golden fur, who heard him and took pity.
He entered a cool spring, came over, and embraced him.
After a while, the man regained strength, and Mṛga led him to the water.
He bathed him and gathered fruit for him to eat.
Once his body had recovered,
he thought to himself,
'Now I have seen this beast, the very one the king seeks.
Yet when I was near death, I relied on him to save my life.
I have not repaid his kindness; how could I bear to harm him?
But if I do not capture him,
those hunters will surely be executed.'
Thinking this, he grieved.
Mṛga asked, 'Why are you unhappy?'
He answered, revealing his thoughts.
Mṛga said,
'Do not worry about this matter. My skin is easily obtained.
I have given up my body countless times, yet never for merit.
Now, with my body and skin, I can save the lives of many.
If you wish to gain something,
just peel off my skin; do not take my life immediately.
I give it to you without regret or resentment.'
The hunter peeled off the skin.
Mṛga then made a vow:
'Now I give my skin to this person,
saving those beloved lives.
With this merit, I dedicate it to all sentient beings,
to attain Buddhahood and universally liberate all.'
After making this vow, the three thousand lands shook six times.
After the skin was peeled off, his flesh was exposed, blood flowing freely.
Furthermore, eighty thousand flies and ants
gathered on his body, feeding on him simultaneously.
Wishing to return to his den but fearing he might harm them,
he endured the pain, holding himself still without moving.
He died there.
The flies and ants that fed on him died and were reborn in heaven.
The hunter carried the skin to the king.
The king, seeing its rarity, often spread it out to sleep on.
His body and mind were at ease and happy.
The beast Mṛga is now my body.
King Brahmadatta is now Devadatta.
The eighty thousand insects—when I first attained Buddhahood and turned the Dharma wheel,
the eighty thousand devas who attained the path were they.
There was a wild fox who went to beg food from a lion.
Each time he got leftovers, he kept going without cease.
Once, the lion was hungry and had not yet eaten,
so he called the wild fox, sniffed him, took him, and swallowed him.
Before dying, in the throat, the fox cried out,
'Master, spare my life!'
The lion thought,
'I have fed you until you are fat and sleek, intending to keep you as a reserve.
What more do you have to say?'
A woman left her infant in one place.
A wolf carried the child away.
People pursued and caught up, saying to him,
'Why are you taking this child away?'
The wolf replied,
'This child's mother is my enemy.
For five hundred lifetimes, she has always eaten my children.
I, too, for five hundred lifetimes, have always killed her children.
If she can abandon her old grudge,
I can also abandon mine.'
The people told the child's mother,
'You should abandon your grudge.'
The child's mother replied,
'I have now abandoned it.'
The wolf observed the child's mother.
Although she said she had abandoned it, her heart did not let go.
He killed the child and left.
In the past, there was a Brahmin, one hundred twenty years old.
From youth, he did not marry and was without lust.
He dwelled in solitude deep in the mountains, in a hut of thatch,
with wormwood for a mat, and fruits and melons for food.
He did not accumulate wealth or treasures.
When the king summoned him, he did not go, remaining serene and unattached.
For several thousand years, he amused himself with birds and beasts.
There were four kinds of animals:
first, a fox;
second, a monkey;
third, an otter;
fourth, a hare.
These four animals listened to the ascetic's sutra recitations and precept teachings.
After a long time like this,
the fruits and melons they ate were all exhausted.
Later, the ascetic intended to leave.
These four great animals were sad and unhappy.
They discussed together, saying,
'Each of us should seek offerings.'
The monkey fetched sweet fruits to offer to the ascetic.
The fox also sought food and obtained a bag of rice to offer to the ascetic.
The otter entered the water and caught a big fish to offer to the ascetic.
The hare thought to himself,
'What shall I use to make an offering to the ascetic?'
He thought,
'I shall offer my own body.'
So he went to gather firewood, lit a fire to make charcoal,
and went to tell the ascetic,
'Now I am of little worth.
Please make charcoal, and I will enter the fire.
I offer my body to the ascetic.'
The fire would not burn.
The ascetic, moved by his righteousness and compassion,
pitted him and stopped him.
That Brahmin was the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.
The hare was my body.
The monkey was Śāriputra.
The fox was Ānanda.
The otter was Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
The Buddha and the bhikṣus
accepted the invitation of the Brahmin Śreṣṭhin.
Returning to Vulture Peak,
they washed their bowls by the river.
In the Aśoka grove, there was a monkey.
Walking, he saw a tree without bees but with ripe honey.
He came to Ānanda to ask for a bowl.
Ānanda did not give it.
The Buddha said, 'Just give it to him.'
The monkey got the bowl, filled it with honey, and offered it to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One did not accept it, telling him to purify it with water.
The monkey did not understand,
thinking there were insects.
He took it to the water's edge to wash the bowl.
The water swirled into the honey; he brought it back and offered it to the Buddha. The Buddha distributed it among the assembly of monks, all receiving a share.
The monkey, overjoyed, leaped and danced, fell into a pit, and died.
He was conceived in the womb of Śreṣṭhin's wife.
Later, a son was born, handsome in form and features. The Buddha said,
'In the past, at the time of the Buddha Kāśyapa,
there was a young śramaṇa.
Seeing an Arhat leap across a stream,
he said to an ordinary bhikṣu,
"You are as swift as a monkey."
For five hundred lifetimes thereafter, he was always a monkey.'
The Tathāgata attained parinirvāṇa in the country of Mathurā.
A hundred years later, on Mount Urumaṇḍa,
on one side there were five hundred pratyekabuddhas.
On another side there were five hundred ṛṣis.
On another side there were five hundred monkeys.
The leader of the monkeys went among the pratyekabuddhas and saw them.
He felt joy.
He took flowers and fruits from trees to make offerings to the pratyekabuddhas.
He paid homage and sat at the end of the assembly.
He did this every day.
Later, all the pratyekabuddhas entered parinirvāṇa.
The monkey continued making offerings as before.
Seeing that the pratyekabuddhas did not accept them,
he tugged at their robes and grasped their feet, but they still did not move.
The monkey thought,
"They have all died."
He wept and grieved.
He then went to where the five hundred ṛṣis were.
They all went into a thicket of thorns.
The monkey also went in.
The ṛṣis went onto a patch of ash and dirt.
The monkey also went onto the ash and dirt.
The ṛṣis practiced the fivefold asceticism of scorching their bodies.
The monkey also did likewise.
A ṛṣi hung himself from a tree by his hands.
The monkey knocked his hands loose, causing him to fall to the ground.
He constantly taught the ṛṣis the four dignified deportments.
After teaching them,
he sat upright among the ṛṣis and cultivated concentration.
He said to the ṛṣis,
"All of you should sit like this."
Then the five hundred ṛṣis followed him in sitting in meditation.
The ṛṣis, without a teacher expounding the Dharma,
contemplated the thirty-seven aids to enlightenment,
attained realization, and achieved the path of the pratyekabuddha.
They all thought,
"I attained the noble path because of this monkey."
They then made offerings of incense, flowers, and food to the monkey.
When the monkey died, they cremated his body with fragrant wood.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"That monkey was Upagupta.
In the evil destinies, he brought benefit to many beings.
More than a hundred years after my parinirvāṇa,
these events will occur."
Formerly, when the Buddha was in the country of Rājagṛha,
he sent an arhat named Sumana,
carrying the Buddha's hair and nails, to the southern mountains of the country of Kapiśa to build a stūpa.
Five hundred arhats constantly resided in the monastery there.
Morning and evening they burned incense, circumambulated the stūpa, and paid homage.
At that time, there were five hundred monkeys in those mountains.
Seeing the monks making offerings to the stūpa and monastery,
they immediately went together to a deep ravine,
carried mud and stones on their backs, and imitated building a stūpa.
They erected a wooden pole, set up a flagstaff, and tied a tattered banner to the top.
Morning and evening they paid homage, just like the monks.
At that time, mountain waters suddenly flooded.
The five hundred monkeys were all swept away and drowned.
Their spirits were immediately reborn in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
There were palaces of the seven treasures, and food and clothing appeared spontaneously.
Each thought to himself,
"From where have I come to be born in this heaven?"
Using their divine eye, they saw their former bodies,
the bodies of monkeys,
who had playfully imitated the monks in making a stūpa and monastery.
Although their bodies were swept away, their spirits were reborn in heaven.
Now they should descend to repay the kindness of their former corpses.
Each, with his attendants, bringing flowers, incense, and musicians, descended to their former corpses.
They scattered flowers, burned incense, and circumambulated them seven times.
At that time, there were five hundred brahmins in the mountains.
They studied heterodox views and did not believe in karmic retribution.
Seeing the devas scattering flowers, making music, and circumambulating the monkey corpses,
they were astonished and asked,
"Your divine radiance is so majestic.
Why do you condescend to make offerings to these corpses?"
The devas said,
"These corpses are our former bodies."
They fully recounted the previous events.
"Because of this small merit, we were reborn in heaven.
Therefore, we now scatter flowers to repay the kindness of our former bodies.
Playfully making a stūpa and monastery brought such reward.
If one were to serve the Buddha with utmost sincerity,
the virtue gained would be beyond description.
You, with your heterodox views, do not believe in the true Dharma.
For a hundred kalpas of diligent hardship, you gain nothing.
It would be better to go together to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to pay homage and make offerings, gaining limitless merit."
They all gladly went together to where the Buddha was.
They prostrated themselves on the ground with five limbs, scattered flowers, and made offerings.
The devas addressed the Buddha,
"We were recently in the bodies of monkeys.
Through the World-Honored One's grace,
we were reborn in heaven.
We regret not having seen the Buddha, so now we take refuge."
They further addressed the Buddha,
"In our past lives, what evil deeds did we commit that we received monkey bodies?
Although we made a stūpa and monastery, our bodies were swept away."
The Buddha told the devas,
"It did not arise from emptiness.
In a past age, there were five hundred young brahmins who went together into the mountains seeking the path of the ṛṣis.
At that time, there was a śramaṇa on the mountain.
He wished to plaster a vihāra on the mountain.
He went down into the valley to fetch water, his body light as if flying.
The five hundred brahmins, feeling jealous, laughed at him in unison, saying,
'This śramaṇa goes up and down swiftly like a monkey.
What is so remarkable about that?'
He continued fetching water without stopping.
Soon, mountain waters came and drowned them."
The Buddha told the devas,
"The śramaṇa going up and down was my former body.
The five hundred young brahmins were the five hundred monkey bodies.
Making jokes creates offense, and one receives the retribution in body."
The Buddha spoke a verse.
The five hundred devas, hearing the Buddha's words, immediately attained the path.
The five hundred brahmins, hearing about the retribution of offense and merit,
sighed to themselves, saying,
"We have studied to become ṛṣis for many years,
yet have received no fruit.
It is not as good as the monkeys who playfully created merit and were reborn in heaven.
The Buddha's virtue is truly sublime."
They bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet, wishing to become his disciples.
The Buddha said,
"Welcome, bhikṣus."
They immediately became śramaṇas, diligently practiced, and attained the path.
Formerly, there was a monk
sitting in meditation under a tree, reciting sūtras.
There was a monkey in the tree imitating him.
Unaware, it fell from the tree and died.
It was reborn in heaven.
Formerly, there was a king who had a monkey.
It constantly played with a maidservant, repeatedly without stopping.
A brahmin said to the king,
"You should separate this maidservant from the monkey."
The king said,
"What harmony is there to disrupt that I should separate them?"
Later, the maidservant came from outside carrying a rice vessel and a large stick.
The monkey ran up and tugged at the maidservant.
The maidservant, angry, kicked it and struck it with the stick.
The monkey fell into a fire, which burned its fur.
It ran into a pile of firewood.
The fire spread to the houses and palace.
The treasuries all turned to ashes.
Only then did the king realize the truth of the brahmin's words.
Formerly, there was a rabbit king who wandered in the mountains.
He ate fruits and drank water together with his group.
He practiced the four immeasurables: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
He taught his retinue to be entirely benevolent and harmonious, and not to commit any evils.
"After leaving this body, you may obtain human form
and be able to receive the Buddha's teaching."
At that time, his retinue was joyful
and followed his teaching, not daring to disobey.
There was a ṛṣi dwelling in the forest trees.
He ate fruits and drank water, cultivating the path alone.
He never strayed, but established the four brahmavihāras:
loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, reciting sūtras and contemplating the path.
His voice was clear and fluent, harmonious and elegant; all who heard it rejoiced.
Then the rabbit king went near him.
Listening to him recite sūtras, his mind was filled with joyful excitement and he never grew weary.
Together with his retinue, he brought fruits and melons to make offerings to the ascetic.
Thus days accumulated, passing through months and years.
When winter's cold arrived,
the ṛṣi wished to return to the human world.
The rabbit king saw this and was saddened, unhappy.
His heart was filled with longing and regret; he did not wish him to leave.
He asked where he was going.
"Here we see each other daily for enjoyment.
We forget hunger and thirst as if relying on parents.
We beg you to stay, do not go."
The ṛṣi replied,
"I have the four great elements which I must carefully protect.
Now winter's cold has come, fruits and melons are exhausted.
The mountain waters are frozen, and there are no caves in which to dwell.
Therefore, I wish to leave and rely on the human world,
going on alms rounds for food and staying temporarily in a vihāra.
After this winter cold passes, I will return to you.
Do not be distressed."
The rabbit king replied,
"We, your retinue, will go seek fruits.
We will search far and wide and will certainly provide enough.
We beg you to bend your will, have compassion, and help us.
If you leave, the sorrow of longing may cause us not to survive.
If today we have no offering to present,
then I will offer my own body to the ascetic."
The ascetic saw this and was moved, feeling pity and concern.
His compassion was utmost, but what could he do?
The ṛṣi maintained a sacred fire; before him were live coals.
The rabbit king thought to himself,
"The ascetic is silent for my sake." He then lifted his own body and threw it into the fire.
The fire blazed greatly; the ascetic wished to save him,
but he had already died and was reborn in the Tuṣita heaven.
As a bodhisattva, his merit and virtue were especially honored, his majestic spiritual power towering.
The ṛṣi saw this.
For the sake of the Dharma, he did not spare his body or life.
Feeling pity and compassion for him, he also blamed himself.
He abstained from food and did not eat.
Soon after, his spirit departed and he was also reborn in the Tuṣita heaven.
The Buddha said,
"The rabbit king at that time was I.
The ṛṣi was the Buddha Dīpaṃkara."
In a past age, there was a wildcat.
Hungry, thirsty, and emaciated,
it lay in wait for young mice in a hole.
When a young mouse emerged, it swiftly seized and swallowed it.
The young mouse, being small, entered its belly alive.
It ate the cat's internal organs.
The cat, confused and distressed, ran wildly in all directions.
It then died.
A foolish, ignorant mendicant, lacking virtue,
did not guard his body and mind. Seeing various women,
he grasped at their forms and appearances.
The Buddha said:
"Jiālán Tuó" is the name of a mountain rat.
At that time, King Píshèlí,
leading his female entertainers, entered the mountains to amuse himself.
The king, weary, slept beneath a tree.
The female entertainers scattered left and right, running and playing.
In a burrow under the tree was a large venomous snake.
Smelling the king's wine-laden breath, it emerged intending to bite the king.
A rat in the tree came down from above, crying out to wake the king.
The snake then withdrew.
After waking, the king slept again.
The snake emerged once more.
The rat again cried out, descending to wake the king.
The king rose and saw the large venomous snake.
He was immediately terrified.
He sought his female entertainers, but they were nowhere to be seen.
The king thought to himself:
"I have survived today
due to the rat's kindness.
I wish to repay it."
There was a village by the mountain.
He summoned the village,
declaring, "From now on, all my provisions and taxes shall be redirected to supply the rats."
Because of this rat, the village was named Jiālán Tuó.
At that time, there was an elder in the village.
He possessed four billion gold coins.
The king then bestowed upon the elder a position.
Because of the village's name, he was called Elder Jiālán Tuó.
Long ago, in an elder's household, there was a ghee jar.
Placed in a high loft, its cover was not secure.
A rat entered the ghee jar, eating day and night.
Its body consequently grew. The ghee was soon exhausted,
and the rat filled the jar, its appearance resembling the color of ghee.
Someone came to buy ghee.
At that time, the elder took the ghee and placed it over a fire.
The rat inside the jar then died within the jar.
It transformed into ghee.
It was sold to the buyer.
When measuring out by the peck and bushel, its bones sank to the bottom,
its skull and limb bones each separating and disintegrating.
Garuda birds are of four kinds:
first, egg-born;
second, womb-born;
third, moisture-born;
fourth, transformation-born.
All previously had minds of great generosity, soaring loftily in the sky.
But with minds harboring much anger and arrogance towards suffering beings,
they were born among these birds.
They possess wish-fulfilling jewel necklaces.
They can transform in myriad ways, accomplishing any task.
Their bodies are forty *li* tall.
Their garments are eighty *li* wide
and forty *li* long,
weighing only two and a half *liang*.
They eat turtles, alligators, fish, and tortoises as coarse food; bathing and fine garments serve as their delicate food.
They also have marriages.
The two bodies touch to achieve union.
Their lifespan is one kalpa, or sometimes less.
On the northern shore of the great ocean is a tree named Jiūluó Chēnmó, one hundred *yojanas* tall,
shading fifty *yojanas*. East of the tree are the palaces of egg-born dragons and egg-born Garudas.
South of the tree are the palaces of womb-born dragons and womb-born Garudas.
West of the tree are the palaces of moisture-born dragons and moisture-born Garudas.
North of the tree are the palaces of transformation-born dragons and transformation-born Garudas.
Each palace measures six thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth.
Their adornments are as described above.
If an egg-born Garuda flies down to the sea and strikes the water with its wings,
the water parts two hundred *yojanas* deep.

It takes egg-born dragons and eats them at will. The same applies to womb-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born dragons. There is a transformation-born dragon prince who observes the eight precepts on the three fasting days.
At that time, a Garuda bird wanted to seize and eat him.
It carried him up to a large iron tree north of Mount Sumeru,
one hundred sixty thousand *li* high.
It sought his tail but could not find it at all.
The bird, hearing this, also received the five precepts.
The Garuda king,
named Zhèngyīn,
was joyful and at ease among the feathered tribes.
In Jambudvīpa, he daily ate one dragon king and five hundred small dragons.
Throughout the four continents, he ate in turn,
the daily number being as above.
This cycle repeated continuously.
After eight thousand years, signs of death appeared.
The dragons spewed poison, so he could no longer eat.
Driven by hunger and panic, he found no peace.
He went to the Vajra Mountains.
From the Vajra Mountains, he descended straight to the surface of the great waters.
Reaching the realm of the wind circle, he was blown by the wind back to the Vajra Mountains.
This happened seven times, after which he died.
Due to his poison, ten jeweled mountains simultaneously caught fire.
The dragon king Nàntuó, fearing this mountain would burn,
immediately sent down heavy rain, with drops as large as cart wheels.
The bird's flesh completely dissolved, leaving only its heart intact.
The heart also descended straight down seven times as before, then rested at the Vajra Mountains.
The dragon king Nàntuó took it and made it into a bright pearl.
A wheel-turning sage king obtained it as a wish-fulfilling pearl.
If a person contemplates the Buddha, their mind is also like this.
Qiānqiū,
with a human face and bird body,
gave birth to offspring that then harmed their mother.
Later, she attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Animals lack such wisdom and the concept of seniority and juniority.
They do not incur the five heinous crimes.
By the Míhóu River in Píshèlí, there was a garlic garden.
The bhikṣuṇī Tōuluó Nántuó
was not far from the garden.
The garden owner asked,
"Auntie, do you need garlic?"
The bhikṣuṇī then, along with śrāmaṇerikās and śikṣamāṇās,
repeatedly went to ask for garlic.
It was eventually all exhausted.
The owner abandoned the garden and left.
The Buddha told a Jātaka tale:
Long ago, there was a Brahmin,
one hundred twenty years old, with an emaciated body.
His wife was incomparably beautiful.
They had many sons and daughters.
This Brahmin's mind was attached to his wife and children,
never parting from them.
Due to this deep affection and clinging,
he died and was reborn as a goose.
Its body and feathers were entirely golden.
Because of his previous meritorious karma, he remembered his past lives.
He thought, "By what means can I support these children so they do not suffer poverty?"
Each day he returned, dropped one feather, and left.
The children saw this but did not know the reason.
They discussed together, saying,
"We should wait for his arrival,
find a way to catch him, and take all his golden feathers."
As they plotted, they plucked all the golden feathers.
When the feathers were gone, white feathers grew back.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Know that the Brahmin who died and became a goose—
is he someone else?
He is none other than the garden owner.
His beautiful wife is none other than the bhikṣuṇī.
The sons and daughters are none other than the śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇerikās, and others."
The Buddha was in the country of Bōluónài.
In a forest and marsh,
he expounded the wonderful Dharma for the devas, humans, and the fourfold assembly.
At that time, in the sky, a flock of five hundred geese
hearing the Buddha's voice, deeply delighted, circled wishing to descend.
A hunter spread his net, and the geese fell into it.
Killed by the hunter, they were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
They appeared on their parents' knees like eight-year-old children,
incomparably dignified and radiant like a golden mountain.
They then thought to themselves,
"By what cause am I born here?"
They immediately remembered their past lives and the karmic result of their love for the Dharma.
Together, holding flowers, they descended to Jambudvīpa.
They came before the World-Honored One, paid homage at his feet, and said,
"We, hearing the Dharma's sound, were born in this wonderful heaven.
We beseech you to expound it again."
The Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths.
They attained the fruit of Stream-enterer.
They then returned to heaven.
A king's consort, ascending a high tower,
saw geese flying in the sky and desired their meat.
She informed the king.
The king dispatched hunters,
who took nets and spread them, searching everywhere.
They caught several dozen and kept them in cages.
Among them were some that did not eat.
The other geese said to them,
"Now that we are alive, what good is not eating?"
The non-eating ones said,
"Worried, we cannot eat."
After seven days, emaciated, they escaped through the cage holes and flew away.
From afar, they called to the fat ones, saying,
"You, greedy for food, will suffer pain later."
In Amitābha Buddha's land,
there are always various wonderful, multi-colored birds:
white swans, peacocks, parrots, śārikas, kalaviṅkas, and jīvajīvas.
Day and night, at the six periods, they produce harmonious and elegant sounds.
The sounds they utter speak of
the five faculties,
the five powers,
the seven factors of enlightenment,
the eightfold noble path,
and such Dharmas.
The beings of that land, hearing these sounds,
all contemplate the Three Jewels.
Long ago, on Snow Mountain, there was a pigeon.
At that time, heavy snow fell.
A person lost his way, destitute and suffering,
with hunger and cold imminent, his life hanging by a thread.
The pigeon flew to seek fire,
gathered firewood for him, and lit it.
Once lit, it threw itself into the fire,
offering itself to this starving person.
The Buddha was walking in meditation in the Jìhuán Grove during the afternoon.
Śāriputra followed him.
At that time, a hawk was chasing a dove.
The dove flew to the Buddha's side.
The Buddha's shadow covered it as he walked.
The dove's body became peaceful and secure, its fear was immediately dispelled, and it no longer made a sound.
Later, when Śāriputra's shadow reached it,
the dove made sounds and trembled in terror as before.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Both the Buddha and I are free from the three poisons.
When the Buddha's shadow covered the dove, the dove was not terrified.
When my shadow covered it, it trembled in fear as before."
The Buddha said:
"It is because you still have the habit of the three poisons.
You observe this dove's past karmic connections—for how many lifetimes has it been a dove?"
Śāriputra immediately entered the samādhi of knowing past lives.
He observed and saw that this dove
had been a dove for eighty thousand great kalpas.
Beyond that, I cannot see."
The Buddha said:
"If you cannot fully know the past,
try to observe when this dove will be liberated."
Śāriputra then entered the samādhi of knowing future aspirations.
He observed and saw that this dove
would not be liberated from its dove body for eighty thousand great kalpas.
Beyond that, I do not know.
For as many great kalpas as the sands of the Ganges River, it will always be a dove."
Long ago, a wildfire burned a forest.
In the forest, there was a pheasant.
It diligently exerted itself, flying into the forest
and sprinkling water on it. Though it went back and forth until exhausted, it did not consider it suffering.
At that time, the god Śakra came and asked:
"What are you doing?"
It replied:
"I am saving this forest out of compassion for all beings.
This forest provides extensive shade, is cool and pleasant.
All my kind and relatives depend on it.
Since I have physical strength, how can I be lazy and not save it?"
Śakra asked:
"How long will you persevere with such diligence?"
The pheasant said:
"Until death."
Śakra said:
"Who will bear witness for you?"
It then made a vow:
"If my heart is sincere and my words are not false, may the fire extinguish itself."
At that time, the pure abode gods, knowing the pheasant's great vow,
extinguished the fire.
The forest remained lush and was never burned by fire."
King Prasenajit had four great ministers.
He appointed them as generals.
They assembled four armies to attack a small country.
The four ministers saw the Buddha and bowed at his feet.
The World-Honored One asked them:
"Where are you going?"
They fully explained the matter.
"We, with our bodies, have accomplished much for this king and often fear for our lives. Now we are about to go to war."
The World-Honored One praised them:
"Excellent, virtuous ones.
This is repaying kindness and showing loyalty.
Not only in this life have you served this king.
In a past age, in the country of Shājié,
a flock of crows gathered and settled in that country.
The crow king was named Gānzhè.
He ruled eighty thousand crows.
The crow king had a wife named Jiùlíní.
She was pregnant and had a craving. She sincerely told the king:
'I have a slight desire and wish to have tender
deer king meat to survive; otherwise, I will die.'
Thereupon, the crow king, hearing her words, assembled the crow flock.
'You must go to the country of Shājié.
In Shājié, the king has a great deer king
named Xūjù.
I want its meat.'
Four crows volunteered.
'We are capable.
We will not spare our lives to accomplish this task.'
Then the four crows repeatedly went to the gathering place.
The prince of the country saw the crows and became fearful.
He hurried back and reported to the king:
'I saw four crows of such appearance.
They repeatedly come to the deer park.'
The king then ordered people to capture them.
The bird-catchers devised a method, set up nets, and caught the crows.
They were captured alive and presented to the king.
The king questioned the four crows and scolded them:
'Why do you repeatedly come here?
You violate my territory.'
The crows said:
'Indeed, heavenly king, it is not our wish.
There is a king named Ānzhù.
His wife is pregnant
and desires the tender meat of the deer king Xūjù.
That king sent us.
We obey our lord's command.'
The king was astonished and found it strange.
'To receive the king's command and devise such a plan,
casting aside one's own life—this is truly beyond compare.
To seek such loyalty among ordinary people
who receive the teachings of ruler and father is hardly possible,
let alone among birds and beasts.'
The king told the crows:
'Now I pardon your offense.'"
"Long ago, there was a crow named Jūqí who lived in a thicket and laid eggs, raising its young in a tree.
At that time, Jūqí and a monkey were close friends.
In the thicket, there was a poisonous snake.
It waited until the crow was away
and ate all of Jūqí's offspring, leaving none.
Jūqí, having lost its young, cried out in sorrow, not knowing where they were.
After careful consideration,
it realized the snake had eaten them.
When the monkey returned and asked what was wrong,
it replied:
'The snake ate all my children, completely.'
The monkey said:
'I will take revenge.'
When the poisonous snake was moving,
the monkey went before it and encircled it.
The snake angrily coiled around the monkey.
The monkey seized its head and dragged it,
grinding it on a rock until it broke and died.
It discarded the snake and returned.
Jūqí leaped for joy."
"In a past age,
a flock of chickens lived by a hazel forest.
A wildcat invaded and ate them, leaving only one hen.
A crow came and covered her, and they produced one offspring together.
When the offspring made a sound, the crow spoke a verse:
In a distant past age,
a eunuch died.
His body was discarded among paper mulberry trees.
A fox and a crow
came together to eat the flesh.
They praised each other.
The crow said:
The fox said:
At that time, a great sage dwelt in seclusion.
He cultivated purity and practiced the Way.
Hearing this, he spoke a verse and asked:
The crow said:
'There are four kinds of dragons:
first, egg-born;
second, womb-born;
third, moisture-born;
fourth, transformation-born.
All previously had much hatred and crooked minds.
But because they greatly practiced generosity, they now receive this form.
Their palaces are made of seven treasures, their bodies are forty miles tall,
their robes are forty miles long,
eighty miles wide,
and weigh two and a half ounces.
With divine power, they enjoy food of a hundred flavors at will.
The last mouthful turns into a toad.
If they transform their own retinue and arouse the mind of the Way,
and give black robes to beggars, they can cause all dragons to make offerings.
Sand does not rain on their bodies, and they are free from various afflictions. They eat turtles, alligators, fish, and soft-shelled turtles
as coarse food, and bathing and clothing as fine food.
They also have marriages.
Through bodily contact, they achieve yin and yang.
Their lifespan is one kalpa,
or sometimes less.
They avoid being eaten by garuḍa birds.
There are only sixteen kings:
first, Suōjié;
second, Nántuó;
third, Bónántuó;
fourth, Yīnàpóluó;
fifth, Títóulàizhà;
sixth, Shànjiàn;
seventh, Āxū;
eighth, Jiājùluó;
ninth, Jiāpíluó;
tenth, Ābōluó;
eleventh, Jiānú;
twelfth, Qújiānú;
thirteenth, Ānòudá;
fourteenth, Shànzhù;
fifteenth, Yōushàngāpōtóu;
sixteenth, Déchājiā.
The dragon king Suōjié
dwells north of Mount Sumeru at the bottom of the great sea.
His palace measures eighty thousand yojanas in length and width.
It is made of seven treasures, with walls of seven layers,
balustrades, nets, and adorned above.
There are gardens, groves, bathing pools, and birds singing in harmony.
Gold walls and silver gates.
The gates are twenty-four hundred miles high,
twenty-two hundred miles wide,
beautifully painted.
They are constantly guarded by five hundred spirits.
He can rain according to his will,
which other dragons cannot match.
The abyss where he dwells flows into the sea,
blue as lapis lazuli."
The dragon king said to the Buddha,
"Since the beginning of the kalpa, I have dwelled in the great sea.
From the time of Krakucchanda Buddha,
there were very few wives and children in the great sea.
But now, the dragon kinsmen in the sea are numerous.
The Buddha told the dragon king,
"Those who leave home under the Buddha's Dharma,
violate the precepts, commit offenses, and do not abandon their broken precepts are mostly reborn as dragons.
They do not directly fall into hell.
Such beings, after their lifespan ends, are all reborn as dragons.
The Buddha told the dragon king,
"During the time of Krakucchanda Buddha,
nine billion eight hundred million householders and those who had left home,
violated his prohibitions and were all reborn as dragons.
During the time of Kanakamuni Buddha,
eight billion householders and those who had left home,
destroyed the precepts and indulged their minds.
After their lifespan ended, they were all reborn as dragons.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha,
six billion four hundred million householders and those who had left home,
violated the precepts and were all reborn as dragons.
In my era,
nine hundred ninety billion householders,
who quarreled, slandered, and violated the sutras and precepts, died and were reborn as dragons.
Some have already been born.
For this reason,
in the great sea, the wives, children, and kinsmen of the dragons are beyond calculation.
After my nirvāṇa, there will be many evil upāsakas [lay male devotees]
who violate and lose the prohibitions and will be reborn as dragons.
Or they will fall into hell.
Greatly powerful poisonous dragons
can kill the weak just by looking at them with their eyes.
By exhaling their breath, they can also kill the strong.
At that time, a dragon received the one-day precepts.
He left home and entered the forest among the trees to contemplate.
After sitting for a long time, he grew weary and slackened, and fell asleep.
When dragons sleep, their form is like that of a snake.
They are of variegated colors like the seven treasures.
A hunter saw him and exclaimed with surprise and joy, saying,
'With this rare and hard-to-obtain skin,
I can offer it to the king,
would it not be fitting to use it as ornamentation for his ship?'
He then pressed the dragon's head with a stick and skinned him with a knife.
The dragon thought to himself,
'My power can overturn a kingdom.
How can this small creature trouble me?
But now, because I uphold the precepts, I will not consider this body.
I should follow the Buddha's words and endure myself.
I will close my eyes and not look, hold my breath and not exhale.
I will have compassion for this person.
For the sake of upholding the precepts, I will wholeheartedly accept being skinned without regret.'
After losing his skin, his bare flesh lay on the ground.
At that time, the sun was very hot, and he writhed in the soil.
Wanting to go to a large body of water, he saw many small insects coming to eat his body.
For the sake of upholding the precepts, he did not dare to move again.
He thought to himself,
'Now I give this body to these insects.
For the sake of the Buddha's path,
I now give my flesh to fill their bodies.
Later, I will give the Dharma to benefit their minds.'
When his body dried up and his life ended, he was immediately reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
There was a dragon king,
first named Xīqì [Inhaling Breath],
second named Dà Xīqì [Great Inhaling Breath],
third named Néngluó [Able to Encompass],
fourth named Wúliàngsè [Immeasurable Color],
who said to the World-Honored One,
'In this sea, there are countless kinds of dragons.
There are four kinds of garuḍa birds that constantly eat the dragons in the sea.
We wish the Buddha would protect us so that we may attain peace and security, free from sorrow and fear.'
The World-Honored One took off his black robe and told the sea dragon king,
'You should take this Tathāgata's black robe,
divide it among all the dragons so that it reaches everywhere.
In the great sea, any who obtain even a single thread of it
cannot be harmed by the garuḍa bird kings.
The Buddha's established, inconceivable, majestic virtue is like this.'
At that time, the sea dragon king took the Buddha's robe and divided it among the dragon kings.
According to their needs, whether broad or narrow, large or small, it was naturally provided.
The robe remained as before, never exhausted.
Then the sea dragon king told the dragon kings,
'You should revere this robe as you revere the World-Honored One.
After his nirvāṇa, make offerings to his relics,
and with all offerings, serve the World-Honored One.'
The four garuḍa bird kings, hearing what the Buddha had established, became alarmed and fearful.
They quickly went to the Buddha's place, prostrated themselves at his feet,
and said, 'Why has the World-Honored One taken away our food?'
The Buddha said,
'There are four kinds of food [livelihoods]
that lead to three destinations.
What are the four?
First, using nets to hunt birds and beasts, harming herds and flocks, killing living beings and taking lives wrongfully to make a living.
Second, carrying weapons, knives, spears, hacking and stabbing, forcing, fighting, shooting, robbing, and seizing others' wealth to make a living.
Third, being stingy, greedy, flattering, deceitful, violating prohibitions, holding wrong views, and being deceitful to obtain food.
Fourth, claiming to be a teacher when one is not,
claiming to be a World-Honored One when one is not,
following what is wrong and calling it right,
claiming to be a tranquil ascetic when one is not,
claiming to be pure when one is not,
claiming to practice brahmacarya when one is not,
boasting and fraudulently seeking to obtain food.
These are the four kinds of food.
They lead to the three evil destinations: hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
The Dharma I teach eliminates these four kinds of food.
One should not sustain one's body by harming living beings.
If you wish to protect yourself, you should protect others.
What should not be done, be careful not to do.'
At that time, the four garuḍa bird kings,
each with a thousand followers, said to the Buddha,
'Today we take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
We confess and repent our past offenses.
We will uphold the prohibitions from today onward.
We will give fearlessness to all dragon kings.
We will protect the true Dharma until the Dharma remains and is transmitted.
We will follow the path of Dharma until its extinction, not violating the Buddha's teaching.'
Once in Jambudvīpa, there was a country named Bōluónài [Vārāṇasī].
There was a man
who especially loved gold.
He toiled his body to seek it and obtained seven jars of gold.
He buried them in the ground and never used them for food or clothing.
He fell ill and died.
His greed and attachment were so heavy
that he was reborn as a poisonous snake,
coiling around the gold jars. He died and was reborn again for tens of thousands of years.
Later, he thought to himself and suddenly was able to awaken.
'It is precisely because of the gold that I have received this evil retribution.
I should give it away as a field of merit and seek a good place.'
At that time, he went out to the roadside and saw a brāhmaṇa.
He then said,
'I have a jar of gold. I entrust you to provide a meal for the Saṅgha.
If you do not do it for me, I will kill you.'
The brāhmaṇa said,
'I can do it for you.'
The snake brought out the gold and gave it to him.
The brāhmaṇa then took it to the monastery,
fully explaining to the monks,
conveying the snake's intention to make an offering.
The monks agreed.
He handed the gold to the karmadāna [distributing monk].
The karmadāna managed the preparations for the meal as the day approached.
The brāhmaṇa took a small basket and went to where the snake was.
The snake saw him and was joyful.
He then coiled onto the basket.
The brāhmaṇa covered him with a cloth and carried him toward the monastery.
People on the road saw this and gave many财物 to send to his home.
A specific day was chosen,
and the noble Saṅgha was invited for a meal.
After the gathering,
the snake went before the Saṅgha and stood in the street,
having the brāhmaṇa look at each one in turn.
With sincere faith, he observed those receiving the meal.
He gazed intently without shifting.
After the event, the snake felt even more reverence and was not satisfied.
After the monks finished eating, they again expounded the Dharma for him.
The snake then gave all seven jars of gold, having the karmadāna take them for offerings.
He then left his evil form and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
Once there was a snake whose head and tail quarreled with each other.
The head said to the tail,
'I should be the greater.'
The tail said to the head,
'I should be the greater.'
The head said,
'I have ears that can hear,
eyes that can see,
a mouth that can eat.
When moving, I go in front.
Therefore, I should be the greater.
You do not have these abilities.'
The tail said,
'I make you go,
so you can go.
If I coil around a tree three times with my body,
for three days you will not be able to seek food.
You will starve and nearly die.'
The head said to the tail,
'You can release it. I will listen to you being the greater.'
The tail, hearing these words, immediately released it.
The head again said to the tail,
'Since you are the greater, I will listen to you going in front.'
The tail went in front.
Before it had gone many steps, it fell into a fire pit and died.
Once there was a snake,
a frog, and a turtle in a pond together, becoming close friends.
Later, the pond water dried up,
and they were hungry, destitute, and troubled, with nowhere to turn.
At that time, the snake sent the turtle to call the frog, saying,
The frog said,
'Tell the bhikṣus,
in the great sea there is a blind turtle,
with a lifespan of immeasurable kalpas,
which surfaces once every hundred years.
There is also a floating log with just one hole,
drifting on the ocean waves, going east and west with the wind.
The blind turtle surfaces once every hundred years; if it encounters this hole, it reaches the eastern sea.
The floating log may go to the western sea, and missing each other is also like that.
Although there may be deviation, sometimes they do meet.
Ordinary beings drift in the sea of the five destinies,
and regaining a human body is even more difficult than this.'
The Buddha and the bhikkhus
headed toward Vaiśālī.
They arrived at the Líyuè River.
By the riverside, there were five hundred cowherds and five hundred fishermen.
The Buddha sat down to rest not far from the river.
At that time, the fishermen caught a fish in their net.
Five hundred men pulled but could not bring it out.
They then called upon the cowherds.
A thousand men joined forces and caught a huge fish.
Its body had a hundred heads of various kinds:
donkey, horse, camel, tiger, wolf, pig, dog, ape, monkey, fox, and the like.
The crowd was greatly astonished and gathered to look at it.
The World-Honored One immediately went to where the fish was.
He asked the fish,
"Are you Kǎpílí?"
He asked three times, and each time the answer was yes.
He asked again,
"Where are those you taught now?"
The answer was,
"They have fallen into the Avīci Hell."
Ānanda asked,
"Why do you now call this hundred-headed fish Kǎpílí?"
The Buddha said,
"During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a brāhmaṇa
who had a son
named Kǎpílí.
He was intelligent and learned,
the most knowledgeable among his kind.
Only the śramaṇas surpassed him.
On his deathbed, his father earnestly admonished him,
'Be careful not to debate the Dharma with the śramaṇas of Kāśyapa.
Why?
Their wisdom is profound; you are certainly not their equal.'
After his father passed away, his mother asked,
'You were originally highly intelligent; is there anyone now who surpasses you?'
He replied,
'The śramaṇas are superior to me.'
His mother asked again,
'In what way are they superior?'
He answered, 'When they have doubts, they go to ask the Buddha and receive explanations.
If they ask me, I cannot answer.'
His mother then said,
'Why not learn their teachings?'
He replied,
'To respectfully learn their teachings, one must become a śramaṇa.
I am a layperson; how can I learn them?'
His mother said,
'Pretend to be a śramaṇa, learn until you master their teachings, then return home.'
Following his mother's instruction, he became a bhikkhu.
After a short time, he studied the Tripiṭaka and thoroughly understood its principles.
His mother asked him,
'Have you surpassed them now?'
He replied,
'In learning, I have surpassed them, but not in meditation.
How do I know?
When I ask them, they can explain everything.
When they ask me, I cannot answer.
Because of this, I am not yet their equal.'
His mother said,
'From now on, if you engage in debates,
and if you are not equal to them, you may insult them.'
Kǎpílí said,
'The śramaṇas have no faults.
How can I insult them?'
She answered,
'Just insult them, and you will win.'
At that time, Kǎpílí could not bear to disobey his mother.
Later, when debating again,
if he was at a disadvantage, he would insult them, saying,
'You are foolish and ignorant, worse than animals.'
He compared them to the heads of various beasts.
He did this repeatedly.
Because of this karma, he is now reborn as a fish with a hundred heads.
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
'When will he be freed from this fish body?'
The Buddha told Ānanda,
'Even after a thousand Buddhas have passed in this Bhadrakalpa, he will still not be freed.'
At that time, Ānanda and the crowd,
hearing what the Buddha said,
all spoke in unison, saying,
'One must be careful in bodily, verbal, and mental actions.'
Then the fishermen and cowherds,
all together, joined their palms toward the Buddha,
seeking to leave home and cultivate pure conduct.
The Buddha said, 'Welcome.'
Their hair and beards fell off, and the Dharma robes appeared on their bodies.
The Buddha preached the wonderful Dharma to them, and they became arhats.
The southern sea suddenly surged, with towering waves flooding the land.
Three large fish flowed into a small channel.
They said to each other,
'We are trapped here, and before the water recedes,
we should swim upstream and return to the sea.'
But they were blocked by a water channel and could not cross.
The first fish exerted all its strength, leaped over the channel, and crossed.
The second fish relied on grass and managed to cross.
The third fish exhausted its strength
and was caught by a hunter.
The Buddha saw this and spoke a verse:
In the Jiāluó Pond, there was a clam.
Hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma,
it emerged from the pond and hid under grass roots.
At that time, there was a cowherd
who saw a large crowd gathered around listening to the Buddha preach the Dharma.
He went to where the Buddha was
and, wanting to hear the Dharma, stuck his staff into the ground.
He accidentally struck the clam's head.
The clam died and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Seeing the heavenly maidens and hearing the music,
it immediately thought,
'I was originally an animal.
For what reason was I reborn in this heavenly palace?'
Using its heavenly eye, it observed
that it had previously listened to the Buddha preach the Dharma by the pond.
Because of this merit, it attained this reward.
The clam deity then rode its palace
to where the Buddha was, bowed at his feet,
and the Buddha preached the Dharma to it, enabling it to attain the fruit of Stream-Entry.
Long ago, a wealthy household stored a thousand hú of grain
and buried it in the ground.
When spring warmth arrived, they opened it to take seeds,
but found no grain.
Instead, there was a worm as large as a cow's basket,
without limbs, head, or eyes, like a lump of dull flesh.
Everyone in the household was astonished.
They placed it on flat ground
and asked,
'What are you?'
It gave no answer.
They then pierced it with an iron awl.
It said,
'If you want to know my name, place me by the main road.
Someone who knows me will name me.'
So they placed it by the roadside.
For three days, no one could name it.
Then came several hundred yellow horse-drawn carriages,
with yellow-clothed attendants.
They stopped the carriage and called out,
'Grain thief, why are you here?'
It replied,
'I ate someone's grain, so they placed me here.'
After speaking for a long time, it bid farewell and left.
The householder asked the grain thief,
'Who was that just now?'
It replied,
'That was the essence of gold and treasure.
It resides under a large tree about three hundred paces west of here.
There is a hundred-dàn jar filled with gold.'
The householder immediately took dozens of people to dig and found the jar of gold.
The family rejoiced, loaded the gold onto carts, and brought it home.
They bowed to the grain thief,
saying, 'Today we obtained gold thanks to your great divine kindness.
Please stay and return with us so we can make offerings to you.'
The grain thief said,
'Earlier, when I ate your grain and did not reveal my name,
it was so that you could obtain this gold as repayment.
Now I must travel to spread blessings throughout the world.
I cannot stay any longer.'
Having said this, it suddenly disappeared.
Southeast of Rājagṛha, there is a corner with a pool of water.
Within the city, the ditches and drains are filthy.
All excrement and urine flow into it.
The stench is unbearable to approach.
There is a large creature born in the pool.
Its body is several zhang long, without hands or feet.
Yet it twists and turns, lowering and raising itself, playing in the pool.
Thousands of people watch it.
Ānanda, while going on alms round, saw it and went to look.
The creature immediately leaped, causing waves to surge and swell.
Ānanda fully reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha, together with the bhikṣus, went to the pond.
The people saw the Buddha.
Each thought to themselves:
Today, the Tathāgata
will surely explain the origins and end of this creature to the assembly, resolving everyone's doubts—how wonderful that will be!
The Buddha said:
After the parinirvāṇa of Buddha Vipaśyin,
there was a stūpa temple.
Five hundred bhikṣus passed by the temple.
The temple master saw them and was greatly delighted.
He invited them to stay and receive offerings for three months, and all accepted the invitation.
The temple master wholeheartedly provided meals, leaving nothing out.
Later, five hundred merchants went to sea to gather treasures and, upon returning, passed by the stūpa temple.
Seeing the five hundred bhikṣus diligently practicing the path,
they each generated a mind of faith.
Happily, they discussed together:
"A field of merit is hard to encounter; we should offer a humble feast."
They then informed the temple master.
The temple master replied:
"I have invited them for three months; only five more days remain.
Only then can we arrange a grand feast."
The merchants said:
"We must leave and cannot wait until the end."
The five hundred merchants each donated one pearl,
obtaining five hundred maṇi pearls.
They entrusted them to the temple master,
instructing him:
"When the days are complete, use our pearls to make offerings to the saṅgha."
The bhikṣu said, "Agreed,"
and accepted them all.
Later, he gave rise to an unwholesome mind,
plotting to take them all for himself.
In the end, he did not make the offerings.
The saṅgha asked:
"Master, previously the merchants donated pearls; should you not arrange the offerings
and then send them off?"
The temple master said:
"That was a donation to me.
If you want to seize it, I might as well give you my excrement.
If you do not leave promptly,
I will cut off your hands and feet and throw you into the latrine pit."
The assembly, pitying his folly, silently departed.
Long ago in the past,
after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata who should appear,
during the period of the semblance Dharma, there was a meditating bhikṣu
alone in the forest, constantly troubled by lice.
He then made an agreement with them:
"When I meditate, you should remain silent."
His body hidden in stillness, the lice followed the rule well.
Later, at one time,
a flea came to the side of a louse.
It asked:
"How is it that you are so plump and thriving?"
The louse said:
"The master I rely on constantly practices meditation.
He taught me the times for feeding.
I follow the rule, hence I am fresh and plump."
The flea said:
"I also wish to practice this method."
The louse said, "As you wish."
The flea, smelling the scent of flesh and blood, immediately bit and fed.
The bhikṣu was distressed.
He then took off his robe and burned it with fire.
That meditating bhikṣu was Buddha Kāśyapa.
The flea was Devadatta.
The louse was I.
As for King Yama,
he was formerly the king of Piśāca Kingdom.
Because he fought with King Vidāśī,
his military strength was no match.
Thus he made a vow:
"May I become the lord of hell."
His eighteen ministers, leading a million troops, with horns on their heads and ears, were all filled with wrath.
Together they vowed:
"Later we will assist in punishing these sinners."
The king of Piśāca is now Yama.
The eighteen men are the various minor kings.
The million troops are the various attendants.
They are subordinate to the northern guardian king, Vaiśravaṇa.
South of Jambudvīpa, there is a great vajra mountain.
Within it is the palace of King Yama.
It measures six thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Three times a day and night, a large bronze cauldron naturally appears before him.
If the cauldron enters the palace,
the king sees it and is terrified.
He flees outside the palace.
If the cauldron goes outside the palace, the king enters inside.
There are great hell guards.
They lay the king on the hot cauldron,
pry open his mouth with iron hooks,
and pour molten copper into it.
From his throat down, everything is scorched and rotten.
After this is done, he returns to amuse himself with his court ladies.
Those ministers who shared in his blessings also suffer the same.
There are three messengers:
first, old age;
second, sickness;
third, death.
If there are beings who commit evil through the three karmas,
when their bodies perish and lives end, they should fall into hell.
The king asks:
"Were you summoned by the heavenly messengers?"
The king says:
"Did you see the first messenger?
When you were among humans,
did you see those with white hair, fallen teeth, dim eyesight,
loose skin, wrinkled muscles, bent backs leaning on canes, moaning as they walked—did you see such people?"
The sinner says, "I saw."
The king says:
"Why did you not reflect,
'I too shall be like that'?"
The sinner says:
"At that time, I was heedless and did not realize it."
The king says:
"Now I shall make you know the suffering of heedlessness.
It is not the fault of parents, brothers, the heavenly emperor, ancestors, friends, servants, or śramaṇas.
You yourself committed evil; now you shall receive it yourself."
He asks again, "Did you see the second messenger?
When you were human,
did you see those gravely ill, lying in their own foul excrement and urine,
needing others to feed them, every joint aching, shedding tears, moaning, unable to speak—did you see such?"
He answers, "I saw."
The king asks:
"Why did you not reflect?" He asks further, "Did you perceive the third messenger?
Did you see people dead, bodies perished, lives ended, faculties forever extinguished,
bodies stiff and straight like dry wood, discarded in burial grounds, eaten by birds and beasts—did you see such?"
He answers, "I saw." After speaking, he hands them over to the hell guards to be taken to the great hell.
As for the eighteen minor kings:
first, Jiāyán oversees the Niraya hell;
second, Qūzūn oversees the Mountain of Knives;
third, Fèishā Shòu oversees the Boiling Sand;
fourth, Fèidiǎn oversees the Boiling Excrement;
fifth, Jiāshì oversees the Black Ear;
sixth, Luósuō oversees the Fire Cart;
seventh, Tāngwèi oversees the Cauldron of Boiling Water;
eighth, Tiějiārán oversees the Iron Bed;
ninth, Èshēng oversees the Luó Mountain;
tenth, Hánbīng; eleventh, Píjiā oversees the Flaying;
twelfth, Jìngtóu oversees the Animal [hell];
thirteenth, Tíbó oversees the Weaponry;
fourteenth, Yídà oversees the Iron Mill;
fifteenth, Yuètóu oversees the Icy Hell;
sixteenth, Tiě [gap]; seventeenth, Shēn oversees the Maggots;
eighteenth, Guānshēn oversees the Molten Copper.
The first is King Píngcháo.
He presides over the Avīci Great Mud.
The second is King Jìnpíng.
He presides over the Black Rope Heavy Prison.
The third is King Túdū.
He presides over the Mortar and Pestle Prison.
The fourth is King Fǔtiān.
He presides over the Assembly Prison.
The fifth is King Shèngdū.
He presides over the Great Mountain Prison.
The sixth is King Xuándū.
He presides over the Fire City Prison.
The seventh is King Guǎngwǔ.
He presides over the Sword Tree Prison.
The eighth is King Wǔyáng.
He presides over the Howling Prison.
The ninth is King Píngyáng.
He presides over the Eight Paths Prison.
The tenth is King Dūyáng.
He presides over the Thorn Tree Prison.
The eleventh is King Xiāoyáng.
He presides over the Boiling Ash Prison.
The twelfth is King Tǐngwèi.
He presides over the Great Screaming Prison and the Small Screaming Prison.
The thirteenth is King Guǎngjìn.
He presides over the Great Avīci Prison.
The fourteenth is King Gāodū.
He presides over the Iron Cart Prison.
The fifteenth is King Gōngyáng.
He presides over the Iron Fire Prison.
The sixteenth is King Píngjiě.
He presides over the Boiling Excrement Prison.
The seventeenth is King Zhùyáng.
He presides over the Burning Ground Prison.
The eighteenth is King Píngqiū.
He presides over the Mílí Prison.
The nineteenth is King Liánshí.
He presides over the Mountain Stone Prison.
The twentieth is King Lángyé.
He presides over the Duōhuán Prison.
The twenty-first is King Dūguān.
He presides over the Mud Prison.
The twenty-second is King Xuánxī.
He presides over the Flying Insect Prison.
The twenty-third is King Tàiyī.
He presides over the Yáng'ā Prison.
The twenty-fourth is King Héshí.
He presides over the Great Millstone Prison.
The twenty-fifth is King Liángwú.
He presides over the Cold Snow Prison.
The twenty-sixth is King Wúyuán.
He presides over the Iron Pestle Prison.
The twenty-seventh is King Zhèngzhì.
He presides over the Iron Pillar Prison.
The twenty-eighth is King Gāoyuǎn.
He presides over the Pus and Blood Prison.
The twenty-ninth is King Dūjìn.
He presides over the Burning Stone Prison. The thirtieth is King Yuándū.
He presides over the Iron Wheel Prison.
These are the thirty great and severe mud prisons.
The divine spirits listen, investigate, and record sins and blessings without regard to status.
They report six times a month and review four times a year.
On the days of the four reviews, all eight kings are used.
On the eight kings' days, the heavenly kings inspect and compare the subjects among the heavens and the common people.
Those with blessings have their lifespans increased; those with sins have their allotted years reduced.
They determine the length of life down to the smallest detail without error.
People are blind and ignorant, completely unaware.
If they do not prepare by doing good, they are collected and delivered to hell.
The five officials are:
first, the Fresh Official, who prohibits killing;
second, the Water Official, who prohibits stealing;
third, the Iron Official, who prohibits lust;
fourth, the Earth Official, who prohibits duplicity;
fifth, the Heaven Official, who prohibits alcohol.
To the east, west, and south of King Yánluó's city are arrayed various hells.
There is sunlight and moonlight, but they are not bright and pure.
Only the Black Ear Hell is not illuminated by light.
When a person's life ends, the spirit gives rise to the intermediate state.
The intermediate state means having already abandoned the dead shade but not yet reached the living shade.
Those who are sinners ride on the intermediate state body.
They enter the mud prison city.
The mud prison city is where all sinners
gather together before receiving their punishments.
Blown by skillful winds, they receive bodies large or small according to the weight of their karma.
Blown by foul winds, they achieve the coarse and ugly forms of sinners.
Blown by fragrant winds, they achieve the subtle and fine bodies of blessed people.
Whether ascending to heaven or falling into hell,
each has someone to welcome them.
When a person is sick and about to die,
their eyes see those coming to welcome them.
Those destined to be born in heaven see heavenly beings holding heavenly garments and music coming to welcome them.
Those destined to be born in other realms see respected people speaking wonderful words to them.
Those destined to fall into hell see soldiers holding knives, shields, spears, halberds, and ropes surrounding them.
What is seen differs.
The mouth cannot speak.
Each receives their retribution according to their deeds.
Heaven is not unjust or excessive.
It is impartial and without duality.
According to what one has done, the net of heaven governs them.
The eight kings say:
referring to the thirty-two ministers of the heavenly emperor Śakra,
the four great guardian kings, the directors of fate and records,
the five great kings of retribution, and the messengers of the eight kings.
They all go out and spread everywhere, covering and patrolling.
Again, they coincide with the reports made by the four kings on the fifteenth and thirtieth days.
They examine and compare the people's established conduct of good and evil.
The kings of hell also dispatch assistant ministers and lesser kings.
They go out simultaneously, and if there is sin, it is recorded immediately.
On the previous fasting day of the eight kings,
if offenses were committed but blessings were strong, there is rescue and safety; there is no other use of blessings to pardon originally.
If by the later fasting day there is re-offense,
and the number of sins is many, lifespan is reduced, names are listed, and death is decreed.
The year, month, day, and hour are sent down to hell.
Hell receives the document and immediately dispatches hell demons holding the name register to summon.
Hell demons have no mercy; if the death date has not arrived,
they force and push to do evil, causing life to be cut short and exhausted.
Those with many blessings have their lifespan increased and years added.
Heaven dispatches good spirits to protect and guard their bodies.
They send down to hell to remove and erase the charges.
They eliminate death and establish life.
Later, they are born in heaven.
What is hell?
Answer: it is the borderlands of cold and heat.
There are immeasurable kinds.
Now I shall briefly explain.
Cold hells are:
conscious screaming,
unconscious screaming,
and non-screaming.
These three characteristics are extremely evil cries.
Conscious screaming has three:
first, Arbuda;
second, Nirarbuda;
third, Aṭaṭa.
In the Arbuda hell, due to cold, bodies grow something like boils.
In the Nirarbuda hell, the wind blows and causes swelling and fullness.
In the Aṭaṭa hell, an extremely cold wind blows, stripping the body's skin and flesh until they all fall off.
All shiver urgently and cry out.
These three are conscious.
Unconscious screaming are:
first, Hahava;
second, Utpala.
Hahava is also blown by an extremely cold wind.
Skin and flesh are stripped off, crying "Hahava."
Utpala: an extremely great cold wind blows and strips the body's skin and flesh; iron leaves from within the body wind around and bind it themselves.
Like an Utpala flower.
Because of slandering the wise and saints, one falls into this hell.
Non-screaming are:
first, Kumbhīpa;
second, Sūkaramukha;
third, Gahanapriya;
fourth, Gahanapratipūrṇa.
An extremely cold wind blows, causing the body to swell and become full.
Like the four kinds of appearances, suffering and groaning.
Because of slandering the wise and saints, one falls into those four kinds of hells.
At all times, they suffer immeasurable pain.
These are all the great cold hells.
They are located between the four continents.
Attached to the bottom of the Iron Ring Mountains.
Facing upward, dwelling in darkness.
Cold winds destroy the body.
Burned by great fires.
Like burning bamboo groves.
Sounds and coughs touch each other.
There are also other beings suffering within.
All slandered and defamed the wise and saints, thus suffering such pain.
As the World-Honored One said in verse:
These are called the cold hells.
Question: What are the hot hells?
Answer: First, those with rulers;
second, those with few rulers;
third, those without rulers.
These three characteristics of rule refer to torture.
With rulers:
first, Reviving;
second, Black Rope;
third, Crushing.
The Reviving Hell:
Hell wardens use sharp knives and axes to dismember, flay, chop, and slice sinful beings like cutting grass heads.
Skin and flesh disintegrate, but the sin's cause is not yet exhausted.
Blown by a cold wind, they revive as before.
Again, due to evil deeds, hands grow iron claws sharp as knives.
Each gives rise to resentment and conflict, striking and cutting each other further.
Like cutting bamboo and reeds.
Hearing each other, harboring hatred until death, thus born here.
The Black Rope Hell:
Stretch the sinner on the ground.
Use black ropes to mark and then saw and cut.
Because of cutting beings, they are born in that hell.
Furthermore, with red-hot
copper plates wrapped around the body, bones shattered, marrow and blood flowing.
For striking sentient beings and monastics with whips and staves,
and not diligently accepting and wearing the robes offered in faith, one is born there.
Extremely great darkness and suffering from smoke inhalation.
Hanging upside down to inhale smoke.
This is due to dwelling in smoke-filled caves among sentient beings.
Those who traverse hells.
Rows of sinful beings like in a slaughterhouse.
Severing hands, feet, ears, nose, and head.
Originally being a butcher, one suffers this torment.
Furthermore, on a hot iron ground, driving an iron fire-cart.
Hell guards ride it, eyes wide open, shouting and scolding.
For driving elephants and horses to exhaustion, one falls into this.
For committing adultery with another’s wife, driven onto a sword tree, naturally burned by fire, suffering such torment.
It is said there are lords who govern hells and hell guards.
Due to karmic causes, they are not burned by fire.
Lesser lords who govern hells.
One: Saṃghāta, two: Mahāraurava, three: Tapana.
The Saṃghāta hell:
Sinful beings fear hell guards.
Countless hundreds of thousands flee into the mountains.
Before and behind, fire naturally arises.
Two mountains come together like grinding stones.
Blood flows like a river, flesh and bones completely pulverized.
This is due to delighting in grinding sentient beings.
Furthermore, burning a large iron mortar, pounding with a pestle.
Passing through a hundred years, due to karmic causes, their lives do not end.
This is due to pounding and killing fleas and lice, and killing recklessly.
The Mahāraurava hell:
A large iron mountain entirely ablaze, surrounded with no place to go.
Evil hell guards without compassion.
Angrily saying:
“Where do you think you’re going?”
Burning an iron pestle with fire to smash their heads.
For oppressing the myriad people, one is born here.
The Tapana hell:
A large iron mountain with flames clashing.
Shoveled with an iron shovel.
All around leaning against the scorching, one side just cooked.
The shovel naturally turns, tumbling over and over.
For impaling and killing people, one is born here.
The Avīci hell:
An iron ground entirely ablaze, measuring a hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
Four gates like a city, covered with thin copper above, flames continuously linked.
All sinful beings gathered like firewood.
Flames unobstructed, scorching and burning their bodies, suffering without lack.
For killing parents or arhats,
harboring evil intent toward the Buddha, causing his blood to flow,
causing strife among the saṅgha,
and committing the ten unwholesome deeds to an extreme degree, one is born here.
The Pṛthagjana hell:
Located in homes, waters, mountains, and wilderness.
Alone receiving the retribution of evil karma, this is called the Pṛthagjana hell.
Outside the four continents are eighty thousand continents surrounding them.
Outside the eighty thousand continents is again a great ocean.
Outside the ocean is again a great vajra mountain.
Outside that mountain is another mountain also called vajra; between these two mountains, the sun, moon, and divine heavens’ majestic light does not shine.
There are eight great hells.
First: Saṃjīva.
Second: Kālasūtra.
Third: Saṃghāta.
Fourth: Raurava.
Fifth: Mahāraurava.
Sixth: Tapana.
Seventh: Pratāpana.
Eighth: Avīci. Each great hell
has sixteen smaller hells.
The sixteen of the Saṃjīva hell:
First: Black Sand.
Second: Boiling Excrement.
Third: Five Hundred Nails.
Fourth: Hunger.
Fifth: Thirst.
Sixth: Single Copper Cauldron.
Seventh: Multiple Copper Cauldrons.
Eighth: Stone Mill.
Ninth: Pus and Blood.
Tenth: Measuring Fire.
Eleventh: Ash River.
Twelfth: Iron Balls.
Thirteenth: Axes.
Fourteenth: Jackals and Wolves.
Fifteenth: Sword Tree.
Sixteenth: Cold Ice.
Among them, beings
grow iron claws on their hands, mutually hostile and angry.
Clawing each other, flesh falls off with each touch.
Thinking they have died.
Furthermore, among them, beings harbor thoughts of harm.
Holding knives and swords, they hack and stab each other.
Skinning, slicing, cutting their bodies, shattered on the ground.
Saying to each other they have died.
A cold wind blows, and they quickly revive.
They say to themselves, “Now I am alive.”
After long suffering, they leave the Saṃjīva hell.
Panicked, seeking rescue, unknowingly suddenly arrive at the Black Sand hell.
Hot storm winds arise, blowing hot black sand onto their bodies.
Burning skin through to the bone, flames arise within the body.
Whirling around, burning and scorching the body.
Their sins not yet exhausted, thus they do not die.
After long suffering, leave the Black Sand hell, arrive at the Boiling Excrement hell.
There are boiling excrement and iron balls naturally filling before them.
Driving the sinners, making them embrace iron balls, burning their hands and bodies.
Again making them grab and put into their mouths.
From throat to abdomen, through and out below, all is scorched.
There are iron-mouthed worms gnawing flesh to the marrow, suffering immeasurably.
Retribution not finished, again unwilling to die.
After long suffering, leave the Boiling Excrement hell, arrive at the Iron Nails hell.
Guards throw them down on hot iron.
Stretching out their bodies, nailing hands and feet.
All over the body, five hundred nails in total.
Suffering and wailing, yet still not dying.
After long suffering, leave the Iron Nails hell, arrive at the Hunger hell.
Immediately thrown on hot iron, molten copper poured into the mouth.
From throat to abdomen, through and out below, all is scorched.
Remaining sins not exhausted, still not dying.
After long suffering, leave the Hunger hell, arrive at the Thirst hell.
Immediately thrown on hot iron, hot iron balls placed in their mouths.
Burning lips and tongue, through and out below, all is scorched, suffering and crying.
After long suffering, leave the Thirst hell, arrive at the Single Copper Cauldron hell. Hell guards angrily grab the sinners’ feet, throwing them headfirst into the cauldron.
Following the boiling broth, surging up and down, whirling around.
Body ruined, cooked thoroughly, ten thousand torments arriving, thus they do not die.
After long suffering, leave the Single Copper Cauldron, arrive at the Multiple Copper Cauldrons hell.
Grab the sinners’ feet, throwing them headfirst into the cauldron.
Following the boiling broth, surging up and down, whirling around, the whole body ruined and cooked.
Taking with iron hooks, placing in another cauldron.
Wailing in suffering, thus they do not die.
After long suffering, leave the Multiple Copper Cauldrons, arrive at the Stone Mill hell.
Seize those sinners, throw them on hot stones.
Stretching out hands and feet, with large hot stones grinding their bodies.
Turning and rubbing, bones and flesh pulverized.
Suffering intensely, thus they do not die.
After long suffering, leave the Stone Mill hell, arrive at the Pus and Blood hell.
Pus and blood boiling, sinners running east and west within.
Scalding their bodies, heads and faces ruined.
Also taking pus and blood to eat.
Through and out below, suffering unbearable, thus they do not die.
After long suffering, then leave Pus and Blood, arrive at the Measuring Fire hell.
There is a great fire mass, its flames blazing, driving the sinners.
Holding iron measures, measuring the fire mass.
Burning all over the body, suffering intense heat and pain.
Moaning and wailing, thus they do not die.
After long suffering, leave the Measuring Fire hell, arrive at the Ash River hell.
Length, breadth, depth each five hundred yojanas.
